. Professional Nursing Practice: Concepts and Perspectives (5th ed.). Upper
Saddle River, NJ: Pearson Education, Inc., p. 11. Reproduced with permission of Pearson Education, Inc.
26 Blais, K. K. & Kozier, B. J. (2006). Professional Nursing Practice: Concepts and
Perspective (6th ed.). Upper Saddle River, NJ: Pearson Education.
Watson’s human caring theory
Jean Watson  believes the practice of caring is central to nursing; it
is the unifying focus for practice. Her major assumptions about
caring are shown in Box 3.1
.
27 Watson, J. (2005). Caring Science as Sacred Science. Philadelphia: F. A. Davis.
BO X
3.1 Watson’s assumptions of caring
Human caring in nursing is not just an emotion, a concern,
an attitude or a benevolent desire. Caring connotes a
personal response.
26
27


Caring is an inter-subjective human process and is the
moral ideal of nursing.
Caring can be effectively demonstrated only
interpersonally.
Effective caring promotes health and individual or family
growth.
Caring promotes health more than does curing.
Caring responses accept a person not only as they are
now but also for what the person may become.
A caring environment offers the development of potential
while allowing the person to choose the best action for the
self at a given point in time.
Caring occasions involve action and choice by nurse and
person. If the caring occasion is transpersonal, the limits
of openness expand, as do human capacities.
The most abstract characteristic of a caring person is that
the person is somehow responsive to another person as a
unique individual, perceives the other’s feelings and sets
one person apart from another.
Human caring involves values, a will and a commitment to
care, knowledge, caring actions and consequences.
The ideal and value of caring is a starting point, a stance
and an attitude that has to become a will, an intention, a
commitment and a conscious judgment that manifests
itself in concrete acts.
Source: © Dr Jean Watson, <www.watsoncaringscience.org>; jean @watsoncaringscience.org.


Nursing interventions related to human care originally referred to as
carative factors have now been translated into clinical caritas
processes (Watson ):
28 Watson, J. (2007). Watson’s Theory of Human Caring and Subjective Living Experiences:
Carative Factors/Caritas Processes as a Disciplinary Guide to the Professional Nursing
Practice. Retrieved from <www.scielo.br>.
1. Formation of humanistic–altruistic system of values becomes
‘practice of loving-kindness and equanimity within context of
caring consciousness’.
2. Instillation of faith–hope becomes ‘being authentically present,
and enabling and sustaining the deep belief system and
subjective life world of self and one-being-cared-for’.
3. Cultivation of sensitivity to one’s self and to others becomes
‘cultivation of one’s own spiritual practices and transpersonal
self, going beyond ego self’.
4. Development of a helping–trusting, human caring relationship
becomes ‘developing and sustaining a helping–trusting,
authentic caring relationship’.
5. Promotion and acceptance of the expression of positive and
negative feelings becomes ‘being present to, and supportive
of, the expression of positive and negative feelings as a
connection with deeper spirit of self and the one-being-cared-
for’.
6. Systematic use of a creative, problem-solving caring process
becomes ‘creative use of self and all ways of knowing as part
of the caring process; to engage in artistry of caring–healing
practices’.
28


7. Promotion of transpersonal teaching–learning becomes
‘engaging in genuine teaching–learning experience that
attends to unity of being and meaning attempting to stay
within other’s frame of reference’.
8. Provision for a supportive, protective and/or corrective
mental, physical, societal and spiritual environment becomes
‘creating healing environment at all levels (physical as well as
non-physical), subtle environment of energy and
consciousness, whereby wholeness, beauty, comfort, dignity,
and peace are potentiated’.
9. Assistance with gratification of human needs becomes
‘assisting with basic needs, with an intentional caring
consciousness, administering “human care essentials”, which
potentiate alignment of mind–body–spirit, wholeness and
unity of being in all aspects of care’, tending to both embodied
spirit and evolving spiritual emergence.
10. Allowance for existential–phenomenological–spiritual forces
becomes ‘opening and attending to spiritual– mysterious and
existential dimensions of one’s own life–death; soul care for
self and the one-being-cared-for’.
Watson’s theory of human caring has received worldwide recognition
and is a major force in redefining nursing as a caring–healing health
model. Watson has also explored how her theory and that of Rogers
can be integrated and synthesised to form a unitary caring science
(Watson & Smith ).
29 Watson, J. & Smith, M. C. (2002). Caring science and the science of unitary human
beings: A trans-theoretical discourse for nursing knowledge development. Journal of
29


Advanced Nursing, 37, 452–461.
King’s goal attainment theory
Imogene King’s theory of goal attainment
 was derived from her
conceptual framework (see Figure 3.4
). King’s framework shows
the relationship of personal systems (individual), interpersonal
systems (groups such as the nurse and individuals) and social
systems (such as educational system, health care system). She
selected 15 concepts from the nursing literature (self, role,
perception, communication, interaction, transaction, growth and
development, stress, time, personal space, organisation, status,
power, authority and decision making) as essential knowledge for
use by nurses.
30 King, I. M. (1981). A Theory for Nursing: Systems, Concepts, Process. Albany, NY:
Delmar.
Figure 3.4
30


King’s conceptual framework for nursing: dynamic interacting
systems.
Ten of the concepts in the framework were selected (self, role,
perception, communication, interaction, transaction, growth and
development, stress, time and personal space) as essential
knowledge for nurses in concrete nursing situations.


Within this theory, a transaction process model was designed (see
Figure 3.5
). This process describes the nature of and standard
for nurse–person interactions that lead to goal attainment—that
nurses purposefully interact and mutually set, explore and agree to
means to achieve goals. Goal attainment represents outcomes.
When this information is recorded in the individual’s record, nurses
have data that represent evidence-based nursing practice.
Figure 3.5


King’s model of transactions.
King’s theory offers insight into nurses’ interactions with individuals
and groups within the environment. It highlights the importance of a
person’s participation in decisions that influence care and focuses on
both the process of nurse–person interaction and the outcomes of
care. King believes that her theory, used in evidence–theory-based
practice, blends the art and the science of nursing .
31 King, I. M. (2006). Imogene M. King’s theory of goal attainment. In M. E. Parker, Nursing
Theories and Nursing Practice (2nd ed.), pp. 235–244. Philadelphia: F. A. Davis.
Research note
What are the implications of nursing models for
professional practice?
31


N. McCrae
. Whither nursing models? The value of nursing theory in the context of evidence-based
practice and multidisciplinary health care. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 68(1), 222–229.
32 McCrae, N. (2012). Whither nursing models? The value of nursing theory in the context of
evidence-based practice and multidisciplinary health care. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 68(1), 222–
229. Doi: 10.1111/j.1365-2648.2011.05821.x.
This research paper discusses the role of nursing models and
theories in the contemporary clinical environment. It contends
that while existing models of nursing and nursing theories
were intended to provide a framework for nursing knowledge
and practice, they have not been used successfully to bridge
the theory–practice gap.
The paper was informed by literature on nursing models and
theories from the 1950s to date. The author explains that the
use of literature was not guided by a structured search
strategy but as a qualitative selection of the major
contributions to nursing theory and papers that have
contributed to the debate about nursing theories and
contemporary practice. In the paper, published discussion
and arguments against nursing theories that have been
proposed by authors are scrutinised. These arguments
suggest that nursing definitions, and therefore models and
theories, cannot be applied to practice. Others contend that
models and theories do not ameliorate a lack of prescription
for practice. Other authors suggest theories are incompatible
with evidence-based practice and are irrelevant to modern
health care. These arguments are examined in detail.
32


Implications Using arguments against models and theories
of nursing practice, the author concludes that, of late, broad
theories and conceptual models have been overshadowed by
empirical evidence in the knowledge of nursing. That is,
evidence and science have become the accepted norm in the
pursuit of legitimising and explaining nursing practice, and
attempts to infuse a theoretical and philosophical perspective
in the human-centred activity of nursing have been measured
and largely unsuccessful. However, the author contends that
the operational and philosophical challenges of incorporating
nursing theory are not so constraining that nursing theory
should be completely ignored.
The paper argues for the recognition and explanation of
nursing theory in nursing preregistration curricula in order to
understand its place in the cycle of nursing knowledge, thus
helping practitioners to assert, apply and evaluate their
unique role in health care.
An example of how this can be achieved is demonstrated in
research conducted by McAllister and Moyle (2008). The
findings of their research paper imply that nurses should
adopt and make explicit models of care based on clearly
articulated nursing theory that highlight nursing’s contribution
to the wellbeing of the people cared for by nurses. By doing
so, it helps nurses articulate and justify the unique role and
place they have in the health care system.
McCrae (2012) concludes by asserting that in the
contemporary practice environment of multidisciplinary health


care and the axiom of evidence-based practice that is driving
nursing practice, a unique theoretical standpoint based on
nursing theory should be considered. This, McCrae (2012)
argues, would allow nurses to more clearly articulate the art
and science of nursing. This proposition is also considered in
the context of the doctoral preparation of nurse scholars.
Grace et al.
 contend that the maturation of the profession
may be in peril, with an emphasis on empirical studies
becoming the norm at the expense of conceptual/theoretical
inquiry. They contend that to ignore the latter is to disregard
the dimensions that have permitted the development of core
disciplinary knowledge.
33 Grace, P., Willis, D., Roy, C. & Jones, D. (2016). Profession at the crossroads: A
dialogue concerning the preparation of Nursing Scholars and leaders. Nursing
Outlook, 64(1), 61–70. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.outlook.2015.10.002.
Parse’s human becoming theory
Rosemarie Parse  proposes three assumptions about human
becoming:
34 Parse, R. R. (Ed.) (1999). Illumination: The Human Becoming Theory in Practice and
Research. Boston: Jones & Bartlett.
33
34


1. Human becoming is freely choosing personal meaning in
situations in the inter-subjective process of relating value
priorities.
2. Human becoming is co-creating rhythmic patterns or relating
in mutual process with the universe.
3. Human becoming is co-transcending multidimensionally with
the emerging possibilities (p. 6).
These three assumptions focus on meaning, rhythmicity and co-
transcendence:
Meaning arises from a person’s interrelationship with the world
and refers to happenings to which the person attaches varying
degrees of significance.
Rhythmicity is the movement towards greater diversity.
Co-transcendence is the process of reaching out beyond the self.
Parse’s model of human becoming emphasises how individuals
choose and bear responsibility for patterns of personal health. Parse
contends that the person, not the nurse, is the authority figure and
decision maker. The nurse’s role involves helping individuals and
families in choosing the possibilities for changing the health process.
Specifically, the nurse’s role consists of illuminating meaning
(uncovering what was and what will be), synchronising rhythms
(leading through discussion to recognise harmony) and mobilising
transcendence (dreaming of possibilities and planning to reach
them). The goal of nursing from the human becoming perspective is
quality of life (Parse ).
35


35 Parse, R. R. (2006). Rosemarie Rizzo Parse’s human becoming school of thought. In M.
E. Parker, Nursing Theories and Nursing Practice (2nd ed.) (pp. 187–194). Philadelphia: F. A.
Davis.
The Parse nurse uses ‘true presence’ in the nurse–person process.
‘In true presence the nurse’s whole being is immersed with the client
as the other illuminates the meanings of his or her situation and
moves beyond the moment’ (Parse , p. 18).
36 Parse, R. R. (1994). Quality of life: Sciencing and living the art of human becoming.
Nursing Science Quarterly, 7(1), 16–21.
36


Nursing theorists in Australia
Although much of the work for nursing theory development has
occurred in North America, a number of Australian nursing
academics have also attempted to contribute to knowledge
development in this area. Jocelyn Lawler is an Australian nurse
academic who has developed a mid-range theory of nursing from
her doctoral studies to explain how nurses deal with problems of the
body. Jocelyn Lawler believes that nurses are able to assist people
to live in their body during illness. She contends that this is achieved
through the ways nurses manage the body, which is usually done
behind ‘closed doors’ to minimise embarrassment or
misinterpretation of activities that occur during nursing care
practices. This she contends means that nursing work is often
hidden from view (Lawler
).
37 Lawler, J. (2006). Behind the Screens—Nursing, Somology, and the Problem of the Body.
Sydney: Sydney University Press.
Many other Australian nurse academics are working to develop
theories through research to explain or guide nursing practice and
education. Many are using postmodern concepts, and future
publication of this research should see Australian nurse academics
recognised for postmodern nursing theory development
(Greenwood ).
37
38


38 Greenwood, J. (2000). Nursing Theory in Australia (2nd ed.). Frenchs Forest, NSW:
Pearson Education Australia.


Critique of nursing theory
Several nurse scholars have developed strong critiques of twentieth-
century nursing theories, choosing to ground their work in philosophy
or the social sciences (Munhall ). The best theories in philosophy
and the social sciences are often used in the humanities for the
insights and perspectives that can be brought to literature and art.
So far, other disciplines have not discovered a sufficiently unique or
interesting perspective on the human condition in nursing theories.
39 Munhall, P. L. (Ed.) (2006). Nursing Research: A Qualitative Perspective (4th ed.). Boston:
Jones & Bartlett.
Nursing scholars continue to debate whether grounding our research
in the best theories from other disciplines is good or bad. Some think
this detracts from the development of nursing as a separate
discipline; others argue that nursing research becomes more
relevant when informed by scholarship that addresses larger social
concerns. Recently, the noted nurse theorist Rosemarie Parse
(2016) responded to a call for nursing research to become more
embedded in the positivist paradigm of technology, omics and
symptom science. Parse argued that these are ancillary to nursing
science and should not be considered as such. She contends that
nursing science should reflect the theories and frameworks
developed over the past 100 years that describe the unique
39


knowledge that focuses on the human–universe–health processes
that are embedded in nursing theories and frameworks.
Most things in the world have both positive and negative
implications. Technology can be used for good or for evil. Theory
can be used to broaden our perspectives in nursing and facilitate the
altruistic and humanistic values of the profession. At the same time,
rational and predictive theory can produce language and social
practices that are superimposed onto the lives of vulnerable people
and do violence to the fragility of human dignity. As a lens, theory
can either illuminate or obscure. As a tool, theory can either liberate
or enslave.
Case study
Sarah is a 28-year-old woman with newly diagnosed irritable
bowel syndrome (IBS). Over the past 6 months, her episodes
of discomfort and diarrhoea have become more frequent and
intense, causing her weight to drop from 70 kg to 55 kg due
to intractable diarrhoea and poor appetite. The doctor thought
kilojoule intake was of primary importance and urged Sarah
to eat whatever she could tolerate and supplement with high-
kilojoule liquids. The doctor also prescribed codeine for the
diarrhoea, but Sarah hated the codeine because it made her
feel out of control and sleepy. Since Sarah was getting worse,
her nurse argued that she needed intravenous nutrition and
should eat only those foods that Sarah knew would not


exacerbate her condition until the diarrhoea stopped and she
was well enough to work with a dietitian to work out the
dietary modifications to manage her IBS. The nurse
suggested adding other foods one at a time and only as
tolerated. Sarah’s family and friends offered to take control of
Sarah’s food preparation.
The doctor compared IBS to HIV due to the similar symptoms
of weight loss and diarrhoea and argued he would not
prescribe intravenous nutrition for HIV. The nurse argued that
this was Sarah’s first hospitalisation and that her condition
was different from someone with HIV as Sarah required
education about dietary modification and needed time for the
new medications to work. The nurse’s primary focus was on
stopping the diarrhoea and supplementing nutrition with
intravenous therapy. Sarah’s friends preferred the nurse’s
approach but Sarah and her doctor were not as easily
convinced.

context

Chapter 3 Review


Chapter highlights
In the natural sciences, the main function of theory is to guide
research. In the practice disciplines, the main function of theory
(and research) is to provide new possibilities for understanding
the discipline’s focus (music, art, management, nursing).
To Nightingale, the knowledge required to provide good nursing
was neither unique nor specialised. Rather, Nightingale viewed
nursing as a central human activity grounded in observation,
reason and commonsense health practices.
During the latter half of the twentieth century, disciplines seeking
to establish themselves in universities had to demonstrate
something that Nightingale had not envisaged for nursing—a
unique body of theoretical knowledge.
Theories articulate significant relationships between concepts in
order to point to something larger, such as gravity, the
unconscious or the experience of pain.
Paradigms include our notions of reality that are largely
unconscious or taken for granted. Most theories reflect the
dominant paradigm of a culture, although some may grow out of
a developing rival paradigm.
In the late twentieth century, much of the theoretical work in
nursing focused on articulating relationships between four major
concepts: person, environment, health and nursing. Since these
four concepts can be superimposed on almost any work in
nursing, they are sometimes collectively referred to as a
‘metaparadigm’ for nursing.


Debates about the role of theory in nursing practice and nursing
research continue to provide evidence that nursing is maturing as
both an academic discipline and a clinical profession. However,
concern is expressed at the diminution of the relevance of
nursing theory.
Australian nursing academics are contributing to the
development of nursing theories to help explain what it is that
nurses do.

Legal aspects of nursing
It is important for nurses to understand the basics of legal concepts
because nurses are accountable for their professional decisions and
actions. In Australia, nurses are also accountable for their
professional practice under the National Law that provides an
individual with the right to be registered as a health care
professional. Accountability
 is an essential component of
professional nursing practice and the law. Knowledge of laws that
regulate and affect nurses and their practice is needed to:
ensure the safety of the public in the nurse’s care
ensure that the nurse’s decisions and actions are guided by
standards
protect the nurse from liability
practise nursing with, knowledge, understanding and confidence.


General legal concepts
The rule of law
 is a fundamental doctrine of law that supports the
notion that society is governed by abstract rules and principles,
rather than by people or groups of people in a position of power. In
society, all people are compelled to abide by the law because if they
do not there are usually repercussions such as fines or
imprisonment (Forrester & Griffiths ). This means that everyone,
regardless of their position, is subject to the law of the land equally
(Savage ).
1 Forrester, K. & Griffiths, D. (2015). Essentials of Law for Health Professionals (4th ed.).
Sydney: Elsevier.
2 Savage, P. (2015). Legal Issues for Nursing Students: Applied Principles (3rd ed.). Frenchs
Forest: Pearson Australia.
Law
 is defined as rules that society deems as enforceable
because they are considered by most to be morally and socially
acceptable. Although laws also may appear to be ethical, this may
not always be the case as societies have different values on a
variety of issues such as abortion and euthanasia (Johnstone ;
Forrester & Griffiths 2015). Law creates not only a set of boundaries
to establish order in society but is also used by lawyers to formulate
and apply those boundaries (Forrester & Griffiths 2015). It is
important to note that law, like society, is constantly evolving and is
influenced by trends such as current political, social and economic
1
2
3


considerations. A recent example of this is laws that have been
added to the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) amended 2019 (Criminal
Code) about counter- terrorism (Attorney-General’s Department ).
While it is convenient to narrowly define law as being concerned with
rules and regulations, the reality is that in a sophisticated society the
application of law is much more complex. Areas of legal inquiry, such
as jurisprudence (legal philosophy), are concerned with answering
questions such as ‘What is law?’. It is not always easy to pinpoint an
exact answer to legal questions because the issues are rarely ‘black
and white’; there are numerous ‘shades of grey’ as well. However,
for nurses, the main consideration is that they have enough
knowledge to adequately identify legal issues and have the
necessary skills to assist in decision making (Savage 2015). See
Box 4.1
 for functions of the law in nursing.
3 Johnstone, M. J. (2019). Bioethics: A Nursing Perspective (7th ed.). Sydney: Elsevier.
4 Attorney-General’s Department (2019). Administrative Law. Retrieved from
<www.ag.gov.au>.
BO X
4.1 Functions of the law in nursing
The law serves a number of important functions in nursing:
It provides a legal framework for establishing nursing
actions that are provided.
4


It differentiates the nurse’s responsibilities from those of
other health professionals.
It helps establish the boundaries of independent nursing
action.
It assists in maintaining a standard of nursing practice by
making nurses accountable under the law (accountability).
The nature of law
The legal system in Australia has its origin in the British common law
system. Table 4.1
 provides the sources of Australian law.
Table 4.1 Sources of Australian law
The Australian Constitution forms the rules about how Australia is
run. There are three distinctive groups that have the ability to
instigate and manage federal law—the Parliament, the Executive
and the Judiciary—with the division between these groups being
known as the ‘separation of powers’.
The Australian governments (federal and state) are generally
described as ‘representative democracies’. This political approach
has its origins in the ‘Western’ democratic system of government
with representatives of government duly elected by the majority of
voters at an election held at both federal and state levels. Judges,


on the other hand, are appointed to their position permanently, or
until they retire, and are not subject to citizen elections.
The head of the Commonwealth of Australia is not democratically
elected but is a hereditary monarch (presently Queen Elizabeth II of
the United Kingdom). Australia’s government is referred to as a
‘constitutional monarchy’ because the head of state is a monarch
but we derive our laws from the Australian Constitution
. There
is continuing debate in Australia (the Republic argument) about the
relevance of having a foreign head of state and her representatives
(Governor-General and governors).
The main sources of law originate from statutory authority (Acts of
Parliament
) and common law
 principles (judge-made law).
Statutory law is often referred to as ‘written law’ and judge-made law
as ‘unwritten law’. The origins of law are important because
members of state and federal parliaments (politicians) are elected
via a democratic process and thus have the vote and authority of
citizens to represent them and make laws. The theory of
‘parliamentary sovereignty or supremacy’ was described by Dicey
(p. 37) as the dominant characteristic of English political institutions.
Its main purpose is to emphasise the ‘supremacy’ of the Australian
Parliament as the major institution of government and law-making
within our legal system. Judges are appointed to their position by the
Australian Governor-General (Commonwealth Courts) or State
Governor (state or territory) on the advice of the government. Their
ability is limited in scope to interpreting, rather than making the law.
5


5 Dicey, A. V. (1926). An Introduction to the Study of Law of the Constitution. London:
Macmillan.
Australia has evolved from earlier individual colonies to a system
based on states, territories and Commonwealth authorities. This was
achieved by Federation
 in 1901. This system preserved most
law-making state powers and added an extra layer to law-making
authority by creating the Commonwealth government. The authority
that allows the federal government to make law is found in the
Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900 (the Constitution).
There are six Australian states: New South Wales (NSW), Victoria
(Vic), Western Australia (WA), South Australia (SA), Queensland
(Qld) and Tasmania (Tas), and nine territories. External territories
include Christmas Island, Ashmore and Cartier Islands, Cocos
(Keeling) Islands, Coral Sea Islands, Norfolk Island, Heard Island
and McDonald Island, and the Australian Antarctic Territory. Internal
territories include the Northern Territory and the Australian Capital
Territory. The Australian Capital Territory, Northern Territory and
Norfolk Island are self-governing by virtue of federal legislation. The
significance of this is that in Australia there are 10 separate
governments with law-making powers (counting the Commonwealth
government and the state and territory governments). This situation
can make the system of government in Australia quite complex and
difficult. Federal legislation is superior to state legislation in as much
that a federal law can overrule any law made at the state level.
Section 122 of the Constitution permits Parliament to repeal a law
made at territory level at any time. An example of this is in 1998
when the Northern Territory had its voluntary euthanasia Act Rights


of the Terminally Ill Act 1995 overturned by the Commonwealth
government Euthanasia Laws Act 1997 (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Generally, however, each of the levels of governments has specific
responsibilities and makes the laws that relate to those areas of
responsibility.
Understanding the history behind Federation and the system of
government it set up is important because it is still relevant today.
The original framers of the Constitution were keen to preserve state
powers as well as create Commonwealth powers. What this means
in practical terms is that when considering the law, it is important to
identify its particular source—Commonwealth, state or territory.
Jurisdiction
The question of jurisdiction
 is important because this decides
where laws are made and who will be bound by them. The courts
are also bound by questions of jurisdiction; for example, not all
courts in the hierarchy are able to hear serious criminal offences.
Because Australia is a nation it has its own laws and is able to
enforce them. If an overseas tourist visits Australia, they are subject
to the laws of this country. Citizens are also bound by the laws of the
place they reside in, visit or work in. For example, if a crime is
committed in Victoria the criminal is subject to the legal system in
that state even though they may live in Queensland.


Clinical consideration
On 1 July 2010, the Health Practitioner
Regulation National Law Act came into effect.
This law regulates health practitioner practice in
each state and territory (the National Law). In
Australia, 15 health professions are regulated by
nationally consistent legislation under the
National Registration and Accreditation Scheme,
the most recent of the professions to become
accredited being paramedicine in 2017
(Australian Health Practitioner Regulation
Agency (AHPRA) ).
6 Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA)
(2019). Notifications and Outcomes. Retrieved from
<www.ahpra.gov.au>.
Constitutional law—Federation
Australia became a nation on 1 January 1901 when it became a
Federation of states. This system involves two tiers of
government––state and Commonwealth. Under Australia’s federal
system, the Commonwealth government and the state governments
6


have their own institutions such as parliamentary and judicial
systems. Both tiers of government are constrained by the text of the
Australian Constitution (Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act
1900). It is the High Court’s role to ensure that these rules are
followed and to strike down unauthorised federal or state laws.
The Constitution provides the authority for Commonwealth powers.
It establishes the general organisation of the Commonwealth
government, grants certain powers to the government and places
limits on what Commonwealth and state governments may do. It
also established a federal judicial system (courts). Section 71 of the
Constitution established the High Court, the most important superior
court in this country, with appellate jurisdiction (appeals from other
courts) over all judicial decisions, including those handed down by
state Supreme Courts. The High Court is made up of the Chief
Justice and a maximum of six judges. Not all judges sit on the High
Court bench at the same time; however, where there is an important
legal issue being decided it is likely that all seven judges will sit to
hear the case and render a decision. An important function of the
High Court is to interpret constitutional questions and make
decisions regarding the division of powers between the states and
the Commonwealth.
An example of the High Court’s importance and decision- making
ability is demonstrated by the decision in New South Wales and
Others v Commonwealth [2006] HCA 52. In this case, a number of
states challenged the validity of the Howard government’s workplace
relations ‘Work Choices
’ legislation (2005). The states argued


that the federal government did not have the necessary authority
under the Constitution to pass these particular laws (i.e. the
legislation was ‘ultra vires
’, meaning ‘beyond the power’ or ‘an
act in excess of the authority conferred by law’). It was held by a
majority of High Court judges (5 to 2) that the Work Choices
legislation was constitutionally valid in every aspect.
Although the federal government enacts legislation covering health
issues, it is the state governments that make the majority of laws
covering health services. For example, before 1946 the Constitution
did not give the Commonwealth government authority to deliver a
wide range of health and welfare services (this was primarily left to
the states).
The preferred method of state, territory and Commonwealth
implementation of policy and law is to cooperate with each other for
the mutual benefit of the country. State, territory and federal
government health ministers meet annually in an effort to respond to
community needs. Following on from the National Health Reform Act
2011 (Cth) amended 2016, to gain funding for each state, reports
are required at a national, state or territory level as well as for each
local hospital network within each state and territory. The funding is
then deposited into a state pool account before being distributed
according to service categories or local hospital networks (National
Health Reform Public Hospital Funding ).
7 National Health Reform Public Hospital Funding (2019). National Health Reform Funding
Reports. Retrieved from <www.publichospitalfunding.gov.au>.
7


The Constitution is not a particularly long document and the main
Commonwealth powers to legislate can be found in s 51. Unlike the
United States and other democratic countries (e.g. Charter of Rights
and Freedoms (Canada), Human Rights Act 1998 (UK), Bill of Rights
Act 1990 (NZ)), the Australian Constitution does not specifically
mention or protect human rights
. The protection of human rights
in Australia can be located in a number of sources, including
international conventions and treaties such as United Nations
obligations (e.g. European Convention on Human Rights), specific
legislation (e.g. Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission
Act 1986 (Cth) amended 2019, Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW)
amended 2019, Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) amended 2018)
and common law. However, it is worth noting that the ACT does
have a Human Rights Act 2004 (ACT) and Victoria has a Charter of
Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (Vic), but these
represent the exception rather than the rule.
It is also important to mention and note that Australian states have
their own constitutions under which they operate and function; for
example, New South Wales Constitutional Act 1853, Constitution Act
1975 (Vic), Constitution Act 1934 (SA), Constitution Act 1867 (Qld).
Indigenous law in Australia
The Indigenous peoples who originally occupied Australia were
literally overwhelmed when British settlers inhabited the land at the
end of the eighteenth century and throughout the nineteenth


century. Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
have a history dating back some 50 000–100 000 years, making
their culture one of the oldest in the world. It has been estimated
that there were around 500 Indigenous groups with 750 000
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people at the time of European
colonisation (Behrendt ). There are numerous examples of foreign
settlement around the world and the adverse effect this had, and
continues to have, on Indigenous populations; for example, in
Canada, the United States and New Zealand, as well as in Australia.
8 Behrendt, L. (2012). Indigenous Australia for Dummies. Milton: Wiley Publishing Australia
Pty Ltd.
There are two principles that apply to Australian Indigenous people
from the time of colonisation. They are:
1. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are subject to the
same law as non-Indigenous people.
2. There are some circumstances, however, where customary
Indigenous Australian law is considered due to The
Recognition of Aboriginal Customary Laws Report published
in 1986 and modified in 2010. This report outlines that where
an offence could be subject to tribal punishment this will be
taken into consideration. It also reflects statutory recognition
about traditions including cultural aspects such as marriage,
placement of children, hunting, fishing or gathering (Australian
Law Reform Commission ).
9 Australian Law Reform Commission (2010). Aboriginal Customary Laws.
Canberra: Australian Government. Retrieved from <www.alrc.gov.au>.
8
9


Common law native title has been an impediment for Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander people as, unlike other property-related rights,
it vests ownership or authority in a group of people rather than in an
individual and these rights cannot be alienated to anyone but the
Crown. Any claim must be defined on a case-by-case basis with
reference to the group’s pre-existing traditional law and customs,
which make up the rights, for example, in relation to hunting grounds
and sacred sites. The Native Title Act 1993 was amended in 2012
and again in 2015 to clarify some meanings, such as what
constituted ‘traditional’, as well as to reconsider native title historical
ownership of areas such as parks and reserves (Australian Law
Reform Commission ). Following the review of the Native Title Act
1993, further recommendations were put forward to ensure that the
system is efficient, fair and equitable, and that the law has flexibility
to facilitate the beneficial purposes of the Act. They are:
10 Australian Law Reform Commission (2015). ALRC Recommendations for Reform of the
Native Title Act. Media release. Retrieved from <www.alrc.gov.au>.
Traditional laws and customs, under which native title rights and
interest are possessed, may adapt, evolve or otherwise develop.
Acknowledgment of traditional laws and customs need not have
continued substantially uninterrupted since sovereignty; nor is
acknowledgment required by each generation.
It is not necessary that a society, united by acknowledgment of
traditional laws and customs, has continued since sovereignty;
and succession of native title rights and interests may be
recognised (Australian Law Reform Commission 2015).
10


New Zealand has the Treaty of Waitangi (Tiriti o Waitangi), which
was signed on 6 February in 1840 by Maˉori chiefs from the North
Island of New Zealand and representatives of the British Crown. It
resulted in the declaration of British sovereignty but established that
a British Governor of New Zealand recognised Maˉori ownership of
their lands, forests and other properties, and gave the Maˉori the
rights of British subjects. In return, the Maˉori people ceded New
Zealand to Queen Victoria, giving her government the sole right to
purchase land.
Unlike New Zealand, Australian Indigenous people did not have a
treaty, and the British assumed sovereignty unilaterally under the
presumption of ‘terra nullius’ (meaning ‘empty land’). Thus, in a
single episode, an entire continent was legally claimed and
possessed by settlers, effectively denying Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander people their right to traditional lands. In Milirrpum v
Nabalco Pty Ltd (1971) 17 FLR 141 (Gove Land Rights case), the
claim regarding land failed for a number of significant reasons,
including the fact that Australian Aboriginal people were accorded no
legal rights by virtue of their Indigenous status. It was noted that no
treaties were signed and recognition of common law native title was
not acknowledged until the Australian Native Title Act 1993
(Australian Law Reform Commission 2015).
However, the situation dramatically changed in Mabo v Queensland
(No. 2) (1992) 175 CLR 1 (Mabo case). The High Court overturned
the earlier Milirrpum decision and acknowledged the existence of
common law native title. The recognition of native title by the High


Court provoked a legislative response by the Commonwealth
government: the Native Title Act 1993. Other cases that were
significant include The Wik People v The State of Queensland
(1996) 187 CLR 1. The Wik case helped refine the ‘perimeters’ of
native title claims.
Indigenous justice in Australia is an ongoing issue and, despite
numerous reports and international covenants (e.g. Law Reform
Commission (LRC) (NSW) 2000, Report 96 Sentencing: Aboriginal
Offenders; International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1980,
Article 27); Covenant on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial
Discrimination), the problems have not been resolved.
Recommendations relating to ‘rights’ such as self-determination and
recognition of Aboriginal customary law (LRC (NSW)
) have been
highlighted, and it is recognised that Aboriginal law is encoded in
each group’s religious tradition (LRC, p. 3). There is, however, a
fusion of law and religion in Indigenous culture, which can give rise
to problems when defining that law.
11 Law Reform Commission (LRC) (NSW) (2000). Report 96 Sentencing: Aboriginal
Offenders. Retrieved from <www.lawreform.justice.nsw.gov.au>.
One area of significant concern for Indigenous people, apart from
social justice issues, is health care and the provision of services,
particularly in remote areas of Australia. Nurses are often seen as
very important frontline workers in this area. Australian remote area
nurses (RANs) are specialist advanced practice nurses. Their work
is unique and often extremely challenging, providing a diverse range
of health care services to remote, often Indigenous, communities.
11


There are a number of government websites, such as the Australian
Indigenous HealthInfoNet <www.healthinfonet.ecu.edu.au> and
the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare report on Australia’s
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people (<www.aihw.gov.au/
reports-data/health-welfare-overview/indigenous-health-
welfare/overview>), which can be viewed for more information
about this important area.
Patient safety competency framework
3 Cultural competence
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must
demonstrate cultural competence by respecting
each person’s values, beliefs, life experiences
and health practices (Levett-Jones et al.
).
12 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Separation of powers
12


Separation of powers
 theory emerged in Britain and France in
the eighteenth century and is an important concept in the exercise of
government in Australia. The principle of the ‘separation of powers’
comes from liberal democracy theory and requires that there be a
separation between the three arms of government: the executive,
legislature and judiciary. The reasoning behind this lies with the
notion that by separating law-making powers it is less likely that a
repressive government will emerge (autocrats, dictatorship). It is
argued that if power is concentrated in the same hands, there is the
potential for wide-ranging abuse of authority and political power
(Parliamentary Education Office
).
13 Parliamentary Education Office (2019). Separation of Powers: Parliament, Executive and
Judiciary. Retrieved from <www.peo.gov.au>.
Legislation (statutory law)
Laws enacted by any legislative body (Parliament) are called
statutory laws
. When federal and state laws conflict, federal law
prevails, as reflected in s 109 of the Constitution. Likewise, state
laws take precedence over local laws.
Regulation of nurses
The regulation of nursing is primarily a function of national law.
Nursing, like other health professions, is regulated under the Health
Practitioner Regulation National Law Act 2009, which sets out the
13


legal requirements for nurse registration. Nurses and midwives who
satisfy the minimum criteria (education, skills, English language
competence, recency of and fitness for practice) have their names
entered into the national nursing register and as a result are
considered to be ‘registered’. Prior to this, state-based nursing Acts
regulated nursing practice individually in each state and territory. The
nursing regulation authority known as the Nursing and Midwifery
Board of Australia (NMBA)
 is responsible for registering nursing
and midwifery practitioners and students, and developing standards,
codes and guidelines for the nursing and midwifery profession, as
well as handling notifications, complaints, investigations and
disciplinary hearings. The NMBA approves accreditation standards
and courses of study for nurses and midwives after they have been
assessed by the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Accreditation
Council (ANMAC)
. ANMAC is also responsible for assessing
overseas-trained nurses and midwives who wish to work in Australia
before they seek registration. Nurses and midwives must comply
with professional codes and guideline requirements including
policies, professional standards, guidelines, position statements,
frameworks and fact sheets (NMBA 2019).
14 Australian Nursing and Midwifery Accreditation Council (ANMAC) (2019). Retrieved from
<www.anmac.org.au>.
The Health Practitioner Regulation National Law Regulation 2010 is
a second piece of legislation that was enacted by the
Commonwealth at the same time as the Health Practitioner
Regulation National Law Act 2009. This regulation applies other
federal law requirements, such as freedom of information and
14


privacy, to the new legislation, and establishes a role for the
Commonwealth Ombudsman to act in issues of complaint or conflict
across all the national health practice areas.
Nurses and midwives are regulated under drugs and poisons
legislation in the particular state or territory in which they practise. It
is the responsibility of individual health practitioners to understand
the requirements of the legislation that applies to their practice in
any given state or territory. The Patient Safety Competency
Framework indicates that nursing students must demonstrate the
ability to administer and monitor the therapeutic use of medications:
and respond appropriately to medication errors and adverse drug
reactions (Levett-Jones et al. 2017).
Assistant in Nursing, support worker,
carer, personal care assistant
There are assistants working in nursing who are not on the nursing
register but who work in areas of health care, including aged care,
residential aged care, community aged care and other areas of the
health industry. Generally, people who undertake this level of work
hold a vocational qualification (Australian Qualifications Framework
Certificate III or IV) in the discipline area in which they work: aged
care, mental health, disability services.
Undergraduate nursing students often work as Assistants in Nursing
as a way of gaining valuable clinical experience, as well as


supplementing their income when studying.
Administrative law
Administrative law is made up of the body of principles, practices
and institutions that provide mechanisms for the supervision,
regulation and structuring of the executive power of government.
Administrative law is used when a person disputes a decision or
action made by government officials. This could relate to decisions
about a policy, contract, employment, delegated legislation by an
official or even a criminal case if civil prosecution is warranted
(Attorney-General’s Department 2019).
When a legislature passes a statute, an administrative agency is
given the authority to create rules and regulations to enforce the
statutory laws. The Health Practitioner Regulation National Law Act
2009 provides the authority for the NMBA to set education,
registration and practice standards for nursing practice that are
legally enforceable.
Administrative law in Australia has developed over many years and
there are well-established legal and ethical practices attached to this
area. Many of the common law concepts found in administrative law
reflect the ‘rule of law’ principle and support the ‘separation of
powers’ principle. Administrative law is mainly concerned with the
administration of public agencies, organisations and institutions such
as hospitals, health centres and community health care facilities.


However, the recent growth of government executive power and
private sector involvement in the health area has prompted the
government to exercise greater control over public and private
sector organisations. This has been achieved in a number of ways,
including specific legislation (e.g. Health Records and Information
Privacy Act 2002 (NSW), Aged Care Act 1997 (Cth)), as well as
continuing government funding control attached to payment
schemes such as Medicare, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme
(PBS), health insurance and aged care. Where public money (i.e.
Medicare, PBS) is used by government to provide health services,
the recipient of those funds (i.e. medical practitioners, pathology
services etc.) must comply with public accountability requirements
(under the scrutiny of the Auditor-General or ombudsmen)
(Department of Human Services ).
15 Department of Human Services (2019). Medicare. Retrieved from
<www.humanservices.gov.au>.
Clinical consideration
It is an offence under law for a person to
represent themselves as a Registered Nurse
unless they meet the legal requirements under
the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law
Act 2009.
15


Common law
A major source of law comes from common law. Unlike statutory law
(legislation) that is passed by Parliament, common law evolves from
judge-made court decisions. The courts are frequently asked to
resolve disputes between two parties. Judges make laws indirectly in
a very different way from legislators. In deciding specific
controversies, courts generally adhere to the doctrine of stare
decisis—‘to stand by things decided’—usually referred to as
‘following precedent’. This means to make a ruling, and in order to
maintain consistency in a case, the court applies the same rules and
principles applied in previous, similar cases. The effect of the
doctrine of precedent
 is that, over time, decided cases
contribute to our legal body of knowledge. Judges do not generally
see themselves as ‘making law’ but only ‘interpreting it’, arguing that
it is the legislator who makes law (Fallon ).
16 Fallon, M. (Ed.) (2009). The Law Handbook (11th ed.). Redfern: Redfern Legal Centre
Publishing; Pyrmont: Thomson Reuters Australia.
Common law principles provide a valuable source of legal
understanding for nurses and midwives. This is because it is virtually
impossible for any statutory Act to cover every possible situation
that could develop. This is particularly relevant given the rapid
advances in areas such as information technology and biomedical
technology.
16


Novel situations frequently arise where legislation does not provide
the solution and the only redress is in the courts. An example of this
position can be seen in the British conjoint twin’s separation case. In
2000, the distraught parents of conjoint twin girls (Jodie and Mary)
went to Britain from the Maltese island of Gozo for medical
assistance for the girls. Despite the parents’ refusal, an operation to
separate the twins was proceeded with after the court intervened to
allow the operation. There were a number of legal and ethical issues
to be considered in this case. One such issue concerned the
unavoidable death of one of the separated babies. The alternative to
this was that if the twins were not separated the likelihood of both
babies dying was very high. Of course, it is only recently that the
medical technology necessary to separate the twins has been
available. The decision regarding the plight of the children and the
overriding of the parents’ requests was made by three judges with
no previous case (precedent) to guide them. They did, however,
refer to two other cases (Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993] 1 All ER
821 HL and R v Dudley and Stephens [1884] 14 QBD 273 DC) for
assistance in deciding the case.
The doctrine of precedence means that all lower courts are bound
by a higher court’s decision and must follow it (Fallon 2009). Only
superior Australian courts are able to set precedence. If a decision is
given in, for example, a magistrate’s court (a lower court), a higher
court is not required to follow the ruling. If a superior court in another
country decides a case, Australian courts do not have to follow the
decision. Some overseas decisions will be ‘persuasive’; however,


they do not have to be followed. This is one reason why ‘jurisdiction’
and ‘source’ must be considered when studying law.
Clinical consideration
When studying law, current Australian resources
should be used for reference. Overseas
references may not be relevant to Australian
law.
Australia has numerous courts consisting of judges and magistrates.
The type of case heard by individual courts will depend on the
relevant constitution and the jurisdiction. There is a separate court
system for the Commonwealth and each state and territory.
The courts in each particular system (Commonwealth, state or
territory) are ranked in a strict hierarchy, according to their particular
power to determine a case and make orders (see Figure 4.1
).
The lower-level or ‘inferior’ courts are known as magistrate’s courts.
The intermediate courts are referred to as the local, county or
district courts. Superior courts are found in both the state and
federal systems—the state court is known as the Supreme Court.
Figure 4.1


Hierarchy of courts in Australia.
Types of laws
While statutory and common law is an important division of law, laws
can be further classified into different types (see Table 4.2
). The
two main types are public law and private or civil law.
Table 4.2 Traditional categories of Australian law
Public law
 refers to the body of law that deals with relationships
between and among individuals and the government and
governmental organisations. An important segment of public law is
criminal law
, which deals with actions against the safety and
welfare of the public. Examples are murder, manslaughter and theft.
Each state and territory, as well as the Commonwealth, has
legislation establishing criminal offences and penalties (e.g. Crimes
Act 1900 (NSW), Crimes Act 1914 (Cth)). When a person is
accused of a criminal offence, it is the state (or Crown) that brings
the action and prosecutes the perpetrator. The Crown must show
(has the onus of proving) ‘beyond reasonable doubt’ that the
accused is guilty of the crime.
Criminal actions deal with the prosecution of offenders by the state
for conduct against people or property. The objective in this
proceeding is that the offender is punished, not that the victim is
compensated (Forrester & Griffiths 2015). The state brings an action


against an individual and the interest of criminal law is to punish the
perpetrator; for example, if a woman shoots her husband, the state
(Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP)) will charge her with murder
and society will bring her to trial for judgment by her peers (jury).
Private law, or civil law
, is the body of law that deals with
relationships between private individuals. It can be categorised into a
variety of legal specialties such as contract law and tort law. An
important difference between civil and criminal law is the potential
outcome for the defendant. In a civil action such as negligence or
contract, the defendant will have to pay a sum of money
(compensation) if the judgment goes against them. If the accused is
found guilty in a criminal action, they may be fined money, be
required to perform community service, be given a good behaviour
bond or be sent to prison. Unlike some states in the United States
and other countries, Australia does not sanction capital punishment.
Equity
In the past, the rules associated with common law could be very
harsh and occasionally outcomes were rigid; for example, ownership
of land recognises that a person whose name is on the title deed to
land is the person who owns it at law. Hence, if the person sells the
land, they may have sole rights to the proceeds of the sale. This
may cause hardship, especially if there is another person who has
contributed to the acquisition or improvement of the property but
whose name is not on the title deed. An appeal to common law
courts for relief by the aggrieved person did not necessarily


guarantee justice. A set of alternative approaches has now been
developed, aimed at the prevention of unjust enrichment at
another’s expense. These principles are known as the ‘principles of
equity’ (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Equitable principles are now incorporated into the jurisdiction of
common law courts. This means that courts can consider both
common law and equitable remedies when determining the outcome
of a decision. Where there is a conflict between the rules of equity
and common law, equity
 will be triumphant (Forrester & Griffiths
2015). From a Registered Nurse perspective, equitable principles
could relate to actions such as a mistake, undue influence or
coercion, breach of confidence or fraud (Savage 2015).
The civil judicial process
The term ‘litigation’ generally refers to the formal legal system of
resolving disputes, and lawyers who participate in lawsuits may be
referred to as ‘litigators’. While this process is important, there are
other or alternative dispute resolution mechanisms that are also
important in the health area that need considering.
The formal judicial process primarily functions to settle disputes
peacefully and in accordance with the law. A lawsuit has strict
procedural rules. There are a number of steps to this process:


1. Commencement. A document referred to as the originating
process (statement of claims or summons) is filed by a
person referred to as the plaintiff (the person making the
complaint), who claims that their legal rights have been
infringed by one or more people or entities, referred to as the
defendants.
2. Service. The defendant is served with a summons and the
complaint.
3. A written response, called a defence, is made by the
defendant. The defendant may also make a counterclaim. If
the defendant does not respond, judgment by default may be
entered in favour of the plaintiff by the court.
4. Both parties engage in pre-trial activities, referred to as
discovery, in an effort to obtain all the facts of the situation.
This consists of information gathering and getting witnesses
to provide dispositions (written reports), interrogatories
(verbal examination of key people) and examining medical
records or research data.
5. Pre-trial hearings. The court can order or direct the parties
(plaintiff and defendant) to prepare for the hearing. It is at this
time that the court may, if appropriate, refer the matter to
arbitration or mediation.
6. In the trial/hearing of the case, all the relevant facts are
presented either to a judge and jury, or only to a judge. This is
when the opportunity arises for each side to present its case
through testimony of witnesses. The judge will direct legal
proceedings during the trial. Rules of evidence and courtroom
procedure must be followed by lawyers representing the


parties; for example, in examination- in-chief, cross-
examination, expert witness testimony and closing
statements.
7. Jury instruction and deliberation. If there is a jury (most
civil cases do not have a jury), the judge takes time to instruct
the jury on points of law that are important. Members of the
jury review the facts (evidence) of the case and render their
verdict on the strength of the facts (who they believe). They
do not consider legal questions (the judge does this).
8. The judge renders a decision or the jury renders a
verdict. The legal question of sentence or compensation is
made by the judge.
9. Appeal. If there is a ‘legal question’ (e.g. regarding evidence
presented) associated with how the trial was conducted or the
outcome of the trial (e.g. sentencing), one of the parties can
lodge an appeal. The case is not reheard, but points of law,
procedure and fairness are reviewed.
10. Enforcement. Once a judgment has been ordered, there are
procedures available to the court for ensuring that those
orders are carried out. An example of this is where a person
has been ordered to pay compensation (money); it may be
possible to obtain a court order for this money to be taken out
of the person’s wages (Savage 2015, p. 41).
During a trial, a plaintiff must offer evidence of the defendant’s
wrongdoing. This duty of proving an assertion of wrongdoing is
called the burden of proof
.


Negligence
A plaintiff must be able to prove all the elements of an action to
determine the ‘burden of proof’.
There are three particular elements that constitute a negligence
action in law. They are:
1. that a person was owed a duty of care
2. that that duty of care has been breached through an act or
omission
3. that the act or omission (causative link) caused a physical,
mental or financial harm (harm). The causative link and harm
together are called the ‘damage’.
The above three elements must be proved to the satisfaction of the
court before negligence can be asserted. The injured person
(plaintiff) must prove all three elements; the defendant does not
have to disprove and only has to cause doubt that any one of the
three elements is not present (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Alternative dispute resolution
(ADR)
Disputes can often be resolved without an appeal to formal litigation
processes. ADR is an umbrella term for processes other than judicial


determination. There are a number of ways that this can happen,
including:
Prevention—be open to other people’s views in the first place.
Respectfully communicate and appreciate that some people may
have a reason to have a differing opinion.
Negotiation (negotiated agreements)—to confer for the purpose
of mutual agreement; to bargain; to manage.
Mediation—the process in which the parties to a dispute, with
the assistance of a ‘neutral third party’ (dispute resolution
practitioner), identify the disputed issues, develop options and
consider alternatives to help the parties reach an agreement.
Conciliation—a process by which a conciliator (dispute
resolution practitioner) helps the parties identify the issues in the
dispute, consider options and alternatives, and try to reach an
agreement. The conciliator may have an advisory role on the
content of the dispute but does not determine the outcome.
Neutral evaluation—a process that may occur before a court or
tribunal hearing begins. Professional advisors can refer
participants to an independent legally trained evaluator who will
make decisions about how a dispute can be resolved.
Arbitration—a process in which the parties to the dispute
present their arguments to an arbitrator (dispute resolution
practitioner) who makes the determination (Attorney-General’s
Department
).
17 Attorney-General’s Department (2016). Alternative Dispute Resolution. Retrieved from
<www.ag.gov.au>.
17


Other important mechanisms for
handling health care complaints
Statutory authorities
There are a number of different ways that complaints (by people
receiving care, carers or health care professionals) can be handled
by government. One such method is via statutory authorities that
are specifically set up to deal with certain health care complaints.
Examples of these authorities include Health Care Complaints
Commissions or similar bodies in all states and the National Health
and Medical Research Council (NHMRC). The specific authority and
function of these bodies is set out in the legislation (e.g. Health Care
Complaints Act 1993 (NSW) amended 2018, Health Ombudsman
Act 2013 (Qld), Human Rights Commission Act 2005 (ACT)
amended 2018 and National Health and Medical Research Council
Act 1992 (Cth) amended 2014).
Health research—standards and
complaints
Ongoing medical research into evidence-based ‘best’ practice
represents an important government initiative in the health area. The


main monitoring body is the NHMRC. There are legal as well as
ethical duties that arise from conducting human research. Human
research ethics committees (HRECs) are to be found in most health
organisations and it is their function to implement the National
Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research as it applies to
new and ongoing research applications.
Nurses have many opportunities to be actively involved in research
as primary researchers, as part of a research team/institute or as
participants in research. Postgraduate nursing education is likely to
involve nurses in research activities and to require an understanding
of their legal and ethical obligations when it comes to conducting
medical research (see Tobacco Institute of Australia Ltd v National
Health and Medical Research Council (1996) 142 ALR 1).


Regulation of nursing practice
As citizens of Australia, health care providers, including nurses, are
subject to the laws of the land. As with other professions (lawyers,
medical practitioners, accountants), nurses are subject to a system
of regulation imposed by the national regulator but primarily
determined by the profession. What this means is that the
profession is able to implement a self-regulatory system that
establishes nursing standards and disciplinary procedures. However,
the regulator has the authority to step in under certain
circumstances where a breach of the criminal law or negligence has
resulted.
In order to practise nursing in Australia, the nurse or midwife must
be registered with the NMBA (NMBA ). The NMBA defines nursing
practice and its scope, with protection of the public as its primary
concern. This responsibility is reflected in the legal purpose of
registration requirements and adherence by practitioners to
minimum standards of care. Nurses are expected to know and
practise nursing according to the professional codes and guidelines
established by the professional board (NMBA ). See Box 4.2
 for
some features of the NMBA.

BO X
4.2 Some features of the nursing and
midwifery board of Australia
Composition. The Board is composed of members
appointed by government, members elected by the
profession and representative bodies (i.e. members of the
public, other health professionals etc.).
Education and research. The Registration Board sets
the standard of education and practice for the different
classes of practitioners. It also has additional powers to
carry out research into the profession and practice. This
includes advising the government on matters relevant to
the profession, disseminating information and developing
codes of practice. ANMAC is the independent accrediting
body for nursing and midwifery courses and providers in
Australia (ANMAC 2019).
Registration. The NMBA is legally obliged to maintain a
register of those who have qualified for registration. This
includes registers for different levels of practice
(midwives, Registered Nurses, Enrolled Nurses, Nurse
Practitioners). The requirements to maintain registration
include yearly review by complying with mandatory


standards expected, including completing an updated
criminal history check, information about professional
indemnity insurance if required, recency of practice and
continuing professional development (CPD). It also
requires payment of an annual fee (NMBA 2019a).
Registration of endorsement and notation. An
additional part of registration identifies nurses and
midwives with additional qualifications and specific
expertise. For Registered Nurses who work in regional or
isolated practice, endorsement can be gained to supply
and administer scheduled medicines. Nurse Practitioners
and eligible midwives may also prescribe some scheduled
medicines. Some nurses who were previously registered
in a specialty area only receive a notation on their general
registration indicating that they are solely qualified in that
specialty area. Some Nurse Practitioners also may
practise as an advanced practice nurse able to work
within a scope of practice specific to that area (NMBA
2019a).
Discipline. AHPRA takes complaints for all registered
health care professionals. Complaints about nurses and
midwives from the public are referred to the Health Care
Complaints Commission, from where decisions then can
be referred to the Civil and Administrative Tribunal New
South Wales and, if necessary, the Director of Public
Prosecutions. Other health practitioners, employers or
education providers report directly to AHPRA. In
Queensland, consumers and health care professionals


refer to the Office of the Health Ombudsman. The
tribunals make decisions based on the professional codes
and guidelines that are available on the NMBA website.
Nurses and midwives are expected to abide by these
standards to maintain and uphold the reputation of their
profession. Notifications or concerns can be received
about a health practitioner’s health, conduct or
performance. Registered health care practitioners have
mandatory reporting
 obligations imposed by national
law (AHPRA 2019).
There are many professional nursing organisations that represent
nurses at both a state and national level and relate to the practice of
nursing in Australia. For example:
Australian Nursing College (ACN)—key national professional
organisation for nurses as well as the Australian member of the
International Council of Nurses
Australian College of Mental Health Nurses
Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation (ANMF)
Australian Primary Health Care Nurses Association (APNA)
Congress of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Nurses and
Midwives (CATSINaM)
National Enrolled Nurses Association (NENA)
Australian College of Nurse Practitioners (ACNP)
Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA)
Council of Deans of Nursing and Midwifery (CDNM)


Australian Nursing and Midwifery Accreditation Council (ANMAC)
Coalition of National Nursing Organisations (CoNNO)
Council of Remote Area Nurses of Australia (CRANAplus)
International Council of Nurses (ICN)
Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI)
Australian Nurse Teachers’ Society (ANTS).
Legislation relevant to nursing
practice
It is a requirement that nurses and midwives behave lawfully.
Legislation that is applicable to nursing practice originates in both
federal, and state and territory jurisdictions. The following are
examples of the types of legislation nurses may be required to follow
when working in their professional practice:
Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act 1966 (NSW) amended 2018
Aged Care Act 1997 (Cth) amended 2020
Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission Act (Cth) 2018
amended 2020
Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 (Cth) amended 2020
My Health Records Act 2012 (Cth) amended 2019
Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) amended 2014
Australian Immunisation Register Act 2015 (Cth) amended 2017
Queensland Human Rights Act 2019
Human Tissue Act 1982 (Vic) amended 2014


Freedom of Information Act 1982 (Cth) amended 2019
Public Health Act 2010 (NSW) amended 2019
Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1995 (NSW)
amended 2018
Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998
(NSW) amended 2019

Mandatory reporting requirements
Notifiable conduct
All registered health practitioners have a professional and ethical
obligation to protect and promote public health and safe health care.
Under the National Law, health practitioners, employers and
education providers are required to contact AHPRA or a national
board if they have formed a reasonable belief that a health
practitioner has behaved in a way that constitutes notifiable conduct
in relation to the practice of their profession. This includes concerns
that a practitioner is working or providing care in an unsafe way,
such as:
serious or repeated mistakes in carrying out procedures, in
diagnosis or in prescribing medications for a patient
a failure to examine a person properly or to respond reasonably
to a person’s needs


serious concerns about the way in which a practitioner managed
someone’s personal information
serious concerns about the way a practitioner is prescribing
medication
serious concerns about the practitioner’s ability to understand
and communicate in English
serious concerns about the practitioner’s skills, knowledge or
judgment in their profession (AHPRA 2019).
Concerns can also be raised about the way a practitioner behaves,
including:
a practitioner abusing their professional position; for example, by
engaging in a sexual or personal relationship with a patient or
someone close to a patient
inappropriate examinations of a patient
acts of violence, sexual assault or indecency
acts of fraud or dishonesty
any serious criminal acts
any other behaviour that is inconsistent with the practitioner
being fit and proper to be a registered health practitioner
(AHPRA 2019).
Child abuse and neglect
It is a legislative requirement for people working in selected
professions (including nurses) to report suspected cases of child
abuse and neglect to government authorities. There are differences


between the various states and territories, such as the state of mind
that activates the reporting duty. The variations on state of mind
might be having a concern, suspicion or belief on reasonable
grounds. There may also be differences about where the mandatory
report must be lodged. However, it is important that nurses are
aware of the requirements for the jurisdiction they are working in
(Australian Institute of Family Studies ).

Aged care
The Aged Care Amendment (Residential Care) Act 2007(Cth), which
amended the Aged Care Act 1997, protects residents in aged care
facilities. Older-person abuse (sometimes referred to as elder
abuse) can be physical, psychological or emotion, sexual or
financial. It can also be neglect of an older person— intentional or
otherwise. While older-person abuse often occurs in families, there
is recognition that it can also occur in aged care facilities (My Aged
Care ). The new Aged Care Quality Standards commenced on 1
July 2019. These Standards were introduced following information
that was revealed during the Royal Commission into Aged Care in
2018. In addition to the Standards, older people now have a specific
Older Persons Advocacy Network which can assist and support
older people who have a complaint or want to resolve an issue
(Older Persons Advocacy Network (OPAN)
. It is compulsory for
approved providers and their services to report suspicions or
20
21
22


allegations of assaults of residents to local police and the Australian
Department of Health (Ageing and Aged Care ). There is also a
requirement to report unexplained absences or missing residents to
police and the Australian Department of Health (Ageing and Aged
Care ).

Other reporting situations
Other situations where nurses are required to provide notification
are:
Notifying relevant public health units about outbreaks of
infectious disease.
Informing the coroner if there is a sudden or unexpected death.
In a hospital environment, this may be reported by team leaders
or other staff, but it may be required when working in the
community or in regional/remote communities.
23
24


In the interests of public safety, health professionals including
nurses are required to report a person to the relevant authority if
they believe that person has a mental or physical condition that
will affect their driving abilities.
Open disclosure
Open disclosure
 is the open discussion of incidents that have
resulted in harm to a person while receiving health care, with the
person, their family, carers and other support people. Open
disclosure is:
a patient and consumer right
a core professional requirement and institutional obligation
a normal part of an episode of care should the unexpected occur
and a critical element of clinical communications
an attribute of high-quality health service organisation and
important part of health care quality improvement.
The open disclosure framework has eight guiding principles:
1. open and timely communication
2. acknowledgment
3. apology or expression of regret
4. supporting and meeting the needs and expectations of
people, their family and carers
5. supporting and meeting the needs of those providing health
care


6. integrated clinical risk management and systems
improvement
7. good governance
8. confidentiality (Australian Commission on Safety and Quality
in Health Care (ACSQHC)
).
25 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2014).
Open Disclosure Framework. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Nurses as witnesses
A nurse may be called to testify in a legal action. It is advisable that
any nurse who is asked to testify in such a situation should seek the
advice of a lawyer before providing testimony. In most cases, the
lawyer for the employer will provide support and counsel during the
legal case. If the nurse is the defendant, however, it is advisable for
the nurse to seek independent legal advice to protect the nurse’s
own interests. If the nurse belongs to a union, it is advisable to
approach this organisation for support before deciding what action to
take in this situation.
A nurse may also be asked to provide testimony as an expert
witness. There are strict rules associated with who may be
appointed as an expert witness and such action entails special
training, experience or skill in a relevant area. Once the court has
accepted the nurse as an expert, they can offer an opinion on an
issue within their area of expertise. The nurse’s credentials and
expertise help a judge or jury understand the appropriate standard
25


of care. For example, a nurse expert will have the ability to critically
analyse the facts or evidence and draw inferences about whether
the standard of care was met.
Professional governance
Professional discipline
The Health Practitioner Regulation National Law Act 2009 protects
the public by legally defining and describing the scope of nursing
practice. An important feature associated with self- regulation of
nursing practice is the ability of the profession to determine
standards of nursing practice. This is achieved in some respects by
board-appointed disciplinary committees and tribunals that are
authorised to investigate and carry out disciplinary action against
practitioners if required.
The standards that determine the framework for practice of nurses
and midwives in Australia are the professional codes and guidelines
provided by the NMBA. These include all the associated policies,
professional standards, guidelines, position statements, frameworks
and fact sheets.
One important feature of these guidelines (and the Act) is the
mandatory requirement for nurses and midwives to notify the NMBA
of improper or below-standard professional behaviour of another
health practitioner that places the public at risk of harm; this includes


students. Additional to mandatory reporting is voluntary reporting of
any professional behaviour that falls short of minimum professional
expectations. Voluntary notifications can be made by any person or
organisation that has reason to believe there are grounds for
concern.
There are a range of outcomes resulting from a complaint or
concern (see Table 4.3
).
Table 4.3 Possible outcomes from a complaint or concern about
practice

process/Possible-outcomes.aspx> where further information is available about each of the listed outcomes.
Unprofessional conduct and unsatisfactory
professional performance
There is a difference between unprofessional conduct and
unsatisfactory professional performance.
Unprofessional conduct
, of a registered health practitioner,
