means professional conduct that is of a lesser standard than that
which might reasonably be expected of the health practitioner by the
public or the practitioner’s professional peers, and includes:
a. a contravention by the practitioner of this Law, whether or not
the practitioner has been prosecuted for, or convicted of, an


offence in relation to the contravention; and
b. a contravention by the practitioner of—
i. a condition to which the practitioner’s registration was
subject; or
ii. an undertaking given by the practitioner to the National
Board that registers the practitioner; and
c. the conviction of the practitioner for an offence under another
Act, the nature of which may affect the practitioner’s
suitability to continue to practise the profession; and
d. providing a person with health services of a kind that are
excessive, unnecessary or otherwise not reasonably required
for the person’s well-being; and
e. influencing, or attempting to influence, the conduct of another
registered health practitioner in a way that may compromise
patient care; and
f. accepting a benefit as inducement, consideration or reward
for referring another person to a health service provider or
recommending another person use or consult with a health
service provider; and
g. offering or giving a person a benefit, consideration or reward
in return for the person referring another person to the
practitioner or recommending to another person that the
person use a health service provided by the practitioner; and
h. referring a person to, or recommending that a person use or
consult, another health service provider, health service or
health product if the practitioner has a pecuniary interest in
giving that referral or recommendation, unless the practitioner


discloses the nature of that interest to the person before or at
the time of giving the referral or recommendation.
Unsatisfactory professional performance
, of a registered
health practitioner, means that the knowledge, skill or judgment
possessed, or care exercised by, the practitioner in the practice of
the health profession in which the practitioner is registered is below
the standard reasonably expected of a health practitioner of an
equivalent level of training or experience, according to the Health
Practitioner Regulation National Law Act 2009.
There are various discretionary penalties available to the disciplinary
tribunal as a result of findings that support disciplinary proceedings
as outlined in Table 4.3. There is an embedded democratic ‘right’
that seeks to protect the individual from injustice by supporting the
availability of an appeal process against the original decision of a
case. This is available only if certain essential legal criteria are met
by the complainant. For example, if crucial ‘evidence’ was omitted
from the original hearing, or the board overstepped its legal authority
(ultra vires), or the punishment was too extreme given the
circumstances, a complainant may seek a review by the court of the
original case. Legislation is clear as to the limits of the registration
board’s authority and powers, processes and procedures that can
be utilised (substantive and procedural obligations).
The case of Andrew Moses (Health Care Complaints Commission v
Moses [2019] NSWCATOD 64), a Registered Nurse, was that he
had failed to observe proper professional boundaries with a patient


at a clinic at a private hospital in 2015. Moses developed a
relationship with the former patient after termination of treatment.
He was alleged to have communicated extensively and
inappropriately via phone and text message with the former patient,
who was considered highly vulnerable due to having a significant
mental health history.
The decision handed down in this case was that Moses was found
guilty of unsatisfactory professional performance because he:
engaged in conduct that demonstrates the knowledge, skill or
judgment possessed, or care exercised, by the practitioner in the
practice of nursing is significantly below the standard reasonably
expected of a practitioner of an equivalent level of training or
experience; and/or
engaged in improper or unethical conduct relating to the practice
or purported practice of nursing.
Clinical consideration
Remember, professional disciplinary bodies
have the power to investigate, discipline and
deregister a nurse.
Health and performance assessment


There are provisions included in the Health Practitioner Regulation
National Law Act 2009 that outline how the NMBA must respond
after receiving notification about a health practitioner. The Board
must within 60 days conduct a preliminary assessment of the
notification. If the Board decides that there is a case that requires
further investigation, the nurse or midwife will be notified by the
Board, in writing, of the nature of the notification (s 152). If there are
no real grounds for complaint, the complainant will be informed of
the Board’s decision to take no further action (s 151).
Impaired nurses
If the Board reasonably believes that the nurse or midwife has an
impairment that relates to the notification, it may require the person
to undergo a health assessment (s 169).
Performance assessment
If the Board reasonably believes that the nurse or midwife practises
the profession in an unsatisfactory way, it may require the person to
undergo a performance assessment (s 170).
Accreditation/approval of basic nursing
education programs
One important function of the NMBA is to ensure that education
providers preparing nurses maintain minimum standards of
education. The NMBA has appointed ANMAC as the independent


accrediting authority. ANMAC accredits all nursing and midwifery
courses and education providers.
The education programs for pre-registration nursing courses must
provide a broad foundation in nursing. This includes the
management of a person across the lifespan and health/illness
continuum. Courses must encompass a wide range of practices
such as health promotion, medical/surgical nursing, mental health
and disabilities nursing, and aged care nursing. Students must also
learn about cultural safety, in particular in relation to Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander people, and develop awareness of the cultural
diversity that exists in the Australian community.
Standard of care
The purpose of standards of care is to protect the consumer.
Standards of care
 are the knowledge, skills, attitude and
judgment expected by members of a profession to practise safely.
These standards are used to evaluate the quality of care nurses
provide and, therefore, they become guidelines for nursing practice
upon which other authorities, including legal authorities, can depend
as a minimum expectation.
Nursing standards of care can include the requirements of a job
description, educational knowledge and expertise as well as
individual institutional or organisational policies and procedures.


Other professional expectations are that of registration entities and
affiliated professional organisations.
Accreditation of health service organisations in Australia commenced
in 2011. The accreditation associated with the National Safety and
Quality Health Service (NSQHS) Standards
 was implemented
by the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC) to ensure safety and quality systems were introduced to
improve health care delivery in Australia. The primary aims of the
NSQHS Standards are to protect the public from harm and to
improve the quality of health service provision. They provide a
quality assurance mechanism that tests whether relevant systems
are in place to ensure minimum standards of safety and quality are
met, and a quality improvement mechanism that allows health
services to realise aspirational or developmental goals.
All health service organisations are required to provide a consistent
statement about the level of care people should expect or receive,
no matter where they are located in Australia. There is an
expectation that all nurses provide best practice clinical care related
to the NSQHS Standards (ACSQHC ). The Patient Safety
Competency Framework (Levett-Jones et al. 2017) has been
introduced to assist nursing students to understand and practise
safely within the context of the NSQHS Standards.
26 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2017). National
Safety and Quality Health Service Standards. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
26


In order to comply with professional standards, it is important for
nurses to be familiar with organisational, local, state and
Commonwealth policies and procedures as well as legislative
requirements under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law
Act 2009. Nurses also need to remain competent through self-
improvement, by reading professional journals and attending
continuing education and in-service programs. These are continuing
professional development (CPD) activities required by law under the
regulations for all health practitioners. The purpose of understanding
and practising standards of care is to protect the public, as well as to
ensure ‘professional’ practice.
In addition to the professional codes and guidelines available
through the NMBA website, other standards to adhere to are:
evidence-based practice guidelines
research organisations
complementary therapies used in nursing and midwifery practice.


Contractual arrangements in
nursing
Agreements are entered into for many reasons. Some agreements
are legally enforceable and some are not. The word ‘contract’ is
used to describe a legally enforceable agreement between two or
more people (parties). When a contract is made, the parties are
legally obliged to do what they promised. It is important for a person
who enters into an agreement with another person to understand
the implications of this arrangement.
There are some essential features in contract law. The main points
are that it is an ‘agreement’ and as such must have the elements
essential to agreements. For example, if the terms of the contract
are understood and consented to by the parties, the subject, terms
and so on are legal. Once the terms of the contract have been
agreed upon by two or more people (parties), if there is a breach
(wrong) by a party to the contract the person who is claiming this
breach may have a legal remedy available against the other party
(Forrester & Griffiths 2015). There is a difference between a
promise to do something and a contract. The main criteria for
distinguishing between a ‘promise’ and a ‘legal contract’ are the
intentions of the parties to formalise the agreement. For example, a
friend may ask you to help move furniture on a particular day and


you make a promise to help but don’t show up. Your friend may be
angry with you but this is not a legally enforceable contract.
A contract is the basis of the relationship between a nurse and an
employer—for example, a nurse and a hospital, or a nurse and a
doctor. A contract
 is an agreement between two or more
competent people, on sufficient consideration
(remuneration/service), to do or not to do some lawful act. A
contract may be verbal, written or even implied (Forrester & Griffiths
2015). An oral contract is as equally binding as a written contract.
The terms of the oral contract, however, may be more difficult to
prove in a court of law. A written contract cannot be changed legally
by an oral agreement. If two people wish to change some aspect of
a written contract, the change must be written into the contract
because one party cannot hold the other to an oral agreement that
differs from the written one.
A contract is considered to be expressed when the two parties
discuss and agree, orally or in writing, to terms and conditions during
the creation of the contract. For example, a nurse will work at a
hospital for a stated length of time and under stated conditions. An
implied contract
 is one that has not been explicitly agreed to by
the parties but that the law nevertheless considers exists (Forrester
& Griffiths 2015). For example, the nurse is expected to be
competent and to follow hospital policies and procedures even
though these expectations were not written or discussed. Likewise,
the hospital is expected to provide the necessary supplies and


equipment needed to provide competent nursing care (Savage
2015).
Legal role of nurses
Nurses have three separate, interdependent legal roles, each with
rights and associated responsibilities: provider of service, employee
or contractor for service and citizen (see Table 4.4
).
Table 4.4 Legal roles, rights and responsibilities
These roles can be further viewed as independent, interdependent
and dependent roles. For example, nurses who are providers of a
service (independent contractors) would be independent in that they
would carry out their duties relying on their own judgment and skills.
Employees, on the other hand, would be dependent practitioners in
the sense that they would be employed by an employer and subject
to the employer’s directions (old master/servant relationship). As a
citizen, you have the rights and obligations that all citizens possess
(receive health care services, pay tax, subject to the law etc.).
Citizen
The rights and responsibilities of the nurse in the role of citizen are
the same as those of any individual under the legal system. Rights
of citizenship protect people from harm and ensure consideration for


their personal property rights, rights to privacy, confidentiality and
other rights discussed later in this chapter. These same rights apply
to nurses.
Nurses move in and out of these roles when carrying out
professional and personal responsibilities. An understanding of these
roles and the rights and responsibilities associated with them
promotes legally responsible conduct and practice by nurses. A
right
 is a privilege or fundamental power to which an individual is
entitled unless it is revoked by law or given up voluntarily; a
responsibility
 is the obligation associated with a right.
However, it must be appreciated that the responsibilities associated
with independent and dependent actions can include
‘interdependent’ requirements as well. A nurse is a recognised
‘professional’, so to a very large extent is accountable not only for
workplace performance but also for practice requirements. The fact
that nurses are employees or independent contractors does not
necessarily mean that they are free to determine their own
‘standards’ of practice outside the profession itself as they have
professional standards expected of them in order to maintain
registration. There are also expectations that, as a professional, the
values held during a professional capacity are also upheld in private
life.
Provider of service


The nurse is expected to provide safe and competent care. Implicit
in this role are several legal concepts: liability, standards of care and
contractual obligations.
Liability
 is the quality or state of being legally responsible for
one’s obligations and actions, and for making financial restitution for
wrongful acts. A nurse, for example, has an obligation to practise
and direct the practice of others under their supervision so that harm
or injury is prevented and standards of care are maintained. Even
when a nurse carries out treatments ordered by the doctor, the
responsibility for the nursing activity belongs to the nurse. When a
nurse is asked to carry out an activity that they believe will be
injurious to a person, the nurse’s responsibility is to refuse to carry
out the order and report this to their supervisor.
The standards of care by which a nurse acts or fails to act are
defined by the NMBA in respect of the legal requirements laid out in
the Heath Practitioner Regulation National Law Act 2009 and by the
rule of reasonable and prudent action—what a reasonable and
prudent professional with similar preparation and experience would
do in similar circumstances. Contractual obligations
 refer to the
nurse’s duty of care (i.e. duty to render care) established by the
presence of an expressed or implied contract.
Employment contracts
The workplace is constantly changing. Traditional contractual
relationships (e.g. having a job for life, living and working in one


location) between employees and employers no longer dominate the
way we approach work. There is a need to be flexible from both the
employee and the employer point of view. The trend towards short-
term fixed contract arrangements, employment agency relationships
and casual and part-time employment are common features of our
society. Continuing debate about the need for a flexible and
productive workforce resonates politically and via the media; we are
constantly reminded that workers must be economically productive
in order to be ‘globally’ competitive. This has significantly changed
the way we think about and approach work. Nurses have not been
immune to these changes, although shortages in the workforce allow
nurses some political sway. The progressive erosion of workplace
conditions (penalty rates, maternity leave etc.), wages and
professional recognition is still an ongoing problem for many workers
including nurses.
In employment law there is an important distinction between the
contract for service and independent contracts; this is because
different legal obligations flow from this distinction and are important
for nurses to understand. There are numerous ways in which
employment relationships are organised; for example, full time,
casual, part time, specific contract and permanent part time, as well
as agency.
An important job of the law of employment is to categorise the
different types of relationship that may arise in order to determine
how they should be regulated. The application of the term
‘employee’ gradually replaced the term ‘servant’. Over the years, a


body of law developed which suggested a common and identifiable
distinction between two categories of those performing paid work—
employees and independent contractors:
1. Employees are those who perform work under the ‘control’ of
another person (employer) and are dependent on that other
for remuneration.
2. An independent contractor is a person who is considered to
be supplying services as businesses in their own right (Fair
Work Ombudsman ).
27 Fair Work Ombudsman (2019). National Employment Standards (NES).
Retrieved from <www.fairwork.gov.au>.
Who is an employer?
The question of employment relationships and how they are
structured is far more important these days because of the push
towards the privatisation of health services by government. There is
an assumption in employment relationships and employment
contracts that if a person has an employer it is not necessarily the
person with whom they contract to perform the work. This has
become important in a number of situations; for example, where the
business is operated through a related entity and a labour hire
service (agency) is used.
It is not uncommon for a business to split up its operation so that
workers are employed by one entity while the trading operations
27


they are supporting are carried out by another. These arrangements
can be deliberately structured so that the employing entity (often
referred to as a ‘service company’) is kept separate from the main
trading entity.
A common form of labour hire is through employment agencies. The
popularity of this type of entity has grown over the years. Some
agencies do no more than ‘broker’ employment contracts. They
introduce a worker and an employer and leave them to make the
necessary contract. However, there is another agency set-up that
operates as a ‘labour hire service’, which involves a triangular or
trilateral relationship between the agency, the worker and the host
firm.
The usual relationship of agency is where the agency enters into an
agreement with the worker and arranges to hire out the worker’s
services to the host or series of hosts. Even though the worker
generally performs these services at the host’s premises (hospital,
clinic, private home, nursing home etc.), the worker is paid by the
agency. Thus, issues of worker ‘dismissal’ will often be determined
by the contractual relationship between the parties (employee,
employer or agency).
A nurse who is employed by an agency works as a representative of
the agency, and the nurse’s contract with people who are cared for
in the facility is an implied one. However, a nurse who is employed
directly by a person, for example a private nurse, may have a
written contract with that person in which the nurse agrees to


provide professional services for a certain fee. A nurse might be
prevented from carrying out the terms of the contract because of
illness or death. However, personal inconvenience and personal
problems, such as the nurse’s car failure, are not legitimate reasons
for failing to fulfil a contract.
Another consideration here is regards midwives who provide
services to women and their babies in their homes. In this situation,
midwives are required to have professional indemnity insurance as a
legal requirement, per s 129(1) of the National Law.
Contractual relationships
 vary between practice settings (see
Box 4.3
). An independent Nurse Practitioner is a contractor for
service whose contractual relationship with the person requiring care
is an independent one. The nurse employed by a hospital functions
within an employer–employee relationship in which the nurse
represents and acts for the hospital, and therefore must function
within the policies of the employing organisation. This type of legal
relationship creates the ancient legal doctrine known as respondeat
superior (‘let the master answer’). In other words, the master
(employer) assumes responsibility for the conduct of the servant
(employee) and can also be held responsible for negligence by the
employee. This relationship is given legal standing via the doctrine of
‘vicarious liability’. This doctrine makes an employer responsible for
the acts of the employee. If a nurse is an employee of a hospital,
they are the hospital’s responsibility.


BO X
4.3 Elements of contract
There is an intention by both parties to assume legally binding
obligations.
1. Domestic agreements that are reached between close
family members are inferred from the facts not to be
legally binding unless otherwise proved: Balfour v
Balfour [1919] 2 KB 571, Merritt v Merritt [1970] 2 All
ER 760.
2. The likely inference of an agreement between friends
or volunteers is that it is not intended to be binding
unless proved otherwise: Teen Ranch Pty Ltd v Brown
(1995) 11 NSWCCR 197.
3. If the agreement is made in a commercial context, it is
usually inferred that the parties intended to be legally
bound.
4. The parties can agree that the creation of a contract
can be delayed until some event has taken place.
5. Agreements can be characterised as formal and
informal. Formal agreements are those that are
executed in a ‘deed’. An agreement that is not
executed in a deed is called an ‘informal’ agreement.


This doctrine does not imply that the nurse cannot be held liable as
an individual. Nor does it imply that an employee’s actions will prevail
if the behaviour is extraordinarily inappropriate; that is, beyond those
expected or foreseen by the employer. For example, if the nurse hits
a person in the face, the employer could disclaim responsibility
because this behaviour is beyond the bounds of expected behaviour.
Criminal acts, such as assisting with illegal surgical procedures or
taking tranquillisers or other drugs from a person’s supply for
personal use, would also be considered extraordinarily inappropriate
behaviour. Nurses can be held liable for failure to act. These are
examples of situations requiring mandatory reporting (AHPRA 2019).
For example, a nurse who sees another nurse hitting someone and
fails to do anything to protect the person may be considered
negligent.
The nurse in the role of employee or contractor for service has
obligations to the employer, the person requiring care and other
personnel. The nursing care provided must be within the limitations
and terms specified (see Box 4.4
). The nurse has an obligation to
contract only for those responsibilities that the nurse is competent to
discharge. For example, the nurse must practise according to the
federal and state legislation and the policies and procedures of the
facility or organisation.
BO X


4.4 Key principles in contract of
employment
1. There must be a clear and definite offer of
employment made between the parties.
2. The terms of the agreement between the parties need
to be certain.
3. There must be valid consideration.
4. The employment contract must be for a legal purpose.
The nurse is expected to respect the rights and responsibilities of
other health care participants. For example, although the nurse has
a responsibility to explain nursing activities to a person requiring
care, the nurse does not have the right to comment on medical
practice in a way that disturbs that person or denounces the doctor.
At the same time, the nurse has the right to expect reasonable and
prudent conduct from other health professionals.
The following elements underpin the finding that the parties intend
that their arrangement will have legal consequences.
The nature and scope of an employee’s duties under contract of
employment in Australia must include:
maximum weekly hours
requests for flexible working arrangements


parental leave and related entitlements
annual leave
personal carers’ leave and compassionate leave
community service leave
long-service leave
public holidays
notice of termination and redundancy pay
Fair Work Information Statement (Fair Work Ombudsman 2019).
It must also include the position title (classification), remuneration
and terms of employment.
The existence of a bilateral duty of ‘trust and confidence’ in the
employment area has been accepted in Australian law.
Workplace awards
From the early twentieth century (1904), the Australian industrial
relations system and the terms of employees within it have been
based on the compulsory settlement of industrial disputes by means
of conciliation and arbitration under s 51(35) of the Constitution. The
federal system has been dominated by the Commonwealth Court of
Conciliation and Arbitration. States manage their own industrial
relations matters, with the Northern Territory and Australian Capital
Territory being covered by Commonwealth legislation. Industrial
legislation is important to protect issues such as payment of wages,
sick leave, provision of holiday or other leave, contract or


employment conditions, and notice of termination and redundancy
pay.
An award is a declaration of future rights and responsibilities
between the employer and employee. Contracts can involve
bargaining by both parties before an award if agreed to. The Fair
Work Act 2009 (Cth) amended 2018 was introduced to become the
national workplace relations tribunal. It has been established to
assist in setting minimum wages and working conditions, facilitating
good faith bargaining for enterprise agreements, regulating industrial
action, workplace dispute resolution, termination of employment and
determining outcomes for unfair dismissal (Fair Work Ombudsman
2019).
Work Choices
The Fair Work System was established by the Fair Work Act 2009.
The Fair Work System sets the minimum employment laws and
agency bodies that were instituted from the Fair Work Act 2009. It
demands that there are 10 minimum National Employment
Standards, awards that are regulated for specific industries and
occupations, a national minimum wage and protection from unfair
dismissal (Fair Work Ombudsman 2019).
Enterprise bargaining and
agreements


Enterprise bargaining
 and agreements have played and
continue to play an important role in Australian industrial relations.
Workplace bargaining assists in fostering change to improve
productivity and efficiency of a company and can lead to
improvements in the workplace. It involves reviewing the specific
needs and circumstances of a particular industry (nursing, teachers,
clerical etc.). Generally, the process involves the recognition of a
bargaining representative for the employees. This representative
can be a union, a trade association or a professional organisation. If
a majority of employees want to bargain with an employer, an
application can then be made to the Fair Work Commission for a
majority support determination (s 236) of the Fair Work Act 2009
(Fair Work Commission ). It is still possible for an employer and an
employee to directly negotiate an employment agreement at the
workplace.
28 Fair Work Commission (2019). Australia’s National Workplace Relations Tribunal.
Retrieved from <www.fwc.gov.au/>.
When enterprise bargaining breaks down because an agreement
cannot be reached, in limited situations, employees can call a strike
or impose work bans. This is known as ‘protected industrial action’.
The Fair Work Commission can prohibit strike activities by essential
services personnel, including health practitioners (nurses, doctors
and paramedics) (Fair Work Commission 2019). Because nursing
practice is a service to the ill or vulnerable, strikes present a moral
dilemma as their actions can affect the safety and wellbeing of the
public.
28


Selected legal aspects of nursing
practice
Nurses need to know and apply legal aspects in their many different
roles. For example, as an advocate for people in their care, nurses
ensure the right to informed consent or refusal. They can also
identify and report violent behaviour or neglect of vulnerable people.
Legal aspects include the duty to report any health practitioner who
poses a threat to the safety of a person due to lack of knowledge or
skills or poor health, or who is suspected of being under the
influence of drugs or alcohol while in the workplace (AHPRA 2019).
Informed consent
Consent may be spoken, written or implied; it must be voluntary and
related only to the specific procedure consented to. The person
giving consent must have the ‘legal capacity’ to do so. This means
that the person is an adult of sound mind and is competent to make
decisions about their treatment or their refusal of treatment (Savage
2015).
The Australian Charter of Healthcare Rights determines who has the
authority to consent on behalf of people who do not have the mental


capacity to consent. Factors such as a life-threatening situation,
mental illness, intellectual disability and age can constitute reasons
why a person may not be able to fully consent (ACSQHC 2017).
The use of consent provides the health practitioner with a legal
defence against unlawful touching of a person requiring their care. It
also protects the bodily and psychological integrity of that person by
supporting important ethical considerations such as autonomy
and/or rights. It can be argued that proper consent to a treatment or
procedure should be informed. The term informed consent
 is a
tautology because in order for consent to be a valid defence it must
be informed. In Rogers v Whitaker (1992) 175 CLR 479, a woman
(W) underwent elective surgery on her right eye. The woman had
had a penetrating injury as a child and was blind in her right eye but
could see out of her ‘good left eye’. Dr Rogers, an ophthalmic
surgeon, performed surgery on her right eye as a cosmetic
procedure (although it was hoped that she might get some sight
back again). Subsequent to surgery, complications developed in the
right eye and spread to the left eye, resulting in total blindness,
known as ‘sympathetic ophthalmia’, a very rare complication of the
surgery. The woman sued for negligence on a number of grounds.
The case was appealed to the High Court from the Supreme Court
of New South Wales on several important points and still remains
legally relevant today. The outcome from this case is that medical
practitioners are now required by law to inform people about
potential risks from surgery and medical procedures (Savage 2015).


The High Court in Rogers v Whitaker applied the test of ‘material
risks’ regarding what information about the treatment needed to be
communicated to a person receiving care in order to discharge this
duty. This information would include the benefits and risks of
treatment, alternatives to the treatment and prognosis if not treated
by a doctor. Communication is the key to consent. Usually a person
requiring care signs a form provided by the organisation. The form is
a record of the informed consent, not the informed consent itself
(Savage 2015).
There are two types of consent: express and implied. Express
consent may be either an oral or a written agreement. It is generally
expected that the more invasive a procedure and/or the greater the
potential for risk to the person requiring care, the greater the need
for written permission. Implied consent exists when the individual’s
non-verbal behaviour indicates agreement. For example, people who
position their bodies for an injection or cooperate with the taking of
vital signs infer implied consent. Consent is also implied in a medical
emergency when an individual cannot provide express consent
because of a physical condition (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Obtaining valid consent for specific medical and surgical treatments
is the responsibility of the person who is going to perform the
procedure (see Box 4.5
). Generally, it is the medical practitioner;
however, it could also be a Nurse Practitioner, nurse midwife, clinical
nurse specialist or the doctor’s assistant who is performing the
procedure in their advanced practices.


BO X
4.5 Three major elements of valid
consent
There are three major elements of valid consent:
1. The consent must be given voluntarily.
2. The consent must be given by a person who has the
capacity and competence to understand.
3. The person requiring care must be given enough
information to be the ultimate decision maker.
Informed consent also applies to nurses who are not independent
practitioners and are performing direct nursing care for such
procedures as nasogastric tube insertion or medication
administration. The nurse relies on orally expressed consent or
implied consent for most nursing interventions. It is imperative to
remember the importance of communicating by explaining nursing
procedures and ensuring the person understands before obtaining
permission (Johnstone 2019).
To give valid consent voluntarily, a person must not feel coerced
(see Box 4.5
). Sometimes fear of disapproval by a health
professional can be the motivation for giving consent; such consent
is not voluntarily given. Coercion invalidates the consent. It is
important, therefore, for the person obtaining the consent to invite


and answer questions a person may have (Johnstone 2019). It is
also important to remember that a person may not understand what
they are being asked to consent to. Poor understanding about a
procedure and expected recovery can lead to unnecessary stress to
all involved as well as possible legal action (ACSQHC 2017). Another
consideration can be the technique of ‘nudging’, which is where
surgeons might be accused of providing a variety of options for
people requiring surgery, even though there may not be a
requirement for those options. An example of this is where a small
breast lump is found and although there is not a very high chance of
the lump being cancer, the surgeon would suggest an open surgical
incision. Douglas and Proudfoot
 suggest that people requiring care
look for nuances in the way doctors present information that might
imply a certain course of action or management. This course of
action may be reasonable; however, the doctor may not have
provided all the information that could have provided the person with
an opportunity to make an informed decision.
29 Douglas, C. & Proudfoot, E. (2013). Nudging and the complicated real life of ‘informed
consent’. The American Journal of Bioethics, 13(6), 16–17.
Cultural perspective
 also needs to be considered when people
are asked to make decisions about a procedure or treatment. For
example, informed consent in Australia is based on the principle of
autonomy. That is, each person has the right to decide what can or
cannot be done to their person. It is expected that the competent
adult will have the autonomy to make their own health care
decisions. In contrast to this individual perspective, people from
some cultures (e.g. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Middle
29


Eastern) may have a group perspective for decision making. They
may believe that another member of their family or group should
make the decision. The nurse can provide culturally competent care
by asking people who are requiring care if there is someone they
would like to be present when information or discussion of their
health care treatment occurs (Johnstone 2019).
Informed consent relies heavily on moral principles most often
referred to when thinking about ethical decision making. They are:
autonomy—that people be respected for being self-determining
choosers and that they be able to have options about accepting
risks
non-maleficence—that people be protected from battery, assault,
trespass, exploitation, or any detriment that may result from
inadequate or inappropriate consent processes (including the
inadequate or inappropriate disclosure of information)
beneficence—that people be treated kindly and that their
wellbeing be maximised using the consent process
justice—that all people be treated fairly and not be unnecessarily
burdened by the consent process (Johnstone 2019).
Clinical consideration
When considering consent there are legal and
moral obligations that the nurse must take into
account to validly discharge this duty. Evidence


of consent is a recognised defence to a civil
action in negligence, assault or battery (defence
of volenti).
If given sufficient information, a competent adult can make decisions
regarding health. Under common law, a competent adult is a person
over 18 years of age who is conscious and oriented. A person who
is confused, disoriented or sedated is not considered functionally
competent. A legal guardian or representative can provide or refuse
consent for the incompetent adult.
Informed consent regulations were originally written with acute care
settings in mind. Nonetheless, ensuring informed consent is equally
important in providing nursing care in the home. Because the
provision of home care often occurs over an extended period of
time, the nurse has multiple opportunities to ensure that a person
agrees to the proposed plan of treatment. A challenge to informed
consent in the home, however, is that the plan may affect other
members of the family and, if so, they need to be consulted. For
example, in New South Wales, the Guardianship Act 1987 (NSW)
amended 2018 may need to be used in certain circumstances and
provides process about identifying a substitute decision maker or
providing consent to specialised medical treatments. These might be
particular medications required or treatments that affect fertility. The
Guardianship Act may also be used in instances where treatment
needs to be given without the person’s consent.


Exceptions to consent
The law recognises that an adult who is conscious and capable of
making decisions has a right to accept or refuse treatment.
However, there are some groups of people who cannot provide
consent. The first is minors
. In most areas, a parent or guardian
must give consent before minors can obtain treatment. Generally, a
person is a minor or child at law for most reasons until the age of 18
unless that person marries. This general common law requirement
has been modified in the health area by legislation. For example, s
49 of the Minors (Property and Contracts) Act 1970 (NSW)
amended 2015 sets the age at which a child can consent to medical
treatment at 14 years and s 6 of the Consent to Medical Treatment
and Palliative Care Act 1995 (SA) amended 2014 sets it at 16 years.
In other jurisdictions, the right to consent to treatment is vested in:
a parent of the child or a person in whose favour a parenting
order by the Family Court under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth)
amended 2019 has been made
the nominated person to whom the parent has given authority to
make such a decision
a legally appointed guardian of the child (e.g. a foster parent,
welfare officer)
a court with the jurisdiction to make such a decision for the child
(exercising parens patriae jurisdiction) (Forrester & Griffiths
2015).


Mature minor
A mature minor means that a child may consent to treatment if they
are capable of understanding the nature and consequences of that
treatment. The legal requirements for this ruling can be found in the
High Court decision in Department of Health and Community
Services (NT) v JWB and SMB (Marion’s case) (1992) 175 CLR 218.
The majority of the court followed the English decision in Gillick v
West Norfolk and Wisbech Area Health Authority [1986] AC 112. The
rationale behind Gillick’s case is that once a child achieves sufficient
understanding and intelligence to understand the proposed
treatment and consequences of that treatment, their parent’s right to
consent on their behalf ceases. This supports the concept of the
diminishing parent’s role as a child matures (Marion’s case)
(Forrester & Griffiths 2015, p. 154).
Adults who cannot consent
The capacity and competency to consent may be short term or long
term depending on the condition and circumstances of each case.
For temporary situations (non-urgent) the carer may need to wait
until a person has regained the capacity to consent, if this is
possible. This will guard against ‘blanket labelling’ of such a person
as ‘incompetent’, which can have significant legal and ethical
consequences (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Intellectual disability


The term ‘intellectual disability’ is used to describe a person who has
a permanent or long-term intellectual deficit that renders them
incapable to some extent of leading a normal life without assistance
from others. The impairment may be mild to severe. A person who
suffers from this type of disability may be unable to consent to
treatment. Health care providers generally will not be able to legally
give consent on their behalf without a substitute decision maker who
is authorised by law. Legislation such as the Guardianship Act 1987
(NSW) amended 2018 (other states and territories also have similar
laws) will determine who this person is. It should be noted that there
is no common law authority that allows relatives to consent to
treatment on behalf of an incompetent adult (Forrester & Griffiths
2015).
Mental illness
All states and territories have legislation (mental health Acts) setting
out the obligations of people who have a mental illness (as defined
under the various Acts). Generally, there are strict procedural and
‘rights’ obligations attached to consent requirements when it comes
to mental illness. The general proposition is that just because a
person has an identifiable mental illness, it does not mean that they
cannot or are unable to consent to treatment. There are a number
of legal categories that are used for access to treatment criteria,
such as ‘voluntary’ and ‘involuntary’ admission. These categories
refer to the status of the person seeking admission to the clinic or
hospital for treatment. There are many legal and ethical checks and
balances, such as the opportunity to attend a magistrate’s hearing,


courts, mental health boards and tribunals, which regulate this
important area of health care.
However, where a person is scheduled under an Act, there may be
an exception to the normal consent rule when it comes to necessary
treatment and hospitalisation.
Box 4.6
 sets out warning signs for mental illness (see also
Chapter 45
).
BO X
4.6 Warning signs—mental illness
There are a number of signs that may indicate a person
requires a mental health assessment. These may include:
erratic mood swings (depression or elation)
hearing voices, inappropriately talking to oneself
inappropriate or bizarre behaviour and/or speech.
Drugs and alcohol
This is a complicated and very important area of health concern,
especially for those nurses who are constantly exposed to people


who misuse drugs or alcohol. There are a number of reasons why
drugs may affect a person with a substance misuse disorder:
side effects of prescribed medication
sedation due to medications, such as narcotics or tranquillisers
hormones
illegal drug use—speed, crack cocaine or heroin
alcohol use
combination of drugs and alcohol
combination of drugs.
In this situation, consideration should be given to the decision-
making capacity. If a person was asked to sign a consent form for
an operation after a pre-medication had been given, it is likely that
any consent would be rejected by the court. It would also be rejected
if a person was considered to be incapacitated by drugs, felt
pressure to sign, was not given enough information or felt unable to
question and consider the treatment.
Drug and alcohol problems are not just confined to people who
require care; nurses and other health care providers can be
susceptible to substance misuse (see Box 4.7
). It is important
that nurses become knowledgeable about the risk factors of
chemical abuse and its early warning signs.
BO X


4.7 Some warning signs of drug and
alcohol misuse in health care workers
Mood swings and irritability
Deterioration in behaviour (increased isolation, unkempt
appearance etc.)
Memory problems (temporary amnesia) and even
blackouts
Impaired motor coordination (slurred speech, flushed
face, bloodshot eyes, unsteady gait, excessive sweating)
Smell of alcohol
Frequent absences from ward or keenness to work
overtime
Increased somatic complaints
Signs out a large amount of controlled drugs
Often offers to administer medication to people not in their
direct care
May wear long sleeves all the time
People in their care who should have received pain
medication complain that the medication has not been
effective or deny having received their medication.
Not all characteristics need to be present. It is important to
look for changes or patterns in behaviour.
Emergency situations and consent


The doctrine of necessity is recognised in emergency situations.
Where a person who is unconscious or injured in such a way that
they are unable to give consent arrives at hospital, it is usual
practice that consent is obtained from the closest adult relative if
existing statutes permit. In a life-threatening emergency, if consent
cannot be obtained from a person requiring care or from a relative,
the law generally agrees that consent is implied to provide
necessary care for the emergency situation.
Statutory exceptions
The law recognises a number of statutory exceptions to the consent
rule. An example of this is an enduring power of attorney. A person
has a right in some jurisdictions to appoint a person as an agent to
make decisions on their behalf when they are unable to do so
through some form of physical or mental impairment.
An enduring power of attorney allows a person to authorise the legal
representative to:
consent to medical treatment
refuse medical treatment
consent to the donation of an organ, blood or tissue on their
behalf.
In New South Wales, the Guardianship Act 1987 amended 2018
allows competent adults to appoint an enduring guardian. In
Queensland, the Power of Attorney Act 1998 amended 2017


provides that competent adults may appoint an ‘enduring attorney’ to
make health care decisions.
Consent forms
As previously mentioned, not every procedure requires written
consent: it can be verbal or implied. Although not a legal
requirement, health practitioners and institutions will usually require
written consent forms because they provide evidence should a
dispute arise. Hospital policy sets out the process and who is
responsible for obtaining written consent from people requiring care.
It is essential that the words used in the consent form can be
understood by the person, that consent is voluntarily given and that
the process follows ‘best practice’. This means that the information
is explained and signed by the clinician performing the procedure
(Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
The right of consent also involves the right of refusal. People have a
right to change their minds and cancel a procedure or treatment.
Consent is a continual process and, particularly for those who are
undergoing long-term treatment or treatment that changes, people
should be reminded of their prerogative to alter the consent initially
given by them (Griffith & Tengnah ). Similar to informed consent, it
is important to educate the person about any possible benefits or
risks associated with the refusal. The court can deny adults the right
to refuse treatment if it risks the life or health of others; for example,
the court can intervene to order a caesarean section to save a baby
if the mother refuses. Based on the Children (Care and Protection)
30


Act 1987 (NSW) amended 2019, in February 1994 a Supreme Court
of Australia judge ordered that a child have a life- saving blood
transfusion even though the parents did not consent due to religious
beliefs (Savage 2015). If a person does refuse treatment, the nurse
should document the circumstances before notifying the health
provider.
30 Griffith, R. & Tengnah, C. (2012). Consent to care: Patients who demand or refuse
treatment. British Journal of Community Nursing, 17(3), 139–142.
Nurse’s role
Generally, it is not the nurse’s responsibility to obtain written consent
from a person requiring care. It is the responsibility of the person
performing the procedure (e.g. medical practitioner, surgeon) to
obtain valid consent from the person (see Figure 4.2
).
Figure 4.2


Obtaining consent is the responsibility of the person performing the
procedure.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
There may be occasions, however, when a nurse is asked to witness
the person’s signature on the consent form. This does not mean that
the nurse is responsible for explaining the procedure or for obtaining
valid consent. This remains the legal responsibility of the particular
medical practitioner. The nurse’s signature confirms three things:
1. The person requiring care gave consent voluntarily.
2. The signature is authentic.
3. The person requiring care appears competent to give
consent.
The issue of witnessing a signature of a person requiring care may
also arise in other clinical situations, such as when a person decides
to execute a new will while in hospital. Many employers have a policy
on witnessing documents and nurses should be discouraged to sign
as a witness unless they fully understand the document they are
signing (Starr
).
31 Starr, K. T. (2016). Should you witness a signature on a patient’s personal legal document?
Nursing2019, 46(12), 14.
Clinical consideration
31


Obtaining consent is the responsibility of the
person performing the procedure. The nurse
may be asked to witness a signature of a
person requiring care on the consent form.
The common law Doctrine of Necessity supports the notion that if a
person has a life-threatening injury and cannot consent, and there is
a likely outcome of death or greater injury, then the consent rule can
be overridden.
The nurse advocates for a person by verifying that enough
information has been provided to give consent. If the person
requiring care has questions, or if the nurse has doubts about the
person’s understanding, the nurse must notify the health provider.
Again, the nurse is not responsible for explaining the medical or
surgical procedure. In fact, the nurse could be liable for giving
incorrect or incomplete information or interfering with the relationship
the person has with the provider.
Clinical consideration
Ask a person requiring care to state in their own
words what they have been told about the
procedure or treatment.


Documentation
Documentation is a very important part of providing care. It is
necessary to obtain information from people and record
observations and test results. This is generally achieved via medical
health records.
The function of documentation is that it is a source of
communication between members of the health team and contribute
to effective care. Documentation provides a contemporaneous
record of events that have taken place. Appropriate documentation
is critical in negligence or other cases in establishing the facts of
treatment. The professional standards case, HCCC v Selby &
Phillips ([2016] NSWNMPSC 5), highlights a lack of effective
communication, including documentation by two Registered Nurses.
These nurses were working in an emergency department where they
failed to provide adequate information about the recent history of
deterioration of a 6-month-old infant to the treating medical officer
and ambulance service staff transporting the child. Due to the poor
documentation that failed to indicate significant issues, the child
deteriorated further during road transfer. This required a helicopter
to expedite him to advanced care and surgery; however, the child
subsequently suffered neurological damage and died.
For many reasons, medical records are important and they have
many uses outside as well as inside the clinical area; for example,
as court documents. They may be used to refresh a witness’s


memory or challenge the accuracy of the particular event under
consideration; therefore, ideally they should be written
contemporaneously and not retrospectively (Forrester & Griffiths
2015).
Documentation should:
be adequate—it should be carefully completed. Adequate time
should be made available for this requirement
be accurate—it should reflect as closely as possible the event
being reported
be objective—other than in the context of ‘expert witnesses’,
opinions are generally not accepted in courts, nor is hearsay. The
health care professional must directly hear, see, feel, smell or
taste something
be legible and clear as to meaning
not be rewritten or transcribed—errors could be made in the
process
not be written on behalf of another health care professional
be error-free, but errors should not be obliterated—when a
mistake occurs, rule neatly through the mistake, then initial and
date it (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Controlled substances
Laws in Australia (Narcotic Drugs Act 1967 (Cth) amended 2016,
Therapeutic Goods Act 1989 (Cth) amended 2018, Poisons and


Therapeutic Goods Act 1966 (NSW) amended 2018, Health (Drugs
and Poisons) Regulation 1996 (Qld) amended 2017) regulate the
distribution and use of controlled substances such as narcotics,
depressants, stimulants and hallucinogens. Misuse of controlled
substances leads to criminal penalties (Forrester & Griffiths 2015)
(see Chapter 36
).
Clinical consideration
It is important that nursing students and nurses
become knowledgeable about the risk factors of
substance misuse and its early identification and
interventions.
Sexual harassment
Sexual harassment
 is a violation of the individual’s rights and a
form of discrimination. Sexual harassment is any unwanted or
unwelcome sexual behaviour that makes a person feel offended,
humiliated or intimidated. It is not about interaction, flirtation or
friendship that is mutual or consensual. Sexual harassment
continues to be one of the most common types of complaints in the
workplace, even though the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth)
amended 2018 was introduced more than 30 years ago. The Sex


and Age Discrimination Legislation Amendment Act 2011 amended
the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 in May 2011 to expand the
protections against sexual harassment; however, the extensive use
of technologies such as mobile phones, email and social networking
sites make sexual harassment more prevalent (Australian Human
Rights Commission ).
32 Australian Human Rights Commission (2016a). Sexual Discrimination. Retrieved from
<www.humanrights.gov.au>.
Sexual harassment can take many different forms—it can be
obvious or indirect, physical or verbal, repeated or one-off, and
perpetrated by males and females against people of the same or
opposite sex.
Sexual harassment may include:
staring or leering
unnecessary familiarity, such as deliberately brushing up against
someone, or unwelcome touching
suggestive comments or jokes
insults or taunts of a sexual nature
intrusive questions or statements about a person’s private life
displaying posters, magazines or screen savers of a sexual
nature
sending sexually explicit emails or text messages
inappropriate advances on social networking sites
accessing sexually explicit internet sites
32


requests for sex or repeated unwanted requests to go out on
dates
behaviour that may also be considered to be an offence under
criminal law, such as physical assault, indecent exposure, sexual
assault, stalking or obscene communications.
Sexual harassment disproportionately affects women, with 1 in 4
women aged 15 years and over experiencing sexual harassment in
the workplace at some time. The harasser is most likely to be a co-
worker and the most common forms of sexual harassment include
sexually suggestive comments/jokes, intrusive questions/comments
about private life or appearance, and inappropriate staring or leering
(Australian Human Rights Commission 2016a). Sexual harassment
can undermine women’s opportunities for equal participation in
organisations or business, reduce the quality of their working life and
impose costs on organisations (Australian Human Rights
Commission ).
40 Australian Human Rights Commission (2016b). Workplace Bullying: Violence, Harassment
and Bullying Factsheet. Retrieved from <www.humanrights.gov.au>.
Workplace bullying
Bullying is different from sexual harassment. Bullying can be
anything from a sarcastic remark by a work colleague to intentionally
being provided with the wrong person’s chart (Gaffney et al.
).
Workplace bullying is verbal, physical, social or psychological abuse
40
33


by an employer (or manager) or another person or group of people
at work (Safe Work Australia ). Bullying in the workplace is not
tolerated and should be reported if it occurs. All staff have a moral
responsibility to support colleagues if they think they are being
bullied.
33 Gaffney, D. A., DeMarco, R. F., Hofmeyer, A., Vessey, J. A. & Budin, W. C. (2012). Making
things right: Nurses’ experiences with workplace bullying—A grounded theory. Nursing
Research and Practice, 2012, 243210. Doi: 10.1155/2012/243210.
34 Safe Work Australia (2019). Safe Work Australia Leads the Development of National Policy
to Improve Work Health and Safety and Workers’ Compensation Arrangements across
Australia. Retrieved from <www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au>.
Workplace bullying can include:
repeated hurtful remarks or attacks, or making fun of your work
or you as a person (including your family, sex, sexuality, gender
identity, race or culture, education or economic background)
sexual harassment, particularly unwelcome touching, sexually
explicit comments and requests that make you uncomfortable
excluding you or stopping you from working with people or taking
part in activities that relate to your work
playing mind games, ganging up on you or other types of
psychological harassment
intimidation (making you feel less important and undervalued)
giving you pointless tasks that have nothing to do with your job
giving you impossible jobs that cannot be done in the given time
or with the resources provided
34


deliberately changing your work hours or schedule to make it
difficult for you
deliberately holding back information you need to get your work
done properly
pushing, shoving, tripping, grabbing you in the workplace
attacking or threatening with equipment, knives, guns, clubs or
any other type of object that can be turned into a weapon
initiation rituals or hazing—where you are made to do humiliating
or inappropriate things in order to be accepted as part of the
team.
Workplace bullying may affect your work and cause you to:
be less active or successful
be less confident in your work
feel scared, stressed, anxious or depressed
have your life outside work affected (e.g. study, relationships)
want to stay away from work
feel like you can’t trust your employer or the people you work
with
have a lack in confidence and happiness about yourself and your
work
have physical signs of stress such as headaches, backaches and
sleep problems (Australian Human Rights Commission 2019b).
Death and related issues


The nurse’s role in legal issues related to death is prescribed by the
laws of the state and the policies of the health care institution. A
person must be pronounced dead by a medical officer. Any tubes or
cannulae should be left in situ if there is to be an autopsy. When a
person dies unexpectedly in a hospital, it is most likely that there will
be an autopsy or investigation of the body. The family may agree to
a medico-legal autopsy; although this could be to determine death,
sometimes this may be in the interests of research. A post-mortem
looks at all the events and circumstances related to the death
(Savage 2015). It is also important to consider that there may be
religious or cultural practices that the family should be allowed to
follow as long as the practice does not distress other people
receiving care nearby.
Coronial inquest
Each state or territory has specific legislation that sets out the legal
requirements of investigating a suspicious death (Coroners Acts). An
inquest
 is a legal inquiry into the cause or manner of a death.
The coroner is involved when a death:
is sudden and of unknown cause
occurs under suspicious circumstances
occurs during or shortly after surgery or other invasive process
occurs in custody
occurs when a person was in or temporarily absent from a
mental health facility where they were receiving involuntary
treatment.


The inquest is conducted under the jurisdiction of a coroner or
pathologist. A coroner is a magistrate appointed to inquire into the
causes of death, when appropriate. A pathologist usually has
advanced education in pathology or forensic medicine.
Organisational policy dictates who is responsible for reporting deaths
to the coroner (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).


Areas of potential liability in
nursing
Nursing liability is usually involved with tort law. It is important for the
nurse to know the differences between negligence (an unintentional
tort) and intentional torts.
Crimes and torts
A crime is an act committed in violation of public (criminal) law and
punishable by a fine or imprisonment. A crime does not have to be
intended in order to be a crime. For example, a nurse may
accidentally give a person an additional and lethal dose of a narcotic
to relieve discomfort.
Crimes are classified as either felonies or misdemeanours. A felony
is a crime of a serious nature, such as murder, punishable by a term
in prison. In some areas, second-degree murder is called
manslaughter. A nurse who accidentally gives an additional and
lethal dose of a narcotic can be accused of manslaughter.
Crimes are punished through criminal action by the state against an
individual. A misdemeanour is an offence of a less serious nature


and is usually punishable by a fine or short-term jail sentence, or
both. A nurse who slaps the face of a person who is in their care
could be charged with a misdemeanour.
Tort law
A tort
 is a civil wrong committed against a person or a person’s
property. Torts are usually litigated in court by civil action between
individuals. In other words, the person, or people, claimed to be
responsible for the tort is sued for damages. Tort liability almost
always is based on fault; that is, something that was done incorrectly
(an unreasonable act of commission) or something that should have
been done but was not (an act of omission).
Torts may be classified as unintentional or intentional. It is important
to distinguish between intentional and unintentional torts because
the legal actions and requirements are different.
Unintentional torts
Negligence is an example of an unintentional tort that may occur in
the health care setting. Negligence
 is misconduct or practice that
is below the standard expected of an ordinary, reasonable and
prudent person (Donohue v Stevenson—the ‘snail in the ginger beer
bottle’ case—[1932] AC 562). Such conduct places another person
at risk of harm. Both non-medical and professional people can be


liable for negligent acts. Criminal negligence
 occurs when the
health care professional’s action has been so grossly negligent as to
be deliberately reckless of life or limb, and there is a possibility that
the health care professional may be prosecuted by the criminal
court. As discussed earlier in this chapter, in Australia, nurses can
be found guilty of professional misconduct or unprofessional
conduct.
Duty of care
 means the nurse must have (or should have had) a
relationship with the person that involves providing care and
following an acceptable standard of care. Such duty of care, for
example, is evident when the nurse has been assigned to care for
that person in the home or hospital. A nurse also has a general duty
of care, even if they haven’t been specifically assigned to a
particular person, if that person needs assistance.
Clinical consideration
It is a nurse’s duty to respond to all call lights or
buzzers, not just those of people assigned to
them for their shift.
Breach of duty of care. There must be a standard of care that
is expected in the specific situation but that the nurse did not
observe. For example, something was done that should not have


been done or nothing was done when it should have been done.
This is the failure to act as a reasonable, prudent nurse under
the circumstances. The standard can come from the professional
codes and guidelines outlined by the NMBA, organisational
policies and procedures, textbooks or journals, general
knowledge and practice of the profession, or it may be stated by
expert witnesses (Rogers v Whitaker (1992) 175 CLR 479).
Foreseeability. A link must exist between the nurse’s act and
the injury suffered (Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v The Miller
Steamship Co Pty Ltd (‘The Wagon Mound’) (No. 2) [1967] 1 AC
617 (Privy Council England)).
Causation. It must be proved that the harm occurred as a direct
result of the nurse’s failure to follow the standard of care and the
nurse could have (or should have) known that failure to follow the
standard of care could result in such harm (Froom v Butcher
[1976] QB 291).
Harm or injury. The plaintiff must demonstrate some type of
harm or injury (physical, financial or emotional) as a result of the
breach of duty owed. The plaintiff will be asked to document
physical injury, medical costs, loss of wages, ‘pain and suffering’
and any other damages (Miller v Royal Derwent Hospital Board
of Management [1992] Aust Torts Reports ¶81-175 (SC Tas)).
Damages. If negligence caused the injury, the nurse is held liable
for damages that may be compensated. The goal of awarding
damages is to assist the injured party to their original position so
far as financially possible (Safety, Rehabilitation and
Compensation Act 1988 (Cth) amended 2019; Safety,
Rehabilitation and Compensation Regulations 2002) (Guido ).
35


There are different types of damages, including economic and
non-economic damages (e.g. loss of wages, medical expenses,
pain and suffering).
35 Guido, G. W. (2005). Legal and Ethical Issues in Nursing (4th ed.). Upper Saddle
River, NJ: Prentice Hall.
Clinical consideration
The best defence against a negligence claim is
to know your nursing responsibilities and the
scope of practice of members of your health
team.
In order to establish negligence as a cause of action under the law
of torts, a plaintiff must prove that the defendant had a duty to the
plaintiff, the defendant breached that duty by failing to conform to
the required standard of conduct, the defendant’s negligent conduct
was the cause of the harm to the plaintiff and the plaintiff was, in
fact, harmed or damaged.
Several legal doctrines or principles are related to negligence. One
such doctrine is vicarious liability; this doctrine shifts the
responsibility for monetary compensation from a negligent employee
to the employer (institution). Hospitals and other health service
providers are responsible for people in their care; this is referred to


as non-delegable duty of care. What non-delegable duty of care
means is that a hospital (health service) owes certain obligations
(that cannot be delegated away to someone else) to people in their
care, including providing a safe environment, competent staff,
appropriate record keeping and adequately maintained equipment
(see Ellis v Wallsend District Hospital (1989) 17 NSWLR 553)
(Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Another doctrine or principle is res ipsa loquitur (‘the thing speaks for
itself’). In some cases, the harm cannot be traced to a specific
health care provider or standard but does not normally occur unless
there has been a negligent act. An example is harm that results
when surgical instruments or bandages are accidentally left in a
person during surgery.
To defend against a negligence action, the nurse must prove that
one or more of the required elements (duty, breach, causation,
scope of liability, damages) is not met. There is also a limit to the
amount of time that can pass between recognition of harm and the
bringing of a suit. This is referred to as the Statute of Limitations.
The exact time limitation varies by type of suit and state, but
typically plaintiffs have 1 to 2 years from the time that they knew of
the injury or had reason to believe that an injury had been sustained
to file a negligence lawsuit. In some cases, an additional defence is
‘contributory or comparative negligence’ on the part of the injured
person. In these situations, the person was at least partly
responsible for their injury. When people who have received care
choose not to follow health care advice, such as remaining in bed


while recovering from a treatment, the court may reduce any verdict
against the nurse by an amount considered to be the plaintiff’s own
contribution.
To avoid charges of negligence, nurses must recognise those
nursing situations in which negligent actions are most likely to occur
and take measures to prevent them. The most common situation is
the medication error. Because of the large number of medications on
the market today and the variety of methods of administration, these
errors may be on the increase. Nursing errors include failing to read
the medication label, misreading or incorrectly calculating the
dosage, failing to correctly identify the correct person, preparing the
wrong concentration or administering a medication by the wrong
route (e.g. intravenously instead of intramuscularly). Some
medication errors are very serious and can result in death (Forrester
& Griffiths 2015). For example, administering an anticoagulant to a
person recently returned from surgery could cause that person to
have a haemorrhage. Nurses must check medications very carefully.
Even after checking, the nurse is wise to recheck the medication
order and the medication before administering it if a person states,
for example, ‘I did not have a green pill before’.
Nurses should also recognise situations that may be potential areas
of legal concern. For example, a prescribing medical practitioner
might order medication and the order is ambiguous (not written
clearly) or it is not within acceptable or therapeutic ranges (dosages
or times) according to evidence, and could potentially be a risk to
the person receiving care. The nurse must question the order, not


give the medication (until sure) and seek support and assistance
from the manager. Remember that giving the incorrect dose
according to orders and having the person receiving care suffer an
adverse reaction puts the nurse in a position of legal accountability,
despite the fact or defence that the nurse was ‘carrying out the
doctor’s orders’. Nurses are legally responsible for carrying out
orders, even if they are incorrect.
Clinical consideration
To be an advocate for people in your care, you
must know about the medications being
administered. Know why the person is receiving
the medication, the dosage range, possible
adverse effects, toxicity levels and
contraindications.
Clinical consideration
Assess people in your care for falls risk.
Document all nursing measures taken to protect
that person (e.g. instructed person in my care
how to use the buzzer).


The nurse who does not report a person’s complaint of acute
abdominal pain is negligent and may be found guilty of professional
misconduct if ensuing appendix rupture and death occur. By failing
to take the blood pressure and pulse and to check the dressing of a
person who has just had abdominal surgery, a nurse has omitted
important assessments. If that person haemorrhages and dies, the
nurse may be held responsible for the death as a result.
Incorrectly identifying people receiving care can occur, particularly in
busy hospital units. Unfortunate occurrences, such as removal of a
healthy gallbladder from the wrong person, have resulted from
nurses preparing the wrong person for surgery. This situation would
be considered professional misconduct and negligence by the nurse.
Clinical consideration
The nurse must monitor both the physical and
psychosocial status of the person in their care
and document observations and interventions.
Statutory considerations
It should be noted that the above discussion mainly focuses on the
common law development of negligence. Numerous concerns and
subsequent reports into the negligence area have resulted in the


implementation of legislation in all jurisdictions. In New South Wales,
the Civil Liability Act 2002 amended 2019 attempts to codify and in
some instances changes the requirements of areas such as
negligence. Nurses need to supplement their knowledge not only
with common law principles but also with statutory changes.
Clinical consideration
Nurses must be aware of current legislation that
may override or modify the common law in the
tort area.
Intentional torts
Several differences distinguish unintentional torts from intentional
torts. Unintentional torts (e.g. negligence) do not require intent but
do require the element of harm. In contrast, with intentional torts the
defendant executed the act on purpose or with intent. No harm need
be caused by intentional torts for liability to exist. Also, because no
standard is involved, no expert witnesses are needed. Four
intentional torts related to nursing will be discussed: assault and
battery, false imprisonment (trespass to people), defamation (libel or
slander) and confidentiality.


The terms assault and battery are often heard together, but each
has its own meaning. Assault
 can be described as an attempt or
threat to touch another person unjustifiably (Candutti v ACT Health
and Community Care [2003] ACTSC 95). Assault precedes battery;
it is the act that causes the person to believe a battery is about to
occur. For example, the person who threatens someone by making
a menacing gesture with a club or a closed fist is guilty of assault. A
nurse who threatens a person in their care with an injection after
that person refuses to take the medication orally would be
committing assault (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Battery
 is the wilful touching of a person (or the person’s clothes
or even something the person is carrying) that may or may not
cause harm. To be actionable at law, however, the touching must be
wrong in some way; for example, touching without permission or that
is embarrassing or that causes injury. In the example of the nurse
threatening a person in their care with an injection, if the nurse
followed through on the threat and gave the injection without
consent, the nurse would be committing battery. Liability applies
even though the medical practitioner ordered the medication or the
activity, and even if the person ultimately benefits from the nurse’s
action (Hart v Herron [1984] Aust Torts Rep 80-201 (SC NSW),
Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Consent is required before procedures are performed. Battery exists
when there is no consent, even if the plaintiff was not asked for
consent. Unless there is implied consent, such as in life-threatening
emergencies, a procedure performed on an unconscious person


without informed consent is battery. Another requirement for consent
is that the person receiving care be competent to give consent. It
can be very difficult to determine if older people, people who have
specific mental disorders or people who take particular medications
are actually competent to agree to treatments. If the nurse is
uncertain whether a person refusing a treatment is competent, the
supervisor and doctor should be consulted so that ethical treatment
that does not constitute battery can be provided. Determination of
competency is not a medical decision; it is one made through court
hearings (Savage 2015).
False imprisonment
 is when someone makes an allegation that
they have been denied their freedom and can lead to criminal
charges (Savage 2015). False imprisonment accompanied by
forceful restraint or threat of restraint is battery. Actions such as
stopping a person from leaving their bed or administering sedatives
or tranquillisers that restrict freedom of movement are considered
false imprisonment (Forrester & Griffiths 2015). Although nurses
may suggest under certain circumstances that a person in their care
remain in the hospital room or in bed, that person must not be
detained against their will unless under a mental health Act. The
person has a right to discharge themself against medical advice. As
with assault or battery, the cognitive capacity of a person is a factor
in determining whether there is a case of false imprisonment or a
situation of protecting a person from injury. To guide nurses in such
dilemmas, agencies should have clear policies about the application
of restraints (see Chapter 33
).


Defamation
 is communication that is false, or made with a
careless disregard for the truth, and results in injury to the reputation
of a person. It is illegal in all states and territories of Australia to
defame someone. Both libel and slander are wrongful actions that
come under the heading of defamation. Libel
 is defamation by
means of print, writing or pictures. Writing in the nurse’s notes that a
doctor is incompetent because they did not respond immediately to
a call is an example of libel. Slander
 is defamation by the spoken
word, stating unprivileged (not legally protected) or false words by
which a reputation is damaged. An example of slander would be for
the nurse to tell a person in their care that another nurse is
incompetent (Savage 2015).
Only the person defamed may bring the lawsuit. The defamatory
material must be communicated to a third party such that the
person’s reputation may be harmed. For example, a comment made
in private criticising that person’s competence is not defamation
because a third party did not hear it.
Nurses need to be familiar with their professional obligations related
to social media under the National Law and Code of Conduct. For
example, posting unauthorised photographs of patients in any
medium is a breach of a patient’s privacy and confidentiality,
including on a personal Facebook site or group even if the privacy
settings are set at the highest setting (such as for a closed, ‘invisible’
group) (NMBA ).
36 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2014). Social Media Policy. Retrieved
from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
36


Nurses have a qualified protection to make statements that could be
considered defamatory, but only as a part of nursing practice and
