only to a doctor or another health team member who is directly
involved in the care. This is referred to as qualified privilege (Savage
2015). The communication must be made in good faith with the
intent to protect the quality of care; for example, when a nurse
manager provides a prospective employer with information about a
nurse’s professional practice.
Confidentiality
 is the protection of personal information. There is
a duty to maintain information that is received in confidence. It
should be noted that there is no common law duty to protect privacy
in Australia, although there are statute requirements found in
legislation such as the Privacy Act 1988 amended 2019 (as well as
state and territory equivalents). The ‘right’ to privacy is the right of
individuals to withhold themselves and their lives from public
scrutiny. It can also be described as the right to be left alone.
Liability can result if the nurse breaches confidentiality by passing on
confidential information about a person in their care to others or
intrudes into a person’s private domain.
The tort of breach of confidentiality has three elements:
1. The information is confidential in nature.
2. It has been imparted in circumstances giving rise to an
obligation of confidence.
3. It is used without authority to the detriment of the person who
gave it (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).


There are a number of remedies that are available for breach of
confidentiality. They include:
equity (equitable remedy)
action in negligence
action in contract (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Exceptions to confidentiality
There are a number of defences and exceptions that a defendant
may argue to a breach of confidentiality. These include:
The person receiving care agrees to the disclosure.
Disclosure is compelled by law: see Royal Women’s Hospital v
Medical Practitioner’s Board of Victoria [2006] VSCA 85.
There is a duty to the public to disclose.
The interests of one of the parties is involved (e.g. a carer or
hospital) (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
In this context, there is a delicate balance between the need for a
number of people to contribute to the diagnosis and treatment of a
person, and their right to confidentiality. Necessary discussion about
a person’s medical condition is considered appropriate; however,
unnecessary discussion and gossip are considered a breach of
confidentiality. Necessary discussion involves only those engaged in
the direct care.


Clinical consideration
Never discuss situations involving a person in
your care in the lift, cafeteria or other public
areas.
Most jurisdictions of the country have a variety of statutes that
impose a duty to report certain confidential information. Four major
categories are: (1) vital statistics, such as births and deaths; (2)
infections and communicable diseases, such as diphtheria, syphilis,
HIV and typhoid fever; (3) child or older person abuse; and (4)
violent incidents, such as gunshot wounds and knife wounds.
Privacy of personal health information
The Privacy Act 1988 amended 2019 regulates how organisations
collect and handle personal information, including how a person can
access their own personal health information. Australia now has a
digital health record system containing online summaries of a
person’s health information. The My Health Records Act 2012
amended 2019, My Health Records Rule 2016 and My Health
Records Regulation 2012 are the legislative framework for how
health information in My Health Record can be collected, used and
disclosed (Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
(OAIC)
).
37


37 Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) (2019a). Privacy Law. Retrieved
from <www.oaic.gov.au>.
Freedom of information
Freedom of information in Australia is regulated by the Office of the
Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC). Anyone can request
that a government agency or minister access their individual
personal information, or documents about a policy or information
relating to a decision. This request can be refused; however, if
applicants believe that their request is reasonable and it has been
denied, there is an appeal process. This legislation is known as the
Freedom of Information Act 1982 amended 2018 (FOI Act) and
provides the mechanism by which a person may access information
that is located in public institutions (hospitals, clinics etc.). Access to
information kept by private sector health providers may also be
achieved through specific legislation requirements (e.g. Privacy
Amendment (Private Sector) Act 2000 (Cth)).
Medical records under common law are owned by the maker of the
record; that is, the organisation, the institution or the sole
practitioner (as the case may be). Although made by an employee,
written notes (including computer-generated notes) would be owned
by the employer. In order to overcome this, the Freedom of
Information Act 1982 amended 2018 has been changed to allow
access to notes about care by the person receiving the care
(OAIC ). Any complaints relating to how an agency has dealt with
38


an individual’s FOI request is handled by the Commonwealth
Ombudsman (OAIC 2019b).
38 Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) (2019b). FOI Act. Retrieved
from <www.oaic.gov.au>.


Legal protections in nursing
practice
Laws and strategies are in place to protect the nurse against
litigation. ‘Good Samaritan’ Acts are an example of laws designed to
help protect nurses when assisting at the scene of an emergency.
Providing safe, competent practice by following the Health
Practitioner Regulation National Law Act 2009, legislation that
applies to nursing practice and organisational policies, and abiding
by professional codes or guidelines about standards of practice
ensure a legal safeguard for nurses. Accurate and complete
documentation is also a critical component of legal protection for the
nurse.
Being a Good Samaritan
A rescuer/Good Samaritan is a person who is acting without
expectation of reward in order to come to the aid of another person.
A person who performs this act should not be liable for assisting in
an emergency if the rescuer/Good Samaritan was exercising all
reasonable care and skill (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).


Common law does not require citizens to render aid to people in
distress. Such assistance is considered more of an ethical than a
legal duty. All jurisdictions except Tasmania have enacted ‘Good
Samaritan’ laws that protect nurses and doctors who provide
medical assistance at the scene of an accident or other emergency.
Guidelines for nurses who choose to render emergency care are as
follows:
Limit actions to those normally considered first aid, if possible.
Do not perform actions that you do not know how to do.
Offer assistance but do not insist.
Have someone call or go for additional help.
Do not leave the scene until the injured person leaves or another
qualified person takes over.
Do not accept any compensation (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Professional indemnity insurance
Because of the increase in the number of negligence lawsuits
against health professionals, nurses must be aware of issues such
as professional indemnity insurance, particularly if they are
independent practitioners. In fact, indemnity insurance is mandatory
for Enrolled Nurses, Registered Nurses and midwives who work in
independent practice in Australia. Organisations must have liability
insurance that covers employees; however, contractors who are paid
to carry out specific work are required to have their own insurance.


To determine if someone is a contractor, the ‘control test’ should be
established. This is about how much control the employer has about
work conditions, the workplace and tools that they use to complete
the work. Other factors may be about remuneration, provision and
maintenance of equipment, obligation to work, provision of holidays,
deduction of income tax and delegation of work (Forrester & Griffiths
2015).
Carrying out doctors’ orders
Nurses are expected to analyse procedures and medications
ordered by doctors. It is the nurse’s responsibility to seek
clarification of ambiguous or seemingly erroneous orders from the
prescriber. Clarification from any other source is unacceptable and
regarded as a departure from competent nursing practice.
If an order is ambiguous or erroneous, the nurse is responsible to
ensure that the order is legally correct by questioning the prescriber
before administering. Examples of situations when nurses should
question the prescriber include:
Question any order a person in your care questions. For
example, if a person who has been receiving an intramuscular
injection tells the nurse that the doctor changed the order from
an injectable to an oral medication, the nurse must recheck the
order before giving the medication.


Question any order if the condition of a person in your care
has changed. The nurse is considered responsible for notifying
the doctor of any significant changes in a person’s condition,
whether the doctor requests notification or not. For example, if a
person who is receiving an intravenous infusion suddenly
develops a rapid pulse, chest pain and a cough, the nurse must
notify the doctor immediately and question continuance of the
ordered rate of infusion. If a person who is receiving morphine
for pain develops severely depressed respirations, the nurse
must withhold the medication and notify the doctor.
Question and record verbal orders to avoid
miscommunications. In addition to recording the time, the date,
the doctor’s name and the orders, the nurse documents the
circumstances that occasioned the call to the doctor, reads the
orders back to the doctor and documents that the doctor
confirmed the orders as the nurse read them back.
Question any order that is illegible, unclear or incomplete.
Misinterpretations in the name of a drug or in the dose, for
example, can easily occur with handwritten orders. The nurse is
responsible for ensuring that the order is interpreted the way it
was intended and that it is a safe and appropriate order.
Where a treatment order (written or verbal) is ambiguous, the
nurse must seek advice from an appropriate authority (manager
etc.).
Methods of legal protection are summarised in the following ‘Practice
Guidelines’.


Clinical consideration
Nurses must be aware of their own professional
capabilities and limitations and act accordingly.
The incident report
An incident report
 (also called an ‘unusual occurrence’ report) is
an employment record of an accident or unusual occurrence.
Incident reports are used to make all the facts available to the
employer to contribute to statistical data about accidents or
incidents, and to help health personnel prevent future incidents or
accidents. It is also a requirement under the Work Health & Safety
Act 2011 (Cth) amended 2018 and workers compensation Acts in all
states and territories of Australia (Safe Work Australia 2019). All
accidents are reported on incident forms. Other incidents, such as
the occurrence of infection or the loss of personal effects of
someone in your care, may also need to be reported.
The nurse should include the following information in an incident
report:
Identification of the person by name, initials, organisation or
identification number.
Date, time and place of incident.


The facts of the incident avoiding any conclusions or blame.
Describe the incident as witnessed even if different from others’
descriptions.
Incorporate the person’s own account of the incident. Write
comments by using direct quotes.
Identify all witnesses to the incident.
Identify any equipment by number and any medication by name
and dosage.
The report should be completed as soon as possible and filed
according to organisational policy. Because incident reports are not
part of a person’s medical record, the facts of the incident should
also be noted in the medical record. Do not record in the person’s
record that an incident report has been completed because the facts
are already documented in the chart. The purpose of the report form
is to alert the risk manager to the event.
The person who identifies that the incident occurred should complete
the incident report. This may not be the same person actually
involved with the incident. For example, the nurse who discovers
that an incorrect medication has been administered completes the
form even if it was another nurse who administered the medication.
In addition, all witnesses to an incident, such as a fall, are listed on
the incident form even if they were not directly involved.
Incident reports are reviewed by an organisation’s risk management
committee, which decides whether to investigate the incident further.
Incidents and near misses are summarised in categories by


organisations to inform safety alerts and reviews of care processes.
Nurses are required to answer questions about what they believe
precipitated an incident, how it may have been prevented and
whether any equipment should be adjusted or not used.
When an incident occurs, the nurse should first assess the person
and intervene to prevent injury. If a person is injured, nurses must
take steps to protect the person involved, themselves and their
employer. Organisations have policies regarding incidents. It is
important to follow policies and not assume someone is negligent.
Although negligence may be involved, accidents can and do happen
even when every precaution has been taken to prevent them.


Reporting crimes, torts and unsafe
practices
Nurses are required by law (Health Practitioner Regulation National
Law Act 2009) to report nursing colleagues or other health
professionals for practices that endanger the health and safety of
people in their care. For instance, alcohol and drug use, theft from a
person receiving care or the organisation, as well as unsafe nursing
practice should be reported. Reporting a colleague is not easy. The
person reporting may feel disloyal, incur the disapproval of others or
perceive that chances for promotion are endangered. When
reporting an incident or series of incidents, the nurse must be
careful to describe observed behaviour only. The following ‘Practice
guidelines’ box summarises the procedure to be followed for
reporting a crime, tort or unsafe practice.
Practice guidelines
Legal protection for nurses
Function within the scope of your education, job
description and the Health Practitioner Regulation National
Law Act 2009, any subordinate legislation and state and
other legislation that applies to nursing practice.


Follow the procedures and policies of the employing
organisation.
Build and maintain good rapport with people in your care.
Always check the identity of a person receiving care.
Observe and monitor a person in your care accurately.
Communicate to the doctor and record significant
changes in their condition.
Ensure that you plan and provide care using evidence-
based practice.
Promptly and accurately document all assessments and
care given.
Be alert when implementing nursing interventions and give
each task your full attention and skill.
Perform procedures correctly and appropriately.
Make sure the correct medications are given in the
correct dose, by the right route, at the scheduled time and
to the right person.
When delegating nursing responsibilities, ensure that the
person who is delegated a task understands what to do
and that the person is working within their scope of
practice with the knowledge and skill required.
Protect people in your care from injury.
Report all incidents.
Check any order that a person in your care questions.
Know your scope of practice as well as your strengths and
weaknesses. Ask for assistance or supervision in
situations for which you feel inadequately prepared.


Maintain your clinical competence. For students, this
demands study and practice before caring for people. For
graduate nurses, it means continued study to maintain
and update clinical knowledge and skills.
Practice guidelines
Reporting a crime, tort or unsafe practice
Write a clear description of the situation being reported.
Make sure that statements are factual and complete.
Make sure information is credible.
Obtain support from at least one trustworthy person
before filing the report.
Report the matter starting at the lowest possible level in
the agency hierarchy.
Assume responsibility for reporting the individual by being
open about it. Sign the letter.
See the problem through once reported.
Another situation that may arise is where the nurse encounters
practices that may not be technically ‘negligent’ but are below the
expected standard. It is advisable that the nurse seek advice from a
senior member of staff about the action that should be taken in this
situation and how best to deal with the problem.
Whistle-blowing


Reporting these events is referred to as ‘whistle-blowing
’. Many
states have laws that prevent wrongful termination of whistle-
blowers by employers. In Australia it is mandatory for a nurse with
knowledge of unprofessional conduct to report that behaviour to the
NMBA. One example of mandatory reporting or ‘whistle-blowing’ is
the case of the Bundaberg nurse who reported surgeon Jayant Patel
for unsafe practice. This reporting resulted in a manslaughter charge
against Patel (ABC News ).
39 ABC News (2013). Court Agrees to Extra Jury Scrutiny for Jayant Patel Trial. Retrieved
from <www.abc.net.au>.
39


Legal responsibilities of students
Nursing students are responsible for their own actions and liable for
their own acts of negligence committed during the course of clinical
experiences. When they perform duties that are within their scope of
practice, such as administering an injection, they are legally held to
the same standard of skill and competence as a registered
professional nurse. Lower standards are not applied to the actions of
nursing students (Forrester & Griffiths 2015).
Nursing students need to be aware that the NMBA will require
reporting of prior criminal history when applying for registration. A
person with a criminal record and/or some misdemeanour offences
may be denied registration even though that individual has
graduated from an approved nursing program. Universities, colleges
and training organisations now require students to provide evidence
of criminal checks prior to commencing education programs that
lead to registration as a nurse or midwife. Nursing students who are
unsure of their personal situation are advised to contact the NMBA
for more information.
It is worth noting that the issue of prior criminal record reporting
often refers to the judgment of good character. The fact that
someone has a criminal event in their past is not the issue; what is
important is their probity (honesty) in declaring their transgression.
This can determine how the profession ultimately views the offence


and the potential impact on future registration of the student. Many
cases in Australia have been heard on the issue of not declaring a
criminal record up-front—not declaring a misdemeanour is
potentially more damaging.
Students in clinical situations must be assigned learning experiences
within their capabilities and be given reasonable guidance and
supervision. Nursing educators are responsible for assigning
students to Registered Nurses who are responsible for providing
supervision. There is a professional expectation that Registered
Nurses supervise students; failure to provide reasonable supervision
or asking a student to care for a person when they are not
adequately prepared and/or competent can be a basis for liability.
To fulfil responsibilities to people in our care and to minimise the
potential for liability, nursing students need to:
ensure they are prepared to carry out the necessary care for the
people they are assigned to for the shift
ask for help or supervision in situations for which they feel
inadequately prepared
comply with the policies of the organisation in which they obtain
their clinical experience
comply with the policies and definitions of responsibility supplied
by the education provider.
Students who work as nursing assistants or Enrolled Nurses must
also remember that legally they can perform only those tasks that


appear in the job description of the role they are working in. Even
though a student may have received instruction and acquired
competence in administering injections or suctioning a tracheostomy
tube, the student cannot legally perform these tasks while employed
as an Enrolled Nurse or assistant. While acting as a paid employee,
the student is covered for negligent acts by the employer, not the
education provider.
Case study
An adult female who has had vision impairment since birth is
admitted to the surgical unit. She is to have surgery the next
morning. The doctor has written an order for her to sign the
surgical consent form. Her husband is in the room when the
nurse approaches the woman to sign the consent form. Her
husband says that he will sign for his wife.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. What question(s) should the nurse ask before
addressing the signing of the form?
2.
 Can someone who has vision impairment give
consent? Consider the dimension ‘context of care’
from the Fundamentals of Care Framework when
answering this question.


3.
 How can the nurse ensure that the woman in
their care is aware of what she is signing? Consider
the dimensions ‘relationship established’ and
‘integration of care’ from the Fundamentals of Care
Framework when answering this question.
4. What else should the nurse consider when obtaining a
signature?
5. What would the nurse include in the documentation?


Chapter 4 Review


Chapter highlights
Accountability is an essential concept of professional nursing
practice under the law.
Nurses need to understand laws that regulate and affect nursing
practice to ensure that the nurses’ actions are consistent with
current legal principles and to protect themselves from liability.
Acts legally define and describe the scope of nursing practice
that the law seeks to regulate.
Standards of practice published by the NMBA, legislation that
applies to nursing practice, organisational policies and
procedures, and job descriptions further delineate the scope of a
nurse’s practice.
Nurses have specific legal obligations and responsibilities to
people in their care and employers. As citizens, nurses have the
rights and responsibilities shared by all individuals in the society.
Workplace relations legislation can improve nurses’ working
conditions and economic welfare.
Informed consent implies that: (a) the consent was given
voluntarily; (b) the person was of age and had the capacity and
competency to understand; and (c) the person was given enough
information on which to make an informed decision.
Chemical dependence in health care workers is a problem, in
part because of the high levels of stress involved in many health
care settings and the easy access to addictive drugs. Chemical
impairment includes abuse of alcohol and addictive drugs. The
nurse needs to know correct reporting procedures about health


care practitioner colleagues whose practice is chemically
impaired.
Nurses must be knowledgeable about responsibilities concerning
legal issues surrounding death: ‘Do not resuscitate’ orders,
inquests and organ donation.
Nurse negligence, an unintentional tort, can be established when
the following criteria are met: (a) the nurse (defendant) owed a
duty to the person receiving care; (b) the nurse failed to carry out
that duty according to standards; (c) there was foreseeability of
harm; (d) the person’s injury was caused by the nurse’s failure to
follow the standard; and (e) the person receiving care (plaintiff)
was injured. The nurse is liable for damages that may be
compensated.
Nurses can be held liable for intentional torts, such as assault
and battery, false imprisonment, invasion of privacy and
defamation.
Good Samaritan acts performed by health professionals are
protected from claims of negligence when they offer assistance
at the scene of an emergency, provided that there is no wilful
wrongdoing or gross departure from normal standards of care.
When a person is accidentally injured or involved in an unusual
situation, the nurse’s first responsibility is to take steps to protect
that person and then to notify the appropriate organisation
personnel.
Nurses need to understand that it is important they ask for help
or supervision in situations for which they feel inadequately
prepared.


Concept check
1. A doctor’s orders indicate that a surgical consent form needs
to be signed. Because the nurse was not present when the
doctor discussed the surgical procedure, which statement
best illustrates the nurse fulfilling the advocate role for the
person in their care?
1. ‘The doctor has asked that you sign this consent form.’
2. ‘Do you have any questions about the procedure?’
3. ‘What were you told about the procedure you are going
to have?’
4. ‘Remember that you can change your mind and cancel
the procedure.’
2. Although the person refused the procedure, the nurse
insisted and inserted a nasogastric tube in the right nostril.
The hospital decides to settle the lawsuit because the nurse is
most likely to be found guilty of which of the following?
1. An unintentional tort.
2. Assault.
3. False imprisonment.
4. Battery.
3. A nurse discovers that a doctor has prescribed an unusually
large dosage of a medication. Which of the following is the
most appropriate action?
1. Administer the medication.


2. Notify the prescriber.
3. Call the pharmacist.
4. Refuse to administer the medication.
4. A doctor prescribes one tablet but the nurse accidentally
administers two. After notifying the doctor, the nurse monitors
the person carefully for possible side effects, of which there
are none. Is the person likely to be successful in suing the
nurse for negligence?
1. No, the person was not harmed.
2. No, the nurse notified the doctor.
3. Yes, a breach of duty exists.
4. Yes, foreseeability is present.
5. The doctor wrote a ‘Do not resuscitate’ (DNR) order. Which of
the following should the nurse recognise will apply in the
planning of nursing care for this person?
1. The person may no longer make decisions regarding
their own health care.
2. The person and their family know that they will most
likely die within the next 48 hours.
3. The nurses will continue to implement all treatments
focused on comfort and symptom management.
4. A DNR order from a previous admission is valid for the
current admission.
6. The nurse’s partner/spouse undergoes exploratory surgery at
the hospital where the nurse is employed. Which of the


following practices is most appropriate?
1. Because the nurse is an employee, access to the chart
is allowed.
2. The relationship with the partner/spouse provides the
nurse special access to the chart.
3. Access to the chart requires a signed release form.
4. The nurse can ask the surgeon to discuss the outcome
of the surgery.
7. Following a car accident, a nurse stops and offers assistance.
Which of the following actions is/are most appropriate? Select
all that apply.
1. The nurse needs to know the Good Samaritan
protection for the state or territory they are in.
2. The nurse is not held liable unless there is gross
negligence.
3. After assessing the situation, the nurse can leave to
obtain help.
4. The nurse can expect compensation for helping.
5. The nurse offers to help but cannot insist on helping.
8. The nurse notices that a colleague’s behaviours have
changed during the past month. Which of the following
behaviours could indicate signs of impairment? Select all that
apply.
1. Increased absences from the nursing unit during the
shift.
2. Interacts well with others.


3. ‘Forgets’ to sign out for administration of controlled
substances.
4. Offers to administer medication for people who are in
the care of other nurses.
5. Is able to say ‘no’ to requests to work more shifts.
9. Which of the following nursing actions could result in
negligence? Select all that apply.
1. Learns about a new piece of equipment.
2. Forgets to complete the assessment of a person in
their care.
3. Does not follow up on a complaint made by a person in
their care.
4. Charts drug allergies of people in their care.
5. Questions doctor about an illegible order.
Focus on critical thinking
1. How could nurses ensure that they have up-to-date
knowledge about changes in legislation that may affect their
practice and responsibilities to people in their care?
2. How might a person’s cultural background affect their
understanding of informed consent?
3. What is the responsibility of the nurse if they suspect that a
colleague has come to work under the influence of drugs or
alcohol? Who should they report this situation to and why?


4. Why do you think negligence is the most likely reason that
litigation may occur against a nurse?
5. Think of factors in a nurse’s busy work day that may influence
the chance of a claim in negligence being brought against
them.
6. What is the purpose of accurate documentation in the health
care environment? Consider the potential legal and
professional risks and implications of poor documentation for
the nurse.
7. What are the likely effects on teamwork that result from a
culture of bullying in the workplace?

advocacy

When presented with an ethical situation, identify the moral
issues and principles involved.

professionals.

making and practice.

Health care delivery and practice is constantly
changing and evolving in partnership with
technology and developments in diagnosis and
treatment. Like all health care professionals,
nurses are required to remain cognisant of their
changing environment together with the ethical
challenges that changes and developments may
engender. Changes in health care delivery are
not restricted to technology, treatment
modalities and processes alone as, importantly,
in recent years there have been changes to the
philosophy of health care delivery, leading to a
much more person-centred approach.
A person-centred approach has distinct
characteristics that enable nurses to include and
support individuals in their health-related
decisions. Every day nurses support and care
for people during intimate and fundamental
human experiences such as birth, illness,
recovery and death. These experiences do not
happen in isolation but are situated in the
cultural, social and personal world of the
individual. Nurses support and advocate for
people and families who are facing difficult
choices, and for those who are living with the


outcomes of choices that others make for and
about them.
The modern health care working environment is
often governed by budget restraints and nursing
shortages and tends to emphasise business
values. Substantial workloads and
organisational issues can sometimes impede
nurses’ ability to respond appropriately and
compassionately to the individual needs of
people in their care. This dilemma creates new
moral problems and intensifies old ones, making
it more critical than ever for nurses to make
mindful, ethical decisions. Nurses, therefore,
need to develop sensitivity to the ethical
dimensions of nursing practice by first
examining their own values and beliefs, and by
considering how these may influence their
decisions and thinking about the kinds of moral
problems they are likely to face.
Values and beliefs guide thoughts and actions
and form the basis for our attitudes towards
things. It is important to understand and be
transparent about what these mean. In some
ways, beliefs are about what matters to us and
values are about what matters most to us, so it


has a value placed on it. People have many
different attitudes and beliefs, but a smaller
number of values. This chapter explores the
influences of values and moral frameworks on
the ethical dimensions of nursing practice.


Attitudes
Attitudes
 are feelings towards a person, object or idea, such as
acceptance, compassion and openness. Typically, an attitude lasts
over time, whereas a belief may last for less time. Attitudes are
often judged as bad or good, positive or negative, whereas beliefs
are judged as correct or incorrect. Attitudes have thinking and
behavioural aspects and vary greatly among individuals. For
example, a nurse might have the attitude that good time
management is fundamental to practice.


Beliefs
Beliefs
 are interpretations or conclusions that people accept as
true and are often about something that matters to them. They may
be based more on faith than on fact and may or may not be true.
Beliefs do not necessarily involve values. For example, the
statement ‘If I study hard I will get a good grade’ expresses a belief
that does not overtly involve a value. By contrast, the statement
‘Good grades are really important to me, I must study hard to obtain
good grades’ involves both a value and a belief.


Values
Values
 are enduring beliefs or attitudes about the worth of a person, object, idea or action. Person-
centred care requires the nurse to recognise people as individuals and to take into consideration their
beliefs and values. Values influence decisions and actions, including a nurse’s ethical decision making.
Even though they may be unspoken, questions of value underlie all moral dilemmas. Not all values are
moral values. For example, people hold values about work, family, religion, politics, money and
relationships. Values are often taken for granted. In the same way people are not aware of their
breathing, they usually do not consciously think about their values; they simply accept and act on them.
Nurses do need to consciously think about their values and, if their personal values are in conflict with
their professions values, they may need to question or reflect on their personal values. Clinical
supervision helps with reflective practice.
A value set
 is the group of values held by an individual. People organise their set of values internally
along a continuum from most important to least important, forming a value system
. Value systems
are basic to a way of life, give direction to life and form the basis of behaviour—especially behaviour
that is based on decisions or choices.
Values transmission
Values are learned through observation and experience and are influenced by a person’s societal
traditions, cultural, ethnic and religious groups, and by family and peer groups. For example, if a parent
consistently demonstrates honesty in dealing with others, the child will probably value honesty.
Personal values
Patient safety competency framework
4 Teamwork and collaborative practice
The Patient Safety Competency Framework indicates that nursing students must
demonstrate teamwork and collaborative practice, which is a key aspect of effective
care (Levett-Jones et al. ).
1 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady, T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P.
(2017). Patient Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students. Sydney. Retrieved from
<http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
1


Although people derive values from society and their individual subgroups, they internalise some or all
of these values to become personal values
. People need societal values to have a sense of
belonging and they need personal values to have a sense of individuality. Shared personal values are
important when working in team environments to ensure nursing care is provided in a collaborative and
collegiate manner.
Values clarification
Values clarification
 is a process by which people identify, examine and develop their own values. A
principle of values clarification is that no single set of values is the same for everyone. When people
identify their values, they can retain or change them, and thus act based on freely chosen, rather than
unconscious, values. Values clarification seeks to make visible what may be invisible to an individual and
others. Values clarification promotes personal growth by fostering self-awareness, empathy and insight.
Nurses need to clarify their values by being reflective clinicians.
Raths, Harmin and Simon  describe values clarification as a ‘valuing process’ of thinking, feeling and
behaviour that they termed ‘choosing’, ‘prizing’ and ‘acting’ (see Box 5.1
). Values clarification
exercises are useful in helping people become more aware of how their values influence their actions.
For example, asking a person in their care to agree or disagree with a list of statements or to rank a list
of beliefs in order of importance can assist the nurse and the person to make their values explicit. This
can enable the nurse and the individual to more easily plan care in partnership. See Table 5.1
 for an
example of a general values clarification exercise.
2 Raths, L., Harmin, M. & Simon, S. (1978). Values and Teaching: Working with Values in the Classroom (2nd ed.). Columbus, OH: Merrill.
BO X
5.1 Values clarification
Choosing (cognitive) Beliefs are chosen
freely, without outside pressure
from alternatives
after reflecting and considering consequences.
Example: A person learns about energy resources, production and consumption; the
greenhouse effect; and other environmental issues, including ways to minimise and recycle the
use of limited resources.
Prizing (affective) Chosen beliefs are prized and cherished
2


Example: The person is proud of the belief that they have an obligation to participate in some
way in reducing environmental waste.
Acting (behavioural) Chosen beliefs are
affirmed to others
incorporated into one’s behaviour
repeated consistently in one’s life.
Example: The person participates in their community recycling program for household waste,
uses public transportation rather than driving a car when possible, helps organise recycling in the
workplace and is active in legislative and political activities related to environmental issues.

Professional values and behaviours
A nurse’s professional values
 are acquired during nursing education, socialisation into nursing from
clinical practicums, the national professional standards, codes of ethics, nursing experiences, teachers
and peers. In Australia, a Code of Ethics for Nurses and Nursing Competency Standards was first
formulated following the Australasian Nurse Registering Authorities Conference (ANRAC) held in . The
Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia’s (NMBA) (2016a) Registered Nurse Standards for Practice
outline seven standards in which Registered Nurses must be competent (see Chapter 1
). These
standards are:

1. Thinks critically and analyses nursing practice
2. Engages in therapeutic and professional relationships
3. Maintains the capability for practice
4. Comprehensively conducts assessments
5. Develops a plan for nursing practice
6. Provides safe, appropriate and responsive quality nursing practice
7. Evaluates outcomes to inform nursing practice.

RNs, as regulated health professionals, are responsible and accountable for ensuring they are
safe and have the capability for practice. This includes ongoing self-management and
responding when there is concern about other health professionals’ capability for practice. RNs
are responsible for their professional development and contribute to the development of others.
They are also responsible for providing information and education to enable people to make
decisions and take action in relation to their health.
The Registered Nurse
Standard 6: Provides safe, appropriate and responsive
quality nursing practice
RNs provide and may delegate quality and ethical goal-directed actions. These are based on
comprehensive and systematic assessment and the best available evidence to achieve planned
and agreed outcomes.

Clarifying health-related values
Nurses need to reflect on the values they hold about life, death, health and illness together with their
professional values and codes. One strategy for gaining awareness of personal values is to consider
one’s attitudes about specific issues such as termination of pregnancy or euthanasia, asking ‘Can I
accept this or live with this?’, ‘Why does this bother me?’, ‘What would I do or want done to me in this
situation?’. Nurses use critical thinking to reflect on various viewpoints and previous experiences that
may have influenced their own current values. Reflective practice that incorporates critical thinking as
well as peer support and feedback may help nurses explore, understand and refine their own health-
related personal values.
accepts accountability for decisions, actions, behaviours and responsibilities inherent in
their role, and for the actions of others to whom they have delegated responsibilities
identifies and promotes the integral role of nursing practice and the profession in
influencing better health outcomes for people.

A person-centred approach enables individuals to make informed health care decisions that are aligned
with their own values and beliefs. To plan effective care in partnership with the individual, nurses need
to work with them to understand their values as they influence and relate to a particular health problem.
Understanding a person’s values and beliefs will help nurses make fewer assumptions about people in
their care. A person who has been admitted to hospital in acute pain may value the comfort of pain
analgesia, but their most important value may be knowing that their pet at home is safe. Nurses
sometimes take for granted what the person in their care values most. Clinical reasoning does not only
demand the question ‘What can be done?’ but also begs the question ‘What should be done?’.
Patient safety competency framework
5 Clinical reasoning
The Patient Safety Competency Framework indicates that nursing students must
demonstrate clinical reasoning, which is a key aspect of both effective and safe
care (Levett-Jones et al. 2017).
As treatment modalities become more advanced, successful and expensive in an age of health care
rationing, the question ‘What should be done?’ is becoming more frequently asked. For example, a
person with end-stage cancer and advanced-stage cognitive decline could be given aggressive
chemotherapy for their cancer, but should they be? A person- centred approach and therapeutic
communication facilitate clarification of what is valuable to that person. When individuals hold unclear or
conflicting values that may be detrimental to their health, the nurse may assist the person in clarifying
values by using the following process. (Examples of behaviours that may indicate the need for
clarification of health values are listed in Table 5.2
.)
Table 5.2 Behaviours that might indicate unclear or contested values
1. Seek to understand what is important to the individual. Ask: ‘What does this person value?’
2. List and discuss alternative courses of action. Ask: ‘Are you considering other courses of
action?’, ‘Tell me about them.’
3. Examine possible implications of choices. Ask: ‘What do you think you will gain from doing
that?’, ‘What benefits do you foresee from doing that?’
4. Choose freely. Ask: ‘Do you feel you had any say in that decision?’, ‘Did you have choices?’
5. Feel good about the choice. Ask: ‘Some people feel good after a decision is made, others feel
bad. How do you feel?’
6. Affirm the choice. Ask: ‘How will you discuss this with others (family, friends)?’
7. Act on the choice. Ask: ‘Will it be difficult to tell your (partner, family, friends) about this?’
8. Act with a pattern. Ask: ‘How many times have you done that before?’ or ‘If that happens again,
would you do the same thing?’.


When implementing these eight steps to clarify values, the nurse assists the person to think each
question through, but does not impose personal values. The nurse rarely, if ever, offers an opinion when
the person asks for it—and then only with great care or when the nurse is an expert in the area.
Instead, the nurse guides the discussion back to explore what the individual wants or feels is best for
them in their own specific circumstances. Because each situation is different, what the nurse would
choose in their own life may not be relevant to this individual’s circumstances and the nurse cannot
possibly share exactly the same beliefs, values or experiences of the person in their care. Thus, if the
individual asks ‘What would you have done in my situation?’ it is best to redirect the question back to
them rather than answering from your personal view.
The previous section examined the differences between attitudes, beliefs and values in relation to
individuals and groups. The focus was on individual nurses’ attitudes and values as well as those held
by those in their care. The emphasis was on how to clarify values for the best outcomes. The following
section builds on this by examining morality and ethics and moral frameworks and principles to assist in
resolving clinical dilemmas.


Morals
Morality (or morals) is similar to ethics and many people use the
terms interchangeably. Morality
 usually refers to private, personal
standards of what is right and wrong in conduct, character and
attitude. Sometimes the first clue to the moral nature of a situation is
an aroused conscience or an awareness of feelings such as guilt,
hope or shame. Another indicator is the tendency to respond to the
situation with words such as ought, should, right, wrong, good and
bad. It is not appropriate for nurses to impose their own moral
standards on people in their care.
Nurses need to distinguish between morality and law. Laws reflect
the moral values of a society; they offer guidance in determining
what is moral. However, an action can be legal but not moral. For
example, an order for full resuscitation of a person who is dying is
legal, but one could question whether the act is moral. This is an
example of what could be done versus what should be done.
Alternatively, an action can be moral but illegal. For example, if a
child at home stops breathing, it is moral but not legal to exceed the
speed limit when driving the child to the hospital. Legal aspects of
nursing practice are covered in Chapter 4
.
Nurses also need to distinguish between morality and religion as
they link to health practices, although the two concepts are related.
For example, according to some religious beliefs, women may


undergo procedures such as female circumcision that may cause
physical mutilation. Other religions or groups may consider this
practice to be an ethical violation of the human right to self-
determination. In some countries, it is illegal. Additional common
instances of differences in moral perspectives on health involving
religious beliefs include blood transfusions, abortion, contraception
and euthanasia.
Clinical consideration
In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
communities, local protocols exist to guide
behaviours. In relation to grieving and death
(Sorry Business), Aboriginal team leaders
involved in contributing to the book Binan Goonj:
Bridging Cultures in Aboriginal Health stated:
Our custom is when somebody is dying it’s important for as
many of the members of the family to see that person before
he or she dies . . . it doesn’t matter what the hospital rules are.
That’s probably a custom in many Aboriginal communities in
the same way that it’s our custom to attend the funeral.
(Eckermann et al. , p. 132)

Moral development
Ethical decisions require individuals to think and reason. Reasoning
is a cognitive function and is, therefore, developmental. Moral
development
 is the process of learning to tell the difference
between right and wrong, and learning what ought and ought not be
done. It is a complex process that begins in childhood and continues
throughout life.
Theories of moral development attempt to answer complex
questions such as: How does a person become moral? What factors
influence the way a person behaves in a moral situation? Two well-
known theorists of moral development are Lawrence Kohlberg  and
Carol Gilligan . Kohlberg’s theory emphasises rights and formal
reasoning; Gilligan’s theory emphasises care and responsibility,
although it points out that people use the concepts of both theorists
in their moral reasoning. For a full discussion of these two theories,
see Chapter 23
.
6 Kohlberg, L. (1969). Stage and sequence: The cognitive-developmental approach to

Moral frameworks
Moral theories provide frameworks through which nurses can view
and clarify challenging care situations. Nurses can use moral
theories in developing explanations for their ethical decisions and
actions, and in discussing problem situations with others. Three
types of moral theories are widely used and are differentiated by
their emphasis on (a) consequences, (b) principles and duties, or (c)
relationships.
Consequence-based (teleological) theories
 look to the
outcomes (consequences) of an action in judging whether that
action is right or wrong. Utilitarianism
, one form of
consequentialist theory, views a good act as one that brings the
most good and the least harm to the greatest number of people. For
example, if a person’s behaviour was disturbing others, the nurse
would focus on alleviating the behaviour of the disruptive individual in
order to minimise the impact on others. This is called the principle of
utility
 and is an approach often used in making decisions about
funding and delivery of health care (i.e. the greater good).
Teleological theories focus on issues of fairness as an end result
(Johnstone ) and ask questions such as ‘What is the best thing to
do?’, ‘What are the consequences of this action?’.
8 Johnstone, M. J. (2015). Bioethics: A Nursing Perspective (6th ed.). Chatswood, NSW:
Elsevier.
8


Principles-based (deontological) theories
 involve logical and
formal processes and emphasise individual rights, duties and
obligations. The morality of an action is determined not by its
consequences but by whether it is done according to an impartial,
objective principle. For example, following the rule ‘Do not lie’, a
nurse might believe that they should tell the truth to a dying person,
even though instructions have been given not to do so. There are
many deontological theories; each justifies the rules of acceptable
behaviour differently. Deontological ethics ask questions such as
‘What is the right thing to do?’.
Relationships-based (caring) theories
 stress courage,
generosity, commitment and the need to nurture and maintain
relationships. Unlike the two preceding theories, which frame
problems in terms of justice (fairness) and formal reasoning, caring
theories (see Chapter 25
) judge actions according to a
perspective of caring and responsibility. Care ethics are sometimes
considered to be a subset of virtue ethics. Virtue ethics ask
questions such as ‘How should I live my life?’ and largely appeal to
the values of relationships and integrity. A person-centred approach
implies a caring (virtue ethics) ethical practice, as the notion of
person-centredness focuses on the person’s values and beliefs, and
a negotiated care pathway.
Moral frameworks guide moral decisions, but do not determine the
outcome. Imagine that a frail, elderly man has made it clear he does
not want further surgery, but the family and surgeon insist. Three
nurses have each decided that they will not help with preparations


for surgery and that they will work through proper channels to try to
prevent it. Using consequence-based reasoning, Nurse A thinks,
‘Surgery will cause him more suffering; he probably will not survive it
anyway, and the family may even feel guilty later’. Using principles-
based reasoning, Nurse B thinks, ‘This violates the principle of
autonomy. This man has a right to decide what happens to his body’.
Using caring-based reasoning, Nurse C thinks, ‘My relationship to
this person in my care commits me to protecting him and meeting
his needs, and I feel such compassion for him. I must advocate for
him and try to help the family understand that he needs their
support’. Each of these perspectives is based on the nurse’s moral
framework.
Moral principles
Moral principles are statements about broad, general, philosophical
concepts such as autonomy and justice. They provide the foundation
for moral rules
, which are specific prescriptions for actions. For
example, the rule ‘People should not lie’ is based on the moral
principle of respect for individuals (autonomy). Principles are useful
in ethical discussions because even if people disagree about which
action is right in a situation, they may be able to agree on the
principles that apply. Such an agreement can serve as the basis for
a mutually acceptable solution. Most people would agree with the
principle that nurses are obligated to respect people in their care,
even if they disagree as to whether the nurse should deceive a
particular individual about their prognosis.


Ethics
Ethics
 refer to moral principles that guide behaviour and decision
making. It is the branch of knowledge and inquiry that deals with
moral principles.
Guiding moral principles arise from a variety of beliefs about right
and wrong and behaviour. For example, a social code (in my society
stealing is wrong); a professional code (e.g. the International Council
of Nurses (ICN) Code of Ethics for Nurses); or a philosophical code
(rules based, such as a religion or utilitarian: the greatest good for
the greatest number).
Bioethics
 is ethics as applied to human life or health (such as
decisions about abortion or euthanasia). Beauchamp and Childress
identified four essential bioethical principles which guide health care
practice:
9 Beauchamp, T. L. & Childress, J. F. (2015). Principles of Biomedical Ethics (8th ed.). New
York: Oxford University Press.
1. Autonomy
 refers to the right to make one’s own decisions.
Person-centredness recognises that each individual is unique
and has the right to be what they want to be and to choose
personal goals. People have ‘inward autonomy’ if they have
9


the ability to make choices; they have ‘outward autonomy’ if
their choices are not limited or imposed by others.
Honouring the principle of autonomy means that nurses
respect an individual’s right to make decisions even when
those choices do not seem to be in the person’s best interest
and treat others with consideration. This principle is violated,
for example, when a person with mental illness is admitted to
hospital against their will. Respect for autonomy means that
people should not be treated as an impersonal source of
knowledge or training. This principle comes into play in the
requirement that the person who requires care provides
informed verbal or written consent before tests, procedures
or when participating in a research project. See ‘Informed
consent’ in Chapter 4
.
2. Non-maleficence
 means to ‘do no harm’. Although a
seemingly simple principle to follow, in reality it is complex.
Harm can mean intentionally causing harm, placing someone
at risk of harm and unintentionally causing harm. However,
placing a person at risk of harm has many facets. A person
may be at risk of harm as a known consequence of a nursing
intervention intended to be helpful. For example, an individual
may react adversely to a medication. Unintentional harm
occurs when the risk could not have been anticipated. For
example, while supporting an individual who loses their
balance, the nurse grips them tightly enough to cause
bruises. It is difficult for caregivers to agree on the degree of
risk that is morally permissible in order to attempt the
beneficial result.


3. Beneficence
 means ‘doing good’. Nurses are obligated to
do good; that is, to implement actions that benefit individuals.
However, doing good can also pose a risk of doing harm. For
example, a nurse may advise a person about a strenuous
exercise program to improve general health, but not if it is
known that this may impact on the person’s health or
wellbeing.
4. Justice
 is often referred to as fairness. Nurses face
decisions where a sense of justice should prevail. For
example, a nurse making home visits finds one individual
tearful and depressed and knows she could help by staying
for 30 more minutes to talk. However, that would take time
from the person scheduled for her next visit, whose blood
glucose levels are elevated. The nurse will need to carefully
weigh up the facts in order to prioritise and allocate time.
Two important additional ethical principles most relevant in health
care are fidelity and veracity.
Fidelity
 means to be faithful to agreements and promises. By
virtue of their professional standing, nurses have responsibilities to
people in their care, employers, society and themselves. Nurses
often make promises such as ‘I’ll be right back with your pain
medication’ or ‘I’ll find out for you’. Individuals take such promises
seriously and nurses are obliged to respond within appropriate time
frames.


Veracity
 refers to telling the truth. Although this seems
straightforward, in practice choices are not always clear. Should a
nurse tell the truth when it is known that it will cause harm? Does a
nurse lie when it is known that the lie will relieve anxiety and fear?
Lying to sick or dying people is rarely justified. The loss of trust in
the nurse and the anxiety caused by not knowing the truth usually
outweigh any benefits derived from lying.
Accountability
 means that nurses answer to the people in their
care, the nursing regulatory authority, their employers and the
public. The NMBA Registered Nurse Standards for Practice state
that while care can be delegated, accountability cannot, and so the
nurse who delegates care to be undertaken by another person
retains accountability for that care (NMBA ).
10 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016b). Registered Nurse Standards
for Practice Fact Sheet. Australia: NMBA. Retrieved from
<www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
The ethical nurse is able to explain the rationale behind every action
and recognises the standards to which they will be held. Nursing
ethics
 refer to ethical issues that occur in nursing practice.
10


Nursing ethics
No one profession holds responsibility for ethical decisions, nor does
expertise in one discipline such as nursing or social work necessarily
make a person an expert in ethics. As situations become more
complex, input from all stakeholders becomes increasingly
important.
Various ethical issues occur for different health care disciplines with
differing levels of complexity. For example, nurses may consider an
individual’s privacy while undertaking a complex dressing as an
important ethical issue, whereas a doctor may consider the right
time to give a person a diagnosis an important ethical issue. Some
ethical issues are of public concern and are discussed in the media,
such as cloning or stem cell research. Nurses may or may not be
directly involved in this work. The day-to-day care that nurses
provide can often be fraught with ethical concerns that do not attract
public or media attention. Privacy, confidentiality, individual choice
and even clinical interventions, such as hydration or performing a
painful procedure, are all part of the nurse’s professional and ethical
domains.
To address the particular ethical issues and practice standards
nurses face, the ICN developed a code of ethics. In March 2018, the
NMBA adopted the ICN Code of Ethics for Nurses (2012). This is
now in effect for all nurses in Australia and replaces the NMBA Code


of Ethics for Nurses (2008). The International Confederation of
Midwives Code of Ethics for Midwives is in effect for all midwives in
Australia.
Nursing codes of ethics
A code of ethics
 is a formal statement of a group’s ideals and
values. This set of ethical principles (a) is shared by members of the
group, (b) reflects their moral judgments over time, and (c) serves
as a standard for their professional actions. Codes of ethics usually
have higher requirements than legal standards and are never lower
than the legal standards of the profession. Nurses are responsible
for being familiar with the codes that govern their practices. The ICN
first adopted a code of ethics in 1953, and the current (2012)
version can be found at <www.icn.ch/sites/default/files/inline-
files/2012_ICN_Codeofethicsfornurses_%20eng.pdf>.
The ICN Code of Ethics for Nurses comprises four elements: nurses
and people, nurses and practice, nurses and the profession, and
nurses and co-workers (see Box 5.3
). The document provides
guidance on how to apply the elements into different practice
contexts such as practitioners, educators and national associations
of nurses.
BO X


5.3 Elements of the ICN Code of
Ethics for Nurses
Nurses and people
1. The nurse’s primary professional responsibility is to
people requiring nursing care.
2. In providing care, the nurse promotes an environment
in which the human rights, values, customs and
spiritual beliefs of the individual, family and community
are respected.
3. The nurse ensures that the individual receives
accurate, sufficient and timely information in a
culturally appropriate manner on which to base
consent for care and related treatment.
4. The nurse holds in confidence personal information
and uses judgment in sharing this information.
5. The nurse shares with society the responsibility for
initiating and supporting action to meet the health and
social needs of the public, in particular those of
vulnerable populations.
6. The nurse advocates for equity and social justice in
resource allocation, access to health care and other
social and economic services.
7. The nurse demonstrates professional values such as
respectfulness, responsiveness, compassion,
trustworthiness and integrity.


Nurses and practice
1. The nurse carries personal responsibility and
accountability for nursing practice and for maintaining
competence by continual learning.
2. The nurse maintains a standard of personal health
such that the ability to provide care is not
compromised.
3. The nurse uses judgment regarding individual
competence when accepting and delegating
responsibility.
4. The nurse at all times maintains standards of personal
conduct which reflect well on the profession and
enhance its image and public confidence.
5. The nurse, in providing care, ensures that use of
technology and scientific advances is compatible with
the safety, dignity and rights of people.
6. The nurse strives to foster and maintain a practice
culture promoting ethical behaviour and open dialogue.
Nurses and the profession
1. The nurse assumes the major role in determining and
implementing acceptable standards of clinical nursing
practice, management, research and education.
2. The nurse is active in developing a core of research-
based professional knowledge that supports evidence-
based practice.


3. The nurse is active in developing and sustaining a core
of professional values.
4. The nurse, acting through the professional
organisation, participates in creating a positive practice
environment and maintaining safe, equitable social and
economic working conditions in nursing.
5. The nurse practises to sustain and protect the natural
environment and is aware of its consequences on
health.
6. The nurse contributes to an ethical organisational
environment and challenges unethical practices and
settings.
Nurses and co-workers
1. The nurse sustains a collaborative and respectful
relationship with co-workers in nursing and other fields.
2. The nurse takes appropriate action to safeguard
individuals, families and communities when their health
is endangered by a co-worker or any other person.
3. The nurse takes appropriate action to support and
guide co-workers to advance ethical conduct.
