Chapter 6 Health care delivery
systems
Majella Hales
Learning outcomes
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Differentiate between health services based on primary,
secondary and tertiary health care categories.
Describe the functions and purposes of the health care agencies
outlined in this chapter.
Identify the roles of various health care professionals.
Describe the factors that affect health care delivery.


Compare various systems of funding for health care services.
Key terms
case management
 125
critical pathways
 125
differentiated practice
 125
health care system
 113
Medicare
 122
person-centred care
 125
skill mix
 125
team nursing
 126
A health care system
 is the totality of
services offered by all health disciplines. The
health system is one of the largest industries in
Australia. In the past, the major purpose of a
health care system was to provide care to the ill
and injured. However, in contemporary times,
with increasing awareness of health promotion,
illness prevention and levels of wellness, health
care systems are changing, as are the roles of
nurses in these areas. The services provided by


a health care system are commonly categorised
according to type and level.


Types of health care services
Health care services are often described in three classifications: (a)
primary health care, which includes health promotion and illness
prevention; (b) secondary health care, which encompasses
diagnosis, treatment and prevention of further disability; and (c)
tertiary health care, which consists of rehabilitation, health
restoration and palliative care, with a focus on minimising chronic or
permanent effects.
Primary health care: health
promotion and illness prevention
Before the 1970s, health care in Australia was primarily aimed at
treating illness and, to some extent, preventing infection via
immunisation programs. Health care was mostly the domain of
medical practitioners. During the 1970s, however, in Australia and
other developed countries, there was an increasing realisation that
health and illness were determined not only by biophysiological
changes but also by the effects of external factors or ‘social
determinants’, such as poverty and poor nutrition and living
conditions. Health and illness are now consequently viewed as being
more than medical issues.


From 1978 to 1986, two milestone events occurred as a
consequence of this changing perception. The first of these was the
Alma Ata Declaration, which was developed as a result of a primary
health care conference staged by the World Health Organization
(WHO) in 1978. This declaration identified 10 principles for primary
health care, the most critical one being the concept of ‘health for all
by the year 2000’. Other important principles in health care include
the notion of equity, access, affordability and community
participation (Wakerman & Humphreys ; Wakerman et al. ).
1 Wakerman, J. & Humphreys, J. (2019). ‘Better health in the bush’: Why we urgently need a
national rural and remote health strategy. MJA, 210(5), 202–204 Retrieved from
<www.mja.com.au>.
2 Wakerman, J., Humphreys, J., Lyle, D., McGrail, M. & Lavey, L. (2015). Overcoming
Access and Equity Problems Relating to Primary Health Care Services in Rural and Remote
Australia. Retrieved from <http://aphcri.anu.edu.au>.
Despite this progress, the concept of health promotion was slow to
develop until the advent of the second milestone, the Ottawa
Charter. This Charter also arose out of a WHO conference on health
promotion, in 1986, and it identified five action areas for health
promotion. Two of these action areas were to create environments
that support healthy living and to develop personal skills (Talbot &
Verrinder ).
3 Talbot, L. & Verrinder, G. (2017). Promoting Health: The Primary Health Care Approach (6th
ed.). Sydney: Elsevier/Churchill Livingstone.
1
2
3


Since that time, more and more people are recognising the
advantages of staying healthy and avoiding illness. Primary
prevention programs address areas such as adequate and proper
nutrition, weight control and exercise, and stress reduction. Health
promotion activities emphasise the important role individuals play in
maintaining their own health and encourage people to maintain the
highest level of wellness they can achieve.
Illness prevention programs may be directed at the individual or the
community, and involve such practices as providing immunisations,
identifying risk factors for illnesses and helping people take
measures to prevent these illnesses from occurring. Illness
prevention also includes environmental programs that can reduce
the incidence of illness or disability. For example, steps to decrease
air pollution include requiring inspection of vehicle exhaust systems
to ensure acceptable levels of fumes. Environmental protective
measures are frequently legislated by governments and lobbied for
by citizen groups.
As Australia’s health care system matures, more funding is being
provided both by government and non-government sources for
primary health care services. According to the Australian Institute of
Health and Welfare (AIHW) , primary health care services exceeded
$62 billion dollars in 2016–17. This figure equates to 34% of the total
health funding in that year. However, this figure includes
pharmaceutical costs and dental services, and as such, does not
represent the pure health promotion and illness prevention dollar.
The majority of this figure includes costs associated with the
4


provision of goods and services to reduce the chance of an
individual’s admission to an acute care facility for the management
of an exacerbation of their current medical condition.
4 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019a). Hospital Resources 2017–18:
Australian Hospital Statistics. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Clinical consideration
As private health funds have realised that
keeping people healthy is less expensive than
treating illnesses, their insurance plans have
begun to pay for preventive health care
activities; for example, gym memberships and
massage sessions.
Secondary health care: diagnosis
and treatment
In the past, the largest segment of the health care services has
been dedicated to the diagnosis and treatment of illness, and this
continues to be the case in Australia. Hospitals and general practice
clinics have been the major agencies offering these complex


secondary prevention services. Hospitals continue to focus
significant resources on individuals requiring emergency, intensive
and around-the-clock acute care. According to the Australian Bureau
of Statistics (ABS) (ABS ; ), public hospital services in accounted
for approximately $54 billion dollars (31%) of the total annual
recurrent health expenditure in 2017–18.
5 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018a). 5204.0. Australian System of National
Accounts, 2017–18. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
6 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2019a). 3238.0. Estimates and Projections, Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander Australians, 2006 to 2031. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Freestanding diagnostic and treatment facilities also have evolved
and serve ever-growing numbers of individuals. For example,
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and related radiological
diagnostic procedures are commonly performed at day surgeries or
local medical centres.
Early detection of disease is also included as a health promotion
service in secondary care. This is accomplished through routine
screening of the population and focused screening of those at
increased risk of developing certain conditions. Examples of early
detection services include regular dental exams from childhood
throughout life and bone density studies for women at menopause to
evaluate for early osteoporosis. Community-based agencies have
become instrumental in providing these services. For example,
clinics in some communities provide mammograms and education
regarding the early detection of cancer of the breast. Voluntary HIV
5 6


testing and counselling is another example of the shift in services to
community-based agencies. Some malls and shopping centres also
have walk-in clinics that provide diagnostic tests, such as screening
for cholesterol, high blood pressure and skin cancer.
Tertiary health care: rehabilitation,
health restoration and palliative
care
The goal of tertiary health care is to help people move to their
previous level of health (i.e. to their previous capabilities) or to the
highest level they are capable of given their current health status.
Rehabilitative care emphasises the importance of assisting
individuals to function adequately in the physical, mental, social,
economic and vocational areas of their lives. For example, someone
with an injured neck or back from a motor vehicle accident may have
restrictions in the ability to perform work or daily activities. If the
injury is temporary, rehabilitation can assist in return to former
function. If the injury is permanent, rehabilitation assists the person
to learn how to perform activities in order to achieve maximum
abilities. Rehabilitation may begin in the hospital but will eventually
lead individuals back into the community for further treatment and
follow-up once health has been restored.


Sometimes, people cannot be returned to health. A growing field of
nursing and tertiary health care services is that of palliative care—
providing comfort and treatment for symptoms. End-of-life care may
be conducted in many settings, including the home.


Types of health care agencies and
services
Health care agencies and services in Australia are both varied and
numerous. Some health care agencies or systems provide services
in different settings; for example, a hospital may provide acute
inpatient services, outpatient clinic or ambulatory care services, and
emergency room services. Hospice services may be provided in the
hospital, the home, or another agency within the community (see
Figure 6.1
). Because the array of health care agencies and
services is so great, nurses often need to help a person choose the
one that best suits their needs. Individuals may be seen by any
number and type of nurses and other providers, depending on their
care and ability to pay for the services.
Figure 6.1


Various health care settings.
Sources: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo; vividpixels/123RF; © wavebreakmedia ltd/Shutterstock.com; Tyler
Olson/123RF; Katarzyna Bialasiewicz/123RF.
Primary health care services
Government (official) agencies are established at the state and
federal government levels to provide primary health care services.
Such health agencies vary according to the need of the area. These
services complement those provided by the secondary and tertiary
health services such as medical health services, dentists,
optometrists and pharmacists. Primary health care services include
the management and monitoring of food quality, communicable
disease control (largely achieved through immunisation programs),
health education campaigns, injury prevention and harm
minimisation strategies, and screening programs. Primary health
care services are purpose built to meet the health needs of the
community. Programs provide the necessary nursing and allied
health staff and facilities to operate. The programs should be
evaluated frequently to ensure that effectiveness is maintained.
Primary health care services also need to monitor the need for
change and institute modifications where necessary to ensure the
programs’ success.
Public health in Australia incorporates health protection, illness
prevention, health promotion and infrastructure development. Other
functions include conducting research and providing training in the


health field. Public health is administered via federal, state and
territory governments; however, it is largely the responsibility of the
state, territory and local governments.
The federal government arm of public health and primary health
care in Australia is the responsibility of the Department of Health and
the Department of Social Services. Other organisations that support
the department are the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA),
the Office of Health Protection (OHP) and Food Standards Australia
New Zealand (FSANZ, formerly the Australian New Zealand Food
Authority), to name a few. Also at the national level are research
institutions such as the National Health and Medical Research
Council (NHMRC) and the AIHW.
The public health environment is changing significantly in Australia.
The division of public health spending between states and federal
government is still fluid. In comparison with the other 35
Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)
member countries, Australia ranks thirtieth in relation to spending on
disease prevention and public health as a percentage of current
health expenditure at 1.9%, whereas Costa Rica (ranked first)
spends 15.2%, and Canada (ranked second) spends 6.1%. The
average country in the OECD spends 2.7% (OECD 2019). Since
2000, Australia has averaged 1.8%, never spending more than 2.1%
(in 2006 and 2007).
Primary Health Networks (PHN)


Australia’s primary health care system has undergone significant
change for two decades. The latest Australian government initiative
to improve primary health care is called the Primary Health Network.
In July 2015, 31 Primary Health Networks, organised by
geographical regions, were established (see Figure 6.2
).
Figure 6.2


31 Primary Health Networks identified by region.
Source: Information extracted from Department of Health . 31 Primary Health Network Boundaries—September,
2015. Retrieved from
www.health.gov.au/internet/main/publishing.nsf/Content/03F3D39E5C44403DCA257FB000095CA8/$File/phnN
atSep15.pdf. © Commonwealth of Australia 2016.
7 Department of Health (2015). 31 Primary Health Network Boundaries—September, 2015.
Retrieved from <www.health.gov.au>.
The key objective for the inception of the Primary Health Networks is
to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of health services and
improve the coordination of care (Department of Health ). The six
key areas of focus within this initiative are related to mental health,
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health, population health, the
health workforce, eHealth and aged care. Hopefully, this program will
help improve these services which need National Health Priority
status.
8 Department of Health (2018). Evaluation of the Primary Health Networks Program Final
Report 2018. Retrieved from <www.health.gov.au>.
For more information on community health, see Chapter 7
.
7
8


Aboriginal Community Controlled
Health Services (ACCHSs)
An important consideration in the provision of community health
services is ensuring that not only are they medically appropriate and
responsive to need, but also they are culturally appropriate. In 2019,
there was an estimated Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
population of 847 200 people in Australia (ABS 2019a). As a
population, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians
experience a significant disparity in mobility and mortality when
compared with non-Indigenous Australian health statistics. To this
end, there are in excess of 150 entities initiated by the community
delivering comprehensive, holistic and culturally appropriate local
health care services. These entities are represented by a national
peak body called the National Aboriginal Community Controlled
Health Organisation (NACCHO). NACCHO is governed by a board
comprised of two directors from each state and territory who are
elected from member organisations.
General practitioners’ offices
In Australia, the general medical practitioner’s (GP) office is also a
primary care setting. The majority of GPs either have their own
offices or work with several other GPs in a group practice.
Individuals usually go to a GP’s office for routine health screening,


lifestyle management, health education, illness diagnosis and
treatment.
A recent innovation in Australia in some medical practices, such as
those of family practice GPs or specialists such as dermatologists or
surgeons, is to have general practice nurses (GPNs), who are
Registered Nurses (RNs) working alongside GPs. These GPNs have
a variety of roles and responsibilities, including administrative tasks,
preparing the individual for an examination and obtaining and
providing health information. Other functions may include obtaining
specimens, assisting with procedures and providing some
treatments. In offices without RNs, these tasks are performed by the
GP.
Privately owned day hospitals
Privately owned day hospitals are used in many communities. Most
of these have diagnostic and treatment facilities providing medical,
nursing and allied health care, and laboratory and radiological
services, and they may or may not be associated with an acute care
hospital. These privately owned clinics also provide services to
people who require minor surgical procedures that can be performed
at the centre. After surgery, the person returns home the same day.
These centres offer two advantages: they permit the person to live
at home while obtaining necessary health care and they free up
costly hospital beds for people who are seriously ill. In 2016–17,


there were 357 of these clinics dispersed throughout Australia
(ABS ).
9 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018b). 4390.0. Private Hospitals, Australia, 2016–17.
Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Occupational health and safety
clinics
The occupational (industrial) health clinic is gaining importance as a
setting for employee health care. Employee health has long been
recognised as important to productivity. Today, more companies
recognise the value of healthy employees and encourage healthy
lifestyles by providing exercise facilities and coordinating health
promotion activities.
Community health nurses in the occupational setting have a variety
of roles. Worker safety has always been a concern of occupational
nurses. Today, nursing functions in industrial health care include
work safety and health education, annual employee health screening
and maintaining immunisation information. Other functions may
include screening for such health problems as hypertension and
obesity, caring for employees following injury and counselling.
9


Hospitals
Hospitals vary in size from the 12-bed regional and remote hospital
to the large metropolitan hospital which might have more than 800
beds. In 2017–18, there were 1350 hospitals (95 986 beds) in
Australia, and 693 of these were in acute public hospitals (AIHW
2019a). Hospitals can be classified according to their ownership or
control as governmental (public) or non-governmental (private). In
Australia, public hospitals are funded both by federal and state
governments but their management and monitoring is a state
responsibility. In some cases, the federal government provides
hospital facilities in the form of residential care for older people.
Private hospitals are operated by churches, companies,
communities or charitable organisations. Private hospitals may be
for profit or not for profit. Although hospitals are chiefly viewed as
institutions that provide care, they have other functions, such as
providing sources for health-related research and teaching. This is
particularly the case in public hospitals.
Hospitals are also classified by the services they provide. General
hospitals admit individuals requiring a variety of services, such as
medical, surgical, obstetric, paediatric and psychiatric services.
Other hospitals offer only specialty services, such as psychiatric or
paediatric care. In general, an acute care hospital provides
assistance to individuals whose illness and need for hospitalisation
are relatively short term; for example, a day to a couple of weeks.


The variety of health care services that hospitals provide depends
on their size and location. The large urban hospitals usually have
inpatient beds, emergency services, diagnostic facilities, ambulatory
surgery centres, pharmacy services, intensive and coronary care
services, and multiple outpatient services provided by clinics. Some
large hospitals have other specialised services such as spinal cord
injury and burns units, oncology services and infusion and dialysis
units. In addition, some hospitals have substance abuse treatment
units and health promotion units. Small regional and remote
hospitals are often limited to inpatient beds, radiology and laboratory
services, and basic emergency services. The number of services a
regional or remote hospital provides is usually directly related to its
size and its distance from an urban centre (see also Chapter 9
).
Hospitals in Australia have undergone organisational changes in
order to contain costs and/or to attract individuals. This has been
achieved by reducing bed numbers, increasing throughput of
individuals, changing the skill mix of staff on units and management
restructuring. The focus of hospital care also has changed to include
innovative outpatient services, such as diabetes outreach services,
nutrition classes and alternative birth centres.
Aged care/extended
care/residential care facilities


There are more than 3.79 million Australians aged 65 years or older,
which equates to 15.4% of the population (ABS ). Aged, extended
or residential care facilities, formerly called nursing homes, are now
often multilevel buildings that include independent living quarters for
seniors, assisted living facilities, skilled nursing facilities
(intermediate care) and extended care (long-term care) facilities that
provide levels of personal care for those who are chronically ill or are
unable to care for themselves without assistance. Traditionally,
extended care facilities only provided care for older people, but they
now provide care to individuals of all ages who require rehabilitation
or custodial care. Because individuals are being discharged earlier
from acute care hospitals, some individuals may still require
supplemental care in a skilled nursing or extended care facility
before they return home.
10 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2019b). 31010. Australian Demographic Statistics,
Dec 2018. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Currently, there are approximately 125 aged care places per 1000
people (aged over 70 years) (Office of the Royal Commission ).
11 Office of the Royal Commission (2019). Navigating the Maze: An Overview of Australia’s
Current Aged Care System. Retrieved from <https://agedcare.royalcommission.gov.au>.
Because chronic illness occurs most often in the elderly, long-term
care facilities have programs that are oriented to the needs of this
age group. Facilities are intended for people who require not only
personal services (such as assistance with mobilising, hygiene and
nutrition) but also some regular nursing care and occasional medical
10
11


attention. However, the type of care provided varies considerably.
Some facilities admit and retain only residents who are able to dress
themselves and are ambulatory. Other extended care facilities
provide bed care for people who are more incapacitated. These
facilities can, in effect, become the person’s home, and
consequently the people who live there are frequently referred to as
residents rather than patients.
Specific guidelines govern the admission procedures for individuals
admitted to an extended care facility. Insurance criteria, treatment
needs and nursing care requirements must all be assessed
beforehand. Extended care and skilled nursing facilities are
becoming an increasingly popular means for managing the health
care needs of individuals who do not meet the criteria for remaining
in the hospital. Nurses in extended care facilities assist individuals
with their daily activities, provide care when necessary and
coordinate rehabilitation activities.
Clinical consideration
Older adults may move between levels of care
several times—from independent living, to a
hospital, to a rehabilitation centre, to long-term
care, and hopefully back to independent or
assisted living. The sequence varies, as will the
length of time in each setting.


Retirement villages and
assisted living centres
Retirement villages or assisted living centres consist of separate
houses, townhouses or apartments for residents. Residents live
relatively independently; however, many of these facilities offer
meals, laundry services, nursing care, transportation and social
activities. Some centres have a separate hospital to care for
residents with short-term or long-term illnesses. Often, these
centres also work collaboratively with other community services,
including case managers, social services and a hospice, to meet the
needs of the residents who live there. The retirement or assisted
living centre is intended to meet the needs of people who are unable
to remain at home but do not require hospital or nursing home care.
Nurses in retirement and assisted living centres provide limited care
to residents, usually related to the administration of medications and
minor treatments, but conduct significant health promotion activities.
Rehabilitation centres
Rehabilitation centres usually are independent community centres or
special units. However, because rehabilitation ideally starts the
moment a person enters the health care system, nurses who are
employed on paediatric, psychiatric or surgical units of hospitals also
help to rehabilitate individuals. Rehabilitation centres play an


important role in assisting individuals to restore their health and
recuperate. Drug and alcohol rehabilitation centres, for example,
help free individuals of drug and alcohol dependence and assist
them to re-enter the community and function to the best of their
ability. Today, the concept of rehabilitation is applied to all illness and
injury (physical and mental). Nurses in the rehabilitation setting
coordinate a person’s activities and assist the individual to
understand and adhere to their rehabilitation regimen. This type of
nursing often requires specialised skills and knowledge.
Home health care agencies
Early discharge of individuals from hospitals has made home care
an essential aspect of the health care delivery system. As concerns
about the cost of health care have escalated, the use of the home
as a care delivery site has increased. In addition, the scope of
services offered in the home has broadened. Home health care
nurses and other staff offer education to individuals and families,
and also provide comprehensive care to acute, chronic and
terminally ill individuals.
Day care and community
health centres


Day care centres serve many functions and many age groups.
Some day care centres provide care for infants and children while
parents work. Other centres provide care and nutrition for adults
who cannot be left at home alone but do not need to be in an
institution. Senior citizen care centres often provide care involving
socialising, exercise programs and stimulation. Some centres
provide counselling and physical therapy. Nurses who are employed
in day care or community health centres may provide medications,
treatments and counselling, thereby facilitating continuity between
day care and home care.
Regional and remote care
Regional and remote health care is a particular challenge in Australia
due to a number of complex factors associated with isolation and
access. Cost inefficiencies have resulted in a contraction of acute
care services with an emphasis on centralisation over the past few
decades. However, the biggest challenge by far is recruitment and
retention of health professionals, specifically suitably qualified
doctors.
As a response to this challenge, the federal government developed
the Rural Retention Program (RRP) in 2000 which, in 2010, was
replaced by the General Practice Rural Incentive Program (GPRIP)
as a way of encouraging doctors to remain in regional and remote
areas. In July 2015, the GPRIP program altered its classification
system to the Modified Monash Model (MMM). This model uses the


Australian Statistical Geography Standards Remoteness Areas
(ASGS-RA) to determine degree of remoteness, which is then used
to direct the incentive payments the GP will receive per annum.
Incentive payments range between $4000 and $60 000 per annum.
In January 2020, GPRIP will transition to the Workforce Incentive
Program in an attempt to support the needs of the community by
strengthening multidisciplinary models of care (Department of
Health ).
12 Department of Health (2019). Fact Sheet—Workforce Incentive Program Factsheet.
Retrieved from <www1.health.gov.au>.
As a consequence of the shortage of doctors and other health
professionals, nurses in regional and remote settings must be
generalists who are able to manage a wide variety of individuals and
health care problems. Due to their training in providing
comprehensive primary care across the lifespan, Nurse Practitioners
(NPs) are particularly suited to these roles. Their only support is
often the Royal Flying Doctor Service, which is dispatched on
request when the person’s acuity exceeds the resources or skills
available. An expanded discussion of regional and remote nursing
appears in Chapter 9
.
Hospice (palliative care) services
Originally, a hospice was a place for travellers to rest. Recently, the
term has come to mean interdisciplinary health care service for the
12


dying, provided in the home or another health care setting. The
hospice movement subsumes a variety of services given to the
terminally ill, their families and support people. The central concept
of the hospice movement, as distinct from the acute care model, is
not saving life but improving or maintaining the quality of life until
death. Individuals in hospice programs are cared for at home, in the
hospital or in skilled nursing facilities. The place of health care
delivery may vary as the person’s condition declines or the ability of
the family to care for the person changes. The hospice nurse
performs ongoing assessments of the needs of the person and their
family and helps to find the appropriate resources and additional
services for them as needed.
Crisis centres
Crisis centres provide emergency services to individuals
experiencing life crises. These centres may operate out of a hospital
or in the community, and most provide a 24-hour telephone service.
Some also provide direct counselling to people at the centre or in
their homes. The primary purpose of the centre is to help people
cope with an immediate crisis and then provide guidance and
support for long-term therapy.
Nurses working in crisis centres need well-developed communication
and counselling skills. The nurse must immediately identify the
person’s problem, offer assistance to help the person cope and


perhaps later encourage the person to access resources for long-
term support.
Mutual support and self-help
groups
In Australia today, there are more than 100 mutual support or self-
help groups that focus on nearly every major health problem or life
crisis people experience. Such groups arose largely because people
felt their needs were not being met by the existing health care
system. Alcoholics Anonymous, which formed in 1935, served as the
model for many of these groups.


Providers of health care
The providers of health care, also referred to as the health care
team or health professionals, are nurses and health personnel from
different disciplines who coordinate their skills to assist individuals
and their support people (see Figure 6.3
). Their mutual goal is to
restore a person’s health and promote wellness. The choice of
personnel for a particular person depends on the needs of the
individual. Health teams commonly include the nurse and several
different personnel. Nurses’ roles are described in Chapter 1
 and
throughout this textbook. The non-nurse providers that are
discussed below are examples of some possible providers.
Figure 6.3


Although all members of the health care team individualise care for
the person based on their own discipline, there are areas that
overlap which are facilitated through teamwork.
Nurse
The role of the nurse varies with the needs of the person, the
nurse’s credentials and the type of employment setting. An RN
(Division 1) assesses a person’s health status, identifies health
problems and develops and coordinates care. An Enrolled Nurse


(EN) (Division 2) provides direct care under the direction of an RN or
a doctor. As nursing roles have expanded, new dimensions for
nursing practice have been established. Nurses can pursue a variety
of practice specialties (e.g. critical care, mental health, oncology).
Advanced practice nurses (APNs) provide direct care as NPs and
clinical nurse specialists. These nurses have education and
qualifications that—depending on state regulations—may allow them
to provide primary care, prescribe medications and make referrals.
In some states, NPs also have hospital admission rights and
corresponding Medicare provider numbers.
Case manager
The case manager’s role is to ensure that individuals receive fiscally
sound, appropriate care in the best setting. This role is often filled by
the member of the health care team who is most involved in the
person’s care. Depending on the nature of the individual’s concerns,
the case manager may be a nurse, a social worker, an occupational
therapist, a physical therapist or any other member of the health
care team.
Dentist
Dentists diagnose and treat dental problems. Dentists are also
actively involved in preventive measures to maintain healthy oral


structures (e.g. teeth and gums). Many hospitals, especially public
hospitals, have dentists on staff.
Dietitian or nutritionist
A dietitian has special knowledge about the diets required to
maintain health and to treat disease. Dietitians in hospitals generally
are concerned with therapeutic diets, may design special diets to
meet the nutritional needs of individuals and supervise the
preparation of meals to ensure that individuals receive the proper
diet.
A nutritionist is a person who has special knowledge about nutrition
and food. The nutritionist in a community setting recommends
healthy diets and gives broad advice about the purchase and
preparation of foods. Community nutritionists often function at the
preventive level. They promote health and prevent disease; for
example, by advising families about balanced diets for growing
children and pregnant women.
Occupational therapist
An occupational therapist (OT) assists individuals with impaired
function to gain the skills to perform activities of daily living. For
example, an OT might teach a man with severe arthritis in his arms


and hands how to adjust his kitchen utensils so that he can continue
to cook. The OT can also make splints and provide appliances to
assist the individual to function better without assistance.
Social worker
A social worker counsels individuals and their support people
regarding problems such as finances, marital difficulties and
adoption of children. It is not unusual for health problems to produce
problems in day-to-day living and vice versa. For example, an older
woman who lives alone and has a stroke resulting in impaired
mobility may find it impossible to continue to live in her third-floor
apartment. Finding a more suitable living arrangement can be the
responsibility of the social worker if the person has no support
network in place.
Health technicians
Laboratory technicians, radiographers and sonographers, and
nuclear medicine technicians are just a few kinds of health
technicians in the expanding field of medical technology. Laboratory
technicians examine specimens such as urine, faeces, blood and
discharge from wounds to provide exact information that facilitates
the medical diagnosis and the prescription of a therapeutic regimen.
The radiographers assist with a wide variety of x-ray procedures,


from simple chest radiography to more complex fluoroscopy.
Sonographers also assist in the production of ultrasound scans vital
for gaining more information for the person’s management. The
nuclear medicine technicians use radioactive substances to provide
diagnostic information and can administer therapeutic doses of
radioactive materials as part of a therapeutic regimen.
Pharmacist
A pharmacist prepares and dispenses pharmaceuticals in hospital
and community settings. The role of the pharmacist in monitoring
and evaluating the actions and effects of medications on individuals
is becoming increasingly prominent. A clinical pharmacist is a
specialist who guides doctors in prescribing medications. A
pharmacy assistant is also recognised in some states. This person
administers medications to individuals or works in the pharmacy
under the direction of the pharmacist.
Clinical consideration
Significant overlap may occur between those
providers who can perform certain health care
activities. For example, an anaesthetist, midwife
or neonatal care nurse may be responsible for
assisting a newborn baby with breathing


problems. All providers undertake education
sessions specific to the needs of the individual.
Physiotherapist
The physiotherapist assists individuals with musculoskeletal
problems. Physiotherapists treat movement dysfunctions by means
of heat, water, exercise, massage and electric current. The
physiotherapist’s functions include assessing the person’s mobility
and strength, providing therapeutic measures (e.g. exercises and
heat applications to improve mobility and strength) and teaching new
skills (e.g. how to walk with a prosthetic leg). Some physiotherapists
provide their services in hospitals; however, independent
practitioners establish offices in communities and serve individuals
either at the office or in the home.
Medical officer
The medical officer is responsible for medical diagnosis and for
determining the therapy required by a person who has a disease or
injury. The doctor’s role has traditionally been the treatment of
disease and trauma (injury); however, many doctors are now
including health promotion and disease prevention in their practice.
Some doctors are general practitioners (GPs) while others are


physicians, dermatologists, neurologists, oncologists, orthopaedic
specialists, paediatricians, psychiatrists, radiologists or surgeons—to
name a few.
Physician assistant (doctor’s
assistant)
Physician assistants (PAs) perform certain tasks under the direction
of a doctor. They diagnose and treat certain diseases, conditions
and injuries. In the United States, PAs have been part of the health
workforce for some years. However, in Australia, they are a recent
addition to the health care team. Research and trials have not
resulted in a significant embrace of this type of health care
professional. There are approximately 40 Australian-trained PAs;
however, they cannot register with Australian Health Practitioner
Regulation Agency and are not recognised under the Medicare
Benefits Schedule nor the Pharmaceutical Benefit Scheme. As the
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) does not
support the increase or implementation of the PA’s role in the
Australian health care landscape, this role is unlikely to grow.
Perioperative nurse surgeon’s assistants (PNSAs) are specialist
advanced practice perioperative Registered Nurses who can function
as an assistant to the surgeon. They have at least 5 years
postgraduate experience in a surgical specialty and postgraduate
qualifications. Currently, they do not have a provider number for


Medicare so that patients can access a rebate; however, discussions
are still progressing (Australian Association of Nurse Surgical
Assistants ).
13 Australian Association of Nurse Surgical Assistants (2019). Scope of Practice. Retrieved
from <www.aansa.org.au>.
Podiatrist
Podiatrists diagnose and treat foot conditions. In some cases,
appropriately qualified podiatrists (with postgraduate qualifications),
referred to as podiatric surgeons, are able to perform surgery and
prescribe medications.
Assistants in Nursing
Assistants in Nursing (AINs) are health care staff who assume
delegated aspects of basic care. These tasks include bathing,
assisting with feeding, collecting specimens and transporting
individuals. Other AIN titles include personal care attendant (PCA),
patient support assistant (PSA) and orderly. Some of these
categories of provider may have standardised education and job
duties (e.g. personal care attendants), while others do not. The
parameters regarding delegation to unregulated nursing roles must
be undertaken with care to ensure that the delegated task remains
13


within their scope of practice. Failure to observe scope appropriately
when delegating can put an RN’s registration at risk.
Spiritual support personnel
Chaplains, pastors, rabbis, priests and other religious or spiritual
advisors serve as part of the health care team by attending to the
spiritual needs of the person. In most facilities, local clergy volunteer
their services on a regular or on-call basis. Hospitals affiliated with
specific religions, as well as many large medical centres, have full-
time chaplains on staff. They usually offer regularly scheduled
religious services. The nurse is often instrumental in identifying the
person’s desire for spiritual support and notifying the appropriate
person.
Alternative (complementary)
care provider
Alternative or complementary health care refers to those practices
not commonly considered part of Western medicine. See Chapter
20
 for a detailed description of these. Chiropractors, herbalists,
acupuncturists, massage therapists, reflexologists and other health
care providers are playing increasing roles in the contemporary
health care system. These providers may practise alongside


Western health care providers, or individuals may use their services
in conjunction with, or in lieu of, Western therapies.


Factors affecting health care
delivery
Today’s health care consumers have greater knowledge about their
health than in previous years, and they are increasingly influencing
health care delivery. Formerly, people expected a doctor to make
decisions about their care; today, however, consumers expect to be
involved in making any decisions. Consumers have also become
aware of how lifestyle affects health. As a result, they desire more
information and services related to health promotion and illness
prevention. A number of other factors affect the health care delivery
system.
Increasing number of older people
Currently, those aged 65 years and over account for 15.4% of
Australia’s population. This proportion is projected to increase to
approximately 23% in 2063 (ABS ). Long-term illnesses are
prevalent in this group, and older people frequently require special
housing, treatment services, financial support and social networks.
The frail older person, considered to be people over age 85, is
projected to be the fastest-growing population. Because only a small
percentage of these people live in residential aged car facilities,
14


substantial home management and nursing support services are
required to assist those living in their homes and communities.
14 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2014). 4102.0. Australian Social Trends, 2014. Does
Size Matter? Population Projections 20 and 50 Years from 2013. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au>.
Older people also need to feel they are part of a community even
though they are approaching the end of their lives. The feeling of
being a useful, wanted and productive citizen is essential to every
person’s health. Special programs are being designed in
communities so that the talents and skills of this group will be used
and not lost to society.
Advances in technology
Scientific knowledge and technology related to health care are
rapidly increasing. Improved diagnostic procedures and
sophisticated equipment permit early recognition of diseases which
might otherwise have remained undetected. New antibiotics and
medications are continually being manufactured to treat infections
and multidrug-resistant organisms. Surgical procedures involving the
heart, lungs and liver that were non-existent 20 years ago are
common today. Laser and microscopic procedures streamline the
treatment of diseases that required surgery in the past.


Computers, bedside charting and the ability to store and retrieve
large volumes of information in databases are commonplace in
health care organisations. In addition, as a result of the internet and
World Wide Web access from numerous public and private
locations, individuals now have access to medical information similar
to that of health care providers (although not all websites provide
accurate information).
Individuals are now more likely to be treated in the community,
utilising resources, technology and treatments available outside the
hospital. For example, years ago a person having cataract surgery
had to remain in bed in the hospital for 10 days; today, most
cataract surgeries are performed on an outpatient basis.


The Australian health system
The health care system funding arrangements in Australia are
changing. Efficiency reviews have identified that there are significant
issues resulting in money being wasted on duplicative, excessive or
irrelevant health interventions which, in some instances, provide little
to no benefit (Productivity Commission ). There have been shifts in
the responsibilities between federal and state governments in health
care management and funding arrangements. Irrespective of new
systems and attempts to improve efficiencies that will be
implemented, health care costs in Australia will still consume a
significant volume of the gross domestic product. Like its
counterparts in other Western countries, it is a very large, complex
system that at the beginning of the twenty-first century is stretched
to the limit.
15 Productivity Commission (2015). Efficiency in Health. Commission research paper.
Canberra. JEL codes: I10, I18. Retrieved from <www.pc.gov.au>.
The system operates as a combination of public and private
ownership. A federal government system called Medicare
,
introduced in the early 1980s, provides the funds for public health
care services. The finances for this system are obtained from a
percentage of income tax that is levied on most wage earners. In
addition to Medicare, funding relationships exist between the
individual states and territories to enable the functioning of the public
15


health care systems across Australia. For more information
regarding funding and health care service arrangements, see
Chapter 7
.
Regulation and administration of the health system starts at a state
ministerial level and is led by an elected Member of Parliament who
is appointed as the minister by the incumbent state Premier. The
minister is advised by experts from within specific health disciplines
who hold executive positions within the central health service. The
primary functions at this level are to table and pass Acts of
Parliament and develop relevant policy which regulates professional
practice within the health system. The central health service also
accredits courses, ensures professional standards are maintained
and registers and licenses health practitioners.
The next strata within the hierarchy takes place at the local level
within the state and is usually focused within the administration of a
large public hospital that also incorporates all the surrounding
community health services. This level is led by chief executive
officers (CEOs) and directors of nursing (DONs). At this level, these
individuals and their associates interpret the Acts, Regulations and
policies developed at ministerial level and apply them to their local
requirements. They also recruit and manage large numbers of staff,
provide educational courses, support medical research and ensure
that individuals have access to the highest-quality care.
The number of remaining levels within the system depends on the
size of the organisation but, generally, they all have a middle-


management level and a clinical level. For nurses, the middle-
management level consists of assistant directors of nursing
(ADONs) and nurse unit managers (NUMs). The ADONs act as a
conduit between the wards/health care units and the nursing
directors, who then report to the executive officers on issues
surrounding these units and act as a gatekeeper of information from
the DON to the units. The NUMs manage the ward/units by ensuring
safe, high-quality care is implemented while concurrently improving
efficiencies and cost effectiveness. In addition, they advocate for
their staff and act as a gatekeeper between them and the ADONs.
Finally, the clinical level is composed of RNs and ENs who
implement the care using the policies and procedures developed at
the first two levels as a guide.
The Australian government spent an estimated $180.7 billion on total
health expenditure in 2016–17, which was approximately 10% of the
gross domestic product (GDP) (AIHW
). On the whole, however,
Australia compares well with other OECD countries in relation to
health expenditure, where the range is from 4.2% in Turkey to
16.9% in the United States (OECD ).
16 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018a). Health Expenditure Australia
2016–17. Health and welfare expenditure series no. 64. Cat. no. HWE 74. Canberra: AIHW.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
17 Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) (2019). Health
Expenditure and Financing Statistics. Retrieved from <www.oecd.org>.
16
17


The major reasons for cost increases include:
Existing equipment and facilities are continually becoming
obsolete as research uncovers new and better methods in health
care. Health care providers and consumers want the newest and
the best, and these services cost more each year.
Inflation increases all costs.
The total population is growing, especially the segment of older
adults who tend to have greater health care needs than younger
people.
As more people recognise that health is everyone’s right, large
numbers of people are seeking assistance in health matters.
According to the RACGP , 38% of Australians visit their GP 2–3
times a year; however, 1 in 8 Australians (12%) sees their GP
more than 12 times a year. This figure accounts for 42% of the
Medicare out-of-hospital benefits fund. The average out-of-
pocket costs for individuals visiting their GP has increased to
$37.39 per visit, which is more than double the increase in the
Consumer Price Index over the preceding year.
18 Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) (2018). The General
Practice: Health of the Nation 2018 Report. Retrieved from <www.racgp.org.au>.
The relative number of people who provide health care services
has increased.
Women’s health
18


There are more than 12.4 million women in Australia, of whom
400 000 identify as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
(AIHW
). The women’s movement has been instrumental in
changing health care practices. Examples are the provision of
childbirth services in more relaxed settings, such as birthing centres,
and the provision of overnight facilities for parents in children’s
hospitals. Until recently, women’s health issues focused on the
reproductive aspects of health, disregarding many health care
concerns that are unique to women. Investigators are beginning to
recognise the need for research that examines women equally to
men in health issues such as osteoporosis, heart disease and
responses to various treatment modalities. Current provision of
health care shows an increased emphasis on the psychosocial
aspects of women’s health, including the impact of career, delayed
childbearing, role of caregiver to older family members and extended
lifespan.
19 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019b). The Health of Australia’s
Females. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Men’s health
There are more than 12.2 million men in Australia, of whom almost
400 000 identify as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
(AIHW
). In this age where male suicide is three times higher than
for females, and ranks as the tenth highest cause of death, it is time
to bring men’s health into focus (ABS ). Seventy per cent of adult
19
20
21


males are obese (60% of women), 17% smoke daily (11% of
women) and 24% are rated as lifetime risky drinkers (10% of
women) (AIHW 2019b; AIHW 2019c). There is an urgent need to
ensure that primary health services and health care practitioners
who provide health education to men have the knowledge and
resources to address these issues, not only for the benefit of men,
but also to reduce Australia’s health care burden.
20 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019c). The Health of Australia’s Males.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
21 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018c). 3303.0. Causes of Death, Australia, 2017.
Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Uneven distribution of services
Serious problems in the distribution of health services exist in
Australia. Two facets of this problem are (a) uneven distribution, and
(b) increased specialisation.
In some areas, particularly remote and very remote locations, there
are insufficient health care professionals and services available to
meet the health care needs of individuals. Specifically, only 1.9% of
the nursing workforce practise in remote areas and a mere 1.2% in
very remote areas (AIHW
). Consequently, individuals in regional
and remote areas may need to drive large distances to obtain the
services they require. Uneven distribution is also evidenced by the
22


disparity in numbers of nurses across states. For example, in 2015,
New South Wales had approximately 1036 nurses per 100 000
population compared with the Northern Territory where there were
1534 nurses per 100 000 population (AIHW
; ABS ) (see Figure
6.4
).

Workforce Data and Additional Material—Table 23: Employed Midwives: Selected
Characteristics, Remoteness Area(s), 2015. Canberra: AIHW. Retrieved from
<www.aihw.gov.au>.

Dataset 2014. Retrieved from <http://analytics.aihw.gov.au>.

An increasing number of health care personnel provide specialised
services. Specialisation can lead to fragmentation of care and, often,
increased cost of care. To individuals, it may mean receiving care
RNs = Registered Nurses RMs = Registered midwives
ENs = Enrolled Nurses FTE = full-time equivalent


from 5 to 30 people during their hospital experience. This seemingly
endless stream of personnel and the paperwork required is often
confusing and frightening.
The socioeconomically
disadvantaged
Because of the conditions for those who are socially disadvantaged
and, particularly, those who are homeless (who live in shelters, on
the streets, in parks, in tents, under temporary covers and dwellings,
in railway stations or in cars), their health problems are often
exacerbated and sometimes become chronic. Physical, mental,
social and emotional factors can create health care challenges for
these individuals (see Box 6.1
) as they may lack physical access,
such as convenient or timely transportation, to health care facilities.
Financial burdens may also impact on their health and wellbeing.
According to Harris , disadvantaged Australians are less likely to
access preventive medical services, are more likely to exhibit the
common health risk factors and consequently have shorter lives
than those who are more economically advantaged. One specific
group of people who suffer from these disadvantages is Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander people.
25 Harris, M. (2016). The interface between primary health care and population health:
Challenges and opportunities for prevention. Public Health Research and Practice, 26(1),
e2611601. Doi: http://dx.doi.org/10.17061/phrp2611601. Retrieved from <www.phrp.com.au>.
25


BO X
6.1 Factors contributing to health
problems of the socioeconomically
disadvantaged
Poor physical environment resulting in increased
susceptibility to infections.
Inadequate rest and privacy.
Improper nutrition.
Poor access to facilities for personal hygiene.
Exposure to the elements.
Lack of social support.
Few personal resources.
Questionable personal safety (physical assault is a
constant threat for the homeless).
Inconsistent health care.
Difficulty with adherence to treatment plans.
In 2016, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people comprised
3.3% of the total population (AIHW
). However, comparative
population statistics of the time indicate the disparities in health
between non-Indigenous and Indigenous people:
26


26 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018b). Australia’s Health 2018.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander babies are twice as likely as
all other Australian babies to be born prematurely or to be of low
birth weight (weighing under 2500 g).
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults are 2.7 times more
likely than non-Indigenous Australians to report experiencing
significant psychological distress.
The mortality rate of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
is approximately twice that of non-Indigenous people.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are approximately
1.6 times more likely to be obese and 1.8 times more likely to
have diabetes than non-Indigenous Australians.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are approximately
2.1 times more likely to have chronic kidney disease and 1.9
times more likely to have anaemia than non-Indigenous
Australians.
The life expectancy of an Indigenous male is 67.5 and a female
is 73.1, which is approximately 10 years less than non-
Indigenous Australians (AIHW
).
27 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2015b). The Health and Welfare of
Australia’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples 2015. Cat. no. IHW 147 2015.
Canberra: AIHW. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Lower educational status, lower employment levels and thus lower
income levels certainly contribute to these sobering statistics;
however, the evidence indicates that economic disadvantage is only
one of many factors affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
27


people’s health status. Complex and variable factors may be causing
this disparity, such as lack of Indigenous health professionals or
cultural pressures. Consequently, despite increasing government
expenditure on Indigenous people’s health, the overall gap in
mortality and morbidity between Indigenous and non-Indigenous
Australians continues to widen (AIHW 2015b).
Experts now believe that living conditions, such as overcrowded,
poorly maintained housing; entrenched violence; early exposure to
illicit drugs and alcohol; depression; and suicide are the greatest
causes of ill health in this group. These factors are all associated
with a sense of limited control over their lives that many Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander people experience. Therefore, the problem
is multifaceted and complex, and is not able to be solved exclusively
by any one government department such as the health system.
However, one strategy that has been implemented is to set up
health services that are considered to be more culturally safe and
therefore more likely to be accessed by the Indigenous community.
These are services that are generally initiated and operated by
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander personnel; so far, they are
proving to be quite successful.
Demographic changes
The characteristics of the Australian family have changed
considerably in the past few decades. The numbers of single-parent
families and alternative family structures have increased markedly.


Most of the single-parent families are headed by women, many of
whom work and require assistance with child care or when a child is
sick at home.
Recognition of the cultural and ethnic diversity of the population is
also increasing. Health care professionals and agencies are aware
of this diversity and are employing means to meet the challenges it
presents. For example, more agencies are employing nurses who
are bilingual and who can communicate with individuals whose
primary language is not English.


Frameworks for care
A number of configurations for the delivery of nursing care support
continuity of care and cost effectiveness. These include case
management, person-centred care, differentiated practice, shared
governance, the case method, the functional method, team nursing
and primary nursing. These have evolved, some from each other, for
reasons such as the need to decrease health care costs and to
improve the utilisation of limited human and physical resources. A
particular agency may use more than one configuration—for
example, team nursing on the medical/surgical units and primary
nursing on the cardiac surgery unit.
Research note
Barriers/enablers to quality of care in Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander Australians with chronic kidney
disease
R. Reily, K. Evans, J. Gomersall, G. Gorham, M. Peters, S. Warren, R. O’Shea, A. Class & A. Brown
.
Effectiveness, cost effectiveness, acceptability and implementation barriers/enablers of chronic
kidney disease management. BMC Health Services Research, 16(149), 1−13. Doi: 10.1186/s12913-
016-1363-0.
28 Reily, R., Evans, K., Gomersall, J., Gorham, G., Peters, M., Warren, S., O’Shea, R., Class, A. &
Brown, A. (2016). Effectiveness, cost effectiveness, acceptability and implementation
28


barriers/enablers of chronic kidney disease management. BMC Health Services Research, 16(149),
1−13. Doi: 10.1186/s12913-016-1363-0.
This literature review involving 10 studies examines factors
that influence the success of programs designed to manage
chronic kidney disease in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people. Factors such as ensuring culturally competent
designs that are embedded into existing health care services
is important in the design of successful kidney health
programs. The researchers found that other common
features of effective programs included structure supporting
community ownership with a central role for Indigenous
health workers, robust systems and communications, and
intensive follow-up.
Implications This research demonstrates the critical need
for nurses and other health care professionals to understand
the factors that may influence the best possible design
structure to maximise the initiation and delivery of effective
community health programs. Community health programs are
a critical element in the provision of comprehensive and
effective health care services. However, they can be
expensive to develop and therefore it is critical that nurses
equip themselves with the knowledge and resources
necessary to enable every opportunity for the program to
succeed in the first instance.


Case management
Case management
 describes a range of models for integrating
health care services for individuals or groups. Generally, case
management involves multidisciplinary teams that assume
collaborative responsibility for planning, assessing needs and
coordinating, implementing and evaluating care for groups of
individuals from pre-admission to discharge or transfer and
recuperation. A case manager, however, may be a nurse, social
worker or other appropriate professional. In some areas of Australia,
case managers may be referred to as discharge planners or pre-
admission nurses. Key responsibilities for case managers are shown
in Box 6.2
.
BO X
6.2 Responsibilities of case
managers/discharge planners
Assessing individuals and their homes and communities.
Coordinating and planning care.
Collaborating with other health professionals.
Monitoring a person’s progress.
Evaluating outcomes.


Case management may be used as a cost-containment strategy in
managed care. Both case management and managed care systems
often use clinical or critical pathways
 to track the person’s
progress. A critical pathway is an interdisciplinary plan or tool that
specifies interdisciplinary assessments, interventions, treatments
and outcomes for health-related conditions across a timeline. Critical
pathways are also called critical paths, interdisciplinary plans,
anticipated recovery plans, interdisciplinary action plans and action
plans.
Person-centred care
Person-centred care
 is a delivery model that brings all services
and care providers to the individuals. The supposition is that if
activities normally provided by auxiliary personnel (e.g.
physiotherapy, ECG testing and phlebotomy) are moved closer to
the individual, the number of personnel involved and the number of
steps involved to get the work done are decreased. Cross-training
and development of multiskilled workers who can perform tasks or
functions in more than one discipline are essential elements of
person-focused care.
Differentiated practice (skill mix)


Differentiated practice
 is a system in which the best possible
use of nursing personnel is based on their educational preparation
and resultant skill sets. This is often referred to as ‘skill mix
’.
Thus, differentiated practice models consist of specific job
descriptions for nurses according to their education or training; for
example, AIN, EN or RN. The model is customised within each
health care institution by the nurses employed there. The institution
must first identify the nursing competencies required by the
individuals within the specific practice environment. This model
further requires the delineation of roles between AINs, ENs and
RNs. This enables nurses to progress and assume roles and
responsibilities appropriate to their level of experience, capability and
education. As with managed care and case management,
differentiated nursing practice seeks to provide quality care at an
affordable cost.
Shared governance
The shared governance model can be used in concert with other
models of nursing delivery. It is an organisational model in which
nursing staff are cooperative with administrative personnel in
making, implementing and evaluating care policies. The focus of this
model is to encourage participation of nurses in decision making at
all levels of the organisation. Individuals may participate either at
their own request or as part of their job role criteria. More commonly,
nurses participate through serving in decision-making groups, such
as committees and task forces. The decisions made may also


address employment conditions, cost effectiveness, long-range
planning, productivity and wages and benefits. The underlying
principle of shared governance is that employees will be more
committed to the organisational goals if they have had input into
planning and decision making.
Case method/total person care
The case method, also referred to as total person care (formerly
total patient care), is one of the earliest nursing models developed
and it is still one of the most common models utilised in Australia. In
this person-centred method, one nurse is assigned to and is
responsible for the comprehensive care of a group of individuals
during an 8- or 12-hour shift. For each person, the nurse assesses
needs, makes nursing plans, formulates diagnoses, implements care
and evaluates the effectiveness of care. In this method, a person
has consistent contact with one nurse during a shift but may have
different nurses on other shifts. The case method, considered the
precursor of primary nursing, continues to be used in a variety of
practice settings such as intensive care nursing.
Functional method
The functional nursing method focuses on the jobs to be completed
(e.g. bed making, temperature measurement). In this task-oriented


approach, personnel with less preparation than the professional
nurse perform less complex care requirements. It is based on a
production and efficiency model that gives authority and
responsibility to the person assigning the work; for example, the
nurse. Clearly defined job descriptions, procedures, policies and
lines of communication are required. The functional approach to
nursing is economical and efficient and permits centralised direction
and control. Its disadvantages are fragmentation of care and the
possibility that non-quantifiable aspects of care, such as meeting the
person’s emotional needs, may be overlooked. In Australia, this
model is often utilised in residential care facilities.
Team nursing
Team nursing
 is the delivery of individualised nursing care to
people by a team most often led by a Registered Nurse. A nursing
team consists of RNs, ENs and unlicensed assistive personnel. This
team is responsible for providing coordinated nursing care to
numerous individuals.
The RN (the team leader) retains responsibility and authority for an
individual’s care but delegates appropriate tasks to the other team
members. Proponents of this model believe the team approach
increases the efficiency of the RN. Opponents state that inpatients’
high acuity of illness leaves little to be delegated. This nursing
practice model is often utilised in environments where individuals are
bed-bound, such as in orthopaedic wards. The rationale for this is


the need for more than one person to implement many of the
required nursing interventions for each person. In addition, due to
the complexity of the skill mix and issues arising as a consequence
of the nursing shortage in Australia, this model is now becoming
increasingly utilised.
Primary nursing
Primary nursing is a system in which one nurse is responsible for
overseeing the total care of a number of individuals 24 hours a day,
7 days a week, even if they don’t deliver all the care personally. It is
a method of providing comprehensive, individualised and consistent
care.
Primary nursing uses the nurse’s technical knowledge and
management skills. The primary nurse assesses and prioritises an
individual’s needs, identifies nursing diagnoses, develops a plan of
care with the person and evaluates the effectiveness of care.
Unregulated health care workers (AINs, PCAs) provide some care,
but the primary nurse coordinates it and communicates information
about the person’s health to other nurses and other health
professionals. Primary nursing encompasses all aspects of the
professional role, including teaching, advocacy, decision making and
continuity of care. The primary nurse is the first-line manager of the
individual’s care with all its inherent accountabilities and
responsibilities. Nurse Practitioners, independent midwives and
advanced practice nurses often implement the primary care model.


Financing health care
Although efforts have been made to control the costs of health care,
these costs continue to increase. Employers, legislators, insurers
and health care providers continue to collaborate in efforts to resolve
the issues surrounding how to best finance health care costs.
Among these efforts, the Australian government has implemented
some cost-containment strategies including health promotion and
illness prevention activities.
Health care funding in Australia
The nature of health care funding in Australia is complex.
Figure 6.5
 illustrates the responsibilities of the different
stakeholders.

Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.

Government sources
Government sources of health care funding are provided primarily
via Medicare, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme and a number of
other small special assistance schemes (AIHW 2018a). In addition,
the Department of Veterans’ Affairs (DVA) provides funding for
medical services provided by GPs registered with the DVA and
specialists for war veterans and their dependants. Veterans entitled
to the full range of services receive a gold health card to access
these benefits (DVA ).
30 Department of Veterans’ Affairs (DVA) (2019). Veterans’ Health Cards. Retrieved from
<www.dva.gov.au>.
In 1984, the Australian government introduced a universal health
system, Medicare, which was designed to provide access to high-
quality, affordable health care for all Australian citizens. Similar to
that described by the Declaration of Alma Ata, the basic philosophy
underpinning the introduction of Medicare was egalitarian and was
based on the belief that access to health care is a basic human
right, not a privilege (Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in
Health Care ).
31 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2019).
Australian Health Charter of Rights (2nd ed.). Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
One component of the finances that support the operation of
Medicare is raised via taxation as a levy. The levy amounts to 2.5%
30
31


of the taxable income of all Australians (Australian Taxation Office
(ATO)
). In addition, there is a further sliding-scale surcharge that is
levied on high-income earners who choose not to take private health
insurance cover, and a reduction for low income earners (ATO
;
2019).
32 Australian Taxation Office (ATO) (2019). Medicare Levy Surcharge. Retrieved from
<www.ato.gov.au>.
33 Australian Taxation Office (ATO) (2017). Increase in the Medicare levy—National Disability
Insurance Scheme. Retrieved from <www.ato.gov.au>.
Medicare Australia works in partnership with the Department of
Health to provide services, such as treatment by GPs, optometrists,
practice nurses, eligible dentists and some allied health practitioners,
as well as public hospital care, diagnostic services and many
pathology tests (Department of Human Services ).
34 Department of Human Services (2018). Medicare Information for Health Professionals.
Retrieved from <www.humanservices.gov.au>.
Non-government sources
Non-government sources of funding come from expenses paid by
individuals for services that either are not totally covered by
Medicare or health insurance, or are not covered at all (such as
some cosmetic surgery). They also come from benefits paid by
private health insurance companies, providers of compulsory third-
32
33
34


party insurance for vehicles and workers’ compensation insurance
providers.
Private insurance
Since the advent of Medicare in 1984, private health insurance
companies have also offered insurance cover for services that are
offered mostly in private hospitals and community clinics, as well as
non-hospital related services and also some public health services.
Almost 55% of the Australian population was covered by private
health insurance in 2016 (AIHW
).
35 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018c). Private Health Insurance
Expenditure 2015–16. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
The funds that are distributed via these companies are usually
tailored to meet the specific needs of contributors and are often
shaped in relation to the needs of individuals of particular age
groups, marital status or family composition. The premiums charged
for particular packages therefore vary according to what is included
in or excluded from the package (i.e. dental care). In addition,
contributors can reduce their premiums by opting to pay an excess
for hospital care services.
Private health insurers are regulated by federal government
legislation and their performance is independently monitored. They
are also registered as either open or restricted membership
organisations. Open membership organisations are available for
anyone to join. Restricted membership organisations (such as Police
35


Health or Teachers Health Limited) are only available to specific
groups through unions, professional associations or employment
groups.
Lifespan considerations
Assessing functional levels of older
people
Assessing the functional levels of older people on an ongoing
basis will provide guidelines for detecting needs for special
care, resources and services. It helps to determine their level
of independence and changes as they occur. The two most
common assessments are to evaluate the following activities
of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living:
Activities of daily living
Bathing
Dressing
Toileting
Transferring
Continence
Feeding.
Instrumental activities of daily living


Ability to use the telephone
Shopping
Food preparation
Housekeeping
Laundry
Mode of transportation
Responsibility for own medication
Ability to handle finances.
The following case study is an example of how these
assessments and needs might change for older people.
Mobilising appropriate resources to help maintain the older
person’s functioning ability is important in providing nursing
care.
Case study
Mr Mendel is an 83-year-old married man. He has a history
of severe osteoarthritis, leading to bilateral hip replacements
and one knee replacement. He has mild hypertension
controlled by oral medication. His last orthopaedic surgery
was to replace a hip component that failed due to repeated
dislocations. At that time, he developed a severe urinary tract
infection resulting in weight loss, fatigue and weakness. After
stabilisation, he was sent to the rehabilitation unit of the
hospital for two weeks until ready to go back home.


Occupational therapists consulted with him and his wife
during his hospitalisation.
He lives in a three-storey house with the bedrooms on the top
floor, kitchen and living room on the middle/main floor and
family room on the bottom floor. He has not driven since the
last operation, but would like to. He has smoked cigars for
years and sits on the front porch to smoke. Physiotherapists
have come to the house three times a week for several
months. A home health nurse has also been consulted
periodically to assist with nutrition and elimination difficulties.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. In what ways has Mr Mendel used (a) health
promotion and illness prevention (primary health care),
(b) diagnosis and treatment (secondary health care),
and (c) rehabilitation and health restoration services
(tertiary health care)?
2. Name three types of health care agencies he has
used. What are the strengths of each of these?
