 What other members of the health care
profession would most likely be on the case manager’s
team and why? If you were the nurse providing care,
how would you work with the multi-disciplinary team to
advocate and provide care for Mr Mendel?


Chapter 6 Review


Chapter highlights
Health care delivery services can be categorised by the type of
service: (1) primary: health promotion and illness prevention; (2)
secondary: diagnosis and treatment; and (3) tertiary:
rehabilitation, health restoration and palliative care.
Hospitals provide a wide variety of services on an inpatient and
outpatient basis. Hospitals can be categorised as for profit or not
for profit, public or private, acute care or long-term care. Many
other settings, such as clinics, offices and day care centres, also
provide care.
Various providers of health care coordinate their skills to assist a
person. Their mutual goal is to restore a person’s health and
promote wellness.
The role of the nurse in providing care to individuals will vary
depending on the employment setting, the nurse’s credentials
and the needs of the person.
The many factors affecting health care delivery include the
increasing number of older people, advances in knowledge and
technology, economics, increased emphasis on women’s health,
uneven distribution of health services, access to health care,
health care for those who are socioeconomically disadvantaged
and demographic changes.
Delivery of nursing care that supports continuity of person-
focused care and is cost effective may be implemented by any of
the following methods: case management, person-centred care,
differentiated practice/skill mix, shared governance, case


method/total person care, functional method, team nursing or
primary nursing.
In Australia, health care is financed largely through government
agencies and private organisations that provide health care
insurance and federally funded programs. Government-financed
plans include Medicare and the Pharmaceutical Benefits
Scheme. Private plans consist of open membership and
restricted membership organisations including Medibank Private,
BUPA and Colonial Mutual to name just a few.

family history of high cholesterol.
4. Removal of tonsils for a person with recurrent
tonsillitis.

2. Health care agencies only run health programs funded
by the government.

setting.
4. Various health care services can be provided in an

1. Number of children according to the family’s income.
2. Number of uninsured and underinsured people.

nationwide.
4. Competition between drug and medical equipment
manufacturers.

Discuss primary health care reform in Australia.

Explain essential aspects of collaborative health care.

Health care reform
Australia’s health care system is undergoing significant change. In
2011, the National Health Reform Agreement 2011 (NHR
Agreement), describing the framework on which the various levels of
government will work in partnership to effect an improved and
sustainable health care system for Australia’s future, was
formulated.
The four principal primary health care (PHC) outcomes associated
with this framework are:
building a consumer-focused and integrated PHC system
improving access and reducing inequity
increasing the focus on health promotion and prevention,
screening and early intervention
improving quality, safety, performance and accountability
(Department of Health and Ageing ).
1 Department of Health and Ageing (2013). National Primary Health Care Strategic
Framework. Retrieved from <www.health.gov.au>.
Various issues are driving factors for change including escalating
health care costs, expanding technology, changing patterns of
demographics, shorter hospital stays, increased acuity and health
care access issues. The concept of care is expanding out of
traditional settings into the community and neighbourhoods. Health
1


care activities such as intravenous fluid or drug administration,
mechanical ventilation or even dialysis, once considered safe only in
hospital settings, are now available for individuals in their homes or
community-based health care facilities (see Chapter 8
).
Many factors influence a person’s choice to have their care in
hospitals or in community settings. Some variables include
individuals’ knowledge and awareness of community resources,
cost, availability of home care and perceived safety of care within
the home.
Although it is difficult to document care shifting from hospitals to the
community, tracking the distribution of state and federal government
health expenditure can elicit some important information and the
new transparency commitments of the federal and state
governments will demonstrate improvements tracking fund
allocation. The Australian government is expecting to spend an
estimated $89.5 billion on health in 2022–23 (Commonwealth of
Australia ). The fiscal burden of health care increases with the cost
of drugs, equipment and many other aspects outside the control of
the health care system.
2 Commonwealth of Australia (2019). Budget 2019–20—Overview. Retrieved from
<www.budget.gov.au>.
Internationally, it has been demonstrated that an increase in
spending on health promotion reduces overall health care costs.
More focus on preventable health issues and control of the
progression of chronic disease can improve efficiency in the health
2


dollar. This shift from health care facilities to community care also
brings changes in the roles and responsibilities of health care
professionals involved. This chapter will focus on community health
(public health—the health of the community as an entity). It is
important that a distinction is made between community care
(nursing individuals in their home, see Chapter 8
) and promoting
the health of the community (aka primary health care, discussed
later in this chapter).
Both consumers and health care professionals have been
dissatisfied with Australia’s health care system, which focuses on
acute, hospital-based care. However, over the past 5 years Australia
has experienced many changes associated with attempts to institute
significant health care reform, with many changes and new initiatives
planned over the next few of years.
Since 1997, the Divisions of General Practice Network, which
included the Australian General Practice Network (AGPN) of 112
divisions of general practice organised geographically, aimed to link
health care professionals to provide health care at a local level. This
was replaced by a new system in 2011 called Medicare Locals in
which 61 independent companies, led by the group Australian
Medicare Local Alliance (AML), managed community health services
within regions. In 2013, this system was reviewed and by 2015 was
replaced with Primary Health Networks. This system has 31 groups
organised geographically (see Figure 6.2
 in Chapter 6
),
responsible for implementing relevant health promoting programs to
local communities.


Nurses, professional organisations and consumers influence health
care reform. Nurses provide a unique perspective on the health care
system because of their constant presence in a variety of settings,
and their contact with consumers who receive the benefits of the
system’s most complex services and with those who have problems
with the system’s inefficiencies.
Nurses are well positioned to influence change in health structure
and expenditure. In 2008, the Australian Nursing Federation, along
with several other key nursing groups, organised a meeting with the
federal Minister for Health and Ageing (see Box 7.1
).

Consumers are also effecting major changes in health care delivery
systems. Consumers are adopting health-related values that include
the following:
Health means more than the absence of disease; it
encompasses wellbeing and quality of life.
Quality of life is related to a healthy community that includes
healthy families and a healthy environment.
*
*
*
*


Individuals can actively participate in promoting and maintaining
their health through behaviour and lifestyle changes.
Disease prevention is important.
Another substantial change in Australia’s community health funding
landscape is the creation and institution of the National Disability
Insurance Scheme (NDIS). As a result of the 2010 Productivity
Commission review on long-term disability support, this funding
model was developed to assist individuals (under 65 years of age at
the time of application) with significant and permanent disability to
receive support and services across their lifetime. This scheme aims
to assist over 460 000 people in Australia who require significant
support to live and participate in an ordinary life (NDIS ).
3 National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) (2018). What Is the NDIS? Retrieved from
<www.ndis.gov.au>.
The National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 was passed in
March 2013 and, after successful trials in selected sites around
Australia from 2013, the NDIS was formally introduced in July 2016.
The National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) is the group
responsible for administration of the NDIS.
This community health initiative is designed to tailor funding to the
health needs of the individual; however, it is not a health scheme per
se. Participants are funded on an annual basis to support services,
aids, equipment and care which can be provided by a number of
services on a voucher arrangement, so services are consumer
3


directed. The system concept is a step in the right direction towards
person-centred care.
However, the distinction between approved goods and services and
limitation of the scheme is arbitrary, resulting in obvious teething
problems detracting from an efficient implementation process. One
example involves a profoundly deaf man who was seeking $10 000
to upgrade an old speech processor for his cochlear implant. He was
originally granted $30 000, $10 000 of which was for the processor,
$5000 for speech pathology services and $15 000 for ‘core
supports’, which included social and community activities.
Unfortunately, within a short time after the grant letter came, the
NDIS rescinded the $10 000 for the speech processor funding, yet
was more than willing to provide the ‘core supports’ funding for
which he didn’t actually ask. On appeal, the speech processor
funding was still rejected on the grounds that the guidelines do not
allow for replacement of equipment under 5 years of age
(Stünzner ). There is clearly a flaw in the distribution decisions when
this arbitrary decision suggests that the actual medical assistance
device sought by the individual has been deemed less important
than financial support for social interaction (and for which he felt he
needed no assistance). Another limiting factor of the scheme is that
it only covers people with disabilities of non-traumatic origin,
whereas another scheme—the National Injury Insurance Scheme
(NIIS)—is responsible for the funding and provision of goods and
services for those incurring trauma-related injuries. More information
regarding the differences between these two schemes can be found
in Table 8.1
 (Chapter 8
).
4


4 Stünzner, I. (2019). NDIS denies deaf man $10k for hearing aid upgrade, grants him $15k
for coffee and social outings. ABC News. Retrieved from <www.abc.net.au>.
The funding scheme aims to enable participants to receive support
that will assist them to live in their own home in the community. This
may include goods or services such as equipment, home
modification and personal care or domestic assistance. However,
clinical or medical treatment is excluded and will be the responsibility
of the public or private health system (NDIS 2018).
The NDIS is supported by both state and federal funds. The budget
for 2019–20 was $21.5 billion, which equates to approximately 1.1%
of Australia’s gross domestic product (GDP), to be spent on
disability services. This figure is expected to increase to 1.3% of
GDP by 2044–45 (Parliament of Australia ).
5 Parliament of Australia (2019). Paying for the National Disability Insurance Scheme.
Retrieved from <www.aph.gov.au>.
However, despite this positive move towards better funding for
people with disability, financial issues remain in this new government
health service. In 2018–19, an estimate of $16.9 billion was
budgeted, yet there was a massive underspend of $3.7 billion,
angering many including the support group People with Disability
Australia (PWDA). PWDA suggests that these funds should have
been spent to assist with the logistical difficulties experienced by
NDIS consumers such as delayed applications, long wait times for
review and inadequate funding packages for individuals (PWDA ).
5
6


6 People with Disability Australia (PWDA) (2019). 2019 Federal Budget. Retrieved from
<https://pwd.org.au>.
Primary health care and primary
care
In 1978, the term primary health care (PHC)
 was coined in the
World Health Assembly by the World Health Organization (WHO)
and the United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund
(UNICEF).
PHC is defined as:
essential health care based on practical, scientifically sound and socially acceptable
methods and technology made universally accessible to individuals and families in the
community through their full participation and at a cost that the community and country
can afford to maintain at every stage of their development in the spirit of self-reliance and
self-determination. (WHO , p. 35)
7 World Health Organization (WHO) (1978). Primary Health Care. Report of the
International Conference on Primary Health Care. Retrieved from <www.who. int>.
PHC incorporates five principles:
1. equitable distribution
2. appropriate technology
3. a focus on health promotion and disease prevention
7


4. community participation
5. a multisectoral approach.
Deep concern about health care for the majority of the world’s
population, specifically low life expectancies and high mortality rates
among children, led to the global health strategy of PHC. The WHO
declaration emphasised health or wellbeing as a fundamental right
and a worldwide social goal. It attempted to address inequality in the
health status of people in all countries and to target government
responsibility for policies that would promote economic, social and
health development. Both economic and social development were
considered basic to the achievement of health for all. Thus, PHC
extends beyond the boundaries of traditional health care services. It
involves issues of the environment, agriculture, housing and other
social, economic and political issues such as poverty, transportation,
unemployment, economic development to sustain the population and
so on. A major feature of PHC is that consumers, governments and
public institutions such as public health departments and city
councils should be involved in the planning and delivery of health
care.
In Australia, the principles of PHC include the prevention of illness
through personal care and health promotion. The focus is on
access, equity and collaboration through service providers, and the
importance of self-determination and development by the
community. Ultimately, it encompasses an understanding of the
various determinants of health including social, cultural, economic


and political determinants of health (Australian Primary Health Care
Nurses Association (APNA) ).
8 Australian Primary Health Care Nurses Association (APNA) (2017). Definition of Primary
Health Care Nursing. Retrieved from <www.apna.asn.au>.
Clinical consideration
Terminology review
Community health. Targeted services that may
be provided to support groups of people within
the community. They may be broad services
similar to primary health care or more narrow
services similar to primary care (e.g. aged
care).
Population health. The study of health and
disease in a group of people (e.g. tracking
hepatitis C infection statistics).
Primary care. A more focused concept of
health promotion of community services
individuals can access (e.g. general
practitioners (GPs)).
Primary health care. A broad concept of
promoting health encompassing various
methods and technologies to support
8


population-based health issues (e.g.
immunisation programs).
Public health. A broad concept of undertakings
to promote health and prevent disease. It is
often used interchangeably with the term
primary health care.
Although often used interchangeably, PHC differs from primary care.
Primary care (PC)
 addresses personal health services and not
population-based public health services. PC is generally a reference
to the first point where health services are sought. Because of the
structure of Australian health care, this is most often the GP or local
medical officer (LMO).
In Australia, health care funding is split between the state, territory
and federal governments. Some not-for-profit groups also assist with
promoting population health within limited communities. The National
Healthcare Agreement between the Commonwealth government and
the states and territories distributes the Australian health care costs
differently from previous funding arrangements (see Figure 7.1
).
Without a collaborative, planned approach by all funding bodies, this
scattering of health care funds can contribute to the major
inefficiencies that Australia is currently experiencing. Distribution of
PHC funding is generally focused on providing services to promote
health and preventing chronic illness or disease that is targeted as a


priority area. Unfortunately, since 2011, the Australian government
has stopped releasing the Public Health Expenditure Series and data
cubes. The last itemised and searchable data available is from 2009.
Figure 7.1


National Healthcare Agreement between Commonwealth and state
and territory governments.
Source: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) . Australia’s Health 2018. Retrieved from
<www.aihw.gov.au/getmedia/7c42913d-295f-4bc9-9c24-4e44eff4a04a/aihw-aus-221.pdf>.
9 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018). Australia’s Health 2018. AIHW cat.
no. AUS 221. Canberra: AIHW. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
9


Community-based health care
Community-based health care (CBHC)
 is a PHC system that
provides health-related services within the context of people’s daily
lives. Examples of this include services in their own home, in
shelters, in long-term care residences, at work, in schools, in senior
citizens’ centres and in ambulatory settings. The care is directed
towards a specific group within the geographical neighbourhood (see
Figure 7.2
). The group may be established by a physical
boundary, an employer, a school district or a specific medical need.
In contrast to the traditional health care system that focuses
primarily on the ill and the injured, community-based care is holistic.
It involves a broad range of services designed not only to restore
health but also to promote health, prevent illness and protect the
public.
Figure 7.2


Communities may consist of several types of neighbourhoods.
Source: © wanderworldimages/Alamy Stock Photo.
To be truly effective, a CBHC system needs to (a) provide easy
access to care, (b) be flexible in responding to the care needs that
individuals and families identify, (c) promote care between and
among health care agencies through improved communication
mechanisms, (d) provide appropriate support for family caregivers,
and (e) be affordable.
As far back as , de Tornyay suggested that an ideal health care
system needed to:
10 de Tornyay, R. (1992). Reconsidering nursing education: The report of the Pew Health
Professions Commission. Journal of Nursing Education, 31, 296–301.
be more oriented to health and emphasise health promotion and
disease prevention
focus on individual responsibility for health practices and
behaviour
be population-based and focus more attention on risk factors in
the physical and social environment
use electronic information systems for health histories and
research findings to support diagnostic decisions and treatment
recommendations
have a stronger focus on consumers who would have increased
information and be informed participants in decisions about their
health care
base decisions on outcomes
10


provide care more efficiently by means of integrated or
coordinated teams of providers
balance technology with non-technical interventions and weigh
the benefits against its effects on human values and
interpersonal processes
have health care providers who will be increasingly accountable
to consumers and society for a wide range of outcomes of care.


Community health
A community
 is a collection of people who share some attribute
of their lives and interact with each other in some way. They may live
in the same locale, attend a particular church or even share a
particular interest such as art. Groups that constitute a community
because of common member interests are often referred to as
communities of interest (e.g. religious and cultural groups). A
community can also be defined as a social system in which the
members interact formally or informally and form networks that
operate for the benefit of all people in the community. Five of the
main functions of a community are described in Box 7.2
. In
community health, the community may be viewed as having a
common health problem, such as a high incidence of infant mortality
or tuberculosis, HIV infection or another communicable disease. Box
7.3
 lists the characteristics of a healthy community. A
population
 is composed of people who share some common
characteristic but who do not necessarily interact with each other.
Community health nursing
 focuses on promoting and
preserving the health of population groups.
BO X


7.2 Five main functions of a
community
1. Production, distribution and consumption of
goods and services. These are the means by which
the community provides for the economic needs of its
members. This function includes not only the supplying
of food and clothing but also the provision of water,
electricity and police and fire protection, and the
disposal of refuse.
2. Socialisation. Socialisation refers to the process of
transmitting values, knowledge, culture and skills to
others. Communities usually contain a number of
established institutions for socialisation: families,
churches, schools, media, voluntary and social
organisations.
3. Social control. Social control refers to the way in
which order is maintained in a community. Laws are
enforced by the police; public health regulations are
implemented to protect people from certain diseases.
Social control is also exerted through the family,
church and schools.
4. Social interparticipation. Social interparticipation
refers to community activities that are designed to
meet people’s needs for companionship. Families and
churches have traditionally met this need; however,


many public and private organisations also serve this
function.
5. Mutual support. Mutual support refers to the
community’s ability to provide resources at a time of
illness or disaster. Although the family is usually relied
on to fulfil this function, health and social services may
be necessary to augment the family’s assistance if
help is required over an extended period.
BO X
7.3 Ten characteristics of a healthy
community
A healthy community:
1. is one in which members have a high degree of
awareness of being a community
2. uses its natural resources while taking steps to
conserve them for future generations
3. openly recognises the existence of subgroups and
welcomes their participation in community affairs
4. is prepared to meet crises
5. is a problem-solving community; it identifies, analyses
and organises to meet its own needs


6. possesses open channels of communication that allow
information to flow between all subgroups of citizens in
all directions
7. seeks to make each of its system’s resources
available to all members
8. has legitimate and effective ways to settle disputes
that arise within the community
9. encourages maximum citizen participation in decision
making
10. promotes a high level of wellness in all its members.
In Australia, programs targeting behaviours that contribute to
chronic ill health are attempting to reduce serious risk factors such
as harmful alcohol use, obesity and smoking (see Table 7.1
).
However, as a community, we still have a long way to go before we
can significantly reduce the preventable chronic disease burden.
Table 7.1 Comparisons of risk factors contributing to
preventable chronic ill health.

risk factor.

and risk factor.

Communities, like individuals and families, are living entities. A
strategic approach to determining the health care needs of a
community should be embraced to maximise the assessment,
planning and implementation of programs to support a community’s
health needs. Figure 7.3
 identifies an approach used by the
Primary Health Networks to determine an economical yet functional
plan for the needs of the community.
Figure 7.3


A structured approach for assessing and planning the health needs
of a community—the PHN Commissioning Framework.
Source: Data extracted from Department of Health
. Needs Assessment Guide. Retrieved from
<www.health.gov.au/internet/main/publishing.nsf/Content/98D184E26BF30004CA257F9A000718F4/$File/PHN
%20Needs%20Assessment%20Guide.pdf>.
12 Department of Health (2015). Needs Assessment Guide. Retrieved from
<www.health.gov.au/>.
In Australia, a nurse may be part of a multidisciplinary team
responsible for planning community health. The plan may be
oriented towards improved crisis management, disease prevention
and health maintenance or health promotion.
12


In community health, evaluation determines whether the planned
interventions have led to the achievement of the established goals
and objectives; for example, was there an improvement in the
immunisation rate of preschool children? Because community health
is usually a collaborative process between health providers,
community leaders, politicians and consumers, all may be involved
in the evaluation process. Often the community health nurse is the
agent of evaluation, collecting and assessing the data that determine
the effectiveness of implemented programs.


Community health and primary
health care
Nurses have a role in promoting community health through PHC.
Many nurses perform PHC functions as part of their daily routine. As
the health care reform attitude strengthens towards PHC, the
development of more programs will lead to the prevention of chronic
illness or assist in the early diagnosis of targeted health issues that
persistently burden Australia’s health care dollar. Nurses may work
in areas of PHC, including as a practice nurse, in centres directly
responsible for immunisation or control of communicable disease,
women’s health, men’s health, environmental health and any
number of other areas offering health promotion and community
initiatives.
Research note
Are we missing the overall picture? Should we re-
evaluate our current ‘single disease’ focus in light of
prevalent combinations of complex comorbidities when
considering health care in Australia?
C. Harrison, J. Henderson, G. Miller & H. Britt
. The prevalence of complex multimorbidity in
Australia. Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health, 40(3), 239−244. Doi: 10.1111/1753-
13


6405.12509.
13 Harrison, C., Henderson, J., Miller, G. & Britt, H. (2016). The prevalence of complex multimorbidity
in Australia. Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health, 40(3), 239−244. Doi:
10.1111/1753-6405.12509.
In this research, the authors reviewed the records of 8707
individuals to determine cluster patterns and prevalence of
multiple chronic conditions. They found that two-thirds (66%)
of individuals had more than one chronic condition. Nearly
half (45%) of the people visiting the GP had complex
multimorbidity with the most common combination being
hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and osteoarthritis. The next
most common, yet probably more predictable combination,
was hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and
hyperlipidaemia.
Implications Currently, the focus in the Australian health
care system is one of single disease. It is important for
nurses to understand not only the interrelationship between
disease processes and treatments, but also the implications
of the complexity of a person’s health status in relation to
health education, access and funding implications when
caring for individuals with complex and severe illness.
Structured, well-thought-out and innovative PHC plans are
required to promote a person’s health and reduce the risk of
exacerbation of their disease/s, catapulting them into the
acute health care system.


Nurse immuniser
Two immunisation advisory bodies facilitate technical and operational
implementation of the National Immunisation Program: the
Australian Technical Advisory Group on Immunisation (ATAGI) and
the National Immunisation Committee (NIC). The National
Immunisation Program is a critical component of PHC. Registered
Nurses are able to undertake extra education in order to gain
endorsement to administer immunisations to individuals without a
drug order from a medical officer. This PHC arrangement provides a
more cost effective and efficient system for health care consumers.
Nurse immunisers must follow the National Immunisation Program
Schedule and maintain current knowledge of schedule changes and
other important associated information. In Australia, immunisations
are offered by many different health care providers. Irrespective of
the location, nurses are often primarily responsible for the
management and administration of these programs.
Women’s health nurse
Nurses developing specialist knowledge about women’s health
issues may work in a community centre or as a practice nurse
working with a doctor in a general practice. They often assist women
with issues relating to breastfeeding, breast cancer, gynaecological
issues, menopause, osteoporosis, pregnancy and sexual health. The
focus is generally on health, wellness, disease prevention or early


diagnosis. The type and breadth of a PHC initiative are normally
informed by public health statistics and dictated by local, state,
territory or federal government funding. The biannual Pap smear
screening program is an example of a targeted health care issue. In
Australia, an increasing number of practice nurses are qualified to
perform Pap smears.
Men’s health nurse
As in women’s health, nurses may develop knowledge and skills
permitting their contribution to PHC for men. Education, screening,
research or clinical assistance with men’s health issues may include
nutrition and methods to manage weight, prostate cancer, mental
health and sexual health issues. Teaching men about testicular self-
examination or the importance of understanding risk factors and
indicators of prostate problems are critical tasks for nurses involved
in men’s health.
Work health and safety
Nurses are often employed by large industries to assist with work
health and safety issues for their staff. This role would entail not only
education, screening and monitoring of staff for injury and illness
specific to the risk associated with the particular industry, but they
may also perform various other functions.


School nurse
Although the role of a school nurse could be considered one of
acute care, assisting children and adolescents with illness and injury
while they are at school, it can also be one of education and
screening. Position descriptions vary between states and even
between schools. However, nurses employed in schools are well
positioned to promote healthy behaviours, effect change and provide
true preventive interventions.
Child and adolescent health nurse
Individuals with specialist skills and knowledge of child and
adolescent development and health care issues often work in the
community assisting families with various difficulties. Many education
institutions offer courses that result in tertiary qualifications. Several
professional nursing bodies also exist to support education,
networking and research, and to influence policy at local, state and
federal levels. Health promotion takes a critical place in the role of
child and adolescent health nurses.
Remote area nurses


Nurses who work in regional and remote areas often take on tasks
that would normally be performed by other health care professionals
(see Chapter 9
 for more on the role of nurses in regional and
remote communities). The skill set and knowledge required by
nurses in regional and remote areas is remarkably different from
those in metropolitan areas. The paucity of equipment, personnel
and funds complicates an already difficult task. Significant
inequalities exist between health care services offered to
metropolitan and regional and remote communities (Rural Doctors
Association of Australia ; Alston et al.
).
14 Rural Doctors Association of Australia (2018). Submission to the Senate Economic
References Committee Inquiry into Regional Inequality in Australia. Retrieved from
<www.rdaa.com.au>.
15 Alston, L., Allender, S., Peterson, K., Jacobs, J. & Nichols, M. (2017). Rural inequalities in
the Australian burden of ischaemic heart disease: A systematic review. Heart, Lung and
Circulation, 26(2), 122–133.
Clinical consideration
The health and welfare of Australia’s Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander peoples is a major
concern. The past decade has seen significant
improvement in the collection and analysis of
statistical information directly quantifying health
in Indigenous Australians. However, despite
improvements, the gap between Indigenous and
14
15


non-Indigenous Australians remains. (For more
information regarding regional and remote
nursing see Chapter 9
 and for information
regarding Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people’s health see Chapter 19
.)
Some significant inequalities exist as a result of
living in regional, remote and very remote
communities, where primary and secondary
health care services are more difficult to access.
However, there are clearly reasons beyond
geography for this inequity as 79% of
Indigenous Australians live in urban areas
(Australian Bureau of Statistics ).
16 Australian Bureau of Statistics (2018). 2071.0. Census of
Population and Housing: Reflecting Australia—Stories from the
Census, 2016. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Chronic disease educator
Individuals functioning as diabetic nurse educators and enterostomal
nurses have been around for a very long time. As more diseases
and illnesses become the focus of the government, different types of
chronic disease educators may emerge.
16


Practice nurse
In Australia, the role of the practice nurse is still developing. A
practice nurse can work in a range of community and institutional
settings and is responsible for providing PHC within their scope, with
a focus on scientifically sound, socially appropriate and universally
accessible care (APNA 2017). Responsibilities of a practice nurse
often include health promotion and illness prevention, assistance
with end-of-life care or rehabilitation, and provision of midwifery,
antenatal and postnatal care. They may also have significant
influence in education, research, policy development and advocacy
(APNA 2017).
Recent success in the acceptance and value of practice nurses has
resulted in some services provided by practice nurses being given
Medicare Benefits Schedule item numbers.
Community-based frameworks
Various approaches are emerging to address community health.
Some of these are an integrated health care system, community
initiatives, community coalitions, managed care, case management
and outreach programs using lay health workers.
An integrated health care system
 makes all levels of care
available in an integrated form—PC, secondary care and tertiary


care. Its goals are to facilitate care across settings, recovery,
positive health outcomes and the long-term benefits of modifying
harmful lifestyles through health promotion and disease prevention.
Community initiatives are being sponsored by some hospitals or
local community agencies. These initiatives involve members of the
community establishing health priorities, setting measurable goals
and determining actions to reach these goals. If a community
agency is initiating this project, the associated hospital may
contribute human resources to assist in the endeavour.
Community coalitions bring together individuals and groups for the
shared purpose of improving the community’s health. Nurses are
major participants and contributors in these coalitions and often
assume leadership positions. Community coalitions may focus on a
single or a multifaceted problem. Examples include establishment of
an abuse program, a gang prevention program, an older adults’
assessment program or an immunisation program for high-risk
groups.
Infection-control initiatives
Communicable diseases are managed at local, state, territory and
federal levels in Australia, and various programs exist to contribute
to infection control in the community (see Table 7.2
).


Table 7.2 Selected major programs for surveillance of some
communicable diseases
Source: Developed using information from the Department of Health
.
17 Department of Health (2019). National Surveillance Systems Reported in Communicable
Diseases Intelligence. Retrieved from <www.health.gov.au>.
A nurse’s influence on PHC through communicable disease control
extends across many domains, including education, research,
monitoring and notification. A nurse can improve the accuracy of
these surveillance systems through ensuring that individuals in the
community are appropriately assessed when signs and symptoms
warrant. Education of the community can also impact on early
detection. Ultimately, improved surveillance systems can assist the
safety of others in the community.
Managed care
In managed care, which is a common model in health care
restructuring, health care providers (hospitals, doctors, Nurse
Practitioners, practice nurses and allied health care professionals)
join to meet health needs across the care continuum. The managed
care organisation serves as a ‘go-between’ or ‘gatekeeper’ between
the person, provider and payer. Providers are organised into groups
and the person must select one from the group to which they
belong. Managed care aims in this way to enhance the quality and
cost effectiveness of health care.
17


Case management is an integrative health care model that tracks a
person’s needs and services through a variety of care settings to
ensure continuity. The case manager is familiar with the person’s
health needs and resources available through their insurance
coverage so they can receive cost-effective care. Another important
aspect of case management is assisting the person and family to
understand and navigate their way through the complex health care
system.
Outreach programs using lay health workers are a method of linking
under-served or high-risk populations with the formal health care
system. They can minimise or reduce barriers to health care,
increase access to services and thus improve the health status of
the community. They involve partnerships between nurses and
members of the community. Interested and committed lay health
workers are identified who will assist their neighbours through
outreach networks. Nurses provide training, consultation and
support to these individuals.


Community-based nursing
Community-based nursing (CBN)
 is nursing care directed
towards specific individuals.
Clinical consideration
CBN and community health nursing are not the
same concept. CBN focuses on care of
individuals in geographically local settings
whereas community health nursing emphasises
the promotion and preservation of the health of
groups (or populations).
Collaborative health care
Collaboration
 between health care professionals becomes
increasingly important as more practitioners specialise in
progressively more narrow areas of expertise, while others take on
the generalist role. Over time, the boundaries and legal scope of
practice of each health care profession may change. To deliver


optimal health care for the individual, nurses must work as a
member of the team providing comprehensive health care.
The nurse as a collaborator
Nurses collaborate with nurse colleagues and other health care
professionals. They frequently collaborate to optimise an individual’s
care needs but also may be involved, for example, in collaborating
on bioethical issues, on legislation, on health-related research and
with professional organisations. Box 7.4
 outlines selected aspects
of the nurse’s role as a collaborator.
BO X
7.4 The nurse as a collaborator with
nurse colleagues
With nurse colleagues
Shares personal expertise with other nurses and elicits
the expertise of others to ensure quality person-centred
care.
Develops a sense of trust and mutual respect for peers,
recognising everyone’s unique contributions.


With other health care professionals
Recognises the contribution that each member of the
interdisciplinary team can make by virtue of their expertise
and view of the situation.
Listens to each individual’s views.
Shares health care responsibilities in exploring options,
setting goals and making decisions with individuals and
their families.
Participates in collaborative interdisciplinary research to
increase knowledge of a clinical problem or situation.
With professional nursing
organisations
Seeks opportunities to collaborate with and within
professional organisations.
Serves on committees in state/territory and national
nursing organisations or specialty groups.
Supports professional organisations in political action to
create solutions for professional and health care
concerns.
With legislators


Offers expert opinions on legislative initiatives related to
health care.
Collaborates with other health care providers and
consumers on health care legislation to best serve the
needs of the public.
To fulfil a collaborative role, nurses need to assume accountability
and increased authority in practice areas. Education is integral to
ensuring that the members of each professional group understand
the collaborative nature of their roles, specific contributions and the
importance of working together. Each professional needs to
understand how an integrated delivery system centres on the
person’s health care needs rather than on the particular care given
by one group.
Competencies basic to collaboration
Key elements necessary for collaboration include effective
communication skills, mutual respect, trust and a decision-making
process.
Communication
Collaborating to solve complex problems requires effective
communication skills. Effective communication can occur only if the
involved parties are committed to understanding each other’s
professional roles and appreciating each other as individuals.


Additionally, they must be sensitive to differences in communication
styles. Instead of focusing on distinctions, a group of professionals
needs to centre on their common ground: the individual’s needs.
Mutual respect and trust
Mutual respect occurs when two or more people show or feel honour
or esteem towards one another. Trust occurs when a person is
confident in the actions of another person. Both mutual respect and
trust imply a mutual process and outcome. They must be expressed
both verbally and non-verbally.
Decision making
The decision-making process at the team level involves shared
responsibility for the outcome. To create a solution, the team must
follow each step of the decision-making process, beginning with a
clear definition of the problem. Team decision making must be
directed at the objectives of the specific effort. It requires full
consideration of and respect for diverse viewpoints. Members must
be able to verbalise their perspectives in a non-threatening
environment.
An important aspect of decision making is satisfied when the
interdisciplinary team focuses on the person’s priority needs and
organises interventions accordingly. The discipline best able to
address the person’s needs is given priority in planning and is
responsible for providing its interventions in a timely manner. For


example, a social worker may first direct attention to an individual’s
social needs when these needs interfere with the person’s ability to
respond to therapy. Nurses, by the nature of their holistic practice,
are often able to help the team identify priorities and areas requiring
further attention.
Case study
Nurses take an active role in influencing the direction of
health care. Recognising that there are finite limits to the
amount of money and health care providers available,
desirable outcomes often compete for resources. One PHC
initiative discussed in this chapter was community health
through immunisation. Consider the situation where a nurse
immuniser informs a parent that the next set of
immunisations are due for their child (as per the National
Immunisation Program Schedule) and the parent refuses to
allow the immunisations to be administered.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. In relation to PHC, how might this action affect
community health?
2. Which is more important: the parent’s right to decide
what chemicals should be injected into their child or
‘herd immunity’ for the community?


3.
 Taking into consideration the psychosocial
element of ‘respecting values and beliefs’ within the
Fundamentals of Care Framework, how should the
nurse respond? What should the nurse’s next step be?


Chapter 7 Review


Chapter highlights
Health care costs, access to health care and the quality of health
care are major areas of concern about the current health care
system.
A community is a collection of people who share some attribute
of their lives.
The significant changes to funding arrangements for community
health programs will have an impact on the community health
environment for several years. Community health nurses will
need to be vigilant and creative to ensure that the logistical
effects of implementation will not affect individuals in their care.
Primary health care is an established method of reducing
escalating health spending. Prevention and early detection are
also better for the individual.
Consumers support an increased emphasis on health care
measures that promote wellness.
Approaches are emerging to address community-based care.
These include an integrated health care system, community
initiatives, community coalitions, managed care, case
management and outreach programs using lay health workers.
To practise in community health care systems, nurses need
knowledge and understanding of primary and secondary
preventive strategies, health promotion strategies, collaborative
and interdisciplinary teamwork, determinants of an accessible
and cost-effective health care system, a decision-making
process that involves consumers and information management.


Education in public health policy and strategies to influence and
effect change are essential.
Collaboration between health care providers is key to maintaining
continuity of care as individuals move through the health care
system.
Concept check
1. Which of the following is characteristic of nursing care
provided in community-based health?
1. Individuals are primarily those with identified illnesses.
2. Individuals are individuals in groups according to their
geographical commonalities.
3. Care is paid for by the community as a whole rather
than by individuals.
4. All individuals are case managed.
2. When performing collaborative health care, the nurse must
implement which of the following?
1. Assist in facilitating coordinated care.
2. Rely on the expertise of other health care team
members.
3. Be physically present for the implementation of all
aspects of the care plan.
4. Delegate decision-making authority to each health care
provider.


3. A large disaster in a community resulted in the destruction of
many family homes and many individuals were injured. The
assistance of community health nurses and home health
nurses is needed. The home health nurse is most likely to
perform which of the following?
1. Provide for a safe water supply.
2. Monitor for communicable diseases.
3. Establish communication and support systems.
4. Assess and treat individuals.
Focus on critical thinking
1. How does concerted spending on disease prevention reduce
the national burden of health care costs?
2. How can nurses and midwives directly influence health
promotion at the ‘coal face’?
3. Should individuals have a right to choose whether their
children are immunised or does the concept of ‘herd
immunity’ have a greater right as this decision directly
influences the health of other people in the community?
4. The ‘Green’ movement ‘Helping improve the health of the
earth’ has achieved a significant increase in followers and in
public knowledge and education about the cause. How can
health care professionals learn from the techniques of the
‘Green’ movement to make primary health more appealing?

care for people in regional and remote communities?

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Define home health care.
Compare the characteristics of home health nursing with those of
institutional nursing care.
Describe the types of home health organisations, including

Describe the roles of the home health nurse.
Identify the essential aspects of the home visit.


Discuss the safety and infection-control dimensions associated
with the home care setting.
Identify ways the nurse can recognise and minimise caregiver
role strain.

home care

Historically, Australian home nursing
commenced in Victoria in 1885 (Boulton
Clarke ). Since that time, numerous groups
have developed similar services in the other
states and territories (see Figure 8.1
).
1 Boulton Clarke (2019). Our Future Is in Our History.
Retrieved from <www.boltonclarke.com.au/about-us/our-
history>.
1


Figure 8.1


A timeline representing important landmarks in
the Australian history of home health nursing.
The terminology for the provision of nursing care
in a person’s home is diverse. It can be known
as domiciliary nursing, ambulatory care,
community health nursing, district nursing and
hospice nursing, to name but a few. Irrespective
of its name, community nursing consists
primarily of nurses providing care in a person’s
home. Originally, only basic care was performed;
however, changes, especially in the past few
decades, have led to nursing services in home
settings increasing in frequency, scope and
complexity.
Home care
 today involves a wide range of
health care professionals providing services to
people recovering from acute illness or injury,
those who are disabled, those who have a
chronic condition or those for whom end-of-life
support is required. Nurses are responsible for a
significant majority of this work. Home care
nursing is a specialty and individuals working in
this field must develop a highly advanced skill


set. The individuals requiring care often have
chronic illness which can be confounded by
complex comorbidities. Because of the nature of
their work, the breadth and depth of knowledge
and skill required for this occupation, and the
fact that it is a developing role, home care
nurses have significantly more scope in their
practice and a higher degree of autonomy than
colleagues working in acute care facilities.
In 2016–17, Australia’s health expenditure was
approximately 10% of the gross domestic
product (Australian Institute of Health and
Welfare (AIHW) ). With an ageing population,
this figure continues to increase. Since 1901,
the number of people aged 65 years or older
has increased from 5% of the population in
1927 to 15% in 2017, with projections to 2061
citing 20.7% (Australian Bureau of Statistics
(ABS) ; AIHW ) (see Figure 8.2
). In the past
50 years, the population has doubled, and by
2042, the number of people of aged 85 and
over will double (ABS 2018a). There are over
25.4 million people currently living in Australia.
With this increase in population and the
increasing age of the population, more demands
are being placed on the health dollar. Caring for
individuals in acute care institutions is
2
3
4


expensive, and both state and federal
governments are trying to reduce the number of
inpatients within the hospital system, yet
individuals still require assistance to manage
their health concerns. Therefore, pressures on
home care nursing services are also mounting.
2 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW)
(2018a). Health Expenditure Australia 2016–17. Health and
welfare expenditure series no. 64. Cat. no. HWE 74.
Canberra: AIHW. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
3 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018a). Population
Projections, Australia, 2017 (Base)—2066. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au>.
4 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW)
(2018b). The Health and Welfare of Australia’s Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander Peoples—An Overview 2011.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Figure 8.2


A graph representing the increasing population
trend in Australians 65 years of age and over.

and ABS . Australian Demographic Statistics, Dec 2015. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>. © Commonwealth
of Australia.
5 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2016). 3101.0.
Australian Demographic Statistics, Dec 2015. Retrieved

Other factors have also contributed to rising
health care costs, such as a growing emphasis
on managing chronic illness, reducing stress,
preventing illness and enhancing the quality of
life. In the not-too-distant past, home health
care occurred at the end of the individual’s care
continuum, after discharge from an acute care
facility. Today the trend is changing to the use of
home health care services to avoid
hospitalisation.
Because home health nurses must function
independently in a variety of home settings and
situations, the knowledge and skills required to
be a successful home health nurse have led to
employers preferring to employ nurses with at
least a few years postgraduate experience.
Although there is no credential or endorsement
required to practise as a community nurse in
5


Australia, many tertiary education institutions
offer postgraduate qualifications (e.g. Graduate
Certificate or Graduate Diploma) in community
health nursing. Registered Nurses work as part
of a team that often also includes Enrolled
Nurses and sometimes Assistants in Nursing
(also known as personal care attendants). The
home care nurse’s role includes the
coordination of services, the provision of direct
care, health assessment, consulting, education,
administration and research activities.


Home health nursing
Home health nursing
 includes the nursing services and products
provided to individuals to maintain, restore or promote their physical,
psychological and social wellbeing in their homes. The individuals
and their families are the focus of home health care nursing. This
differs somewhat from public health nursing whose broader focus is
individuals, families and aggregate groups (see Chapter 7
).
Palliative care nursing
 (or hospice nursing), support and care of
the dying person and family, is often considered a subspecialty of
home health nursing because hospice services are frequently
delivered to terminally ill individuals in their residence. See Chapter
44
 for further information about palliative care.
Unique aspects of home
health nursing
Home care nurses must function independently in a variety of
unfamiliar home settings and situations. Because the home is the
family’s territory, power and control issues in delivering nursing care
differ from those in the hospital. For example, entry into a home is
granted, not assumed; the nurse must therefore establish trust and


rapport with the person and family. Due to the limited time for visits
and the possibly lengthy interval between visits, this process does
not always occur as quickly as it might when nursing within an acute
care facility.
Health care that is provided in the home is often given with other
family members present. Families may feel freer to question advice,
ignore directions, do things differently and set their own priorities
and schedules.
Home health nurses have identified significant advantages in caring
for individuals and families in the home. The home setting is
intimate; this intimacy fosters familiarity, sharing, connections and
caring between individuals, families and their nurse. Behaviours are
more natural, cultural beliefs and practices are more visible and
multigenerational interactions tend to be displayed. Nurses often get
to know the person and their family well as they may care for them
over weeks or months.
Home health nurses have also identified issues negatively affecting
care in the home. More than any other care providers, these nurses
have first-hand knowledge and experience about the burden of
caregiving and the role of family dynamics in health care practices.
In the interest of cutting health care costs, policy makers and
medical providers are placing increasingly complex responsibilities
on individuals’ families and significant others. Family caregiving
demands may go on for months or years, placing the caregivers
themselves (many of whom are older adults) at risk of physiological


and psychosocial problems. Additionally, nurses enter homes where
the living conditions and support systems may be inadequate.
Nurses caring for individuals in rural home settings have challenges
different from those in urban or suburban environments. These
include the need for flexibility, as individuals may live great distances
from the nurse and require care in the evening or at night, creativity
and the ability to practise independently as fewer resources
(including other nurses) are available, and the ability to work in an
environment over which there is little nurse control and increased
chances of injury (Terry et al. ). In 2016, a rural area nurse in South
Australia was murdered after being abducted en route to a midnight
call-out in a remote community (Cremin ). This resulted in numerous
nursing organisations around Australia petitioning for the abolition of
single-nurse posts in rural areas. Although this circumstance is an
extreme situation where the safety of a nurse was severely
compromised, it does illustrate an added risk to which community
and home care nurses are potentially exposed. Hypervigilance and
the ability to undertake and respond to risk analysis is critical.
Nurses who require a high degree of certainty, structure and
consistency are less likely to be successful in a rural home health
environment.
6 Terry, D., Le, Q., Nguyen, U. & Hoang, H. (2015). Workplace health and safety issues
among community nurses: A study regarding the impact on providing care to rural
consumers. BMJ Open, 5(e008306), 1–10. Doi: 10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008306.
7 Cremin, G. (2016). Remote Area Nurses Scared for Their Safety as Violence Is ‘Brushed
under the Carpet’. Retrieved from <www.news.com.au>.
6
7


Research note
Safety in a person’s home
D. Terry, Q. Le, U. Nguyen & H. Hoang (2015). Workplace health and safety issues among community
nurses: A study regarding the impact on providing care to rural consumers. BMJ Open, 5(e008306)
1–10. Doi: 10.1136/bmjopen-2015-008306.
This qualitative research of 15 community nurses who worked
in rural community home care settings attempted to
determine the type of workplace health and safety issues
experienced by rural community home care nurses. The
researchers determined that numerous issues existed
including the need to drive long distances between individuals’
homes and their offices, sustained periods of inadequate
communication, risks associated with concerning individual or
carer behaviour, and exposure to poor environmental
conditions in individuals’ homes, such as cigarette smoke,
animals and violence. The researchers also cited issues
surrounding workload, burnout and work-related stress.
Implications Knowledge gained from research such as this
can help individuals, organisations and government bodies to
understand and develop procedures, programs and systems
in order to reduce home health nurses’ occupational risks.
Practice of home health nursing


The home health nurse will practise a variety of roles. Direct hands-
on care for complex health conditions occurring in individuals from
birth to death is becoming common in home settings. Home health
nurses routinely perform physical assessments, change wound
dressings, insert and maintain intravenous access for various
therapies, establish and monitor indwelling urinary catheters, monitor
exercise or nutritional therapies, and, in short, perform many nursing
functions formerly thought of as being confined to acute care
facilities.
Home health nurses serve as health educators. They clarify
misconceptions about the course of the illness, the treatment plan
and medications, and potential interactions with over-the-counter
drugs. They also educate the person and their family on how to
access the health care system appropriately. Because of the
demands of this specialty, the home health nurses work hard to
develop their knowledge and keep abreast of a broad range of
current research. Consultation and liaison with other health care
professionals regarding a person’s care is often led by the home
health nurse. They must have confidence in their knowledge and
ability to function as an advocate.
The Registered Nurse working in home health care will be
responsible for the direction and supervision of many unregulated
health care workers. These workers have only sufficient training and
education to assist them to function in the limited roles for which
they are employed, and they make up the majority of the workforce.
The Registered Nurse needs to possess management and


supervisory skills to facilitate relationships with these workers.
Advanced interpersonal skills such as negotiation, leadership and
role modelling are required to ensure competent functioning of the
team promoting the best outcome for the person.


The home health care system in
Australia
The provision of home health support is heavily funded by the
federal government and supported by state and local government.
Services provided by home health nurses and organisations through
these funding arrangements include:
programs which delay the transition to aged care facilities by
providing support for older adults to stay living in their own home
for longer
respite care which provides support for full-time carers to have a
short time out from the care relationship
after-hospital (transition) care for individuals who have recently
been discharged from hospital and still require assistance with
things such as wound care, medications, personal care and
rehabilitation (Department of Health ).
8 Department of Health (2019). Transition Care Programme. Retrieved from
<https://agedcare.health.gov.au>.
Following changes brought about by the National Health Reform and
2015–16 Budget announcements, significant improvements have
been made to how home care services are delivered to older people
(see Figure 8.3
). A budget of $25.4 billion has been allocated to
aged care expenditure in 2022–23. The principle of the new reform
8


is to enable the health care consumer to determine what care they
require and by whom. The new system is called consumer-directed
care. As in the previous arrangement, there are four levels of care
offered by the Home Care Package
 system:
1. Home Care Level 1—to support people with basic care needs
~ $8750 a year
2. Home Care Level 2—to support people with low-level care
needs ~ $15 250 a year
3. Home Care Level 3—to support people with intermediate care
needs ~ $33 500 a year
4. Home Care Level 4—to support people with high care needs
~ $50 750 a year (Australian Government ).
9 Australian Government (2019a). Home Care Packages. Retrieved from
<www.myagedcare.gov.au>.
Figure 8.3
9


Australian government total budgeted aged care expenditure 2017–
18.
Source: Aged Care Financing Authority
. 2019 ACFA Annual Report (Seventh report on the Funding and
Financing of the Aged Care Sector), Chart 2.1, p. 21. Retrieved from
<https://agedcare.health.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/07_2019/2019_acfa_annual_report_on_funding_a
nd_financing_of_the_aged_care_sector.pdf>.
10 Aged Care Financing Authority (2019). 2019 ACFA Annual Report (Seventh report on the
Funding and Financing of the Aged Care Sector). Retrieved from
<https://agedcare.health.gov.au>.
10


The Home Care Packages system attempts to drive three main
areas of change in aged care funding arrangements. These include:
1. The funding will follow the eligible consumer (instead of being
assigned to individuals’ home health care providers). This
attempts to improve the choice and portability of services
sought.
2. The system aims to facilitate a consistent and national
approach to home care access.
3. The system aims to streamline the process for health care
providers to be approved as a result of the amendments to
the Aged Care Act 1997 and Aged Care (Transitional
Provisions) Act 1997 (Australian Government 2019a).
The goal was to remove complicating bureaucratic limitations
preventing individuals from seeking the providers or services of their
choice to streamline the process. However, the transition was not
without issues as despite government promises that individuals
would be no worse off, some participants found that their current
level of funding did not cover the same services offered by the
providers in the new system. They were forced to find alternatives to
fund the shortfall themselves or cope with reduced home care
support. Conversely, other individuals who were unable to access
sufficient care services under previous systems have fortunately had
either the type and/or volume of care increased.
Support at home in the form of a Home Care Package is not entirely
free. It is expected that a consumer will contribute to the cost of


their own care, if they are so placed to do so. The service provider is
permitted to charge a daily fee of up to 17.5% of the single basic
age pension or, if the individual has an income, an income-tested
care fee may be calculated. However, this calculation does not take
into account the value of the person’s home or other assets. If
individuals are unable to pay, there is a financial hardship provision
permitting the fees to be reduced or waived (Australian
Government
).
11 Australian Government (2019b). Aged Care Home Costs and Fees. Retrieved from
<www.myagedcare.gov.au>.
Two other changes developed to significantly improve community
care and home support are the National Disability Insurance
Scheme (NDIS) and the National Injury Insurance Scheme (NIIS).
Currently, the NDIS is rolling out nationally; however, at this stage,
the NIIS is being instituted only in Queensland. See Table 8.1
 for
more details of the schemes.
Table 8.1 National disability insurance scheme and national
injury insurance scheme comparisons
