scheme/faqs/>.
There are several not-for-profit organisations functioning to assist
individuals to stay in their own home. These important organisations
and their staff, who are often volunteers, provide selfless and
significant support to individuals and families in order to assist
11


people to stay in their own home. Various government bodies are
responsible for the provision and funding of home care. These
organisations differ between states and may even change names
and structure depending on the state and national political party in
power. Table 8.2
 lists some organisations responsible for
implementation and funding of home and community care services.
Table 8.2 Federal and state organisations responsible for
funding home care
Some individuals may have extremely complicated needs. These
needs may include the use of complex equipment. An assessment
process will identify the individual’s needs, permitting a coordinated
approach between medical equipment companies, home nursing
organisations, not-for-profit community organisations and other
organisations to provide the individual with the services and
equipment to enable them to stay in their home. The expenses
related to these services differ depending on the financial means,
the complexity of care required and the services available in the
area.
Referral process
The referral process differs depending on the needs and the
services to be provided. Generally speaking, a person is referred to
community care organisations through their doctor, a medical officer
from the hospital of discharge, a discharge care planner or an


assessment team member. Families often initiate the process by
approaching one of these referral sources or by directly contacting a
home health organisation in order to make inquiries. With the new
system, processes start when contact is made through the My Aged
Care contact centre where a screening process undertaken by the
operator will determine if the person requires a basic home support
assessment by a Regional Assessment Service (RAS) or a
comprehensive assessment by a member of an Aged Care
Assessment Team (ACAT) (Aged Care Guide ).
12 Aged Care Guide (2019). Assessing Your Needs and Eligibility. Retrieved from
<www.agedcareguide.com.au>.
After the evaluation visit (often undertaken by a nurse), a decision
regarding what level of care the individual requires is determined. In
keeping with the concept of consumer-directed care, the person can
be assisted to find a home health provider and tailor a range of
cares and services appropriate for the individual’s requirements.
Home health organisations
Home health organisations offer coordinated professional, skilled
and paraprofessional services. Because a person often requires the
services of several professionals, case management is essential.
This responsibility generally rests with the Registered Nurse.
Depending on the organisation, additional providers may include
Nurse Practitioners, practical nurses, nursing assistants, personal
12


care assistants, occupational therapists, speech therapists, social
workers, dietitians and a pastoral care minister or chaplain. In
addition, it is not unusual for home health organisations to offer the
services of specialised nurses such as enterostomal nurses,
continence nurses or diabetes educators. The care plan
implemented by the home health agency may require services once
or twice a day, up to 7 days a week. Although the time of care
depends on the person’s needs, another influencing factor is the
service package.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Partnering with Consumers
‘Leaders of a health service organisation develop, implement
and maintain systems to partner with consumers.’ (Australian
Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC)
, p. 14)
13 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health
Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved by
encouraging and supporting health care
consumers to actively participate in the planning
of their own care. This can be implemented by
embracing governance structures that promote
13


consumer-directed care and by monitoring its
progress and adjusting the approach.
Experience shows us that there are significant
benefits to be gained by ensuring care is person
centred and consumer driven. Collaborative
care assists individuals to embrace activities to
promote health, adhere to treatment regimens
and, ultimately, experience more positive health
outcomes. Although this concept is a substantial
shift away from historical health care, home
care is an area where collaborative consumer-
driven care is heavily supported by the health
reform process.
There are several different types of home health organisations,
including the following:
Official or public organisations are operated by state or local
governments and financed primarily by tax funds.
Voluntary or private not-for-profit organisations are supported by
donations, endowments or charities.
Private, proprietary organisations are for-profit organisations and
are governed by either individual owners or national corporations.
Some of these organisations participate in co-contribution; others
rely on government funding sources.


Institution-based organisations operate under a parent
organisation, such as a hospital, funded by the same sources as
the parent.
Regardless of the type of organisation, all home health organisations
must meet specific standards for licensing, certification and
accreditation.
Medical equipment supply
companies
Medical equipment supply companies provide health care equipment
for the person at home. The types of equipment can range from
hospital beds and bedside commodes to ventilators and apnoea
monitors. Most states have a medical aids subsidy scheme to assist
with the costs of hire or purchase of medical equipment and
consumables. Home health nurses should be fully aware of the
equipment supply and funding options necessary to support people
requiring home health services.


Roles of the home health nurse
Historically, nurses who provided direct services in the home were
strong generalists who focused on long-term preventive, educational
and rehabilitative outcomes. Today many home health nurses
possess high-technology skills that were formerly used only in acute
care settings. For example, nurses provide a variety of intravenous
therapies in the home setting and monitor individuals who are
dependent on technologically complex medical equipment, such as
ventilators and central venous lines. These nurses collaborate with
medical officers and other health care professionals in providing
care. They play a key role in facilitating an effective plan of care as
individuals move between hospitals, home, school, work and other
care settings such as clinics or long-term care.
Major roles of the home health nurse are those of advocate,
caregiver (provider of direct care), educator and care coordinator.
Advocate
Advocacy begins on the first visit. The nurse explores and supports
the person’s choices in health care; all viable options are considered.
Advocacy includes having discussions about the person’s rights,
advanced health care directives, living wills and enduring power of


attorney for health care. It also usually involves assistance to access
community resources, make informed decisions, recognise and cope
with necessary changes in lifestyle and understand ways to
effectively use the complex medical system. Advocacy can be a
particular challenge when family members’ or other caregivers’ views
differ from those of the individual. In the event of conflict, the nurse,
being the person’s primary advocate, ensures that the individual’s
rights and desires are upheld.
Caregiver
The home health nurse’s major role as caregiver is to assess and
determine the person’s actual and potential health problems, plan
care and evaluate the person’s outcomes. Direct personal care
activities such as bathing, changing linens, feeding and light
housekeeping activities to maintain a clean and safe home
environment are usually provided by a family member or a personal
care assistant arranged by the nurse. The home health nurse,
however, will provide direct care for specific procedures and
treatments such as enterostomal care, wound care, intravenous
therapy and so on according to organisation policies and practices.
Much of the home health nurse’s time is spent teaching others to
provide the required care.
Educator


The educator role of the home health nurse focuses on teaching
illness care, the prevention of problems and the promotion of optimal
wellness or wellbeing. A common example is that of guiding the
health and development of newborns. Some people have acute
illnesses that will resolve while others have chronic conditions that
will last the lifetime. Most individuals visited by a home health care
nurse experience chronic health care issues. The nurse’s health
teaching methods will vary based on the need of these individuals.
The nurse may also be involved in teaching others with whom the
person interacts, such as the schoolteachers of special-needs
children. Education is ongoing and can be considered the crux of
home care practice; its goal is to help individuals learn to manage as
independently as possible. All home health nurses need to
understand the concepts of teaching and learning and strategies
that facilitate learning. (See Chapter 28
 for detailed information.)
Care coordinator
The home health nurse coordinates the activities of all other home
health team members involved in the individual’s treatment plan.
Coordination can occur individually, in person or by telephone, with a
specific team member such as the occupational therapist, dietitian or
physiotherapist, or during a team conference where each team
member provides information about the person’s health status. The
nurse is the main contact to report any changes in the person’s
condition and to bring about a revision in the plan of care as needed.


Documentation of care coordination is a legal requirement and must
be recorded on the person’s medical record.


Perspectives of home care
Individuals requiring home care include a diverse population that
encompasses all ages, a variety of health problems and families of
different structures and cultural backgrounds. A home care nurse
may provide care for people with a wide range of health problems
that include disabilities, perinatal problems, mental illnesses and
acute and chronic illnesses. The nurse should not assume that the
person understands the various personnel and their roles in
providing home health care. Individuals and their carers can be very
reliant on the services provided by home care personnel.
Although the person receiving care is considered the centre of home
care needs, the person’s family may have needs as well as they are
often associated with caregiving and have a major impact on the
person’s wellness status. The home health nurse will encounter
many different family structures ranging from single families to
extended families, and dwellings that house multiple families. In the
home setting, family members may include not only persons related
by birth and marriage but also friends, other significant individuals
and animals.
Various cultural influences also affect a person’s health care beliefs
and practices. The home health nurse needs to be culturally
sensitive; that is, to become aware of the person’s culture and
develop a nursing care plan accordingly. See Chapter 19
 for


detailed information about making cultural assessments and
providing culturally competent care.


Selected dimensions of home
health nursing
Selected dimensions of home health care include assessing the
home for safety features, infection control and caregiver support.
Safety considerations
Hazards in the home are major causes of falls, fire, poisoning and
other accidents, such as those caused by improper use of
household equipment (e.g. tools and cooking utensils). The appraisal
of such hazards and suggestions for remedies is an essential
nursing function. See the ‘Home care considerations
’ box for a
home hazard appraisal and Chapter 33
 for a discussion of
potential hazards and preventive actions for individuals of all ages.
Obviously, home health nurses cannot expect to change a family’s
living space and lifestyle. However, they can express their concern
and react appropriately when a situation suggests that an injury is
imminent. Nurses must document information they provide and the
family’s response to instruction, and make ongoing assessments
about the family’s use of safety precautions.


Other aspects of a person’s safety relate to emergency situations.
The home health nurse can assist the person and caregivers as
follows:
Post a list of all emergency telephone numbers (ambulance, fire,
police, MedicAlert  and home care nursing contacts) at each
telephone.
Post a list of all the person’s medications and potential side
effects in a central location, such as on the refrigerator.
Help the person and family apply for a MedicAlert  system such
as a bracelet or necklace (see Figure 8.4
). Information on the
MedicAlert  system can be obtained by contacting the Australia
MedicAlert  Foundation.
Figure 8.4
®
®
®
®


MedicAlert  systems.
Source: © Australia MedicAlert  Foundation. MedicAlert  is a registered trademark and service mark.
Recommend and/or assist with the acquisition of an emergency
response system. These systems provide a small device with a
help button that attaches to a wrist or neck chain. The home
base station can require the person to send a signal daily that
indicates that they are okay. If the signal is not sent or if the
portable device is activated, the system automatically calls the
person and then dials a previously established list of emergency
contacts. This system is particularly useful for people who are
alone because if they should fall, for instance, and be unable to
reach a telephone, they might be left helpless for an extended
period of time.
Home care considerations
Home hazard appraisal for adults
The environment
Walkways and stairways (inside and outside):
note uneven sidewalks or paths, broken or loose
steps, absence of handrails or placement on only
one side of stairways, insecure handrails,
®
®
®


congested hallways or other traffic areas, and
adequacy of lighting at night.
Floors: note uneven and highly polished or slippery
floors and any unanchored rugs and mats.
Furniture: note hazardous placement of furniture
with sharp corners. Note chairs or stools that are
too low to get into and out of or that provide
inadequate support.
Bathroom(s): note presence of grab bars around
tubs and toilets, non-slip surfaces in baths and
showers, hand-held showerhead, adequacy of night
lighting, need for a raised toilet seat or bath chair in
tub or shower, ease of access to shelves and water
temperature regulated at a maximum of 50°C.
Kitchen: note inaccessible storage areas and
hazardous furniture or slippery surfaces.
Bedrooms: note adequacy of lighting, in particular
the availability of night lights and accessibility of
light switches; ease of access to commode, urinal
or bedpan; and need for a hospital bed or bed rails.
Electrical: note unanchored or frayed electrical
cords and outlets that are overloaded or near
water.
Fire protection: note presence or absence of
smoke detectors, fire extinguisher and fire escape
plan; and improper storage of combustibles (e.g.
petrol or kerosene) or corrosives (e.g. rust
remover).


Toxic substances: note improperly labelled
cleaning solutions.
Communication devices: note presence of
method to call for help, such as a telephone or
intercom in the bedroom and elsewhere (e.g.
kitchen), and access to emergency telephone
numbers.
Medications: note medications kept beyond date
of expiration, adequacy of lighting for medication
cabinet or storage, and method of disposal of sharp
objects such as needles used for injections.


Nurse safety
Some less desirable living locations pose additional personal safety
concerns for the nurse. In some countries, home health
organisations have contracts with security firms to escort nurses
needing to see individuals in potentially unsafe neighbourhoods;
however, this is not common in Australia. The nurse should avoid
taking any personal belongings during these visits and have a pre-
established mechanism to signal for help. Home health organisations
should provide training for nurses in ways to decrease personal risk.
Although little formal research has been published regarding
violence to home care nurses, the mainstream media periodically
reports various incidences where nurses have been attacked. An
article published in NT News on 4 May 2016 entitled ‘Wadeye health
clinic in danger of closing after second nurse attacked in a week’
reports that health staff could be removed from the community
following two separate, unrelated assaults on nursing staff in one
week. One of the attacks resulted in a home health nurse who was
undertaking a house call allegedly being punched and kicked
repeatedly while on the ground (Poulsen ).
14 Poulsen, J. (2016). Wadeye health clinic in danger of closing after second nurse attacked
in a week. NT News. Retrieved from <www.ntnews.com.au>.
Violence against health care workers is rising. Between 36% and
65% of nurses have been physically assaulted (Pandey, Bhandari &
14


Dangal ; Rodwell & Demir
) by individuals, residents or family
members. The Registered Nurse is responsible for assessing the
environment for the safety of the other patients and health workers
who may assist in care.
15 Pandey, M., Bhandari, T. & Dangal, G. (2018). Workplace violence and its associated
factors among nurses. Journal of Nepal Health Research Council, 15(3), 235–241.
16 Rodwell, J. & Demir, D. (2014). Addressing workplace violence among nurses who care
for the elderly. Journal of Nursing Administration, 44(3), 152–157. Doi:
10.1097/NNA.0000000000000043.
Infection control
The goal of infection control in the home is to protect individuals,
caregivers and the general community from the transmission of
disease. This is particularly important for people who are
immunocompromised, who have infectious or communicable
diseases or who have draining wounds, drainage tubes or other
invasive access devices. The nurse’s major role in infection control is
health teaching. Individuals and caregivers need to learn about
effective hand washing, use of gloves, handling of linens, disposal of
wastes and soiled dressings, and the practice of infection control
(standard precautions). Infection control can present a challenge to
the home health nurse, especially if the home care facilities are not
conducive to basic aseptic requirements such as the availability of
running water for hand washing.
15
16


An important aspect of infection control involves handling the home
health nurse’s equipment and supplies. Supplies may include
materials for hand cleansing; assessment equipment such as
stethoscope, sphygmomanometer, thermometer and tape measure;
infection-control items such as gowns, eye protection, masks, gloves
and blood spill kit; and antimicrobial cleaning agents. Yet the
transport of any equipment between homes brings with it infection
control issues too. The home health nurse must be cognisant of the
impact their practice will have on infection control.
Although some modifications in technique may be indicated in the
home setting, such as the use of clean rather than sterile technique
in caring for chronic wounds, all the basic principles still apply.
Nurses need to follow organisation protocol about aseptic practice in
the home. Evidence-based practice is important as beneficial
research and understanding about methods to better improve
infection control are occurring all the time. The National Health and
Medical Research Council (NHMRC ) produced a 68-page
pocketbook document outlining the guidelines for the prevention and
control of infection in residential and community aged care. It is a
mini guide with important content and concepts taken from an older
283-page document written in 2010, which contains guidelines for
the prevention and control of infections within a health care facility.
The document was updated in 2019 (NHMRC ). These documents
should be a starting point for all community care nurses.
17 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) (2014). Prevention and Control
of Infection in Residential and Community Aged Care. Retrieved from
<https://agedcare.health.gov.au>.
17
18


18 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) (2019). Australian Guidelines for
the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare. Retrieved from <www.nhmrc.gov.au>.
Caregiver support
Caregiving may be directed to individuals of any age and varies from
short term to long term according to the physical or mental
disabilities of the care receivers. For example, some children who
have permanent disabilities, and adults who experience progressive
deterioration such as those with Alzheimer’s disease or multiple
sclerosis, require care on a permanent basis. Others who are
recovering from a surgical procedure require care only on a
temporary basis. Most caregivers have close relationships with the
care receiver; that is, a spouse/partner, parent, child, friend or other
significant relationship. Many caregiving relationships, therefore,
represent changes from the caring and caregiving that is intrinsic to
all close relationships to becoming an extraordinary and unequal
burden for the caregiver. Caregivers may experience caregiver role
strain
 when they have physical, emotional, social and financial
burdens that can seriously jeopardise their own health and wellbeing.
This situation may lead to considerable risk to the person because
frustration, stress and lack of coping skills by the carer can lead to
aggression, violence and an unsafe environment for the person or
home health nurse.


Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Preventing and Controlling
Healthcare-Associated Infection
The intention of this standard is to ‘reduce the risk of patients
acquiring preventable healthcare-associated infections,
effectively manage infections if they occur, and limit the
development of antimicrobial resistance through prudent use
of antimicrobials as part of antimicrobial stewardship’
(ACSQHC 2017, p. 22).
Implementing this standard is achieved by
employing strategies to control the spread of
infection, managing individuals who currently
have infections or are colonised with pathogens,
implementing an antimicrobial stewardship
program, ensuring appropriate cleaning,
disinfection and sterilisation processes are
occurring and promoting communication to
educate consumers and carers.
Because of rapidly developing antimicrobial
resistance, we are quickly heading towards a
time when we may have no effective antibiotics
left to treat even basic infections. If we descend
to a post-antibiotic era, it will not be fanciful to
imagine significant loss of life from infections we
once were able to control easily. This situation
would be a travesty and would mark a


considerable backwards step in our ability to
care for individuals. Even in a home care
setting, it is critical that we understand the
gravity of this problem and embrace policy,
methods and systems that will reduce the
spread of healthcare-associated infections.
The home health nurse needs to recognise signs of caregiver role
strain and suggest ways to minimise or alleviate this problem. Signs
of caregiver overload include the following:
difficulty performing routine tasks for the person in their care
reports of declining physical energy and insufficient time for
caregiving
concern that caregiving responsibilities interfere with other roles
such as those of parent, spouse, worker, friend
anxiety about their ability to meet the person’s future care needs
feelings of anger and depression
dramatic change in the home environment’s appearance.
The nurse needs to encourage caregivers to express their feelings
and at the same time convey understanding about the difficulties
associated with caregiving and acknowledge the caregivers’
competence. The nurse can obtain a realistic appraisal of the
situation by asking a caregiver to describe a typical day and daily or
weekly leisure and social activities. It is also helpful to identify


activities for which assistance is desired. These activities may
include activities of daily living, such as hygiene, mobility, feeding or
treatments, house cleaning, laundry, shopping, house repairs,
gardening, transportation, doctor’s or hairdresser’s appointments or
respite care.
Activities that are commonly completed by nurses and unlicensed
assistant personnel, such as changing an occupied bed and
transferring a person from bed to chair, may be overwhelming to a
caregiver who has not performed them before. Demonstrating them
in the home and allowing caregivers to perform them with the
nurse’s supervision increases their confidence and increases the
likelihood of caregivers asking for assistance in other situations.
Arranging the provision of appropriate transfer equipment can also
reduce the caregiver’s burden.
When activities for which assistance is required are identified, the
nurse and caregiver need to identify possible sources of help. Both
volunteer and organisation sources need to be explored. Volunteer
sources of help may include family members (cousins, siblings),
neighbours, friends, church associates or caregiver support groups
in the community. Other sources include, for example, a home
health aide for light housekeeping and grocery shopping, Meals on
Wheels, day care, transportation and counselling and social
services. Families with a chronically ill member may benefit from
weekend respite—a program some hospitals provide in which the
person is admitted to a skilled unit for observation and care,


enabling the caregiver to have a break from ongoing health care
needs.
Caregivers need to be reminded of the importance of caring for
themselves by getting adequate rest, eating nutritious meals, asking
for help, delegating household chores and making time for leisure
activities or simply some time alone. Family members other than the
caregiver may also need instruction in ways to support the caregiver.
The nurse may discuss the importance to the caregiver of regular
phone calls, cards, letters and visits; offer encouragement to take
day trips or a holiday; listen without giving advice; and acknowledge
the burden of caregiving and the need to feel appreciated.
A particular challenge exists when the nurse is in a position to be a
caregiver to a family member. Although the nurse’s clinical expertise
and familiarity with the individual and setting can be especially
useful, negotiating the professional distancing that is sometimes
needed when providing care to individuals can be difficult with family.
The nurse may feel obligated to provide care, even when this is over
and above regular employment responsibilities. The nurse must
have the opportunity to step back and experience the role and
emotions of being a family member—not only those of being a
nurse.
Research note


Nurses can assist ‘lay carers’ to safely manage
subcutaneous injections for breakthrough pain
management for home-based palliative care patients.
S. Healy, F. Israel, M. Charles & L. Reymond
. Laycarers can confidently prepare and administer
subcutaneous injections for palliative care patients at home: A randomized controlled trial. Palliative
Medicine, 32(7), 1208–1215. Doi: 10.1177/0269216318773878.
19 Healy, S., Israel, F., Charles, M. & Reymond, L. (2018). Laycarers can confidently prepare and
administer subcutaneous injections for palliative care patients at home: A randomized controlled trial.
Palliative Medicine, 32(7), 1208–1215. Doi: 10.1177/0269216318773878.
Individuals receiving home palliative care support services
often require the administration of subcutaneous medications
to provide adequate pain relief for some time during their
end-of-life experience. Logistical and financial barriers may
often reduce the availability of sufficient nursing support for
these people. However, if relatives or partners are educated
to provide this support, their loved one has the opportunity to
experience optimal symptom control.
The researchers surveyed 93 carers from 24 community
services who were taught how to safely administer and
manage breakthrough subcutaneous injections for home-
based palliative care patients following participation in a
structured Registered-Nurse-delivered education session or
package. The lay carers, who were spouses, partners or
daughters of individuals receiving palliative care support
services, identified that the package was useful to assist
them to feel confident in undertaking the task. The research
was randomised into three intervention arms depending on
19


whether the carer, nurse or pharmacist prepared the injection
for later administration by the carer. There was no statistical
difference detected in the confidence of the carer between
the three intervention arms of the study.
Implications With increasing strain on the health care dollar,
nurses may be able to use their education skills to assist
loved ones to undertake cares traditionally reserved for
health care professionals. This will not only reduce financial
burdens, but may also result in individuals in a home-care
palliative environment receiving safe, timely pain control.


The practice of nursing in
the home
The home health nurse assesses the health care demands of the
person requiring care, their family, and the home and community
environment. This process actually begins when the nurse contacts
the person for the initial home visit and reviews documents received
from the referral organisation. The goal of the initial visit is to obtain
a comprehensive clinical picture of the person’s needs.
Most organisations have a kit that includes forms for consent to
treatment; physical, psychosocial and spiritual assessment;
medications; pain assessment; family data; a charter of rights; care
plan; and daily visit notes. During the initial home visit, the home
health nurse obtains a health history (see Figure 8.5
), examines
the person, observes the relationship of the person requiring care
and their caregiver, and assesses the home and community
environment. Parameters of assessment of the home environment
include the person’s mobility and ability to perform self-care, the
cleanliness of the environment, availability of caregiver support,
safety, food preparation, financial support and the emotional status
of the person and their caregiver.
Figure 8.5


Interviewing a person for a home care assessment.
Source: Monkey Business Images, Shutterstock.
Following this initial examination, the nurse determines whether
further consultations and support personnel are needed. Some
questions that a home health nurse may consider are: ‘Would the
person benefit from a dietary consultation or Meals on Wheels?’, ‘Is
a home health aide needed to assist with activities of daily living or
domestic tasks?’, ‘Is a social worker needed to help with financial
resources or future care needs such as placement in a nursing
home?’, ‘What additional supplies does the person need?’.
Before completing the initial interview, the nurse also discusses what
the individual and family can expect from home care, what other
health care providers may be needed to help the person achieve
independence and the frequency of home visits.
Establishing health issues
As in other care environments, the nurse identifies both actual and
potential problems. One of the most common examples of health
issues that nurses address in home care settings is the person’s
lack of knowledge related to their own health conditions and self-
care.


Planning and delivering care
The nurse needs to encourage and permit individuals to make their
own health management decisions. Alternatives may need to be
suggested for some decisions if the nurse identifies potential harm
from a chosen course of action.
Strategies to meet goals generally include teaching the person and
their family techniques of care and identifying appropriate resources
to assist the person and their family in maintaining self-sufficiency.
To implement the plan, the home health nurse performs nursing
interventions, including teaching; coordinates and uses referrals and
resources; provides and monitors all levels of technical care;
collaborates with other disciplines and providers; identifies clinical
problems and solutions from research and other health literature;
supervises ancillary personnel; and advocates for the person’s right
to self-determination. Technical skills commonly performed by home
health nurses include blood pressure measurement; body fluid
collection (blood, urine, stool, sputum); wound care; respiratory
care; and all types of intravenous therapy, enteral nutrition, urinary
catheterisation, enterostomal care and renal dialysis (see Figure
8.6
).
Figure 8.6


The nurse monitors the person’s response to treatments and
therapy.
Source: iofoto. Shutterstock.
A large part of the nurse’s role involves teaching the person
requiring care and their caregiver the necessary skills for self-care—
for example, administering insulin injections, measuring blood
glucose and administering medications. Medication instruction about
dosage, frequency of administration and possible side effects is of
particular concern for many people. (See Chapter 36
 for more
information.) Individuals who are receiving high-technology
interventions are often anxious about their ability to manage such
sophisticated equipment. The home health nurse is challenged to
alleviate the person’s fears and to provide thorough instruction,
demonstration and periodic evaluation of the person requiring care
and their family’s performance of such skills.
Although all situations will require some education, some disease
processes, disabilities or even health deterioration from ageing will
require the home health nurse to focus on reducing strain and
burden by instituting plans to assist the provision of care. Continued
assessment is required with each visit to ensure that the needs,
situation and health status are still being satisfied by the planned
care.
Even though the person and their family may become independent
in self-care skills, the home health nurse still has the ultimate
responsibility to ensure the person is receiving the prescribed


therapy at the appropriate timed intervals. Ongoing communication
with the medical officer about the person’s progress is critical, and
the nurse must make ongoing assessments to ensure that all
aspects of the care are being followed.
On subsequent home visits, the nurse observes the same
parameters assessed on the initial home visit and relates findings to
the expected outcomes or goals (see Figure 8.7
). The nurse can
also teach caregivers parameters of evaluation so that they can
obtain professional intervention if needed. Documentation of care
given and the person’s progress towards goal achievement at each
visit is essential. Notes must also reflect plans for subsequent visits
and when the person may be sufficiently prepared for self-care and
discharge from the facility or program.
Figure 8.7


Determining the success of a care plan includes comparing
assessment findings with previous values. Weighing this tube-fed
baby provides critical data about her progress.
Source: Travis Manley/123RF.


The future of home health care
What is the future for home health care? More studies are needed
to determine the practicality, safety, effectiveness, cost and
satisfaction with home care—especially new models of ‘hospital-at-
home’ care. Trends in the home health care industry include:
ethics committees to handle ethical issues that arise in the home.
These committees may be necessary for organisations to receive
accreditation
nurse pain specialists to assess and manage pain in the home,
thus avoiding costly hospitalisations and procedures
electronic home visits—telemedicine. A computerised system
can obtain information, such as blood pressure readings, allowing
care coordinators to review a person’s progress from off-site.
Lifespan considerations
Home care
Children


Ideally, all children with disabilities would live in a secure,
‘permanent’ family environment. Such an environment
supports family strengths, connects families to their
community and fosters ongoing, secure relationships. At
times, children with disabilities may need to be placed in
adoptive or medical foster homes. Home health nurses can
strengthen family functioning by:
providing information, advice and instruction on the care
of the  child
identifying natural support systems (e.g. extended family,
neighbours, friends)
helping families find community resources to meet their
needs (e.g. respite care, technical and equipment
services)
assisting families with alternative placement options as
needed (e.g. medical foster care)
advocating for families with other health care providers
and policy makers.
Older adults
Individuals who have been hospitalised are often discharged
after short stays and may still be acutely ill. This becomes a
challenge for home health nurses in planning and
implementing care. Special areas of concern for older adults
in this situation include the following:


Healing time is slower due to changes that normally occur
in ageing, such as impaired circulation and alteration in
immune response.
Changes in medications or lingering traces of anaesthesia
may alter cognitive status, even though it is usually
temporary.
Weakness and fatigue create safety issues, such as risk
for falling.
Chronic diseases already present may have been
complicated by other conditions acquired while
hospitalised.
Assessment should be initiated while the person is in the
hospital to determine the need for assistive devices or
environmental changes when the person returns home.
Some examples of these devices are walkers, raised toilet
seats, safety bars in the bathroom and better lighting.
Good planning eases the transition to home care for the
individual and caregiver.
In the future, although the number of older adults will
increase, fewer family caregivers may be available.
Unfortunately, fewer family members are willing or able to
assist in the care of their relative. However, whenever it is
possible, older adults could receive care from family
members. Where achievable, nurses should facilitate and
encourage this option.


Indigenous health considerations
Home care
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
peoples
It is well established that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
peoples have less access to health care in Australia. In part,
this disparity is related to distance from services, availability
of health care professionals and the services available within
the community. In 2019, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
nurses or midwives totalled 0.97% of the total number of
nurses or midwives in Australia. Education and training of
Indigenous individuals to work in health and community
services is also a factor. Students from Indigenous
backgrounds totalled 1.3% of the population of students
completing any degree course in 2018 (Department of
Education ).
20 Department of Education (2019). Higher Education Student Enrolment: 2018 First
Half Year Student Summary. Retrieved from <https://docs.education.gov.au>.
Home care nurses face challenges in every environment. The
AIHW reports that Indigenous people in remote areas are
twice as likely as Indigenous people in non-remote areas to
20


consult an Indigenous health care worker or nurse (AIHW
).
It is not necessary that home care nurses are Indigenous;
however, it is likely that in remote communities they will be.
21 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2015). The Health and Welfare
of Australia’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples: 2015. Retrieved from
<www.aihw.gov.au>.
Home health nurses need to understand the special needs
that accompany the health care management of Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander Australians. Although Indigenous
Australians are estimated to account for only 3.3% of the
Australian population (ABS ), home health nurses will
undoubtedly meet and facilitate Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander peoples’ care needs. More research, education and
publications to facilitate understanding the culture, language
and special needs of this community are warranted.
22 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018b). Estimates of Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander Australians. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Case study
Mr Madden is a 67-year-old male with a 20-year history of
hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He has recently
undergone amputation of three toes due to poor circulation.
21
22


Because he is progressing well and his diabetes is under
control, he is being discharged from the acute care setting to
his home. He has been referred to the community health
nursing organisation, which will assign a nurse to change his
foot dressings, administer IV antibiotics and monitor his blood
glucose levels.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. Compare and contrast the community nurse’s role to
that of the acute care nurse’s role.
2. What rights does Mr Madden have when being cared
for at home that may not be afforded him while in a
health care facility?
3. What factors could negatively affect the care of Mr
Madden in his own home?
4. Speculate about personal benefits derived by people
being cared for at home rather than in a hospital or
other institution.
5.
 Speculate about financial savings derived by
people being cared for at home rather than in a
hospital or other institution.


Chapter 8 Review


Chapter highlights
Home health care is an alternative to acute and subacute health
care facilities. The trend has changed from using home health
care after hospitalisation to using it to avoid hospitalisation.
Palliative nursing, often considered a subspecialty of home
nursing, supports terminally ill individuals and their families during
the last stages of life and bereavement.
Home health organisations offer skilled professional and
paraprofessional services. Because individuals often require the
services of several professionals simultaneously, case
coordination is essential.
There are several types of home health organisations: official or
public organisations, voluntary or private not-for-profit
organisations, private organisations and institution-based
organisations. All home health organisations must meet specific
standards for licensing, certification and accreditation.
Although significant health reforms are occurring in Australia,
home and community care programs can provide assistance but
may require co-contribution from the person, depending on their
financial status. However, no person will be refused care for
reasons of inability to pay.
Referrals for home health services may be made by the person’s
doctor, a discharging medical officer, a discharge planner or an
assessment team member.
Major roles of the home health nurse are those of advocate,
caregiver, educator and care coordinator.


The home health nurse assesses the care needs of individuals in
their home; plans, implements and supervises that care; teaches
the person requiring care and their family self-care techniques;
and mobilises the resources of hospitals, doctors and community
organisations in meeting the needs of the person and their
families.
Home care individuals include a diverse population that
encompasses all ages, a variety of health problems and families
of different structures and cultural backgrounds. The home
health nurse needs to be culturally sensitive; that is, become
aware of the individual’s culture and form a nursing care plan that
incorporates that culture.
Important dimensions of home health nursing include the home
visit in which the nurse assesses the person and they make
plans for care, the safety of both the individual and the nurse,
infection control and caregiver support.
Concept check
1. Care in the home is an alternative to hospital placement.
Which of the following is one major difference associated with
in-home care?
1. Does not focus on curative and life-saving approaches.
2. Is less able to manage complex symptoms.
3. Facilitates extensive involvement of significant
others/family.


4. Permits use of pain medication regimens not allowed in
the hospital.
2. After the nurse instructed an individual about the rationale for
sitting with feet elevated to enhance venous return, the
person refused to perform the activity. Which statement by
the nurse would be most useful?
1. ‘If you won’t cooperate, I can’t help you.’
2. ‘Tell me the reasons you won’t put your feet up.’
3. ‘It is essential that you do this.’
4. ‘I’ll notify your doctor that you are unable to keep your
feet up.’
3. A home health nurse is providing care for a person who is
hemiplegic and whose spouse provides most of the care.
Which of the following may be a sign of caregiver role strain?
1. The caregiver loses weight and has insomnia.
2. The caregiver asks other family and friends for help.
3. The caregiver asks the nurse what other ways they
can help the person.
4. The caregiver seems sad whenever the person’s
prognosis is discussed.
Focus on critical thinking
1. How does a home care nurse’s day differ from a nurse in an

2. How will the National Health Reform impact on home and

Nursing practice in Australia is guided by the
professional codes and guidelines approved by
the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia
(NMBA) . The Registered Nurse Standards for
Practice are used in conjunction with other
NMBA standards, codes and guidelines to
ensure that nursing practice is safe and
1


coordinated. (NMBA 2016). There are
professional standards for Registered Nurses,
Nurse Practitioners, Enrolled Nurses and
midwives (NMBA 2016). All nursing practice at
any level is subject to the same guidelines and
professional standards. This chapter discusses
how these guidelines can provide guidance to
nurses working in regional and remote nursing
in Australia.
1 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016).
Registered Nurse Standards for Practice. Retrieved from
<www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.


Overview
It is important to clarify the term ‘regional and remote nursing’, which
is often used to describe nursing practice that involves the provision
of nursing care in any centre geographically removed from a major
city.
One of the most complex tasks when discussing regional and
remote issues relating to any discipline is to identify and apply
common definitions. To assist in providing a consistent guide, the
Australian government uses systems which incorporate many of the
factors impacting on an individual’s access to health services as a
result of their location. These systems include the
Accessibility/Remoteness Index of Australia (ARIA+) (Australian
Bureau of Statistics (ABS) ) and the Australian Statistical Geography
Standard (ASGS) (ABS ).
2 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018a). Remoteness Structure. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au>.
3 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018b). Australian Statistical Geography Standard
(ASGS). Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
ARIA+ is a score measuring remoteness based on road distance
from a locality (where there is known to be a population) to a service
centre (where the population exceeds 1000 people as per statistics
from the ABS). A service centre is assumed to have a greater level
2
3


of service provision (health, education or retail) and is rated by
categories depending on the population at that location (Hugo
Centre for Migration and Population Research ). The values range
from 0 (high accessibility) to 15 (high remoteness). This is now being
replaced by the Modified Monash Model (MMM) that defines
whether a location is a city, rural, remote or very remote
(Department of Health ). The model measures remoteness and
population size on a scale of Modified Monash (MM) category MM 1
to MM 7. MM 1 is a major city and MM 7 is very remote.
Understanding the MMM classifications helps us distribute the health
workforce better in regional and remote areas. MMM classifications
are based on the Australian Statistical Geography Standard—
Remoteness Areas (ASGS-RA) framework (see Table 9.1
).
4 Hugo Centre for Migration and Population Research (2016). Accessibility/Remoteness
Index of Australia (ARIA+). Retrieved from <www.adelaide.edu.au>.
5 Department of Health (2019a). Modified Monash Model (MMM). Retrieved from
<www1.health.gov.au>.

Clinical consideration
4
5


When reviewing any element of nursing practice
or care it is essential to identify and
acknowledge our individual interpretation and
understanding, which can inevitably be
influenced by our life experiences both
personally and professionally. These
preconceptions may be highlighted even more
when discussing nursing practice and care in
regional or remote Australia, as pre-existing
knowledge and experiences can inform our
understanding of issues, challenges and
rewards associated with working in these areas.
Therefore, before embarking on the content of
this chapter, take a moment to consider your
knowledge about living and working in regional
and remote areas of Australia. How has that
knowledge and understanding been informed?
Is it from a lived experience of regional or
remote Australia? Would this knowledge
influence your ability to discuss nursing practice
in these areas?
Accurate assessment of individual and community health needs and
subsequent implementation of appropriate interventions can be
influenced by the nurse’s ability to identify challenges that might
arise in the delivery of care when working in isolated or remote


communities. Having an understanding of the unique challenges can
assist in organising acute or follow-up health care for people in these
settings. Thus a sound understanding of the remoteness
classifications
 is essential to effectively fulfil nursing
responsibilities.
It has long been understood that people who live in regional and
remote areas of Australia have different life expectancies and are at
greater risk of different health challenges than their counterparts
residing in urban or city centres. For example, people living in
regional and remote areas have one or more chronic diseases
compared to 48% of those in major cities. This is possibly due to
higher levels of disease and injury and poorer access to and use of
health services compared to people living in major cities (Australian
Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) ). More than 2 in 3 people
living in outer regional areas overweight or obese and nearly 3 in 4
people living in outer regional areas do not get enough exercise
(AIHW 2018). There are 5.4 times the rate of deaths due to land
accidents in remote and very remote areas compared to remote
areas (AIHW 2018).
6 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018). Australia’s Health 2018. Australia’s
health series no. 16. Cat. no. AUS 221. Canberra: AIHW.
There are many defining characteristics that make up a community,
each of which reflects the geographical, cultural and philosophical
diversity of the individual communities. Distance from metropolitan
city centres is a major factor for determining access to health
services, but this must be considered in context.
6


It is impossible to clearly define the lines of regional and remote
communities, especially in a country with the geographical, cultural
and population diversity of Australia. Geography cannot be the
single determinant. As previously highlighted, the current accepted
classification system is based on road distance from a locality to the
closest service centre in each of five classes of population size.
Areas are classified as major cities, inner regional, outer regional,
remote and very remote (ABS 2018a). If regionality and remoteness
were determined by distance or population alone, these towns, and
many more like them, would be grouped into classifications that may
not necessarily reflect the challenges the nursing workforce and
communities within them face when accessing health care.
As a nurse, awareness of these classifications is necessary for a
range of reasons. Possibly of greatest importance is the statistical
evidence that people who live in regional and remote Australia have
overall poorer mortality and morbidity than those who live in more
populated, less remote areas (AIHW ). It is statistically significant
that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples make up a higher
percentage of the remote area population than of the urban
population. Indigenous people in regional and remote areas are also
over-represented in poorer health outcomes data overall, which is
consistent with the lower life expectancy rates for Indigenous people
in Australia. Furthermore, it has been proposed that the lower life
expectancy of Indigenous people living in remote areas is more
suggestive of their Indigenous status than their locality (AIHW 2017).
7 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2017). Rural and Remote Health.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
7


Remoteness is a social determinant of health; however, it seems to
be a subjective term influenced by many factors. Geography which
causes difficult access, extreme distance and weather may result in
remoteness. Lack of resources, including access to relevant health
care professionals, poor infrastructure and limited communication
can impact on access to health care. People living and/or working in
an environment where they are not within their normal family or
community networks, and are socially and/or culturally isolated,
should also be considered as remote. Health provision in regional
and remote areas is achieved through the implementation of a range
of models of care modified for use in localities with specific health
care needs. The terms ‘regional and remote health’ and ‘primary
health’ are not always interchangeable and, in fact, may refer to a
regional and remote health model underpinned by primary health
care principles.
The terms ‘regional’ and ‘remote’ invoke impressions of distance but,
in reality, the communities, people and available health services in
these areas vary greatly. So, too, do the responsibilities, roles and
philosophies employed when providing nursing care for people in
these areas. Therefore, any discussion about regional and remote
nursing requires acknowledgment of the fact that there is no single
definition of ‘regional’ or ‘remote’, and awareness of the specific
areas being discussed is required to ensure accurate and consistent
representation.
Understanding regional and remote nursing is not exclusively the
domain of the local workforce, health department officials or


government policy advisers. All nurses, including those working in
major cities or inner regional areas, need to possess a sound
knowledge of the associated challenges and barriers. The ability to
recognise health issues relevant to particular regions has increased
with the development of Primary Health Networks (PHNs). PHNs are
a government initiative to improve health services and coordination
of care for people who may be at risk of poor health outcomes
(Department of Health ). Nurses provide a greater percentage of
health care than any other health-related discipline, and regional and
remote nursing encompasses a vast range of nursing skills,
including the ability to accurately identify the health needs of people
in these communities and to refer and/or transfer people to major
centres as appropriate.
8 Department of Health (2016a). Primary Health Networks (PHNs). Retrieved from
<www.health.gov.au>.
The further away people live from major cities, the less healthy they
are likely to be. People living in outer regional, remote and very
remote areas are more likely to visit the emergency department
compared to those living in major cities (AIHW 2017). People living
in inner regional Australia are more likely to be admitted to hospital
than those living in major cities (AIHW 2017).
The health of Australians in outer regional and remote areas is
generally poorer than that of people who live in major cities and
towns. People living in outer regional and remote areas have less
access to health services and are required to travel greater
distances for medical attention.
8


The AIHW’s report Australia’s Health 2018 identifies the following
areas of concern for people living in outer regional and remote
areas:
higher mortality rates and lower life expectancy
higher road injury and fatality rates
higher reported rates of hypertension, hypercholesteraemia,
diabetes and obesity
higher death rates from chronic disease
higher prevalence of mental health problems
higher rates of alcohol abuse and smoking
poorer dental health
higher incidence of poor antenatal and postnatal health
higher incidence of babies born with low birth weight to mothers
in very remote areas
lower rates of regular exercise.
Another serious issue is the higher risk of injury associated with
agricultural production in regional and remote areas, particularly with
the use of alcohol (AIHW 2018). There have been problems related
to safety performance, a reduction in workers’ compensation claim
rates and the number of deaths in the agriculture industry compared
with other high-risk industries such as construction, manufacturing
and transport (Carrington et al. ). Moreover, the risk of unintentional
injury in settings outside metropolitan areas often results in
psychological stress and high-level use of alcohol (Fragar et al.
).
9
10


9 Carrington, K., McIntosh, A., Hogg, R. & Scott, J. (2011). Safeguarding Rural Australia:
Addressing Masculinity and Violence in Rural Settings: Unintentional Violent Harm Including
Injuries in an Australian Rural Context: Analysis of Secondary Data Analysis. Retrieved from
<http://eprints.qut.edu.au>.
10 Fragar, L., Inder, K. J., Kelly, B. J., Coleman, C., Perkins, D. & Lewin, T. J. (2012).
Unintentional injury, psychological distress and depressive symptoms: Is there an association
for rural Australians? The Journal of Rural Health, 29(1), 12–19.


What is regional and remote
nursing?
Remote area nurses (RANs) and remote area midwives (RAMs)
work in a multitude of settings such as Indigenous communities,
outback and isolated towns, farm communities, islands, tourist
locations, mines and railways. These nurses must have skills that
facilitate a primary health care response which ranges from covering
an emergency, to administering a variety of medications, to providing
health education encompassing a generalist approach to health. The
scope of practice required of a RAN or RAM can be quite diverse
and, depending on a number of factors, can become quite broad
when required (CRANAplus ). A RAN/RAM is required to work
collaboratively with others to ensure a continuous, coordinated and
comprehensive approach to individuals and people in their
community (CRANAplus 2016).
11 CRANAplus (2016). Framework for Remote Practice. Retrieved from
<https://crana.org.au>.
11


The regional and remote nursing
workforce
Of all the health care disciplines in Australia, nursing is one of the
most stable and equally distributed across the country, with many
nurses working in a diverse range of settings within regional and
remote areas (AIHW 2018). In remote areas, Registered Nurses
and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health workers/health
practitioners constitute a large percentage of all health care
professionals and are therefore the usual point of first contact for
people seeking health advice or intervention.
However, the nursing workforce in very remote Australia is like the
rest of Australia in that it is ageing. In 2016, the number of employed
nurses and midwives aged 20–34 and over 55 increased; however,
the group aged 35–54 decreased slightly (AIHW 2018). This is
compared to the national average age of nurses aged 50 years or
over (37.2%) (AIHW 2018). Currently, many remote communities
are relying on health professionals who have not trained in Australia
and on locums or fly in/fly out services (O’Sullivan et al.
).
12 O’Sullivan, B., McGrail, M., Joyce, C. & Stoelwinder, J. (2016). Service distribution and
models of rural outreach by specialist doctors in Australia: A national cross-sectional study.
Australian Health Review, 40, 330–336. Retrieved from <www.publish.csiro.au>.
12


Staff working in these areas rely heavily upon each other, requiring
the development of effective interprofessional relationships and the
presence of a strong collegial working environment.
Anecdotally, communities in remote or isolated parts of Australia
recruit new staff quite well. The difficulty has been retaining those
staff members in the long term due to issues such as burnout,
professional isolation and working and living in a different social and
cultural environment. Burnout and feelings of professional isolation
are two of the key issues cited when practitioners choose to leave
small health services. While these phenomena are not unique to
working in regional or remote areas, the geographical isolation and
long distances to various levels of support can exacerbate the
situation and make working in these communities particularly
difficult.
There are some considerable differences between the daily life
experiences of living and working in an isolated area and those of a
city. Likewise, there can be notable differences in lifestyles between
states and territories resulting from historical and climatic influences.
Experiences with general practitioner (GP) care vary by remoteness.
In 2016–17, 21% of people in outer regional/remote/very remote
areas waited longer than they felt was acceptable to get an
appointment with a GP (compared with 19% in inner regional areas
and 18% in major cities), 33% of people in outer
regional/remote/very remote areas reported they could not see their
preferred GP on one or more occasion (compared with 28% in inner


regional areas and 25% in major cities), 11% of people in outer
regional/remote/very remote areas reported their GP sometimes,
rarely or never spent enough time with them (compared with 8.9% in
inner regional areas and 9.3% in major cities) and 4.8% of people in
inner regional areas reported that they at least once delayed seeing,
or did not see, a GP when they needed to because of cost
(compared with 4.6% in outer regional/remote/very remote areas
and 3.9% in major cities) (AIHW 2018).

As with doctors, the average per capita ratio of nurses and midwives
to population in regional areas was lower than in major cities. People
living in outer regional, remote and very remote regions tend to have
a higher level of visiting hospital emergency departments, which is
believed to be related to the lack of specialists and primary care
specialists in those areas.

of 40.5 hours a week, compared with 32.6 hours for those working in
inner regional areas where nurse to population ratios are much
higher (Department of Health ).

Incentives
Over the past 20 years or so, there has been a trend for medical
practitioners to leave regional areas; however, many universities are
13


now providing education and support for new medical practitioners
and other health care professionals to make a transition into regional
and remote health. The Stronger Rural Health Strategy has
implemented the Workforce Incentive Program to encourage
doctors, nurses and other allied health professionals to relocate to
regional and remote areas. GPs are provided with incentives to
assist them in establishing practices in regional and remote areas
and gain further benefits if they employ practice nurses and allied
health professionals, including non-dispensing pharmacists and
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health workers or practitioners
(Department of Health ).
14 Department of Health (2018). Stronger Rural Health Strategy—Factsheets. Retrieved from
<www1.health.gov.au>.
The Australian government has established programs to improve the
adequacy and quality of Australia’s health workforce. The
Department of Health (2016b) health workforce program offers
information for all health professionals, including students, about all
communities or organisations who want to recruit or retain health
professionals in regional and remote areas. For example, for nurses,
there is information about opportunities to expand their knowledge,
skills and practice as a Nurse Practitioner or how to work as an
independent practitioner and be eligible for access to the Medicare
Benefits Schedule. There is information for overseas-qualified
nurses to assist with registration requirements for Australia and on
how to learn about the Australian eHealth record system. This site
also offers health care professionals information about particular
programs relevant to specific communities such as locum (medical,
14


nursing, allied health) scholarship or training opportunities
(Department of Health ).
15 Department of Health (2016b). Health Workforce Program. Retrieved from
<https://hwd.health.gov.au>.
15


Primary health care
Discussions pertaining to regional and remote health often include
reference to primary health care
. Contemporary health care in
Australia has adopted primary health care principles which
acknowledge the individual needs of communities and address the
World Health Organization’s (WHO) goal for equity in access to
high-quality health care services. These principles include the full
spectrum of health care, from prevention and early detection to
curative and rehabilitative services to palliative services, which
ideally should be available and accessible to all people regardless of
geographical location. In 2015, the Australian government
introduced the Primary Health Network (PHN). PHNs have been
established in areas throughout Australia with the aim of working
with GPs, other primary health care providers, secondary care
providers and hospitals to assist in providing improved outcomes for
people (Department of Health 2016a). There are six key priority
areas targeted including mental health, Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander health, population health, health workforce, eHealth and
aged care (Department of Health 2016a).
There can be some differences in terminology, philosophy and
strategic approaches between conventional health services and
primary health care models. Table 9.3
 shows a comparison
between conventional health services and primary health care
approaches.

Upskilling and professional development are essential requirements
for every Registered Nurse; however, for nurses in regional and
remote Australia, this can assist nurses in establishing their
professional identity and smoothly facilitate their integration into
small communities. Many scholarships are available to provide
support should nurses wish to gain postgraduate qualifications in
regional and remote nursing.
Nursing registration in Australia underwent historic change in 2010
with the move to registration under one national body, the Nursing
and Midwifery Board of Australia, under the auspices of the
Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency. This change from
state to national registration provided the platform for
implementation of change across a range of professional standards
and requirements for registration.
Some of the changes to professional registration requirements
include the Registered Nurse being required to provide documented
evidence of ongoing professional development. In 2010, national
16


registration for health care practitioners was introduced, and in the
interests of public safety, student nurses also are now required to be
registered with the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia
(NMBA). Accordingly, nurses practising in regional and remote
Australia also have essential registration requirements linked to
ongoing professional education which are reliant on equitable access
to quality skills development and knowledge growth. Thus,
awareness of, and access to, professional education, forums,
conferences and networking are core components of working in
regional and remote areas. CRANAplus, the Australian Rural Health
Education Network and the Australian College of Nursing are some
of the organisations other than government departments providing
ongoing support for nurses working in regional or remote areas. This
support may be through scholarships, education and/or short
courses. Table 9.4
 provides some examples of the organisations
and the professional development opportunities offered specifically
for nurses practising in regional and remote areas of Australia.

The health of regional and remote
Australia
The health profile of residents of regional and remote Australia is
different in some elements from the health profile of those
Australians who reside in cities in Australia. Mortality rates are
known to increase with remoteness (AIHW 2017). Health care for
people living in regional and remote areas, and especially for
Indigenous people, has a long way to go to have a noticeable impact
on outcomes. The recent introduction of the PHN implements an
analysis and assessment of the health and service needs of people
within each region. PHN employees from each network are required
to identify opportunities, synthesise the evidence and then set
priorities for planning around health care needs. It is anticipated that
the health needs of Australians living in regional and remote
Australia might be more adequately met with this system
(Department of Health 2016a).
There are more males than females living in outer regional and in
remote areas. Where there were only 98 and 99 males for every
100 females in major cities and inner regional areas, there were 104,
112 and 113 males for every 100 females in outer regional, remote
and very remote areas (AIHW 2017).


Regional Australians are reported to have poorer health associated
with a number of factors including socioeconomic status, such as
lower levels of education, income and employment; risks specific to
occupation and livelihood, such as farming and mining; increased
rates of alcohol consumption and smoking; reduced access to and
availability of health services, including preventive programs; and the
risks associated with long-distance road travel (AIHW 2017). Not
eating enough fruit and vegetables and not doing enough exercise
each day are extremely common issues for males living in regional
and remote areas. Additionally, psychosocial factors such as
increased personal safety, community interaction and increased
generalised wellbeing reported by residents of regional and remote
areas can impact significantly on the health profile and health
outcomes. The harshness often linked to living in more isolated
areas can also impact on the health of the residents. For example,
prolonged drought can have debilitating psychological effects on the
farmer or grazier resulting from financial stress, emotional stress
and family disturbance. In some areas of Australia, drought has had
an effect, imposing substantial stressors on the local population.
Other uncontrollable challenges for regional and remote
communities include flooding, bushfires, plagues and disease
outbreaks in flora and fauna (AIHW 2017). When the property
owners are affected, there is a flow-on effect to the local community,
local businesses and the general identity of the community. People
who live in these areas are expected to ‘tough it out’ and failure to
do so may have long-term psychological and/or physical effects.


Research note
The regional and remote women’s perspective: the
impact of drought on mental health in regional and
regional Australia
B. Edwards, M. Gray & B. Hunter
. The impact of drought on mental health in rural and regional
Australia. Social Indicators Research, 121, 177–194.
17 Edwards, B., Gray, M. & Hunter, B. (2015). The impact of drought on mental health in rural and
regional Australia. Social Indicators Research, 121, 177–194.
This study questions whether the impact of drought has had
an effect on the mental health of people on farms in regional
areas of Australia. The more severely the drought has
affected the productivity, the more significantly it has affected
the farmers. This study surveyed 8000 people living in
agricultural areas of Australia. Equal numbers of participants
were interviewed from below-average rainfall and above-
average rainfall areas; however, at the time of the interviews
the average rainfall for Australia was quite low. Farmers were
experiencing severe financial hardship with dramatic
reductions in their income from the previous year.
Participants were surveyed in order to understand their
overall wellbeing while under the influence of drought
conditions. The findings showed that although the drought
was a meteorological event, the impact affected a person
socially and economically. A farmer or farm worker felt
17


responsible for the animals that were also being affected by
the drought, which then had an impact on mental health.
These findings support the evidence that mental health
problems are significant in regional and remote settings and
that adequate mental health services are required to support
groups that are vulnerable and may be at risk.
Implications Nurses need to be aware that occurrences
such as drought can have a devastating effect on farmers
and their families living in regional and remote regions. It is
important to remember that rates of suicide are also
significantly higher in regional and remote areas of Australia
(Kolves et al.
).
18 Kolves, K., Milner, A., McKay, K. & De Leo, D. (2012). Suicide in Rural and
Remote Areas of Australia. The Australian Institute for Suicide Research and
Prevention Griffith University. Retrieved from <www.griffith.edu.au>.
Tending to non-life-threatening injuries sustained in regional and
remote areas is often undertaken onsite using available resources
(see Figure 9.2
). The long trip to medical services and the limited
access can mean that people in regional and remote areas self-
treat, only seeking further advice if complications arise.
