Health information
Self-service in the world of health
Historically, nurses, midwives and other health care professionals
were the source of health care information. Health education is
pivotal in ensuring that the individual is able to move closer to a
state of health, whether in the context of discharge instruction
information for an acute illness or for primary health care guidance
from community health professionals. Nowadays, health information
is readily available in many places. Some sources such as
pharmacies have quality, appropriate information, yet other sources
such as the internet have voluminous content, much of which is not
necessarily valid or reliable.
The internet, World Wide Web and
health information
The internet
 is a worldwide network that connects other
networks. Connections between networks and PCs via the internet
allow for almost instantaneous transmission between distant sites


and can include text, audio and video data. The World Wide Web
(www)
 refers to the complex links between web pages or
websites, accessed through ‘addresses’ called universal resource
locators (URLs). URLs often begin with the designation http://
followed by www. URLs end with a designation that denotes the type
of site. For example, .com is for commercial sites, .org for
organisations, .edu for educational institutions and .gov for
government sites.
Tens of thousands of health-related websites exist, with many new
ones appearing daily and others becoming ‘dead links’. No
standardised controls exist to ensure that the information provided is
current or accurate. Nurses and midwives should evaluate health
websites as they access them and assist individuals in doing the
same. Uninformed belief of information from questionable sites can
cause individuals significant distress. There are countless tools for
evaluating internet health information, including a website produced
by the State Library of New South Wales  informing health care
consumers how to analyse and assess online health information
(see Figure 10.5
).
38 State Library of New South Wales (2019). How to Analyse and Assess Online Health
Information. Retrieved from <https://guides.sl.nsw.gov.au>.
Figure 10.5
38


Considerations in assessing legitimacy of online health information.
Source: Developed using website content from the State Library of New South Wales (2019). How to Analyse
and Assess Online Health Information. Retrieved from <https://guides.sl.nsw.gov.au/c.php?
g=671834&p=4728885>.


Lifespan considerations
Computer use
Children and adults
Computer programs are available for children and adults to
learn everything from a foreign language to algebra.
There are many issues of concern related to frequent and
extended use of computers by all ages. In particular,
repetitive motion injuries (especially of the hand) can occur
with extensive typing and use of the computer mouse, eye
strain can occur from computer monitor viewing and
musculoskeletal damage is related to inadequate ergonomic
arrangement of desk chairs, surface height and monitor
placement. Students and adults who use computers daily
should be thoroughly evaluated and instructed in the
prevention of these conditions.
Parents need to be reminded of potential risks to children
from internet contact with strangers and adults-only websites.
They also need to monitor schoolchildren’s use of computers
to ensure they are not being side-tracked from homework
into computer games and messaging.


All people should protect their financial and personal
information when conducting business via computer.
Older adults
Computer classes are being taught to increasing numbers of
older adults. Use of the computer provides them with an
avenue of communication and exposure to a vast amount of
health care information. Although nurses and midwives have
little control over what internet sites will be accessed, it is
important to teach individuals and the general public to
evaluate information from the site and to be aware that
misinformation can also be presented. Important guidelines
that increase the validity of a site are as follows:
The article or information lists the author and credentials
and/or the institution from which the information came.
A date is listed that states when information was updated.
If health care information is presented, a disclaimer
should be included. The disclaimer presents limitations of
the information and should say that it is not medical
advice.
Computer-assisted programs can be very effective teaching
aids for older adults. They may provide audio and visual
instruction and may even be interactive. They are useful for
teaching about medical conditions and medications, and for
providing information about procedures and surgeries to be
performed.


Buying drugs online
When the internet changed the face of shopping and enabled
individuals to purchase products online, pharmacies soon lost their
monopoly on drug sales. Unfortunately, with this increased
availability came reduced quality control, resulting in inferior or
counterfeit drugs from non-reputable sources seeping into the online
market. Added to this is the ability to purchase almost any drug
without a prescription. The internet environment is practically
impossible to regulate and although individual countries have
attempted to do so, the borderless presence of online companies
has made enforcement relatively difficult. Many of these drugs are
counterfeit, do not contain the identified drug and/or are
contaminated with other potentially dangerous substances
(Ghanem
; Hensey & Gwee ). Nurses, midwives and other health
care professionals must ensure that individuals understand the
significant risks associated with purchasing online drugs. Although
there is information on the internet relating to online purchase of
drugs, many individuals remain naïve and do not understand that
they may be breaking the law.
39 Ghanem, N. (2019). Substandard and falsified medicines: Global and local efforts to
address a growing problem. Clinical Pharmacist. Retrieved from <www.pharmaceutical-
journal.com>.
39
40


40 Hensey, C. & Gwee, A. (2016). Counterfeit drugs: An Australian perspective. Medical
Journal of Australia, 204(9), 344. Doi: 10.5694/mja16.00105.


Technology in nursing and
midwifery practice
Many activities of a nurse’s and midwife’s day involve collecting,
recording and using data. Computers are well suited to assist in
these functions. Specifically, the nurse may record information in
computer records, access other departments’ information on
individuals from centralised computers and manage scheduling,
among many other functions.
Documentation and medical
record keeping
Numerous studies have identified that a nurse spends a lot of time
on tasks other than direct care of the individuals (Penoyer et al.
;
Westbrook et al.
). Some of this time could be reduced by
improving access to medical records, policies and procedures, and
other important information. Computers can be used to assist with
each of these.
41 Penoyer, D., Cortelyou-Ward, K., Noblin, A., Bullard, T., Talbert, S., Wilson, J.,
Schafhauser, B. & Briscoe, J. (2014). Use of electronic health record documentation by
41
42


healthcare workers in an acute care hospital system. Journal of Healthcare Management,
59(2), 130–144.
42 Westbrook, J., Duffield, C., Li, L. & Creswick, N. (2011). How much time do nurses have
for patients? A longitudinal study quantifying hospital nurses’ patterns of task time distribution
and interactions with health professionals. BMC Health Services Research, 11(319), e1–e12.
Retrieved from <http://bmchealthservres.biomedcentral.com>.
Bedside data entry
There are several different types of computerised bedside data entry
systems. These allow recording of an individual’s assessments,
medication administration progress notes, care plan updating, acuity
and accrued charges. The terminal can be fixed or hand-held,
hardwired to the central system or cordless, and have the ability to
transmit the data to distant sites, such as from the person’s home to
the organisation’s office. A slightly different type of bedside terminal
is the point-of-care or point-of-service computer.
Irrespective of the system, the health care staff will need to master
the interface in order to obtain and enter critical data. A longitudinal
study by Zadvinskis, Garvey Smith & Yen  suggests that investing
in quality equipment, refining policies to improve practice and
ensuring systems can focus on patient safety are critical to the
success of health care technology.
43 Zadvinskis, I. M., Garvey Smith, J. & Yen, P. Y. (2018). Nurses’ experience with health
information technology: Longitudinal qualitative study. JMIR Medical Informatics, 6(2), e38.
Doi: 10.2196/medinform.8734.
43


E-health records
As previously discussed, e-health records (EHRs)
 permit e-
health data retrieval by caregivers, administrators, creditors and
other people who require the data.
EHRs can improve individuals’ safety and standard of care. Reduced
delay in gaining complete information can result from multiple
sources of information converging into a common area for ease of
access. The benefits of an EHR include assisting with tracking of
medications, immunisations and allergies, and also can be realised
by a reduction in duplication of investigations (ADHA 2019). This is
not only less taxing to the individual but also consumes less of the
health care budget. Above all, improved communication between
health care providers can only help to improve an individual’s care.
Because of the way computers provide access to the EHR,
providers easily retrieve specific data such as trends in vital signs,
immunisation records and current problems. The system can be
designed to warn providers about conflicting medications or
parameters that indicate dangerous conditions. Sophisticated
systems allow replay of audio, graphic or video data for comparison
with current status. All text is legible and can be searched for
keywords.


Health care monitoring and
diagnostic technology
Besides computers designed for record keeping, other technology is
used extensively in health care to assess and monitor a person’s
condition. The data accumulated from various electronic devices can
be part of the EHR and also stored for research purposes.
Electronic records take up much less space than paper records and
may be stored more securely. Copies can be made easily onto
different electronic media that are more compact and durable than
paper. Data can also be transmitted to a consulting specialist in
another location.
Nursing and midwifery has benefited greatly from the myriad
personal monitors. In everyday practice, nurses and midwives use
digital or tympanic thermometers, digital scales, pulse oximetry,
ECG/telemetry/haemodynamic monitoring, apnoea monitors, fetal
heart monitors, blood glucose analysers, ventilators and intravenous
(IV) pumps. Although most of these monitors are applied externally,
implanted electronic monitors are also proving to have great value.
For example, a surgically placed wireless sensor can measure the
pressure inside a bulging weakened blood vessel (aneurysm) and
warn of potential rupture. These instruments can be used in any
care setting, from intensive care to the home. Most instruments
keep a record of the recent values and some can transmit their data
to a more sophisticated computer or print out a paper record. Some


have digital displays that ‘talk’ to the user, giving instructions or
results. Most instruments also have error detection or alarms that
indicate either that the instrument is malfunctioning or the assessed
value is outside predetermined parameters. These devices, with
their minute but powerful computer chips, make it possible to extend
observations to previously immeasurable valid and reliable data.
In various specialty areas of health care, individuals undergo
diagnostic procedures in which computers play a major role.
Computed axial tomography (CAT) scans, magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans use
computers extensively to perform tests and analyse the findings.
Blood gas analysers, pulmonary function test machines and
intracranial pressure monitors all use computer processing.
Telemedicine/telehealth
One of the most exciting areas being developed in computer-
assisted health care is telemedicine
. Telemedicine uses
technology to transmit electronic data about an individual to health
care professionals at distant locations. In one example, two-way
audiovisual communication allows an expert to examine and consult
on a person’s case from thousands of kilometres away. X-rays,
scans, stored computer data and almost anything imaginable can be
sent using computers.


Health care improvements to individuals in regional and regional
areas have been realised by the use of techniques and equipment
permitting exchange of information via telephone, mobile, fax or
computer in the person’s own home (see Chapter 9
).
Concerns regarding telemedicine relate to legal and ethical issues.
The Nursing and Midwifery Telehealth Consortia is a collection of
nursing and midwifery peak bodies who responded to the
Commonwealth invitation to undertake the Telehealth, Nursing and
Midwifery: Education and Support Project. One of the project’s
objectives was to develop and disseminate a set of professional
standards and clinical guidelines to assist nurses, midwives and
Nurse Practitioners who use telehealth technology (see Box 10.1
for Consortia structure). As a result, the Telehealth Standards:
Registered Nurses were written. As time has progressed, the
Standards have developed into separate entities, one for Registered
Nurses and one for registered midwives. These documents outline
concepts related to telehealth, make specific reference to issues
such as consent, privacy and confidentiality, and also outline broad
principles to assist nurses and midwives across the domains (10
domains for nursing and 14 domains for midwives). The documents
identify specific considerations for practice with respect to each of
the domains (Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation ).
44 Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation (2014). Telehealth. Retrieved from
<http://anmf.org.au>.
BO X
44


10.1 Membership bodies of the
Nursing and Midwifery Telehealth
Consortia
The Australian Practice Nurses Association
The Australian College of Midwives
The Australian College of Nurse Practitioners
CRANAplus (Council of Remote Area Nurses of Australia
and all remote health professionals)
Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation
Practice management
Beyond functions related to direct care, computers also assist
nurses and midwives in many other ways. In hospitals, data
terminals are commonly used to order supplies, tests, meals and
services from other departments. Tracking these orders allows
analysis to determine the most frequently used or most costly items
used by a particular unit. This information may lead to decisions to
modify a budget, provide different staffing, move supplies to a
different location or make other changes for more efficient and
higher-quality care.


Computers are used extensively for scheduling. Appointments can
be easily entered or changed. Special notes or tags can be applied
to the appointment as a reminder to the provider to perform
particular services. The schedule for a single day can be printed so
that all personnel have a copy. Staffing patterns must also be
coordinated. Special requests for days off or continuing education
classes can be entered and the schedule can be viewed for a day,
week, month or year.
Each practice needs to keep track of procedures health care
workers perform, diagnoses and time spent with a person so that
billing can be accurate. The use of computerised databases filled
with unique codes for each medication, medical diagnosis, treatment
and supply allows for accurate and timely management of this data.
Specific applications of computers
in nursing and midwifery practice
As previously described, numerous systems are in use for collecting
and classifying the various types of data used. Some of these
systems have been found particularly useful in specific settings.
Research note
Can technology reduce medication errors?


J. Callen, A. Hordern, K. Gibson, L. Li, I. Hains & J. Westbrook
. Can technology change the work of
nurses? Evaluation of a drug monitoring system for ambulatory chronic disease patients. International
Journal of Medical Informatics, 82(3), 159–167. Doi: 10.1016/j.ijmedinf.2012.11.009.
45 Callen, J., Hordern, A., Gibson, K., Li, L., Hains, I. & Westbrook, J. (2013). Can technology change
the work of nurses? Evaluation of a drug monitoring system for ambulatory chronic disease patients.
International Journal of Medical Informatics, 82(3), 159–167. Doi: 10.1016/j.ijmedinf.2012.11.009.
This article reports on the benefits of an electronic drug-
monitoring system for people experiencing care in an
ambulatory rheumatology unit of a large Australian
metropolitan hospital. The results of this single site study
involving more than 3000 nursing tasks demonstrated that
after the implementation of the technology, the nurses were
able to spend less time on drug-monitoring tasks and more
time with individuals, performing care activities and
participating in education.
Implications The results of this study demonstrate that when
implemented well and embraced by users and consumers,
technology can help improve health care by nurses.
Community and home health
Computer networks are being used in innovative ways in home
settings. A computer placed in a home allows the person to access
information on a variety of topics, search the internet or email a
health care provider with questions or concerns. Individuals also can
record data about their health status that can be transmitted to the
45


health care provider at the central network computer. Examples that
have been successful using this approach include monitoring women
at risk for pre-term labour, people with HIV/AIDS and people with
Alzheimer’s disease. Home alert systems that allow the person to
signal the base station in an emergency are also widely used.
Cultural consideration
Process for achieving cultural safety
The Australian Bureau of Statistics  has identified that one-
third of the Australian population were born overseas, nearly
1 in 2 Australians have an overseas-born parent and 21% of
Australians speak a language other than English at home.
With such diversity, it is important that we consider
individuals’ reactions to the knowledge that their information
may be kept and stored electronically. Many people fear
governments, especially those who have fled from
dictatorships and authoritarian countries. Perceptions that
health data may be collected and used against individuals
may become a barrier to seeking appropriate or necessary
care.
46 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2017). Cultural Diversity in Australia: 2016
Census Data Summary. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Data storage and retention of health care research
information should be undertaken with a degree of cultural
awareness and understanding of the perceptions held by
some individuals and groups. Peak groups such as the
46


Federation of Ethnic Communities’ Councils of Australia
(FECCA) are attempting to show that technology such as the
My Health Record System will have benefits for culturally and
linguistically diverse (CALD) individuals such as the removal
of language barriers in communicating past health
challenges, medication allergies and current medications
(FECCA ). However, these groups do recognise the
concerns regarding data security and hope that they can
work with CALD consumers and the government to build trust
in the e-health information system.
47 Federation of Ethnic Communities’ Councils of Australia (FECCA) (2018). My
Health Record: A Resource for CALD Australians. Retrieved from
<http://fecca.org.au>.
The benefits from increased communication and information
retrieval can assist in improving the health of Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander people; however, this needs to be
approached in a safe and culturally competent way (Cafferty
et al.
). Due consideration for individuals from Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander communities and other cultures should
be paramount in the design of the process; otherwise, the
technology could have detrimental effects on a person’s
health and their anxiety levels may rise from concern
regarding collection and use of their personal information.
48 Caffery, L. J., Bradford, N. K., Smith, A. C. & Langbecker, D. (2018). How
telehealth facilitates the provision of culturally appropriate healthcare for Indigenous
Australians. Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare, 24(10), 676–682.
https://doi.org/10.1177/1357633X18795764.
47
48


Nurses and midwives who visit people in their homes may use
notebook computer systems or tablet computers to record
assessments and transmit data to the main office. Similar systems
have been developed for nursing and midwifery students in
community health courses to communicate with the academic staff.
Case management
Case managers must be able to track the people for whom they are
responsible—the caseload. Software programs allow the case
manager to enter a person’s data and integrate this with
predesigned case-tracking templates. In addition, the case manager
must keep abreast of the latest regulations affecting eligibility for
health care benefits, the reporting requirements of the private health
funds and detailed facts about the variety of service providers the
person may need to access. All this data can be placed in integrated
computer software programs. Finally, the case manager must
document quality; that is, demonstrate outcomes related to dollars
spent.


Computers in nursing and
midwifery education
Just as computers have become standard instructional tools in the
primary and secondary school systems, they are used extensively in
all aspects of nursing and midwifery education. Nursing and
midwifery programs require computerised libraries and academic
staff use technological teaching strategies in the classroom and
outside assignments, as well as to demonstrate and use applications
in clinical rotations. Further, academic record keeping is facilitated by
database programs.
Teaching and learning
Computers enhance the teaching and learning experience for
students and faculty in at least four ways: access to literature,
computer-assisted learning, classroom technologies and strategies
for learning at a distance.
Literature access and retrieval
In the information age, it is a challenge to keep abreast of the
information on any subject. Computers have significantly improved


our abilities in this area by presenting catalogues and the text of
materials in a way that can be searched systematically. Previously,
users needed to leaf through numerous collections of printed
indexes, one keyword or topic at a time. Now continuously updated
cumulative indexes of related materials can be searched
electronically in a fraction of the time. The searcher can specify the
recency, language, document type and other characteristics of the
citation for desired materials. Once a list of search matches is
displayed on the computer screen, users can select all or certain
citations and either print them or store them on their own local
computers.
In addition to searching lists of documents, complete publications
and materials are available in computerised formats. These include
medical textbooks, the full text of journals, drug references, digitised
x-rays or scans, and graphics, including clip art. Through the internet
and the World Wide Web, both classic and the most current
information can be found on any topic. Users can access statistics
from the Australian Bureau of Statistics or any number of other
organisations that publish their data on the internet.
Computer-assisted learning
Nursing and midwifery have enjoyed the computer revolution in the
form of computer-assisted learning (CAL). Dozens of software
programs help nursing and midwifery students and nurses learn and
demonstrate learning. These have been created by individuals,
educational institutions, technology companies or print publishers.


Programs cover topics from drug dosage calculations to ethical
decision making and are classified according to format: tutorial, drill
and practice, simulation, or testing. CAL can contain diagrams,
graphics, animation, video and audio and may be accessed on CD-
ROMs or downloaded from the internet. All forms of CAL allow
almost instant access to any section of the program and can be
designed to branch to different sections depending on the user’s
responses.
Anti-plagiarism software is also used in education not only to detect
episodes of plagiarism but also to educate students on the important
need either to cite quoted sources directly or to paraphrase and thus
represent a more processed and integrated version of information
sources.
Tutorials on electrocardiograph (ECG) interpretation, drug
interactions and the legal aspects of care are examples of these
programs. Course syllabi that contain worksheets or activities that
students can complete on the computer may be distributed on disk,
through the university network or via the internet. Students who
become familiar with CAL will also find that they have an easier time
adjusting to the software programs many employers require them to
use for annual competency testing mandated by accrediting bodies
in certain areas (e.g. drug calculations and fire safety). Completion
of CAL programs may also be an acceptable means of
demonstrating continuing education activities required for
registration renewal.


Classroom technology
Most new educational buildings are wired to accommodate
technology. This includes adequate electrical outlets for students to
plug in laptop computers and wiring (or wireless technology) for
network or internet access. For educators, projectors and liquid
crystal display (LCD) panels that allow computer screens to be
displayed to the entire classroom are becoming standard. These
enhancements allow educators to use the full text, video and audio
capabilities of computers instead of overhead transparencies, slides
or writing on the board. Computer tablets and smartphones are also
becoming widely used by both academics and students alike.
Distance learning
There are several different models of distance learning
. In one
model, the student receives course materials, communicates with
the educator and other students, and submits assignments
completely through the mail, phone or fax, email, website and
electronic ‘dropbox’ (a server folder accessible from the internet).
This may be referred to as an asynchronous mode because the
people involved are not interacting at the same ‘real’ time. Another
model of distance education involves groups of students in
classrooms at different sites participating in a class session through
two-way audio and video transmission. Computers are used to code
and decode the sounds and visuals for transmission. Students who
are not at the site where the educator is located can also
communicate via voice-activated microphones or response devices.


These devices permit the students to indicate that they wish to ask a
question or even to respond to multiple-choice test questions.
Synchronous distance learning can be accomplished through the
use of chat and instant messaging. Another computerised delivery of
knowledge is through computer tablets, netbooks, personal digital
assistants (PDAs) and ebooks—where an entire textbook is
available on a computer, tablet or PDA and can be annotated and
searched. Hand-held, portable devices can also contain reference
materials such as drug handbooks for instant, up-to-date
information. As computer technology becomes more cost effective
and increases its transmission quality and speed, it is anticipated
that more schools will use distance learning strategies to reach
students around the globe.
Clinical consideration
Distance education courses held entirely on
computer are called online courses, whereas
part computer-based and part classroom-based
courses are often referred to as web-enhanced
or hybrid courses. Learning management
system software (such as Blackboard, Moodle
and SharePoint) provides an organising
framework for delivery of the internet content of
distance courses.


Testing
The computer is ideal for conducting certain types of learning
evaluations. Surveys can be completed online, including anonymous
questionnaires. For testing, large banks of potential items can be
written and the computer can generate different exams for each
student depending on the selection criteria designated by the
educator. In addition, the students’ answers can be stored
electronically and the overall exam results analysed quickly.
Student and course record
management
Computers are also very useful for maintaining results of students’
grades or attendance using spreadsheets
. Often educators are
able to import student exam answer sheets directly into a grade
book on the computer. The program can then calculate percentages,
sort student scores in order and print results for both students and
staff. Grades from multiple exams plus scores on essays or other
projects can be calculated into final grades.
Students are frequently asked to evaluate staff and courses using
machine-readable forms. These data are also scanned into the
computer so that cumulative results can be calculated and stored.
That is an example of what is called data warehousing
—the


accumulation of large amounts of data that are stored over time and
can be examined for output in different types of reports (charts and
tables).
Most nursing and midwifery schools now have all student records on
computer. From application to graduation, the registrar’s office
keeps track of names, addresses, units taken, grades and all other
pertinent student data. Students may be able to sign up for classes,
check their tuition costs and see their transcripts on computer
terminals on campus or from anywhere that has a computer with
internet access.


Computers in administration
As indicated in the section of this chapter on computers in nursing
and midwifery practice, the volume of data that nurses and midwives
need to have available and the additional volume of data generated
can and must be managed electronically. Administrators require this
data to develop strategic plans for the organisation.
Human resources
All employers must maintain a database on each employee. In
addition to the usual demographics and wage data, the database for
personnel has unique fields for areas such as competencies’
currency, health requirements (e.g. tuberculosis testing, hepatitis
immunisation, rubella titres) and performance appraisals.
Administrators can use this human resources database to
communicate with employees, examine staffing patterns and create
budget projections.
Medical records management
Costs are inherent in and reflected by medical records. It is
expensive to keep records, but it is even more expensive not to be


able to access what is in them. Therefore, nurses and midwives
require computer programs that allow a person’s record to be
searched for trends such as the most common presenting
diagnoses, number of cases by diagnosis-related groups, most
expensive cases, length of stay or total number of days the case
was open, and a person’s clinical outcomes.
Facilities management
Many aspects of managing buildings and non-nursing/midwifery
services can be facilitated by computer. Heating, air-conditioning,
ventilation and alarm systems are computer controlled. Security
devices, such as readers that scan identification cards, barcodes or
magnetic strips, permit only authorised personnel to enter secure
areas. Computers can also manage and report inventory, tracking
everything from pillowcases to syringes.
Budget and finance
Advantages of computerised billing are that claims are transmitted
much more quickly and have a greater likelihood of being complete
and accurate compared with handwritten documents. If this is the
case, claims will be paid sooner and the health care organisation will
have better control over its financial status. Computers can also


contribute to cost savings by reducing the time needed for
processing accounts payable and receivable.
The budget itself is generally a spreadsheet program. This software
allows tracking as well as forecasting and planning. In uncertain
times, the ability to perform ‘what if’ calculations is especially
valuable.
Quality assurance and utilisation
reviews
Both internal and external stakeholders in health care organisations
need to know that the services and activities of the organisation
have positive results. Once standards, pathways, key indicators and
other vital data have been identified and described, computers can
facilitate the accumulation of data for individuals and also for groups
enabling rapid analysis of the data. Quality is considered a process
and not an end point. Applying this perspective, computerised
systems are ideal for taking a snapshot of the institution’s quality
indices at any time.
Utilisation review consists of examining trends and proposing
advantageous disposition of resources (specifically, length of stay).
For example, might a person who has had a fractured hip repaired
have equivalent outcomes at lesser cost if they are discharged
home and commenced on a rehabilitation program sooner? Studies


can be conducted with computer analyses to answer such
questions.
Accreditation
The Australian Council on Healthcare Standards (ACHS) requires
significant monitoring of quality indicators. Health care agencies
must maintain databases of policies and procedures, standards of
care, continuing education/in-service and employee accomplishment
as part of the accreditation process. Acuity statistics, length of stay
and many other pieces of information need to be collected, tracked,
reviewed and interpreted. Such volume of information needs to be
organised, stored and easily retrieved. To perform these tasks with
as little time and effort as possible, a collection of computer systems
working both independently and as part of a bigger system is
required.


Computers in nursing and
midwifery research
Computers are invaluable assistants in the conduct of both
quantitative and qualitative nursing and midwifery research in each
step of the research process—problem identification, literature
review, research design, ethics application, grant proposals, data
collection and analysis, and results dissemination. Computer
resources are an important component of the planning phase of any
research project. The size of the computer and its storage capacity
must be adequate for the amount of data that will be collected, and
the appropriate software programs must be in place to manage and
analyse the data. Computerised word processing is also an integral
component in the publication and dissemination of research.


The future: Technology and health
care
As exciting as technology in health care is today, individuals can
probably expect even more exciting, effective and expensive devices
and science knowledge in years to come. The complexity and
breadth of technology is expanding exponentially. Computer access
is rapidly increasing while the cost is trending downwards.
Technology is evolving in the areas of virtual reality, remote access,
task automation, robotics and bioengineering. Simultaneously,
however, concerns continue to arise regarding privacy, access for
people with disabilities, intellectual property debates (who owns web
content), destructive programs (computer viruses), ergonomic
injuries and, in underdeveloped countries, piracy.
Finally, although nurses, midwives and other health care workers are
becoming more and more reliant on technology, it is critical that we
do not lose sight of the person for whom we care.
Case study
As a nurse (or midwife) working for a home care agency in a
small town, you would like to receive up-to-date and accurate
health information regarding all the people in your care. High-


speed computer access is available in your office, and many
residents have a computer in their homes as it provides a
low-cost way of communicating with friends and relatives who
are far away (e.g. using email and sending digitised photos).
Fundamentals of care framework in
context


1. You have a difficult clinical case and want to
investigate possible interventions. What are some of
the ways computers could assist in this endeavour?
2. You decide that sending photos of the person would be
useful to your colleagues in providing input. Since time
is an issue, you determine that sending them
electronically would be most expeditious. The person
agrees to the photos but is worried about privacy in
sending them through the computer. What are the
issues with sending confidential data electronically?
What mechanisms could you institute to reduce the
risks associated with digital transfer of information?
3. An individual shares with you a website that states it
can guarantee a cure to their illness. How would you
respond?
4. How would you establish a relationship with someone
when providing care through an online medium (e.g.
email)? Consider the elements from the ‘Relationship
Established’ dimensions of the Fundamentals of Care
Framework: Trust, Focus, Anticipate, Know and
Evaluate.
5.
 You are considering enrolling in a postgraduate
degree program that is offered online. What would be
some of the advantages and disadvantages of such a
program?


Chapter 10 Review


Chapter highlights
Australia is progressing towards the development of a national e-
health record that will increase the efficiency of all facets of care
that health care facilities can provide.
A hospital information system (HIS) organises data from various
areas in the hospital such as admissions, medical records,
clinical laboratory, pharmacy and finance.
E-health records (EHRs) enable longitudinal health assessment
and treatment data to be collected and made available to all
health care providers who require it. Such data warehousing also
enables research to be conducted on quality of care, a person’s
clinical outcomes and a variety of other parameters.
Nurses need to participate in the creation of taxonomies and
classifications of electronic data.
Concerns regarding privacy and confidentiality of health records
have arisen as electronic databases and communications have
proliferated.
Smart technologies are used commonly by nurses to access
apps to assist them with their clinical practice or to search
websites to inform their knowledge.
Nurses can benefit from the use of social media but can also risk
breaching principles of confidentiality and conduct.
Computers are used extensively to locate and access data
through online databases and internet searching. Many nursing
journals are in electronic formats.


Computer-assisted learning programs include tutorial, drill and
practice, and simulations.
In distance learning, the educator and student may be located far
apart and communicate via computer, phone, fax and video
technologies.
Bedside entry of nursing and midwifery data is becoming more
prevalent. Studies on whether these systems save nursing time
have conflicting results.
Computer monitoring and diagnosing of a person’s conditions are
widespread. Examples include digital or tympanic thermometers,
digital scales, pulse oximetry, ECGs, telemetry, haemodynamic
monitoring, apnoea monitors, fetal heart monitors, blood glucose
analysers, ventilators, IV pumps, CAT scans and MRI.
Telehealth, which allows the health care profession to use
electronic means of communication in diagnosis and care
activities, is a growing area that generates both excitement and
concerns.
Computers are used by home health nurses and midwives to
record data and to communicate with the central office.
Individuals can also have computers in the home that allow them
to monitor their own health status and send information about
their condition.
Specialised computer software programs enable case managers
to track a person’s needs, resources and health care outcomes.
Computers are used in nursing and midwifery administration to
manage personnel, human resources, facilities, budgets, quality
assurance, utilisation review, staffing and scheduling, and
accreditation.


Each step of the research process makes use of computer
technology. In particular, computers are used to access literature,
analyse data and report findings.
Concept check
1. The challenge most associated with the use of an e-health
record system is which of the following?
1. Cost.
2. Accuracy.
3. Privacy.
4. Curability.
2. One disadvantage associated with electronic (e.g. internet-
based) courses includes which of the following?
1. They take longer.
2. Interpersonal communication is not possible.
3. Everyone has to ‘log on’ at the same time.
4. It is harder to establish a sense of community.
3. Which of the following is an advantage of using computers
while conducting nursing research?
1. Designing the steps of the research plan.
2. Analysing the quantitative data.
3. Disseminating the research findings.
4. All of the above.


4. A person insists that the health care professional uses a
treatment method discovered on an internet website. Which
of the following is the most appropriate response?
1. ‘The treatment must be examined to see if it is
appropriate.’
2. ‘Most website treatments have not been studied or
researched.’
3. ‘The person who set up the website is the only one
who can use it on individuals.’
4. ‘Websites are like advertising; they are biased and may
not be legitimate.’
Focus on critical thinking
1. Can information technology benefit nurses and those for
whom they care in day-to-day care activities? If so, how?
2. If a health care system relied heavily on information
technology and computerised systems, how could nurses and
midwives function in times of extended power failure?
3. Which cultures fear storage of personal data? Why? How can
a nurse assist an individual with their fears regarding storage
of medical information?
4. Technology is advancing at tremendous speed. Information
technology and infrastructure are expensive. Do systems
have a use-by date? How would health care providers
resource the upgrades? What effect may this have on a
person’s care?


5. The evolution of e-health records means that a ‘data
receptacle’ will hold incredible amounts of information. This
data could be aggregated and ‘de-identified’. How could
having such a volume of information benefit medical and
nursing research?


Unit 3 The nursing process
The nursing process is a systematic, person-
centred method for structuring the delivery of
nursing care. The nursing process entails
gathering and analysing data in order to identify
the person’s strengths and potential or actual
health problems, and developing and continually
reviewing a plan of nursing interventions to
achieve mutually agreed goals or outcomes. At
every stage of the process, the nurse works
closely with the person to individualise care and
build a relationship based on respect and trust.

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Discuss the definition, skills and attitudes of critical thinking.
Describe the significance of developing critical-thinking abilities in
order to practise safe, effective and professional nursing care.
Discuss the relationships between the nursing process, critical
thinking, the problem-solving process, the strength identification
process and the decision-making process.


Apply the critical-thinking process to the provision of person-
centred, culturally competent care.
Explore ways of demonstrating critical thinking.

Analysing complex data about people, making
decisions about problems, identifying a range of
possible interventions and deciding on the most
appropriate actions are all integral aspects of
nursing practice. Nurses must be informed and
inquisitive. In addition, nurses must ensure they
base their practice on high-quality evidence.


Critical thinking uses
Critical thinking
 is a complex collection of cognitive skills and
affective habits of the mind and can be described as the process of
analysing and assessing thinking with a view to improving it. Critical
thinking is essential to safe, competent, skilled nursing practice
requiring open-mindedness, the consideration of alternatives,
inquisitiveness and self-confidence in analytical skills (Kim et al. ).
1 Kim, D., Moon, S., Kim, E., Kim, Y. & Lee, S. (2013). Nursing students’ critical thinking
disposition according to academic level and satisfaction with nursing. Nurse Education Today.
Doi: http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2013.03.012.
In the clinical setting, critical thinking involves the use of scientific
knowledge and the nursing process to consider a person’s particular
situation and make clinical judgments about what to do in that
context. Nurses need to develop their thinking and reasoning skills in
order to meet the patient’s and family’s caring needs in collaboration
with other health care professionals (Popil (2011) cited in Azizi-Fini,
Hajibagheri & Adib-Hajbaghery ).
2 Azizi-Fini, I., Hajibagheri, A. & Adib-Hajbaghery, M. (2015). Critical thinking skills in nursing
students: A comparison between freshmen and senior students. Nursing and Midwifery
Studies, 4(1), e25721.
1
2


Nurses use knowledge from other
disciplines to enhance their
critical-thinking skills
As nurses respond holistically to human needs, they must draw
meaningful information from other subject areas (i.e. interdisciplinary
connections) in order to understand the meaning of data and to plan
effective interventions. Nursing curricula often includes biological and
social sciences as well as the humanities so that nurses can acquire
a strong foundation on which to build their professional knowledge
and skills. For example, the nurse might use knowledge from
nutrition, physiology and physics to promote wound healing and
prevent further injury to a person with a pressure ulcer; or draw from
psychology and sociology to provide effective, culturally competent
care.
Nurses need critical-thinking skills
to respond to dynamic clinical
environments
Nurses work in a variety of settings such as hospital wards,
emergency departments and community health facilities. Many of


these environments are associated with rapidly changing situations.
Further to this, treatments, medications and technology change
constantly and a person’s condition may change from minute to
minute. Routine actions may therefore not be adequate to respond
to the situation at hand. Familiarity with the routine for giving
medications, for example, does not help the nurse care for a person
who is frightened of injections or someone who does not wish to
take a medication. When unexpected situations arise, critical
thinking enables the nurse to recognise important cues, reflect on
past similar experiences, draw on their diverse knowledge bank,
respond quickly and adapt interventions to meet a person’s specific
needs.
Nurses need critical-thinking skills
to inform their clinical decisions
Nurses use critical thinking and judgment to collect and interpret
relevant information needed to make decisions, often in complex
and rapidly changing situations. They must use good judgment, for
example, to decide which observations must be reported to the
doctor immediately and which can be noted in the person’s record
for the doctor to address later. Critical thinking should also be
informed by relevant health care policies, local protocols and the
advice of clinical experts such as clinical nurse consultants.


Practice guidelines
Critical thinking and analysis
The Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) has
developed the Registered Nurse Standards for Practice
(NMBA ) which specify that nurses must critically think about
patient care and have the skills to contribute to evidence-
based care through application of research in practice.
3 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016). Registered Nurse
Standards for Practice. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Critical thinking and analysis (see below) is the first of the
seven Standards for Practice (NMBA 2016). It relates to self-
appraisal, professional development and the value of
evidence and research for practice.
Standard 1: Thinks critically and
analyses nursing practice
RNs use a variety of thinking strategies and the best available
evidence in making decisions and providing safe, quality
nursing practice within person-centred and evidence-based
frameworks.

Skills in critical thinking
Complex mental processes such as analysis, synthesis, problem
solving and decision making require the use of critical-thinking skills
(Parker ) such as reflection, creativity, critical analysis, clinical
reasoning, divergent thinking and clarifying, making valid inferences,
differentiating facts from opinions, evaluating the credibility of
information sources, clarifying concepts and recognising
assumptions.
4 Parker, S. (2017). Becoming a critical thinker. In J. Daly, S. Speedy & D. Jackson (Eds),
Contexts of Nursing (5th ed.). Australia: Elsevier.
Reflection
Intrinsic to learning and professional nursing practice is critical
reflection. This process is not merely introspection but a deliberate,
orderly and structured activity. Reflection is the key to learning from
nursing practice; it enables nurses to process their experiences,
explore their understanding of their actions and evaluate their
experiences. Reflection involves evaluating the outcomes of nursing
care interventions and is essential to clinical reasoning and the ability
to provide safe and holistic nursing care (NMBA 2016).
4


Creativity
Creativity
 is a major component of critical thinking as it allows
nurses to identify unique solutions to unique problems. Creativity in
problem solving and decision making is the ability to develop and
implement new and improved solutions. Creativity is required when
the nurse encounters a new situation or a situation in which
traditional interventions have not been effective. For example, a
paediatric nurse is caring for a 9-year-old girl who has ineffective
breathing following abdominal surgery. The doctor has ordered
incentive spirometry (a treatment device that promotes alveolar
expansion). The child is frightened by the equipment and tires
quickly during the treatments. The nurse offers her a bottle of soapy
water and a blowing wand. She is delighted with blowing bubbles.
The nurse knows that the respiratory effort in blowing bubbles will
promote alveolar expansion and suggests that the child blow
bubbles between incentive spirometry treatments.
Creative thinkers must have knowledge of the problem. They must
have assessed the present problem and be knowledgeable about
the underlying facts and principles that apply. For example, in the
previous situation, the paediatric nurse knew the anatomy and
physiology of respiratory function and was aware of the purpose of
incentive spirometry. The nurse also understood paediatric growth
and development. In trying to assist the child, the nurse built on this
knowledge and came up with a creative solution. Using creativity,
nurses:


can generate news ideas rapidly
are flexible and are able to change perspectives or directions in
thinking quickly and easily
create original solutions to problems
tend to be independent and self-confident, even when under
pressure.
Critical analysis
Critical analysis
 is the application of a set of questions to a
particular situation or idea to determine relevant from irrelevant
information and ideas. Nurses can use a number of key questions in
critical analysis. Not all questions will need to be applied to every
situation, but nurses must be familiar with all the questions in order
to choose those questions that are appropriate to a given situation.
Socrates (c.470–399 BC) was a Greek philosopher who developed
the Socratic method of questioning. Box 11.1
 lists some Socratic
questions that can be used in critical analysis. Socratic
questioning
 is a technique that can be used to look beneath the
surface, recognise and examine assumptions, search for
inconsistencies, examine multiple points of view, and differentiate
what a person knows from what they merely believe. Nurses should
employ Socratic questioning when listening to an end-of-shift report,
reviewing a person’s history or progress notes, planning care or
discussing a person’s care with colleagues.


BO X
11.1 Socratic questioning
Questions about the question (or problem)
Is this question clear, understandable and correctly
identified?
Is this question important?
Could this question be broken down into smaller parts?
Can you rephrase the question?
Questions about assumptions
You seem to be assuming?
Please explain why?
Can you verify or prove your assumption?
Questions about point of view
What would someone who disagrees with your
perspective say?
Can you see this any other way?
Questions about evidence and reasons
What evidence do you have for that?


Is there any reason to doubt that evidence?
How do you know?
Would your evidence hold up in court?
What would change your mind?
Questions about implications and
consequences
What effect would that have?
What is the probability that will actually happen?
Are there any alternatives?
What are the implications of that?
Reasoning
Two other critical-thinking skills are inductive and deductive
reasoning. In inductive reasoning
, generalisations are formed
from a set of facts or observations. When viewed together, pieces of
information indicate a particular interpretation. Inductive reasoning
moves from specific examples (premises) to a generalised
conclusion—for example, after touching several hot flames
(premise), we conclude that all flames are hot. A nurse who
observes a person who has dry skin, poor turgor, sunken eyes and
dark amber urine, and who is dehydrated (premise), concludes that


the presence of those signs indicates dehydration in other
individuals.
Deductive reasoning
, by contrast, is reasoning from the general
premise to the specific conclusion. If you begin with the premise that
the sum of the angles in any triangle is always 180 degrees, you can
then conclude that the sum of the angles in the triangle you happen
to have is also 180 degrees. A nurse might start with a premise that
all Australian children love Vegemite sandwiches. This is an example
in which the premise is not always valid and, thus, the conclusion
may not be valid. Nurses use critical thinking to help analyse
situations and establish which premises are valid.
Divergent thinking and clarifying
In critical thinking, the nurse differentiates between statements of
fact, inference, judgment and opinion. Table 11.1
 shows how
these may be applied. Evaluating the credibility of information
sources is an important step in critical thinking. Unfortunately, we
cannot always believe what we read or are told. The nurse may
need to ascertain the accuracy of information by checking other
documents or checking with other informants as effective
communication and documentation are critical to patient safety
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care ).
5 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (2017). National Safety and
Quality Health Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
5


Table 11.1 Differentiating types of statements
To comprehend a situation clearly, the nurse and person must agree
on the meaning of terms. For example, if the person says to the
nurse, ‘I haven’t broken my arm, the doctor said it’s a fracture’, the
nurse needs to clarify what the word fracture means to the person
and explain that the two words have the same meaning in this
situation.
People commonly live their lives under certain assumptions. Inherent
values, biases, attitudes and beliefs of a nurse can potentially
negatively affect care. Difficulty arises when people do not take the
time to consider what assumptions underlie their attitudes, values,
beliefs and actions. It is essential for a nurse to have self-awareness
and insight into their own personal beliefs, attitudes and values to
ensure that they do not negatively influence the care they provide.


Attitudes for critical thinking
Certain attitudes are believed to be crucial to critical thinking. These
attitudes are based on the presumption that a rational person is
motivated to develop, learn and grow. There are many things to
consider when thinking critically, including the purpose of the
thinking; the nurse’s current level of knowledge, biases, assumptions
and personal values, and beliefs influencing the nurse’s thinking; and
what information is required from other sources. As well, nurses
must be able to identify all the possible options, evaluate the
alternatives and reach a conclusion. Nurses must have the following
attitudes and traits: independence/interdependence, fair-
mindedness, insight, intellectual humility, intellectual courage,
curiosity, integrity, perseverance, confidence and, importantly,
reflection.
Independence and
interdependence
Critical thinking requires both autonomous and interdependent
thinking. Interdependent thinking is essential to interprofessional
health care and the ability to work as a team to make judgments and


decisions collaboratively, particularly in complex and dynamic
situations (Turpin & Higgs ).
6 Turpin, M. & Higgs, J. (2017). Clinical reasoning and evidence-based practice. In T.
Hoffmann, S. Bennett & C. Del Mar (Eds), Evidence-based Practice across the Health
Professions (3rd ed.). Sydney: Churchill Livingstone, Elsevier.
Fair-mindedness
According to Paul and Elder , critical thinkers are fair-minded,
assessing all viewpoints with the same standards and not basing
their judgments on personal or group bias or prejudice. Fair-
mindedness helps a person to consider opposing points of view and
try to understand new ideas and evidence fully before rejecting or
accepting them. Critical thinkers are open to the possibility that new
evidence could change their minds.
7 Paul, R. & Elder, L. (2009). Critical thinking: Ethical reasoning and fairminded thinking, part
1. Journal of Developmental Education, 33(1), 38–39.
Insight
Critical thinkers are aware that personal biases or social pressures
and customs can affect their thinking. They actively try to examine
their own biases and bring them to awareness when making a
decision. For example, a nurse spends extensive time trying to
6
7


teach a person in their care how to prevent a future recurrence of
some problem but is mystified when the person appears
disinterested and does not follow the advice provided. The nurse’s
tendency to assume that all people are motivated and interested in
preventive care (because the nurse is) has resulted in an inaccurate
assessment of the person’s desire to learn; and both the nurse’s
and the individual’s time has been wasted. Had the nurse assessed
the person’s background and beliefs about the problem and
collected sufficient evidence, the nurse might have identified a
problem more relevant to the person’s priorities and, thus,
developed a better care plan.
Critical thinking requires a sense of balance and understanding of a
situation. Nurses need to be curious about what happens in
particular situations and their part in it. For example, they need to
ask themselves, ‘What were the steps in my thinking as I engaged in
that episode of care?’. This approach helps nurses to be alert to how
their beliefs, values and biases inform their thinking about the
nursing care they provide.
Intellectual humility
Intellectual humility means having an awareness of the limits of a
person’s own knowledge. Critical thinkers are willing to admit what
they do not know; they are willing to seek new information and to
rethink their conclusions in light of new knowledge. They never
assume that what everybody believes to be right will always be right,


because new evidence may emerge. A nurse might be unable to
imagine how the older woman will care for her husband who has
recently had a stroke. However, the nurse also recognises that it is
not really possible to know what the couple can achieve.
Intellectual courage
Courage is needed to change the status quo and move away from
‘ritual’ practice. For example, many nurses previously believed that
allowing family members to observe an emergency, such as
cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), would be psychologically
harmful to the family. However, research has demonstrated that
family presence during CPR is associated with positive results on
psychological variables and does not interfere with medical efforts or
increase stress in the health care team (Jabre et al. ).
8 Jabre, P., Belpomme, V., Azoulay, E., Jacob, L., Bertrand, L., Lapostolle, F., . . . Adnet, F.
(2013). Family presence during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. New England Journal of
Medicine, 368(11), 1008–1018.
Curiosity
The curious nurse has the courage to examine traditions to be sure
they are still valid. Ask these questions: Why do we believe this?
What causes that? Does it have to be this way? Could something
8


else work? What would happen if we did it another way? Who says
that is so?
Integrity
Critical thinkers question any inconsistencies in their own knowledge
and beliefs as quickly and thoroughly as they challenge those of
another person. To have integrity in nursing practice involves
embracing new evidence and adapting practice.
Perseverance
Nurses who are critical thinkers show perseverance in finding
effective solutions to nursing problems. This determination enables
them to clarify concepts and sort out related issues in spite of
difficulties and frustrations. Critical thinkers resist the temptation to
find a quick and easy answer. Important questions tend to be
complex and confusing, and often require a great deal of thought
and research to arrive at an answer.
Confidence


Critical thinkers believe that well-reasoned thinking will lead to
trustworthy and confident conclusions, and they often ask questions
such as: Is that argument fair? Is it based on sufficient evidence?
The critical thinker develops skill in both inductive reasoning and
deductive reasoning. As the nurse gains greater awareness of the
thinking process and more experience in improving such thinking,
confidence in the process will grow.


Applying critical thinking to nursing
practice
Not all decisions require in-depth crucial thinking, and many small
decisions are based primarily on habit with minimal thinking involved.
Such examples include selecting what uniform to wear, choosing
which route to take to work, and deciding what to eat for lunch.
Higher-order critical-thinking and clinical-reasoning skills are needed
when a new idea is encountered or a non-routine decision must be
made.
The phases of the nursing process
—assessing, diagnosing,
planning, implementing and evaluating—provide a systematic and
rational method of planning and care (see Table 11.2
). This
involves a cycle of comprehensive assessment of the person,
identification of actual and potential problems from this data,
designing interventions and providing rationales for each, organising
these interventions and applying them to the person, evaluating the
success of the care provided and altering necessary aspects. Each
phase is dependent on the accuracy of the other phases and relies
on critical thinking.

application to a clinical example of critical thinking are shown in

. This demonstrates the use of critical thinking with
individuals. In addition, a nurse often employs critical thinking when
setting priorities for the day, working with groups and dealing with
situations or critical incidents.
Table 11.3 Applying critical thinking to the nursing process
Problem solving
In problem solving
, the nurse obtains information that clarifies
the nature of the problem and suggests possible solutions. Possible
solutions, however, require an understanding of the person or people
being cared for, including their strengths, resources and resilience. It
also involves an assessment of the nurse’s own strengths, those of
the multidisciplinary team, other resources at hand and, importantly,
the credibility of evidence available. Only then is the nurse able to
carefully evaluate the possible solutions and choose the best one to
implement. The situation is carefully monitored over time to ensure
its initial and continued effectiveness. The nurse does not discard
the other solutions but holds them in reserve in the event that the
first solution is not effective. The nurse may also encounter a similar
problem with a different set of strengths and resources in different
situations where an alternative solution is determined to be the most
effective. Therefore, problem solving and strength/resource


identification for one situation may contribute to the nurse’s body of
knowledge for problem solving in similar situations.
Patient safety competency framework
5 Clinical reasoning
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must know that,
when engaged in clinical reasoning, nurses refer
to a range of patient data, including handover
reports, medical records, the person’s social
and medical history and evidence-based
guidelines, as well as eliciting the person’s
concerns and understanding of the situation
(Levett-Jones et al. ).
9 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Decision making
9


Decision making
 is a critical-thinking process for choosing the
best actions to meet a desired goal. Decisions must be made
whenever several mutually exclusive choices are available or when
there is an option to act or not.
Nurses make decisions in the course of solving problems. Decision
making, however, is also used in situations that do not involve
problem solving. Nurses often do the following:
make value decisions (e.g. to keep the person’s information
confidential)
make time-management decisions (e.g. taking clean linen to the
person’s room at the same time as the medication in order to
save steps)
make scheduling decisions (e.g. to bathe the person before
visiting hours)
make priority decisions (e.g. which interventions are most urgent
and which can be delegated)
make decisions for building strengths and resources (such as
improving social, networking and communication skills, family
bonding and so on).
Nurses must make decisions and assist and encourage individuals
to make decisions. When faced with several people’s needs at the
same time, the nurse must prioritise and decide which person to
assist first. The nurse may:
look at advantages and disadvantages of each option


apply Maslow’s hierarchy of needs (see Figure 17.3
 on page
284) (Maslow )
10 Maslow, A. H. (1968). Towards a Psychology of Being (2nd ed.). New Jersey:
Princeton.
consider which tasks can be delegated to others
use another priority-setting framework.
When a person is trying to make a decision about what course of
treatment to follow, the nurse may need to provide them with
information, resources and guidance. Table 11.4
 outlines the
sequential steps involved in the decision-making process.

nurse uses critical thinking in each step or phase of these processes
so that decisions and care are well considered and delivered with the
highest possible quality.

Developing critical-thinking skills
Some people make better evaluations than others do; some people
believe information from nearly any source; and others seldom
believe anything without carefully evaluating the credibility of the
information. Critical thinking is not easy. Solving problems, identifying
and harnessing strengths and making decisions are risky.
Sometimes the outcome is not what was desired. With effort,
however, everyone can improve their critical-thinking skills to
become an effective problem solver and decision maker.
Self-assessment
The nurse should consider some of the attitudes discussed earlier
that facilitate critical thinking, such as curiosity, fair-mindedness,
humility, courage and perseverance.
Reflection at every step of critical thinking and nursing care helps
the nurse examine the ways in which they gather and analyse data,
make decisions and determine the effectiveness of interventions.
Reflection requires the nurse to assess their beliefs, knowledge,
values, attitudes and abilities in the particular situation at hand. The
purpose of this reflection is to determine if the current course of
action is the best one and to improve future actions. Figure 11.1


‘Mind map for critical thinking in nursing’ is a visual depiction of the
interactive loops of concepts used in critical thinking.

Tolerance
The nurse needs to take deliberate efforts to cultivate critical-
thinking attitudes. For example, to develop fair-mindedness a nurse
could deliberately seek out information that is in opposition to their
own views; this provides practice in understanding and learning to be
open to other viewpoints. Nurses should increase their tolerance for
ideas that contradict previously held beliefs and they should practise
suspending judgment until ambiguity is explored, evidence properly
examined and a solution proposed on that basis.
Creating supportive environments
11


Nurses in leadership positions must be particularly aware of the
climate for thinking that they establish, and they must actively create
a stimulating environment that encourages differences of opinion
and fair examination of ideas, evidence and options. Nurses must
embrace exploration of the perspectives of people from different
ages, cultures, religions, socioeconomic levels and family structures.
Lifespan considerations
Health care decisions
Children
Parents most often make decisions about the health care of
children. Growing children can participate in those decisions
in age-appropriate ways. The ability of children to reason and
critically think about themselves and their situation develops
gradually. At each stage, nurses should be aware of the ways
children think and be sensitive as to how they can be involved
in health care decisions:
Infants progress from reflexive behaviour to simple,
repetitive behaviour and then to imitative behaviours,
learning the concepts of cause and effect and object
permanence. Although not involved in making decisions,
they need to be comforted and secure as care is given.


Toddlers and preschoolers are very egocentric and
engage in magical thinking. They cannot reason out the
implications of care but need explanations in language
they can understand. Play therapy and use of dolls and
toys can help them adjust to care, and they can
sometimes be given options (e.g. ‘Do you want your
dressing changed before breakfast or after?’).
School-age children tend to be concrete thinkers. They
benefit from simple, direct explanations; hands-on
exploration of equipment and materials; and helping the
care provider as appropriate during procedures. Involving
these children in care can increase cooperation and
decrease anxiety.
Adolescents are increasingly able to think abstractly and
may make many of their own health care decisions. They
should be actively consulted as a part of the family
system.
Older adults
It is important to include all adults in decision making and
planning nursing care, but it is especially difficult to do this
when working with older adults who have impaired cognitive
abilities, such as those with Alzheimer’s disease. The nurse
should allow them as much control and input as possible,
keeping things simple and direct so they understand. Older
adults with impairments are usually unable to perform
multiple tasks or even to think of more than one step at a


time. Keeping things simple (one step at a time) and direct to
maximise understanding is important in allowing some degree
of independence. The nurse must have patience, show
respect and dignity, and be willing to calmly repeat
instructions if necessary. Presenting and discussing issues in
basic terms helps to maintain respect and dignity, and allows
older adults to participate in their own care for as long as
possible. If the older person is unable to perform self-care
activities such as bathing or health-related activities such as a
dressing change, the nurse should seek appropriate
alternative methods for assisting the older adult with these.
Case study
Mr Williams is a 53-year-old recently retired engineer with a
history of irritable bowel syndrome that causes frequent
diarrhoea and rectal bleeding. It is mid-December when he
comes to your clinic complaining about ‘not feeling good’. You
conclude his intestinal problem is recurring.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. What questions would you ask yourself to check this
assumption?
2.
 What questions would you ask Mr Williams in
relation to his physical fundamental needs to check
this assumption?


3. How would you demonstrate that you are using the
critical-thinking attitude of ‘confidence in reasoning’?
4. What are the implications of your thinking? Consider
the implications if you are correct and if you are
incorrect in your assumption.
5. Critical thinkers look for subtle cues. Which cues in this
situation require follow-up?


Chapter 11 Review


Chapter highlights
Nurses need critical-thinking skills and attitudes to be safe,
competent, skilful practitioners.
Critical thinking is a process that guides a nurse in generating,
implementing and evaluating approaches for dealing with person
care and professional concepts.
Nurses use critical thinking as they apply knowledge from other
subjects and fields to nursing practice, deal with change in
stressful environments and make important decisions related to
health care. When nurses incorporate creativity into their
thinking, they are able to find unique solutions to unique
problems.
Creativity enhances critical thinking. Creative nurses generate
many ideas rapidly, are flexible and natural, create original
solutions to problems, tend to be independent but acknowledge
interdependence, and are self-confident.
Critical-thinking skills include the ability to perform critical
analyses, perform inductive and deductive reasoning, make valid
inferences, differentiate facts from opinions, evaluate the
credibility of information sources, clarify concepts and recognise
assumptions.
Critical thinkers have the attitudes of independence, inter-
dependence, fair-mindedness, insight, intellectual humility,
intellectual courage to challenge the status quo and rituals,
integrity, perseverance, confidence and curiosity.


Critical thinking consists of high-level cognitive processes that
include problem solving, strength resource identification and
harnessing, and decision making. There are several problem-
solving methods: trial and error, intuition, the nursing process,
the scientific method and the modified scientific method. Nurses
use the scientific method or research process when they
participate in nursing and health research.
The nursing process and critical thinking are interrelated and
interdependent but they are not identical. Both involve problem
solving, strength and resource recognition, decision making and
creativity.
Steps of the decision-making process used by nurses include
identifying the purpose of the decision, setting the criteria,
weighting the criteria, seeking alternatives, examining
alternatives, projecting, implementing and evaluating the action.
Concept check
1. A person with diarrhoea also has a doctor’s order for a bulk
laxative daily. The nurse, not realising that bulk laxatives can
help solidify certain types of diarrhoea, concludes: ‘The doctor
does not know the person has diarrhoea’. This statement is
an example of:
1. A fact.
2. An inference.
3. A judgment.
4. An opinion.


2. A person reports feeling hungry but does not eat when food is
served. Using critical-thinking skills, the nurse should perform
which of the following?
1. Assess why the person is not ingesting the food
provided.
2. Continue to leave the food at the bedside until the
person is hungry enough to eat.
3. Notify the doctor that tube feeding may be indicated
soon.
4. Believe the person is not really hungry.
3. Although one nurse feels the manager prepared the holiday
work schedule unfairly, the manager states that it is the same
type of schedule used in the past and other nurses have no
problems with it. The nurse continues to feel uncomfortable
about how the schedule was created. Which response
indicates the nurse is displaying an attitude of critical
thinking?
1. Accepting the preferences of the other nurses because
there are several of them.
2. Recognising that the nurse must have reached a false
conclusion.
3. Considering going to a higher authority than the
manager for an explanation.
4. Continuing to query the manager until the nurse
understands the explanation.


4. The person who is short of breath benefits from the head of
the bed being elevated. As this position can result in skin
breakdown in the sacral area, the nurse decides to study the
amount of sacral pressure occurring in other positions. This
decision is an example of which of the following?
1. The scientific method.
2. The trial-and-error method.
3. Intuition.
4. The nursing process.
5. In the decision-making process, the nurse sets and weights
the criteria, examines alternatives and performs which of the
following before implementing the plan?
1. Re-examines the purpose for making the decision.
2. Consults the person and family members to determine
their view of the criteria.
3. Identifies and considers various means for reaching
the outcomes.
4. Determines the logical course of action should
intervening problems arise.
Focus on critical thinking
1. Consider the many, varied roles in nursing. Why is critical
thinking an essential element of nursing practice?
2. What do you think are the core components of critical
thinking? Why?


3. How would you prepare to care for a new patient? Consider
why you would choose this approach.
4. In your own words, describe the cyclical nature of the nursing
process and how critical thinking is involved in this.
