The nursing process is a dynamic, systematic
and cyclical process of problem solving in
clinical practice. The purpose of the nursing
process is to identify and assess a person’s
health status and actual or potential health care
problems/needs/strengths, to establish plans to
meet the identified needs, to deliver specific
nursing interventions to meet those needs and
to evaluate the care provided. A key feature of
the nursing process is that it focuses not only on
ways to improve the person’s physical needs,
but also on social, cultural, emotional and
spiritual needs. The nursing process is therefore
person centred, interpersonal, collaborative and
universally applicable.
Person-centred communication has been linked
to better adherence to treatment regimens and
improved health outcomes (Iedema & Manidis ).
Person-centred care encompasses qualities of
compassion, empathy and responsiveness to
the needs, values and expressed preferences of
the individual person (Australian Commission on
Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) ).
Person-centred care also means forming
1
2


partnerships between the person, their family,
carers and health care providers.
1 Iedema, R. & Manidis, M. (2013). Patient-Clinician
Communication: An Overview of Relevant Research and
Policy Literatures. Sydney: Australian Commission on
Safety and Quality in Health Care and UTS Centre for
Health Communication.
2 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health
Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Patient safety competency
framework
1 Person-centred care
The Patient Safety
Competency Framework
indicates that nursing
students must demonstrate
person-centred care by
providing holistic care that


takes into account the
person’s current situation,
previous experiences and
life history (Levett-Jones et
al. ).
3 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T.,
Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L.,
Flenady, T., Applegarth, J.,
Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017).
Patient Safety Competency
Framework (PSCF) for Nursing
Students. Sydney. Retrieved from

m>.
3


Overview of the nursing process
The use of the nursing process in clinical practice is embedded in
the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia’s  Registered Nurse
Standards for Practice, specifically Domain 5: Develops a plan for
nursing practice. The nursing process directs nurses to assess,
diagnose, plan, implement and evaluate nursing care in collaboration
with individuals and the interprofessional healthcare team, so as to
achieve goals and improve health outcomes. See Figure 12.1
 for
an illustration of the nursing process in action.
4 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (2016). Registered Nurse Standards for Practice.
Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Figure 12.1
4


The nursing process in action.
Images source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Each phase of the nursing process is interrelated and affects the
others. For example, if inadequate data are obtained during the
assessment phase, the nursing diagnosis will be incomplete or
incorrect; inaccuracy will also be reflected in the planning,
implementing and evaluation phases. The components of the
nursing process follow a logical sequence, but more than one
component may be involved at one time. At the end of the first
cycle, care may be terminated if goals are achieved, the cycle may
continue with reassessment or the plan of care may be modified to
meet a person’s changing needs.
Phases of the nursing process
An overview of the five-phase nursing process is shown in
Table 12.1
. Each of the five phases is discussed in depth in this
and subsequent chapters. The phases of the nursing process are
not separate entities but overlapping, continuing subprocesses (see
Figure 12.2
). For example, assessing, which may be considered
the first phase of the nursing process, is also carried out during the
implementing and evaluating phases. For example, while actually
administering medications (implementing), the nurse may also
observe the person’s ability to swallow and communicate.
Table 12.1 Overview of the nursing process


Figure 12.2


The five overlapping phases of the nursing process. Each phase
depends on the accuracy of the other phases. Each phase involves
critical thinking.
Characteristics of the nursing
process
The nursing process has distinctive characteristics that enable the
nurse to respond to the person’s changing health status. These
characteristics include its cyclical and dynamic nature, person
centredness, focus on problem solving and decision making,
interpersonal and collaborative style, universal applicability and use
of critical thinking.
Data from each phase provide input into the next phase. Findings
from evaluation feed back into assessment. Hence, the nursing
process is a regularly repeated event or sequence of events (a
cycle) that is continuously changing (dynamic) rather than
staying the same (static).
The nursing process is person centred. The nurse organises the
plan of care in partnership with, and according to, the person’s
needs and strengths rather than nurse-initiated goals. In the
assessment phase, the nurse collects data to understand the
person’s habits, health beliefs, routines and needs. This practice
enables the nurse to incorporate the person’s lifestyle and
routines into the care plan as much as possible.


The nursing process is an adaptation of problem solving (see
Chapter 11
) and systems theory (see Chapter 25
). It can
be viewed as parallel to, but separate from, the process used by
doctors. Both processes (a) begin with data gathering and
analysis, (b) base action (intervention or treatment) on a problem
statement (nursing diagnosis or medical diagnosis), and (c)
include an evaluative component. Interprofessional health care
means that all health care professionals are focused on the
provision of person-centred care. However, the medical model
focuses primarily on physiological systems and the disease
processes, whereas the nursing process is directed towards a
person’s responses to disease and illness.
Decision making is involved in every phase of the nursing
process. Nursing practice is informed by the principles of
evidence-based practice; however, nurses can be creative in
determining when and how to use data to make decisions. While
they are bound by standards of practice, in practising person-
centred care nurses apply their repertoire of skills and knowledge
to meet the person’s needs by designing individualised care
plans.
The nursing process is interpersonal and collaborative. It requires
the nurse to communicate directly and consistently with
individuals and their families to meet their needs. It also requires
that nurses collaborate, as members of the healthcare team, in a
joint effort to provide quality care.
The universally applicable characteristics of the nursing process
mean that it is useful as a framework for nursing care in all types
of health care settings with people of all age groups.


Nurses use a variety of critical-thinking skills during the nursing
process to develop and guide a plan of care for the person,
incorporating evidence-based practice concepts. Table 12.2
provides examples of critical thinking in the nursing process (see
also Chapter 11
).
Table 12.2 Examples of critical thinking in the nursing process

reproduced by permission of Pearson Education, Inc., Upper Saddle River, New Jersey. ISBN: 9780132242868,.
p. 67.

River, NJ: Prentice Hall.

Assessing
Assessing
 is the systematic and continuous collection,
organisation, validation and documentation of data
 (information).
It is undertaken during all phases of the nursing process. For
example, in the evaluation phase, assessment is done to determine
the effectiveness of nursing actions and to evaluate whether specific
patient care goals have been achieved. There are different types of
assessments including: initial assessment, problem-focused
assessment, emergency assessment and time-lapsed reassessment
(see Table 12.3
). Assessments vary according to their purpose,
timing, time available and the status of the person.
Table 12.3 Types of assessment
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: Comprehensive care
The National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards advocate that each person has an
initial assessment consisting of a history and
physical examination performed and
documented on presentation and when required
during hospitalisation (ACSQHC 2017, p. 42).


Nursing assessments focus on examining a person’s responses to a
health problem and should include the person’s perceived needs,
health problems, related experience, health practices, values and
lifestyle. To be most useful, the data collected should be relevant to
a particular health problem. Therefore, nurses need to think critically
about what to assess.
The assessment process involves four closely related activities:
collecting data, organising data, validating data and documenting
data (see Figure 12.3
).
Figure 12.3


Assessing. The assessment process involves four closely related
activities.
Collecting data
Data collection is the process of gathering information about a
person’s health status; it includes the nursing health history (see
Box 12.1
), physical assessment and physical examination
findings, results of laboratory and diagnostic tests, and material
contributed by other health personnel.
BO X
12.1 Components of a nursing health
history
Biographical data
The person’s name, language/s spoken, address, age, sex,
marital status, next of kin, occupation, religious preference,
health insurance and general practitioner or usual source of
medical care.
Chief complaint or reason for visit


The answer given to the question ‘What is troubling you?’ or
‘Can you tell me the reason you came to the hospital or clinic
today?’. The chief complaint should be recorded in the
person’s own words.
History of present illness
Ask:
When did the symptoms start?
Was the onset of symptoms sudden or gradual?
How often does the problem occur?
Where is the exact location of the distress?
What is the character of the complaint (e.g. intensity of
pain or quality of sputum, emesis or discharge)?
What, if any, activity was the person involved in when the
problem occurred?
What phenomena or symptoms are associated with the
chief complaint?
What factors aggravate or alleviate the problem?
History
Childhood illnesses, such as chickenpox, mumps,
measles, rubella (German measles), streptococcal
infections, scarlet fever, rheumatic fever and other
significant illnesses.
Childhood immunisations and the date of the last tetanus,
flu vaccination, others.


Allergies to drugs, animals, insects or other environmental
agents, the type of reaction that occurs and how the
reaction is treated.
Accidents and injuries: how, when and where the incident
occurred, type of injury, treatment received and any
complications.
Hospitalisation for serious illnesses: reasons for the
hospitalisation, dates, surgery performed, course of
recovery and any complications.
Medications: all currently used prescription and over-the-
counter medications, such as ‘pain killers’ (e.g. Panadol),
nasal spray, vitamins, tonics, laxatives or herbal remedies;
medicines prescribed by a complementary therapist.
Family history of illness
To identify risk factors for certain diseases, the ages of
siblings, parents and grandparents and their current state of
health or, if they are deceased, the cause of death are
obtained. Particular attention should be given to disorders
such as heart disease, cancer, diabetes, hypertension,
obesity, allergies, arthritis, tuberculosis, bleeding, alcoholism
and any mental health disorders.
Lifestyle
Personal habits: ask about substance use; if yes, ask
the amount, frequency and duration of substance use


(tobacco, alcohol, coffee, cola, tea, caffeinated energy
drinks, and illicit or recreational drugs).
Diet: description of a typical diet on a normal day or any
special diet, number of meals and snacks per day, who
cooks and shops for food, culturally distinct food patterns
and allergies.
Sleep/rest patterns: usual daily sleep/wake times,
difficulties sleeping and remedies used for difficulties.
Activities of daily living (ADLs): any difficulties
experienced in the basic activities of eating, grooming,
dressing, elimination and mobility.
Instrumental activities of daily living: any difficulties
experienced in food preparation, shopping, transportation,
housekeeping, laundry and ability to use the telephone,
handle finances and manage medications.
Recreation/hobbies: exercise activity and tolerance,
hobbies and other interests, and holidays.
Social data
Family relationships/friendships: who the person lives
with; the person’s support system in times of stress (who
helps in time of need?); what effect the person’s illness
has on the family and whether any family problems are
affecting the person. See also the discussion of family
assessment in Chapter 25
.
Cultural affiliation: health customs and beliefs; cultural
practices that may affect health care and recovery. See


also cultural assessment considerations in Chapter 19
.
Educational history: data about the person’s highest
level of education attained and any past difficulties with
learning or reading.
Occupational history: current employment status, the
number of days missed from work because of illness, any
history of accidents on the job, any occupational hazards
with a potential for future disease or accident, the
person’s need to change jobs because of past illness, the
employment status of spouses or partners and the way
child care is handled, and the person’s overall satisfaction
with the work.
Economic status: information about how the person is
paying for medical care (including what kind of health
insurance the person has) and whether the person’s
illness presents financial concerns.
Home and neighbourhood conditions: home safety
measures and adjustments in physical facilities that may
be required to help the person manage a physical
disability, activity intolerance and activities of daily living;
the availability of neighbourhood and community services
to meet the person’s needs.
Psychological data
Major stressors experienced and the person’s perception
of them.


Usual coping pattern with a serious problem or a high
level of stress.
Communication style: ability to voice appropriate emotion;
non-verbal communication—such as eye movements,
gestures, use of touch and posture; interactions with
support people; and the congruence between non-verbal
behaviour and verbal expression.
Patterns of health care
All health care resources the person is currently using and
has used in the past. These include the general practitioner,
specialists (e.g. ophthalmologist or gynaecologist), dentist,
alternative or complementary practitioners (e.g. herbalist,
Ayurvedic practitioner or acupuncturist), traditional cultural
healers (e.g. Ngangkari), health clinic or health centre;
whether the person considers the care being provided
adequate; and whether access to health care is a problem.
The person’s data should include past history as well as current
problems. For example, a history of an allergic reaction to penicillin
is a vital piece of historical data. Past surgical procedures,
alternative or complementary medicines and health practices, and
chronic diseases are also examples of historical data. Current data
relate to present circumstances, such as pain, nausea, sleep
patterns and religious practices. To collect data accurately, both the
person and the nurse need to actively participate. Data can be of


subjective or objective and constant or variable types, and from a
primary or a secondary source.
Types of data
Subjective data
, also referred to as symptoms
, are apparent
only to the person affected and can be described or verified only by
that person. Itching, pain and feelings of worry are examples of
subjective data. Subjective data include the person’s sensations,
feelings, values, beliefs, attitudes and perception of personal health
status and life situation.
Objective data
, also referred to as signs
, are detectable by
an observer or can be measured or tested against an accepted
standard. They can be seen, heard, felt or smelled, and they are
obtained by observation or physical examination. For example, a
discolouration of the skin or a blood pressure reading is objective
data. During the physical examination, the nurse obtains objective
data to validate subjective data and to complete the assessment
phase of the nursing process. Examples of subjective and objective
data are shown in Table 12.4
.
Table 12.4 Examples of subjective and objective data
*Blood pressure obtained using an external cuff and manometer
may be considered secondary or indirect data since it does not
directly measure the pressure within the arteries.


Sources of data
Sources of data are primary or secondary. The person is the primary
source of data. Family members or other support people, other
health professionals, records and reports, laboratory and diagnostic
analyses and relevant literature are secondary or indirect sources.
All data from secondary sources should be validated if possible.
The person
The best source of data is usually the person who is the recipient of
care, unless the person is too ill, young or confused to communicate
clearly. The person can provide subjective data that no one else can
offer. Most often, primary data refers to statements made by the
person but also includes objective data that can be directly obtained
by the nurse from the person, such as gender. Some people cannot
or do not wish to provide accurate data.
Support people
Family members, friends and caregivers who know the person well
can often supplement or verify information provided to them. They
might convey information about the person’s response to illness, the
stresses the person was experiencing before the illness, family
attitudes on illness and health, and the person’s home environment.
Care must always be taken to respect the person’s privacy and
confidentiality. Where possible, permission should be sought from
the person to discuss their health concerns with others, including


family members. Particular care must be taken when seeking
information from support people about individuals who are culturally
and/or linguistically different from the nurse (see Chapter 19
 for a
detailed discussion).
Support people are an especially important source of data for a
person who is very young, unconscious or confused. In some cases
—where someone is physically or emotionally abused, for example
—the person giving information may wish to remain anonymous.
Before eliciting data from support people, the nurse should ensure
that the person, if mentally able, accepts such input. The nurse
should also indicate on the nursing history that the data were
obtained from a support person.
Information supplied by family members, significant others or other
health professionals is considered subjective if it is not based on
fact. If the person’s daughter says, ‘Dad is very confused today’,
that is secondary subjective data because it is an interpretation of
the father’s behaviour by the daughter. The nurse should attempt to
verify the reported confusion by interviewing the person directly.
However, if the daughter says, ‘Dad said he thought it was the year
1941 today’, that may be considered secondary objective data since
the daughter heard her father state this directly.
Clinical records
Clinical records include information documented by various
healthcare professionals. Clinical records also contain data regarding


the person’s language preferences, occupation, religion and marital
status. By reviewing such records before interviewing the person,
the nurse can avoid asking questions for which answers have
already been supplied. Repeated questioning can be stressful and
annoying, and cause concern about the lack of communication
between health professionals. Types of clinical records include
medical records, records of therapies and laboratory records.
Medical records (e.g. medical history, physical examination, surgical
report, progress notes and consultations undertaken by doctors) are
often a source of a person’s present and past health and illness
patterns. These records can provide nurses with information about
the person’s coping behaviours, health practices, previous illnesses
and allergies.
Records of therapies provided by other health professionals, such as
social workers, dietitians or physiotherapists, help the nurse obtain
relevant data already recorded about the person. For example, a
community nurse’s report on a person’s living conditions can also be
helpful to a nurse conducting a hospital-based assessment.
Laboratory records also provide pertinent health information. For
example, the determination of blood glucose level allows nurses to
monitor the administration of oral hypoglycaemic medications. Any
laboratory data about a person must be compared with the
diagnostic laboratory’s norms for that particular test and for the
person’s age, sex and other significant data. Diagnostic studies
commonly ordered are discussed in Chapter 35
.


The nurse must always consider the information in clinical records in
light of the present situation. For example, if the most recent
medical record is 10 years old, the person’s health practices and
coping behaviours are likely to have changed. Older people may
have numerous previous records. These are very useful and
contribute to a full understanding of the health history, especially if
the person’s memory is impaired.
Health care professionals
Because assessment is an ongoing process, verbal reports from
other health care professionals serve as additional sources of
information about a person’s health. Nurses, social workers, doctors,
Nurse Practitioners, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health
workers and physiotherapists, for example, may have information
from either previous or current contact with the person. Sharing
information between professionals is especially important to ensure
continuity of care when people are transferred to and from home
and health care services.
Data collection methods
The principal methods used to collect data are observing,
interviewing and examining. Observation occurs whenever the nurse
is in contact with the person or their support people. Interviewing is
used mainly while taking a nursing health history. Examining is the
major method used for a physical health assessment.


A nurse often uses all three methods simultaneously when
assessing people. For example, during the interview the nurse
observes, listens, asks questions and mentally retains information to
explore in the physical examination.
Observing
To observe is to gather data by using the senses. Observation is a
conscious, deliberate skill that is developed through effort and with
an organised approach. Examples of clinical data observed through
the senses are shown in Table 12.5
.
Table 12.5 Using the senses to observe clinical data
Observation has two aspects: (1) noticing the data; and
(2) selecting, organising and interpreting the data. A nurse who
observes that a person’s face is flushed should relate that
observation to findings such as body temperature, activity,
environmental temperature and blood pressure.
Errors can occur in selecting, organising and interpreting data; for
example, when a nurse overlooks certain signs, either because they
are unexpected or because they do not conform to preconceptions
about a person’s illness. Nurses often need to focus on specific data
in order not to be overwhelmed by a multitude of data. Observing,
therefore, involves distinguishing data in a meaningful manner. For
example, nurses caring for newborns learn to ignore the usual


sounds of machines in the nursery but respond quickly to an infant’s
cry or movement.
An experienced nurse is often able to attend to an intervention (e.g.
give a bed bath or monitor an intravenous infusion) and at the same
time make important observations (e.g. note a change in respiratory
status or skin colour). A beginning student must learn to make
observations and complete tasks simultaneously; this practice takes
time, patience and attention.
Nursing observations must be organised so that nothing significant is
missed. Most nurses develop a particular sequence for observing
events, usually focusing on the person first. For example, a nurse
may walk into a person’s room and observe, in the following order:
1. clinical signs of distress (e.g. pallor or flushing, laboured
breathing and behaviour indicating pain or emotional distress)
2. threats to the person’s safety, real or anticipated (e.g. a
lowered side rail)
3. the presence and functioning of associated equipment (e.g.
intravenous equipment and oxygen)
4. the immediate environment, including the people in it.
Interviewing
An interview
 is a planned communication or a conversation with
a purpose; for example, to get or give information, identify problems
of mutual concern, evaluate change, teach, provide support or


provide counselling or therapy. One example of the interview is the
nursing health history, which is a part of the nursing admission
assessment.
There are two approaches to interviewing: directive and non-
directive. The directive interview
 is highly structured and elicits
specific information. The nurse establishes the purpose of the
interview and controls the interview, at least at the outset. The
person responds to questions but may have limited opportunity to
ask questions or discuss concerns. Nurses frequently use directive
interviews to gather and to give information when time is limited (e.g.
in an emergency situation).
During a non-directive interview
, or rapport-building interview,
the nurse allows the person to control the purpose, subject matter
and pacing. Rapport
 is an understanding between two or more
people.
A combination of directive and non-directive approaches is usually
appropriate during the information-gathering interview. The nurse
begins by determining areas of concern for the person. If, for
example, a person expresses worry about surgery, the nurse pauses
to explore the person’s worry and to provide support. Simply noting
the worry, without dealing with it, can leave the impression that the
nurse does not care about the person’s concerns or dismisses them
as unimportant.
Types of interview questions


Questions are often classified as closed or open-ended. Closed
questions
, used in the directive interview, are restrictive and
generally require only ‘yes’ or ‘no’ or short factual answers giving
specific information. Closed questions often begin with ‘when’,
‘where’, ‘who’, ‘what’, ‘do (did, does)’ or ‘is (are, was)’. Examples of
closed questions are ‘What medication did you take?’, ‘Are you
having pain now? Show me where it is’, ‘How old are you?’, ‘When
did you fall?’. The highly stressed person and the person who has
difficulty communicating will find closed questions easier to answer
than open-ended questions.
Open-ended questions
 invite the person to discover and
explore, elaborate, clarify or illustrate their thoughts or feelings. An
open-ended question specifies only the broad topic to be discussed
and invites answers longer than one or two words. Such questions
give people the freedom to divulge only the information that they are
ready to disclose. The open-ended question is useful at the
beginning of an interview or to change topics and to elicit attitudes.
Open-ended questions may begin with ‘what’ or ‘how’. Examples of
open-ended questions are ‘How have you been feeling lately?’,
‘What brought you to the hospital?’, ‘How did you feel in that
situation?’, ‘Would you describe more about how you relate to your
child?’, ‘What would you like to talk about today?’.
The type of question a nurse chooses depends on the needs of the
person at the time. Nurses often find it necessary to use a
combination of closed and open-ended questions throughout an
interview to accomplish the goals of the interview and obtain needed


information. See Box 12.2
 for advantages and disadvantages of
open-ended and closed questions.
BO X
12.2 Selected advantages and
disadvantages of open-ended and
closed questions
Open-ended questions
Closed questions
Source: C. J. Stewart & W. B. Cash Jr . Interviewing: Principles and Practices (14th ed.). New York:
McGraw-Hill. © 2014. Reprinted with permission from The McGraw-Hill Companies.
6 Stewart, C. J. & Cash, Jr, W. B. (2013). Interviewing: Principles and Practices (14th ed.). New York:
McGraw-Hill.
Planning the interview and setting
Before beginning an interview, the nurse reviews available
information; for example the operative report, information about the
6


current illness or literature about the person’s health problem. The
nurse also reviews the laboratory’s data collection form to identify
which data must be collected and which data are within the nurse’s
discretion to collect based on the specific person. If a form is not
available, most nurses prepare an interview guide to help them
remember areas of information and determine what questions to
ask. The guide includes a list of topics and subtopics rather than a
series of questions.
Both nurses and patients are made comfortable in order to
encourage an effective interview by balancing several factors. Each
interview is influenced by many things, including the time, place,
seating arrangement or distance, and language.
Time. Nurses need to plan interviews when the person is physically
comfortable and free of pain and when interruptions by friends,
family and other health professionals are minimal. Nurses should
schedule interviews with people in their homes at a mutually
convenient time.
Place. A well-ventilated, well-lit room that is relatively free of noise,
movements and distractions encourages communication. In addition,
a place where others cannot overhear or see the discussion is
desirable.
Seating arrangement. By standing and looking down at a person
who is in bed or in a chair, the nurse risks intimidating the person.
When a person is in bed, the nurse can sit at a 45-degree angle to


the bed. This position is less formal than sitting behind a table or
standing at the foot of the bed.
A seating arrangement with the nurse behind a desk and the person
seated on the other side creates a formal setting that suggests a
business meeting between a superior and a subordinate. In contrast,
a seating arrangement in which the parties sit on two chairs placed
at right angles to a desk or table, or a metre apart with no table
between, creates a less formal atmosphere and the nurse and the
person tend to feel on equal terms. In groups, a horseshoe or
circular chair arrangement can avoid a superior or head-of-the-table
position.
Distance. The distance between the interviewer and interviewee
should be neither too small nor too great, because people feel
uncomfortable when talking to someone who is too close or too far
away. Most people feel comfortable maintaining a distance of a half
to one metre during an interview. Some people require more or less
personal space, depending on their cultural and personal needs. See
Box 12.3
. For additional information, see Chapter 19
.
BO X
12.3 Culturally responsive care:
personal space variables
Accepted distance between individuals in conversation
varies with cultural affiliation. For example, it is


commonly about one-third of a metre in Arab countries,
half a metre in the United States, two-thirds of a metre in
Australia and Britain, and one metre in Japan.
Men of all cultures usually require more space than
women.
Anxiety increases the need for space.
Direct eye contact increases the need for space.
Physical contact is used only if it has a therapeutic
purpose. Touch, even a simple hand on the shoulder, can
be misinterpreted—especially between people of
opposite gender and in some intercultural interactions.
Language. Cultural competence in an interview is the ability to
understand, accept, appreciate and work with individuals of cultures
different from one’s own. In this context, the word ‘culture’ is used
broadly to include ethnicity, race, sexual orientation and gender (see
also Chapter 19
). Because culture drives a person’s values and
beliefs regarding health and illness, and expectations of health care
providers and treatments, it is important that nurses find ways in the
interview to draw out the person’s interpretation of their health and
illness. Failure to communicate in words the person can understand
is a form of racial discrimination. The nurse must convert
complicated medical terminology into common English usage, and
interpreters or translators should be used if the person and the
nurse do not speak the same language or dialect (a variation in a
language spoken in a particular geographical region).


There may be differences in understanding terminology even
between people who speak English. People from different parts of
the English-speaking world may have strong accents, or people who
are less educated and young people may ascribe different meanings
to words. For example, ‘cool’ may imply something ‘good’ to one
person and something ‘not warm’ to another. The nurse must always
confirm accurate understandings.
Examining
The physical examination or physical assessment is a systematic
data collection method that uses observation (i.e. the senses of
sight, hearing, smell and touch) to detect health problems. To
conduct the examination the nurse uses techniques of inspection,
auscultation, palpation and percussion (see Chapter 31
).
Patient safety competency framework
2 Therapeutic communication
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must
communicate in a way that is appropriate to the
person’s level of health literacy and avoids
jargon and complex terms (Levett-Jones et al.
2017).


The physical examination is carried out systematically. It may be
organised according to the examiner’s preference in a head-to-toe
approach or a body systems approach. Usually, the nurse first
records a general impression about the person’s overall appearance
and health status; for example, age, body size, mental and
nutritional status, speech and behaviour. Then the nurse takes such
measurements as vital signs, height and weight. The head-to-toe
approach begins the examination at the head, progresses to the
neck, thorax, abdomen and extremities, and ends at the toes. The
nurse using a body systems approach investigates each system
individually; that is, the respiratory system, the circulatory system,
the nervous system and so on. During the physical examination, the
nurse assesses all body parts and compares findings on each side
of the body (e.g. lungs). These techniques are discussed in detail in
Chapters 30
 and 31
.
Practice guidelines
Communication during an interview
Listen attentively, using all your senses, and speak slowly
and clearly.
Use language the person understands and clarify points
that are not understood. Remember, communication is
non-verbal, so observe body language and facial
expressions closely and clarify where necessary.
Avoid making assumptions.
Plan questions to follow a logical sequence.


Ask only one question at a time. Multiple questions limit
the person to one choice and may confuse the person.
Acknowledge the person’s right to look at things the way
they appear to them and not the way they appear to the
nurse or someone else (this is a mark of person-centred
care).
Do not impose your own beliefs and values on the person.
Avoid using personal examples, such as saying, ‘If I were
you ...’.
Non-verbally convey respect, concern, interest and
acceptance.
Be aware of the person’s and your own body language.
Be conscious of the person’s and your own voice
inflection, tone and affect.
Sit down to talk with the person (be at an even level).
Use and accept silence to help the person search for
more thoughts or to organise them.
Use eye contact appropriately and be calm, unhurried and
sympathetic.
Instead of giving a complete examination, the nurse may focus on a
specific problem area noted from the nursing assessment, such as
the inability to urinate. On occasion, the nurse may find it necessary
to resolve a complaint or problem (e.g. shortness of breath) before
completing the examination. Alternatively, the nurse may perform a
screening examination. A screening examination
 is a brief
review of essential functioning of various body parts or systems.
Data obtained from this examination are measured against norms or


standards, such as ideal height and weight standards or norms for
body temperature or blood pressure levels.
Organising data
The nurse uses a written or electronic format that organises the
assessment data systematically. This is often referred to as a
nursing health history, nursing assessment or nursing database
form. The format may be modified according to the person’s
physical status, such as one focused on musculoskeletal data for
orthopaedic patients.
Conceptual models/frameworks
Most schools of nursing and health care agencies have developed
their own structured assessment format. Many of these are based
on selected nursing models or frameworks; others do not use any
one particular nursing model (see Chapter 3
). There is much
critical debate in Australia about the use of nursing models (e.g. see
Winch, Henderson & Creedy ). However, three examples are
provided here for students to explore: (1) Gordon’s functional health
pattern framework; (2) Orem’s self-care model; and (3) Roy’s
adaptation model.
7 Winch, S., Henderson, A. & Creedy, D. K. (2013). The growth of ideas and theories in
nursing. In J. Daly, S. Speedy & D. Jackson (Eds), Contexts of Nursing (4th ed.) (Ch. 6, pp.
87−100). Chatswood, NSW: Elsevier.
7


Gordon  provides a framework of 11 functional health patterns (see
Box 12.4
) and uses the word pattern to signify a sequence of
recurring behaviour. The nurse collects data about dysfunctional as
well as functional behaviour. Thus, by using Gordon’s framework to
organise data, nurses are able to discern emerging patterns.
8 Gordon, M. (2014). Manual of Nursing Diagnosis (13th ed.). Boston: Jones & Bartlett.
BO X
12.4 Gordon’s typology of 11
functional health patterns
1. Health perception/health management pattern.
Describes the person’s perceived pattern of health and
wellbeing and how health is managed.
2. Nutritional–metabolic pattern. Describes the
person’s pattern of food and fluid consumption relative
to metabolic need and pattern indicators of local
nutrient supply.
3. Elimination pattern. Describes the patterns of
excretory function (bowel, bladder and skin).
4. Activity–exercise pattern. Describes the pattern of
exercise, activity, leisure and recreation.
5. Sleep–rest pattern. Describes patterns of sleep, rest
and relaxation.
8


6. Cognitive–perceptual pattern. Describes cognitive
and sensory–perceptual patterns.
7. Self-perception/self-concept pattern. Describes the
person’s self-concept pattern and perceptions of self
(e.g. self-conception/worth, comfort, body image,
feeling state).
8. Role–relationship pattern. Describes the person’s
pattern of role participation and relationships.
9. Sexuality–reproductive pattern. Describes the
person’s patterns of satisfaction and dissatisfaction
with sexuality pattern; describes reproductive patterns.
10. Coping/stress-tolerance pattern. Describes the
person’s general coping pattern and the effectiveness
of the pattern in terms of stress tolerance.
11. Value–belief pattern. Describes the patterns of
values, beliefs (including spiritual) and goals that guide
the person’s choices or decisions.
Source: M. Gordon (2014). Manual of Nursing Diagnosis (13th ed.). Boston: Jones & Bartlett, pp. 2–5.
Orem  delineates eight universal self-care requisites of humans (see
Box 12.5
). Roy and Andrews
 outline the data to be collected
according to the Roy adaptation model and classify observable
behaviour into four categories: physiological, self-concept, role
function and interdependence (see Box 12.6
).
9 Orem, D. E. (2001). Nursing: Concepts of Practice (6th ed.). St Louis, MO: Mosby.
9
10


10 Roy, C. & Andrews, H. A. (2008). The Roy Adaptation Model (3rd ed.). Upper Saddle
River, NJ: Prentice Hall.
BO X
12.5 Orem’s self-care model
Universal self-care requisites
1. The maintenance of a sufficient intake of air.
2. The maintenance of a sufficient intake of water.
3. The maintenance of a sufficient intake of food.
4. The provision of care associated with elimination
processes and excrement.
5. The maintenance of a balance between activity and
rest.
6. The maintenance of a balance between solitude and
social interaction.
7. The prevention of hazards to human life, human
functioning and human wellbeing.
8. The promotion of human functioning and development
within social groups in accord with human potential,
known human limitations, and human desire to be
normal. (Normalcy is used in the sense of that which is
essentially human and that which is in accord with the
genetic and constitutional characteristics and the
talents of individuals.)


Source: Adapted from D. E. Orem (2001). Nursing: Concepts of Practice (6th ed.). St Louis, MO:
Mosby, p. 225.
BO X
12.6 Roy’s adaptation model
Adaptive modes
1. Physiological needs
Activity and rest
Nutrition
Elimination
Fluid and electrolytes
Oxygenation
Protection
Regulation: temperature
Regulation: the senses
Regulation: endocrine system
2. Self-concept
Physical self

Source: C. Roy & H. A. Andrews (2008). The Roy Adaptation Model (3rd ed.). Upper Saddle River,
NJ: Pearson Education, Inc., p. 68. © 2008. Reproduced with permission.
Non-nursing models
Frameworks and models from other disciplines may also be helpful
for organising data. These frameworks may be different from the
model required in nursing; therefore, the nurse usually needs to
combine these with other approaches to obtain a complete history.
Validating data
The information gathered during the assessment phase must be
complete, factual and accurate because the nursing diagnoses and
interventions are based on this information. Validation
 is the act
of ‘double-checking’ or verifying data to confirm that it is accurate
and factual. Validating data helps the nurse complete these tasks:
ensure that assessment information is complete
ensure that objective and related subjective data agree
obtain additional information that may have been overlooked
differentiate between cues and inferences. Cues
 are
subjective or objective data that can be directly observed by the
nurse; that is, what the person says or what the nurse can see,
hear, feel, smell or measure. Inferences
 are the nurse’s


interpretation or conclusions made based on the cues (e.g. a
nurse observes the cues that an incision is red, hot and swollen;
the nurse makes the inference that the incision is infected)
avoid jumping to conclusions and focusing in the wrong direction
to identify problems.
Not all data require validation. For example, data such as height,
weight, birth date and most laboratory studies that can be measured
with an accurate scale can be accepted as factual. As a rule, the
nurse validates data when there are discrepancies between data
obtained in the nursing interview (subjective data) and the physical
examination (objective data), or when the person’s statements differ
at different times in the assessment. Guidelines for validating data
are shown in Table 12.6
.
Table 12.6 Validating assessment data
To collect data accurately, nurses need to be aware of their own
biases, values and beliefs and to separate fact from inference,
interpretation and assumption (see Chapter 11
). For example, a
nurse seeing a man holding his arm to his chest might assume that
he is experiencing chest pain, when in fact he has a painful hand.
Nurses must validate assumptions regarding the person’s physical
or emotional behaviour. In the previous example, the nurse should
ask the person why he is holding his arm to his chest. The person’s
response may validate the nurse’s assumptions or prompt further
questioning. Failure to validate assumptions can lead to an


inaccurate or incomplete nursing assessment and could compromise
the person’s safety.
Documenting data
To complete the assessment phase, the nurse records the person’s
data. Accurate documentation is essential and should include all
data collected about the person’s health status. Data are recorded in
a factual manner and not interpreted by the nurse. For example, the
nurse records the person’s breakfast intake (objective data) as
‘coffee 240 mL, juice 120 mL, 1 egg and 1 slice of toast’, rather than
as ‘appetite good’ (a judgment). A judgment or conclusion such as
‘appetite good’ or ‘normal appetite’ may have different meanings for
different people. To increase accuracy, the nurse records subjective
data in the person’s own words, using quotation marks. Restating in
other words what someone says increases the chance of changing
the original meaning (see Chapter 16
).
Lifespan considerations
Children
Consider this example: A 4-year-old girl is admitted to your
ward following emergency surgery for a ruptured appendix.


She is awake and alert, but refuses to talk. Her parents have
had little sleep for over 24 hours and are extremely anxious.
Gathering assessment data in this situation requires the
nurse to be sensitive to the parents’ need for rest and
assurance; at the same time, the nurse must collect
information to compile an adequate database for
appropriate nursing care decisions. Assessment will be
problem focused, monitoring the condition of the child as
she recovers from surgery and being alert to potential
problems.
The parents become the major source of subjective data,
although the child should be encouraged to tell the nurse
how she is feeling.
Objective data collected include vital signs; level of and
response to pain (often called the fifth vital sign); bleeding
or discharge from the incision; mobility; integrity of
dressings, intravenous lines, catheters, nasogastric tubes
or other medical devices; and affect.
As children are a part of families, assessment will include
observation of the whole family and the interpersonal
dynamics between family members.
Case study


Eighty-two-year-old Ms Tyson is in the hospital for hip
replacement surgery.
Fundamentals of care framework in
context


1.
 What are the key areas of information, in
relation to both Ms Tyson’s physical and psychosocial
needs, that you must obtain regarding her past
history?
2. Which physiological systems are the most important
for data collection before her surgery?
3. What exactly would you say to her to determine if
someone will be at home to assist her after discharge?
4. What other sources of data might be appropriate to
access in her case?


Chapter 12 Review


Chapter highlights
The nursing process is a systematic, rational method of planning
and providing individualised nursing care for individuals, families,
groups and communities.
The goals of the nursing process are to identify a person’s actual
or potential health care needs, to establish plans to meet the
identified needs and to deliver and evaluate specific nursing
interventions to meet those needs in a culturally appropriate
manner.
The nursing process can be used in all health care settings. It is
cyclical and dynamic, person centred, interpersonal and
collaborative, and universally applicable, and it focuses on
problem solving and decision making.
The nursing process is organised into five interrelated,
interdependent phases: assessing, diagnosing, planning,
implementing and evaluating.
Assessing involves collecting, organising, validating and
recording data.
Diagnosing is the process of making a clinical judgment (nursing
diagnosis) about a person’s potential or actual health problems.
Planning involves setting priorities, writing goals/desired
outcomes and establishing a written plan for nursing
interventions.
Implementing is carrying out the nursing interventions. It
incorporates all the activities performed to promote health,


prevent complications, treat present problems and facilitate the
person’s coping with chronic alterations in health status.
Evaluating is the process of comparing the person’s responses
with preselected outcomes to determine whether goals have
been met. It includes review and modification of the care plan.
Assessment involves active participation by the person and nurse
in obtaining subjective and objective data about the person’s
health status.
The person is the primary source of data. Secondary sources are
family, friends, health team members, the health record and
pertinent literature.
Subjective data are the person’s personal perceptions, often
gathered during the nursing health history.
Objective data (e.g. data observed and collected during the
physical examination) are detectable by an observer.
The primary methods of data collection are observing,
interviewing and examining.
Observation is a conscious, deliberate skill involving use of the
senses.
The nurse uses closed and open-ended questions to obtain the
nursing health history.
Nursing models provide formats for collecting and organising a
person’s data.
The nursing assessment must be complete and accurate
because nursing diagnoses and interventions are based on this
information.
Some data must be validated. Subjective data can be used to
validate objective data, and vice versa. Primary and secondary


data can also be used to validate each other.
Data must be recorded in a factual manner without interpretation
or inferences.
Concept check
1. Which of the following behaviours is most representative of
the nursing diagnosis phase of the nursing process?
1. Identifying major problems or needs.
2. Organising data in the person’s family history.
3. Establishing short-term and long-term goals.
4. Administering an antibiotic.
2. Which of the following behaviours would indicate that the
nurse was utilising the assessment phase of the nursing
process to provide nursing care?
1. Proposes hypotheses.
2. Generates desired outcomes.
3. Reviews results of laboratory tests.
4. Documents care.
3. Which of the following elements is best categorised as
secondary subjective data?
1. The nurse measures a weight loss of 10 kg since the
last clinic visit.
2. Spouse states the person has lost all appetite.
3. The nurse palpates oedema in lower extremities.


4. Person states severe pain when walking up stairs.
4. The nurse wishes to determine the person’s feelings about a
recent diagnosis. Which interview question is most likely to
elicit this information?
1. ‘What did the doctor tell you about your diagnosis?’
2. ‘Are you worried about how the diagnosis will affect
you in the future?’
3. ‘Tell me about your reactions to the diagnosis.’
4. ‘How is your family responding to the diagnosis?’
5. The use of a conceptual or theoretical framework for
collecting and organising assessment data ensures which of
the following?
1. Correlation of the data with other members of the
health care team.
2. Demonstration of cost-effective care.
3. Utilisation of creativity and intuition in creating a plan of
care.
4. Collection of all necessary information for a thorough
appraisal.
6. Which of the following is the purpose of assessing?
1. Establish a database of a person’s responses to their
health status.
2. Identify the person’s strengths and problems.
3. Develop an individualised plan of care.
4. Implement care, prevent illness and promote wellness.


7. In the validating activity of the assessing phase of the nursing
process, the nurse performs which of the following?
1. Collects subjective data.
2. Applies a framework to the collected data.
3. Confirms data is complete and accurate.
4. Records data in the person’s record.
8. A major characteristic of the nursing process is which of the
following?
1. A focus on the individual’s needs.
2. Its static nature.
3. An emphasis on physiology and illness.
4. Its exclusive use by and with nurses.
9. Which of the following would be true regarding use of the
observing method of data collection?
1. When observing, the nurse uses only the visual sense.
2. Observing is done only when no other nursing
interventions are being performed at the same time.
3. Data should be gathered as it occurs, rather than in
any particular order.
4. Observed data should be interpreted in relation to
other sources of collected data.
10. Which of the following represent effective planning of the
interview setting? Select all that apply.
1. Keep the lighting dimmed so as not to stress the
person’s eyes.


2. Ensure that no one can overhear the interview
conversation.
3. Stand near the person’s head while they are in the bed
or chair.
4. Keep approximately 1 metre away from the person
during the interview.
5. Use a standard form to be sure all relevant data are
covered in the interview.
Focus on critical thinking

Why is communication an essential element of nursing

Diagnosing is the second phase of the nursing
process and the fourth stage of the clinical-
reasoning cycle (Levett-Jones ; Levett-Jones et
al. ) (see Figures 13.1
 and 13.2
). Nurses
use critical-thinking skills to process the clinical
data they collect in order to identify the person’s
problem/s and formulate a specific, clear and
individualised nursing diagnoses. At all times
the nurse adopts a person-centred approach
and works in partnership with the person who is
experiencing ill health. This ensures that the

person’s goals and needs remain central to the
nursing process. Diagnosing is a pivotal step as
care planning and nursing interventions follow
directly from this phase. Safe and effective
health care depends on an accurate nursing
diagnosis.
