Nursing diagnoses
Definitions
A diagnosis
 is a statement or conclusion regarding the nature of
a phenomenon. A nursing diagnosis consists of the person’s
problem, the related aetiology
 (causal relationship between a
problem and its related or risk factors) and supporting evidence (e.g.
cues). A nursing diagnosis is a judgment made after thorough,
systematic data collection of objective and subjective cues.
An appropriate plan of care depends on the accuracy of the nursing
diagnosis, and it is important that nurses communicate the
assessment data used to support the diagnoses so that others
caring for the person know why a particular diagnosis was reached.
Terms such as ‘related to’ and ‘evidenced by’ are effective in
providing this clarity. It is also important that nurses document the
person’s nursing diagnosis accurately and completely in order to
makes their thought processes clear to other staff.
Types of nursing diagnoses


There are different types of nursing diagnoses; for example:
1. An actual diagnosis
 is a problem that is present when the
nurse assesses the person. An actual nursing diagnosis has a
specific aetiology and is based on the presence of associated
signs and symptoms identified through collection, analysis
and synthesis of objective and subjective cues. An actual
nursing diagnosis will be written in three parts: Problem,
aetiology and signs and symptoms. For example: Dehydration
related to post-operative nausea and vomiting evidenced by
dry mucous membranes, oliguria, poor skin turgor,
hypotension and tachycardia.
2. A risk nursing diagnosis
 is a clinical judgment about a
potential problem where the presence of risk factors
indicates that a problem has the potential to develop unless
nurses intervene appropriately. For example, all people
admitted to a hospital have some possibility of acquiring an
infection; however, a person with diabetes or a compromised
immune system is at higher risk than others. Therefore, a risk
diagnosis is written in two parts and does not include signs
and symptoms; for example, Risk of infection related to type
2 diabetes.
Prioritising nursing diagnosis
Prioritisation of the diagnosis is essential to ensure that the person
receives care and management of the issues that are most


important in an appropriate time frame. For example, if a person
was experiencing both hypoxia and constipation the nurse would
ensure the hypoxia was managed before the constipation. Both
diagnoses are important, but one takes priority over the other.
Priority diagnoses
 are those nursing diagnoses that, if not
managed immediately, may cause significant deterioration or delay
improvement in the person’s condition. Realistically, a nurse cannot
hope to address all of the nursing diagnoses that can apply to an
individual, family or community. By prioritising one or a group of
nursing diagnoses that take precedence over others, the nurse can
best direct care towards goal achievement. Importantly, nurses must
recognise diagnoses associated with airway, breathing and
circulation as priorities and address them accordingly.
Patient safety competency framework
5 Clinical reasoning
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
states that nurses must identify priority patient
problems based on accurate and complete
interpretation of available patient data (Levett-
Jones et al. ).
4 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
4


Components of a nursing
diagnosis
A nursing diagnosis generally has three components: (1) the
problem; (2) the aetiology; and (3) the defining characteristics. Each
component serves a specific purpose.
Problem
The problem statement clearly describes the person’s health
problem for which nursing care is needed. The problem statement
needs to be specific; for example, knowledge deficit related to
current medications rather than just knowledge deficit. Qualifiers are
often used to give additional meaning and clarification to the nursing
diagnosis; for example:
Deficient (inadequate in amount, quality or degree; not sufficient;
incomplete)
Impaired (made worse, weakened, damaged, reduced,
deteriorated)
Decreased (lesser in size, amount or degree)
Ineffective (not producing the desired effect)
Compromised (to make vulnerable to threat).


Aetiology (related factors and risk factors)
The aetiology component of a nursing diagnosis identifies one or
more probable causes of the health problem, gives direction to the
required nursing interventions and enables the nurse to individualise
the person’s care. Differentiating between possible causes in the
nursing diagnosis is essential because each may require different
nursing interventions. Table 13.1
 provides an example of a
problem that has different aetiologies and therefore requires
different interventions.
Table 13.1 Example of a problem that has different aetiologies
and therefore requires different nursing interventions
Defining characteristics
Defining characteristics
 are the signs and symptoms (cues)
that indicate the presence or risk of a particular nursing diagnosis.
For an actual nursing diagnosis, the defining characteristics are the
person’s signs and symptoms. The defining characteristics of a risk
diagnosis are those that relate to other diagnoses; for example, Risk
of infection related to poor nutritional state or Risk of falls related to
incontinence of urine.
Real-world practice


Example of diagnosis in a clinical setting
Mrs Milingu is a 61-year-old Aboriginal woman with
stage II heart failure secondary to a myocardial
infarction that she experienced 3 years ago. She has
been treated for hypertension for the past 6 years. Mrs
Milingu is overweight, with a BMI of 31. Two years ago,
she was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. She found
this illness difficult to understand and manage, and
consequently her BGLs were often elevated and
unstable. Mrs Milingu was experiencing symptoms of
increased fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, persistent
cough and palpitations. Her BP was 150/92, HR 124,
RR 28 and
 91% on room air. Mrs Milingu’s
blood glucose level (BGL) was 13.0 mmol/L.
With these data, a nurse may formulate the following
nursing diagnoses:
1. Unstable blood glucose level (problem) related
to knowledge deficit (aetiology) evidenced by
elevated BGL (defining characteristic)
2. Impaired mobility (problem) related to
breathlessness on exertion (aetiology)
evidenced by fatigue, tachypnoea and hypoxia
(defining characteristics).
Source: M. Lunney . Use of critical thinking in the diagnostic process. International
Journal of Nursing Terminologies and Classifications, 21, 82–88.
SpO2
5


5 Lunney, M. (2010). Use of critical thinking in the diagnostic process. International
Journal of Nursing Terminologies and Classifications, 21, 82–88.
Differentiating nursing diagnoses
from medical diagnoses
Both nurses and medical practitioners formulate a diagnosis by
gathering information from the person through a range of sources:
physical examination, collecting a history, reviewing clinical findings
and diagnostic results, and so on. However, a medical diagnosis
deals with a medical condition or disease. For example, a medical
diagnosis of cerebrovascular attack (CVA or stroke) provides
information about the person’s pathology and directs the medical
interventions that are required. A complementary nursing diagnosis,
for example Impaired verbal communication, provides a more
complete understanding of the impact of the stroke on this particular
person and directs nursing interventions. Using a medical diagnosis
alone does not provide enough information to develop a
comprehensive and person-centred nursing care plan.
Nursing diagnoses and types of
interventions


The interventions that follow on from a nursing diagnosis will require
(a) independent (nurse-initiated) nursing interventions, (b)
collaborative (working with other health professionals) nursing
interventions and/or (c) dependent (those that rely on a doctor’s
order) interventions. For example, a person who has persistent pain
(nursing diagnosis) as a result of rheumatoid arthritis (medical
diagnosis) may require the nurse to apply heat or ice packs
(independent nursing intervention) while consulting with the
physiotherapist to organise an exercise regimen (collaborative
intervention) and to contact the doctor so that an order for non-
steroidal anti-inflammatory or analgesic medication can be obtained.
Nursing diagnoses involve human responses, which vary greatly
from one person to the next. They take into account the person’s
beliefs, goals and priorities. Therefore, the same set of nursing
diagnoses cannot be applied to all people who have a particular
disease or condition. For example, postoperative individuals may be
at risk of different complications depending on their age,
comorbidities and previous history and will therefore have different
nursing diagnoses.


The diagnostic process
The diagnostic process uses clinical-reasoning and critical-thinking
skills to analyse and synthesise objective and subjective cues in
order to come to an understanding of the person’s problem (Levett-
Jones 2018). Analysis is the separation into components; that is, the
breaking down of the whole into its parts (deductive reasoning). In
this stage of the process, each element of the assessment data is
examined and aberrations from normal identified. Synthesis is the
opposite; that is, the putting together of parts into the whole
(inductive reasoning), identifying gaps or inconsistencies in the data
and looking for patterns or cue clusters. For example, a person may
present with confusion, hypertension, drowsiness, sensitivity to light,
nausea, vomiting and headache—the nurse would first analyse each
of these signs and symptoms; they would then look for patterns or
trends in the clinical data to help to determine a tentative nursing
diagnosis such as increased intracranial pressure. Further cue
collection to help confirm this diagnosis would then include an
assessment using the Glasgow Coma Scale. (See Chapter 11
 to
review the concepts of deductive and inductive reasoning.)
The diagnostic process is used continuously by competent nurses.
An experienced nurse may enter a person’s hospital room and
immediately observe significant data and draw conclusions about the
person. As a result of their knowledge, skill and expertise, the expert
nurse may seem to perform these mental processes automatically


and intuitively. However, it should be noted that the critical-thinking
and clinical-reasoning processes that underpin a competent nurse’s
ability to diagnose and to initiate appropriate interventions are highly
sophisticated. Experienced nurses select relevant and specific cues
and know what to pay attention to and what questions to ask (Hardy
et al. ). Novice nurses are less focused in the selection of cues and
tend concentrate on the most obvious symptoms only (Levett-Jones
et al. 2010). They need guidelines and repeated opportunities to
develop their critical-thinking and clinical-reasoning skills in order to
become skilled in formulating nursing diagnoses.
6 Hardy, S., Garbett, R., Titchen, A. & Manley, K. (2002). Exploring nursing expertise: Nurses
talk nursing. Nursing Inquiry, 9(3), 196–202.
The diagnostic process has three steps:
1. analysing data
2. identifying health problems and risks
3. formulating a nursing diagnosis.
Analysing data
In the diagnostic process, analysing involves the following steps:
1. comparing data (cues such as signs and symptoms) with
norms and standards to identify aberrations from normal, and
distinguishing relevant from irrelevant data
6


2. clustering cues, pattern matching and identifying relationships
(to generate tentative hypotheses)
3. identifying gaps and inconsistencies in the data collected.
Note that, for experienced nurses, these activities usually occur
continuously rather than sequentially.
Comparing data with standards and
norms
Nurses draw on knowledge and experience to compare clinical data
with standards and norms and to identify significant and relevant
cues. A standard
 or norm
 is a generally accepted measure,
rule, model or pattern. The nurse uses a wide range of standards,
such as growth and development patterns, normal vital signs and
pathology values. A cue is considered significant if it:
Points to a negative or positive change in a person’s health
status or pattern. For example, the person states: ‘I have
recently experienced shortness of breath while climbing stairs’ or
‘I have noticed blood in my urine over the last few days’.
Varies from norms of the population. The person’s pattern may fit
within cultural norms but vary from norms of the general society.
For example, a person eating very small meals and having little
appetite may consider this to be normal. This pattern, however,
may not be healthy and may require further exploration.


Indicates a developmental delay. For example, by age 12 months
an infant is usually able to crawl. The infant who has not
accomplished this task needs further assessment for possible
developmental delays.
Table 13.2
 lists specific examples of cues, and norms with which
they may be compared.
Table 13.2 Comparing cues with standards and norms
Clustering cues
Cue clustering is a process of determining the relatedness of data
and determining whether any patterns in the cues are present,
whether the data represent isolated incidents and whether the data
are significant. This is the beginning of synthesis.
The nurse may cluster data inductively by combining data from
different assessment areas to form a pattern. Experienced nurses
may cluster data as they collect and interpret it simultaneously, as
evidenced in remarks such as ‘I’m getting a sense of . . .’ or ‘This
cue doesn’t fit the picture’. The novice nurse may not always have
the knowledge base or the clinical experience to pattern match and
to compare what they are seeing with previous encounters. They
must therefore be vigilant in conducting evidence-informed clinical
assessments, consulting with more experienced staff and using
reliable resources for comparing the person’s signs and symptoms
with norms and standards.


Data clustering is followed by making inferences about the data. The
nurse interprets the possible meaning of the cues and labels the cue
clusters with tentative hypotheses (Levett-Jones 2018).
Identifying gaps and inconsistencies in
data collected
Skilful assessment minimises gaps and inconsistencies in data.
However, data analysis should include a final check to ensure that
data are complete and correct. During the cue-clustering process it
may become evident that the cues are pointing towards a certain
problem, but it may be necessary to collect additional cues before a
final diagnosis may be made. For example, an adult has a persistent
productive cough and a respiratory rate of 24; however, the person’s
breath sounds have not been auscultated and this needs to occur in
order to determine a diagnosis.
Inconsistencies are conflicting data. Possible sources of conflicting
data include measurement error, expectations and inconsistent or
unreliable reports. For example, a nurse may learn from the nursing
history that a person has a haemoglobin level of 8.0 g/L but there is
no evidence of recent blood loss. All inconsistencies must be
clarified before a valid pattern can be established and the diagnosis
determined.


Identifying health problems and
risks
After grouping and clustering the data, the nurse identifies problems
that support a possible diagnosis. While some data may indicate a
possible problem, when clustered with other data the problem may
change. For example, a person may have decreased urinary output
indicating a potential urinary elimination problem but when this
information is clustered with a history of inadequate fluid, the nursing
diagnosis must be reviewed.
Formulating a nursing diagnosis
Most nursing diagnoses are written as two- or three-part
statements, but there are variations of these.


Basic two-part risk nursing diagnosis
The basic two-part statement includes the following components
within the nursing diagnosis:
1. problem: statement of the presenting issue
2. aetiology: factors contributing to or probable causes of the
problem.
The two parts are joined by the words related to rather than due to.
The phrase due to implies that one part causes or is responsible for
the other part. By contrast, the phrase related to merely implies a
relationship. There is an increase in clarity about the person’s
problem when the nurse uses critical thinking skills to clarify the
nature of the problem by using a two-part nursing diagnosis which
includes the factors that are contributing to the problem. A two-part
nursing diagnosis is used for a risk diagnosis about a potential
problem where the presence of risk factors indicates that a problem
has the potential to develop unless nurses intervene appropriately.
Some examples of how the two-part nursing diagnoses influence
subsequent nursing interventions are shown in Table 13.3
.


Table 13.3 Basic two-part risk nursing diagnosis and relevant
nursing interventions


Basic three-part actual nursing diagnosis
The three-part nursing diagnosis is used when there is a specific
aetiology and is based on the presence of associated signs and
symptoms. An actual three-part nursing diagnosis includes the
following:
1. problem: statement of the person’s issue
2. aetiology: factors contributing to or probable causes of the
problem
3. signs and symptoms: defining characteristics manifested by
the person and cues collected by the nurse.
An actual nursing diagnosis can be documented by using the three-
part statement (see Table 13.4
) because the signs and symptoms
have been identified. This format cannot be used for risk diagnoses
because the person does not exhibit signs and symptoms of the
diagnosis.


Table 13.4 Basic three-part nursing diagnosis
Variations of basic formats
Variations of the basic two- and three-part statements include the
following:
1. Writing unknown aetiology when the defining characteristics
are present but the nurse does not know the cause or
contributing factors. One example is Non-compliance with
medication regimen with unknown aetiology. Nurses need to
be sure that all cues have been explored prior to making this
diagnosis.
2. Using the word possible or potential to describe either the
problem or the aetiology. A thorough assessment must be
conducted prior to using this phrasing. Examples are Anxiety,
possibly related to recent retrenchment from job.
Evaluating the accuracy of nursing
diagnoses
Nursing diagnoses should be accurate, concise, descriptive and
specific (see Table 13.5
). The nurse needs to be confident that all
relevant cues have been collected prior to confirming the diagnosis.
Table 13.5 Guidelines for ensuring accuracy of nursing
diagnoses


Avoiding errors in diagnostic
reasoning
Some error is inherent in any human undertaking, and diagnosis is
no exception. However, it is important that nurses make nursing
diagnoses with a high level of accuracy. Errors can occur at any
point in the diagnostic process and be caused by conflicting
assessment information, failure to consider other possible diagnosis
and clinging to first impressions even as conflicting data
accumulates (Redelmeier ). Nurses can, however, avoid some
common errors of reasoning by recognising them and applying the
appropriate clinical-reasoning and critical-thinking skills.
7 Redelmeier, D. A. (2005). Improving patient care. The cognitive psychology of missed
diagnosis. Annals of Internal Medicine, 18 January, 142(2), 115–120.
The following suggestions help to minimise diagnostic error:
Verify. Hypothesise possible explanations of the data, but realise
that all diagnoses are only tentative until they are verified. Begin
and end the diagnostic process by including the person and their
family as active participants in care provision. When collecting
data, ask the person what their health problems are and what
they believe the causes to be. At the end of the process, ask
them to confirm the accuracy and relevance of your diagnoses.
Build a good knowledge base and acquire clinical
experience. Nurses must apply knowledge from many different
7


areas to recognise significant cues and patterns and generate
hypotheses about the data. Nurses need to be able to recall their
knowledge of physiology, pathophysiology, pharmacology,
epidemiology, therapeutics, culture, ethics, law and so on in order
to understand and accurately interpret clinical data. Should the
nurse have minimal experience, clarification and confirmation of
information from reliable sources is advised.
Have a working knowledge of what is normal. Nurses need to
know the population norms; for example, vital signs, laboratory
tests, speech development and breath sounds. In addition,
nurses must determine what is usual for a particular person,
taking into account age, physical make-up, lifestyle, culture and
the person’s own perception of what their normal status is. For
example, normal blood pressure for adults is in the range of
110/60 mm Hg to 140/80 mm Hg. However, a nurse might obtain
a reading of 90/50 mm Hg that is perfectly normal for a particular
person. The nurse should compare actual findings with the
person’s baseline when possible and take into account additional
objective and subjective information that could be obtained.
Consult resources. Both novices and experienced nurses
should consult appropriate evidence-based resources whenever
in doubt about a diagnosis. Professional literature, nursing
colleagues and other professionals are all appropriate resources.
Base diagnoses on patterns and trends. Wherever possible
collect and analyse cues such as behaviours and assessment
findings over time rather than on an isolated incident.
Develop critical-thinking and clinical-reasoning skills. These
skills assist the nurse in thoroughly assessing and sorting


carefully through the relevant cues that lead the nurse to draw a
supported inference. Preconceptions, assumptions, biases,
stereotypes and stigmatisation can negatively influence the
clinical-reasoning process and prevent accurate diagnostic
reasoning (Crosskerry ). In preparation for clinical reasoning,
nurses should reflect on and question their assumptions and
prejudices in order to become ‘self-aware’. Failure to do so may
impair the accuracy of diagnostic reasoning and consequently
the individual’s outcomes (Levett-Jones 2020).
8 Crosskerry, P. (2003). The importance of cognitive errors in diagnosis and strategies to
minimise them. Academic Medicine, 78(8), 1–6.
Lifespan considerations
Diagnosing
Children
Many developmental issues in paediatrics are not considered
problems or illnesses, yet they can benefit from nursing
intervention. When applied to children and families, nursing
diagnoses may reflect a condition or state of health. For
example, parents of a newborn infant may be excited to learn
all they can about infant care and child growth and
development. Assessment of the family system might lead
the nurse to conclude that the family is ready and able, even
8


eager, to take on the new roles and responsibilities of being
parents. An appropriate diagnosis for such a family could be
Readiness for learning, and nursing care could be directed to
educating and providing encouragement and support to the
parents.
Older adults
Older adults may have multiple problems with complex
physical and psychosocial needs when they are ill. If the
nurse has conducted a thorough, accurate assessment,
nursing diagnoses can be selected to cover all problems and,
at the same time, prioritise special needs. For example, if a
person is admitted with severe congestive heart failure,
prompt attention will be focused on Decreased cardiac output
and Hypervolaemia, with interventions selected to improve
these concerns quickly. As these conditions improve, other
nursing diagnoses, such as Limited mobility and Knowledge
deficit related to medication regimen, might require more
attention. They are all part of the same medical problem of
congestive heart failure, but each nursing diagnosis has
specific expected outcomes and nursing interventions.
Case study
Mr Huong has a medical diagnosis of lung cancer. Someone
has written the nursing diagnosis of Anxiety on his care plan.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. Is this a complete nursing diagnosis? If not, why not?
2. What data/defining characteristics would support this
nursing diagnosis?
3. Which related factors might exist in his situation?


4.
 Why and how might you develop a relationship
with Mr Huong in order to gather the potentially
sensitive data and information relating to both the
medical and the nursing diagnosis?
5. Which other nursing diagnoses might you expect to
find in Mr Huong’s case?
6. Another nursing diagnosis on the care plan reads Lung
cancer related to smoking. Is this an appropriate
nursing diagnosis? If not, why not?


Chapter 13 Review


Chapter highlights
Accurate nursing diagnoses depend on clinical-reasoning and
critical-thinking skills.
Registered Nurses are responsible for formulating nursing
diagnoses, even though others may contribute data or implement
care.
A nursing diagnosis is a clinical judgment about a person’s
responses to actual and potential health problems or life
processes.
A nursing diagnosis provides the basis for selecting nursing
interventions to achieve outcomes for which the nurse is
accountable.
Nursing diagnoses differ from medical diagnoses in orientation,
duration and nursing focus.
It is essential to prioritise nursing diagnosis in the order of care
that needs to be addressed first to prevent deterioration of the
person’s condition.
The three phases of the diagnostic process are data analysis,
identification of the person’s health problems and health risks,
and formulation of a nursing diagnosis.
In data analysis and processing, the nurse compares data
against standards and norms to identify significant cues, clusters
the data and identifies gaps and inconsistencies in the data
collected.
Significant cues are those that (a) point to change in a person’s
health status or pattern, (b) vary from norms of the population,


or (c) indicate a developmental delay.
The basic format for an actual nursing diagnosis is ‘Problem
related to Aetiology’ as ‘evidenced by ...’.
The basic format for a risk nursing diagnosis is ‘Problem related
to Aetiology’.
Concept check
1. The nurse is formulating a nursing diagnosis for a person with
a seizure disorder. Which of the following should occur
between cue collection and determining the nursing
diagnosis?
1. Undertaking relevant nursing interventions.
2. Cue clustering.
3. Goal planning.
4. Evaluation of the person’s outcomes.
2. In the nursing diagnosis Excess fluid volume related to
decreased venous return as evidenced by lower leg oedema
(swelling), the aetiology of the problem is which of the
following?
1. Excess fluid volume.
2. Decreased venous return.
3. Oedema.
4. Unknown.


3. Which of the following risk nursing diagnoses contains the
proper components?
1. Recent CVA.
2. Risk of falls.
3. Risk of falls related to CVA.
4. Risk of falls related to right hemiparesis.
4. One of the primary advantages of using a three-part
diagnostic statement such as the problem–aetiology–
signs/symptoms format includes all but which of the following:
1. Increases accuracy and specificity of diagnosis.
2. Standardises organisation of a person’s data.
3. Improves nursing communication and documentation.
4. Provides clear guidance for nursing interventions.
5. A collaborative intervention occurs when:
1. The nurse liaises or works with members of the
interprofessional team to manage the problem.
2. The nurse independently initiates care to manage the
problem.
3. Care is delivered independently by the person’s doctor.
Focus on critical thinking
Address these questions in relation to the following case:


Mrs Akbar is an elderly Muslim woman who has a leg ulcer
secondary to peripheral vascular disease and requires daily
dressings.
1. What actual and potential nursing diagnosis could be
developed for Mrs Akbar?
2. What collaborative interventions may be needed for Mrs
Akbar?
3. What are the benefits in utilising the language ‘related to’
when developing a nursing diagnosis?

including initial planning, ongoing planning and discharge
planning.
Discuss the differences between care plans and clinical
pathways.
Identify key elements of nursing care plans.

the nursing diagnoses.

Introduction to care planning
When nurses use nursing diagnoses (see Chapter 13
) to develop
goals and nursing interventions, the result is a holistic, individualised
plan of care that will meet each person’s unique needs while
respecting their individual dignity, culture, values and beliefs (Nursing
and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) ).
1 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016). Registered Nurse Standards for
Practice. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Care planning is the third phase of the nursing process and is linked
to the fifth stage of the clinical-reasoning cycle (Levett-Jones ) (see
Figure 14.1
). Care planning can be defined as a systematic goal-
based approach formulated in response to a specific nursing
diagnosis and identified patient problems or needs. Therefore,
planning care involves nurses logically assessing (Chapter 12
)
and identifying a nursing diagnosis (both actual or risk), problems or
needs; setting goals/outcomes; establishing interventions
(considering options, constraints and resources); and evaluating the
results (see Chapter 15
).
2 Levett-Jones, T. (2018). Clinical reasoning—What it is and why it matters. In T. Levett-Jones
(Ed.), Clinical Reasoning: Learning How to Think Like a Nurse (2nd ed.). Frenchs Forest:
Pearson.
Figure 14.1
1
2


Establish goals. The fifth stage of the clinical-reasoning cycle.
Source: T. Levett-Jones et al. . The ‘five rights’ of clinical reasoning: An educational model to enhance nursing
students’ ability to identify and manage clinically ‘at risk’ patients. Nurse Education Today, 30(6), 515−520.
3 Levett-Jones, T., Hoffman, K., Dempsey, Y., Jeong, S., Noble, D., Norton, C., Roche, J. &
Hickey, N. (2010). The ‘five rights’ of clinical reasoning: An educational model to enhance
nursing students’ ability to identify and manage clinically ‘at risk’ patients. Nurse Education
Today, 30(6), 515–520.
Planning care is an important part of the nursing process that
requires critical thinking to ensure competent decision making and
problem solving (see Chapter 11
 for an exploration of critical
thinking in nursing). When planning care, the nurse refers to the
person’s assessment data and nursing diagnosis to formulate goals
and design nursing interventions
 required to address or prevent
the person’s health problems (see Figure 14.2
).
Figure 14.2
3


Planning. The third phase of the nursing process, in which the nurse
and patient develop patient goals/desired outcomes and nursing
interventions to prevent, reduce or alleviate the patient’s health
problems.
A care plan refers to a tool that is used to document nursing care
provided to patients. It facilitates communication between caregivers
to ensure there is continuity of care. A care plan is a dynamic
document and, as interventions are evaluated or new problems are


identified, the plan should be updated. If expected outcomes are not
achieved, the patient must be reassessed.


Types of care planning
The end product of the planning phase is a plan of care. Although
planning is the nurse’s responsibility, input from the patient and their
support people should also be sought whenever possible. While in a
hospital setting care planning begins on admission and continues
until discharge, it is also an important aspect of the role of
community nurses. The perspective of both patients and members
of the interprofessional team should inform care plan development
(Levett -Jones et al. ; Van Dongen et al. ).
4 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady, T., Applegarth, J., Guinea,
S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing
Students. Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
5 Van Dongen, J. J. J., Lenzen, S. A., van Bokhoven, M. A., Daniëls, R., van der Weijen, T. &
Beurskens, A. (2016). Interprofessional collaboration regarding patients’ care plans in primary
care: A focus group study into influential factors. BMC Family Practice, 17, 58.
Initial planning
The nurse who performs the admission assessment usually
develops the initial plan of care, taking into account subjective and
objective data. Initial planning will be based on the person’s actual
and potential nursing diagnoses (see Chapter 13
) as well as the
4
5


person’s medical diagnosis. For example, a nurse may identify the
nursing diagnosis of Impaired mobility (problem) related to
breathlessness on exertion evidenced by fatigue, tachypnoea and
hypoxia. Alongside this, the medical diagnosis may be asthma. With
both the nursing and medical diagnoses in place, the nurse can plan
the care to be provided to the person.
Ongoing planning
Ongoing planning is done by all nurses who work with the person. As
nurses obtain new information and evaluate the person’s responses
to care, they continue to update and individualise the initial care
plan. Ongoing planning also occurs at the beginning of each shift
when nurses:
1. determine whether the patient’s health status has changed
2. set priorities for care during the shift
3. decide which problems to focus on during the shift.
Discharge planning
Discharge planning
, the process of anticipating and planning for
needs after discharge, is a crucial part of comprehensive health care
and should be addressed in each care plan. As the average stay in
acute care hospitals has become shorter, people are sometimes


discharged who still require nursing care. They may be transferred
to other health care organisations (e.g. rehabilitation or residential
aged care facilities) or to their own home where community nurses
may provide care.
The Cochrane Collaboration (Shepperd et al. ) suggests that a
comprehensive and structured discharge plan tailored to each
individual results in a reduction in hospital length of stay and
readmission rates.
6 Shepperd, S., Lannin, N. A., Clemson, L. M., Cameron, I. D. & Barras, S. L. (2013).
Discharge Planning from Hospital to Home (Review), The Cochrane Collaboration. John
Wiley & Sons Ltd. Retrieved from <www.thecochranelibrary.com>.
Discharge planning can be improved by including both the person
and the family in planning required interventions, ensuring
interprofessional collaboration and communicating with the required
community-based services. Discharge planners are often employed
in larger health facilities to act as a guide and consultant for the
implementation of discharge plans.
6


Developing nursing care plans
The end product of the planning phase of the nursing process is a
formal or informal plan of care. An informal nursing care plan
 is
a strategy for action that exists in the nurse’s mind. For example,
the nurse may think, ‘Mrs Evans is very tired. I will need to
encourage her to do her breathing exercises after she has rested’. A
formal nursing care plan
 is written or electronic documentation
about a person’s care. The most obvious benefit of a formal written
care plan is that it provides for communication and continuity of
care.
A standardised care plan
 is a formal plan that outlines the
nursing care for groups of people with common needs (e.g. all those
with myocardial infarction). An individualised care plan
 is
tailored to meet the unique needs of a specific person—needs that
are not addressed by the standardised plan. It is important that all
health professionals work towards the same outcomes. Nurses also
use formal care plans to guide what they document in the person’s
progress notes and to inform the staffing requirements.
Care plans include the actions nurses must take to address the
person’s nursing diagnoses and produce the desired outcomes. The
complete plan of care for a person is made up of several different
documents that (a) describe the routine care needed to meet basic
needs (e.g. bathing, nutrition), (b) address the nursing diagnoses


and collaborative problems and (c) specify nursing responsibilities in
carrying out the medical plan of care (e.g. keeping the person from
eating or drinking before surgery; scheduling a pathology test). A
complete plan of care integrates dependent and independent
nursing functions into a meaningful whole and provides a central
source of information about the person.
Standardised approaches to
care planning
Most health care organisations provide clinicians with ready access
to best-practice guidelines, integrated care pathways, clinical
pathways and decision support tools relevant to their clinical practice
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care ).
These include a variety of pre-printed, standardised plans and
pathways for providing essential nursing care to people who have a
similar diagnosis (e.g. total hip replacement, acute coronary
syndrome). These documents are developed, reviewed and
accepted by the nursing staff in order to (a) ensure that minimally
acceptable standards are met, and (b) promote efficient use of
nurses’ time by removing the need to unnecessarily repeat writing
care outcomes for common activities for many of the people on a
nursing unit.
7 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (2017). National Safety and
Quality Health Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
7


Standardised care plans are written from the perspective of what
care the person can expect. Figure 14.3
 shows a standardised
care plan for Dehydration.
Figure 14.3


A standardised care plan for the nursing diagnosis of Dehydration.
Standardised care plans:
are kept with the person’s individualised care plan on the nursing
unit; when the person is discharged, the plans become part of
the permanent nursing and medical record
provide detailed interventions and contain additions or deletions
from the standards of care of the organisation
typically are written in the nursing process format:
Problem/nursing diagnosis → Goals/desired outcomes →
Nursing interventions → Evaluation
frequently include checklists, blank lines or empty spaces to allow
the nurse to individualise goals and nursing interventions.
Like standardised care plans, protocols
 are pre-printed to
indicate the actions commonly required for a particular group of
people. For example, a hospital may have a protocol for admitting a
person to the intensive care unit or for caring for a person receiving
continuous epidural analgesia. Protocols may include both the
doctor’s orders and nursing interventions. Depending on the
institution, protocols may or may not be included in the person’s
permanent record.


Policies
 and procedures
 are developed to govern the
management of frequently occurring situations. For example, a
hospital may have a policy specifying the number of visitors a
person may have. Some policies and procedures are similar to
protocols and specify what is to be done; for example, in the case of
clinical review or a rapid response (Clinical Excellence
Commission ). Policies are institutional records and do not become
a part of the care plan or permanent record.
8 Clinical Excellence Commission (2019). Between the Flags. Retrieved from
<www.cec.health.nsw.gov.au>.
A standing order
 is a written document with orders regarding
patient care. Standing orders give nurses the authority to carry out
specific actions under certain circumstances, often when a doctor is
not immediately available. In a hospital critical care unit, a common
example is the administration of emergency antiarrhythmic
medications when a person’s cardiac monitoring pattern changes. In
a home care setting, a doctor may write a standing order for the
nurse to obtain blood tests for a person who has been on a certain
medication regimen for a prescribed amount of time.
Regardless of whether care plans are handwritten, computerised or
standardised, nursing care must be individualised to fit the unique
needs of each person. In practice, a care plan usually consists of
both pre-printed and nurse-created sections. The nurse uses
standardised care plans for predictable, commonly occurring
problems and creates an individual plan for unusual problems or
problems needing special attention.
8


Formats for nursing care plans
Although formats differ between hospital/care facilities, the care plan
is often organised into four sections: (1) nursing diagnoses or
problems; (2) goals/desired outcomes; (3) nursing interventions; and
(4) evaluation. Some institutions use a three-section plan in which
evaluation is done in the goals section or in the nurses’ notes. Other
institutions have a five-section plan that adds a space for
assessment data preceding the nursing diagnosis section.
Electronic care plans
Computers are increasingly used to generate and store both
standardised and individualised nursing care plans. Nurses access
the person’s stored care plan from a centrally located terminal at the
nurses’ station or from a terminal in the person’s room. The nurse
chooses goals and interventions appropriate for the individual and
adds additional goals and interventions or nursing actions not listed.
Multidisciplinary (collaborative)
care plans


A multidisciplinary care plan
 is a standardised plan that
outlines the care required for people with common, predictable—
usually medical—conditions. Such plans, also referred to as
collaborative care plans
 and clinical pathways
, sequence
the care that must be given on each day during the projected length
of stay for the specific type of condition (e.g. total hip replacement
pathway). A multidisciplinary care plan can specify outcomes and
nursing interventions to address patient problems (including nursing
diagnoses). However, it includes therapies to be performed by other
health care professionals such as physiotherapists and occupational
therapists. A multidisciplinary care plan is usually organised with a
section for each day, listing the interventions that should be carried
out and the care goals to be achieved on that day.
Guidelines for writing nursing
care plans
Nurses should use the following guidelines when writing nursing care
plans:
1. Date and sign the plan. The date the plan is written is
essential for evaluation, review and future planning. The
nurse’s signature demonstrates accountability to the person
and to the nursing profession.
2. Use category headings: ‘Nursing diagnoses’, ‘Goals/desired
outcomes’, ‘Nursing interventions’ and ‘Evaluation’. Include a


date for the evaluation of each goal.
3. Use standardised/approved medical terminology and
abbreviations where appropriate. For example, ‘Clean
wound with normal saline bd’ rather than ‘Clean the person’s
wound with normal saline twice a day, morning and evening’.
Table 16.5
 on page 274 provides a list of commonly used
abbreviations.
4. Be specific. Document specific times using the 24-hour clock
to clarify when nursing interventions are required.
5. Refer to protocols or other sources of information rather
than including all the steps on a written plan. For
example, write ‘See protocol for tracheostomy care’ or attach
a standard nursing plan about such procedures as radiation
implantation care and preoperative or postoperative care.
6. Tailor the plan to the unique needs of the person. Ensure
the person’s preferences are included on the plan. This
reinforces the person’s individuality and sense of control. For
example, the written nursing intervention ‘Provide prune juice
at breakfast rather than any juice’ indicates that the person
was given a choice of beverages.
7. Ensure that the nursing plan incorporates preventive and
health maintenance aspects as well as restorative ones.
For example, carrying out the intervention ‘Provide active
assistance ROM (range-of-motion) exercises to affected
limbs q2h’ prevents joint contractures and maintains muscle
strength and joint mobility.
8. Ensure that the nursing plan contains interventions for
ongoing assessment (e.g. ‘Inspect incision q8h’).


9. Include collaborative activities in the plan. For example,
the nurse may document that a referral to a dietitian or
physiotherapist is required.
10. Include plans for discharge and home care needs. The
nurse begins discharge planning as soon as the person has
been admitted. It may be necessary to consult and make
arrangements with a community health nurse, social worker
or other health care agencies that supply information or
medical equipment. Include patient teaching requirements as
part of the discharge plan if needed.


The planning process
In the process of developing care plans, the nurse engages in the
following activities:
setting priorities
establishing patient goals
selecting nursing interventions
writing individualised nursing interventions on care plans.
Setting priorities
Priority setting
 is the process of establishing a preferential
sequence for addressing nursing diagnoses and initiating
interventions. The nurse and patient begin by deciding which nursing
diagnosis requires attention first, second and so on. Instead of rank-
ordering diagnoses, nurses can group them as having high, medium
or low priority. Serious problems, such low oxygen saturation levels,
are designated as high priority. A low-priority problem is one that
requires only minimal nursing support.
It is not necessary to resolve all high-priority diagnoses before
addressing others. The nurse may partially address a high-priority
diagnosis and then take care of a diagnosis of lesser priority.


Furthermore, because the person may have several problems, the
nurse often manages more than one diagnosis at a time. Priorities
change as the person’s responses, problems and therapies change.
The nurse must consider a variety of factors when assigning
priorities, including the following:
Person’s health values and beliefs: values concerning health
may be more important to the nurse than to the person as the
nurse must ensure they provide safe and competent nursing
care. For example, a person may believe being home for the
children to be more urgent than a health problem. When there is
such a difference of opinion, the person and nurse should
discuss it openly to resolve any conflict. However, in a life-
threatening situation the nurse MUST take the initiative.
Person’s priorities: involving the person in prioritising and care
planning enhances cooperation. Sometimes, however, the
person’s perception of what is important conflicts with the nurse’s
knowledge of potential problems or complications. For example,
an elderly person may not regard turning and repositioning in bed
as important, preferring to be undisturbed. The nurse, however,
aware of the potential complications of prolonged bed rest (e.g.
muscle weakness and pressure sores), needs to inform the
person and carry out these necessary interventions.
Resources available to the nurse and person: if the necessary
resources are not available, the solution to that problem might
need to be postponed or the person may need a referral. Patient
resources, such as finances or coping ability, may also influence
the setting of priorities. For example, a person who is


unemployed may defer dental treatment; a person whose
husband is terminally ill and dependent on her may feel unable to
cope with nutritional guidance directed towards losing weight.
Urgency of the health problem: regardless of the framework
used, life-threatening situations require that the nurse assign
them high priority. Situations that affect the integrity of the
person (i.e. those that could have a negative or destructive effect
on the person) also have high priority. Such health problems as
drug abuse and radical alteration of self-concept due to
amputation can be destructive both to the individual and to the
family.
Medical treatment plan: the priorities for treating health
problems must be congruent with treatment by other health
professionals. For example, a high priority for the person might
be to become ambulatory; however, if the doctor’s therapeutic
regimen calls for extended bed rest, ambulation must assume a
lower priority in the nursing care plan. The nurse can provide or
teach exercises to facilitate ambulation later, provided the
person’s health permits. The nursing diagnosis related to
ambulation is not ignored; it is merely deferred.
Patient safety competency framework
5 Clinical reasoning
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nurses plan and implement
nursing care both autonomously and in


consultation with other members of the health
care team (Levett-Jones et al. 2017).
Establishing patient goals/desired
outcomes
After establishing priorities, the nurse and person set goals for each
nursing diagnosis. On a care plan, the goals/desired outcomes
describe, in terms of observable patient responses, what the nurse
hopes to achieve by implementing the nursing interventions. When
goals are stated broadly, the care plan must include both goals and
desired outcomes. They are sometimes combined into one
statement linked by the words ‘as evidenced by’.
Writing the broad, general goal first may help nurses to think of the
specific outcomes that are needed, but the broad goal is just a
starting point for planning. It is the specific, observable outcomes
that must be written on the care plan and used to evaluate the
person’s progress. Table 14.1
 shows both broad goals and
specific outcomes.
Table 14.1 Deriving desired outcomes from nursing diagnoses
Purpose of desired goals/outcomes


Desired outcomes/goals serve the following purposes:
Provide direction for planning nursing interventions. Ideas for
interventions come more easily if the desired outcomes state
clearly and specifically what the nurse hopes to achieve.
Serve as criteria for evaluating the person’s progress. Although
developed in the planning step of the nursing process, desired
outcomes serve as the criteria for judging the effectiveness of
nursing interventions and the person’s progress in the evaluation
step (see Chapter 15
).
Enable the person and nurse to determine when the problem has
been resolved.
Help motivate the person and nurse by providing a sense of
achievement. As goals are met, both the person and the nurse
can see that their efforts have been worthwhile. This provides
motivation to continue following the plan, especially when difficult
lifestyle changes need to be made.
Long- and short-term goals
Goals may be short term or long term. A short-term goal might be
‘Patient will raise right arm to shoulder height by Friday’. In the same
context, a long-term goal might be ‘Patient will regain full use of right
arm in 6 weeks’. Short-term goals are useful (a) for people who
require health care for a short time, and (b) for those who are
frustrated by long-term goals that seem difficult to attain and who
need the satisfaction of achieving a short-term goal. In an acute


care setting, much of the nurse’s time is spent on the person’s
immediate needs, so most goals are short term. However, people in
acute care settings also need long-term goals to guide planning for
their discharge to long-term care facilities or home care, especially in
a managed care environment. Long-term goals are often used for
people who live at home and have chronic health problems, and for
people in nursing homes, extended care facilities and rehabilitation
centres.
Relationship between desired
goals/outcomes and nursing
diagnoses
Goals are derived from the nursing diagnoses. For example, if the
nursing diagnosis is Risk of dehydration related to diarrhoea and
nausea evidenced by hypotension, tachycardia, poor skin turgor, dry
mucous membranes and oliguria, the goal might be:
The patient’s fluid status will improve within 8 hours, as evidenced by urine output of
greater than 30 mL/hour, normal skin turgor and moist mucous membranes.
For every nursing diagnosis, the nurse must write the desired
outcome or outcomes that, when achieved, directly demonstrate
resolution of the problem. When developing goals/desired outcomes,
ask the following questions:


What is the person’s problem?
How will the person look or behave if the healthy response is
achieved? (What will I be able to see, hear, measure, palpate,
smell or otherwise observe with my senses?)
What must the person do and how well must the person do it to
demonstrate that the problem has resolved?
Components of goals/desired
outcome statements
Goals/desired outcome statements should specify both action and
time. The action is the observable behaviour that the person is to
perform. The time specifies when the behaviour is to be performed
to demonstrate achievement of the goal. Table 14.2
 illustrates the
format that should be used to write outcomes.
Table 14.2 Components of goals/desired outcomes
Guidelines for writing goals/desired
outcomes
The following guidelines can help nurses write useful goals and
desired outcomes:


Goals and outcomes should be specific, measurable and written
in terms of the person’s responses, not nursing actions. For
example:
Correct: The patient will drink 100 mL of water per hour (patient
behaviour).
Incorrect: Maintain patient hydration (nursing action).
Be sure that desired outcomes are realistic for the person’s
capabilities, limitations and designated time span. ‘Limitations’
refers to finances, equipment, family support, social services,
physical and mental condition, and time. For example, the
outcome ‘Measures insulin accurately’ may be unrealistic for a
person who has poor vision due to cataracts or diabetic
retinopathy.
Ensure that the goals and desired outcomes align with the
requirements of other professionals. For example, the outcome
‘Will increase the time spent out of bed by 15 minutes each day’
is not compatible with a doctor’s order of bed rest.
Make sure that each goal is derived from only one nursing
diagnosis. For example, the goal ‘The patient will increase the
amount of nutrients ingested and show progress in the ability to
feed self’ is derived from two nursing diagnoses and should have
two goals. Keeping the goal statement related to only one
diagnosis makes it easier to evaluate care by ensuring that
planned nursing interventions are clearly related to one specific
diagnosis.
Use observable, measurable terms for outcomes. Avoid words
that are vague and require interpretation or judgment by the


observer. For example, non-specific phrases such as increase
daily exercise and improve knowledge of nutrition can mean
different things to different people. If used in outcomes, these
phrases can lead to ambiguity in determining whether the
outcome was met.
Make sure the goals/desired outcomes are important to the
person. Some outcomes, such as those for problems related to
self-esteem, parenting and communication, involve choices that
are best made by the person themself.
Some people may know what they wish to accomplish with regard to
their health problem; others may not know all the outcome
possibilities. The nurse must actively listen to the person to
determine personal values, goals and desired outcomes in relation
to current health concerns. People are usually motivated and
expend the necessary energy to reach goals they consider
important.
Selecting nursing interventions
and actions
Nursing interventions and actions are identified to facilitate
achievement of patient goals. The specific interventions chosen
should focus on eliminating or reducing the aetiology (related cause)
of the nursing diagnosis.


When it is not possible to change the aetiological factors, the nurse
chooses interventions to treat the signs and symptoms. Examples of
this situation would be Pain related to surgical incision and Anxiety
related to unknown aetiology.
Interventions for risk nursing diagnoses should focus on measures
to prevent or reduce the person’s risk factors.
Correct identification of the aetiology during the diagnosing phase
provides the framework for choosing successful nursing
interventions. For example, the nursing diagnosis Inability to tolerate
sustained activity may have several aetiologies (causes): pain,
weakness, sedentary lifestyle, anxiety or cardiac arrhythmias.
Nursing interventions will vary according to the cause of the
problem.
Types of nursing interventions
Nursing interventions are identified and written during the planning
stage of the nursing process; however, they are actually performed
during the implementing stage. Nursing interventions include both
direct and indirect care, as well as nurse-initiated, doctor-initiated
and other-provider-initiated treatments. Direct care is an intervention
performed through interaction with the person. Indirect care is an
intervention performed away from but on behalf of the person, such
as interprofessional collaboration or management of the care
environment.


Independent interventions
 are those activities that nurses are
permitted to undertake on the basis of their knowledge and skills.
They include physical care, ongoing assessment, emotional support
and comfort, teaching, counselling, environmental management and
making referrals to other health care professionals. Recall from
Chapter 13
 that nursing diagnoses are patient problems that can
be treated primarily by independent nursing interventions. In
performing an autonomous activity, the nurse determines that the
person requires certain nursing interventions, either carries these
out or delegates them to other nursing personnel and is accountable
or answerable for the decision and the actions (NMBA 2016). An
example of an independent action is planning and providing oral care
for a person after diagnosing Dry oral mucous membranes.
Dependent interventions
 are activities carried out under the
doctor’s orders or supervision, or according to specified routines.
Doctors’ orders commonly direct the nurse to provide medications,
intravenous therapy, diagnostic tests, treatments, diet and activity.
The nurse is responsible for assessing the need for, explaining and
carrying out the medical orders. Nursing interventions may be
written to individualise the medical order based on the person’s
status. For example, for a medical order of ‘Progressive ambulation,
as tolerated’, a nurse might write the following:
1. Dangle feet over bedside for 5 mins, 12 hours postop.
2. Stand at bedside for 5 mins 24 hours postop; observe for
pallor, dizziness and weakness.


3. Check pulse before and after ambulating. Do not continue if
.
Collaborative interventions
 are actions the nurse carries out in
collaboration with other team members, such as physiotherapists,
social workers, occupational therapists, dietitians, psychologists and
doctors. Collaborative nursing activities reflect the overlapping
responsibilities of, and collegial relationships between, health care
professionals. For example, the doctor might order physiotherapy so
that the physiotherapist can teach the person how to walk with
crutches. The nurse would be responsible for informing the
physiotherapy department and for coordinating the care to include
the physiotherapy sessions. When the person returns to the nursing
unit, the nurse would assist the person to walk with crutches and
collaborate with the physiotherapist to evaluate the person’s
progress.
The amount of time the nurse spends in an independent versus a
collaborative or dependent role varies according to the clinical area,
type of health care institution and role of the nurse.
Considering the consequences of
each intervention
Usually several possible interventions can be identified for each
nursing goal. The nurse’s role is to choose those that are most likely
to achieve the desired patient outcomes. The nurse begins by
pulse > 110


considering the risks and benefits of each intervention. An
intervention may have more than one consequence. For example,
‘Provide accurate information’ could result in the following patient
behaviours:
increased anxiety
decreased anxiety
wish to talk with the doctor
desire to leave the hospital
relaxation.
Determining the consequences of each intervention requires nursing
knowledge and experience. For example, the nurse’s experience
may suggest that providing information the night before the person’s
surgery may increase their worry and tension, whereas maintaining
the usual rituals before sleep is more effective. The nurse might
then consider providing information several days before surgery.
Criteria for choosing nursing interventions
After considering the consequences of the alternative nursing
interventions, the nurse chooses one or more that are likely to be
most effective. Although the nurse bases this decision on knowledge
and experience, the patient’s input is also important.
The following criteria can help the nurse choose the best nursing
interventions. The plan must be:


safe and appropriate for the individual’s age, health and condition
achievable within the resources available. For example, a
community nurse might wish to include an intervention for an
older person to ‘Check blood glucose daily’ but in order for that to
occur, either the person must have adequate vision, cognition
and memory to carry this out independently, or daily visits from a
nurse must be available and affordable
congruent with the person’s values, beliefs and culture
appropriate with other concurrent treatments and therapies (e.g.
some foods are contraindicated with some medications)
based on an appropriate rationale and informed by the best
available evidence (NMBA 2016)
within established standards of care as determined by state laws,
professional associations, best practice guidelines and the
policies of the institution. Many organisations have policies to
guide the actions of health professionals and to safeguard
people.
Writing individualised nursing
interventions
After choosing the appropriate nursing interventions, the nurse
documents them on the care plan. They must be reviewed regularly
at intervals that depend on the individual’s needs. In an intensive
care unit, for example, the plan of care will be continually monitored


and revised. In a community clinic, weekly reviews may be
appropriate.
The format of written interventions is similar to that of outcomes and
includes both actions and time. The action starts the intervention
and must be precise. For example, ‘Explain (to the patient) the
actions of insulin’ is a more precise statement than ‘Teach (the
patient) about insulin’. ‘Measure and record ankle circumference
daily at 0900 hrs’ is more precise than ‘Assess oedema of left ankle
daily’. The time element specifies when, how long or how often the
nursing action is to occur. Examples are ‘Assist patient with bath at
0700 daily’ and ‘Administer analgesia 30 minutes prior to
physiotherapy’. In some settings, the intervention (and other
segments of the nursing care plan) is signed. The signature of the
nurse prescribing the intervention shows the nurse’s accountability
and has legal significance.
Relationship of nursing
interventions to problem status
Depending on the type of patient problem, the nurse writes
interventions for observation, prevention, treatment and health
promotion (see Table 14.3
).
Table 14.3 Care planning considerations


Observations include assessments made to determine whether a
complication is developing, as well as observation of the person’s
responses to nursing and other therapies. The nurse should write
observations for both real problems and those for which the person
is at risk. Some examples are ‘Auscultate lungs eight hourly’,
‘Observe for redness over sacrum 2nd hourly’, and ‘Record intake
and output hourly’.
Prevention interventions prescribe the care needed to avoid
complications or reduce risk factors. They are needed mainly for
potential nursing diagnoses and collaborative problems. Examples
are ‘Coughing and deep breathing exercises 2nd hourly’ (to prevent
respiratory complications) and ‘Keep bed rails raised and bed in low
position’ (to prevent falls).
Treatments include teaching, referrals, physical care and other care
needed for an actual nursing diagnosis. Some interventions may
accomplish either prevention or treatment functions, depending on
the nature of the problem. In the preceding examples, ‘Coughing
and deep breathing exercises 2nd hourly’ can also be intended to
treat an existing respiratory problem.
Health promotion interventions are appropriate when the nursing
interventions are aimed at helping the person identify areas for
improvement that will lead to a higher level of wellness and actualise
the person’s overall health potential. Examples are ‘Discuss the
importance of daily exercise’ and ‘Explore possibility of yoga
classes’.


Delegating implementation
Delegating is another activity that often occurs during the planning
phase of the nursing process. While identifying nursing interventions
for the person’s care plan, the nurse must also determine who
should actually perform the activity and provide adequate
supervision of the delegated activity. The ability to delegate care and
assign tasks is a vital skill for Registered Nurses because many
health care institutions use assistive personnel (e.g. an Assistant in
Nursing (AIN) or Personal Care Attendant (PCA)). To delegate
appropriately, the nurse must be aware of the scope of practice for
each member of the nursing team as determined by their regulatory
authority (NMBA 2016), as well as the background, experience,
knowledge, skills and strengths of each person.


Concept map: Amanda Szirom
Amanda is a 50-year-old woman admitted with a potential medical
diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia. The following concept
maps and care plan provide examples of Amanda’s nursing care.
Lifespan considerations
Nursing care plan
Older adults
When a person is in a residential aged care facility,
interventions and medications often remain the same for a
number of days. However, it is still important to review the
care plan on a regular basis because changes in the
condition of older people may be subtle and go unnoticed.
Changes in improvement or deterioration should receive
attention so that appropriate revisions can be made to
expected patient outcomes and nursing interventions.
Outcomes need to be realistic, with consideration given to the
person’s physical condition, emotional condition, support
systems and mental status. Outcomes may need to be


achieved in very small steps. For instance, a person who has
had a cerebrovascular accident may spend weeks learning to
brush their own teeth or dress themself. When these small
steps are successfully completed, it gives the person a sense
of accomplishment and motivation to continue working
towards increasing self-care. This particular example also
demonstrates the need to work collaboratively with other
health professionals, such as physiotherapists and
occupational therapists, to develop the nursing care plan.

Chapter 14 Review


Chapter highlights
Planning is the process of designing nursing actions required to
prevent, reduce or address a person’s health problems.
Planning involves the nurse, the person, support people and
other health professionals.
Shorter acute care hospitalisation necessitates careful discharge
planning.
Standardised care plans should be adapted and used with
individualised plans to meet individual patient needs.
The nursing care plan provides direction for individualised care of
the person.
Nursing diagnoses are assigned high, medium and low priorities
in consultation with the person, if health permits.
The planning process includes determining priorities to address
the nursing diagnosis, establishing patient goals/desired
outcomes, selecting nursing interventions and documenting
individualised nursing interventions.
The nurse consults with other nurses or health professionals to
verify information, implement changes or obtain additional
knowledge to aid in patient goals.
Patient goals/desired outcomes are used to plan nursing
interventions that will achieve anticipated changes in the person’s
condition.
Desired outcomes describe specific and measurable patient
responses and help the nurse evaluate the effectiveness of the
nursing interventions.


Patient goals/desired outcomes are derived from, and based on,
the nursing diagnosis.
Goal statements and desired outcomes are written in terms of
the person’s behaviour.
Nursing interventions are focused on alleviating problems
identified through nursing diagnosis.
Independent nursing interventions are those the nurse is licensed
to prescribe or delegate.
Projecting the consequences of each nursing strategy requires
nursing knowledge and experience.

1. Pain.
2. Nausea.
3. Constipation.
4. Potential for wound infection.

Measure patient’s fluid intake and output. F. Jenkins, RN’.
What element of a proper nursing intervention has been

1. Action verb.
2. Content.
