The nursing process is action oriented, person
centred and outcome directed. After developing
a plan of care based on the assessing and
diagnosing phases, nurses implement the
interventions and evaluate the desired
outcomes. On the basis of this evaluation, the
plan of care is continued, modified or
terminated. As in all phases of the nursing
process, the person and their support people
are encouraged to participate as much as
possible.


Implementing
In the nursing process, implementing is the action phase in which
the nurse performs the nursing interventions. Implementing
consists of doing and documenting the activities that are the specific
nursing actions needed to carry out the interventions, while at the
same time engaging in critical thinking. Nurses perform or delegate
the nursing activities for the interventions that were developed in the
planning step and then conclude the implementing step by
documenting nursing activities and the resulting responses.
Although nurses may act on the person’s behalf (e.g. referring to a
community health nurse for home care), professional standards
support a person- and family-centred approach in all phases of the
nursing process. The degree of participation depends on the
person’s health status. For example, while an unconscious man is
unable to participate in his care and therefore needs to have care
provided for him, this care should be developed in consultation with
his family. By contrast, an ambulatory person’s care would be
developed collaboratively and may require very little direct input from
the nurse.


Relationship of implementing to
other nursing process phases
The first three phases of the nursing process—assessing,
diagnosing and planning—provide the basis for the nursing actions
performed during the implementing step. In turn, the implementing
phase refers to the actual nursing activities. This is followed by an
evaluation of the person’s responses to the activities— this is the
final phase of the nursing process. Using data acquired during
assessment, the nurse individualises the care delivered in the
implementing phase, tailoring the interventions to fit the specific
person’s needs rather than applying them routinely to categories of
people (e.g. all people with pneumonia).
While implementing nursing care, nurses continue to reassess the
person regularly, gathering data about their needs and responses to
the nursing activities and any new problems that may have
developed. A nursing activity on the care plan for Airway
management might read ‘Auscultate breath sounds q4h’. When
performing this activity, the nurse is both carrying out the
intervention (implementing) and performing an assessment. Some
routine nursing activities are, themselves, assessments. For
example, while assisting an older adult with bathing, the nurse can
observe skin integrity and may detect any abnormality such as a
reddened area on the person’s sacrum. Or, when emptying a urinary


catheter bag, the nurse assesses the urine and may record ‘200 mL
of offensive-smelling, brown urine’.
Implementing skills
To implement a person-centred care plan successfully, nurses need
critical-thinking, interpersonal and technical skills. Although these
may be distinct from one another, in practice nurses use them in
various combinations and with a different emphasis depending on
the activity. For instance, when inserting a urinary catheter, the
nurse needs to critically review the need for this intervention, have
knowledge of the principles and steps of the procedure, employ
interpersonal skills to inform, reassure and protect the dignity of the
person, and have the technical or psychomotor skills needed to
drape the person, manipulate the equipment and correctly adhere to
principles of asepsis.
The cognitive skills
 (intellectual skills) include problem solving,
decision making, critical thinking and clinical reasoning. They are
crucial to safe and effective nursing care (see Chapter 11
).
Interpersonal skills
 are all the activities, verbal and non-verbal,
people use when interacting directly with one another. The
effectiveness of nursing actions often depends largely on the nurse’s
ability to communicate with others. The nurse uses therapeutic
communication to understand the person and, in turn, be
understood. One of the recommendations of the Special


Commission of Inquiry: Acute Care Services in NSW Public
Hospitals (Garling ) is that the health care team provides person-
centred ‘shared’ care. In order to offer effective shared care, nurses
also need to work effectively with other members of the
interprofessional health care team (Paliadelis et al. ). The
importance of effective communication is further reinforced by the
findings of the New South Wales Health Patient Survey . This survey
of over 70 000 health care consumers in New South Wales found
that an individual’s satisfaction is linked to the availability of nurses
and doctors and, in particular, that people felt more satisfied when
they had the opportunity to discuss their anxieties and fears with
nurses.
1 Garling, P. (2008). Special Commission of Inquiry: Acute Care Services in NSW Public
Hospitals. Sydney: New South Wales Government.
2 Paliadelis, P., Parmenter, G., Parker, V., Giles, M. & Higgins, I. (2012). The challenges
confronting clinicians in rural acute care settings: A participatory research project. Rural and
Remote Health Research, Education, Practice and Policy, 12(2), 1–12.
3 New South Wales Health (2008). Health Patient Survey 2007: State-wide Report. Sydney:
New South Wales Health.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: partnering with consumers
The National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2017) require that the health care
workforce partner with consumers (or their
1
2
3


carers) when developing their care (Australian
Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) , p. 14).
4 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Interpersonal skills are necessary for all nursing activities: caring,
comforting, advocating, referring, counselling and supporting, to
name just a few. Interpersonal skills include conveying knowledge,
attitudes, feelings, interest in and appreciation of the person’s
cultural values and lifestyle. Before nurses can be highly skilled in
interpersonal relations, they must have self-awareness and
sensitivity to others (see Chapters 26
 and 40
).
Technical skills
 are purposeful ‘hands-on’ skills, such as
manipulating equipment, giving injections, bandaging and moving
and repositioning. These skills are also called tasks, procedures or
psychomotor skills. The term psychomotor refers to physical actions
that are controlled by critical thought and clinical decision making,
which means that they are not just reflexive actions.
Technical skills require knowledge and, frequently, manual dexterity.
The number of technical skills expected of nurses has greatly
4


increased in recent years because of the pervasive use of
technology, especially in acute care hospitals.
Process of implementing
Before implementing, the nurse must inform the person and seek
their consent. The process of implementing (see Figure 15.1
)
normally includes the following:
Reassessing the person.
Determining the nurse’s need for assistance.
Implementing the nursing interventions.
Supervising the delegated care.
Documenting nursing activities.
Figure 15.1


Implementing. The fourth phase of the nursing process, in which the
nurse implements the nursing interventions and documents the care
provided.
Reassessing the person
Just before implementing an intervention, nurses must reassess the
person to make sure the intervention is still needed. Even though a
problem is included on the care plan, the person’s condition may
have changed. For example, a person has a Disturbed sleep pattern
related to anxiety and unfamiliar surroundings. During rounds, the
nurse discovers that the person is sleeping and therefore defers the
back massage that had been planned as a relaxation strategy.
New data may indicate a need to change the priorities of care or the
nursing activities. For example, a nurse begins to teach an adult who
has diabetes how to self-administer insulin injections. Shortly after
beginning the teaching, the nurse realises that the person is not
concentrating on the lesson. Subsequent discussion reveals that this
adult is worried about his eyesight and fears he is going blind.
Realising that the person’s anxiety is interfering with his learning, the
nurse ends the lesson and arranges for an eye test to be performed.
The nurse also engages in supportive communication to help
alleviate the person’s anxiety.
Determining the nurse’s need for
assistance


When implementing some nursing interventions, nurses may require
assistance for one or more of the following reasons:
The nurse is unable to implement the nursing activity safely or
efficiently alone (e.g. ambulating an unsteady, obese person).
Assistance would reduce the person’s discomfort (e.g. turning a
person who experiences acute pain when moved).
The nurse lacks the knowledge or skills to implement a particular
nursing activity (e.g. a nurse who is not familiar with a particular
model of traction equipment needs assistance the first time it is
applied). The implementation may not fall into the nurse’s scope
of practice and therefore assistance from a more senior
Registered Nurse or other health professional is required.
Implementing the nursing interventions
It is important to discuss any interventions with the person to ensure
there is mutual understanding of what interventions will be
undertaken, what sensations to expect, what they are expected to
do and what the expected outcome is. For many nursing activities it
is also important to ensure the person’s privacy; for example, by
closing doors, pulling curtains or draping. The number and kind of
direct nursing interventions are almost unlimited. Nurses also make
appropriate referrals; this involves scheduling the person’s contacts
with other staff or departments (e.g. laboratory, x-ray technicians or
physiotherapy) and serving as a liaison between the various
members of the health care team.


When implementing interventions, nurses should follow these
guidelines:
Base nursing interventions on scientific knowledge, nursing
research and professional standards of care (evidence-based
practice). Critically review the intervention with the person,
paying particular attention to current best-practice evidence and
the cultural safety of the person. The nurse must be aware of the
scientific rationale as well as possible side effects or
complications of all interventions. For example, a person may
prefer to take an oral medication after meals; however, evidence
shows that this medication is not absorbed well in the presence
of food. Therefore, the nurse will need to discuss why this
preference is not advisable and negotiate an acceptable
alternative for this person.
In Australia, nurses have access to a number of national and
state health-department-sponsored websites that provide easy
access to evidence-based information. Similarly, a national
database, the Joanna Briggs Institute <www.joannabriggs.org>,
compiles evidence and produces systematic reviews in single-
sheet form, called Best Practice Information Sheets, as well as
clinical procedure manuals that are available to health care
professionals.
Ensure that they understand the interventions to be implemented
and ask questions about any aspects they do not understand.
The nurse is responsible for intelligent implementation of plans of
care. This requires critical thought about each intervention, its
purpose in the person’s plan of care, any contraindications (e.g.


allergies) and changes in the person’s condition that may affect
the intervention.
Adapt activities in consultation with the individual. A person’s
beliefs, cultural background, values, age, health status and
environment are factors that can affect the success of a nursing
action. For example, the nurse identifies that a person believes
he will choke when swallowing pills, so the nurse can consult with
the medical officer to change the order to a liquid form of the
medication. Or the nurse recognises that many people from
Asian countries prefer to drink warm water rather than iced water
and, after confirming this with the individual, supplies this at the
bedside. Nurses must also recognise that Indigenous Australians
have particular cultural needs and these must be addressed in
order to provide appropriate and quality nursing care in a
culturally safe manner (Marmot ).
5 Marmot, M. (2011). Social determinants and the health of Indigenous Australians.
Medical Journal of Australia, 194(10), 512–513.
Implement safe care. For example, when changing a sterile
dressing, the nurse practises sterile technique to prevent
infection; when giving a medication, the nurse administers the
correct dosage by the ordered route and adheres to the five
rights of medication administration:
1. The right person.
2. The right drug.
3. The right dose.
4. The right route.
5. The right time (Kim & Bates ).
5
6


6 Kim, J. & Bates, D. W. (2013). Medication administration errors by nurses:
Adherence to guidelines. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 22(3–4), 590–598. Doi:
10.1111/j.1365-2702. 2012.04344.x.
In some parts of Australia, nurses are taught to adhere to six,
seven, eight or even nine rights, with the added ones commonly
being about the ‘right documentation’ (Elliott & Liu ; Evans ), ‘the
right to refuse’ or the ‘right response’ (Wakefield ).
7 Elliott, M. & Liu, Y. (2010). The nine rights of medication administration: An overview.
British Journal of Nursing, 19(5), 300−305.
8 Evans, J. (2009). Prevalence, risk factors, consequences and strategies for reducing
medication errors in Australian hospitals. Contemporary Nurse, 31(2), 176–189.
9 Wakefield, J. (2008). Patient Safety: From Learning to Action 11. Queensland:
Queensland Health.
Provide teaching, support and comfort. See Chapter 28
 for
details of person-centred teaching and Box 28.5
 for examples
of verbs used in writing learning outcomes. The nurse should
always discuss the purpose of interventions, identifying what the
person will experience and how the person can participate. The
nurse must seek the person’s agreement to the plan of care and
encourage the person to assume responsibility for as much self-
care as possible. These independent nursing activities enhance
the effectiveness of nursing care plans (see Figure 15.2
).
Be holistic. The nurse must always view the person as a whole
and consider the person’s needs and responses in that context.
For example, whenever possible, nurses honour the person’s
7
8
9


preference that interventions be planned for times that fit with the
person’s usual schedule of visitors, work, rest, prayer or eating.
Respect the dignity of the person and enhance the person’s self-
esteem. Providing privacy and collaborating with people to
encourage them to make their own decisions are ways of
respecting dignity and enhancing self-esteem.
Encourage people to participate actively in implementing the
nursing interventions. Active participation enhances the person’s
sense of independence and control. However, people vary in the
degree of participation they desire. Some want total involvement
in their care, whereas others prefer little involvement. The
amount of desired involvement may be related to the severity of
the illness, the person’s culture or fear about the illness and the
intervention. Cultural issues must also be considered in relation
to the degree of involvement the person wishes to have.
Figure 15.2


Amanda agrees to deep-breathing exercises q3h during the day. In
addition, she verbalises awareness of the need to increase fluid
intake.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Patient safety competency framework
3 Cultural competence
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nurses demonstrate cultural
empathy by seeking to understand the person’s
cultural and spiritual values, needs, practices
and perspectives (Levett-Jones et al.
).
10 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Supervising delegated care
If care has been delegated to other health care personnel, the nurse
remains responsible for coordinating the person’s overall care and
must ensure that activities have been implemented according to the
care plan and in collaboration with the person. The Registered Nurse
10


is also responsible for ensuring other care workers are performing
within their scope of practice. For example, many Enrolled Nurses
give medications (usually excluding Schedule 8) by any route,
provided this is written into local area health policy and the overall
responsibility remains under the supervision of a Registered Nurse
(Australian Nursing and Midwifery Accreditation Council ). However,
it is noted in the national framework for the development of decision-
making tools for nursing and midwifery practice (Nursing and
Midwifery Board of Australia ) that Enrolled Nurses may not
delegate medication administration to other Enrolled Nurses or non-
nurses. Other caregivers, including unregulated nursing assistants,
are required to discuss their activities with the Registered Nurse and
document them on the person’s health record. The nurse validates
and responds to any adverse findings or responses. This may
involve modifying the nursing care plan.
11 Australian Nursing and Midwifery Accreditation Council (ANMAC) (2012). Strategic
Statement 2018-2021. Retrieved from <anmac.org.au>.
12 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (2013). A National Framework for the
Development of Decision-Making Tools for Nursing and Midwifery Practice. Retrieved from
<www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Documenting nursing activities
After carrying out nursing activities, nurses complete the
implementing phase by recording the interventions and the person’s
responses in the nursing progress notes. These are a part of
organisations’ permanent record for the person. Nursing care must
11
12


not be recorded in advance because the nurse may determine on
reassessment of the person that the intervention should not or
cannot be implemented. For example, if a person had a legal
medication order for 10 mg of subcutaneous morphine sulfate, but
the nurse finds that the person’s respiratory rate is 4 breaths per
minute, the nurse would withhold the morphine and report the
person’s low respiratory rate to the nursing unit manager and/or the
medical officer.
The nurse may record routine or recurring activities (e.g. mouth
care) in the person’s record at the end of a shift. However, in most
instances it is preferable to record any nursing interventions
immediately after they are implemented. According to Staunton and
Chiarella (
, p. 204), ‘entries in reports should be made at the time
a relevant incident occurs. This is known as “contemporaneous
reporting”’. This is particularly true of the administration of
medications and treatments. Recorded data about a person must be
up to date, accurate and available to other nurses and health care
professionals. Immediate recording helps safeguard the person, for
example, from receiving a duplicate dose of medication.
13 Staunton, P. & Chiarella, M. (2017). Law for Nurses and Midwives (8th ed.). Sydney:
Elsevier.
Nursing activities are communicated verbally as well as in writing.
When a person’s health is changing rapidly, the nursing unit
manager and/or the medical officer may want to be kept up to date
with frequent verbal reports. Nurses also report a person’s status at
a change of shift and on a person’s discharge to another unit or
13


health organisation in person, via a voice recording or in writing.
Shift handover is best conducted at the person’s bedside as this
practice assists in developing more effective person-centred care.
For further information on documenting and reporting, see Chapter
16
.


Evaluating
To evaluate is to judge or to appraise. Evaluating is the fifth and last
phase of the nursing process. In this context, evaluating
 is a
planned, ongoing, purposeful activity in which health care
professionals use a person-centred approach to determine (a) the
person’s progress towards achievement of goals/outcomes, and (b)
the effectiveness of the intervention(s). Evaluation is an important
aspect of the nursing process because conclusions drawn from the
evaluation determine whether the nursing interventions should be
terminated, continued or changed.
Evaluation is continuous. Evaluation performed during or
immediately after implementing a nursing order enables nurses to
make on-the-spot modifications in interventions. Evaluation
performed at specified intervals (e.g. once a week for the person
needing home care) shows the extent of progress towards goal
achievement and enables nurses to correct any deficiencies and
modify care plans accordingly. Evaluation continues until the person
achieves the agreed health goals or is discharged from nursing care.
Evaluation at discharge includes the status of goal achievement and
the person’s self-care abilities with regard to follow-up care. Most
health care organisations have a special discharge record for this
evaluation.


Through evaluating, nurses demonstrate responsibility and
accountability for their actions, indicate the results of the nursing
activities and demonstrate a desire not to perpetuate ineffective
actions, but to adopt more effective ones.
Relationship of evaluating to other
nursing process phases
Successful evaluation depends on the effectiveness of the steps that
precede it. Assessment data must be accurate and complete so that
nurses can formulate appropriate nursing diagnoses and desired
outcomes. The desired outcomes must be stated concretely in
behavioural terms if they are to be useful for evaluating a person’s
responses. Finally, without the implementing phase in which the plan
is put into action, there would be nothing to evaluate.
The evaluating and assessing phases overlap. As previously stated,
assessment (data collection) is ongoing and continuous at every
contact between the health care professional and the person.
However, data are collected for different purposes at different points
in the nursing process. During the assessment phase, the nurse
collects data for the purpose of making clinical decisions. During the
evaluation step, the nurse collects data for the purpose of
comparing them with agreed goals and judging the effectiveness of
the nursing care. The act of assessing (data collection) is the same;


the differences lie in (a) when the data are collected, and (b) how
the data are used.
Process of evaluating responses
to care
Before evaluation, the nurse discusses with the person the desired
outcomes that will be used to measure goal achievement. Desired
outcomes serve two purposes: (1) they establish the kind of
evaluative data that need to be collected; and (2) they provide a
standard against which the data are judged. For example, given the
following expected outcomes, any nurse caring for the person would
know what data to collect:
Daily fluid intake will not be less than 2500 mL.
Urinary output will balance with fluid intake.
Residual urine will be less than 100 mL.
The evaluation process has five components (see Figure 15.3
):
1. Collecting data related to the desired outcomes.
2. Comparing the data with desired outcomes.
3. Relating nursing activities to outcomes.
4. Drawing conclusions about problem status.
5. Continuing, modifying or terminating the nursing care plan.


Figure 15.3


Evaluating. The final phase of the nursing process, in which the
nurse determines the person’s progress towards goal achievement
and the effectiveness of the nursing care plan. The plan may be
continued, modified or terminated.
Collecting data related to the desired
outcomes
Using the clearly stated, precise and measurable desired outcomes
as a guide, the nurse collects data so that conclusions can be drawn
about whether goals have been met. It is usually necessary to
collect both objective and subjective data.
Some data may require interpretation. Examples of objective data
requiring interpretation are the degree of tissue turgor of a
dehydrated person or the degree of restlessness of a person with
pain. Examples of subjective data needing interpretation include the
person’s symptoms of nausea or pain. When interpreting subjective
data, the nurse must use critical thinking and rely on either (a) the
person’s statements (e.g. ‘My pain is worse now than it was after
breakfast’), or (b) objective indicators of the subjective data, even
though these indicators may require further interpretation (e.g.
decreased restlessness, decreased pulse and respiratory rates, and
relaxed facial muscles as indicators of pain relief). Data must be
recorded concisely and accurately to facilitate the next part of the
evaluating process.


Comparing data with desired outcomes
If the first two parts of the evaluation process have been carried out
effectively, it is relatively simple to determine whether a desired
outcome has been met. Both the nurse and the individual play an
active role in comparing the actual responses with the desired
outcomes. Did the person drink 3000 mL of fluid in 24 hours? Did
they walk unassisted the specified distance per day? When
determining whether a goal has been achieved, the nurse can draw
one of three possible conclusions:
1. The goal was met; that is, the person’s response is the same
as the desired outcome.
2. The goal was partially met; that is, either a short-term goal
was achieved but the long-term goal was not, or the desired
outcome was only partially attained.
3. The goal was not met.
In consultation with the person, a nurse determines whether a goal
has been met and writes an evaluative statement (either on the care
plan or in the person’s progress notes). An evaluation statement
consists of two parts: a conclusion and supporting data. The
conclusion is a statement that the goal/desired outcome was met,
partially met or not met. The supporting data are the list of
responses that support the conclusion, for example:
Goal met: oral intake 300 mL more than output; skin turgor resilient; mucous membranes
moist.


See the ‘Nursing care plan
’ at the end of the chapter for
evaluation statements for Amanda Szirom. Data in the ‘Evaluation
statements’ column of this table represent Ms Szirom’s responses to
care as observed by the night nurse on the morning after her
admission to the unit. In practice, care plans often do not have a
column for evaluation statements; rather, these are recorded in the
nurse’s notes.
Relating nursing activities to outcomes
The third aspect of the evaluating process is determining whether
the nursing activities had any relation to the outcomes. It should
never be assumed that a nursing activity was the cause of, or the
only factor in, meeting, partially meeting or not meeting a goal. For
example, a person was obese and needed to lose 14 kg. When the
nurse and the person drew up a care plan, one goal was ‘Lose 1.4
kg in 4 weeks’. A nursing strategy in the care plan was ‘Discuss how
to plan and prepare a 1200 calorie a day diet’. Four weeks later, the
person weighed herself and had lost 1.8 kg. The goal had been met
—in fact, exceeded. It is easy to assume that the nursing strategy
was highly effective. However, it is important to collect more data
before drawing that conclusion. On questioning the person, the
nurse might find any of the following: (a) the person planned a 1200
calorie diet and prepared and ate the food; (b) the person planned a
1200 calorie diet but did not prepare the correct food; (c) the person
did not understand how to plan a 1200 calorie diet, so she did not
bother with it.


If the first possibility is found to be true, the nurse can safely judge
that the nursing strategy ‘Explain how to plan and prepare a 1200
calorie diet’ was effective in helping the person lose weight.
However, if the nurse learns that either the second or third possibility
actually happened, it must be assumed that the nursing strategy did
not affect the outcome. The next step for the nurse is to collect data
about what the person actually did to lose weight. Therefore, it is
important to establish the relationship (or lack thereof) of the nursing
actions to the person’s responses.
Drawing conclusions about problem
status
Nurses use critical thinking to make clinical judgments about goal
achievement to determine whether the care plan was effective in
resolving, reducing or preventing the person’s problems. In order to
do this, the nurse would critically review the stated problem, and the
subjective and objective data related to each goal, and compare this
to the desired outcomes to determine whether the goals have been
met. When goals have been met, the nurse can draw one of the
following conclusions about the status of the person’s problem:
The actual problem stated in the care planning stage has been
resolved or the potential problem is being prevented and the risk
factors no longer exist. In these instances, the nurse documents
that the goals have been met and discontinues the care for the
problem.


The potential problem is being prevented but the risk factors are
still present. In this case, the nurse keeps the problem on the
care plan.
The actual problem still exists even though some goals are being
met. For example, a desired outcome on a person’s care plan is
‘Will drink 3000 mL of fluid daily’. Even though the data may
show this outcome has been achieved, other data (dry oral
mucous membranes) may indicate that the person is still
dehydrated. Therefore, the nursing interventions must be
continued even though this one goal was met.
When goals have been partially met or when goals have not been
met, two conclusions may be drawn:
1. The care plan may need to be revised in consultation with the
individual and the health care team because the problem is
only partially resolved. The revisions may need to occur
during assessing, diagnosing or planning phases, as well as
implementing.
OR
2. The care plan does not need revision because the person
merely needs more support or time to achieve the previously
established goal(s). To make this decision, the nurse must
assess why the goals have only been partially achieved,
including whether the evaluation was conducted too soon
(see Figure 15.4
).
Figure 15.4


Upon assessment of respiratory excursion, the nurse detects failure
of the person to achieve maximum ventilation. The nurse and
Amanda re-evaluate the care plan and modify it to increase
coughing and deep-breathing exercises to q2h.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Continuing, modifying or terminating the
nursing care plan
After drawing conclusions about the status of a person’s problems,
nurses modify the care plan as indicated. Depending on the health
care organisation, modifications may be made by drawing a line
through portions of the care plan, marking portions using a
highlighting pen or writing ‘Discontinued’ (dc’d), ‘goal met’ or
‘problem resolved’ and the date.
Whether or not goals were met, a number of decisions need to be
made about continuing, modifying or terminating nursing care for
each problem. See Table 15.1
 for a checklist to use when
reviewing a care plan. Although the checklist uses a closed-ended
Yes/No format, its only intent is to identify areas that require the
nurse’s further examination.
Table 15.1 Evaluation checklist
Before making modifications, the nurse must critically review
whether the plan as a whole was completely effective. This requires


a review of the entire care plan and a critique of each step of the
nursing process involved in its development.
Assessing
Incomplete or incorrect data influences all subsequent steps of the
nursing process and care plan. If data are incomplete, the nurse
needs to reassess the person and record the new data. In some
instances, new data may indicate the need to identify new, actual
and potential problems, new goals and new nursing interventions.
Diagnosing
If the data were incomplete, new problem statements may be
required. If the data were complete, the nurse needs to analyse
whether the problems were identified correctly and whether they
were relevant to those data. After making judgments about problem
status, the nurse revises or adds new actual and potential problems
as needed to reflect the most recent evaluative data.
Planning: desired outcomes
If an actual or potential problem was inaccurate, obviously the goal
statement will need revision. If the problem statement was
appropriate, the nurse checks if the goals were realistic and
attainable. Unrealistic goals require correction. The nurse should
also determine whether priorities have changed and whether the
person still agrees with the priorities. For example, the amount of


time required to achieve a specific amount of weight loss was
possibly too short and should be extended. Goals must also be
written for any new nursing diagnoses.
Planning: nursing interventions
The nurse investigates whether the nursing interventions were
related to goal achievement and whether the best nursing
interventions were selected. Even when problem statements and
goals are appropriate, the nursing interventions selected may not
have been the best ones to achieve the goal. It is particularly
important to develop goals in consultation with the person, taking
into consideration their needs and expectations. New nursing
interventions may reflect changes in the amount of nursing care the
person needs, scheduling changes or rearrangement of nursing
activities to group similar activities or to permit longer rest or activity
periods for the person. For example, for a person who wishes to
stop smoking, there are many potential interventions. If medication
was prescribed but the person is still smoking, possibly a
behavioural intervention such as group counselling could be added.
If new problem statements have been written, new nursing
interventions will also be necessary.
Implementing
Even if all sections of the care plan appear to be satisfactory, the
manner in which the plan was implemented may have interfered with
goal achievement. Before selecting new interventions, the nurse


should check whether they were carried out. Other personnel may
not have carried them out, either because the interventions were
unclear or because they were unreasonable in terms of external
constraints such as staff time and resources. It is also important for
Registered Nurses to understand their role in the delegation of
nursing interventions to Enrolled Nurses and non-nurse caregivers to
ensure that no worker exceeds their scope of practice.
After making the necessary modifications to the care plan, the nurse
implements and/or delegates nursing care according to the modified
plan and begins the nursing process cycle again. Refer to the
‘Nursing care plan
’ at the end of this chapter to see how the plan
for Amanda Szirom was modified after evaluation of goal
achievement and review of the nursing process. A line has been
drawn through portions the nurse wished to delete; additions to the
care plan are shown in italics.
Evaluating the quality of nursing
care
In addition to evaluating goal achievement for individuals, nurses are
also involved in evaluating and modifying the overall quality of the
person-centred care delivered. This is an essential part of
professional accountability and is mandated in the National Safety
and Quality Health Service Standards (ACSQHC 2017). In each of
the processes described, nurses and all other health care providers


work together as an interprofessional team focused on improving
person-centred care. The activities both use and contribute to
evidence-based practice.
Quality assurance
A quality-assurance (QA) program
 is an ongoing, systematic
process designed to evaluate and promote excellence in the health
care provided to people. Quality assurance frequently refers to
evaluation of the level of care provided in a health care organisation.
It may be limited to the evaluation of the performance of one nurse
or more broadly involve the evaluation of the quality of the care in an
organisation, or even in a country. In Australia, the agency charged
with conducting an evaluation of the continuous quality improvement
of health care facilities is the Australian Council on Healthcare
Standards (ACHS)
. Another agency involved in the quality of
health care is the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality
in Health Care (ACSQHC)
, which is responsible for the National
Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (2017) for Australia.
The ACHS undertakes comprehensive reviews of health care
standards using a four-year cycle of self-assessment and an
organisation-wide survey. The current version of the Evaluation and
Quality Improvement Program (EQuIP)
 is EQuIP6, which
focuses on three topic areas:
1. clinical
2. support


3. corporate.
Within each of these focus areas are mandatory criteria that must
be met for the facility to gain accreditation. For example, under the
clinical heading one of the mandatory criteria is ‘care is planned and
delivered in partnership with the consumer/client and, where
relevant, the carer, to achieve the best possible outcomes’
(ACHS ).
14 Australian Council on Healthcare Standards (ACHS) (2016). EQuIP6. Retrieved from
<www.achs.org.au>.
Clinical consideration
Bad systems—and not bad people—lead to
most errors.
There are also currently strong state-based and national efforts
focused on evaluating and improving the quality of health care based
on internal assessment by health care providers and increasing
awareness by the public that medical errors are not uncommon and
can be lethal. For example, the New South Wales Health Care
Complaints Commission <www.hccc.nsw.gov.au> provides a code of
practice and publishes decisions regarding health care complaints on
its website. In addition, publications are available to download that
14


address issues such as how to lodge a complaint and how to resolve
health concerns. Other states have similar departments that
investigate health care concerns and complaints.
The National Patient Safety Education Framework was released by
the ACSQHC; the ACSQHC  has assumed responsibility for this
document. The ACSQHC is charged with identifying the knowledge
and performance required by all health care workers in relation to
safety and quality. These are presented in the National Safety and
Quality Health Service Standards (2017). The ACSQHC  has also
produced a useful discussion paper titled Patient-centred Care:
Improving Quality and Safety by Focusing Care on Patients and
Consumers (available from
<https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/dce8/582215a272b0a1ee7d5fad43
fb1e15a59e85.pdf>).
15 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2005). National
Patient Safety Education Framework. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
16 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2010). Patient-
centred Care: Improving Quality and Safety by Focusing Care on Patients and Consumers.
Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au/>.
In most states, systems are in place to record errors or ‘near
misses’; for example, in New South Wales, the Incident Information
Management System (IIMS) is the database for all reported
incidents. An evaluation of this system has been published by the
University of New South Wales (Braithwaite et al.
). A similar
system in use in the Queensland Health Department is called
15
16
17


Human Error and Patient Safety (HEAPS), while all other states and
territories have their own systems of collating incidents in an effort to
improve the quality of health care in Australia.
17 Braithwaite, J., Travaglia, J., Westbrook, M., Jorm, C., Hunter, C., Carroll, K., Iedema, R.
& Ekambareshwar, M. (2006). Evaluation of the Incident Information Management System in
New South Wales: Overview of Studies. Centre for Clinical Governance Research. Australia:
University of New South Wales.
Health care organisations must respond to incidents by assessing
the cause, identifying a plan for intervention and evaluating the
results of the plan. Often assessment involves a root cause
analysis. Root cause analysis
 is a process for identifying the
factors that brought about deviations in practices that led to the
event or incident. It focuses primarily on systems and processes
rather than individual performance. It begins with an examination of
the single event but with the goal of determining which organisational
improvements are required to decrease the likelihood of such events
occurring again.
Research note
Nurses’ experience of ethical issues
J. Rankin
. The rhetoric of patient and family centred care: An institutional ethnography into what
actually happens. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 71(3), 526–534.
18 Rankin, J. (2015). The rhetoric of patient and family centred care: An institutional ethnography into
what actually happens. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 71(3), 526–534.
18


This article explores the tensions between the nurses’ desire
to deliver person-centred care and the organisational
pressures that make it difficult for nurses to collaborate with
people to provide the care they need.
Implications Nurses need to become more critically aware of
the role that technology, funding models and hospital
agendas have in shaping the care they provide.
Unlike quality assurance, quality improvement (QI)
 follows the
individuals’ care rather than organisational structure, which focuses
on processes rather than individuals and uses a systematic
approach with the intention of improving the quality of care rather
than ensuring the quality of care. QI studies often focus on
identifying and correcting a system’s problems, such as duplication
of services in a hospital. QI is also known as continuous quality
improvement (CQI), total quality management (TQM), performance
improvement (PI) or persistent quality improvement (PQI).
Nursing audit
An audit
 means the examination or review of records. A
retrospective audit
 is the evaluation of a person’s records after
discharge from a health care facility. Retrospective means ‘relating
to past events’. A concurrent audit
 is the evaluation of a
person’s health care while the person is still receiving care from the
facility. These evaluations use the techniques of interviewing, direct
observation of nursing care and review of clinical records to
determine whether specific evaluative criteria have been met.


Another type of evaluation of care is peer review. In nurse peer
reviews, nurses functioning in the same capacity (i.e. as peers)
appraise the quality of care or practice performed by other equally
qualified nurses. A peer review is based on pre-established
standards or criteria.
There are two types of peer reviews: individual and nursing audits.
The individual peer review focuses on the performance of an
individual nurse. The nursing audit focuses on evaluating nursing
care through the review of records. The success of these audits
depends on accurate documentation.
Lifespan considerations
Evaluation of goals, selected outcomes and interventions
needs to be continuous, with ongoing assessment and
reassessment of the situation. Priority needs can change
quickly and must be reprioritised when problems occur.
Children
Infants and young children are vulnerable to rapid change in
their condition due to their small body size, disproportionate
size of organs and immaturity of body systems. Also, they
may not be able to verbalise how they are feeling so it is vital
to consult with their family members to set goals.


Older adults
Older adults may have conditions that impair communication,
such as aphasia from a cerebrovascular accident, dementia,
multiple sclerosis or other neurological conditions. In such
cases, the nurse needs to be even more astute in performing
non-verbal assessments, being alert to potential problems,
and detecting changes in the person’s condition, again in
consultation with the person’s family. If evaluations are
performed often and thoroughly, changes can be made
quickly to intervene more effectively and improve outcomes.
Constant assessment, communication and interpersonal skills
are as essential in the evaluation phase as they are in the
initial assessment.

Chapter 15 Review


Chapter highlights
Implementing is putting planned person-centred nursing
interventions into action.
Reassessing occurs simultaneously with the implementing phase
of the nursing process.
Successful implementing and evaluating depend in part on the
quality of the preceding phases of assessing, diagnosing and
planning.
Cognitive, interpersonal and technical skills are used to
implement nursing strategies.
Before implementing an intervention, the nurse reassesses the
individual to be sure that the intervention is person-centred and
still appropriate.
The nurse must determine whether assistance is needed to
perform a nursing intervention knowledgeably, safely and
comfortably for the person.
The implementing phase terminates with the documentation of
the nursing activities and the person’s responses.
After the care plan has been implemented, the nurse evaluates
the person’s health status and the effectiveness of the care plan
in achieving the person’s goals.
The desired outcomes formulated during the planning phase
serve as criteria for evaluating the person’s progress and
improved health status.
The desired outcomes determine the data that must be collected
to evaluate the person’s health status.


Re-examining the care plan is a process of making decisions
about problem status and critiquing each phase of the nursing
process.
Professional standards of care hold that nurses are responsible
and accountable for implementing and evaluating the plan of
care.
Quality assurance evaluation includes consideration of the
structures, processes and outcomes of nursing care.
Quality improvement is a philosophy and process internal to the
institution, and does not rely on inspections by an external
agency.
Concept check
1. When initiating the implementation phase of the nursing
process, the nurse performs which of the following steps
first?
1. Carries out nursing interventions.
2. Determines the need for assistance.
3. Reassesses the person.
4. Documents interventions.
2. Under what circumstances is it considered acceptable
practice for the nurse to document a nursing activity before it
is carried out?
1. When the activity is routine (e.g. raising the bed rails).


2. When the activity occurs at regular intervals (e.g.
turning the person in bed).
3. When the activity is to be carried out immediately (e.g.
a stat (once-only) medication).
4. It is never acceptable.
3. The primary purpose of the evaluating phase of the care
planning process is to determine whether:
1. Desired outcomes have been met.
2. Nursing activities were carried out.
3. Nursing activities were effective.
4. The person’s condition has changed.
4. The person has a high-priority nursing diagnosis of Risk for
impaired skin integrity related to the need for several weeks
of imposed bed rest. The nurse evaluates the person after 1
week and finds the skin integrity is not impaired. When the
care plan is reviewed, the nurse should perform which of the
following?
1. Delete the diagnosis because the problem has not
occurred.
2. Keep the diagnosis because the risk factors are still
present.
3. Modify the nursing diagnosis to Impaired mobility.
4. Demote the nursing diagnosis to a lower priority.
5. If the nurse planned to evaluate the length of time people
must wait for a nurse to respond to their needs, reported over


the intercom system on each shift, which of the following
processes does this reflect?
1. Structure evaluation.
2. Process evaluation.
3. Outcome evaluation.
4. Audit.
Focus on critical thinking
1. The importance of effective communication to the delivery of
person-centred care is evident. One suggestion is that
handover should be conducted at the person’s bedside. Do
you think that this practice would have any impact on the
maintenance of confidentiality?
2. The implementation of safe nursing care in relation to the

propose six or more rights, how do you think this might affect

3. During your evaluation of a person’s goals, you identify that

Effective communication between health
professionals is vital to the quality of patient
care. Such communication allows exchange of
information between all the members of the
interprofessional team and facilitates effective,
person-centred care. Generally, health
personnel communicate through discussion,
reports and records. A discussion
 is an
informal oral consideration of a subject by two or
more health care personnel to identify a problem


or to establish strategies to resolve a problem. A
report  is oral, written or electronic
communication intended to convey information
to others. The process of making an entry in a
patient’s record is called recording
,
charting
 or documenting
.
A clinical record, also called a chart  or patient
record
, is a formal, legal document that
provides evidence of a person’s care. Although
health care organisations use different systems
and forms for documentation, all patient records
contain similar information.
Each health care organisation has policies
about recording and reporting patient data, and
each nurse is accountable for practising
according to these standards. Organisations
also indicate which nursing assessments and
interventions can be recorded by registered
health professionals and unregulated health
care workers. In addition, the Australian Council
on Healthcare Standards (ACHS) specifies that
documentation must be timely, complete,
accurate, confidential and specific to the
individual person (ACHS ).
1


1 Australian Council on Healthcare Standards (ACHS)
(2019). Retrieved from <www.achs.org.au>.


Ethical and legal considerations
The Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA)  states that
‘nurses treat personal information obtained in a professional capacity
as confidential’ (p. 4). The confidentiality and privacy of health
information is protected by statutory or common law requirements.
However, in Australia, these precise requirements vary between
states and territories. Access to the record is restricted to health
care professionals involved in providing care, together with other key
agencies including the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation
Agency, which may access records as a component of
investigations. Although the institution or agency is often the rightful
owner of the patient’s record, there has been an emergence of
patient-held records. No matter where the record is held, any person
has a right to access their records.
2 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2018). Code of Conduct for Nurses in
Australia. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: communicating for safety
The importance of effective documentation to
patient safety is emphasised in the National
Safety and Quality Health Service Standards,
2


where it is specified that health service
organisations must have health care records
available to clinicians at point of care and
support the workforce to maintain accurate and
complete health care records while complying
with security and privacy regulations. It is noted
that systems and processes must be in place to
support effective documentation at high-risk
times, such as when critical information about a
person’s care emerges or changes and when it
is important to ensure that a person is correctly
identified and matched to their intended care,
discharge planning and transfer of care
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in
Health Care (ACSQHC) , pp. 48, 54).
3 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
The Health Records and Privacy Information Act 2002 (NSW)
provides for the privacy and confidentiality of health information held
in both public and private agencies. This Act specifies that any
information regarding a person’s health or health care in the
possession or control of a health care organisation should be kept
confidential. This applies to health information that is transmitted or
3


maintained in any form or medium, including verbal discussions,
electronic communications with or about patients and written
communications.
For purposes of education and research, most health care
organisations allow health care students access to records with
permission. The records may be de-identified and used in case
conferences, clinics, rounds, case studies and written papers.
However, students are bound by a strict ethical code and legal
responsibility to hold all information in confidence and maintain the
person’s privacy by not using a name or any identifying information.
Clinical consideration
Strict measures are required to ensure privacy
and confidentiality when sharing clinical
information to outside agencies via fax or
electronic means, such as email. For example,
a fax cover sheet should contain instructions
that the faxed material is to be given only to the
named recipient. Consent is needed from the
person to share information with outside
agencies via fax or electronic means.


Ensuring confidentiality of
electronic medical records
Because of the increased use of electronic medical records, health
care organisations have developed policies and procedures to
ensure the privacy and confidentiality of patient information stored in
computers. The provisions of the Health Records and Privacy
Information Act 2002 (NSW) also apply to the health information that
is stored electronically. The following are some guidelines for
ensuring the confidentiality and security of electronic records:
A personal password is required to enter and sign off computer
files. Do not share this password with anyone, including other
staff.
After logging on, never leave a computer terminal unattended.
Do not leave personal information displayed on the monitor
where others may see it.
Shred all unneeded computer-generated worksheets.
Know the facility’s policy and procedure for correcting an entry
error.
Follow agency procedures for documenting sensitive material,
such as a diagnosis of AIDS.
Information technology (IT) systems managers must install a
firewall to protect the server from unauthorised access.


Purposes of patient records
Patient records are kept for a number of purposes.
Communication
The record serves as the vehicle by which different health
professionals who interact with the person can communicate with
each other. This prevents fragmentation, repetition and delays in
care of the person.
Patient safety competency framework
4 Teamwork and collaborative practice
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must have the
ability to collaborate and communicate
effectively with members of the health care
team in ways that facilitate mutual respect and
shared decision making (Levett-Jones et al. ).
4 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
4


Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Planning patient care
Each health professional uses data from the patient’s record to plan
care for that person. A medical practitioner, for example, may order
a specific antibiotic after establishing that the person’s temperature
is steadily rising and that laboratory tests reveal the presence of a
certain micro-organism. Nurses use baseline and ongoing data to
evaluate the effectiveness of the nursing care plan.
Auditing health organisations
An audit is a review of records for quality-assurance purposes (see
Chapter 15
). Accrediting agencies, such as ACHS, may review
patient records to determine if a particular health agency is meeting
its stated standards.
Research


The information contained in a record can be a valuable source of
data for research. The treatment plans for a number of people with
the same health problems can yield helpful data and can be utilised
with provision of ethical and organisational approval.
Education
Students in health disciplines often use patient records as
educational tools. A record can frequently provide a comprehensive
view of the individual, their illness, effective treatment strategies and
factors that affect the outcome of the illness.
Reimbursement
Documentation also helps a facility receive reimbursement from the
government. ‘Under Medicare, the Australian and State
governments jointly fund public hospital services so they are
provided free of charge to people who are treated as public patients’
(Department of Human Services ). To ensure correct payment to the
facility through Medicare, the person’s clinical record must contain
the correct diagnosis-related group (DRG) codes and reveal that the
appropriate care has been given.
5 Department of Human Services (2013). Medicare Services. Retrieved from
<www.humanservices.gov.au>.
5


Codeable diagnoses, such as DRGs, are supported by accurate,
thorough recording by nurses and other health care professionals.
This not only facilitates reimbursement from the government but
also facilitates reimbursement from health insurance companies and
other third-party payers. If additional care, treatment or length of
stay becomes necessary for the person’s welfare, thorough charting
will help justify these needs.
Legal documentation
The person’s record is a legal document and is admissible in court
as evidence in both civil and criminal proceedings. Such records can
be used to investigate allegations made against the health care
service; in such cases the records are subject to close scrutiny.
Therefore, it is very important that entries in these records are of a
high standard and made with the assumption that they will be
examined at some time (Staunton & Chiarella ).
6 Staunton, P. & Chiarella, M. (2017). Nursing and the Law (8th ed.). Sydney: Elsevier.
Health care analysis
Information from records may assist health care planners to identify
organisational needs, such as over-utilised and under-utilised
hospital services. Such review of records also supports
6


benchmarking between organisations related, for example, to length
of stay, postoperative infection rates or unplanned readmission
rates. Records can be used to establish the costs of various
services and to identify those services that cost the organisation
money and those that generate revenue.
Professional conduct
The nursing profession has developed The NMBA Registered Nurse
Standards for Practice (NMBA ) to guide professional conduct and
to ensure safe and competent nursing care. In relation to
documentation and reporting, the Standards in Box 16.1
 are of
particular relevance. These Standards reinforce the integral role that
documentation and communication play in teamwork and the
delivery of quality patient care.
7 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016). Registered Nurse Standards for
Practice. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
