Documentation systems
A number of different documentation approaches and systems are
in current use; for example, integrated record keeping; source-
oriented records; problem-oriented medical records; the problems,
interventions, evaluation (PIE) model; focus charting; charting by
exception (CBE); electronic documentation; and case management.
The choice of system will depend on a number of factors, such as
the policy of the particular health care agency, the purpose of the
documentation and the requirements of regulatory bodies.
Regardless of the system used, it must be borne in mind that the
ultimate aim is to communicate clearly and succinctly the manner in
which individuals have been assessed, how these assessments
have been acted on and the outcomes of these actions. The
following sections provide some possibilities for documentation that
may be used alone or in combination to achieve the aims of
particular health care settings.
Integrated record keeping
Most hospitals in Australia have introduced a system of integrated
report writing
. In this system, a single patient record contains
chronological entries made by all health care professionals involved
in the person’s care. These notes allow for open and accessible


communication between all staff concerned with the care and
provide a holistic approach to such care. The notes support and
encourage interprofessional teamwork, allowing staff to read others’
contributions to the care and to ‘determine, document and
communicate patients’ priorities, goals and outcomes’ (NMBA 2016,
p. 5). Each entry is made contemporaneously (as close to the time
of the activity as possible) and by the health care professional who
undertook the activity.
Source-oriented record
The traditional patient record is a source-oriented record
. Each
health care professional or professional staff member makes
notations in a separate section or sections of the person’s chart. For
example, the admissions department has an admission sheet; the
doctor has a doctor’s order sheet, a doctor’s history sheet and
progress notes; nurses use the nurses’ notes; and other
departments or personnel have their own records.
In this type of record, information about a particular problem is
distributed throughout the record. For example, if a person had left
hemiplegia (paralysis of the left side of the body), data about this
problem might be found in the doctor’s history sheet, on the doctor’s
order sheet, in the nurses’ notes, in the physiotherapist’s record and
in the social worker’s record. Table 16.1
 lists some of the
components of a source-oriented record.


Table 16.1 Components of the source-oriented record
Narrative charting
 is a traditional part of the source-oriented
record. It consists of written notes that include routine care, normal
findings and patient problems. There is no right or wrong order to
the information, although chronological order is preferred. Today,
narrative recording is being replaced by other systems, such as
charting by exception and focus charting. However, narrative
charting is expedient in emergency situations. Many organisations
combine narrative charting with another system. For example, an
organisation using a charting by exception system (discussed later)
may use narrative charting when describing abnormal findings.
When using narrative charting, it is important to organise the
information in a clear, coherent manner. Using the nursing process
as a framework is one way to do this. See Box 16.2
.
BO X
16.2 Example of organising narrative
charting
Situation: person is postop day #2
after abdominal surgery
Critical thinking and clinical reasoning


Questions to ask yourself:
What assessment data are relevant?
What nursing interventions have I completed?
What is my evaluation of the result of the interventions
and/or what is the person’s response to the interventions?
Example
Source-oriented records are convenient because care providers
from each discipline can easily locate the forms on which to record
data and it is easy to trace the information specific to one’s
discipline. The disadvantage is that information about a particular
problem is scattered throughout the chart, so it is difficult to find
chronological information on a person’s problems and progress. This
can lead to decreased communication in the health care team, poor
coordination of care and adverse patient outcomes.
Problem-oriented medical record
In the problem-oriented medical record
, or problem-oriented
record
, the data are arranged according to the problems the
person has rather than the source of the information. Members of
the health care team contribute to the problem list, plan of care and
progress notes. Plans for each active or potential problem are drawn
up and progress notes are recorded for each problem.


The advantages of the problem-oriented medical record are that (a)
it encourages collaboration, and (b) the problem list in the front of
the chart alerts caregivers to the person’s needs and makes it easier
to track the status of each problem. Its disadvantages are that (a)
caregivers differ in their ability to use the required charting format,
(b) it takes constant vigilance to maintain an up-to-date problem list,
and (c) it can be inefficient because assessments and interventions
that apply to more than one problem must be repeated.
The problem-oriented medical record has four basic components:
1. Database.
2. Problem list.
3. Plan of care.
4. Progress notes.
In addition, flow sheets and discharge notes are added to the record
as needed.
Database
The database consists of all information known about the person
when they first enter the health care facility. It includes the nursing
assessment, the doctor’s history, social and family data, and the
results of the physical examination and baseline diagnostic tests.
Data are constantly updated as health status changes.


Problem list
The problem list (see Figure 16.1
) is derived from the database.
It is usually kept at the front of the chart and serves as an index to
the numbered entries in the progress notes. Problems are listed in
the order in which they are identified and the list is continually
updated as new problems are identified and others resolved. All
caregivers may contribute to the problem list, which includes the
person’s physiological, psychological, social, cultural, spiritual,
developmental and environmental needs. Doctors write problems as
medical diagnoses, surgical procedures or symptoms; nurses write
problems as nursing diagnoses.
Figure 16.1


A patient’s problem list in the problem-oriented medical record. Note
that problems 1B, 1C and 2 were redefined on the dates indicated
and listed subsequently.
As the person’s condition changes or more data are obtained, it may
be necessary to ‘redefine’ problems. Figure 16.1
 illustrates how
this has been done for problems 1B, 1C and 2. When a problem is
resolved, a line is drawn through it and the number is not used again
for that person.
Plan of care


The initial list of orders or plan of care is made with reference to the
active problems. Care plans are generated by the health
professional who lists the problems. Doctors write doctor’s orders or
medical care plans; nurses write nursing orders or nursing care
plans. The written plan in the record is listed under each problem in
the progress notes and is not isolated as a separate list of orders.
Progress notes
A progress note
 in the problem-oriented medical record is a
chart entry made by all health professionals involved in a person’s
care; they all use the same type of sheet for notes. Progress notes
are numbered to correspond to the problems on the problem list and
may be lettered for the type of data. For example, the SOAP format
is frequently used. SOAP
 is an acronym for subjective data,
objective data, assessment and planning.
S—Subjective data consist of information obtained from what the
person says. It describes the person’s perceptions of and
experience with the problem (see Chapter 12
). When possible,
the nurse quotes the person’s words; otherwise, they are
summarised. Subjective data are included when they are important
and relevant to the problem.
O—Objective data consist of information that is measured or
observed by use of the senses (e.g. vital signs, laboratory and x-ray
results).


A—Assessment is the interpretation or conclusions drawn about the
subjective and objective data. During the initial assessment, the
problem list is created from the database, so the ‘A’ entry should be
a statement of the problem. In all subsequent SOAP notes for that
problem, the ‘A’ should describe the person’s condition and level of
progress rather than merely restating the diagnosis or problem.
P—The plan is the plan of care designed to resolve the stated
problem. The initial plan is written by the person who enters the
problem into the record. All subsequent plans, including revisions,
are entered into the progress notes.
Over the years, the SOAP format has been modified with the
acronyms SOAPIE and SOAPIER referring to formats that add
interventions, evaluation and revision.
I—Interventions refer to the specific interventions that have actually
been performed by the caregiver.
E—Evaluation includes responses to nursing interventions and
medical treatments. This is primarily reassessment data.
R—Revision reflects care plan modifications suggested by the
evaluation. Changes may be made in desired outcomes,
interventions or target dates.
Newer versions of this format eliminate the subjective and objective
data and start with assessment, which combines the subjective and
objective data. The acronym then becomes AP, APIE or APIER. See
Figure 16.2
.


Figure 16.2


Examples of nursing progress notes using SOAP, SOAPIER and
APIE formats.
PIE
The PIE
 documentation model groups information into three
categories. PIE is an acronym for problems, interventions and
evaluation of nursing care. This system consists of a patient care
assessment flow sheet and progress notes. The flow sheet
 uses
specific assessment criteria in a particular format, such as human
needs or functional health patterns. The time parameters for a flow
sheet can vary from minutes to months. In a hospital intensive care
unit, for example, a person’s blood pressure may be monitored by
the minute, whereas in an ambulatory clinic a person’s blood glucose
level may be recorded once a month.
After the assessment, the nurse records specific problems on the
progress notes, often using a nursing diagnosis to word the problem
(see Chapter 13
). The evaluation of the effectiveness of the
nursing interventions should also be documented.
The PIE system eliminates the traditional care plan and incorporates
an ongoing care plan into the progress notes. Therefore, the nurse
does not have to create and update a separate plan. A disadvantage
is that the nurse must review all the nursing notes before giving care


to determine which problems are current and which interventions
were effective.
Focus charting
Focus charting
 is intended to ensure that the focus of care is on
a person’s individual problems, concerns and strengths. Three
columns for recording are usually used: date and time, focus and
progress notes (see Table 16.2
). The focus may be a condition, a
nursing diagnosis, a behaviour, a sign or symptom, an acute change
in the person’s condition or a person’s strength. The progress notes
are organised into data, action and response. The data category
reflects the assessment phase of the nursing process and consists
of observations of the person’s status and behaviours, including data
from flow sheets (e.g. vital signs, pupil reactivity). The nurse records
both subjective and objective data in this section.
Table 16.2 Example of focus charting
The action category reflects planning and implementation and
includes immediate and future nursing actions. It may also include
any changes to the plan of care. The response category reflects the
evaluation phase of the nursing process and describes the response
to any nursing and medical care.
The focus charting system provides a holistic perspective of the
person and their needs. It also provides a nursing process


framework for the progress notes. The three components do not
need to be recorded in order and each note does not need to have
all three categories. Flow sheets and checklists are frequently used
on the person’s chart to record routine nursing tasks and
assessment data.
Charting by exception
Charting by exception (CBE)
 is a documentation system in
which only abnormal or significant findings or exceptions to norms
are recorded. Charting by exception incorporates three key
elements:
1. Flow sheets. Examples of flow sheets include a graphic
record, fluid balance record (see Chapter 55
), daily nursing
assessment record (see Figure 16.3
), patient teaching
record (Chapter 28
), patient discharge record and skin
assessment record (see Figure 16.4
).
2. Standards of nursing care. Documentation by reference to
the organisation’s printed standards of nursing practice
eliminates much of the repetitive charting of routine care. An
organisation using charting by exception must develop its own
specific standards of nursing practice that identify the
minimum criteria for care of the person regardless of clinical
area. Some units may also have unit-specific standards
unique to their type of patient. For example, ‘The nurse must
ensure that the unconscious person has oral care at least


q4h’. Documentation of care according to these specified
standards involves only a check mark in the routine standards
box on the graphic record. If all of the standards are not
implemented, an asterisk on the flow sheet is made with
reference to the nurses’ notes. All exceptions to the
standards are fully described in narrative form on the nurses’
notes.
3. Bedside access to chart forms. In the charting by exception
system, all flow sheets are kept at the person’s bedside to
allow immediate recording and to eliminate the need
to transcribe data from the nurse’s worksheet to the
permanent record.
Figure 16.3


Sample of a daily nursing assessment form used in charting by
exception.
Figure 16.4


Sample skin assessment flow sheet.
The advantage of this system is the elimination of lengthy, repetitive
notes; it also makes changes in condition more obvious. Inherent in
charting by exception is the presumption that the nurse did assess
the person and determined what responses were normal and
abnormal. Many nurses believe in the saying ‘not charted, not done’
and subsequently may feel uncomfortable with the charting by
exception documentation system. N/A should be written on flow


sheets where the items are not applicable. This would then avoid the
possible misinterpretation that the assessment or intervention was
not done by the nurse.
Electronic information systems for
documentation
The Australian government Australian Digital Health Agency
(ADHA)  provides information on different types of electronic health
records. It describes electronic medical records (EMRs) as
containing information that is created and resides within a single
health care organisation or service. Electronic health records (EHRs)
are similar but are shared across organisations or services. Personal
health records (PHRs) are held by individuals and can be shared
with permission at point of care—providers can add to these also.
(See Chapter 10
 for further information.)
8 Australian Digital Health Agency (ADHA) (2019). Retrieved from
<https://conversation.digitalhealth.gov.au>.
One of the drawbacks evident is the use of different systems and
data sets leading to difficulties in sharing information with multiple
health care providers (e.g. government and non-government
providers; community and acute care). In electronic documentation,
nurses use computers to store the person’s database, add new
data, create and revise care plans and document the person’s
8


progress. The underpinning principles of nursing documentation
remain the same but are kept in electronic form. Some institutions
have a computer terminal at the bedside or nurses carry a small
hand-held terminal, enabling the nurse to document care
immediately after it is given.
Multiple flow sheets are not needed in computerised record systems
because information can be retrieved in a variety of formats. For
example, the nurse can obtain results of a person’s blood test, a
schedule of all people on the unit who are to have surgery during the
day, a suggested list of interventions for a nursing diagnosis, a
graphic chart of vital signs or a printout of all progress notes for a
person. Many systems can generate a work list for the day, with a
list of all treatments, procedures and medications needed by the
person. One of the challenges for nurses is that in many acute care
settings, patient records or information are partially computerised
and not fully integrated.
The computerisation of clinical records has made it possible to
transmit information from one care setting to another. Many
Australian hospitals currently use computerised records for
recording and storing information. The National E-Health Transition
Authority (NEHTA ) was initially established to lead the take up and
adoption of e-health in Australia; this has now become the remit of
the ADHA.
9 National E-Health Transition Authority (NEHTA) (2013). Retrieved from
<www.nehta.gov.au/>.
9


The aim of such electronic systems is to give health care providers
access to a person’s health history and to improve person-centred
care through improved knowledge sharing and the promotion of
interprofessional teamwork. The focus within the Australian context
is twofold and is being progressed through strategies to ensure
integration of infrastructure and standards, together with personally
controlled electronic health records. Selected pros and cons of
electronic documentation are shown in Box 16.3
.
BO X
16.3 Pros and cons of electronic
documentation
Pros
Electronic records can facilitate a focus on a person’s
outcomes.
Bedside terminals can synthesise information from
monitoring equipment.
Electronic documentation allows health care professionals
to use their time more efficiently.
The system links various sources of a person’s
information.
A person’s information, requests and results are sent and
received quickly.


Links to monitors improve accuracy of documentation.
Bedside terminals eliminate the need to take notes on a
worksheet before recording.
Bedside terminals permit the nurse to check an order
immediately before administering a treatment or
medication.
Information is legible.
The system incorporates and reinforces standards of
care.
Standard terminology improves communication.
Cons
People’s privacy may be compromised if security
measures are not used.
Breakdowns make information temporarily unavailable.
The system is expensive.
It is dependent on individual knowledge, skills and
confidence utilising systems—updates to systems require
training to maintain expertise.
Access may be assigned only to employees of
organisations, therefore limiting access for students or
visiting professionals.


Case management
The case management model emphasises quality, cost-effective
care delivered within an established length of stay. This model uses
an interprofessional approach to planning and documenting care of
the person using critical pathways. These forms identify the
outcomes that certain groups of people are expected to achieve on
each day of care, along with the interventions necessary for each
day. See Figure 16.5
 and Chapter 6
 for more information
about critical pathways.
Figure 16.5


Excerpt from a critical pathway documentation form.
Along with critical pathways, the case management model
incorporates graphics and flow sheets. Progress notes typically use
some type of charting by exception. For example, if goals are met,
no further charting is required. A goal that is not met is called a
variance
. A variance is a deviation from what is planned on the
critical pathway—unexpected occurrences that affect the planned
care or the person’s responses to care. When a variance occurs,
the nurse writes a note documenting the unexpected event, the
cause and actions taken to correct the situation or justify the actions
taken. See Table 16.3
 for an example of how a variance might be
documented.


Table 16.3 Example of variance documentation (critical
pathway)
The case management model promotes collaboration and teamwork
between caregivers, helps to decrease length of stay and makes
efficient use of time. Because care is goal focused, the quality may
improve. However, critical pathways work best for people with one or
two medical diagnoses and few individualised needs. People with
multiple diagnoses (e.g. a person with a hip fracture, pneumonia,
diabetes and compromised skin integrity, or those with an
unpredictable course of symptoms such as a neurological patient
with seizures) are difficult to document on a critical path.


Documenting nursing activities
The patient record should describe the person’s ongoing status and
reflect the full range of the nursing process. Regardless of the
records system used in a facility, nurses document evidence of the
nursing process on a variety of forms throughout the clinical record
(see Table 16.4
).
Table 16.4 Documentation for the nursing process
All steps are recorded on discharge/referral summaries.
Admission nursing assessment
A comprehensive admission assessment, also referred to as an
initial database, nursing history or nursing assessment, is completed
when the person is admitted to the nursing unit. As discussed in
Chapter 12
, these forms can be organised according to health
patterns, body systems, functional abilities, health problems and
risks, nursing model or type of health care setting (e.g. labour and
delivery, paediatrics, mental health). The nurse generally records
ongoing assessments or reassessments on flow sheets or on
nursing progress notes.
*


Nursing care plans
The ACHS (2019) requires that the clinical record include evidence
of patient assessments, nursing diagnoses and/or patient needs,
nursing interventions, patient outcomes and evidence of a current
nursing care plan. Depending on the records system being used, the
nursing care plan may be separate from the person’s chart,
recorded in progress notes and other forms in the patient record, or
incorporated into a multidisciplinary plan of care.
There are two types of nursing care plans: traditional and
standardised. The traditional care plan is written for each person.
The form varies from organisation to organisation according to the
needs of the person and the department. Most forms have three
columns: one for nursing diagnoses, a second for expected
outcomes and a third for nursing interventions. See Chapter 14
for additional information.
Standardised care plans were developed to save documentation
time. These plans may be based on an institution’s standards of
practice, thereby helping to provide a high quality of nursing care.
For further information, see Chapter 14
. Standardised plans must
be individualised by the nurse in order to adequately address an
individual’s needs.
Flow sheets


A flow sheet enables nurses to record nursing data quickly and
concisely and provides an easy-to-read record of the person’s
condition over time.
Graphic record
This record typically indicates body temperature, pulse, respiratory
rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturations, pain, and weight. Such
charting integrates use of early-warning scores to assist with
recognition of the deteriorating patient (ACSQHC ). Charting often
includes additional clinical data such as daily fluid balance and bowel
movements.
10 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2009).
Recognising and Responding to Clinical Deterioration: Use of Observation Charts to Identify
Clinical Deterioration. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Intake and output record
All routes of fluid intake and all routes of fluid loss or output are
measured and recorded on this form. See Chapter 55
 for more
information.
Medication administration record
Medication flow sheets usually include designated areas for the date
of the medication order, the expiration date, the medication name
and dose, the frequency of administration and route, and the nurse’s
10


signature. The ACSQHC  has developed a suite of national
medication charts and guides that all nurses should be familiar with.
In aged care, and increasingly in acute care, electronic systems of
medication management are in use in order to support safety in
resident or patient care. See, for example, Autumn Care
(<https://autumn.care>) or iCare (<www.icarehealth.com.au>).
11 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2019). National
Inpatient Medication Chart. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Skin assessment record
A skin or wound assessment is often recorded on a flow sheet such
as the one shown in Figure 16.4
. These records may include
categories related to stage of skin injury, drainage, odour, culture
information and treatments.
Progress notes
Progress notes made by nurses provide information about the
progress a person is making towards achieving desired outcomes.
Therefore, in addition to assessment and reassessment data,
progress notes include information about problems and nursing
interventions. The format used depends on the documentation
system in place in the institution. Various kinds of nursing progress
notes are discussed in the ‘Documentation systems’ section earlier
in this chapter.
11


Nursing discharge/referral
summaries
A discharge note and referral summary are completed when the
person is being discharged and transferred to another institution or
to a home setting where a visit by a range of other health care
providers is required. In many organisations, such referrals are now
sent via electronic data systems that decrease risk associated with
facsimile transfer of information. Some records combine the
discharge plan, including instructions for care, and the final progress
note. Many are designed with checklists to facilitate data recording.
If the discharge plan is given directly to the person and their family, it
is imperative that instructions be written in terms that can be readily
understood. For example, medications, treatments and activities
should be written in layman’s terms and use of medical
abbreviations (such as ‘tid’ instead of ‘three times a day’) should be
avoided.
If a person is transferred within the facility or from a residential aged
care facility to a hospital, a report needs to accompany them to
ensure continuity of care in the new area. It should include all
components of the discharge instructions but also describe the
condition of the person before the transfer. Any teaching or
instruction that has been done should also be described and
recorded.


If the person is being transferred to another institution or to a home
setting where a visit by health care providers is required, the
discharge note takes the form of a referral summary. Regardless of
format, discharge and referral summaries usually include some or all
of the following:
description of person’s physical, mental and emotional status at
discharge or transfer
resolved and unresolved continuing health problems and care
needs; may include a review-of-systems checklist that considers
integumentary, respiratory, cardiovascular, neurological,
musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, elimination and reproductive
problems
long-term health goals and treatments to be continued (e.g.
wound care, oxygen therapy) or limited (e.g. consider the
person’s directive for limitation of treatment, including transfer to
hospital for management of care)
current medications
restrictions that relate to (a) activity such as lifting, stair climbing,
walking, driving, work, (b) diet and (c) bathing such as sponge
bath, tub or shower
functional/self-care abilities in terms of vision, hearing, speech,
mobility with or without aids, meal preparation and eating,
preparing and administering medications, and so on
comfort level
support networks, including family, significant others, religious
advisor, community self-help groups, home care and other
community agencies available and so on


education provided in relation to disease process, activities and
exercise, special diet, medications, specialised care or
treatments, follow-up appointments and so on
discharge destination (e.g. home, nursing home) and mode of
discharge (e.g. walking, wheelchair, ambulance)
referral services (e.g. social worker, community nurse, Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander health worker).


Documentation in residential aged
care facilities
Residential aged care facilities usually provide care to a range of
people with varied needs that are assessed by nurses considering
three broad domains: activities of daily living, behaviour and complex
health care. The level of care is assessed using a funding tool called
the Aged Care Funding Instrument (ACFI).
Requirements for documentation in residential aged care settings
are based on professional standards, federal and state regulations
and the policies of the health care organisation. This documentation
must provide evidence of meeting residents’ care needs, which is
linked to Commonwealth government funding. Therefore, it is
important that documentation is a clear reflection of the actual care
that the resident receives.
Nurses need to familiarise themselves with regulations influencing
the kind and frequency of documentation required in residential aged
care facilities by referring to accreditation standards and
requirements of individual organisations. Nurses make an entry into
every resident’s notes related to nursing care and also record any
change in resident condition or care needs in a contemporaneous
manner as needed.


Home care documentation
The Commonwealth Home Support Program provides a range of
community-based services for older people who need assistance to
remain living independently. The services provided include nursing
care, allied health care, food services, domestic assistance,
personal care, home modification and maintenance, respite care,
counselling and support and assessment (Department of Health ).
Nursing care provided is usually sourced from public and/or private
nursing organisations and includes services such as wound care,
chronic disease management and palliative care. In addition, older
people can access Home Care Packages with a focus on the person
determining priorities for support that may include transport and
domestic support, personal care, allied health or clinical services,
and case management. Providers of home support or care
packages maintain documentation and submit data to the funding
agency using agreed data sets that describe, evaluate and plan for
service provision.
12 Department of Health (2019). About the Commonwealth Home Support Programme.
Retrieved from <https://agedcare.health.gov.au>.
Many community nursing agencies provide nurses with a laptop or
hand-held computer to make records available in multiple locations.
With the use of a modem, the nurse can add new information to
records at the agency without travelling to the office.
12


Practice guidelines
Residential aged care documentation
Complete the assessment and screening forms and plan
of care within the time period specified by regulatory
bodies.
Write nursing summaries and progress notes that comply
with the frequency and standards required by regulatory
bodies.
Review and revise the plan of care when the resident’s
health status changes, including after admission/discharge
from acute care.
Document and report any change in the resident’s
condition to the medical officer and the resident’s family
as soon as possible.
Document all measures implemented in response to a
change in the resident’s condition.
Ensure progress notes address the resident’s progress in
relation to the goals or outcomes defined in the plan of
care.
Practice guidelines
Community-based care documentation
Complete a comprehensive nursing assessment and
develop a plan of care.


Write a progress note at each visit, noting any changes in
the person’s condition, nursing interventions performed
(including education and instructional brochures and
materials provided), responses to nursing care and vital
signs as indicated.
Liaise with other health care professionals also providing
care.
Report changes in the plan of care to the medical officer
and document that these were reported.
Write a discharge summary for the doctor. Include all
services provided, the person’s health status at discharge,
outcomes achieved and recommendations for further
care.


General guidelines for recording
Because the person’s record is a legal document and may be used
to provide evidence in court, many factors are considered in
recording. Health care personnel must not only maintain the
confidentiality of the person’s record but also meet legal standards in
the process of recording.
Date and time
Document the date and time of each recording. This is essential not
only for legal reasons but also for the person’s safety. Record the
time in the conventional manner (e.g. 9.00 a.m. or 3.15 p.m.) or
according to the 24-hour clock (military clock), which avoids
confusion about whether a time was a.m. or p.m. (see Figure
16.6
). Note that many electronic health records automatically time
stamp entries. However, it remains the nurse’s responsibility to
ensure this is recorded.
Figure 16.6


The 24-hour clock.


Timing
Follow the organisation’s policy about the frequency of documenting
and adjust the frequency as a person’s condition indicates; for
example, a person whose blood pressure is changing requires more
frequent documentation than a person whose blood pressure is
constant. As a rule, documenting should be done as soon as
possible after an assessment or intervention. No recording should
be done before providing nursing care.
Lifespan considerations
Transfer from residential aged care or
home care to acute care
Older people can have complex care needs and generally
experience subtle small changes in their condition. However,
when problems do occur that cannot be managed in the
facility or service, there may be a requirement for transfer to
acute care. The ACSQHC  recognises transfer to hospital
from aged care as a high-risk clinical activity where handover
requirements involve multiple modalities and staff. This
highlights the importance of up-to-date and comprehensive
record keeping in aged care facilities and community care.
Transfer of older people to the acute care sector from
13


residential aged care or home care presents multiple
challenges where they are at higher risk of adverse events
than the general population.
13 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2008).
Public Report on Pilot Study. Aged Care Home Transfer-to-Hospital Envelope Trial.
Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
In order to facilitate such communication, many facilities have
identified minimum data that must accompany residents on
transfer. They include medication chart, care plan, advanced
care directive, nursing summary of the presenting problem
and any assessments undertaken. The North Eastern Valley
Division of General Practice  developed a Transfer to
Hospital Envelope that contains the resident’s medical and
nursing documentation and a checklist of important
information that should be sent to the hospital. This form of
documentation has become known as the ‘Yellow Envelope’
and is recommended as ‘a worthwhile process to continue
when using a paper-based system’ (Hoare , p. 15).
14 North Eastern Valley Division of General Practice (2007). Clinical Handover
Initiative: Aged Care Home Transfer to Hospital Envelope. Retrieved from
<www.nevdgp.org.au>.
15 Hoare, H. (2009). What’s Missing? Linking Patient Information to Patient Care—
Public Report on Pilot Study. Brisbane: GP Partners Australia.
Source: North Eastern Valley Division of General Practice (2007). Clinical Handover Initiative: Aged
Care Home Transfer to Hospital Envelope.
14
15


Legibility
All entries must be legible and easy to read to prevent interpretation
errors. Hand printing or easily understood handwriting is usually
permissible. Follow the organisation’s policies about handwritten
recording.
Permanence
All entries on the person’s record are made in black ink so that the
record is permanent and changes can be identified. Also, black ink
reproduces well in duplication processes. Follow the organisation’s
policies about the type of pen and ink used for recording.
Accepted terminology
Use only commonly accepted abbreviations, symbols and terms that
are specified by the organisation. Many abbreviations are standard
and used universally; others are used only in certain specialty areas.
Many health care facilities supply an approved list of abbreviations
and symbols to prevent confusion. When in doubt about whether to
use an abbreviation, write the term out in full until certain about the
abbreviation. Table 16.5
 lists some common abbreviations


(except those used for medications, which are described in Chapter
36
).
Table 16.5 Commonly used abbreviations
Care should be taken with the use and interpretation of
abbreviations. Most hospitals and specialties have their own lists of
accepted abbreviations or refer to national guidelines. The above
examples are generally widely accepted although there is often more
than one meaning for an abbreviation.
Correct spelling
Correct spelling is essential for accuracy in recording. If unsure how
to spell a word, look it up in a dictionary or other resource. Two
decidedly different medications may have similar spellings; for
example, Fosamax and Flomax.
Clinical consideration
Incorrect spelling can lead to serious adverse
events and gives a negative impression to the
reader, thereby decreasing the nurse’s
credibility.
*
*


Signature
Each recording on the nursing notes is signed by the nurse making
it. The signature includes the name and title; for example, ‘Susan J.
Green, RN’ or ‘S. J. Green, RN’. Some agencies have a signature
sheet and after signing this signature sheet nurses can use their
initials. Note that student nurses are required to have any entries
countersigned by the supervising nurse. With electronic charting,
each nurse has their own code, which allows the documentation to
be identified.
The following title abbreviations are often used, although nurses
need to follow hospital policy about how to sign their names.
Accuracy
The person’s name and identifying information and medical record
label should be attached to, or written on, each page of the clinical
record. Before making any entry, check that it is the correct chart.
Do not identify charts by room number only; check the person’s
name. Special attention is needed when caring for people with the
same last name.


Notations on records must be accurate and correct. Accurate
notations consist of facts or observations rather than opinions or
interpretations. It is more accurate, for example, to write that the
person ‘refused medication’ (fact) than to write that the person ‘was
uncooperative’ (opinion); to write that a person ‘was crying’
(observation) is preferable to noting that the person ‘was depressed’
(interpretation). Similarly, when a person expresses worry about the
diagnosis or problem, this should be quoted directly on the record:
‘Stated: “I’m worried about my leg”’. When describing something,
avoid general words, such as large, good or normal which can be
interpreted differently. For example, chart specific data such as
 rather than ‘large bruise’.
When a recording mistake is made, draw a line through it and write
the words mistaken entry above or next to the original entry with
your initials or name (depending on hospital policy). Do not erase,
blot out or use correction fluid. The original entry must remain
visible. When using electronic charting, the nurse needs to be aware
of the hospital’s policy and process for correcting documentation
mistakes. (See Figure 16.7
 for an example.)
Figure 16.7
‘2 cm × 3 cm bruise’


Correcting a charting error.
Write on every line but never write between lines. If a blank appears
in a notation, draw a line through the blank space so that no
additional information can be recorded at any other time or by any
other person, and sign the notation.
Sequence
Document events in the order in which they occur; for example,
record assessments, then the nursing interventions and then the
person’s responses. Update or delete problems as needed.
Appropriateness


Record only information that pertains to the person’s health
problems and care. Any other personal information that the person
conveys is inappropriate for the record. Recording irrelevant
information may be considered an invasion of the person’s privacy
and/or libellous. A person’s disclosure that she was addicted to
heroin 15 years ago, for example, would not be recorded on the
medical record unless it had a direct bearing on the person’s current
health problem. In addition, the use of appropriate language is
required. For example, it is important to use inclusive language that
does not demean, exclude, stereotype or trivialise people on the
basis of disability, race or gender.
Completeness
Not all data that a nurse obtains about a person can be recorded.
However, the information that is recorded needs to be complete and
helpful to the person and health care professionals.
Nurses’ notes need to reflect the nursing process. Record all
assessments, dependent and independent nursing interventions,
problems, the person’s responses to interventions and tests,
progress towards goals and communication with the person and
other members of the health team.
Care that is omitted because of the person’s condition or because
they declined treatment must also be recorded. Document what was
omitted, why it was omitted and who was notified.


Clinical consideration
Do not assume that the person reading your
charting will know that a common intervention
(e.g. pressure area care) has occurred because
you believe it to be an ‘obvious’ component of
care.
Clinical consideration
Complete charting—for example, by using the
steps of the nursing process as a framework—is
the best defence against malpractice.
Conciseness
Recordings need to be brief as well as complete to save time in
communication. The person’s name and the word patient are
omitted. For example, write ‘Perspiring profusely. Respirations
shallow, 28/min’. End each thought or sentence with a full stop.


Research note
The impact of language in nursing documentation
D. Jefferies, M. Johnson & D. Nicholls
. Nursing documentation: How meaning is obscured by
fragmentary language. Nursing Outlook, 59(6), E6−E12.
16 Jefferies, D., Johnson, M. & Nicholls, D. (2011). Nursing documentation: How meaning is
obscured by fragmentary language. Nursing Outlook, 59(6), E6−E12.
A multitude of publications in scholarly literature exists in
relation to nursing documentation predicated on
understandings of the importance of documentation as it
relates to ethico-legal principles, person-centredness and
communication to other nurses and health care professionals.
This research initiative describes the examination of nursing
documentation in 10 hospitals participating in a larger study.
Sixty-seven individual entries were examined using a textual
analysis approach to further understand grammatical and
linguistic aspects of the text. Four key areas are discussed in
detail: (1) use of abbreviations; (2) expressions that are not
quantifiable; (3) fragmentation of language; and (4) poor
sentence structure. The challenges of making sense of such
documentation are discussed and risk of adverse events
highlighted. Importantly, the research is linked to ongoing
work with clinicians utilising a range of strategies including
audit (Johnson, Jefferies & Langdon ), practice development
and coaching programs (Jefferies et al.
) in order to ensure
continuous and sustainable improvements.
16
17
18


17 Johnson, M., Jefferies, D. & Langdon, R. (2010). The Nursing and Midwifery
Content Audit Tool (NMCAT): A short nursing documentation audit tool. Journal of
Nursing Management, 18(7), 832–845.
18 Jefferies, D., Johnson, M., Nicholls, D. & Lad, S. (2012). Award-based writing
coach program to improve the quality of nursing documentation. Nurse Education
Today, 32(6), 647–651.
Implications The research highlights risks to patient safety
and care planning that can result from use of language that
can be understood at a local level but not by those outside
the setting. The authors also suggest such documentation
may obscure nurses’ contribution to care planning and
assessment. All nurses should be cognisant of the findings
and be encouraged to attend ongoing education, recognising
documentation as a central aspect of care.
Practice guidelines
Documentation
Do
Chart a change in a person’s condition and show that
follow-up actions were taken and who was notified.
Read the nurses’ notes prior to care to determine if there
has been a change in the person’s condition.
Be timely. A late entry is better than no entry; however,
the longer the period of time between actual care and
charting, the greater the suspicion.


Use objective, specific and factual descriptions.
Correct charting errors.
Chart all teaching.
Record the person’s actual words by putting quote marks
around the words.
Chart the person’s response to interventions.
Review your notes. Are they clear and do they reflect
what you want to say?
Don’t
Leave a blank space for a colleague to chart later.
Chart in advance of the event (e.g. procedure,
medication).
Use vague terms (e.g. ‘Appears to be comfortable’, ‘Had a
good night’).
Chart for someone else.
Alter a record even if requested by a superior or a doctor.
Record assumptions or words reflecting bias (e.g.
‘complainer’, ‘disagreeable’).
Legal prudence
Admissible in court as a legal document, the clinical record provides
information about care delivered to a person. Documentation is


usually viewed by juries and lawyers as the best evidence of what
really happened to the person. Hence accurate, complete
documentation that adheres to professional standards and
articulates the delivery of nursing care aligned with organisational
policy and procedure and practice guidelines is central to
understanding an individual case. It will provide protection for the
nurse, other health care providers and the health care facility. It will
also provide clear information to others who have an interest in
understanding episodes of care provided. For example:


Reporting
The purpose of reporting is to communicate specific information to a
person or group of people. A report, whether oral or written, should
be concise, including pertinent information but no extraneous detail.
In addition to change-of-shift reports (see Chapter 27
) and
telephone reports, reporting can also include the sharing of
information or ideas with colleagues and other health professionals
about some aspect of a person’s care. Examples include the care
plan conference and nursing rounds.

pain. He has a past medical history of hypertension. He told
the admitting nurse that he has lost interest in many of his
normal activities because of the constant pain.

Chapter 16 Review


Chapter highlights
Patient records are legal documents that provide evidence of a
person’s care.
The nurse has a legal and ethical duty to maintain confidentiality
of the person’s record; this includes special measures to protect
personal information stored electronically.
Patient records are kept for a number of purposes, including
communication, planning care, auditing health care facilities,
research, education, reimbursement, legal documentation and
health care analysis.
In source-oriented clinical records, each health care professional
group provides its own record. Recording is oriented to the
source of the information.
In problem-oriented clinical records, recording is organised
around patient problems.
Examples of documentation systems include PIE, focus charting,
charting by exception (CBE), electronic documentation and case
management.
Computers make care planning and documentation relatively
easy. The use of computer terminals at the bedside enables
immediate documentation of nursing actions.
The case management model emphasises quality and cost-
effective care delivered within an established length of stay.
Nursing progress notes provide information about the progress
the person is making towards desired outcomes. The format for


the progress note depends on the documentation system at the
facility.
Community-based services are provided by a range of health
professionals who all keep separate records. A solution to this
problem is to keep a common record at the person’s home.
Legal guidelines for the process of recording in a patient record
include documenting date and time, legible entries, using dark
ink, using correct terminology and spelling, accuracy,
appropriateness, completeness, conciseness and adding an
appropriate signature.
The purpose of reporting is to communicate specific information
for the goal of improving quality of care. Examples include
handover reports, telephone reports, telephone orders, care plan
conferences and nursing rounds.

Unit 4 Health beliefs and practices
As increasingly knowledgeable health care
consumers, people expect and deserve quality
care. While assisting people—whether as an
individual, family or entire community—quality
nursing care should emphasise illness
prevention and health promotion. Nurses
recognise that people’s health state and
wellness encompass many dimensions,
including social, spiritual, cultural, sexual and
environmental, as well as physical and
psychological. Each encounter affords the nurse
an opportunity to influence and encourage both
traditional and innovative health-seeking
behaviours.

Health promotion is an important component of
nursing practice. It is a way of thinking that
revolves around a philosophy of wholeness,
wellness and wellbeing. In the past three
decades, the public has become increasingly
aware of and interested in health promotion.
Many people are aware of the relationship
between lifestyle and illness and are developing
health-promoting habits, such as getting
adequate exercise, rest and relaxation;
maintaining good nutrition; and controlling the
use of tobacco, alcohol and other drugs.
Assessing and planning health care of the
individual is enhanced when the nurse
understands the concepts of individuality,
holism, homeostasis and human needs. The
beliefs and values of each person and the
support they receive come in large part from the
family and are reinforced by the community. The
reverse is also true—the health of a community
is affected by the beliefs, attitudes and
behaviours of the individuals in the community.


Individual health
Dimensions of individuality include the person’s total character, self-
identity and perceptions. The person’s total character encompasses
behaviours, emotional state, attitudes, values, motives, abilities,
habits and appearances. The person’s self-identity encompasses
perception of self as a separate and distinct entity alone and in their
interactions with others. The person’s perceptions encompass the
way the person interprets the environment or situation, directly
affecting how they think, feel and act in any given situation.
Concept of individuality
To help people attain, maintain or regain an optimal level of health,
nurses need to understand each individual and support a person-
centred approach to care. Each individual is a unique being who is
different from every other human being with a different combination
of genetics, life experiences and environmental interactions.
When providing care, nurses need to focus on the person within
both a total care and an individualised care context. In the total care
context, the nurse considers all the principles and areas that apply
when taking care of any person of that age and condition. In the
individualised care context, the nurse becomes acquainted with the


person as an individual, using the total care principles that apply to
this person at this time. For example, a nurse who is advising the
mother of a preschooler understands that the child’s desire to
explore their world is a developmental stage that all preschoolers
experience. However, the preschooler diagnosed with attention
deficit hyperactivity disorder may have an increased risk of accidents
and injuries when interacting with the environment due to their
impulsive behaviour or poor self-control.
Concept of holism
Nurses are concerned with the individual as a whole (a holistic
approach), not as an assembly of parts and processes. When
applied in nursing, the concept of holism
 emphasises that nurses
must keep the whole person in mind and strive to understand how
one area of concern relates to the whole person. The nurse must
also consider the relationship of the individual to the external
environment and to others. For example, in helping a man who is
grieving over the death of his spouse, the nurse explores the impact
of the loss on the whole person (i.e. on the man’s appetite, rest and
sleep pattern, energy level, sense of wellbeing, mood, usual
activities, family relationships and relationships with others). Nursing
interventions are directed towards restoring overall harmony so they
depend on the man’s sense of purpose and meaning of his life. For
additional information about holistic practices, see Chapter 20
.


Concept of homeostasis
The concept of homeostasis
 was first introduced by Cannon  to
describe the relative constancy of the internal processes of the body,
such as blood oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, blood pressure,
body temperature, blood glucose and fluid and electrolyte balance.
To Cannon, the word homeostasis did not imply something stagnant,
set or immobile; it meant a condition that might vary but remained
relatively constant. Cannon viewed the human being as separate
from the external environment and constantly endeavouring to
maintain physiological equilibrium
, or balance, through
adaptation to that environment. Homeostasis, then, is the tendency
of the body to maintain a state of balance or equilibrium while
continually changing.
1 Cannon, W. B. (1939). The Wisdom of the Body (2nd ed.). New York: Norton.
Physiological homeostasis
Physiological homeostasis means that the internal environment of
the body is relatively stable and constant. All cells of the body
require a relatively constant environment to function; thus, the
body’s internal environment must be maintained within narrow limits.
Homeostatic mechanisms have four main characteristics:
1. They are self-regulating.
2. They are compensatory.
1


3. They tend to be regulated by negative feedback systems.
4. They may require several feedback mechanisms to correct
any physiological imbalance.
Self-regulation
 means that homeostatic mechanisms come into
play automatically in the healthy person. However, if a person is ill,
or if a respiratory organ such as a lung is injured, the homeostatic
mechanisms may not be able to respond to the stimulus as they
would normally. Homeostatic mechanisms are compensatory
(counterbalancing) because they tend to counteract conditions that
are abnormal for the person. An example is a sudden drop in air
temperature. The compensatory mechanisms are that the peripheral
blood vessels constrict, thereby diverting most of the blood
internally, and increased muscular activity and shivering occur to
create heat. Through these mechanisms the body temperature
remains stable despite the cold.
Homeostasis occurs within the physiological system
, a set of
interacting identifiable parts or components. The fundamental
components of a system are matter, energy and communication.
Without any one of these, a system does not exist. The individual is
a human system with matter (the body), energy (chemical or
thermal) and communication (e.g. the nervous system). The
boundary
 of a system, such as the skin in the human system, is
a real or imaginary line that differentiates one system from another
system or a system from its environment.


There are two general types of systems: closed and open. A closed
system
 does not exchange energy, matter or information with its
environment; it receives no input from the environment and gives no
output to the environment. An example of a closed system is a
chemical reaction that takes place in a test tube. In reality, outside
the laboratory no closed systems exist. In an open system
,
energy, matter and information move into and out of the system
through the system boundary. All living systems, such as plants,
animals, people, families and communities, are open systems
because their survival depends on a continuous exchange of energy.
They are, therefore, in a constant state of change.
An open system depends on the quality and quantity of its input,
output and feedback. Input
 consists of information, material or
energy that enters the system. After the input is absorbed by the
system, it is processed in a way useful to the system. This
transformation is called throughput
. For example, food is input to
the digestive system; it is digested (throughput) so that it can be
used by the body. Output
 from a system is energy, matter or
information given out by the system as a result of its processes.
Output from the digestive system includes caloric energy, nutrients,
urine and faeces.
Feedback
 is the mechanism by which some of the output of a
system is returned to the system as input. Feedback enables a
system to regulate itself by redirecting the output back into the
system, thus forming a feedback loop (see Figure 17.1
). This
input influences the behaviour of the system and its future output.


Negative feedback
 inhibits change; positive feedback
stimulates change. Most biological systems are controlled by
negative feedback to bring the system back to stability. This type of
feedback system senses and counteracts any deviations from
normal. The deviations may be greater or less than the normal level
or range. For example, an increase in the production of parathyroid
hormone is stimulated by a drop in blood calcium, but when
additional parathyroid hormone raises the level of blood calcium, the
hormone’s production is then inhibited (see Figure 17.2
). With
hypoxia (shortage of oxygen), the concentration of red blood cells
increases and the heart rate becomes faster to transport the blood
and available oxygen around the body adequately. People interact
with the environment by adjusting themselves to it or adjusting it to
themselves. This premise directs the nurse to look at environmental
factors influencing the system, to think critically and to plan nursing
interventions to help the person maintain homeostasis. For example,
the individual who is experiencing severe anxiety may be taught a
variety of stress management techniques.
Figure 17.1


An open system with a feedback mechanism.
Figure 17.2


The homeostatic regulator of the body: autonomic nervous system,
endocrine system and specific organ systems.
Psychological homeostasis
The term psychological homeostasis
 refers to emotional or
psychological balance or a state of mental wellbeing. It is maintained
by a variety of mechanisms. Each person has certain psychological
needs, such as the need for love, security and self-esteem, which
must be met to maintain psychological homeostasis. When one or
more of these needs is not met or is threatened, certain coping
mechanisms are activated to protect the person and provide
psychological homeostasis.
Psychological homeostasis is acquired or learned through the
experience of living and interacting with others. In addition, societal
norms and culture influence behaviour. Some prerequisites for a
person to develop psychological homeostasis are:
a stable physical environment in which the person feels safe and
secure. For example, the basic needs for food, shelter and
clothing must be met consistently
a stable psychological environment so that feelings of trust and
love develop. Growing children and adolescents also need kind
but firm and consistent discipline, encouragement and support to
be their own unique selves
a social environment that includes adults who are healthy role
models. Children learn the customs and values of society from


these individuals
a life experience that provides satisfaction. Throughout life,
people encounter many frustrations. People deal with these
better if enough satisfying experiences have occurred to
counterbalance the frustrating ones.
Assessing the health of individuals
A thorough assessment of the individual’s health status is basic to
health promotion. Components of this assessment are the health
history and physical examination, physical fitness assessment,
lifestyle assessment, health risk appraisal, health beliefs review and
life stress review. Details of these assessments are discussed in
Chapters 12
 and 31
.


Applying theoretical frameworks
A variety of theoretical frameworks provide the nurse with a holistic
overview of health promotion for the individual and families across
the lifespan. Two major theoretical frameworks that nurses use in
promoting the health of the individual are needs theories and
developmental stage theories.
Needs theories
In needs theories, human needs are ranked on an ascending scale
according to how essential the needs are for survival. Abraham
Maslow , perhaps the most renowned needs theorist, ranks human
needs on five levels (see Figure 17.3
 and Box 17.1
).
2 Maslow, A. H. (1970). Motivation and Personality (2nd ed.). New York: Harper & Row.

17.1 Maslow’s characteristics of a
self-actualised person
Is realistic, sees life clearly and is objective about their
observations.
Judges people correctly.
Has superior perception, is more decisive.
Has clear notion of right and wrong.
Is usually accurate in predicting future events.
Understands art, music, politics and philosophy.
Possesses humility, listens to others carefully.
Is dedicated to some work, task, duty or vocation.
Is highly creative, flexible, spontaneous, courageous and
willing to make mistakes.
Is open to new ideas.
Is self-confident and has self-respect.
Has low degree of self-conflict; personality is integrated.
Respects self, does not need fame, possesses a feeling
of self-control.
Is highly independent, desires privacy.
Can appear remote and detached.
Is friendly, loving and governed more by inner directives
than by society.
Can make decisions contrary to popular opinion.
Is problem-centred rather than self-centred.
Accepts the world for what it is.


Source: A. H. Maslow . Toward a Psychology of Being (2nd ed.). Reproduced with permission from
John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
4 Maslow, A. H. (1968). Toward a Psychology of Being (2nd ed.). New York: John Wiley & Sons Inc.
Maslow’s hierarchy of needs
The five levels in ascending order are as follows:
1. Physiological needs. Needs such as air, food, water, shelter,
rest, sleep, activity and temperature maintenance are crucial
for survival.
2. Safety and security needs. The need for safety has both
physical and psychological aspects. The person needs to feel
safe, both in the physical environment and in relationships.
3. Love and belonging needs. The third level of needs includes
giving and receiving affection, attaining a place in a group and
maintaining the feeling of belonging.
4. Self-esteem needs. The individual needs both self-esteem
(i.e. feelings of independence, competence and self- respect)
and esteem from others (i.e. recognition, respect and
appreciation).
5. Self-actualisation. When the need for self-esteem is
satisfied, the individual strives for self-actualisation, the innate
need to develop one’s maximum potential and realise one’s
abilities and qualities.
4


Kalish’s hierarchy of needs
Richard Kalish (1983) adapted Maslow’s hierarchy of needs into six
levels rather than five. He suggests an additional category between
the physiological needs and the safety and security needs. This
category, referred to as stimulation needs, includes sex, activity,
exploration, manipulation and novelty (see Figure 17.3
). Kalish
emphasises that children need to explore and manipulate their
environments to achieve optimal growth and development. He notes
that adults, too, often seek novel adventures or stimulating
experiences before considering their safety or security needs (e.g.
skydiving).
Characteristics of basic needs
All people have the same basic needs; however, each person’s
needs and reactions to those needs are influenced by the culture
with which the person identifies. For example, professional
achievement, independent functioning and privacy may be important
in one culture or subculture and unimportant in another.
People meet their own needs relative to their own priorities. For
example, an impoverished mother might give up food so that her
child might have sufficient food to live.
Although basic needs generally must be met, some needs can
be deferred. An example is the need for independence, which an
ill person can defer until well.


Failure to meet needs results in one or more homeostatic
imbalances, which can eventually result in illness.
A need can make itself felt by either external or internal stimuli.
An example is the need for food. A person may experience
hunger as a result of physiological processes (internal
stimulation) or as a result of seeing a beautiful cake (external
stimulation).
A person who perceives a need can respond in several ways to
meet it. The choice of response is largely a result of learned
experiences, lifestyle and the values of the culture. For example,
many people’s food choices at mealtimes and snack times are
based on past experiences, lifestyle and culture.
Needs are interrelated. Some needs cannot be met unless
related needs are also met. The need for hydration can be
influenced by the need for elimination of urine. Likewise, the
need for security can be markedly altered if the need for oxygen
is threatened by a respiratory obstruction.
Needs can be satisfied in healthy and unhealthy ways. Ways of
meeting basic needs are considered healthy when they are not
harmful to others or to self, conform to the individual’s sociocultural
values and are within the law. Conversely, unhealthy behaviour may
be harmful to others or to self, does not conform to the individual’s
sociocultural values or is not within the law. People who satisfy their
basic needs appropriately are healthier, happier and more effective
than those whose needs are frustrated.


Knowledge of the theoretical bases of human needs assists nurses
in responding therapeutically to a person’s behaviours and in
understanding themselves and their own responses to needs.
Human needs serve as a framework for assessing behaviours,
assigning priorities to desired outcomes and planning nursing
interventions. For example, an adult with poor self- esteem would
have difficulty accomplishing self-actualisation. Therefore, nursing
interventions would focus on increasing the person’s self-esteem.
Developmental stage theories
Developmental stage theories categorise a person’s behaviours or
tasks into approximate age ranges or in terms that describe the
features of an age group. The age ranges of the stages do not take
into account individual differences; however, the categories do
describe characteristics associated with the majority of individuals at
periods when distinctive developmental changes occur and with the
specific tasks that must be accomplished. See Chapter 21
 for
further information about developmental stages.
Developmental stage theories allow nurses to describe typical
behaviours of an individual within a certain age group, explain the
significance of those behaviours, predict behaviours that might occur
in a given situation and provide a rationale to control behavioural
manifestations. Individuals can be compared with a representative
group of people at the same point in time or compared at different
points in time. The nurse’s knowledge of developmental stage


theories can be used in education, counselling and anticipatory
guidance.


Defining health promotion
Considerable differences appear in the literature regarding the use
of the terms health promotion, primary prevention, health protection
and illness prevention. Edelman and Mandle  state that ‘prevention,
in a narrow sense, means avoiding the development of disease in
the future and, in the broader sense, consists of all interventions to
limit progression of a disease’ (p. 13). The levels of prevention occur
at various points in the course of disease progression. Leavell and
Clark  define three levels of prevention: primary, secondary and
tertiary.
5 Edelman, C. L. & Mandle, C. L. (2017). Health Promotion throughout the Lifespan (9th ed.).
St Louis, MO: Mosby.
6 Leavell, H. R. & Clark, E. G. (1965). Preventive Medicine for the Doctor in the Community
(3rd ed.). New York: McGraw-Hill.
Five steps describe these levels: primary prevention
 focuses on
(a) health promotion, and (b) protection against specific health
problems (e.g. immunisation against hepatitis B). The purpose of
primary prevention is to decrease the risk or exposure of the
individual or community to disease. Secondary prevention
focuses on (a) early identification of health problems, and (b) prompt
intervention to alleviate health problems. Its goal is to identify
individuals in an early stage of a disease process and to limit future
disability. Tertiary prevention
 focuses on restoration and
5
6


rehabilitation with the goal of returning the individual to an optimal
level of functioning. Table 17.1
 provides examples of activities for
each level of prevention. The three levels of prevention may overlap
in practice. For example, a person may have experienced a heart
attack and a goal of secondary prevention is to limit disability. The
teaching (e.g. lifestyle changes) for the person’s rehabilitation will be
similar to health education activities in primary prevention.
Table 17.1 Levels of prevention
Pender, Murdaugh and Parsons  consider health promotion to be
different from disease prevention or health protection. They define
health promotion
 as a ‘central strategy for improving health that
has shifted from defining health as a dichotomy (presence or
absence of illness or disease) to a multidimensional definition of
health with social, economic, cultural and environmental dimensions’
(p. 9) and disease prevention
, or health protection
, as ‘the
use of regulatory measures to promote health’ (p. 31). The
individual’s underlying motivation for the behaviour, and the
involvement of government through regulation, is the major
difference (p. 31).
7 Pender, N. J., Murdaugh, C. L. & Parsons, M. A. (2015). Health Promotion in Nursing
Practice (7th ed.). Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice Hall.
The difficulty in separating the terms health promotion and disease
prevention/health protection lies in the fact that an activity may be
carried out for numerous reasons. For example, a 40-year-old male
may begin a program of walking 5 km each day. If the goal of his
7


program were to ‘decrease the risk of cardiovascular disease’, the
activity would be considered disease prevention or health protection.
By contrast, if the motivation for his walking regimen were to
‘increase his overall health and feeling of wellbeing’, then the activity
would be considered a health promotion behaviour. It is most helpful
to think of health promotion and health protection as being
complementary processes because both affect quality of health.
Health promotion can be offered to all people regardless of their
health and illness status or age. For example, weight- control
measures can benefit both overweight people without disease and
people with cardiac or joint disease. Age-specific health promotion
activities are discussed in Chapters 22
, 23
 and 24
. See
‘Lifespan considerations
’ for examples of health promotion
topics.
