This chapter aims to provide the beginnings of
an understanding of culture, nursing and


Indigenous Australian health. It is centred on
the following philosophical belief: ‘If we take the
time to develop enough trust to learn from each
other how not to be Binan Goonj—that is,
“hearing but not listening”—we can arrive at a
shared understanding of how best to
communicate’ (Eckermann et al. , p. 104). It is
acknowledged from the outset that Indigenous
Australian cultures are unique to the Australian
continent and Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander peoples (known collectively throughout
this text as Indigenous Australians) have a
specific mention in this chapter as they are the
First peoples of Australia and there is evidence
of significant disparities in health outcomes for
Indigenous Australian people. The National
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Plan
2013–2023 seeks a culturally respectful and
non-discriminatory health system with nurses
playing a critical role in transforming the health
system (Department of Health and Ageing
(DoHA) ).
1 Eckermann, A. K., Dowd, T., Chong, E., Nixon, L., Gray,
R. & Johnson, S. (2006). Binan Goonj: Bridging Cultures in
Aboriginal Health (2nd ed.). Marrickville: Churchill
Livingstone.
1
2


2 Department of Health and Ageing (DoHA) (2013).
National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Plan
2013–2023. Retrieved from <www.health.gov.au>.
To provide quality culturally responsive
care
, nurses must become informed about
and be sensitive to the culturally diverse
subjective meanings of health, illness, caring
and healing practices. It is essential for nurses
(who themselves will come from a wide range of
cultural backgrounds) to understand their own
culture and the impact that culture has on their
nursing work. Critical self-exploration, which
includes awareness and a willingness to learn,
is required to provide culturally responsive care
(Blackman ). Culture
 can be defined as the
knowledge and characteristics of a particular
group of people, including their language,
religion, cuisine, social habits, arts and music
(Zimmerman ). Culture defines how health is
perceived, how health care information is
received, how rights and protections are
exercised, what is considered to be a health
problem, how symptoms and concerns about
the health problem are expressed and
interpreted, who should provide treatment and
how and what kind of treatment should be
3
4


given. For example, scarification is practised in
several cultures as a way of ridding the body of
impurities, even if this intervention may interfere
with other medical practices and limited
evidence has been found to support the
practice. Cultural beliefs may dominate, with
local or traditional health providers being sought
for treatment over more evidence-based
Western medical interventions.
3 Blackman, R. (2011). Understanding culture in practice:
Reflections of an Australian Indigenous nurse.
Contemporary Nurse, 37(1), 31–34.
4 Zimmerman, K. A. (2017). What is culture? Definition of
culture. LiveScience. Retrieved from
<www.livescience.com>.
Nurses must be aware that although people
from a cultural group share certain beliefs,
values and experiences, often there are
subcultures within the group, and that each
person brings a unique perspective that should
be considered in health care delivery. Major
differences within cultural groups may be due to
such factors as age, gender, sexuality, level of


education, socioeconomic status and area of
origin in the home country (rural or urban). Such
factors influence the person’s beliefs and
perspectives about health and illness, health
practices, help-seeking behaviours and
expectations of nurses. For these reasons,
conscious effort must be made and care taken
to avoid stereotyping people from specific
cultural groups.
Australia is a multicultural society and, while
English is Australia’s national language, the
cultural diversity within the population has
resulted in over 300 languages being spoken
(Australia Bureau of Statistics (ABS) ). People
in Australia come from a rich variety of cultural,
ethnic, linguistic and religious backgrounds.
Most Australians are immigrants who have
arrived during the past two centuries from more
than 200 countries and have brought with them
practices of their heritage—things passed down
from previous generations (Department of
Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) ). In addition,
Indigenous Australian peoples have inhabited
Australia for tens of thousands of years and
offer a host of different languages and tribal
groups, and wide cultural diversity.
5
6


5 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2013). Australian
Social Trends, April 2013. Cat. no. 4102.0. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au>.
6 Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) (2016).
Australia in Brief. Retrieved from <http://dfat.gov.au>.
Clinical consideration
Culture and language are
vital factors in how clinical
nursing care is delivered
and received.


National organisations and trends
The demographic changes in the overall population of Australia,
including Indigenous Australians’ unique needs and the influence of
immigration and the arrival of refugees on health services, are the
major reasons for the need for culturally focused nursing care. The
Australian initiatives described in Box 19.1
 and nurse-specific
initiatives described in Box 19.2
 are evidence of increased
emphasis on providing culturally appropriate health care.
BO X
19.1 Australian initiatives focused on
culturally appropriate health care
The National Aboriginal Community Controlled Health
Organisation (NACCHO) is the national peak body for
Aboriginal health. A principle objective of the organisation
is to deliver holistic and culturally appropriate health care
to Aboriginal communities. See <www.naccho.org.au>.
The Department of Home Affairs manages permanent
and temporary entry of people to Australia and brings
together Australia’s federal law enforcement, national and
transport security, criminal justice, emergency


management, multicultural affairs and immigration and
border-related functions, working together to keep
Australia safe. See <www.homeaffairs.gov.au>.
The Implementation Plan for the National Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander Health Plan 2013–2023 was
prepared by the Department of Health  and outlines the
actions to be taken by the Australian government, the
Aboriginal community controlled health sector and other
key stakeholders to give effect to the vision, principles,
priorities and strategies of the National Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander Health Plan 2013–2023. See
<www.health.gov.au/internet/main/publishing.nsf/Content/i
ndigenous-implementation-plan>.
7 Department of Health (2015). Implementation Plan for the National Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander Health Plan 2013–2023. Retrieved from
<www.health.gov.au>.
The National Health and Hospital Reform Commission’s
report entitled Beyond the Blame Game: Accountability
and Performance Benchmarks for the Next Australian
Health Care Agreements highlights the need for the health
care system to be more person-centred and equitable.
The commission identified 12 health care challenges, the
first of which was to ‘Close the Gap’ in Indigenous health
status. Other challenges include meeting the needs of
people with mental illness, those who are socially
marginalised and those who live in regional and remote
areas.
7
8


8 National Health and Hospitals Reform Commission (2008). Beyond the Blame

Health Care Agreements. Retrieved from <www.health.gov.au>.
Originating from the ‘Close the Gap’ campaign, a
‘statement of intent’ has been developed between the
government of Australia and the Aboriginal and Torres
Islander peoples of Australia (supported by non-
Indigenous Australians and Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander and non-Indigenous health organisations) to work
together to achieve equality in health status and life
expectancy between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
peoples and non-Indigenous Australians by the year 2030
(Australian Human Rights Commission ).
9 Australian Human Rights Commission (2008). National Indigenous Health
Equality Summit Outcomes. Canberra: Author.
The ‘Close the Gap’ initiative is monitored by the
Department of Health via the Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander Health Performance Framework. This framework
monitors progress in Indigenous Australian health
outcomes, health system performance and broader
determinants of health. See
<www.health.gov.au/internet/main/publishing.nsf/Content/o
atsih_heath-performanceframework>. In 2017, the report
showed encouraging improvements in aspects of
Indigenous health. See <www.pmc.gov.au/sites/default/
files/reports/closing-the-gap-2017/sites/default/files/
ctg-report-2017.pdf>.
9


The National Advisory Group on Aboriginal and Torres

established in 2000 by the Australian Health Ministers’

Information Management Principle Committee on health

people. The plan was updated in 2011 (AIHW
). See
<www.aihw.gov.au/reports/indigenous-australians/
national-advisory-group-on-aboriginal-and-torres-s/
contents/table-of-contents>.
10 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2011). National Advisory
Group on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Information Strategic Plan

The Congress of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
Nurses and Midwives (CATSINaM) was established in
1997 and is the sole representative body for Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander nurses and midwives in
Australia. See <http://catsinam.org.au>.
The Australian Indigenous Doctors’ Association (AIDA) is

See <www.aida.org.au>.

The National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health

19.2 Documents relevant for nurses
working with people from diverse
cultures
In 2018, the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia
(NMBA), the Congress of Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islanders Nurses and Midwives, the Australian College of
Midwives, the Australian College of Nursing and the
Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation published a
joint statement outlining appropriate culturally safe care to
be employed by nurses and midwives in Australia. See
<www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au/News/2018-03-
23-joint-statement.aspx>.
From March 2018, the International Council of Nurses
(ICN) Code of Ethics for Nurses (2012) replaced the
NMBA Code of Ethics for Nurses in Australia . In the ICN
11


document, it is proposed that the first principle is that
nurses, ‘provide care that respects human rights and is
sensitive to the values, customs and beliefs of people’
(ICN , p. 6).
11 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2013). Code of Ethics for

The NMBA Registered Nurse Standards for Practice :
‘Standard 1: Thinks critically and analyses nursing
practice’ (NMBA 2016, p. 3) states in Standard 1.3 that
the Registered Nurse ‘respects all cultures and
experiences, which includes responding to the role of
family and community that underpin the health of
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and people
of other cultures’. In addition, ‘Standard 2: Engages in
therapeutic and professional relationships’ indicates in
Standard 2.2 that the Registered Nurse ‘communicates
effectively, and is respectful of a person’s dignity, culture,
values, beliefs and rights’ (NMBA 2016, p. 3). These
Standards, first published in 2006 and updated in 2016,
provide a framework for culturally competent and person-
centred care.
13 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016). Registered Nurse
Standards for Practice. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
12
13


Demographics
Statistics on the ethnicity of the population can be difficult to
interpret. Australia’s population in 2018 was 25.1 million (ABS ). In
2011, the median age of Australians was 37.8 years, compared with
23 years for Indigenous Australians, and 71% of people living in
Australia were born here (ABS 2018). Of those born overseas,
England (4.0%) is the largest represented group of immigrants,
followed by China (2.6%), India (2.4%), New Zealand (2.3%) and
then the Philippines (1.1%) (ABS 2018).
14 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018). Demographic Statistics. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au>.
In the 2016 Census, 3.3% of the total population of Australia
identified themselves as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
(ABS ). This comprised 798 400 people, of which 50% were male
and 50% were female (ABS 2016a). Of the 3.3% of people that
identified as Indigenous, around 91% identified as Aboriginal, 5% as
Torres Strait Islanders and 4% as both Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander descent (ABS 2018).
15 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2016a). Population Clock. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au/>.
Immigration
14
15


Migration has increased Australia’s population. It is estimated that in
2018, overseas migration resulted in a net increase in the Australian
population by approximately 237 200 people. Australia has a long
history of immigration, even before European colonisation in 1788.
Since the end of World War II in 1945, over 7.3 million people have
migrated to Australia. The number of new migrants in 2018 was,
however, 10% fewer than in 2017 (ABS 2018), with New South
Wales recording the highest migration at 36%; 30.5% arrived in
Victoria and 16.3% in Queensland (ABS 2018). Humanitarian
arrivals to Australia (refugees) made up only a small percentage of
arrivals, with Australia taking only 0.65% of the 3.5 million displaced
people across the world in 2017 (United Nations High Commissioner
for Refugees ).
16 United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (2018). UNHCR Global Trends 2017—
How Australia Compares with the World. Retrieved from <www.refugeecouncil.org.au>.
Lifespan considerations
Ageing population
Older adults
Australia (with the exception of Indigenous Australians)
has the second longest life expectancy in the world, with
Australia’s older population expected to grow from 2.5
16


million people over the age of 65 in 2002 to 6.2 million by
2042 (Productivity Commission ; Commonwealth of
Australia ). In acknowledgment of this the Australian
government, through local state and territory initiatives, is
responding to the opportunities and challenges of
population ageing in a diverse and multifaceted way. As
such, in 2011, the Productivity Commission released a
government report called Caring for Older Australians with
the aim of developing detailed options for redesigning
Australia’s aged care system to ensure that it can meet
the challenges facing it in coming decades.
17 Productivity Commission (2011). Caring for Older Australians. Productivity
Commission Inquiry Report. No. 53. Retrieved from <www.pc.gov.au>.
18 Commonwealth of Australia (2004). Australia’s Demographic Challenges,
Social Policy Division. Retrieved from <http://demographics.treasury.gov.au>.
The life expectancy for non-Indigenous Australian males
in 2010–12 was 79.7 years and for females was 83.1
years; in contrast, at the same time the life expectancy for
Indigenous males was 67.5 years and for females 73.1
years (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare
(AIHW)
). This equates to, on average, 11.1 years less
life expectancy for Indigenous Australians. The life
expectancy gap is a priority for the National Indigenous
Health Equality Summit and has decreased from 17 years
to 11.1 years since 2008 (ABS 2018; Australian Human
Rights Commission 2008). Nurses will need to continue to
17
18
19


respond to the challenges that come with caring for an
ageing population in a culturally responsive way.
19 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018). Deaths in Australia.
Canberra: AIHW. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.


Cultural nursing care
Nurses’ responsibility for cultural health care is supported by the ICN
Code of Ethics for Nurses (2012) which suggests that professional
nursing care be culturally sensitive, appropriate, safe and
competent. This type of nursing is critical to meeting the complex
nursing care needs of a given person, family and community. It is
the provision of nursing care across cultural boundaries and takes
into account the context in which the person lives as well as the
situations in which the person’s health problems have arisen:
‘Culturally sensitive
’ implies that nurses possess some basic
knowledge of and constructive attitudes towards the health
traditions observed in the diverse cultural groups found in the
setting in which they are practising. Cultural responsiveness
refers to the practitioner being able to undertake clinical actions
that acknowledge the person’s cultural background and consider
this to enhance their therapeutic relationship.
‘Culturally appropriate
’ implies that nurses apply the
underlying background knowledge that must be possessed to
provide an individual with the best possible health care.
‘Cultural competence
’ suggests that within the delivered care
nurses understand and attend to the total context of the person’s
situation and use a complex combination of knowledge, skills,
behaviours and attitudes. Cultural competence implies that care
incorporates the importance of culture, an assessment of cross-


cultural relations, the expansion of cultural knowledge, cultural
respect, vigilance towards the dynamic nature of culture and
cultural differences, and the adaption of care and services to
meet unique cultural needs (Bainbridge et al.
). The term
‘cultural competence’ first emerged in the 1980s in the United
States during a time where specific disciplines were attempting to
transform their practices to meet the needs of an increasingly
multicultural population. In the context of health care provision,
there was growing evidence that people from non-dominant
cultural groups (ethnic and racial minorities) continued to
experience significantly poorer health outcomes than people from
the majority/dominant culture. The concept of cultural
competence has since been taken up in a number of other
English-speaking countries, particularly those with significant
immigrant and Indigenous populations.
20 Bainbridge, R., McCalman, J., Clifford, A. & Tsey, K. (2015). Cultural Competency in
the Delivery of Health Services for Indigenous People. Issues Paper No. 13. Closing the
Gap Clearinghouse. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Cultural safety
 is ‘the effective nursing practice of a person or
family from another culture and is determined by that person or
family. Cultural includes, but is not restricted to, age or
generation; gender; sexual orientation; occupation and
socioeconomic status; ethnic origin or migrant experience;
religious or spiritual belief; and disability. The nurse delivering the
nursing service will have undertaken a process of reflection on
their own cultural identity and will recognise the impact that their
personal culture has on professional practice. Unsafe cultural
practice comprises any action which diminishes, demeans or
20


disempowers the cultural identity and well-being of an individual’
(Nursing Council of New Zealand , p. 4).
21 Nursing Council of New Zealand (2005). Guidelines for Cultural Safety, the Treaty of
Waitangi and Māori Health in Nursing Education and Practice. Wellington: Author.
Cultural safety is a model of care based on the work of Irihapeti
Ramsden, a Maori nurse educator and scholar. To achieve cultural
safety, nurses need to participate in the following steps described by
the Nursing Council of New Zealand (2005, p. 5):
1. Cultural awareness is the beginning step towards
understanding that there is a difference in the social,
economic and political context in which people exist.
2. Cultural sensitivity alerts the nurse to the legitimacy of
difference and begins a process of self-exploration of their
own life experiences and realities, and the impact these may
have on others.
3. Cultural safety is an outcome of nursing and midwifery
education that enables safe service to be defined by those
who receive the service.
The term ‘transcultural nursing’ has been promulgated by nurse
Madeleine Leininger since the 1950s. Transcultural nursing
focuses on providing care within the differences and similarities of
the beliefs, values and patterns of cultures (Leininger &
McFarland ). Leininger created the theory of culture care diversity
and universality. Her transcultural research has involved international
studies that have served the nursing profession by providing a
21
22


framework for understanding the needs of immigrants and
multicultural populations in Australia and around the world.
22 Leininger, M. M. & McFarland, M. R. (2005). Culture Care Diversity & Universality: A
Worldwide Nursing Theory (2nd ed.). Boston: Jones & Bartlett.
Countless conflicts in the health care delivery arenas are predicated
on people misunderstanding another’s cultural beliefs and practices.
Although many of these misunderstandings are related to universal
situations, such as verbal and non-verbal language
misunderstandings, the conventions of courtesy, sequencing of
interactions, phasing of interactions, objectivity and so forth, many
cultural misunderstandings are unique to the delivery of nursing
care. Cultural nursing care is essential and demands that nurses be
able to assess and interpret a person’s health beliefs and practices
and cultural needs and apply this information to their health care
practice. One way of understanding the complexities of another’s
culture is demonstrated by the iceberg model. Just as the iceberg
has visible and hidden aspects above and below the water line, so
does a person’s culture (Stanley ). Refer to Figure 19.1
 for a
diagrammatical representation of the iceberg model. Cultural nursing
care alters the perspective of nursing care delivery because it
enables the nurse to understand, from a cultural perspective, the
manifestations of the person’s health care beliefs and practices.
23 Stanley, D. (Ed.) (2019). Clinical Leadership for Nurses and Healthcare: Values into Action.
East Sussex: Wiley Blackwell.
Figure 19.1
23


Iceberg model of culture.
Source: Based on G. Rocher
. Introduction à la Sociologie Générale, Tome 1.
24 Rocher, G. (1969). Introduction à la Sociologie Générale, Tome 1. Montreal: Editions
Hurtubise HMH.
24


Concepts related to
cultural nursing care
All groups of people face issues in adapting to their environment:
providing nutrition and shelter, caring for and educating children,
dividing labour, developing social organisations, expressing
themselves sexually, controlling disease and maintaining health.
Humans adapt to varying environments by developing cultural
solutions to meet these needs. Culture is a universal experience, but
no two cultures are exactly alike. Cultural patterns are learned and it
is important for nurses to note that members of a particular group
may not share identical cultural experiences. Thus, each member of
a cultural group will be somewhat different from their own cultural
counterparts.
Subculture
Large cultural groups often have cultural subgroups or subsystems.
A subculture
 is usually composed of people who have a distinct
identity and yet are related to a larger cultural group. A subcultural
group generally shares ethnic origin or physical characteristics with
the larger cultural group. Examples of cultural subgroups include
occupational groups (e.g. nurses), societal groups (e.g. feminists,


emos) and ethnic groups (e.g. within the Indigenous culture there
are 250 language subculture groups).
Bicultural
‘Bicultural
’ is used to describe a person who has dual patterns of
identification and crosses two cultures, lifestyles and sets of values
(Dunn ). For example, a young man whose father is of Indigenous
descent and whose mother is of non-Indigenous descent may
honour his traditional Indigenous heritage while also being influenced
by his mother’s cultural values.
25 Dunn, A. M. (2009). Health perception and health management patterns. In C. E. Burns, A.
M. Dunn, M. A. Brady, N. Starr & C. G. Blosser (Eds), Pediatric Primary Care: A Handbook
for Nurse Practitioners (4th ed., pp. 182−185). Philadelphia: W. B. Saunders.
Diversity
Diversity
 refers to the fact or state of being different. Many
factors account for diversity: race, gender, sexual orientation,
culture, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, educational attainment,
religious affiliation and so on. Diversity therefore occurs not only
between cultural groups but also within a cultural group.
25


Acculturation
While becoming participants in the dominant culture, members of a
non-dominant cultural group are always identified as members of the
culture from which they originate. People immigrating to Australia
from any country will be associated with their home countries for
many years, if not for all their lives. The involuntary process of
acculturation
 occurs when people adapt to or borrow traits from
another culture. The member of the non-dominant cultural group is
often forced to learn the new culture to survive. Acculturation can
also be defined as the changes of one’s cultural patterns to those of
the host country (Spector
).
26 Spector, R. E. (2013). Cultural Diversity in Health and Illness (8th ed.). Upper Saddle
River, NJ: Pearson Prentice Hall.
Assimilation
Assimilation
 is the process by which an individual develops a
new cultural identity. Assimilation means becoming like the members
of the dominant culture. The process of assimilation encompasses
various aspects, such as behavioural, marital, identification and
community. The underlying assumption is that the person from a
given cultural group loses their original cultural identity to acquire the
new one. In fact, because this is a conscious effort, it is not always
possible and the process may cause severe stress and anxiety.
26


Assimilation can also be described as a collection of subprocesses:
a process of inclusion through which a person gradually ceases to
conform to any standard of life that differs from the dominant group
standards and, at the same time, a process through which the
person learns to conform to all the dominant group standards. The
process of assimilation is understood in Australia in two ways: (1)
through the experience of migrants to Australia; and (2) from the
perspective or history of Indigenous Australians. Migrants are seen
as completely assimilated when the ‘foreigner’ is fully merged into
the dominant cultural group (McLemore & Romo ). With Indigenous
Australians, assimilation has been linked with detrimental health
effects due to a lack of recognition of the central place of Indigenous
Australian culture (Australian Human Rights Commission ).
27 McLemore, S. D. & Romo, H. D. (2005). Racial and Ethnic Relations in America (7th ed.).
Boston: Allyn & Bacon.
28 Australian Human Rights Commission (1997). Bringing Them Home Report. Canberra:
Commonwealth of Australia.
The concepts of assimilation and acculturation are complex and
sensitive. The dominant society may expect that all immigrants are
in the process of acculturation and assimilation, and that the world
view that we have as nurses is commonly shared by all people.
Because we live in a society with many cultures and many variations
of health beliefs and practices, assimilation and acculturation are not
always embraced or required.
27
28


Race
Race
 is commonly defined as a set of shared biological
characteristics (i.e. skin colour, bone structure, hair texture), genetic
markers or features of a group of people. However, research has
shown that defining race only on biological characteristics is
unfounded (Saggers, Walter & Gray ). In Australia, the term race is
more commonly used as a social construction of a particular group
of people and is influenced by social determinants such as education
and income level. These social determinants provide different ‘races’
with life chances that may be positive as well as negative (Saggers
et al. 2010).
29 Saggers, S., Walter, M. & Gray, D. (2010). Culture, history and health. In R. Thackrah
(Ed.), Indigenous Australian Health and Cultures (pp. 1–21). Frenchs Forest, NSW: Pearson
Australia.
Prejudice
Prejudice
 is a negative belief or preference that is generalised
about a group and that leads to ‘prejudgment’. Prejudice occurs
either because the person making the judgment does not
understand the particular person or their heritage, or because the
person making the judgment generalises an experience of one
individual from a culture to all members of that group. It may also be
29


referred to as racism. A related concept is xenophobia
—the fear
or dislike of people different from one’s self.
Stereotyping
Stereotyping
 is assuming that all members of a culture or ethnic
group are alike. For example, a nurse may assume that all Italians
verbally express pain loudly or that all Chinese people like rice.
Stereotyping may be based on generalisations founded in research
or it may be unrelated to reality. For example, while some Italians
express pain verbally, not all will. Stereotyping that is unrelated to
reality is frequently an outcome of racism or discrimination. Not all
people of a specific group have the same health beliefs, practices
and values, and it is essential to identify a specific person’s beliefs,
needs and values rather than assume they are the same as those
attributable to the larger group.
Ethnocentrism
Ethnocentrism
 is the belief that one’s own culture or way of life is
better than that of others. Ethnocentric individuals tend to view the
world from their own cultural perspective and may have difficulty
recognising that others view the same world differently. Other
viewpoints are considered to be not only different, but wrong or of
lesser importance.


Discrimination
Discrimination
, the differential treatment of individuals or groups
based on categories such as race, ethnicity, gender, social class or
exceptionality occurs when a person or organisation acts on
prejudice and denies other people one or more of their fundamental
rights.
Culture shock
Culture shock
 is a disorder that occurs in response to transition
from one cultural setting to another. A person’s former behaviour
patterns are ineffective in such a setting and basic cues for social
behaviour are absent (Spector 2013). This phenomenon may occur
when a person moves from one geographical location to another or
when a person migrates to a new country. It may occur when a
person is admitted into a hospital and has to adapt to an unfamiliar
environment. Expressions of culture shock may range from
confusion and anxiety, to silence and immobility, to agitation, rage or
fury.


Heritage consistency
Heritage consistency
 relates to the observance of beliefs and
practices of a person’s traditional cultural system (Spector 2013).
The concept has been expanded in an attempt to study the degree
to which a person’s lifestyle reflects their traditional culture, whether
English, Asian, New Zealander or Indigenous Australian. The values
indicating heritage consistency exist on a continuum and a person
can possess characteristics of both heritage consistency
(traditional
)—observance of the beliefs and practices of one’s
traditional cultural belief system—and evolved heritage
—the
observance of the beliefs and practices of one’s acculturated (or
modern) belief system. The model of heritage consistency has four
overlapping components: culture, ethnicity, religion and socialisation.
Culture
Culture is a complex whole in which each part is related to every
other part. It is learned and the capacity to learn culture is genetic,
but the subject matter is not genetic and must be learned by each
person in their family and social community. Culture also depends on
an underlying social matrix, including knowledge, belief, art, law,
morals and custom. Nursing involves the identification of cultural


traits and the integration of such cultural elements in the delivery of
care.
Ethnicity
Cultural background is a fundamental component of one’s ethnic
background or ethnicity, a group within the social system that claims
to possess variable traits such as a common religion or language.
For example, collectively, Australians speak over 300 languages. In
2016, Mandarin was the most popular language other than English.
It was spoken at home by 2.5% of the population, followed by Arabic
(1.4%), Cantonese (1.2%), Vietnamese (1.2%) and Italian (1.2%)
(ABS ).
30 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2016b). Community Profiles. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au>.
Religion
The third major component of a person’s heritage is religion.
Although the word has many definitions, religion
 may be
considered a system of beliefs, practices and ethical values about
divine or superhuman power or powers worshipped as the creator(s)
and ruler(s) of the universe. In Australia, the proportion of people
belonging to any religion has fallen from 88% in 1966 to 70% in
30


2016, with Christianity remaining the most common religion (52%);
of these, 22.6% identify as Catholic. Islam and Buddhism make up
2.6% and 2.4% respectively of the religions practised in Australia
(ABS 2016b). The practice of religion is revealed in numerous cults,
sects, denominations and churches. Ethnicity and religion are clearly
related and one’s religion quite often is determined by one’s ethnic
group (see Figure 19.2
). Religion gives a person a frame of
reference and a perspective with which to organise information.
Religious teachings about health help to present a meaningful
philosophy and system of practices within a system of social controls
having specific values, norms and ethics. Illness is sometimes seen
as the punishment for the violation of religious codes and morals. It
is not possible to isolate the aspects of culture, religion and ethnicity
that shape a person’s world view. Each is part of the other and all
three are united within the person. See Chapter 42
 for more
information on spirituality.
Figure 19.2


Celebrations of the passage to adulthood are often based on culture
or religion.
Sources: © Penny Tweedie/Alamy; Andrii Shevchuk/123RF.
Socialisation
Socialisation
 is the process of being raised within a culture and
acquiring the characteristics of that group. Education—be it in
primary school, high school or university—is a form of socialisation.
For many people who have been socialised within the boundaries of
a traditional culture or a non-modern culture, developed-world
culture becomes a second cultural identity. Those who immigrate
here from non-Western or developing countries may find
socialisation into the Australian culture an extremely difficult and
painful process. As time passes, many people experience
biculturalism and divided loyalties. In addition, many people who
have been socialised in cultures wherein traditional health care
resources are used may prefer to use this type of care even though
they are residing within a cultural setting with modern health care
resources.


Selected parameters for cultural
nursing care
This section outlines selected phenomena of significance to nursing.
Information about cultural aspects of death and dying are found in
Chapter 44
 and about pain management in Chapter 48
.
Health traditions model
The health traditions model (Spector 2013) is predicated on the
concept of holistic health and describes what people do from a
traditional perspective to prevent illness and maintain, protect and
restore health. Imagine health as a complex, interrelated, threefold
phenomenon; that is, the balance of all aspects of the person—the
body, mind and spirit:
The body includes all physical aspects, such as genetic
inheritance, body chemistry, gender, age, nutrition and physical
condition.
The mind includes cognitive processes, such as thoughts,
memories and knowledge of such emotional processes as
feelings, defences and self-esteem.


The spiritual facet includes both positive and negative learned
spiritual practices and teachings, dreams, symbols, stories,
protecting forces and metaphysical or native forces.
These aspects are in constant flux and change over time, yet each
is completely related to the other and also related to the context of
the person. The context includes the person’s family, culture, work,
community, history and environment (Spector 2013).
The health traditions model (see Table 19.1
) consists of nine
interrelated facets, represented by the following:
traditional methods of maintaining health—physical, mental
and spiritual—include following a proper diet and wearing proper
clothing, concentrating and using the mind and practising one’s
religion
traditional methods of protecting health—physical, mental
and spiritual—include wearing protective objects, such as
amulets, avoiding people who may cause illness or trouble, and
placing religious objects in the home
traditional methods of restoring health—physical, mental and
spiritual—include the use of herbal remedies, exorcism and
healing rituals.
Table 19.1 The nine interrelated facets of health (physical,
mental and spiritual) and personal methods of maintaining
health, protecting health and restoring health


Source: R. E. Spector (2013). Cultural Diversity in Health and Illness (8th ed.). Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice
Hall, p. 93. © 2013. Adapted with permission.
Symbolic examples
Symbolic, health-related images may be used to maintain, protect or
restore physical, mental or spiritual health by people of different
heritages:
‘Thousand-year-old’ eggs from China represent traditional foods
that may be eaten daily to maintain physical health.
The enjoyment of nature, the natural environment, may be a
universal way of maintaining mental health.
The Islamic prayer from East Jerusalem represents prayer, a
way of maintaining spiritual health.
Red string from the Tomb of Rachel in Bethlehem, Israel, may be
worn to protect physical health.
The eye from Cuba represents the plethora of eye-related
objects that may be worn or hung in the home to protect the
mental health of people by shielding them from the envy and bad
wishes of others.
The thunderbird from the Hopi nation may be worn for spiritual
protection and good luck.
The herbal remedy from Africa represents aromatic plants that
may be used by people from all ethnocultural traditional
backgrounds as one method of restoring physical health.
Tiger balm from Singapore represents substances that are used
in massage therapy as a way of restoring mental health.


Rosary beads from Italy symbolise prayer and meditation
methods used in the spiritual restoration of health.
The snake in Indigenous cultures is a creator being and is a
symbol of health and healing.
There are an infinite number of examples one could present. A
major aspect of conducting the cultural assessment of a person is to
determine what items are used by a specific person and their
meaning to the person.
Health beliefs and practices
Three views of health beliefs include spiritual, scientific and holistic.
In the spiritual health
 belief view, health and illness are
controlled by supernatural forces. The person may believe that
illness is the result of ‘being bad’ or opposing God’s will.
Getting well is also viewed as dependent on God’s will. The person
may make statements such as ‘If it is God’s will, I will recover’ or
‘What did I do wrong to be punished with cancer?’. Some cultures
believe that magic can cause illness. A sorcerer or witch may put a
spell or hex on the person. Some people view illness as possession
by an evil spirit. Although these beliefs are not supported by
empirical evidence, people who believe that such things can cause
illness may in fact become ill as a result. Such illnesses may require
alternative treatments in addition to scientific treatments. For
example, a man who experiences gastric distress, headaches and


hypertension after being told that a spell has been placed on him
may recover only if the spell is removed by the culture’s healer.
The scientific
 or biomedical health belief
 is based on the
belief that life and life processes are controlled by physical and
biochemical processes that can be manipulated by humans. The
person with this view will believe that illness is caused by germs,
viruses, bacteria or a breakdown of the human machine, the body.
This person will expect a pill or treatment or surgery to cure health
problems.
The holistic health belief
 holds that the forces of nature must be
maintained in balance or harmony. Human life is one aspect of
nature that must be in harmony with the rest of nature. When the
natural balance or harmony is disturbed, illness results.
The Indigenous Australian definition of health incorporates holistic
health beliefs with clear evidence to show that the social, cultural
and spiritual determinants of health add to an individual’s ill health
(NACCHO
). This includes such factors as their early life
experiences, social and economic position in society, exposure to
stress, educational attainment and exclusion from participation in
society, which all have a powerful influence on their health
throughout their life. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people see
health as a whole-of-life view that contributes to the total wellbeing
of their community, not only the individual. This view also includes
the concept of life–death–life (Australian Indigenous
HealthInfoNet
).
31
32


31 National Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (NACCHO) (2013). Healthy
Futures 2013–2030: NACCHO 10 Point Plan. Canberra: NACCHO.
32 Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet (2018). Summary of Australian Indigenous Health.
Retrieved from <https://healthinfonet.ecu.edu.au>.
The concept of yin and yang in the Chinese culture and the hot–cold
theory of illness in many Spanish cultures are examples of holistic
health beliefs. When a Chinese person has a yin illness or a ‘cold’
illness, such as cancer, the treatment may include a yang or ‘hot’
food (e.g. hot tea).
What is considered hot or cold varies considerably across cultures.
In many cultures, the mother who has just delivered a baby should
be offered warm or hot foods and kept warm with blankets because
childbirth is seen as a ‘cold’ condition. Conventional scientific thought
recommends cooling the body to reduce a fever. The doctor may
order liquids for the person and cool compresses to be applied to
the forehead, the axillae or the groin. Many cultures believe that the
best way to treat a fever is to increase elimination of toxins through
sweat baths. People from these cultures may want to cover up with
several blankets, take hot baths and drink hot beverages. The nurse
must keep in mind that a treatment strategy that is consistent with
the person’s beliefs may have a better chance of being successful.
Sociocultural forces, such as politics, economics, geography, religion
and the predominant health care system, influence the person’s
health status and health care behaviour. For example, people who
have limited access to scientific health care may turn to traditional


medicine or healing. Traditional healing
 is defined as those
beliefs and practices relating to illness prevention and healing that
derive from cultural traditions rather than from modern medicine’s
scientific base. Many people have special teas or ‘cures’ (such as
chicken soup) used by older family members to prevent or treat
colds, fevers, indigestion and other common health problems.
Western medicine tends to concentrate on the physical aspect of
health, including treatment of disease symptoms, infections, and
injury. It uses a science-based approach towards treatment and
prevention from an evidence-based perspective. Traditional healing
practices are more centred on a holistic approach that looks at the
individual and their community.
Healing is not just physical: it’s mental, emotional and spiritual as well. For Indigenous
people a positive outlook and in-look was considered necessary to be healthy: if you feel
good inside regardless of your health, it will help you in any medical problems. (Shahid et
al.
, cited in Hampton & Toombs 2013)
33 Shahid, S., Finn, L., Bessarab, D. & Thompson, S. C. (2011). ‘Nowhere to room ...
nobody told them’: Logistical and cultural impediments to Aboriginal peoples’ participation
in cancer treatment. Australian Health Review, 35, 235–241 as cited in Hampton &
Toombs (Eds) (2013), Indigenous Australians and Health: The Wombat in the Room.
Melbourne: Oxford University Press.
Indigenous Australian people from all areas have developed their
own approaches to illness, medicine and healing, utilising knowledge
developed over many generations as well as traditional or
metaphysical approaches. Clever Men (aka ‘medicine men’, e.g.
Ngangkari among the Anangu) deliver both types of treatment, often
associated with ritual, such as herbal mixtures and substances.
33


Many of the substances used are beneficial and based in long-held
knowledge of their effects.
Why do individuals use traditional healing methods? Traditional
healing is thought to be more humanistic than biomedical health
care. The consultation and treatment often take place in the
community of the recipient, frequently in the home of the healer. It
may be less expensive than scientific or biomedical care. The healer
often prepares the treatments, such as herbs to be ingested,
poultices to be applied or charms or amulets to be worn. A frequent
component of treatment is some ritual practice on the part of the
healer or the recipient to cause healing to occur. Because traditional
healing is more culturally based, it is often more comfortable and
less frightening for the person. Traditional healing from an Australian
Indigenous perspective could include ‘bush’ medicines, traditional
foods, a focus on family ties and links to ‘country’, or practices
related to loss and grief, such as Sorry Business.
Clinical consideration
Treatments once considered to be alternative
treatments, including acupuncture, therapeutic
touch, herbal remedies and massage, are now
being investigated for their therapeutic effect.
The Australian Traditional Medicine Society
provides up-to-date information on this line of
research.


It is important for the nurse to obtain information about traditional or
family healing practices that may have been used before or while the
person used Western medical treatment. Often people are reluctant
to disclose the use of home remedies with health care professionals
for fear of being laughed at or rebuked. von Conrady and Bonny
report that approximately two-thirds of Australian adults use some
form of complementary and alternative medicine and that 60%
believe it aids their wellbeing (see also Chapter 20
).
34 von Conrady, D. M. & Bonney, A. (2017). Patterns of complementary and alternative
medicine use and health literacy in general practice patients in urban and regional Australia.
Australian Family Physician, 46(5), 316–320.
Family patterns
In Western society, the family is the basic unit of society. Cultural
values can determine communication within the family group, the
norm for family size and the roles of specific family members. In
some families, the man is considered the provider and decision
maker. The woman may need to consult the male before making
decisions about her medical treatment or the treatment of her
children. Some families are matriarchal; that is, the mother or
grandmother is viewed as the leader of the family and is usually the
decision maker. Many families do not follow ‘traditional’
34


wife/husband/children configurations, with some families being made
up of a rich variety of partners, adopted children, same-sex parents,
step-children and a host of other configurations. The nurse needs to
identify who has the ‘authority’ to make decisions in a person’s
family. If the decision maker is someone other than the patient, the
nurse needs to include that person in health care discussions.
The value placed on children and older adults within a society is
culturally derived. In some cultures, children are not disciplined by
smacking or other forms of physical punishment. Rather, children
are allowed to interact with their environment while caregivers
provide subtle direction to prevent harm or injury. In other cultures,
older adults are considered the holders of the culture’s wisdom and
are therefore highly respected. In the Indigenous Australian culture,
an older adult who has achieved the status of holder of the culture’s
wisdom is referred to as an ‘Elder’. Responsibility for caring for older
relatives is also determined by cultural practices. In some cultures,
older relatives who cannot live independently live with a married son
or daughter and family.
Cultural gender-role behaviour may also affect nurse– person
interactions. In some cultures, men dominate and women have little
status. Men from these cultures may not accept advice from a
female nurse or doctor but will be receptive to the same advice
given by a male doctor, family member or nurse. Some cultures
have a prevailing concept of machismo, or male superiority. The
positive aspects of machismo require that the adult man provide for


and protect his family, including extended family members. The
woman is expected to maintain the home and raise the children.
Cultural family values may also dictate the extent of the family’s
involvement in the hospitalised person’s care. In some cultures, only
the nuclear and the extended family will want to visit for long periods
and participate in care. In other cultures, the entire community may
want to visit and participate in the person’s care. This can cause
concern in health care facilities that have strict visiting policies. The
nurse should evaluate the positive benefits of family participation in
the person’s care and modify visiting policies as appropriate.
Cultures that value the needs of the extended family as much as
those of the individual may believe that personal and family
information must stay within the family. For cultural reasons, some
cultural groups are reluctant to disclose family information to
outsiders, including health care professionals. This scenario can
present difficulties for health care professionals when conducting
assessment of the individual. For example, in Indigenous Australian
culture, men’s and women’s business are kept very separate; in
Asian culture, mental health illness is often left untreated due to the
social stigma and family shame.
Communication style
Communication and culture are closely interconnected. Through
communication, the culture is transmitted from one generation to the


next and knowledge about the culture is transmitted within the group
and to those outside the group. Communicating effectively with
people of various ethnic and cultural backgrounds is critical to
providing culturally competent nursing care. There are cultural
variations in both verbal and non-verbal communication.
Verbal communication
The most obvious cultural difference is in verbal communication:
vocabulary, grammatical structure, voice qualities, intonation,
rhythm, speed, pronunciation and silence. In Australia, the dominant
language is English; however, immigrant groups who speak English
still encounter language differences because English words can
have different meanings in different English-speaking cultures. For
example, in New Zealand, a container to keep items cold is referred
to as a chilly bin; in Australia, it is referred to as an esky. Spanish is
spoken by people in several regions of the world: Spain, South
America, Central America, Mexico, the Caribbean and the
Philippines, for example. Nevertheless, each cultural group that
speaks Spanish may use different vocabulary, apply rules of
grammar differently and use different phonology so that often two
people of different Latino cultures, speaking Spanish together, may
not completely understand each other.
Initiating verbal communication may be influenced by cultural values.
While being busy is not an excuse for nurse-centric care, the busy
nurse may need to complete nursing admission assessments
quickly. The person, however, may be offended when the nurse


immediately asks personal questions. In most cultures, social
courtesies should be established before business or personal topics
are discussed. Discussing general topics can convey that the nurse
is interested and has time for the person. This enables the nurse to
develop a rapport with the person before progressing to discussion
that is more personal. Refer to Chapter 27
 for additional
information on communication.
Verbal communication becomes even more difficult when an
interaction involves people who speak different languages. Both
people seeking health care and health professionals experience
frustration when they are unable to communicate verbally with each
other. Techniques for therapeutic communication with people who
have different cultural and ethnic backgrounds are shown in the
following ‘Practice guidelines
’.
For the person whose language is not the same as that of the health
care provider, an intermediary may be necessary. A translator
converts written material (such as health education pamphlets) from
one language into another. An interpreter
 ensures accurate
communication between two people who have different language
needs. The Department of Immigration and Citizenship  provides a
translating and interpreting service to most Australians, facilitating
access to vital information. A professional interpreter is bound by the
Australian Institute of Interpreters and Translators Code of Ethics.
The National Accreditation Authority for Translators and Interpreters
(NAATI) is the national standards and accreditation body funded by
the Australian government and state and territory governments to
35


aid with language translation. When using interpreters and
translators, it is advisable to use those accredited by NAATI to
ensure they have the necessary skills and credentials (Queensland
Health ). Asking a family member or other non-professional to
interpret can create difficulties. Cultural rules often dictate who can
discuss what with whom. Guidelines for using an interpreter are
shown in the following ‘Practice guidelines
’.
35 Department of Immigration and Citizenship (2013). Fact Sheet 91—Translating and
Interpreting Service (TIS National). Canberra: Commonwealth of Australia.
36 Queensland Health (2012). Interpreter Services. Retrieved from <www.health. qld.gov.au>.
Practice guidelines
Verbal communication with people from different cultural
and ethnic backgrounds
Consult communication guides and health service tools for
effective communication.
Avoid slang words, medical terminology, jargon and
abbreviations.
Augment spoken conversation with gestures or pictures to
increase the person’s understanding.
Speak slowly, in a respectful manner and at a normal
volume. Speaking loudly does not help the person
understand and may be offensive.
Frequently validate the person’s understanding of what is
being communicated. Do not automatically interpret a
person’s smiling and nodding to mean that they
36


understand; the person may only be trying to please the
nurse and not understand what is being said.
Practice guidelines
Using an interpreter
Avoid asking a member of the person’s family, especially a
child or spouse, to act as interpreter. The person, not
wishing family members to know about their problem, may
not provide complete or accurate information.
Be aware of gender and age differences; it is preferable to
use an interpreter of the same gender as the person to
avoid embarrassment and cultural customs.
Avoid an interpreter who is politically or socially
incompatible with the person. For example, a Bosnian
Serb may not be the best interpreter for a Muslim, even if
they speak the language.
Address the questions to the person, not to the
interpreter.
Ask the interpreter to translate as closely as possible the
words used by the nurse.
Speak slowly and distinctly. Do not use idiomatic
expressions such as, ‘Does it swell like a grapefruit?’ or ‘Is
the pain stabbing like a knife?’.
Observe the facial expressions and body language that
the person assumes when listening and talking to the
interpreter.


Become aware of the individual expressions and colloquial
words used in specific regions and acknowledge them
when using interpreting services.
When caring for Indigenous Australians (where English may be their
third or fourth language), nurses need to work in partnership with
Indigenous Australian health workers who can assist with
appropriate communication during assessment, identify culturally
appropriate interventions and provide essential insight regarding the
person, family and community (Hooper, Thomas & Clarke ). The
New South Wales Department of Health’s  Communicating
Positively guide is a useful tool for supporting professionals in
appropriate communication with Indigenous Australians.
37 Hooper, K., Thomas, Y. & Clarke, M. (2007). Health professional partnerships and their
impact on Aboriginal health: An occupational therapist’s and Aboriginal health worker’s
perspective. Australian Journal of Rural Health, 15, 46–51.
38 New South Wales Department of Health (2004). Communicating Positively: A Guide to
Appropriate Aboriginal Terminology. Sydney: NSW Government.
Nurses and other health care providers must remember that people
who have used English comfortably for years in social and business
communication may revert back to their primary language when they
are ill or distressed. It is important for the nurse to promote
behaviours to facilitate verbal communication, such as taking more
time, providing an environment where the person is comfortable and
feels safe, and reassure the person that this is normal.
37
38


Clinical consideration
Nurses who speak a second language may be
asked to interpret for others. Nursing schools
and health care facilities may not permit nursing
students to interpret for consent for a procedure
because limited knowledge about the procedure
may lead the student to give inaccurate
information. Check the health care facility’s
policy before agreeing to interpret for health
care staff.
Non-verbal communication
To communicate effectively with culturally diverse people, the nurse
needs to be aware of two aspects of non-verbal communication
behaviours: what non-verbal behaviours mean to the person and
what specific non-verbal behaviours mean in the person’s culture.
Before assigning meaning to non-verbal behaviour, the nurse must
consider the possibility that the behaviour may have a different
meaning for the person and their family. To provide safe and
effective care, nurses who work with specific cultural groups should
learn more about cultural behaviour and communication patterns
within these cultures.


Non-verbal communication can include the use of silence, touch, eye
movement, facial expressions and body posture. Some cultures are
quite comfortable with long periods of silence whereas others
consider it appropriate to speak before the other person has finished
talking. Many people value silence and view it as essential to
understanding a person’s needs or use silence to preserve privacy.
Some cultures view silence as a sign of respect whereas to other
people, silence may indicate agreement.
Touching involves learned behaviours that can have both positive
and negative meanings. In the Australian culture, a firm handshake
is a recognised form of greeting that conveys character and
strength. In some European cultures, greetings may include a kiss
on one or both cheeks. In some societies, touch is considered
magical and, because of the belief that the soul can leave the body
on physical contact, casual touching is forbidden. In some Middle
Eastern cultures, it is not considered appropriate for men and
women to touch (e.g. shake hands) as a form of greeting. In
addition, in some Asian cultures (e.g. people from India, Sri Lanka,
Thailand and Laos), some older adults are permitted to touch the
head of others and children are never patted on the head. Nurses
should be mindful of non-verbal communication styles used in
different cultures.
Cultures dictate what forms of touch are appropriate for individuals
of the same and opposite gender. In many cultures, for example, a
kiss is not appropriate for a public greeting between people of the
opposite sex, even those who are family members; however, a kiss


on the cheek is acceptable as a greeting between individuals of the
same sex. The nurse should watch interaction between people
requiring health care and their families for cues to the appropriate
degree of touch in that culture. The nurse can also assess the
person’s response to touch when providing nursing care; for
example, by noting the person’s reaction to the physical examination
and other nursing care.
Facial expression can also vary between cultures and convey a
meaning opposite to what is felt or understood. Eye movement
during communication has cultural foundations. In some Western
cultures, direct eye contact is regarded as important and generally
shows that the other is attentive and listening. It conveys self-
confidence, openness, interest and honesty. Lack of eye contact
may be interpreted as secretiveness, shyness, guilt, lack of interest
or even a sign of mental illness. However, other cultures may view
eye contact as impolite or an invasion of privacy. In the Hmong
culture, continuous direct eye contact is considered rude but
intermittent eye contact is acceptable. Additionally, within some
Indigenous Australian communities (and other cultural groups), eye
contact is considered disrespectful and therefore the nurse should
not misinterpret the character of the person who avoids eye contact.
Nurses should carefully assess the cultural norms in relation to eye
contact before avoiding direct eye contact with a patient or their
relatives.
Body posture and hand gestures are also culturally learned. For
example, the ‘V’ sign means victory in some cultures but is an


offensive gesture in other cultures. Tapping the index finger on one’s
temple may mean someone is intelligent in Australia but crazy in The
Netherlands.
Communication is an essential part of establishing a relationship with
a person and their family. It is also important for developing effective
working relationships with health care colleagues. To enhance their
practice, nurses can observe the communication patterns of people
and be aware of their own communication behaviours.
Space orientation
Space is a relative concept that includes the individual, the body, the
surrounding environment and objects within that environment. The
relationship between the individual’s own body and objects and
people within space is learned and is influenced by culture. For
example, in nomadic societies, space is not owned; it is occupied
temporarily until the tribe moves on. In Western societies, people
tend to be more territorial, as reflected in phrases such as ‘This is
my space’ or ‘Get out of my space’. In Western cultures, spatial
distances are defined as the intimate space, the personal space and
the social and public spaces (see Chapter 27
). The size of these
areas may vary with the specific culture. Nurses move through all
four spaces as they provide care for people. The nurse needs to be
aware of the person’s response to movement towards them. The
person may physically withdraw or back away if the nurse is
perceived as being too close. The nurse will need to explain to the


person why there is a need to be close. To assess the lungs with a
stethoscope, for example, the nurse needs to move into the
person’s intimate space. The nurse should first explain the
procedure and await consent to continue.
People who reside in long-term care facilities or who are hospitalised
for an extended time may want to personalise their space. They may
want to arrange their room differently or control the placement of
objects on their bedside cabinet or overway table. The nurse should
be responsive to the person’s needs to have some control over their
space. When there are no medical contraindications, people should
be permitted and encouraged to have objects of personal
significance. Having personal and cultural items in one’s
environment can increase self-esteem by promoting not only one’s
individuality but also one’s cultural identity.
Time orientation
Time orientation refers to an individual’s focus on the past, the
present or the future. Most cultures include all three time
orientations but one orientation is likely to dominate. The Australian
focus on time tends to be directed to the future, emphasising time
and schedules. Nursing students know what times they must be in
lectures and tutorials. They know what courses they will take in
future semesters. Australians often plan for next week, their holidays
or their retirement. Other cultures may have a different concept of
time. For example, ‘most (Indigenous Australian) people live for


today. It could be hypothesised that the “here and now” approach to
survival was all that was relevant traditionally (in hunter–gatherer
times) and the future as a “material” or liveable concept was more or
less irrelevant’ (Janca & Bullen , p. S41).
39 Janca, A. & Bullen, C. (2003). Aboriginal concept of time and its mental health implications.
Australasian Psychiatry, 11, S40–S44.
The culture of nursing and health care values time. Appointments
are scheduled and treatments are prescribed with time parameters
(e.g. changing a dressing once a day). Medication orders include
how often the medicine is to be taken and when (e.g. digoxin 0.25
mg, once a day, in the morning). Nurses need to be aware of the
meaning of time for individuals. When caring for people who are
‘present oriented’, it is important to avoid fixed schedules. The nurse
can offer a time range for activities and treatments. For example,
instead of educating the person to take digoxin every day at 10
a.m., the nurse might tell the person to take it every day in the
morning or every day after getting out of bed.
Nutritional patterns
Most cultures have staple foods that are plentiful or readily
accessible in the environment. For example, the staple food of many
Asian countries is rice; of Italians, pasta; and of Eastern Europeans,
wheat. Even people who have been in Australia for several
39


generations often continue to eat the staple foods of their cultural
homeland.
The way in which staple foods are prepared also varies. For
example, some Asian cultures prefer steamed rice; others prefer
boiled rice. Southern Asians from India prepare unleavened bread
from wheat flour rather than the leavened bread of Australians.
Food-related cultural behaviours can include whether to breastfeed
or bottle-feed infants and when to introduce solid foods to them.
Food can also be considered part of the remedy for illness. Foods
classified as ‘hot’ foods or foods that are hot in temperature may be
used to treat illnesses that are classified as ‘cold’ illnesses. For
example, corn meal (a ‘hot’ food) may be used to treat arthritis (a
‘cold’ illness). Each culture group defines what it considers to be hot
and cold entities.
Religious practice associated with specific cultures also affects diet.
Some Catholics avoid meat on certain days, such as Ash
Wednesday and Good Friday, and some Protestant faiths prohibit
meat, tea, coffee and alcohol. Both Orthodox Judaism and Islam
prohibit the ingestion of pork or pork products. Orthodox Jews
observe kosher customs, eating certain foods only if they have been
inspected by a rabbi and prepared according to dietary laws. For
example, the eating of milk products and meat products at the same
meal is prohibited. Some Buddhists, Hindus and Sikhs are strict
vegetarians. The nurse must be sensitive to such religious dietary


practices and incorporate appropriate interventions and actions into
their care.


Indigenous Australian
health issues
Understanding Indigenous
Australian cultural competence
in relation to nursing care
Indigenous Australian communities are made up of many different
nations, tribes and groups, and represent a diverse range of cultural
expression. As a result, a ‘one size fits all’ approach is not suitable
when working with, treating or addressing the health needs of
Indigenous Australians. Durey  suggests that Indigenous Australian
people are more likely to access providers where communication is
respectful and providers have some understanding of Indigenous
Australian culture, build good relationships and have Indigenous
Australian health workers as a part of the health care team. This
suggests that there is a link between health practitioner behaviours,
skill and attitudes to patient outcomes. Internationally, there has
been reported research suggesting that cultural competence training
does lead to positive changes in health outcomes (D’Silva et al.
;
Cook et al.
).
40
41
42


40 Durey, A. (2010). Reducing racism in Aboriginal health care in Australia: Where does
culture education fit in? Australia and New Zealand Journal or Public Health, 34(S1), 87–92.
41 D’Silva, J., Schillo, B., Sandman, N., Leonard, T. & Boyle, R. (2011). Evaluation of a tailored
approach for tobacco dependence treatment for American Indians. American Journal of
Health Promotion, 25(5 Suppl), 66–69.
42 Cook, A., Grothaus, C., Gutierrez, C., Kehoe, K. & Valentin, M. (2010). Closing the gap:
Disparity in Native Hawaiian cardiac care. Hawai‘i Medical Journal, 69(5 Suppl 2), 7–10.
One model in Indigenous Australian cultural competence specific to
nursing practice has suggested a non-linear progressive journey that
involves nurses making a connection with Indigenous Australian
culture and actively seeking their truth, stimulating a change in
individual world views (Biles et al.
). Indeed, seeking out or asking
about an Indigenous person’s ‘truth’ should be considered a priority
for health care providers in order to facilitate culturally competent
care. Other models suggest a linear journey that incorporates an
understanding of culture, Indigenous Australian culture and
professional reflexivity, leading to cross-cultural and professional
skills in cultural competence. The Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander Health Curriculum Framework (Commonwealth of
Australia ) refers to cultural competence more broadly as cultural
capabilities encompassing a variety of skills required to build a
culturally responsive workforce.
43 Biles, J., Coyle, J., Bernoth, M. & Hill, B. (2016). I am looking for my truth: A hermeneutic
phenomenological study focusing on undergraduate nursing students’ journeys in Indigenous
Australian cultural competence. Journal of Australian Indigenous Issues, 19(1–2), 161–175.
43
44


44 Commonwealth of Australia (2014). Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Curriculum
Framework. Canberra: Commonwealth of Australia.
A little history: how historical
background, legislation,
government policies and practices
have impacted on Indigenous
Australian identity, culture and
health
For over 60 000 years or more (Behrendt
), Indigenous people
have populated the land and islands on and about what is now
known as Australia. For these people and their descendants, little
had changed over this period. However, during the sixteenth and
seventeenth centuries, European people came into contact with
Indigenous Australians and eventually settled and permanently
colonised the area around what is now Sydney, New South Wales,
before Europeans spread out across the continent and islands of
Australia. This initiated a profound period of rapid change for
Indigenous Australian people and has resulted in a dramatic
influence on the health, social, political and cultural aspects of
Indigenous Australian people’s lives.
45


45 Behrendt, L. (2012). Indigenous Australia for Dummies. Milton: Wiley Publishing.
From the very first contact between Europeans and Indigenous
Australian people, there has existed a sense of mistrust and
uncertainty, even though many individuals have acted and
encountered each other with good grace and the best of intentions.
Seldom have words such as ‘intervention’ and ‘protection’ resulted in
positive outcomes for Indigenous Australians and many of the
colonising power’s actions have resulted in devastating personal and
cultural consequences (see Box 19.3
 Redfern speech).
BO X
19.3 Redfern speech
The following excerpt is from the then Prime Minister Paul
Keating’s 1992 Redfern speech.
... in truth, we cannot confidently say that we have succeeded as we would like
to have succeeded ... Redfern is a good place to contemplate these things. Just
a mile or two from the place where the first European settlers landed, in too
many ways it tells us that their failure to bring much more than devastation and
demoralisation to Aboriginal Australia continues to be our failure ... We simply
cannot sweep injustice aside. Even if our own conscience allowed us to, I am
sure, that in due course, the world and the people of our region would not ...
There should be no mistake about this—our success in resolving these issues
will have a significant bearing on our standing in the world ... However intractable
as the problems seem, we cannot resign ourselves to failure ... the starting point
might be to recognise that the problem starts with us non-Aboriginal Australians.


It begins, I think with that act of recognition. Recognition that it was we who did
the dispossessing. We took the traditional lands and smashed the traditional way
of life. We brought the diseases. The alcohol. We committed the murders. We
took the children from their mothers. We practised discrimination and exclusion.
It was our ignorance and our prejudice. And our failure to imagine these things
being done to us. With some noble exceptions, we failed to make the most basic
human response and enter into their hearts and minds. We failed to ask—how
would I feel if this were done to me? As a consequence, we failed to see that
what we were doing degraded all of us ... For all this, I do not believe that the
Report should fill us with guilt. Down the years, there has been no shortage of
guilt, but it has not produced the responses we need. Guilt is not a very
constructive emotion. I think what we need to do is open our hearts a bit. All of us
... Where Aboriginal Australians have been included in the life of Australia they
have made remarkable contributions. Economic contributions, particularly in the
pastoral and agricultural industry. They are there in the frontier and exploration
history of Australia. They are there in the wars. In sport to an extraordinary
degree. In literature and art and music. In all these things they have shaped our
knowledge of this continent and of ourselves. They have shaped our identity ...
We should never forget—they have helped build this nation.
Source: P. Keating
. Transcript: Redfern speech. Retrieved from <https://antar.org.au/sites/
default/files/paul_keating_speech_transcript.pdf>.
46 Keating, P. (1992). Transcript: Redfern speech (Year for the World’s Indigenous People).
Delivered in Redfern Park by Prime Minister Paul Keating, 10th December 1992. Retrieved
from <https://antar.org.au>.
Expansion over the continent brought European settlers into conflict
with resident Indigenous Australian peoples, resulting in sometimes
violent conflict, brutality, exploitation, marginalisation and the
46


subsequent forced removal of children from their families. The
removal of children (known as the Stolen Generations) was an
Australian government policy until 1969 and is still regarded as one
of the most devastating ‘interventions’, with consequences from this
policy still being felt by Indigenous Australians today.
Other factors also influence a history of mistrust and ill will. These
include failure of the European settlers to recognise Indigenous
occupation of the land prior to European settlement, a lack of legal
power, underrepresentation in government positions and denial of
the right to vote prior to 1962 (1965 in Queensland), with the
generally remote and isolated locations of many Indigenous
communities and the variety of tribal and cultural groups
compounding many attempts to bring a united Indigenous voice to
the attention of the federal and state governments.
This said, progress has been made on many fronts. Governments
and non-government organisations are building more effective
collaborative relationships with Indigenous Australians and the
positive outcome of the Australian Human Rights Commission report
entitled Bringing Them Home in May 1997 laid the groundwork for
the New South Wales Premier, Bob Carr, to issue a formal apology
in 1997. In his speech, Bob Carr stated that the New South Wales
government ‘apologises unreservedly to the Aboriginal people of
Australia for the systematic separation of generations of Aboriginal
children from their parents, families and communities’.


In February 2008, the then Prime Minister Kevin Rudd issued a
formal apology to all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples on
behalf of the Commonwealth government. Things have changed and
many improvements are evident, but it is acknowledged that past
government legislation and practices forced on Indigenous
Australians have contributed to their social/cultural/health/political
and economic disadvantage, with many of these impacts still being
felt in Indigenous communities and by individual Indigenous
Australians today.
Figure 19.3
 shows the flags that represent the Australian
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations.
Figure 19.3


The Aboriginal flag and the Torres Strait Island flag.
Sources: Peter Etchells/123RF; Alan Cotton/123RF.
The context of Indigenous
Australian health and nursing
The history and the background of European interaction with
Indigenous Australians and the past and more recent federal and
state government interventions have all impacted on the context or
lens through which nurses should view their care and treatment
interactions with Indigenous Australian people.
In addition to the historical context, two key issues should be
considered when supporting the health and wellbeing of Indigenous
Australians. These are a recognition of Indigenous Australians’
connection to their land or ‘country’ and the impact of being
separated from either the traditional lands or family during episodes
of ill health. Health services that are not accessible (not on
traditional lands) or user-friendly (i.e. not always culturally
appropriate) for Indigenous Australians place them at a
disadvantage from the outset. These factors alone will increase
feelings of marginalisation, isolation, insecurity and fear, and
approaching an Indigenous Australian’s health concerns needs to be
addressed in light of these contextual issues.


There are a number of factors that may positively impact on
improving health services for Indigenous Australians, including
offering more accessible funding models to allow Indigenous
Australians to access health services, offering more health services
in regional and remote locations, employing culturally competent
non-Indigenous health care staff, providing culturally appropriate
health educational or health promotional information, and, where
possible, recruiting and employing Indigenous Australian health care
staff.
Reflecting on our own values
and beliefs in respect to
Indigenous Australian culture
Achieving cultural competence is a lifelong journey and may be
challenging. We are all influenced by our own unique world views
formed, for example, during our upbringing, in childhood, at school,
while reading literature or through the influence of the visual media
and social media. These influences may not all have been positive,
and it is suggested that care needs to be taken when approaching
any cultural group other than our own so that we can check and
reflect upon the nature of our insight or views and ensure that our
