views do not impact on the care we provide.


Here, it is suggested that prior to engaging in clinical care it is useful
to stop and reflect on what may have contributed to your own
perspectives or views about, in this case, Indigenous Australians
(see Box 19.4
).
BO X
19.4 Questions to ask about views
of Indigenous Australians
Ask yourself these questions:
What do I know about Indigenous Australian culture?
What engagement or interaction have I had with
Indigenous Australian people?
Where have I met Indigenous Australians? How did I feel?
What was the context of the meeting?
What do my friends, family, the media and fellow students
say about Indigenous Australians?
Are there gaps in my knowledge of Indigenous Australian
culture?
Where has my knowledge of Indigenous Australian culture
come from?
Is there more I need to learn or are there questions I
should seek answers to?
Have I explored my biases?


Do I have all the more relevant information? Who has
provided this information? Can I trust the source?
How would I feel about the history, treatment and others’
perceptions from the perspective of an Indigenous
Australian?
The realities of contemporary
Indigenous Australian health
The practices and interactions by government agencies of the past
have had negative consequences for Indigenous Australians. As
such, Indigenous Australians remain over-represented in areas such
as the welfare system, criminal and juvenile justice systems, child
protection system and homelessness. These challenges can be
compounded by lower levels of literacy and numeracy, higher levels
of unemployment and the impact of a range of debilitating and
damaging health consequences. However, within Indigenous
Australian communities, there is evidence of strength in areas such
as higher rates of childhood immunisation than for non-Indigenous
people, strong links with extended family and skills in building
community development and social capacity building, to name just a
few.


Indigenous Australian population profile
In 2018, the percentage of Indigenous Australians was
approximately 3.1% (fewer than the 2016 Census data of 3.3%) of
the total population of Australia. However, percentages differ in
regional and remote communities and larger city populations, with
37% of Indigenous Australians living in major cities (Australian
Indigenous HealthInfoNet 2018). The Indigenous Australian
population is much younger overall than the non-Indigenous
population and in 2018, more than 33% of Indigenous Australians
were under the age of 15. Indigenous Australians are also
underrepresented in the aged community, with only 4% of
Indigenous Australians being over 65 years of age compared with
14% of non-Indigenous Australians (Australian Indigenous
HealthInfoNet 2018).
Indigenous Australians are much more likely than non-Indigenous
Australians to die before they reach old age. In general, Indigenous
Australian children born between 2010 and 2012 could expect to live
to an age, on average, 10 years younger than a non-Indigenous
Australian. The leading causes of death of Indigenous Australians
are cardiovascular disease, cancer and injury (including vehicle
accidents and self-harm) (Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet
2018).
Mental and emotional health issues


The impact and consequence of historical interactions and
encounters has resulted in a greater burden of mental health
concerns and issues for Indigenous Australians, with issues of grief,
loss and trauma continuing to impact on many Indigenous
Australians, their families and communities. Underlying
socioeconomic factors, past issues of mistrusting governments, the
history of forced removal and long-held cultural coping strategies
have meant that grief and loss issues have become cyclical and
impact on new generational groups.
Adult Indigenous Australians report 2.7 times the level of anxiety and
emotional distress as non-Indigenous Australians, and around 7 in
10 Indigenous Australians report significant stressors impacting on
their lives (Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet 2018). As well, in
2017, the death rate for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
living in New South Wales, Queensland, Western Australia, South
Australia and the Northern Territory was twice the rate reported for
non-Indigenous people (Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet 2018).
Stressors cited were death of a family member or friend with a
serious illness, trouble with the police, inability to find work, alcohol
or drug problems, and mental illness issues.
Nurses and other health professionals need to increase their
awareness and understanding of the ongoing impact of these issues
and learn to work more effectively with Indigenous Australians,
families and communities in a sensitive and respectful manner.
Cardiac health


Indigenous Australians are around 1.2 times more likely than other
Australians to be affected by heart disease and suffer a heart attack
(Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet 2018). They are seven times
more likely to be hospitalised for rheumatic heart disease or
rheumatic fever. They are 10.5 times more likely to die from
coronary heart disease and 1.5 times more likely to have high blood
pressure than non-Indigenous Australians (Heart Research
Institute ). As much of the burden of disease for cardiovascular
health is preventable, risk factors such as smoking, high blood
cholesterol, decreased physical activity, diabetes, poor nutrition and,
as a result, being overweight and obese, could all be addressed with
lifestyle and behavioural changes.
47 Heart Research Institute (2016). Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People. Retrieved
from <www.hri.org.au>.
Infant mortality
Between 1998 and 2015, there was a 15% reduction in the death
rate of Indigenous people (Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet
2018), and in general, there have been some improvements in the
birth and pregnancy outcomes for Indigenous women and babies.
Overall, Indigenous Australians have more children (on average 2.3
births compared with 1.9 births for all other Australian women) and
have them at a younger age than non-Indigenous Australians.
Indigenous Australian babies have an average birth weight lower
than non-Indigenous Australian babies (although this parameter is
improving) and these babies are twice as likely to be of low birth
47


weight, increasing the risk of the child developing health problems.
Babies born to Indigenous Australians are twice as likely as those of
non-Indigenous Australians to die in their first year of life.
Cancer
Cancer describes a wide range of malignant conditions and affects a
number of body systems. Indigenous Australians have a higher rate
of specific cancers than non-Indigenous Australians. These cancers
are liver cancer, lung cancer, cervical cancer and uterine cancer (in
women), pancreatic cancer and cancer of unknown origin. Some
cancers are less common in Indigenous Australians, including bowel,
breast, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma and prostate cancer. Indigenous
Australians are more likely to die from the specific cancers cited
above because in remote areas diagnosis and treatment are less
accessible, the cancer may be more advanced by the time it is
diagnosed and the types of cancers that are prevalent are more
likely to be fatal (especially if diagnosed late).
Respiratory health
Indigenous Australians are about 1.2 times more likely than non-
Indigenous Australians to die from a respiratory disease. The most
common respiratory illnesses impacting on Indigenous Australians
are asthma (particularly in women) and chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease (at five times the non-Indigenous Australian
rate), and they are around three times more likely than non-


Indigenous Australians to suffer from or be admitted to hospital for
influenza or pneumonia (Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet 2018).
Eye health
Issues with poor eye health are common for Indigenous Australians,
with about one-third of adults (more commonly women) and 1 in 11
children reporting problems with their vision although, again,
outcomes are improving, with the rate of eye health problems
reducing from six times the non-Indigenous average to three times
the non-Indigenous average since 2008 (Australian Indigenous
HealthInfoNet 2018). Eye health is affected by environmental factors
(e.g. dust and lack of access to running/clean water), cataracts,
complications of diabetes (retinopathy) and trachoma (although
rates of this eye condition are decreasing). Because most eye health
issues are treatable, it is commonly a lack of specialist eye care or
ophthalmology services that continue to negatively impact on
improving Indigenous Australian’s eye health. Healthy vision is
essential for learning, driving, play, effective social engagement and
everyday life, and a loss of sight compounds marginalisation and
increases vulnerability, already significant determinates of
Indigenous Australians’ health.
Ear health
Although there are a number of ear-related medical conditions,
Indigenous Australians most commonly suffer from otitis media (an
infection of the middle ear) at a greater rate than non-Indigenous


Australians, with 1 in 8 Indigenous Australian adults and 1 in 5
children reporting ear problems or hearing difficulties. In remote
communities, the problem can impact on as many as 80% of the
children under 3 years of age (Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet
2018).
Communicable disease
Communicable diseases are those that are commonly passed from
person to person indirectly via dirty or contaminated food or water,
through the air or by direct person-to-person contact. Examples of
communicable disease are tuberculosis, hepatitis, sexually
transmitted diseases and HIV/AIDS. In each of these examples,
Indigenous Australians are diagnosed with and suffer at greater
rates than non-Indigenous Australians.
Disability
Around 6.7% of Indigenous Australians reported a profound or
severe disability in 2016. A significant number of Indigenous
Australians required support with mobility, communication or daily
home help, with older Indigenous Australians and males requiring
the most help (Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet 2018).
Diabetes
Approximately 13% of Indigenous Australian reported having
diabetes between 2012 and 2013 (Australian Indigenous


HealthInfoNet 2018). Diabetes mellitus results when high levels of
sugar (glucose) accumulate in the blood because of a lack of or
inability to use insulin (a hormone that transports sugar into the
cells). In the Indigenous Australian population, the prevalence of
type 2 diabetes is common, at about 3.5 times the rate of the non-
Indigenous Australian population. Diabetes can lead to life-limiting
and life-threatening complications and, for many Indigenous
Australians, diagnosis often takes place late and after serious
symptoms have developed. Diabetes is the second leading cause of
death for Indigenous Australians with a death rate seven times that
of non-Indigenous Australians (Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet
2018). As a complication of diabetes, end-stage renal disease is
about 6.8 times more common than for non-Indigenous Australians
and impacts on younger Indigenous Australians (Australian
Indigenous HealthInfoNet 2018).
Alcohol and drug use
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are more likely non-
Indigenous people not to drink alcohol, with 38% of Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander people reporting in 2012–13 that they did not
drink alcohol in the previous 12 months (Australian Indigenous
HealthInfoNet 2018). However, for those Indigenous people who do
drink, they are more likely than non-Indigenous Australians to drink
alcohol in binge events (short-term/single occasions). Although long-
term alcohol consumption rates for non-Indigenous people and
Indigenous people who drink are very similar, alcohol drinking is
more of an issue for Indigenous people in inner city or inner regional


areas than in remote locations (Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet
2018).
Most Indigenous people do not use illicit drugs, with 69% of
Indigenous people over the age of 15 indicating that they have never
used illicit drugs. Of the illicit drugs used by Indigenous people,
marijuana was the most common (19%); next were analgesics and
sedatives for non-medical use (13% which were the only group used
in higher levels by females); ‘other’ drugs (e.g. heroin, cocaine,
petrol, LSD, ecstasy and ice) accounted for only 4% (Australian
Indigenous HealthInfoNet 2018).
Strengths-based approaches
to improving Indigenous health
Indigenous Australian health can, at first glance, appear to be overly
negative. However, as touched on previously in this chapter, the
complete picture also includes growing evidence of programs that
are helping to build Indigenous Australians’ resilience with a
strength-based focus. Five key strengths are identified as (1) the
extended family, (2) a commitment to community, (3) extensive
neighbourhood networks, (4) community organisation, and (5)
common community events. Focusing on these strengths and
building on them through community development activities are seen
as powerful tools for enhancing the cultural advantages already
evident in Indigenous communities (Brough, Bond & Hunt,
). As
48


well, strength for Indigenous people comes from the care provider
seeking out, recognising or asking about the Indigenous person’s
‘truth’. Gaining a personal world view will enhance care, facilitate
greater understanding and lead to more robust culturally competent
care.
48 Brough, M. K., Bond, C. & Hunt, J. (2004). Strong in the city: Toward a strength-based
approach in Indigenous health promotion. Health Promotion Journal of Australia, 15(3), 215–
220.
Summary
Multiple interrelated factors contribute to the poorer health status of
Indigenous Australian people. There is a clear relationship between
socioeconomic inequalities and the health gap. An appreciation of
the social determinants of Indigenous Australian health, including the
contributions of historical factors, education, employment, housing,
environmental factors, social and cultural capital, and racism, is
critically important to closing the health gap between Indigenous and
non-Indigenous Australians. Health policies, programs and services
must be designed and delivered in ways that take account of the
socioeconomic disadvantage experienced by many.
Despite a disparity in health remaining, we have seen some
improvement in statistics of health outcomes of Indigenous
Australian people with a growing emphasis on strengths-based
models that focus on bringing Indigenous Australians’ resilience and


community support to the fore. Government initiatives for ‘closing
the gap’ have worked in some areas better than in others. The
health system can make a positive contribution to the social
determinants including training and employment of Indigenous
Australian people, supporting Aboriginal community controlled health
services and building on the strengths of Aboriginal communities in
general (DoHA 2013). Further improvements in the health of
Indigenous Australians is dependent on a multitude of factors, such
as a greater focus on strengths-based models of intervention,
improving access to education, stable employment and associated
income growth, improved socioeconomic factors and improved
access to health care, diagnosis and treatment, as well as health
practitioners who understand and are culturally responsive to
Indigenous Australians’ needs.
The implications of Australian
Indigenous health for nursing
and nursing care practices
Some practical tips for working or engaging with Indigenous
Australians in a culturally sensitive way are:
Focus on the strengths evident in Indigenous Australian culture
and apply the principles of person-centred care with each
interaction (see Box 19.5
).


Become familiar with the Indigenous Australian cultural group(s)
of the area you are (will be) working in.
If not already on display, obtain images that have cultural
legitimacy (such as maps of the Indigenous Australian cultural
groups in the area where you work or local artworks) and display
them prominently in your practice/workplace. Working with the
local community or the local Aboriginal Land Council in your area
will offer opportunities for individual growth (professionally and
personally) and provide future opportunities to improve access to
health services for Indigenous Australians.
Arrange for Indigenous Australian colleagues or experts in
Indigenous health to hold information sessions to outline local or
community history and discuss the specific local issues or
Indigenous group/cultural dynamics in your practice/work
location.
Attend local Indigenous Australian cultural events.
Research local Indigenous Australian organisations and
resources. There are usually a number that can be accessed if
you seek them out (e.g. local Aboriginal Land Councils,
community resource groups, local libraries and local council
services).
Respect cultural values, protocols and ways of doing business.
An example of this is respecting Sorry Business by discussing
local protocols. These should be followed regarding the
scheduling of meetings or events after the death of a community
member.
Consider the language and communication approach used
(verbal, non-verbal and written), respect the use of silence and


be patient when communicating verbally. As with other patients,
avoid jargon, use uncomplicated language and speak clearly
(New South Wales Department of Community Services ).
49 New South Wales Department of Community Services (2009). Working with
Aboriginal People and Communities: A Practice Resource. Ashfield, NSW: NSW
Department of Community Services. Retrieved from <www.comunity.new.gov.au>.
Build a dialogue with individual Indigenous people and seek out
their cultural ‘truth’.
Understand the implications and importance of building
relationships between extended family and community structures
and concepts. Indigenous Australians have strong family values
and an extended family structure that places the ‘family as
community’. Children are seen as the responsibility of the entire
family with kinship bonds being responsible for sharing family
roles and responsibilities. Indigenous Australian families are
commonly complex and imply an overarching set of obligations
and shared roles that go well beyond the traditional Western
nuclear family structure. Ensure that the extended family is
included in important meetings and care practice decisions (New
South Wales Department of Community Services 2009).
In the care environment, respect and acknowledgment should be
offered for all people but specifically for Elders and community
leaders. However, referring to an Elder or leader as Aunty or
Uncle may not be appropriate unless a strong relationship has
been established.
Indigenous Australians are the traditional custodians of the land
and it is important that their special position is recognised and
incorporated into official events. It is common practice when
49


organising a meeting, event or conference that Indigenous
Australian culture is acknowledged in a respectful and
appropriate way.
It is common in traditional Indigenous Australian culture for many
issues related to men and women to be dealt with separately.
Commonly referred to ‘men’s and women’s business’, these
practices have regulations and penalties for breaking these rules.
It is important that care staff recognise that for a range of health
issues, appropriately gendered staff are required for different-
gendered Indigenous Australians. As well, specific staff may
need to take part in different aspects of care provision and
offence should not be taken if men or women leave the
treatment environment if Indigenous Australians feel there is a
breach of ‘men’s or women’s business’ (New South Wales
Department of Community Services 2009).
BO X
19.5 The strengths evident in
contemporary Indigenous Australian
health
The 26th of January (Australia Day) is not a day of
celebration for Indigenous Australians. It is commonly known
as ‘Survival Day’ but it is not a day of sadness because, in
spite of the injustice and problems of the past, Indigenous


Australians have survived and continue to thrive and make a
valuable contribution to Australia’s future. The 26th of May is
known as National Sorry Day, a day that was established
following the Bringing Them Home Report, and is regarded as
a day of healing for all Australians. This is followed by
Reconciliation Week between the 27th of May and the 3rd of
June. In addition, the National Aborigines and Islanders Day
of Observance Committee (NAIDOC) Week occurs in July,
allowing all Australians to recognise and bring to their
consciousness the significant and vital place Indigenous
Australians have in a modern and growing nation.
Great gains have been made by Indigenous Australians with
many non-Indigenous Australians celebrating the progress
that has been made in reconciliation. More and more
Indigenous Australians are appearing on mainstream
television, in the media and in the sporting and national
consciousness. As well, greater respect and understanding of
the history and trauma evident following the clash of cultures
that resulted from European colonisation is acknowledged by
a wider spectrum of non-Indigenous Australians. Changes in
legislation, policy and attitudes are taking place across the
landscape of Australia with much of this being led by
empowered and strong Indigenous Australian leadership.
Positive steps are being made as Indigenous Australians are
approaching their health with strength-based strategies and
empowering approaches to doing ‘what works’ as a way
towards a healthier and more promising future, with genuine


health gains being seen to be made (Australian Indigenous
HealthInfoNet 2018).
Research note
Developing a culturally safe antenatal clinic for
Australian Indigenous women
S. Kildea, H. Stapleton, R. Murphy, N. Billy Low & K. Gibbons
. The Murri clinic: A comparative
retrospective study of an antenatal clinic developed for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women.
BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth, 12, 159−169.
50 Kildea, S., Stapleton, H., Murphy, R., Billy Low, N. & Gibbons, K. (2012). The Murri clinic: A
comparative retrospective study of an antenatal clinic developed for Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander women. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth, 12, 159−169.
The purpose of the study was to evaluate the strengths and
challenges of the Murri clinic by undertaking an evaluation of
maternal and neonatal health data. Service users and staff
were also interviewed individually and in focus groups. The
Murri clinic women (n = 367) were compared with women
attending standard care (n = 414). The results found that
continuity of carer was a major attraction, with one participant
reporting, ‘It’s good coming here too because you know
you’re going to see the same people all the time ... she
knows your full history’ (p. 6). Culturally responsive care was
reported by 92%. Future considerations include ongoing
cultural competency training for staff, combining multi-agency
resources and working in partnership.
50


Implications Nurses need to be aware of their experiences
with people from diverse cultural backgrounds and how these
experiences shape their views, understandings, attitudes and
behaviours in providing person-centred cultural care.
Additionally, health care facilities should develop
organisational policy and guidelines regarding cultural
diversity and focused cultural care for nurses working in
clinical settings.


Providing cultural nursing care
All phases of the nursing process are affected by the person
requiring health care and the nurse’s cultural values, beliefs and
behaviours. As the unwell individual’s culture and the nurse’s culture
come together in the nursing care relationship, a unique cultural
environment is created that can improve or impair the unwell
person’s health outcome. Self-awareness of personal biases can
enable nurses to develop modifying behaviours or (if they are unable
to do so) to remove themselves from situations where care may be
compromised. Nurses can become more aware of their own culture
through values clarification (see Chapter 5
). The nurse must also
consider the cultural values dominant in the health care setting
because those, too, may influence the person’s outcome.
Leininger’s model of transcultural nursing care entitled ‘Leininger’s
sunrise model to depict the theory of cultural care diversity and
universality’ (Leininger
) depicts human beings as inseparable from
their cultural background and their social structure. Briefly, the model
provides the nurse with four different levels to comprehend the
health care beliefs of different cultures. The four levels are (1)
culture care, world view and cultural and social structure dimension
systems; (2) individuals, families, groups, communities and
institutions in diverse health systems; (3) the generic (folk) systems,
nursing care and professional systems; and (4) nursing care
decisions and actions (Leininger 1997). There are many other
51


models of cultural care that you may like to consider in your
practice.
51 Leininger, M. (1997). Overview of the theory of culture care with the ethnonursing research
method. Journal of Transcultural Nursing, 8(2), 32–52.


Nursing management
Assessing
There are many cultural assessment tools that provide a guide for
conducting a cultural assessment. Tools and guides can be used as
prompts when interviewing and facilitating communication with
individuals and their families. They are designed to enhance the
process in order to determine if the person is identifying with their
traditional cultural heritage (heritage consistent) or if they have
acculturated into the dominant culture of the modern society they
reside in (heritage inconsistent). Tools may be used in any setting,
facilitate conversation, provide prompts for the nurse and help in the
planning of cultural care. Once a conversation begins and the
person describes aspects of cultural heritage, it becomes possible to
develop an understanding of the person’s unique health and illness
beliefs, practices and cultural needs. See Figure 19.4
 for cultural
assessment considerations.
Examples of heritage consistency
The following factors and examples indicative of heritage
consistency can be explored to determine the depth to which a


person identifies with their traditional heritage; that is, the cultural
beliefs and practices of their family heritage:
The person’s childhood development occurred in the person’s
country of origin or in an immigrant neighbourhood of like ethnic
groups in Australia. For example, the person was raised in a
specific ethnic neighbourhood, such as an Italian, Asian, Greek
or Jewish one, in a given part of a city, and was exposed only to
the culture, language, foods and customs of that particular
group.
Extended family members encouraged participation in traditional
religious and cultural activities. For example, the parents sent the
person to religious (parochial) school and most social activities
were church related.
The individual engages in frequent visits to the country of origin
or returns to the ‘old neighbourhood’ in Australia. The desire to
return to the old country or to the old neighbourhood is prevalent
in many people; however, many people, for various reasons,
cannot return. Reasons why people may not return to their native
country include political conditions in the homeland or lack of
relatives or friends in that land.
The individual’s family home is within the ethnic community of
which they are a member. As adults, people elect to live with
their families in the ethnic neighbourhood wherein the people are
from a similar heritage.
The individual participates in ethnic cultural events, such as
religious festivals or national holidays, sometimes with singing,


dancing and costumes. For example, the person is active in
social and cultural groups and participates in family festivities.
The individual was raised in an extended family setting. For
example, when the person was growing up, grandparents or
aunts and uncles may have been living in the same house or
close by. The person’s social frame of reference was the family.
The individual maintains regular contact with the extended family.
For example, the person maintains close ties with family
members of the same generation, the surviving members of the
older generation and members of the younger generation.
The individual’s name has not been ‘Westernised’. For example,
the person has restored the family name to its original if it had
been changed at the time the family immigrated or at a later time
in an attempt to assimilate to the dominant culture more fully.
The individual was educated at a private school with a religious or
ethnic philosophy similar to the family’s background. The
person’s education plays an enormous role in socialisation and
the major purpose of education is to socialise a person into the
dominant culture. Children learn English and the customs and
norms of Australian life at school. In private schools, they not
only learn English but also are socialised in the culture and
norms of the particular religious or ethnic group that is
sponsoring the school.
The individual engages in social activities primarily with others of
the same religious or ethnic background. For example, the major
portion of the person’s personal time is spent attending meetings
and events sponsored by those with whom they identify.


The individual has knowledge of the culture and language of
origin. For example, the person has been socialised in the
traditional ways of the family and expresses this as a central
theme of life.
The individual expresses pride in their heritage. For example, the
person may identify themself as ethnic Australian and display
flags, wear clothing or participate in ethnic activities to a great
extent.
Conveying cultural sensitivity
The process of cultural and health tradition assessment is important.
How and when questions are asked requires sensitivity and clinical
judgment. The timing and phrasing of questions need to be adapted
to the individual. Timing is important in introducing questions.
Sensitivity is needed in phrasing questions. Trust must be
established before people can be expected to volunteer and share
sensitive information. The nurse therefore needs to spend time with
the person, introduce some social conversation and convey a
genuine desire to understand their values and beliefs. If the nurse
does not spend the time to complete a comprehensive assessment,
incorporating cultural considerations, the quality of nursing care is
compromised. See Figure 19.4
 for cultural assessment
considerations.
Figure 19.4


Cultural assessment considerations.


Before a cultural assessment begins, determine what language the
person speaks and the person’s degree of fluency in the English
language. It is also important to learn about the person’s
communication patterns and space orientation. This is accomplished
by observing both verbal and non-verbal communication. For
example:
Does the person do the speaking or defer to another?
What non-verbal communication behaviours does the person
exhibit (e.g. touching, eye contact)?
What significance do these behaviours have for the nurse–
person interaction?
What is the person’s proximity to other people and objects within
the environment?
How does the person react to the nurse’s movement towards
them?
What cultural objects within the environment have importance for
health promotion or health maintenance?
It is vital for nurses to be culturally sensitive and to convey this
sensitivity to the person requiring health care, support people and
other health care personnel. Some ways to do so follow:
Always address the person, support people and other health care
personnel by their last names (e.g. Mrs Bourne, Dr Stewart) until
they give you permission to use other names. In some cultures,
the more formal style of address is a sign of respect, whereas
the informal use of first names may be considered disrespectful.


However, it is important to ask people how they wish to be
addressed.
When meeting a person for the first time, introduce yourself by
your full name and then explain your role (e.g. ‘My name is Alicia
Bernett and I am a student nurse at Nightingale School of
Nursing’). This helps establish a relationship and provides an
opportunity for each person to learn the pronunciation of one
another’s names and their roles.
Be authentic with people and be honest about the knowledge you
lack about their culture. When you do not understand a person’s
actions, politely and respectfully seek information.
Use language that is culturally sensitive; avoid using slang or
derogatory terms.
Find out what the person thinks about their health problems,
illness and treatments. Assess whether this information is
congruent with the dominant health care culture. If the beliefs
and practices are incongruent, establish whether this will have a
negative effect on the person’s health.
Do not make any assumptions about the person and always ask
about anything you do not understand.
Show respect for the person’s values, beliefs and practices, even
if they differ from your own or from those of the dominant
culture. If you do not agree with them, it is important to respect
the person’s right to hold these beliefs.
Show respect for the person’s support people. In some cultures,
men in the family make decisions affecting other family members
while in other cultures women make the decisions.


Make a concerted effort to obtain the person’s trust but do not
be surprised if it develops slowly or not at all. The culture
assessment takes time and usually needs to extend over several
meetings.
Diagnosing
The nursing diagnoses are focused on nursing care and are based
on Western cultural beliefs. It is essential to expand the
understanding of nursing practice to include all cultural beliefs.
Nurses must provide appropriate care to people of any culture. This
is accomplished through developing cultural safety and considering
how a person’s culture influences their responses to health
conditions, much as the nurse considers how a person’s age or
gender influences a nursing diagnosis, plan and delivery of nursing
care.
Planning
Cultural competence in nursing involves delivering care that
integrates the mind, the body, the spirit and the cultural values of the
individual. A potential outcome is that the person can maintain,
foster and/or regain mutually desired and reasonable levels of health
within the scope of their life circumstances.


There are several steps involved in the process that lead to the
development of cultural competency. The knowledge and skills
necessary to incorporate cultural care into standard nursing require
the acquisition of a broad base of knowledge about different cultures
and social structures. It is an ongoing process and the skills and
knowledge base grow over time. As one’s knowledge base grows,
the ability to convey cultural sensitivity also grows.
The following are examples of the necessary steps:
1. Become aware of one’s own culture. Where were your
parents and grandparents born? What are examples of their
traditional health and illness beliefs and practices? Do they
value stoic behaviour in relation to pain or is it permissible to
state that you are in pain? Are the rights of the individual
valued over and above the rights of the family? Only by
knowing one’s own culture (values, practices and beliefs) can
a person be ready to learn about another’s.
2. Become aware of the person’s culture and health traditions as
described by the individual. It is important to avoid assuming
that all people of one ethnic background have the same
cultural beliefs and values. When the nurse has knowledge of
the person’s culture, mutual respect between the person and
nurse is more likely to develop.
3. Become aware of adaptations that the person made to live in
Australia’s culture. During this part of the interview, a nurse
can also identify the person’s preferences in health practices,
diet and hygiene.


4. Develop a nursing plan with the person that incorporates their
cultural beliefs regarding the maintenance, protection and
restoration of health. In this way, cultural values, practices
and beliefs can be incorporated into the necessary nursing
care.
Implementing
The implementation of cultural nursing care includes (a) cultural
preservation and maintenance, and (b) cultural accommodation and
negotiation. Cultural preservation may involve the use of cultural
health care practices, such as giving herbal tea, chicken soup or ‘hot
foods’ to the ill person. Accommodation of the person’s viewpoint
and negotiating appropriate care require expert communication
skills, such as responding empathetically, validating information and
effectively summarising content. Negotiation is a collaborative
process. It acknowledges that the nurse–person relationship is
reciprocal and that different views exist of health, illness and
treatment. The nurse’s role is to provide education and information
on evidence-based practice while respecting the person’s cultural
perspectives.
Negotiation occurs when cultural treatment practices conflict with
those of the health care system. It must be determined precisely
how the person is managing the illness, what practices could be
harmful and which practices can be safely combined with Western
medicine. For example, reducing dosages of an antihypertensive


medication or replacing insulin therapy with herbal measures may be
detrimental. Some herbal remedies are synergistic with Western
medicines and others are antagonistic; therefore, it is necessary to
fully inform the person about the possible outcomes. Consider these
examples of potential conflicts between cultural beliefs or practices
and the dominant Australian health care system:
The decision to circumcise male infants is often made based on
cultural and family beliefs and can occasionally conflict with
medical advice.
Members of the Jehovah’s Witness faith do not accept blood
transfusions, even in life-threatening situations.
Indigenous Australian people may refuse nursing care if they
believe their illness is a result of cultural beliefs. Both the
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health Plan 2013–2023
(DoHA 2013) and the Implementation Plan for the National
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Plan 2013–2023
(Department of Health 2015) clearly articulate the centrality of
culture and wellbeing in the health of Indigenous Australian
people.
When a person chooses to follow only cultural practices and declines
all prescribed medical or nursing interventions, the nurse and person
must adjust their health care goals. Monitoring the person’s
condition to identify changes in health and to recognise impending
crises before they become irreversible may be all that is realistically
achievable. At a time of crisis, the opportunity may arise to
renegotiate care.


Providing cultural nursing care is challenging. It requires discovery of
the meaning of the person’s behaviour, flexibility, creativity and
knowledge to adapt nursing interventions. A conscious effort must
be made to learn from each experience. This knowledge will improve
the delivery of culturally safe care to future individuals seeking health
care. The following box offers suggestions for providing such care to
people.
Evaluating
Evaluating nursing care of individuals that incorporates the concepts
of culture and ethnicity is performed in the same way as with any
individual. The person’s outcomes are compared with the goals and
expected outcomes established following comprehensive
assessment that includes sensitivity to cultural diversity. However, if
the outcomes are not achieved and the person and nurse are from
different cultures, the nurse should be especially careful to consider
whether the person’s belief system has been adequately included as
an influencing factor.
Culturally competent care
Families
Include cultural assessment of the person and family as
part of overall assessment.


Discover customs and practices of the major cultural
groups with whom you come into contact.
Respect the richness of diversity and consider it an asset
rather than a hindrance in your practice. This is the
basis of strengths-based models of Indigenous
Australian care.
Don’t make assumptions about beliefs or practices.
Ask about the person’s use of cultural or alternative
approaches to healing.
Identify your personal biases, attitudes, prejudices and
stereotypes.
Recognise that it is the person’s (or family’s) right to make
their own health care choices. Explain in detail the
person’s condition and the treatment plan if the person
consents for you to do this.
Convey respect for and cooperate with traditional healers
and caregivers.
Case study
Jedda was born to an Australian Aboriginal mother and a
New Zealand European father. Although the family
participated in Western traditions, Jedda’s mother taught her
many Aboriginal traditions as well so that her culture would be
preserved. Jedda is now 58 years old, practises traditions
from both her Australian Aboriginal and Western upbringing


and is dying of cancer. You are the nurse caring for Jedda
during her final days.
Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. Differentiate between Jedda’s culture, ethnicity and
race.
2. How might Jedda’s mixed cultural background pose a
dilemma for you as her nurse or for her family?


3. How might Jedda’s culture affect her approach to
death and the care of her body following her death?
4. Of what benefit would a cultural assessment be to
Jedda or her family considering she is dying?
5.
 How would you support and involve Jedda’s
family when planning and delivering her nursing care?
6. How could nurses’ race, culture or religion influence
their care of people who are racially or culturally
different?


Chapter 19 Review


Chapter highlights
Australian health care initiatives impact on the nursing care of
culturally diverse people. The ‘Close the Gap’ campaign is an
example of a significant Australian initiative that was developed
between the government of Australia and the Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander peoples of Australia and is supported by
Indigenous and non-Indigenous health organisations. The
intention is to work together to achieve equality in health status
and life expectancy between Indigenous Australians and non-
Indigenous Australians by the year 2030.
Cultural safety is a model of care which originated in New
Zealand that incorporates cultural awareness and cultural
sensitivity, which can lead to culturally safe practice.
A comprehensive nursing assessment, incorporating a cultural
assessment, is paramount to ensuring culturally safe nursing
practice.
People in Australia come from a variety of backgrounds and
many retain at least some of their traditional values, including
health beliefs and practices.
People may live within their traditional culture or they may
embrace both their original ethnocultural traditional heritage(s)
and the modern culture of Australia.
An individual’s heritage and cultural background can influence
health beliefs and practices.
Through acculturation, most groups in Australia modify some of
their traditional cultural characteristics.


Personal characteristics also modify an individual’s cultural
values, beliefs and practices.
Health professionals need to recognise their own perspectives,
beliefs and values about cultural engagement and take into
consideration their own perspectives before engaging with people
from other cultures.
Indigenous Australians face a multitude of health challenges in a
range of health areas. Nurses and other health professionals
need to acknowledge the history and background impacting on
Indigenous Australians’ health circumstances and respond with
cultural sensitivity and in culturally competent ways that will
enhance the nurse–client relationship and have a positive impact
on the person’s health outcomes.
Health beliefs and practices, family patterns, communication
style, space and time orientation, and nutritional patterns may
influence the relationship between the nurse and a person who
has a different cultural background.
Build care on a resilience model or strengths-based model that
recognises strong health factors impacting on Indigenous
Australians’ potential to be empowered in the face of their health
issues.
When assessing an individual, the nurse considers the
individual’s cultural values, beliefs and practices related to health
and health care.
Concept check


1. Which of the following is the major factor contributing to the
increased emphasis on the need for proficiency in cultural
nursing practice in Australia?
1. The nursing shortage.
2. Limited access to health care services.
3. Demographic changes.
4. A decreasing rate of immigration.
2. Which of the following behaviours is most indicative of

1. The nurse helps the person recognise the need to
adapt health practices to fit commonly accepted
practices.
2. The nurse provides education and information on

cultural perspectives.
3. The nurse informs the person that lack of adherence to
the medical regimen may be detrimental.
4. The nurse asks a person from the same culture to

statement?
1. ‘Because, in your culture, people don’t drink iced water,
I will bring you hot tea.’
2. ‘Do you have any books I could read about people of

4. ‘You will need to set aside your usual customs and

4. Which of the following behaviours is most representative of a

It is important to begin by stating that in many
parts of the world, what we call complementary
and alternative therapies (CATs) (also called
complementary and alternative medicine (CAM))
are indeed practised as primary therapeutic
interventions. However, in most Western
countries (Australia, New Zealand, the United
States, Canada and Europe), nursing education
has been influenced by and offered under the
umbrella of the biomedical model of health.
Thus, nurses from these parts of the world are
familiar and comfortable with biomedical beliefs,
theories, practices, strengths and limitations.
Fewer nurses have studied alternative
therapeutic interventions and practices and, as
a result, many lack information or even harbour


misinformation about CATs’ impact on health
and wellbeing. In this chapter, the terms
conventional medicine
 and biomedicine
are used to describe Western medical
therapeutic practices. The terms alternative
medicine
 or complementary medicine
 are
used to describe as many as 1800 other
therapies practised all over the world. Many of
these have been handed down over thousands
of years, both orally and as written records.
They are based on the healing and therapeutic
systems of ancient cultures, including Egyptian,
Chinese, Indian, Greek and many others. Other
therapies, such as Pilates and chiropractic
therapies, evolved in the Western world over the
past two centuries. Still others, such as some of
the mind–body and bioelectromagnetic
approaches, are on the frontier of scientific
knowledge and understanding.
Clinical consideration
What constitutes traditional,
complementary or
alternative therapies (CAT)


for one person may be
considered mainstream by
another. Do not assume
anything about an
individual’s belief system—
be sure to assess. It is also
important to note that with
some CATs, such as
meditation, guided imagery
and hypnotherapy, the
active participation of the
person is vital; however,
with other therapies such as
acupuncture it is the
practitioner who is most
actively involved in the
therapy.
The conventional medical community cannot
ignore complementary and alternative therapies.
The public interest is extensive and growing,
along with evidence to support the effectiveness
of many of the therapies practised. One has
only to look at the proliferation of popular health
books, health food stores and clinics offering


healing therapies to realise this. The Australian
College of Nursing (ACN) and the Australian
Medical Association (AMA) have position
statements about complementary medicine or
complementary therapies that support and
comment on the value and growth of
complementary therapies. Health insurance
companies too have recognised the benefits of
supporting complementary therapies and their
preventive, prophylactic and therapeutic
benefits. von Conrady & Bonney  suggest that
60% of Australians access some form of CAT,
with 68% of this number being female. This is
supported by Reid et al. . The Australian
Bureau of Statistics  indicate that the use of
complementary health increased by 51% in the
10 years to 2005. The integration of CATs into
mainstream medical treatment options is also
reflected by the growing number of general
practitioners (GPs) who are referring people for
complementary and alternative therapy, with
Bensoussan et al.  suggesting that 30–40% of
GPs subscribe, administer and use
complementary therapies and 59% of GPs
report an increased demand for complementary
therapies.
