The adult phase of development encompasses
the years from the end of adolescence to death.
Because the developmental tasks of young
adults differ from those of older adults,
adulthood is often divided into three phases:
young adulthood, middle adulthood and late
adulthood. In this book, young adults are
defined as people 20 to 40 years of age and
middle-aged adults as 40 to 65 years of age.
There is some discrepancy with names and
exact dates for each generation, but the
following are relatively widely recognised as the
more common terms and age ranges. They are:
the Baby Boomers
 (birth years 1946–64);
Generation X
 (birth years 1965–79);
Generation Y
 (birth years 1980–94);
Generation Z
 (birth years 1995–2009); and
Generation Alpha
 (birth years 2010–24)
(McCrindle Research ). Each cohort has shared
specific life events and has its own world view,
1


making them quite diverse in some ways. Life
expectancy has increased over time, with males
on average living until 83 years old and females
86 years old (Australian Bureau of Statistics
(ABS) ). Currently, just over half of Australia’s
population fall between 24 and 64 years old,
with the median age being 37.2 years old (ABS
2018a). Understanding each generation, what
major events affected their lives and how they
best learn and interact, especially in this
technologically advanced age, will be important
in providing holistic person-centred care.
1 McCrindle Research (2019). Generation Next: Meet Gen
Z and the Alphas. Retrieved from
<www.mccrindle.com.au>.
2 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018a). Population
Projections, Australia, 2017 (Base)—2066. Cat. no. 3222.0.
Canberra: ABS.
This chapter applies the concepts of growth and
development introduced in Chapter 21
 to the
young and middle-aged adult. Each
developmental stage includes physical,
psychosocial, cognitive, moral and spiritual
2


aspects. The main health problems for each
group are identified and health assessment and
promotion guidelines have been provided.


Young adults (20 to 40 years)
The age at which a person is considered an adult depends on how
adulthood is described in the social context of the individual; this
defining age is changing. Legally a person in Australia can vote at 18
years of age. The legal age for alcohol consumption outside the
home is also 18 years of age. Another criterion of adulthood is
financial independence, which is also highly variable. Some
adolescents support themselves as early as 16 years of age, usually
because of family circumstances. By contrast, some adults are
financially dependent on their families for many years, for example,
during prolonged periods of education.
Adulthood may also be indicated by moving away from home and
establishing one’s own living arrangements; yet this independence
also varies greatly. Some adolescents leave home because of family
problems. Regardless of whether the adolescent leaves home or
not, they often value the emotional support and advice that parents
give as they transition from adolescence to adulthood (Vassallo,
Sanson & Olsson ). It is not uncommon for young adults to move
back into their parents’ homes after an initial period of independent
living; the expression ‘boomerang kids
’ evolved to represent this
phenomena. This finding is supported by Australian Institute of
Family Studies (AIFS) , which states that in 2016, approximately
68% of young adults (of which 43.4% were in the 20–24 year age
group, 17.1% in the 25–29 year age group and 7.1% in the 30–34
3
4


year age group) were still residing at home with their parents. The
factors contributing to this trend include high unemployment and
divorce rates, tertiary education and housing costs, and problems
resulting from substance abuse and maladaptive behaviours. Some
young people who are employed full-time receive only a minimum
wage and are unable to earn enough money to be self-supporting,
and thus remain at home.
3 Vassallo, S., Sanson, A. & Olsson, C. (2014). 30 years on: Some key insights from the
Australian Temperament Project. Family Matters, 94, 29–34.
4 Australian Institute of Family Studies (AIFS) (2019a). More Young Adults Living at Home
with Their Parents. Retrieved from <www.aifs.gov.au>.
Young adults typically are busy people who face many challenges.
They are expected to assume new roles at work and in the home
and community, and to develop interests, values and attitudes
related to these roles.
Physical development
People in their early 20s are in their prime physical years. The
human body is at its most efficient functioning at about age 25. The
musculoskeletal system is well developed and coordinated. This is
the period when athletic endeavours reach their peak. All other
systems of the body (e.g. cardiovascular, visual, auditory and
reproductive) are also functioning at peak efficiency. Emerging


adults, however, tend to be high risk takers (Berk ), placing their
high-functioning bodies at substantial risk of serious injury.
5 Berk, L. (2014). Development through the Lifespan (6th ed.). Boston: Pearson.
Although physical changes are minimal during this stage, weight and
muscle mass may change as a result of diet and exercise. Health
outcomes in older adulthood may have their beginnings in younger
adult behaviours. In addition, extensive physical and psychosocial
changes occur in pregnant and lactating women (Rankin ).
6 Rankin, J. (Ed.) (2017). Physiology in Childbearing with Anatomy and Related Biosciences
(4th ed.). London: Elsevier.
Psychosocial development
In contrast to the minimal physical changes, psychosocial
development of the young adult is great. Young adults face a
number of key transitions as they progress towards maturity and
become independent of their parents. During young adulthood, new
experiences and changes in lifestyle are characterised by their
choices in education and employment or career, decisions about
whether to marry or remain single, starting a family and rearing
children. Social responsibilities often include forming new friendships
and social networks, adopting new roles and assuming community
activities. Box 23.1
 reviews this psychosocial development
according to the theories of Freud, Erikson and Havighurst.
5
6


Developmental tasks for young adults centre on having a firm sense
of self and establishing intimacy
 or very close friendships. Choice
of a lifelong partner, considerations of childbearing and forming new
friendships depend on the successful negotiation of intimacy and the
ability to reach out to others and develop loving, intimate
relationships.
BO X
23.1 Psychosocial development:
young adult
The young adult
Is in the genital stage in which energy is directed towards
attaining a mature sexual relationship, according to
Freud’s theory.
Is in the intimacy versus isolation phase of Erikson’s
stages of development.
7 Erikson, E. H. (1963). Childhood and Society (2nd ed.). New York: Norton.
Has the following developmental tasks, according to
Havighurst :
8 Havighurst, R. J. (1972). Developmental Tasks and Education (3rd ed.). New
York: Longman.
selecting a mate
7
8


learning to live with a partner
starting a family
rearing children
managing a home
getting started in an occupation
taking on civic responsibility
finding a congenial social group.
While these are generally the most prominent psychosocial changes
experienced during young adulthood, not all individuals take the
same developmental path, and experiences and choices will vary
between individuals. Variations may be related to earlier life
experiences and socioeconomic and cultural factors. For example,
many young adults have experienced the divorce of their parents
and being raised in blended families or stepfamilies. As children of
divorce, feelings of being ‘caught’ between two divorced parents
may be a heavy burden as they move into young adulthood.
Common problems among young adults raised in blended families
include concerns about adequate financial resources, difficulty
deciding how much personal information to share with others and
worries about loyalty and disloyalty to family members. These added
concerns have obvious implications for the development of intimate
and long-lasting relationships in young adults. South’s  study on
adult children of divorce reported that children who experienced
multiple parental divorces found it harder to establish intimate
relationships than children who had experienced none or one
9


parental divorce. Couples are also choosing to live together without
being married and getting married later in life (AIFS ).
9 South, A. (2013). Perceptions of romantic relationships in adult children of divorce. Journal
of Divorce and Remarriage, 54(2), 126–141.
10 Australian Institute of Family Studies (AIFS) (2019b). Marriage Rates in Australia.
Retrieved from <www.aifs.gov.au>.
Occupational choice and education are largely inseparable.
Education influences occupational opportunities; conversely, an
occupation, once chosen, can determine the education required and
undertaken. Education enhances employment opportunities and
usually ensures economic survival. As the role of women has
changed, many women now choose to assume active careers and
civic roles in society in addition to their roles as mother and/or wife.
Some women work out of necessity rather than choice (see Figure
23.1
).
Figure 23.1
10


Many young women combine active careers with motherhood.
Source: pictrough/123RF.
Remaining single is becoming the lifestyle of more and more young
adults. Many people choose to remain single, perhaps to pursue an
education and then to have the freedom to pursue their chosen
occupation. Some unmarried individuals choose to live with another
person of the opposite or same sex and share living arrangements
and certain expenses.
Although non-traditional lifestyles are becoming more acceptable in
society, attitudes towards these various lifestyles can contribute
social pressures that lead to stress responses. The multiple roles of
adulthood (citizen, worker, taxpayer, homeowner, wife/husband,
daughter/son, brother/sister, parent, friend and so on) may also
create role conflict, which can cause stress.
Cognitive development
Young adults are able to use formal operations, characterised by the
ability to think abstractly and employ logic. For example, young
adults are able to generate hypotheses about what will happen given
a set of circumstances and do not have to engage in trial-and-error
behaviour.
Researchers in the field of psychology have suggested that Piaget’s
formal operational stage is not the last stage of human


development. Some have proposed a concept of post-formal
thought. Post-formal thought includes creativity, intuition and the
ability to consider information in relationship to other ideas (Murray,
Zentner & Yakimo ). Post-formal thinkers possess an
understanding of the temporary or relative nature of knowledge.
They can proceed from abstract reasoning to practical
considerations. They are aware that most problems have more than
one cause and more than one answer, and some solutions will work
better than others (Murray et al. 2014). They are able to
comprehend and balance arguments created by both logic and
emotion. Meditation and other insight-oriented practices facilitate
becoming a post-formal thinker.
11 Murray, R. B., Zentner, J. P. & Yakimo, R. (2014). Pearson New International Edition:
Health Promotion Strategies through the Life Span (8th ed.). Harlow, England: Pearson
Education Limited.
Moral development
Young adults who have mastered the previous stages of
Kohlberg’s
 theory of moral development enter the post-
conventional level. At this time, the person is able to separate self
from the expectations and rules of others and to define morality in
terms of personal principles. When individuals perceive a conflict
with society’s rules or laws, they judge according to their own
principles. For example, a person may intentionally break the law
and join a protest group to stop hunters from killing wild animals,
11
1213


believing that the principle of wildlife conservation justifies the protest
action. This type of reasoning is called principled reasoning. See
also Gilligan’s ethic of care in Chapter 21
. Gilligan  argues that
as individuals approach young adulthood, men and women tend to
define moral problems somewhat differently. Men often use an ‘ethic
of justice’ and define moral problems in terms of rules and rights.
Women, by contrast, often define moral problems in terms of
obligation to care and to avoid hurt.
12 Kohlberg, L. (1981). The Psychology of Moral Development: Moral Stages and the Idea of
Justice. San Francisco: Harper & Row.
13 Kohlberg, L. (1984). The Psychology of Moral Development: The Nature and Validity of
Moral Stages. San Francisco: Harper & Row.
14 Gilligan, C. (1982). In a Different Voice: Psychological Theory and Women’s Development.
Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.
Spiritual development
According to Fowler (1981), the individual enters the individuating
reflective period some time after 18 years of age. During this period,
the individual focuses on reality. A 27-year-old adult may ask
philosophical questions regarding spirituality and may be self-
conscious about spiritual matters. The religious teaching that the
young adult had as a child may now be accepted or redefined. Anye
et al.
 purport that religion and spirituality can be protective factors
against risky health behaviour in young adults; a view shared by
14
15


many others. In a study they conducted involving college students in
the United States, they found spiritual wellbeing made a significant
contribution to health-related quality of life.
15 Anye, E., Gallien, T., Bian, H. & Moulton, M. (2013). The relationship between spiritual well-
being and health-related quality of life in college students. Journal of American College Health,
61(7), 414–421.
Health risks
Young adulthood is generally a healthy time of life and health risk is
often related to lifestyle and behaviour choices. People in this age
group can put themselves at greater risk of developing chronic
conditions later in life by making poor lifestyle choices (i.e. smoking,
risky alcohol use) and not eating a nutritional diet or exercising
regularly (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW)
).
Health risks that are common in this age group include injuries,
suicide, substance abuse, hypertension, diabetes, sexually
transmitted infections (STIs), abuse of women and certain cancers.
Leading causes of ‘burden’ between the ages of 25 years and 44
years are reported to be anxiety disorders, back pain and back
problems, suicide and self-inflicted injuries, depressive disorders and
other musculoskeletal disorders (AIHW 2018a). Some of these
problems are related to behaviours that could potentially be
prevented or modified through education and other primary
prevention strategies. For young adults, education and establishing
healthy behaviours during this time can help reduce health risks in
16


later life. Promotion of primary health care by nurses is vital so that
young adults can actively engage with their own health-related
behaviours and make healthy choices. This approach can encourage
young adults to manage their health and to make choices that suit
their lifestyle and behaviours. This facilitates an individualised
approach to health promotion and a focus on the person’s needs
within their own context.
16 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018a). Australia’s Health 2018.
Australia’s health series no. 16. AUS 221. Canberra: AIHW.
Injuries
The AIHW (2018a) reports that injury (i.e. land transport accidents)
and accidental poisoning are both leading causes of death in
Australia for young adults aged between 25 and 44 years old. As the
majority of young adults are employed, workplace injury is also
prominent, particularly for males. Injury can lead to long-term
disability and impairment resulting in significant disruptions in growth,
development and quality of life for young adults, and the need for
lifetime care and support. This may then also greatly affect the lives
of the young person’s parents and family who may need to resume
or take on a care-giving role.
Indigenous Australians in the 35–44 years age group died at about
five times the rate of non-Indigenous Australians (ABS ). Rates of
injury for Indigenous Australians rise in younger adulthood, with the
biggest difference noted between 20 and 44 years of age and
17


peaking in the 30−34 years age group. Injury inflicted by another
person is a common cause of hospitalisation for Indigenous
Australians, second only to hospitalisation for care involving dialysis
(Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet
). Education about safety
precautions and injury prevention is a major role of the nurse in
promoting the health of young adults. For a further discussion of
safety education for young adults, see Chapter 33
.
17 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2017a). Deaths, Australia, 2016. Cat. no. 3302.0.
Canberra: ABS.
18 Australian Indigenous HealthInfoNet (2016). Overview of Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander Health Status 2015. Retrieved from <www.healthinfonet.ecu.edu.au>.
Suicide
Suicide rates continue to be a serious health concern (AIHW 2018a).
Myriad factors are associated with the increased risk of suicide in
young Australians. Some include the mental health of the person;
family dynamics (parental separation, relationship breakdowns,
abuse); social circumstances (drug use, bullying, friendships); and
socioeconomic situation (education levels, living arrangements,
unemployment). In 2011, suicide deaths accounted for 21% of
deaths of people aged 25–44 years and males were more likely to
die from suicide than females (AIHW 2018a). The rate of suicide for
Indigenous males and females is reported to be at least three times
higher than that of their non-Indigenous counterparts in this age
group (ABS ). Many suicides may actually be mistaken for
accidental death (motor vehicle accidents, the result of combining
18
19


alcohol and drugs, or falls). Suicide may result from problems with
close relationships such as those with marriage partners or parents,
or from depression related to perceived occupational, academic or
financial failure. In general, suicide can result from the young adult’s
inability to cope with the pressures, responsibilities and expectations
of adulthood.
19 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018b). Causes of Deaths, Australia, 2017. Cat. no.
3303.0. Canberra: ABS.
The nurse’s role in the prevention of suicide includes identifying
behaviours that may indicate potential problems: depression; a
variety of physical complaints, including weight loss, sleep
disturbances and digestive disorders; and decreased interest in
social and work roles along with an increase in isolation. Nurses can
participate in educational programs that provide information and skill
development in assessing and identifying early signs of suicide. A
young adult identified as at risk for suicide should be referred to a
general practitioner (GP), the emergency department or a mental
health specialist. Most importantly, a suicide threat should never be
ignored and development of communication skills to make it easier
for young adults to discuss and seek help is critical for nurses in the
prevention of suicide.
Hypertension
Hypertension is a problem for young Australian adults and is listed
as one of the main problems managed by the GP (AIHW 2018a).
Many of the causes for this higher incidence of hypertension are


unknown. In addition to biological inheritance, contributing factors
may include smoking, obesity, a diet high in salt and high stress
levels. Hypertension is a major risk factor in the development of
stroke (cerebrovascular accidents) or chronic heart disease.
Indigenous Australians are diagnosed with hypertension 1.2 times
more commonly than non-Indigenous Australians (Australian
Indigenous HealthInfoNet 2016). Blood pressure measurements are
usually advised at least every 2 years for young adults to screen for
hypertension. Nurses can provide nutrition advice and referral to
relevant health professionals for those requiring further support in
addressing hypertension issues.
Diabetes
Diabetes is a chronic disease that can have severe complications. In
Australia, 30 543 people aged 21–39 are registered as having type 1
diabetes and 37 575 people aged 21–39 are registered as having
type 2 diabetes with the National Diabetes Services Scheme (NDSS)
(NDSS
). A person with diabetes is at greater risk of developing
cardiovascular, eye and kidney diseases and in 2017, diabetes
contributed to about 17 000 deaths in Australia (AIHW
). The
prevalence of diabetes has increased significantly over the past two
decades. However, since 2014–15, it has remained relatively stable
(ABS ). Worldwide, it is estimated that 1 in 11 adults have diabetes,
or 425 million people (International Diabetes Federation ).
20 National Diabetes Services Scheme (NDSS) (2019a). Type 1 Diabetes: As at 30 June
2019. Retrieved from <www.ndss.com.au>.
2021
22
23
24


21 National Diabetes Services Scheme (NDSS) (2019b). Type 2 Diabetes: As at 30 June
2019. Retrieved from <www.ndss.com.au>.
22 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019a). Diabetes. Cat. no. CVD 82.
Canberra: AIHW.
23 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018c). National Health Survey: First Results,
2017–18. Cat. no. 4364.0.55.001. Canberra: ABS.
24 International Diabetes Federation (2017). IDF Diabetes Atlas (8th ed.). Brussels, Belgium:
International Diabetes Federation.
Type 2 diabetes is most prevalent and more prominent in middle-
aged people, although in recent years it has started to appear in
adolescence. Type 1 diabetes is more common in childhood but can
occur at any age. The 2017–18 data indicates that there are more
males than females diagnosed with diabetes in the age range of 18
to 44 years (AIHW 2019a). The data also demonstrates a link
between low socioeconomic groups and an increase in diabetes; the
rates were around twice as high in this group. Furthermore, people
who lived in remote or very remote locations were two times more
likely to be hospitalised or die from diabetes than their city
counterparts (AIHW 2019a). Childbearing females in this age group
are also at risk of diabetes in pregnancy. In 2019, 40 799 women
registered as having gestational diabetes with NDSS and, of that
number, 37 364 were under 40 years old (NDSS ).
25 National Diabetes Services Scheme (NDSS) (2019c). Gestational Diabetes: As at 30 June
2019. Retrieved from <www.ndss.com.au>.
25


Women who have gestational diabetes are at a higher risk of
developing type 2 diabetes later in life than women who do not have
gestational diabetes (AIHW 2018a). Indigenous Australians are also
at least three times more affected than non-Indigenous Australians
(AIHW 2018a). The risk factors that contribute to diabetes include
being overweight and obese, being physically inactive and having
impaired glucose regulation. While diabetes is more prevalent in
people over 55 years, it is still important to monitor as the
occurrence of key risk factors, overweight and obesity, is increasing.
Of all adults aged 18 years or over in 2017–18, 36% were
overweight and 31% were obese (ABS 2018c). The diagnosis of
diabetes will increase as the numbers of young people being
overweight or obese increase, leading to a higher number of
individuals entering adulthood with a long-term chronic illness that
can lead to more serious health issues and disability. A diagnosis of
diabetes is likely to have an impact on their development and ability
to manage the many transitions, changes and adjustments
associated with young adulthood.
Nurses, alongside other health professionals, are well positioned to
instigate interventions that will increase awareness, detect and
diagnose diabetes early, manage care and support, and promote
research into finding a cure. Nurse strategies include remaining up
to date with current screening tools, prevention strategies and
treatment options. The nurse can assist the person with diabetes to
take responsibility and manage their diabetes self-care. By the nurse
developing an understanding of psychosocial factors that influence
young adults, coupled with knowledge of cultural influences and


barriers to healthy behaviour, the nurse will help ensure individuals
receive optimal care, education and support that is specific to their
needs.
Substance abuse
Substance abuse is a major threat to the health of young adults.
Substances used may be legal (such as tobacco, alcohol and
prescribed medications) or illegal (such as amphetamines or
opioids). Young adulthood is a time of many adjustments and
transitions, making it a vulnerable age for some individuals. This can
cause some young adults to seek these avenues to help them cope.
Substances such as alcohol, marijuana, amphetamines and cocaine
can bring about feelings of wellbeing that may be highly valued by
people with adjustment problems. The level of Australians who
smoked tobacco has remained stable over the past number of
years: 12.8% in 2013 to 12.2% in 2016. The most commonly used
illegal drugs are cannabis, cocaine, ecstasy and methamphetamines
(AIHW
). Methamphetamine, or ‘ice’, has significantly increased in
usage between 2010 (22%) and 2016 (57%) (AIHW 2017a).
26 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2017a). National Drug Strategy
Household Survey 2016: Detailed Findings. Drug statistics series no. 31. Cat. no. PHE 214.
Canberra: AIHW.
According to the 2016 National Drug Strategy Household Survey,
people in their early 20s had a significant decline in the number of
cigarettes smoked per week and were more likely than an older
person to have tried an e-cigarette (AIHW 2017a). In 2016, people
26


drinking at risky levels in the 18–24 years and 25–29 years age
groups were significantly less than in 2010 (AIHW 2017a). Alcohol is
associated with many serious social issues, such as violence, drink
driving and child abuse and neglect, as well as being a causative
factor in about 60 different heath conditions. In 2016, there was a
decline in the number of risky activities that people undertook when
drinking compared to previous data; for example, driving a motor
vehicle (12.2% to 9.9%), verbally abusing another person (4.0% to
2.7%), going swimming (7.5% to 6.5%) and physically abusing
another person (0.7% to 0.4%) (AIHW 2017a). There are also
marked differences in substance use for Indigenous Australians
compared with non-Indigenous Australians. The 2016 National Drug
Strategy Household Survey found that smoking and illicit drug use
by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people was higher than for
other Australians. Indigenous Australians were 2.3 times as likely as
non-Indigenous Australians to smoke tobacco daily and Indigenous
Australians used cannabis nearly twice as much as non-Indigenous
Australians (AIHW 2017a). Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people are less likely than non-Indigenous people to drink alcohol;
however, for those who do consume alcohol, they tend to do so at
harmful levels (AIHW 2017a).
Smoking and excessive alcohol consumption or binge drinking
continue to pose health risks for young adults. Prolonged use of
substances can lead to physical and psychological dependency and
subsequent health problems. For example, drug abuse during
pregnancy can lead to fetal damage/defects. Prolonged use of
alcohol can lead to such diseases as cirrhosis of the liver and cancer


of the oesophagus, and smoking is a known risk factor for all types
of cancer and chronic respiratory diseases such as emphysema.
Addiction, or physical and psychological dependence on a
substance, is related to properties of the substance, the individual
user and the social network of the person (Mathre ).
27 Mathre, M. L. (2016). Alcohol, tobacco and other drug problems. In M. Stanhope & J.
Lancaster (Eds), Public Health Nursing: Population-Centered Health Care in the Community
(9th ed.). St Louis, Missouri: Elsevier.
It is likely that nurses will come across people who have used
substances so it is important that the nurse consider the individual’s
personal and clinical implications associated with substance use.
Nursing strategies related to substance use include screening and
assessment of the young adult to detect problems early and assist
the young adult to access intervention services. For those nurses
providing care to young adults, having knowledge of health
promotion campaigns and available resources and support services
that can assist in managing situations leading to substance use is
important. Young adults who understand the effects and
consequences of substance abuse are more likely to change their
attitudes towards harmful substance use. The nurse may be able to
suggest resources or counselling services related to lifestyle and
behaviour modification for those who desire to cease substance use.
Sexually transmitted infection
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as genital herpes, HIV,
syphilis and gonorrhoea are common infections in young adults.
27


Chlamydia is the most prevalent STI in Australia, with those under
30 years being most at risk (Australian Sexual Health Alliance ).
The rates for STIs are much higher in the Indigenous population,
with infectious syphilis being six times higher, chlamydia three times
higher and gonorrhoea 10 times higher (The Kirby Institute ). Poor
access to health services, lack of awareness and stigma are some
of the reasons Indigenous people experience higher rates of STIs.
28 Australian Sexual Health Alliance (2018). Australian STI Management Guidelines for Use
in Primary Care: Chlamydia. Retrieved from <www.sti.guidelines.org.au>.
29 The Kirby Institute (2019). Sexually Transmissible Infections. Retrieved from
<www.kirby.unsw.edu.au>.
STIs can have a significant impact on a young adult’s ability to
achieve key milestones associated with young adulthood, such as
intimacy and finding a long-term partner, marriage and childbearing.
Some STIs, such as gonorrhoea, are becoming resistant to multiple
antibiotics and therefore cause long-term implications for future
health outcomes, growth and development; therefore, early
detection and treatment are important. Nursing functions are largely
educational and relate to safe sex practices, promotion of regular
health checks and provision of information on the disease,
transmission, management and consequences. Simple suggestions
such as the use of condoms can help reduce the transfer of
infectious microorganisms from one partner to another. Knowledge
about the symptoms of these diseases can help the individual obtain
early treatment. In dealing with young adults with an STI, the nurse
must be non-judgmental and accepting of individual lifestyle choices,
28
29


and treat any information obtained as confidential (see Chapter
41
).
Overweight, obesity and eating disorders
Either being underweight or having excess weight (overweight and
obesity) has associated health risks for young adults. In recent
years, excess weight rates have steadily increased and become a
major health issue for the Australian population, particularly adults,
with 63% of Australians aged 18 years and over being overweight or
obese (AIHW
). Prevalence of overweight and obesity for adults
living outside major cities is higher than those living in major cities,
for both men and women (AIHW 2017b).
30 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2017b). A Picture of Overweight and
Obesity in Australia 2017. Cat. no. PHE 216. Canberra: AIHW.
Excess weight affects a young adult’s psychosocial wellbeing and
increases the risk of developing chronic conditions, including
diabetes, cardiovascular disease, osteoarthritis and some cancers.
Obesity affects the whole life spectrum, and in Australia many key
primary health care initiatives are being aimed at the young (AIHW
2017b). Recommendations to address overweight and obesity
issues include up-skilling and supporting the public health workforce
to support individuals in making healthier choices, become more
self-reliant and manage their own health care needs. Some
examples of projects and social marketing campaigns are The
National Healthy School Canteens Project, Kids at Play, Healthy
30


Workers Project and Girls Make Your Move Campaign (AIHW
2017b).
Eating disorders such as bulimia and anorexia are also major health
issues for young adults. Being underweight results in a number of
poor health outcomes, including dental problems, dehydration,
fertility problems, impaired kidney function and sometimes death
(Butterfly Foundation for Eating Disorders ). It is hard to determine
how many Australians are affected by eating disorders; however, it is
estimated to be around 4% of the total population, or approximately
1 million people (Butterfly Foundation for Eating Disorders 2019).
31 Butterfly Foundation for Eating Disorders (2019). Understanding Eating Disorders.
Retrieved from <www.thebutterflyfoundation.org.au>.
Nutritional assessment, including physical, psychosocial, cultural,
lifestyle and behavioural aspects, is fundamental in identifying and
addressing nutritional status. Being responsive to individual
differences, stage of life, cultural diversity and a person’s
preferences is important. The nurse can assess nutritional concerns
and discuss diet and exercise patterns with the young adult for the
subsequent development of an individualised wellness plan. It is
important that nurses have knowledge of nutritional and exercise
requirements and can share information about the consequences of
being underweight or overweight with this age group. As well, the
nurse needs to understand the physical changes that may affect
nutritional status during young adulthood. Specific areas of
nutritional needs particularly for young women, such as meeting
calcium requirements and proper nutrition during the childbearing
31


years, are also important aspects to consider and discuss (see
Chapter 50
).
Abuse of women
The problem of battering or abuse of women affects families at all
socioeconomic levels. Violence against women is a significant
financial burden for the Australian government, state and territory
governments, costing $4.1 billion in 2015–16 (KPMG
). The first
National Plan to Reduce Violence against Women and their Children
was introduced in Australia in 2011. It is a long-term plan (ends
2022) and targets both domestic and family violence as well as
sexual assault (Department of Social Services (DSS)
). In 2019, the
fourth and final action phrase of the plan commenced (DSS 2019).
Nurses need to become familiar with health policy screening tools
and guidelines for assessing and managing domestic violence, and
community resources such as adult protective services, shelters,
LifeLine and Relationships Australia, advocacy programs, victim
assistance programs and hotlines. A nurse can explicitly ask about
safety issues or whether the woman is frightened or hurt by
someone they know (Ali ).
32 KPMG (2016). The Cost of Violence against Women and Their Children in Australia: Final
Report. Retrieved from <www.dss.gov.au>.
33 Department of Social Services (DSS) (2019). The National Plan to Reduce Violence
against Women and Their Children 2010–2022. Retrieved from <www.dss.gov.au>.
32
33
34


34 Ali, P. (2018). Gender-based violence and the role of healthcare professionals. Nursing
Open, 5(1), 4–5. Doi. 10.1002/nop2.120.
Stresses that predispose families to abuse may include financial
problems, separation from family and community support, and
physical as well as social isolation. Intimate partner violence is a
leading cause of illness, disability and premature death for women
aged 18–44 years (Ayre et al.
). In Australia, 1 in 4 women have
experienced emotional abuse by a current or former partner since
the age of 15 years and 1 in 5 have been the victim of sexual
violence (ABS ). Indigenous women are 32 times more likely to end
up in hospital because of family violence (AIHW
).
35 Ayre, J., Lum On, M., Webster, K., Gourley, M. & Moon, L. (2016). Examination of the
Burden of Disease of Intimate Partner Violence against Women in 2011: Final Report. Sydney:
Australia’s National Research Organisation for Women’s Safety (ANROWS).
36 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2017b). Personal Safety Survey. Cat. no. 4906.3
Canberra: ABS.
37 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018b). Family, Domestic and Sexual
Violence in Australia 2018. Cat. no. FDV 2. Canberra: AIHW.
Cancer
Cancer is a major cause of illness in Australia and accounts for 3 in
10 deaths (AIHW
). In 2019, the most commonly diagnosed
cancers in Australia were cancer of the breast, prostate, colorectal,
melanoma of the skin and lung (AIHW 2019b). Even though cancer
is not common in people aged 25–49, it is estimated there were
35
36
37
38


16 715 new cases of cancer in this age group in 2019 (AIHW
2019b). For this age group, breast cancer is estimated to be the
most common cancer diagnosis in 2019, followed by melanoma of
the skin and colorectal cancer (AIHW 2019b).
38 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019b). Cancer in Australia 2019.
Cancer series no. 119. Cat. no. CAN 123. Canberra: AIHW.
Melanoma of the skin is the fourth most common cancer diagnosed
in Australia. Australia, along with New Zealand, has the highest
incidence of melanoma in the world (AIHW 2019b; Cancer Council
Australia (CCA)
). While generally the highest prevalence is noted
in older adults, incidence increases with age, making this a health
risk for young and middle-aged adults. For more than a decade,
much has been done to educate the Australian public about the
harmful effects of the sun. Health prevention messages aimed at
preventing skin cancers include: avoiding the sun, especially in the
middle of the day; covering up or seeking shade; applying sun
protection factor 30+ sunscreen regularly; wearing a hat that covers
the head, neck and ears; wearing protective close-fitting sunglasses;
and avoiding solariums (CCA 2019a).
39 Cancer Council Australia (CCA) (2019a). Melanoma. Retrieved from <www.cancer.org.
au>.
Cervical cancer also continues to be an important consideration in
the health of young adult women. Greater awareness, improved
screening and early detection have led to a drop in the prevalence of
cervical cancer over the past two decades, but it continues to be a
39


health risk (AIHW 2019b). The national cervical screening program
originally targeted adult women aged 20–69 years, 2 yearly, but at
the end of 2017, changed the screening protocol to 5 yearly and
amended the age range to 25 to 74 years. The new Cervical
Screening Test
 was implemented due to the introduction of the
human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination program in 2007, as well as
having more effective testing techniques. The new cervical
screening test detects the HPV, whereas the Papanicolaou (Pap)
smear
 only looked at cell changes in the cervix (AIHW 2019b).
Participation in cervical screening is vital and education targeting this
age group is required to improve screening rates. Many young
adults are reluctant to have screenings; therefore, it is important for
nurses to promote and encourage women to have cervical screening
testing performed as recommended, to explain the purpose of the
test and to encourage all young women to begin this preventive
measure by 25 years of age. For more information on the vaginal
exam, see Chapter 31
.
When working with young adults, the nurse needs to be aware of
high-risk factors for cervical cancer, which include sexual activity at
an early age, multiple sexual partners or a history of syphilis, herpes
genitalis or Trichomonas vaginitis.
While treatments and survival rates are improving, some sections of
the Australian population have poorer survival rates and cancer
outcomes. These include Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islanders, those
who are socioeconomically disadvantaged and those living in
regional and remote areas (AIHW 2019b).


With better diagnostic methods, earlier detection and improvements
in treatment, more than half of all cancers diagnosed in Australia are
successfully treated. In 2011–15 in Australia, the 5-year survival rate
for all cancers combined was 69% (AIHW 2019b). This survival rate
improved from 50% in 1986–90. The earlier a cancer is discovered,
the greater the effectiveness of treatment. Screening for cancers
and public awareness campaigns are key preventive mechanisms
targeting early detection of cancers. The most prominent national
population-based screening programs for cancer screening in
Australia are for bowel (National Bowel Cancer Screening Program)
breast (BreastScreen Australia) and cervical cancer (National
Cervical Screening Program).
While screening programs for bowel, breast and prostate cancer are
targeted at those aged 40 years and over (middle-aged adults), this
does not exclude young adults. Breast cancer is rare under the age
of 25 but can occur at any age (CCA ), making it vital to educate
young adults about the risk factors and encourage them to discuss
these with a health professional and to be screened if required. For
young adult women in high-risk groups for breast cancer, screening
by computed tomography (CT) and/or magnetic resonance imaging
(MRI) can be used (CCA 2019b). In addition to this, an annual
breast exam performed by a doctor is also recommended, but
breast self-exam is no longer recommended for all women.
40 Cancer Council Australia (CCA) (2019b). Breast Cancer. Retrieved from
<www.cancer.org. au>.
40


Nurses need to be aware of potential malignancies young adults
could face, cancer risk factors and the available screening and
health promotion measures specifically aimed at young adults. For
detailed information on cancer screening, see Chapter 31
. It is
important that young adults are encouraged to have regular health
checks and report unusual or abnormal symptoms to their health
practitioner. Identifying malignancies early and managing them
effectively can avoid long-term consequences and poor health
outcomes that may disrupt development and impact on future
health.
Health assessment and promotion
Assessment guidelines for the growth and development of the young
adult are shown in the accompanying ‘Developmental assessment
guidelines
’. Young adults are in the prime of their physical health;
therefore, this period provides the platform for developing
behaviours that can reduce health risks in later life. Generally, they
are interested in meeting their health needs. Due to the many
stresses and changes that occur throughout this 20-year period, the
nurse may need to offer information and guidance in several health
care areas. During a health assessment, considering individual
preferences, socioeconomic and cultural factors, as well as an
individual’s knowledge and attitude about health can affect the
choices the young adult makes in the developing health-protective
behaviours. The nurse may wish to discuss some or all of the health


promotion topics outlined in Box 23.2
. These topics are discussed
in detail in subsequent chapters throughout the book.

The young adult

Middle-aged adults (40 to
65 years)
The middle years, from 40 to 65, have been called the years of
stability and consolidation. Middle-aged adults may experience
changing responsibilities and have greater self-satisfaction. For
most, it is a time when children have grown and moved away or are
moving away from home. Thus, partners generally have more time
for and with each other and time to pursue interests they may have
deferred for years (see Figure 23.2
). A number of relationship
changes and transitions can occur during middle age. These may
include changes as a result of divorce, sexuality issues, remarriage
and grandparenting. Some individuals may change their careers as
a result of reassessing unaccomplished goals or financial
achievements. Thus, this period can often become a time of career
and financial readjustment for both men and women. Specific
challenges may also arise as a result of children leaving the home,
while others may be dealing with late parenting.
Figure 23.2


Middle-aged adults often have more time available to pursue
interests and hobbies once their children are older and more
independent.
Source: PaylessImages/123RF.
Most middle-aged adults are said to have reached maturity.
Maturity
 is the state of maximal function and integration, or the
state of being fully developed. Many other characteristics are
generally recognised as representative of maturity. Mature
individuals are guided by an underlying philosophy of life. They take
many perspectives into account and are tolerant of the views of
others. A comprehensive philosophy allows a person to make sense
out of life and thus helps that person maintain a sense of purpose
and hope in the face of human tragedies. Mature people are open to
new experiences and continued growth; they can tolerate ambiguity,
are flexible and can adapt to change. In addition, mature people
have the quality of self-acceptance; they are able to be reflective
and insightful about life and to see themselves as others see them.
Mature people also assume responsibility for themselves and expect
others to do the same. They confront the tasks of life in a realistic
and mature manner, make decisions and accept responsibility for
those decisions.
Physical development
A number of changes that start when young adults are in their mid-
20s become noticeable as the fifth decade approaches. At 40, most


adults can function as effectively as they did in their 20s; however,
during ages 40 to 65 many physical changes take place that may
affect functional capacity. These are summarised in Table 23.1
.
Table 23.1 Physical changes of the middle-aged adult
Both men and women experience decreasing hormonal production
during the middle years. For women, one of the most significant
physical changes occurs with menopause
, or the so-called
change of life, when menstruation ceases. It is said to have
occurred when a woman has not had a menstrual period for 12
months. Menopause usually occurs some time between ages 45 and
55; the average is about 51 years of age (Australasian Menopause
Society ). At this time, ovarian activity declines until ovulation
ceases. Common symptoms, related to a decline in oestrogen, are
hot flushes, chills, a tendency of the breasts to become smaller and
less dense and a decrease in metabolic rate that may lead to weight
gain. Insomnia and headaches may also occur (Australasian
Menopause Society 2019). Psychologically, menopause can be an
anxiety-producing time, especially if the ability to bear children is an
integral part of the woman’s self-concept. For other women,
menopause may produce few symptoms, physically or
psychologically.
42 Australasian Menopause Society (2019). Fact Sheets. Retrieved from
<www.menopause.org.au>.
Sexual arousal in both men and women takes longer after midlife
than in younger adulthood. In men, there is no change comparable
42


to the menopause in women, although the term climacteric
(andropause) has been used to denote the change in sexual
response in men. Androgen levels decrease very slowly; however,
men can father children even in late life. Some men may have
difficulties achieving sexual arousal for psychological reasons, such
as anxiety. See Chapter 41
 for further details about sexual health.
Psychosocial development
Before the mid-1990s, the developmental tasks of middle-aged
adults received little attention. Havighurst (1972) outlined seven
tasks for this age group (see Box 23.3
). Erikson (1963) viewed
the developmental choice of the middle-aged adult as generativity
versus stagnation. Generativity
 is defined as the concern for
establishing and guiding the next generation. In other words, the
concern about providing for the welfare of humankind is equal to the
concern of providing for self. People in their 20s and 30s tend to be
self and family centred. In middle age, the individual collaborates
with others (Murray et al. 2014). Marriage partners have more time
for companionship and recreation; thus, marriage may be more
satisfying in the middle years of life. Partners have time to work
together in volunteer activities and hobbies or have the time to focus
on their own individual pursuits. Generative middle-aged people are
able to feel a sense of comfort in their lifestyle and receive
gratification from charitable endeavours.

23.3 Psychosocial development:
middle-aged adult
The middle-aged adult
Is in the generativity versus stagnation phase of
Erikson’s  stages of development.
43 Erikson, E. H. (1982). The Life Cycle Completed: A Review. New York:
Norton.
According to Havighurst (1972), has the following
developmental tasks:
achieving adult civic and social responsibility
reaching and maintaining satisfactory performance in
one’s occupational career
assisting teenage children to become responsible and
happy adults
developing adult leisure-time activities
relating oneself to one’s spouse as a person
accepting and adjusting to the physiological changes of
middle age
adjusting to ageing parents.
According to Slater
, has the additional developmental
tasks of:
43
44


44 Slater, C. L. (2003). Generativity versus stagnation: An elaboration of
Erikson’s adult stage of human development. Journal of Adult Development, 10,
53–65.
inclusivity versus exclusivity
pride versus embarrassment (in children, work or
creativity)
responsibility versus ambivalence (making choices
about commitments)
career productivity versus inadequacy
parenthood versus self-absorption
being needed versus alienation
honesty versus denial (with oneself).
Erikson (1963; 1982) wrote that people who are unable to expand
their interests at this time and who do not assume the
responsibilities of middle age suffer a sense of boredom and
impoverishment; that is, stagnation. These people have difficulty
accepting their ageing bodies and become withdrawn and isolated.
They are preoccupied with self and unable to give to others. Some
may regress to younger patterns of behaviour; for example,
adolescent behaviour.
Middle adulthood is the time when most people become increasingly
aware of the gradual changes in their bodies that mark the ageing
process. People usually accept the fact that they are ageing;
however, some try to defy the years by changing their dress and
even their actions. A new freedom to be independent and follow


one’s individual interests arises. Prior to this period, the marriage
partner or lover and other people were crucial to a definition of self.
Now the middle-aged person does not make comparisons with
others, often no longer fears ageing or death, relaxes the sense of
competitiveness and enjoys the independence and freedom of
middle age. Other people’s opinions become less important and the
earlier habit of trying to please everyone is overcome. The person
establishes ethical and moral standards that are independent of the
standards of others. The focus shifts from inner self and being to
others and doing. Religious and philosophical concerns become
important.
The ‘midlife crisis’ is a popular idea and one that is the source of
many jokes and humorous anecdotes. This crisis occurs when
individuals recognise that they have reached the halfway mark of
life. Midlifers begin to recognise that time is at a premium and that
life is finite. Youthfulness and physical strength can no longer be
taken for granted.
Cognitive development
The middle-aged adult’s cognitive and intellectual abilities change
very little. Cognitive processes include reaction time, memory,
perception, learning, problem solving and creativity. Reaction time
during the middle years stays much the same or diminishes during
the later part of the middle years. Memory and problem solving are


maintained through middle adulthood. Learning continues and can
be enhanced by increased motivation at this time in life.
Genetic, environmental and personality factors in early and middle
adulthood account for the large difference in the ways in which
individuals maintain mental abilities (Murray et al. 2014). The
experiences of the professional, social and personal life of middle-
aged people will be reflected in their cognitive performance. Thus,
approaches to problem solving and task completion will vary
considerably in a middle-aged group.
Moral development
According to Kohlberg (1981; 1984), the adult can move beyond the
conventional level to the post-conventional level (see
Chapter 22
). Kohlberg believed that extensive experience of
personal moral choice and responsibility is required before people
can reach the post-conventional level. Kohlberg found that few of his
subjects achieved the highest level of moral reasoning. To move
from stage 4, a law-and-order orientation, to stage 5, a social
contract orientation, requires that the individual move to a stage in
which rights of others take precedence. Research demonstrates that
moral development continues through adulthood and that few
individuals attain stage 5 before age 40 (Dawson ).
45 Dawson, T. L. (2002). New tools, new insights: Kohlberg’s moral judgement stages
revisited. International Journal of Behavioral Development, 26(2), 154–166.
45


Spiritual development
Not all adults progress through to Fowler’s  fifth stage called the
paradoxical–consolidative stage. At this stage, the individual can
view ‘truth’ from a number of viewpoints. Fowler’s fifth stage
corresponds to Kohlberg’s fifth stage of moral development. Fowler
believes that only some individuals after the age of 30 years reach
this stage.
46 Fowler, J. W. (1981). Stages of Faith: The Psychology of Human Development and the
Quest for Meaning. New York: Harper & Row.
In middle age, people tend to be less dogmatic about religious
beliefs and religion often offers more comfort to the middle-aged
person than it did previously. People in this age group often rely on
spiritual beliefs to help them deal with illness, death and tragedy.
Health problems
Many middle-aged adults remain healthy; however, due to general
physical and functional decline associated with ageing, the risk of
developing a health problem is greater than for the young adult. As
age increases, causes of death are more likely to relate to chronic
conditions such as heart disease and cancers. According to the
AIHW (2018a), leading causes of burden for middle-aged adults
aged 45–64 years include coronary heart disease, osteoarthritis and
46


other musculoskeletal, back pain and problems, lung cancer and
anxiety disorders. Vision and hearing changes also start to affect
people in this age group more profoundly. Leading causes of death
in the 45–64 age group include coronary heart disease, lung cancer,
suicide, breast cancer and colorectal cancer (AIHW 2018a). Again,
variations are seen with Indigenous populations where cultural,
socioeconomic and lifestyle factors greatly influence outcomes
(AIHW 2018a).
Injuries
Changing physiological factors, as well as concern over personal
and work-related responsibilities, may contribute to the injury rate of
middle-aged people. Decreased reaction times and visual acuity may
make the middle-aged adult prone to injury. Motor vehicle accidents
are the most common cause of unintentional death in this age
group. Other unintentional causes of death for middle-aged adults
include falls, fires, burns, poisonings and drowning. Across this age
group, males were involved in more injury-related deaths than
females. Work-related injuries continue to be a significant safety
hazard during the middle years. Intentional self-harm (suicide) is
also a problem for this group; however, more so for those in early
middle adulthood (45−54 years). In 2017, the median age of death
from suicide was 44.0 years for males and 45.7 years for females
(ABS 2018b). Physiological and developmental transitions can
increase stress levels and create altered mental states such as
anxiety and depression—known risk factors for suicide.


Cancer
Cancer accounts for considerable mortality and morbidity in both
men and women in this age group. It was estimated that 16 715 new
cases of cancer were diagnosed in people aged 50–64 years in 2019
(AIHW 2019b). Breast cancer is the most common cancer for this
age group, followed by prostate cancer and melanoma of the skin
(AIHW 2019b). The large number of cancers diagnosed in this age
group is often attributed to the improved screening and detection
programs that are now in place, such as BreastScreen Australia.
Screening initiatives, while not the only way to detect cancers, are
important strategies in the early detection and treatment of cancer
for middle-aged adults. Women between the ages of 25 and 74 are
advised to have a Cervical Screening Test every 5 years; this has
replaced the Pap smear test. Mammographic screening for breast
cancer is available to women from 40 years of age; women aged
50−74 years are invited every 2 years for a free mammogram
(Department of Health ). Those aged 50–74 are recommended to
screen for bowel cancer with a faecal occult blood test every 2
years; this test will be free for all Australians every 2 years from
2020 (CCA ).
47 Department of Health (2016). BreastScreen Australia. Retrieved from
<www.cancerscreening.gov.au>.
48 Cancer Council Australia (CCA) (2019c). Bowel Cancer. Retrieved from
<www.cancer.org. au>.
47
48


Currently, there is no population-based screening for prostate
cancer, as testing measures are not definitive of a diagnosis and
therefore not effective for population-based screening; however,
tests are available that may help pick up the disease (CCA ). Public
awareness campaigns for early detection focus on raising
awareness of risk factors such as family history, providing
information on the possible symptoms of prostate cancer and the
importance of regular health checks and reporting of unusual
symptoms. Nurses can work with middle-aged adults to encourage
participation in regular screening, attending regular health checks
and reducing known risk factors for cancer such as smoking. CCA
has a helpful website (see Web links
 at the end of the chapter).
49 Cancer Council Australia (CCA) (2019d). Prostate Cancer. Retrieved from
<www.cancer.org. au>.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Partnering with Consumers
The intention of this standard is ‘to create an organisation in
which there are mutually beneficial outcomes by having:
consumers as partners in planning, design, delivery,
measurement and evaluation of systems and services; and
patients as partners in their own care, to the extent that they
choose’ (Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in
Health Care
, p. 14).
49
50


50 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved by
involving people who have been diagnosed with
cancer, their families and loved ones in the
decision making about their care so that the
care is responsive to the needs and inputs of
the person and/or their family.
Cancer affects many people directly and
indirectly. A diagnosis of cancer will affect every
aspect of a person’s life. Providing the person
who has cancer with a ‘toolkit’ of resources will
empower them to better care for themselves.
There is an excellent consumer involvement
toolkit available on the Cancer Australia website.
People living with cancer have provided
feedback and suggestions that have led to
major improvements in quality and safety, which
is precisely what this standard espouses.
Cardiovascular disease
Coronary heart disease (CHD), or ischaemic heart disease (IHD), is
the leading cause of burden in adults aged 45–64 (AIHW 2018a).


Several factors contribute to risk of CHD. These include smoking,
obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes mellitus, sedentary
lifestyle, a family history of myocardial infarction or sudden death in
a father less than 55 years old or in a mother less than 65 years old,
and the individual’s age. A recognised cluster of risk factors that
often occur together, termed metabolic syndrome, increases the risk
for CHD. This syndrome includes the following risk factors:
excessive abdominal fat, hypertension, high lipid levels and insulin
resistance. Lifestyle modifications, such as healthy diet with caloric
restriction and increase in exercise, can help prevent the
development of metabolic syndrome (Dietitians Association of
Australia (DAA)
).
51 Dietitians Association of Australia (DAA) (2019). What Is Metabolic Syndrome? Retrieved
from <www.daa.asn.au>.
Men over 45 years of age and women over 55 years of age are at
greater risk of developing CHD than younger adults. Physical
inactivity places individuals at greater risk of developing CHD and
midlife adults should be helped to incorporate some physical activity
in activities of daily living. Recent statistics indicate that prevalence
of two risk factors, diabetes and obesity, has increased particularly
for middle-aged adults. This puts them at greater risk of the
development of cardiovascular disease and disability associated with
chronic illness in later life (AIHW 2018a).
Research note
51


Stroke care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
peoples: culturally responsive and inclusive care
R. Quigley, J. Mann, J. Robertson, S. Bonython-Ericson
. Are we there yet? Exploring the journey to
quality stroke care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in rural and remote Queensland.
Rural and Remote Health, 19(3), 4850. Doi: org/10.22605/RRH4850.
52 Quigley, R., Mann, J., Robertson, J. & Bonython-Ericson, S. (2019). Are we there yet? Exploring
the journey to quality stroke care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in rural and remote
Queensland. Rural and Remote Health, 19(3), 4850. Doi: org/10.22605/RRH4850.
The aim of this study was to identify the needs of Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander stroke survivors who live in rural
and remote Queensland and to develop a model of care
responsive to those needs. The study site was Far north
Queensland; 18 diverse communities agreed to participate in
the study. Participants included stroke survivors, carers and
stakeholders. Key findings of this study include: the care
needs to be inclusive and culturally responsive to the patient,
the family and community; an Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander liaison officer should be included as a vital member
of the multidisciplinary team; and wherever possible, an
appropriate language interpreter should be sought to assist
with health literacy and advocacy.
Implications Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are
more likely than non-Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people to have a stroke at a younger age and it is twice as
likely the stroke will result in death. Nurses need to involve
the family in all stages of the stroke recovery process to best
support the person and help reduce associated disability.
52


Nurses should advocate for an Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander heath worker to be part of the multidisciplinary team
and work collaboratively to provide culturally responsive care
to the stroke survivor and their family. Information and
education need to be provided to the stroke survivor, the
family and community and shared in a way that is
understandable and crosses language barriers. It is important
to provide ongoing support to the person, their family and the
community after the person is discharged from hospital.
Patient safety competency framework
4 Teamwork and collaborative practice
Caring for people with chronic illnesses requires
a team approach. Nurses need to work in
partnership with patients, doctors, allied health
professionals, families and communities to
deliver person-centred, culturally responsive
care. Nurses should seek and value the
perspective of all team members and ensure
clear communication and reporting lines are in
place to avoid misunderstandings between team
members (Levett-Jones et al.
).
53 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
53


Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Overweight and obesity
Similar to young adults, obesity in middle-aged adults has become a
major public health challenge for Australia, reflecting worldwide
trends in obesity for developed countries (AIHW 2017b). Australians
in their 50s and 60s are gaining weight as they gain years. Women
aged 55–64 years are more likely than men to be obese. Waist
circumference tends to increase for both men and women with age,
with approximately 77% of men and 81% of women aged 55 years
having a waist circumference that puts them at risk for poor health
(AIHW 2017b). Overweight and obesity increases the likelihood of
developing some cancers, CHD, back pain and problems, dementia,
diabetes, osteoarthritis and chronic kidney disease (AIHW 2017b).
Middle-aged adults who gain weight may not be aware of some
common facts about this age period. Decreased metabolic activity
and decreased physical activity mean a decrease in caloric need.
The Australian Dietary Guidelines, as recommended by the DAA ,
encourage nutrient intake based on physical activity, age and gender
and guidance on a healthy diet. The nurse’s role in nutritional health
promotion is to encourage individuals to prevent obesity by providing
information on life-stage changes and to find avenues to reduce
kilojoule intake and participate in regular exercise. Identifying
54


personal and cultural factors that affect nutrition is important in
ensuring wellness plans target individual lifestyles. Highlighting the
risks associated with being overweight, such as the potential to
develop a chronic illness, reduced mobility and physical functioning,
needs to be incorporated into discussions about health care needs
and choices. Middle-aged adults can be directed to the DAA website
(see Web links
 at the end of this chapter) to design a
customised, healthy diet plan for themselves. While it is important
that middle-aged adults are self-sufficient and direct their own health
care, medical advice should be sought before considering any major
changes in their diets.
54 Dietitians Association of Australia (DAA) (2018). The Australian Dietary Guidelines.
Retrieved from <www.daa.asn.au>.
Alcoholism
The excessive use of alcohol is a prominent health risk in Australia
and can result in unemployment, disrupted homes, injuries and
diseases. There has been a significant increase in alcohol
consumption for people aged 50–59 years; there was nearly a 3%
increase between 2013 and 2016 of people in this age group
consuming 11 or more standard drinks on a single occasion (AIHW
2017a). Women in their 50s are now more likely than those in their
late teens or early 20s to drink at risky levels (AIHW 2017a).
Nursing strategies related to alcohol use include screening and
assessment similar to those explained earlier in the chapter for


young adults. Identifying problems early and enabling adults to
access interventions and support services is a key factor. Being
knowledgeable on guidelines related to alcohol consumption and the
health risks associated with drinking at various levels can help
nurses provide individual support with specific health needs. Nurses
can provide middle-aged adults with general information about the
dangers of excessive alcohol use and, where appropriate, refer
them to relevant health professionals for specialised support. For
early-stage alcohol problems, using brief interventions as a
preventive measure can help to reduce the need for later treatment
and reduce the risk of developing chronic conditions associated with
long-term alcohol consumption.
Mental health alterations
Developmental stressors, such as the menopause, the climacteric,
ageing and impending retirement, and situational stressors, such as
divorce, unemployment and death of a spouse, can precipitate
increased anxiety and depression in middle-aged adults. Individuals
may benefit from support groups or individual therapy to help them
cope with specific crises. Discussing lifestyle choices and health
behaviours, providing information on available support networks and
other resources allows middle-aged adults the opportunity to choose
avenues that suit their individual needs. Understanding an
individual’s personal circumstances, lifestyle and culture will help the
nurse direct conversation about mental health alterations towards
achieving outcomes that best meet their personal circumstances.


Health assessment and promotion
Assessment guidelines for the growth and development of the
middle-aged adult are shown in the accompanying ‘Developmental
assessment guidelines
’. Middle-aged adults usually take care of
their health needs and are interested in maintaining health and
preventing the acceleration of the ageing process.
The nurse may choose to discuss some or all of the health
promotion topics with the middle-aged adult (see Box 23.4
).
These topics are discussed in detail in subsequent chapters
throughout the book.
BO X
23.4 Health promotion guidelines for
middle-aged adults
Health tests and screening
Physical examination (every 1 to 5 years until age 40,
then annually).
Immunisations: 65 years and over: pneumococcal
vaccine (Pneumovax 23 ) and annual influenza
vaccination. Also, as recommended: tetanus–diphtheria–
®


pertussis boosters (Boostrix  or Adacel ) (Department of
Health 2019).
Regular dental assessments (e.g. every 6 to 12 months).
Tonometry for signs of glaucoma and other eye diseases
every 2 to 3 years or annually if indicated.
Breast examination annually by health practitioner.
Testicular examination annually by health practitioner.
Screenings for cardiovascular disease (e.g. blood
pressure measurement, electrocardiogram and
cholesterol test as directed by the health practitioner).
Screenings for colorectal, breast, cervical, uterine and
prostate cancer (see cancer screening guidelines in
Chapter 31
).
Screening for type 2 diabetes.
Smoking: history and counselling, if needed.
Safety
Motor vehicle safety reinforcement, especially when
driving at night.
Workplace safety measures.
Home safety measures: keeping hallways and stairways
well lit and uncluttered, using smoke detectors, using non-
slip mats and handrails in the bathrooms.
Nutrition and exercise
®
®


Importance of adequate protein, calcium and vitamin D in
diet.
Nutritional and exercise factors that may lead to
cardiovascular disease (e.g. obesity, cholesterol and fat
intake, lack of vigorous exercise).
An exercise program that emphasises skill and
coordination.
Social interactions
The possibility of a midlife crisis: encourage discussion of
feelings, concerns and fears.
Providing time to expand and review previous interests.
Retirement planning (financial and possible diversional
activities), with partner if appropriate.
Developmental assessment
guidelines
The middle-aged adult
In these three developmental areas, does the middle-aged
adult do the following?


Physical development
Exhibit weight within normal range for age and sex.
Manifest vital signs (e.g. blood pressure) within normal
range for age and sex.
Manifest visual and hearing abilities within normal range.
Exhibit appropriate knowledge and attitudes about
sexuality (e.g. about menopause).
Verbalise any changes in eating, elimination or exercise.
Psychosocial development
Accept ageing body.
Feel comfortable and respect self.
Enjoy new freedom to be independent.
Accept changes in family roles (e.g. having teenage
children and ageing parents).
Interact effectively and share companionable activities
with life partner.
Expand and renew previous interests.
Pursue charitable and altruistic activities.
Have a meaningful philosophy of life.
Development in activities of daily living
Follow preventive health practices.


Case study
Daniel Graham, a 22-year-old plumber, comes into a health
centre for a ‘physical’. He states that the last time he saw a
health care provider was during high school and he is only
here today because his employer required that he be
examined prior to returning to work. Mr Graham has been off
the job for 2 weeks following an accident in which he fell off a
ladder, sustaining multiple contusions and a concussion. He
mentions that he and ‘his mates’ have enjoyed his 2 weeks
off from work and have used the time to ‘drink beer and
chase women’.

Chapter 23 Review


Chapter highlights
Five distinct generations are included in adulthood: Baby
Boomers, Generation Xers Generation Ys, Generation Zs and
Generation Alphas. Each has its own world view.
Emerging and young adults develop a self-identity and prepare
for intimate relationships with others.
Moral development continues throughout adulthood.
Health risks for young adults are primarily related to lifestyle and
behaviour.
Midlife adults begin to notice physical changes associated with
ageing.
The developmental issue for midlife adults is generativity.
Adults in midlife must balance the needs of many, including their
own parents and children.
Health decisions made by midlife adults may affect their health in
later life.
A variety of health threats, including cancer and heart disease,
begin to affect people in their middle age.
Physical activity, healthy nutrition choices and routine care by a
health provider are important throughout the adult years.

In 2017, approximately 3.8 million (15%) of the
Australian population were aged 65 years or
over; this number is expected to more than
double to approximately 8.9 million (21%) by
2066 (Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) ).
The ABS (2018) further projects that people

by 2042 and close to 2 million (3.6%) by 2066.
1 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018). Population

Canberra: ABS.
At the end of 2018, the Australian government
announced a Royal Commission into Aged Care
Quality and Safety. The final report was due to
be released at the end of 2020.
1


Characteristics of older adults in
Australia
Older adults represent an increasingly diverse population in
Australia. A review of the major characteristics of the older
population includes demographic, socioeconomic, cultural and
linguistic profile and health characteristics.
Demographic
At one time, all individuals over the age of 65 were considered old.
With advancements in disease control, living conditions and health
technology, people are living longer. On average, men and women
aged 65 years in 2014–16 can expect to live to around 85 years and
87 years respectively (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare
(AIHW) ). Life expectancy for non-Indigenous Australian males born
in 2015–17 is 80.5 years and for females is 84.6 years; in contrast,
the life expectancy for Indigenous males born in 2015–17 is 71.6
years and for females is 75.6 years—this equates to, on average, 9
years less (AIHW ). People aged 85 years and over are the fastest
growing of all age groups in the country, with the number predicted
to increase from 493 000 in 2017 to 1.0 million by 2036 and 2.0
million by 2062 (ABS 2018). Because chronic illness and disability
2
3


increase in this age group, there will be a corresponding need for an
increase in services and government funding to support the ageing
population. Older adults are as heterogeneous as any other age
group that spans 40 years or more. As a result, there are three
categories to describe the older population, each one having a
distinct set of interests and health care needs. See Box 24.1
2 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018). Older Australia at a Glance. Cat.
no. AGE 87. Canberra: AIHW. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
3 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019a). Deaths in Australia. Cat. no. PHE
229. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
BO X
24.1 Categorising the ageing
population
1. Young-old: 65 to 74 years.
2. Old: 75 to 84 years.
3. Oldest-old: 85+ years.
Source: C. Eliopoulos . Gerontological Nursing (9th ed.). Philadelphia, PA: Wolters Kluwer.
4 Eliopoulos, C. (2018). Gerontological Nursing (9th ed.). Philadelphia, PA: Wolters Kluwer.
4


Socioeconomic
Socioeconomic characteristics such as gender, marital status,
education, income and living arrangements vary in people over 65
years old (AIHW 2018). Women outnumber men—over half of older
Australians aged 65 and over are women (AIHW 2018). With the
increase in life expectancy for men in recent years, this is expected
to even out in future years (AIHW 2018).
Level of education can affect the socioeconomic status of the older
adult. Higher education is usually associated with higher incomes.
According to Hunter , educational levels for older adults are
gradually increasing, as indicated by the increasing percentage rates
of people 65 years and older who have completed high school.
However, there is significant variation among cultural and
linguistically diverse (CALD) groups. Usually, older adults have lower
incomes than younger adults and people 65 years and older have
the lowest median income (ABS ).
5 Hunter, S. (2015). Miller’s Nursing for Wellness in Older Adults (2nd Australian and New
Zealand ed.). Sydney: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins Australia.
6 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2019). Householder Income and Wealth, Australia,
2017–2018. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov>.
Living arrangements of older adults are linked not only to income,
but also to health status. In 2016, 68% of older people aged 65–74
lived with a spouse or partner in a private dwelling, while people
5
6


aged 85 years and over were more likely to live alone (35%) (ABS ).
Older women were more likely than older men to live alone,
especially for the 85 years and over age group (ABS 2017). Most
people aged 65–74 (98%) live in a private dwelling; however, this
percentage does decline as the person ages. Approximately 25% of
people 85 years and older reside in non-private dwellings, such as
residential aged care facilities (ABS 2017). Older people who live
alone are more likely to live in poverty than people in the same age
category who are married (ABS 2019). Living arrangements vary
according to an individual’s cultural background (see Table 24.1
).
The rate of living alone increases as age increases.

Australia—Stories from the Census, 2016. Cat. no. 2071.0. Canberra: ABS.
