Cultural diversity
The growing population of older adults in Australia consists of
increasing numbers of people from culturally and linguistically
diverse backgrounds. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people,
with their own diversity in terms of the 150 languages spoken by
tribal groups at home in 2016, comprise approximately 4.8% of the
Australian population over the age of 65; less than 1% were aged 85
and over (AIHW 2018; ABS 2017). In addition, population estimates
suggest that approximately 37% of the Australian population aged
65 years and over were born in countries other than Australia (ABS
2017). In 2016, the most common countries of birth of migrants
from non-main English-speaking backgrounds were China and India,
and from English-speaking backgrounds were England and New
Zealand (ABS 2017). Other common countries include Italy, Greece,
Germany and the Netherlands. This information provides some
indication of the cultural richness and diversity of Australian society
and emphasises the importance of nurses being culturally sensitive
and competent. See Figure 24.1
 for a comparison of the older
population growth.
Figure 24.1


Older people, by age, sex and cultural and linguistic background, 30
June 2011.
Source: Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) . Australian Demographic Statistics, Sep 2011. Cat. no. 3101.0.
Canberra: ABS. © Commonwealth of Australia.
9 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2012). Australian Demographic Statistics, Sep 2011.
ABS. Cat. no. 3101.0. Canberra: ABS.
9


Health
Chronic health problems and disabilities increase as age increases.
However, disease is not a normal outcome of ageing. Research
shows that older Australians today are generally healthier than
previous generations and are living longer (AIHW 2018). The vast
majority (73%) of older Australians rated their health as either good,
very good or excellent (AIHW 2018), even though most have chronic
health conditions and report a severe or profound core disability,
meaning that they sometimes or always require assistance with
activities such as self-care, mobility and/or communication. In recent
years, there is a clear trend towards having more disability-free
years than a decade or more ago, with men aged 65 years or older
gaining 9 years and women 65 years or older gaining 10 years more
of disability-free living (AIHW 2018). With that said, in 2015, almost
33% of people aged 65 years and over reported needing some
assistance with activities of daily living (ABS ). Nurses need to be
aware that promoting health and wellness and assessing and
promoting functional abilities for activities of daily living continue to
be valid and important for 65-year-old individuals who have 19.6 to
22.3 more years to enjoy life (AIHW 2018).
10 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2016). Disability, Ageing and Carers, Australia:
Summary of Findings, 2015. Canberra: ABS.
10


Attitudes towards ageing
Because older adults are increasing in number, most nurses will be
caring for older adults at some point. It is important for nurses to be
aware of their own values and attitudes towards ageing and older
people and to examine whether myths or stereotypes influence
those attitudes. It is also crucial to recognise that older Australians
are not a homogeneous group but are as diverse in their interests
and needs as any population of people. Indigenous Australians,
older Australians with culturally diverse backgrounds and those with
a mental illness or disability comprise only some of the special needs
groups recognised in this population. Also worthy of mention are
ageing older people of gay, lesbian, bisexual, transgender or intersex
orientation (AIHW 2018), who face possible discrimination and
marginalisation in their later years.
Ageism
Australian society values youth. See the ‘Culturally competent
care
’ box to see how different cultures view older people.
Ageism
 is a term to describe the deep and profound prejudice in
Western societies against older adults. It is a form of discrimination
based solely on age (COTA for Older Australians ). Unfortunately,
this negative attitude towards ageing or older people exists among
11


some health care professionals (Wyman, Shiovitz-Ezra & Bengel ).
This attitude is another reason for nurses to reflect on their personal
beliefs and values regarding older people. Central to the care of
older people, and to ameliorating some of this discrimination, is the
concept of person-centred care. This is, in part, about health
professionals interacting with older people as individual human
beings to be respected and cared for, rather than as ‘sick old people’
upon whom tasks such as showering or dressing are performed in
impatient or disrespectful ways.
11 COTA for Older Australians (2019). Ageism and Discrimination. Retrieved from
<www.cota.org.au>.
12 Wyman, M., Shiovitz-Ezra, S. & Bengel, J. (2018). Ageism in the health care system:
Providers, patients, and systems. In L. Ayalon & C. Tesch-Romer (Eds), Contemporary
Perspectives on Ageism (Vol. 19). Switzerland: Springer Open.
Myths and stereotypes
Ageism contributes to the development of negative stereotypes
about older adults. Stereotypes occur when younger people do not
understand or identify with older people as unique human beings.
Instead, they generalise undesirable characteristics (e.g. senile, old
fashioned, unproductive, inflexible) to all older people. Many
negative attitudes about ageing are based on myths and incorrect
information. See Table 24.2
 for some myths and realities of
ageing. As a result, it is important for nurses to provide accurate
information about ageing. This has been found to be an effective
12


intervention for reducing negative stereotypes and improving
attitudes about ageing (Hunter 2015).
Table 24.2 Myths and realities of ageing

Gerontological nursing
The growth of the older population is characterised by unique and
diverse individuals who may require a variety of health care
professionals to meet their health and social care needs.
Gerontology
 is a term used to define the study of ageing and
older adults. Gerontology is multidisciplinary and is a specialised
area within various disciplines such as nursing, psychology and
social work. Geriatrics
 is associated with the medical care (e.g.
diseases and disabilities) of older adults.
Development
Gerontological nursing involves advocating for the health of older
people at all levels of prevention (Eliopoulos 2018). In the 1960s,
gerontological nursing became a subspecialty of nursing. In the
1980s, gerontological nursing leaders stated that most practising
nurses did not have sufficient knowledge about gerontology. This
prompted discussion of how to prepare nurses for gerontological
nursing. Since the late 1990s, the nursing profession has recognised
the importance of preparing all practising nurses with basic
gerontological knowledge. As a result, schools of nursing now
provide classes or courses about the nursing care of older adults.
Practising gerontological nurses can obtain specialist qualifications in


advanced practice in gerontological nursing through postgraduate
studies in nursing at universities across Australia.
Roles
The gerontological nurse has many roles: healer, caregiver,
educator, advocate and innovator (Eliopoulos 2018). As a healer, the
nurse uses a holistic approach, recognising that the person must be
viewed in the context of their biological, emotional, social, cultural
and spiritual parts and that people are active participants in the
maintenance of their own health. As a caregiver, the nurse gives
direct care to older adults in a variety of settings. The gerontological
nurse educator shares knowledge and skills related to the care of
the older adult, both to the general community and to other health
professionals. As an advocate, the nurse can assist the older person
to assert their rights and obtain services that they require. This can
also extend to advocating on behalf of a community for resources or
activities that promote the health of the older person. Aged care
nursing is evolving and will continue to do so to meet the demands
of an ageing population. The gerontological nurse needs to be an
innovator, seeking opportunities to develop new technologies or
models of care that will best meet the needs of the ageing
population.


Care settings for older people
Gerontological nurses practise in a variety of settings, including
acute care, rehabilitation, palliative, residential aged care facilities
and the community. Older adults are regular users of health care
services, from acute care facilities to rehabilitation, long-term
residential care and the community. No matter the setting, older
adults require health assessment and promotion.
Culturally competent care
How different cultures view older people
Indigenous Australians
Traditionally, older people are respected for their wisdom,
experience and knowledge.
Older Indigenous Australians assume significant roles as
teachers, role models and caretakers of the young.
Chinese
Traditional Chinese values place the family and society
over the individual. Many Australian-born Chinese may not


be as traditional but still hold values of respect for older
adults and authority.
The oldest son has obligations towards the family and is
expected to respect and care for parents.
The tradition of ‘filial piety’ is the value of total respect for
the family, especially older people. This respect for older
people was advocated by Confucius, the famous Chinese
philosopher, and many Chinese and Chinese-Australian
families choose to follow these ancient principles.
Vietnamese
Older people are given high respect in Vietnamese
society. They are considered the carriers of tradition,
knowledge and wisdom. Age is considered an asset, not a
liability.
Ageing grandparents and parents stay with the family for
support and care.
Older people may prepare meals and care for
grandchildren if both the husband and wife work.
In Vietnam, older people are the leaders and decision
makers in the family and are often sought for advice.
When these older people move to Australia, they can
become socially and culturally isolated for many reasons
(e.g. lack of English, age, lack of training for work). In
contrast, the younger family members become more
accustomed to Australian culture and may behave in ways
their ageing parents do not approve of. This can create


tension in families where the ageing parents feel ignored
and not respected.
Italian and Greek
Older people are held in high esteem.
Old age is viewed as a positive time in the life of the older
person.
Care for older people is often provided by the extended
family. It is expected that children will be integrally
involved in the care of their ageing parents.
Acute care facilities
Older adults account for a large proportion of people cared for in the
acute care hospital setting. For example, in 2017–18, people aged
65 years and older accounted for about 22% of all emergency
department presentations (AIHW
) and 42% of inpatient
hospitalisations (AIHW
).
14 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019b). Hospitals at a Glance 2017–18.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
15 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019c). Admitted Patient Care 2017–18.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.

15


Nurses in an acute care setting focus on protecting the health and
wellbeing of the older adult, with the goal of the older adult returning
to their prior level of independence. Examples include:
preventing nosocomial infections (e.g. urinary tract infections,
pneumonia)
preventing therapy-related problems (e.g. confusion,
sleeplessness, dehydration, decreased nutrition)
treating the health problem that resulted in the older adult’s
admission plus assessing for potential undiagnosed health
problems (e.g. depression, drug and/or alcohol abuse)
preventing complications (e.g. decubitus ulcer).
Older adults often perceive that being in the hospital could change
their ability to be autonomous and independent. As a result, nurses
need to assess the older adult’s stage or perception of need for
control and autonomy during hospitalisation and their fears and
hopes about being discharged from the hospital setting.
Residential aged care facilities
The objective of residential aged care facilities (RACFs) is to provide
a place of safety and care to attain optimal wellness and
independence for each individual whose care needs can no longer
be met within their own home (AIHW 2018). Older people who live in
RACFs are generally referred to as ‘residents’. In 2017–18, 234 798
people aged 65 years and over were permanently living in RACFs in


Australia and a further 60 278 received respite care in an RACF
(Productivity Commission ). There are two types of care offered by
a RACF: permanent care and respite care. Permanent care
facilities offer ongoing care in an RACF, with no distinction between
high-level and low-level care needs. Respite care
 is short-term
care offered in an RACF to allow carers and older people time to
regenerate so that they may live at home for as long as possible.
Unlike permanent care, respite care is offered as either high or low
care.
16 Productivity Commission (2019). Report on Government Services 2019: Aged Care
Services. Retrieved from <www.pc.gov.au>.
In response to the increased government emphasis on the provision
of community care, the acuity level of older people living in RACFs is
increasing. For example, it is not unusual in today’s residential care
environment to care for an older person with a tracheostomy or
percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG). The number of
people with dementia in residential care is also increasing. Nurses
therefore need specialist knowledge to meet the complex needs of
these individuals and their families. There is also an increased need
for people requiring palliative care.
Admission into an RACF can only occur after an Aged Care
Assessment Team (ACAT) assessment has been conducted and a
decision has been made as to the level of care required. An ACAT is
comprised of a range of health professionals, such as geriatricians
and other doctors, nurses, social workers, physiotherapists,
occupational therapists and psychologists; in 2017–18, ACATs
16


completed 180 493 assessments (Productivity Commission 2019).
There is a high demand for the places in residential care, and
decisions have to be made by the family and the older person within
a very short time, otherwise the place may be taken. The majority of
aged care facilities are regulated by the Commonwealth government
and thus funded by it. The funding for each older person is
determined by the Aged Care Funding Instrument (ACFI)
assessment undertaken by the nurse (Productivity Commission
2019). The ACFI measures care needs across three different areas
of care: activities of daily living; cognition and behaviour; and
complex health care (AIHW 2018). Once the individual is assessed
and categorised for ACFI funding, the information is submitted to the
Commonwealth to acquire the funding for that person.
Palliative care
Gerontological nurses may also work in palliative care, also known
as hospice care, and care for dying people and their families. The
majority of people cared for in palliative care are older people.
Palliative care
 is a concept that includes coordinated care and
support by health professionals to terminally ill individuals and their
families for the purpose of improving quality of life for the person
and family. Palliative care requires a great deal of patience,
expertise, understanding, interdisciplinary communication and
compassion on the part of gerontology nurses (Department of
Health ).
17


17 Department of Health (2016). Palliative Care. Retrieved from <www.health.gov.au>.
Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation may be found in several settings: acute care hospitals,
subacute or transitional care, residential aged care facilities and the
community. Many older people benefit from a rehabilitation program
where the goal is to maintain physical independence (e.g. after
orthopaedic surgery, stroke or amputation). The nurse is an
important member of the interdisciplinary rehabilitation team. The
role of the nurse is often as a health care coordinator, manager and
counsellor for older people and their families. For example, nurses
monitor the older person’s health care, assist with activities of daily
living and facilitate the person’s adjustment and coping with the
disability.
Home care and community care
Home care is provided through two main programs: the
Commonwealth Home Support Programme (CHSP)
 and the
Home Care Packages program (Parliamentary Budget Office ). The
CHSP provides a basic level of aged care services to assist people
who are 65 years and over to live independently and remain in their
own homes (AIHW 2018). The Home and Community Care (HACC)
program was incorporated into the CHSP in 2015. In 2017–18, more
18


than 830 272 people aged 65 and over accessed these services
(Productivity Commission 2019). The CHSP provides a range of
services and support, such as centre-based daycare, domestic
assistance, respite care and social support (Productivity Commission
2019). Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people can access
CHSP/HACC services from the age of 50 and over.
18 Parliamentary Budget Office (2019). Australia’s Ageing Population: Understanding the
Fiscal Impacts over the Next Decade. Canberra: Commonwealth of Australia.
The biggest provider of home care services is the not-for-profit
sector, such as religious, charitable and community-based
organisations. The Australian government provides a number of
Home Care Packages
 that providers help older individuals to
access so they can stay in their home longer (known as ‘ageing in
place
’) (Rantz et al.
). Help is offered, for example, with
showering, dressing and mobility or with house cleaning and basic
home maintenance activities (Productivity Commission 2019). There
are four levels of care available, ranging from low-level care (level 1)
to high-level care (level 4). All Home Care Packages are delivered
on a consumer-directed care basis. This promotes greater
autonomy for the older person and takes a person-centred approach
to providing resources that are ideally suited to the person’s
situation. As of 30 June 2018, 91 847 people were recipients of
Home Care Packages; the level 2 package was the most accessed
(Productivity Commission 2019).
19 Rantz, M., Popejoy, L., Galambos, C., ... Miller, S. (2014). The continued success of
registered nurse care coordination in a state evaluation of aging in place in senior housing.
19


Nursing Outlook, 62(4), 237–246.
Real-world practice
Working in an aged care facility has offered some of
the most poignant moments of my nursing career. It is
a place that, as a nurse, you need to be able to make
considered autonomous decisions and it is a place that
has great joy and great sorrow.
Recently, while holidaying with my family, I took a
number of pictures and videos of the stunning
landscape we visited, which included running
waterfalls, lush rainforests and historical buildings. I did
this with the purpose of sharing these images and
videos with the residents of the aged care facility
where I work, particularly the residents who were
unable to travel any longer. The sounds and sights of
the waterfalls and the various other images of the
holiday, many of which depicted places the residents
had visited themselves in their earlier lives, brought
them such delight and curiosity; it was a wonderful
moment shared.
Caring for the older person helps you as a nurse to
become an advocate for that person in a strong and
‘person-centred’ way. It is easy to say that you will be


an advocate for ‘patients’, but in reality, it is often
challenging to do. When you look after someone long
term and develop a therapeutic relationship with them,
it provides you with the courage to be an advocate
when needed.
Recently I received a card from the daughter of one of
our beautiful residents who passed away and in her
card she said, ‘I knew this place was special—more a
family than a nursing home’. There are immense
opportunities in aged care nursing to make a
difference to a person’s and their family’s life and to be
part of a team that provides the human touch and care
that our older population deserves. I hope you find a
nursing career that will provide you with the rewards,
challenges, excitement, decision making and
leadership opportunities that aged care nursing has
provided for me.
—Michelle Yanner, RN, RM, BNSc, PGDipMid, GradDipNurs (Dementia) Loreto Home for
the Aged, Townsville, Queensland
Research note
Are trained volunteers making a difference?


A. Blair, C. Bateman & K. Anderson
. ‘They take a lot of pressure off us’: Volunteers reducing staff
and family care burden and contributing to quality of care for older patients with cognitive impairment
in rural hospitals. Australasian Journal on Ageing, 38(Suppl 2), 34–45. Doi: 10.1111/ajag.12612.
20 Blair, A. Bateman, C. & Anderson, K. (2019). ‘They take a lot of pressure off us’: Volunteers
reducing staff and family care burden and contributing to quality of care for older patients with
cognitive impairment in rural hospitals. Australasian Journal on Ageing, 38(Suppl 2), 34–45. Doi:
10.1111/ajag.12612.
The purpose of this study was to explore the ability of trained
volunteers to help provide person-centred care to older
people living with dementia and/or delirium in hospital. The
study also explored the enablers and barriers to having
trained volunteers working alongside hospital staff and how
this impacted on the family of the person with dementia and
on hospital staff. Caring for a person with a cognitive
impairment is very time consuming and challenging and
places hospital staff under additional stress. The risk of
wandering behaviours is high and the care burden for staff is
great.
This mixed methods study, conducted in a rural hospital in
New South Wales, developed a program where volunteers
were recruited and trained to provide one-to-one practical
assistance with nutrition, hydration, encouraging the use of
hearing aids, mobilising, therapeutic activities and emotional
support—the role was similar to that of a family carer.
Volunteers were screened and interviewed for
appropriateness and became part of the care team. They
wore gold t-shirts and worked 4-hour shifts across 5 days of
the week.
20


People living with dementia reported they had reduced
episodes of distress, improved quality of care (i.e.
nutrition/hydration), improved emotional wellbeing, improved
person-centred care, improved safety and reduced
readmissions. The family of the person living with dementia
reported reduced family care burden, having a break
(respite), emotional support and developing an enjoyable
relationship with the volunteer themselves, which aided in
information sharing. Hospital staff reported improved time to
plan and prioritise clinical care, upskilling in dementia, access
to person-centred strategies and reduction in staff care
burden. Many nurses felt they could do a ‘better job’ as they
had more time to deliver clinical care more effectively and
equitably. They considered the volunteers as an important
member of the health team.
Implications Volunteer programs such as this have many
benefits for the person living with dementia, family members
and hospital staff. However, these programs must have a
designated volunteer program coordinator, careful screening
and selection processes and adequate training to ensure safe
person-centred care is provided. Furthermore, volunteers
should have clearly defined roles and reporting frameworks.
Similar programs could be implemented in other hospitals and
residential aged care facilities across Australia.


Flexible care
Flexible care provides an option other than RACFs and home care.
There are four types of flexible care options available: (1) transition
care program, (2) short-term restorative care (STRC) program, (3)
multipurpose services (MPS) program, and (4) Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander flexible aged care program. The transition care
program aids older people to return home after a hospital stay; the
STRC program is similar to transition care, but without the person
having been in hospital; the MPS program provides services to
regional or remote areas where mainstream services are not
available or viable; and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
program provides culturally safe aged care that is a mix of
residential and home care services (Productivity Commission 2019).


Physiological ageing
In the past half-century, scientists have proposed numerous theories
of why people age. More recently, as both the absolute number and
the population percentage of older people increase, there is renewed
scientific interest in why people age, how people age and what
factors affect the physical, psychological and functional status of
older people. There are nearly 40 different theories of ageing in the
biological, psychological and social sciences and many in
gerontological nursing. Clearly, there are more questions as to how
people age than there are answers. At this point, it is helpful to
distinguish between normal or usual ageing (the typical ageing
course with concomitant diseases and disabilities) and successful
ageing (the ageing course without disease). Unfortunately, it is
extremely difficult to know one from the other.
The most promising theories for explaining physical ageing include
genetics (Kirkwood & Austad ), oxidative stress (Finkel &
Holbrook ) and cellular changes (De Pinto ). These theories may
be grouped generally into: (a) theories that hypothesise ageing as a
consequence of accumulated damage to informational molecules,
and (b) theories that hypothesise ageing as a consequence of
regulation by specific genes (Kane, Ouslander & Abrass ). Table
24.3
 describes some of the various biological theories of ageing.
