As the person ages, a number of physical changes occur; some are
visible, some are not. In general, lean body mass is reduced, fat
tissue increases and bone mass decreases. Extracellular fluid
remains constant; however, intracellular fluid decreases and leads to
reduced total body fluid. Thus, older people are at risk for developing
dehydration (Eliopoulos 2018). Table 24.4
 provides a summary of
the normal physical changes associated with ageing.
Table 24.4 Normal physical changes associated with ageing
Source: Based on C. Eliopoulos (2018). Gerontological Nursing (9th ed.). Philadelphia, PA: Wolters Kluwer.
Integument
Obvious changes occur in the integumentary system (skin, hair,
nails) with age. The skin becomes drier, less elastic and more
fragile, making the older person more susceptible to skin tears and


shearing injuries. The hair loses colour, the fingernails and toenails
become thickened and brittle and, in women over 60, facial hair
increases.
Responses to these changes vary among individuals and cultures.
For example, one person may feel distinguished with grey hair
whereas another may feel embarrassed or depressed, interpreting
grey hair as a sign of losing one’s youth.
These integumentary changes accompany progressive losses of
subcutaneous fat and muscle tissue, muscle atrophy and loss of
elastic fibre, resulting in a ‘double’ chin, sagging of eyelids and
earlobes and wrinkling of skin, especially in areas exposed to sun.
Bony prominences may become visible. In older women, the breasts
become less firm and may sag. Loss of subcutaneous fat also
decreases older people’s tolerance of cold.
Health promotion teaching about skin care for older people can
include the following:
maintaining healthy skin
ensuring optimal nutrition
maintaining adequate hydration
preventing skin dryness by using emollient lotions after bathing or
showering, when the skin is still moist
avoiding skin products that contain perfume or alcohol
assessing the frequency of bathing/showering
avoiding sun damage


using sunscreen lotions with sun protection factor (SPF) of 15 or
higher
wearing wide-brimmed hats, sun visors and sunglasses when
exposed to the sun
observing for any skin changes (e.g. new lesions, change in mole
size or colour) and seeking medical evaluation
preventing skin injury
avoiding strong detergent to wash clothes
avoiding rough texture in clothing
avoiding highly starched linens
using soft washers, towels and bed linen.
Neuromusculoskeletal
With ageing comes gradual reduction in the speed and power of
skeletal or voluntary muscle contractions and sustained muscular
effort. Exercise can strengthen weakened muscles and, up to about
age 50, the skeletal muscles can increase in bulk and density. After
that time, there is a steady decrease in muscle mass, strength and
function (sarcopenia
), mainly seen in older adults who do not
exercise (Eliopoulos 2018). Therefore, it is important for nurses to
encourage exercise to minimise loss of muscle tone and strength.
Often, balance is impaired with age and is related to loss of muscle
strength. Muscle endurance diminishes with age, resulting in muscle
fatigue after short periods of exercise for the older adult. There is
substantial evidence, however, that the muscles that do remain in


the older adult can be strengthened through exercise and training
with resulting improvements in functional status.
The person’s reaction time slows with age. Reaction time can be
delayed further by decreased muscle tone as a result of diminished
physical activity. Older adults compensate for this reaction difference
by being exceptionally cautious, for instance in their driving habits,
which exasperates some impatient younger drivers.
Loss in overall stature occurs with age. This can be exaggerated by
muscular weakness resulting in a stooping posture and kyphosis
(humpback of the upper spine). Imbalance in the rates of absorption
and formation of bone tissue occurs with ageing; therefore, older
adults have more porous and fragile bones than younger adults,
making older people prone to serious fractures. Osteoporosis
, a
pathological decrease in bone density that is more common in older
than younger adults, may lead to spontaneous (i.e. without a fall or
other trauma to the bone) fractures that are called pathological
fractures
. Osteoporosis occurs more frequently in people with
insufficient intake of dietary calcium, in women after menopause, in
Caucasians and Asians, and in individuals who are immobilised or
physically inactive. Even though it is often considered a woman’s
disease, it is important to remember that osteoporosis affects men
also (Osteoporosis Australia ).
25 Osteoporosis Australia (2015). About Osteoporosis. Retrieved from
<www.osteoporosis.org.au>.
25


Joints and their supporting structures change with age, including
decreased elasticity, strength and hydration of the tendons and
ligaments, making movement stiffer and more restricted. Stiffness is
aggravated by inactivity; for example, if a person sits too long, the
joints become stiff and the person has difficulty standing and
walking. These changes may be compounded by osteoarthritis. A
continual program of physical activity and proper nutrition will slow
bone density loss and decrease muscle atrophy and stiffness (see
Figure 24.2
).
Figure 24.2


A regular program of exercise is important for maintenance of joint
mobility and muscle tone and can promote socialisation.
Source: Pressmaster/Shutterstock.
As indicated, these age-related changes may affect the mobility and
safety of the older adult. For example, decreased muscle strength,
decreased balance and osteoporosis put the older adult at risk for
falls and fractures. For health promotion, the nurse assesses the
musculoskeletal functioning of the older adult and identifies any risk
factors that may contribute to falls or hinder the ability to perform
activities of daily living. Health promotion interventions often include
providing information about the risk factors for osteoporosis and the
importance of adequate intake of calcium and vitamin D.
Sensory/perceptual
Each of the five senses becomes less efficient in older adulthood.
Changes in vision associated with ageing include the obvious
changes around the eye, such as the shrunken appearance of the
eyes due to loss of orbital fat, the slowed blink reflex and the
looseness of the eyelids, particularly the lower lid, due to poorer
muscle tone. Other changes result in loss of visual acuity, less
power of adaptation to darkness and dim light, a decrease in
accommodation to near and far objects, loss of peripheral vision,
atrophy of lacrimal glands resulting in dry eyes and difficulty in
discriminating similar colours, especially blues, greens and purples.


Presbyopia
, the inability to focus or accommodate due to a loss
of elasticity of the lens, causes a decrease in near vision. This
generally starts around age 40. Visual acuity lessens gradually after
age 50 and more rapidly after age 70 (Eliopoulos 2018).
By the age of 80, nearly all older adults have some lens opacity
(cataracts
) that reduces visual acuity and causes glare to be a
problem. In addition to cataracts, three other conditions result in
visual impairment and blindness in older adults: age-related macular
degeneration (ARMD), glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy (Vision
2020 Australia ). It is important for the nurse to promote health by
informing older adults to schedule routine eye examinations to
maintain and protect their vision. Also, wearing sunglasses will help
avoid the damaging effect of ultraviolet light.
26 Vision 2020 Australia (2015). Eye Health by Numbers. Retrieved from
<www.vision2020australia.org.au>.
The loss of hearing ability related to ageing, called presbycusis
,
affects people over age 65. Gradual loss of hearing is more
common in men than women, perhaps because men are more
frequently in noisy work environments. Hearing loss is greater in the
higher frequencies than the lower. Thus, older adults with hearing
loss usually hear speakers with low, distinct voices best. Hard
consonants (e.g. , , ) and long vowel sounds (e.g.
,
) are
more easily recognised and sibilant sounds ( ,
, ) are the most
difficult to hear. Older adults may have more difficulty compensating
for hearing loss than the young, who pay closer attention to the lip
movements of the speaker.
26
k d t
ay ee
s th f


If family members notice communication problems or social
withdrawal of the older adult, the nurse should provide health
promotion teaching by suggesting that the older adult be referred for
hearing screening. Also, the older adult’s ears should be checked for
impacted earwax. If hearing has diminished, hearing aids are
available and the nurse can provide information to the older adult
and their family. To help avoid increased hearing loss, inform the
older adult to use ear protection devices when working in or around
activities that give off loud noise.
Older people have a poorer sense of taste and smell and are less
stimulated by food than the young. It is common for the sense of
smell to decline more than the sense of taste. These changes
significantly affect appetite in the older adult, contributing to poor
nutrition. Decreased or absent sense of smell and taste also add to
the health hazard of increased salt usage and safety issues (e.g.
being unable to smell a gas leak). It is important for the nurse to
teach the older adult and their family about the safety issues
involved with a decreased sense of taste and smell and what
strategies can be implemented to promote the older adult’s safety
(e.g. dating and labelling foods, using smoke alarms).
Loss of skin receptors takes place gradually, producing an increased
threshold for sensations of pain, touch and temperature. The older
person may not be able to distinguish hot from cold or the intensity
of heat. Stimuli causing severe pain in a younger person may cause
only minor sensation or pressure in older people. This places the
older adult at higher risk for burns and other injuries. Again, it is


important for the nurse to teach about the involved safety risks and
subsequent interventions (e.g. setting the temperature of the water
heater to 43°C to prevent scalding).
Respiratory
Respiratory efficiency is reduced with age. Tidal volume (the amount
of air moved in and out during normal respiration) remains the same
but the older adult has a decreased vital capacity. This means the
older adult is unable to compensate for increased oxygen need by
significantly increasing the amount of air inspired. Dyspnoea
(difficult breathing) occurs frequently with increased activity, such as
running for a bus or carrying heavy parcels upstairs. A greater
volume of residual air is left in the lungs after expiration and the
capacity to cough efficiently decreases because of weaker
expiratory muscles. Mucus secretions tend to collect more readily in
the respiratory tree. Thus, susceptibility to respiratory infections
increases in older adults.
Health promotion teaching includes information about the following:
cessation of smoking, if appropriate
preventing respiratory infections by washing hands
ensuring the influenza and pneumonia vaccinations are up to
date.


Cardiovascular
The working capacity of the heart diminishes with age. This is
particularly evident when increased demands are made on the heart,
such as during periods of exercise or emotional stress. The heart
rate at normal rest may decrease with age. However, the heart rate
of the older person is slower to respond to stress and slower to
return to normal after periods of physical activity.
Changes in the arteries occur concurrently. Reduced arterial
elasticity may result in diminished blood supply to, for instance, the
legs and the brain, resulting in pain on exertion in the calf muscles
and dizziness, respectively. In addition, there may be a delay in the
circulatory adjustments required when a person quickly stands up
from a lying or sitting position. The delay results in an abrupt drop in
systolic blood pressure known as orthostatic hypotension.
For blood pressure measurements, it is not unusual to have a slight
increase in the systolic pressure while the diastolic pressure remains
the same. A significant increase in blood pressure is more likely the
result of other factors such as diet, weight or stress, rather than age
alone. Hypertension is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease and
should be treated following validated guidelines, such as the
Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Hypertension in
Adults released in 2016 (National Heart Foundation of Australia ).
27


27 National Heart Foundation of Australia (2016). Guideline for the Diagnosis and
Management of Hypertension in Adults—2016. Melbourne: National Heart Foundation of
Australia.
Health promotion activities involve detecting and reducing risks for
cardiovascular disease. To detect risks, the older adult should have
their blood pressure checked regularly. The older adult should be
aware of their cholesterol level and have it rechecked at appropriate
intervals, depending on the results of the blood test (e.g. the higher
the level, the more frequently it should be rechecked). To reduce
risks of cardiovascular disease, the nurse should inform the older
adult about the importance of the following: smoking cessation (if
applicable), maintaining ideal body weight, exercising daily, avoiding
foods high in sodium and fat, and eating fruits and vegetables, and
discussing relaxation therapies and the use of low-dose aspirin
therapy with the older adult’s general practitioner (Hunter 2015).
Gastrointestinal
Age-related changes in the gastrointestinal system include:
periodontal disease, which can lead to tooth loss. With age, tooth
enamel becomes harder and more brittle, making teeth more
susceptible to fractures. The root of the tooth shrinks and the
gingival retracts. The bones that support the teeth decrease in
density and height, all leading to tooth loss (Eliopoulos 2018)


reduced saliva, which may lead to xerostomia (dry mouth) and
make the oral mucosa of the older adult more susceptible to
infection
decreased oesophageal motility slowing the oesophageal
emptying process
decreased stomach motility and emptying time. Also, a higher pH
of the stomach contributes to increased incidence of gastric
irritation in the older adult
decreased production of intrinsic factor leading to pernicious
anaemia
decreased intestinal absorption, motility and blood flow.
Health promotion teaching for older adults includes effective oral
hygiene and preventive dental care (e.g. half-yearly teeth cleaning).
Nutrition is important, including appropriate diet as needed by the
older adult and sufficient fluid intake. Maintenance of a regular bowel
routine is helpful and screening for colorectal cancer is important
(e.g. annual faecal occult blood test, colonoscopy every 5 years).
Urinary
The excretory function of the kidney diminishes with age but usually
not significantly below normal levels unless a disease process
intervenes. The kidney’s filtering abilities may also be impaired; thus,
waste products may be filtered and excreted more slowly. For this
reason, the nurse should be aware of whether medications that are
administered are excreted via the kidney or liver. Drugs that are


metabolised predominantly in the kidney may accumulate in the
older adult and the nurse needs to watch for signs of toxicity.
More noticeable changes are those related to the bladder.
Complaints of urinary urgency and urinary frequency are common.
The capacity of the bladder and its ability to completely empty
diminish with age. Many older people need to rise during the night to
void (nocturia) and may experience retention of residual urine,
predisposing the older adult to bladder infections.
Although older people are susceptible to urinary incontinence (UI)
because of changes in the kidney and bladder, UI is never normal.
The nurse must promptly investigate UI, particularly when of new
onset. Urinary incontinence has many ill effects on older adults,
including social isolation, falls and skin breakdown.
The nurse can teach the following health promotion activities for
good urinary function in the older adult:
Drink sufficient fluids daily (e.g. 8 to 10 glasses of non-
caffeinated liquid).
Drink fluids even if you do not feel thirsty. (The thirst mechanism
in older people is diminished.)
Avoid foods that can irritate the bladder (e.g. sugar, caffeine,
alcohol, chocolate, artificial sweeteners and spicy and acidic
foods).
Practise pelvic muscle exercises to stop or control stress
incontinence.


The nurse should also explain that incontinence is not a normal
change related to ageing.
Genitals
Degenerative changes in the gonads are gradual in men. Production
of testosterone continues and the testes can produce sperm well
into old age, although there is a gradual decrease in the number of
sperm produced. In women, the degenerative changes in the
ovaries are noticed by the cessation of menses in middle age during
the menopause.
Changes in the gonads of older women result from diminished
secretion of the ovarian hormones. Some changes, such as the
shrinking of the uterus and ovaries, go unnoticed. Other changes
are obvious. The breasts atrophy and lubricating vaginal secretions
are reduced. Reduced natural lubrication may be the cause of
painful intercourse, which may be addressed through the use of
lubricating gels.
The older man will notice several age-related changes in his sexual
response and performance, but it is important for the nurse to
reassure the man that sexual response and performance should be
present in the older adult. For both men and women, the major age-
related change in sexual response is timing: it takes longer to
become sexually aroused, longer to complete intercourse and longer
before sexual arousal can occur again (Nusbaum, Lenahan &


Sadovsky ). In general, the older man’s libido may decrease but not
disappear. If an older man reports a loss in sexual interest, the
nurse should be as concerned as when a younger man reports a
loss of interest in sexual activity. Older men achieve an erection that
is less firm than in younger men but still capable of penetration.
Ejaculation may take longer to occur and the older man may have
difficulty anticipating or delaying ejaculation.
28 Nusbaum, M., Lenahan, P. & Sadovsky, R. (2005). Sexual health in aging men and
women: Addressing the physiological and psychological sexual changes that occur with age.
Geriatrics, 60(9), 18–23.
Older women also experience changes in their sexual responses. It
takes longer for an older woman to become sexually aroused and
produce vaginal lubrication, and the labia and uterus do not fully
elevate, making penetration slightly more difficult (Nusbaum et al.
2005). The clitoris remains an important part of orgasm but may
become irritated more easily because the clitoral hood is less
protective than in younger women. During orgasm, the uterus will
contract less frequently but the contractions remain vigorous and
orgasm is as intense as in younger women.
The nurse needs excellent communication skills when providing
health education about sexual function in older people.
A survey of older people found that they prefer the health care
professional to be open, respectful, non-judgmental and use plain
English when discussing sexuality (Hunter 2015). The nurse should
also not assume that all older people are heterosexual (Eliopoulos
28


2018), needing to be open to the possibility that they are interacting
with homosexual older people. Older people are fully capable of
enjoying sexual activity. If they experience problems with sexual
function, they should seek professional advice from their general
practitioner or another appropriate health care professional.


Psychosocial ageing
A number of theories have attempted to explain psychosocial
ageing. These theories focus on behaviour and attitude changes
during the ageing process. One of the earliest, disengagement
theory
, developed in the early 1960s by Cumming and Henry ,
proposed that ageing involves mutual withdrawal (disengagement)
between the older person and others in the older person’s
environment. It has been widely criticised for the assumptions that
disengagement is appropriate for the older adult. According to
Havighurst’s  activity theory
, the best way to age is to stay
active physically and mentally and, according to Atchley’s
continuity theory
, people maintain their values, habits and
behaviour in old age. A person who is accustomed to having people
around will continue to do so and the person who prefers not to be
involved with others is more likely to disengage. This theory
accounts for the great variety of behaviour seen in older people.
29 Cumming, E. & Henry, W. E. (1961). Growing Old: The Process of Disengagement. New
York: Basic Books.
30 Havighurst, R. J. (1963). Successful aging. In R. H. Williams, C. Tibbitts & W. Donohue
(Eds), Processes of Aging: Social and Psychological Perspectives (Vol. 1, pp. 299–320). New
York: Atherton.
31 Atchley, R. C. (1989). A continuity theory of normal aging. Gerontologist, 29, 183–190.
29
30
31


According to Erikson , the developmental task at this time is ego
integrity versus despair. People who attain ego integrity view life with
a sense of wholeness and derive satisfaction from past
accomplishments. They view death as an acceptable completion of
life. People who develop integrity accept ‘one’s one and only life
cycle’ (Erikson 1963, p. 263). By contrast, people who despair often
believe they have made poor choices during life and wish they could
live life over.
32 Erikson, E. H. (1963). Childhood and Society (2nd ed.). New York: Norton.
Acknowledging that the ‘young-old’ and ‘oldest-old’ differ not only in
physical characteristics but also in psychosocial responses, many
people have difficulty with Erikson’s singular developmental task.
Peck
 proposed the following three developmental tasks of the
older person in contrast to Erikson’s task of ego integrity versus
despair:
33 Peck, R. (1968). Psychological development in the second half of life. In B. L. Neugarten
(Ed.), Middle Age and Aging. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
1. ego differentiation versus work-role preoccupation
2. body transcendence versus body preoccupation
3. ego transcendence versus ego preoccupation.
For details about these tasks, see Chapter 21
. See Box 24.2
for further developmental tasks of the older adult.
32
33


BO X
24.2 Developmental tasks of the older
adult
65 to 75 years
Adjusting to decreasing physical strength and health.
Adjusting to retirement and lower and fixed income.
Adjusting to the death of parents, spouses and friends.
Adjusting to new relationships with adult children.
Adjusting to leisure time.
Keeping active and involved.
Making satisfying living arrangements as ageing
progresses.
75 years and older
Adapting to living alone.
Safeguarding physical and mental health.
Adjusting to the possibility of moving into a residential
aged care facility or supported accommodation.
Remaining in touch with other family members.
Finding meaning in life.
Adjusting to one’s own death.


Source: R. B. Murray, J. P. Zentner & R. Yakimo
. Pearson New International Edition: Health
Promotion Strategies through the Life Span (8th ed.). Harlow, England: Pearson Education Limited.
34 Murray, R. B., Zentner, J. P. & Yakimo, R. (2014). Pearson New International Edition: Health
Promotion Strategies through the Life Span (8th ed.). Harlow, England: Pearson Education Limited.
Retirement
After 65 years of age, the demographic patterns of those remaining
in the workplace change significantly. The highest proportions of
men remaining in the workforce after 65 years of age are
professionals, administrators or managers, and there is a similar
profile for women. Retirement age in Australia will increase by 6
months every 2 years, reaching 67 years by 1 July 2023
(Department of Human Services ).
35 Department of Human Services (2019a). Age Pension. Retrieved from
<www.humanservices.gov.au>.
It is important to remember that the retirement age and the
qualifying age for the age pension has no relationship to the abilities
of the worker. As a result, although the number of people working in
paid positions over 65 years is small, the numbers of older people
volunteering in a variety of settings is significant and this adds
appreciably to the social capital of Australia. Recreational pursuits
are frequently encouraged by local and state governments through
34
35


assistance with a variety of special interest groups (see Figures
24.3
 and 24.4
).
Figure 24.3


Many older people find creative outlets during retirement.
Source: ©Sylvie Bouchard/Shutterstock.com.
Figure 24.4


Retirement provides time for enjoying hobbies and travelling.
Economic change
Many people in the Australian workforce prior to the 1980s
contributed to private or work-supported pensions. Those in casual
work and homemakers were not eligible for these pension schemes,
so to amend this discrepancy the government implemented a
national superannuation scheme in 1985. As a result, increasing
numbers of Australians are able to self-fund their retirement. In the
event of them experiencing hardship, a government pension is
available.
Many older Australians have been accustomed to the Australian
universal health system, which began in the 1970s; however,
medical bills often are not met entirely by the health care subsidy
(Medicare) and private health insurance schemes do not cover all
health care costs. Older people can investigate their eligibility for a
Commonwealth Seniors Health Card and, if caring for someone with
a disability, may qualify for a Carer Payment or Carer Allowance.
Nurses should be aware of the costs of health care, and of issues
concerning the ‘safety net’, which assists older individuals on low
incomes to access pharmaceuticals at an affordable cost
(Department of Human Services ).
36 Department of Human Services (2019b). Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme. Retrieved
from <www.humanservices.gov.au>.
36


Specialised diets and healthy eating styles may also impact on the
older adult’s budget. Health professionals need to consider the
availability of specialised and healthy foods and the costs of such
foods when planning diets for older individuals.
Grandparenting
Grandparents provide a valuable contribution to the extended family
unit and grandparenting is associated with active and healthy ageing
(Campbell, Burn & Szoeke ). Campbell et al. believe that
grandparents and grandchildren share a unique bond that is
mutually beneficial. However, grandparenting can also produce
additional stress on the older adult, especially if the amount of time
spent with grandchildren is excessive. If the older adult is taking on
the primary caregiver role for children due to the parent(s) working
full time, this may lead to an increase in morbidity for the older
person due to the additional stress it places on them. A study
conducted by Brennan and Cass  found that Indigenous
grandparents cared for their grandchildren for a number of reasons;
for example, socioemotional problems of the parents, including
mental illness and imprisonment. Also commonly reported was drug
and alcohol misuse by the parents, resulting in the grandchildren
relocating to live with their grandparents.
37 Campbell, S., Burn, K. & Szoeke, C. (2016). Grand-parenting for healthy ageing in women:
Fact or fiction? Maturitas, 92, 130–133.
37
38


38 Brennan, D. & Cass, B. (2014). Grandparents as primary carers of their grandchildren:
Policy and practice insights from research. In A. Hayes & D. Higgins (Eds), Families, Policy
and the Law: Selected Essays on Contemporary Issues for Australia. Melbourne: Australian
Institute of Family Studies.
Maintaining independence and
self-esteem
Most older Australians thrive on independence. It is important to
them to be able to look after themselves even if they have to
struggle to do so. Although it may be difficult for younger family
members to watch an older person completing tasks in a slow,
determined way, older adults need this sense of accomplishment.
Children might notice that their ageing father or mother with failing
vision cannot keep the kitchen as clean as before. The ageing
parent may be slower and less meticulous in carpentry tasks or
gardening. To maintain the older person’s sense of self-respect,
nurses and family members need to encourage independence within
a safe environment. Many young people, including nurses,
mistakenly think that they are helpful to older people when they take
over for them and do the job much faster.
Nurses need to acknowledge the older person’s ability to think,
reason and make decisions. While most older people are willing to
listen to suggestions and advice, they like to maintain their
autonomy and appreciate the same thoughtfulness, consideration


and acceptance as the rest of the populace. As has been
mentioned, older adults do not represent as a homogeneous group;
there is as much diversity as there is in any other population group
and the nurse should be just as wary of stereotyping older adults as
of stereotyping any other group. The values and standards held by
older people need to be accepted, whether they are related to
ethical, religious or household matters. The health industry has
previously discriminated against the older adult both in the
community and in acute care. Nurses should reflect on why this has
happened.
Facing death and grieving
Well-adjusted ageing couples usually thrive on companionship. Many
couples rely increasingly on their partners for this company and may
have few outside friends. Great bonds of affection and closeness
can develop during this period of ageing together and nurturing each
other. When a mate dies, the remaining partner inevitably
experiences feelings of loss, emptiness and loneliness. Many are
capable of living alone and can manage to do so; however, reliance
on younger family members may increase as age advances and ill
health occurs.
Older adults are often reminded of the brevity of life by the death of
friends. It is a time when they review their life with happiness or
regret. Feelings of serenity or guilt and inadequacy can arise.
Independence established prior to the loss of a partner makes this


adjustment period easier. A person who has some meaningful
friendships, economic security, ongoing interests in the community,
private hobbies and a peaceful philosophy of life copes more easily
with bereavement. Successful relationships with children and
grandchildren are also of inestimable value. See Chapter 44
 for a
discussion about facing death.
Nurses help people who are alone to adjust to their living
arrangements or lifestyle so that they have more companionship.
Moving to a retirement village that has other people in similar
circumstances and organised social activities is one example. Many
communities provide social centres for older people; for example,
community centres.


Cognitive abilities and ageing
Piaget’s  phases of cognitive development end with the formal
operations phase. However, considerable research on cognitive
abilities and ageing is currently being conducted. Intellectual capacity
includes perception, cognitive agility, memory and learning.
39 Piaget, J. (1966). The Origins of Intelligence in Children. New York: Norton.
Perception
Perception
, or the ability to interpret the environment, depends
on the acuteness of the senses. If the ageing person’s senses are
impaired, the ability to perceive the environment and react
appropriately is diminished. Changes in the nervous system may
also affect perceptual capacity.
Changes in the cognitive structures occur as a person ages. The
brain loses mass with ageing. In addition, blood flow to the brain
decreases, the meninges thicken and brain metabolism slows. As
yet, little is known about the effects of these physical changes on
the cognitive functioning of the older adult. Lifelong mental activity,
particularly verbal activity, may help the older person retain a high
level of cognitive function and maintain long-term memory.
39


Cognitive ability
In older adults, changes in cognitive abilities are more often a
difference in speed than in ability. Overall, the older adult maintains
intelligence, problem solving, judgment, creativity and other well-
practised cognitive skills. Intellectual loss generally reflects a disease
process such as atherosclerosis, which causes the blood vessels to
narrow and diminishes perfusion of nutrients to the brain. It is
important to note that memory impairment increases exponentially
with age, being more prevalent in people over age 85. Cognitive
impairment that interferes with normal life is not considered part of
normal ageing. A decline in intellectual abilities that interferes with
social or occupational functions should always be regarded as
abnormal and investigated thoroughly.
Memory
Memory is also a component of intellectual capacity that involves the
following steps:
1. Momentary perception of stimuli from the environment
referred to as sensory memory
.
2. Storage in short-term memory
 (information held in the
brain for immediate use or what one has in mind at a given
moment). An example of this type of memory is when you call
information for a telephone number and remember the


number only for the brief time needed to dial the number.
Short-term memory is also referred to as recent memory
and includes memories from events or activities that the
person did, from a few minutes to a few hours beforehand.
3. Encoding, in which the information leaves short-term memory
and enters long-term memory
, the repository for
information stored for periods longer than 72 hours and
usually weeks and years. Memories of childhood friends,
teachers and events are stored in long-term memory. Older
people who remember the flowers in their wedding bouquet or
the names of friends from school are drawing from long-term
memory.
In older people, retrieval of information from long-term memory can
be slower, especially if the information is not used frequently. Most
age-related differences, however, occur in short-term memory.
Learning
Older people need additional time for learning, largely because of
the problem of retrieving information. Motivation is also important.
Older adults need to consider the learning experience meaningful;
therefore, the nurse should be particularly careful to discover what is
meaningful to the older adult before attempting education. See
Chapter 28
.


Moral reasoning
Much of the theoretical and empirical work related to moral
development in older adults was conducted in the 1980s and few
current studies can be found. According to Kohlberg , moral
development is completed in the early adult years. Kohlberg
hypothesised that an older person at the preconventional level obeys
rules to avoid pain and the displeasure of others. At stage 1, a
person defines good and bad in relation to self, whereas older
people at stage 2 may act to meet another’s needs as well as their
own. Older adults at the conventional level follow society’s rules of
conduct in response to the expectations of others. Pratt et al.
found that moral reasoning does not decline in old age.
40 Kohlberg, L. (1984). The Psychology of Moral Development: The Nature and Validity of
Moral Stages. San Francisco: Harper & Row.
41 Pratt, M. W., Diessner, R., Pratt, A., Hunsberger, B. & Pancer, S. M. (1996). Moral and
social reasoning and perspective taking in later life: A longitudinal study. Psychology and
Aging, 11(1), 66–73.
Gilligan , however, challenged Kohlberg’s stages as not being
applicable to women. She developed a theory of moral reasoning
based on the concept of caring. She believed that women base
moral judgments on connectedness to others and the value of
relationships, while Kohlberg based his stages on concepts of
justice, objectivity and preservation of rights. Subsequent research
40
41
42


has demonstrated that men and women do make moral decisions
differently and represent Kohlberg (men) and Gilligan (women) along
gender lines. Older adults, however, begin to make moral decisions
that are consistent with both Kohlberg and Gilligan (Pinch &
Parsons
). Older men consider relationships, as well as justice, in
moral decisions and older women add justice to the factors they
consider in moral situations.
42 Gilligan, C. (1982). In a Different Voice: Psychological Theory and Women’s Development.
Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.
43 Pinch, W. J. E. & Parsons, M. E. (1997). Moral orientation of elderly persons: Considering
ethical dilemmas in health care. Nursing Ethics, 4(5), 380–393.
The value and belief patterns that are important to older adults may
be different from those held by younger people because they
developed during a time that was very different from today. In
addition, a large number of today’s older adults are first-generation
immigrants to Australia from culturally or linguistically diverse
backgrounds (CALD). Cultural background, life experiences, gender,
sexual orientation, religion and socioeconomic status all influence
one’s values. The nurse must identify and consider the specific
values of the older person when nursing care is planned.
43


Spirituality and ageing
Older adults can contemplate new religious and philosophical views
and try to understand ideas missed previously or interpreted
differently. The older person may derive a sense of worth by sharing
experiences or views. In contrast, the older adult who has not
matured spiritually may feel impoverishment or despair as the drive
for economic and professional success lessens.
Many older people take their faith and religious practice very
seriously and display a high level of spirituality. They have strong
religious convictions and continue to attend religious meetings or
services. Involvement in religion often helps the older adult to
resolve issues related to the meaning of life, to adversity or to good
fortune. Religion may also be an important coping resource, leading
to enhanced wellbeing. The ‘oldest-old’ person who cannot attend
formal services often continues religious participation in a more
private manner. Assisting the older person to participate in religious
and spiritual practices is an important nursing responsibility.
Today, however, there is an increasing awareness that spirituality is
not always interpreted within a formal religious context. This tends to
make caring all the more complex when attempting to meet the
holistic needs of an individual. Ross , reviewing literature
concerning spiritual care in aged care facilities, found that the term
‘spirituality’ encompasses all of the following: faith and belief;
44


meaning and purpose; love, belonging and forgiveness; peace,
harmony, guidance and hope. As many of the oldest-old adults are
reaching the end of their natural lifespan, meeting the spiritual needs
of the person is a key issue (Ross 2006).
44 Ross, L. (2006). Spiritual care in nursing: An overview of the research to date. Journal of
Clinical Nursing, 15(7), 852–862.


Health problems
Health problems that older adults may experience include injuries,
chronic disabling disease such as hypertension and arthritis, drug
abuse and misuse, alcoholism, dementia and abuse. Leading
causes of death in people aged 65 years and over are chronic
diseases rather than acute or infectious diseases (AIHW 2018). The
leading causes of death are coronary heart disease, dementia,
cerebrovascular disease (stroke), lung cancer and chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease (AIHW 2018). Dementia is the
number one leading cause of death for those aged 85 and over
(AIHW 2018).
Injuries
Injury prevention is a major concern for older people. The nurse and
family are often overwhelmed not only by the intrinsic risks but also
by the extrinsic risks associated with falls. This risk of falls is
multifactorial and includes intrinsic factors such as osteoporosis,
sarcopenia, decreasing exercise and vision impairment as well as
extrinsic factors such as safety concerns within the person’s
environment. As a result, careful documentation of living conditions
and social and medical history will assist in preparing a falls
prevention program. Driving, particularly night driving, requires


caution because accommodation of the eye to light is impaired and
peripheral vision is diminished. The older person needs to learn to
turn their head before changing lanes and should not rely on side
vision; for example, when crossing a street.
Fires are a hazard for the older person because of reduced
sensitivity to pain and heat, and care must be taken to prevent
burns when the person bathes or uses heating devices. Older adults
with cognitive changes are also at risk as a result of short-term
memory loss, which can lead to the older adult leaving on an
appliance, such as an iron, or forgetting to extinguish a cigarette.
Nurses can help older people make the home environment safe by
identifying and correcting specific hazards; for example, installing
handrails on staircases. People with Alzheimer’s disease
 or
disease of the Alzheimer’s type need to have an ongoing risk
assessment as their condition alters and deteriorates. Older adults
experiencing vascular dementia may have a more fluctuating
cognitive condition and monitoring of potential hazards and risks is
vital.
Guidelines for injury prevention for the older adult are detailed in
Chapter 33
.
Chronic disabling illness


Many older adults function well within the community without
impairments; others are afflicted with one or more chronic illnesses
that may seriously impair their functioning. Examples of these are
arthritis, osteoporosis, heart disease, stroke, obstructive lung
disease, hearing and visual alterations and cognitive dysfunctions. In
addition, acute illnesses such as pneumonia, fractures, trauma from
falls, motor vehicle accidents or other incidents may create chronic
health problems. Chronic illness brings many changes to the older
person and the family members. The older adult, for example, may
need increasing help with the activities of daily living such as
ambulation, nutrition, hygiene and so on; expenses concerning
support and health care often escalate and may become an
economic concern; family roles may need to be altered; and family
members may need to change their lifestyle to meet caregiving
needs.
Drug use and misuse
The older adult is at greater risk for adverse drug events (ADEs),
partly because they are more likely to be taking one or more
medicines and partly because they take more drugs with known
contraindications (Manias, Kusljic & Luu Lam
). Older people need
to understand the importance of reporting to their pharmacist and
general practitioner all medication they ingest, including
prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines and complementary or
alternative medicines, as some agents ingested have not been
45


adequately tested for side effects or interactions with other
medications.
45 Manias, E., Kusljic, S. & Luu Lam, D. (2015). Use of the Screening Tool of Older Persons’
Prescriptions (STOPP) and the Screening Tool to Alert doctors to The Right Treatment
(START) in hospitalised older people. Australasian Journal on Ageing, 34(4), 252–258. Doi:
10.1111/ajag.12186.
Research note
When things go bump in the night
G. Rose, V. Decalf, K. Everaert & W. Bower
. Toileting-related falls at night in hospitalised patients:
The role of nocturia. Australasian Journal on Ageing. (Online.) Doi: 10.1111/ajag.12696.
46 Rose, G., Decalf, V., Everaert, K. & Bower, W. (2019). Toileting-related falls at night in hospitalised
patients: The role of nocturia. Australasian Journal on Ageing. (Online.) Doi: 10.1111/ajag.12696.
The purpose of this study was to determine the prevalence
and characteristics of toileting-related falls in hospitalised
older people, across seven medical and aged care wards at a
Melbourne hospital. The researchers conducted a
quantitative retrospective analysis of all falls that occurred at
a tertiary-level hospital in Melbourne during July 2016 and
June 2017. People who were 60 years or over were included
in the study sample. Primarily, information about the fall was
obtained via the incident report and, where the incident report
was poorly completed, the patient chart was reviewed for
additional information. Data included the date and time of the
fall, the location of the fall, the activity the person was doing
46


when the fall occurred and any injuries as a result of the fall.
Over the 12-month period there were 402 total fall incidents
and, of these, 135 falls were associated with toileting. Further
analysis showed that 59 falls were related to toileting at night
(between 9 p.m. and 6.59 a.m.) and 76 falls related to
toileting at other times of the day. The median age of the
person who fell was 82 years (range 74–87 years) and just
over half of the falls related to night-time toileting by males. In
terms of the timing of the falls at night, there were more falls
between 11 p.m. and 1.59 p.m. (18 falls) and 5 a.m. and 5.59
a.m. (15 falls). The most common location was bedside (46%
of falls), followed by bathroom (27%) and the middle of the
room (20%). Approximately 80% of the night-time falls
associated with toileting happened in the early stages of
mobilising. Of the 59 people who fell at night while going to
the toilet, 37 (63%) sustained a physical injury. Most were
classified as minor; however, three were classified as
moderate and included a displaced fractured neck of femur,
inferior pubic rami fracture and a lateral rib fracture. No falls
resulted in death. Interestingly, 88% of the people who fell at
night were recommended to have assistance/supervision
while mobilising. Of these, 80% chose to mobilise without the
recommended assistance. This may be due to reduced
staffing at night, the person not being able to wait to go to the
toilet or lack of education about asking for help.
Implications Upon admission to hospital or a residential
aged care facility, older people should be assessed for
nocturia, gait and mobilisation needs. Having to toilet during


the night can increase risk of falls for older people. Education
about asking for assistance and showing the person where
the nurse call bell is can help minimise people attempting to
mobilise on their own and therefore reduce the risk of a fall.
The complexities involved in the self-administration of medication
may lead to a variety of misuse situations, including taking too much
or too little medication, combining alcohol and medication, combining
prescribed medications with over-the-counter drugs, taking
medications at the wrong time or taking someone else’s medication.
Other potential misuse situations occur when more than one doctor
prescribes medications and the person fails to tell each health care
provider what has been previously prescribed. Additionally, the
pharmaco-dynamics of drugs are altered in older adults. The
variations in absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion of
drugs are related to physiological changes associated with ageing.
These variations are discussed in Chapter 36
.
Most older people living independently in the community take their
medications with no supervision. Therefore, education about
medications is important for safe medication-taking behaviours
(Eliopoulos 2018). The following strategies, taught by the nurse, can
promote safe medication use by the older person:
Write a list of all the medications you are taking, including over-
the-counter drugs and herbal supplements. Include any
medication allergies on the list.


Know the reason you are taking each medication. Ask your
general practitioner the reason for any new medication.
Consider using a ‘pill organiser’ system to help you remember to
take your medications (this can be discussed with your
pharmacist). This is helpful if you have many medications to take
each day.
Ask your pharmacist for easy-to-open containers if you have
difficulty opening the medications.
If possible, obtain all medications from the same pharmacy. This
allows the pharmacist to monitor for drug duplications and
interactions.
Alcoholism
There are two types of older alcoholics: those who began drinking
alcohol in their youth and those who began excessive alcohol use
later in life to help them cope with the changes and problems of their
older years. Many late-onset alcoholics are widowers.
Chronic drinking has major effects on all body systems, causes
progressive liver and kidney damage, damages the stomach and
related organs and slows mental response, frequently leading to
injuries and death. Alcohol interacts with various drugs, altering the
normal effect of the medication on the body. Some medications have
an increased effect when taken with alcohol (e.g. anticoagulants and
narcotics), whereas the action of other medications (e.g. antibiotics)
is inhibited. For the older adult who has a chronic illness and takes


many medications, the combination of drugs and alcohol can lead to
serious drug overdose.
The nurse should assess the number and type of alcoholic
beverages consumed as well as the pattern and frequency of
consumption. It is important that the nurse discusses this topic in a
sensitive manner and takes a comprehensive medicines history to
determine the side effects and interaction effects of alcohol with the
medications that the person is taking. The role of the nurse is to act
as the person’s advocate and facilitate the treatment of the drinking
problem at any age, in addition to the prevention of possible
complications.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Medication Safety
The intention of this standard is to ‘ensure clinicians are
competent to safely prescribe, dispense and administer
appropriate medicines and to monitor medicine use; and to
ensure consumers are informed about medicines and
understand their individual medicine needs and risks’
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC)
, p. 30).
47 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) (2017a). National Safety and Quality Health
Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
47


Implementing this standard is achieved by
taking and recording a comprehensive
medication history when the person is admitted
to hospital, and regularly reviewing the person’s
medications and keeping them informed of the
various medicines they are taking.
Older Australians frequently are taking multiple
medications to manage their health conditions;
because of this, they are more prone to
medication-related errors and complications.
Nurses have an important role in providing
education as well as helping the older population
to manage their medicines to minimise and
prevent complications. For example, some
medicines can lead to a greater risk of falls and
confusion, which can be distressing for the older
person. Nurses can identify where
polypharmacy may put the person at risk
through a comprehensive assessment and
ensure regular medicine reviews and necessary
referrals are in place.
Dementia


Dementia
 is a neurodegenerative disorder which causes a
progressive loss of cognitive function. The most common types of
dementia are Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia (AIHW
2018). Dementia is an umbrella term that is used to describe
impairment of brain function, including language, memory,
perception, personality and cognitive skills (Wicking Dementia
Research & Education Centre ).
48 Wicking Dementia Research & Education Centre (2019). About Wicking Dementia Centre:
What is Dementia. Retrieved from <www.utas.edu.au>
In 2016, 354 000 people were estimated to have dementia in
Australia, almost all of whom were aged 65 and over (AIHW 2018).
This figure is expected to grow significantly over the next few
decades and is projected to more than double by 2046 to 833 000
(AIHW 2018).
Alzheimer’s disease is the most common type of dementia and
cannot be definitively diagnosed until after death at autopsy
(Dementia Australia ). Other forms of dementia are dementia with
Lewy bodies, dementia due to Parkinson’s disease, dementia due to
Huntington’s disease and dementia due to progressive supranuclear
palsy, all of which are relatively uncommon forms of dementia
(Eliopoulos 2018).
49 Dementia Australia (2017). Alzheimer’s Disease. Retrieved from <www.dementia.org.au>.
Once the person no longer recognises family members or close
friends, caregiving is complicated. The nurse’s responsibility is to
48
49


provide supportive nursing care, accurate information and support if
placement in a nursing care facility becomes necessary. Respite
services may also be very helpful to the caregiver. It is important for
the nurse to do an ongoing assessment of both the older person and
the caregiver because changes will occur as the person’s condition
deteriorates.
Patient safety competency framework
9 Medication safety
Medication errors are a problem in Australia,
costing about 1.2 billion annually (ACSQHC ).
Nurses are ideally placed to help educate
members of the health care team about the
principles of safe medication management and
to help identify factors that may compromise
these practices. Administering the wrong
medication/s to a person is one of the most
common errors recorded. It is essential that the
nurse correctly identify they have the ‘right
person’ before administering any medication/s.
For people over 85 years old, where dementia is
prevalent, this can pose a high risk. Facility
processes and checks need to be in place and
complied with to minimise such errors (Levett-
Jones et al.
).
50
51


50 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC) (2017b). Australia Joins International Push to Halve
Medication Errors. Retrieved from
<www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
51 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Mistreatment of older people
Abuse of older people was a term in common usage in the last
century. Koch and Nay  note that ‘abuse’ is a highly emotive word
and overuse or inappropriate use may result in issues becoming
hidden. Terms such as ‘mistreatment’ may present a more accurate
picture of the incident (Koch & Nay 2003). Mistreatment may involve
physical, psychological, emotional, sexual or financial mistreatment,
and includes violation of human or civil rights as well as active or
passive neglect.
52 Koch, S. & Nay, R. (2003). Reducing abuse of older people with dementia and their carers.
Australasian Journal of Ageing, 22(4), 191–194.
When mistreatment of an older person involves physical neglect,
victims may suffer from dehydration, malnutrition and over-sedation.
52


The victim may be deprived of necessary articles such as glasses,
hearing aids or walkers. Psychologically, the person may suffer
verbal assaults, threats, humiliation or harassment. Abuse may also
include failure to provide appropriate medications or medical
treatment, isolation, unreasonable confinement, lack of privacy, an
unsafe environment and involuntary servitude. Some are financially
exploited by relatives who steal from them or misuse their property
or funds.
Drug capsule
Aricept (donepezil hydrochloride)—acetylcholinesterase
inhibitor
The person with Alzheimer’s disease
Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors improve cholinergic function by
inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, thus increasing the amount of
acetylcholine in the brain.
In normal brain function, acetylcholine is an essential
neurotransmitter and plays an important role in cognitive
function, including memory storage and retrieval (NPS
MedicineWise ).
53 NPS MedicineWise (2018). Aricept Tablets: Donepezil Hydrochloride. Retrieved
from <www.nps.org.au>.
Cholinesterase inhibitors do not alter Alzheimer’s disease but
may stabilise the older adult at the current level of dementia
53


and/or lessen symptoms for a short period of time (e.g.
average of 6 months).
Nursing responsibilities
Assess cognitive ability of the person.
Monitor heart rate as bradycardia may occur.
Person- and family-centred teaching
Explain that donepezil may cause dizziness and they may
want to take the medication in the evening before going to
bed.
Educate the person that the medication can be taken with
or without food.
Educate to swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of
water.
Emphasise the importance of taking the medication every
day. A missed dose should be skipped and the person
should return to the regular schedule the next day.
Explain that the medication is started at a lower dose with
a gradual increase in dosage. Higher doses may not
increase the effects but may increase the side effects
(gastrointestinal disturbance, sleep disturbance and
sedation).
Note: Prior to administering any medication, review all
aspects with a current drug handbook or other reliable


source.
Older person abuse or neglect may occur in private homes,
retirement homes or aged care facilities as well as in hospitals.
Many of the abusers are sons or daughters; others include spouses,
relatives (grandchildren, siblings, nieces and nephews) and, in some
instances, health care providers.
Older adults living at home may fail to report abuse or neglect for
many reasons. They may be ashamed to admit that their children
have mistreated them or fear retaliation if they seek help. They may
fear being sent to an institution. They frequently lack financial
resources or lack the mental capacity to be aware of abuse or
neglect and to report the situation. Examples of crimes are assault
and financial abuse of an older person who is physically or mentally
incompetent and has no trustworthy friend or relative to help. In
some instances, nurses can intervene by educating caregivers about
the needs of older adults and available resources to provide
increased home support.
Nurses should be familiar with the laws of their particular state or
territory regarding the reporting of suspected or known abuse. The
legally competent adult cannot be forced, however, to leave the
abusive situation and in many cases may decide to stay. If the
person is not legally competent, court proceedings to attain
guardianship can be initiated.


Developmental assessment
guidelines
The older adult
In these three developmental areas, does the older person
do the following?
Physical development
Adjust to physiological changes (e.g. appearance,
sensory/perceptual, musculoskeletal, neurological,
cardiovascular).
Adapt lifestyle to diminishing energy and ability.
Maintain vital signs (especially blood pressure) within
normal range for age and sex.
Psychosocial development
Manage retirement years in a satisfying manner.
Participate in social and leisure activities.
Have a social network of friends and support people.
View life as worthwhile.
Have high self-esteem.
Gain support from value system and/or spiritual
philosophy.
Accept and adjust to the death of significant others.


Development in activities of daily
living
Exhibit healthy practices in nutrition, exercise, recreation,
sleep patterns and personal habits.
Have the ability to care for self or to secure appropriate
help with activities of daily living.
Have satisfactory living arrangements and income to meet
changing needs.


Health assessment and promotion
Assessment guidelines for the development of the older adult are
shown in the accompanying ‘Developmental assessment guidelines’.
Assessment activities include measurement of weight, height and
vital signs; observation of the skin for hydration status or presence
of lesions; examination of visual acuity using the Snellen chart;
examination of hearing acuity (see Chapter 31
); and questions
about the following:
usual dietary pattern
any problems with bowel or urinary elimination
activity/exercise and sleep/rest patterns
family and social activities and interests
any problems with reading, writing or problem solving
adjustment to retirement or loss of partner.
Health care professionals should also be alert for these signs:
symptoms of depression
risk factors for suicide
signs of abnormal bereavement
changes in cognitive function
medications that increase risk of falls
signs of physical abuse or neglect
skin lesions (malignant and peripheral)


tooth decay, gingivitis, loose teeth
peripheral arterial disease.
Older people are usually concerned about their health and interested
in information and behavioural strategies directed towards improving
it. The nurse may wish to discuss some or all of the health
promotion topics outlined in Box 24.3
. These topics are discussed
in detail in subsequent chapters throughout the book.
BO X
24.3 Health promotion guidelines for
older adults

Total cholesterol and high-density lipid protein
measurement every 2 to 5 years until age 75.
Aspirin, 100 mg daily, if in high-risk group.

group.
Smoking cessation.

Annual digital rectal exam.

Safety
Home safety measures to prevent falls, fire, burns, scalds
and electrocution.
Working smoke detectors in the home.
Motor vehicle safety reinforcement, especially about
driving at night.
Precautions to prevent pedestrian accidents.
Nutrition and exercise
®
®
54


Importance of a well-balanced diet with fewer calories to
accommodate lower metabolic rate and decreased
physical activity.
Importance of sufficient amounts of vitamin D and calcium
to prevent osteoporosis.
Nutritional and exercise factors that may lead to

Importance of 30 minutes of moderate physical activity

Encouraging personal relationships that promote

Assessment of risk factors for maltreatment.
Availability of community centres and programs for older

Case study
Imagine you are a student nurse on clinical placement in the
emergency department (ED) of the local hospital. You are
assisting the Registered Nurse (RN) to assess an older
woman who has arrived at the ED by ambulance. The
ambulance officer has provided the following information
about the woman and her situation: Mrs Georgiou is a 79-
year-old woman who lives alone in a small rented unit. She
has burnt her hands this morning on the stove while
preparing her breakfast and a neighbour called the
ambulance upon finding her on her front step crying with
pain. The neighbour told the ambulance officer that this has
happened before and that Mrs Georgiou has also sustained
several falls at home in the past few weeks. Mrs Georgiou
tells you in accented, broken English that she is frightened
and does not know where she is. Using Figure 11.1
 ‘Mind
map for critical thinking in nursing’ on page 199, develop a
series of questions you and the RN need to ask yourselves or
Mrs Georgiou to best assess her situation. You will be
provided with several questions to commence the process
and need to complete the necessary questions as far as you
can.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. What immediate treatment does Mrs Georgiou require
for her burn injury?
2. Does Mrs Georgiou understand what is being said to
her?
3. Is Mrs Georgiou confused from the pain of her injury
or is something else going on in relation to her


confusion about where she is?
4. Does Mrs Georgiou have family or friends who need to
be contacted?
5. Does Mrs Georgiou have a regular GP?

 Apart from the burn injury, how is Mrs

Chapter 24 Review


Chapter highlights
The older population is steadily growing and projected to
outnumber young people by the middle of the twenty-first
century.
Older adults are categorised into young-old (65 to 74 years), old
(75 to 84 years) and oldest-old (85+ years).
Older people represent a diverse population in Australia. For
example, women outnumber men and the majority of older adults
rate their health as good even though most have at least one
chronic health condition.
It is important for nurses to be aware of their own values and
attitudes towards ageing and older people, to avoid ageism and
to examine whether myths or stereotypes influence their
personal attitudes and beliefs about the older adult.
The gerontological nurse has many roles: healer, caregiver,
educator, advocate and innovator.
The gerontological nurse has a major role in providing care that
is person-centred and culturally competent.
Older people are primary users of health care services in
different types of care settings, including acute care,
rehabilitation, residential aged care facilities, home care and the
community. No matter the setting, the older person requires
health assessment and health promotion.
Several theories have been proposed to account for the
biological ageing process: wear-and-tear, neuroendocrine, free-


radical, genetic, cross-linking, immunity and environmental
theories.
Older people experience many physical changes associated with
ageing. All body systems undergo change: integumentary,
neuromuscular, sensory/perceptual, pulmonary, cardiovascular,
gastrointestinal and genitourinary.
Psychosocial theories about ageing include the disengagement,
activity and continuity theories.
The older person has to adjust to possible psychosocial changes,
including retirement (which necessitates financial and social
adjustments), grandparenting, increasing dependence on others
and coping with losses and death.
The cognitive abilities of the healthy older person undergo some
changes in perception, short-term memory and learning.
In the realm of moral reasoning, most older people begin to
blend concepts of justice and caring relationships into their moral
decision making.
Many older people take their faith and religious practice seriously
and display a high level of spirituality.
Health problems of older people include injuries, chronic disabling
disease, drug use and misuse, alcoholism, dementia and older
person mistreatment.
Health promotion information for all adults needs to include
positive health practices that can promote health and wellness.
These include (a) recommended physical, visual, hearing and
dental assessments, (b) screenings for cardiovascular disease
and tuberculosis, (c) breast and testicular self-examinations, (d)
immunisations, (e) Cervical Screening Test for some older


women, (f) safety precautions to prevent injuries, (g) the
importance of appropriate nutrition and exercise and (h) the
importance of measures to prevent constipation.
Concept check
1. The nurse provides care for an older adult whose husband
died 8 months ago. Which of the following behaviours
indicates that the person is experiencing ineffective coping?
1. She always shows the nurse photographs of her family.
2. She no longer has her hair done by the hairdresser.
3. She visits the cemetery and her husband’s grave every
2 weeks.
4. She is Catholic and goes to mass on a regular daily
basis.
2. A nurse in an aged care facility is caring for several older
adults with noticeable hearing losses. The best way to
communicate with these individuals includes which of the
following?
1. Speak slowly using the proper volume and as few
words as possible.
2. Write the information using large lettering.
3. Speak in a low and distinct voice tone.
4. Have the person increase the volume in the hearing
aid.


3. The nurse notices that an 85-year-old man at an adult care
centre frequently tells stories about when he was younger
and how he came to Australia after the war in Germany. His
stories are told in a very positive manner. How would the
nurse assess his behaviour?
1. Would refer him for a geriatric psychiatric evaluation.
2. Would consider this a normal response for his
developmental level.
3. Would converse with him but distract him and change
the conversation.
4. Would perceive a need to involve him in more social
activities.
4. A 70-year-old woman with Alzheimer’s disease becomes
agitated every evening, pacing and insisting on leaving to go
‘home’. Which of the following is/are most appropriate nursing
intervention(s) to assist this person? Select all that apply.
1. Take her to her room, turn the lights out and leave her
alone.
2. Allow her to pace and inform her that she is at home.
3. Turn on the television and encourage her to watch it
with you.
4. Touch her in a gentle way.
5. While being admitted to a rehabilitation unit, an 82-year-old
woman mentions to the nurse that she ‘has trouble holding
her water’, and adds ‘if I could have that tube back in me like


I had in the hospital, I wouldn’t have so many accidents’.
What is the best response to this woman?
1. ‘Don’t worry, the staff will bring plenty of pads to keep
you dry.’
2. ‘I’ll put the tube back in you so you will stay dry.’
3. ‘Tell me more about your “leaking” problem.’
4. ‘Just call the staff and we’ll help you to the bathroom in
time.’
6. The nurse notices that when an 80-year-old man rises from a
seated position, he uses both arms to push himself up and
also ‘rocks’ back and forth before finally standing. What is the
most appropriate intervention for this man?
1. Suggest a referral to physical therapy for strengthening
exercises.
2. Suggest a waist restraint to remind him not to stand by
himself.
3. Praise him for his attempts to remain independent.
4. Assist him to rise by grasping both his shoulders and
pulling forward.
7. A healthy 78-year-old woman who is considering marriage to
a healthy 79-year-old neighbour tells the nurse she wonders if
they will be able to have sexual intercourse. Which of the
following is the most appropriate response?
1. Sexual activity may be too demanding for the cardiac
systems.


2. Older women maintain sexual function but most older
men are impotent.
3. Most older people are not interested in sexual activity.
4. Older men and older women may have slower
responses to sexual stimulation.
8. Mr Dawson informs the nurse that he has difficulty clearly
seeing the words in the newspaper unless he places the
newspaper an arm’s length away. The nurse documents this
age-related change as:
1. Presbycusis.
2. Xerostomia.
3. Presbyopia.
4. Presbyoesophagus.
9. The nurse integrates the theories of psychosocial ageing into
nursing care of older people by applying which of the following
principles? Older adults:
1. Experience physical changes at a predictable rate.
2. Are as individual as younger adults.
3. Are best supported in long-term facilities.
4. Cause an economic drain on society.
10. The nursing student is planning care for an older person who
had a total knee replacement yesterday evening. Which of
the following interventions would be most appropriate?
1. Ask the person how much of his bath he can perform.


2. Ask the person about his thoughts regarding discharge
from the hospital.
3. Tell the person that he needs to decide when he wants
his medications.
4. Tell the person that he needs to rest and that he (the
nursing student) will bathe him today.
Focus on critical thinking
1. A major focus for the gerontological nurse is to provide
individualised person-centred care in an environment that is
culturally safe. List at least five different nursing interventions
that would be appropriate in helping to achieve this goal.
2. Research has shown that older married couples and/or
females are more likely to remain in their own home longer
compared with older people who live on their own (i.e.

Chapter 25 Promoting family
health
Tanya Langtree
Learning outcomes
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Describe the functions of the family.
Describe different types of families.
Identify theoretical frameworks used in family health promotion.
Identify the components of a family health assessment.


Identify common risk factors regarding family health problems.
Develop nursing diagnoses, outcomes and interventions
pertaining to family functioning.
Key terms

Nurses assess and plan health care for three
types of people: the individual, the family and
the community. The beliefs and values of each
person and the support they receive largely
come from their family and are reinforced by the
community. Thus, an understanding of family
dynamics and the context of the community
assists the nurse in planning care. When a
family is the recipient of care, the nurse
determines the health status of the family and
its individual members, the level of family
functioning, family interaction patterns and
family strengths and weaknesses.


Family health
The family
 is a basic unit of society. It consists of those
individuals, male or female, youth or adult, legally or not legally
related, genetically or not genetically related, who are considered by
the person to represent their significant people. In the nursing
profession, interest in the family unit and its impact on the health,
values and productivity of individual family members is expressed by
family-centred nursing
: nursing that considers the health of the
family as a unit in addition to the health of individual family
members.
Functions of the family
The economic resources needed by the family are secured by adult
members. The family protects the physical health of its members by
providing adequate nutrition, shelter and health care services.
Nutritional and lifestyle practices of the family also directly affect the
developing health attitudes and lifestyle practices of the children.
In addition to providing an environment conducive to physical growth
and health, the family creates an atmosphere that influences the
cognitive and the psychosocial growth of its members. Children and
adults in healthy, functional families receive support, understanding


and encouragement as they progress through predictable
developmental stages, as they move in or out of the family unit and
as they establish new family units. In families where members are
physically and emotionally nurtured, individuals are challenged to
achieve their potential in the family unit. As individual needs are met,
family members are able to support other members of the family
and can contribute to the broader community.
Families from different cultures are an integral part of Australia’s
population mix (see Figure 25.1
). Each family has values and
beliefs that are unique to their culture of origin and that shape the
family’s structure, methods of interaction, health care practices and
coping mechanisms. These factors interact to influence the health of
families.
Figure 25.1


Australian society is made up of a mix of cultures.
Source: © Richard Baker/Alamy Stock Photo.
Religion can form a significant component of a family’s cultural
practices. While the dominant religion in Australia is Christianity,
Buddhism (2.4% of the total Australian population) and Islamic faiths
(2.6%) are steadily becoming more popular (Australian Bureau of
Statistics (ABS) ). Approximately 30% of the Australian population
do not affiliate with any religion (ABS 2017a). This rising trend of
individuals reporting no religious affiliation is being replicated in other
Western countries.
1 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2017a). Census of Population and Housing: Australia
Revealed, 2016. Cat. no. 2024.0. Canberra: ABS.
Becoming acculturated is a slow, stressful process of learning the
language and customs of a new country. Approximately 73% of
permanent migrants speak a language other than English at home
(ABS ). However, it is important to note that this data does not
reflect the person’s ability to speak English, with 83% of permanent
migrants reporting they can speak English very well (ABS 2018a).
Children in cultural clusters often have greater contact with the world
around them than do adults. Through school, children become more
proficient in their second language and more comfortable with new
customs and behaviours. However, sometimes children create
conflict in the family when they bring home new ideas and values.
For more information about cultural aspects of health of individuals
and families, see Chapter 19
.

2

from the Australian Census and Migrants Integrated Dataset, Australia, 2016. Cat. no. 3417.0.
Canberra: ABS.
Patient safety competency framework
3 Cultural competence
Nursing students must be able to discuss how
the life experiences of migrants and refugees
can impact on their health and wellbeing
(Levett-Jones et al. ).
3 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
