Types of families in today’s society
Families consist of people (structure) and their responsibilities within
the family (roles). Government data are grouped by ‘household
composition’. The structure of the ‘household composition’ integrates
with the concept of ‘family composition’ and reflects the complexity
of Australian family constructs. A family structure of parents and
3


their offspring is known as the nuclear family
. The relatives of
nuclear families, such as grandparents, aunts and uncles, compose
the extended family
. In some families, members of the extended
family live with the nuclear family. Members of the extended family
often provide a source of emotional, physical and/or financial
support, despite living at a different location. For example, a
grandparent may care for their grandchildren, thereby enabling their
child—the parent—to resume employment.
Some families live in houses, some in apartments; some live in
urban areas, some in regional towns; and some are homeless. The
ABS  defines homelessness as when an individual’s current living
arrangement is in an inadequate lodging, the period of tenancy is
constrained or non-existent, or the individual has limited privacy or
space for social relations. The latter category incorporates the
concept of severe ‘overcrowding’, where the number of people living
in a shelter exceeds adequate sleeping arrangements. Importantly,
homelessness is not equivalent to ‘roof-lessness’ and homelessness
is not a choice made by the individual or family (ABS 2018b).
4 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018b). Census of Population and Housing:
Estimating Homelessness, 2016. Cat. no. 2049.0. Canberra: ABS.
In Australia on any given night, 50 out of every 10 000 people are
considered homeless, with the Northern Territory reporting the
highest rates of homelessness (ABS 2018b). The rates of
homelessness are higher among Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander people, with 1 in 28 Indigenous Australians being homeless
on Census night in 2016 (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare
4


(AIHW) ). In 2017–18, the majority of people seeking assistance
from specialist homelessness services in Australia were single-
parent families (AIHW 2018a). Escaping family violence or
overwhelming financial strain are primary reasons for Australian
families becoming homeless (AIHW 2018a).
5 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018a). Specialist Homelessness
Services Annual Report 2017–18. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Australian society consists of many types of family (see Figure
25.2
).
Figure 25.2
5


Definitions about what constitutes a ‘family’ are broad in a society
such as Australia.
Source: Scott Griessel/123RF.
Traditional family
Traditionally, the Australian family was viewed as an autonomous
unit in which both parents resided in the home with their children, the
mother often assuming the nurturing role and the father providing
the necessary economic resources. In today’s society, both males
and females are less bound to traditional role patterns. For example,
fathers are more likely to be involved with the household chores,
their children and family life. However, Australian women,
irrespective of their primary role in the family unit, still assume the
majority of household chores (Foster & Stratton ).
6 Foster, G. & Stratton, L. S. (2019). What women want (their men to do): Housework and
satisfaction in Australian households. Feminist Economics, 25(3), 23–47. Doi:
10.1080/13545701.2019.1609692.
The structure of families within Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
communities often differs from what is viewed as the traditional
Australian family unit. This perspective includes a wider sense of
family than the typical nuclear family and frequently leads to
dynamic, complex and multigenerational household structures
(Newton ). One of the major benefits of this family structure is there
is a shared responsibility for child-rearing by all community
members.
6
7


7 Newton, B. (2019). Understanding child neglect in Aboriginal families and communities in the
context of trauma. Child & Family Social Work, 24(2), 218–226. Doi: 10.1111/cfs.12606.
Two-career family
In two-career (or dual-career) families, both partners are employed.
They may or may not have children. Couple families with children
are the most common type of family in Australia, with this trend
predicted to continue in coming years (ABS ). Two-career families
have become the norm in Australia. In 2016, the ABS identified that
62.4% of all couple families had both partners who were working
(ABS ). The changes in career profiles may account for women
having children later in life, with 4.3% of babies being born to women
over 40 in 2017, compared with 3.4% of babies born to the same
age group in 2006 (ABS ).
8 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2019). Household and Family Projections, Australia,
2016 to 2041. Cat. no. 3236.0. Canberra: ABS.
9 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2017b). 2016 Census QuickStats. Retrieved from
<https://quickstats.censusdata.abs.gov.au>.
10 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018c). Births, Australia, 2017. Cat. no. 3301.0.
Canberra: ABS.
Single-parent family
Single-parent families account for 15.8% of all household
compositions and this figure continues to increase (ABS 2017b). Of
8
9
10


these families, 81.8% are headed by women (ABS 2017b). There
are many reasons for single parenthood: the death of a spouse,
separation or divorce from a partner, a committed lifestyle choice or
adoption of a child by a single man or woman. Single parents without
a support network may face additional stresses of parenthood, such
as childcare concerns, financial concerns, role overload, role fatigue
in managing daily tasks and social isolation. Consequently, a single
parent is at greater risk of experiencing a mental health issue
compared with a couple family with children (ABS ).
11 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2015). General Social Survey: Summary Results,
Australia, 2014. Cat. no. 4159.0. Canberra: ABS.
Adolescent family
Birth rates for teenagers have dropped significantly over the past
two decades, with approximately 2.4% of Australian children in 2017
being born to women aged 19 years and under (ABS 2018c).
Despite the lower rate of teenage pregnancies, the incidence of
teenage births is higher (approximately 14%) for Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander people (ABS 2018c). Adolescent pregnancies
frequently interrupt or stop formal education. Children born to an
adolescent are often at greater risk of health and social problems
and they may have fewer role models to assist in breaking out of the
cycle of poverty.
Foster family
11


Children who can no longer live with their birth parents may require
placement with a family who has agreed to include them temporarily.
The legal agreement between the foster family and the court to care
for the child includes the expectations of the foster parents and the
financial compensation they will receive. The foster parents (with or
without their own children) may house more than one foster child at
a time or different children over many years. At some time in the
future, the fostered child might return to the birth parent(s) or be
legally and permanently adopted by other parents.
Blended family
Existing family units who join together to form new families are
known as blended families or step-families. Family integration
requires time and effort. Stresses occur as blended families get
acquainted with each other, respect differences and establish new
patterns of behaviour. When blended families with children form
following the divorce or death of a parent, adjustment can be
particularly challenged by the normal processes of grief and loss
(see Chapter 44
).
Intra-generational family
In some cultures, and as people live longer, more than two
generations may live together. Children may continue to live with
their parents after having their own children or the grandparents
may move in with their grown children’s families after some years of
living apart. In other situations, a generation is skipped or missing;


that is, grandparents live with and care for their grandchildren but
the children’s parents are not a part of this family. Many life events
and choices can lead to this type of family.
Cohabiting family
Cohabiting (or communal) families consist of unrelated individuals or
families who live under one roof. A common time for cohabitation is
when adolescents move out of home for the first time into a shared
house. Another common reason for cohabitation in Australia is when
a young couple decide to test their commitment to each other
through moving in together. In recent years, the incidence of couples
living together prior to marriage has increased to 81%, reflecting the
changing social norms of Australian culture (Australian Institute of
Family Studies ; ABS ).
12 Australian Institute of Family Studies (2019). Marriage Rates in Australia. Retrieved from
<https://aifs.gov.au>.
13 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018d). Marriages and Divorces, Australia,
2017.Cat. no. 3310.0. Canberra: ABS.
Cohabitating can also help individuals and families to share
household expenses. In Australia, a significant proportion of a family
unit’s collective income goes towards household expenses
(Warren ). With rising living and housing costs being experienced in
Australia, new patterns of cohabitating are beginning to emerge
(Warren 2018). These include: room sharing, where individuals who
are unrelated and not in a relationship share a room; ‘couch surfing’,
12
13
14


where an individual regularly moves between temporary living
arrangements (e.g. staying with different friends); and ‘garage
sleeping’, where an individual may rent the garage space of a house
(Nasreen & Ruming ; Curry et al.
).
14 Warren, D. (2018). Children’s housing experiences. In D. Warren & G. Daraganova (Eds),
Growing up in Australia—The Longitudinal Study of Australian Children, Annual Statistical
Report 2017 (pp. 9–24). Melbourne: Australian Institute of Family Studies. Retrieved from
<https://growingupinaustralia.gov.au>.
15 Nasreen, Z. & Ruming, K. (2018). Room sharing in Sydney: A complex mix of affordability,
overcrowding and profit maximisation. Urban Policy and Research, 37(8), 1–19. Doi:
10.1080/08111146.2018.1556632.
16 Curry, S. R., Morton, M., Matjasko, J. L., Dworsky, A., Samuels, G. M. & Schlueter, D.
(2017). Youth homelessness and vulnerability: How does couch surfing fit? American Journal
of Community Psychology, 60(1–2), 17–24. Doi: 10.1002/ajcp.12156.
Overcrowding is also becoming more common in Australia (ABS
2018b). It can impact on effective parenting, stress levels and
emotional wellbeing of family members (Cant et al.
). The difficulty
in maintaining sanitation standards in severely overcrowded
households can also lead to an increased risk of infections spreading
between family members.
17 Cant, R. L., O’Donnell, M., Sims, S. & Harries, M. (2019). Overcrowded housing: One of a
constellation of vulnerabilities for child sexual abuse. Child Abuse & Neglect, 93, 239–248.
Doi: 10.1016/j.chiabu.2019.05.010.
15
16
17


Research note
Family-centred care for families living with cystic
fibrosis in a rural setting: a qualitative study
M. Jessup, W. Smyth, G. Abernethy, L. Shields & T. Douglas
. Family-centred care for families living
with cystic fibrosis in a rural setting: A qualitative study. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 27(3–4), e590–
e599. Doi: 10.1111/jocn.14105.
18 Jessup, M., Smyth, W., Abernethy, G., Shields, L. & Douglas, T. (2018). Family-centred care for
families living with cystic fibrosis in a rural setting: A qualitative study. Journal of Clinical Nursing,
27(3–4), e590–e599. Doi: 10.1111/jocn.14105.
This article discusses the findings of a qualitative study
exploring parents’ perceptions of family-centred care with
respect to cystic fibrosis (CF) management in regional
Australia. Data was collected using semi-structured interviews
with parents of children with CF. Five themes emerged from
the interview data: (1) Daily care: A family affair; (2) Family-
centred care: Seeking inclusion; (3) Control versus
collaboration: Seeking mutual trust; (4) Future projections;
and (5) The CF circle. The first theme, Daily care: A family
affair, described the daily balancing act parents must face
when meeting the care needs of the child with CF and the
broader needs of the family unit. Within the second and third
themes, the need for parents to feel involved and have a say
in their child’s care were identified as being pivotal in
maintaining family-centred care. The fourth theme, Future
projections, explored the parents’ fears and hopes for the
18


child’s future. In the final theme, The CF circle, the unique
positioning of parents with children with CF was explored—
their existence in a ‘normal world’ and a world that is
dominated by CF.
Implications Negative interactions with staff and restrictive
health care processes can interfere with the delivery of
family- centred care.
Same-sex family
Over the past decade, same-sex couples have steadily become
more socially accepted in Australia. With this growing acceptability,
Australian same-sex couples now have equal entitlements and rights
as heterosexual couples, including the right to legally marry
(Commonwealth of Australia ). The number of same-sex families in
Australia is steadily increasing, with 15% of same-sex couples now
having children (ABS ; ABS 2017a; Qu, Knight & Higgins
). While
children raised in same-sex families develop gender role orientations
and behaviours similar to children in the general population, they
may experience increased levels of social stigma (Qu et al. 2017).
Nurses therefore need to be mindful of the negative effects of such
stigma and other forms of discrimination (Perales & Campbell ).
19 Commonwealth of Australia (2019). Getting Married. Retrieved from <www.ag.gov.au>.
20 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018e). Census of Population and Housing:
Reflecting Australia—Stories from the Census, 2016. Cat. no. 2071.0. Canberra: ABS.
19
20
21
22


21 Qu, L., Knight, K. & Higgins, D. (2017). Same-sex Couple Families in Australia (Fact
Sheet). Retrieved from <https://aifs.gov.au>.
22 Perales, F. & Campbell, A. (2018). Who supports equal rights for same-sex couples?
Evidence from Australia. Family Matters, 100, 28–41. Retrieved from <https://aifs.gov.au>.
Real-world practice
Family-centred care involves encompassing the entire
family dynamic when providing care, especially for
newborns and children. It provides an opportunity for
nurses and parents to work in partnership to ensure
the optimal outcome is achieved for all involved. As
health professionals, we need to look at the whole
picture, not just a small section, to truly understand the
situation and provide holistic care.
The following is an example of family-centred care.
Jane and her baby Cooper drop in to a community
baby clinic for a weight check. During this encounter,
the nurse observes that Jane is quick to hand over
Cooper and appears disinterested when discussing his
milestones, feeding and sleeping patterns. It is noted
that Cooper has mild plagiocephaly (asymmetrical
head shape) but Jane does not easily engage when
discussing this feature and appears more interested in
her phone. Initially, the nurse could assume that Jane
is disinterested and reluctant to take on board the


nurse’s information and recommendations for Cooper.
Consequently, the nurse may feel frustrated with Jane
as her behaviour is not what the nurse thinks it should
be.
If approached with family-centred care in mind, the
nurse will take the time to talk to Jane and find out
more information about her family’s situation. When
talking to Jane, the nurse discovers that Cooper is
Jane’s first baby and she has no private transport
available to her so she walks to the clinic. Additionally,
the nurse discovers that Jane has just moved to this
town, her husband works away and all of Jane’s
support networks are down south. Jane divulges that
she does not know what she should be doing with
Cooper and feels very lonely and isolated. Jane then
states that her mother calls around this time every day
to speak to her and she does not like to miss her calls.
This information sheds a completely new light on the
assumptions made by the nurse. Knowing this
information allows the nurse to create opportunities to
engage Jane with local support services and activities
to assist her with her parenting. Thus, a therapeutic
relationship is established between Jane and the
nurse. This mutual respect facilitates Jane and the
nurse to set achievable, realistic goals for Cooper. In
turn, this increases Jane’s compliance with ongoing


treatment recommendations as they are individualised
to her family’s needs.
Tamlyn Brice, RN, RM, BNSc, PGDipMid, PGCertCHN The Townsville University Hospital,
Queensland
Single adults living alone
Individuals who live by themselves represent a significant portion of
today’s society. The 2016 Census identified that 24% of family units
are single-person households (ABS 2017a). Singles include young
self-supporting adults who have recently left the nuclear family as
well as older adults living alone. Young adults typically move in and
out of living situations and may have membership in family, non-
family household and living alone categories at several different
times. Older adults may find themselves single through divorce,
separation or the death of a spouse and often remain living alone for
the remainder of their lives.


Applying theoretical frameworks to
families
A variety of theoretical frameworks provide the nurse with a holistic
overview of health promotion for families across the lifespan. Major
theoretical frameworks that nurses use in promoting the health of
families are systems theory and structural–functional theory.
Systems theory
A system
 is a set of interacting identifiable parts or components.
The basic concepts of general systems theory were proposed in the
1950s. One of its major proponents, von Bertalanffy , introduced
systems theory as a universal theory that could be applied to many
fields of study. Nurses are increasingly using systems theory to
understand not only biological systems but also systems in families,
communities, and nursing and health care. General systems theory
provides a way of examining interrelationships and deriving
principles.
23 von Bertalanffy, L. (1980). General System Theory (revised from original 1969). New York,
NY: George Braziller.
23


Systems may be complex and the systems’ components are often
studied as subsystems
. For family systems, the subsystems
would be individuals. Looking back up the hierarchy, the systems
above other systems are referred to as suprasystems
—the
family is the suprasystem of the individual. See Figure 25.3
 for a
hierarchy of the human system.
Figure 25.3


A common system hierarchy.
A system depends on the quality and quantity of its input,
throughput, output and feedback. Input
 consists of information,
material or energy that enters the system. After the input is
absorbed by the system, it is processed in a way useful to the
system. This transformation is called throughput
. For example,
food is input to the digestive system; it is digested (throughput) so
that it can be used by the body. Output
 is energy, matter or
information given out by the system as a result of its processes.
Output from the digestive system includes caloric energy, nutrients,
urine and faeces.
Feedback
 is the mechanism by which some of the output of a
system is returned to the system as input. Feedback enables a
system to regulate itself by redirecting the output of a system back
into the system as input, thus forming a feedback loop (see Figure
25.4
). This input influences the behaviour of the system and its
future output. Negative feedback
 inhibits change; positive
feedback
 stimulates change.


Figure 25.4
A system with a feedback mechanism.


The interrelatedness of all the parts of a system is the basis for
nursing’s holistic view of the person. A tumour of the liver affects the
whole individual; that is, the person may be nauseated, tired and
anxious. A psychological problem such as stress or anxiety may also
manifest itself by physiological symptoms, such as sleeplessness,
nausea or changes in cardiac function.
The family unit can also be viewed as a system. Its members are
interdependent, working towards specific purposes and goals.
Families, as open systems, are continually interacting with and
influenced by other systems in the community. Boundaries regulate
the input from other systems that interact with the family system;
they also regulate output from the family system to the community
or to society. Boundaries protect the family from the demands and
influences of other systems. Families are likely to welcome input
from others, encourage their individual members to adapt beliefs
and practices to meet the changing demands of society, seek out
health care information and use community resources.
Using a systems theory for the health promotion of a family, the
nurse considers how each element of the system may affect the
other elements. For example, if a child is seriously injured in a home
accident, other siblings may feel left out of the considerable attention
devoted to the child, a parent may withdraw if there are feelings of
guilt for not preventing the accident and other family members may
be recruited to assist with finances or chores while the nuclear family
focuses on the injured child. The nurse will need to facilitate a care


plan that includes diagnoses and problems affecting the different
components of the family system.
Structural–functional theory
The structural–functional theory focuses on family structure and
function. The structural component of the theory addresses the
membership of the family and the relationships between family
members. Intra-family relationships are complex because of the
numerous relationships that exist within the family structure:
mother–daughter, brother–sister, spouse– partner and so on. These
relationships are constantly evolving as children mature and leave
the family nest and adults age and become more dependent on
others to meet their daily needs.
The functional aspect of the theory examines the effects of intra-
family relationships on the family system, as well as their effects on
other systems. Some of the main functions of the family include
developing a sense of family purpose and affiliation, adding and
socialising new members, and providing and distributing care and
services to members. A healthy family organises its members and
resources in meeting family goals; it functions in harmony, working
towards shared goals.
The nurse can use this theory to examine how the family functions.
Questions nurses may need to clarify include: Who is/are the
primary decision maker(s) in the family? How does communication


occur between family members? What is the economical and
emotional stability of the family members? The nurse will need to
facilitate a care plan that stabilises or enhances the family structure
and function during the episode of disruption.


Nursing management
Assessing
The purpose of family assessment is to determine the level of family
functioning, clarify family interaction patterns, identify family
strengths and weaknesses, and describe the health status of the
family and its individual members. Also important are family living
patterns, including communication, child-rearing, coping strategies
and health practices. Family assessment gives an overview of the
family process and helps the nurse identify areas that need further
investigation. Nurses carry out a detailed assessment in specific
target areas as they become more acquainted with the family and
begin to understand family needs and strengths more fully. In
planning interventions, nurses need to focus not only on problems
but also on family strengths and resources as part of the nursing
care plan (see Box 25.1
).
BO X
25.1 Family assessment guide


Family structure
Size and type: nuclear, extended or other type of family.
Age and gender of family members.
Family roles and functions
Family members working outside the home; type of work
and satisfaction with it.
Household roles and responsibilities and how tasks are
distributed.
Ways child-rearing responsibilities are shared.
Major decision maker and methods of decision making.
Family members’ satisfaction with roles, the way tasks are
divided and the way decisions are made.
Physical health status
Current physical health status of each member.
Perceptions of own and other family members’ health.
Preventive health practices (e.g. status of immunisations,
oral hygiene practices, regularity of visual examinations).
Routine health care, when and why doctor last seen.
Screening for and knowledge of any genetic disorders.
Adherence to recommended management plans (e.g.
asthma management plan, medication regimen
adherence).


Interaction patterns
Ways of expressing affection, love, sorrow, anger and so
on.
Most significant family member in person’s life.
Openness of communication with all family members.
Family values
Cultural and religious orientations; degree to which cultural
and religious practices are followed.
Use of leisure time and whether leisure time is shared with
total family unit.
Family’s view of education, teachers and the school
system.
Health values: how much emphasis is put on exercise,
diet, preventive health care.
Coping resources
Degree of emotional support offered to one another.
Availability of support people and affiliations outside the
family (e.g. friends, church memberships).
Sources of stress (e.g. if a member of the family has a
disability).
Methods of handling stressful situations and conflicting
goals of family members.


Ability to meet current and future financial needs.
The assessment begins with a complete health history. The nurse
focuses first on the family unit and then on the individuals in that
family. The health history is one of the most effective ways of
identifying existing or potential health problems. The health history is
followed by a physical assessment of each of the family members.
Employment of a genogram will help the nurse to visualise how all
family members are genetically related to each other and to grasp
how patterns of chronic conditions are present within the family unit.
A genogram
 is composed of visual representations of gender and
lines of birth descent through the generations (see Figure 25.5
).
Figure 25.5


An example of a family genogram with accompanying legend
(symbols used in genograms).
The nurse should also develop an ecomap for family members
individually and as a group to document the family unit’s energy
expenditures within the community setting. An ecomap
 provides a
visualisation of how the family unit interacts with the external
community environment such as schools, religious commitments,
occupational duties and recreational pursuits (see Figure 25.6
).
When the focus is on health, the appraisal includes information on
lifestyle behaviours and health beliefs. The nurse uses data from the
health appraisal to formulate a health profile. The health profile


provides the data necessary to determine wellness or to establish a
nursing diagnosis and to plan appropriate nursing interventions to
promote optimal health through lifestyle modification.
Figure 25.6


An example of a family ecomap. Many more components may be
added to the map.
Health beliefs
To promote health, the nurse must understand the health beliefs of
individuals and families. Health beliefs may reflect a lack of
information or misinformation about health or disease. They may
also include folklore, alternative and complementary therapies and
practices from different cultures. The nurse is frequently in a position
to give updated information or correct misconceptions. This function
is an important component of the nursing care plan. For additional
information on health beliefs, see Chapter 18
.
Family communication patterns
The effectiveness of family communication determines the family’s
ability to function as a cooperative, growth-producing unit. Messages
are constantly being communicated between family members, both
verbally and non-verbally. The information transmitted influences
how members work together, fulfil their assigned roles in the family,
incorporate family values and develop skills to function in society.


Intra-family communication plays a significant role in the
development of self-esteem, which is necessary for the growth of
personality.
Families who communicate effectively transmit messages clearly.
Members are free to express their feelings without fear of
jeopardising their standing in the family. Family members support
one another and have the ability to listen, empathise and reach out
to one another in times of crisis. When the needs of family members
are met, they are more able to reach out to meet the needs of
others in society.
When patterns of communication between family members are
dysfunctional, messages are often communicated unclearly. Verbal
communication may be incongruent with non-verbal messages.
Power struggles may be evidenced by hostility, anger or silence.
Members may be cautious in expressing their feelings because they
cannot predict how others in the family will respond. When family
communication is impaired, the growth of individual members is
stunted. As a result, individual members may turn to other systems
to seek personal validation and gratification.
The nurse needs to observe intra-family communication patterns
closely. Nurses should pay special attention to who does the talking
for the family, which members are silent, how disagreements are
handled and how well the members listen to one another and
encourage the participation of others. Observation of non-verbal


communication is also important as it can reveal valuable clues
about what individual family members are feeling.
Family coping mechanisms
Family coping mechanisms are the behaviours families use to deal
with stress or changes imposed. Coping mechanisms can be viewed
as an active method of problem solving developed to meet life’s
challenges. The coping mechanisms families and individuals develop
reflect their individual resourcefulness. Families may use coping
patterns rather consistently over time or may change their coping
strategies when new demands are made on the family. The success
of a family largely depends on how well it copes with the stresses it
experiences.
Nurses working with families realise the importance of assessing
coping mechanisms as a way of determining how families relate to
stress. Also important are the resources available to the family.
Internal resources, such as knowledge, skills, effective
communication patterns and a sense of mutuality and purpose within
the family, assist in the problem-solving process. In addition,
external support systems promote coping and adaptation. These
external systems may be extended family, friends, religious
affiliations, health care professionals or social services. The
development of social support systems is particularly valuable today
because many families, due to stressors such as disability, mobility
or poverty, are isolated from the resources that would traditionally
have helped them cope.


The National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) is one example of
how support services are now being targeted to meet the needs for
support of the person with a disability and their family (National
Disability Insurance Agency ). Through the NDIS, each eligible
person has an individualised plan of care implemented that meets
the goals of the person and their family. Hence, this holistic
approach not only maximises the person’s functionality but it also
increases the family’s access to services.
24 National Disability Insurance Agency (2018). How the NDIS Works. Retrieved from
<www.ndis.gov.au>.
Family violence
The incidence of family violence has increased in recent years.
Fortunately, Australians have a growing awareness of this serious
issue due to the 2015 Australian of the Year Rosie Batty’s own story
of family violence and her commitment to change the culture of
domestic and family violence in Australia.
In its report Family, Domestic and Sexual Violence in Australia,
2018, the AIHW
 defines family violence as ‘violence between
family members as well as between current or former intimate
partners’ (p. 3). This definition of family violence may include, but is
not limited to, physical violence, sexual assault, financial abuse,
verbal abuse, emotional and psychological abuse, serious neglect in
a relationship of dependence, damage to property, causing injury or
death to an animal, spiritual or cultural abuse and exposing a child to
24
25


the effects of these behaviours. Early symptoms are evident in
burns, cuts, fractures and even death. Other manifestations often
seen are depression, alcohol and substance abuse and suicide
attempts. Nurses should be alert to the symptoms of family violence
and act appropriately to report it and obtain resources for the family.
Most states and territories have mandatory reporting requirements
for suspected child abuse.
25 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018b). Family, Domestic and Sexual
Violence in Australia, 2018. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Risk for health problems
Risk assessment helps the nurse identify individuals and groups at
higher risk than the general population of developing specific health
problems, such as stroke, diabetes and lung cancer. The
vulnerability of family units to health problems may be based on the
maturity level of individual family members, heredity or genetic
factors, gender, ethnicity, sociological factors and lifestyle practices.
Maturity factors
Families with members at both ends of the age continuum are at risk
of developing health problems. Families entering childbearing and
child-rearing phases experience many changes in roles,
responsibilities and expectations. The many conflicting demands on
the family often cause stress and fatigue, which may impede growth
of individual family members and the functioning of the group as a


unit. For example, adults who simultaneously care for both their
ageing parents and their own children may be at risk of caregiver
role strain. Alternatively, older adults may feel a lack of purpose and
decreased self-esteem. These feelings in turn reduce their
motivation to engage in health promoting behaviours, such as
exercise or community and family involvement.
Hereditary factors
People born into families with a history of certain diseases, such as
diabetes or cardiovascular disease, are at greater risk of developing
these conditions. A detailed family health history, including
genetically transmitted disorders, is crucial to the identification of
people and families at risk. These data are used not only to monitor
the health of individual family members but also to recommend
modifications in health practices that potentially reduce the risk,
minimise the consequences or postpone the development of
genetically related conditions.
Gender or ethnicity
Some family units or family members may be at risk of developing a
disease by reason of gender or ethnicity. Males, for example, are at
greater risk of having cardiovascular disease at an earlier age than
females, and females are at greater risk of developing osteoporosis,
particularly after menopause. Although it is sometimes difficult to
separate genetic factors from cultural factors, certain risk factors
seem to be related to ethnicity. Tay-Sachs, for example, is a


neurodegenerative disease that occurs primarily in descendants of
Eastern European Jews.
Sociological factors
Poverty is a major problem that affects not only the family but also
the community and society. Despite improvement in the health of the
people in Australia, partially through the implementation of Medicare
and through public health initiatives during the previous century,
there still remains a disparity in the availability of health services.
Regional and remote populations and the lower socioeconomic
sector are often disadvantaged (see Chapter 9
).
Lifestyle factors
Many diseases are preventable, the effects of some diseases can
be minimised or the onset of disease can be delayed through
lifestyle modifications. Lifestyle diseases include certain cancers,
cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus and tooth decay.
The incidence of lung cancer, for example, would be greatly reduced
if people stopped smoking. Good nutrition, dental hygiene and the
use of fluoride—in the water supply and in toothpaste—have been
shown to reduce dental decay or caries. Many diseases, such as
pertussis and hepatitis B, can be prevented by immunisations. Other
important lifestyle considerations are exercise, stress management
and sleep. A nurse’s role is to disseminate information about
prevention and to motivate families to make lifestyle changes prior to
the onset of illness.


Identifying nursing diagnoses,
outcomes and interventions
Individuals with disruption in family health
History Mr and Mrs Gibson’s 9-year-old son Harry has just
been diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus. Harry is
currently in hospital for the stabilisation of his blood glucose
levels. The Gibsons also have an 11-year-old daughter and a
4-year-old son.
Diagnosing and Planning
Data gathered during a family assessment may lead to the following
nursing diagnoses:
Interrupted family processes: a change in family relationships
and/or functioning.
Readiness for enhanced family coping: effective management
of adaptive tasks by family member involved with the individual’s
health challenge, who now exhibits desire and readiness for
enhanced health and growth in regard to self and in relation to
the family member requiring health care.
Disabled family coping: behaviour of significant person (family
member or other primary person) that disables their capacity to


effectively address tasks essential to either person’s adaptation
to the health challenge.
Impaired parenting: inability of the primary caretaker to create,
maintain or regain an environment that promotes the optimum
growth and development of the child.
Impaired home maintenance: inability to independently
maintain a safe, growth promoting, immediate environment.
Caregiver role strain: difficulty in performing family caregiver
role.
Examples of contributing factors for one selected diagnosis, desired
outcomes to evaluate the achievement of goals and the
effectiveness of nursing interventions are listed in ‘Identifying nursing
diagnoses, outcomes and interventions’.
Being sensitive to cultural differences is important in assessment
and planning care. Knowing who makes most of the decisions in the
family, especially in health care, helps the nurse to know who to ask
in order to obtain information and also who to give instructions to.
The extended family unit is found in many cultures and there may be
a difference in health beliefs and health practices within the family.
Older members of the family may use their traditional practices while
younger members may have had more exposure to modern
practices. Building a trusting relationship with these families is the
first step towards planning more effective care by being able to talk
to them about their beliefs and practices.


Nurses need to focus on assisting the family to plan realistic
goals/outcomes and strategies that enhance family functioning, such
as improving communication skills, identifying and utilising support
systems and developing and rehearsing parenting skills. Anticipatory
guidance may assist well-functioning families in preparing for
predictable developmental transitions that occur in the life of
families.
The family experiencing a health crisis
Illness of a family member is a crisis that affects the entire family
system. The family is disrupted as members abandon their usual
activities and focus their energy on restoring family equilibrium.
Roles and responsibilities previously assumed by the ill person are
delegated to other family members, or those functions may remain
undone for the duration of the illness. The family experiences
anxiety because members are concerned about the sick person and
the resolution of the illness. This anxiety is compounded by
additional responsibilities when there is less time or motivation to
complete the normal tasks of daily living. See Box 25.2
 for some
factors that determine the impact of illness on the family unit.
BO X


25.2 Factors determining the impact
of illness on the family
The nature of the illness, which can range from minor to
life threatening.
The duration of the illness, which ranges from short term
to long term.
The residual effects of the illness, including none to
permanent disability.
The meaning of the illness to the family and its
significance to family systems.
The financial impact of the illness, which is influenced by
factors such as loss of income and ability of the ill
member to return to work.
The effect of the illness on future family functioning (e.g.
previous patterns may be restored or new patterns may
be established).
The family’s ability to deal with the stress of illness depends on the
members’ coping skills. Families with good communication skills are
better able to discuss how they feel about the illness and how it
affects family functioning. They can plan for the future and are
flexible in adapting these plans as the situation changes. An
established social support network provides strength,
encouragement and services to the family during the illness. During
health crises, families need to realise that it is a sign of strength, not


a sign of weakness, to turn to others for support. Nurses can be part
of the support system for families or they can identify other sources
of support in the community.
During a crisis, families are often drawn together by a common
purpose. In this time of closeness, family members have the
opportunity to reaffirm personal and family values and their
commitment to one another. Indeed, illness may provide a unique
opportunity for family growth.
The nurse’s role with families
experiencing illness
Nurses committed to family-centred care involve both the ailing
individual and the family in the nursing process. Through their
interaction with families, nurses can give support and information.
Nurses make sure that not only the individual but also each family
member understands the disease, its management and the effect of
these two factors on family functioning. The nurse also assesses the
family’s readiness and ability to provide continued care and
supervision at home when warranted. After carefully planned
instruction and practice, families are given an opportunity to
demonstrate their ability to provide care under the supportive
guidance of the nurse. When the care indicated is beyond the
capability of the family, nurses work with families to identify available
resources that are socially and financially acceptable.


In helping families reintegrate the ill person into the home, nurses
use data gathered during family assessment to identify family
resources and deficits. By formulating mutually acceptable goals for
reintegration, nurses help families cope with the realities of the
illness and the changes it may have brought about, which may
include new roles and functions of family members or the need to
provide continued medical care to the ill or recovering person.
Working together, nurses and families can create environments that
restore or reorganise family functioning during illness and throughout
the recovery process.
Death of a family member
The death of a family member usually has a profound effect on the
family. After the death of a family member, families may need
counselling to deal with their feelings and to talk about the person
who died. Individual members may experience a sense of loss. They
grieve for the lost person and they grieve for the family that once
was. The structure of the family is altered and this change may in
turn affect how it functions as a unit. They may also want to talk
about their fears and hopes for the future. At this time, families often
derive comfort from their religious beliefs and their spiritual advisors.
Support groups are also available for families experiencing the pain
of death. However, as the family begins to recover, a new sense of
normalcy develops, the family reintegrates its roles and functions
and it comes to grips with the reality of the situation.


Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Partnering with Consumers
The intention of this standard is ‘to create an organisation in
which there are mutually valuable outcomes by having:
consumers as partners in planning, design, delivery,
measurement and evaluation of systems and services; [and,]
patients as partners in their own care, to the extent that they
choose’ (Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in
Health Care
, p. 14).
26 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved by
creating a health service that is responsive to
the needs and inputs of the person and/or their
family.
Nurses caring for young children in hospital are
in an ideal position to promote family-centred
care principles. The nurse should involve
parents in decision making and allow parents to
be active partners in the care of their child.
Such actions can help to allay family members’
fears and anxieties regarding hospitalisation.
26


It can be difficult for a nurse to deal with grieving families because
the nurse may also feel the loss and feel inadequate in knowing
what to say or do. By understanding the effect death has on
families, nurses can help families resolve their grief and move ahead
with life. (See Chapter 44
 for a discussion of loss and grieving.)
Implementing and evaluating
Nursing interventions are based on medical diagnoses, nursing
diagnoses and selected goals or outcomes (see ‘Identifying nursing
diagnoses, outcomes and interventions’). In evaluating the success
of the family care plan, the nurse assesses for the presence of the
indicators identified for the chosen outcomes. If the indicators are
present, it is likely that the outcome has been achieved. If the
indicators or outcomes are partially or not met, all aspects of the
family situation must be re-examined: Have the intervention activities
been carried out? Are the indicators and outcomes appropriate? Is
the nursing diagnosis accurate? Has the medical condition or
diagnosis changed?
Recognition of individual and family strengths helps to maintain
wellness and also directs behaviour in crisis situations. If a plan of
care has to be modified to be more effective, these strengths should
be identified and utilised.


Case study
Lauren is a 42-year-old mother of four young children who
has developed a chronic back condition that has affected her
ability to work and adequately care for her family. Her illness
has created a financial hardship for the family. Lauren and
her current partner have custody of their children from
previous marriages as well as a daughter of their own. They
are reluctant to seek assistance from outside sources due to
ongoing custody issues with their ex-spouses.


1. How else may Lauren’s current physical condition be
impacting on the family unit?
2. Explain why Lauren’s family is considered to be in a
health crisis when only Lauren is experiencing an
illness.
3. What are the advantages or disadvantages of facing
illness as a member of a family as opposed to
individually?
4. Describe Lauren’s family from the perspective of
general systems theory.
5.
 When providing care, consider why and how you
would develop a relationship with Lauren as well as her
family.


Chapter 25 Review


Chapter highlights
The family is the basic unit of society.
Family-centred nursing addresses the health of the family as a
unit, as well as the health of family members.
Many types of families exist: traditional, two-career, single-
parent, those headed by one or more adolescent parents, foster,
blended, intra-generational, cohabiting and same-sex. In
addition, many single adults live alone.
Theoretical frameworks provide the nurse with a holistic overview
of health promotion of families across the lifespan.
The purpose of family assessment is to determine the level of
family functioning, clarify family interaction patterns, identify
family strengths and weaknesses and describe the health status
of the family and its individual members.
Information on how family members are genetically related is
gathered via a genogram. An ecomap allows the nurse to see
where the family’s energy is being expended.
Families at risk for health problems may be considered on the
basis of family maturity level, presence of hereditary factors, sex
or race, lifestyle practices and sociological factors such as
poverty.
Nursing diagnoses that relate to family health needs and
problems include Interrupted family processes, Readiness for
enhanced family coping, Disabled family coping, Impaired
parenting, Impaired home maintenance and Caregiver role strain.

Focus on critical thinking
1. How would you ensure that your nursing care was delivered in
a culturally safe way when faced with a family structure that is
very different from what you perceive as ‘normal’? What is
meant by the term ‘cultural safety’ and what will it mean to
you as a nurse?
2. Is family-centred nursing care reserved only for families with

3. After sensing negative perceptions from nursing and medical
staff, a father threatens to leave the emergency department
with his young daughter who has had an accident at home.
How do you think staff have caused ‘negative perceptions’
from the father’s point of view? What stereotypes could be
influencing their interaction with the child’s father? Why is the
doctor’s first question after examining the child, ‘Where is

encounter have on this family’s future visits to the emergency
department?


Unit 6 Integral aspects of nursing
Caring and effective communication are
essential for optimal interpersonal relationships,
especially in health care. Nurses respond not
only to the factual content of a message, but
also to the feelings expressed through verbal
and non-verbal modes. Nurses should therefore
be attuned to all forms of communication,
recognising that gestures, expressions and
other kinds of body language often convey a
message more powerfully and accurately than
mere words. Establishing rapport with people
also facilitates another vital nursing role—the
process of teaching, a structured form of
communication designed to enhance learning.

In this age of technological competence and
efficiency, the knowledge and skills embedded
in caring practices can be overlooked. We live in
a world where technology is ever-present and,
as Gracia  reminds us, ‘changing at a dizzy
pace’ (p. 231). This global trend presents an
ethical challenge for nurses to maintain a culture
of caring amid the ever-present complexity
(Tatsumi ). However, as early as , Phillips and
Benner identified a ‘crisis in caring’ across
society, manifested in health care. For this
reason, theories and practices of caring have
been studied extensively in nursing (Watson ;
Bourgeois ; Leininger ). Simply stated, caring
1
2
3
4
5
6


means that people, relationships and things
matter (Benner & Wrubel ). In nursing, this
means we have a responsibility to engage
empathically with both the people we care for
and those we work with.

This chapter addresses theories and practices
of caring along with strategies to create a
culture of caring in nursing. Throughout this
chapter, there are numerous ‘Real-world
practice’ exemplars to assist students to more
fully understand this complex phenomenon.


Professionalisation of caring
Caring practice
 requires connection, a person-centred approach,
empathy, mutual recognition and involvement. In person-centred
care, there is a strong focus on the individual and respect for their
personal beliefs, values, needs and desires (McCance, Slater &
McCormack ; Landers ). The language we use is often a good
indicator of whether we are person centred. For example, referring
to a person as ‘the appendix in room 32 needing analgesia’
constructs the person as an object with a symptom and a task that
has to be attended to.
8 McCance, T., Slater, P. & McCormack, B. (2009). Using the caring dimensions as an
indicator of person-centred nursing. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 18, 409–417.
9 Landers, M. (2007). Person-centred nursing with older people in Ireland. Nursing Science
Quarterly, 20(1), 78–84.
Consider the following examples of caring involving a person-centred
approach:
A person experiencing postoperative pain is given medication to
control their symptoms and then the nurse talks quietly and holds
their hand for a few minutes as the pain resolves. The nurse’s
presence provides comfort to the person.
Nurses care for each other. The cost of caring for people and
their relatives can make nurses feel vulnerable and distressed.
8
9


The following example highlights how nurses can care for each
other. A nurse working night duty in a coronary care unit had
been caring for Mr Teo, a long-term patient, and his distressed
wife. At the end of the difficult 10-hour shift, Mr Teo died as a
result of heart failure. Following his death, the nurse sat with Mr
Teo’s wife and comforted her. The nurse was exhausted and
about to leave the unit when the nurse in charge of the shift said,
‘You did a beautiful job looking after Mr and Mrs Teo’ and gave
her a hug. This feedback made the nurse feel that her colleagues
both recognised her efforts and were supportive of her at a time
when she was emotionally and physically exhausted.
Just as people benefit from caring practices, nurses experience
caring through knowing that they have made a difference.
Nursing students can develop their understanding of the importance
of caring by studying the meaning of caring in nursing and seeking
to understand how caring is defined, understood and described by
both patients and nurse researchers. Nurses must also understand
the importance of culture as a dimension of care (Nursing and
Midwifery Board of Australia ).
10 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (2016). Registered Nurse Standards for Practice.
Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Caring as ‘helping the other grow’
10


Milton Mayeroff
, a noted philosopher, proposed that to care for
another person is to help the person grow and become actualised.
Caring is a process that develops over time, resulting in a deepening
and transforming relationship. Recognising the other as having
potential and the need to grow, the carer does not impose direction
but allows the direction of the other person’s growth to help
determine how to respond.
11 Mayeroff, M. (1990). On Caring. New York: HarperCollins.
Elements of caring include:
Knowing another person’s needs and understanding how best to
respond to those needs.
Patience enables another person to grow in their own way and
time.
Honesty includes awareness and openness to one’s own feelings
and a genuineness in caring for the other.
Trust involves letting go and allowing the person to grow in their
own way and own time.
Humility means acknowledging that there is always more to learn
and that learning may come from any source.
Hope is belief in the possibilities of the person’s growth.
Courage is the sense of going into the unknown, informed by
insight from past experiences.
11


Nursing theories on caring
Caring is a multidimensional concept underpinned by the ethical
principle of respect for human dignity (Wolf & France ). Theories
and models of caring are often grounded in humanism and the idea
that caring is the basis for effective human interactions. Over
decades, nursing theorists have focused on caring from various
perspectives; for example, Leininger, Ray, Roach, Watson, and
Benner and Wrubel. Many of these theories have been underpinned
by Nightingale’s philosophy of caring.
12 Wolf, Z. & France, N. (2017). Caring in nursing theory. International Journal of Human
Caring, 21(2), 95–108.
Culture care diversity (Leininger)
Based on studies in nursing and anthropology, Leininger defines
caring as ‘assisting, supporting, or enabling another individual or
group with evident or anticipated needs to ameliorate or improve a
human condition or lifeway, or to face death’ (2001, p. 46). Leininger
proposed that ‘caring is the essence of nursing and the distinct,
dominant, central and unifying focus of nursing’ (Leininger 2001, p.
35). Her theory of transcultural nursing is based on the assumption
that nurses must understand different cultures in order to provide
care and practise effectively.
12


Transcultural nursing focuses on both the differences and the
similarities among people in diverse cultures. While cultures have
different ways of caring for others, there are also some universal
behaviours that transcend cultural differences. In order to provide
care that is congruent with a person’s cultural values, beliefs and
practices, the nurse must understand these differences and
similarities. When the nursing care provided is not congruent with a
person’s beliefs and values, there may be conflict, non-compliance
and stress.
Real-world practice
A healing haven Fairy Garden
The following excerpt from a student’s reflective journal
during a tour in northern Thailand highlights culturally
congruent care.
I enjoyed working and observing people in the
Lampang Hospital Fairy Garden immensely. During our
time there it became clear to me that the benefits of
the Fairy Garden are multi-faceted. My initial
expectation was that the paediatric patients, and
perhaps their siblings or visiting friends, would be the
ones who would benefit from the Fairy Garden;


however, I soon discovered it was more complex than I
had expected.
Lampang Hospital is an 800-bed tertiary hospital. The
Fairy Garden is central to the ground floor of the
hospital and is a place where all types of people gather
to spend time together, eat or simply enjoy the area. I
witnessed young and old utilising the garden and its
surrounds as a place to escape the clinical
environment and have some time away from the ward.
Elderly patients and visitors gather together, sharing
food and smiling as they watch children playing on the
playground equipment; mothers sit together sharing
stories and supporting each other; and children run
around playing and interacting with one another. The
Fairy Garden helps to reinforce the sense of
community that I feel is so central to the Thai culture,
and for a while I forgot I was in a hospital environment.
The Fairy Garden is also used by parents and staff to
motivate and reward the paediatric patients . . . I
believe the Fairy Garden has fostered a connection
between Australia and Thailand and shows we are a
caring country comprised of people who look beyond
their own borders.
It was an absolute privilege to work in the Fairy
Garden and explore the people, country and culture of


Thailand. Many of my experiences there will help
strengthen my nursing skills, particularly in terms of
compassionate, person-centred, holistic nursing care.
Figure 26.1


Lampang hospital fairy garden.
—Lucinda Whitehouse, nursing student, University of Newcastle Source: © Lucinda
Whitehouse.
Culturally congruent care is provided in three major ways: (1) by
preserving the person’s familiar lifeways; (2) by making
accommodations in care that are satisfying to people; and (3) by
repatterning nursing care to help the person move towards wellness
(Leininger 2001).
Theory of bureaucratic caring
(Ray)
Ray’s theory of bureaucratic caring  focuses on caring in
organisations (e.g. hospitals) as cultures. This theory suggests that
caring in nursing is contextual and is influenced by the organisational
structure. In Ray’s research, the meaning of caring varied in the
emergency department, intensive care unit, oncology unit and other
areas of the hospital. For example, an intensive care unit may have
a dominant value of technological caring (i.e. monitors, ventilators,
treatments and pharmacokinetics) and an oncology unit may have a
value of a more intimate, spiritual caring (i.e. family focused,
comforting, compassionate). Furthermore, the meaning of caring is
influenced by the role and position a person holds. For example,
13


nurses may value caring in terms of its relatedness to people, while
administrators consider caring as more system related, such as
safeguarding the economic wellbeing of the hospital (Coffman ).
13 Ray, M. (2001). The theory of bureaucratic caring. In M. Parker (Ed.), Nursing Theories
and Nursing Practice (pp. 422–431). Philadelphia: F. A. Davis.
14 Coffman, S. (2006). Marilyn Anne Ray: Theory of bureaucratic caring. In A. Tomey & M.
Alligood (Eds), Nursing Theorists and Their Work (6th ed., pp. 116–139). St Louis, MO:
Mosby.
Real-world practice
A person-centred approach to care
As a Registered Nurse working in palliative care, I had
the opportunity to look after a 32-year-old male by the
name of Sam,
 who had been admitted to our
palliative care unit for end-of-life care.
Sam had multiple malignant fungating melanomas all
over his body. His face was covered in ulcerating
melanomas that he constantly picked at, causing them
to bleed. The nursing staff frequently advised him not
to touch them. However, mostly he ignored us. Sam
was non-communicative to staff and others and when
he did communicate, he expressed anger.
14
*


There were a number of reasons why he would have
been angry. His business was in financial difficulties
(bankruptcy), his partner, who was also his business
partner, had left him and he was dying. His elderly
mother had flown in from another country to spend the
past few weeks with her dying son. It was a Sunday
and I had given Sam a hot towel bath and had been
thinking about shaving him; however, I was worried
about making his face bleed. Sam had not had a
shave for many weeks and there were tufts of hair on
his face that made him look almost extraterrestrial. His
mother took a photo from her purse that showed Sam
as a very handsome young man. It was at this point
that I decided I would shave Sam. Seeing this photo
was a reminder that I could do more for him and
perhaps provide him with a sense of esteem and
dignity. I checked in with Sam and asked him if he
would like a shave. Expecting a sullen response, I was
surprised by his enthusiastic reaction.
Shaving Sam took time and patience. I must have
spent at least an hour and a half gently shaving his
disfigured face. During the time I was shaving his face,
it would bleed and I would gently apply a dressing to
stop the bleeding. A few times I asked him if I should
stop and he replied gruffly, ‘No, keep going’. All the
time I was shaving Sam, he insisted on holding a
mirror so he could see what I was doing.


At the end of the shave, the look of pleasure and
delight in Sam’s eyes made the effort worthwhile. His
face was relaxed and the tension gone. His mother
had tears in her eyes. That afternoon all the nursing
staff came to admire and comment on how good he
looked. Sam just smiled.
Two days later Sam died and his mother thanked me
for making him feel good about himself in his last few
days of life. As I reflect on this practice experience, I
am reminded that caring is about making a difference
to a person’s life but it can also involve risk taking. It is
important that nurses project a persona of caring.
Sam’s mother expected this and Sam certainly wanted
his nurse to be caring. The action of shaving Sam was
a simple activity; however, using knowledge about his
life expectations, engaging him and showing Sam
through this activity that he was valued, supported his
sense of identity, self-esteem and self-worth. While
Sam was experiencing end-of-life care, the care
allowed him to feel respected, dignified and valued.
—Associate Professor Pamela Van der Riet School of Nursing and Midwifery University of
Newcastle
Name changed for privacy.
*


Patient safety competency framework
1 Person-centred care
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
states that students must demonstrate an ability
to provide holistic care that takes into account
the person’s current situation, previous
experiences and life history, and demonstrate
empathy by seeking to understand the person’s
perspective (Levett-Jones et al.
).
15 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Caring, the human mode of being
(Roach)
Roach focuses on caring as a philosophical concept and proposes
that caring is the human mode of being or the ‘most common,
authentic criterion of humanness’ (Roach , p. 28). People develop
their caring abilities by being true to self, being real and being who
they truly are. Thus, caring is not unique to nursing.
15
16


16 Roach, M. S. (2002). Caring, the Human Mode of Being (2nd ed.). Ottawa, Ontario,
Canada: CHA Press.
However, Roach visualises caring as central to nursing because
caring is the centre of all attributes used to describe nursing. Roach
defines these attributes as the six Cs of caring: compassion,
competence, confidence, conscience, commitment and
comportment. See Box 26.1
 for definitions of each characteristic.
The six Cs are used as a broad framework, suggesting categories of
behaviour that describe professional caring. Each category reflects
specific values and includes virtuous actions by which a nurse can
demonstrate caring.
BO X
26.1 The six Cs of caring in nursing
Compassion
Awareness of one’s relationship to others, sharing their joys,
sorrows, pain and accomplishments. Participation in the
experience of another.
Competence
Having the knowledge, judgment, skills, energy, experience
and motivation to respond adequately to others within the
demands of professional responsibilities.


Confidence
The quality that fosters trusting relationships. Comfort with
self, person and family.
Conscience
Morals, ethics and an informed sense of right and wrong.
Awareness of personal responsibility.
Commitment
Convergence between one’s desires and obligations and the
deliberate choice to act in accordance with them.
Comportment
Appropriate bearing, demeanour, dress and language that are
in harmony with a caring presence. Presenting oneself as
someone who respects others and demands respect.
Source: Adapted from M. S. Roach (2002). Caring, the Human Mode of Being (2nd ed.). Canadian
Health Association (CHA Press). Reproduced with permission.
Theory of human caring (Watson)


Watson’s theory of human caring views caring as the essence and
the moral ideal of nursing. Human caring is the basis for nursing’s
role in society; indeed, nursing’s contribution to society lies in its
moral commitment to human care. Health professionals need a
deep, philosophical value-based approach. Watson’s theory is
recognised internationally as providing a theoretical, ethical and
moral framework to inspire and transform nursing (Watson ). Pai
points out that Watson’s theory of caring involves mind–body–soul
engagement and advises that people will not heal when viewed as
tasks or objects. Riegel, Crossetti and Siqueira  remind us that
Watson’s theory of caring also contributes to nurses’ critical thinking
and holistic practice.
17 Watson, J. (2009). Caring science and human caring theory: Transforming personal and
professional practices of nursing and health care. Journal of Health and Human Services
Administration, 31(4), 466−482.
18 Pai, H. (2015). The effect of self-reflection and insight program on the nursing competence
of nursing students: A longitudinal study. Journal of Professional Nursing, 31(5), 424–431.
19 Riegel, F., Crossetti, M. & Siqueira, D. (2018). Contributions of Jean Watson’s theory to the
holistic critical thinking of nurses. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem (Brazilian Journal of
Nursing), 71(4), 2072–2076.
The primacy of caring (Benner and
Wrubel)
17
18
19


As Benner and Wrubel (1989) listened to expert nurses’ stories and
analysed their meanings, caring emerged as the essence of
excellence in nursing. Nursing is described as a relationship in which
caring is primary because it sets up the possibility of giving and
receiving help (Benner & Wrubel 1989). Caring practice requires
attending to the particular person over time, determining what
matters to the person and using this knowledge in clinical judgments.
As nurses gain expertise, they are more effective in focusing on
what the person brings to the health care encounter. Caring
facilitates the nurse’s ability to problem solve and to implement
individualised solutions.
Caring is interactive in that the strengths and abilities of the person
being cared for are as important as the skills of the nurse. A caring
relationship requires a certain amount of openness and capacity to
respond to care on the part of the person. In caring practice, being
with someone may be just as important as doing something for that
person, if not more so. As the nurse gains expertise, they learn how
to be with people, to respect who they are and where they are at
and to stop doing for them.


Types of knowledge in nursing
Nursing involves different types of knowledge that are integrated to
guide caring practices. Nurses require scientific competence
(empirical knowledge), therapeutic use of self (personal knowing),
moral/ethical awareness (ethical knowing) and creative action
(aesthetic knowing). These four types of knowledge were identified
by Carper
 from her observations of nurses’ activities. Figure
26.2
 illustrates the interconnection of these different types of
knowledge.
20 Carper, B. (1978). Fundamental patterns of knowing in nursing. Advances in Nursing
Science, 1(1), 13–23.
Figure 26.2
20


The four ways of knowing.
Empirical knowing: the science of
nursing
Knowledge about the empirical world is systematically organised into
laws and theories for the purpose of describing, explaining and
predicting phenomena of special concern to the discipline of nursing.
Empirical knowing
 ranges from factual, observable phenomena
(e.g. anatomy, physiology, chemistry) and identifying what can be
measured (such as temperature, blood pressure) to theoretical
analysis (e.g. developmental theory, adaptation theory).
Aesthetic knowing: the art of
nursing
Aesthetic knowing
 is the art of nursing and is expressed by the
individual nurse through their creativity and style when meeting the
needs of others. The nurse uses aesthetic knowing to provide care
that is both effective and satisfying. Empathy, compassion, holism
and sensitivity are important in the aesthetic pattern of knowing. It is
intuitive knowledge and subjective. Refer to ‘Research note
’.


Personal knowing: the therapeutic
use of self
Personal knowledge is concerned with the knowing, encountering
and actualising of the concrete, individual self. Because nursing is an
interpersonal process, the way in which nurses view their own selves
and the person is of primary concern in any therapeutic relationship.
Personal knowing
 promotes wholeness, self-awareness and
integrity in the personal encounter, achieves engagement rather
than detachment and denies the manipulative or impersonal
approach. As Mantzoukas and Jasper(
, p. 320) state, ‘personal
practice knowledge is grasped in a conscious moment of
encountering and interacting with a specific patient’. The earlier story
about Sam and his experience in palliative care was about a
purposeful and personal encounter involving personal knowing.
21 Mantzoukas, S. & Jasper, M. (2008). Types of nursing knowledge used to guide care of
hospitalized patients. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 62(3), 318–326.
