Visualisation and massage were used creatively to create
comfort for Wendy, who was dying.
After her visualisation and massage session, Wendy muses
about its soothing and relaxing effects:
I enjoyed the neck.
I like the feet too,
maybe more than the hands.
That was a wonderful massage.
I’ve been thinking about the rainforest,
trees and waterfalls.
I left the snow.
Yes I went into the rainforest.
That was lovely. I really enjoyed it.
Yes.
I’m feeling relaxed,
contented,
nice and peaceful.
Soothing.
Just relaxed.
No stress.
I could drift off into the rainforest.


For Wendy, the visualisation and massage session enabled
her to experience her body as stress-free and peaceful. Prior
to this, she had only experienced the stress of having cancer
and being told that she had a life expectancy of 3 to 6
months, while at the same time she was caring for her
dependent son who had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.
Hart
 supports the idea of visualisation for reducing a
person’s stress.
24 Hart, J. (2008). Guided imagery. Alternative and Complementary Therapies,
14(6), 295−299.
Michie(
, p. 83) says that ‘visualisations are extremely
flexible and can be developed and applied to deal with a
range of physical and psychological needs’. In this exemplar,
visualisation created a personal change in both the person
and the nurse.
25 Michie, D. (2008). Hurry Up and Meditate. Sydney: Allen & Unwin.
Ethical knowing: the moral
component
Goals of nursing include the conservation of life, alleviation of
suffering and promotion of health. Ethical knowing
 focuses on
24
25


what is right and just. There is a strong focus on matters of
obligation or what ought to be done, along with promoting dignity
and rights. It goes beyond simply following the ethical codes of the
discipline. Nursing care involves a series of deliberate actions or
choices that are subject to the judgment of right or wrong.
Occasionally, the principles and norms that guide choices may be in
conflict. The more sensitive and knowledgeable the nurse is to these
issues, the more ‘ethical’ they will be.
Developing ways of knowing
The methods for developing each type of knowledge are unique
(Chinn & Kramer
). The methods that are required for developing
one pattern cannot be used to develop knowledge within another
pattern. For example, personal knowing is developed through critical
reflection on one’s own actions and feelings in practice. Empirical
knowing is gained from studying scientific models and theories and
from making objective observations. Ethical knowing involves
confronting and resolving conflicting values and beliefs. Aesthetic
knowing arises from a deep appreciation of the uniqueness of each
individual and the meanings that an individual ascribes to a given
situation. The nurse who practises effectively is able to integrate all
types of knowledge to understand situations more holistically.
26 Chinn, P. & Kramer, M. (2015). Knowledge Development in Nursing (9th ed.). St Louis,
MO: Mosby.
26


Caring encounters
How does a nurse demonstrate caring? Given similar situations, why
is one nurse judged to be ‘caring’ while another is said to be
‘uncaring’? Nurse theorists and researchers have studied this
question and identified caring attributes and behaviours. Because
caring is contextual, a nursing approach used with a person in one
situation may be ineffective in another. Caring responses should be
cognisant of individual needs, environmental resources and nurses’
imaginations. Caring encounters are influenced by the diversity of
human responses, the nurse’s workload and the preferences of the
nurse and person. When people perceive the encounter to be
caring, their sense of dignity and self-worth is increased and feelings
of connectedness are experienced.
Knowing the person being cared
for
Caring attends to the totality of the person’s experience. The nurse
asks: Who is this person? What is their history? What are their
needs, desires, dreams, spiritual beliefs? Who loves and cares for
this person at home? Where is home and what resources are there?


What does this person need today, from me, right now? Can they
tell me what is needed?
Personal knowledge of the person is a key in the caring relationship
between nurse and person. The nurse aims to know who the person
is in their uniqueness. This knowledge is gained by observing and
talking with the person and family using listening and communication
skills. The nurse cannot remain detached but is actively engaged
with the person.
Take, for example, an older man experiencing postoperative pain
after removal of a cancerous prostate. The nurse assesses his pain,
using an appropriate pain scale. The man’s position, hygiene,
amount of rest and other physiological variables are assessed for
their effect on pain. In addition, there are a multitude of other factors
that affect the person’s perception of pain. Is this surgery likely to
cure the cancer or is it primarily palliative? The meaning to this
person of the diagnosis and surgery affects his pain experience. The
nurse discovers that this man lost his wife to cancer 2 years ago.
His daughter, at the bedside, is his primary support. The nurse
discusses with his daughter how she can make her father more
comfortable.
Knowing the person and family ultimately involves the nurse and
person in a caring transaction. By attending broadly to personal,
ethical, aesthetic and empirical knowledge, the nurse understands
events as they have meaning in the life of the person. The nurse


knowing the person ultimately increases the possibilities for
therapeutic interventions to be perceived as relevant.
Nursing presence
Caring in nursing always takes place in a relationship. Watson
describes the transpersonal caring relationship in which the nurse
enters into the life space of another person. Establishment of a
caring relationship depends on a moral commitment by the nurse
and the nurse’s ability to assess and realise another person’s state
of being. Being fully present involves mindfulness; that is, being in
the present moment with the person the nurse is caring for. It is not
operating on autopilot; instead, it is the essence of engagement in
the moment.
27 Watson, J. (2002). Intentionality and caring-healing consciousness: A practice of
transpersonal nursing. Holistic Nursing Practice, 16(4), 12–19.
Empowering the person being
cared for
Through knowing the person and engaging in a mutual relationship,
the nurse is able to identify and build upon their strengths. This
empowering relationship includes mutual respect, trust and
27


confidence in the other’s abilities and motives. According to
Swanson , the caring behaviour of enabling is defined as ‘facilitating
the other’s passage through life transitions and unfamiliar events’ (p.
356). Enabling also includes coaching, informing, explaining,
supporting, assisting, guiding, focusing and validating. There are
times when enabling involves substitutive care, but doing no more
than is needed at the time. At other times, enabling involves
providing an environment in which the person can function safely
and effectively. The nurse should remain mindful of professional
boundaries and responsibilities. The goal is always to facilitate
growth and development.
28 Swanson, K. (1993). Nursing as informed caring for the well-being of others. IMAGE:
Journal of Nursing Scholarship, 25(4), 352–357.
Nurses both advocate for (verb) and are advocates (noun) for
people and families. Crook  points out that even though advocacy
is an important responsibility of all nurses, it can be challenging. The
two key components of advocacy are evidence-based practice and a
healthy practice environment (Crook 2016). Through advocacy,
nurses are champions for others. They empower people and families
through activities that enhance wellbeing, understanding and self-
care.
29 Crook, C. (2016). Advocacy: How far would you go to protect your patients? AORN
Journal, 103(5), 522–526.
28
29


Compassion
Universally, people equate compassion with caring. The caring nurse
is described as warm and empathic, compassionate and concerned.
In order to demonstrate empathy, the nurse must be able to identify
with the person, appreciating the pain and discomfort of illness, or
imagine ‘walking in their shoes’ in regard to some part of the
person’s life experience. Compassion is fundamental to nursing (van
Zyl & Noonan ) and includes kindness and a desire to alleviate
suffering (Gracia 2017).
30 van Zyl, A. & Noonan, I. (2018). The Trojan war inside nursing: An exploration of
compassion, emotional labour, coping and reflection. British Journal of Nursing, 27(20), 1192–
1196.
Dewar
 defines compassion as the way in which we relate to each
other and implies a level of reciprocity for others who are suffering
(p. 49). Compassion involves participating in the person’s experience
with sensitivity to the person’s pain or discomfort and a willingness to
share in their experience. Compassion is given as part of the caring
relationship as the nurse shares the person’s joys, sorrows, pain and
accomplishments (Tierney, Bivins & Seers ). Compassion is a gift
from the heart rather than an advanced skill or technique; it involves
the nurse being present both physically and emotionally
(Hudacek ).
31 Dewar, B. (2013). Cultivating compassionate care. Nursing Standard, 27(34), 48–54.
30
31
32
33


32 Tierney, S., Bivins, R. & Seers, K. (2019). Compassion in nursing: Solution or stereotype?
Nursing Inquiry, 26(1), e12271.
33 Hudacek, S. (2008). Dimensions of caring: A qualitative analysis of nurses’ stories. Journal
of Nursing Education, 47(3), 127–129.
Attention to spiritual needs is part of compassionate care,
particularly in the face of death and bereavement. The nurse is
aware that spiritual and religious beliefs are important coping
mechanisms in dealing with issues of mortality (see Chapter 42
).
The nurse does not impose their own spiritual beliefs but rather
assists the person and family in drawing upon their own beliefs as
spiritual resources. Pesut
 suggests that spirituality has attempted
to redress difference, to find meaning and to be ‘good in a world of
uncertain morality’ (p. 5), and as such spirituality is important when
caring for people worldwide.
34 Pesut, B. (2013). Nursing’s need for the idea of spirituality. Nursing Inquiry, 20(1), 5–10.
Comfort is often associated with compassionate care, and many
nursing interventions are carried out to provide comfort. Comfort
care can be used to describe both physical and emotional comfort
(Hudacek 2008; Williams & Irurita ). For example, bathing,
positioning, talking, touching and listening are often performed to
increase the person’s comfort level. Just like pain or discomfort,
comfort is subjective and is thought about in terms of ‘whatever the
person says it is’ based on the individual’s perceptions. Despite this
subjectivity, comfort care is often the basis for nursing in settings
ranging from intensive care to hospice and serves as a motivator for
nursing interventions. Nurses are challenged to be creative and
34
35


innovative, basing interventions on their knowledge of the person’s
preferences in order to provide appropriate comfort care.
35 Williams, A. M. & Irurita, V. (2006). Emotional comfort: The patient’s perspective of a
therapeutic context. International Journal of Nursing Studies, 43, 405–415.
Competence
The competent nurse employs the necessary knowledge, critical
thinking, clinical reasoning, skills, attitudes and motivation to respond
adequately to the person’s needs. Just as competence without
compassion is cold and inhumane, compassion without competence
is meaningless and dangerous. Competent nurses are emotionally
intelligent, combining knowledge, skills and attitudes. They are also
aware of the importance of National Safety and Quality Health
Service Standards.
Lejonqvist, Eriksson and Meretoja  point out that caring should be
the core of clinical competence, and without this, nursing is only
tasks and skills. In order to practise competently, one also needs to
care for self.
36 Lejonqvist, G., Eriksson, K. & Meretoja, R. (2016). Educating clinical competence during
nursing education: A comprehensive integrated lit review. International Journal of Nursing
Practice, 22, 142–151.
36


Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: Partnering with consumers
The Partnering with Consumers standard of the
National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (Australian Commission on Safety
and Quality in Health Care ) emphasises that
competent practice requires effective
communication and partnerships between
patients, carers, families and clinicians.
37 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards
(2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
37


Maintaining caring practice
The concept of caring for self seems almost foreign to many nurses
and nursing students because of the professional emphasis on
meeting others’ needs. Yet, as nurses take on multiple commitments
to family, study, community and shift work, they risk exhaustion,
burnout, stress and compassionate fatigue.
In their professional life, nurses witness human conditions of frailty,
vulnerability and human suffering (Sacco et al.
; Sobrinho, Radunz
& da Rosa ). Such commitment or challenges can place great
stress upon nurses’ abilities to cope with the unpredictability of
human morbidity (Mercer & Halliwell ). The very act of caring can
leave nurses vulnerable to compassion fatigue (Cross ).
38 Sacco, T., Ciurzynski, S., Harvey, M. & Ingersoll, G. (2015). Compassion satisfaction and
compassion fatigue among critical care nurses. Critical Care Nurse, 35(4), 32–44.
39 Sobrinho, A., Radunz, V. & da Rosa, L. (2015). Caring for self to promote health:
Transforming nursing care. Cienc Cuid Saude, 14(1), 941–947.
40 Mercer, A. & Halliwell, D. (2006). Nursing as caring science: A position threatened by
health care modernization. International Association for Human Caring, 10(2), 49.
41 Cross, L. (2019). Compassion fatigue in palliative care nursing. Journal of Hospice and
Palliative Care Nursing, 21(1), 21–28.
38
39
40
41


In this section, we provide some self-care strategies to prevent
compassion fatigue and burnout. Many of these strategies are
common sense and not demanding. Obstacles to self-care may be
related to the demands of a particular work setting or they may be
personal, such as poor health habits or unrealistic expectations of
self (see Chapter 43
 for more information on stress and coping).
Despite these challenges, it is imperative that nurses attend to their
own needs because caring for self is central to caring for others.
Caring for self involves having a healthy lifestyle and an appropriate
work–life balance. Sitzman(
, p. 66) points out that ‘self-care has
been shown to mitigate job stress and ease emotional stress
through the creation and maintenance of physical, emotional and
spiritual reserves’.
42 Sitzman, K. (2017). Theory-guided self-care for mitigating emotional strain in nursing:
Watson’s caring science. International Journal of Human Caring, 21(2), 66–67.
It is important for nurses that they are happy within themselves, as
happiness is linked to wellbeing and health (Bekhet, Zauszniewski &
Nakhla ). Nurses who are positive role models are advocates for
health and wellbeing and are in a position to be more caring for
others.
43 Bekhet, A., Zauszniewski, J. & Nakhla, W. (2008). Happiness: Theoretical and empirical
considerations. Nursing Forum, 43(1), 12–23.
Caring for self
42
43


Caring for self means taking the time to nurture oneself. This
involves initiating and maintaining behaviours that promote healthy
living and wellbeing. Different activities may be helpful to different
people. Examples include:
a balanced diet that is high in fibre and low in fat content
regular exercise (e.g. walking or going to the gym)
adequate rest and sleep (most people need at least 7 hours
sleep a night)
recreational activities
meditation and prayer
a regular massage as therapy for body, mind and spirit
gardening and enjoying nature
yoga or tai chi
taking time to be with friends and family
listening respectfully and carefully to the messages your body is
telling you.
Self-care focuses on care of the self in the deepest sense. Self-
awareness and self-esteem are intimately connected to self-care.
Each person is unique and possesses individual strengths and
weaknesses. Self-care practices are intentionally created by the self
and vigilantly maintained. This is a lifelong unfolding process, leading
to wholeness that comes from and contributes to self-esteem.
Individuals with high self-esteem can critically problem solve and
tackle obstacles more effectively. Self-care practices build self-
esteem, leading to feelings of comfort and accomplishment.


A healthy lifestyle
Everyone needs to pay attention to nutrition and exercise and to
avoid unhealthy lifestyle practices. Key words for a healthy lifestyle
are balance and moderation. These lifestyle practices are
supplemented by regular physical examinations and health
screenings.
Nutrition
Healthy eating is important for everyone. A nutritionally balanced
eating plan provides more energy, builds endurance to carry out
daily activities and reduces the risk of certain health problems.
Healthy eating means learning to make good choices in the foods
eaten, preparing foods appropriately and eating in moderation. It is
important to select a variety of foods, to eat regular meals and to
eat the correct amount to maintain a healthy weight. Determining a
healthy weight depends on several factors, including age, activity
level and the presence of weight-related medical problems such as
high blood pressure. An abundance of fresh and raw vegetables and
fruit is essential to keep you healthy. Dietary guidelines and
standards for a healthy diet are included in Chapter 50
.
Activity and exercise
Exercise is recognised as a lifetime endeavour that is essential for
energetic, active and healthy living (see Figure 26.3
). The
benefits of exercise have been linked to many physiological and


psychological responses, from a reduced feeling of stress to an
increased sense of wellbeing. Exercise strengthens the heart, lungs
and blood vessels to prevent heart disease, keeps the joints flexible
and helps many people deal with sad or unhappy feelings. For
people who are overweight, exercise has the added benefit of
burning kilojoules, resulting in weight loss or maintenance. Whatever
the exercise, whether walking or working out in a gym, 30 minutes
per day three to four times a week is generally recommended.
Figure 26.3


Regular activity and exercise is an effective self-care practice.
Nurses participate in strenuous activities that call for specialised
knowledge of body mechanics and movement techniques to prevent
self-injuries. It is important to keep your body fit. Consider activities
such as yoga or tai chi to keep your body and mind strong and fit so
that you are able to cope with the strenuous physical and mental
activities of nursing.
Recreation
Self-care also includes taking time to do the things that bring joy and
stimulate creativity. Ask yourself ‘What do I want to do?’ rather than
‘What should I do?’. Nurses need to reward themselves, experience
spontaneity and even take downtime or time to do nothing and
simply just ‘be’. Defending the right to this time may take courage
and conviction in the face of others’ demands. Box 26.2
 is
intended to help people recapture a sense of joy and self-reward.
BO X
26.2 Twelve things you would love to
do
We often put off doing the simple things that bring us joy and
happiness.


Make a list of 12 things you would love to do after reviewing
the list on the left. Post your list where you can see it.
Resolve to carry out one activity by a specified time. Enjoy!
Avoiding unhealthy patterns
Part of staying healthy is avoiding unhealthy life patterns. This
means avoiding activities or thought patterns that contribute to
negative health outcomes. Negative thinking can create a stress
response with all its physiological, mental and emotional outcomes.
It is not what happens but how events are perceived that determines
an individual’s reaction. Practices such as identifying negative
feelings, refocusing on the positive and using humour are helpful to
avert the stress response by changing thought patterns. Using
positive affirmations, as listed in Box 26.3
, can lead to greater
self-esteem and control self-doubt. It is also important to avoid
destructive lifestyle choices such as smoking, abuse of alcohol or
drugs and misusing medications.
BO X
26.3 Positive affirmations
Begin the day with positive statements about how you want to
think and act:
I am a person of worth and goodness.


I am happy to be alive.
I am in the right place at the right time.
I am prepared to do a good job today.
I am surrounded by people I love who love me.
I make myself my fulfilment.
I am doing what brings me joy.
This is an opportunity to grow.
I appreciate my own uniqueness.
Mind–body therapies
The interconnectedness of the mind and body is the basis for
complementary therapies. Imagery, meditation, storytelling, music
therapy and yoga are complementary therapies that bring balance to
thoughts and emotions. Practising one or more mind–body therapies
is an effective self-care strategy to help restore peace and balance.
More in-depth information on different types of complementary
therapies is included in Chapter 20
.
Guided imagery
Imagery is a mind–body intervention that uses the power of the
imagination as a therapeutic tool. Imagery is used to promote
relaxation, decrease anxiety and enhance psychological or spiritual
insight. Through forming mental images of an object, event or


situation, the individual can reframe negative responses into positive
images, thus enhancing healing and emotional wellbeing.
Mindfulness and meditation
Mindfulness involves total attention to the moment. This could be, as
mentioned previously, being fully present in the moment with the
person you are caring for. It could also simply mean that while
washing your hands at work, you take three slow deep breaths and
focus on that moment of washing your hands to help calm and move
you through the busyness of your shift (Sitzman 2017).
Meditation is a tool for mindfulness. It is defined by Tang, Hölzel and
Posner(
, p. 1) ‘as a form of mental training that aims to improve an
individual’s core psychological capacities, such as attentional and
emotional self-regulation’. By quietening the mind and focusing it on
the present, meditation assists the individual in releasing fears,
worries and doubts. The technique involves both relaxation and
focused attention. Meditation is a process of focusing the mind on
an object or specific activity. This might involve prayer, the repetitive
action of a hobby or practising mindful meditation.
44 Tang, Y., Hölzel, B. & Posner, M. (2015). The neuroscience of mindfulness meditation.
Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 16(4), 213–225.
A qualitative pilot study on mindfulness meditation with
undergraduate nursing students identified improvement in sleep,
concentration and clarity of thought and a reduction in negative
thoughts (van der Riet et al.
). Research indicates that mindfulness
44
45


meditation has the potential to reduce compassion fatigue and
improve empathy among nurses (van der Riet, Levett-Jones &
Aquino-Russell ). Guidelines for mindfulness meditation include
choosing a quiet space, sitting comfortably, achieving progressive
relaxation through deep breathing, regular practice and focusing
attention on breathing or a mental image.
45 van der Riet, P., Rossiter, R., Kirby, D., Dluzewska, T. & Harmon, C. (2015). Piloting a
stress management and mindfulness program for undergraduate nursing students: Student
feedback and lessons learned. Nurse Education Today, 35, 44–49.
46 van der Riet, P., Levett-Jones, T. & Aquino-Russell, C. (2019). The effectiveness of
mindfulness meditation for nurses and nursing students: An integrated literature review. Nurse
Education Today, 65, 201–211. Doi: 10.1016/j.nedt.2018.03.018.
Storytelling
Telling stories is a natural component of everyday conversation that
can be utilised as a powerful tool to communicate with others
(Struthers ; Adamski, Parsons & Hooper
). As expressions of
human consciousness, stories help individuals move towards
wholeness. Indigenous groups often conduct storytelling sessions
with the participants sitting in talking circles and, in this way, they are
able to establish a strong sense of connectedness and belonging as
they share their stories with confidence.
47 Struthers, R. (2013). Storytelling as a healing tool. In M. Snyder & R. Lindquist (Eds),
Complementary/Alternative Therapies in Nursing (7th ed., pp. 124–134). New York: Springer.
46
47
48


48 Adamski, M., Parsons, V. & Hooper, C. (2009). Internalizing the concept of caring: An
examination of student perceptions when nurses share their stories. Nursing Education
Perspectives, 10(6), 358–362.
Music therapy
Using music as therapy includes listening, singing and body
movement. Quiet, soothing music is often used to induce relaxation.
Active rhythms can awaken feelings of power and control. Familiar
music allows the listener to recall past events or feelings. Music can
also serve as an effective distraction technique. Each person’s likes
and dislikes should be taken into account in order to achieve the
desired emotional response.
Yoga
The practice of yoga unites the body, mind and spirit (see
Figure 26.4
). The popularity of yoga has increased in recent
years as a means of reducing stress and anxiety and improving
mood and overall wellbeing (Desai, Tailor & Bhatt
). Through daily
practice of the various postures and breathing practices of yoga, an
individual can achieve increased balance and flexibility, mental
alertness and calmness. Yoga can facilitate health and happiness
and reduce tension in everyday living. The bending, stretching and
holding properties of the postures help to relax and tone the muscles
and improve the function of the internal organs. Breath control is
designed to still the mind and enhance awareness.
49


49 Desai, R., Tailor, A. & Bhatt, T. (2015). Effects of yoga on brain waves and structural
activation: A review. Complementary Therapies in Clinical Practice, 21, 112–118.
Figure 26.4


Yoga is a mind–body self-care strategy to help restore peace and
balance.
Reflection on practice
Critical thinking, self-analysis and reflection are required in order to
learn from one’s experience. The student matures as a practitioner
by thinking about how values and standards guide practical
experience. Research has shown that nurses who engage in self-
reflection improve their self-awareness and clinical competence and
have an overall reduction in stress (Pai 2015). Reflection
 is
thinking from a critical point of view, analysing why one acted in a
certain way and assessing the results of one’s actions. In order to
develop oneself as a caring practitioner, reflection on practice must
be personal and meaningful.
Reflective practice is a method of self-examination that involves
thinking back over what happened in a nursing situation. It involves
the whole person, including emotions. Reflectivity includes becoming
aware of how one feels about oneself and recognising how one
thinks and acts. This exploration of experiences leads to new
understandings and appreciations. Through reflection, nurses can
become more comfortable with an authentic way of being in the
world and can participate more fully in caring–healing relationships
(Cumbie ).
50


50 Cumbie, S. (2001). The integration of mind–body–soul and the practice of humanistic
nursing. Holistic Nursing Practice, 15(3), 56–62.
Using four ways of knowing
Reflection provides a method to explore alternative forms of nursing
knowledge, including empirical, aesthetic, personal and ethical types.
Johns suggests the following questions for exploration of different
ways of knowing (2013):
Empirical knowing: What knowledge informed me in this
situation? What additional information did I need? Was I
prepared to deal with this situation?
Personal knowing: What were my thoughts and emotions in this
situation? Why did I feel the way I did? To what extent was I
concerned for the person? To what extent was I preoccupied with
self?
Aesthetic knowing: What was I trying to achieve? Why did I
respond as I did? What were the consequences for the
person/family? How were others feeling and how did I know this?
Ethical knowing: Did I act for the best? What standards were
relevant in this situation? Was there conflict of values between
different people’s perspectives?
Reflective practice requires discipline, action, openness and trust. It
is a form of self-evaluation. Reflective journal writing, as a tool for
learning in educational settings, is sometimes shared with a mentor
or teacher who works in partnership with students. A guideline, such


as the one in Box 26.4
, provides structure for the journal writing
process. Writing reflections in a journal provides a space for
students to look at and acknowledge the deeper self. Guidance from
a mentor or teacher can help students view a nursing situation from
many different perspectives. It helps students find meaning in the
event, understand and learn through it and emerge at a higher level
of understanding.
BO X
26.4 Guideline for reflective journal
writing
Reflection is a window through which the student can view
and focus on self in ways that enable them to understand,
confront and work towards resolving the contradictions
between actual and desirable practice. Reflection facilitates
learning through everyday lived experiences. This guideline
focuses on the concept of being available, which is the
essence of effective holistic practice (Johns ). The following
outline can be used as a guide for journal writing after each
clinical experience or for creating electronic reflective practice
portfolios:
51 Johns, C. (2013). Becoming a Reflective Practitioner (4th ed.). Oxford: Blackwell
Science.
1. Knowing what is desirable (ethical knowing)
51


What are your beliefs and values in relation to the
situation?
Describe the contradictions between your values and
the reality of the situation.
2. Knowing the person/family
What is the meaning of the health event to each
person?
What are each person’s values and needs?
What behaviours did you assess to reveal these
meanings and needs?
How did your relationship (trust) with each person
influence your knowing?
3. Concern for the person/family
Evaluate your level of concern for the person/family.
How easy or difficult was it to care about each person?
How did your personal reactions influence your
concern?
4. The aesthetic response to the person (aesthetic
knowing)
Assess the extent to which you were able to interpret
the situation, envisage what needed to be done and
respond appropriately to the person/family.


Were you able to expand on your ability to be available
to the person and respond effectively?
5. Knowing and managing self’s involvement with
the person (personal knowing)
In what ways did you feel vulnerable in the situation?
How did you manage negative influences such as
anxiety, stress, prejudice, loss of concern,
preoccupation with self?
What did you feel you did well or improved upon from
previous experiences?
6. Creating and sustaining an environment where
being available is possible
Were there environmental factors that constrained
your availability to work with others (norms, ways of
relating, lack of resources, time, etc.)?
Source: Based on C. Johns (2013). Becoming a Reflective Practitioner (4th ed.). Oxford: Blackwell
Science. Reproduced with permission.
Case study
Madeline started university in February and was soon feeling
overwhelmed by the amount of reading and studying that was


required. Her anxiety level began to rise, but at the same
time, she became more aware of her feelings and reactions
to situations. In her nursing courses, she was studying
nursing as caring and in the clinical setting she focused on
applying these ideas in her practice. She was surprised how
genuinely people responded to a kind word of
encouragement, the attention of personal care and her
concern for their wellbeing. Boosted by the responses from
the people she cared for, Madeline became more confident
and was motivated to learn more about her patients’
conditions and needs.
Each week Madeline analysed and described the clinical
situations encountered in practice in a reflective journal.
Through reflecting on her clinical experiences and with
feedback from her clinical facilitator, she was able to identify
her personal strengths and areas for growth. She began to
think about how she could better organise her study
schedule, plan time with her friends and family, and provide
the same level of caring for herself that she desired to give
them.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1.


 Being a nursing student is often an
overwhelming experience. How do you relate to
Madeline’s situation?
2. Using the Fundamentals of Care Framework to help
you, think about the ideas on caring in nursing that


interest you most. How have you implemented these
ideas in your own practice as a nursing student?
3. Give examples of how you practised each of Carper’s
four ways of knowing in your care of people.
4. What value do you see in keeping a reflective journal?
As you reflect on practice situations, have you written
down your thoughts?
5. What changes can you make in your weekly schedule
to be more efficient with studying and also plan time
for self-care?
6. What self-care activities would be most helpful to you
right now? Changes in diet? Scheduled exercise or
recreation? Meditation, yoga or another mind–body
therapy?
7. Do you have unhealthy patterns that you need to work
on, such as smoking or negative thinking? Develop an
action plan to change these behaviours.


Chapter 26 Review


Chapter highlights
Caring practice involves connection, mutual recognition and
involvement between nurse and person. Caring is central to
nursing practice.
To care for another person is to help the person grow and
actualise themself. By helping the other grow, the caregiver
moves towards self-actualisation. Caring behaviours described
by Mayeroff (1990) include knowing, alternating rhythms,
patience, honesty, trust, humility, hope and courage.
Caring is a multidimensional concept underpinned by the ethical
principle of respect for human dignity.
Various theorists have focused on caring as the essence of
nursing. Each theory develops different aspects of caring,
describing how caring is unique in nursing.
Research into caring is diverse and contributes to nursing
knowledge.
Nursing involves different types of knowledge that are integrated
to guide nursing practice. Empirical knowing includes scientific
competence, personal knowing focuses on the self, ethical
knowing requires moral/ethical awareness and aesthetic knowing
is the creative art of nursing.
Caring encounters are influenced by the diversity of human
responses. Common caring patterns include knowing the person,
nursing presence, empowering the person, compassion and
competence.


Caring for self is central to caring for others. Nurse self-care
includes a balanced diet, regular exercise, adequate rest and
sleep, recreational activities and mind–body therapies.
The nurse matures as a practitioner by reflecting on practice.
Through reflection, nurses can grow and participate more fully in
caring–healing relationships.
Concept check
1. Which of the following examples illustrates the principle of
knowing the person?
1. The nurse provides a back rub to help the person relax
and then makes the bed with clean linen.
2. The nurse listens as the person describes how he has
been caring for his diabetes at home.
3. The nurse administers a piggyback antibiotic for a
person with pneumonia.
4. The nurse collects a urine specimen to send to the lab
and explains to the person the reason for the test.
2. The nurse teaches a person with diabetes how to make
decisions about insulin management after discharge. This
teaching most clearly reflects which caring activity?
1. Empowering the person being cared for.
2. Compassion.
3. Knowing the person being cared for.
4. Nursing presence.


3. Mayeroff (1990) described allowing the other to grow in their
own way and time. This behaviour most clearly reflects which
major ingredient of caring?
1. Humility.
2. Knowing.
3. Patience.
4. Courage.
4. Leininger’s (2001) theory, culture care diversity, would provide
the best framework for assessing which of the following
nursing situations?
1. Because the Indonesian parents of an infant prefer to
use hot/cold therapies to prevent seizures, they
withhold the prescribed phenobarbital medication.
2. Staff nurses on a hospital unit discuss how to
reorganise person-centred care to provide more
continuity.
3. Nurses in a community agency search for learning
resources about intravenous therapy in the home
setting.
4. A nurse manager explores ways to assist new nursing
graduates to develop clinical skills on the hospital unit.
5. In a reflective journal, a nursing student writes this statement
about a comatose person on the hospice unit: ‘The do-not-
resuscitate order was not on the chart and none of the nurses
knew what measures should be taken if the person stopped


breathing.’ This statement most clearly reflects which of the
four ways of knowing?
1. Empirical.
2. Personal.
3. Ethical.
4. Aesthetic.
6. The nurse sits with the person and holds his hand as his pain
decreases. This situation is an example of the following caring
practice:
1. Nursing presence.
2. Assessment.
3. Knowing the person being cared for.
4. Empowering the person being cared for.
7. The nursing student reviews the pathophysiology of
myocardial infarction in preparation for the next day’s clinical
experience. This activity is an example of which type of
knowledge development?
1. Empirical knowing.
2. Aesthetic knowing.
3. Personal knowing.
4. Ethical knowing.
8. Which mind–body therapy is described by the following
activity: ‘The person sits quietly in a chair, breathing deeply
and focusing on the mental image of a crystal’?
1. Storytelling.


2. Yoga.
3. Music therapy.
4. Meditation.
9. A 40-year-old person who comes to the clinic for a routine

recommended for a healthy lifestyle. Which answer is most
appropriate?
1. 10 minutes daily.
2. 30 minutes three to four times a week.
3. 20 minutes two or three times a week.
4. 1 hour every other day.

1. In your role as a nurse, reflect on a time when you were

2. How do you ensure the nursing care you provide is congruent
