Communication is a nursing skill critical to safe,
collaborative and effective nursing care. It is
used to gather, share and validate assessment
data, to build an understanding of each
individual person and their health experiences,
and to express caring and comfort.
Communication is also an integral part of
developing and maintaining a therapeutic
nurse–patient relationship and working
collaboratively with members of the health care
team.


Communicating
Communication is a dynamic process which aims to elicit a
response. Its purpose is to influence others and to obtain
information. However, the term communication
 has various
meanings, depending on the context in which it is used. To some,
communication is the interchange of information between two or
more people; in other words, the exchange of ideas or thoughts.
This kind of communication uses methods such as talking and
listening or writing and reading. However, symbols, painting, dancing
and storytelling are also methods of communication. In addition,
thoughts are conveyed to others not only by spoken or written words
but also by gestures or body language.
In nursing, communication has a more personal connotation than
only the interchange of ideas or thoughts. It can be a transmission
of feelings. For the purpose of this text, communication refers to any
means of exchanging information or feelings between two or more
people.
Communication is a basic component of human relationships,
including relationships developed by nurses with the person being
cared for and their families, and other health care professionals.
Communication can be described as therapeutic or helpful when it
encourages sharing information, thoughts or feelings between
nurses and the person they are caring for. Alternatively,


communication is referred to as unhelpful or non-therapeutic when it
hinders or blocks the transfer of information and feelings.
Effective communication helps the nurse to develop an
understanding of the patient as a person, to develop trust and work
collaboratively in a therapeutic relationship (Stein-Parbury ). The
development of trust is essential for the relationship to move beyond
a superficial level; without trust, self-disclosure is limited and the
nurse is unlikely to develop a true understanding of the person’s
health experiences and needs (Stein-Parbury 2018).
1 Stein-Parbury, J. (2018). Patient and Person: Interpersonal Skills in Nursing (6th ed.).
Marrickville, NSW: Elsevier.
Nurses who communicate effectively are better able to collect, share
and validate assessment data, think critically, initiate interventions,
evaluate intervention outcomes, initiate change and prevent unsafe
practice (Levett-Jones ). Therefore, effective communication is
central to safe person-centred care and effective therapeutic
relationships, as reflected in the Nursing and Midwifery Board of
Australia (NMBA ) Registered Nurse Standards for Practice, where it
is stated that Registered Nurses must communicate effectively and
be respectful of each person’s dignity, culture, values, beliefs and
rights.
2 Levett-Jones, T. (2020a). The relationship between communication and patient safety. In T.
Levett-Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient Safety: An Essential Guide for Health
Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
1
2
3


3 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016). Registered Nurse Standards for
Practice. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Communicating for Safety
The importance of effective communication to
patient safety is also emphasised in the National
Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS)
Standards (Australian Commission on Safety
and Quality in Health Care ), where it is
specified that health professionals must facilitate
structured and effective communication
between health service organisations, within
health service organisations, between clinicians
and between clinicians and consumers.
Additionally, the NSQHS Standards highlight the
importance of structured clinical handovers,
interprofessional communication of critical
information in a timely manner, and accurate
and legally appropriate documentation.
4 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards
(2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
4


All nurses need to be fully aware of and put into practice the intent
of these professional expectations when engaging in therapeutic
relationships with patients. Effective communication is also central to
respectful and purposeful relationships with colleagues, a dimension
of practice explored later in this chapter.
Communication levels
Communication occurs at different levels. These levels are
described in the adult communication management model proposed
by Kaye ( ; ). This model has an appearance similar to Russian
matryoshka dolls (see Figure 27.1
), symbolising communication
as a synthesis of four interdependent perspectives or
communication levels: self, interpersonal, people in systems and
competence. All of these are at play in the way nurses relate to the
people in their care, their families and colleagues.
5 Kaye, M. (1994a). Adult communication management: A new perspective on
communication processes and practices in vocational education. In M. Kaye & S. Saunders,
Communication in Vocational Education and Training: Monograph Series. Sydney: University
of Technology.
6 Kaye, M. (1994b). Communication Management. Sydney: Prentice Hall.
Figure 27.1
5 6


A: Russian matryoshka dolls. B: Adult communication management
model.
Sources: A: Olena Makovey/123RF; B: M. Kaye (1994b). Communication Management. Sydney, NSW: Prentice
Hall.
Intrapersonal communication
The innermost doll in Kaye’s (1994a; 1994b) adult communication
model is the ‘self’ and represents the importance of knowing and
understanding your own self as part of being an effective
communicator and nurse. This level is also known as intrapersonal
communication
 and calls for self-awareness. Self-awareness
is being consciously aware of aspects of your own self, such as your
thoughts, feelings, beliefs, biases, prejudices, behaviours and
values. These aspects of the self can interfere with the nurse’s
ability to hear the intended message, to share meaning, to
understand context and perspective, to accurately assess the
person they are caring for and to engage in effective clinical
reasoning (Levett-Jones ). For example, confusion is often
incorrectly viewed as a typical symptom of ageing. However, this
ageist and stereotypical view of older people can negatively
influence the way nurses assess and relate to people in their care.
This can result in the provision of inaccurate nursing care which
does not take into account the potentially life-threatening nature of
acute confusion in older people.
7 Levett-Jones, T. (2018). Clinical reasoning—What it is and why it matters. In T. Levett-Jones
(Ed.), Clinical Reasoning: Learning to Think Like a Nurse (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
7


Developing self-awareness requires an ongoing ability to accurately
assess and become increasingly conscious of your own self (Stein-
Parbury 2018). Its development is important to nurses because our
ability to help other people, to work within professional boundaries
and to relate to colleagues is influenced by the understanding we
have of ourselves, by what we think and feel, what we want and how
we act. Self-awareness is therefore the basis on which emotional
intelligence
 develops (Goleman ). One way that nurses can
improve their self-awareness is by applying the Johari Window (Luft
1969 cited in Candlin ) (see Figure 27.2
).
8 Goleman, D. (1998). Working with Emotional Intelligence. New York: Bantam Books.
9 Candlin, S. (2008). Therapeutic Communication: A Lifespan Approach. Frenchs Forest,
NSW: Pearson.
Figure 27.2
8
9


The Johari Window.
Source: Adapted from J. Luft
. Group Processes: An Introduction to Group Dynamics (3rd ed.). Palo Alto, CA:
McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc. (Mayfield), March 1984. ISBN: 9780874845426. Figure 5.1, p. 60.
10 Luft, J. (1984). Group Processes: An Introduction to Group Dynamics (3rd ed.). Palo Alto,
CA: McGraw-Hill Companies, Inc.
Interpersonal communication
The next doll in Kaye’s (1994a; 1994b) communication model is the
interpersonal communication
 level and represents how the self
10


relates to other people. This refers to the way those engaged in
communication can affect each other and bring about change in
themselves and those interacting with them. Interpersonal
interactions represent most of the communication that occurs
between a nurse and the person they are caring for; however,
interpersonal interactions may also occur using information
communication technologies, such as email, social media, Skype
and text messaging. Interpersonal communication occurs within a
setting or context (i.e. at the bedside) and often includes verbal and
non- verbal communication.
In some situations, there are significant challenges that need to be
overcome to communicate effectively. For example, when caring for
people who are intubated or sedated, nurses must ensure that they
communicate effectively, as this is critical to people’s emotional and
psychological health (see Box 27.1
).
BO X
27.1 Nurse communication in
intensive care
The ICU setting, where sedation and mechanical ventilation
are common, impedes normal communication processes by
unavoidably affecting people’s ability to communicate verbally.
The inability to speak as a result of endotracheal intubation is
a frightening experience which may trigger episodes of
TM


anxiety, agitation and numerous other adverse physiological
and psychological effects that impact on the person’s
recovery (Rotondi et al.
). Research indicates that an ICU
patient’s inability to communicate their needs can result in
fretfulness, fear, frustration, distress and pain (Patak et al.
).
These unpleasant experiences are exacerbated by
inadequate or ineffective communication.
11 Rotondi, A. J., Chelluni, L., Sirio, C., . . . Pinsky, M. R. (2002). Patients’
recollections of stressful experiences while receiving prolonged mechanical
ventilation in an intensive care unit. Critical Care Medicine, 30(4), 746–752.
12 Patak, L., Gawlinski, A., Fung, I., Doering, L. & Berg, J. (2004). Patients’ reports
of health care practitioner interventions that are related to communication during
mechanical ventilation. Heart & Lung, 33(5), 308–320.
An absence of verbal communication interactions with
unconscious people can lead to sensory overload, resulting in
an inability to process all the environmental information they
are exposed to; or sensory deprivation, the feeling of being
socially or physically isolated (Merchant
). Evidence
suggests that difficulty in communication is the most
commonly reported cause of distress for ICU patients who
are mechanically ventilated (Rotondi et al. 2002). Additionally,
patients often remember their ICU experiences and
sometimes experience post-traumatic stress as a result
(Elliott & Wright
).
13 Merchant, S. (2011). Nature of nurses’ verbal communication with unconscious
or sedated patients in an intensive care unit at a tertiary care hospital, Karachi,
11
12
13
14


Pakistan. Paper presented at the Sigma Theta Tau international 41st Biennial
Convention, Grapevine, Texas, US.
14 Elliott, R. E. & Wright, L. (1999). Verbal communication: What do critical care
nurses say to their unconscious or sedated patients? Journal of Advanced Nursing,
29(6), 1412–1420.
—Natalie Govind, ICU nurse and academic
People in systems
The people in systems doll in Kaye’s (1994a; 1994b) communication
model represents how individuals at work function and influence
work colleagues and the organisation itself. Nurses usually work
within organisations and groups or teams. Group communication is
concerned with interactions that occur when a number of people
meet and communicate. This communication is usually goal or task
directed and requires an understanding of group dynamics and
group goals. Communication in groups is effective when the group
achieves its goals in a manner that is inclusive of all members of the
group. Effective and respectful group and organisational
communication are important in creating a care and work
environment which considers patient safety to be paramount
(Croker, Grotowski & Tasker
).
15 Croker, A., Grotowski, M. & Tasker, D. (2020). Interpersonal communication for
interprofessional collaboration. In T. Levett-Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient
Safety: An Essential Guide for Health Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
15


Communication competence
The outermost doll in Kaye’s (1994a; 1994b) communication model
is the communication competence doll. This doll is conceptualised as
an ‘x-ray doll’ penetrating through all the dolls, highlighting the
importance and interconnectedness of communication competence
at all levels. Nurses who display communication competence
possess empathy and emotional intelligence, a capacity to
recognise, respect and manage their own emotions and those of
others they relate to (Goleman 1998). Being emotionally intelligent
means engaging in nursing interactions with both heart and head
(Stein-Parbury 2018).
The interpersonal communication
process
Interpersonal communication involves a sender
, a message
, a
receiver
 and a response
, or feedback
 (see Figure
27.3
). In its simplest form, communication is a two-way process
that involves the sending and the receiving of a message. Because
the intent of communication is to elicit a response, the process is
ongoing and dynamic; the receiver of the message becomes the
sender of a response and the original sender becomes the receiver.
Figure 27.3


The communication process. The dashed arrows indicate
intrapersonal communication. The solid lines indicate interpersonal
communication.
Sender
The sender, a person or group who wishes to express or convey a
message to other people, can be considered the source encoder.
This term suggests that the person or group sending the message
must have an idea or reason for communicating (source) and must


put the idea or feeling into a form that can be transmitted. Encoding
involves the selection of specific signs or symbols (codes) to
transmit the message, such as the language and words to use, how
to arrange the words and what tone of voice and gestures to use.
For example, if the receiver speaks English, the sender usually
selects English words. If the message is ‘Mr Johnson, you can have
your pain medication now’, the tone of voice selected and a nod of
the head or smile can confirm and reinforce the message. When
sending messages, the nurse must not only deal with different
languages but with different language skills and vocabularies, such
as those of a child, an adolescent, an adult layperson or a colleague.
Message
The second component of the communication process is the
message itself—what is actually said or written/typed, the body
language that accompanies the words and how the message is
transmitted. The medium used to convey the message is the
channel and it can target any of the receiver’s senses. It is important
that the channel is appropriate for the message and the person
receiving the message. When nurses use non-visual electronic
communication methods non-verbal cues may be lost, making it
difficult to ensure the receiver has the message the nurse intended.
Talking face to face with a person may be more effective in some
instances than telephoning, writing a message, texting or emailing.
The non-verbal channel of touch
 is often highly effective and is
used extensively in nursing. Asynchronous communication, where
there is a delay between the message being sent and received, such


as a written message or email, can be appropriate for long
explanations or for a message that needs to be preserved or
reinforced (e.g. discharge self-care instructions after surgery).
Receiver
The receiver, the third component of the communication process, is
the listener who must attend, listen and observe. This person is the
decoder, who must perceive what the sender intended
(interpretation) by the message. To decode means to relate the
message perceived to the receiver’s storehouse of knowledge and
experience and to sort out the meaning of the message. Perception
uses all of the senses to receive verbal and non-verbal messages.
Whether the message is decoded accurately by the receiver,
according to the sender’s intent, depends largely on their similarities
in knowledge, experience and sociocultural background. If the
meaning of the decoded message matches the intent of the sender,
the communication has been effective. Ineffective communication
occurs when the message sent is misinterpreted by the receiver. For
example, Mr Johnson may perceive the verbal message accurately:
‘I can have my pain medication now’. However, if experience has
taught him that receiving his pain medication is always a lengthy
process because he has to ask repeatedly for analgesia before
receiving it, he may interpret the intent of the message differently.
This is also true of electronic communication where the receiver may
not be able to decode the message or, as the message may have
few contextual cues, its meaning may be misconstrued.


Response
The fourth component of the communication process, the response,
is the message that the receiver returns to the sender. It is also
called feedback. Feedback can be verbal, non-verbal or both. Non-
verbal examples include a nod of the head or a smile. Feedback
allows the sender to correct or reword a message. In the case of Mr
Johnson, the receiver may appear irritated or say, ‘Well, it always
takes a long time for my pain medication to actually come’. The
sender then knows their intended message was not interpreted
accurately. However, now the original sender becomes the receiver,
the one who is required to decode and respond. In nurse–patient
relationships, the nurse assumes a primary responsibility for seeking
message clarification. As non-verbal cues and visual feedback are
often absent during electronically supported communication,
particular attention is needed to ensure the correct message has
been received.
Modes of interpersonal
communication
Interpersonal communication generally has two different modes—
verbal and non-verbal—and can occur in face-to-face
communication or through electronic communication technologies.
Verbal communication
 uses the spoken or written/typed word;
non-verbal communication
 is harder to control and uses other


forms of communication such as gestures, facial expressions, eye
contact, posture and touch. Communication received non-verbally
adds depth to verbal communication and helps the nurse to better
understand the person they are caring for or their colleagues.
Learning about non-verbal communication assists nurses in
developing therapeutic communication patterns with people in their
care and collegial relationships within the health care team.
Verbal communication
Verbal communication is largely conscious because people choose
the message they want to send and the words they use. The words
used vary between individuals according to factors such as role,
culture, socioeconomic background, age and education. As a result,
countless possibilities exist for the way ideas are verbally
exchanged. In addition, a wide variety of feelings can be conveyed
when people talk or respond. At times, nurses will encounter verbal
communication by the people they care for that is disjointed and at
odds with their context. While difficult to understand, this verbal
communication can provide assessment information that is
important for the person’s care. When choosing words to say or
write/type, nurses need to consider pace and intonation, simplicity,
clarity and brevity, timing and relevance, adaptability, credibility and
humour.
Pace and intonation


The meaning of a nurse’s message is modified by the pace and
intonation of their verbal communication. The intonation or tone of
voice can express enthusiasm, sadness, irritation, anger or
amusement. Intonation might be modified by a nurse to prevent an
unintended message from being sent. The pace or speed of speech
may indicate interest, anxiety, boredom or fear. For example,
speaking slowly enough to enunciate clearly and speaking softly to
an excited person may have a calming effect. Speaking quickly and
firmly may have the negative effect of blocking the person from
providing important assessment information or asking questions
about their care.
Simplicity
Simplicity includes the use of commonly understood words. Many
complex technical terms become natural to nurses and are
sometimes referred to as professional jargon. Within some specialty
care areas, nurses use highly specific and technical language. This
can lead to the development of language-based power and authority
within nursing and health care services (Allen et al.
). The person
the nurse is caring for and their colleagues can misunderstand these
specific terms. Words such as preop, vasoconstriction or
cholecystectomy may be meaningful to the nurse and easy to use
but when used with other people the meaning needs to be shared
and checked.
16 Allen, S., Chapman, Y., O’Connor, M. & Francis, K. (2007). The importance of language for
nursing: Does it convey commonality of meaning and is it important to do so? Australasian
Journal of Advanced Nursing, 24(4), 47–51.
16


Nurses need to learn to select appropriate, understandable language
based on variables such as health status, health literacy level, age,
knowledge, culture and education. For example, instead of saying,
‘The nurses will be catheterising you tomorrow for a urinalysis’, it
may be more appropriate and understandable to say, ‘Tomorrow we
need to get a sample of your urine to test. To do this we will need to
insert a small tube into your bladder to collect the urine’. The latter is
more likely to elicit a response as to why it is needed and whether
the person agrees because they understand the language used.
Some words also have different meanings to different people: having
your medication with dinner may mean the midday meal to one
person but the last meal of the day to another. (See Box 27.2
 for
another example of the importance of using language that is
appropriate to each person being cared for.)
BO X
27.2 Appropriate assessment
language
In the Pilbara, an Aboriginal man was asked by his nurse
whether he had passed water; he replied that he had not.
This question was asked a number of different times during
the shift, always with the same response by the man. The
nurses were becoming increasingly concerned, to the point
where they were contemplating whether the man should be
catheterised. Eventually one of the nurses, in conversation


with the Aboriginal liaison officer, worked out that the man
thought that passing water referred to passing a creek on his
way to the hospital. The nurse did not know that in this man’s
language the word for urine was koomp and had not
considered the effect of language on the effectiveness of
their communication and the safety of the man’s care.
Source: Strobel et al.
. Communicating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples. In T.
Levett-Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient Safety: An Essential Guide for Health
Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
17 Strobel, N., Rudd, C., Hayward, C., McAullay, D. & Sim, M. (2020). Communicating with Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander Peoples. In T. Levett-Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient Safety:
An Essential Guide for Health Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
Clarity and brevity
A message that is brief, direct and simple is often the most effective.
Clarity is saying precisely what is meant and brevity is using the
fewest words necessary. The result is a message that is simple and
clear. To ensure clarity, nurses also need to enunciate clearly and
ensure that their verbal pace is appropriate to the person they are
caring for.
Timing and relevance
Nurses need to be aware of both relevance and timing when
communicating with the person they are caring for. No matter how
17


clearly or simply words are stated or written/typed, the timing needs
to be appropriate to ensure that the message can be heard.
Moreover, the message needs to relate to the person or to their
interests and concerns at that time. This requires sensitivity to
individual needs and concerns. For example, a person who is
enmeshed in fear of cancer may not hear the nurse’s explanations
about procedures before and after surgery. In this situation, the
nurse can encourage the person to talk about their concerns, the
necessary procedural explanations occurring afterwards when the
person is receptive and ready to listen. Another aspect of poor
timing is to ask a question and then not wait for an answer. For
example, a nurse says in one breath, ‘Good morning, Mrs Brody.
How are you this morning? Did you sleep well last night? Your
husband is coming to see you before your surgery, isn’t he?’. Mrs
Brody is left to wonder which question to answer first and if any of
the responses are of importance to her care.
When using information communication technologies, the electronic
format should be relevant for the person and for the information
being communicated. For example, the selection of asynchronous
methods, such as email, to relay a message allows the recipient to
reply in their own time or simply review the message when they are
ready.
Adaptability
Spoken messages need to be altered in accordance with
behavioural cues, an adjustment known as adaptability. What the


nurse says and how it is said must be individualised, requiring astute
nurse assessment and sensitivity. For example, a nurse who usually
smiles, appears cheerful and greets the person they are caring for
with an enthusiastic ‘Hi, Mrs Brown!’ notices Mrs Brown is not
smiling and appears distressed. It is important for the nurse to then
modify their tone of speech and express concern through facial
expressions while moving towards the person.
Equally, the nurse can use cues to adapt to personal preferences for
electronic or face-to-face communication. If the relationship has
been established via telephone but the person prefers to use
internet software (e.g. Skype
), the communication medium should
be modified when possible.
Credibility
Credibility means worthiness of belief, trustworthiness and reliability.
Credibility may be the most important criterion of effective
communication. Nurses foster credibility by being consistent,
trustworthy and honest. The nurse needs to be knowledgeable about
what is being discussed and to have accurate information. Nurses
should convey confidence and certainty in what they are saying
while being able to acknowledge their limitations. For example, ‘I
don’t know the answer, but I will find someone who does’.
Humour
TM


Humour can be a positive and powerful communication tool in
nurse–patient and collegial relationships, but it must be used with
sensitivity and respect for the other person. The physical act of
laughter can be an emotional and physical release, reducing tension
by providing a different perspective and promoting a sense of
wellbeing. Humour can also help people to adjust to difficult and
painful situations. However, MacDonald (
, p. 23) warns that while
humour and laughter can help reduce stress and anxiety in the early
and recovery stages of a crisis, humour can be considered offensive
or distracting at a peak crisis period. When used inappropriately,
humour can result in affront, disrespect or a lack of trust, and be
detrimental to the development or maintenance of therapeutic
relationships. When using humour, it is important to consider the
person’s perception of what is considered humorous. Where non-
verbal cues are unreliable or lost, for example, in email and text
communication, attempts at using humour to support the therapeutic
relationship may be misinterpreted.
18 MacDonald, C. M. (2004). A chuckle a day keeps the doctor away: Therapeutic humour
and laughter. Journal of Psychosocial Nursing and Mental Health Services, 42(3), 18–25.
Non-verbal communication
Non-verbal communication is sometimes called body language and
occurs without the use of words. It includes gestures, body
movements, use of touch and physical appearance. Because non-
verbal behaviour is controlled less consciously than verbal behaviour,
it often tells others more about what a person is feeling than what is
18


actually said (see Figure 27.4
). Non-verbal communication is
displayed by both the person being cared for and the nurse, and
may either reinforce or contradict what is said verbally. When the
verbal and non-verbal messages contradict each other, a ‘mixed
message’ results and miscommunication may occur. For example, if
a nurse says, ‘I’d be happy to sit here and talk to you for a while’,
yet glances repeatedly at her watch, the non-verbal communication
is contradicting the verbal message. The person the nurse is caring
for is more likely to believe the non-verbal behaviour, which conveys,
‘I don’t have time for this’, and they may even defer telling the nurse
important information because of perceived ‘busyness’. In this case,
the person being cared for has received a mixed or non-congruent
message because the verbal and non-verbal communication are
inconsistent.
Figure 27.4


Non-verbal communication sometimes conveys meaning more
effectively than words. In the picture on the left, the people’s
postures indicate openness to communication. In the picture on the
right, the speaker’s posture is more closed and the listener’s posture
reflects caution.
Source: © Alexander Raths, Shutterstock.
Observing and interpreting non-verbal behaviour is an essential
nursing skill. To observe non-verbal behaviour efficiently requires a
systematic assessment of the person’s overall physical appearance,
posture, gait, facial expressions and gestures. However, the nurse
cannot always be sure of the correct interpretation of the feelings
expressed non-verbally. The same feeling can be expressed in more
than one way, even within the same cultural group. For example,
anger may be communicated by aggressive or excessive body
motion, or it may be communicated by stillness.
Acceptable non-verbal communication varies widely across cultures.
Cultures differ in greeting behaviours, such as smiling and
handshaking, not only between broad cultural groups, such as
Indigenous and non-Indigenous cultures, but also within cultural
groups (Eckerman et al.
). For example, the use of eye contact
varies across cultural groups. The non-verbal channel of touch is
often highly effective and is used extensively in nursing but should
be carefully considered in the context of culture, gender and age.
19 Eckerman, A. K., Dowd, T., Chong, E., Nixon, L., Gray, R. & Johnson, S. (2006). Binan
Goonj: Bridging Cultures in Aboriginal Health (2nd ed., pp. 103–145). Marrickville, NSW:
Elsevier.
19


People who have altered thought processes, such as in delirium or
dementia, may experience times when expressing themselves
verbally is difficult or impossible. During these times, the nurse
needs to be able to interpret what the person is expressing non-
verbally. A nurse who attends to and clarifies non-verbal and verbal
communication displays interest, caring and acceptance of the
person. This can be the beginning or consolidation of a trusting
relationship between the nurse and the person they are caring for,
even when there are communication difficulties.
Personal appearance
Clothing and adornments can be sources of information about a
person. Although choice of apparel is highly personal, it may convey
social and financial status, culture, religion, group association and
self-concept. Charms and amulets may be worn for decorative,
religious, cultural or health protection purposes. When the symbolic
meaning of an object is unfamiliar, the nurse can sensitively inquire
about its significance, fostering rapport with the person they are
caring for.
How a person dresses may be an indicator of how well the person
feels. Someone who is tired or unwell may not have the energy or
the desire to maintain their normal grooming. When a person known
for immaculate grooming becomes lax about their appearance, the
nurse may suspect a loss of self-esteem or a physical or mental
illness. For an acutely ill person, a self-initiated change in grooming
habits may signal they are feeling better; for example, a man may


request a shave or a woman may request a mirror and hairbrush.
The nurse must validate this observed non-verbal data by asking if
the person is feeling better.
Nurses also send messages through their own personal
appearance. Careful grooming may convey a message of
professionalism, supporting trust and competence. Lax attire may
have a negative effect on therapeutic and collegial relationships.
Posture and gait
The way people walk and carry themselves is often a reliable
indicator of self-concept, current mood and health. Erect posture
and an active, purposeful stride suggest a feeling of wellbeing.
Slouched posture and a slow, shuffling gait suggest physical
discomfort. Tense posture and a rapid, determined gait suggest
anxiety or anger. The posture when sitting or lying can also indicate
feelings or mood. Again, the nurse clarifies the meaning of the
observed behaviour by describing what they see and then asking for
clarification or confirmation of its meaning. For example, ‘It looks like
it really hurts to move today. Is your pain worse?’.
Facial expression
No part of the body is as expressive as the face (see Figure
27.5
) and many facial expressions convey a universal meaning.
For example, a smile expresses pleasure. Contempt is conveyed by
the mouth turned down, the head tilted back and the eyes directed


down the nose. Feelings of surprise, fear, anger, disgust, happiness
and sadness can also be conveyed by facial expressions. Although
the face may express the person’s genuine emotions, it is also
possible to control these muscles, so the emotion expressed does
not fully reflect what the person is feeling. No single expression can
be interpreted accurately, however, without considering other
reinforcing physical cues, the setting in which it occurs, the
expression of others in the same setting and the cultural background
of the person being cared for. Some people will have an
expressionless face or a ‘flat affect’, making it difficult for the nurse
to confirm verbal messages. When the message is not clear, it is
important to get feedback to be sure of the intent of the expression.
Figure 27.5


The child’s facial expression is part of non-verbal communication
with the nurse.
Nurses need to be aware of their own expressions and what they
are communicating to others. People being cared for are quick to
notice the nurse’s facial expression, particularly when they feel
unsure or uncomfortable. The person who questions the nurse about
a feared diagnostic result will watch whether the nurse maintains eye
contact or looks away when answering. The person who has had
disfiguring surgery will examine the nurse’s face for signs of rejection
or disgust. It is impossible to control all facial expressions, but the
nurse must learn to control the expression of feelings that may
disturb or upset the people they care for.
Eye contact is an essential element of facial communication. In
many cultures, mutual eye contact acknowledges the other person
and indicates a willingness to maintain communication. Often a
person initiates contact by a glance, capturing the person’s attention
prior to verbal communication. A person who feels weak or
defenceless often averts the eyes or avoids eye contact; the
communication received may be too embarrassing or too
dominating. However, even behaviours such as eye contact differ
between cultures. For example, to traditional Yolnu, an Indigenous
people of Australia, strong eye contact makes them feel threatened,
very uncomfortable and vulnerable (Trudgen ), and in response
they look away or down. They prefer to sit side by side, looking
ahead or over the shoulder of the person, as though there was
something or someone there to look at. For non-Indigenous
20


Australians, this behaviour is seen as different from what they
expect, and they may even turn to see what is being looked at
(Trudgen 2000).
20 Trudgen, R. (2000). Why Warriors Lie Down and Die: Towards an Understanding of Why
the Aboriginal People of Arnhem Land Face the Greatest Crisis in Health and Education Since
European Contact. Darwin, NT: Aboriginal resources and Development Services Inc.
Gestures
Hand and body gestures may emphasise and clarify the spoken
word or they may occur without words to indicate a particular feeling
or to give a sign. A father waiting for information about his daughter
after surgery may wring his hands, tap his foot, pick at his nails or
pace back and forth. A wave goodbye and the motioning of a visitor
towards a chair are gestures that have relatively universal meanings.
Some gestures, however, are culturally specific and require the
nurse to clarify their meaning before using them to communicate
across cultures; for example, extending your arm to shake hands as
a greeting. Advice on the cultural appropriateness of gestures can
be sought from qualified health care interpreters or health care
workers.
For people with communication problems, such as deafness, the
hands are invaluable in non-verbal communication. Many people
who are deaf learn sign language. People who are unable to reply
verbally can similarly devise a communication system using their
hands; for example, they may be able to raise an index finger once
for ‘yes’ and twice for ‘no’. Signals can often be devised to denote


other meanings and care needs. Devices such as a communication
board or applications in electronic devices can also be used (see
Figure 27.6
).
Figure 27.6


Using communication boards to aid understanding.
Factors influencing the
communication process
Many factors influence the dynamic nature of the communication
process. Some of these are human development, gender, values
and perceptions, culture, personal space, roles and relationships,
environment, congruence and attitudes.
Development
Language, psychosocial and intellectual development all develop
across the lifespan. Knowledge of a person’s developmental stage
will allow the nurse to modify the message and communicate
effectively (see ‘Lifespan considerations’). The use of dolls, puppets
and games with simple language may help explain a procedure to a
child (see Figure 27.7
). With adolescents who have developed
more abstract thinking skills, more detailed explanations can be
given, whereas an adult may need more detailed technical or
research information. Older people may have had a wider range of
health care experiences that may influence their response or
understanding. Ageing changes to the acuity of vision and hearing
may also affect communication.


Figure 27.7


The nurse uses a soft toy to explain an operation to a child.
Source: © Elisabeth Schneider/Look at Sciences/Science Photo Library.
Gender
From an early age, females and males communicate differently.
Girls tend to use language to seek confirmation, minimise
differences and establish intimacy. Boys use language to establish
independence and negotiate status within a group. These
differences can continue into adulthood so that the same
communication may be interpreted differently by a man and a
woman. Although differences exist, it remains important to consider
each person as unique and not stereotype communication strategies
and understanding based on gender.
Lifespan considerations
Communication
The ability to communicate is directly related to the
development of thought processes, the presence of intact
sensory and motor systems and the extent and nature of an
individual’s opportunities to practise communication skills. As
children grow, their communication abilities change markedly.
Infants


Infants communicate non-verbally, often in response to
body feelings rather than in a conscious effort to be
expressive.
Infants’ perceptions are related to sensory stimuli, so a
gentle voice or touch is soothing, for example, while
tension and anger around them can create distress.
Toddlers and preschoolers
Toddlers and young children gain skills in both expressive
(i.e. telling others what they feel, think, want, care about)
and receptive communication (hearing and understanding
what others are communicating to them).
Allow time for them to complete verbalising their thoughts
without interruption.
Provide a simple response to questions because their
attention span is short.
Drawing a picture or engaging the child in play can provide
other ways for the child to communicate.
School-age children
Talk to the child at eye level to help decrease intimidation.
Include the child in the conversation when communicating
with the parents.
Nurses can use the following communication techniques to
work effectively with children and their families:


Play, the universal language, allows children to use other
symbols, not just words, to express themselves.
Drawing, painting and other art forms can be used by
even non-verbal children.
Storytelling, in which the nurse and child take turns adding
to a story or putting words to pictures, can help the child
feel safer in expressing emotions and feelings.
Word games that pose hypothetical situations or put the
child in control, such as ‘What if . . .?’, ‘If you could . . .’,
‘If a genie came and gave you a wish . . .’, can help a
child feel more powerful or explore ideas about how to
manage the illness.
Read books with a theme similar to the child’s condition or
problem, then discuss the meaning, characters and
feelings generated by the book. Movies, DVDs or
electronic games can also be used in this way.
Writing can be used by older children to reflect on their
situation, develop meaning and gain a sense of control.
Adolescents
Take time to build rapport with the adolescent.
Use active listening skills.
Project a non-judgmental attitude and non-reactive
behaviours, even when the adolescent makes challenging
remarks.
In all interactions with children and adolescents, it is
important to provide opportunities for expression, to listen


openly and respond honestly, using words and concepts that
can be understood and that focus on their concerns.
Values and perceptions
Values are the standards that influence behaviour and perceptions
are the personal view of an event. Because each person has unique
personality traits, values and life experiences, each will perceive and
interpret messages and experiences differently. For example, if the
nurse draws the curtains around a crying woman and leaves her
alone, the woman may interpret this as ‘The nurse thinks that I will
upset others and that I shouldn’t cry’ or ‘The nurse respects my
need to be alone’. It is important for the nurse to be aware of each
person’s perceptions and values and the need to validate or correct
perceptions to avoid barriers in their relationships with people in their
care and also colleagues.
Culture
Culture has an influence on communication (see Chapter 19
) as it
teaches us communication rules which, over time, are taken for
granted. However, there are a large number of cultural variables to
both verbal and non-verbal communication which nurses need to
consider when communicating. Communicating across cultures is
known as transcultural, cross-cultural or intercultural communication,
and, while it is often used to refer to communication between people


from different countries, it also relates to communication between
different subgroups. Australia is known for its culturally diverse
population and in this context all nurses need transcultural
communication
 skills. Nurses who are respectful of cultural
dimensions during communication show respect for the person and
display one aspect of culturally safe practice.
Personal space
Personal space is the invisible distance people prefer to have
between them and another person when engaged in interpersonal
communication. The distance chosen varies, influenced by factors
such as the circumstances, culture and status of the relationship.
When this space is threatened, the person may behave defensively,
and the effectiveness of communication usually decreases. Nurses
will often move into the personal space of a person by virtue of the
caring activities they perform. When this happens, it is important for
the nurse to acknowledge what they are doing by forewarning the
person, seeking permission and communicating respect, gentleness
and confidence. Circumstances may dictate whether personal space
is appropriate. Personal space is thought to have different distance
zones: intimate, personal, social and public (Tamparo & Lindh , p.
31).
21 Tamparo, C. T. & Lindh, W. Q. (2000). Therapeutic Communications for Health
Professionals (2nd ed.). Albany, NY: Delmar Thomson Learning.
Intimate distance communication is characterised by body contact,
heightened sensations of body heat and smell, and vocalisations
21


that are low. Vision is intense and is restricted to a small body part.
It is a natural protective instinct for people to maintain a certain
amount of space immediately around them and the amount varies
with individuals and cultures. When someone steps too close when
they want to communicate, the receiver automatically steps back to
re-establish a comfortable distance (Tamparo & Lindh 2000, p. 31).
In their therapeutic roles, nurses are often required to work within
the intimate distance. Examples include cuddling a baby, positioning
or bathing, and holding a toddler during a procedure. In many
instances, the nurse can respect (not come too close to) a person’s
intimate distance. In other instances, the nurse may come within
intimate distance to communicate warmth and caring.
Personal distance is less overwhelming than intimate distance. Voice
tones are moderate and body heat and smell are noticed less.
Physical contact such as a handshake or touching a shoulder is
possible. More of the person is perceived at a personal distance so
that non-verbal behaviours such as body stance or full facial
expressions are seen with less distortion (Tamparo & Lindh 2000, p.
31). Much communication between nurses and the person they are
caring for occurs at this distance. Examples occur when nurses are
sitting with the person they are caring for, giving medications or
establishing an intravenous infusion. Communication at a close
personal distance can convey involvement by facilitating the sharing
of thoughts and feelings.
Social distance is characterised by a clear visual perception of the
whole person. Body heat and odour are imperceptible, eye contact is


increased and vocalisations are loud enough to be overheard by
others. Communication is therefore more formal and is limited to
seeing and hearing. The person is protected and out of reach.
Adopting a social distance is expedient when communicating with
several people at the same time or within a short time, and to
accomplish the business of the day (Tamparo & Lindh 2000, p. 31).
However, it is frequently misused. For example, the nurse who
stands in the doorway and asks, ‘How are you today?’ will receive a
more non-committal reply than the nurse who moves to a personal
distance from the person in their care.
Public distance requires loud, clear vocalisations with careful
enunciation. Although the faces and forms of people are seen at
public distance, individuality is lost. Instead, the perception is of a
group of people or the community (Tamparo & Lindh 2000, p. 31).
Public distance is not used in therapeutic relationships in nursing
care but may be used with colleagues; for example, presenting a
paper at a nursing conference.
Roles and relationships
The roles and relationships between sender and receiver affect the
communication process. Roles such as nursing student and clinical
educator, patient and nurse, nurse and colleague, or parent and
child affect communication content and responses. Choice of words,
sentence structure and tone of voice vary considerably from role to
role. In addition, the specific relationship between the
communicators is significant. The nurse who meets a person for the


first time communicates differently from a nurse who has an
established therapeutic or collegial relationship. Observing
communication between the person and their family can provide
valuable assessment cues about relationships and need for support.
Environment
People usually communicate most effectively in an environment that
meets their needs for comfort and safety. Temperature extremes,
excessive noise and a lack of privacy can all interfere with
communication. Environmental distractions in the busy hospital
environment can also impair and distort communication. A lack of
privacy may interfere with a person’s communication about matters
considered private or sensitive. For example, a man who is worried
about his wife’s ability to care for him after hospital discharge may
not wish to discuss this concern when family members or other
people can hear their conversation.
Congruence
In congruent communication, verbal and non-verbal messages
match and miscommunication is minimised. However, if there is
incongruence the nurse needs to identify the content and feeling of
messages and explore the true meanings with the person.
Sometimes people can convey a thought in words while their
emotions contradict the words; that is, words and feelings are
incongruent. For example, a woman says, ‘I am glad he has left me;
he was very violent’. However, the nurse observes tears in her eyes


as she speaks. To respond to the words, the nurse might simply
rephrase, saying, ‘You are pleased that he has left you’. To also
respond to the feelings, the nurse would acknowledge the person’s
tears, saying, for example, ‘You seem saddened by him leaving but
also relieved’.
Interpersonal attitudes
Attitudes convey beliefs, thoughts and feelings about people and
events and are communicated to others. Attitudes such as caring,
warmth, respect and acceptance facilitate communication, whereas
condescension and disinterest inhibit communication.
Caring involves feelings, thoughts, skill and knowledge. It is often
considered fundamental to nursing and involves both caring about
and for the person (Stein-Parbury 2018) (see Chapter 26
). Caring
conveys deep and genuine concern for the person and a feeling of
emotional closeness, and contrasts with an impersonal approach. It
requires psychological energy and poses the risk of gaining little in
return. Yet, by caring, the benefits of greater communication and
understanding are achieved. Warmth is similar to caring and
conveys approachability, friendliness, interest in and regard for the
person (Stein-Parbury 2018). It helps the person to feel at ease and
is mainly conveyed through non-verbal communication (Stein-
Parbury 2018).
Respect is an attitude that emphasises the other person’s worth and
individuality. It conveys that the nurse considers the person’s hopes


and feelings to be special and unique even though they may be
similar to others in many ways. Egan  suggests that being
competent, committed and genuine, and working with the person to
achieve their goals are ways nurses show respect for the person
they are caring for. Nurses also convey respect by listening open-
mindedly to the other person, even if they disagree, and ensuring
their practice is focused on doing no harm (Egan 2013). See Box
27.3
.
22 Egan, G. (2013). The Skilled Helper: A Problem-Management and Opportunity-
Development Approach to Helping (10th ed.). Belmont, CA: Brooks/Cole.

. Toward Culturally Competent Care: A Toolbox for

Communication Strategies. San Francisco, CA: Center for the Health Professions, University of
California, San Francisco.
23


Nurses may unknowingly use speech that they believe shows caring
and respect but is perceived as demeaning or patronising by the
person in their care. This can happen in settings that provide health
care to older people and/or people with physical or intellectual
disabilities. This style of communication can be referred to as
‘elderspeak’ or ‘baby talk’ and sends a message of dependence and
incompetence rather than respect. The characteristics of this
communication style include use of diminutives (inappropriate terms
of endearment such as ‘dearie’ and ‘sweetie’), inappropriate use of
plural pronouns (such as using ‘we’ when referring to an
independent older adult), tag questions, which prompt the answer to
the question and imply that the adult can’t decide for themselves
(such as ‘You would rather wear the blue socks, wouldn’t you?’) and
slow, loud speech (Williams, Kemper & Hummert
, p. 22). In an
Australian study by Gardner et al.
, participants commented on the
language used by nurses and they resented being called ‘love’,
‘honey’ or ‘sweetie’ (p. 36). Many health care providers are not
aware that they use this inappropriate communication style and that
it adversely affects the development and maintenance of a
therapeutic relationship.
24 Williams, K., Kemper, S. & Hummert, M. L. (2004). Enhancing communication with older
adults: Overcoming elderspeak. Journal of Gerontological Nursing, 30(10), 17–25.
25 Gardner, A., Goodsell, J., Duggan, T., Murtha, B., Peck, C. & Williams, J. (2001). ‘Don’t
call me sweetie!’ Patients differ from nurses in their perceptions of caring. Collegian, 8(3), 32–
38.
24
25


Acceptance emphasises neither approval nor disapproval. An
accepting attitude allows other people to express personal feelings
freely and to be themselves. The nurse may, however, need to
restrict acceptance in situations where behaviours are harmful to the
person or to others. Helping people to appropriately express their
feelings may be an education strategy used to set therapeutic
relationship boundaries or to establish safe collegial relationships.
Therapeutic communication
Therapeutic communication
 occurs when the nurse uses
communication techniques and processes in ways that effectively
promote understanding, are therapeutic for the person being cared
for and are developmental in relation to the therapeutic relationship.
Therapeutic communication is therefore different from collegial and
social communication.
The person being cared for and their family members notice when
communication is not therapeutic and may sometimes identify
communication as a reason for complaint (Kable & Farmer
). In the
2016–17 NSW government Health Care Complaints Commission’s
(HCCC) report on complaints, approximately 17% of complaints
related to communication by health professionals (HCCC ).
26 Kable, A. & Farmer, W. (2020). Why do patients complain about how health professionals
communicate? In T. Levett-Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient Safety: An
Essential Guide for Health Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
26
27


27 Health Care Complaints Commission (HCCC) (2017). Annual Report 2016–17. Retrieved
from <www.hccc.nsw.gov.au>.
Patient safety competency framework
2 Therapeutic communication
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students should share
information with the person in a way that is
understandable and that encourages
participation in decision making (Levett-Jones et
al.
).
28 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
In therapeutic communication, nurses need to respond not only to
the content of a person’s verbal message but also to the feelings
expressed. It is important to understand how the person views the
situation and feels about it before responding. People usually need
to deal with feelings before they can cope with other matters, such
as learning new skills or planning for the future. For example, when
a person learns that they have a terminal illness, they may require
28


hours, days or even weeks before they are ready to start other
tasks. Some need time to themselves; others need someone to
listen or assistance to identify and verbalise feelings before making
decisions about their care or future courses of action. Box 27.4
lists the benefits of therapeutic communication.

Positive clinical outcomes
Higher levels of patient satisfaction
Higher levels of patient compliance with treatment
programs
Lower levels of patient frustration/anger
