The key verbal and non-verbal communication techniques that
facilitate communication, assist with relationship development and
help the nurse focus on the person’s concerns are described in
Table 27.1
. The techniques of active listening
 and
attending
 are explored in the following paragraphs as these
techniques are central to effective therapeutic communication.
Table 27.1 Verbal and non-verbal communication techniques
Active listening
When nurses listen actively, they attend to the person, hear what is
being said and communicate that they have heard the person’s
message. Active listening includes verbal and non-verbal techniques
and is probably the most important communication technique in
nursing. In an Australian study, patients rated ‘listens to me’ as the
third most important caring nurse behaviour (Gardner et al. 2001).
Active listening is a dynamic process that requires energy and
concentration. It involves paying attention to the total message, both
verbal and non-verbal, and noting whether these communications
are congruent. Active listening means interpreting both the content
and the feeling the person is conveying without bias or judgment.
The nurse does not select or listen solely to what the nurse wants to
hear; the nurse focuses not on their own needs but rather on the
needs of the person they are caring for. Active listening conveys an
attitude of caring and interest, thereby encouraging the person to
communicate further and more deeply.


Active listening involves listening for key themes in the
communication. The speaker should not be interrupted and the
nurse should take time to think about the message before
responding. As a listener, the nurse should also ask questions to
obtain additional information, to clarify content or emotions and to
explore incongruous messages.
To be an effective active listener nurses need to be aware of their
own biases, be able to suspend judgment about the person and their
message and be able to spend time listening. The message should
not be filtered through the nurse’s own biases, including
stereotypical views of different groups (e.g. unmarried mothers,
Indigenous peoples, teenage girls). A message that reflects different
values or beliefs should not be discredited for this reason.
A nurse can reinforce that they are actively listening by using
minimal encouragement. Minimal encouragement is the use of
verbal and non-verbal communication techniques that lets the
person know the nurse is listening and is following what they are
saying and indicates that the nurse wants the person to continue.
Common examples of minimal encouragement are nodding the head
or uttering ‘Yes’, ‘Uh huh’ or ‘Mmm’. Each nurse has characteristic
ways of responding with minimal encouragement; however, the
nurse must take care not to sound insincere or appear to be
responding automatically and without thought.
Attending


Attending, or ‘tuning in’, is defined by Egan (2013) as a manner of
being present to or being with another person. Listening, in Egan’s
frame of reference, is what a person does while attending (see
Figure 27.8
). Egan (2013) outlines five key non-verbal behaviours
to convey that you are tuned in to the person. These are known by
the acronym SOLER and are described in Box 27.5
. When
adopting these actions in nursing, care is needed to ensure that
cultural considerations and variation in a person’s need for personal
space are taken into account.
Figure 27.8


The nurse conveys active listening through an attending posture.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
BO X
27.5 Non-verbal tuning in: using
SOLER
S: Face the other person squarely. This position says, ‘I
am available to you’. Turning away lessens the degree of
involvement.
O: Adopt an open posture. This non-defensive position is
one in which neither arms nor legs are crossed. It
conveys that the person wishes to encourage ongoing
communication and is open or receptive to what is going
to be said.
L: If possible, lean towards the person. People move
naturally towards one another when they want to say or
hear something—by moving to the front of a class, by
moving a chair nearer a friend or by leaning across a table
with arms propped in front. The nurse conveys
involvement by leaning forward, closer to the person they
are caring for.
E: Maintain good eye contact. Mutual eye contact,
preferably at the same level, recognises the other person
and denotes willingness to maintain communication. Eye


contact neither glares at nor stares down another but is
natural.
R: Try to be relatively relaxed and natural in the way you
use your body. Total relaxation is not feasible when the
nurse is listening with intensity, but the nurse can show
relaxation by taking time in responding, allowing pauses
as needed, balancing periods of tension with relaxation
and using gestures that are natural.
These five attending postures need to be adapted to the
specific needs of the person in a given situation. For
example, leaning forward may not be appropriate at the
beginning of an interview. It may be reserved until a closer
relationship develops between the nurse and the person they
are caring for. The same applies to eye contact, which is
generally uninterrupted when the communicators are very
involved in the interaction.
Source: Adapted from G. Egan (2013). The Skilled Helper: A Problem-Management and Opportunity-
Development Approach to Helping (10th ed., pp. 77–78). Belmont, CA: Brooks/Cole.
Barriers to communication
Communication barriers are factors that prevent meaning from being
effectively understood during communication. Nurses need to
recognise barriers or non-therapeutic communication responses in


their practice (see Table 27.2
). Failure to listen, improperly
decoding the intended message and placing the nurse’s needs or
opinions above other people’s are major communication barriers
which impede the development of therapeutic relationships and
effective and safe person-centred care.
Table 27.2 Barriers to communication


Therapeutic relationships
Nurse–patient relationships are referred to by some as therapeutic
relationships
, by others as helping relationships and by still
others as interpersonal relationships. The development of a
therapeutic relationship supports the nurse in being person centred
(Bolster & Manias ). For the therapeutic relationship to be effective
in meeting the person’s goals and needs, the nurse needs to earn
the person’s trust and respect, often through demonstration of
sound nursing knowledge and use of effective communication skills.
In addition, the nurse needs to show respect for the person they are
caring for (Egan 2013). The therapeutic relationship is not, however,
the same as a social relationship. In a therapeutic relationship, the
nurse assumes professional responsibility for the person they are
caring for and focuses on their needs and goals. The person trusts
that the nurse will act in their best interest and will base care on an
assessment of their individual needs and collaborative decision
making. Characteristics of therapeutic relationships are listed in Box
27.6
.
30 Bolster, D. & Manias, E. (2010). Person-centred interactions between nurses and patients
during medication activities in an acute hospital setting: Qualitative observation and interview
study. International Journal of Nursing Studies, 47(2), 154–165.
BO X
30


27.6 Characteristics of therapeutic
relationships
A therapeutic relationship:
is a partnership between the nurse and the person they
are caring for which is focused on the person’s health
needs/goals
respects the person being cared for as an individual,
including:
maximising the person’s ability to participate in
decision making and health care activities
consideration of ethnic and cultural aspects
consideration of family relationships and values
maintaining privacy
respects confidentiality
focuses on the promotion of self-care and independence
is based on mutual trust, respect, empathy and
acceptance
is characterised by phases of development: pre-
introductory, introductory, working and termination phases.
The therapeutic relationship is influenced by the personal and
professional characteristics of the nurse and characteristics of the
person they are caring for. Willingness, age, sex, appearance,
diagnosis, education, values, self-awareness, ethnic and cultural
background, personality, expectations and setting can all affect the


development of the relationship. Consideration of all of these
factors, combined with good communication skills and sincere
interest in helping the person, enable the nurse to develop and work
within a therapeutic relationship.
Real-world practice
Over many years one the most troubling and recurring
practices I’ve witnessed have been during clinical
handover. Nurses who at the end of their shift were
tired, impatient and frustrated, would sometimes make
offhand, negative and disparaging comments about
the people they were caring for, such as, ‘He has been
on the bell and whinging about pain all night . . . he’s
got a PCA but he just won’t let up’ or ‘That’s all you
can expect of “that lot” . . . Some people don’t deserve
to have kids’ or ‘She is so demanding . . . I’ll be glad
when she’s discharged . . . nothing we do is good
enough’. These types of comments made me feel
uncomfortable; they would influence the views and
practice of the nurses coming on duty and as a
consequence patient care would sometimes suffer. By
contrast, some of the very best nurses I’ve seen
ignore these prejudicial comments and deliberately set
out to spend time talking with and coming to
understand the person’s needs and concerns. These


nurses are transformative. By actively listening and
attending they are able to discern and address the
person’s real concerns, fears and needs, even with
people from different cultures. Those so-called
demanding patients trusted these nurses and felt safe.
Their level of anxiety reduced and they were able to
focus on getting well, secure in the knowledge that
their nurse was compassionate, professional and
engaged.
—Registered Nurse
The nursing profession has expectations about how nurses will work
in therapeutic relationships. These expectations help to protect the
person’s interests and balance the positional power nurses have in
their relationships with patients. A Nurse’s Guide to Professional
Boundaries (NMBA ) describes a continuum of behaviour in
relationships between nurses and the people they care for. See
Figure 27.9
. In this continuum, nurses who develop relationships
that display the characteristics of a therapeutic relationship are
working in the ‘zone of helpfulness’ and accept responsibility for
ensuring that their nurse–patient relationships are, and remain,
therapeutic and safe. Nurses who are unwilling or unable to engage
in a safe and therapeutic nurse–patient relationship are described as
under-involved and the relationship as non-therapeutic. For
example, a nurse who is opposed to the reason a person needs
nursing care (e.g. termination of pregnancy or attempted suicide)
31


may be consequently unable to engage effectively with the person to
assess their needs and plan appropriate and safe care. When
under-involvement
 is evident, the nurse is not responding to all
of the person’s needs and care is likely to be characterised by
disinterest or neglect. At the other end of the continuum, the nurse–
patient relationship displays over-involvement
 with the person
and may be characterised by favouritism. Over-involvement may
also include inappropriate personal or sexual relationships with the
person or their family members. In severe circumstances, nurses
practising in ways that display under- or over-involvement may be
referred to the appropriate regulatory body for professional
misconduct (NMBA 2010).
31 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2010). A Nurse’s Guide to Professional
Boundaries. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Figure 27.9


A continuum of professional nursing behaviours in nurse therapeutic
relationships.
Source: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
. A Nurse’s Guide to Professional Boundaries, p. 4.
Retrieved from <www.ncsbn.org/ProfessionalBoundaries_Complete.pdf>. © 2000 National Council of State
Board of Nursing, used with permission.
32


32 National Council of State Boards of Nursing (2000). A Nurse’s Guide to Professional
Boundaries. Retrieved from <www.ncsbn.org>.
The NMBA Registered Nurse Standards for Practice (2016) state
that Registered Nurses must establish, sustain and conclude
relationships in a way that differentiates the boundaries between
professional and personal relationships. All nurses need to be fully
aware of and put into practice the intent of these professional
expectations when engaging in therapeutic relationships.
Phases of the therapeutic
relationship
The therapeutic relationship can be described in terms of four
sequential phases, each characterised by identifiable tasks and
skills. The relationship usually progresses through the stages in
succession, each building on the one before. Nurses can identify the
progress of a relationship by understanding these phases, though
not all relationships will successfully negotiate the entire process.
The four phases are: pre-interaction phase, introductory phase,
working (maintaining) phase and termination phase. Table 27.3
summarises the tasks and skills required in each phase.
Table 27.3 Tasks and skills for each phase of the therapeutic
relationship


Pre-interaction phase
The pre-interaction phase is similar to the planning stage before an
interview. In most situations, the nurse has information about the
person they are caring for before the first face-to-face meeting.
Such information may include the person’s name, address, age,
medical history, social history and/or reason for seeking help.
Planning for the initial interview may generate some anxious feelings
in the nurse. If the nurse recognises these feelings, identifies
specific information to be discussed and utilises collegial support
from within the health care team, positive outcomes can evolve.
Alternatively, failure to successfully negotiate this pre-interaction
stage may limit the amount of information the person is willing to
divulge or the nurse is able to gather. If the person doesn’t feel
respected or safe, they may withhold important details about their
health, particularly if they feel they could be judged by revealing
information that the nurse may not approve of (Rossiter, Scott &
Walton ). Without the correct and complete information, the nurse
is unable to effectively engage in clinical reasoning as all the
decisions and actions that follow on will be ill informed, placing the
person’s safety at risk (Levett-Jones 2018).
33 Rossiter, R., Scott, R. & Walton, C. (2020). Key attributes of therapeutic communication. In
T. Levett-Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient Safety: An Essential Guide for Health
Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
Introductory phase
33


The introductory phase, also referred to as the orientation phase or
the pre-helping phase, is important because it sets the tone for the
rest of the relationship. During this initial encounter, the person being
cared for and the nurse closely observe each other and form
judgments about each other. The three components of this
introductory phase are opening the relationship, clarifying the
problem and structuring and formulating the contract. Other
important tasks of the introductory phase include getting to know
each other and developing trust.
After introductions, the nurse may initially engage in some social
interaction to put the person at ease. For example, they may talk
about what a nice day it is and what they would like to do if at home.
By encouraging the person to respond to social talk, the nurse
develops rapport which can help facilitate effective communication
and develop the therapeutic relationship.
During the introductory phase, the person may display some
resistive behaviours. Resistive behaviours are those that inhibit
involvement, cooperation or change. These may be due to difficulty
in acknowledging the need for help and thus a dependent role, fear
of exposing and facing feelings, anxiety about the discomfort
involved in changing problem-causing behaviour patterns, and fear
or anxiety in response to the nurse’s approach, which may, in the
person’s opinion, be inappropriate.
Resistive behaviours can be overcome by conveying a caring
attitude, genuine interest in the person and competence. These


nurse behaviours also foster the development of trust in the
relationship. Trust can be described as a reliance on someone
without doubt or question, or the belief that the other person is
capable of assisting in times of distress and in all likelihood will do
so. To trust another person involves risk; people become vulnerable
when they share thoughts, feelings and attitudes with the nurse.
Trust, however, enables the person to express thoughts and feelings
openly and without fear of adverse consequences.
By the end of the introductory phase, the person being cared for by
the nurse should begin to:
develop trust in the nurse
view the nurse as a competent professional capable of helping
view the nurse as honest, open and concerned about their
welfare
believe the nurse will understand and respect their cultural values
and beliefs
believe the nurse will respect their confidentiality
feel comfortable talking with the nurse about feelings and other
sensitive issues
understand the purpose of the relationship and the roles
feel that they are active participants in developing a mutually
agreeable plan of care.
Working phase


During the working phase of a therapeutic relationship, the nurse
and the person they are caring for begin to view each other as
unique individuals. The nurse helps them to explore thoughts,
feelings and actions and helps them to plan care to meet pre-
established goals. They begin to appreciate and care about each
other. Caring includes a genuine concern about the welfare of the
other person. Once caring develops, the potential for empathy
increases.
The working phase has two major stages:
1. exploring and understanding thoughts and feelings
2. facilitating and taking action.
Exploring and understanding thoughts and
feelings
The nurse requires the following skills for this phase of the
therapeutic relationship:
Empathetic listening and responding. Nurses must listen
actively and respond in ways that indicate they have listened to
what was said and understand how the person feels. The nurse
responds to content or feelings or both, as appropriate. The
nurse’s non-verbal behaviours are also important. Non-verbal
behaviours indicating empathy include moderate head nodding, a
steady gaze, moderate gesturing and little activity or body
movement. Empathetic listening focuses on a kind of ‘being with’


that encourages continued expression. It develops an
understanding of the person and their world in order to decrease
the person’s sense of isolation. The understanding that develops,
however, must also be communicated effectively through an
empathetic response. The end result of empathy is comforting
and caring for the person and a helping, healing relationship.
Respect. Nurses must show respect for the person, their
willingness to be available and a desire to work with the person.
The nurse’s manner should convey that they take the person’s
point of view seriously.
Genuineness. Nurses show genuineness through their attitudes
and behaviours. They present their true thoughts and feelings
and are seen to be comfortable with themselves when they are
with the people they care for. Egan (2013) has outlined
behaviours that communicate genuineness (see Box 27.7
).
When used effectively, genuineness benefits both the nurse and
the person in their care.
BO X
27.7 Components of genuineness
The genuine person:
does not take refuge in or overemphasise the role of
counsellor
is spontaneous
is non-defensive
displays few discrepancies—that is, the person is
consistent and does not think or feel one thing but say


another
is capable of self-disclosure (sharing self) when it is
therapeutic for the person they care for.
Concreteness. The nurse must assist the person to be concrete
and specific rather than to speak in generalities. When the
person says ‘I’m stupid and clumsy’, the nurse narrows the topic
to the specific by pointing out, ‘You tripped on the rug’.
Confrontation. The nurse points out discrepancies between
thoughts, feelings and actions that inhibit the person’s self-
understanding or exploration of specific areas. This should be
done sensitively and not judgmentally.
During this stage of the working phase, the intensity of interaction
increases and feelings such as anger, shame or self-consciousness
may be expressed. If the nurse is skilled in this stage, and if the
person in their care is willing to pursue self-exploration, the outcome
is a beginning understanding about their needs, behaviour and
feelings.
Research note
Can a therapeutic relationship be developed during short
hospital stays?
A. Mottram
. Therapeutic relationships in day surgery: A grounded theory study. Journal of Clinical
Nursing, 18, 2830−2837.
34


34 Mottram, A. (2008). Therapeutic relationships in day surgery: A grounded theory study. Journal of
Clinical Nursing, 18, 2830-2837.
Time constraints and rapid patient throughput are sometimes
considered to be barriers to the development of a therapeutic
relationship. Mottram (2008) explored patients’ perception of
therapeutic relationships in a day surgery clinic. The
researcher interviewed 145 day surgery patients in the United
Kingdom and identified that people who were admitted for
day surgery often spoke highly of the relationships they
developed with their nurses. The core category revealed was
therapeutic relationships. Subcategories were ‘presence’,
‘extra special’, ‘befriending’ and ‘comfort giving’. The
researcher concluded that it is possible to develop
therapeutic relationships with people despite the short
duration of nurse–patient contact in fast-paced day surgery
units. Highlighted is the importance of routine interaction with
people in their care; that is, interactions that may be
dismissed by nursing staff as unimportant.
Implications It has been surmised that nurses who have
limited time to interact with people in their care are unable to
develop therapeutic relationships and engage with people in a
therapeutic manner. However, this study highlights the
potential for nurses who work in contexts characterised by
limited nurse–patient interaction time to develop therapeutic
relationships and realise their therapeutic potential.


Facilitating taking action
Ultimately, the person in the nurse’s care must make decisions and
take action to progress. The responsibility for action belongs to
them. The nurse, however, collaborates in these decisions, provides
support and may offer options or information. There is a risk here
that the nurse may feel a responsibility to ‘do something’ and may
inappropriately take on the person’s problems. When this occurs, it
is a warning sign that the nurse has become over-involved and may
have crossed boundaries in the therapeutic relationship.
Termination phase
The termination phase of the relationship may be difficult or filled
with ambivalence. However, if the previous phases have evolved
effectively, the person in the nurse’s care generally has a positive
outlook and feels able to handle problems independently. On the
other hand, because caring attitudes have developed, it is natural to
expect some feelings of loss and each nurse needs to develop a
way of saying goodbye.
Many methods can be used to terminate therapeutic relationships.
Summarising can produce a sense of accomplishment. This may
include sharing reminiscences of how things were at the beginning of
the relationship and comparing them with how they are now. It is
also helpful for both the nurse and the person to express their
feelings about termination openly and honestly. Thus, termination
discussions need to start in advance of actual separation. This


allows time for the person to adjust to independence. In some
situations, referrals are necessary, or it may be appropriate to offer
a follow-up meeting to give support and monitor independence.
Follow-up phone calls are another intervention that ease the
person’s transition to independence.
Box 27.8
 provides examples of how to conduct an interview with
a patient during different phases.
BO X
27.8 Example of how to conduct an
interview with a patient
The introductory phase
Nurse: ‘Hello, Mr Brown, I’m Alicia Johnson. I’m a nursing
student, a second-year nursing student who will be caring for
you today. What would you like me to call you?’ (This
introduction should generally be followed by a smile and a
handshake if culturally appropriate.)
Patient: ‘Hi. Call me David. What university are you from?’
Nurse: ‘I’m studying at xxx University. Do you know where it
is?’


Patient: ‘Yes, my daughter went there and studied teaching
quite a long time ago. She loved it there.’
Nurse: ‘Well, the uni has changed quite a bit over the years,
but it is still a terrific place to study.’
The working phase
Nurse: ‘May I sit with you for a few minutes and ask you a
few questions?’
Patient: ‘Yes, OK. What do you want to know?’
Nurse: ‘Well, to plan your discharge, could I ask you about
your home situation? Who you live with and whether you will
have the support you need when you get home?’
Patient: ‘No problem, let’s go.’
Nurse: ‘If there are questions you’d prefer not to answer, that
is fine. Your answers will be documented in your chart but
only accessed by health professionals involved in your care.’
Patient: ‘Sure, that will be fine.’
The termination phase
The following are examples of questions and approaches that
can be used to conclude a patient interview:
‘Do you have any questions?’ (Allow time for the person to
answer and listen carefully—the patient’s ‘real’ needs


often surface at the end of a well-conducted interview.)
‘Thank you, that’s all I need to know for now.’
‘Thank you for your time. Your answers have been really
helpful and will help me get your discharge process
started.’ Shake the person’s hand, if culturally appropriate.
Summarise any concerns that arose during the interview
and what you will do to address them. ‘I understand that
you are anxious about going home because you have a
lot of steps that will be difficult to negotiate with your
crutches. I’ll talk to the Registered Nurse and make sure
your physiotherapist is aware. We will probably need to
speak to the occupational therapist and she may want to
do a home visit before you are discharged.’


Communication and the nursing
process
Communication is an integral part of the nursing process, with
nurses using communication skills in each phase of the nursing
process. Communication skills take on even more importance when
caring for people who have communication problems such as
sensory, language or cognitive impairments.


Nursing management
Assessing
To assess the person’s communication, the nurse determines
communication impairments or barriers, and communication style.
Remember that culture may influence when and how a person
communicates verbally and non-verbally, and language may also
vary.
Impairments to communication
Various barriers may alter a person’s ability to send, receive or
comprehend messages. These include language deficits, sensory
deficits, cognitive impairments, structural deficits and paralysis. The
nurse must assess each person to determine if a barrier is present
and to clearly identify the barrier type.
Language deficits
Determine the person’s primary language and whether an interpreter
is required. Some people, for whom English is a second language,
may have language skills that are inadequate for health care
communication, particularly for giving a valid consent for care.


Sensory deficit
The ability to hear, see, feel and smell are important adjuncts to
communication. Deafness can significantly alter the message the
person receives; impaired vision alters the ability to observe non-
verbal behaviour, such as a smile or a gesture; inability to feel and
smell can impair the person’s capacity to report injuries or detect the
smoke from a fire. For people with severe hearing impairments, the
following steps can be used:
Look for a medical alert bracelet (or necklace or tag) indicating
hearing loss.
Determine whether the person wears a hearing aid and whether
it is functioning (batteries need to be checked). If functioning but
hearing is not present, assess the person for wax build-up in the
external ear canal.
Observe whether the person is attempting to see your face to
read lips or write messages.
Observe whether the person is attempting to use their hands to
communicate with sign language or gestures.
Cognitive impairment
Any disorder that involves an acute or chronic impairment of
cognitive functioning (e.g. cerebrovascular disease, Alzheimer’s
disease and brain tumours or injuries) may affect a person’s ability
to use and understand language. These people may develop total
loss of speech, impaired articulation or the inability to find or name


words. Certain medications such as sedatives, antidepressants and
neuroleptics may also impair speech, causing the person to use
incomplete sentences or to slur words.
The nurse assesses whether the person can respond when asked a
question and, if so, assesses the following: Is the person’s speech
fluent or hesitant? Does the person use words correctly? Can the
person comprehend instructions as evidenced by following
directions? Can the person repeat words or phrases? In addition,
the nurse assesses the person’s ability to read and understand
written words: Can the person follow written directions? Can the
person respond correctly by pointing to a written word? Can the
person read aloud? Can the person recognise words or letters if
unable to read whole sentences? The nurse uses large, clearly
written words when trying to establish abilities in this area.
When the person is unconscious, the nurse looks for any indication
that suggests comprehension of what is communicated (e.g. tries to
arouse the person verbally and through touch). The nurse asks a
closed question such as ‘What is your name?’ or asks the person to
complete a task such as ‘Open your eyes’ and watches for both
verbal and non-verbal responses.
Structural deficit
Structural deficits of the oral and nasal cavities and respiratory
system can alter a person’s ability to speak clearly and
spontaneously. Examples include cleft palate, artificial airways such


as an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy and laryngectomy
(removal of the larynx). Extreme dyspnoea (shortness of breath)
can also impair speech patterns.
Paralysis
If verbal impairment is combined with paralysis of the upper
extremities that impairs the person’s ability to write, the nurse should
determine whether the person can point, nod, shrug, blink or
squeeze a hand. Any of these could be used to devise a beginning
communication system.
Style of communication
In assessing the person’s communication style, the nurse considers
both verbal and non-verbal communication. As well as physical
barriers, some psychological illnesses (e.g. depression or psychosis)
influence the ability to communicate. The person may demonstrate
constant verbalisation of the same words or phrases, a loose
association of ideas or flight of ideas.
Verbal communication
When assessing verbal communication, the nurse focuses on three
areas: the content of the message, the themes and the verbalised
emotions. In addition, the nurse considers the following:


whether the communication pattern is slow, rapid, quiet,
spontaneous, hesitant or evasive
the vocabulary of the individual, particularly any changes from
the vocabulary normally used (e.g. a person who normally never
swears may indicate increased stress or illness by an
uncharacteristic use of swearing)
the presence of hostility, aggression, assertiveness, reticence,
hesitancy, anxiety or loquaciousness (incessant verbalisation) in
communication
difficulties with verbal communication, such as slurring,
stuttering, inability to pronounce a particular sound, lack of clarity
in enunciation, inability to speak in sentences, loose association
of ideas, flight of ideas or the inability to find or name words or
identify objects
refusal or inability to speak.
Non-verbal communication
Consider non-verbal communication in relation to the person’s
culture. Pay particular attention to facial expression, gestures, body
movements, affect, tone of voice, posture and eye contact.
Diagnosing
Impaired verbal communication may be used as a nursing diagnosis
when an individual experiences a decreased, delayed or absent
ability to receive, process, transmit and use a system of symbols—


anything that has meaning (i.e. transmits meaning). Communication
problems may be receptive (e.g. difficulty hearing) or expressive
(e.g. difficulty speaking).
Lifespan considerations
Communication with older people
It is important to assess older people for physical or cognitive
problems that necessitate nursing interventions for changes
to communication skills. Some problems experienced by older
people include:
sensory deficits, such as vision and hearing
cognitive impairment, as in dementia
neurological deficits from strokes or other neurological
conditions, such as aphasia (expressive and/or receptive)
and lack of movement
psychosocial problems, such as depression.
Recognition of specific needs and obtaining appropriate
resources can greatly increase socialisation and quality of life.
Interventions directed towards improving communication for
people with these special needs are as follows:
Make sure that assistive devices, glasses and hearing
aids are being used and are in good working order.


Make referrals to appropriate resources, such as speech
therapy or audiometry.
Make use of communication aids, such as communication
boards, computers or pictures, when possible.
Keep environmental distractions to a minimum.
Allow enough time to communicate with the person and
support people.
Speak in short, simple sentences, one subject at a time—
reinforce or repeat what is said when necessary.
Use touch to communicate your presence and caring.
Always face the person when speaking—coming up
behind someone may be frightening.
With the person’s consent include family and friends in
conversations.
Use reminiscing, either in individual conversations or in
groups, to maintain memory connections and to enhance
self-identity and self-esteem in the older adult.
When verbal expression and non-verbal expression are
incongruent, believe the non-verbal. Clarification of this
and attentiveness to a person’s feelings will help promote
a feeling of caring and acceptance.
Find out what has been important and has meaning to the
person and try to maintain these things as much as
possible. Even simple things such as bedtime rituals
become important if they are lost in a hospital or
residential care.


The nursing diagnosis of Impaired verbal communication may not be
useful when an individual’s communication problems are caused by
a mental illness or a coping problem. In those instances, the nursing
diagnoses of Fear or Anxiety may be more appropriate. Other
nursing diagnoses relevant to people experiencing communication
problems that involve impaired verbal communication as the
aetiology could include the following:
Anxiety related to impaired verbal communication
Powerlessness related to impaired verbal communication
Social isolation related to impaired verbal communication
Impaired social interaction related to impaired verbal
communication.
Planning
When a nursing diagnosis related to impaired verbal communication
has been made, the nurse and person in their care determine
outcomes and begin planning ways to promote effective
communication. The overall outcome for people with Impaired verbal
communication is to reduce or resolve the factors impairing the
communication. Specific nursing interventions will be planned based
on impairment aetiology. Examples of outcome criteria to evaluate
the effectiveness of nursing interventions and achievement of the
person’s goals follow below.
The person receiving care:


communicates that needs are being met
begins to establish a method of communication:
– signals yes/no to direct questions using vocalisation or agreed-
on physical cue (i.e. eye blink, hand squeeze)
– uses verbal or non-verbal techniques to indicate needs
perceives the message accurately, as evidenced by appropriate
verbal and/or non-verbal responses
communicates effectively:
– using dominant language
– using health care interpreter
– using sign language
– using word board or picture board
– using a computer
regains maximum communication abilities
expresses minimum fear, anxiety, frustration and depression
uses resources appropriately.
Implementing
Nursing interventions to facilitate communication with people who
have problems with speech or language include manipulating the
environment, providing support, employing measures to enhance
communication and educating the person and their support person.


Manipulate the environment
A quiet environment with limited distractions will make the most of
the communication efforts of both the person and the nurse and
increase the possibility of effective communication. Sufficient light
will help in conveying non-verbal messages, which is especially
important if visual or auditory acuity is impaired. Initially, the nurse
needs to provide a calm, relaxed environment, which will help reduce
any anxiety the person may have. Remember that for the person
receiving care any factor that affects communication can create
feelings of frustration, anxiety, depression or hostility.
Communication normally contributes to a person’s sense of security
and feelings that they are not alone, so communication problems
may cause some people to feel isolated and confused. To further
reduce these emotions the nurse should acknowledge and praise
the person’s attempts at communication.
Research note
Can patients with advanced dementia participate in a
social conversation?
Based on J. Perry, S. Galloway, J. L. Bottorff & S. Nixon (2005). Nurse–patient communication in
dementia. Improving the odds. Journal of Gerontological Nursing, 31(4), 43–52.
The nursing literature provides general principles for
communicating with people who have dementia. However,
there is little research that documents the effectiveness of
the principles or strategies. The purpose of this study by


Perry et al.
 was to describe the communication strategies
used by expert nurses in communicating with residents with
advanced dementia and to assess the effectiveness of the
strategies in supporting participation in social conversations.
35 Perry, J., Galloway, S., Bottorff, J. L. & Nixon, S. (2005). Nurse–patient
communication in dementia: Improving the odds. Journal of Gerontological Nursing,
31(4), 43–52.
The researchers used a descriptive study design. Two of the
researchers led a weekly socialisation group over a 10-week
period for eight women with dementia. The socialisation
group sessions were audiotaped and transcribed verbatim.
These data resulted in the formation of two taxonomies: one
represented the nurses’ communication and the other
represented the participants’ communication repertoire.
The research supported the use of a greater number of
conversational strategies than is often stated in the nursing
literature. The findings also suggested that residents with
advanced dementia are able to engage in social conversation
beyond what was expected given their Mini-Mental State
Examination (MMSE) score.
Implications This study suggests that residents with
advanced dementia are able to participate in a conversation
when nurses use a broad range of conversational strategies.
Moreover, the use of socialisation groups to encourage
residents with advanced dementia to interact with others is an
effective way of enhancing their quality of life.
35


Provide support
The nurse should encourage the person and provide non-verbal
reassurance, perhaps by touch if appropriate. If the nurse does not
understand, it is critical to let the person know so that the person
can provide clarification with other words or through some other
means of communication. When speaking with a person who has
difficulty understanding, the nurse should check frequently to
determine what the person has heard and understood. Using open-
ended questions will assist the nurse in obtaining accurate
information about the effectiveness of communication. For example,
Mrs Ng, who has limited English skills, is being taught about diet for
self-management of her Crohn’s disease. If the nurse asks, ‘Do you
understand what to eat?’, Mrs Ng may nod her head. However, this
does not give the nurse confirmation that the message given has
been received and understood. Rather the nurse needs to say,
‘What do you think will be good for you to eat when you go home?’.
The nurse’s body language (e.g. gestures, posture, facial expression
and eye contact) should convey acceptance and approval.
Employ measures to enhance
communication
First, determine how the person can best receive messages: by
listening, by looking, through touch or through an interpreter. Ways
to help communication include keeping words simple and concrete


and discussing topics of interest to the person. It is often helpful to
use alternative communication strategies such as word boards,
pictures or paper and pencil (Tasker & De Bortoli ). Strategies for
enhancing communication with people who have communication
deficits are listed in Box 27.9
.
36 Tasker, D. & De Bortoli, T. (2020). Communicating with people who have limited or no
verbal communication ability. In T. Levett-Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient
Safety: An Essential Guide for Health Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
BO X
27.9 Enhancing communication with
people who have communication
deficits
People who have a hearing
impairment
Gain the person’s attention by saying the person’s name
or gently touching the person’s arm. This helps the person
to focus attention and concentrate on your words.
Check that available hearing aids are operational and in
use.
Reduce environmental interference.
36


Face the person and don’t cover your mouth. Don’t turn or
lower your head, as this reduces the volume of sound
reaching the person’s ears.
Try to be within one metre of the person so your voice is
not faint and interference is reduced.
Use pencil and paper. If you have an unfamiliar accent or
you are not being understood, try writing the message.
Auslan (Australian Sign Language) may be used by the
person. It incorporates signs, body movements, facial
expressions, mime and gesture. A professional Auslan
interpreter should be used.
People who are unable to speak
fluent English
Provide an interpreter and avoid using family/other health
care staff as interpreters. Hospitals have policies indicating
who should interpret for people who are unable to speak
fluent English and they have procedures for accessing trained
health care interpreters (telephone or face to face).
Utilise the interpreter to discuss with the person how best
to communicate with them when the interpreter is not
available.
In circumstances where family members are used as an
interpreter, obtain the person’s permission before
commencing a detailed discussion with the person in their


family member’s presence. Instruct the family member to
translate as precisely as possible, without interpretation or
judgment, and to indicate to you if they do not understand
what you or the person has said. Extra attention to
clarifying that messages have been understood may be
necessary.
To help with basic nursing care, develop a communication
or picture board. Use words translated into English or
images.
Teach the person to use the nurse call bell with the help of
the interpreter.
Use a normal intonation.
Combine gestures with verbal communication.
Provide health information in translated form.
People who have a cognitive
impairment
Attend to the person and allow enough time for them to
respond.
Ask one question at a time and use appropriate language.
Reduce environmental distractions.
Avoid lengthy instructions and explanations; pace the
information and check that the person understands.
Ensure that the person and/or family knows how to call for
a nurse.
Avoid frequent changes of topic.


If confused consider providing reassurance rather than
orientation.
Communicate with the support person.
People who are unresponsive
Use the person’s name and speak as though they are
able to hear you.
Use your time with the person to orientate them to your
name and role and to time and place.
Explain what you are doing and why while attending to
nursing care and being near the person.
Communicate through verbal and non-verbal techniques;
for example, touch.
Avoid talking to the person while leaning over them.
Provide support people with advice about communication
with the person.
Educate the person and their support
people
Sometimes people and their family or support people can be
prepared in advance for communication problems; for example,
before intubation or throat surgery. By explaining anticipated
problems, the person is often less anxious when problems arise.


Communication options can be demonstrated and practised before
communication is lost. This helps the person to be familiar with and
manage the new communication strategy when the need arises.
Evaluating
Evaluation is useful for reflecting on the two-way nature of human
communication and for reviewing communication progress.
Communication by the person receiving
care
To establish whether planned outcomes have been met in relation to
communication, the nurse must listen actively, observe non-verbal
cues and use therapeutic communication skills to determine that
communication was effective. Examples of statements indicating
outcome achievement include, ‘Using picture board effectively to
indicate needs’ or ‘The person stated, “I listened more closely to my
daughter yesterday and found out how she feels about the divorce”’.
Nurse–patient communication
For nurses to evaluate the effectiveness of their own communication
with the people they care for, a mentor may be used. Nurses will
often ask a colleague to act as their mentor and to observe their
interactions during nursing care. Consent of the people receiving


care is sought and the mentor silently observes the interactions.
After the interaction, the mentor gives the nurse feedback on
communication skills. The outcome for nurses should be increased
awareness and insight regarding their communication strengths, as
well as identification of areas for future skills development.


Group and team communication
People are born into a family group and interact in various groups
throughout all stages of life: play groups, peer groups, work groups,
recreational groups, religious groups and so on. Groups can be
thought of as gatherings of two or more people who work together
but do not necessarily have a sense of connectedness, an identity
as a group or a sense of purpose. Rather, they meet to get a task
done or are brought together by a personal attribute/interest or as
an elected committee member. It is important to note, however, that
a health care team is not just a group of people who are co-located
or caring for the same group of people. A health care team
 is a
group of people who do collective work and are mutually committed
to a common purpose. Being in a group or team means that nurses
do not have to cope alone; there is always someone who can offer
support or expertise. In the best performing teams, members
appreciate each other’s abilities and limitations, know how to use
complementary abilities within the team, have a common purpose
and communicate effectively.
As a team member, the nurse may be required to fulfil different
roles: member, leader, teacher, learner, advisor or advisee and so
on. Despite these different roles, there are attributes that help
nurses to be effective team members. Consider your own attributes
as a team member and compare these with those listed in Box
27.10
.


BO X
27.10 Attributes of effective team
members
Committed to the goals and values of the team; for
example, continuum of care for people discharged from
the ward.
Effective communication skills, including team
communication.
Enjoy working collaboratively and collectively with others.
Use cooperative rather than competitive approaches.
Willingly communicate openly with team members.
Listen actively to others.
Suspend judgment and consider the views of others
without personal bias.
Trust and respect colleagues, team members and
themselves.
Expertise that complements team-member expertise.
Readiness to applaud the work of others.

. Key attributes of ‘patient safe’ communication. In T. Levett-
Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient Safety: An Essential Guide for Health Professionals
(2nd ed.). Pearson: Sydney.

Critical Conversations for Patient Safety: An Essential Guide for Health Professionals (2nd ed.).
Sydney: Pearson.
37


Group dynamics
The communication that takes place between members of any group
or team is known as group dynamics. A number of interrelated
factors and variables will influence each group’s dynamics. Each
member of the group will have an effect on group dynamics, based
on their motivation for participating, similarity to other group
members, level of maturity, ability to appropriately express ideas and
feelings, and the goal of the group.
The unique dynamics of each group will influence its maturation or
group process as well as the effectiveness of the group. Three main
functions are required for any group to be effective. It must maintain
a degree of group unity or cohesion, it needs to develop and modify
its structure to improve its effectiveness and it must accomplish its
goals. The characteristics of effective and ineffective groups are
shown in Table 27.4
. Facilitating health care team members to
work effectively together to provide high-quality care for people and
their families has been a long-standing problem and continues to be
a challenge within health services. Lefton  explains that ‘relationship
issues [between colleagues] are real obstacles to the development
of work environments in which patients and their families can receive
safe, excellent care’ (p. 13).
38


38 Lefton, C. (2007). Improve your environment through communication and change. Nursing
Management, 38(1), 13–14.
Table 27.4 Comparative features of effective and ineffective
groups


Communication with colleagues
Effective communication between colleagues is as important to safe,
caring and effective patient care as the promotion of therapeutic
communication between the nurse and the person being cared for
(Levett-Jones 2020a). Communication between colleagues is based
on an understanding of communication concepts and techniques
such as attending, listening, probing and instructing discussed earlier
in this chapter. However, unlike communication between the person
being cared for and their nurse, communication between colleagues
is not based on therapeutic communication and the formation of a
therapeutic relationship. Rather these relationships are known as
collegial relationships. The terms multidisciplinary, interdisciplinary,
cross-disciplinary, transdisciplinary, interprofessional and
intercollegial are also used, each reflecting variations on group
approaches to achieving quality care for health care consumers and
their families. Deficiencies in communication between colleagues
and recommendations for improvement are major findings in many
health care quality improvement investigations.
Nurse–nurse communication
A particularly important nurse−nurse communication event is the
nursing handover
, shift report or nursing report. Handover usually


occurs at the end and beginning of each shift, and its purpose is to
formally hand responsibility and accountability for the people
receiving care to another nurse or team of nurses (Connell ).
During handover, information about the people receiving care is
passed from one nurse to another, often including age, diagnosis,
tests and procedures, vital signs and significant changes in health
status or planned care. Various communication techniques are used
to achieve handover, including verbal accounts which are delivered
face to face, or indirectly via tape or digital recorder. Another
technique is the written report.
39 Connell, T. (2010). Nursing: Handover. Evidence summary. The Joanna Briggs Institute.
Retrieved from <http://joannabriggs.org>.
Handover is the time when each nurse is focused on achieving
continuity of care (Nykolyn & McHugh-Schuster
), a key component
of care safety (Connell 2010). Despite this, handover has been
identified as a time when continuity of care can fail as the receiving
nurse may not understand or act upon the information provided
(Yee, Wong & Turner
). During handover, it is important that
communication gaps which lead to breakdowns in continuity of care,
inappropriate treatment and harm to the person do not occur.

Harmful Events and Promote Patient Safety. Oregon: F. A. Davis.
41 Yee, K. C., Wong, M. C. & Turner, P. (2009). ‘Hand me an ISOBAR’: A pilot study of an
evidence-based approach to improving shift-to-shift clinical handover. Medical Journal of
Australia, 190(11), S121–S124.
39
40
41


Acronyms such as ISBAR (refer to Table 27.5
) have been
reported as effective in streamlining the way doctors and nurses
communicate during telephone calls and handover, and in increasing
safety for people receiving care (Moroney ). Acronyms such as
ISBAR provide a framework to communicate in a consistent way and
play a particularly important role in facilitating communication of
critical information to colleagues when the patient is deteriorating
and immediate attention and action is required (Levett-Jones et
al.
).

Bullying
During the past few decades nursing, as a profession, has
undergone significant change; however, not all aspects of nursing
practice have moved forward. In Australia, workplace bullying
(sometimes called horizontal violence) is prevalent. It seriously
42
43
44


undermines the effectiveness of communication between colleagues
and, as a consequence, the safety of people receiving nursing care.
Unfortunately, most nurses either witness or personally experience
workplace bullying at some stage during their nursing career, often
despite ‘zero tolerance’ policies. Workplace cultures that are lacking
in respect are also thought to promote bullying behaviours.
Workplace bullying involves inter-group conflict (Curtis, Bowen &
Reid ) and hostile or aggressive behaviour by one or more group
members. It includes behaviours such as excessive criticism,
innuendo, withholding information, intimidation, ridicule, making
excessive demands, inequitable rosters, spreading rumours,
scapegoating, removing responsibility or blocking opportunities for
learning or promotion (Jackson, Clare & Mannix ). Evidence has
emerged that nurses are major perpetrators of workplace bullying of
other nurses (Jackson et al. 2002) and that nursing students may
experience bullying while on clinical placement. Students are
especially vulnerable to workplace bullying during their clinical
placement experiences, and being bullied prevents students from
feeling as if they are accepted or fit in (Levett-Jones & Reid-Searl ).

Communicating with colleagues
49
50


All members of the health care team are focused on improving the
health status of people in their care and achieving their health goals.
Historically, doctors were considered to be superior to the other
members of the team and assumed a leadership role, with nurses
and allied health professionals taking a more subordinate role. Over
time, this has changed, with nurses and other health professionals
now asserting legitimate and equal voices in collaborative care and
health service management. Even with this change, the potential for
health care errors as a result of communication problems with
colleagues continues, with possible reasons relating to differing
communication styles and expectations between different members
of the team. See Box 27.13
 for a list of some of the factors that
undermine collaborative practice.
BO X
27.13 Factors that can undermine
interprofessional communication and
collaborative practice
Disruptive behaviours and lack of interprofessional respect
Passive–aggressive behaviours exerted by health
professionals who consider themselves to be
disempowered
Feeling of ‘being taken for granted’ with work and roles
not understood or valued by other team members


Different focus and orientation for different professions;
for example, ‘care’ as opposed to ‘cure’
Gender differences and power differentials; for example,
nursing and allied health being mainly female professions
Nurses (and others) unwilling to ‘rock the boat’ by
challenging authority
The diverse and ever-increasing array of health
professions, specialties and subcultures, each with its own
terminology and norms
Different professions training separately leading to
misunderstandings and miscommunication
Source: Adapted from L. Ebert
. An historical and cultural overview of health professionals’ evolving

for Health Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
51 Ebert, L. (2020). An historical and cultural overview of health professionals’ evolving team
dynamics. In T. Levett-Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient Safety: An Essential Guide for
Health Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
Assertive communication
Assertive communication
 promotes care safety by minimising
miscommunication with colleagues. People who use assertive
communication are honest, direct and appropriate while being open
to ideas and respecting the rights of others.
51


An important characteristic of assertive communication includes the
use of ‘I’ statements versus ‘you’ statements. The ‘you’ statement
places blame and puts the listener in a defensive position. On the
other hand, the ‘I’ statement encourages discussion. For example, a
nurse who states ‘I am concerned about . . .’ to a doctor will be
gaining the attention of the doctor while also giving the message of
the importance of working together for the benefit of the person. It is
important for the nurse to be clear, concise, organised and fully
informed when verbally presenting the person’s concern to the
doctor.
Non-assertive communication
Two types of interpersonal behaviours are considered non-
assertive
: submissive and aggressive.
Submissive
When people use a submissive communication style, they allow their
rights to be violated by others. They meet the demands and
requests of others without regard to their own feelings and needs as
they believe their own feelings are not important. Some experts
believe that people who use the submissive behaviours or
communication styles are insecure and try to maintain their self-
esteem by avoiding conflict (e.g. negative criticism and
disagreement from others). For nurses, being submissive can mean
that important information about the person is not communicated to
colleagues and the person’s condition may suffer as a result.


Research note
Silence kills
D. Maxfield, J. Grenny, R. McMillan, K. Patterson & A. Switzler (2005). Silence Kills. The Seven
Crucial Conversations in Health Care. VitalSmarts, L. C. Copyright Adesse Pty Ltd.
A 2004 research study collected survey data from over
17 000 nurses, doctors, clinical care staff and administrators.
This study explored the respondents’ concerns and difficulties
in communicating with each other and how this can lead to
errors and poor care outcomes. The findings resulted in a
compelling report entitled Silence Kills. As Maxfield et al.
reported, the study identified the categories of conversations
that were difficult but, at the same time, essential for people
in health care to master. The effectiveness of health care
professionals’ communication was related to medical errors,
patient safety, quality of care, staff satisfaction and staff
turnover. The seven areas of concern were broken rules,
mistakes, lack of support, incompetence, poor teamwork,
disrespect and micromanagement (p. 3).
52 Maxfield, D., Grenny, J., McMillan, R., Patterson, K. & Switzler, A. (2005).
Silence Kills. The Seven Crucial Conversations in Health Care. VitalSmarts, L. C.
Retrieved from <www.silencekills.com>.
The report indicates, for example, that many of the health
care workers observed colleagues taking dangerous
shortcuts, showing poor clinical judgment and exhibiting
verbal abuse and/or intimidating behaviours. However, very
52


few discussed their concerns with their colleagues directly
and their silence was strongly related to poor health
outcomes for people in their care. On the other hand, the
study also showed that those health care workers who were
confident in their ability to discuss their concerns with their
colleagues were more satisfied and committed to staying in
health care. Moreover, better patient outcomes (i.e. fewer
errors) were observed.
Aggressive
There is a fine line between assertive and aggressive
communication. Assertive communication is an open expression of
ideas and opinions while respecting the rights, opinions and ideas of
others. Aggressive communication strongly asserts the person’s
legitimate rights and opinions with little regard or respect for the
rights and opinions of others. Aggressive communication is often
perceived as a personal attack by the other person because
aggressive communication attempts to humiliate, dominate, control
or embarrass the other person. By lowering the other person’s self-
esteem, the person using aggressive communication may feel
superior, which helps increase their self-esteem. Aggressive
communication can take several different forms, including
screaming, sarcasm, rudeness, belittling jokes and direct personal
insults.


Aggressive communication by nurses can mean colleagues withdraw
from involvement with the nurse and/or the person receiving their
care, miss important clinical information or engage in conflict at the
expense of directing attention to care.
Case study
You are the nursing student assigned to care for Mr
Manasovitz, a 45-year-old man who will be returning from the
recovery room after undergoing the removal of a mass from
his abdomen. While you are preparing his room for his return,
the Registered Nurse and surgeon arrive to talk with Mrs
Manasovitz about her husband’s surgery. The surgeon
explains that the mass was malignant and invasive. Mr
Manasovitz is a candidate for chemotherapy, but his
prognosis is guarded because of the extent of the tumour
growth. Mrs Manasovitz looks away, closes her eyes and only
nods her head, ‘Yes’.
As the surgeon leaves, the Registered Nurse approaches
Mrs Manasovitz, sits next to her and puts her arm around
her. Mrs Manasovitz begins to cry. The Registered Nurse
uses a gentle voice to tell Mrs Manasovitz that it is okay to
cry and assures her she will remain with her. They sit in
silence until Mrs Manasovitz is able to express her feelings.
The nurse listens actively. Later the nurse offers to get a cup
of coffee for Mrs Manasovitz and asks if there is anything she
can do to assist Mrs Manasovitz at this difficult time.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. Interpret Mrs Manasovitz’s non-verbal behaviour in
response to the news about her husband’s surgery.
2. Evaluate the nurse’s response towards Mrs
Manasovitz based on the concepts of caring and
comforting. Use the Fundamentals of Care Framework
to help you.


3. Why is it important for the nurse to effectively
communicate with Mrs Manasovitz at this time and
how might the nurse do so?
4.

 The nurse was described as listening
actively to Mrs Manasovitz. Describe actions that
portray active listening.


Chapter 27 Review


Chapter highlights
Communication is a critical nursing skill which is directly related
to patient safety, person-centred care and the development of a
therapeutic relationship.
Effective communication is critical to gathering assessment data
for nursing diagnoses, to developing understandings of the
person receiving care, to instructing and cooperating in care
delivery, to teaching, to expressions of caring and comfort and to
collaboration with health colleagues.
Communication is a dynamic two-way interpersonal process
involving the sender of the message and the receiver of the
message. It also involves intrapersonal messages which can
affect the message, the interpretation of the message and the
response.
Because the sender must encode the message and determine
the appropriate channels for conveying it and because the
receiver must perceive the message, decode it and then
respond, the communication process includes four elements:
sender, message, receiver and feedback.
Verbal communication will be more effective when the criteria of
pace, intonation, simplicity, clarity, brevity, timing, relevance,
adaptability and credibility are met.
Non-verbal communication often reveals more about a person’s
thoughts and feelings than verbal communication; it includes
personal appearance, posture and gait, facial expressions and
gestures.


Communication with the person in the nurse’s care or colleagues
is effective when the receiver and sender accurately perceive the
meaning of each other’s message.
When assessing verbal and non-verbal behaviours, the nurse
needs to consider cultural influences and be aware that a single
non-verbal expression can indicate any of a variety of feelings
and that words can have various meanings.
When communication is effective, verbal and non-verbal
expressions are congruent.
The use of electronic communication in nursing practice
continues to evolve, requiring nurses to understand how to
effectively communicate using these methods.
Many factors influence the communication process:
development, gender, culture, values and perceptions, personal
space (intimate, personal, social and public distance),
territoriality, roles and relationships, environment, congruence
and interpersonal attitudes.
Many techniques facilitate therapeutic communication:
expressing empathy, prompting, instructing, using silence,
probing—using open and closed questions, using touch, restating
or paraphrasing, seeking clarification, perception checking or
seeking consensual validation, offering self, providing
information, encouraging, focusing, reflecting, summarising,
confronting and self-disclosure.
Techniques that inhibit communication include stereotyping, being
defensive, testing, rejecting, false reassurance, passing
judgment, arguing, patronising, agreeing and disagreeing,
excessive questioning and giving common advice.


The effective nurse–patient relationship is a therapeutic
relationship that facilitates patient growth.
Four phases of the therapeutic relationship include the pre-
interaction phase, the introductory phase, the working phase and
the termination phase; each has a specific goal and tasks, with
each phase requiring specific skills of the nurse.
When a person experiences a deficit in their communication,
careful nursing assessment is needed to identify the deficit and
to implement appropriate nursing actions to restore nurse–
patient communication.
To help people with communication problems, the nurse
manipulates the environment, provides support, employs
measures to enhance communication and educates the person
and support people.
Mentor feedback is used by nurses to evaluate their own
communication. Nurses can review both the process and the
content of the communication and identify both communication
strengths and areas for improvement.
Effective communication between health professionals is vital for
safe care.
Handover is an important communication event between nurses.
Its aim is to hand over responsibility for the care of the person to
the next nurse/shift and to ensure a safe continuity of care. Use
of acronyms such as ISBAR are effective tools in promoting clear
communication and maintaining care safety.
Assertive communication promotes care safety by minimising
miscommunication with colleagues. An important characteristic of
assertive communication is the use of ‘I’ statements.


Non-assertive communication includes two types of interpersonal
behaviours: submissive and aggressive.
Concept check
1. A student nurse is caring for a 72-year-old woman who is
very confused and has a medical diagnosis of Alzheimer’s
disease. The most appropriate communication strategy
should include which of the following?
1. Written directions for bathing.
2. Speaking very loudly.
3. Gentle touch while providing activities of daily living.
4. Flat facial expression.

framework, place the following descriptions in the correct

1. After introductions, the nurse asks, ‘What plans do you
have for the upcoming holiday weekend?’.
2. The nurse states, ‘It sounds like you are concerned
about the possible complications of having diabetes.
What would be most helpful for you at this time?’.
3. The nurse reads in the medical record that the person
was diagnosed with diabetes 1 week ago.
4. The nurse states, ‘When we met, you knew very little
about diabetes and now you are able to use your new
information and apply it to your own personal situation’.

2. Presumption of an understanding of the person’s
needs.
3. An open professional posture during communication.

3. Concreteness.
4. Confrontation.

2. ‘I am concerned about Mr Black’s blood pressure. It is

Teaching is an essential and highly valued
aspect of the role of the nurse. The Nursing and
Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA)  illustrates
the importance of both patient education and
professional education in the Registered Nurse
Standards for Practice, where it is stated that
Registered Nurses provide ‘the information and
education required to enhance people’s control
1


over health’ and use ‘a lifelong learning
approach for continuing professional
development of self and others’ (p. 4).
1 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016).
Registered Nurse Standards for Practice. Retrieved from
<www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Patient education is multifaceted and involves
promoting, protecting and maintaining health. It
involves teaching about reducing health risk
factors, increasing a person’s level of wellness
and taking specific protective health measures.
Box 28.1
 lists examples and specific areas of
patient education.

Teaching
Teaching
 is a planned series of actions intended to produce
specific learning outcomes. The teaching–learning process involves
a dynamic interaction between teacher and learner. Each participant
in the process communicates information, emotions, perceptions
and attitudes to the other. The teaching process and the nursing
process are similar (see Table 28.1
) and both require
sophisticated critical thinking skills and a person-centred approach.
As a nurse, you will be presented with multiple opportunities for
teaching the people you care for as well as other health
professionals. Teaching is not a role that only a select group of
nurses take on; it is an inherent part of the role for all nurses and for
this reason developing effective teaching skills is essential.
Table 28.1 Comparison of the teaching process and the nursing
process
Nurses are responsible for teaching a variety of learners in a variety
of settings. They teach people in the hospital, in clinics and in the
home. Nurses teach large and small groups of learners in
community health education programs, in schools and in
rehabilitation units. Despite this diversity, it is essential that the nurse
respects and values each person and supports their individual
learning needs and motivations.


Nurses also teach students, professional colleagues and other
health care personnel in academic institutions such as universities
and TAFE colleges, and in health care facilities such as hospitals or
nursing homes.
Teaching patients and families
Nurses often teach individuals in one-to-one teaching episodes. For
example, the nurse may teach about wound care while changing a
person’s dressing or may teach about diet, exercise and other
lifestyle behaviours that minimise the risk of a heart attack for a
person who has a cardiac problem. The nurse may also be involved
in teaching family members or other support people who are caring
for the person. Nurses working in maternity and paediatric areas
teach parents and sometimes grandparents how to care for babies
and children.
Because of the decreased length of hospital stays, time constraints
may impact on teaching sessions. Nurses need to provide education
that will ensure the person’s safe transition from one level of care to
another and make appropriate plans for follow-up education in their
home. Discharge plans must include information about what the
person has been taught before transfer or discharge, and what
remains for them to learn in order to perform self-care in the home
or other residence.


Teaching in the community
Nurses are often involved in community health education programs.
Such teaching activities may be voluntary as part of the nurse’s
involvement in organisations, such as the Red Cross or CanTeen, or
they may be part of the nurse’s work role, such as for practice
nurses and school nurses. Community teaching activities may be
aimed at large groups of people who have an interest in some
aspect of health, such as nutrition classes, cardiopulmonary
resuscitation or bicycle or swimming safety programs. Community
education programs can also be designed for small groups of
learners, such as childbirth classes or family planning sessions.
Teaching health care
professionals
Nurses are frequently involved in the instruction of professional
colleagues through continuing education, in-service programs and
staff development. Experienced nurses function as mentors or
preceptors for students, new graduate nurses or newly employed
nurses, and may also be involved in the teaching of other health
care professionals such as medical or allied health students. Nurses’
teaching responsibilities are diverse and require high-level skills,
knowledge and expertise, as well as a genuine desire to empower
and educate others. Box 28.2
 lists the Australian Nurse Teachers’


Society’s Australian Nurse Teacher Competencies 2010. These
standards provide a clear and detailed overview of the skills required
of a nurse teacher. However, it is important to understand that all
nurses need to develop these attributes as they will be required
across contexts and in all nursing roles.
