Real-world practice
The challenges that face nurses who work closely with
people with chronic diseases, such as end-stage
kidney disease, are extensive. Not least is the risk of
apathy that may come with continuing education and
supporting effective health maintenance behaviours.
People undergoing haemodialysis are required to
follow multifaceted treatment regimens that frequently
involve dietary and fluid restrictions. These regimens
are complex, difficult to comprehend and often require
the individual to make profound adjustments to their
current way of living.
I remember one person with end-stage kidney disease
who I cared for a few years ago. He was a 28-year-old
single male who continuously presented for his
haemodialysis sessions with fluid overload. It was
Demonstrates the ability to use deductive and
inductive reasoning.
3.3.4
2


challenging to watch the interactions between this
young man and the nurses. The conversation typically
went: ‘Jock,  you’re 5 kilograms over your dry weight;
don’t you know what you’re doing to your heart?’.
Needless to say, this patronising approach was
ineffective and only served to create a tense and
confrontational clinical environment.
I spoke with Jock one day after we had stabilised him
after he came in with fluid overload and pulmonary
oedema. I acknowledged the difficulty I could see he
was having with managing his fluid balance between
dialysis sessions. He instantly became defensive: ‘I
know, I know, it’s stuffing up my heart’. I responded, ‘I
don’t care about your heart . . . well I do, but at the
moment I care more about how you are coping when
you aren’t here with us’. Jock had been on
haemodialysis for 6 months, he had developed end-
stage kidney disease after a short illness and it was
clear the long-term damage to his heart was not a
priority for him at this stage of his life. I asked him to
give me some words to describe this life-changing
experience. He gave me one: ‘Loss . . . I’ve lost my
job, I’ve lost the function of my kidneys and the ability
to eat and drink what I want and I’m stuck in this place
three times a week and all you nurses do is nag me
about my fluids when you have no idea what it is like to
be me’. He was right—we had no idea.
*


We had a long discussion about the gulf between ‘our’
ideas to help him achieve ‘our’ health goals and how
ineffective this was because he could not identify with
such measures or how they related to his own
perceptions of his experience. The concept of
adherence to a given health behaviour and the
consequences of poor management need to be
relevant to those we care for in order for them to
understand their importance. Behavioural adherence is
a multidimensional phenomenon and we need to
recognise this when teaching. Effective person-centred
education needs to start with understanding and
respecting the individual, not some didactic,
regimented or formulaic ritual.
That day Jock was in a bad way. He was dyspnoeic,
tachycardic, hypertensive and very scared. This was
an ideal place to start identifying how he felt and how
he might avoid further distressing episodes of acute
pulmonary oedema and really impress upon him the
need to take ownership of his health management. We
worked on this together, but Jock’s challenges were far
deeper and were related to the destruction this disease
process had caused his identity.
It seemed that one of the biggest hurdles Jock faced
was the idea of not going out socialising and drinking
with his mates. He felt that he would be ostracised


from his mates if he gave up this part of who he was. I
asked him to identify some strategies he could use to
better handle this situation. He struggled to come up
with any, so I suggested two things: one, that he spoke
with his mates about how he was feeling, and
secondly, on a more practical front, to switch from beer
to something like whisky which contained less fluid
volume . . . there was no reason why he had to
completely stop this social activity with his mates. He
figured both were worth trying in order to get ‘us’ off
his back!
This interaction impressed upon me the need to
continuously ask myself: ‘Do I make assumptions
about understanding the life experiences of my
patients?’. I now consciously remind myself to
circumvent the natural tendency to assume that I
‘know’ what the patient needs.
This was the start, but ‘we’ had a long way to go. Jock
talked with his mates and they proved to be incredibly
supportive. He enjoyed the challenge of working in
partnership with us and was able to decrease his
interdialytic fluid gain remarkably.
Promoting self-efficacy should be our express goal
when working with people with chronic disease.
Avoiding the use of negative and paternalistic language


in our interactions will enhance our partnership in
health management and the attainment of mutually
acceptable health maintenance behaviour. We need to
appreciate our patients’ experiences, health beliefs,
attitudes and expectations of both their illness and
their treatment. This understanding will enhance
educational and care delivery strategies.
—Pete Sinclair Lecturer, The University of Newcastle, New South Wales
Name changed for privacy.
*


Learning
Whether you are engaged in patient education or the education of
other health professionals, it is essential to remember that people
have a variety of learning needs and learning styles. A learning
need
 is a desire or a requirement to know something that is
presently unknown to the learner. Learning needs include new
knowledge or information but can also include new skills or physical
activities, or new behaviours or a need to change current
behaviours. Learning
 is a change in human disposition or
capability that persists and that cannot be solely accounted for by
growth. Learning is represented by a change in attitude and/or
behaviour/s. See ‘Patient education’ for attributes of learning.
An important aspect of learning is the individual’s motivation to learn
and to act on the learning; this is referred to as compliance
. In
the health care context, compliance is the extent to which a person’s
behaviour coincides with medical or health advice. Compliance is
best illustrated when the person recognises and accepts the need to
learn and then follows through with the appropriate behaviours that
reflect the learning. For example, a person diagnosed as having
diabetes learns about the need for a special diet and then plans and
follows the learned diet. Many people, however, view the term
‘compliance’ in a negative way because it implies that the learner is
submissive and forced to comply by changing behaviour and this is
in conflict with the learner’s right to determine their own health care


decisions. For some, the term compliance denotes ‘power over’
rather than ‘power with’. It is important not to label a person as ‘non-
compliant’ without obtaining further information. For example, a
person might want to comply but is unable to do so because they
cannot afford the cost of the medications or special dietary
requirements, or because they are unable to read the written
instructions provided.
Another term seen in the health care literature is adherence
,
which is a commitment or an attachment to a regimen. Bastable
explains that both compliance and adherence refer to the person’s
‘ability to maintain health-promoting regimens’ (p. 169).
3 Bastable, S. B. (2008). Nurse as Educator: Principles of Teaching and Learning for Nursing
Practice (3rd ed.). Massachusetts: Jones and Bartlett.
Patient education
Attributes of learning
Learning is:
an experience that occurs inside the learner
the discovery of the personal meaning and relevance of
ideas
a consequence of experience
a collaborative and cooperative process
an evolutionary process that builds on past learning and
experiences
a process that is both intellectual and emotional.
3


Andragogy
Andragogy
 is often referred to as the art and science of teaching
adults; it contrasts with pedagogy, which refers most often to
teaching practices related to children. Knowles , sometimes known
as the ‘father of andragogy’, chanced upon the term ‘andragogy’ in
1967 and then adopted it to describe his developing ideas about
self-directed adult learning. Over time, ‘andragogy’ came to be
accepted as the term that encapsulated the wealth of knowledge
that had been accumulated about the education of adults (see Box
28.3
).
4 Knowles, M. S. (1984). Andragogy in Action. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.
BO X
28.3 Andragogy and self-directed
learning
Knowles  suggests that the main purpose of education is to
develop independent skills of inquiry to learn to exploit every
educational experience, both in formal education settings and
in everyday life. Knowles (p. 18) defines self-directed learning
as:
5 Knowles, M. S. (1975). Self-directed Learning: A Guide for Learners and Teachers.
Chicago: Follet.
4
5


A process in which individuals take the initiative, with or without the help of
others, in diagnosing their learning needs, formulating learning goals, identifying
human and material resources for learning, choosing and implementing
appropriate learning strategies and evaluating learning outcomes.
Knowles (p. 14) outlines the advantages of self-directed
learning by suggesting that learners who take the initiative:
learn more things and learn better than those who wait
passively to be taught
enter into learning more purposefully and with greater
motivation
tend to retain and make use of what they learn, better and
longer.
Many adult education writers agree with Knowles’
understanding of the advantages of self-directed learning,
suggesting that when given the opportunity adults prefer to
be in charge of their own learning and actually thrive under
such conditions (Galbraith ). In fact, Knox  asserts that
adults rarely learn, remember or utilise answers for which
they did not formulate the question. Proponents of self-
directed learning suggest it is a model in which learning
progresses from being merely a transmission of information
to being a meaningful, memorable, relevant and motivating
educational experience (Levett-Jones ).
6 Galbraith, M. (Ed.) (1991). Facilitating Adult Learning: A Transactional Process.
Malabar, FL: Kreiger.
6
7
8


7 Knox, A. (1979). Helping Adults Learn. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.
8 Levett-Jones, T. (2005). Self-directed learning: Implications and limitations for
undergraduate nursing education. Nurse Education Today, 25, 363–368.
It is not appropriate to apply the same teaching skills to the teaching
of children and adults. Most often the intent and motivation to learn
are different and the needs of adult learners must be considered.
Nurses can use the following adult learning concepts to guide their
work as health educators (Knowles 1984):
As people mature, they move from dependence to
independence.
An adult’s previous experiences can be used as a resource for
learning.
An adult’s readiness to learn is often related to a developmental
task or social role (i.e. perceive a need in their life situation).
An adult is more committed to learning when the material is
meaningful, purposeful and immediately useful.
Learning theories
Learning theories help us to better understand how people learn.
Three main theoretical constructs are behaviourism, cognitivism and
humanism.


Behaviourism
Major behaviourist theorists include Thorndike, Pavlov, Skinner and
Bandura. In the behaviourist school of thought, an act is called a
response when it can be traced to the effects of a stimulus.
Behaviourists closely observe responses and then manipulate the
environment to bring about the intended change. Thus, to modify a
person’s attitude and response, a behaviourist would either alter the
stimulus condition in the environment or change what happens after
a response occurs (Bastable 2008).
Skinner’s  and Pavlov’s  work focused on conditioning behavioural
responses to a stimulus that causes the response or behaviour. To
increase the probability of a response, Skinner introduced the
importance of positive reinforcement
 (e.g. a pleasant
experience such as praise and encouragement) in fostering
repetition of an action. Bandura , however, claims that most
learning comes from observational learning and instruction.
Bandura’s research focuses on imitation
, the process by which
individuals copy or reproduce what they have observed;
modelling
, the process by which a person learns by observing
the behaviour of others; and self-efficacy
 beliefs, which
determine how people think, feel, motivate themselves and behave.
9 Skinner, B. F. (1953). Science and Human Behavior. New York: Macmillan.
10 Pavlov, I. P. (1927). Conditioned Reflexes (G. V. Anrep, trans.). London: Oxford University
Press.
9
10
11


11 Bandura, A. (1997). Self-efficacy: The Exercise of Control. New York: W. H. Freeman and
Company.
Nurses applying behaviouristic theory will:
select teaching strategies that avoid distracting information and
that evoke the desired response
praise the learner for correct behaviour and provide positive
feedback at intervals throughout the learning experience
provide opportunities for learners to solve problems by trial and
error
help learners develop a sense of self-efficacy
provide role models of desired behaviour.
Cognitivism
Cognitivism
 depicts learning as a complex cognitive activity. In
other words, learning is largely a mental, intellectual or thinking
process whereby the learner structures and processes new
information. Perceptions are selectively chosen by the individual and
personal characteristics have an impact on how a cue is perceived.
Cognitivists also emphasise the importance of social, emotional and
physical contexts in which learning occurs, such as the teacher–
learner relationship and the environment. Developmental readiness
and individual readiness (expressed as motivation) are other key
factors associated with cognitive approaches.
Major cognitive theorists include Piaget
, Lewin  and Bloom
.
Piaget’s five major phases of cognitive development include the
12
13
14


sensorimotor phase, the preconceptual phase, the intuitive phase,
the concrete operations phase and the formal operations phase.
Each phase is discussed in Chapter 21
. According to Lewin,
learning involves four different types of changes: change in cognitive
structure, change in motivation, change in one’s sense of belonging
to the group and improvement in voluntary muscle control. His
widely known theory of change has three basic stages: unfreezing,
moving and refreezing.
12 Piaget, J. (1966). Origins of Intelligence in Children. New York: Norton.
13 Lewin, K. (1951). Field Theory in Social Science. New York: Harper & Row.
14 Bloom, B. S. (Ed.) (1956). Taxonomy of Education Objectives. Book 1, Cognitive Domain.
New York: Longman.
Bloom (1956) identified three domains or areas of learning:
cognitive, affective and psychomotor. The cognitive domain
, the
‘thinking’ domain, includes six intellectual abilities and thinking
processes: knowing, comprehending, applying, analysing,
synthesising and evaluating. Importantly, it involves problem solving.
The affective domain
, known as the ‘feeling’ domain, is divided
into categories that specify the degree of a ‘person’s depth of
emotional response to tasks’ (Bastable 2008). It includes feelings,
emotions, interests, attitudes and appreciations. The psychomotor
domain
, the ‘skill’ domain, includes fine and gross motor skills
such as giving an injection.
Nurses should include each of Bloom’s three domains in patient
education. For example, educating a person on how to self-


administer insulin is in the psychomotor domain. But an important
part of an educating plan for a person with diabetes is to teach why
insulin is needed and what to do when not feeling well; this is in the
cognitive domain. Helping the person accept the chronic implications
of diabetes and develop self- efficacious beliefs in managing the
diabetes is in the affective domain.
Nurses applying cognitive theory will:
provide a social, emotional and physical environment conducive
to learning
encourage a positive teacher–learner relationship
select multisensory teaching strategies because perception is
influenced by the senses
recognise that personal characteristics and beliefs have an
impact on how information is perceived and develop appropriate
teaching approaches to target different learning styles
assess a person’s developmental and individual readiness to
learn and adapt teaching strategies to the learner’s
developmental level
select behavioural objectives and teaching strategies that
encompass the cognitive, affective and psychomotor domains of
learning.
Humanism
Humanistic learning theory focuses on both cognitive and affective
qualities of the learner. Prominent members of this school of thought


include Maslow  and Rogers
. According to humanistic theory,
learning is believed to be self-motivated, self-initiated and self-
evaluated. Each individual is viewed as a unique composite of
biological, psychological, social, cultural and spiritual factors.
Learning focuses on self-development and achieving full potential.
15 Maslow, A. H. (1968). Toward a Psychology of Being (2nd ed.). New York: John Wiley
Sons.
16 Rogers, C. R. (1969). Freedom to Learn. Columbus, OH: Chas. E. Merrill.
Autonomy and self-determination are important; the learner is an
active participant who identifies the individual learning needs and
takes the initiative (and responsibility) to meet these needs.
Nurses applying humanistic theory will:
convey empathy in the nurse–patient relationship
encourage the learner to establish goals and promote self-
directed learning
encourage active learning by serving as a facilitator, mentor or
resource for the learner
use active learning strategies to assist the person’s adoption of
new behaviour
expose the learner to new information and ask appropriate
questions to encourage the learner to seek answers.
Using learning theories
15
16


Nurses using the behaviourist theory
 identify what is to be
taught and immediately identify and reward correct responses.
However, the theory is not easily applied to complex learning
situations and limits the learner’s role in the teaching process. Users
of cognitive theory
 recognise the developmental level of the
learner and acknowledge the learner’s motivation and environment.
However, some of the motivational and environmental factors may
be beyond the teacher’s control. Using humanism
, the nurse
focuses on the feelings and attitudes of learners, on the importance
of the individual in identifying learning needs and in taking
responsibility for them, and on the self-motivation of the learners to
work towards self-reliance and independence.
Being aware of the focus and limitations of the various learning
theories allows the nurse to use one or more of them when
developing a teaching plan for a patient or peer. Knowing what is
important (e.g. knowledge, motivation, beliefs, feelings, attitudes)
assists the nurse in choosing the appropriate learning theory or
theories. The nurse also needs to be aware of the different factors
that can affect learning.
Factors affecting learning
Many factors can facilitate or hinder learning. The nurse should be
aware of these factors, particularly when available teaching time is
limited.


Motivation
Motivation
 is the desire to learn. It greatly influences how quickly
and how much a person learns. Motivation is generally greatest
when a person recognises a need and believes the need will be met
through learning. It is not enough for the need to be identified and
verbalised by the nurse; it must be experienced by the learner. Often
the nurse’s task is to help a person work through the problem and
identify the learning need. Sometimes people need help to identify
information relevant to their situation before they can see a need.
For instance, people with heart disease may need to know the
effects of smoking before they recognise the need to stop smoking,
or adolescents may need to know the consequences of an untreated
sexually transmitted disease before they see the need for treatment.
Readiness
Readiness
 to learn is the demonstration of behaviours or cues
that reflect the learner’s motivation and ability to learn at a specific
time. For example, a person may want to learn self-care during a
dressing change, but if the person experiences pain or discomfort
they may not be able to learn. The nurse can provide analgesia to
make the person more comfortable and ready to learn.
Active involvement
When the learner is actively involved in the process, learning
becomes more meaningful. If the learner actively participates in


planning and discussion, learning is faster and retention is better
(see Figure 28.1
). Active learning promotes critical thinking,
enabling learners to problem solve more effectively. People who are
actively involved in learning about their health care are enabled to
apply the learning to their own situation. For example, when actively
involved in learning about therapeutic diets a person may be more
able to apply the principles being taught to their cultural food
preferences and their usual eating habits. Passive learning, such as
listening to a lecture or watching a film, does not foster optimal
learning.
Figure 28.1


Learning is facilitated when the person is interested and actively
involved.
Relevance
The knowledge or skill to be learned must be personally relevant and
meaningful to the learner. People learn more easily if they can
connect the new knowledge to existing knowledge. For example, if a
person is diagnosed with hypertension, is overweight and has
symptoms of headaches and fatigue, they are more likely to
understand the need to lose weight if they remember having more
stamina when they weighed less. The nurse needs to validate the
relevance of learning with the person throughout the learning
process.
Feedback
Feedback is information regarding a person’s performance towards
a desired goal. It has to be meaningful to the learner. Feedback that
accompanies the practice of psychomotor skills helps the person to
learn those skills. Support of desired behaviour through praise,
positively worded corrections and suggestions of alternative
methods are ways of providing positive feedback. Negative feedback
such as ridicule, anger or sarcasm can lead people to withdraw from
learning. Such feedback, viewed as a type of punishment, may
cause the learner to avoid the teacher in order to avoid punishment.


Non-judgmental support
People learn best when they believe they are accepted and will not
be judged. The person who expects to be judged as ‘poor’ or ‘good’
will not learn as well as the person who feels no such threat. Once
learners have succeeded in accomplishing a task or understanding a
concept, they gain self-confidence in their ability to learn. This
reduces their anxiety about failure and can motivate greater
learning.
Simple to complex
Learning is facilitated by material that is logically organised and
proceeds from the simple to the complex. Such organisation enables
the learner to comprehend new information, assimilate it with
previous learning and form new understandings. Of course, simple
and complex are relative terms, depending on the level at which the
person is learning. What is simple for one person may be complex
for another.
Repetition
Repetition of key concepts and facts facilitates retention of newly
learned material. Practice of psychomotor skills, particularly with
feedback, improves performance of those skills and facilitates their
transfer to another setting.


Timing
People retain information and psychomotor skills best when the time
between learning and active use of the learning is short; the longer
the time interval, the easier it is to forget the learning. For example,
a person who is only shown literature and videos about
administering insulin but is not permitted to practise insulin
administration until discharge from the hospital is unlikely to
remember what was learned. However, administering their own
injections while in the hospital with support and guidance from the
nurse will enhance the person’s learning.
Environment
An optimal learning environment facilitates learning by reducing
distraction and providing physical and psychological comfort. It has
adequate lighting that is free from glare, a comfortable room
temperature and good ventilation. Most students know what it is like
to try to learn in a hot, stuffy room; the consequent drowsiness
interferes with concentration. Noise can also distract the student and
interfere with listening and thinking. To facilitate learning in a hospital
setting, nurses should choose a time when no visitors are present
and interruptions are unlikely. Privacy is also essential for some
learning activities. For example, when a person is learning to change
a colostomy bag, the presence of others can be embarrassing and
thus interfere with learning. However, when a person is particularly
anxious, having a support person present may give added
confidence.


Many factors inhibit learning. Some of the most common barriers to
learning are described next and in Table 28.2
.
Table 28.2 Barriers to learning
Emotions
Emotions such as fear, anger and depression can impede learning.
A high level of anxiety or stress resulting in agitation and the inability
to focus or concentrate can also inhibit learning. Patients or families
who are experiencing extreme emotional states may not hear
spoken words or may retain only part of the communication.
However, emotional responses such as fear and anxiety may be
decreased when information is provided that relieves uncertainty.
Physiological events
Physiological events such as a critical illness, pain or sensory deficits
inhibit learning. Because the person cannot concentrate and apply
energy to learning, the learning itself is impaired. The nurse should
try to reduce physiological barriers to learning as much as possible
before teaching. For example, providing analgesics and rest before
teaching is often helpful; and teaching a person how to use a PCA
(patient-controlled analgesia) should be undertaken prior to surgery,
not in the postoperative period when the person’s ability to learn
may be impeded by pain.


Cultural aspects
There are cultural barriers to learning, such as language or values.
Western medicine may conflict with a person’s cultural healing
beliefs and practices. To be effective, nurses must be culturally
sensitive; otherwise the person may not comply with or participate in
recommended treatments. Another impediment to learning is
differing values held by the patients and the health care team. For
example, if a person comes from a culture that views being
overweight as positive, the nurse will need to negotiate with the
person to determine an acceptable weight and develop a plan
together.
Psychomotor ability
It is important that the nurse is aware of a person’s psychomotor
skills when planning teaching. Psychomotor skills can be affected by
health. For example, an older adult who has severe osteoarthritis of
the hands may not be able to wrap a bandage. The following
physical abilities are important for learning psychomotor skills:
Muscle strength. For example, an older adult who cannot rise
from a chair because of insufficient leg and muscle strength
cannot be expected to learn to lift herself out of a bathtub.
Motor coordination. Gross motor coordination is required for
movements such as walking, and fine motor coordination is
needed when using utensils such as a fork for eating. For
example, a person who has advanced motor neurone disease


involving the lower limbs will probably be unable to use a walking
frame.
Energy. Energy is required for most psychomotor skills and
learning these skills uses more energy. People who are frail, ill or
elderly often have limited energy resources; learning and carrying
out these skills must be timed for when the person’s energy
sources are at their peak.
Sensory acuity. Sight is used for most learning (i.e. walking with
crutches, changing a dressing, drawing a medication into a
syringe). People who have a vision impairment may need the
assistance of a support person to carry out such tasks. Similarly,
people with a hearing impairment may need communication
support to help understand the instructions given to them.
See Box 28.4
 for ten tips to help learning.
BO X
28.4 Ten tips to help learning
1. The content ‘makes sense’ to the learner.
2. The content relates to the role of the learner.
3. The content can be realistically applied.
4. The content is presented in manageable pieces.
5. The presenter has credibility.
6. The presentation is engaging and interesting.
7. Potential obstacles to implementation are addressed.


8. Opportunities exist for implementation of new or
reinforced knowledge and skills.
9. Opportunities exist for reflection during the
implementation on the implementation process.
10. The learner is continually challenged to grow and
learn.
Source: Based on P. Dickerson
. Ten tips to help learning. Journal for Nurses in Staff Development,
19(5), 244–250.
