244–250.
17


The internet and health
information
The use of information and communication technology (ICT) and the
internet has become a part of the lives of many Australians, allowing
them to communicate and obtain information quickly and easily. ICT
has dramatically changed the activities of health care (see Chapter
10
). E-health is defined as the use of the internet and other
related technologies in health care to improve the access, efficiency,
effectiveness and quality of clinical care in an effort to improve the
health status of patients. Use of ICT in health care includes
electronic medical records, point-of-use documentation, medication
administration and the use of smartphones and other mobile
devices. In contemporary clinical practice environments, ICT skills
are advantageous, not only to nurses but also to the people they are
caring for. There is good evidence that ICT competence,
appropriately utilised, can have a significant impact on health
outcomes (Staggers, Gassert & Curran ).
18 Staggers, N., Gassert, C. & Curran, C. (2001). Informatics competencies for nurses at four
levels of practice. Journal of Nursing Education, 40(7), 303–316.
Online health information
18


ICT is increasingly evident in our everyday lives, with 91% of
Australian households reporting access to a computer and 86%
reporting internet access (Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS)
).
The proportion of people accessing the internet for health services
or health research has increased from 22% in 2014–15 to 46% in
2016–17 (ABS 2017). The following groups are less likely to use and
be competent in the use of ICT (ABS 2017):
19 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2017). Household Use of Information Technology,
Australia, 2016–17. Cat. no. 8146.0. Canberra: Commonwealth of Australia. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au>.
lower-income people and the unemployed
those without a tertiary education
those living in regional and remote locations
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
people with a disability.
Implications
ICT and the internet are important sources of health information for
many adults in Australia. Therefore, nurses need to know and be
able to integrate this technology into teaching plans for people who
use the internet. On the other hand, nurses also need to apply
effective teaching strategies for people who do not use the internet.
19


Nurse as educator
Being an educator or a teacher is an important and essential nursing
role of all nurses. Health care consumers and their families have the
right to health education in order to make informed decisions about
their health. The nurse is in a position to promote healthy lifestyles
through the application of health knowledge, the change process,
learning theories and the nursing and teaching process when
teaching people and their families.


Nursing management
Assessing
A comprehensive assessment of learning needs incorporates data
from the nursing history and physical assessment and addresses
the person’s support system. It also considers individual
characteristics that may influence the learning process: readiness to
learn, motivation to learn and reading and comprehension level, for
example. Assessing a person’s stage of change and any barriers to
change are also important and often overlooked (see Chapter
17
).
The nurse’s awareness of common learning needs for people
experiencing similar health problems is another source of
information. Learning needs change as the person’s health status
changes, so nurses must constantly reassess them.
Nursing history
Several elements in the nursing history provide cues to learning
needs. These elements include (a) age, (b) the person’s
understanding and perceptions of the health problem, (c) health
beliefs and practices, (d) cultural factors, (e) economic factors, (f)


learning style and (g) the person’s support systems. Examples of
interview questions to elicit this information are shown in the
‘Assessment interview
’ (note the number of open-ended
questions).
Age
Age provides information on the person’s developmental status that
may indicate distinctive health teaching content and teaching
approaches. Simple questions to school-age children and
adolescents will elicit information on what they know. Observing
children at play provides information about their motor and
intellectual development as well as relationships with other children.
For older people, conversation and questioning may sometimes
reveal slow recall or limited psychomotor skills, sensory deficits and
learning difficulties (see ‘Lifespan considerations’); however, broad
assumptions about older people’s abilities should not be made as
each person is different.
Individual understanding of health problems
People’s perceptions of their current health problems and concerns
may indicate deficient knowledge or misinformation. In addition, the
effects of the problem on the person’s usual activities can alert the
nurse to other areas requiring instruction. For example, people who
cannot manage self-care at home often need information about
community resources and services.


Health beliefs and practices
A person’s health beliefs and practices are important to consider in
any teaching plan. The health belief model described in Chapter
18
 provides a predictor of preventive health behaviour. However,
even if a nurse is convinced that a person’s health beliefs should be
changed, doing so may not be possible because of the individual’s
health beliefs.
Cultural factors
Many cultural groups have their own traditional and spiritual beliefs
and practices, a number of which are related to diet, health, illness
and lifestyle. It is therefore important to discuss the person’s cultural
perspective on illness and related treatments. Cultural practices and
values will affect each person’s learning needs. For example, a
person may understand the health care information being taught but
this learning might not be used if it contradicts their beliefs about
traditional healing practices (see Chapter 19
).
Economic factors
Economic factors can also affect a person’s learning. For example, a
person who cannot afford to obtain a new sterile syringe for each
injection of insulin may find it difficult to learn to administer the
insulin when the nurse teaches that a new syringe should be used
each time. Similarly, a person brought up in the post-war period may
have learnt to live frugally and ‘economising’ may be a way of life.


Learning styles
The term ‘learning styles’ refers to the ways individuals and
members of cultural groups prefer to receive, process and present
information and ideas. Considerable research has been done on
people’s learning styles. Each individual learns in a unique way.
Some people are visual learners and learn best by watching. Other
people do not visualise an activity well; they learn best by actually
manipulating equipment and discovering how it works. Other people
can learn well from reading things presented in an orderly fashion.
Some learn best in groups where they can relate to other people.
For some, stressing the thinking part of a skill and its logic will
promote learning. For others, stressing the feeling part or
interpersonal aspect motivates and promotes learning.
There is a considerable debate among education researchers about
the main influences on learning styles. These influences may include
personality, life experiences and the purpose of the learning. A
person’s learning style may also be based in their cultural
background. For example, people from cultures that have a strong
oral tradition, such as Indigenous Australians, may prefer to learn in
groups with opportunities for ‘yarning’ (storytelling) and asking
questions, instead of individualised or didactic teaching approaches.
Most people will not have an exclusive learning style; rather, they will
adjust to what is offered. However, there is a strong theoretical
argument for teachers to try to match their teaching methods with
the preferred way that individuals learn.


The nurse seldom has the time or the skills to assess each learner,
identify the person’s particular learning style and then adapt teaching
accordingly. What the nurse can do, however, is to ask the person
how they have learned things best in the past or how they like to
learn. Many people know what helps them learn and the nurse can
use this information in planning the teaching. Using a variety of
teaching techniques and varying activities during teaching are good
ways to match learners with learning styles. One technique will be
most effective for some people, whereas other techniques will be
suited to people with different learning styles.
Support systems
The nurse should explore the person’s support system to determine
the extent to which others may enhance learning and offer support.
Family members or a close friend may help the person perform
required skills at home and maintain the required lifestyle changes.
Physical examination
A physical examination provides useful cues about the person’s
learning needs, such as mental status, energy level and nutritional
status. Other parts of the physical examination reveal data about the
person’s physical capacity to learn and to perform self-care
activities. For example, visual ability, hearing ability and muscle
coordination affect the selection of content and approaches to
teaching.


Readiness to learn
People who are ready to learn often behave differently from those
who are not. A person who is ready may search out information by
asking questions, reading books or articles, talking to others and
generally showing interest. The person who is not ready to learn is
more likely to avoid the subject or situation. In addition, the person
who is not ready may change the subject when it is brought up by
the nurse. For example, the nurse might say, ‘I was wondering about
a good time to show you how to change your colostomy bag’, and
the person responds, ‘Oh, my wife will take care of everything’.
To ascertain the person’s readiness to learn the nurse assesses for
these characteristics:
Physical readiness. Is the person able to focus on things other
than physical status or are pain, fatigue and immobility
consuming all their time and energy?
Emotional readiness. Is the person emotionally ready to learn
self-care activities? People who are extremely anxious,
depressed or grieving over their health status are not ready.
Cognitive readiness. Can the person think clearly at this point?
Are the effects of anaesthesia and analgesia altering their level
of consciousness?
Assessment interview


Learning needs and characteristics
Primary health problem
Can you tell me what you know about your current health
problem? What do you think caused it?
What concerns do you have about it?
How has the problem affected what you can or cannot do
during your usual activities (e.g. work, recreation, sleep,
shopping and housework)?
What do you or did you do at home to relieve the
problem? How helpful was it?
How have the treatments you have started helped your
problem?
What, if any, difficulties have the treatments caused you
(e.g. inconvenience, cost, discomfort)?
Can you tell me about the tests (surgery, treatments) you
are going to have?
Health beliefs
How would you describe your health generally?
What things do you usually do to keep healthy?
What health problems do you think you may be at risk of
because of family history, age, diet, occupation,
inadequate exercise or other habits, such as smoking?
What changes would you be willing to make to decrease
your risk for these problems or to improve your health?


Cultural factors
What language do you use most often when speaking and
writing?
Do you seek the advice of another health practitioner?
Do you use herbs or other medications or treatments
common to your cultural group?
Does your doctor know about these?
What advice or treatments given previously by your doctor
conflicted with values or beliefs you consider important?
When a conflict arose, what did you do?
Learning ability
Note the person’s age and developmental level.
What level of education have you received?
Do you like to read?
Where do you obtain health information (e.g. doctor,
nurse, magazines, books, pharmacist and so on)?
Learning style
How do you best learn new things?
– By reading about them.
– By talking about them.
– By watching a movie or demonstration.
– By computer.


– By listening to the teacher.
– By first being shown how something works and then
doing it.
– On your own or in a group.
Support systems
Would you like a family member or friend to help you learn
about things you need to do to take care of yourself?
Who do you think would be interested in learning with
you?
Lifespan considerations
Special teaching considerations
Older adults
Older adults often have chronic illnesses that require multiple
treatments and/or medications. Health teaching will focus on
the same areas as with other ages—health and wellness
promotion and prevention of illness and accidents—but often
the needs of the older adults are greater when learning to
manage their lives in order to live with their chronic health
conditions and to maintain optimal health and functioning. For


older adults to be motivated to learn, the material must be
practical and have meaning for them individually, especially if
the information is new to them. Special considerations in
teaching older adults include the following:
Health promotion is a priority and should include these
areas:
– exercise
– nutrition
– safety habits
– having regular health check-ups
– understanding medications
– setting achievable goals and involving the person and
their and family
– determining where they currently obtain most of their
health information (e.g. newspapers, magazines,
television)
– investigating the cause of non-compliance if it is a
problem. It could be due to lack of finances, transportation
problems, poor access to health care and so on.
If developing written materials:
– use large print (e.g. at least 14 point font) in bulleted
format


– use buff-coloured paper (avoids the glare of white
paper).
If providing teaching using a verbal approach:
– increase the time provided and allow for rest periods as
processing of information may be slower
– ensure material is well organised
– ensure that there is minimal distraction
– repeat information if necessary
– use return demonstrations with psychomotor skills, such
as teaching someone to learn to give insulin injections
– use examples that older adults can relate to in their daily
lives
– be aware of sensory deficits, such as hearing and vision
– use a setting in which the individual is most comfortable
— either a group or a one-on-one setting.
Older adults come with a lifetime of experiences and a
repertoire of skills and knowledge. Prior to commencing
health teaching, it is essential that you identify what the older
person already knows and work from that basis. It is also
important that you make sure that their current knowledge is
correct. Positive reinforcement and ongoing evaluation of
what has been taught are important factors in effective health
teaching of older people (Stanley, Blair & Beare ).
20


20 Stanley, M., Blair, K. A. & Beare, P. G. (2005). Gerontological Nursing: Promoting
Successful Aging with Older Adults (3rd ed.). Philadelphia: F. A. Davis.
Children
It has often been said that the parent is a child’s first and
most important teacher. Every interaction between a child
and parent (or other adults and children) is a moment in
which teaching and learning occurs, often unconsciously. In
order to make parents more aware of the teaching they are
doing, nurses can point out how the parent is using the
concept of a ‘teaching loop’ and how that ‘informal’ teaching
strategy can be applied more consciously to many parent–
child interactions.
The teaching loop consists of four specific teaching
behaviours that give children verbal instruction, role modelling
and positive feedback. These include:
1. Alerting: get children’s attention by calling their name,
touching them or making a noise.
2. Instructing: give the child a short, specific instruction
about what is to be done; modelling or demonstrating
behaviour can also be done (e.g. ‘Try it like this . . .’).
3. Performing: give the child opportunity to practise the
task, play with the toy and explore the materials being
used. Provide ‘enough’ time, but with some structure
or direction.
4. Reinforcing: give the child feedback; a positive or
negative comment (e.g. ‘You poured the milk very well’
or ‘No, that’s not quite right; try turning it this way’) that


is specific to the task lets children know how they have
done and encourages them to continue to learn.
Nurses can promote readiness to learn by providing physical and
emotional support during the critical stage of recovery. As the
person stabilises physically and emotionally, the nurse can provide
opportunities to learn.
Motivation
Motivation relates to whether the person wants to learn and is
usually greatest when the person is ready, the learning need is
recognised and the information being offered is meaningful.
Assessment of motivation, however, may be difficult. Communication
skills used by the nurse can obtain helpful information indicating a
readiness for change, such as ‘I’m really ready to lose weight this
time’. On the other hand, non-verbal behaviours such as disinterest,
lack of attention and missed appointments can indicate a decreased
motivation to learn.
Nurses can increase a person’s motivation in several ways:
by relating the learning to something the person values and
helping them see the relevance of the learning
by helping to make the learning situation pleasant and non-
threatening
by encouraging self-direction and independence


by demonstrating a positive attitude about the person’s ability to
learn
by offering continuing support, encouragement and constructive
feedback as the person attempts to learn (i.e. positive
reinforcement)
by creating a learning situation in which the person is likely to
succeed (succeeding in small tasks motivates them to continue
learning)
by assisting the person to identify the benefits of changing
behaviour.
Health literacy
Health literacy
 is the ability to read, understand and act on
health information, including such tasks as comprehending
prescription labels, interpreting appointment slips, completing
medical forms and following instructions for diagnostic tests (Dean &
Saunders ). To achieve optimal health outcomes, people must be
able to understand and act on health care advice. When people
have this capacity, they are described as health literate. However,
almost 60% of Australian adults have a low level of health literacy
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care ), a
factor that can significantly impact on their health and wellbeing; for
example, a person may not be able to read a prescription to know
how many tablets to take (e.g. ‘once’ means ‘eleven’ in Spanish).
People with low literacy skills have less information about health
promotion and/or management of a disease process for themselves
21
22


and their families because they are unable to read the educational
materials.
21 Dean, S. & Saunders, C. (2020). An introduction to communication skills. In T. Levett-
Jones (Ed.), Critical Conversations for Patient Safety: An Essential Guide for Health
Professionals (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
22 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (2014). Health Literacy:
Taking Action to Improve Safety and Quality. Sydney: ACSQHC.
Patient safety competency framework
2 Therapeutic communication
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students should
communicate in a way that is appropriate to the
person’s level of health literacy and avoids
jargon and complex terms (Levett-Jones et
al.
).
23 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
23


Limited health literacy skills are often greater among certain groups:
people with limited education, socioeconomically disadvantaged
people, minority groups and those with limited English proficiency. As
a result, they have higher rates of hospitalisation than people with
adequate health literacy. While it may be challenging for nurses to
teach people with limited reading and writing skills, such teaching is
vitally important because they are in need of learning opportunities
to improve their health practices.
Nurses are responsible for assessing patients’ health literacy skills
and ensuring that patient education is aligned with these
assessment results (Brach et al.
). When nurses do not consider a
person’s health literacy level when teaching them, communication
can be ineffective and unclear (Cafiero ). However, it is sometimes
difficult to assess a person’s literacy skills because the shame and
stigma associated with limited health literacy skills may present
major barriers. Many people with low reading levels may still report
that they ‘read well’ as they may be too embarrassed to admit they
cannot read. The following behaviours may be indicative of a literacy
problem:
24 Brach, C., Keller, D., Hernandez, L., ... Schillinger, D. (2012). Ten Attributes of Health
Literate Health Care Organizations. National Academy of Sciences. Retrieved from
<https://nam.edu>.
25 Cafiero, M. (2013). Nurse practitioners’ knowledge, experience, and intention to use health
literacy strategies in clinical practice. Journal of Health Communication, 18(Suppl 1), 70–81.
pattern of non-compliance
24
25


insisting that they already know the information
having a friend or family member read the document for them
pattern of excuses for not reading the instructions (e.g. glasses
broken, stating they will read later or when they get home).
There are many formulas for assessing the reading level of written
material. Most word processing programs have a feature that will
calculate the readability for you. Nurses involved in developing
written health teaching materials should write for reading levels of a
Year 5 or 6 student (see ‘Patient education: Developing written
teaching aids’). People with good reading skills are not offended by
simple reading material and prefer easy-to-read information. Even
the simplest written directions, however, won’t be helpful for the
person with low or no reading skills. See the ‘Patient education:
Teaching people with low literacy levels’ box for suggestions on how
to teach people with low literacy levels.
Diagnosing
Nursing diagnoses for people with learning needs can be designated
in two ways: as the person’s primary concern or problem, or as the
aetiology of a nursing diagnosis associated with the person’s
response to health alterations or dysfunction.
Patient education
Developing written teaching aids


Keep language level at or below the Year 5 level.
Use active voice, not passive voice.
Use easy, familiar words of one or two syllables (e.g. use
instead of utilise or give instead of administer).
Use the second person (you) rather than the third person
(the person).
Use a large size font (14 to 16 point).
Write short sentences.
Avoid using all capital letters.
Place priority information first and repeat more than once.
Use bold for emphasis.
Use simple pictures, drawings or cartoons, if appropriate.
Leave plenty of white space.
Patient Eeducation
Teaching people with low literacy levels
Use multiple teaching methods: show pictures. Read
important information. Lead a small group discussion.
Role play. Demonstrate a skill. Provide hands-on practice.
Emphasise key points in simple terms and provide
examples.
Limit the amount of information in a single teaching
session. Instead of one long session with a great deal of
information, it is better to have more frequent sessions
with a major point at each session.
Associate new information with something the person
already knows and/or associates with their job or lifestyle.


Reinforce information through repetition.
Involve the person in the teaching.
Obtain feedback: ask the person specific questions about
the information presented or ask the person to repeat it in
their own words.
Avoid handouts with many pages and classroom lecture
format with a large group.
Planning
Developing a teaching plan is accomplished in a series of steps.
Involving the person at this time promotes the formation of a
meaningful plan and stimulates motivation. The person who helps
develop the teaching plan is more likely to achieve the desired
outcomes (see ‘Patient education: sample teaching plan for wound
care’).
Determining teaching priorities
The person’s learning needs must be ranked according to priority.
This should be done together, with the person’s priorities always
being considered. Once a person’s priorities have been addressed,
they are generally more motivated to concentrate on other identified
learning needs. For example, a man who wants to know all about
coronary artery disease may not be ready to learn how to change


his lifestyle until he understands more about the disease. Nurses
can also use theoretical frameworks, such as Maslow’s hierarchy of
needs, to establish priorities (see Chapter 17
).
Setting learning outcomes
Learning outcomes can be considered the same as desired
outcomes for other nursing diagnoses. They are written in the same
way. Learning outcomes should be structured using the SMART
criteria (specific, measurable, achievable. realistic and timely. In
addition, they should:
State the learner behaviour or performance, not nurse behaviour.
For example, ‘Identify personal risk factors for heart disease’
(learner behaviour), not ‘Teach the person about cardiac risk
factors’ (nurse behaviour).
Reflect an observable, measurable activity. The performance
may be visible (e.g. walking) or invisible (e.g. adding a column of
figures). It is necessary, however, to be able to evaluate whether
an unobservable activity has been mastered from some
performance that represents the activity. For example, the
performance of an outcome might be written: ‘Selects low-fat
foods from a menu’ (observable), not ‘Understands low-fat diet’
(unobservable). Examples of measurable verbs used for learning
outcomes are shown in Box 28.5
. Avoid using words such as
knows, understands, believes or appreciates because they are
neither observable nor measurable.


BO X
28.5 Examples of verbs for writing
learning outcomes
Patient education
Sample teaching plan for wound care
Assessment of learner: a 24-year-old male university
student suffered a 7 cm laceration on the left lower
anterior leg during a hockey game. The laceration was
cleaned, sutured and bandaged. He was given an
appointment to return to the medical centre in 10 days for
suture removal. He states that he lives in university
accommodation and is able to do wound care if given
instructions. The student is able to understand and read
English.
Nursing diagnosis: inadequate knowledge about care of
a sutured wound.
Long-term goal: the person’s wound will heal completely
without infection or other complications.
Intermediate goal: at clinic appointment, the person’s
wound will be healing without signs of infection, loss of


function or other complication.
Short-term goals: the person will (a) correctly list three
signs and symptoms of wound infection, and (b) correctly
demonstrate wound cleansing and dressing.
Evaluation: to determine the effectiveness of the
teaching session the nurse evaluates the extent to which
the short-term goals have been achieved by:
asking the person to describe the signs and symptom
of wound infection
allowing the person to demonstrate wound cleansing
and dressing
asking the person if he can recall the contact person
and telephone number to obtain assistance, as well
as date, time and location of follow-up appointment.
Add conditions or modifiers as required to clarify what, where,
when or how the behaviour will be performed. Examples are
‘Demonstrates four-point crutch gait correctly’ (condition),
‘Administers own insulin independently (condition) as taught’ or
‘States three (condition) factors that affect blood sugar level’.
Include criteria specifying the time by which learning should have
occurred. For example, ‘The patient will state three things that
affect blood sugar level by end of second diabetic teaching
session’.


In writing learning outcomes, the nurse must be specific about what
behaviours and knowledge (cognitive, psychomotor and affective)
learners must have to be able to positively influence their health
state. In most cases, the learning needs are more complex than
simple acquisition of knowledge and also include the application of
that knowledge.
Choosing content
The content, or what is to be taught, is determined by learning
outcomes. For instance, ‘Identify appropriate sites for insulin
injection’ means that the nurse must include content about the body
sites suitable for insulin injections. Nurses can select from many
sources of information, including books, nursing journals, anatomical
models and the internet. Whatever sources the nurse chooses,
content should be:
accurate
current
based on learning outcomes
adjusted for the learner’s age, culture and ability
consistent with information the nurse is teaching
selected with consideration of how much time and what
resources are available for teaching.
Selecting teaching strategies


The method of teaching that the nurse chooses should be suited to
the individual and to the material to be learned (see Figure 28.2
).
For example, the person who cannot read needs material presented
in non-written forms; a discussion is usually not the best strategy for
teaching how to give an injection; and a nurse using group
discussion for teaching should be a competent group leader. As
stated earlier, some people are visually oriented and learn best
through seeing; others learn best through hearing and having the
skill explained. Table 28.3
 lists selected teaching strategies.
Figure 28.2


Teaching materials and strategies should be suited to the person’s
age and learning abilities.
Source: saiyood srikamon/123RF.
Table 28.3 Selected teaching strategies
Clinical consideration
Leave a notepad and pen at people’s bedsides
and encourage them to write down their
questions for their nurse or doctor.
Organising learning experiences
To save nurses time in constructing their own teaching guides, some
health care organisations have developed guides for teaching
sessions that nurses commonly give. These guides standardise
content and teaching methods and make it easier for the nurse to
plan and implement education. Standardised teaching plans also
ensure consistency of content for the learner, thereby decreasing
the risk of confusion if different practices are taught. For example,
when teaching infant bathing, the nurse should be consistent about
which soaps are appropriate for the infant’s bath and distinguish
those that are not. Whether the nurse is implementing a plan


devised by another or developing an individualised teaching plan,
guidelines can help the nurse sequence the learning experience:
Start with something the learner is most concerned about; for
example, before learning how to administer insulin to himself, an
adolescent male may want to know how to adjust his lifestyle so
that he can still play sport.
Discover what the learner knows and then proceed to the
unknown. This gives the learner confidence. Sometimes you will
not know the person’s knowledge or skill base and will need to
elicit this information either by asking questions or by having
them fill out a form, such as a pre-test.
Address early on any area that is causing the person anxiety. A
high level of anxiety can significantly impair concentration and
learning. For example, a woman highly anxious about her fear of
injections may not be able to learn how to self-administer an
insulin injection until her fear is resolved.
Teach the basics before proceeding to the variations or
adjustments (e.g. simple to complex). It is confusing to learners
to have to consider possible adjustments and variations before
they master the basic concepts. For example, when teaching a
female about self-catheterisation, it is best to teach the basic
procedure before teaching any adjustments that might be
needed if the catheter stops draining after insertion.
Schedule time for review of content and questions the person
may have to clarify information.


Clinical consideration
If the person has no questions, you can help
introduce questions by saying, ‘A few frequently
asked questions are . . .’.
Implementing
The nurse needs to be flexible in implementing any teaching plan
because the plan may need revising. The person may tire sooner
than anticipated or be faced with too much information too quickly,
their needs may change or external factors may intervene. For
instance, the nurse and the patient plan to change his dressing at
1000 hours but when the time comes, the person wants to observe
the nurse once more before actually doing it himself.
In this case, the nurse alters the teaching plan and discusses any
desired information, provides another demonstration and defers
teaching the psychomotor skill until the next day. It is also important
for nurses to use teaching techniques that enhance learning and
reduce or eliminate any barrier to learning such as pain or fatigue
(see Table 28.2
 earlier in this chapter).


Clinical consideration
Many nurses find that they teach while
performing nursing care (e.g. giving
medications). Remember to also document this
informal but important teaching.
Guidelines for teaching
Knowledge alone is not enough to motivate a person to change
behaviour. Do not assume that providing information will
automatically result in a change of behaviour. Learning what needs
to be done to change behaviour and acting on that knowledge are
two different processes. The stages of change, the person’s
willingness and perceived need to change and barriers to change
are important elements to reflect on when implementing a teaching
plan (see Chapter 17
). When a person is ready to change health
behaviour and when implementing a teaching plan, the following
guidelines are helpful:
Rapport between teacher and learner is essential. A relationship
that is both accepting and constructive will best assist learning.
Understanding the learner and being aware of the previously
described factors that affect learning is essential before planning
the teaching.


The teacher who draws on the person’s life experiences, skills
and knowledge when teaching facilitates self-efficacy and the
confidence to learn new skills. For example, a person who
already knows how to cook can use this knowledge when
learning to prepare food for a special diet.
The optimal time for each session depends largely on the learner.
Whenever possible, ask the person to choose the best time; for
example, when they feel most rested or when no other activities
are scheduled. Look for ‘teachable moments’ that may occur
during normal routine care. For example, if a person asks you
why he needs a certain medication (e.g. warfarin), it is an
opportunity to explain the reason for the medication, signs to
watch for and if follow-up laboratory work is needed.
The nurse−teacher must be able to communicate clearly and
concisely. The words used need to have the same meaning to
the person as to the teacher. A person having radiotherapy who
is taught not to put water on an area of skin may think a wet
washcloth is permissible for washing the area. In effect, the
nurse needs to explain that no water or moisture should touch
the area.
Using plain English and avoiding jargon enhances
communication. Often nurses use terms and abbreviations that
have meaning to other health professionals but make little sense
to patients. Even words such as urine or faeces may be
unfamiliar and abbreviations such as ICU (intensive care unit) or
PACU (post-anaesthesia care unit) are often misunderstood.
The pace of each teaching session also affects learning. Nurses
should be sensitive to any signs that the pace is too fast or too


slow. A person who appears confused or does not comprehend
material when questioned may be finding the pace too fast.
When the person appears bored and loses interest, the pace
may be too slow, the learning period may be too long or they
may be tired.
The environment can detract from or assist learning; for
example, noise or interruptions usually interfere with
concentration, whereas a comfortable environment promotes
learning. If possible, the person should be out of bed and in a
private area for learning activities. Most people associate their
bed with rest and sleep, not with learning. Placing the person in a
position and location associated with activity or learning may
influence the amount of learning that takes place. For instance, a
person who is shown a YouTube video while in bed may be more
likely to become drowsy during instruction than someone who is
sitting in a bedside chair.
Teaching aids can foster learning and help focus a learner’s
attention. To ensure the transfer of learning, the nurse should
use the types of supplies or equipment the person will eventually
use. Before the teaching session, the nurse needs to assemble
all equipment and visual aids and ensure that all audiovisual
equipment is functioning effectively. See ‘Patient education’ for
teaching tools for children.
Patient education
Teaching tools for children
Visits. Visiting the hospital and treatment rooms;
seeing people dressed in uniforms, scrubs, protective


gear.
Dress-up. Touching and dressing up in the clothing
they will see and wear.
Colouring books. Using colouring books to prepare
for treatments, surgery or hospitalisation to show what
rooms, people and equipment will look like.
Story books. Story books describe how the child will
feel, what will be done and what the place will look like.
Parents can read these stories to children several
times before the experience. Younger children like this
repetition.
Dolls. Practising on dolls or teddy bears procedures
that they will later experience gives a sense of mastery
of the situation. Custom dolls are often available for
inserting tubes and giving injections, for example.
Puppet play. Puppets can be used in role play
situations to provide information and show the child
what the experience will be like; they help the child
express emotions.
iPads and apps. Many children have highly developed
technical skills and are familiar with the online learning
environment. There are numerous readily available
health education apps and e-learning programs for
children of all ages.
Teaching that involves a number of the learner’s senses often
enhances learning. For instance, when teaching about changing
a surgical dressing, the nurse can tell the person about the


procedure (hearing), show how to change the dressing (sight)
and show how to manipulate the equipment (touch).
Learning is more effective when the learners discover the
content for themselves. Ways to increase learning include
stimulating motivation and self-direction, for example, (a) by
providing specific, realistic, achievable outcomes; (b) by giving
feedback; and (c) by helping the learner derive satisfaction from
learning. The nurse may also encourage self- directed
independent learning by encouraging the person to explore
sources of information, such as reliable websites. If certain
activities do not assist the learner to attain outcomes, these need
to be reassessed; perhaps other activities can replace them.
Explanation alone may not be able to teach a person to handle a
syringe. Actually handling the syringe may be more effective (see
Figure 28.3
).
Repetition reinforces learning. Summarising content, rephrasing
(using other words) and approaching the material from another
point of view are ways of repeating and clarifying content. For
instance, after discussing the kinds of foods that can be included
in a diet, the nurse describes the foods again, but in the context
of the three meals eaten during one day.
It is helpful to employ ‘organisers’ to introduce material to be
learned. Advanced organisers provide a means of connecting
unknown material to known material and generating logical
relationships. The following statement can be an advanced
organiser: ‘You understand how urine flows down a catheter from
the bladder. Now I will show you how to inject fluid so that it flows


up the catheter into the bladder’. The details that follow are then
seen within a framework that adds meaning.
The anticipated behavioural changes that indicate learning has
taken place must always be within the context of the person’s
lifestyle and resources. It would be unreasonable to expect a
woman to soak in a tub of hot water two times a day if she does
not have a bathtub or has to heat water on a stove.
Figure 28.3


Teaching activities may need to include hands-on patient
participation.
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.
Special teaching strategies
One-on-one discussion is the most common method of teaching
used by nurses. However, nurses can choose from a number of
special teaching strategies: contracts, group teaching, e-learning,
discovery/problem solving and behaviour modification. Any strategy
the nurse selects must be appropriate for the learner and the
learning objectives.
Learning contracts
This involves establishing a learning contract with a patient that
specifies certain outcomes and when they are to be met. Here is an
example of a learning contract:
I, Amy Martin, will exercise strenuously for 20 minutes three times per week for a period of
2 weeks and will then buy myself six yellow roses.
Amy Martin
Jennifer Ward, RN 30 July 2020
The contract, drawn up and signed by the person and the nurse,
may specify the learning outcomes, the responsibilities of the person
and the nurse, and the methods of follow-up and evaluation. The


contract can be changed in two ways: if the person meets the
contract outcomes and wants to negotiate new learning outcomes,
and if the person decides that they are unable to meet the existing
learning outcomes and wants to revise them. The learning contract
allows for freedom, mutual respect and mutual responsibility.
Group teaching
Group instruction is economical and provides members with an
opportunity to share with and learn from others. A small group
allows for discussion in which everyone can participate. A large
group often necessitates a lecture technique or use of films,
PowerPoint presentations or role playing by teachers.
It is important that all members involved in group instruction have a
common need (e.g. prenatal health or preoperative instruction). It is
also important that sociocultural factors be considered in the
formation of a group.
E-learning
E-learning
 approaches have become increasingly popular over
the past decade. Initially, the primary use of electronic educational
methods was learning of facts. When done well, e-learning
encourages critical thinking and independent learning practices
(Lees, Price & Andrews ). Computers, iPads and other similar
technologies can also be used to teach the following:
26


26 Lees, L., Price, D. & Andrews, A. (2010). Developing discharge practice through education.
Module development, delivery and outcomes. Nurse Education in Practice, 10, 210–215.
application of information (e.g. answering questions after reading
the information about a health subject)
psychomotor skills (e.g. filling a syringe on the computer screen
to the correct dosage line on the syringe)
complex problem-solving skills (e.g. responding to questions
based on a patient situation).
Computers can be used in a variety of ways:
individual health care professionals or patients using one
computer
families or small groups of three to five people gathering around
one computer taking turns to run the program and answering
questions together
large groups with a PowerPoint presentation, and a teacher or
one learner using the keyboard
individuals or small groups at computers using programs through
shared network platforms or through internet websites.
Individuals using a computer are able to set the pace that meets
their particular learning needs. Learners can read and view
informational material, answer questions and receive immediate
feedback. The correct answer is usually indicated by the use of
colours, flashing signs or written praise. When the learner selects an
incorrect answer, the computer may respond with an explanation of
why that was not the best answer and encouragement to try again.


Some computer programs feature simulated situations that allow
learners to manipulate objects on the screen to learn psychomotor
skills. When used to teach such skills, e-learning must be followed
up with practice on actual equipment supervised by the teacher.
Some people may have a negative attitude about computers that
could act as a barrier to learning. In order to successfully introduce
e-learning, it is essential to understand the person’s ICT
competence, confidence, attitudes and access to resources. The
nurse can help people who display resistance by explaining how the
computer can help meet their needs. Matching a computer program
or website to the person’s individual health circumstances may
encourage computer use. Providing a resource list of free available
community sites for training and access may also help. It is also
important for the nurse to teach people how to evaluate whether
websites provide relevant and credible sources of health information.
E-learning materials are also available for people with different
language needs, for people with special visual needs and for those
at different growth and development levels.
Discovery/problem solving
In using the discovery/problem- solving technique, the nurse
presents some initial information and then asks the learner a
question or presents a situation related to the information. The
learner applies the new information to the situation and decides what
to do. Learners can work alone or in groups. This technique is well


suited to family learning. The teacher guides the learners through
the thinking process necessary to reach the best solution to the
question or the best action to take in the situation. This may also be
referred to as anticipatory problem solving. For example, the nurse
educator might present information on diabetes and glucose
management. Then the nurse might ask the learners how they think
their insulin and/or diet should be adjusted if their morning glucose
was too low. In this way, the person and their family learn what
critical components they need to consider to reach the best solution
to the problem.
Behaviour modification
The behaviour modification system has as its basic assumptions: (a)
that human behaviours are learned and can be selectively
strengthened, weakened, eliminated or replaced; and (b) that a
person’s behaviour is under conscious control. Under this system,
desirable behaviour is rewarded and undesirable behaviour is
ignored. The person’s response is the key to behaviour change. For
example, people trying to quit smoking are not criticised when they
smoke, but they are praised or rewarded when they go without a
cigarette for a certain period of time. For some people, a learning
contract is combined with behaviour modification and includes the
following pertinent features:
Positive reinforcement (e.g. praise) is used.
The person participates in the development of the learning plan.
Undesirable behaviour is ignored, not criticised.


The expectation of the patient and the nurse is that the task will
be mastered (i.e. the behaviour will change).
Cultural considerations for teaching
Nurses and people from different cultural and ethnic backgrounds
have additional barriers to overcome in the teaching–learning
process. These barriers include language and communication
problems, differing concepts of time, conflicting cultural healing
practices, beliefs that may positively or negatively influence
compliance with health teaching and unique high-risk or high-
frequency health problems (see Chapter 19
). Nurses should
consider the following guidelines when teaching people from various
ethnic backgrounds:
Obtain teaching materials, pamphlets and instructions in
other languages. Nurses who are unable to read the foreign
language material for themselves can have the translator read
the material to them. The nurse can then evaluate the quality of
the information and update it with the translator’s help as
needed.
Use visual aids, such as pictures, charts, diagrams or films
to communicate meaning. Audiovisual material may be helpful
if the English is spoken clearly and slowly. Even if understanding
the verbal message is a problem for the person, seeing a skill or
procedure may be helpful. In some instances, a translator can be
asked to clarify the content of the DVD. Alternatively, the DVD


may be available in several languages and the nurse can request
the necessary version from the company.
Use concrete rather than abstract words. Use simple
language (short sentences, short words) and present only one
idea at a time.
Allow time for questions. This helps the person mentally
separate one idea or skill from another.
Avoid the use of medical terminology/jargon or health care
language, such as ‘taking your vital signs’ or ‘apical pulse’.
Rather, nurses should say they are going to take the person’s
blood pressure or listen to the person’s heart.
Do not use slang words or colloquialisms. These may be
interpreted literally.
If understanding a person’s pronunciation is a problem,
validate brief information in writing. For example, during
assessments, write down numbers, words or phrases and have
the person read them to verify accuracy.
Use humour very cautiously. Meaning can change in the
translation process.
Do not assume that a person who nods, uses eye contact or
smiles is indicating an understanding of what is being
taught. These responses may simply be the person’s way of
indicating respect. They may feel that asking the nurse questions
or stating a lack of understanding is inappropriate because it
might embarrass the nurse or cause the nurse to ‘lose face’.
Invite and encourage questions during teaching. Let people
know they are welcome to ask questions. When asking questions
to evaluate understanding, avoid asking negative questions.


These can be interpreted differently by people for whom English
is a second language. ‘Do you understand how far you can bend
your hip after surgery?’ is better than the negative question ‘You
don’t understand how far you can bend your hip after surgery, do
you?’. With particularly difficult information or skills teaching, the
nurse might say, ‘Most people have some trouble with this. May I
please help you go through this one more time?’. In some
cultures, expressing a need is not appropriate and expressing
confusion or asking to be shown something again is considered
rude.
When explaining procedures or functioning related to personal
areas of the body, it may be appropriate to have a nurse of the
same sex do the teaching. Because of modesty concerns in
many cultures and beliefs about what is considered appropriate
and inappropriate male–female interaction, it is often wise to
have a nurse of the same sex teach about issues such as
personal care, birth control, sexually transmitted diseases and
other potentially sensitive areas. If a translator is needed during
explanation of procedures or teaching, the translator should also
be the same sex.
Include the family in planning and teaching. This promotes
trust and mutual respect. Identify the authoritative family
member (when appropriate) and incorporate that person into the
planning and teaching to promote compliance and support of
health teaching. In some cultures, the male head of household is
the critical family member to include in health teaching; in other
cultures, it is the eldest female member.


Consider the person’s time orientation. The person may be
more oriented to the present than the nurse. Preventing future
problems may be less significant for some people than for
others, so teaching prevention may be more difficult. For
example, teaching a person why and when to take medications in
order to prevent long-term complications may be more difficult if
the person is oriented to the present. In such instances, the
nurse can emphasise preventing short-term problems rather than
long-term problems. Failure to keep clinic appointments or to
arrive on time is common in people who have a present-time
orientation. The nurse can help by accommodating these people
when they do arrive for their appointment.
Schedules may be very flexible in present-oriented societies, with
sleeping and eating patterns varying greatly. Teaching people to
take medications at bedtime or with a meal does not necessarily
mean that these activities will occur at the same time each day.
For this reason, the nurse should assess the person’s daily
routine before teaching them to pair a treatment or medication
with an event the nurse assumes occurs at the same time every
day. When teaching when to take medication, the nurse should
determine whether a clock or watch is available to the person
and whether they can tell the time.
Identify cultural health practices and beliefs. Non-compliance
with health teaching may be related to conflict with traditional
healing beliefs. Non-compliance may also be related to lack of
understanding or fatalism, a belief system in which life events are
held to be predestined or fixed in advance and the individual is
powerless to change them. To encourage compliance, the nurse


needs to learn the person’s explanation of why the illness
developed and how it might be treated. See ‘Culturally competent
care’ below.
The nurse should treat cultural healing beliefs with respect and try to
identify whether any are in agreement or in conflict with what is
being taught. The nurse can then focus on the ones in agreement to
promote the integration of new learning with the familiar health
practices. The goal is to arrive at a mutually agreeable plan, decide
which instructions must be followed and negotiate less traditional
healing practices.
Culturally competent care
For Indigenous Australians
Nurses need to be mindful of cultural differences when
teaching Indigenous Australians:
Be sensitive to the nuances in language. For example, if
an Indigenous Australian complains that ‘His spirit locates
in his navel’, this may mean that there are problems in the
abdominal area such as nausea or pain.
Do not mention the names of deceased people.
Be aware that ‘nodding of the head’ may be to please a
person and not necessarily about agreement with what
has been said.
The use of educational materials should encourage
‘yarning’ or, in other words, ‘storytelling’.


Be respectful of physical space and confidentiality for
‘women’s business’ and ‘men’s business’.
Some Indigenous Australians believe that it is polite to
avert one’s eyes when communicating.
Source: Summarised from M. Cribbes & K. Glaister
. ‘It’s not easy’: Caring for Aboriginal clients with
diabetes in remote Australia. Contemporary Nurse, 25, 163–172.
27 Cribbes, M. & Glaister, K. (2007). ‘It’s not easy’: Caring for Aboriginal clients with diabetes in
remote Australia. Contemporary Nurse, 25, 163–172.
Evaluating
Evaluating is both an ongoing and a final process in which the
person receiving care, the nurse and often the support people
determine what has been learned.
Evaluating learning
Learning is measured against the predetermined learning outcomes
selected in the planning phase of the teaching process. Thus, the
outcomes serve not only to direct the teaching plan but also to
provide outcome criteria for evaluation. For example, the learning
outcome ‘The patient will be able to select foods that are low in
carbohydrates’ can be evaluated by asking the person to name such
foods or to select low-carbohydrate foods from a list.
27


The best method for evaluating depends on the type of learning. In
cognitive learning, the person demonstrates acquisition of
knowledge. Examples of the evaluation tools for cognitive learning
include the following:
direct observation of behaviour (e.g. observing the person
selecting the solution to a problem using the new knowledge)
written measurements (e.g. tests)
oral questioning (e.g. asking the person to restate information or
correct verbal responses to questions)
self-reports and self-monitoring. These can be useful during
follow-up phone calls and home visits. Evaluating individual self-
paced learning, as might occur with computer-assisted
instruction, often incorporates self-monitoring.
The acquisition of psychomotor skills is best evaluated by observing
how well the person carries out a procedure such as self-
administration of insulin.
Affective learning is more difficult to evaluate. Whether attitudes or
values have changed may be inferred by listening to the person’s
responses to questions, noting how they speak about relevant
subjects and observing behaviours that express feelings and values.
For example, have parents learned to value health sufficiently to
have their children immunised? Do people who state that they value
safe sex actually use condoms every time they have sex with a new
partner?


Following evaluation, the nurse may find it necessary to modify or
repeat the teaching plan if the objectives have not been met or have
been met only partially. Follow-up teaching in the home or by phone
may be needed following discharge from a health facility.
Behaviour change does not always take place immediately after
learning. Often individuals accept change intellectually first and then
change their behaviour only periodically (e.g. a person who knows
that she must lose weight, diets and exercises off and on). If the
new behaviour is to replace the old behaviour it must emerge
gradually, otherwise the old behaviour may prevail. The nurse can
assist people with behaviour change by allowing for vacillation and
by providing encouragement.
Evaluating teaching
It is important for nurses to evaluate their own teaching and the
content of the teaching program, just as they evaluate the
effectiveness of other nursing interventions. Evaluation should
include a consideration of all factors—the timing, the teaching
strategies, the amount of information, whether the teaching was
helpful and so on. The nurse may find, for example, that the person
was overwhelmed with too much information, was bored or was
motivated to learn more.
Both the person and the nurse should evaluate the learning
experience. The person may tell the nurse what was helpful,


interesting and so on. Feedback questionnaires and recording the
learning sessions for later review can also be helpful.
The nurse should not feel ineffective as a teacher if the person
forgets some of what is taught. Forgetting is normal and should be
anticipated. Having the person write down information, repeating it
during teaching, giving handouts on the information and allowing the
person to be active in the learning process all promote retention.
Documenting
Documentation of the teaching process is essential because it
provides a legal record that the teaching took place and
communicates the teaching to other health professionals. If teaching
is not documented, legally it did not occur.
It is also important to document the responses of the person to
teaching activities. What did the person and/or their support person
say or do to indicate that learning occurred? Have they
demonstrated mastery of a skill or the acquisition of knowledge? The
nurse records this in the person’s chart as evidence of learning. An
example of documentation follows:
The parts of the teaching process that should be documented in the
person’s chart include the following:
diagnosed learning needs


learning outcomes
topics taught
achievement (or not) of learning outcomes
need for additional teaching
resources provided.
Case study
Mrs Huang is a 59-year-old Chinese bank chief executive
officer. Three days ago, she was admitted to the hospital with
complaints of shortness of breath and mild chest pain. She is
diagnosed with significant coronary artery disease but has not
yet suffered a myocardial infarction (heart attack). Her doctor
has indicated that Mrs Huang will need to make significant
lifestyle changes to reduce her cardiac risk factors. As her
nurse, you have been requested to teach Mrs Huang about
her disease process, diet, exercise and stress reduction. As
you begin teaching Mrs Huang, you note that she is very
pleasant and frequently nods her head, but she also seems
preoccupied and is readily distracted.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1.

 Using the Fundamentals of Care
Framework, consider why it is important to establish a
relationship with Mrs Huang in order to provide
education. Think specifically about the relationship
(e.g. trust) and relational aspects (e.g. engaging with
patients) of the Framework.


2. How would you evaluate Mrs Huang’s readiness to
learn?
3. Would a learning needs assessment be of any benefit
considering Mrs Huang is obviously a well-educated
person?
4. You recognise that you have a great deal of
information to deliver to Mrs Huang and you are
concerned that you will not be able to teach it all. What
can you do to help Mrs Huang and still accomplish the
learning outcomes?
5. How will you know if your teaching is effective?
6. How might your teaching differ if you were teaching
Mrs Huang at home rather than in a hospital or acute
care setting?


Chapter 28 Review


Chapter highlights
Teaching people and families about their health needs is an
important nursing role. Nurses also teach colleagues, nursing
students and community groups.
Learning is evidenced by a change in behaviour.
Three main theories of learning are behaviourism, cognitivism
and humanism.
Bloom identified three learning domains: cognitive, affective and
psychomotor.
A number of factors affect learning, including motivation,
readiness, active involvement, relevance, feedback, non-
judgmental support, repetition, timing, environment, emotions,
physiological events, psychomotor ability and cultural aspects.
Teaching, like the nursing process, consists of six activities:
assessing the learner, diagnosing learning needs, developing a
teaching plan, implementing the plan, evaluating learning
outcomes and teaching effectiveness, and documenting
instructional activities.
Teaching strategies chosen by the nurse should be suited to the
person and to the material to be learned.
A teaching plan is a written plan consisting of learning outcomes,
content to teach and strategies to use in teaching the content.
The plan must be revised when the person’s needs change or
the teaching strategies prove ineffective.
Evaluating the teaching–learning process is both an ongoing
(formative) and a final (summative) process in which the patient,


nurse and support people determine what has been learned.
Documentation of education is essential to communicate the
teaching to other health professionals and to provide a legal
record.
Concept check
1. Which of the following activities would be classified as the
affective domain of Bloom’s taxonomy?
1. Teaching how to administer an injection.
2. Learning to accept the loss of a limb.
3. Learning to insert a catheter.
4. Teaching how to read.
2. Which of the following is the best method of helping a newly
diagnosed diabetic person to learn the dietary requirements
associated with the disease?
1. Provide a video that addresses the dietary
requirements associated with the disease.
2. Ask a nutritionist to visit the person to present
information and handouts about the diabetic diet.
3. Ask the person to make a list of her favourite foods
and how to work them into her diet.
4. Have the person attend a group meeting for diabetic
people to discuss their adaptation to this chronic health
condition.


3. A nurse is scheduling a teaching situation. Which of the
following people is most ready to learn?
1. A 45-year-old man whose doctor has just informed him
that he has cancer.
2. A 3-year-old child whose parents are reading a story
book about going to the hospital.
3. A 60-year-old female who received medication 5
minutes ago for relief of abdominal pain.
4. A 70-year-old man recovering from a stroke who has
returned from physical therapy.
4. How can the nurse best assess a person’s style of learning?
1. Ask the person how they learn best.
2. Use a variety of teaching strategies.
3. Observe the person’s interactions with others.
4. Ask the person’s family members.
5. A 74-year-old person who takes multiple medications tells the
nurse, ‘I have no idea what that little yellow pill is for’. What is
the best nursing diagnosis for this person?
1. Knowledge deficit.
2. Health-seeking behaviour.
3. Deficient knowledge (medication information).
4. Non-compliance.
6. A person is scheduled to have a diagnostic procedure. Which
questions by the nurse will most likely produce a ‘teachable
moment’? Select all that apply.


1. ‘Have you ever had this procedure before?’
2. ‘What are your concerns about this procedure?’
3. ‘What would you like to know about the procedure?’
4. ‘Are you prepared for this procedure?’
7. A person needs to learn to self-administer insulin injections.
Which statements reflect possible low literacy skills? Select all
that apply.
1. ‘I will read the information later—I’m too tired right
now.’
2. ‘I’ve watched my brother give his own injections. I
know how to do it.’
3. ‘Just show my wife.’
4. ‘Do you have a video showing how I should give myself
the injection?’
8. A general practitioner admitted a person experiencing
hypertensive crisis because of the failure to ingest prescribed
medications. To determine learning needs, which assessment
would have the highest priority?
1. Person’s age.
2. Person’s perception of the effects of hypertension.
3. Person’s ability to purchase needed medications.
4. Person’s support system.
9. A person has a learning outcome of ‘Select foods that are low
in fat content’. Which of the following statements reflect that
the person has met this learning outcome?


1. ‘I understand the importance of maintaining a low-fat
diet.’
2. ‘I feel better about myself now.’
3. ‘See how I revised my favourite recipe to be lower in
fat.’
4. ‘Since changing my diet, my husband is also losing
weight.’
10. A person’s learning outcome is ‘Patient will verbalise
medication name, purpose and appropriate precautions’.
Which of the following documented statements reflect
evidence of learning?
1. Taught name, purpose and precautions for the new
cardiac medication; seemed to understand.
2. Written information about the medication provided and
reviewed; correct responses were given to follow-up
questions.
3. Written information read to patient; stated he would
read it when he got home.
4. Asked questions about the new cardiac medication;
satisfied with the information.
Focus on critical thinking
1. At times, the people you care for may be resistant to
changing their behaviours or learning new skills. How will you


reconcile the conflict between autonomy/self- determination
and your responsibility to provide health education?
2. Consider three situations when a person may be reluctant or
resistant to learn. For each, identify the key issues and an
appropriate approach.
3. Describe how a person-centred approach influences the way
nurses engage in teaching−learning interactions.

Do you want to become an effective leader?
Becoming an effective leader involves
commitment, passion, education and
experience. Leaders also need a clear vision
and the ability to adapt to change and see the
‘big picture’.
Around the world, nurses are beginning to
realise that leadership is critical to improving the
nursing profession, to reforming health care
systems and, most importantly, to delivering
safe and effective patient care.
Leadership impacts on the workplace culture
and effective and compassionate leaders have
a positive impact on staff retention. Effective
leaders involve and support their staff and
optimise their level of motivation, satisfaction


and performance (World Health Organization
(WHO) ).

Excellent leadership is essential to the delivery
of high-quality, safe and empathetic health care
(West et al. ) and, in contemporary health care,
all nurses need effective leadership skills
(Scully ; Xu ). Safe patient care depends on
nursing graduates having the ability to supervise
and delegate appropriately, communicate
effectively within their team and with other
health professionals, collaborate with patients
and their caregivers, and provide leadership in
the management of patient care (Morrow ).
Even as undergraduates, you are expected to
show effective and compassionate leadership
within your peer group and when on clinical
placements. This chapter provides an
introduction to contemporary nursing leadership
and will help you to reflect on your own
leadership style, attributes and skills. It will also
help you to prepare to become an effective
compassionate nursing leader.

The nurse as leader and manager
Nurses frequently act as both leaders and managers—managers
must have leadership abilities and leaders often manage—but the
roles do differ. Leadership and management are often referred to as
if they are interchangeable terms, but the two are very different
(Kotte ). Leaders
 are visionary; they are informed, articulate,
confident and self-aware, and have outstanding interpersonal skills
and the ability to motivate others to work together towards a
common goal. Leaders communicate effectively and have the ability
and confidence to innovate change, transform current practice,
motivate, facilitate and mentor others. Nurse leaders work in a
variety of positions—from in charge of shift to chief executive
officers. However, it is also important to remember that nursing
students and graduates also assume a wide range of leadership
roles.
6 Kotte, J. (2013). Management Is (Still) Not Leadership. Retrieved from
<http://blogs.hbr.org>.
A manager
 is an employee given authority, power and
responsibility for planning, organising, coordinating and directing
other people’s work, and for establishing and evaluating standards.
Managers understand organisational structure and culture; control
human, financial and material resources; set goals; make decisions
and solve problems; and initiate and implement change.
6


Nursing leaders:
improve the health status of individuals and families
enhance colleagues’ effectiveness and levels of job satisfaction
improve the attitudes and expectations of the general public and
legislators towards the nursing profession.
Nurse managers are responsible for:
efficiently accomplishing the goals of the organisation
use of the organisation’s resources
ensuring compliance with institutional, professional, legal,
regulatory and governmental standards
supporting the professional development of all staff within their
team.

Global leadership and policy
A policy is a declared set of actions, principles or a plan of what to
do in a particular circumstance. Too often nurses have not been
involved in important policy decisions that affect the profession, their
patients and the health care systems. This is sometimes because
nurses have not fully understood the critical importance of being
involved in policy development and implementation. However, this is
changing as nurses learn the leadership skills required to effect
change through policy.
As part of the global initiative to ensure more equitable and equal
health care for the world’s populations, the WHO (2016) has been
setting the agenda for the development of a global strategy for
human resources for health, and global nursing leaders have been
involved in the development of this strategy. With the acute
shortages of nurses, doctors and other health care professions in
many parts of the world, many people miss out on much needed
care, health promotion and education. One of the objectives of the
WHO (2016) global strategy is to build leadership capacity in
national and international institutions to support effective governance
for human health care resources. This involves nurses and other
health care professionals developing core competencies in human
resources policy, planning and management. You have made a start
in developing core competencies by reading this chapter and


attending classes on leadership and management, but this is just the
beginning of your journey to become an effective leader.
In various spheres, nurses are working on developing global nursing
leadership competencies, as well as competencies in global health,
infectious diseases, professional and social issues and many other
specialties. Transformation in health care and within society cannot
take place without effective leaders, and as you become a more
experienced nurse, you will find that you need further development
of your leadership skills.


Leadership
Leadership theory
Some of the key findings from research into leadership over the past
80 years are discussed in this chapter. Research about trait theory,
leadership competencies, leadership behaviours, didactic
approaches and charismatic and transformational leadership
theories are briefly outlined.
An impressive amount of research has provided no clear and
unequivocal understanding of what makes an effective leader.
Theories include the existence of particular distinguishing traits such
as charisma, confidence, integrity, energy, intelligence and
commitment, but none is invariably associated with leadership
because that is so dependent on culture and context. In contrast,
situational leadership theories highlight the importance of context in
deciding the right approach in any given situation. The predominant
theory today is that compassionate leadership has the capacity to
transform the experience of health care professionals as well as
consumers. Given the opportunities, people can choose to be
effective leaders and that leadership skills can be learnt.


The continued interest in leadership is evident from the large
number of books and articles on the subject in both a nursing
context and the corporate world. Influential Australian writer Alistair
Mant  argued that good leadership requires a focus on a goal,
purpose or idea; an ability to view the system as a whole; and a
healthy rather than pathological leadership style. However,
increasing recognition that leaders cannot exist without followers has
focused attention on the extent to which leadership effectiveness is
influenced by the characteristics of the group—the notion of
‘followership
’ (Kouzes & Posner ). Positive workplace culture, or
success of a health care service, may lie in the hands of the
‘followers’, as they exist in an inter-related context with the leader
(Abdel Malak ).
7 Mant, A. (1997). Intelligent Leadership. St Leonards: Allen & Unwin.
8 Kouzes, J. M. & Posner, B. Z. (2007). The Leadership Challenge (4th ed.). San Francisco:
Jossey-Bass.
9 Abdel Malak, R. S. (2016). A concept analysis of ‘follower’ within the context of professional
nursing. Nursing Forum, 51(4), 286–294.

The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that for nursing students to collaborate
and communicate effectively with members of
7
8
9


health care teams, facilitating mutual respect
and shared decision making, they must first
demonstrate the ability to discuss the impact of
effective leadership and followership on team
dynamics (Levett-Jones et al.
).
10 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
