Early leadership theories focused on what leaders are (trait
theories), what they do (behavioural theories) and how they adapt
their style according to the situation (contingency theories).
Behaviourists believe that through education, training and life
experiences leaders develop a particular leadership style
,
characterised as autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire or
bureaucratic.
Likened to a dictator, the authoritarian (autocratic) leader
determines policies, giving orders and directions to the group who
may feel secure under this leadership style because procedures are
well defined, activities are predictable and productivity may be high;
however, members are often dissatisfied with this leadership style.
The group’s needs for creativity, autonomy and self-motivation are
not met, and the degree of openness and trust between the leader
10


and the group members is minimal or absent. At times, however, an
authoritarian style is the most effective: when urgent decisions are
necessary (e.g. a cardiac arrest, a hospital fire or an aggressive
incident), one person must assume the responsibility for making
decisions without being challenged.
A democratic (participative, consultative) leader
 encourages
discussion and decision making, acting as a catalyst or facilitator,
actively guiding people towards achievement of group goals.
Assuming individuals to be internally motivated (their driving force
intrinsic, they desire self-satisfaction) and capable of making
decisions and valuing independence, the participative leader focuses
on providing constructive feedback, offering information, making
suggestions and asking questions; productivity and satisfaction are
high because group members contribute to the work effort. This
leadership style demands faith in the group members’ ability to
accomplish the goals. Democratic leadership allows group self-
motivation and creativity and calls for a great deal of cooperation
and coordination; this style can be extremely effective in health care
settings.
The laissez-faire (non-directive, permissive) leader
 recognises
the group’s need for autonomy and self-regulation, assuming a
‘hands-off’ approach and presupposing internal motivation; however,
group members may act independently and at cross-purposes
because of a lack of cooperation and coordination. The laissez-faire
style is most effective for groups whose members have both
personal and professional maturity, so that once a decision has been


made, they become committed to it and have the ability to
implement it, performing tasks in their area of expertise while the
leader acts as resource person. Table 29.2
 compares the
authoritarian, democratic and laissez-faire leadership styles.
Table 29.2 Comparison of authoritarian, democratic and laissez-
faire leadership styles
The bureaucratic leader
 trusts neither self nor others to make
decisions and relies instead on the organisation’s rules, policies and
procedures to direct work efforts. Such inflexibility and impersonal
relationships can cause the group to be dissatisfied.
According to contingency theorists, effective leaders adapt their
leadership style to the situation. A popular contingency theory
describes situational leaders. They (a) make a conscious choice
between directive and supportive behaviours, (b) consider staff
members’ abilities, (c) know the nature of the task and (d) are
sensitive to the ambient context or environment. Task orientation
focuses on activities that encourage group productivity. The
relationship-orientation style is concerned with interpersonal
relationships and focuses on activities that meet group members’
needs.
Situational leaders
 adapt their leadership style to the readiness
and willingness of the individual or group to perform the assigned
task. When employees are insecure or unable or unwilling to
perform the task, the leader uses a highly directive style, providing


specific instructions and close supervision. If the group is motivated
and willing but unable to perform the task, the leader again uses a
highly directive style, but in this case explains decisions and provides
the opportunity for clarification. When the group is able but unwilling
or lacking in confidence, the leader shares ideas and facilitates
decision making. With a group that is willing, able and confident to
perform the task, the leader delegates, turning responsibility for
decision making and implementation over to the group.
Contemporary leadership theories
Contemporary theorists have described charismatic leaders,
transactional leaders, transformational leaders and shared
leadership. Charismatic leadership
 is rare and is characterised
by an emotional relationship between the group members and the
leader, whose charming personality evokes strong feelings of
commitment to the leader and to the leader’s cause and beliefs.
The transactional leader’s
 relationship with followers is based on
possession of the resources or power to reward them with
incentives, such as promotion, which are used to promote loyalty
and performance; for example, in order to ensure adequate staffing
on the night shift, the nurse manager entices a Registered Nurse to
work it in exchange for a weekend shift off duty. The transactional
leader represents the traditional manager, focused on the day-to-day
tasks of achieving organisational goals and understanding and
meeting the needs of the group.


In contrast, a transformational leader
 fosters creativity, risk
taking, commitment and collaboration by empowering the group to
share in the organisation’s vision. The leader inspires others with a
clear, attractive and attainable goal, and enlists them to participate in
achieving it. Through shared values, honesty, trust and continual
learning, the leader empowers the group; independence, individual
growth and change are facilitated.
Shared leadership
 recognises that a professional workforce is
made up of many leaders. No one person is considered to have
knowledge or ability beyond that of other members of the work
group. Appropriate leadership is thought to emerge in relation to the
challenges that confront the work group. Examples of shared
leadership in nursing are self-directed work teams, co-leadership
and shared governance. Shared governance
 is a method that
aims to distribute decision making among a group of people.
Cross-cultural leadership
 theory has developed over the past
few decades as a way to understand leaders who work in a
globalised world, and this theory can be applied to understand the
work of nurse leaders working across countries or cultures. In
today’s world, we need leaders with the ability to adjust quickly to
different environments and work with partners and employees of
other cultures (House, Javidan & Dorfman ).
11 House, R., Javidan, M. & Dorfman, P. (2001). Project GLOBE: An introduction. Applied
Psychology: An International Review, 50(4), 489−505.
11


A philosophy that has gained some ground among nurse leaders is
that of servant leadership
, the idea that leadership begins with a
motivation to serve others, to communicate and establish shared
goals rather than merely directing (Greenleaf
). The principles of
servant leadership—listening, empathy, healing relationships,
awareness, persuasion, conceptualisation, foresight, stewardship,
commitment to others’ professional development and building
community—can enhance quality patient care and improve staff
satisfaction (Neill & Saunders ).
12 Greenleaf, R. K. (2008). The Greenleaf Center for Servant Leadership. Retrieved from
<www.greenleaf.org>.
13 Neill, M. W. & Saunders, N. S. (2010). Servant leadership: Enhancing quality of care and
staff satisfaction. Journal of Nursing Administration, 38, 395–400.
As the body of research exploring compassion in health care grows,
so too does the concept of compassionate leadership
.
Compassionate leadership falls into the transformational category of
a leader. In the wake of reports of lack of compassion and poor care
quality (Francis ), compassionate leadership has become a
possible remedy. Compassionate, patient-centred nursing is still
expected to flourish in a financially constrained environment where
health care is now commodified (Jakimowicz & Perry ), putting
more pressure than ever on our nursing workforce. A
compassionate nursing leader empowers their followers (patients
and colleagues), makes time and space to listen while embracing
risk, establishes clear expectations and builds team and individual
12
13
14
15


capacity. A compassionate leader is emotionally intelligent,
authentic, open, caring, mindful, kind and respectful.
14 Francis, R. (2001). Learning from Bristol: The Report of the Public Inquiry into Children's
Heart Surgery at the Bristol Royal Infirmary 1984–1995. Bristol Royal Infirmary Inquiry, July
2001. Retrieved from <www.bristol-inquiry.org.uk>.
15 Jakimowicz, S. & Perry, L. (2015). A concept analysis of patient-centred nursing in the
intensive care unit. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 71(7), 1499–1517.
Leadership is a universal phenomenon: wherever people live, work
and play, there are leaders. However, because much of the writing
about leadership (and management) is written from a Western
perspective, the reader is encouraged to think about whether the
leadership styles described in this chapter actually translate across
cultures. The core ingredients of leadership (good judgment,
integrity and people skills) are universal, however (Chamorro-
Premuzic & Sanger
). Different cultures may hold different values,
beliefs and attitudes about what constitutes a good leader, so it
follows that what we may understand in Western cultures as good
leadership may not hold true in other cultures. For example, our
neighbours in south-east Asia value consensus more than we do in
Australia; consequently, decision making may take more time as
leaders aim for unanimous agreement. Leaders working across
cultures therefore need to understand and apply the concepts of
cultural competence, cultural safety and culturally congruent
approaches.
16 Chamorro-Premuzic, T. & Sanger, M. (2016). What leadership looks like in different
cultures. Harvard Business Review, May, 30–31.
16


Effective leadership
Principles of effective leadership include vision, compassion,
influence and acting as a role model. Box 29.1
 lists the
characteristics of effective leaders. How do your own leadership
abilities compare with these ideal characteristics? What evidence do
you have to support your view?
BO X
29.1 Characteristics of effective
leaders
Effective leaders
use a leadership style that is natural to them
use a leadership style appropriate to the task and the
members
assess the effects of their behaviour on others and the
effects of others’ behaviour on themselves
are sensitive to forces acting for and against change
express an optimistic view about human nature
are energetic
are open and encourage openness so that real issues are
confronted
facilitate personal relationships


motivate, empower and inspire
are consistent in behaviour towards group members
delegate tasks and responsibilities to develop members’
abilities, not merely to get tasks performed
involve members in all decisions
value and use group members’ contributions
encourage creativity
encourage feedback about their leadership style
model self-awareness and self-care
assess for and promote use of current technology
Vision
 is a mental image of a possible and desirable future state.
Leaders transform visions into realistic goals and communicate their
visions to others, who may accept them as their own. An example of
a vision would be: ‘Healthy people: healthy communities’.
Compassion
 comprises three components: attentiveness,
empathy and ‘intelligent’ action (West 2015). Compassionate nursing
leaders have the capacity to cultivate a positive workplace,
transforming nurses’, other health professionals’ and patients’
experiences into one of connectedness and optimism.
Influence
 is an informal strategy used to gain the cooperation of
others without exercising formal authority. Influence is exercised
through persuasion and excellent communication skills; it is based
on a trusting relationship with the followers.


An effective leader shows sensitivity about being a positive role
model
, demonstrating compassion towards colleagues and
patients. Appropriately for any health and caring profession,
leadership can also be humanistic, placing stress on individual
dignity and worth. Being a good leader takes thought, care, insight,
commitment and energy, setting the example for others to follow.

What does compassionate care look like to
me?

like to me?


Management
This chapter is focused largely on leadership, but as a beginning
nurse you need to also learn about the key function of a nursing
manager.
Management functions
Four management functions—planning, organising, directing and
coordinating—help to achieve the broad goal of quality patient care.
Planning
Planning
 is an ongoing process of (a) assessing a situation, (b)
establishing goals and objectives based on assessment of current
conditions or future trends and (c) developing a plan of action which
identifies priorities, delineates staff responsibility, determines
deadlines and specifies how the intended outcome is to be achieved
and evaluated. Resource allocation covers distribution of money,
staff, equipment and physical space. A top-level manager spends
considerable time on planning and strategy; frontline managers,
such as nurse unit managers, spend less time planning and more on
the day-to-day functioning of their unit.


Risk management
 forms part of the planning. This means having
in place a system to reduce danger to patients and staff,
embodying, anticipating and seeking possible sources; analysing,
classifying and prioritising risks; developing a plan to avoid and
manage risk; gathering data to indicate success in avoiding or
minimising risk; and evaluating and modifying risk reduction
programs. Communication between everyone involved is central to
the process.
Organising
Organising
 is also an ongoing process: determining
responsibilities, specifying expectations and establishing the chain of
command for authority and communication. After identifying the task
and evaluating human and material resources, the manager
arranges the task into smaller units. Top-level managers delegate
much of the work and responsibility to others, but they retain
accountability and need to clearly communicate departmental
objectives, priorities, job descriptions, lines of communication,
nursing standards, procedures and policies.
Directing
Directing
 is the process of setting strategic directions to be
followed in order to accomplish the organisation’s mission and
objectives. It is an executive function of corporate governors
(leaders) who set the goals for managers to implement; it embraces
establishing a vision, setting goals and managing interfaces between


departments and with other organisations. Directing at this level
generally involves supervision of the next level, such as those in
middle management.
Coordinating
Coordinating
 is the process of implementing execution and
evaluation of plans. The manager measures results or actions
against standards or desired outcomes, then reinforces effective
procedures or changes ineffective ones; for example, an upper-level
manager evaluates the effectiveness of recruitment, staff turnover
and budget performance; the nurse unit manager appraises staff
performance; the Registered Nurse determines whether nursing
interventions have helped the person achieve desired outcomes.
Principles of management
A manager has authority, accountability and responsibility.
Authority
 is defined as the legitimate right to direct the work of
others; it is an integral component of managing.
Accountability
 is ability and willingness to assume responsibility
for one’s actions and accept the consequences of one’s behaviour.
Accountability can be viewed as hierarchical: it is reflected at the
individual level in terms of the nurse’s ethical integrity and
behaviours; at the institutional level in the statement of philosophy


and objectives of the nursing department and nursing audits; at the
professional level in standards of practice developed by nursing
registration boards or professional organisations; and at the societal
level in legislated nurse practice acts.
Responsibility
 is an obligation to complete a task. Managers are
responsible for utilisation of resources, communication to
subordinates and implementation of organisational goals and
objectives.
Skills and competencies of nurse
leaders
Today’s health care environment is incredibly complex and
demanding, especially in acute inpatient settings, and nursing
leadership requires knowledge, critical thinking skills and
interpersonal capabilities. As a student nurse, you will have a unique
opportunity to observe a number of leaders and watch their
interactions with others, and start to model your own behaviours on
those you admire.
To be effective, leaders need emotional intelligence and the ability to
think critically, communicate well, manage resources effectively and
efficiently, delegate, collaborate, enhance the team’s performance
and staff satisfaction, provide clinical leadership, manage conflict,
and initiate and manage change.


Emotional intelligence
Emotional intelligence (EI)
 has been defined as ‘the ability to
perceive accurately, appraise, and express emotion; the ability to
access and/or generate feelings when they facilitate thought; the
ability to understand emotion and emotional knowledge; and the
ability to regulate emotions to promote emotional and intellectual
growth’ (Mayer & Salovey , p. 35). It has been suggested that
emotional intelligence is twice as important as intellectual ability for
effective leadership (Goleman ). Emotional intelligence provides a
framework by which a leader’s behaviours can be measured and has
been researched by Feather
 in relation to its impact on staff
satisfaction and staff retention. Feather found that successful
leaders are attuned to the emotional aspects of workplace issues,
anticipating how their staff will react, and that nurse leaders need to
develop self-awareness, self-management, social awareness and
social skills in order to be successful.
17 Mayer, J. & Salovey, P. (1997). What is emotional intelligence? In P. Salovey & D. Sluyter
(Eds), Emotional Development and Emotional Intelligence: Educational Implications (pp. 3–
31). New York: Perseus Books Group.
18 Goleman, D. (1998). Working with Emotional Intelligence. London: Bloomsbury.
19 Feather, R. (2009). Emotional intelligence in relation to nursing leadership: Does it matter?
Journal of Nursing Management, 17, 376–382.
Critical thinking
17
18
19


Critical thinking is a creative cognitive process that includes problem
solving and decision making. The nurse manager reasons with logic,
exploring assumptions, alternatives and the consequences of
actions. See Chapter 11
 for a more detailed discussion of critical
thinking.
Communicating
Managers spend much of their day communicating. Good
communication, both verbal and written, is essential; it determines
success as a leader and is core to efficient nursing practice.
Effective managers use the ‘five Cs’ to communicate clearly,
concisely, confidently, credibly and in a compelling manner (Lewis &
Mills
). See Chapter 27
 for a more detailed discussion of
communication.
20 Lewis, D. & Mills, G. (2017). The Pin Drop Principle: Captivate, Influence and
Communicate Better Using the Time-Tested Methods of Professional Performers. California:
Jossey-Bass, Wiley Imprint.
Managing resources
One of managers’ greatest responsibilities is accountability for
human, fiscal and material resources; budgeting and determining
variance between actual and budgeted expenses are crucial skills for
any manager.
Delegation
20


Delegation is the transference of responsibility and authority for an
activity to a competent individual. An essential part of delegation is
trust in the ability of the person to whom one is delegating a task
(Anderson ). All involved are accountable for their own actions or
inaction, and are potentially liable if competent and safe care is not
provided (Anderson 2012).
21 Anderson, L. (2012). Guidelines to Effective Nursing Delegation, 2013. Retrieved from
<www.nursetogether.com>.
Delegation is a tool that allows the delegator to devote more time to
strategic initiatives that cannot be delegated. It also enhances the
skills and abilities of the delegate, which builds self-esteem,
promotes morale and enhances teamwork and attainment of the
organisation’s goals.
A Registered Nurse who delegates a task to another health care
worker is accountable for selecting an appropriately skilled caregiver
and for continued evaluation of the nursing care. The Registered
Nurse should understand the role and function of the Enrolled Nurse
and any other non-nurse support workers to ensure that the task
being delegated does not exceed the limits of their education,
competence, experience and legal authority. The Nursing and
Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) Registered Nurse Standards
for Practice  also state that Registered Nurses must use
delegation, supervision, coordination, consultation and referrals in
professional relationships to achieve improved health outcomes.
21
22


22 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016). Registered Nurse Standards for
Practice. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au/>.
Clinical consideration
All students, nurses and other registered or
non-nursing health care providers are
responsible for their own actions; anyone who
feels unqualified to perform a delegated task
must decline to do so.
Enhancing the team’s performance
Several ways to enhance employee performance are available to
nurse leaders, who are responsible for facilitating their team’s
development by providing appropriate learning opportunities through
in-service education, attendance at professional workshops and
conferences, or encouraging achievement of advanced education
such as diplomas or higher degrees. Nursing leaders empower
others by the provision of information, support, resources and
opportunities to participate; empowered staff have greater
commitment to the institution, are more effective in their role, have
increased self-esteem and are better able to meet their goals.
Factors identified by nurses as motivation to perform well include
autonomous practice, good working relationships, resource


accessibility, allocated rostered time, individual nurse characteristics
and leadership practices (Jakimowicz, Perry & Lewis ).
23 Jakimowicz, S., Perry, L. & Lewis, J. (2017). Insights on compassion and patient-centred
nursing in intensive care: A constructivist grounded theory. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 27(7),
1599–1611.
Staff satisfaction
Nursing leaders and managers are responsible for enhancing
teamwork within the organisation. They therefore need to be familiar
with group processes. Groups develop in stages, during which roles
and relationships are established. The purposes of the team as a
whole and the role of each member must be clear: every member
must feel that their contributions are recognised and valued by the
manager and the other members. Some of the factors linked to staff
satisfaction have been summarised by Duffield et al.
 as feeling
valued, working autonomously, being able to provide person-centred
care and having strong nursing leadership, a cohesive working
environment, a fair and appropriate workload and meaning and
purpose in one’s work. Effective leaders see the big picture while
simultaneously considering the individual consequence; this is
demonstrated through understanding and compassion.
24 Duffield, C., Roche, M., O’Brien-Pallas, L., Catling-Paull, C. & King, M. (2009). Staff
satisfaction and retention and the role of the Nursing Unit Manager. Collegian, 16, 11–17.
Clinical leadership
23
24


While there is strong agreement that clinical leadership
 is
critical, there is no agreed definition (Mannix, Wilkes & Luck ).
Clinical nursing leadership has as its priority continuous
improvement through influencing others. Preparation for clinical
leadership should begin in undergraduate nursing programs as
anyone who is coordinating another person’s care is in a leadership
role. There is recognition that clinical leadership is required of all
nurses, not just those in positions of power (Brown, Crookes &
Dewing ). Clinical leadership requires knowledge of the role of the
nurse, safety, care planning, ethics, understanding of the clinical
skills required in a specific work context (e.g. critical care specialty),
cultural diversity and group dynamics (Brown et al. 2016), as well as
skills such as written and verbal communication, ability to deal with
change, computer literacy and conflict management. Clinical leaders
are expected to behave responsibly and be accountable,
appropriately assertive and honest (Brown et al. 2016, p. 110).
25 Mannix, J., Wilkes, L. & Luck, L. (2009). Key stakeholders in clinical learning and teaching
in Bachelor of Nursing programs: A discussion paper. Contemporary Nurse, 32(1–2), 59–68.
26 Brown, A., Crookes, P. & Dewing, J. (2016). Clinical leadership development in a pre-
registration nursing curriculum: What the profession has to say about it. Nurse Education
Today, 36, 105–111. Doi: 10.1016/j.nedt.2015.08.006.
Managing conflict
Nurse leaders frequently find themselves in a position of having to
manage conflict between people, groups or teams with differing
values, philosophies or personalities. In health care, conflict can
25
26


arise also from competition for resources, the pressure for change,
interdisciplinary issues and role confusion.
There are many approaches the manager can use to manage
conflict and each has its advantages and disadvantages. Many
nurses have these demands to deal with in addition to shift work and
continued study. A compassionate leader considers each individual
circumstance. Simple initiatives include scheduling meetings in
normal working hours, encouraging nurses to have a say in rostering
arrangements and flexibility in working hours.
Clinical considerations
When I am involved in conflict with another
person, to what extent do I accurately listen
to, consider and represent viewpoints I
disagree with?
Do I behave in accordance with what I say I
believe, or do I tend to say one thing and do
another?
To what extent do I expect the same of
myself as I expect of others?
Managing time


The competent leader uses time effectively and assists others to do
the same. Many factors inhibit the good use of time, such as a
preference for doing things the way ‘they have always been done’
rather than considering and embracing new approaches. Strategies
for the manager and for all nurses for profitable use of time involve
setting goals and priorities, delegating appropriately, examining how
time is used, minimising paperwork, instituting regular schedules to
avoid interruption and setting time limits on activities (Sullivan &
Decker
).
27 Sullivan, E. J. & Decker, P. J. (2009). Effective Leadership and Management in Nursing
(7th ed.). Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice Hall.
Some helpful strategies include the following:
Ensure that you agree on priorities with your manager.
Decide on the top three goals in your life and take care to spend
the majority of your time working towards these goals.
Schedule time in your day to answer emails; opening them the
minute they arrive can lead to constant interruptions to your train
of thought.
Distinguish between urgent and important items and set aside
time to work on high-priority tasks.
Write a list before you go home of what you need to do the
following day.
Think about what time of day you concentrate best and use that
time to work on important documents.
27


Managers must role-model work–life balance for their own benefit
and their staff and, where possible, provide flexible work
arrangements to enable employees to participate in the workforce
and to fulfil their family and lifestyle commitments (Australian
Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW)
). It is important for
managers and staff alike to practise self-care to maintain the
capability to continue practising clinically. Lack of balance is
associated with stress, alcohol abuse, relationship breakdown and
depression, and work-related issues such as high staff turnover and
low morale.
28 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2017). Australia’s Welfare 2017.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Clinical consideration
Time is such a precious resource that it is
worthwhile thinking about how you can save
time. Ask yourself ‘What am I doing that doesn’t
really need to be done?’, ‘What am I doing that
could be done by someone else?’ and ‘What am
I doing that could be done more efficiently?’.
28


Cultural diversity
It is increasingly recognised that nursing practice and research must
take into account cultural competence, cultural safety and culturally
congruent approaches to ensure establishment of appropriate health
care interventions and practices (Stout & Downey ). Australia is a
culturally diverse nation of around 25.5 million people. Around 28.5%
of Australians were born overseas, and nurse leaders and managers
must keep this fact uppermost in their minds in their daily work.
Indigenous Australians comprise 3% of Australia’s population
(Australian Bureau of Statistics ). The life expectancy of Indigenous
people is 11.1 years less than non-Indigenous people (AIHW
).
They are less likely to finish high school or enter university, are
under-represented in the nursing profession (CATSINaM
) and
make up only 1.2% of health service managers (Martins &
Isouard ). It is important that we use culturally congruent
approaches to reduce barriers for Indigenous people when they
access health care services. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Island
Australians have better health outcomes and are more likely to
access health services when they ‘are respectful and culturally safe’
(CATSINaM 2017).
29 Stout, M. & Downey, B. (2006). Nursing, indigenous peoples and cultural safety.
Contemporary Nurse, 22, 2–5.
29
30
31
32
33


30 Australian Bureau of Statistics (2016). Indigenous Populations of Australia and New
Zealand. Canberra: Commonwealth of Australia. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
31 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018). Deaths in Australia. Canberra:
AIHW. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
32 CATSINaM (2017). Position Statement: Embedding Cultural Safety Across Australian
Nursing and Midwifery. Canberra: Congress of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Nurses
and Midwives. Retrieved from <www.catsinam.org.au>.
33 Martins, J. M. & Isouard, G. (2012). Health Service Managers in Australia part 4: Hours
worked, marital status, country of birth and Indigenous status. Asia Pacific Journal of Health
Management, 7(2), 59−70.
Disparities in care and access to care are evident in the health care
system. Culturally insensitive care is characterised by a lack of
collaboration between care providers and health care consumers.
People from culturally diverse backgrounds may be bewildered by
the lack of information about health and intimidated by culturally
insensitive environments and interactions that discount their health
beliefs and cultural background (Hedlund et al.
, p. 6). Strategies
for improving this include increasing cultural competency training
and increasing diversity in leadership (Dolan ). How well nurses
manage culturally diverse teams will determine whether an
organisation derives benefit from having such teams (Nederveen
Pieterse, van Knippenberg & van Dierendonck ).
34 Hedlund, N., Esparza, A., Calhoun, E. & Yates, J. (2012). The importance of staff diversity
to address disparity. Physician Executive Journal, Sep/Oct, 6–12.

Healthcare Management, 58(2), 84–86.
36 Nederveen Pieterse, A., van Knippenberg, D. & van Dierendonck, D. (2013). Cultural
diversity and team performance: The role of team member goal orientation. Academy of
Management Journal, 56(3), 782–804.
Patient safety competency framework
3 Cultural competence
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must
demonstrate respect for each person’s cultural
values, beliefs, life experiences and health
practices. Nursing students must have a high
level of knowledge and be able to demonstrate
cultural competence skills to ensure safe and
effective clinical practice (Levett-Jones et al.
2017).


Clinical governance
Clinical governance
 refers to a system of policies, processes
and accountabilities directed at improving patient safety and the
quality and effectiveness of patient care.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: clinical governance
The National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards specify that clinical governance is
critical for maintaining and improving the
reliability, safety and quality of health care, and
improving health outcomes for patients
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in
Health Care (ACSQHC ).
37 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC) (2017a). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
In contrast with ‘corporate governance’, which is concerned with
structures, systems and processes that assure the quality,
37


accountability and proper management of an organisation’s
operation and delivery of service, it applies only to care delivery
aspects.
A Clinical Governance Framework developed by the ACSQHC aims
to ensure that ‘the community and health service organisations can
be confident that systems are in place to deliver safe and high-
quality health care, and continuously improve services’ (ACSQHC ,
p. iii). The Clinical Governance Framework supports leaders in
health care bodies to ‘provide leadership to develop a culture of
safety and quality improvement’ (ACSQHC 2017b, p. 20).
38 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2017b). National
Model Clinical Governance Framework. Sydney: ACSQHC.
38


Change and the nurse manager
A major part of a nurse leader’s role is, in a visionary sense, to help
determine what changes need to be made within organisations and
to assist staff to implement policies regarding those changes. People
sometimes resist change, and this can be confronting to nurse
leaders. It is critical therefore that leaders understand change theory
and discover their own thoughts and interpretations of change.
Change can be understood as those events that happen at
microscopic or macroscopic level. For example, changes to a health
system budget might mean that nurses have to use different and
cheaper wound dressings in clinical practice, or they might mean
larger changes such as ward closures or staff cuts.
Change is difficult in a large organisation (Battilana & Casciaro )
and even harder in complex organisations such as health services.
In the contemporary health care environment, change is not the
exception but an ongoing process: it can involve gaining new
knowledge or adapting what is currently known in the light of new
information; it can also involve having to obtain new skills. Change is
an integral aspect of nursing and nurses are often change
agents
: people who initiate, motivate and implement change. Due
to the unprecedented rate of change and its multiple drivers such as
technology, consumer expectations and rapid communication,
organisations are impacted by increased levels of anxiety within
work systems (Kott
). Change agents must:
39
40


39 Battilana, J. & Casciaro, T. (2013). The network secrets of great change agents. Harvard
Business Review, July–August, 63–68.
40 Kott, K. (2014). Applying Bowen theory to work systems. OD Practitioner, 46(3), 76–82.
have excellent communication and interpersonal skills with
individuals, groups, administration and all levels of the
organisation involved in change
have skills in gathering and analysing evidence to ensure that
change is evidence based
have knowledge of available resources and how to use them,
including people, time, money, facilities and information
be skilled in problem solving
be skilled in compassionate and empathetic facilitation
be respected by those involved in the change
have the ability to encourage and nurture those going through
change
be self-confident and able to take risks, and inspire trust in
themselves and others
be able to make decisions
have a broad base of knowledge
have a good sense of timing
ensure that changes are evaluated to understand and assess
their impact
Types of change


Planned change
 is a purposeful attempt by an individual, group,
organisation or social system to influence its own current status.
Problem solving, decision making and interpersonal skills are
important factors in planned change, as well as gathering and
evaluating evidence to underpin planned change.
Change can be covert or overt. A covert change is hidden,
happening unnoticed by the people concerned; for example, a
gradual increase in a hospital’s readmission rates. Overt change is
change of which people are aware, frequently brought about by a
change in policy or function of a health care facility.
Unplanned change
 is an alteration imposed by external events or
people, occurring when unexpected events force a reaction; it is
usually haphazard and the results can be unpredictable. Situational,
or natural, change also may be considered unplanned and occurs
without any control by the person or group affected; for example,
because of a war or natural disaster, or a rapid change in
government policy such as a budget cut in hospital funding. Not all
situational changes are negative: as health services open or close
units, the nurse may have the opportunity to change to a new
workplace.
Models of change
It is rare in today’s health environment for one change process to be
completed before another is started, and this can lead not only to


stress and anxiety but also to an inability to properly embed and
evaluate a change process.
An important aspect of planning change is establishing the likelihood
of the acceptance of the change and then determining the criteria by
which that acceptance can be identified. Accepting change often
takes time, particularly when it does not fit into a person’s attitudinal
framework. The course of acceptance is easier for people if they are
involved in the process. It is important for managers to acknowledge
that change can bring with it high levels of stress, anxiety, anger and
grief for their staff, especially if it involves varying amounts of
ambiguity. Ways of dealing with these reactions should be factored
into the change management process (Kerr
). If possible, change
should be instituted on a small or pilot scale before full
implementation.
41 Kerr, M. (2012). Application of family systems theory to a work system. In R. Sagar & K.
Wiseman (Eds), Understanding Organizations: Applications of Bowen Family Systems
Theory (pp. 121–131). Washington, DC: Georgetown Family Center.
Remember, it is always critical to evaluate changes that have
occurred and to ask searching questions: Was it the right thing to
do? Have our changes been fully implemented? What impact has
the change had on the organisation (staff, patients)? To facilitate
acceptance of the change, the change agent needs to identify
common driving and restraining forces (see Box 29.2
). Guidelines
for dealing with resistance to change are found in Box 29.3
.
41


BO X
29.2 Common driving and restraining
forces
Driving forces
Perception or evidence that the change is challenging.
Economic gain.
Perception that the change will improve the situation.
Visualisation of the future impact of change.
Potential for self-growth, recognition, achievement and
improved relationships.
Restraining forces
Fear that something of personal value will be lost (e.g.
threat to job security or self-esteem).
Grief at letting go.
Misunderstanding of the change and its implications.
Low tolerance for change related to intellectual or
emotional insecurity.
Perception that the change will not achieve goals; failure
to see the big picture.
Lack of time or energy or general indifference.


BO X
29.3 Guidelines for dealing with
resistance to change
1. Communicate with those who oppose the change. Get
to the root of their reasons for opposition.
2. Clarify information and provide accurate information.
3. Be open to revisions but clear about what must
remain.
4. Present the negative consequences of resistance
(threats to organisational survival, compromised
patient care and so on).
5. Emphasise the positive consequences of the change
and how the individual or group will benefit. However,
do not spend too much energy on rational analysis of
why the change is good and why the arguments
against it do not hold up. People’s resistance
frequently flows from feelings that are not rational.
6. Keep resisters involved in face-to-face contact with
supporters. Encourage proponents to empathise with
opponents, recognise valid objections and relieve
unnecessary fears.
7. Maintain a climate of trust, support and confidence.
8. Follow the ‘politics of change’:
a. Analyse the organisational chart; know the
formal lines of authority. Identify informal lines


as well.
b. Identify key people who will be affected by the
change. Pay attention to those immediately
above and below the point of change.
c. Find out as much as possible about these key
people. What interests them, gets them excited,
turns them off? What is on their personal and
organisational agendas? Who typically aligns
with whom on important decisions?
d. Begin to build a coalition of support before you
start the change process. Identify the key
people who will most likely support your idea
and those who are most likely to be persuaded
easily. Talk informally with them to flush out
possible objections to your idea and potential
opponents. What will the costs and benefits be
to them, especially in political terms? Can your
idea be modified in ways that retain your
objectives but appeal to more key people?
Source: E. J. Sullivan & P. J. Decker (2009). Effective Leadership and Management in Nursing (7th
ed.), p. 73. © 2009. Reprinted with permission of Pearson Education, Inc., Upper Saddle River, NJ.
Research note
The influence of generational diversity on health care
teams


In 2014, 1 in 4 nurses were aged over 50, and between 2011
and 2014, there were more employed nurses and midwives in
the 50–54 year age group than any other age group
(AIHW
). The nursing workforce comprises a wide
generational cross-section with each generation having
different expectations, values, goals and motivators (Levett-
Jones & Bourgeois ).
42 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2016). Nursing and Midwifery
Workforce 2014. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
43 Levett-Jones, T. & Bourgeois, S. (2015). The Clinical Placement: An Essential
Guide for Nursing Students (3rd ed.). Marrickville: Elsevier.
Four terms are commonly applied to the generations active in
today’s workplace: Baby Boomers (born 1946–64) comprising
the largest group; Generation X (born 1965–79); Generation
Y (born 1980–94); and Generation Z (born 1995–2009). Baby
Boomers are thought to be highly committed to their
employer, are frequently described as workaholics, may stay
with one employer for an extended period and enjoy personal
recognition for work well done (Hu, Herrick & Hodgin ). In
contrast, Generation Xers believe loyalty to their manager is
of greater importance than length of employment, are more
concerned with finding work–life balance than the previous
generation and prefer public affirmation as a reward for their
work. Generation Y are perceived to be highly aware of their
rights and entitlements at work, want to be continually
learning and challenged, and have short attention spans
(Levett-Jones & Bourgeois 2015). Lastly, Generation Z are
42
43
44


thought to be highly skilled at multitasking, environmentally
aware and able to work autonomously and with self-
confidence (Clark ).
44 Hu, J., Herrick, C. & Hodgin, K. A. (2004). Managing the multigenerational
nursing team. The Health Care Manager, 23(4), 334–340.
45 Clark, D. (2019). 10 Defining Characteristics of Generation Z. Retrieved from
<https://blog.ttisuccessinsights.com/>.
Implications Nurses interact with people of the same and
different generations. Appreciating that such distinctions exist
can help us work together effectively and assist the manager
to delegate and communicate more effectively.
Understanding other people’s viewpoint is a common and
important skill of the nurse in any position—leader, manager
or neither. In your work setting, it will be necessary to
consider how the staff is distributed between different
generations, with their different perspectives.
All nurses are affected by change; nobody can avoid it. Nurses
knowledgeable about the historical and current trends in nursing,
and the present political, social, technological and economic issues
make rational plans to deal with opportunities to initiate and guide
needed change and to respond to change that affects them,
whether it be in the workplace, government, organisations or the
community. Research on major changes in the British National
Health Service found that effective change agents had good informal
networks across the organisation (Battilana & Casciaro 2013).
45


Case study
You have just been interviewed for two nursing positions and
are trying to decide which job to pursue. During your first
interview for a team member position, the nurse unit
manager, Mr Cheung, was cheerful, spoke highly of his
current staff and complimented them for their ability to set
goals and participate in decision making, and he listened to
your ideas and explored ways in which you could contribute
to this team’s effectiveness. At the second interview, the
nurse unit manager, Mrs Turner, was also cheerful and
talkative. She provided you with a job description, explained
her expectations of you as a new employee and spoke of
new programs she was attempting to implement. Both nurse
managers talked about changes taking place in their facilities
and the need for employees to remain flexible.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. Based on the brief data provided, speculate about the
leadership style of each of these nurse managers.
2. Think about managers (or leaders) you have known
and admired. What characteristics did they have that
you would like to integrate into your own management
style should you become a nurse manager?


3. Both nurse managers spoke of changes that were
taking place in their facility. As a nurse, how can you
assist your peers who are unhappy and seem to resist
change even when it is positive?
4.
 How did their leadership style make you feel?
Which leadership style would you like to emulate and
why?
5. How might the delegation of tasks to other nurses or
AINs be different in the two settings?


Chapter 29 Review


Chapter highlights
The professional nurse frequently assumes the roles of leader
and manager. Leaders influence others to accomplish a specific
goal whereas managers have responsibility and accountability for
accomplishing the tasks of an organisation.
It is never too early to learn leadership skills, and it is expected
that all nurses will have effective leadership skills.
Several leadership styles have been described, including
authoritarian, democratic, laissez-faire and bureaucratic. These
styles are often blended to fit the situation. Nurses need to know
which style is most consistent with their behaviour and learn to
incorporate aspects of other styles into their practice. They need
to be aware too that not all cultures may understand or accept
the leadership styles of those that emanate from a Western
perspective. In addition, the world is becoming more globally
connected and nurses are learning that they can influence
change not just locally, but nationally and internationally.
Contemporary leadership theories and concepts include
charismatic, transactional, transformational, shared, cross-
cultural, servant and compassionate leadership. A
compassionate leader is defined as a person who is emotionally
intelligent, authentic, open, caring, empathetic, mindful, kind and
respectful.
Principles of effective leadership include vision, compassion,
influence and acting as a role model.


Nurse managers work in the organisational framework of the
employing agency. Principles of management include authority,
accountability and responsibility.
Four major management functions are planning, organising,
directing and coordinating.
Effective managers need to be skilled at critical thinking,
communication, resource management, enhancing employee
performance and managing teams, conflict, time and change.
Clinical governance is a system of policies, processes and
accountabilities aimed at improving patient safety and the quality
and effectiveness of patient care within a health service.
Nurses function as change agents to initiate, support, motivate
and implement the change process.
Concept check
1. The nurse leader informs the staff of a local emergency and
instructs them to stay at the hospital to prepare for major
casualties. The staff display high levels of anxiety and
disorganisation. The most appropriate leadership style at this
time is which of the following?
1. Authoritarian.
2. Democratic.
3. Laissez-faire.
4. Bureaucratic.


2. Which of the following approaches best illustrates
transformational leadership?
1. The leader stimulates group interest in establishing unit
goals that contribute to the health service’s mission.
2. The leader forms subgroups or task forces that make
decisions about unit problems.
3. The leader provides funding for continuing education
conferences to staff who have not used any sick leave.
4. The leader adjusts strategies to fit the current
situation.
3. Which of the following examples is reflective of a nurse
manager with accountability but not authority?
1. To reduce costs, administrators instruct the manager
to inform the staff to reduce overtime.
2. The manager evaluates the unit staff but cannot
promote or terminate staff.
3. The manager is to recommend a new staffing
procedure to the institution’s nurse manager group.
4. The manager prepares a monthly budget variance
report that includes plans to correct overspending.
4. The nurse manager plans to implement a new method for
scheduling staff annual leave. Senior staff members oppose
the change while newer staff members are more accepting.
Which of the following would be the most effective strategy
for resolving this difference?


1. Provide extensive and detailed rationale for the
proposed change, then implement.
2. Explain that the change will occur as designed,
regardless of the staff’s preference.
3. Withdraw the proposal to prevent a decrease in staff
morale.
4. Encourage interaction between the opposing sides to
attempt resolution.
Focus on critical thinking
1. What are your leadership values, strengths and style?
2. Which style of nursing leadership is best suited to providing
person-centred care in a resource-scarce health care
environment of increasing complexity and clinical challenge?
3. How can you adjust your leadership style to fit the culture you
are working in? What, if anything, do you need to be aware of
or need to change?
4. Think of a time you were treated compassionately by a team
leader or manager. How did it make you feel? How did it
make you feel about your work?


Unit 7 Assessing health
Assessment is an interactive process whereby
nurses consider a person’s situation, collect
cues or information and process that information
in order to identify any problems or issues. A
comprehensive assessment includes
information about a person’s physical,
psychosocial, spiritual, cultural and
environmental health. Nurses also perform
regular focused assessments as indicated by a
person’s needs.

The Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia’s
(NMBA) Registered Nurse Standards for
Practice 2016 specify that the Registered Nurse
‘uses a range of assessment techniques to
systematically collect relevant and accurate
(SaO2)
1


information and data to inform practice’ (NMBA ,
p. 4).
1 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016).
Registered Nurse Standards for Practice. Retrieved from
<www.nursingmidwifery board.gov.au>.
The measurement of a person’s physiological
observations or ‘vital signs
’ is a core nursing
function and key to the recognition of patient
deterioration. Vital signs provide important
information about the interrelationship between
body systems. Vital signs that are within normal
limits reflect a person’s physiological wellbeing,
whereas abnormal vital signs may be an early
warning of clinical deterioration
.
Traditionally, nurses measured the five vital
signs of temperature, pulse, respiration and
blood pressure, with measurement of oxygen
saturation added in the 1980s. However, recent
clinical research indicates the need for closer
and more extensive observation of increasingly
‘sicker’ people in order to predict, prevent,
detect and manage clinical deterioration.
The Standard Adult General Observation
(SAGO) chart is a typical ‘track and trigger’ tool
1


developed by New South Wales Health as part
of its Between the Flags program (New South
Wales Health & Clinical Excellence
Commission ). This chart provides for the
recording of vital signs, such as respiratory rate,
pulse, blood pressure, oxygen saturation (
), oxygen requirement and neurological status.
2 New South Wales Health & Clinical Excellence
Commission (2010). Between the Flags. Retrieved from
<www0.health.nsw.gov.au>.
This chapter will focus on the following vital
signs: respiration, blood oxygenation, blood
pressure, pulse rate and body temperature.
Timely and accurate assessment,
documentation and interpretation of vital signs is
critical to clinical reasoning, accuracy of nursing
diagnoses and implementation of appropriate
interventions. Research has shown that
changes in vital signs commonly precede
serious adverse events such as cardiac or
respiratory arrest, unplanned intensive care unit
(ICU) admission or unexpected death (Barfod et
al. ). Competent nursing practice requires not
only psychomotor and affective skills, but also
complex thinking processes (Levett-Jones ).
2
SpO2
3
4


Accurate clinical reasoning is enhanced by a
sound knowledge base and competence in vital
sign assessment. The monitoring of vital signs
enables a nurse to detect deviations from
normal that may indicate an alteration in the
person’s health status and potential clinical
deterioration. Therefore, nurses need to be
vigilant and recognise the importance of vital
sign monitoring as an essential nursing
responsibility, not simply a routine task.
3 Barfod, C., Lauritzen, M., Danker, J., ... Lange K. (2012).
Abnormal vital signs are strong predictors for intensive care
unit admission and in-hospital mortality in adults triaged in
the emergency department—A prospective cohort study.
Scandinavian Journal of Trauma and Resuscitation
Emergency Medicine, 20(28). Doi: 10.1186/1757-7241-20-
28.
4 Levett-Jones, T. (Ed.). (2018). Clinical Reasoning:
Learning to Think Like a Nurse (2nd ed.). Sydney: Pearson.
A systematic review of nurses’ detection and
management of the deteriorating patient found
that the routine recording of vital signs was seen
as a ritualistic practice that for many has
5


become task oriented (Odell, Victor & Oliver ).
Findings like these are of concern as nurses are
most often the care professionals best
positioned to recognise patient deterioration.
Furthermore, and contradictory to traditional
understanding, strong evidence indicates that
abnormalities in respiratory rate, pulse and
blood pressure are early cues to detecting the
deterioration in a person’s condition (Puskarich
et al. ).
5 Odell, M., Victor, C. & Oliver, D. (2009). Nurses’ role in
detecting deterioration in ward patients: A systematic
literature review. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 65(10),
1992–2006.
6 Puskarich, M., Nandi, U., Long, B. & Jones, A. (2017).
Association between persistent tachycardia and tachypnea
and in-hospital mortality among non-hypotensive
emergency department patients admitted to the hospital.
Clinical and Experimental Emergency Medicine, 4(1), 2–9.
Once vital signs have been assessed, nurses
interpret (compare normal versus abnormal
parameters for this particular person) and
5
6


document the results on the person’s
observation chart. Processing this information in
a systematic manner highlights any
inconsistencies, which then enables the nurse
to recognise changes in the person’s health
status and to discern trends. Vital sign
monitoring and vital sign interpretation should
be considered a thoughtful, scientific process
that facilitates a person-centred and holistic
approach to nursing care.
Many factors such as organisation policy, clinical
guidelines, clinical pathways and patient care
plans can determine timing of vital signs
assessment. However, the person’s clinical
condition and the nurse’s clinical judgment
determine whether observations should be
repeated more frequently. Examples of times to
assess vital signs are listed in Box 30.1
.
BOX


30.1 Times to assess vital
signs
On admission to a health care facility,
to obtain baseline data and monitor a
person’s clinical improvement or
deterioration.
When a person has a change in
health status or reports symptoms
such as chest pain or difficulty
breathing.
Before, during and after surgery or an
invasive procedure.
Before and/or after the administration
of a medication that could affect the
respiratory or cardiovascular systems.
Before and after any nursing
intervention that could affect the vital
signs (e.g. ambulating a person who
has been on bed rest or when a
person is receiving a blood
transfusion).
Following an incident, accident or
injury in the health care setting (e.g.
when a person has fallen or has been
administered an incorrect medication).


Timeliness of vital sign documentation
is also an important factor for safe
patient outcomes. Measures should
be recorded directly at the ‘point of
care’ (e.g. patient bed side) either
electronically or onto a hard-copy
chart. Where nurses need to
document vital sign measures at a
station remote to the person,
transcription errors and time delays
have been found to occur—factors
that could lead to inappropriate
treatment (Fuller et al. ).
7 Fuller, T., Fox, B., Lake, D. & Crawford, K.
(2018). Improving real-time vital signs
documentation. Nursing Management, 49(1),
28–33.
Vital signs must be accurately and immediately
documented. The importance of clear and
comprehensive documentation of vital signs is
emphasised in the National Safety and Quality
Health Service Standards (Australian
Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) ), where it is specified that
7
8


documentation is a professional expectation and
essential way of communicating critical
information to other staff.
8 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health
Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.


Respiration
Respiration
 is the act of breathing. Inhalation
, or
inspiration
, refers to the intake of air into the lungs.
Exhalation
, or expiration
, refers to breathing out or the
movement of gases from the lungs to the atmosphere.
Ventilation
 is also used to refer to the movement of air in and out
of the lungs.
There are basically two types of breathing: costal (thoracic)
breathing
 and diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing
. Costal
breathing involves the external intercostal muscles and other
accessory muscles, such as the sternocleidomastoid muscles. It can
be observed by the movement of the chest upward and outward. By
contrast, diaphragmatic breathing involves the contraction and
relaxation of the diaphragm and is observed by the movement of the
abdomen, which occurs as a result of the diaphragm’s contraction
and downward movement.
Research note
Respiratory rate as a sensitive indicator of patient
deterioration


M. Cretikos, R. Bellomo, K. Hillman, J. Chen, S. Finfer & A. Flabouris (2008). Respiratory rate: The
neglected vital sign. Medical Journal of Australia, 188(11), 657−659.
A raised respiratory rate is a strong and specific predictor of
serious adverse events such as cardiac arrest and unplanned
intensive care unit admission; yet this vital sign is the least
often recorded and the most frequently omitted measure in
hospital documentation (Cretikos et al. ). One approach to
improve the documentation and interpretation of vital signs
was a nationally funded project to develop an evidence-based
adult observation chart. The Standard Adult General
Observation (SAGO) chart and the Adult Deterioration
Detection System (ADDS) chart (see Figure 30.1
) are
examples of ‘track and trigger’ tools that provide for the
recording of vital signs such as respiratory rate, pulse, blood
pressure, oxygen saturation (
), oxygen requirement
and neurological status, and where the respiratory rate has
been relocated to the top of the page.
9 Cretikos, M., Bellomo, R., Hillman, K., Chen, J., Finfer, S. & Flabouris, A. (2008).
Respiratory rate: The neglected vital sign. Medical Journal of Australia, 188(11),
657−659.

chart.

Implications Results from an evaluation of the ADDS and
SAGO charts found that the chart design had a statistically
significant effect on both error rates and response time due
to the graphical representation of clinical data. Furthermore,
the authors contended that these charts are significantly
better at signalling patient deterioration than other currently
available charts that use numerical representation of data
(Missen et al.
).
11 Missen, K., Porter J. E., Raymond, A., de Vent, K. & Larkins, J. (2018). Adult
Deterioration Detection System (ADDS): An evaluation of the impact on MET and
Code blue activations in a regional healthcare service. Collegian, 25, 157–161.
Mechanics and regulation of
breathing
During inhalation, the following processes normally occur: the
diaphragm contracts (flattens), the ribs move upward and outward
and the sternum moves outward, thus enlarging the thorax and
permitting the lungs to expand (see Figure 30.2
). During
exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes, the ribs move downward and
11


inward and the sternum moves inward, thus decreasing the size of
the thorax as the lungs are compressed (see Figure 30.3
).
Normally, breathing is carried out automatically and effortlessly. A
normal adult inspiration lasts 1 to 1.5 seconds, while expiration lasts
2 to 3 seconds.
Figure 30.2


Respiratory inhalation. Left: lateral view, right: anterior view.
Figure 30.3


Respiratory exhalation. Left: lateral view, right: anterior view.
Respiration is controlled by respiratory centres in the medulla
oblongata and the pons of the brain, and by chemoreceptors located
centrally in the medulla and peripherally in the carotid and aortic
bodies. These centres and receptors respond to changes in the
concentrations of oxygen (
), carbon dioxide (
) and hydrogen
(
) in the arterial blood. See Chapter 53
 for further details.
Assessing respirations
Resting respirations should be assessed when the person is relaxed
because exercise affects respirations, increasing their rate and
depth. Anxiety is likely to affect respiratory rate and depth as well.
Respirations may also need to be assessed after exercise to identify
the person’s tolerance to activity. Before assessing a person’s
respirations, a nurse should be aware of the following:
the person’s normal breathing pattern
the influence of the person’s health problems on respirations
any medications or therapies that might affect respirations
the relationship of the person’s respirations to cardiovascular
function.
The rate, depth, rhythm, quality and effectiveness of respirations
should be assessed. The respiratory rate is normally described in
breaths per minute. Breathing that is normal in rate and depth is
O2
CO2
H+


called eupnoea. Abnormally slow respirations are referred to as
bradypnoea
; abnormally fast respirations are called
tachypnoea
. Apnoea
 is the absence of breathing. For the
respiratory rates for different age groups, see Table 30.3
 on page
568.
Clinical consideration
A sleeping adult’s respirations can fall to fewer
than 10 shallow breaths per minute. Use other
vital signs to validate the person’s condition.
Count respirations prior to uncomfortable
procedures so that the respiratory rate is not
artificially elevated by the discomfort.
Factors affecting respirations
Several factors influence respiratory rate. Those that increase the
rate include exercise (increases metabolism), stress (readies the
body for ‘fight or flight’), increased environmental temperature and
lowered oxygen concentration at increased altitudes. Factors that
may decrease the respiratory rate include decreased environmental
temperature, certain medications (e.g. narcotics) and increased
intracranial pressure.


The depth of a person’s respirations can be established by watching
the movement of the chest. Respiratory depth is generally described
as normal, deep or shallow. Deep respirations are those in which a
large volume of air is inhaled and exhaled, inflating most of the
lungs. Shallow respirations involve the exchange of a small volume
of air and often the minimal use of lung tissue. During a normal
inspiration and expiration, an adult takes in about 500 mL of air. This
volume is called the tidal volume
. It is important to note that tidal
volume may vary depending on the age, height and weight of a
person and/or the presence of disease. For further information
about pulmonary volumes and pulmonary capacities, see Chapter
53
.
Clinical consideration
Too often nurses estimate (or worse, guess) a
person’s respiratory rate. It is essential that an
accurate assessment of respiration is conducted
and documented. Because altered respiratory
rate is a significant indication of patient
deterioration, the rate measurement is closely
linked to oxygen flow rate and oxygen saturation
measures
 on adult observation charts
(e.g. SAGO and ADDS charts).
(SpO2)


Body position also affects the amount of air that can be inhaled.
People in a supine position experience two physiological processes
that suppress respiration: an increase in the volume of blood inside
the thoracic cavity and compression of the chest. Consequently,
people lying on their back have poorer lung aeration, which
predisposes them to the stasis of fluids and subsequent infection.
Certain medications also affect the respiratory depth. For example,
narcotics such as morphine and benzodiazepines such as
temazepam depress the respiratory centres in the brain, thereby
depressing the respiratory rate and depth. Hyperventilation
refers to very deep, rapid respirations; hypoventilation
 refers to
very shallow respirations.
Respiratory rhythm
 refers to the regularity of the expirations and
the inspirations. Normally, respirations are evenly spaced.
Respiratory rhythm can be described as regular or irregular. An
infant’s respiratory rhythm may be less regular than an adult’s. See
Chapter 53
 for details about abnormal respiratory rhythms.
Respiratory quality
, or character
, refers to those aspects of
breathing that are different from normal, effortless breathing. Two of
these aspects are the amount of effort a person must exert to
breathe and the sound of breathing. Usually, breathing does not
require noticeable effort. Sometimes, however, people can breathe
only with substantial effort—this is referred to as laboured breathing.
The sound of breathing is also significant. Normal breathing is silent,
but a number of abnormal sounds such as a wheeze are obvious to


the nurse’s ear or with a stethoscope. See Chapter 31
 for
methods used to assess lung sounds. For details about altered
breathing patterns and terms used to describe various patterns and
sounds, see Box 30.2
.
BO X
30.2 Altered breathing patterns and
sounds
Breathing patterns
Rate
Tachypnoea—quick, shallow breaths
Bradypnoea—abnormally slow breathing
Apnoea—cessation of breathing
Volume
Hyperventilation—overexpansion of the lungs,
characterised by rapid and deep breaths
Hypoventilation—underexpansion of the lungs,
characterised by shallow respirations


Rhythm
Cheyne–Stokes breathing—waxing and waning of
respirations, from very deep to very shallow breathing and
temporary apnoea
Ease or effort
Dyspnoea—difficult and laboured breathing during which
the individual has a persistent, unsatisfied need for air and
feels distressed
Orthopnoea—ability to breathe only in upright sitting or
standing positions
Breath sounds
Stridor—a shrill, harsh sound heard during inspiration
with laryngeal obstruction
Stertor—snoring or sonorous respiration, usually due to a
partial obstruction of the upper airway
Wheeze—continuous, high-pitched musical squeak or
whistling sound occurring on expiration and sometimes on
inspiration when air moves through a narrowed or partially
obstructed airway
Bubbling—gurgling sounds heard as air passes through
moist secretions in the respiratory tract
Chest movements


Intercostal retraction—indrawing between the ribs
Substernal retraction—indrawing beneath the
breastbone
Suprasternal retraction—indrawing above the clavicles
Secretions and coughing
Haemoptysis—the presence of blood in the sputum
Productive cough—a cough accompanied by
expectorated secretions
Non-productive cough—a dry, harsh cough without
secretions


Oxygen saturation
During ventilation, oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the
alveolar capillary membrane. These gases diffuse from the area of
high concentration to the area of low concentration. Diffusion of
these gases occurs in the alveoli. Each alveolus is a collection of air
sacs surrounded by a network of capillaries carrying arterial blood
from the right ventricle.
Lifespan considerations
Respirations
Infants
An infant or child who is crying will have an abnormal
respiratory rate and rhythm and will need to be quieted
before respirations can be accurately assessed.
Infants use their diaphragms for both inhalation and
exhalation. If necessary, place your hand gently on the
infant’s abdomen to feel the rapid rise and fall during
respirations.


Most newborns are obligate nasal breathers for at least
the first 6 weeks of life and may be so until up to 3
months of age; consequently, nasal obstruction can be life
threatening.
Some newborns display ‘periodic breathing’ in which they
pause for a few seconds between respirations. This
condition can be normal but parents should be alert to
prolonged or frequent pauses (apnoea) that require
medical attention.
Compared with adults, infants have fewer alveoli and their
airways have a smaller diameter. As a result, infants’
respiratory rate and effort of breathing will increase with
respiratory infections.
Children
Because young children are diaphragmatic breathers,
observe the rise and fall of the abdomen. If necessary,
place your hand gently on the abdomen to feel the rapid
rise and fall during respirations.
Older adults
Ask the person to remain quiet or count respirations after
taking the pulse.
Older people experience anatomical and physiological
changes that cause the respiratory system to be less


efficient. Any changes in rate or type of breathing should
be reported immediately.
Home care considerations
Respirations
Assess the home setting for factors that could
interfere with breathing, such as exhaust, gas or
paint fumes, or people who smoke.
If the person has just come in from another room,
allow them to rest before counting respirations.
Have an adult hold a child gently to reduce
movement while counting respirations.
There is a net movement of oxygen from the air sacs into the
alveolar capillaries, thereby increasing the oxygen concentration of
the blood in these capillaries. This arterial blood has a high carbon
dioxide concentration. Consequently, carbon dioxide diffuses from
the alveolar capillaries into the air sacs.
Oxygen is carried in the blood as either dissolved oxygen or as
oxygen bound to haemoglobin in red blood cells. The concentration


of oxygen dissolved in the plasma is represented as the partial
pressure of arterial oxygen
. In contrast, the saturation of
arterial oxygen
 is a ratio of the oxygen bound to
haemoglobin compared with the oxygen-carrying capacity of the
haemoglobin.
Oxygenation is measured as a correlate of the partial pressure of
arterial oxygen
 and the saturation of arterial oxygen
. The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve demonstrates
the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen. Changes in body
temperature, metabolism and blood pH affect the distribution of
oxygen to the tissues.
An increase in body temperature, partial pressure of arterial carbon
dioxide
) and acidosis decrease the affinity of
haemoglobin for oxygen. Consequently, oxygen is released more
readily to the tissues but is picked up less readily in the lungs. This is
demonstrated as a right shift in the oxygen– haemoglobin
dissociation curve.
In contrast, when body temperature decreases, decreased
and alkalosis increase the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen.
Consequently, oxygen is picked up more readily in the lungs but is
released less readily to the tissues. This is demonstrated as a left
shift in the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve.
A pulse oximeter
 is a non-invasive device that estimates a
person’s arterial blood oxygen saturation
 by means of a
(PaO2)
(SaO2)
(PaO2)
(SaO2)
(PaCO2)
CO2
(SaO2)


sensor attached to the person’s finger, toe, nose, earlobe (see
Figure 30.4
) or forehead (or around the hand or foot of a
neonate). The pulse oximeter can detect hypoxaemia before clinical
signs and symptoms such as cyanosis (dusky-coloured skin and nail
beds) develop.
Figure 30.4


Earlobe oximeter sensor.
Source: © Antonia Reeve/Science Photo Library.
The sensor in the pulse oximeter has two parts:
1. two light-emitting diodes (LEDs)—one red, the other infrared
—that transmit light through nails, tissue, venous blood and
arterial blood
2. a photodetector placed directly opposite the LEDs (e.g. the
other side of the finger, earlobe, toe or nose). The
photodetector measures the amount of red and infrared light
absorbed by oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin in
peripheral arterial blood and reports it as
. Normal
 is 95% to 100% and a measure of
 below 90% is
life threatening. The values for
 and
 are the
same. You will note the SAGO chart reports oxygen
saturation values as
%.
Pulse oximeters with various types of sensors are available from
several manufacturers. The oximeter unit consists of an inlet
connection for the sensor cable and a faceplate that indicates (a)
the oxygen saturation measurement (expressed as a percentage),
and (b) the pulse rate. Cordless units are also available (see Figure
30.5
).
