Factors affecting oxygen
saturation readings
Haemoglobin. If the haemoglobin is fully saturated with oxygen,
the
 will appear normal even if the total haemoglobin level
is low. Thus, the person could be severely anaemic and have
inadequate oxygen to supply the tissues but the pulse oximeter
would return a normal value.
Circulation. The oximeter will not return an accurate reading if
the area under the sensor has impaired circulation, such as
occurs in peripheral vascular disease or if a person is very cold.
Activity. Shivering or excessive movement of the sensor site
may interfere with accurate readings.
Dark-coloured nail polish or discolouration of the nail bed.
False readings typically arise when a person is wearing dark-
coloured nail polish or if the nail bed is discoloured by a
subdermal haematoma or other sources of nail bed
discolouration, such as nicotine stains.
Carbon monoxide poisoning. Pulse oximeters cannot
discriminate between haemoglobin saturated with carbon
monoxide versus oxygen. In this case, other measures of
oxygenation are needed.
SpO2


Blood pressure
Arterial blood pressure
 is a measure of the pressure exerted by
the blood as it flows through the arteries. Because the blood moves
in waves, there are two blood pressure measures. The systolic
pressure
 is the pressure of the blood as a result of contraction of
the ventricles; that is, the pressure of the height of the blood wave.
The diastolic pressure
 is the pressure when the ventricles are at
rest. Diastolic pressure, then, is the lower pressure, present at all
times within the arteries. The difference between the diastolic and
the systolic pressures is called the pulse pressure
. A normal
pulse pressure is about 40 mm Hg, but can be as high as 100 mm
Hg during exercise. A consistently elevated pulse pressure occurs in
arteriosclerosis. A low pulse pressure (e.g. less than 25 mm Hg)
occurs in conditions such as severe heart failure.
Blood pressure is measured in millimetres of mercury (mm Hg) and
recorded as a fraction: systolic pressure over the diastolic pressure.
In clinical practice, parameters are used to assist diagnosis and
clinical decision making. According to the National Heart Foundation
of Australia , optimal blood pressure for an adult is less than 120/80
mm Hg (i.e. systolic blood pressure less than 120 and diastolic blood
pressure less than 80 mm Hg). See Table 30.1
 for the blood
pressure categories and grades of hypertension. A number of
conditions are reflected by changes in blood pressure and, because
blood pressure can vary considerably, it is important for the nurse to
12


know a person’s baseline blood pressure. For example, if a person’s
usual blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg and it is assessed following
surgery to be 110/70 mm Hg, this drop in pressure may indicate
complications and must be reported to the medical officer.
12 National Heart Foundation of Australia (2016). Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management
of Hypertension in Adults. Melbourne: National Heart Foundation of Australia.
Table 30.1 Classification of clinic blood pressure levels in
adults
When a patient’s systolic and diastolic blood pressure levels fall into
different categories, the higher diagnostic category applies.
Determinants of blood pressure
Arterial blood pressure is the result of several factors: the pumping
action of the heart, the peripheral vascular resistance (the resistance
supplied by the blood vessels through which the blood flows) and the
blood volume and viscosity.
Pumping action of the heart
When the pumping action of the heart is weak, less blood is pumped
into arteries (lower cardiac output) and the blood pressure
decreases. When the heart’s pumping action is strong and the
*


volume of blood pumped into the circulation increases (higher
cardiac output), the blood pressure increases.
Peripheral vascular resistance
Peripheral resistance can increase blood pressure. The diastolic
pressure especially is affected. Some factors that create resistance
in the arterial system are the capacity of the arterioles and
capillaries, the compliance of the arteries and the viscosity of the
blood. The internal diameter or capacity of the arterioles and the
capillaries determines the peripheral resistance to the blood in the
body; that is, the smaller the space within a vessel, the greater the
resistance. Normally, the arterioles are in a state of partial
constriction. Increased vasoconstriction, such as occurs with
smoking, raises the blood pressure, whereas decreased
vasoconstriction lowers the blood pressure. If the elastic and
muscular tissues of the arteries are replaced with fibrous tissue, the
arteries lose much of their ability to constrict and dilate. This
condition, most common in middle-aged and older people, is known
as arteriosclerosis
.
Lifespan considerations
Pulse oximetry
Infants


If an appropriate-sized finger or toe sensor (see Figure
30.6
) is not available, consider using an earlobe or
forehead sensor.
The oximeter may need to be taped, wrapped with an
elastic bandage or covered by a stocking to keep it in
place.
Figure 30.6


Fingertip oximeter sensor (child).
Source: © Bork/Shutterstock.com.
Children
Explain to the child that the sensor does not hurt.
Disconnect the probe whenever possible to allow for
movement.
Older adults
Use of vasoconstrictive medications, poor circulation or
thickened nails may make finger or toe sensors
inaccurate.
Blood volume
When the blood volume decreases (e.g. as a result of a
haemorrhage or dehydration), the blood pressure decreases
because of decreased fluid in the arteries. Conversely, when the
volume increases (e.g. as a result of a rapid intravenous infusion),
the blood pressure increases because of the greater fluid volume
within the circulatory system.
Blood viscosity
Blood pressure is higher when the blood is highly viscous
 (thick);
that is, when the ratio of red blood cells to the blood plasma is high.


This proportion is referred to as the haematocrit
. The viscosity
increases markedly when the haematocrit is more than 60% to 65%.
Factors affecting blood pressure
Among the factors influencing blood pressure are age, exercise,
stress, ethnicity, obesity, gender, medications, obesity, diurnal
variations, medical conditions and body temperature.
Age. Newborns have a mean systolic pressure of approximately
75 mm Hg. The pressure rises with age, reaches a peak at the
onset of puberty and then tends to decline somewhat. In older
people, elasticity of the arteries is decreased—the arteries are
more rigid and less yielding to the pressure of the blood. This
produces an elevated systolic pressure. Because the walls no
longer retract as flexibly with decreased pressure, the diastolic
pressure may also be high.
Exercise. Physical activity increases the cardiac output and
hence the blood pressure; thus, 20 to 30 minutes of rest following
exercise is indicated before the resting blood pressure can be
reliably assessed.
Stress. Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system increases
cardiac output and vasoconstriction of the arterioles, thus
increasing the blood pressure reading; however, severe pain can
decrease blood pressure greatly by inhibiting the vasomotor
centre and producing vasodilation.


Ethnicity. Many Indigenous people are affected by
cardiovascular disease (CVD), which includes coronary heart
disease (including heart attack), stroke, heart failure and high
blood pressure (Walsh & Kangaharan ). Indigenous Australians
experience higher rates of hypertension than non-Indigenous
Australians. A review of cardiovascular health among Indigenous
Australians asserted that hypertension (high blood pressure) was
1.5 times more common for males and 1.7 times more common
for females than for their non-Indigenous counterparts across all
age groups, with an earlier age of onset among Indigenous
people (Gray, Brown & Thomson ).
13 Walsh, W. F. & Kangaharan, N. (2017). Cardiac care for Indigenous Australians:
Practical considerations from a clinical perspective. Medical Journal of Australia (MJA),
207(1), 40–45.
14 Gray, C., Brown, A. & Thomson, N. (2012). Review of Cardiovascular Health among
Indigenous Australians. Retrieved from <www.healthinfonet.ecu.edu.au>.
Gender. After puberty, females usually have lower blood pressure
than males of the same age; this difference is thought to be due
to hormonal variations. After menopause, women generally have
higher blood pressure than before.
Medications. Many medications, including caffeine, may
increase or decrease the blood pressure.
Obesity. Both childhood and adult obesity predispose to
hypertension.
Diurnal variations. Pressure is usually lowest early in the
morning, when the metabolic rate is lowest, then rises throughout
the day and peaks in the late afternoon or early evening.
13
14


Disease process. Any condition affecting the cardiac output,
blood volume, blood viscosity and/or compliance of the arteries
has a direct effect on the blood pressure.
Hypervolaemia and hypovolaemia. Fluid overload can increase
a person’s blood pressure and hypovolaemia or dehydration can
reduce blood pressure.
Hypertension
A blood pressure that is persistently above normal is called
hypertension
. A single elevated blood pressure reading indicates
the need for reassessment. Hypertension cannot be diagnosed
unless an elevated blood pressure is found when measured at least
twice at different times. It is usually asymptomatic and is often a
contributing factor to myocardial infarctions and stroke. An elevated
blood pressure of unknown cause is called primary hypertension. An
elevated blood pressure of known cause is called secondary
hypertension.
Hypertension occurs when an adult person has either a diastolic
blood pressure of 90 mm Hg or higher or a systolic blood pressure
higher than 140 mm Hg (see Table 30.1
). The grade of
hypertension is determined by the higher of the two values. For
example, if either the systolic or diastolic values fall in the grade 2
range, a label of ‘grade 2 hypertension’ is assigned. Factors
associated with hypertension include thickening of the arterial walls,
as well as such lifestyle factors as cigarette smoking, obesity, heavy


alcohol consumption, lack of physical exercise, high blood cholesterol
levels and continued exposure to stress. Follow-up care should
include lifestyle changes conducive to lowering the blood pressure as
well as monitoring the pressure itself.
Hypotension
Hypotension
 is a blood pressure that is below normal; that is, a
systolic reading consistently between 85 and 110 mm Hg in an adult
whose normal pressure is higher than this. Postural changes in blood
pressure and heart rate when a person sits or stands is known as
postural
 or orthostatic hypotension
 (OH). OH is defined as a
decline in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mm Hg and/or a
diastolic fall of 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing (30 mm Hg in
hypertensive people), regardless of whether or not symptoms occur
(Wieling & Schatz ). It is usually the result of peripheral vasodilation
in which blood leaves the central body organs, especially the brain,
and moves to the periphery, often causing the person to feel faint.
Hypotension may also be an indicator of autonomic nervous system
disease and is common in people with diabetic neuropathy.
Hypotension can also be caused by analgesics such as morphine,
antihypertensive agents such as angiotensin- converting enzyme
(ACE) inhibitors, bleeding, severe burns, cardiac arrhythmias and
dehydration. It is important to monitor hypotensive people carefully
to prevent falls. When assessing for orthostatic hypotension:
15


15 Wieling, W. & Schatz, I. (2009). The consensus statement on the definition of orthostatic
hypotension: A revisit after 13 years. Journal of Hypertension, 27(5), 935−938. Doi:
10.1097/HJH.0b013e32832b1145.
Place the person in a supine position for 10 minutes.
Record the person’s pulse and blood pressure.
Assist the person to slowly sit or stand. Support the person in
case of faintness.
Immediately recheck the pulse and blood pressure in the same
sites as previously.
Repeat the pulse and blood pressure after 3 minutes.
Record the results. A rise in pulse of 15 to 30 beats per minute or
a drop in blood pressure of 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg
diastolic indicates orthostatic hypotension (Wieling & Schatz
2009).
Assessing blood pressure
Blood pressure is measured with a blood pressure cuff, a
sphygmomanometer and a stethoscope. The blood pressure cuff
consists of the bladder; that is, a rubber bag that can be inflated with
air (see Figure 30.7
). It is covered with cloth and has two tubes
attached to it. One tube connects to a rubber bulb that inflates the
bladder. A small valve on the side of this bulb traps and releases the
air in the bladder.
Figure 30.7


A: Blood pressure cuff and bulb; B: the bladder inside the cuff.
The other tube is attached to a sphygmomanometer. The
sphygmomanometer indicates the pressure of the air within the
bladder. There are two types of sphygmomanometers: aneroid and
digital. The aneroid sphygmomanometer is a calibrated dial with a
needle that points to the calibrations (see Figure 30.8
).
Figure 30.8


An aneroid sphygmomanometer and cuff.
Source: Coprid/Shutterstock.
Most clinical settings use digital (electronic) sphygmomanometers
(see Figure 30.9
); however, manual blood pressure
measurements are more reliable and accurate than electronic blood
pressure devices, which need to be calibrated regularly for accuracy.
All health care facilities should have manual blood pressure
equipment available for use.
Figure 30.9


Blood pressure monitors register systolic and diastolic blood
pressures and often other vital signs.
Source: ronfromyork/Shutterstock.
Doppler ultrasound stethoscopes are also used to assess blood
pressure (see page 569). These are of particular value when blood
pressure sounds are difficult to hear, such as in infants, obese
people and people in shock. Systolic pressure may be the only blood
pressure obtainable with some ultrasound models. Blood pressure
cuffs come in various sizes because the bladder must be the correct
width and length for the person’s arm (see Figure 30.10
). If the
bladder is too narrow, the blood pressure reading will be erroneously
elevated; if it is too wide, the reading will be erroneously low. The
width should be 40% of the circumference, or 20% wider than the
diameter of the midpoint, of the limb on which it is used. The arm
circumference, not the age of the person, should always be used to
determine bladder size. The nurse can determine whether the width
of a blood pressure cuff is appropriate. Lay the cuff lengthwise at the
midpoint of the upper arm and hold the outermost side of the bladder
edge laterally on the arm. With the other hand, wrap the width of the
cuff around the arm and ensure that the width is 40% of the arm
circumference (see Figure 30.11
).
Figure 30.10


Three standard cuff sizes: a small cuff for an infant, small child or
frail adult; a normal adult-size cuff; and a large cuff for measuring
the blood pressure on the leg or on the arm of an obese adult.
Figure 30.11


Determining that the bladder of a blood pressure cuff is 40% of the
arm circumference or 20% wider than the diameter of the midpoint
of the limb.
The length of the bladder also affects the accuracy of measurement.
The bladder should be sufficiently long to cover at least two-thirds of
the limb’s circumference. Blood pressure cuffs are made of non-
distensible material so that an even pressure is exerted around the
limb. Most cuffs are held in place by Velcro.
Blood pressure sites
The blood pressure is usually assessed in the person’s upper arm
using the brachial artery and a standard stethoscope.
Blood pressure is not measured on a particular limb in the following
situations:
The shoulder, arm or hand (or the hip, knee or ankle) is injured or
diseased.
A cast or bulky bandage is on any part of the limb.
The person has had surgical removal of lymph nodes on that
side, such as for cancer.
The person has an intravenous infusion in that limb.
The person has an arteriovenous fistula (e.g. for renal dialysis) in
that limb.


Assessing the blood pressure on a person’s thigh is indicated in
these situations:
The blood pressure cannot be measured on either arm (e.g.
because of burns or other trauma).
The blood pressure in one thigh is to be compared with the blood
pressure in the other thigh.
Methods
Blood pressure can be assessed either directly or indirectly. Direct
(invasive monitoring) measurement, usually performed in critical care
settings, involves the insertion of a catheter into the brachial, radial
or femoral artery. Arterial pressure is represented as wave-like forms
displayed on a monitor. With correct placement, this pressure
reading is highly accurate.
Two non-invasive indirect methods of measuring blood pressure are
the auscultatory and palpatory methods. The auscultatory method is
most commonly used in hospitals, clinics and homes. Required
equipment is a sphygmomanometer, a cuff and a stethoscope. When
carried out correctly, the auscultatory method is relatively accurate.
When taking a blood pressure using a stethoscope, the nurse
identifies phases in the series of sounds called Korotkoff sounds
(see Figure 30.12
). First the nurse pumps the cuff up to about
30mm Hg above the point where the pulse is no longer palpable; that
is, the point when the blood flow in the artery is stopped. Then the


pressure is released slowly (2 to 3 mm Hg per second) while the
nurse observes the readings on the manometer and relates them to
the sounds heard through the stethoscope. Five phases occur but
may not always be audible (see Box 30.3
).
Figure 30.12


Korotkoff sounds can be differentiated into five phases. In the
illustration the blood pressure is 138/90 or 138/102/90.
BO X
30.3 Korotkoff sounds
Phase 1: the pressure level at which the first faint, clear
tapping or thumping sounds are heard. These sounds
gradually become more intense. To ensure that they are
not extraneous sounds, the nurse should identify at least
two consecutive tapping sounds. The first tapping sound
heard during deflation of the cuff is the systolic blood
pressure.
Phase 2: the period during deflation when the sounds
have a muffled, whooshing or swishing quality.
Phase 3: the period during which the blood flows freely
through an increasingly open artery and the sounds
become crisper and more intense, and again assume a
thumping quality, but softer than in phase 1.


Phase 4: the time when the sounds become muffled and
have a soft, blowing quality.
Phase 5: the pressure level when the last sound is heard.
This is followed by a period of silence. The pressure at
which the last sound is heard is the diastolic blood
pressure in adults.
The palpatory method is sometimes used when Korotkoff sounds
cannot be heard and electronic equipment to amplify the sounds is
not available, or to prevent misdirection from the presence of an
auscultatory gap. An auscultatory gap
, which occurs particularly
in hypertensive people, is the temporary disappearance of sounds
normally heard over the brachial artery when the cuff pressure is
high, followed by the reappearance of the sounds at a lower level.
This temporary disappearance of sounds occurs in the latter part of
phases 1 and 2 and may cover a range of 40 mm Hg. If a palpated
estimation of the systolic pressure is not made prior to auscultation,
the nurse may begin listening in the middle of this range and
underestimate the systolic pressure. In the palpatory method of
blood pressure determination, instead of listening for the blood flow
sounds, the nurse uses light to moderate pressure to palpate the
pulsations of the artery as the pressure in the cuff is released. The
pressure is read from the sphygmomanometer when the first
pulsation is felt.


Common errors in assessing blood
pressure
The importance of the accuracy of blood pressure assessments
cannot be overemphasised. Many judgments about a person’s
haemodynamic status and health are made on the basis of blood
pressure. It is an important indicator of the person’s condition and is
used extensively as a basis for nursing interventions. Two possible
reasons for blood pressure errors are haste on the part of the nurse
and subconscious bias. For example, a nurse may be influenced by
the person’s previous blood pressure measurements or diagnosis
and ‘hear’ a value consonant with the nurse’s expectations. Table
30.2
 describes common reasons for obtaining erroneous blood
pressure readings.
Table 30.2 Selected sources of error in blood pressure
assessment
Clinical consideration
Electronic/automatic blood pressure cuffs can be
left in place for several hours, but it is important
that the cuff is removed and the condition of the
skin checked periodically throughout that time
period.


Lifespan considerations
Blood pressure
Infants
Use a paediatric stethoscope with a small diaphragm.
The lower edge of the blood pressure cuff can be closer to
the antecubital space of an infant.
Use the palpation method if auscultation with a
stethoscope or Doppler ultrasound is unsuccessful.
Arm and thigh pressures are equivalent in children under 1
year of age.
One quick way to determine the normal systolic blood
pressure of a child is to use the following formula:
Children
Blood pressure should be measured in all children over 3
years of age and in children under 3 years of age with
certain conditions (e.g. congenital heart disease, renal
malformation, medications that affect blood pressure).
Normal systolic BP = 80 + (2 × child's age in years)


Explain each step of the process and what it will feel like.
Demonstrate on a doll.
Use the palpation technique for children under 3 years old.
Cuff bladder width should be 40% and length should be
80% to 100% of the arm circumference (see Figure
30.13
).
In children, the diastolic pressure is considered to be the
onset of phase 4, where the sounds become muffled.
In children, the thigh pressure is about 10 mm Hg higher
than the arm.
Figure 30.13


Paediatric blood pressure cuffs (with manometers).


Older adults
Skin may be very fragile. Do not allow cuff pressure to
remain high any longer than necessary.
Determine whether the person is taking antihypertensive
medication(s) and, if so, when the last dose was taken.
Medications that cause vasodilation (antihypertensive
medications) along with the loss of baroreceptor efficiency
place older people at increased risk of having orthostatic
hypotension. Measuring blood pressure while the person is
in the lying, sitting and standing positions and noting any
changes can determine this.
If the person has arm contractures, assess the blood
pressure by palpation, with the arm in a relaxed position. If
this is not possible, take a thigh blood pressure.

Pulse or heart rate
The pulse
 is a wave of blood created by contraction of the left
ventricle of the heart. Generally, the pulse wave represents the
stroke volume output or the amount of blood that enters the arteries
with each ventricular contraction. Compliance
 of the arteries is
their ability to contract and expand. When a person’s arteries lose
their distensibility, as can happen with the normal ageing process,
greater pressure is required to pump the blood into the arteries.
Cardiac output
 is the volume of blood pumped into the arteries
by the heart and equals the result of the stroke volume (SV) times
the heart rate (HR) per minute. For example,
 beats
per minute equals 4.55 L per minute. That means when an adult is
resting, the heart pumps about 5 L of blood each minute. In a
healthy person, the pulse reflects the heartbeat; that is, the pulse
rate is the same as the rate of the ventricular contractions of the
heart. Note that observation charts in Australian health care facilities
are increasingly adopting the term ‘heart rate’ instead of ‘pulse’ as it
is considered the most popular term for this vital sign (Preece et
al.
) (see Figure 30.1
).
17 Preece, M., Horswill, M., Hill, A. & Watson, M. (2010). The Development of the Adult
Deterioration Detection System (ADDS) Chart. (Report prepared for the Australian
Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care’s program for Recognising and Responding
to Clinical Deterioration.) Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.

17


Home care considerations
Blood pressure
Readings may be obtained by 24-hour ambulatory
BP monitoring or by self-measurement of BP. It is
useful to obtain BP readings outside the
hospital/clinic because approximately 15% of the
general population show elevated BP when
measured in the clinic but not in other settings
(‘isolated clinic’ or ‘white coat’ hypertension). In a
similar proportion of people, ambulatory BP may be
high while clinic BP is normal (‘isolated ambulatory’,
‘masked’ or ‘reverse white coat’ hypertension)
(National Heart Foundation of Australia 2016).
If the person takes blood pressure readings at
home, use the same equipment or calibrate it
against a system known to be accurate.
Observe the person or family member taking the
blood pressure and provide feedback if further
instruction is needed.
Home blood pressure measurement done by the
patient or family can detect elevated pressures not
identified when the person is seen in a GP clinic.


In some types of cardiovascular disease, the heart and
pulse rates can differ. For example, a person’s heart
may produce very weak or small pulse waves that are
not detectable in a peripheral pulse far from the heart.
In these instances, the nurse should assess both the
apical and the peripheral pulse rates. A peripheral
pulse
 is a pulse located away from the heart; for
example, in the foot or wrist. The apical pulse
, in
contrast, is a central pulse; that is, it is located at the
apex of the heart. It is also referred to as the point of
maximal impulse (PMI)
.
Real-world practice
A 78-year-old man with a history of coronary
artery disease and hypertension was readmitted
to the hospital through the emergency
department after falling at home and fracturing
his right arm. The man’s blood pressure was
154/88 mm Hg. He complained of pain in his
right arm and a feeling of dizziness. He was
admitted to the same medical–surgical unit
where he had received care 2 months ago for
uncontrolled hypertension and a urinary tract
infection (UTI). During this earlier
hospitalisation, the doctor increased the dose of
the man’s antihypertensive medications and


prescribed antibiotics to treat his UTI. On the
second day of the man’s current hospitalisation,
the doctor again increased the dose of
antihypertensives in an effort to manage the
patient’s high blood pressure. The medical
decision was based on his vital signs,
specifically his blood pressure measurements,
which were being assessed every 4 hours.
At this time, a nursing student was assigned to
the man and was responsible for taking his vital
signs. During the student’s initial assessment,
the man complained of being tired all the time
and feeling dizzy and light-headed when he sat
up in bed. The nursing student chose not to use
the available, regular adult-size blood pressure
cuff because it was too small to fit the man’s
upper arm appropriately. Instead, the nursing
student asked the Registered Nurse for a large
adult cuff, which was located in the bottom
drawer of the supply cabinet in the medication
room. When the student used the correct size
cuff and supported the man’s arm at heart
level, his blood pressure measurement was
actually very low; the value was confirmed both
by the Registered Nurse and the clinical
educator. The Registered Nurse withheld the
man’s scheduled antihypertensive medications
and the medical officer was notified. The nurse


was heard saying to the medical officer over the
telephone, ‘We have been using the wrong size
blood pressure cuff for this person and
positioning his arm below his heart the entire
time’.
This scenario illustrates how important the
accurate assessment of a person’s blood
pressure is and how it can have a profound
influence on the management of people and the
quality use of medicines.
Source: B. Tomlinson
. Accurately measuring blood pressure: Factors that
contribute to false measurements. MedSurg Nursing, 19(20), 90−94.
Reproduced with permission of the publisher, Jannetti Publications, Inc.
Pitman, NJ.
18 Tomlinson, B. (2010). Accurately measuring blood pressure: Factors that
contribute to false measurements. MedSurg Nursing, 19(2), 90–94.
Factors affecting the pulse rate
The rate of the pulse is expressed in beats per minute (BPM). A
pulse rate varies according to a number of factors. The nurse should
18


consider each of the following factors when assessing a person’s
pulse:
Age. As age increases, the pulse rate gradually decreases
overall. See Table 30.3
 for specific variations in pulse rates
from birth to adulthood.
Table 30.3 Variations in pulse and respirations by age
Gender. After puberty, the average pulse rate of a male is
slightly lower than that of a female.
Exercise. The pulse rate normally increases with activity. The
rate of increase in the professional athlete is often less than in
the average person because of greater cardiac size, strength
and efficiency.
Pyrexia. The pulse rate increases (a) in response to the lowered
blood pressure that results from peripheral vasodilation
associated with elevated body temperature, and (b) because of
the increased metabolic rate.
Medications. Some medications decrease the pulse rate and
others increase it. For example, cardiac glycosides (e.g. digoxin)
decrease the heart rate, whereas adrenaline increases it.
Hypovolaemia. Loss of blood from the vascular system normally
increases pulse rate. In adults, the loss of circulating volume
results in an adjustment of the heart rate to increase blood
pressure as the body compensates for the lost blood volume.
Adults can usually lose up to 10% of their normal circulating
volume without adverse effects.


Stress. In response to stress, sympathetic nervous stimulation
increases the overall activity of the heart. Stress increases the
rate as well as the force of the heartbeat. Fear and anxiety as
well as the perception of severe pain stimulate the sympathetic
system.
Position changes. When a person is sitting or standing, blood
usually pools in dependent vessels of the venous system.
Pooling results in a transient decrease in the venous blood return
to the heart and a subsequent reduction in blood pressure and
increase in heart rate.
Pathology. Certain diseases such as some heart conditions or
those that impair oxygenation can alter the resting pulse rate.
Pulse sites
A pulse may be measured in the following nine sites (see Figure
30.14
).
Figure 30.14


Nine sites for assessing pulse.
Clinical consideration


Never press both carotid pulses at the same
time because this can cause a reflex drop in
blood pressure or pulse rate.
1. Temporal: where the temporal artery passes over the
temporal bone of the head. The site is superior (above) and
lateral to (away from the midline of) the eye.
2. Carotid: at the side of the neck where the carotid artery runs
between the trachea and the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
3. Apical: at the apex of the heart. In an adult this is located on
the left side of the chest, about 8 cm to the left of the
sternum (breastbone) and at the fourth, fifth or sixth
intercostal space (area between the ribs). In older people, the
apex may be further left if there are conditions that have led
to an enlarged heart. Before 4 years of age, the apex is left of
the mid-clavicular line (MCL); between 4 and 6 years, it is at
the MCL (see Figure 30.15
). For a child 7 to 9 years of
age, the apical pulse is located at the fourth or fifth intercostal
space.
Figure 30.15


Location of the apical pulse for a child under 4 years, a child 4
to 6 years and an adult.
4. Brachial: at the inner aspect of the biceps muscle of the arm
or medially in the antecubital space.


5. Radial: where the radial artery runs along the radial bone, on
the thumb side of the inner aspect of the wrist.
6. Femoral: where the femoral artery passes alongside the
inguinal ligament.
7. Popliteal: where the popliteal artery passes behind the knee.
8. Posterior tibial: on the medial surface of the ankle where
the posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus.
9. Pedal (dorsalis pedis): where the dorsalis pedis artery
passes over the bones of the foot, on an imaginary line drawn
from the middle of the ankle to the space between the big
and second toes.
The radial site is most commonly used in adults as it is easily found
and is readily accessible in most people. Some reasons for use of
each site are given in Table 30.4
.
Table 30.4 Reasons for using specific pulse site
Assessing the pulse
A pulse is commonly assessed by manual palpation (feeling) or
auscultation (listening). The middle three fingertips are used for
palpating all pulse sites except the apex of the heart. A stethoscope
is used for assessing apical pulses. A Doppler ultrasound
stethoscope (DUS) is used for pulses that are difficult to assess.
The DUS headset has earpieces similar to standard stethoscope
earpieces, but it has a long cord attached to a volume-controlled


audio unit and an ultrasound transducer. The DUS detects
movement of red blood cells through a blood vessel. In contrast to
the conventional stethoscope, it excludes environmental sounds.
A pulse is normally palpated by applying moderate pressure with the
three middle fingers of the hand. The pads on the most distal
aspects of the fingers are the most sensitive areas for detecting a
pulse. With excessive pressure one can obliterate a pulse, whereas
with too little pressure one may not be able to detect it. Before the
nurse assesses the resting pulse, the person should assume a
comfortable position. The nurse should also be aware of the
following:
any medication that could affect the heart rate
whether the person has been physically active; if so, wait 10 to
15 minutes until the person has rested and the pulse has slowed
to its usual rate
any baseline data about the normal heart rate for the patient; for
example, a physically fit athlete may have a heart rate below 60
BPM
whether the person should assume a particular position (e.g.
sitting). In some people, the rate changes with the position
because of changes in blood flow volume and autonomic nervous
system activity.
When assessing the pulse, the nurse collects the following data: the
rate, rhythm, volume, amplitude and presence or absence of
bilateral equality. An excessively fast heart rate (e.g. over 100 BPM


in an adult) is referred to as tachycardia
. A heart rate in an adult
of less than 60 BPM is called bradycardia
. If a person has either
tachycardia or bradycardia, the apical pulse should be assessed.
The pulse rhythm
 is the pattern of the beats and the intervals
between the beats. Equal time elapses between beats of a normal
pulse. A pulse with an irregular rhythm is referred to as a
dysrhythmia
 or arrhythmia
. It may consist of random,
irregular beats or a predictable pattern of irregular beats
(documented as ‘regularly irregular’). For example, a ventricular
ectopic beat (VEB) is an extra heartbeat originating in the ventricles.
Similarly, atrial ectopic beats and nodal ectopic beats may also
occur, originating in the atria and sinoatrial node respectively. When
a dysrhythmia is detected, the apical pulse should be assessed. An
electrocardiogram (ECG) is necessary to assess the dysrhythmia.
Pulse volume
, also called the pulse strength or amplitude, refers
to the force of blood with each beat. Usually, the pulse volume is the
same with each beat. It can range from absent to bounding. A
normal pulse can be felt with moderate pressure of the fingers and
can be obliterated with greater pressure. A forceful or full blood
volume that is obliterated only with difficulty is called a full or
bounding pulse. A pulse that is readily obliterated with pressure from
the fingers is referred to as weak or thready.
The elasticity of the arterial wall
 reflects its expansibility or its
deformities. A healthy, normal artery feels straight, smooth, soft and


pliable. An older person often has inelastic arteries that feel twisted
(tortuous) on palpation.
Peripheral pulse assessment
When assessing a peripheral pulse to determine the adequacy of
blood flow to a particular area of the body (perfusion), the nurse
should also assess the corresponding pulse on the other side of the
body. The second assessment gives the nurse data with which to
compare the pulses. For example, when assessing the blood flow to
the right foot, the nurse assesses the right dorsalis pedis pulse
followed by the left dorsalis pedis pulse. If the person’s right and left
pulses are the same, then the dorsalis pedis pulses are said to be
‘bilaterally equal’. The pulse rate does not need to be counted when
assessing for perfusion and equality.
When a peripheral pulse is identified, it indicates that pulses more
proximal to that location will also be present. For example, if the
dorsalis pedis, the most distal pulse of the lower extremity, cannot
be felt, the nurse palpates for the posterior tibial pulse. If it is not
felt, the popliteal pulse must be assessed. If the popliteal pulse is
found, it is not necessary to assess the femoral pulse because it
must also be present in order for the more distal pulse to exist.
Apical pulse assessment
Assessment of the apical pulse is indicated for people whose
peripheral pulse is irregular or unavailable as well as for people with


known cardiovascular, pulmonary and renal diseases. It is commonly
assessed prior to administering medications that affect heart rate,
such as digoxin. The apical site is also used to assess the pulse for
newborns, infants and children up to 2–3 years old.
Home care considerations
Pulse
Assist in obtaining and using an electronic pulse
device if indicated.
Teach the person to monitor the pulse prior to
taking medications that affect the heart rate. Ask
the person to report any notable changes in heart
rate or rhythm (regularity) to the health care
provider.
Apical–radial pulse assessment
An apical–radial pulse
 may need to be assessed for people with
certain cardiovascular disorders. Normally, the apical and radial
rates are identical. An apical pulse rate that is greater than a radial
pulse rate can indicate that the thrust of the blood from the heart is
too weak for the wave to be felt at the peripheral pulse site. It can


also indicate that vascular disease is preventing impulses from being
transmitted. Any discrepancy between the two pulse rates is called a
pulse deficit
 and needs to be reported promptly. In no instance is
the radial pulse greater than the apical pulse.
An apical–radial pulse rate can be taken by one or two nurses,
although the two-nurse technique may be more accurate.


Body temperature
Body temperature
 reflects the balance between the heat
produced and the heat lost from the body and is measured in
degrees Celsius (°C). There are two kinds of body temperature: core
temperature and surface temperature. Core temperature
 is the
relatively constant temperature of the deep tissues of the body, such
as the abdominal cavity and pelvic cavity. The normal core body
temperature is identified in a range (see Figure 30.16
).
Figure 30.16


Estimated ranges of body temperatures in normal people.
Source: E. F. DuBois
. Fever and the Regulation of Body Temperature. Springfield, IL: Charles C. Thomas.
19 DuBois, E. F. (1948). Fever and the Regulation of Body Temperature. Springfield, IL:
Charles C. Thomas.
The surface temperature
 is the temperature of the skin, the
subcutaneous tissue and fat. Surface temperature rises and falls in
response to the environment. The body continually produces heat as
a by-product of metabolism. When the amount of heat produced by
the body equals the amount of heat lost, the person is in heat
balance
 (see Figure 30.17
).
Figure 30.17
19


As long as heat production and heat loss are properly balanced,
body temperature remains constant. Factors contributing to heat
production (and temperature rise) are shown on the left side of the
scale; those contributing to heat loss (and temperature fall) are
shown on the right side of the scale.
Source: E. Marieb & K. Hoehn
. Human Anatomy and Physiology (9th ed.), Fig. 24.24, p. 985. © 2007 Pearson
Education, Inc. Reproduced with permission.
20 Marieb, E. & Hoehn, K. (2012). Human Anatomy and Physiology (9th ed.). Upper Saddle
River, NJ: Pearson.
A number of factors affect heat production in a person’s body. The
five most important are:
20


1. Basal metabolic rate (BMR)
. The BMR is the rate of
energy utilisation in the body required to maintain essential
activities such as breathing. Metabolic rates decrease with
age; the younger the person, the higher the BMR.
2. Muscle activity. Muscle activity, including exercise or
shivering, increases a person’s metabolic rate.
3. Thyroxine output. Increased thyroxine output increases the
rate of cellular metabolism throughout a person’s body. This
effect is called chemical thermogenesis
, the stimulation
of heat production in the body through increased cellular
metabolism.
4. Adrenaline or noradrenaline and sympathetic
stimulation/stress response. The hormones adrenaline and
noradrenaline increase the rate of cellular metabolism in
many body tissues. These hormones directly affect liver and
muscle cells, thereby increasing cellular metabolism.
5. Fever. Fever (also known as pyrexia) increases the cellular
metabolic rate and increases the body’s temperature.
Lifespan considerations
Pulse
Infants


Use the apical pulse for the heart rate of newborns,
infants and children 2 to 3 years old to establish baseline
data for subsequent evaluation, to determine whether the
cardiac rate is within normal range and to determine if the
rhythm is regular.
Place the baby in a supine position and offer a ‘dummy’ if
the baby is crying or restless. Crying and physical activity
will increase the pulse rate. For this reason, take the
apical pulse rate of infants and small children before
assessing body temperatures.
Locate the apical pulse in the fourth intercostal space,
lateral to the mid-clavicular line during infancy.
Brachial, popliteal and femoral pulses may be palpated.
Due to a normally low blood pressure and rapid heart rate
in infants, other distal pulses may be hard to feel.
Newborn infants may have heart murmurs that are not
pathological but reflect functional incomplete closure of
fetal heart structures (ductus arteriosus or foramen
ovale).
Children
To take a peripheral pulse, position the child comfortably
in the adult’s arms or have the adult remain close by. This
may decrease anxiety and yield more accurate results.
To assess the apical pulse, assist a young child to a
comfortable supine or sitting position.


Demonstrate the procedure to the child using a stuffed
animal or doll and allow the child to handle the
stethoscope before beginning the procedure. This will
decrease anxiety and promote cooperation.
The apex of the heart is normally located in the fourth
intercostal space in young children and the fifth intercostal
space in children 7 years of age and over.
Locate the apical impulse along the fourth intercostal
space, between the mid-clavicular line and the anterior
axillary line (see Figure 30.15
).
Older adults
If the older adult has severe hand or arm tremors, the
radial pulse may be difficult to count.
Cardiac changes in older adults, such as decrease in
cardiac output, sclerotic changes to heart valves and
dysrhythmias, often indicate that obtaining an apical pulse
will be more accurate.
Older people often have decreased peripheral circulation,
so pedal pulses should also be checked for regularity,
volume and symmetry.
In the older person, the pulse returns to baseline after
exercise more slowly than with younger people.
Heat is lost from the body via four processes: radiation, conduction,
convection and vaporisation:


1. Radiation
 is the transfer of heat from the surface of one
object to the surface of another without contact between the
two objects, mostly in the form of infrared rays.
2. Conduction
 is the transfer of heat from one molecule to a
molecule of lower temperature. Conductive transfer cannot
take place without contact between the molecules and
normally accounts for minimal heat loss except, for example,
when a body is immersed in cold water. The amount of heat
transferred depends on the temperature difference and the
amount and duration of the contact.
3. Convection
 is the dispersion of heat by air currents. The
body usually has a small amount of warm air adjacent to it.
This warm air rises and is replaced by cooler air, and so
people always lose a small amount of heat through
convection.
4. Vaporisation
 is continuous evaporation of moisture from
the respiratory tract, the mucosa of the mouth and the skin.
This continuous and unnoticed fluid loss is called insensible
fluid loss
, and the accompanying heat loss is called
insensible heat loss
. Insensible heat loss accounts for
about 10% of basal heat loss. When the body temperature
increases, vaporisation accounts for greater heat and fluid
loss.
Drug capsule
Cardiac glycoside


People taking cardiac medications
that affect heart rate
Cardiac glycosides, such as digoxin, increase cardiac
contractility (inotropic effect), which increases cardiac output.
Digoxin also decreases heart rate (chronotropic effect) by
prolonging cardiac conduction, especially at the AV node. As
a result, perfusion to the kidneys is increased, which
increases the production of urine. This dual capacity to
decrease rate and increase contractility ensures that cardiac
output is maintained. Consequently, digoxin is commonly
used for the clinical management of heart failure, atrial
fibrillation, atrial flutter and paroxysmal atrial tachycardia.
Nursing responsibilities
Measure the apical pulse for 1 minute before
administering the cardiac glycoside. If the apical pulse is <
60 BPM or another specific parameter set by the medical
officer, retake the pulse 1 hour later. If pulse remains < 60
BPM, call the medical officer.
Monitor electrolyte levels: low and high potassium, low
magnesium and high levels of calcium place the person at
risk for digitalis toxicity. Check the person’s most recent
electrolyte results before administering the dose.
Avoid giving digoxin with meals as this will delay
absorption.


Monitor for therapeutic drug levels: therapeutic plasma
concentrations of digoxin in adults are generally 0.5 to 2
nanogram/mL (MIMS Online ). Digoxin has a narrow
therapeutic index, which means that there is not a lot of
difference between a therapeutic effect and a toxic effect.
21 MIMS Online (2019). Lanoxin. Retrieved from <www.mims.co.uk>.
Assess for signs of digoxin toxicity such as anorexia,
nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, blurred or ‘yellow’ vision,
unusual tiredness and weakness.
Patient and family teaching
Explain the reason for taking digoxin and the importance
of medical check-ups that may include pathology tests to
evaluate the effects and dosage of the drug.
Teach the person and/or family how to check the radial or
carotid pulse for a full minute. Inform them to take the
pulse at the same time each day and to write it on the
calendar. Provide pulse parameters and tell them when it
is appropriate to call their GP.
Caution the person not to stop taking the digoxin without
approval of the GP.
Caution the person to avoid over-the-counter drugs,
except on the advice of the GP, as many can interact with
digoxin.
Explain the signs and symptoms of digoxin toxicity and the
importance of calling the GP.
21


Note: prior to administering any medication, review all
aspects with a current drug handbook or other reliable source
of drug information.
Regulation of body temperature
Body temperature regulation or thermoregulation is controlled by a
tripartite system consisting of (a) peripheral and central (core)
thermoreceptors, (b) a receiving and analysing area in the
hypothalamus and (c) peripheral and central effector mechanisms
that adjust the production and loss of heat. The hypothalamus
coordinates thermoregulation by synchronising heat production,
dissipation and conservation mechanisms, depending on the body’s
need.
The hypothalamic integrator, the centre that controls the core
temperature, is located in the hypothalamus and maintains the
thermostatic set point at approximately 36.9°C (
) via a
sequence of negative feedback mechanisms. When the sensors in
the hypothalamus detect heat (typically a core temperature greater
than 37.4°C), they send out signals intended to reduce the
temperature; that is, to decrease heat production and increase heat
loss. In contrast, when the cold sensors are stimulated (typically at a
core temperature less than 36.4°C) signals are sent out to increase
heat production and decrease heat loss. The signals from the cold-
sensitive receptors of the hypothalamus initiate effectors, such as
±0. 5∘C


vasoconstriction, shivering and the release of adrenaline, which
increase cellular metabolism and hence heat production. When the
warmth-sensitive receptors in the hypothalamus are stimulated, the
effector system sends out signals that initiate sweating and
peripheral vasodilation. When this system is stimulated, the person
consciously makes appropriate adjustments or engages in
behavioural thermoregulation, such as putting on additional clothing
in response to cold or turning on a fan in response to heat.
Most sensors or sensory receptors to temperature are in the skin.
The skin has more receptors for cold than warmth. Therefore, skin
sensors detect cold more efficiently than warmth. When the skin
becomes chilled over the entire body, three physiological processes
to increase the body temperature take place:
1. Shivering increases heat production.
2. Sweating is inhibited to decrease heat loss.
3. Vasoconstriction decreases heat loss.
Factors affecting body
temperature
An elevated body temperature can be caused by pathological
processes such as infection, inflammatory processes or malignancy.
Nurses should be aware of physiological factors that affect a
person’s body temperature so that they can recognise normal


temperature variations and understand the significance of body
temperature measurements that deviate from normal. Physiological
factors include:
Age. An infant is greatly influenced by the temperature of the
environment and must be protected from extreme changes.
Similarly, a child’s temperature continues to be variable until
puberty. Many older people, particularly those over 75 years of
age, are at risk of hypothermia (temperatures below 36°C) for
reasons such as inadequate diet, loss of subcutaneous fat and
reduced physical activity. The older person is also particularly
sensitive to extremes in the environmental temperature due to a
reduction in the efficiency of their thermoregulatory mechanisms.
Diurnal variations (circadian rhythms). A person’s body
temperature normally changes throughout the day, varying as
much as 1.0°C between the early morning and the late
afternoon. The maximum body temperature is usually reached
between 1600 and 2100 hours (4 p.m. to 9 p.m.) and the
minimum reached between 0400 and 0600 hours (4 a.m. to 6
a.m.). See Figure 30.18
. In a study by Gomolin, Lester and
Pollack , electronic digital thermometers were used to record
variations and the authors found the diurnal rise in body
temperature was less among nursing home residents compared
with high school students.
22 Gomolin, I., Lester, P. & Pollack, S. (2007). Older is colder: Observations on body
temperature among nursing home subjects. Journal of the American Medical Directors
Association, 8(5), 335–337.
Figure 30.18
22


Range of oral temperatures during 24 hours for a healthy young
adult.


Exercise. Hard work or strenuous exercise can increase a
person’s body temperature to levels as high as 40°C.
Hormones. Women usually experience more hormone
fluctuations than men. In women, progesterone secretion at the
time of ovulation raises body temperature by about 0.3°C to
0.6°C above basal temperature.
Stress. Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system can
increase the production of adrenaline and noradrenaline, thereby
increasing metabolic activity and heat production. Nurses can
anticipate that a highly stressed or anxious person could have an
elevated body temperature for that reason.
Environment. Extremes in environmental temperatures can
affect a person’s temperature regulatory systems. If a person’s
temperature is assessed in a very warm room and the body
temperature cannot be modified by convection, conduction or
radiation, the temperature will be elevated. Similarly, if the person
has been outside in cold weather without suitable clothing, or if
there is a medical condition preventing the person from
controlling the environmental temperature (e.g. cognitive
impairment), the body temperature may be low.
Assessing body temperature
The body site where the temperature measurement is made can
greatly affect the reading obtained. The most common sites for
measuring body temperature are the mouth (oral), rectum, axilla,
ear (tympanic membrane) and forehead (temporal artery). Each of


these sites has advantages and disadvantages (see Table 30.5
).
Body temperature is most accurately measured by centrally or
peripherally inserted catheters into blood vessels.
Table 30.5 Advantages and disadvantages of sites for body
temperature measurement
Glass thermometers containing the hazardous substance mercury
were traditionally used to measure body temperature in the mouth
(oral), rectum and axilla, but have been replaced by faster, safer and
more accurate digital thermometers. Few clinical settings in Australia
still use mercury-in-glass thermometers, and in most health care
settings they have been replaced by the use of tympanic
thermometers.
Rectal temperature readings are considered to be very accurate.
However, they are contraindicated in many clinical situations; for
example, people who are undergoing rectal surgery, have diarrhoea
or diseases of the rectum, are immunosuppressed, have a clotting
disorder or have significant haemorrhoids.
The axilla is the preferred site for measuring temperature in
newborns because it is accessible and safe. Axillary temperatures
are lower than rectal temperatures. Nurses should check the
protocol of the clinical setting when taking the temperature of
newborns, infants, toddlers and children. In adults, the axilla is
appropriate when other temperature sites are contraindicated.


The tympanic membrane, or nearby tissue in the ear canal, is a
frequent site for estimating core body temperature. Like the
sublingual oral site, the tympanic membrane has an abundant
arterial blood supply, primarily from branches of the external carotid
artery. Tympanic thermometers detect infrared energy, which is
converted into an electronic temperature reading displayed on an
LCD screen. For infection-control purposes, an appropriate
disposable probe cover is used for each person and the
thermometer usually has an automatic probe cover eject button to
minimise cross-contamination. Even though electronic tympanic
thermometers are found extensively in both inpatient and outpatient
care settings, there is still much debate about the efficacy of ear
thermometry. Most notably, tympanic thermometers are susceptible
to user error, which can result in false low readings due to incorrect
positioning (Davie & Amoore ).
23 Davie, A. & Amoore, J. (2010). Best practice in the measurement of body temperature.
Nursing Standard, 24(42), 42–49.
The temperature may also be measured on the forehead using a
chemical thermometer or a temporal artery thermometer. Forehead
temperature measurements are most useful for infants and children
where a more invasive measurement is not necessary. However,
these devices lack reliability and their efficacy remains largely
unproven.
Types of thermometers
23


Electronic contact thermometers can provide a reading in 2 to 60
seconds, depending on the model. The equipment consists of a
battery-operated portable electronic unit, a probe that the nurse
attaches to the unit, a disposable probe cover and an LCD measure
reading (see Figure 30.19
). Recent technical advancements in
electronic thermometers have produced models that incorporate
options for the selection of oral (see Figure 30.20
), paediatric
axillary or adult axillary modes of measurement as well as a different
circuit and probe for rectal measurement.
Figure 30.19


An electronic thermometer.
Figure 30.20


Oral thermometer.
Source: Welch Allyn.
Infrared thermometers sense body heat in the form of infrared
energy given off by a heat source which, in the ear canal, is primarily
the tympanic membrane (see Figure 30.21
). The infrared
thermometer makes no contact with the tympanic membrane.
Figure 30.21


An infrared (tympanic) thermometer used to measure the tympanic
membrane temperature.
Temporal artery thermometers determine temperature using a
scanning infrared thermometer that compares arterial temperature
in the temporal artery of the forehead with the temperature in the
room and calculates the heat balance to approximate the core
temperature of the blood in the pulmonary artery. The probe is
placed in the middle of the forehead and then drawn laterally to the
hairline. If the person has perspiration on the forehead, the probe is
also touched behind the earlobe so the thermometer can
compensate for evaporative cooling (see Figure 30.22
).
Figure 30.22


A temporal artery thermometer.
Source: © Westend61 GmbH/Alamy Stock Photo.
Clinical consideration
Be sure to record the temperature from an
electronic thermometer before replacing the
probe into the charging unit. With many models,
replacing the probe erases the temperature
from the display.
Oral temperatures are not measured on people
who have diminished consciousness or are
confused, are less than 6 years of age, have an
oral infection or have had oral surgery.
Box 30.4
 shows the placement of different thermometers.
BO X
30.4 Thermometer placement


Alterations in body temperature
There are two primary alterations in body temperature: pyrexia and
hypothermia.
Pyrexia
A body temperature above the usual range is called pyrexia
, or
(in lay terms) fever
. A very high temperature, such as 41°C, is
called hyperpyrexia
 (see Figure 30.23
). A person who has
pyrexia is said to be febrile
 while a person who has a normal
temperature is described as afebrile
.
Figure 30.23


Terms used to describe alterations in body temperature (oral
measurements) and ranges in Celsius scale.
There are four common types of fevers:
1. Intermittent fever
 occurs when the body temperature
alternates at regular intervals between periods of fever and
periods of normal or subnormal temperatures. An example of
when intermittent fever occurs is with the disease malaria.
2. Remittent fever
 occurs typically in conditions such as a
cold or influenza, whereby there is a wide range of above-


normal temperature fluctuations (i.e. more than 2°C) over a
24-hour period.
3. Relapsing fever
 occurs when there are short febrile
periods of a few days interspersed with periods of 1 or 2 days
of normal temperature.
4. Constant fever
 occurs when the body temperature
fluctuates minimally but always remains above normal. This
can occur with typhoid fever.
When a person’s temperature rises to fever level rapidly following a
normal temperature and then returns to normal within a few hours,
the condition is called a fever spike. Bacterial blood infections often
cause fever spikes
.
The clinical signs of fever vary with the onset, course and abatement
stages (see Box 30.5
). These signs occur as a result of changes
in the set point of the temperature control mechanism regulated by
the hypothalamus. Under normal conditions, whenever the core
temperature rises the rate of heat loss increases, resulting in a fall in
temperature towards the set-point level. Conversely, when the core
temperature falls, the rate of heat production is increased, resulting
in a rise in temperature towards the set point. However, in a fever,
the set point of the hypothalamic thermostat changes suddenly from
the normal level to a higher than normal value (e.g. 39.5°C) in
response to the effects of tissue destruction, endogenous and
exogenous pyrogenic substances, or when dehydration is detected
by the hypothalamus.


BO X
30.5 Clinical manifestations of fever
Chill (or cold) phase (onset of fever)
Increased heart rate (tachycardia)
Increased respiratory rate (tachypnoea) and depth
Shivering
Pale, cold skin
Complaints of feeling cold
Cyanotic nail beds
‘Goosebumps’ on the skin
Cessation of sweating.
Plateau phase (course of fever)
Absence of chills
Skin that feels warm
Photosensitivity
Glassy-eyed appearance
Tachycardia and tachypnoea
Increased thirst (polydipsia)
Mild to severe dehydration
Drowsiness, restlessness, delirium or convulsions
Herpetic lesions of the mouth (i.e. an ulceration of the
skin)


Anorexia (persistent loss of appetite) if the fever is
prolonged
Malaise, lethargy, weakness and aching muscles.
Defervescence (or flush) phase
(fever abatement)
Skin that appears flushed and feels warm
Sweating (diaphoresis)
Decreased shivering
Possible dehydration.
There are three phases of fever: the chill, plateau and defervescent
phases. These phases are outlined in Box 30.5
.
The chill (or cold) phase is characterised by heat production
responses that cause elevation of a person’s body temperature such
as chills, feelings of coldness, cold skin due to vasoconstriction and
shivering. This occurs in the interval (typically several hours) during
which the core body temperature (i.e. the blood temperature)
reaches the new set point.
The plateau phase begins when a person’s core temperature
reaches the new set point; the person feels neither cold nor hot and
no longer experiences chills. Depending on the degree of
temperature elevation, other signs may occur during the course of


the fever. Very high temperatures, such as 41°C to 42°C, damage
the parenchyma of cells throughout the body, particularly in the brain
where destruction of neuronal cells is irreversible. Damage to the
liver, kidneys and other body organs can also be great enough to
disrupt functioning and eventually cause death. This situation is
highlighted in cases where children are accidentally locked in a
motor vehicle for extended periods of time.
The defervescent (or flush) phase begins when a person’s body
resolves the cause of the high temperature. The hypothalamic set
point is adjusted to a lower value, perhaps even back to the original
normal level. In this instance, the hypothalamus attempts to lower
the temperature and the usual heat loss responses cause a
reduction of the body temperature; excessive sweating and hot,
flushed skin due to sudden vasodilation occurs.
The three phases of fever and associated clinical manifestations are
shown in Figure 30.24
.
Figure 30.24


The three phases of fever and associated clinical manifestations.
Nursing interventions for a person who has a fever are designed to
support the body’s normal physiological processes, provide comfort
and prevent complications. During the course of a fever, the nurse
needs to monitor and interpret the person’s vital signs closely. The
best practice guidelines for the management of fever are outlined
below.


See Box 30.6
 for symptoms of heat stress and heat stroke.
BO X
30.6 Heat stress and heat stroke
Heat stress and heat stroke are significant health issues in
the Australian community due to the high temperatures and
high levels of humidity. Heat stress occurs when the body
becomes dehydrated and is unable to cool itself enough to
maintain a healthy temperature. If left untreated, this can
lead to heat stroke, which is a life-threatening medical
emergency (Better Health Channel ).
24 Better Health Channel (2010). Heat Stress—Preventing Heat Stroke. Retrieved
from <www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au>.
Heat stroke
 (also known as sunstroke or thermic fever)
occurs when the body’s core temperature rises above 40.5°C
and its internal systems start to shut down. Heat stroke can
be brought on by high environmental temperatures,
strenuous physical activity or other conditions that raise a
person’s body temperature. Whatever the causes, heat
stroke is a life-threatening emergency that requires
immediate medical treatment to prevent brain damage, organ
failure or death.
Symptoms of heat stroke include:
very high body temperature
24


red, hot and dry skin
dry swollen tongue
rapid pulse
shallow, rapid breathing
throbbing headache
confusion or ‘strange’ behaviour
nausea
possible loss of consciousness (New South Wales
Health ).
25 New South Wales Health (2013). Environmental Health Factsheet: Heat
Related Illness Including Heat Stroke. Retrieved from
<www.health.nsw.gov.au>.
People attending large events (concerts, dance parties or
sporting events), working in hot and poorly ventilated or
confined areas, or engaging in vigorous physical activity in
hot weather are at increased risk of dehydration and heat
stroke. Vulnerable groups such as older people and young
children, and those with chronic diseases such as
cardiovascular and respiratory diseases are at increased risk
of both heat stress and heat stroke.
Maintaining a cool environment and the use of fans, cool
baths and showers are key actions to reduce the risk of heat
stroke. It is particularly important to ensure that vulnerable
people are not exposed to excessive heat or humidity. The
maintenance of a stable internal temperature via air-
conditioning and other cooling methods (Bouchama et al.
),
adequate hydration and fluid replacement, and monitoring for
25
26


manifestations of heat stress are important nursing
considerations.
26 Bouchama, A., Dehbi, M., Mohamed, G., Matthies, F., Shoukri, M. & Menne, B.
(2007). Prognostic factors in heat wave related deaths: A meta-analysis. Archives of
Internal Medicine, 167(20), 2170–2176.
Clinical practice guidelines
In many clinical situations, such as the management of fever in
children, a clinical practice guideline has been developed by an
expert clinical group to assist clinicians in their provision of best
possible care. A clinical practice guideline is defined by the National
Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) as ‘systematically
developed statements to assist practitioner and patient decisions
about appropriate healthcare for specific clinical circumstances’
(NHMRC ). For example, in October 2010, New South Wales
Health released Policy Directive: Children and Infants with Fever–
Acute Management based on a clinical guideline.
27 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) (1999). A Guide to the
Development, Implementation and Evaluation of Clinical Practice Guidelines, 1999. Retrieved
from <www.nhmrc.gov.au>.
Levels of evidence for relevant statements are identified within a
clinical guideline. For example, the NHMRC level of evidence in the
New South Wales Health policy directive for the statement ‘methods
of measurement such as axillary and tympanic membrane
27


temperatures are less accurate and less reliable than rectal
temperatures’ is rated level 1; this means that strong evidence was
obtained from a systematic review of all relevant randomised
controlled trials. In contrast, evidence for the following statement is
rated level 1V (evidence obtained from case series, either post test
or pre test and post test): ‘fever is commonly defined as a rectal
temperature > 38°C, which is approximately two standard deviations
above the mean for infants under 3 months old. In some
circumstances, however, a lower temperature will be abnormal’
(NHMRC 1999).
Box 30.7
 lists the clinical recommendations for the management
of fever in infants and children (New South Wales Health ).
28 New South Wales Health (2010). Policy Directive: Children and Infants with Fever—Acute
Management. Retrieved from <www.health.nsw.gov.au>.
BO X
30.7 Children and infants with fever:
acute management
Axillary measurement of temperature is recommended for
routine clinical use, but staff should be aware that axillary
temperatures are up to 1ºC lower than rectal
temperatures. Rectal and oral temperatures are not
recommended because of safety concerns and problems
28


with acceptability. There is also a lack of data for oral
temperatures. Tympanic temperatures are not
recommended as they are unreliable.
All febrile neonates should have a full septic work-up and
be admitted for parenteral antibiotics. Infants aged 1–3
months will generally be managed in a similar fashion, but
there may be a place for outpatient management in
carefully selected infants who are non-toxic, clinically
stable over a period of observation, have reassuring
pathology investigations and in whom close follow-up is
assured.
Any child assessed as being at risk of sepsis should be
admitted to hospital for investigation and, under most
circumstances, parenteral antibiotics should be
administered.
The possibility of urinary tract infection needs to be
considered in all febrile children who do not have an
obvious source of infection. Although urinalysis is a useful
screening investigation in these children, urine culture is
essential prior to the commencement of antibiotics for
suspected urinary tract infection.
The response to antipyretics should not be used as a
diagnostic tool to try to differentiate bacterial from viral
infection.
Source: New South Wales Health (2010). Policy Directive: Children and Infants with Fever—Acute
Management. Retrieved from <www.health.nsw.gov.au/policies/pd/2010/pdf/PD2010_063.pdf>, pp.
13–15.


Nursing measures during the chill phase are designed to help the
person decrease heat loss. At this time, the person’s physiological
processes are attempting to raise the core temperature to the new
set-point temperature. During the flush or crisis phase, the body
processes are attempting to lower the core temperature to the
reduced or normal set-point temperature. At this time, the nurse
takes action to increase heat loss and decrease heat production.
Nursing interventions for adults with fever are shown in Box 30.8
.
BO X
30.8 Nursing interventions for adults
with fever
Monitor vital signs.
Assess skin colour and temperature.
Monitor white blood cell count, haematocrit value and
other pertinent laboratory reports for indications of
infection or dehydration.
Remove excess blankets when the person feels warm,
but provide extra warmth when the person feels chilled.
Provide adequate nutrition and fluids (e.g. 2500–3000 mL
per day) to meet the increased metabolic demands and
prevent dehydration.
Measure fluid intake and output.


Reduce physical activity to limit heat production, especially
during the defervescent phase.
Administer antipyretics (medications that may reduce the
signs and symptoms of fever, such as pain, discomfort
and elevated body temperature) only as indicated or
ordered. This intervention should be considered on the
basis of maintaining the person’s level of comfort rather
than simply reducing an elevated body temperature.
Provide oral hygiene to keep the mucous membranes
moist.
Provide dry clothing and bed linen.
Hyperthermia
Hyperthermia
 is defined as a core temperature greater than
40.6°C. Hyperthermia is a medical emergency which is often fatal
despite intervention. A child or older person with a physical or
developmental disability has a greater risk of hyperthermia and
dehydration than other people. Therefore, leaving a child, an older
person or a person with a physical or developmental disability
unattended in a motor vehicle for even 10 minutes can be
catastrophic (see Box 30.9
).
BO X


30.9 Being inside a locked motor
vehicle
Locked motor vehicles are potential death traps, particularly
during summer. The temperature inside a motor vehicle
during the Australian summer can be 30–40°C higher than
the outside temperature. Therefore, on a 35°C day the
temperature inside a motor vehicle can be 65–75°C.
People who experience a stroke
Fever and hyperthermia can cause morbidity and mortality in those
who are critically ill. A common clinical condition in acute medical
wards where people experience an elevated temperature is stroke.
An Australian study revealed that, along with hyperglycaemia
(elevated blood glucose level) and swallowing dysfunction, fever is
poorly recognised and managed in the admission phase of acute
stroke (Middleton et al.
). The accurate measurement, early
reporting and management of this abnormal physiological variable
can influence the outcomes for a person who has had a stroke
(Middleton et al.
).
29 Middleton, S., Levi, C., Ward, J., ... Cadilhac, D. (2009). Fever, hyperglycaemia and
swallowing dysfunction management in acute stroke: A cluster randomised controlled trial of
knowledge transfer. Implementation Science, 4(16). Doi: 10.1186/1748-5908-4-16.
29
30


30 Middleton, S., McElduff, P., Ward, J., ... Levi, C. (2011). Implementation of evidence-based
treatment protocols to manage fever, hyperglycaemia, and swallowing dysfunction in acute
stroke (QASC): A cluster randomised controlled trial. The Lancet, 378(9804), 1699–1706.
Hypothermia
Hypothermia
 is a core body temperature below the lower limit of
normal. The three physiological mechanisms of hypothermia are
excessive heat loss, inadequate heat production to counteract heat
loss and impaired hypothalamic thermoregulation. The clinical signs
of hypothermia are listed in Box 30.10
.
BO X
30.10 Clinical manifestations of
hypothermia
Decreased body temperature and decreased pulse and
respiration rates.
Severe shivering (initially).
Feelings of cold and chills.
Pale, cool, waxy skin.
Frostbite (nose, fingers, toes).
Hypotension.
Decreased urinary output (oliguria).
Lack of muscle coordination.
Disorientation.


Drowsiness progressing to coma.
Hypothermia may be induced or accidental. Induced hypothermia is
the deliberate lowering of the body temperature to decrease the
need for oxygen by the body tissues, such as during certain
surgeries. Accidental hypothermia can occur as a result of exposure
to a cold environment, immersion in cold water and lack of adequate
clothing, shelter or heat. In the older person, the problem can be
compounded by a decreased metabolic rate and the use of
sedatives. If skin and underlying tissues are damaged by freezing
cold, this results in frostbite. Frostbite most commonly occurs in
hands, feet, nose and ears.
Managing hypothermia involves removing the person from the cold
and rewarming their body by applying blankets. For the person with
severe hypothermia, a hypothermia blanket (an electronically
controlled blanket that provides a specified temperature) is applied
and warm intravenous fluids are given. Wet clothing, which
increases heat loss because of the high conductivity of water, should
be replaced with dry clothing. See Box 30.11
 for nursing
interventions for people who have hypothermia.
BO X


30.11 Nursing interventions for people
with hypothermia
Provide a warm environment.
Remove wet clothing and provide dry clothing.
Apply warm blankets (a space blanket may also be used).
Keep limbs close to body.
Cover the person’s scalp with a cap or beanie.
Supply warm oral or intravenous fluids.
Apply warming pads.

 compares the signs and symptoms indicative of fever,

, heat stroke and hypothermia.
