Home care considerations
Temperature
Teach the person accurate use and reading of the
type of thermometer to be used. Examine the
thermometer used by the person in the home for
safety and proper functioning.


Observe the person/caregiver taking and reading a
temperature. Reinforce the importance of reporting
the site and type of thermometer used and the
value of using one consistently.
Discuss means of keeping the thermometer clean,
such as warm water and soap and avoiding cross-
contamination.
Instruct the person or family member to notify the
health care provider if the temperature is 37.7°C or
higher. It is also important to educate the person,
family and caregivers about the role of core
temperature in fighting infection.
When making a home visit, take a thermometer
with you in case the person does not have a
functional thermometer of their own.
Check that the person knows how to record the
temperature. Provide a recording chart/table if
indicated.
Discuss environmental control modifications that
should be taken during illness or extreme climate
conditions (e.g. heating, air-conditioning,
appropriate clothing and bedding).
Lifespan considerations


Temperature
Infants
The body temperature of newborns is extremely labile,
and newborns must be kept warm and dry to prevent
hypothermia.
Using the axillary site, you need to hold the infant’s arm
against the chest (see Figure 30.25
).
The axillary route may not be as accurate as other routes
for detecting fevers in children.
The tympanic route is fast and convenient but should only
be used when an appropriately shaped and sized
tympanic thermometer (i.e. that suits the shorter and
more horizontal ear canal of the young child) is available.
Place the infant supine and stabilise the head. Pull the
pinna straight back and slightly downward. Direct the
probe tip anteriorly and insert far enough to seal the
canal. The tip will not touch the tympanic membrane.
The tympanic membrane route may be more accurate in
determining temperature in febrile infants.
When using a temporal artery thermometer, touching only
the forehead or behind the ear is needed.
The rectal route is least desirable in infants.
Figure 30.25


Axillary thermometer placement.
Source: © nata-lunata/Shutterstock.
Children
Tympanic or temporal artery sites are preferred.
For the tympanic route, have the child held on an adult’s
lap with the child’s head held gently against the adult for
support. Pull the pinna straight back and upward for
children over age 3 (see Figure 30.26
).
Avoid the tympanic route in a child or infant with active ear
infections or tympanic membrane drainage tubes.
The oral route may be used for children over age 3, but
non-breakable, electronic thermometers are
recommended. When using this method, it is vitally
important to distract the child and incorporate play into the
measuring of the child’s temperature.
For a rectal temperature, place the child prone across
your lap or in a side-lying position with the knees flexed.
Insert the thermometer 2 cm into the rectum.
Figure 30.26


Pull the pinna of the ear back and up for placement of a
tympanic thermometer in a child over 3 years of age, back
and down for children under age 3.
Source: Beau Lark/Corbis/VCG/Getty Images.
Older adults
The core temperature of an older person tends to be
lower than that of a middle-aged adult.
The temperature of an older person is strongly influenced
by both environmental and internal temperature changes.
Their thermoregulation control processes are not as
efficient as those of younger people and they are at
higher risk for both hypothermia and hyperthermia.
The older person can develop significant build-up of ear
cerumen that may interfere with tympanic thermometer
readings.
The temperature of the older person may not be a valid
indication of the seriousness of the pathology of a
disease. They may have pneumonia or a urinary tract
infection and have only a slight temperature elevation.
Other symptoms, such as confusion and restlessness,
may be more accurate indicators of illness and need
follow-up.


Chapter 30 Review


Chapter highlights
Vital signs reflect changes in body function that otherwise might
not be observed.
Respirations are normally quiet, effortless and automatic, and
are assessed by observing respiratory rate, depth, rhythm,
quality and effectiveness.
An alteration in the respiratory rate and rhythm is often an early
sign of patient deterioration.
A pulse oximeter measures the percentage of haemoglobin
saturated with oxygen. A normal result is 95% to 100%.
Pulse oximeter sensors may be placed on the finger, toe, nose,
earlobe or forehead (or around the hand or foot of a neonate).
Blood pressure reflects cardiac output, peripheral vascular
resistance, blood volume and blood viscosity.
Factors influencing blood pressure include age, exercise, stress,
ethnicity, gender, medications, obesity, diurnal variations and
disease processes.
Postural or orthostatic hypotension occurs when the blood
pressure falls as the person assumes an upright position.
A blood pressure cuff that is too large or too small will give false
readings.
During blood pressure measurement, the artery must be held at
heart level.
Pulse rate and volume reflect the stroke volume output, the
compliance of the person’s arteries and the adequacy of blood
flow.


Normally, a peripheral pulse reflects a person’s heartbeat, but it
may differ from the heartbeat in people with certain
cardiovascular diseases; in these instances, the nurse takes an
apical pulse and compares it with the peripheral pulse.
Many factors may affect a person’s pulse rate: age, gender,
exercise, presence of fever, certain medications, hypovolaemia,
stress (in some situations), position changes and pathology.
Although the radial pulse is the site most commonly used, eight
other sites may be used in certain situations.
The difference between the apical and radial pulses is called
pulse deficit.
The nurse selects the most appropriate site to measure
temperature according to the person’s age and condition.
Body temperature is the balance between heat produced by the
body and heat lost from the body.
Factors affecting body temperature include age, diurnal
variations, exercise, hormones, stress and environmental
temperatures.
Four common types of fever are intermittent, remittent, relapsing
and constant.
During a fever, the set point of the hypothalamic thermostat
changes suddenly from the normal level to a higher than normal
level, but several hours elapse before the core temperature
reaches the new set point.
Hyperthermia may be the result of fever, heat stress or heat
stroke. The latter two are serious health issues in the Australian
community because of the high temperatures and humidity in the
Australian spring and summer. It is therefore important to


understand the potential for the development of hyperthermia,
particularly in vulnerable groups such as children and older
adults.
Hypothermia involves three mechanisms: excessive heat loss,
inadequate heat production by body cells and increasing
impairment of hypothalamic thermoregulation.

Assessment is an important nursing role. It is an
ongoing process that requires collection of
baseline information, monitoring and
reassessment of the person’s health for
planning and provision of person- and family-
centred care. In addition to vital signs
(discussed in Chapter 30
), there are other
important aspects of assessment. These include
taking a health history (discussed in Chapter
12
) and the physical examination (discussed
in this chapter).
Patient safety competency
framework
5 Clinical reasoning
The Patient Safety
Competency Framework
indicates that nursing
students must demonstrate
clinical reasoning to
accurately assess, interpret
and respond to individual
patient data in a systematic
and timely way. This


includes conducting
comprehensive and
focused nursing
assessments using
appropriate frameworks and
techniques (Levett-Jones et
al. ).
1 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T.,
Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L.,
Flenady, T., Applegarth, J.,
Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017).
Patient Safety Competency
Framework (PSCF) for Nursing
Students. Sydney. Retrieved from
<http://psframework.wpengine.co
m>.
A physical examination may include one of the
following four approaches depending on the
clinical situation:
1


1. comprehensive physical assessment—
incorporates the gathering of the past
and current health status of the person to
form a baseline against which any future
changes can be measured (e.g. when a
person is admitted to a health care
organisation).
2. focused assessment—the examination of
a cue, one problem or body system (e.g.
the cardiovascular system)
3. ongoing assessment—the appropriate
status evaluation of an identified problem
(e.g. frequent neurovascular observations
for a postoperative patient)
4. primary survey—the initial rapid collection
of data for the emergency management
of potential or actual life-threatening
conditions (e.g. an unconscious patient
with suspected drug overdose).
Note: in this text, the terms assessment and
examination will be used interchangeably—both
referring to a critical investigation and evaluation
of the person’s health status.
The Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia’s
(NMBA) Registered Nurse Standards for


Practice (2016) specify that Registered Nurses
must comprehensively conduct assessments
using a range of assessment techniques to
systematically collect relevant and accurate
information and data to inform practice’ (NMBA ,
p. 4).
2 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016).
Registered Nurse Standards for Practice. Retrieved from
<www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
2


Physical health assessment
In clinical practice, there are several approaches to completing a
physical health assessment used by the interprofessional health
care team. The selected assessment approach guides the sequence
of cue/data collection for the clinician; examples include the head-to-
toe assessment and the body systems approach. The head-to-toe
assessment commences at the head and proceeds in a systematic
manner downward to the toes (see Box 31.1
). The body systems
approach collects cues according to the systems of the body (see
Box 31.2
). The approach may vary according to the age of the
individual, the severity of the illness and/or physical deterioration, the
preferences of the health professionals and the location of the
examination. Regardless of the approach used, the person’s energy
levels need to be considered. The health physical assessment is
therefore conducted in a systematic and efficient manner that
results in the fewest position changes for the person. The person’s
wellbeing, such as privacy, warmth and levels of pain, must be
considered.

A focused physical assessment assesses a specific body area
instead of the entire body, particularly to determine issues in an area
in which the person has health problems. The areas of specific
assessments are chosen in relation to the person’s concerns, the
nurse’s observation of problems, the person’s presenting health
problem, nursing interventions provided and medical therapies.
Examples of these situations and assessments are provided in
Table 31.1
.
Table 31.1 Focused physical assessments addressing selected
situations
A physical examination may be conducted:
to obtain baseline data about a person’s health problem/s
to obtain baseline data about the person’s functional abilities
to supplement, confirm or refute data obtained in the nursing
history
to obtain data that will help establish nursing diagnoses and plans
of care
to evaluate the physiological outcomes of health care and thus
the progress of a person’s health problem
to collect data that will assist the nurse to make clinical
judgments about a person’s health status
to identify areas for health promotion and disease prevention.


Nurses use national guidelines and evidence-based practice to focus
health assessment on specific conditions. For example, when
screening for cancer, nurses should keep in mind the evidence-
based guidelines for early detection. The Department of Health’s
National Bowel Cancer Screening Program is one example of these
guidelines (<www.cancerscreening.gov.au/internet/screening/
publishing.nsf/Content/02E20F41818FE2A7CA257CEC00177989/
$File/
New%20NHMRC%20approved%20Guidelines%20and%20what%
20they%20mean%20for%20the%20National%20Bowel%20Cance
r%20Screening%20Program.pdf>).

<www.cancerscreening.gov.au>.
Patient safety competency framework
6 Evidence-based practice
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must use
evidence-based practice by taking into account
best available evidence, clinical expertise and
patients’ individual needs, values and
preferences (Levett-Jones et al. 2017).
3


Preparing the patient
Most people need an explanation of the physical examination
process and purpose. Often, they are anxious about what the nurse
will find. People can be reassured during the examination by
explanations being provided at each step. The nurse should explain
when and where the examination will take place, why it is important
and what will happen. Advise the person that all information
gathered and documented during the assessment will remain
confidential and that only health care professionals who have a
legitimate need to know the person’s information will have access to
it. Nurses are guided in their practice by the NMBA’s Code of
Conduct for Nurses in Australia  and Code of Conduct for Midwives
in Australia , which specify that all information is treated as
confidential.
4 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2018a). Code of Conduct for Nurses in
Australia. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
5 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2018b). Code of Conduct for Midwives in
Australia. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
The findings from the health assessment must be accurately
documented. The importance of clear and comprehensive
documentation of assessment findings is emphasised in the National
Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (Australian
Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) 2016),
4
5


where it is specified that documentation is critical, especially when a
person’s care changes.
It is important to determine in advance any positions that are
contraindicated or may cause pain for a particular person. The nurse
should assist the person to undress and put on a gown if needed.
The person should empty their bladder before the examination as
doing so helps them feel more relaxed and facilitates palpation of
the abdomen and pubic area. If a urinalysis is required, the urine
should be collected in a container for that purpose. Fully explain to
the person the required procedure for collecting the urine specimen.
When assessing adults, it is important to recognise that people of
the same age differ markedly. Box 31.3
 provides special
considerations for assessing adults, especially older people.
BO X
31.3 Health assessment of the adult
Ask the person how they wish to be addressed, such as
Mrs or Ms.
Be aware of normal physiological changes that occur with
age.
Be aware of stiffness of muscles and joints from ageing
and physiological changes, or history of orthopaedic
surgery or breast surgery. The person may need


modification of the usual positioning necessary for
examination and assessment.
Ensure the area is enclosed to provide maximum privacy.
Expose only areas of the body to be examined in order to
avoid chilling and to maintain privacy.
Permit ample time for the person to answer your
questions and assume the required positions.
Be aware of cultural differences. The person may want a
family member present during disrobing or require care by
health care staff of the same gender.
Arrange for an interpreter if the person’s language differs
from that of the nurse.
Adapt assessment techniques to any sensory impairment;
for example, make sure spectacles or hearing aids are
nearby and used when necessary.
If people are elderly and/or frail, it is wise to plan several
assessment times in order to not overtire them.
Use positive communication techniques to support the
person’s understanding of the assessment process.
The sequence of the assessment of children differs from that of
adults. With children, always proceed from the least invasive or
uncomfortable to the more invasive. Examination of the head and
neck, heart and lungs, and range of motion can be done early in the
process, while the ears, mouth, abdomen and genitals should be left
for the end of the examination.


Preparing the environment
It is important to prepare the environment before starting an
assessment. The time for the physical assessment should be
convenient to both the person and the nurse. The environment
needs to be well lit and the equipment should be organised for
efficient use. A person who is physically relaxed is less likely to
experience discomfort. The room should be warm enough to be
comfortable.
Providing privacy is important. Most people are embarrassed if their
bodies are exposed or if others can overhear or view them during
the assessment. Culture, age and gender of both the person and
the nurse influence how comfortable the person will feel and what
special arrangements might be needed. For example, if the person
and nurse are of different genders, the nurse should ask if it is
acceptable to perform the physical examination or if a nurse of the
same gender is preferred. Family and friends should not be present
unless the person asks for someone. However, a child should have
an adult present.
Clinical consideration
Due to the substantial knowledge and skill
required to undertake formal assessments, they
are not delegated to Assistants in Nursing


(AINs). However, many aspects are observed
during daily patient care and these may be
recorded by people other than the Registered
Nurse. All assessment findings should be
reported to the Registered Nurse and
documented. Enrolled Nurses may undertake
assessments under the delegation of the
Registered Nurse (NMBA 2016). Abnormal
findings must be validated and interpreted by
the Registered Nurse and reported to the
doctor.
Positioning
Several positions may be required during the physical assessment.
It is important to consider the person’s ability to assume a particular
position. The person’s physical condition, energy level and age
should be taken into consideration. Some positions are
embarrassing and uncomfortable and therefore should not be
maintained for long. The assessment is organised so that several
body areas can be assessed in one position, thus minimising the
number of position changes needed (see Table 31.2
).
Table 31.2 Patient positions and body areas assessed


Draping
Drapes or covers should be arranged so that only the area to be
assessed is exposed and other body areas are covered. Exposure
of the body is frequently embarrassing to people. Drapes provide not
only a degree of privacy but also warmth. Specific drapes made of
paper or cloth may be used, or the person’s bed linen can be used.
Instrumentation
All equipment required for the health assessment should be clean, in
good working order and readily accessible. The equipment used will
depend on the purpose of the physical examination. Equipment is
frequently set up on trays, ready for use.
Various instruments are shown in Table 31.3
.
Table 31.3 Equipment and supplies used for a health
examination
Clinical consideration
Not all equipment will be used by the nurse
unless they have been specifically trained to do


so.
Methods of examining
Four primary techniques are used in the physical examination:
inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation. These techniques
are discussed throughout this chapter as they apply to each body
system.
Inspection
Inspection
 is the visual examination or assessment using the
sense of sight. An initial visual assessment should be part of the
procedure of greeting the person, in which such aspects as the
person’s overall demeanour and appearance, hygiene, skin colour
and skin appearance can be noted. Visual examination of physical
indications of pain, the need for assistance such as hearing aids or
spectacles and the overall appearance of health should be
observed. Each aspect of inspection should be documented and
should be deliberate, purposeful and systematic. The nurse inspects
with the naked eye and as required with a lighted instrument to
obtain a clearer visualisation of the inspected area. In addition to
visual observations, olfactory (smell) and auditory (hearing) cues are
noted. For example, the noises of breathing can be noted as
needing further assessment. Nurses frequently use visual inspection


to assess moisture, colour and texture of body surfaces, as well as
shape, position, size and symmetry of the body. Lighting must be
sufficient for the nurse to see clearly and may be either natural or
artificial light. When using the auditory senses it is important to have
a quiet environment to enable accurate hearing. Observation can be
combined with the other assessment techniques.
Palpation
Palpation
 is the examination of the body using the sense of
touch. The pads of the fingers are used because their concentration
of nerve endings makes them highly sensitive to tactile
discrimination. Palpation is used to determine (a) texture (e.g. of the
hair); (b) temperature (e.g. of a skin area); (c) vibration (e.g. of a
joint); (d) position, size, consistency and mobility of organs or
masses; (e) distention (e.g. of the urinary bladder); (f) pulsation; and
(g) tenderness or pain.
General guidelines for palpation include the following:
The nurse’s hands should be clean and warm, and the fingernails
short.
Areas of tenderness should be palpated last.
Deep palpation should be done after light palpation (see below).
There are two types of palpation: light and deep. Light (superficial)
palpation should always precede deep palpation because heavy
pressure on the fingertips can dull the sense of touch. For light


palpation, the nurse extends the dominant hand’s fingers parallel to
the skin surface and presses gently downward while moving the
hand in a circular motion (see Figure 31.1
). With light palpation,
the skin is slightly depressed. If it is necessary to determine the
details of a mass, the nurse presses lightly several times rather than
holding the pressure. See Box 31.4
 for the characteristics of
masses.
Figure 31.1


The position of the hand for a light palpation.
BO X
31.4 Characteristics of masses
Location—site on the body, dorsal/ventral surface
Size—length and width in centimetres
Shape—oval, round, elongated, irregular
Consistency—soft, firm, hard
Surface—smooth, nodular
Mobility—fixed, mobile
Pulsatility—present or absent
Tenderness—degree of tenderness to palpation
Deep palpation is done with two hands (bimanually) or one hand. In
deep bimanual palpation, the dominant hand is extended (for light
palpation), then the finger pads of the non-dominant hand are
placed on the dorsal surface of the distal interphalangeal joint of the
middle three fingers of the dominant hand (see Figure 31.2
). The
non-dominant hand applies pressure while the lower hand remains
relaxed to perceive the tactile sensations. For deep palpation using
one hand, the finger pads of the dominant hand press over the area


to be palpated. Often the other hand is used to support a mass or
organ from below (see Figure 31.3
). Deep palpation is usually not
done during a routine examination and requires significant
practitioner skill. It is performed with extreme caution by doctors
because pressure can damage internal organs. It is usually not
indicated in people who have acute abdominal pain or enlarged
abdominal organs and where the source of pain is yet to be
diagnosed.
Figure 31.2


The position of the hands for a deep bimanual palpation.
Figure 31.3


Deep palpation using the lower hand to support the body while the
upper hand palpates the organ.
To test skin temperature, it is best to use the dorsum or back of the
hand and fingers, where the examiner’s skin is thinnest. To test for
vibration, the nurse should use the palmar surface of the hand.
The effectiveness of palpation depends largely on the person’s
relaxation. Nurses can assist a person to relax by (a) gowning
and/or draping the person appropriately, (b) positioning the person
comfortably and (c) ensuring that their own hands are warm before
beginning. During palpation, the nurse should be sensitive to the
person’s verbal and facial expressions indicating discomfort.
Percussion
Percussion
 is the act of striking the body surface to elicit sounds
that can be heard or vibrations that can be felt. There are two types
of percussion: direct and indirect. In direct percussion, the nurse
strikes the area to be percussed directly with the pads of two, three
or four fingers, or with the pad of the middle finger. The strikes are
rapid and the movement is from the wrist (see Figure 31.4
). This
technique is not generally used to percuss the thorax but is useful in
percussing an adult’s sinuses.
Figure 31.4


Direct percussion. Using one hand to strike the surface of the body.
Indirect percussion is the striking of an object (e.g. a finger) held
against the body area to be examined. In this technique, the middle
finger of the non-dominant hand, referred to as the pleximeter
, is
placed firmly on the person’s skin. Only the distal phalanx and joint
of this finger should be in contact with the skin. Using the tip of the
flexed middle finger of the other hand, called the plexor
, the
nurse strikes the pleximeter, usually at the distal interphalangeal joint
(see Figure 31.5
). The motion comes from the wrist; the forearm
remains stationary. The angle between the plexor and the pleximeter
should be 90 degrees and the blows must be firm, rapid and short to
obtain a clear sound.
Figure 31.5


Indirect percussion. Using the finger of one hand to tap the finger of
the other hand.
Percussion is used to determine the size and shape of internal
organs by establishing their borders. It indicates whether tissue is
fluid filled, air filled or solid. Percussion elicits five types of sound:
flatness, dullness, resonance, hyperresonance and tympany:
1. Flatness is an extremely dull sound produced by very dense
tissue, such as muscle or bone.
2. Dullness is a thud-like sound produced by dense tissue such
as the liver, spleen or heart.
3. Resonance is a hollow sound such as that produced by lungs
filled with air.
4. Hyperresonance is not produced in the normal body. It is
described as booming and can be heard over an
emphysematous lung.
5. Tympany is a musical or drum-like sound produced from an
air-filled stomach.
On a continuum, flatness reflects the most dense tissue (the least
amount of air) and tympany the least dense tissue (the greatest
amount of air). A percussion sound is described according to its
intensity, pitch, duration and quality (see Table 31.4
).
Table 31.4 Percussion sounds and tones
Auscultation


Auscultation
 is the process of listening to sounds produced
within the body. Auscultation may be direct or indirect. Direct
auscultation is the use of the unaided ear; for example, to listen to a
respiratory wheeze or the grating of a moving joint. Indirect
auscultation is the use of a stethoscope, which transmits the sounds
to the assessor’s ears. A stethoscope is used primarily to listen to
sounds from within the body, such as bowel sounds or valve sounds
of the heart and blood pressure.
The stethoscope tubing should be 30 to 35 cm long, with an internal
diameter of about 0.3 cm. It should have both a flat disc diaphragm
and a bell-shaped amplifier. The diaphragm best transmits high-
pitched sounds (e.g. bronchial sounds) and the bell best transmits
low-pitched sounds such as some heart sounds. The amplifier of the
stethoscope is placed firmly but lightly against the person’s skin. If
the person has excessive hair, it may be necessary to dampen the
hairs with a moist cloth so that they will lie flat against the skin and
not interfere with clear sound transmission.
Auscultated sounds are described according to their pitch, intensity,
duration and quality. The pitch is the frequency of the vibrations (the
number of vibrations per second). Low-pitched sounds, such as
some heart sounds, have fewer vibrations per second than high-
pitched sounds, such as bronchial sounds. The intensity (amplitude)
refers to the loudness or softness of a sound. Some body sounds
are loud; for example, bronchial sounds heard from the trachea.
Others are soft; for example, normal breath sounds heard in the
lungs. The duration of a sound is its length (long or short). The


quality of sound is a subjective description of a sound; for example,
whistling, gurgling or snapping.


General assessment
Health assessment begins from the moment you first meet the
person. The general survey provides an overall impression focusing
on the person’s general appearance, mental status, mobility and
measurement of vital signs, height and weight. A number of the
components of the general assessment can be undertaken while
greeting the person or taking the person’s health history, such as the
person’s body build, posture, hygiene and mental status. Touching
the person, such as with a handshake, can also impart valuable
information about the skin.
Clinical consideration
Child development is based on milestones that
are found in the child’s personal health record
booklet provided to each child at birth.
Parents/guardians are asked to ensure all
information related to the child’s health is
entered into the booklet by the attending health
personnel. Most states in Australia provide
these. An example of the child’s health record
with growth charts (NSW Ministry of Health )
can be seen at <www.health.nsw.gov.au/
6


kidsfamilies/MCFhealth/Publications/blue-
book.pdf>. There is a similar booklet published
by the Ministry of Health in New Zealand , Well
Child/Tamariki Ora Health Book, which the
government is encouraging people to use. It is
available online at <www.healthed.govt.nz/
system/files/resource-files/
HE7012_Well%20Child%20Tamariki%20Ora%
20my%20health%20book_0.pdf>.

Retrieved from <www.health.nsw.gov.au>.

Health Book. Retrieved from <www.healthed.govt.nz>.
As well, immunisation records for all children in
Australia can be found at the Australian
Immunisation Register (Department of Human
Services ) and can be accessed by health
professionals <www.humanservices.gov.au/
individuals/services/medicare/australian-
immunisation-register>.
8 Department of Human Services (2019). Australian Immunisation
Register. Retrieved from <www.humanservices.gov.au>.
7
8


Appearance and mental status
The general appearance and behaviour of an individual should be
assessed in relationship to culture, socioeconomic status and
current circumstances. For example, an individual who has recently
experienced a personal loss may appropriately appear depressed
(sad expression, slumped posture). In certain cultures, it is
considered rude to look another person directly ‘in the eye’ and the
person may look away from you. The person’s age, sex and race
are also useful factors in interpreting findings that suggest increased
risk for known conditions. Skill 31.1
 describes how to assess
general appearance and mental status.
Vital signs
Vital signs are measured (a) to establish baseline data against which
to compare future measurements, and (b) to detect actual and
potential health problems. See Chapter 30
 for measurements of
respirations, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, heart rate or pulse,
and temperature. See Chapter 49
 for pain assessment.
Height and weight


In adults, the ratio of weight to height provides a general measure of
health. By asking people about their height and weight before
actually measuring them, the nurse obtains some idea of the
person’s self-image. Excessive discrepancies between the person’s
responses and the measurements may provide cues to actual or
potential problems in self-concept. Ask the person if they have had
any significant unintentional weight gain or loss and, if so, over what
time frame.
The nurse measures height with an appropriate measuring device
attached to weight scales or to a wall. The person should remove
shoes and stand erect, with heels together and the heels, buttocks
and back of the head against the measuring device. Eyes should be
looking straight ahead. The nurse raises the L-shaped sliding arm on
the measuring device until it rests on top of the person’s head, or
places a small flat object such as a ruler or book on the person’s
head. The edge of the flat object should abut the measuring guide.
Weight is usually measured when a person is admitted to a health
organisation, and then regularly; for example, each morning before
breakfast. Scales measure in kilograms (kg); however, if the nurse
needs to convert from the imperial system, 1 kilogram is equal to 2.2
pounds. The nurse should use the same scale each time (because
every scale weighs slightly differently), take the measurements at
the same time each day and make sure the person has on similar
clothing and no footwear. The person stands on a platform and the
weight is read from a digital display panel or a balancing arm. People
who cannot stand can be weighed on a chair (see Figure 31.6
) or


bed scales. The bed scales (see Figure 31.7
) have canvas straps
or a stretcher-like apparatus. A machine lifts the person above the
bed and the weight is reflected either on a digital display panel or on
a balance arm like that of a standing scale. Some hospitals have
beds with built-in scales. Ensure the appropriate equipment is used:
bariatric scales may be need to be sourced.
Figure 31.6


Chair scale.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Figure 31.7


Bed scale.
Body mass index (BMI) can be used to determine underweight,
overweight or obesity in adults by using the person’s weight and
height (see Table 31.5
). The BMI may not be an applicable
measure for all people; for example, children, pregnant women and
those with higher than normal levels of lean body tissue, such as
elite athletes. BMI is defined as the weight in kilograms divided by
the square of the height in metres (
).
 The Australian government’s Department
of Health  provides useful background information about BMIs on its
website <http://healthyweight.health.gov.au/wps/portal/Home/
get-started/are-you-a-healthy-weight/bmi>.

Planning
Prepare the environment and ensure the person
is comfortable.
If necessary (or possible), provide a separate,
quiet and private room.
Obtain the person’s consent after explaining the
assessment to be undertaken.
Equipment
None
Implementation
Performance
1. Initial assessment may be done while

2. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce

The integumentary system
The integumentary system includes the skin, hair and nails. The
examination begins with a generalised inspection using a good
source of lighting, preferably indirect natural daylight.
Skin
Assessment of the skin involves inspection and palpation. The entire
skin surface may be assessed at one time or as each aspect of the
body is assessed. In some instances, the nurse may also use the
olfactory sense to detect unusual skin odours; these are usually
most evident in the skinfolds or in the axillae. Pungent body odour is
frequently related to poor hygiene, hyperhidrosis (excessive
perspiration) or bromhidrosis (foul-smelling perspiration). Ask if the
person has any allergies which may lead to differences noted during
the integument assessment.
Pallor
 is the result of inadequate circulating blood or haemoglobin
and subsequent reduction in tissue oxygenation. In people with dark
skin, it is usually characterised by the absence of underlying red
tones in the skin and may be most readily seen in the buccal
mucosa. In brown-skinned people, pallor may appear as a yellowish-
brown tinge; in black-skinned people, the skin may appear ashen


grey. Pallor in all people is usually most evident in areas with the
least pigmentation, such as the conjunctiva, oral mucous
membranes, nail beds, palms of the hand and soles of the feet.
Cyanosis
 (a bluish tinge) is most evident in the nail beds, lips and
buccal mucosa. In dark-skinned peoples, close inspection of the
palpebral conjunctiva (the lining of the eyelids) and palms and soles
may also show evidence of cyanosis. Jaundice
 (a yellowish tinge)
may first be evident in the sclera of the eyes and then in the mucous
membranes and the skin. Nurses should take care not to confuse
jaundice with the normal yellow pigmentation in the sclera of a dark-
skinned person. If jaundice is suspected, the posterior part of the
hard palate should also be inspected for a yellowish colour tone.
Erythema
 is a redness of the skin associated with inflammation
and may be related to a variety of rashes.
Lifespan considerations
General assessment
Infants
Observation of children’s behaviour can provide important
data for the general assessment, including physical
development, neuromuscular function and social and
interactional skills.
It may be helpful to have parents hold older infants and
very young children for part of the assessment.


Measure height (length) of children under age 2 in the
supine position with knees fully extended.
Weigh without clothing.
Include measurement of head circumference until age 2.
Standardised growth charts include head circumference
up to age 3.
Parents should be able to provide the child’s personal
health record of development, which will assist in
determining any significant changes in health. This will
include birth history, immunisation history and medical
history.
Children
Anxiety in preschool-age children can be decreased by
letting them handle and become familiar with examination
equipment.
School-age children may be very modest and shy about
exposing parts of the body.
Adolescents should be examined without parents present,
unless requested.
Weigh children without shoes and with as little clothing as
possible.
Older adults
Allow extra time for the person to answer questions.
Adapt questioning techniques as appropriate for
individuals with hearing or visual limitations.


Older adults with osteoporosis can lose several
centimetres in height. Be sure to document height and
ask if they are aware of becoming shorter in height.
When asking about weight loss, be specific about amount
and time frame; for example, ‘Have you lost more than
five kilograms in the past two months?’.
Dark-skinned people have areas of lighter pigmentation, such as the
palms, lips and nail beds. Localised areas of hyperpigmentation
(increased pigmentation) and hypopigmentation (decreased
pigmentation) may also occur as a result of changes in the
distribution of melanin (the dark pigment) or in the function of the
melanocytes in the epidermis. An example of hyperpigmentation in a
defined area is a birthmark; an example of hypopigmentation is
vitiligo. Vitiligo
, seen as patches of hypopigmented skin, is
caused by the destruction of melanocytes in the area. Albinism is
the complete or partial lack of melanin in the skin, hair and eyes.
Other localised colour changes may indicate a problem such as
oedema or a localised infection. Oedema
 is the presence of
excess interstitial fluid. An area of oedema appears swollen, shiny
and taut, and tends to blanch the skin colour or, if accompanied by
inflammation, may redden the skin. Generalised oedema is most
often an indication of impaired venous circulation and in some cases
reflects cardiac dysfunction or venous abnormalities.
A skin lesion is an alteration in a person’s normal skin appearance.
Primary skin lesions are those that appear initially in response to


some change in the external or internal environment of the skin (see
Figure 31.8
, 1−8). Secondary skin lesions are those that do not
appear initially but result from modifications such as chronicity,
trauma or infection of the primary lesion. For example, a vesicle or
blister (primary lesion) may rupture and cause an erosion
(secondary lesion). Table 31.6
 illustrates secondary lesions.
Nurses are responsible for describing skin lesions accurately in
terms of location (e.g. face), distribution (i.e. body regions involved)
and configuration (the arrangement or position of several lesions) as
well as colour, shape, size, firmness, texture and characteristics of
individual lesions.
Figure 31.8


Primary skin lesions.
Sources: Dr P. Marazzi/Science Source; Scott Camazine/Alamy; Mediscan/Alamy (3 & 8); BSIP SA/Alamy;
Wellcome Image Library/Custom Medical Stock Photo (5 & 6); Hercules Robinson/Alamy.
Table 31.6 Secondary skin lesions
Clinical consideration
If possible, and the person provides consent,
take a digital or instant photograph of significant
skin lesions for the patient’s record. Include a
measuring guide (ruler or tape) in the picture to
demonstrate lesion size.


Skill 31.2
 describes how to assess the skin.
Lifespan considerations
Assessing the skin
Infants
Physiological jaundice may appear in newborns 2 to 3
days after birth and may last about 1 week. Pathological
jaundice, or that which indicates a disease, appears within
24 hours of birth and may last more than 8 days.
Newborns may have milia (whiteheads), small white
nodules over the nose and face and vernix caseosa (white
cheesy, greasy material on the skin).
Premature infants may have lanugo, a fine downy hair
covering their shoulders and back.
In dark-skinned infants, areas of hyperpigmentation may
be found on the back, especially in the sacral area.
Dermatitis may be seen in the nappy area in infants.
If a rash is present, describe the rash and inquire in detail
about immunisation history.
Assess skin turgor by pinching the skin on the abdomen.
Children


Children normally have minor skin lesions (e.g. bruising or
abrasions) on arms and legs due to their high activity
level. Lesions on other parts of the body may be signs of
disease or abuse and a thorough history should be taken.
Secondary skin lesions may occur frequently as children
scratch or expose a primary lesion to microbes.
With puberty, oil glands become more productive and
children may develop acne. Most people aged 12 to 24
years have some acne.
In dark-skinned children, areas of hyperpigmentation may
be found on the back, especially in the sacral area.
If a rash is present, describe the rash and inquire in detail
about immunisation history.
Older adults
Changes in white skin occur at an earlier age than in dark
skin.
The skin loses its elasticity and wrinkles. Wrinkles first
appear on the skin of the face and neck, which are
abundant in collagen and elastic fibres that become less
elastic with age.
The skin appears thin and translucent because of loss of
dermis and subcutaneous fat.
The skin is dry and flaky because sebaceous and sweat
glands are less active. Dry skin is more prominent over
the extremities.
The skin takes longer to return to its natural shape after
being tented between the thumb and finger.


Due to the normal loss of peripheral skin turgor in older
adults, assess for hydration by checking skin turgor over
the sternum or clavicle.
Flat tan to brown-coloured macules, referred to as senile
lentigines or melanotic freckles, are normally apparent on
the back of the hand and other skin areas that are
exposed to the sun. These macules may be as large as 1
to 2 cm.
Warty lesions (seborrhoeic keratosis) with irregularly
shaped borders and a scaly surface often occur on the
face, shoulders and trunk. These benign lesions begin as
yellowish to tan and progress to a dark brown or black.
Vitiligo tends to increase with age and is thought to result
from an autoimmune response.
Cutaneous tags (acrochordons) are most commonly seen
in the neck and axillary regions. These skin lesions vary in
size and are soft, often flesh coloured and pedicled.
Visible, bright red, fine dilated blood vessels
(telangiectasias) commonly occur as a result of the
thinning of the dermis and the loss of support for the
blood vessel walls.
Pink to slightly red lesions with indistinct borders (actinic
keratoses) may appear at about age 50, often on the
face, ears, backs of the hands and arms. They may
become malignant if untreated.


Assessment tools
Nurses unfamiliar with an assessment may need to follow the
process indicated on an assessment chart. Nurses skilled in
assessment can integrate data collection into their other activities
then fill in the chart. Examples of tools used in the assessment of
the integument are the Waterlow Pressure Ulcer Risk Assessment
Chart (see <www.judy-waterlow.co.uk/waterlow_score.htm>),
the Norton Scale for predicting risk of pressure ulcer or the Braden
Scale risk assessment tool.
Hair
Assessing a person’s hair includes inspecting the hair, considering
developmental changes and ethnic differences, and determining the
individual’s hair care practices and factors influencing them. Much of
the information about hair can be obtained by questioning the
person, especially if there have been recent changes. Rashes and
itchiness on the scalp can be a result of health changes or allergies.
Home care considerations
Assessing the skin


When making a home visit, take a penlight or
examination lamp with you in case the home has
inadequate lighting.
If skin lesions are suggestive of physical abuse,
follow required regulations for follow-up and
reporting. Signs of abuse may include a pattern of
bruises, unusual location of burns or lesions that
are not easily explainable. If lesions are present in
adults or verbal-age children, conduct the interview
and assessment in private.
Document lesions by taking a photo (if the person
consents).
Clinical consideration
Older adults are more likely to develop pressure
ulcers. This is an area of localised damage to
the integument caused by pressure, shear,
friction or a combination of these. Pressure
ulcers occur most often over a bony prominence
and particularly when the person is lying on a
hard surface (such as a trolley, bed, theatre
table). Take note of any reddened areas on
which pressure may have developed. People


are more likely to develop pressure ulcers (in
any setting including at home) if they are less
mobile or have long-term illnesses and pressure
is not regularly relieved.
Normal hair is resilient and evenly distributed. In people with severe
protein deficiency (kwashiorkor), the hair colour is faded and
appears reddish or bleached and the texture is coarse and dry.
Some therapies or health risks cause alopecia
 (hair loss) and
some disease conditions and medications affect the coarseness of
hair. For example, hypothyroidism can cause very thin and brittle
hair.
Skill 31.3
 describes how to assess the hair.
Nails
Nails are inspected for nail plate shape, angle between the nail and
the nail bed (fingernails), nail texture, nail bed colour and the
intactness of the tissues around the nails. The parts of the nail are
shown in Figure 31.9
.
Figure 31.9


The parts of a nail.
The nail plate is normally colourless and has a convex curve. The
angle between the fingernail and the nail bed is normally 160
degrees (see Figure 31.10A
). One nail abnormality is the spoon
shape, in which the nail curves upward from the nail bed (see
Figure 31.10B
). This condition, called koilonychia, may be seen in
people with iron deficiency anaemia. Clubbing
 is a condition in
which the angle between the nail and the nail bed is 180 degrees or
greater (see Figures 31.10C
 and Figures 31.10D
). Clubbing
may be caused by a long-term lack of oxygen.
Figure 31.10


A: A normal nail, showing the convex shape and the nail plate angle
of about 160 degrees; B: a spoon-shaped nail, which may be seen
in people with iron deficiency anaemia; C: early clubbing; D: late
clubbing (may be caused by long-term oxygen lack); E: Beau’s line
on nail (may result from severe injury or illness).


Lifespan considerations
Assessing the hair
Infants
It is normal for infants to have either very little or a great
deal of body and scalp hair.
Children
As puberty approaches, axillary and pubic hair will appear
(see Box 31.9
 on page 660).
Older adults
There may be loss of scalp, pubic and axillary hair.
Hairs of the eyebrows, ears and nostrils become bristle-
like and coarse.
Home care considerations
Assessing the hair


When making a home visit, ask to see the products
the person usually uses on the hair. Assist the
person to determine if the products are appropriate
for the person’s type of hair and scalp; for example,
for dry or oily hair. Provide education regarding
hygiene of the hair and scalp.
When making a home visit, examine the equipment
that the person uses on the hair. Provide education
regarding appropriate combs and brushes, and
regarding safety in using electric hair styling
appliances such as hair dryers.
Nail texture is normally smooth. Excessively thick nails can appear in
older adults, in the presence of poor circulation or in relation to a
chronic fungal infection. Excessively thin nails or the presence of
grooves or furrows can reflect prolonged iron deficiency anaemia.
Beau’s lines are horizontal depressions in the nail that can result
from injury or severe illness (see Figure 31.10E
). The nail bed is
highly vascular, a characteristic that accounts for its colour. A bluish
or purplish tint to the nail bed may reflect cyanosis and pallor may
reflect poor arterial circulation. Should the person report a history of
nail fungus (onychomycosis), a referral to a podiatrist or
dermatologist for treatment of nail fungus may be appropriate.
Symptoms of nail fungus include brittleness, discolouration,
thickening, distortion of nail shape, crumbling of the nail and
loosening (detaching) of the nail.


The tissue surrounding the nails is normally intact epidermis.
Paronychia is an inflammation of the tissues surrounding a nail
(often referred to as an ‘ingrown nail’). The tissues appear inflamed
and swollen and tenderness is usually present. A blanch test
 can
be carried out to test the capillary refill; that is, peripheral circulation.
Normal nail bed capillaries blanch when pressed but quickly turn pink
or their usual colour when pressure is released. A slow rate of
capillary refill may indicate circulatory problems.
Lifespan considerations
Assessing the nails
Infants
Newborns’ nails grow very quickly, are extremely thin and
tear easily.
Children
Bent, bruised or ingrown toenails may indicate shoes that
are too tight.
Nail biting should be discussed with a family member.
Older adults
The nails grow more slowly and thicken.
Longitudinal bands commonly develop and the nails tend
to split.


Bands across the nails may indicate protein deficiency,
white spots indicate zinc deficiency and spoon-shaped
nails indicate iron deficiency.
Toenail fungus is more common and difficult to eliminate
(although not dangerous to health).
Skill 31.4
 describes how to assess the nails.
Home care considerations
Assessing the nails
If indicated, teach the person or family member
about proper nail care, including how to trim and
shape the nails to avoid paronychia.
Refer the person to a podiatrist if they require
assistance with nail care.
If the person has diabetes mellitus they should be
educated on care of the nails or advised to attend a
podiatrist due to the increased risk of infection.


SKILL
31.2 Assessing the skin
Planning
Review characteristics of primary and secondary
skin lesions if necessary (see Figure 31.8
 and
Table 31.6
).
Obtain the person’s consent or the guardian’s
consent.
Ensure that adequate lighting is available.
Equipment
Millimetre ruler
Clean gloves
Magnifying glass
Implementation
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary


and how they can cooperate. Discuss how
the results will be used in planning further
care or treatments.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for the person’s privacy.
4. Inquire if the person has any history of the
following: pain or itching; allergies leading to
skin reactions; presence and spread of
lesions, bruises, abrasions, pigmented spots;
previous experience with skin problems;
associated clinical signs; family history;
presence of problems in other family
members; related systemic conditions; use of
medications, lotions, home remedies;
excessively dry or moist feel to the skin;
tendency to bruise easily; association of the
problem to season of year, stress,
occupation, medications, recent travel,
housing and so on; recent contact with
allergens (e.g. metal paint).
Evaluation
Compare findings with previous skin assessment
data if available to determine if lesions or
abnormalities are changing.


Report significant deviations from normal to the

The head
During assessment of the head, the nurse inspects and palpates
simultaneously, and also auscultates. The nurse examines the skull,
face, eyes, ears, nose, sinuses, mouth and pharynx.
Skull and face
There is a large range of normal shapes of skulls. A normal head
size is referred to as normocephalic
. Names of areas of the
head are derived from names of the underlying bones: frontal,
parietal, occipital, mastoid process, mandible, maxilla and zygomatic
(see Figure 31.11
).
Figure 31.11


Bones of the head.
Many disorders cause a change in facial shape or condition. Kidney
or cardiac disease can cause oedema of the eyelids.
Hyperthyroidism can cause exophthalmos
, a protrusion of the
eyeballs with elevation of the upper eyelids which results in a startled
or staring expression. Hypothyroidism, or myxoedema, can cause a
dry, puffy face with dry skin and coarse features with thinning of
scalp hair and eyebrows. Increased adrenal hormone production or


administration can cause a round face with reddened cheeks,
referred to as moon face, plus excessive hair growth on the upper
lip, chin and sideburn areas. Prolonged illness, starvation and
dehydration can result in sunken eyes, cheeks and temples. Skill
31.5
 describes how to assess the skull and face.
Lifespan considerations
Assessing the skull and face
Infants
Newborns delivered vaginally can have an elongated or
moulded head due to the passage of the baby through the
birth canal. The head usually reverts to a more rounded
shape after a week or two. Infants born by caesarean
section tend to have smooth, rounded heads.
Infants may have a head flatter on one side due to
persistent positioning on that side.
The posterior fontanel (triangle-shaped soft spot) is about
1 cm in size and usually closes by 8 weeks. The anterior
fontanel is a larger diamond shape, about 2 to 3 cm in
size. It closes by 18 months.
Newborns can lift their heads slightly and turn them from
side to side. Voluntary head control is usually well
established by 4 to 6 months.
Older adults


Loss of muscle tone, thinning skin and missing teeth may
change the shape of the face and neck with increasing
wrinkles around the eyes, mouth and forehead.
Pigment changes can occur.
Shape of the nose can change, becoming more elongated
or bulbous.
Eyes and vision
Vision impairment is an important health issue facing the present
and future generations of older Australians—it impacts on their
physical, functional, emotional and social wellbeing and reduces
quality of life. Cataracts and age-related macular degeneration are
the two main causes of blindness and vision loss in Australia
(Foreman et al.
). The prevalence of blindness and vision
impairment among Indigenous Australians is three times that of non-
Indigenous Australians (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare
(AIHW)
).
12 Foreman, J., Keel, S., Xie, J., van Wijingaarden, P., Crowston, J., Taylor, H. & Dirani, M.
(2016). The National Eye Health Survey. Retrieved from <www.vision2020australia.org.au>.
13 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2011). Eye Heath in Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander People. Canberra: AIHW.
12
13


To maintain optimum vision, people need to have their eyes
examined regularly throughout life. It is recommended that people
under age 40 have their eyes tested every 3 to 5 years, or more
frequently if there is a family history of diabetes, hypertension, blood
dyscrasia or eye disease (e.g. glaucoma). After age 40, an eye
examination is recommended every 2 years to rule out the possibility
of glaucoma and macular degeneration.
An eye assessment should be carried out as part of the person’s
initial physical examination; periodic reassessments need to be
made for people in long-term care. Examination of the eyes includes
assessment of the external structures, visual acuity
 (the degree
of detail the eye can discern in an image), ocular movement and
visual fields
 (the area an individual can see when looking straight
ahead). Most eye assessment procedures involve inspection and
most are undertaken by a doctor or optometrist. Consideration is
also given to developmental changes and to individual hygienic
practices, and whether the person wears contact lenses or has an
artificial eye. For the anatomical structures of the eye, see Figures
31.12
 and 31.13
.
Figure 31.12


The external structures and lacrimal apparatus of the left eye.
Figure 31.13


Anatomical structures of the right eye, lateral view.
Many people wear glasses or contact lenses to correct common
refractive errors of the lens of the eye. These errors include
myopia
 (near-sightedness), hyperopia
 (far-sightedness) and
presbyopia
 (loss of elasticity of the lens and thus loss of ability to
see close objects). Presbyopia begins at about 45 years of age.
People notice that they have difficulty reading newsprint. When both
far and near vision require correction, two lenses (bifocals) may be
prescribed. Astigmatism
, an uneven curvature of the cornea that
prevents horizontal and vertical rays from focusing on the retina, is a
common problem that may occur in conjunction with myopia and
hyperopia. Astigmatism may be corrected with spectacles or
surgery.
Three types of eye charts are available to test visual acuity (see
Figure 31.14
). People with denominators of 40 or more on the
Snellen chart with or without corrective lenses need to be referred to
an ophthalmologist.
Figure 31.14


Three types of eye charts: the preschool children’s chart (left), the
Snellen standard chart (centre) and the Snellen E chart for people
unable to read (right).
Common inflammatory visual problems that nurses may encounter
in people include conjunctivitis, dacryocystitis, hordeolum, iritis and
contusions or haematomas of the eyelids and surrounding
structures. Conjunctivitis
 (inflammation of the bulbar and
palpebral conjunctiva) may result from foreign bodies, chemicals,
allergenic agents, bacteria or viruses. Redness, itching, tearing and
discharge occur. During sleep, the eyelids may become encrusted
and matted together. Dacryocystitis
 (inflammation of the lacrimal
sac) is manifested by tearing and a discharge from the nasolacrimal
duct. Hordeolum
 (stye
) is a redness, swelling and tenderness
of the hair follicle and glands that empty at the edge of the eyelids.
Iritis (inflammation of the iris) may be caused by local or systemic
infections and results in pain, tearing and photophobia (sensitivity to
light). Contusions or haematomas are ‘black eyes’ resulting from
injury.
Cataracts
 tend to occur in 11.9% of people over 65 years old in
the Caucasian community (AIHW
). More Indigenous males (5%)
than Indigenous females (2%) reported cataracts (AIHW 2005).
Cataracts are the leading cause of blindness in Indigenous
Australians (32%) (Centre for Eye Research Australia ),
responsible for 32% of the blindness and 27% of the low vision loss
in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults (Taylor et al.
). The
14
15
16


opacity of the lens or its capsule caused by cataracts blocks light
rays. It can be removed and replaced by a lens implant. Cataracts
may also occur in infants due to a malformation of the lens if the
mother contracted rubella in the first trimester of pregnancy.
14 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2005). Vision Problems among Older
Australians. Bulletin (27). Canberra: AIHW.
15 Centre for Eye Research Australia (2009). Indigenous Eye Health Unit, Melbourne School
of Population Health, University of Melbourne.
16 Taylor, H., Xie, J., Fox, S., Dunn, R., Arnold, A-L. & Keeffe, J. (2010). The prevalence and
causes of vision loss in Indigenous Australians: The National Indigenous Eye Health Survey.
Medical Journal of Australia, 192, 312–318.
Glaucoma
 (a disturbance in the circulation of aqueous fluid,
which causes an increase in intraocular pressure) is the most
frequent cause of blindness in people over 40. It can be controlled if
diagnosed early. Danger signs of glaucoma include blurred or foggy
vision, loss of peripheral vision, difficulty focusing on close objects,
difficulty adjusting to dark rooms and seeing rainbow-coloured rings
around lights.
Eyelids that lie at or below the pupil margin are referred to as ptosis
and are usually associated with ageing, oedema from drug allergy or
systemic disease (e.g. kidney disease), congenital lid muscle
dysfunction, neuromuscular disease (e.g. myasthenia gravis) and
third cranial nerve impairment. Eversion, an out-turning of the eyelid,
is called ectropion. Inversion, an in-turning of the lid, is called


entropion. These abnormalities are often associated with scarring
injuries or the ageing process.
Pupils are normally black, equal in size (about 3 to 7 mm in
diameter) and have round, smooth borders. Cloudy pupils are often
indicative of cataracts. Mydriasis
 (enlarged pupils) may indicate
injury or glaucoma or result from certain drugs (e.g. atropine).
Miosis
 (constricted pupils) may indicate an inflammation of the
iris or result from such drugs as morphine or pilocarpine. It is also an
age-related change in older adults. Anisocoria
 (unequal pupils)
may result from a central nervous system disorder; however, slight
variations may be normal. The iris is normally flat and round. A
bulging towards the cornea can indicate increased intraocular
pressure.
Skill 31.6
 describes how to assess a person’s eye structures and
visual acuity.
Lifespan considerations
Assessing the eyes and vision
Infants
Infants 4 weeks of age should be able to gaze at and
follow objects.
Ability to focus with both eyes should be present by 6
months of age.


Infants do not have tears until about 3 months of age.
A cover test and the corneal light reflex (Hirschberg) test
should be conducted on infants to detect misalignment
early and prevent amblyopia.
Visual acuity is about 20/300 at 4 months and
progressively improves.
Children
Epicanthal folds, common in people of Asian cultures,
may cover the medial canthus and cause eyes to appear
misaligned. Epicanthal folds may also be seen in young
children of any race before the bridge of the nose begins
to elevate.
Preschool children’s acuity can be checked with picture
cards or the E chart. Acuity should approach 20/20 by 6
years of age.
A cover test and the corneal light reflex (Hirschberg) test
should be conducted on young children to detect
misalignment early and prevent amblyopia.
Always perform the acuity test with glasses on if a child
wears prescription lenses.
Children may be tested for colour vision deficit. From 8%
to 10% of Caucasian males and from 0.5% to 1% of
Caucasian females have this deficit; it is much less
common in non-Caucasian children. The Ishihara or
Hardy–Rand–Rittler test can be used.
Trachoma is an infectious disease of the eyes that can
lead to blindness. In one study, hyperendemic levels of


trachoma (> 20%) were detected in 17 (13%) of the at-
risk Indigenous communities (The Kirby Institute )
Trachoma was identified in half of the very remote
Indigenous communities, with Australia recognised as the
only developed country in the world to still have endemic
blinding trachoma (AIHW 2011).
17 The Kirby Institute, UNSW Sydney (2011). Australian Trachoma Surveillance
Report 2017. Retrieved from <www1.health.gov.au>.
Older adults
Visual acuity
Visual acuity decreases as the lens of the eye ages and
becomes more opaque and loses elasticity.
The ability of the iris to accommodate to darkness and
dim light diminishes.
Peripheral vision diminishes.
The adaptation to light (glare) and dark decreases.
Accommodation to distant objects often improves but
accommodation to close objects decreases.
Colour vision declines; older people are less able to
perceive purple colours and to discriminate pastel colours.
Many older people wear corrective lenses, which is most
likely due to hyperopia. Visual changes are due to loss of
elasticity (presbyopia) and transparency of the lens.
External eye structures
17


The skin around the orbit of the eye may darken.
The eyeball may appear sunken because of the decrease
in orbital fat.
Skin folds of the upper lids may seem more prominent
and the lower lids may sag.
The eyes may appear dry and lustreless because of the
decrease in tear production from the lacrimal glands.
A thin, greyish-white arc or ring (arcus senilis) appears
around part or all of the cornea. It results from an
accumulation of a lipid substance on the cornea. The
cornea tends to cloud with age.
The iris may appear pale with brown discolourations as a
result of pigment degeneration.
The conjunctiva of the eye may appear paler than that of
younger adults and may take on a slightly yellow
appearance because of the deposition of fat.
Pupil reaction to light and accommodation is normally
symmetrically equal but may be less brisk.
The pupils can appear smaller in size, unequal and
irregular in shape because of sclerotic changes in the iris.
Clinical consideration
A Rosenbaum eye chart may be used by a
doctor to test near vision. It consists of


paragraphs of text or characters in different
sizes on a
 card. Be sure the
person has a literacy level appropriate for the
text used.
Home care considerations
Assessing the eyes and vision
When making a home visit, take your equipment
and charts with you. Also include a tape measure
to measure the 6 m for distance vision testing.
Use the assessment as an opportunity to reinforce
proper eye care and need for regular vision testing.
Ears and hearing
Assessment of the ear includes direct inspection and palpation of
the external ear, inspection of the remaining parts of the ear by an
9 cm × 16.5 cm


otoscope
 (instrument for examining the interior of the ear,
especially the eardrum, consisting essentially of a magnifying lens
and a light) and determination of auditory acuity (see Figure
31.15
). The ear is usually assessed by the doctor during an initial
physical examination; periodic reassessments may be necessary for
long-term patients or those with hearing problems. The person
should also be asked about their use of hearing aids. Otoscopic
examinations are usually only performed by nurses who have been
trained in the procedure, such as advanced practice nurses, Nurse
Practitioners or community nurses.
Figure 31.15


Anatomical structures of the external, middle and inner ear.
Audiometric evaluations, which measure hearing at various decibels,
are recommended for children and older adults. A common hearing
deficit with age is loss of ability to hear high-frequency sounds, such
as f, s, sh and ph. This neurosensory hearing deficit does not
respond well to use of a hearing aid.
Conduction hearing loss
 is the result of interrupted transmission
of sound waves through the outer and middle ear structures.
Possible causes are a tear in the tympanic membrane or an
obstruction, due to swelling or other causes, in the auditory canal.
Sensorineural hearing loss
 is the result of damage to the inner
ear, the auditory nerve or the hearing centre in the brain. Mixed
hearing loss
 is a combination of conduction and sensorineural
loss. Skill 31.7
 describes how to assess the ears and hearing.

and how they can cooperate. Discuss how
the results will be used in planning further
care or treatments.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe

3. Provide for the person’s privacy.


4. Inquire if the person has any history of the

bumps, itching, scaling or dandruff; history of

headache, facial pain or injury; when and how

problem; associated symptoms, treatment
and recurrences.

SKILL
31.6 Assessing the eye
structures and visual acuity
Planning
Place the person in an appropriate room for
assessing the eyes and vision. Natural and
overhead lighting needs to be controlled during
some parts of the examination.
Equipment
Clean gloves
Millimetre ruler
Penlight
Snellen or E chart
Opaque card
Implementation
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using


organisation policy. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can cooperate. Discuss how
the results will be used in planning further
care or treatments.
2. Perform hand hygiene, apply gloves and
observe appropriate infection-control
procedures.
3. Provide for the person’s privacy.
4. Inquire if the person has any history of the
following: family history of diabetes,
hypertension, blood dyscrasia or eye disease,
injury or surgery; the date of the person’s last
visit to an ophthalmologist or optometrist;
current use of eye medications; use of
contact lenses or glasses; hygienic practices
for corrective lenses; current symptoms of
eye problems (e.g. changes in visual acuity,
blurring of vision, tearing, spots, photophobia,

Evaluation
Relate findings to previous assessment data if
available.
Report significant deviations from normal to the
doctor. People with denominators of 40 or more


on the Snellen or character chart, with or without
