Micro-organisms
The human body has 10 times more micro-organisms living in and
on it than the number of human body cells that make us
(Microbiology Society ). We are also exposed to a countless
number of microbes (invisible organisms present in the environment)
as we meander through our existence and everyday life. Microbes
are present in our homes, on the food we eat and on things we
touch. Some micro-organisms perform essential roles in our body,
such as the microbiota in our gastrointestinal tract which help us to
process and absorb nutrients; others inhibit common pathogens;
some perform immunomodulatory functions which can attenuate
autoimmune disease (Durack & Lynch ). These microbiomes may
even possess tumour- suppressive properties. Other micro-
organisms are necessary in the environment and perform critical
tasks such as decomposing and recycling nutrients. Others are used
to produce food; some live on the human body; and, unfortunately,
others cause disease (Lee & Bishop ). Some micro-organisms are
called pathogens (micro-organisms which can cause disease) and
may or may not cause death. Some micro-organisms are harmless.
Health care professionals need to understand the roles, interactions,
benefits, challenges and disadvantages of humans, micro-organisms
and the environment in which we live.
1 Microbiology Society (2019). Microbes and the Human Body. Retrieved from
<www.microbiologyonline.org.uk>.
1
2
3


2 Durack, J. & Lynch, S. (2019). The gut microbiome: Relationships with disease and
opportunities for therapy. The Journal of Experimental Medicine, 216(1), 20–40. Doi:
10.1084/jem.20180448.
3 Lee, G. & Bishop, P. (2016). Microbiology and Infection Control for Health Professionals (6th
ed.). Frenchs Forest, NSW: Pearson.
Knowledge of the relationship between micro-organisms and
infectious diseases developed in the late nineteenth century.
Previously, it was thought infectious diseases were caused by
exposure to ‘bad air’, otherwise known as miasmas (Rose et al. ).
As a result of this naïveté, people had little success in controlling
their spread.
4 Rose, M., Cabral, L., Kezos, J., Barter, T., Phillips, M., Smith, B. & Burnham, T. (2016). Four
steps toward the control of aging: Following the example of infectious disease. Biogerontology,
17(21), 21–31. Doi: 10.1007/s10522-015-9588-6.
There are several thousand micro-organisms known to exist in and
on humans; however, this number represents only about 1% of the
total number of micro-organisms on the earth (Pasolli ; Sender,
Fuchs & Milo ). Micro-organisms can be divided into several major
categories which include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa,
parasites and prions. Bacteria
 are by far the most common
infection-causing micro-organisms. Several hundred species can
cause disease in humans. Bacteria can live in and be transported via
air, water, food, soil, body tissues and fluids, and inanimate objects.
Viruses
 consist primarily of nucleic acid and therefore must enter
living cells in order to reproduce. Common virus families include the
rhinovirus (causes the common cold), hepatitis, herpes and human
4
5
6


immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Fungi
 include yeasts and moulds.
For example, Candida albicans is a yeast considered to be normal
flora in the human vagina. Parasites
 are organisms which live in
or on other living organisms. They include protozoa, such as the one
causing malaria, helminths (worms) and arthropods (scabies, fleas,
ticks). Prions
 are infective particles consisting only of protein and
are responsible for a group of fatal neurological disorders known as
transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (TSEs). For example,
variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (vCJD) is a new prion disease
with evidence of links to ‘mad cow disease’ or, as it should be called,
bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE). This pathogen become
renowned when it caused infections (and subsequent death) in
people after they ate contaminated beef in the United Kingdom.
5 Pasolli, E., Asnicar, F., Manara, S., .?.?. Segata, N. (2019). Extensive unexplored human
microbiome diversity revealed by over 150,000 genomes from metagenomes spanning age,
geography, and lifestyle. Cell, 176(3), 649–662; e20. Doi: 10.1016/j.cell.2019.01.001.
6 Sender, R., Fuchs, S. & Milo, R. (2016). Revised estimates for the number of human and
bacteria cells in the body. PLoS Biology, 14(8), e1002533. Doi:
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533.
As we have identified, micro-organisms exist everywhere: in water,
soil and on body surfaces. Micro-organisms that live on the body
and do not cause disease are known as normal flora (also known as
‘commensal’, meaning having a symbiotic relationship where one
organism benefits; however, the other is unaffected). There are two
types of normal flora—resident and transient. Normal flora are
commonly found in the mouth, upper respiratory tract, vagina and
lower urinary tract, and gastrointestinal tract) (see Figure 32.1
).


Most resident micro-organisms are harmless. Some are even
beneficial, performing essential functions in the body. However, when
environmental conditions alter, these commensal floras can gain
entry to other locations on the host and cause an infection. This is
called opportunism. An example of this is when Escherichia coli (E.
coli)—a normal inhabitant of the large intestine that breaks down
waste and assists in the production of vitamin K—enters the
bloodstream, where it can cause a severe and potentially fatal
infection. E. coli is also a common cause of urinary tract infections.
Figure 32.1


Location of normal flora on the human body.
Source: G. Lee & P. Bishop (2016). Microbiology and Infection Control for Health Professionals (6th ed.). Frenchs
Forest, NSW: Pearson, Figure 7.3, p. 154.
Transient organisms
 cling to the skin’s surface but usually do
not replicate there. They include any micro-organisms with which the
body (particularly the hands) has come into contact during normal
daily activities. Transient micro-organisms are influenced by an
individual’s personal hygiene. For health care workers, the micro-
organisms carried on the hands are important in the transmission of
an infection.


Pathogens: Colonisation
and infection
Over the past century, the pattern of micro-organisms responsible
for infections has changed. For example, in the 1920s, streptococci,
particularly Streptococcus pyogenes, was the most feared bacteria
in hospitals. In the past few years, strains of multidrug- resistant and
methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) with decreased
sensitivity to vancomycin (the only drug available to treat these
bacteria) has been isolated. Now, we also have many bacteria which
are capable of producing an enzyme that inactivates ß-lactam
antibiotics such as penicillins and cephalosporins. Any pathogen
capable of this is called an extended-spectrum ß-lactamase (or
ESBL) and results in a bacterial strain resistant to many antibiotics
available (Munoz-Price ).
7 Munoz-Price, L. (2019). Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases. UpToDate. Retrieved from
<www.uptodate.com>.
A systemic inflammatory response to bacteria (or their toxins) in the
blood stream is known as sepsis
. Clinicians refer to sepsis as the
development of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome
(SIRS) in the presence of infection. The word septicaemia (presence
of bacteria in the bloodstream) is commonly used interchangeably
with the word sepsis.
7


An infection
 is an invasion and proliferation of micro- organisms
into body tissue. These micro-organisms are referred to as
pathogens and such micro-organisms are called infectious agents.
Although some micro-organisms produce little to no clinical evidence
of disease, they can cause considerable damage; for example,
cytomegalovirus (CMV). In an adult, CMV most often causes mild
cold-like symptoms; however, an infection in a pregnant woman can
result in serious congenital malformations to the unborn child.
Many novice health care professionals confuse infection and
colonisation; however, they are distinctly different processes. When
a micro-organism becomes resident flora, it is called
colonisation
. In this state, the micro-organisms may grow and
multiply; however, they do not cause disease. Infection occurs when
newly introduced or resident micro-organisms succeed in invading a
part of the body where the host’s defence mechanisms are
ineffective and the pathogen causes tissue damage.
Pathogenicity
 is the ability of a micro-organism to produce
disease. Micro-organisms causing disease in humans are referred to
as pathogens
. Many micro-organisms that are normally harmless
can cause disease under certain circumstances. A ‘true’ pathogen
has devised means to circumvent the body’s normal controls,
causing disease or infection in a healthy individual. An
opportunistic pathogen
 causes disease only in a susceptible
individual.


Micro-organisms vary in their virulence
 (i.e. the degree to which
they are capable of producing a disease). Micro-organisms also vary
in the severity of the diseases they produce and in their degree of
communicability. For example, a common cold virus is more readily
transmitted than Mycobacterium leprae, the bacillus causing leprosy.
Infectious agents capable of being transmitted from one individual
through direct or indirect contact via a vector (a vehicle) or air-borne
route are called communicable agents. If the infectious agent can be
transmitted to an individual by direct or indirect contact or as an air-
borne infection, the resulting condition is called a communicable
disease
. Communicable diseases include colds, influenza,
measles, chickenpox, rubella, diphtheria and polio, as well as
gastrointestinal and sexually transmitted infections.
Clinical consideration
An individual does not need to have an identified
infection to transfer potentially infective micro-
organisms to another person. Even non-
pathogenic micro-organisms on one person
have the potential to colonise or infect and
become pathogenic in or on another person.


Communicable diseases result from either direct or indirect contact
with an infectious agent such as bacteria, fungi, parasites, prions or
viruses. This concept is discussed later in the chapter.
Communicable diseases are a major cause of death globally. The
control of microbial spread and the protection of people from
communicable diseases and infections are carried out at
international, national, state, community and individual levels.
The World Health Organization (WHO) is the major regulatory
agency at the international level. In Australia, the federal
government’s Department of Health—Office of Health Protection is
the coordinating body in relation to national action in the event of
communicable disease outbreaks and, as the peak body, produces
best practice guidelines and national public health policy. In
association with the Communicable Diseases Network Australia
(CDNA), the National Public Health Partnership helps to provide
national public health leadership and coordination on communicable
disease surveillance, prevention and control (Department of
Health ). The CDNA also offers strategic advice to governments and
other key bodies on public health actions to minimise the impact of
communicable diseases in Australia and the region.
8 Department of Health (2018). Communicable Diseases Information. Retrieved from
<www.health.gov.au>.
8


Types of infection
Infections can be local or systemic. Local infections are limited to the
specific part of the body where the micro-organisms remain. If the
micro-organisms spread and damage different parts of the body, it
becomes a systemic infection. When a culture of the person’s blood
reveals micro-organisms, this is called bacteraemia
. When
bacteraemia results in systemic infection, it is referred to as sepsis.
Infections can also be classed as acute
 or chronic
. Acute
infections generally appear suddenly or last a short time. A chronic
infection occurs slowly, or over a very long period, lasting months or
years. Infections may also be classified as endogenous or
exogenous. Endogenous infections
 are caused by the micro-
organisms already present on the individual’s body, which is acting
as a reservoir. See Table 32.1
 for examples of endogenous
infections. Exogenous infections
 are caused by micro-
organisms from a source external to the individual.
Table 32.1 Examples of endogenous infections


Chain of infection
Six links make up the chain of infection (see Figure 32.2
): the
aetiological agent (or micro-organism); the place where the
organism naturally resides (reservoir); a portal of exit from the
reservoir; a method (mode) of transmission; a portal of entry into a
host; and the susceptibility of the host. Understanding of the chain of
infection is critical for health care professionals, as breaking any link
in the chain of infection can stop the spread of the pathogen and
control the infectious disease.
Figure 32.2


The chain of infection.
Aetiological agent
The extent to which any agent is capable of producing an infection
depends on many factors. These factors include the number of
micro-organisms present (e.g. ‘bacterial load’), the pathogenicity and
virulence of the agent, access to the body, the host’s susceptibility
and the continued ability of the agent to survive in the host (i.e. not
trigger or fend off the host’s immune system).
Reservoir
There are many reservoirs
 or sources of micro-organisms.
Common sources are other humans, the individual’s own micro-
organisms, plants, animals or the general environment. People are
the most common source of infection for others and for themselves.
For example, the person with an influenza virus frequently spreads it
to others. A carrier
 is a person or animal reservoir of a specific
infectious agent that usually does not manifest any clinical signs of
disease. The Anopheles mosquito is a reservoir as it carries the
malaria parasite but is unaffected by it. The carrier state may also
exist in individuals with a clinically recognisable disease; for example,
a person with hepatitis A. Under either circumstance, the carrier
state may be of short duration (temporary or transient carrier) or


long duration (chronic carrier). Food, water sources and faeces also
can be reservoirs.
Over 200 zoonoses (infections in animals that can be transmitted to
humans) are found in wild or domesticated animals (WHO ).
Transmission of many of these diseases from an animal reservoir to
human requires a vector in the form of a blood-sucking insect (e.g.
plague is carried by fleas). However, for other diseases,
transmission is by direct contact with the animal—its fur, feathers or
body secretions. Some Australian zoonoses include Q fever,
brucellosis, psittacosis, leptospirosis and lyssavirus.
9 World Health Organization (WHO) (2019a). Other Neglected Zoonotic Diseases. Retrieved
from <www.who.int>.
Portal of exit from reservoir
Before an infection can establish itself in a host, the micro-
organisms must leave the reservoir. Common human reservoirs and
their associated portals of exit are summarised in Table 32.2
.
Table 32.2 Human body area reservoirs, common infectious
micro-organisms and portals of exit
Method of transmission
9


After a micro-organism leaves its source or reservoir, it requires a
means of transmission to reach another person or host through a
receptive portal of entry. Transmission can be divided into two
mechanisms: direct transmission and indirect transmission.
See Table 32.3
 for an explanation of methods of transmission.
Table 32.3 Methods of transmission of communicable diseases
Portal of entry to the susceptible
host
Before a person can become infected, micro-organisms must enter
the body. The skin is a barrier to infectious agents; however, any
break in the skin can readily serve as a portal of entry. Often, micro-
organisms enter the body of the host by the same route they used
to leave the source. See Table 32.4
 for preferred portal of entry
of some common micro-organisms.
Table 32.4 Preferred portal of entry of some common micro-
organisms
Source: Adapted from G. Lee & P. Bishop (2016). Microbiology and Infection Control for Health Professionals (6th
ed.). Frenchs Forest, NSW: Pearson, Table 8.2, p. 183.


Susceptible host
A susceptible host is any person who is at risk of infection.
Impairment of the body’s immune system, integumentary system
and other biological factors increases susceptibility to infection.
Examples include age (the very young or the very old); individuals
receiving immunosuppression treatment for cancer or chronic illness
or following a successful organ transplant; and those with immune
deficiency conditions.
Incidence of sepsis in individuals with cancer ranges between 7 and
45% (Kochanek et al.
).
10 Kochanek, M., Schalk, E., von Bergwelt-Baildon, M., .?.?. Böll, B. (2019). Management of
sepsis in neutropenic cancer patients: 2018 guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Working
Party (AGIHO) and Intensive Care Working Party (iCHOP) of the German Society of
Hematology and Medical Oncology (DGHO). Annals of Hematology, 98(5), 1051–1069. Doi:
10.1007/s00277-019-03622-0.
10


Body defences against infection
Body defences that exist to reduce the risk of infection can be
categorised as non-specific and specific. Non-specific defences
(also called innate or natural immunity
) protect the individual
against potentially harmful agents, including pathogens and foreign
substances. Non-specific defences do not discriminate one agent
from another, acting in similar ways each time the same agent
enters or attempts to enter the body (Lee & Bishop 2016).
Specific
 (also called acquired-immunity) defences
, by
contrast, are effective against particular identifiable foreign agents
(e.g. bacteria, viruses, fungi or other infectious agents) and develop
in response to that agent. Specific defences assist in eliminating
pathogens that are succeeding in circumventing the non-specific
defences. Once established against a specific pathogen, specific
immunity responds to future exposure to that pathogen by
recognising the structural and chemical features of the pathogen
(Microbiology Society 2019).
Non-specific defences
Non-specific body defences include anatomical and physiological
barriers and the inflammatory response.


Anatomical and physiological barriers
Intact skin and mucous membranes are the body’s first line of
defence against micro-organisms. Intact skin and mucous
membranes serve as relatively effective barriers against many
pathogens. Bacteria are most plentiful in moist areas of the body,
such as the perineum and axillae. Resident bacteria of the skin also
prevent other bacteria from multiplying. They use up the available
nourishment and the end products of their metabolism inhibit other
bacterial growth. Secretions such as sweat which include water, salt
and many acids make the skin somewhat acidic. This forms part of
the non-specific defences by inhibiting bacterial growth and reducing
conditions that may result in cracked skin. This is called the acid
mantle.
The nasal passages have a defensive function. As entering air
follows the tortuous route of the passage, it comes in contact with
moist mucous membranes and cilia. These trap micro-organisms,
dust and foreign materials. The lungs have alveolar macrophages
(large phagocytes). Phagocytes ingest foreign substances and
micro-organisms, which find their way to the lower respiratory tract.
Phagocytes are considered a second line of defence.
Every orifice has protective mechanisms. The oral cavity regularly
sheds mucosal epithelium to rid the mouth of colonisers. The flow of
saliva helps with mechanical flushing, but saliva also contains a
number of antimicrobial substances to control oropharyngeal
microflora and reduce infection risk. Some particularly important


components of saliva include salivary immunoglobin A (sIgA), which
bind to antigens to prevent microbes or viruses from attaching to
dental or mucosal surfaces (Lynge Pedersen & Belstrøm
). It is
important to note that salivary IgA are technically considered third-
line defences (specific defences).
11 Lynge Pedersen, A. & Belstrøm, D. (2019). The role of natural salivary defences in
maintaining a healthy oral microbiota. Journal of Dentistry, 80(S1), S3–S12. Doi:
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdent.2018.08.010.
The eye is protected from infection by tears, which wash micro-
organisms away and contain inhibiting lysozyme.
The gastrointestinal tract also has defences against infection. The
high acidity of the stomach normally prevents microbial growth. The
resident flora of the large intestine helps prevent the establishment
of disease-producing micro-organisms. Peristalsis also tends to
move microbes out of the body.
The vagina also has natural defences against infection. When a
female reaches puberty, Lactobacillus ferments sugars in the vaginal
secretions, creating a vaginal pH of 3.5 to 4.5 (Mirmonsef et al.
).
This low pH inhibits the growth of many disease-producing micro-
organisms. The urethral meatus (entrance to the urethra) harbours
some normal flora including lactobacilli, coagulase-negative
staphylococci, streptococci and corynebacteria (Lee & Bishop 2016).
Low numbers of transient bacteria can include E. coli; however, in
health, the flushing action of the flow of urine occurring in
11
12


intermittent voiding works well to prevent bacteria ascending the
urethra. An intact mucosal surface also acts as a barrier.
12 Mirmonsef, P., Hotton, A. L., Gilbert, .?.?. Spear, G. T. (2016). Glycogen levels in undiluted
genital fluid and their relationship to vaginal pH, estrogen, and progesterone. PLoS ONE,
11(4), e0153553. Doi: http://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0153553.
Inflammatory response
Inflammation is a local and non-specific defensive response of the
tissues to an injurious or infectious agent. It is a mechanism that
destroys or dilutes the injurious agent, prevents further spread of the
injury and promotes the repair of damaged tissue. It is characterised
by five signs: (1) pain; (2) swelling; (3) redness; (4) heat; and (5)
impaired function of the part. Commonly, words with the suffix itis
describe an inflammatory process. For example, appendicitis means
inflammation of the appendix; gastritis means inflammation of the
stomach.
Injurious agents can be categorised as physical agents, chemical
agents and micro-organisms. Physical agents include mechanical
objects causing trauma to tissues, excessive heat or cold, and
radiation. Chemical agents include external irritants (e.g. strong
acids, alkalis, poisons and irritating gases) and internal irritants
(substances manufactured within the body such as excessive
hydrochloric acid in the stomach).
A series of dynamic events is commonly referred to as the three
stages of the inflammatory response:


1. vascular and cellular responses
2. exudate production
3. reparative phase.
Clinical consideration
It is important to understand that infection and
inflammatory response are not always present
at the same time.
A person may be experiencing an
inflammatory response in the presence of a
‘sterile’ or non-infective event such as
destruction of tissue as a result of chemical
injury.
Conversely, a person who is receiving
immunomodifying agents such as steroids or
chemotherapy drugs may not demonstrate a
typical or obvious inflammatory response in
the presence of a developing infection as
their immune system has been manipulated.
Vascular and cellular responses


At the start of the first stage of inflammation, blood vessels at the
site of injury/spasm constrict. This is an attempt to stem any blood
loss and plays a critical role in haemostasis. After the platelet plug
and subsequent clot has brought the haemorrhage under control,
the small blood vessels then undergo vasodilation (as a result of
histamine released by the injured tissues). Thus, more blood flows to
the injured area. This marked increase in blood supply, referred to
as hyperaemia, is responsible for the characteristic signs of redness
and heat.
Vascular permeability increases at the site of injury in response to
cell death, the release of chemical mediators (e.g. histamine,
bradykinin, serotonin and prostaglandin). Fluid, proteins and
leukocytes (white blood cells) leak into the interstitial spaces, leading
to the clinical manifestations of infection oedema (inflammation
swelling) and pain. Pain is caused by the irritation of the nerve
endings by the chemical mediators. Fluid leaking into areas such as
the pleural or pericardial cavity can seriously affect organ function.
In other areas, such as joints, mobility is impaired.
As leukocytes arrive at the site of injury they move to the epithelium
and roll down the inside of the vessel (this is called margination).
The leukocytes then move through the blood vessel wall into the
interstitial space at the site of the injury. This process is called
migration or diapedesis.
In response to leukocytes exiting the blood, the bone marrow
increases leukocyte production and releases these into the


bloodstream. This is called leukocytosis. The normal leukocyte count
of 4.5 to
 can rise to
 or more when
inflammation (or infection) occurs (Royal College of Pathologists of
Australia ).
13 Royal College of Pathologists of Australia (2019). White Cell Count. Retrieved from
<www.rcpa.edu.au>.
Exudate production
In the second stage of inflammation, the inflammatory exudate
 is
produced, consisting of fluid that escaped from the blood vessels,
dead phagocytic cells and dead tissue cells and products they
release. The plasma protein fibrinogen (converted to fibrin when it is
released into the tissues), thromboplastin (released by injured tissue
cells) and platelets form an interlacing network to wall off the area
and prevent spread of the injurious agent. During this stage, the
injurious agent is overcome and the exudate is removed by
lymphatic drainage.
The nature and amount of exudate vary according to the tissue
involved and the intensity and duration of the inflammation. The
major types of exudate are serous, purulent and haemorrhagic
(sanguineous). Descriptions of these exudates are provided in
Chapter 37
.
Reparative phase
13.50 × 109/L
20.0 × 109/L
13


The third stage of the inflammatory response involves the repair of
injured tissues by regeneration or replacement with fibrous tissue
(scar) formation. Regeneration is the replacement of destroyed
tissue cells by cells identical or similar in structure and function.
Damaged cells are replaced one by one. Also, cells are organised so
that the architectural pattern and function of the tissue are restored.
The ability to regenerate cells varies considerably from one type of
tissue to another. For example, epithelial tissues of the skin and of
the digestive and respiratory tracts have a good regenerative
capacity when their underlying support structures are intact. The
same holds true for osseous, lymphoid and bone marrow tissues.
Tissues with limited regenerative capacity include nervous, muscular
and elastic tissues.
When regeneration is not possible, repair occurs by fibrous (scar)
tissue formation. The inflammatory exudate with its interlacing
network of fibrin provides the framework for this tissue to develop.
Damaged tissues are replaced with the connective tissue elements
of collagen, blood capillaries, lymphatics and other tissue-bound
substances. In the early stages of this process, the tissue is called
granulation tissue. It is a fragile, gelatinous tissue, appearing pink or
red because of the many newly formed capillaries. Later in the
process, the tissue shrinks (the capillaries are constricted, even
obliterated) and the collagen fibres contract so that a firmer fibrous
tissue remains. This is called cicatrix or scar.
Specific defences


The specific immune system (adaptive immunity or the acquired
immune system) has two components: antibody-mediated defences
and cell-mediated defences. These two systems provide distinct but
overlapping protection.
Antibody-mediated defences
Another name for antibody-mediated defences is humoral
immunity
 because these defences reside in the blood or lymph
(i.e. ‘humor’, an ancient term for body fluids). This system works
through a process whereby special antibody
-producing cells (B
cells or plasma cells) produce plasma proteins which can defend
against circulating antigens
 (any substance which stimulates the
immune system). Antibodies work by attaching to the specific
antigen and smothering it to inactivate it. This also marks it for
destruction by other cells (Buddiga ). It is important to note that an
antibody can also be called an immunoglobulin
 (Ig).
14 Buddiga, P. (2013). Immune system anatomy. eMedicine. Retrieved from
<http://emedicine.medscape.com>.
Cell-mediated defences
The cell-mediated defences, or cellular immunity, occur as a result of
action by T cells. On exposure to an antigen, the lymphoid tissues
release large numbers of activated T cells into the lymph system.
These T cells pass into the general circulation. There are three main
groups of T cells: (1) helper T cells, which stimulate the immune
14


system; (2) cytotoxic T cells, which attack and kill micro-organisms
and sometimes the body’s own cells; and (3) suppressor T cells,
which calm the immune system once the threat has been controlled.


Types of specific immunity
Immunity can be classified as active or passive (see Table 32.5
).
In active immunity
, the host produces antibodies in response to
natural antigens (e.g. pathogens) or artificial antigens (e.g.
vaccines). Therefore, active immunity is naturally acquired during
microbial infections or artificially as a result of vaccination (Lee &
Bishop 2016). B cells are activated when they recognise the antigen.
They differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete the antibodies
and serum proteins that bind specifically to the foreign substance
and initiate a variety of elimination responses. The B cell may
produce antibody molecules of five classes of immunoglobulins
designated by letters and usually written as IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG and
IgM. Although the clinical situation should be considered when
antibody testing is interpreted, the loose principles can be distilled
simply as the presence of IgM in suggesting a current or recent
infection. The presence of IgG antibodies suggests past infection
and subsequent immunity.
Table 32.5 Types of immunity
Passive (or acquired) immunity
 is the immunity resulting from
the transfer of pre-made antibodies (or immune cells) from an
immune person (or animal) to a non-immune person. Passive
immunity can be naturally or artificially conferred. Naturally passive
immunity is that conferred with the transfer of antibodies to an infant


via the colostrum and breast milk. Passive immunity is artificially
achieved when a person is injected with antibodies produced from
an immune human or from an immune animal. Passive immunity is
generally short-lived because the recipient’s immune system is not
stimulated. See Table 32.5
 for an overview on the types of
immunity.


Factors increasing susceptibility to
infection
Whether a micro-organism causes an infection depends on a
number of factors. One of the most important factors is host
susceptibility, which is affected by age, heredity, level of stress,
nutritional status, current medical therapy and pre-existing disease
processes (see Figure 32.3
). Susceptibility is the degree to which
an individual can be affected; that is, the likelihood of an organism
causing an infection in that person.
Figure 32.3


Factors increasing susceptibility to infection.
Age influences the risk of infection. Newborns and older adults have
reduced defences against infection. Infections are a major cause of
death of newborns with immature immune systems. Although there
is variation in the persistence of maternal antibodies for newborns, it
is thought that some levels of protection may last between 2 and 5
months. This is important for the infant as it does not begin
synthesis of intestinal IgA until several months of age. Even at 12
months, an infant’s serum IgA is only at approximately 14% of the
levels found in an adult (Bayram et al.
).
15


15 Bayram, R., Özdemir, H., Emsen, A., Türk Dagi, H. & Artaç, H. (2019). Reference ranges
for serum immunoglobulin (IgG, IgA, and IgM) and IgG subclass levels in healthy children.
Turkish Journal of Medical Sciences, 49(2), 497–505. Doi: 10.3906/sag-1807-282.
It has been long observed that genetics may play an important role
in influencing susceptibility to certain immune-system- related
disease. A recent example supporting these considerations is a
study demonstrating ethnic variation in immune system response
related to pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) between Indian and Chinese
populations (Oliveira-de-Souza et al.
). This concept is important as
we advance our understanding in disease progression and
appropriate management to ensure improved health care for all
individuals. It suggests that in some instances there may be benefit
in designing treatment determined by a person’s genetic profile. A
number of other research projects highlight the influence of genetics
and heredity on immune system function. Two projects looking at the
influence of evolutionary history on immune system function provide
strong evidence that the interbreeding that occurred thousands of
years ago between humans and Neanderthals provided genetic
variation which ultimately improved innate immune system function
of humans from that lineage (Dannemann, Prüfer & Kelso ).
16 Oliveira-de-Souza, D., Vinhaes, C., Arriaga, M., .?.?. Andrade, B. (2019). Molecular degree
of perturbation of plasma inflammatory markers associated with tuberculosis reveals distinct
disease profiles between Indian and Chinese populations. Scientific Reports, 9(1), 1–10.
17 Dannemann, M., Prüfer, K. & Kelso, J. (2017). Functional implications of Neandertal
introgression in modern humans. Genome Biology, 18(1), 1–11. Doi: 0.1186/s13059-017-1181-
7.
16
17


The primary factor of the influence of stress on immune system
function is the increased release of the hormone cortisol. Cortisol is
a powerful anti-inflammatory agent which will modify macrophage,
dendritic cells and lymphocyte function. Stress will also influence
circadian rhythms, which will impact on the hypothalamic–pituitary–
adrenal endocrine axis, further modifying immune responses.
A review by Vetvicka and Vetvickova  discusses the potential to
manipulate immune system function through a concept of
immunonutrition. The consensus appears to be that nutrition can
influence immune function in three ways: mucosal barrier function,
cellular defences and changes to the inflammatory response.
Nutritional deficiency reduces phagocyte function and the production
of antibodies and inflammatory mediators (such as cytokines).
18 Vetvicka, V. & Vetvickova, J. (2016). Concept of immuno-nutrition. Journal of Nutrition and
Food Sciences, 6(3), 1–3. Doi: 10.4172/2155-9600.1000500. Retrieved from
<www.omicsonline.org>.
Iatrogenic manipulation of the immune system through treatments
such as drugs or other immunosuppressive interventions are
unfortunate but clearly necessary in some circumstances
(Chatham
; Davis & Ballas
). Administration of drugs to prevent
organ rejection, treat cancer and reduce the risk of an asthma
attack or rheumatoid arthritis flares are a mainstay in modern
treatment of these conditions; however, they come with risks,
including a significant increase in susceptibility to an infectious
disease. Even non-pharmacological interventions such as
radiotherapy undermine the immune system changes (through bone
18
19
20


marrow suppression) and surveillance cell function (through natural
killer cell modulation) (Grassberger et al.
). Open surgical
intervention for the treatment of any condition will breach defensive
barriers and increase the risk of developing an infection.
19 Chatham, W. (2019). Glucocorticoid effects on the immune system. UpToDate. Retrieved
from <www.uptodate.com>.
20 Davis, B. & Ballas, Z. (2017). Biologic response modifiers: Indications, implications, and
insights. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology, 139(5), 1445–1456. Doi:
10.1016/j.jaci.2017.02.013.
21 Grassberger, C., Ellsworth, S., Wilks, M., Keane, F. & Loeffler, J. (2019). Assessing the
interactions between radiotherapy and antitumour immunity. Nature Reviews Clinical
Oncology, 16(12), 729–745. Doi: 10.1038/s41571-019-0238-9.
Finally, disease causes a stress response and can result in all of the
previously cited mechanisms which cause immunosuppression. If
the mechanism of the disease itself alters immune system function
(such as cancer), genetic conditions reduce immune system function
(such as DiGeorge syndrome) or there is metabolic dysfunction
(such as metabolic syndrome or diabetes mellitus type 2), the
person’s susceptibility to infection increases even further.
Although it is clear that there are some major improvements
occurring in the context of infectious diseases and Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander health, more research, education and
publications to facilitate understanding the culture, language and
special needs of this community are warranted.
21


Supporting the defences
of a susceptible host
Individuals at an increased risk of developing an infection may
benefit from various measures which can be undertaken to help
reduce a person’s susceptibility:
Hygiene. Having intact skin and mucous membranes is a
significant barrier against micro-organisms entering the body.
Good oral care, including flossing the teeth, reduces the
likelihood of an oral infection. Regular and thorough bathing and
shampooing removes transient micro-organisms and dirt which, if
left unattended, can result in an infection.
Nutrition. A balanced diet enhances the health of body tissues.
It helps with skin integrity and promotes the skin’s ability to repel
micro-organisms. Adequate nutrition encourages tissue health
and provides the vital component required to assist in rebuilding
damaged tissue.
Fluid. Adequate fluid intake keeps cells well hydrated and is
essential to support the metabolic requirements of the cells.
Adequate hydration maintains fluid output, augmenting the
elimination of potentially pathogenic micro-organisms from the
bladder and urethra.
Sleep. Adequate sleep is essential to health and energy renewal.
It is critical in the management of stress and directly influences
immune system function through its effect on the endocrine
system. See Chapter 48
.


Stress. Assisting individuals to develop stress-reducing
techniques will have a very positive effect on health and immune
system function. See Chapter 43
.
Immunisation. The use of immunisations has dramatically
decreased the incidence of infectious diseases. It is
recommended that immunisations begin shortly after birth and be
completed in early childhood, except for boosters. (See
Table 32.7
.) Immunisations may be given by injection,
inhalation, oral solutions or nasal sprays. They are frequently
given in combination to minimise multiple injections. Because
there are frequent changes to immunisation schedules, it is
advisable to update immunisation schedules yearly.

Immunisation programs are available for high-risk groups; for
example, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, health care
personnel, older adults and individuals with chronic illnesses, and
people travelling to foreign countries. For example, hepatitis B
vaccine is recommended for all health care workers.
Vaccine-preventable diseases
The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC)
recommends specific vaccinations for individuals at higher risk of
27


developing vaccine-preventable diseases. These individuals include
all children, all older adults and others (including Indigenous
Australians). The Australian government provides free vaccines for a
number of vaccine-preventable diseases which are set out in the
National Immunisation Program Schedule (Department of Health
2019a). Table 37.2
 lists the vaccinations included in this program.
The WHO states that although immunisation prevents between 2
and 3 million deaths per year, nearly 1 in 5 children worldwide are
still missing immunisations for vaccine-preventable disease and,
subsequently, mortality rates of nearly 1.5 million children under 5
years of age are still attributable to vaccine-preventable diseases
(WHO
).

Herd immunity is the concept that the greater the proportion of
people in a community who are immune to the disease, the less
likely it is susceptible individuals will be exposed to the disease
(Immunisation Coalition ). It is an important concept to control the
28
29
30


spread of disease within a community. Some diseases require very
high herd immunity because of the highly infectious nature and
virulence of the agent. An example of this is measles. The measles
virus requires an estimated herd immunity of between 92% and
94%; therefore, the Australian government is attempting to achieve
national immunisation coverage of 95% (Department of Health ).
Currently, the immunisation rates for fully immunised children are
94.2% of 1-year-old children and 91.4% of all 2-year-old children
(Department of Health ).

Culturally Competent Care
Aboriginal and torres strait islander peoples
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people appear to be
more susceptible to infections compared with non-Indigenous
individuals. Rates for various infections are still high; however,
there has been some ground gained in closing the health
care gap. Some differences between Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander and non-Indigenous people are shown in Table
32.6
.
31
32


The national immunisation numbers improved since the federal
government brought in controversial ‘No Jab, No Pay’ legislation,
which requires parents to fully immunise their children or they will no
longer be eligible for child care benefits, child care rebates or an
end-of-year family tax benefit supplement. It also removed
conscientious objection or objection to vaccination (on non-medical
grounds) as an acceptable exemption (Department of Social
Services ). This legislation, although good for improving herd
immunity and the overall safety of Australians, troubles some
individuals in relation to concerns about governmental control over
what substances can be forced upon and into an individual’s body.

Research note
Can a peer-led, student-centred campaign improve
influenza vaccination rates in student health care
workers at an Australian university?
M. Nyandoro, D. Kelly, D. Macey & D. Mak
. Student-centred interventions the key to student health
care worker influenza vaccination. Infection, Disease & Health, 21(3), 108–115. Doi:
10.1016/j.idh.2016.09.002.
34 Nyandoro, M., Kelly, D., Macey, D. & Mak, D. (2016). Student-centred interventions the key to
student health care worker influenza vaccination. Infection, Disease & Health, 21(3), 108–115. Doi:
10.1016/j.idh.2016.09.002.
33
34


In this Australian study, the need to increase student
vaccination knowledge and improve influenza vaccination
rates in the health care worker student body led to the
development of a research project. Pre-campaign knowledge,
attitudes and vaccination rates were measured. This was
followed by engagement of industry key stakeholders, the
training of ‘peer champions’ and the preparation of materials
to support vaccination knowledge and availability of
vaccination locations. The ‘peer champions’ played pivotal
roles in the design and delivery of the message. Post-
campaign surveys were used to determine vaccination
attitudes and success of the campaign. Apart from
significantly improving vaccination rates across all cohorts
(nursing and midwifery, medicine and physiotherapy), the
project also exposed common reasons for getting vaccinated
and for not getting vaccinated. Of the 1138 students who
participated in the online survey (37.3%), the top three
reasons for getting vaccinated were access to free vaccine,
self-protection and access to affordable vaccine. Interestingly,
patient protection was only cited in 13.2% of the responses.
The three most common reasons for not getting vaccinated
were lack of access, cost and inconvenience to access.
Unfortunately, despite the campaign, some students still cited
perceived lack of need as a reason for non-vaccination.
Implications This research demonstrates that peer
education and influence can have positive effects on changes
in attitudes and behaviours related to important health
messages. The study also highlights reasons why individuals


may choose to participate or exclude themselves from
important infection-control factors. This knowledge can assist
with designing strategies for future campaigns to promote
attitudinal and/or behavioural changes in relation to important
health care messages.
Barriers to achieving full immunisation include distrust of the safety
of the agent, lack of access to medical services or vaccines,
perceived medical contraindications, lack of psychological or social
support, perceived lack of available detailed and balanced
information, and insufficient time provided by health professionals to
work through concerns (Beard & Clark ;
).

Infection control and health care
Health care facilities are a particularly challenging environment when
it comes to controlling pathogenic micro-organisms. Lee and Bishop
(2016) stress that an important aspect of providing quality health
care is to prevent the transmission of infection to susceptible
individuals, health care workers or any other people coming in
contact with an infectious individual in clinical settings. Prevention
and control of infection are the responsibility of everyone working
within the health care system.
In clinical practice, nurses make clinical decisions and deliberate on
moral and ethical considerations to provide individuals with an
environment that is microbiologically safe. If nurses’ behaviours and
clinical practices are of a low standard, then morally and ethically
those nurses are not fulfilling the Nursing and Midwifery Board of
Australia’s  standards for minimising harm to individuals. The
effective implementation of an infection-control program is based on
understanding the nature and properties of the pathogens involved,
their methods of transmission and strategies that can be used to
break the chain of transmission.
40 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA) (2016). Registered Nurse Standards for
Practice. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
40


Clinical consideration
Fever enhances the activity of the immune
system and therefore medications that reduce
fever should be used with care. Common
medications such as aspirin and ibuprofen are
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents which
have analgesic (pain-relieving) and antipyretic
(fever-reducing) activity. Paracetamol, however,
is also an analgesic and antipyretic, but does
not have any anti-inflammatory activity.
In 1996, the National Health and Medical Research Council
(NHMRC) and Australian National Council on AIDS (ANCA) Infection
Control Working Party broadened the scope of the term universal
precautions because it did not include faeces, nasal secretions,
sputum, sweat, tears, urine or vomit. Consequently, the term
standard precautions (work practices required to achieve a basic
level of infection control for the treatment and care of all patients)
was adopted; transmission-based precautions are to be applied for
individuals known or suspected to be infected or colonised with
disease agents causing infections in health care settings which are
not contained by standard precautions alone (NHMRC ).
41 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) (2019). Australian Guidelines for
the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare. Canberra: Commonwealth of Australia.
41


Retrieved from <www.nhmrc.gov.au>.
Lifespan considerations
Infections
Children
Infections are an expected part of childhood, with most
children experiencing some kind of infection from time to
time. The majority of these infections are caused by viruses
and, for the most part, are transient, relatively benign and
able to be overcome by the body’s natural defences and
supportive care. In some cases, however, severe, even life-
threatening, infections occur. Considerations related to
children include the following:
Newborns are born with some naturally acquired immunity
transferred from the mother across the placenta.
Breastfed infants enjoy higher levels of immunity against
infections than formula-fed infants.
Fevers less than 39°C in children should not be treated,
except for comfort of the child.
Children between 6 months and 5 years are at higher risk
for fever-induced (febrile) seizures. Febrile seizures are
not associated with neurological seizure disorders (e.g.
epilepsy).


Children who are immune-compromised (e.g. leukaemia,
HIV) or have a chronic health condition (e.g. cystic
fibrosis, sickle cell disease, congenital heart disease) need
extra precautions to prevent exposure to infectious
agents.
Hand hygiene, comprehensive immunisation, good
nutrition, adequate hydration and appropriate rest are
essential to preventing and/or treating infections in
children.
Hand washing and good hygiene in day care and schools
are important to prevent the spread of infections.
Adolescents are at high risk for sexually transmitted
diseases and should be well educated about how to
prevent infections.
Older adults
Ageing may predispose older adults to increased risk of
infection and delayed healing. Anatomical and physiological
agents that protect a person when younger often change in
structure and function with increasing age, resulting in
decreased protective function. Changes take place in the
skin, respiratory tract, gastrointestinal system, kidneys and
immune system. If unchallenged, these systems work well,
maintaining homeostasis for the individual. When
compromised by stress, illness, infections, treatments or
surgeries, they find it difficult to provide adequate protection.
Special considerations for older adults include the following:


Nutrition is often poor in older adults. Certain components,
especially adequate protein, are necessary to build up and
maintain the immune system.
Diabetes mellitus, which occurs more frequently in older
adults, increases the risk of infection and delayed healing
by causing an alteration in nutrition, and impaired
peripheral circulation decreases the oxygen transported to
the tissues.
The immune system reacts slowly to the introduction of
antigens, allowing the antigen to reproduce itself several
times before it is recognised by the immune system. T cell
effectiveness is often decreased.
The normal inflammatory response is delayed. This often
causes atypical responses to infections with unusual
presentations. Instead of displaying redness, swelling and
fever usually associated with infections, atypical
symptoms such as confusion and disorientation, agitation,
incontinence, falls, lethargy and general fatigue may be
more obvious first.
Recognising these changes in older adults is important in
early detection and treatment of related potential for
infections and delayed healing. Nursing interventions to
promote prevention include the following:
Provide and teach ways to improve nutritional status.
Use aseptic techniques to decrease chance of infections
(especially health-care-associated infections (HAIs)).


Encourage older adults to have regular immunisations for
flu and pneumonia.
Be alert to subtle atypical signs of infection and act
promptly to diagnose and treat.
The Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection
in Healthcare (NHMRC 2019) serve as the national guidelines to be
implemented by health care facilities and should be adopted by all
health care workers. This document outlines the various concepts of
standard precautions and infection control including hand hygiene,
the use of personal protective equipment (PPE), handling and
disposal of sharps and routine cleaning of the environment. There is
also elaboration on the concept of transmission-based precautions
including contact, droplet and air-borne precautions. This document
also contains information on how to manage multidrug-resistant
organisms.
As per the NHMRC national guidelines for infection control, standard
precautions consist of:
hand hygiene, before and after every episode of patient contact
the use of PPE
the safe use and disposal of sharps
routine environmental cleaning
reprocessing of reusable medical equipment and instruments
respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette
aseptic non-touch technique


waste management
appropriate handling of linen (NHMRC 2019).


Standard precautions
Standard precautions
 are the basic precautions that should be
used when caring for all individuals regardless of their diagnosis or
infection status (see Figure 32.5
). It should be remembered that
any person may be infected with a pathogen which could be
potentially harmful to the health care worker or may be spread to the
environment or other health care consumers in the vicinity. An
individual may not display signs or symptoms of an infectious
disease and may not know themself that they are carrying an
infectious disease; therefore, one must work with the assumption
that everyone is potentially infected. This does not mean that health
care professionals need to wrap themselves in impenetrable
materials for every interaction. This would not only be unnecessary
for the vast majority of interactions, it would also be incredibly
consuming of our already stretched health care dollar and could
even potentially be psychologically damaging to those in our care.
Therefore, a sensible approach with an initial analysis of each
interaction will determine what components of precautions are
necessary to undertake the task.
Figure 32.5


Standard precautions poster: national standardised infection-control
and prevention signs.

. Standard Precautions

Standard-Precautions-Photo-PDF-550KB.pdf>.
42 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2012a).
Standard Precautions Poster. Sydney: ACSQHC. Retrieved from
<www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Hand hygiene
Transmission of pathogens is heightened by physical contact.
Therefore, the most basic principle of reducing the spread of
pathogens is hand washing. The WHO identified the 5 moments for
hand hygiene (see Figure 32.6
). Following these
recommendations is critical, and good basic hand hygiene practices
have been shown to significantly reduce the risk of health-care-
associated infections.
Figure 32.6
42


The 5 moments for hand hygiene.
Source: WHO (2019c). 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene. <www.who.int/infection-prevention/campaigns/clean-
hands/5moments/en/>. © World Health Organization. All rights reserved.
Although Figure 32.6
 depicts the application of the ‘5 moments’ in
an acute care setting, these guidelines apply to all health care
settings. Furthermore, these should not be considered the only time


a health care professional should wash their hands; there are
numerous other reasons why one should perform hand hygiene.
Table 32.8
 lists additional situations when hand hygiene should be
performed.
Table 32.8 Non-clinical situations when hand hygiene should be
performed
Source: NHMRC (2019). Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare.
Canberra: Commonwealth of Australia.
Correct hand washing practice is not only about technique, but also
about choosing the correct substance with which to clean. The two
options are use of soap and water or an alcohol-based hand rub
(ABHR). Hand Hygiene Australia reports that ABHRs are superior to
soap and water because they:
result in a significantly greater reduction in bacterial numbers
than soap and water in many clinical situations
require less time to use
cause less irritation to the skin
can be made readily accessible to health care workers
are more cost effective (Ryan, Havers & Grayson , p. 28).
43 Ryan, K., Havers, S. & Grayson, M. (2019). Hand Hygiene Australia Manual (3rd ed.).
Melbourne: Hand Hygiene Australia. Retrieved from <www.hha.org.au>.
However, there are times when the use of ABHRs may not be
appropriate. These include when:
43


hands are visibly soiled
there are suspected or known spore-forming organisms such as
Clostridium difficile
there are suspected or known viral infections such as norovirus,
rotavirus, hepatitis A or polio
there are suspected or known parasitic or protozoan oocyst
infestations/infections (Ryan et al. 2019; WHO
).
44 World Health Organization (WHO) (2019c). 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene. Retrieved
from <www.who.int>.
Although there are times when ABHRs may not be appropriate in the
first instance, in these scenarios it is still acceptable, and often even
sensible, to follow the soap and water hand washing method with an
ABHR, after drying hands well with single-use paper towels (WHO
2019c).
Hand washing technique is important and changes depending on
which solution is used. See Figure 32.7
 for instructions produced
by the WHO demonstrating both techniques.
Figure 32.7a
44


How to Handrub?

Figure 32.7b


How to Handwash?


Source: How to Handwash? Retrieved from <www.who.int/gpsc/5may/How_To_HandWash_Poster.pdf>. ©

Hand Hygiene Australia also states that there is no maximum
number of times that ABHRs can be used before the need to wash
with soap and water (Ryan et al. 2019).
Health care professionals should be aware that skin reactions such
as contact dermatitis can occur as a result of the drying action of the
substances or paper towels. Use of rubs containing emollient has
been found to reduce contact dermatitis in approximately 70% of
health care workers. Also, the use of an oil-containing lotion or
barrier cream is beneficial to reduce skin breakdown from chemical
irritation and drying. Current recommendations suggest that to
reduce skin breakdown and the drying effects of frequent hand
washing, lotion should be applied three times a shift (Ryan et al.
2019). An evidence-based proposal by Hines et al.
 suggests that
on review of the literature, and to assist with improved compliance,
the three lotion applications may be better spaced as once before
work, during work and after work. However, they did also
recommend applying conditioning cream after any hand washing
event. This may be logistically difficult to achieve and not particularly
popular with staff.
45 Hines, J., Wilkinson, S., John, S. et al. (2017). The three moments of skin cream
application: An evidence-based proposal for use of skin creams in the prevention of irritant
contact dermatitis in the workplace. Journal of European Academy of Dermatological
45


Venereology, 31(1), 5–64. Doi: 10.1111/jdv.13851. Retrieved from
<https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com>.
Skill 32.1
 describes correct hand hygiene techniques using soap
and water.
Personal protective equipment
According to international guidelines and, most importantly, the
Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in
Healthcare, along with hand washing, application of personal
protective equipment (PPE) is important to reduce the risk of
exposure to potentially infective materials. PPE for standard
precautions may include gloves, aprons or gowns, face masks and
eye protection.
Gloves
Gloves are worn for three reasons. First, they protect the hands of
nurses when they handle any body substances; for example, blood,
urine, faeces, sputum or exudate from damaged skin. Secondly,
gloves reduce the likelihood of transmitting endogenous micro-
organisms to the individuals receiving care and conversely from the
care recipient to the nurse. Finally, gloves reduce the possibility of
transmitting micro-organisms from an individual or a fomite to
another person. Gloves must be changed between individuals. At no
time should gloves be left on and washed/dried (as one would wash


their own hands). Hands should be washed following removal of
gloves.
Gloves can be made from a variety of materials including latex or
synthetic materials. As latex allergy is on the rise in not only health
care consumers but also health care professionals (Behrman ),
every opportunity to reduce latex exposure should be embraced;
therefore, non-sterile, single-use gloves are more likely to be made
from synthetic materials such as nitrile.
46 Behrman, A. (2016). Latex allergy. eMedicine. Retrieved from <http://emedicine.
medscape.com/article/756632-overview>.
Skill 32.2
 (pages 689–690) describes application and removal of
gloves.
Gowns
Gowns prevent contamination of clothing by body secretions. Choice
of gown or apron depends on the activity and protection required.
Table 32.9
 briefly outlines characteristics for consideration when
selecting an apron or gown.
Table 32.9 Characteristics for consideration when selecting an
apron or gown
Source: Extracted from NHMRC (2019). Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in
Healthcare. Canberra: Commonwealth of Australia.
46


Skill 32.2
 describes how to don and remove a gown. Before
leaving the individual’s room, the nurse performs hand hygiene.
Face masks
Masks are worn by the health care professional to reduce exposure
of the mouth and nose to splashes or sprays. Masks can also be
worn by an individual who is at risk of spreading potentially infected
respiratory secretions through air-borne droplets. There are a
number of mask options and choice depends on the activity and
protection required (wearing masks exceeds standard precautions
and would be in the context of transmission-based precautions).
Table 32.10
 briefly outlines characteristics for consideration when
selecting a mask.
Table 32.10 Characteristics for consideration when selecting a
mask
Source: Extracted from NHMRC (2019). Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in
Healthcare. Canberra: Commonwealth of Australia.
Other important considerations associated with mask use include:
Changing them when they become wet or soiled.
Taking care not to touch the front of the mask (as it is
contaminated).
Discarded masks should never be reapplied.
Masks are either on or off (not dangling around neck) (NHMRC
2019).


Guidelines for donning and removing face masks are shown in Skill
32.2
.
Eyewear
Protective eyewear (goggles, glasses or face shields) and masks
are indicated in situations where body substances may splatter the
face (see Skill 32.2
). Nurses wearing prescription eyeglasses
must still wear goggles over their glasses because the protection
must extend around the sides of the glasses.
Respiratory hygiene and cough
etiquette
Standard precautions include cough etiquette and respiratory
hygiene such as covering sneezes and coughs. Sneezing into
tissues will contain respiratory secretions; however, failing the
availability of tissues, coughing or sneezing can be contained using
the inner elbow rather than the hand. It is critical to perform hand
hygiene following contact with respiratory secretions or objects
contaminated with respiratory secretions (NHMRC 2019).
Disinfecting and sterilising


The links of ‘agent’ and ‘reservoir’ in the chain of infection can be
broken by cleaning (the mechanical removal of material from an
object’s surface). Lee and Bishop (2016) describe two important
concepts in relation to cleaning: disinfection
 (where chemical
agents remove or destroy most pathogens from an object’s surface;
this process is unable to remove all endospores and some viruses)
and sterilisation
 (a process which will remove or destroy all
micro-organisms; sterile objects are free from endospores and
viruses). Table 32.11
 briefly outlines guidelines for sterilisation and
disinfection of equipment.
Table 32.11 Guidelines for sterilisation and disinfection of
equipment
Source: Extracted and modified from G. Lee & P. Bishop (2016). Microbiology and Infection Control for Health
Professionals (6th ed.). Frenchs Forest, NSW: Pearson.
Disinfecting
A disinfectant
 is a chemical preparation capable of killing or
inactivating micro-organisms. The Therapeutic Goods Administration
(TGA) regulates disinfectants. A disinfectant is a chemical to be
used on equipment and on surfaces and an antiseptic is a chemical
which can be used on skin and tissue.
Both disinfectants and antiseptics are said to have bactericidal or
bacteriostatic properties. Bactericidal preparations destroy bacteria
whereas bacteriostatic preparations prevent the growth and
reproduction of some bacteria. Spore-forming bacteria. For


example, Clostridium difficile (a frequent cause of hospital-acquired
diarrhoea) and Bacillus anthracis (anthrax) are inhibited only by a
few agents that are normally effective against other forms of
bacteria.
When disinfecting equipment, nurses must follow organisation policy
and consider the following:
the type and number of infectious organisms; some micro-
organisms are readily destroyed, whereas others require longer
contact with the disinfectant
the recommended concentration of the disinfectant and the
duration of contact
the presence of soap; some disinfectants are ineffective in the
presence of soap or detergent
the presence of organic materials; saliva, blood, pus or
excretions readily inactivate many disinfectants
the surface areas to be treated; the disinfecting agent must
come into contact with all surfaces and areas.
Sterilising
Sterilisation is a process that destroys all micro-organisms, including
spores and viruses. Four commonly used methods of sterilisation
are moist heat, gas, boiling water and radiation.
Moist heat


To sterilise with moist heat (e.g. with an autoclave), steam under
pressure to achieve temperatures higher than boiling point.
Gas
Ethylene oxide gas destroys micro-organisms by interfering with
their metabolic processes. It is also effective against spores. Its
advantages are good penetration and effectiveness for heat-
sensitive items. Its major disadvantage is its toxicity to humans.
Boiling water
This is the most practical and inexpensive method for sterilising in
the home. The main disadvantage is that spores and some viruses
are not killed by this method. Boiling a minimum of 15 minutes is
advised for disinfection of articles in the home.
Radiation
Both ionising (such as alpha, beta and x-rays) and non- ionising
(ultraviolet light) radiation are used for disinfection and sterilisation.
The main disadvantage of ultraviolet light is that the rays do not
penetrate deeply. Ionising radiation is used effectively in industry to
sterilise foods, drugs and other heat-sensitive items. Its main
advantage is that it is effective for items difficult to sterilise. Its chief
disadvantage is that the equipment is very expensive.


Clinical consideration
In the move from intravenous connections that
require needles to the new needleless connector
systems that are more common now, risk of
accidental needle injury for the clinician has
decreased. However, unfortunately, catheter-
associated bloodstream infections (CABSIs)
have increased because of poor adherence to
basic aseptic principles. CABSIs represent a
significant risk to health care consumers and
place an even greater burden on the already
overstretched health care dollar. Simple
disinfection with an appropriate solution (70%
alcohol, chlorhexidine, povidone iodine) prior to
accessing the intravenous connection/port/hub
is a critical step in the prevention of CABSIs.

32.1 Hand washing technique
Effective hand hygiene relies on appropriate
technique as much as on selection of the correct
product (NHMRC 2019).
Purposes
To reduce the risk of cross-contamination among
individuals.
To reduce the risk of transmission of infectious
organisms to oneself.
To reduce the number of micro-organisms on the
hands.
To reduce the risk of transmission of micro-
organisms to individuals
Assessment
Assess
The presence of breaches in skin integrity.
The availability of appropriate products.


The availability of appropriate waste disposal
methods.
Planning
Determine the location of running water and soap or
soap substitutes.
Equipment
Recommended solution of facility
Warm running water
Disposable or sanitised towels
Implementation
Preparation
Assess the hands
Nails should be kept short. Rationale: short,
natural nails are less likely to harbour micro-
organisms, scratch others or puncture gloves.
Most organisations do not permit health care
workers in direct contact with people in their care
to have any type of artificial nails.
Remove all jewellery. Rationale: micro-
organisms can lodge in the settings of jewellery
and under rings. Removal facilitates effective
cleaning of the hands and arms.


Check hands for breaks in the skin, such as
infections or cuts. Rationale: nurses with breaks
or lesions may require a work assignment with
decreased risk for transmission of infectious
organisms due to the increased risk of acquiring
or transmitting an infection.
Performance
1. Turn on the water and adjust the flow.
There are five common types of tap
controls:
a. Hand-operated handles.
b. Knee levers. Move these with the
knee to regulate flow and
temperature. 1


1 A knee-lever tap control
c. Foot pedals. Press these with the
foot to regulate flow and
temperature. 2


2 A foot-pedal tap control
d. Elbow controls. Move these with
the elbows instead of the hands.
e. Infrared control. Motion in front of
the sensor causes water to start
and stop flowing automatically.
Adjust the flow so that the water is warm.
Rationale: warm water removes less of
the protective oil of the skin than hot
water.
2. Wet the hands thoroughly by holding them
under the running water and apply solution to
the hands.
Hold the hands lower than the elbows so
the water flows from the arms to the
fingertips. Rationale: the water should
flow from the least contaminated to the
most contaminated area; the hands are
generally considered more contaminated
than the lower arms. Note that this is a
different technique from the one used
when performing surgical hand washing.
Nurses perform this level of hand washing
when a sterile procedure is required. See
the following variation for hand washing


before a procedure requiring surgical
aseptic non-touch technique.
For liquids, apply 2 to 4 mL (1 tsp) or as
per manufacturer’s recommendations. If it
is granules or sheets, rub them firmly
between the hands.
3. Thoroughly wash and rinse the hands.
Use firm, rubbing and circular movements
to wash the palm, back and wrist of each
hand. Be sure to include the heel of the
hand. Interlace the fingers and thumbs
and move the hands back and forth. 3
Continue this motion for at least
15 seconds. Rationale: the circular action
creates friction that helps remove micro-
organisms mechanically. Interlacing the
fingers and thumbs cleans the interdigital
spaces.


3 Interlacing the fingers during hand
washing
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Rub the fingertips against the palm of the
opposite hand. Rationale: the nails and
fingertips are commonly missed during
hand washing.
Rinse the hands.
4. Thoroughly pat dry the hands and arms.
Dry hands and arms thoroughly with a
paper towel without scrubbing. Rationale:
moist skin becomes chapped readily, as
does dry skin that is rubbed vigorously;
chapping produces lesions.
Discard the paper towel in the appropriate
container.
5. Turn off the water.
Use a new paper towel to grasp a hand-
operated control. 4 Rationale: this
prevents the nurse from picking up micro-
organisms from the tap handles.


4 Using a paper towel to grasp the handle
of a hand-operated tap
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Variation: hand washing before
surgical non-touch aseptic techniques
Apply the antimicrobial solution and wash
as described in step 4, but hold the hands
higher than the elbows during this hand
wash. Wet the hands and forearms under
the running water, letting it run from the
fingertips to the elbows so the hands
become cleaner than the elbows. 5
Rationale: in this way, the water runs
from the area that now has the fewest
micro-organisms to areas with a relatively
greater number.


5 Holding the hands higher than the
elbows during a hand wash before a
surgical non-touch aseptic technique
After washing and rinsing, use a towel to
dry one hand thoroughly in a rotating
motion from the fingers to the elbow. Use
a new towel to dry the other hand and
arm. Rationale: a clean towel prevents
the transfer of micro-organisms from one
elbow (least clean area) to the other hand
(cleanest area).
Evaluation
There is no traditional evaluation of the effectiveness
of the individual nurse’s hand hygiene. Many
organisations routinely audit hand
hygiene compliance. Institutional quality control
departments monitor the occurrence of infections
and investigate those situations in which health care
providers are implicated in the transmission of
infectious organisms. Research has repeatedly
shown that good hand hygiene practice is one of the
most critical factors in infection control.
