32.2 Donning and removing
personal protective equipment
(gloves, gown, mask, eyewear)
Purposes
To protect health care workers and people in their
care from transmission of potentially infective
materials.
Assessment
Consider the activities required to be completed
while the nurse is in the person’s room at this time.
Rationale: this determines which equipment is
required.
Planning
Application and removal of PPE can be time
consuming. Prioritise care and arrange for


personnel to care for other people if indicated.
Determine which supplies are present within the
individual’s room and which must be brought to
the room.
Consider if special handling is indicated for
removal of any specimens or other materials
from the room.
Equipment
As indicated according to which activities will be
performed. Ensure extra supplies are easily
available.
Gown
Mask
Protective eyewear
Clean gloves
Face shield
Implementation
Preparation
Remove or secure all loose items such as name
tags or jewellery.
Performance
1. Depending on the location of the PPE in
relation to the person, prior to performing the


procedure, introduce self and verify the
person’s identity using organisation policy.
Explain to the person what you are going to
do, why it is necessary and how they can
assist.
2. Perform appropriate hand hygiene.
3. Don a clean gown.
Pick up a clean gown and allow it to unfold
in front of you without allowing it to touch
any area soiled with body substances.
Slide the arms and the hands through the
sleeves.
Fasten the ties at the neck to keep the
gown in place.
Overlap the gown at the back as much as
possible and fasten the waist ties or belt.
1 Rationale: overlapping securely covers
the uniform at the back. Waist ties keep
the gown from falling away from the body,
which can cause inadvertent soiling of the
uniform.


1 Overlapping the gown at the back to
cover the nurse’s uniform
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
4. Don the face mask.
Locate the top edge of the mask. The
mask usually has a narrow metal strip
along the edge.


Hold the mask by the top two strings or
loops.
Place the upper edge of the mask over
the bridge of the nose and tie the upper
ties at the back of the head or secure the
loops around the ears. If glasses are
worn, fit the upper edge of the mask
under the glasses. Rationale: with the
edge of the mask under the glasses,
clouding of the glasses is less likely to
occur.
Secure the lower edge of the mask under
the chin and tie the lower ties at the nape
of the neck. 2 Rationale: to be effective,
a mask must cover both the nose and the
mouth because air moves in and out of
both.


2 A face mask and eye protection
covering the nose, mouth and eyes
If the mask has a metal strip, adjust this
firmly over the bridge of the nose.
Rationale: a secure fit prevents both the
escape and the inhalation of micro-
organisms around the edges of the mask
and the fogging of glasses.
Wear the mask only once and do not wear
any mask longer than the manufacturer
recommends or once it becomes damp.
Rationale: a mask should be used only
once because it becomes ineffective when
moist.
Do not leave a used face mask hanging
around the neck.
5. Don protective eyewear if it is not combined
with the face mask.
6. Don clean disposable gloves.
No special technique is required.
If wearing a gown, pull the gloves up to
cover the cuffs of the gown.
7. To remove soiled PPE, remove the gloves
first as they are the most soiled.


If wearing a gown that is tied at the waist
in front, undo the ties before removing
gloves.
Remove the first glove by grasping it on
its palmar surface, taking care to touch
only glove to glove. 3 Rationale: this
keeps the soiled parts of the used gloves
from touching the skin of the wrist or
hand.


3 Plucking the palmar surface below the
cuff of a contaminated glove
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Pull the first glove completely off by
inverting or rolling the glove inside out.
Continue to hold the inverted removed
glove by the fingers of the remaining
gloved hand. Place the first two fingers of
the bare hand inside the cuff of the
second glove. 4 Rationale: touching the
outside of the second soiled glove with the
bare hand is avoided.


4 Inserting fingers to remove the second
contaminated glove
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Pull the second glove off to the fingers by
turning it inside out. This pulls the first
glove inside the second glove. Rationale:


the soiled part of the glove is folded to the
inside to reduce the chance of transferring
any micro-organisms by direct contact.
Using the bare hand, continue to remove
the gloves, which are now inside out, and
dispose of them in the appropriate waste
container. 5


5 Holding contaminated gloves which are
inside out


Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
8. Perform correct hand hygiene.
9. Remove protective eyewear and dispose of
properly or place in the appropriate
receptacle for cleaning.
10. Remove the gown when preparing to leave
the room. Unless a gown is grossly soiled
with body substances, no special precautions
are needed to remove it. If a gown is grossly
soiled:
Avoid touching soiled parts on the outside
of the gown, if possible. Rationale: the
top part of the gown may be soiled; for
example, if you have been holding an
infant with a respiratory infection.
Grasp the gown along the inside of the
neck and pull down over the shoulders.
Roll up the gown with the soiled part inside
and discard it in the appropriate container.
11. Remove the mask at the doorway. If using a
respirator mask, remove it after leaving the
room and closing the door.
If using a mask with strings, first untie the
lower strings of the mask. Rationale: this
prevents the top part of the mask from
falling onto the chest.


Untie the top strings and, while holding the
ties securely, remove the mask from the
face. If side loops are present, lift the side
loops up and away from the ears and
face. Do not touch the front of the mask.
Rationale: the front of the mask through
which the nurse has been breathing is
contaminated.
Discard a disposable mask in the
appropriate waste container.
Perform correct hand hygiene again.
Evaluation
Conduct any follow-up indicated during your care
of the individual.
Ensure there is an adequate supply of equipment
available for the next health care professional.


Asepsis and aseptic technique
Asepsis
 is a term used to indicate freedom from infection
(sepsis) or pathogenic material (NHMRC 2019). During invasive
clinical procedures, there is the potential for transferring micro-
organisms from the surrounding environment or health care worker
into or onto the person receiving care. The Royal College of Nursing
Australia supports the NHMRC Australian Guidelines for the
Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare (2019). In 2016–
17, there were over 60 000 HAIs in Australian acute health care
facilities (ACSQHC ).
47 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2018a). Hospital
Acquired Complications. Sydney: ACSQHC. Retrieved from<www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Techniques health professionals undertake to prevent infections or
manage infection control can be summarised as two broad
categories: (1) those aseptic techniques used for highly invasive
clinical procedures such as open surgery and intravenous central
line placement and generally considered ‘surgical asepsis’; and (2)
all other less invasive procedures, generally considered ‘aseptic
technique
’ or clean or ‘non-touch technique’.
Surgical asepsis
 is typically performed in a surgical (theatre)
environment requiring maximal sterile barrier precautions
(ACSQHC ). This involves keeping the operative area as free of
47
48


micro-organisms as possible by using special environmental cleaning
measures. Surgical instruments and surgical drapes are sterilised
using a variety of processes that destroy the vast majority of micro-
organisms. The whole operative environment is strictly controlled,
including air quality monitoring and the movements of staff.
48 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2017). National
Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
The Australasian College for Infection Prevention and Control
(ACIPC) has developed a set of guidelines to assist health care
professionals understand and practise a standardised approach to
aseptic technique. The guidelines include environmental control
measures, infection-control measures, aseptic field selection and
management, non-touch technique, waste management and
cleaning of equipment (ACIPC ). These guidelines utilise the
aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT ) practice framework developed
by Rowley , which attempts to address the historical confusion in
terminology and wide variability in practice standards.
49 Australasian College for Infection Prevention and Control (ACIPC) (2015). Aseptic
Technique Policy & Practice Guidelines. Retrieved from <www.acipc.org.au>.
50 Rowley, S. (2001). Aseptic non-touch technique. Nursing Times. Infection Control
Supplement Feb 15, 97(7), VI-VIII.
The ANTT  practice framework addresses inconsistencies in the
use, terms and application of the principles of asepsis in clinical
practice. It provides a logical practice structure and educational
materials aimed at minimising variation and developing competence
49
®
50
®


in practice. Notably, ANTT  is based on the fundamental principle
that the aim of all invasive clinical procedures, no matter how
complex, should always be asepsis (ANTT ).
51 Aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT) (2019). ANTT Theory. Retrieved from
<http://antt.org>.
The principles of ANTT  include determination of ‘key part’ and ‘key
site’ protection. During invasive clinical procedures, practitioners
identify and protect the key parts of equipment (e.g. syringe tip and
needle hub) and key sites (such as any portal of entry to the body;
e.g. an open wound). Critically, a key part must only come into
contact with other key parts or key sites (ANTT 2019). It should be
noted that the core principle of ‘non-touch’ still applies in the
operating room setting and in surgical asepsis; sterilised gloves and
other equipment are used to protect equipment and the patient from
direct operator touch.
The ACIPC’s practice guidelines provide general principles of best
practice in relation to aseptic technique (see Box 32.1
). These
guidelines are pivotal in assisting health care professionals to
promote safety and quality in relation to Standard 3 of the
ACSQHC’s National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards of
‘Preventing and Controlling Healthcare-associated Infections’.
BO X
®
51
®


32.1 Aseptic technique practice
guidelines
1. Obtain consent from the patient, check for allergies
and complete patient identification process using three
nationally recognised identifiers.
2. Perform risk assessment and manage environmental
risks.
3. Perform hand hygiene.
4. Clean the tray/trolley/work surface with detergent and
water or detergent wipe.
5. Identify and gather equipment for procedure. Inspect
packaging for damage; check sterility indicators and
expiry dates; ensure any additional equipment, such
as tourniquet, is clean.
6. Perform hand hygiene (clean hands effectively with
soap and water or ABHR).
7. Prepare critical or general aseptic field.
8. Open procedure pack using corners and drop sterile
equipment into sterile field.
9. Prepare patient—use gloves where appropriate to
protect from potential body fluid exposure.
10. Remove gloves if used.
11. Perform hand hygiene.
Note: for standard aseptic procedure, clean hands
effectively with soap and water or ABHR. For surgical
aseptic procedure, a surgical hand scrub is required.


12. Apply gloves if required.
Note: if it is necessary to touch key parts or key sites
directly, sterile gloves are used to minimise the risk of
contamination. Otherwise, non-sterile gloves are
typically the gloves of choice for standard aseptic
procedures. Sterile gloves are used for all surgical
aseptic procedures.
13. Perform procedure ensuring all key parts/components
are protected:
Sterile items are used once and disposed into
waste bag.
Only sterile items contact the key site.
Sterile items do not come into contact with non-
sterile items.
14. Remove gloves (if used) and perform hand hygiene
effectively with soap and water or ABHR.
15. Dispose of all waste (including sharps). Clean
equipment and perform hand hygiene.
Source: ACIPC (2015). Aseptic Technique Policy & Practice Guidelines, p. 4. Retrieved from
<www.acipc.org.au/aseptic-technique-resources/>.
The timing of procedures, such as re-dressing wounds in a ward
area, is an important factor in reducing the risk of infection. Ideally,
these tasks should be carried out at a time when ward activities are
fewer and cleaning activities are suspended. Clean, non-infected
wounds should be dressed first; colostomies and infected wounds


should be dressed last. This minimises environmental contamination
and cross-infection.
Disposal of soiled equipment
and supplies
Many pieces of equipment are supplied for single use only and are
disposed of after use. Some items, however, are reusable.
Organisations have specific policies and procedures for handling
soiled equipment (e.g. disposal, cleaning, disinfecting and
sterilising); nurses must be familiar with these practices in their
employing organisation.
Appropriate handling of soiled equipment and supplies is essential:
to prevent inadvertent exposure of health care workers to articles
contaminated with body substances
to prevent contamination of the environment.
Bagging
Articles contaminated, or likely to have been contaminated, with
infective material such as pus, blood, body fluids, faeces or
respiratory secretions need to be enclosed in a sturdy bag
impervious to micro-organisms before they are removed from the


room of any individual. Some agencies use labels or bags of a
particular colour, designating these as infective wastes.
The Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection
in Healthcare (NHMRC 2019) state that waste should be effectively
segregated according to its category at the point of generation,
using appropriately colour-coded and labelled containers
accordingly:
Clinical waste is to be placed in yellow containers bearing the
international black biohazard symbol and clearly marked ‘clinical
waste’.
Cytotoxic waste is to be placed in purple containers bearing the
telophase symbol and marked ‘cytotoxic waste’.
Radioactive waste is to be placed in red containers with the black
international radiation symbol and marked ‘radioactive waste’.
Outside these categories, the Australian Guidelines for the
Prevention and Control of Infection in Healthcare recommend the
following when handling waste:
Apply standard precautions to protect against exposure to blood
and body fluid during waste handling.
Segregate waste at point of generation.
Contain waste in the appropriate receptacle (identified by colour
and label) and dispose of it according to the facility waste
management plan.


Train the health care worker in the correct procedures for waste
handling.
Ensure that trolleys used for transport of infectious or other
hazardous waste are:
– clearly labelled as such
– used solely for waste transport
– daily
– never overfilled
– fitted with drip trays to contain leaks or spills.
Place visibly soiled non-disposable or reusable equipment in a
labelled bag before removing it from the individual’s bed area and
send it to a central processing area for decontamination. Some
agencies may require glass bottles or jars and metal items be
placed in separate bags from rubber and plastic items. Glass and
metal can be sterilised in an autoclave, but rubber and plastic are
damaged by this process and must be cleaned by other
methods, such as gas sterilisation.
Disassemble specific procedure trays into component parts.
Some components are disposable; others need to be sent to the
laundry or central services for cleaning and decontaminating.
Bag soiled clothing before sending it home or to the
organisation’s laundry.
Regardless of where the waste is generated, the principles of
determining whether it is to be treated as clinical or general waste
remain the same (NHMRC 2019). Where possible, avoid the manual


handling of waste. No special precautions are required for disposal
of uncontaminated equipment.
Linen
Handle soiled linen as little as possible and with the least agitation
possible before placing it in the linen skip. This prevents gross
microbial contamination of the air and people handling the linen.
Close the bag before sending it to the laundry in accordance with
organisational practice.
Laboratory specimens
Laboratory specimens, if placed in a leak-proof container with a
secure lid with a biohazard label, need no special precautions (see
Figure 32.8
). Use care when collecting specimens to avoid
contaminating the outside of the container. Containers visibly
contaminated on the outside should be placed inside a sealable
plastic bag before sending them to the laboratory. This prevents
personnel from having hand contact with potentially infective
material.
Figure 32.8


Biohazard alert.
Source: © jpgon/Fotolia 2004–2010. All rights reserved.


Dishes
Dishes require no special precautions. Soiling of dishes can largely
be prevented by encouraging individuals to cleanse their hands
before eating and providing them with the necessary items. For
convenience, some organisations use paper dishes which are
disposed of in the appropriate waste container.
Blood pressure equipment
Blood pressure equipment needs no special precautions unless it
becomes contaminated with infective material. If it does become
contaminated, follow organisation policy to decontaminate it.
Cleaning procedures vary according to whether it is a wall or
portable unit. In some organisations, a disposable cuff is used for
individuals placed on contact precautions.
Thermometers
Non-disposable used thermometers are generally disinfected after
use. Check organisational practice. Most temperature thermometers
are aural with a disposable ear piece.
Disposable needles, syringes and sharps
Place needles, syringes and ‘sharps’ (e.g. lancets, scalpels and
broken glass) into a puncture-resistant container. To avoid puncture


wounds, use approved safety or needleless systems and do not
detach needles from the syringe or recap the needle before
disposal. See Chapter 36
 for how to prevent needle-stick injuries.
Clinical consideration
National legislation protecting the privacy of
personal health information may extend to the
individual’s label placed on disposable supplies
such as intravenous bags, or individually
labelled disposable waste (Office of the
Australian Information Commissioner
). These
labels might have the individual’s name and the
drug that might be infused. If this waste was not
disposed of appropriately, it would constitute a
breach of personal health information.
Organisations may have or need to develop
policies that require removal of any personal
information before disposal. It is important to
become familiar with the organisation’s policy
which refers to management of disposal of
personal health information.

Guide to Securing Personal Information: ‘Reasonable Steps’ to
Protect Personal Information. Canberra: Australian Government.
Retrieved from <www.oaic.gov.au>.
52


Transmission-based precautions
Transmission-based precautions are specific interventions added
when standard precautions may be insufficient to interrupt
transmission of a pathogen. The additional measures are to target
pathogens easily transmitted by contact, droplet and air-borne
routes.
The three types of transmission-based precautions may be used
alone or in combination but always in addition to standard
precautions. The Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and
Control of Infection in Healthcare (NHMRC 2019) recommended
practices for transmission-based precautions, which are outlined in
Box 32.2
.
BO X
32.2 Transmission-based precautions
The Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of
Infection in Healthcare (NHMRC 2019, pp. 96–120) describe
the transmission of infectious agents in the following ways:


Contact: transmission and
precautions
Contact transmission (indirect or direct) occurs when
environmental surfaces are not appropriately
decontaminated, patient care devices are shared between
individuals, infectious individuals have contact with others or
contaminated health care workers’ hands or clothing come
into contact with other health care consumers (NHMRC
2019). (See Figure 32.9
 for contact precautions
guidelines.)
Figure 32.9


Contact precautions poster (national standardised infection
control and prevention signs).
Source: ACSQHC
. Contact Precautions Poster. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au/
wp-content/uploads/2012/02/Approach-3-Contact-Precautions-Photo-PDF-685KB.pdf>.
53 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC)
(2012b). Contact Precautions Poster. Sydney: ACSQHC. Retrieved from
<www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Droplet: transmission and precautions
Droplet transmission can occur when the hands of health
care workers are contaminated with respiratory droplets
which are transferred to susceptible mucosal surfaces. This
53


type of transfer occurs commonly when respiratory droplets
are expelled by coughing, sneezing or talking. These
pathogen-infected droplets can directly or indirectly come into
contact with someone else’s eyes, nose or mouth. See
Figure 32.10
 for guidelines on droplet precautions.
Figure 32.10


Droplet precautions poster (national standardised infection
control and prevention signs).
Source: ACSQHC
. Droplet Precautions Poster. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au/
sites/default/files/migrated/Approach-1-Droplet-Standard-Precautions-Photo-PDF-790KB.pdf>.
54 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC)
(2012c). Droplet Precautions Poster. Retrieved from
<www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Air-borne precautions
Air-borne transmission occurs when droplet nuclei or small
particles containing infectious agents remain suspended in
the air for a period of time and are inhaled. Lee and Bishop
(2016) suggest that knowledge and implementation of air-
borne precautions is particularly critical, demonstrated by the
fact that in the 2003 worldwide outbreak of SARS, 20% of all
people infected were health care workers. See Figure
32.11
 for guidelines on air-borne precautions.
Figure 32.11
54


Air-borne precautions poster (national standardised infection
control and prevention signs).
Source: ACSQHC
. Air-borne Precautions Poster. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au/
sites/default/files/migrated/Approach-1-Airborne-Standard-Precautions-photo-PDF-519KB.pdf>.
55 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC)
(2012d). Air-borne Precautions Poster. Sydney: ACSQHC. Retrieved from
<www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Lee and Bishop (2016) summarised the various precautions simply
in the following diagram (see Figure 32.12
).
Figure 32.12
55


Standard precautions and transmission-based precautions.
Source: G. Lee & P. Bishop (2016). Microbiology and Infection Control for Health Professionals (6th ed.). Frenchs
Forest, NSW: Pearson, Figure 13.16, p. 349.
Transmission-based precautions are generally a nursing
responsibility based on a comprehensive assessment of the
individual or from information obtained via pathology results.
Assessment should also take into account the person’s possible
susceptibility. Nurses should initiate necessary precautions and,
where possible, identify the mode of transmission of the infectious
agent. Nurses are guided by the institution’s guidelines on
transmission-based precautions and PPE required to be worn.
Irrespective of what care an individual requires, nurses must adhere


to the 5 moments of hand hygiene with particular attention to before
and after care.
Transporting individuals with
infections
Transporting individuals with infections outside their rooms should be
avoided unless absolutely necessary. If a person must be moved,
nurses should implement appropriate precautions and measures to
prevent contamination of the environment. For example, ensure any
draining wound is securely covered or place a surgical mask on the
person with an air-borne infection. In addition, notify the appropriate
staff receiving the person of any infection risk so they can maintain
necessary precautions. Organisation policy should be followed.
Psychosocial needs of individuals
requiring isolation precautions
Individuals requiring isolation precautions can develop problems
associated with separation from others. Two common issues include
sensory deprivation and decreased self-esteem. Sensory deprivation
occurs when the environment lacks normal stimuli for the individual;
for example, communication with others. Nurses must be alert to


common clinical manifestations of sensory deprivation: boredom,
inactivity, slowness of thought, daydreaming, increased sleeping,
thought disorganisation, anxiety, hallucinations and panic.
Chapter 40
 provides information on the development of self-
esteem and self-esteem disturbances. An individual’s feeling of
inferiority can be due to the perception of the infection itself or to the
required precautions. In Australia, many people place a high value
on cleanliness and the idea of being ‘soiled’, ‘contaminated’ or ‘dirty’
can give the person feelings they are at fault and substandard.
Although this is obviously not true, people with infections may feel
‘not as good’ as others and blame themselves.
Nurses need to provide care that prevents these two problems or
deals with them positively. Appropriate nursing interventions include:
use of appropriate level of precautions (i.e. no stricter than are
indicated by the diagnosis or the person’s condition)
explanation of the infection and the associated procedures to
help the person and their support people understand and accept
the situation
demonstration of warm, accepting behaviour; it is important not
to convey to the person any sense of annoyance about the
precautions or any feelings of revulsion about the infection
assessing the individual’s need for stimulation
initiation of measures to help meet the need, including regular
communication with the person and diversionary activities, such
as toys for a child and books, television or radio for an adult;


providing a variety of foods to stimulate the person’s sense of
taste; stimulating the individual’s visual sense by providing a view
or an activity to watch.


Health-care-associated infections
Health-care-associated infections (HAIs)
 are classified as
infections associated with the delivery of services in a health care
facility. HAIs can either develop during an individual’s admission in a
facility or manifest after discharge. HAIs may also be acquired by
health personnel working in the facility and can cause significant
illness and time lost from work.
All health care professionals are directly involved in providing a
biologically safe environment in the clinical or community setting.
Despite the widespread use of standard precautions, aseptic
techniques and educational programs (e.g. hand hygiene), infections
remain a major health problem within clinical settings and in the
community. Institutions, managers and personnel involved in the
prevention, monitoring and control of infection heavily promote these
concepts. It is for this reason that some may argue that part of the
reason compliance to infection-control practices is not absolute is
potentially because the message needs repackaging. Perhaps the
message should not be one of ‘Would you please wash your hands?’
but rather one of ‘Would you please not transmit disease?’ (Kurtz ).
In the light of immense research and activities to increase
compliance, with yet no clearly all-encompassing success, there
may be merit in the concept that attention to the message rather
than isolated focus on a specific task may be beneficial in improving
infection-control practice.
56


56 Kurtz, S. (2016). Are we sending the wrong message when we ask health care workers to
wash their hands? American Journal of Infection Control, 44(10), 1184–1186. Doi:
http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.ajic.2016.01.030.
Infections are more easily acquired in hospital for all the reasons
previously discussed related to factors increasing an ill person’s
susceptibility to infection. Many HAIs are also transferred to the
community because of early discharge and the administration of
treatments in the home. Conversely, residents from aged care units
often bring infections into acute care facilities when they are
admitted. The number of older adults living in residential aged care
facilities is expected to increase substantially as Australia’s
population increases (AIHW 2018a). Residents of aged care facilities
are at increased risk of community-acquired infections and HAIs as
they have close contact with potentially infected or colonised
residents and staff.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: Preventing and controlling
healthcare-associated infection
The intention of this standard is to ‘reduce the risk of patients
acquiring preventable healthcare-associated infections,
effectively manage infections if they occur, and limit the
development of antimicrobial resistance through prudent use
of antimicrobials as part of antimicrobial stewardship’
(ACSQHC 2017, p. 21).


Implementing this standard is achieved by
improving governance and developing enhanced
systems for the prevention and control of HAIs.
Some considerations include promoting
personal, staff and environmental hygiene and
adherence to best practice standards when
reprocessing a device or equipment which has
previously come into contact with another
person. Another critical factor in improving these
standards involves education and development
of ever-advancing protocols for the
management of antibiotics drugs under the
antimicrobial stewardship program.
All interactions with individuals pose a risk for
the transmission of pathogens. Of particular
importance is the control of HAIs. When a
health care consumer permits us to assist them
with their condition, many most likely accept that
the treatment may entail some discomfort or
unpleasant experience as part of the process.
However, as health care professionals, we must
embrace non-maleficence. So failing in our
responsibility to protect the individual from HAIs
is deficiency over which we should most avidly
fight.


The ACSQHC has identified 16 indicators of safety and quality in
health care and has produced a list of hospital-acquired
complications, including a section on HAIs. This list includes:
urinary tract infection
surgical site infection
pneumonia
bloodstream infection
central line and peripheral line associated bloodstream infection
multidrug-resistant organisms
infection associated with prosthetics/implantable devices
gastrointestinal infections
(ACSQHC 2018a).
Post-procedure infection
Australia is moving towards developing a comprehensive national
HAI surveillance program, some HAI data is being tracked. An
example of this is the data collection related to individuals who
developed an infection following a procedure. Figure 32.13
demonstrates comparisons between state and territory post-
procedural infection rates in Australian public hospitals across a
couple of years.

green).

Many individual institutions undertake their own HAI surveillance
programs; however, a coordinated national approach is necessary to
achieve significant reductions in HAIs because without true
quantification and understanding of the problem, significant methods
to address it will fail.
There are a number of HAIs of particular interest. Discussion of
some of these follows.
57
58


Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia
(SAB)
In Australia, since 2009 hospitals have been required to record and
report all SAB infections. In 2017–18, 1493 cases of SAB were
reported in public hospitals, resulting in a national average rate of
0.73 cases per 10 000 days of patient care. The agreed national
benchmark for this particular HAI is no more than 2.0 per 10 000
(AIHW 2017). The percentage of pathogens remaining methicillin
sensitive has continued to be stable at approximately 82% (AIHW
).
This has occurred as a result of the ACSQHC nominating HAIs as a
priority area, and through local and national initiatives such as focus
on hand hygiene; standardisation of infection-control guidelines for
prevention, surveillance and management of SAB; and through a
new Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard to help guide
antibiotic usage.
59 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018b). Staphylococcus aureus
Bacteraemia in Australian Public Hospitals 2016–17: Australian Hospital Statistics. Health
services series no. 83. Cat. no. HSE 198. Canberra: AIHW. Retrieved from
<www.aihw.gov.au>.
There has been a reduction of almost 200 cases since 2013 and,
given that the mortality rate for people with health-care-associated
Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections is approximately
35%, even small reductions mean less people will die from HAIs.
59


Health-care-associated pneumonia
(HCAP)
Pneumonia is often divided into hospital-acquired (nosocomial or
health-care-associated (HCAP)) and community-acquired
pneumonia (CAP). Two types of health-care-associated pneumonia
(HCAP) are hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) and ventilator-
associated pneumonia (VAP). HAPs are not associated with
mechanical ventilation whereas VAP occurs in individuals who
are/were mechanically ventilated (Wu et al.
). In Australia, 17 854
hospital-associated pneumonias were recorded in public hospitals in
2015–16 (ACSQHC 2018a). An unknown percentage of these
people will have developed the pneumonia as a result of the
iatrogenic complication of ventilator use.
60 Wu, D., Wu, C., Zhang, S. & Zhong, Y. (2019). Risk factors of ventilator-associated
pneumonia in critically ill patients. Frontiers in Pharmacology, 10(May), 482. Doi:
10.3389/fphar.2019.00482. Retrieved from <www.frontiersin.org>.
Clostridium difficile infection (CDI)
Another HAI meriting discussion is Clostridium difficile infection
(CDI). C. difficile are bacteria which commonly occur as a
complication of taking antibiotics (for a different infection). Antibiotics
can kill normal gut flora which permits the C. difficile to become
pathogenic and cause an opportunistic infection. The C. difficile
bacteria produce a toxin which is the cause of diarrhoea. C. difficile
can be difficult to kill because it produces pathogenic spores which
60


are unaffected by ABHRs and can remain in the environment for
months to years.
In 2016, Australian public hospitals reported an incidence of
infections of 4.0 per 10 000 bed days, down from a peak in 2012,
where the C. difficile infection rate was 5.0 per 10 000 bed days
(ACSQHC ;
). However, it must be noted that there is a significant
difference in C. difficile infection rates between the states. The
Australian Capital Territory has the highest rate of 6.96 per 10 000;
the Northern Territory has the lowest rate at 0.66 per 10 000
(ACSQHC 2018c). The ACSQHC has established a national
surveillance protocol which will hopefully result in improved tracking,
management and prevention strategies for this potentially life-
threatening HAI (ACSQHC ).

Clostridium difficile Infection: Monitoring the National Burden of Clostridium difficile. Sydney:
ACSQHC. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
62 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2018c).
Clostridium difficile Infection: A Model to Improve the Management and Control of Clostridium
difficile in Australia. Sydney: ACSQHC. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
63 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2018d).
Healthcare Associated Infections. Sydney: ACSQHC. Retrieved
from<www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Transfusion-transmissible infection
61 62
63


Although Australia’s blood supply is among the safest in the world,
there remains a small risk of transfusion-transmissible viral infection.
The chance of receiving HIV, hepatitis C or C virus, human T-
lymphotropic virus or syphilis from a blood transfusion is less than 1
in 1 000 000 units of blood (Khawar et al.
). A part of the reason
the blood is now safer than previously is the pre-donation screening
(via survey) that was undertaken. There is, however, a ‘window
period’ where testing cannot detect some transfusion-transmissible
infections. This accounts for this slight risk which remains an
unpreventable prospect when receiving donated blood. Although the
blood testing cannot detect the window period infections, the pre-
donation survey can be attributed for detecting risk factors which
may increase the likelihood of exposure to blood-borne infections.
There were no HIV, HCV, human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV) or
syphilis transfusion-transmitted infections reported in Australia
between 2008 and 2017 (Khawar et al. 2018).
64 Khawar, L., Seed, C., McGregor, S., Hoad, V. & Guy, R. (2018). Transfusion-transmissible
Infections in Australia: 2018 Surveillance Report. The Kirby Institute, The UNSW and
Australian Red Cross Blood Service. Retrieved from <https://kirby.unsw.edu.au>.
Bacterial contamination of blood components forms the more likely
risk to blood product recipients. The risk of developing a clinically
apparent reaction as a result of receiving a blood product
contaminated by bacteria is approximately 1 in 500 000 when
receiving red blood cells. The risks associated with platelets are
higher at 1 in 75 000 (Khawar et al. 2018). This variation exists
because platelets are stored at room temperature, whereas red
blood cells are refrigerated and plasma is frozen.
64


Finally, the risk of contracting the protozoan disease malaria by
receiving a blood product is extremely low. The Australian Red Cross
Blood Service screens for malaria and tests donated blood for
antibodies, and only approximately 1.3% of donated blood contains
antibodies. None of these donors had detectable malaria DNA,
which suggests that they have had a past infection (Khawar et al.
2018).
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: blood management
The intention of this standard is to guarantee that ‘risks are
identified and strategies are in place to ensure that a patient’s
own blood is optimised and conserved, and that any blood and
blood products the patient receives are appropriate and safe’
(ACSQHC 2017, p. 56).
Implementing this standard is achieved by the
establishment of systems to ensure safe and
appropriate prescription and administration of
blood and blood products. Systems include
processes facilitating accurate documentation,
storage, transport, use and disposal. Effective
communication regarding risks, benefits and use
should exist across all individuals involved in a
person’s care (including the person themself
and their significant others).


Some individuals may develop conditions that
require the administration of blood or blood
products in order to achieve better clinical
outcomes. As with any biological material,
various risks are involved in all facets of this
treatment. These risks include exposure to
pathogens from poorly stored, managed or
contaminated blood or from transmission of
blood-borne infections as a result of blood
administration. Efficient and appropriate
systems are imperative to ensure the safety of
not only the person receiving the product, but
also any other individual involved in their care.
Antimicrobial resistance
The evolution of micro-organisms that are becoming resistant to
antimicrobial drugs has largely occurred as a result of unrestrained
use. Now, we are facing a time reminiscent of pre-antibiotic history
where for some infections, treatment options are slipping away.

 briefly illustrates the discovery and loss (from
resistance) of selected antibiotics across our recent history.
