Vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE)
Enterococci are a species of bacteria which are naturally resistant to
many antimicrobial classes. Enterococci are opportunistic
start of bar = discovery
End of bar = first reported resistance
65
66
67


pathogens. They are most commonly associated with intra-
abdominal and urinary tract infections (ACSQHC ).
68 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2019). AURA
2019: Third Australian Report on Antimicrobial Use and Resistance in Human Health. Sydney:
ACSQHC. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
There are more than 17 species of enterococci; however, few of
them are pathogenic to humans. The two most commonly cultured
are Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium; of these two,
E. faecium has significantly higher rates of resistance to the
antibiotic vancomycin (ACSQHC 2019). Unfortunately, Australia has
one of the highest rates of VRE in the world. Resistance rates differ
significantly between states (see Table 32.12
).
Table 32.12 Rates of vancomycin resistance across states and
territories (2014)
Source: Adapted from ACSQHC (2019). AURA 2019: Third Australian Report on Antimicrobial Use and
Resistance in Human Health. Sydney: ACSQHC. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au/sites/default/
files/2019-06/AURA-2019-Report.pdf>.
Clinically, when individuals have VRE (either colonised or active
infection), the Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control
of Infection in Healthcare recommend transmission-based
precautions including isolation in a single patient room, or at least
with another person with the same strain (NHMRC 2019). See Box
32.2
 earlier for other transmission-based precaution
requirements. As with all multidrug-resistant organisms, good
68


antibiotic stewardship is also critical to help reduce the spread of
VRE.
Other drug resistance being monitored
Various pathogens demonstrate different levels of resistance
between states and even between institutions. The Antimicrobial Use
and Resistance in Australia (AURA) project, along with many other
organisations and groups, assists the ACSQHC to monitor and
report on resistance rates of selected pathogens (see Table
32.13
).
Table 32.13 Summary of antimicrobial resistance rates for
selected high-priority pathogens
Source: Adapted from ACSQHC (2019). AURA 2019: Third Australian Report on Antimicrobial Use and
Resistance in Human Health. Sydney: ACSQHC. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au/sites/default/
files/2019-06/AURA-2019-Report.pdf>.
Preventing HAIs
Many HAIs can be prevented by using proper hand hygiene
techniques and environmental controls and implementing standard
and transmission-based precautions and ANTT  when warranted.
Other considerations include identification and management of
individuals at risk of infection, antibiotic stewardship, monitoring
incidence and managing outbreaks.
®


Nursing management
Assessing
During the assessing phase of the nursing process, the nurse
obtains the person’s history, conducts the physical assessment and
gathers laboratory data.
Health history
During a health history, nurses assess (a) the degree to which an
individual is at risk of developing an infection, and (b) any reports
from the person suggesting the presence of an infection. To identify
individuals at risk, nurses review the individual’s chart and structure
the nursing interview to collect data regarding factors influencing the
development of infection, especially existing disease process, history
of recurrent infections, current medications and therapeutic
measures, current emotional stressors, nutritional status and history
of immunisations and travel to remote areas of Australia or overseas
(see ‘Assessment interview
’).
Physical assessment
Clinical manifestations of an infection vary according to the body
area involved. For example, sneezing, watery or mucoid discharge


from the nose and nasal stuffiness commonly occur with an infection
of the nose and sinuses; urinary frequency and possible cloudy or
discoloured urine often occur with a urinary infection. Commonly the
skin and mucous membranes are involved in a local infectious
process, resulting in the following:
localised swelling
localised redness
pain or tenderness with palpation or movement
palpable heat at the infected area
loss of function of the body part affected, depending on the site
and extent of involvement.
In addition, open wounds may exude drainage of various colours.
Clinical manifestations of systemic infection include the following:
fever
increased pulse and respiratory rate if the fever is high
malaise and loss of energy
anorexia and, in some situations, nausea and vomiting
enlargement and tenderness of lymph nodes draining the area of
infection.
Assessment interview
For individual at risk of infection


When were you last immunised for diphtheria, tetanus,
poliomyelitis, rubella, measles, influenza, hepatitis and
pneumococcal pneumonia?
When did you last have a tuberculin skin test?
What infections have you had in the past and how were
these treated?
Have any of these infections recurred?
Are you taking any antibiotics, anti-inflammatory
medications such as aspirin or ibuprofen, or medications
for cancer?
Have you had any recent diagnostic procedure or therapy
which penetrated your skin or a body cavity?
What past surgeries have you had?
How would you describe your eating habits? Do you eat a
variety of different types of foods?
Do you take vitamins, nutritional supplements or herbal
medications?
On a scale of 1 to 10, how would you rate the stress you
have experienced in the past 6 months?
Have you experienced any loss of energy, loss of appetite,
nausea, headache or other signs associated with specific
body systems (e.g. difficulty urinating, urinary frequency
or a sore throat)?
Have you travelled to remote areas of Australia or
overseas? When?
Note: as with all history taking, nurses must individualise the
specific terms used, examples given to the person and


teaching techniques used to validate agreement on the
meaning of words according to the individual’s culture,
language spoken and education or intellectual abilities.
Laboratory data
The use of laboratory data to indicate the presence of an infection
can include the following:
elevated leukocyte (white blood cell or WBC) count (4.5 to
 normal range)
increases in specific types of leukocytes as revealed in the
differential WBC count; specific types of white blood cells are
increased or decreased in certain infections. See Chapter 35
for normal values for the adult
elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR); red blood cells
normally settle slowly but the rate increases in the presence of
an inflammatory process.
urine, blood, sputum or other drainage cultures
 (laboratory
cultivations of micro-organisms in a special growth medium).
Diagnosing
When considering nursing diagnosis, it is necessary to reflect on
transmission of micro-organisms. What is the risk of infection? Why
11 × 106/mL


is the individual at increased risk of being invaded by pathogenic
micro-organisms.
Possible risk factors that should be identified include:
Inadequate primary defences such as broken skin, traumatised
tissue, decreased ciliary action, stasis of body fluids, change in
pH of secretions or altered peristalsis
Inadequate secondary defences such as leukopenia,
immunosuppression, decreased haemoglobin or suppressed
inflammatory response.
Individuals who have or are at risk of an existing infection are prime
candidates for other physical and psychological problems. Difficulties
arising from the actual presence of an infection include the following:
Potential complication of infection: fever
Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements if the person
is too ill to eat adequately
Acute pain if the individual is experiencing tissue damage and
discomfort
Impaired social interaction or social isolation if the person is
required to be separated from others during a contagious
episode
Anxiety if the individual is apprehensive regarding changes in life
activities resulting from the infection or its treatment, such as
absence from work or inability to perform usual functions.


Planning
The major goals for a person susceptible to infection are to:
maintain or restore defences
avoid the spread of infectious organisms
reduce or alleviate problems associated with the infection.
Desired outcomes depend on the person’s condition. Nursing
strategies to meet the three broad goals generally include using
standard precautions, meticulous aseptic techniques to prevent the
spread of potentially infectious micro-organisms, implementing
measures to support the defences of a susceptible host and
advising the person and their family about protective measures to
prevent infections and the spread of infectious agents when an
infection is present.
Planning for home care
Individuals being discharged following hospital care for an infection
often require continued care to completely eliminate the infection or
to adapt to a chronic state. In addition, such people may be at
increased risk of reinfection or development of an opportunistic
infection following therapy for existing pathogens.
In preparation for discharge, nurses need to know the person and
family’s risks, needs, strengths and resources. The ‘Home care
considerations’ box describes the specific assessment data required


before establishing a discharge plan. Using the data gathered about
the home situation, nurses design a specific teaching plan for the
person and their family (see ‘Patient education’).
Implementing
Whenever possible, nurses implement strategies to prevent
infection. If infection cannot be prevented, nurses’ goal is to prevent
the spread of the infection within and between individuals, and to
treat the existing infection.
Aseptic Fields
Skill 32.3
 describes how to establish and maintain an aseptic
field.
Sterile gloves
Sterile gloves may be donned by the open method or the closed
method. The open method is most frequently used outside the
operating room because the closed method requires the wearing of
a sterile gown. Gloves are worn during many procedures to maintain
the sterility of equipment and to protect an individual’s wound.
Sterile gloves are packaged with a cuff of about 5 cm and palms
facing upward when the package is opened. The package usually


indicates the size of the glove (e.g. size 6 or
).
Home care considerations
Infection
Person and environment
Self-care abilities for wound care: understanding
of rationale of wound care as well as wound care
technique; ability to gather and use supplies for
clean or aseptic technique to change dressings or
care for wounds.
Self-care abilities for hygiene and toileting:
understanding of rationale of hygiene in the home
setting; ability to contain potentially infectious
material, such as that from coughing or sneezing
and body fluids (urine, stool, drainage); ability to
cleanse hands and implement any required
isolation practices.
Self-care abilities for medication
administration: understanding of medication
therapy, expected outcomes and potential side
effects; physical dexterity to take medications and
store medications safely.
7½


Facilities: presence of running water, garbage
containers and disposal, bathroom to facilitate
wound care and contain potentially infectious
materials.
Family
Caregiver availability, skills and responses:
understanding of rationale of wound care as well as
wound care technique; ability to assist with wound
care, medication administration and shopping if the
person has restricted activity; ability to comprehend
infection-control activities without excessive
personal anxiety.
Other susceptible cohabitants: presence and
immunisation status of children, older adults or
others who may be at risk of infection from the
individual.
Community
Resources: availability of and familiarity with
possible sources of assistance for finances,
supplies and home health aid (such as public health
department and community nurses).
Patient education


Infection control
Environmental management
Explore ways to control the environmental temperature
and airflow (especially if the person has an air-borne
pathogen).
Determine the advisability of visitors and family members
in proximity to the person.
Describe ways to manipulate the bed, the room and other
household facilities to prevent additional injury or to
contain possible cross-contamination.
Discuss with the person and their family options available
to clean obviously soiled linen separately from other
laundry. Rinse in cold water, wash in hot water if possible
and add bleach or disinfectant as per the manufacturer’s
safety instructions.
Infection control
Based on assessment of the individual and their family
knowledge, advise on correct hand hygiene (e.g. before
handling foods, before eating, after toileting, before and
after any required home care treatment and after touching
any body substances such as wound drainage) and
related hygiene measures for all family members.


Promote nail care: keep fingernails short, clean and well
manicured to eliminate rough edges or hangnails, which
can harbour micro-organisms.
Discuss with the person and their close family the reasons
for not sharing personal care items such as hairbrushes
and toothbrushes or washing cloths and towels. Provide
the rationale of how infections can be transmitted from
shared personal items.
Discuss the appropriate use of antimicrobial soaps and
effective disinfectants.
Ensure access to and correct use of gloves and other
barriers as indicated by the type of infection or risk.
Discuss the relationship between hygiene, rest, activity
and nutrition in the chain of infection.
Describe the best practice for cleaning reusable
equipment and supplies. Use soap and water and disinfect
with a chlorine bleach solution.
Wound care
Describe to the individual and family the process of wound
healing and the clinical manifestations of wound infection
and why monitoring of the wound is important.
Explain factors promoting wound healing.
Demonstrate the correct technique for changing the
dressing and disposing of the soiled one. Reinforce the
need to place contaminated dressings and other


disposable items containing body fluids in moisture-proof
plastic bags.
Advise the individual and family members to use
appropriate sharps containers and disposal through a
local chemist.
Ask the individual or family questions relating to
instructions. Clarify any points on which they are
uncertain. Ask the person or their family (as appropriate)
to demonstrate skills required to perform as part of care.
Referrals
Provide appropriate information regarding how to access
community resources, home care organisations, sources
of supplies and state and national government
departments as well as local councils for immunisation
information and services.
Home care considerations
Sterile field
Explain to the person and family members the
principles and rationale underlying the use of a
sterile field.


Clean and wipe dry a flat surface for the sterile
field.
Keep pets and non-involved small children out of
the area when setting up for and performing sterile
procedures.
Dispose of all soiled materials in a waterproof bag.
Check with the organisation as to how to dispose of
medical refuse.
Remove all instruments from the home or other
setting where others might accidentally find them.
New or used instruments can be sharp or capable
of causing injury. Used instruments may transmit
infection. Check with the organisation for
instructions on cleansing of reusable supplies and
disposal of single-use instruments.
Latex and latex-free (e.g. nitrile and vinyl) sterile gloves are available
to protect nurses from contact with blood and body fluids. Latex and
nitrile are more flexible than vinyl, mould to the wearer’s hands,
allow freedom of movement and have the added feature of resealing
tiny punctures automatically. Therefore, wear latex or nitrile gloves
when performing tasks (a) demanding flexibility, (b) placing stress on
the material (e.g. turning stopcocks, handling sharp instruments or
tape) and (c) involving a high risk of exposure to pathogens. Vinyl
gloves should be chosen for tasks unlikely to stress the glove


material, requiring minimal precision and with minimal risk of
exposure to pathogens.
Skill 32.4
 describes how to don and remove sterile gloves by the
open method.
Sterile gowns
Sterile gowning and closed gloving are chiefly carried out in
operating or delivery rooms, where surgical asepsis is necessary.
The closed method of gloving can be used only when a sterile gown
is worn because the gloves are handled through the sleeves of the
gown. Before these procedures, the nurse dons a hair cover and a
mask and performs a surgical hand wash.
Skill 32.5
 describes the steps in donning a sterile gown and
sterile gloves by the closed method.


SKILL
32.3 Establishing and
maintaining a critical aseptic
field
Purposes
To ensure asepsis.
Assessment
Review the person’s record or discuss with the
individual or other health care team member exactly
what procedure will be performed requiring a sterile
field. Determine the person’s presence or risk of
infection and ability to cooperate with the procedure.
Planning
Determine, if possible, which supplies and
techniques have been used previously to perform
the procedures for this person. Also, attempt to


determine if the procedure will be performed
again in the future, so the person has
appropriate teaching and adequate supplies will
be available.
Schedule the procedure at a time consistent with
the order, the need for the procedure and the
person’s other activities.
These procedures should not be carried out
when tasks such as bed making are taking place
due to the risk of micro-organisms being
dispersed into the air and potentially
contaminating sterile equipment or a wound.
Delegation
Procedures requiring aseptic technique are not
delegated to Assistants in Nursing (AINs) in most
states.
Equipment
Package containing a sterile drape
Sterile equipment as needed (e.g. wrapped
sterile lint-free gauze, wrapped sterile bowl,
antiseptic solution, sterile forceps)
Implementation
Preparation


Ensure the package is clean and dry; if moisture
is noted on the inside of a plastic-wrapped
package or the outside of a cloth-wrapped
package, it is considered contaminated and must
be discarded.
Check the sterilisation expiration dates on the
package and look for any indications that it has
been previously opened. Spots or stains on cloth
or paper-wrapped objects may indicate
contamination and the objects should not be
used.
Follow organisation practice for disposal of
possibly contaminated packages.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can assist. Discuss how the
results will be used in planning further care or
treatments.
2. Observe other appropriate infection-control
procedures (see Skills 32.1
 and 32.2
).
3. Provide for the person’s privacy.
4. Open the package. If the package is inside a
plastic cover, remove the cover.
To open a wrapped package on a surface


Place the package in the work area so
that the top flap of the wrapper opens
away from you.
Reaching around the package (not over
it), pinch the first flap on the outside of the
wrapper between the thumb and index
finger. 1 Rationale: touching only the
outside of the wrapper maintains the
sterility of the inside of the wrapper. Pull
the flap open, laying it flat on the far
surface.


1 Opening the first flap of a sterile
wrapped package
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Repeat for the side flaps, opening the top
one first. Use the right hand for the right
flap and the left hand for the left flap. 2
Rationale: by using both hands, you
avoid reaching over the sterile contents.


2 Opening the second flap to the side
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Pull the third flap towards you by grasping
the corner that is turned down. 3 Make
sure that the flap does not touch any
object. Rationale: if the inner surface
touches any unsterile article, it is
contaminated.


3 Pulling the last flap towards oneself by
grasping the corner
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Variation: opening a wrapped package
while holding it
Hold the package in one hand with the top
flap opening away from you.
Using the other hand, open the package
as described above, pulling the corners of
the flaps well back. 4 Tuck each of the
corners into the hand holding the package
so that they do not flutter and contaminate
sterile objects. Rationale: the hands are
considered contaminated and at no time
should they touch the contents of the
package.


4 Opening a wrapped package while
holding it
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Variation: opening commercially
prepared packages
If the flap of the package has an unsealed
corner, hold the container in one hand and
pull back on the flap with the other hand. 5


5 Opening a sterile package with an
unsealed corner


If the package has a partially sealed edge,
grasp both sides of the edge, one with
each hand and pull apart gently. 6


6 Opening a sterile package with a
partially sealed edge
5. Establish a critical aseptic field by using a
drape.
Open the package containing the drape as
described above.
With one hand, pluck the corner of the
drape that is folded back on the top,
touching only one side of the drape.
Lift the drape out of the cover and allow it
to open freely without touching any
articles. 7 Rationale: if the drape touches
the outside of the package or any
unsterile surface, it is considered
contaminated.


7 Allowing a drape to open freely without
touching any objects
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
With the other hand, carefully pick up
another corner of the drape, holding it well
away from you and, again, touching only
the same side of the drape as the first
hand.
Lay the drape on a clean and dry surface,
placing the bottom (i.e. the freely hanging
side) furthest from you. 8 Rationale: by
placing the lowermost side furthest away,
you avoid leaning over the critical aseptic
field and contaminating it.


8 Placing a drape on a surface
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
6. Add necessary sterile supplies, being careful
not to touch the drape with the hands.
To add wrapped supplies to a critical
aseptic field
Open each wrapped package as
described in the preceding steps.
With the free hand, grasp the corners of
the wrapper and hold them against the
wrist of the other hand. 9 Rationale: the
sterile wrapper now covers the unsterile
hand.


9 Adding wrapped sterile supplies to a
critical aseptic field
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Place the sterile bowl, drape or other
supply on the critical aseptic field by
approaching from an angle rather than
holding the arm over the field.
Discard the wrapper.
Variation: adding commercially
packaged supplies to a critical aseptic
field
Open each package as previously
described.
Hold the package 15 cm above the field
and allow the contents to drop on the field.
10 Keep in mind that 2.5 cm around the
edge of the field is considered
contaminated. Rationale: at a height of
15 cm, the outside of the package is not
likely to touch and contaminate the sterile
field.


10 Adding commercially packaged gauze
to a sterile field
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Adding solution to a sterile bowl
7. Liquids (e.g. normal saline) may need to be
poured into containers within a critical aseptic
field. Unwrapped bottles containing sterile
solution are considered sterile on the inside
and contaminated on the outside because the
bottle may have been handled. Bottles used
in an operating room may be sterilised on the
outside as well as the inside, however, and
these are handled with sterile gloves.
Before pouring any liquid, read the label
three times to make sure you have the
correct solution and concentration
(strength). Wipe the outside of the bottle
with a damp towel to remove any large
particles that could fall into the bowl or
field.
Obtain the exact amount of solution, if
possible. Rationale: once a sterile bottle
has been opened, its sterility cannot be
ensured for future use. Follow
organisation policy for reuse of opened
sterile solution bottles.


Remove the lid or cap from the bottle and
invert the lid before placing it on a surface
that is not part of the critical aseptic field.
Rationale: inverting the lid maintains the
sterility of the inside surface because it is
not allowed to touch an unsterile surface.
Hold the bottle at a slight angle ensuring
the label is uppermost. Rationale: any
solution flowing down the outside of the
bottle during pouring will not damage or
obliterate the label.


Adding a liquid to a sterile bowl
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Hold the bottle of fluid at a height of 10 to
15 cm over the bowl and to the side of the
field so as little of the bottle as possible is
over the field. Rationale: at this height,
there is less likelihood of contaminating
the sterile field by touching the field or by
reaching an arm over it.
Pour the solution gently to avoid splashing
the liquid. Rationale: if a barrier drape
(one with a water-resistant layer) is not
used and the drape is on a non-aseptic
surface, moisture contaminates the field
by wicking micro-organisms through the
drape.
Tilt the neck of the bottle back to vertical
quickly when finished pouring so that none
of the liquid flows down the outside of the
bottle. Rationale: such drips would
contaminate the field if the outside of the
bottle is not sterile.
If the bottle will be used again, replace the
lid securely and write on the label the date
and time of opening. Rationale: replacing
the lid immediately maintains the sterility


of the inner aspect of the lid and the
solution.
Depending on organisation policy, a sterile
container of solution that is opened might
be used only once and is then discarded
(such as in the operating room). In other
settings, policy may permit recapped
bottles to be reused within 24 hours.
8. Use sterile forceps to handle sterile supplies.
Forceps are usually used to move a sterile
article from one place to another; for
example, transferring sterile gauze from its
package to a sterile dressing tray. Forceps
may be disposable or resterilised after use.
Commonly used forceps include haemostats
and tissue forceps.


Haemostats. Left: straight; Right: curved
Source: Alexandra Truitt & Terry Marshall.


Tissue forceps. Left: plain; Right: toothed
Source: Alexandra Truitt & Terry Marshall.
If forceps tips are wet, keep the tips lower
than the wrist at all times, unless you are
wearing sterile gloves. Rationale: gravity
prevents liquids on the tips of the forceps
from flowing to the unsterile handles and
later back to the tips.


Holding forceps with an ungloved hand,
keeping the tips lower than the wrist
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Hold sterile forceps above waist or table
level, whichever is higher. Rationale:
items held below waist or table level are
considered contaminated.
Hold sterile forceps within sight.
Rationale: while out of sight, forceps may,
unknown to the user, become unsterile.
Any forceps that go out of sight should be
considered unsterile.
When using forceps to lift sterile supplies,
be sure that the forceps do not touch the
edges or outside of the wrapper.
Rationale: the edges and outside of the
sterile field are considered unsterile.
When placing forceps whose handles
were in contact with the bare hand,
position the handles outside the sterile
area. Rationale: the handles of these
forceps harbour micro-organisms from the
bare hand.
Deposit a sterile item on a critical aseptic
field without permitting moist forceps to
touch the field when the surface under the


absorbent field is unsterile and a barrier
drape is not used.
Evaluation
Conduct any follow-up indicated during your care of
the individual. Ensure there are adequate numbers
and types of sterile supplies available for the next
health care provider.


SKILL
32.4 Donning and removing
sterile gloves (open method)
Purposes
To enable the nurse to handle or touch sterile
objects freely without contaminating them.
To prevent transmission of potentially infective
organisms from the nurse’s hands to individuals
at high risk of infection.
Assessment
Review the person’s record and orders to determine
exactly what procedure will be performed that
requires sterile gloves. Check the person’s record
and ask about latex allergies. Use non-latex gloves
whenever possible.
Planning


Think through the procedure, planning which steps
need to be completed before the gloves can be
applied. Determine what additional supplies are
needed to perform the procedure for this person.
Always have an extra pair of sterile gloves available.
Delegation
Procedures requiring aseptic technique are not
delegated to AINs in most states.
Equipment
Packages of sterile gloves
Implementation
Preparation
Ensure the sterility of the package of gloves.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can cooperate. Discuss how
the results will be used in planning further
care or treatments.
2. Observe other appropriate infection-control
procedures (see Skills 32.1
, 32.2 and


32.3
).
3. Provide privacy for the person.
4. Open the package of sterile gloves.
Place the package of gloves on a clean,
dry surface. Rationale: any moisture on
the surface contaminates the gloves.
Some gloves are packed in an inner as
well as an outer package. Open the outer
package without contaminating the gloves
or the inner package. See Skill 32.3
.
Remove the inner package from the outer
package.
Open the inner package as in step 4 of
Skill 32.3
 or according to the
manufacturer’s directions. Some
manufacturers provide a numbered
sequence for opening the flaps and folded
tabs to grasp for opening the flaps. If no
tabs are provided, pluck the flap so that
the fingers do not touch the inner
surfaces. Rationale: the inner surfaces,
which are next to the sterile gloves, will
remain sterile.
5. Put the first glove on the dominant hand.
If the gloves are packaged so that they lie
side by side, grasp the glove for the
dominant hand by its folded cuff edge (on


the palmar side) with the thumb and first
finger of the non-dominant hand. Touch
only the inside of the cuff. 1 Rationale:
the hands are not sterile. By touching only
the inside of the glove, the nurse avoids
contaminating the outside.
or


1 Picking up the first sterile glove
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
If the gloves are packaged one on top of
the other, grasp the cuff of the top glove
as above, using the opposite hand.
Insert the dominant hand into the glove
and pull the glove on. Keep the thumb of
the inserted hand against the palm of the
hand during insertion. 2 Rationale: if the
thumb is kept against the palm, it is less
likely to contaminate the outside of the
glove.


2 Putting on the first sterile glove
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
6. Put the second glove on the non-dominant
hand.


Leave the cuff in place once the unsterile
hand releases the glove. Rationale:
attempting to further unfold the cuff is
likely to contaminate the glove.
Pick up the other glove with the sterile
gloved hand, inserting the gloved fingers
under the cuff and holding the gloved
thumb close to the gloved palm. 3
Rationale: this helps prevent accidental
contamination of the glove by the bare
hand.


3 Picking up the second sterile glove
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Pull on the second glove carefully. Hold
the thumb of the gloved first hand as far
as possible from the palm. 4 Rationale: in
this position, the thumb is less likely to
touch the arm and become contaminated.


4 Putting on the second sterile glove
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Adjust each glove so it fits smoothly and
carefully pull the cuffs up by sliding the
fingers under the cuffs.
7. Remove and dispose of used gloves.
There is no difference in the removal of
sterile gloves to removing unsterile gloves.
If they are soiled with secretions, remove
them by turning them inside out. See
removal of disposable gloves in Skill
32.2
 on pages 689–690.
Document that sterile technique was used
in the performance of the procedure.
Evaluation
Conduct any follow-up indicated during your care of
the person. Ensure there are adequate numbers
and types of sterile supplies available for the next
health care provider.


SKILL
32.5 Donning a sterile gown and
gloves (closed method)
Purposes
To enable the nurse to work close to a sterile
field and handle sterile objects freely.
To protect individuals from becoming
contaminated with micro-organisms on the
nurse’s hands, arms and clothing.
Assessment
Review the person’s record and orders to determine
exactly what procedure will be performed that
requires sterile gloves. Check the person’s record
and ask about latex allergies. Use non-latex gloves
whenever possible.
Planning


Think through the procedure, planning which steps
need to be completed before the gloves and gown
can be applied. Determine what additional supplies
are needed to perform the procedure for this
person. Always have an extra pair of sterile gloves
available.
Delegation
Procedures requiring surgical asepsis are not
delegated to Assistants in Nursing in most states.
Equipment
Sterile pack containing a sterile gown
Sterile gloves
Implementation
Preparation
Ensure the sterility of the package of gloves.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can assist. Discuss how the
results will be used in planning further care or
treatments.


2. Observe other appropriate infection-control
procedures (see Skills 32.1
, 32.2 and
32.3
).
3. Provide for the individual’s privacy.
Donning a sterile gown (closed method)
4. Open the package of sterile gloves.
Remove the outer wrap from the sterile
gloves and leave the gloves in their inner
sterile wrap on the critical aseptic field.
Rationale: if the inner wrapper is not
touched, it will remain sterile. See Skill
32.3
, step 4.
5. Unwrap the sterile gown pack.
6. Perform correct hand hygiene.
See ‘Variation’ at the end of Skills 32.1
and review organisation practice.
7. Put on the sterile gown.
Grasp the sterile gown at the crease near
the neck, hold it away from you and
permit it to unfold freely without touching
anything, including the uniform.
Rationale: the gown will be unsterile if its
outer surface touches any unsterile
objects.
Put the hands inside the shoulders of the
gown without touching the outside of the


gown. 1
1 Putting on a sterile gown


If donning sterile gloves by using the
closed method (see below), work the
hands down the sleeves only to the
beginning of the cuffs.
or
If donning sterile gloves by using the open
method, work the hands down the sleeves
and through the cuffs.
Have a co-worker grasp the neck ties
without touching the outside of the gown
and pull the gown upward to cover the
neckline of your uniform in front and back.
The co-worker ties the neck ties. Gowning
continues at step 11.
Donning sterile gloves (closed method)
8. Open the sterile glove wrapper while the
hands are still covered by the sleeves. 2


2 Opening the sterile glove wrapper
9. Put the glove on the non-dominant hand.
Figures 3 to 5 show a right-handed person.
With the dominant hand, pick up the
opposite glove with the thumb and index
finger, handling it through the sleeve.
Position the dominant hand palm upward
inside the sleeve. Lay the glove on the
opposite gown cuff, thumb side down, with
the glove opening pointed towards the
fingers. 3


3 Positioning the first sterile glove for the
non-dominant hand


4 Pulling on the first sterile glove


5 Extending the fingers into the second
glove of the dominant hand
Use the non-dominant hand to grasp the
cuff of the glove through the gown cuff


and firmly anchor it.
With the dominant hand working through
its sleeve, grasp the upper side of the
glove’s cuff and stretch it over the cuff of
the gown.
Pull the sleeve up to draw the cuff over
the wrist as you extend the fingers of the
non-dominant hand into the glove’s
fingers. 4
10. Put the glove on the dominant hand.
Place the fingers of the gloved hand under
the cuff of the remaining glove.
Place the glove over the cuff of the
second sleeve.
Extend the fingers into the glove as you
pull the glove up over the cuff. 5
Completion of gowning
11. Complete gowning as follows:
Have a co-worker hold the waist tie of
your gown, using sterile gloves or a sterile
forceps or drape. Rationale: this
approach keeps the ties sterile.
Make a three-quarter turn, then take the
tie and secure it in front of the gown.
or


Have a co-worker take the two ties at
each side of the gown and tie them at the
back of the gown, making sure that your
uniform is completely covered.
When worn, sterile gowns should be
considered sterile in front from the waist
to the shoulder. Once the nurse
approaches a table, the gown is
considered contaminated from the waist
or table down: whichever is higher. The
sleeves should be considered sterile from
the cuff to 5 cm above the elbow, since
the arms of a scrubbed person must
move across a sterile field. Moisture
collection and friction areas such as the
neckline, shoulders, underarms, back and
sleeve cuffs should be considered
unsterile.
12. Remove and dispose of used gown and
gloves.
If soiled, remove the attire by turning it
inside out. See removal of disposable
gowns and gloves in Skill 32.2
 for the
sequence of when to remove the gown.
13. If appropriate, document that surgical aseptic
technique was used in the performance of the


procedure.
Evaluation
Conduct any follow-up indicated during your care of
the person. Ensure there are adequate numbers
and types of sterile supplies available for the next
health care provider.


Infection control for health care
workers
Two issues need to be considered in relation to health care workers
and blood-borne infections. First, the worker experiences risks
associated with exposure to potentially contaminated sharps.
Secondly, the infection status of the health care worker needs to be
considered in relation to potential transmission risks of an infectious
condition the worker may have.
The Royal Australian College of Surgeons in 1998 recommended
that sharp instruments not be passed by hand between health care
workers and specified puncture-resistant sharps trays be used to
transfer and/or store all sharp items. Also, using needleless
intravenous systems and blunt needles for drawing up sterile
solutions from ampoules are also recommended.
It has been estimated that 11.2 % of nurses sustain needle- stick
injuries per year (Joseph & Melder
). It has been reported that the
introduction of safety engineered medical devices, along with training
in their use, reduces the risk of needle-stick injury by 69% (Joseph &
Melder 2017). However, despite potential financial and personal
savings, there are many considerations regarding their universal use
in Australia’s health systems.
69


69 Joseph, C. & Melder, A. (2017). Safety Engineered Injection Devices for Intravenous Use
in Healthcare Delivery Settings: A Rapid Review. Centre for Clinical Effectiveness.
Melbourne: Monash Health. Retrieved from <https://monashhealth.org>.
Health care workers have the potential to infect those in their care
when a sharp instrument or needle-stick injury allows the health care
worker’s blood to come in contact with the person’s tissue. The
Australian Guidelines for the Prevention and Control of Infection in
Healthcare advise that health care workers who carry a blood-borne
virus have a clear responsibility to follow the treatment
recommended by their doctor and modify their involvement in direct
patient care. They must not perform exposure-prone procedures
(EPPs) if they are:
HIV antibody positive
hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) positive and/or hepatitis B DNA
positive at high titres
hepatitis C RNA positive (by nucleic acid test).
Health care workers who carry a blood-borne virus and are not in
these categories must not perform EPPs until specialist medical
advice has been sought (NHMRC 2019, p. 204l; CDNA ).
70 Communicable Diseases Network Australia (CDNA) (2018). Australian National
Guidelines for the Management of Healthcare Workers Living with Blood Borne Viruses and
Healthcare Workers Who Perform Exposure Prone Procedures at Risk of Exposure to Blood
Borne Viruses. Retrieved from <www1.health.gov.au>.
70


Australasian college for infection
prevention and control
The Australasian College for Infection Prevention and Control
(ACIPC) is the peak body for infection prevention and control
professionals in the Australasian region. Commencing in January
2012, the College brought together the various state and territory
infection-control associations formerly in the Australian Infection
Control Association to support and encourage collaboration at a
national level (ACIPC ).
71 Australasian College for Infection Prevention and Control (ACIPC) (2018). History of the
College. Retrieved from <www.acipc.org.au>.
In Australia, each state and territory has its own legislation relating
to occupational health and safety concerning exposure to blood,
blood products and blood-borne infections. All employees have a
right to be safe at work. Employers are required to provide
education, equipment and environmental conditions that reduce risks
to workers. Nurses should discuss any concerns with their line
manager or occupational health and safety representative.
Occupational exposure
71


Occupational exposure is defined as skin, eye, mucous membrane
or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious
materials that may result from the performance of an employee’s
duties.
There are three major modes of transmission of infectious materials
in the clinical setting:
1. Puncture wounds from contaminated needles or other sharps.
2. Skin contact, which allows infectious fluids to enter through
wounds and broken or damaged skin.
3. Mucous membrane contact, which allows infectious fluids to
enter through mucous membranes of the eyes, mouth or
nose.
Using correct precautions with aseptic technique, appropriately using
PPE (gloves, masks, gowns, goggles, special resuscitative
equipment) and avoiding carelessness in the clinical area places the
health care worker at significantly less risk for injury. Hepatitis C is of
greatest concern to health care workers as currently there is no
vaccine against the virus or post-exposure prophylaxis. The aim of
follow-up is to detect acute hepatitis C as soon as possible so
appropriate treatment can be commenced (NHMRC 2019).
Prevention remains the primary goal.


Role of the infection-control nurse
All health care organisations must have interdisciplinary infection-
control committees. Representatives from the clinical laboratory,
housekeeping, maintenance, dietary and health care areas are
included. An important member of this committee is the infection-
control nurse. Infection-control nurses are knowledgeable about the
latest research and practices in preventing, detecting and treating
infections. All infections are reported to the nurse in a manner that
allows for recording and analysing statistics, thus assisting in
improving infection-control practices. In addition, the infection-control
nurse may be involved in employee education and implementation of
the blood-borne pathogen exposure control plan put in place by the
organisation.
Evaluating
Using data collected during care (vital signs, lung sounds, skin
status, characteristics of urine or other drainage, laboratory blood
values), nurses can determine whether the individual’s outcomes
have been achieved.
If outcomes are not achieved, nurses may need to consider the
following questions:


Were appropriate measures implemented to prevent skin
breakdown and lung infection?
Was appropriate aseptic technique implemented for invasive
procedures?
Are prescribed medications affecting the immune system?
Is the person’s placement appropriate to reduce the risk of
transmission of micro-organisms?
Did the person and family misunderstand or fail to comply with
necessary instructions?
Case study
Mrs Antonio is an independent 76-year-old woman living
alone who prefers not to rely on others unless absolutely
necessary. She was active and healthy until about 6 months
ago, at which time she developed a persistent upper
respiratory infection. Because she was unable to obtain or
prepare foods, she lost weight and became very weak. Mrs
Antonio finally sought medical attention, but she has not yet
fully recovered. Her general practitioner admitted Mrs Antonio
to the acute care facility for shortness of breath, productive
cough, dehydration and nutritional deficiency.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. Mrs Antonio’s doctor suspects Mrs Antonio has
pneumonia. What data support Mrs Antonio’s
increased risk of such an infection?


2.
 What other information or assessment data
would be helpful to you when planning care for Mrs
Antonio? Think about the physical fundamentals of
care that have been impacted and require attention.
3.
 Using the elements from the Relationship
dimension of the Fundamentals of Care Framework,
how would you establish a relationship with Mrs
Antonio and why is this important?
4. What can you do to prevent the spread of Mrs
Antonio’s infection to other hospitalised individuals and
at the same time prevent Mrs Antonio from getting
infections from others?
5. You see the nursing assistant leaving Mrs Antonio’s
room. The assistant stops to wash her hands. She
turns on the water handles and soaps and rubs her
hands together under running water for about 5
seconds. She then turns off the taps with her bare
hands and proceeds with drying her hands. Should you
intervene and, if so, what should you do?


Chapter 32 Review


Chapter highlights
Micro-organisms are everywhere. Most are harmless and some
are beneficial; however, many can cause infection in susceptible
people.
Effective control of infectious disease is an international, national,
community and individual responsibility.
Asepsis is the freedom from infection or infectious material.
The incidence of health-care-acquired infections is significant.
Major sites for these infections are the respiratory and urinary
tracts, the bloodstream and wounds.
Factors contributing to health-care-acquired infection risks are
invasive procedures, medical therapies, the existence of a large
number of susceptible people, inappropriate use of antibiotics
and insufficient hand cleansing after person-to-person contact
and after contact with body substances.
An infection can develop if the links in the chain of infection—
infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission,
portal of entry and susceptible host—are not interrupted.
Intact skin and mucous membranes are the body’s first line of
defence against micro-organisms.
Some normal body flora release bacteriocins and antibiotic- like
substances that inhibit microbial growth and destroy foreign
bacteria.
Some body secretions (e.g. saliva and tears) contain enzymes
that act as antibacterial agents.


The inflammatory response limits physical, chemical and
microbial injury and promotes repair of injured tissue.
Immunity is the specific resistance of the body to infectious
agents.
Acquired immunity is active or passive and in either case may be
naturally or artificially induced.
Especially at risk of acquiring an infection are the very young or
old; those with poor nutritional status, a deficiency of serum
immunoglobulins, multiple stressors, insufficient immunisations or
an existing disease process; and those receiving certain medical
therapies.
Preventing infections in healthy or ill people and preventing the
transmission of micro-organisms from infected people to others
are responsibilities of all health care professionals.
Nurses must be knowledgeable about sources and modes of
transmission of micro-organisms.
Micro-organisms are invisible and nurses have an ethical
obligation to ensure that appropriate aseptic measures are taken
to protect individuals, support people and health personnel,
including themselves.
All health care providers must apply clean or sterile gloves,
gowns, masks and protective eyewear according to the risk of
exposure to potentially infective materials. Should a health care
worker be exposed to substances with high risk of transmitting
blood-borne pathogens, post-exposure practices and
consideration of prophylactic treatment must be followed
immediately.


Concept check
1. Mrs Jones is a chronic carrier of infection. To prevent the
spread of the infection to others or health care providers,
nurses emphasise interventions that do which of the
following?
1. Eliminate the reservoir.
2. Block the portal of exit from the reservoir.
3. Block the portal of entry into the host.
4. Decrease the susceptibility of the host.
2. The most effective nursing action for controlling the spread of
infection includes which of the following?
1. Thorough hand hygiene.
2. Wearing gloves and masks when providing direct
contact care.
3. Implementing appropriate isolation precautions.
4. Administering broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotics.
3. In caring for Mr Brown with contact precautions for a draining
infected foot ulcer, nurses should perform which of the
following?
1. Wear a mask during dressing changes.
2. Provide disposable meal trays and silverware.
3. Follow standard precautions in all interactions with Mr
Brown.


4. Use surgical asepsis for all direct contact with Mr
Brown.
4. When caring for a single person during one shift, it is
appropriate for the nurse to reuse which of the following
personal protective equipment?
1. Goggles.
2. Gown.
3. Surgical mask.
4. Clean gloves.
5. While donning sterile gloves (open method), the cuff of the
first glove rolls under itself about 5 mm. The best action for
the nurse is to:
1. Remove the glove and start over with a new pair.
2. Wait until the second glove is in place and then unroll
the cuff with the other sterile hand.
3. Ask a colleague to assist by unrolling the cuff.
4. Leave the cuff rolled under.
6. After evaluating progress notes for Ms White aged 65, the
nurse concludes Ms White’s immunisations are current. What
evidence supports this conclusion?
1. Last tetanus booster was at age 50.
2. Receives a flu shot every year.
3. Has not received the hepatitis B vaccine.
4. Has not received the hepatitis A vaccine.


7. Mrs Raymond, aged 56 with poor nutrition, is admitted to
hospital for treatment of a puncture wound. An appropriate
nursing diagnosis would be                     .
8. After teaching Mr Brown and his family strategies to prevent
infection, which statement by Mr Brown indicates effective

1. ‘We will use antimicrobial soap and hot water to wash
our hands at least three times per day.’
2. ‘We must wash or peel all raw fruits and vegetables
before eating.’
3. ‘A wound or sore is not infected unless we see it
draining pus.’
4. ‘We should not share toothbrushes but it is OK to

9. Which of the numbered areas is considered sterile on a

1. Tips of wet forceps are held upward when held in

Focus on critical thinking

2. What reasons are given for not using the terms medical and

3. What actions have taken place for containing difficult-to-treat

All nurses are responsible for ensuring the
provision of safe nursing practice by working to
established national standards of practice (see
Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia
(NMBA) 2016—website details at the end of this

National safety and quality health
service standards
The Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care’s
(ACSQHC) National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS)
Standards were first published in 2012 and were the national
standards used to monitor and evaluate clinical and non-clinical
practices in the health care sector. In 2017, the ACSQHC released
the second edition of the NSQHS Standards (ACSQHC ). There are
eight standards in the second edition. They are listed in Box 33.1
.
4 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2017a). National
Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
BO X
33.1 The eight NSQHCS standards
1. Clinical Governance, which describes the clinical
governance and safety and quality systems that are
required to maintain and improve the reliability, safety
and quality of health care, and improve health
outcomes for patients.
2. Partnering with Consumers, which describes the
systems and strategies to create a consumer-centred
4


health system by including patients in shared decision
making to ensure that patients are partners in their
care and that consumers are involved in the
development and design of quality health care.
3. Preventing and Controlling Healthcare-Associated
Infection, which describes the systems and strategies
to prevent infection, to manage infections effectively
when they occur and to limit the development of
antimicrobial resistance through prudent use of
antimicrobials, as part of effective antimicrobial
stewardship.
4. Medication Safety, which describes the systems and
strategies to ensure that clinicians safely prescribe,
dispense and administer appropriate medicines to
informed patients and monitor use of the medicines.
5. Comprehensive Care, which describes the integrated
screening, assessment and risk identification
processes for developing an individualised care plan to
prevent and minimise the risks of harm in identified
areas.
6. Communicating for Safety, which describes the
systems and strategies for effective communication
between patients, carers and families, multidisciplinary
teams and clinicians, and across the health service
organisation.
7. Blood Management, which describes the systems
and strategies for the safe, appropriate, efficient and


effective care of patients’ own blood, as well as other
supplies of blood and blood products.
8. Recognising and Responding to Acute
Deterioration, which describes the systems and
processes to respond effectively to patients when their
physical, mental or cognitive condition deteriorates.
Source: ACSQHC (2017a). National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (2nd ed.). ©
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care 2017.
The six actions in the NSQHS Standards that focus on meeting the
needs of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are shown in
Table 33.1
Table 33.1 The six actions in the NSQHS Standards that focus
on meeting the needs of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people
ACSQHC (2017a). National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
The core principles underpinning these standards are to protect the
public from harm and to improve the quality of care provision
through innovations to improve efficiencies and health care
outcomes.
The NSQHS Standards require organisations to develop a robust
clinical governance framework supported by risk management
mitigation strategies, policies, procedures, protocols and guidelines.
Nurses have a responsibility to be familiar with the organisational


approach to managing health care risks. These responsibilities are
clearly stated in the nurse practice standards (NMBA 2016). A
definition of clinical governance is provided in Box 33.2
.
BO X
33.2 Definitions of relevant nursing
safety terms
Accreditation
: a status that is conferred on an
organisation or a person when they have been assessed as
having met particular standards. The two conditions for
accreditation are an explicit definition of quality (i.e.
standards) and an independent review process aimed at
identifying the level of congruence between practices and
quality standards (ACSQHC 2017a).
Clinical governance
: structures, systems and standards
applying to create a culture and direct clinical activities.
Clinical accountability and responsibility, a subset of clinical
governance, involves the monitoring and oversight of clinical
activities, including regulation, audit, assurance and
compliance by governors (such as boards of directors),
regulators (such as governments, professional bodies) and
internal and external auditors (Duke ).
5 Duke, N. (2015). Clinical leadership and organizational governance in primary
care. Primary Health Care, 25(9), 34–39.
5


Clinical incident
: any unplanned event that causes or
potentially causes harm to a patient.
Critical incident
: unintended consequences of an action
or actions that may result in harm to recipients of care or
staff involved in care delivery. Critical incidents can, for
example, also involve staff being exposed to violence in the
workplace or to activities that result in needle-stick injuries:
becoming distracted when giving intravenous injections,
vaccinating children/babies, disposing of used needle and
syringe incorrectly.
Incident reporting
: the system or process for reporting
incidents in the health care workplace.
Mandatory competencies
: competencies the nurse must
be able to demonstrate continuously in the health care
workplace.
Patient safety management
: processes and systems of
work used by nurses to minimise harm to patients and to
themselves.
Risk management
: a series of processes developed to
minimise harm to people and staff working in health care
organisations. Risk management also applies to staff—
providing staff with safe systems of work.
Root cause analysis
: a process used for investigating and
categorising unintended consequences of health care


professionals’ actions during the course of their work. It is not
used to apportion blame, but to promote improvement.
Sentinel events
: the unintended consequences of health
professionals’ activities that can result in serious or even fatal
injury to people receiving care. Sentinel events may also
involve staff in incidents that result in psychological injury as
well as physical injury.
Staff safety
: organisational and professional systems of
work designed to minimise harm to staff.
Work health and safety
: national legislation that regulates
and supports safe work practices in all workplaces.
The second edition of the NSQHS Standards maintain an acute care
focus but also include mental health and cognitive impairment,
health literacy, end-of-life care and Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander health. These inclusions were identified as gaps in safety
and quality standards by health care professionals. The ACSQHC
also provides information on the accreditation process which is very
comprehensive and relevant to safe nursing practice (ACSQHC ).
6 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC)(2019). Australian
Health Service Safety and Quality Accreditation Scheme. Retrieved from
<www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Box 33.2
 defines some terms you will encounter as you deliver
nursing care.
6


Keeping nurses safe
As a harm prevention strategy, all nurses working in Australian
health care organisations receive instruction in manual handling
practices. This is supported by organisational policies and
procedures such as a ‘No Lift Policy’, the safe use of lifting devices
for lifting and transporting/transferring people or residents. Manual
handling is not confined to lifting, transferring or transporting people
or residents but includes all physical activities relating to person-
centred care that have the potential to cause physical injury.
Another issue facing all nurses, whether they work in hospitals, the
community or other health service delivery areas, is that of
workplace violence (Pich, Kable & Hazelton ). While there is a clear
acknowledgment of the existence of workplace violence, the
Australian health care industry is yet to produce a consensus
document on workplace violence. Research in this area needs to
define and include physical violence, vertical violence and horizontal
violence (Boyle & Wallis ). This is supported by international studies
showing the variability in experiences of and prevalence of violence,
noting that this is an under-researched area (Park, Cho & Hong ).
7 Pich, J., Kable, A. & Hazelton, M. (2017). Antecedent and precipitants of patient-related
violence in the emergency department: Results from the Australian VENT study (Violence in
Emergency and Triage). Australasian Emergency Nursing Journal, 20(3), 107–113.
7
8
9


8 Boyle, M. J. & Wallis, J. (2016). Working towards a definition for workplace violence actions
in the health sector. Safety in Health, 2(4), 1–6.
9 Park, M., Cho, S. & Hong, H. (2015). Prevalence and perpetrators of workplace violence by
nursing unit and the relationship between violence and the perceived work environment.
Journal of Nursing Scholarship, 47(1), 87–95.
The work, health and safety legislation covers workplace violence,
which remains prominent in the nursing literature (Martinez ).
Health care organisations support nurses and other health
professionals with the skills and knowledge to deal with workplace
violence through the provision of counselling services and
aggression/violence management workshops. Support services for
staff affected should be provided, usually through the organisational
Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
10 Martinez, A. J. S. (2016). Managing workplace violence with evidence-based interventions:
A literature review. Journal of Psychosocial Nursing and Mental Health Services, 54(9), 31–
36.
Horizontal violence or bullying can also impact on person- centred
care outcomes. Holmes, Rudge and Perron  present a critical social
model that relates this phenomenon to such outcomes. Horizontal
violence, workplace incivility and bullying remain prevalent among
nurses working in Australia’s health and aged care sectors
(Mammen, Hills & Lam
).
11 Holmes, D., Rudge, T. & Perron, A. (2016). (Re) Thinking Violence in Health Care Settings:
A Critical Approach. New York: Routledge.
10
11
12


12 Mammen, B., Hills, D. & Lam, L. (2018). Newly qualified graduate nurses’ experiences of
workplace incivility in Australian hospital settings. Collegian, 25(6), 591–599.
Clinical consideration
Safe nursing practice is nursing practice that:
is based on validated standards of practice
and uses evidence (NMBA 2016)
is person centred and knowledge based
complies with legislative and administrative
requirements.


Factors affecting individual safety
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW)
 reported on
trends in the occurrence of injuries requiring hospitalisation in
Australia from 1 July 1999 to 30 June 2015 (see Table 33.2
). The
annual number of cases rose from about 327,000 to 460, 000 during
this period (AIHW 2018). Males had a higher rate of total injury and
highest rates of injury in all ranges from 5 to 64 years of age. From
65 years of age onwards, females experienced higher rates of injury
than males, with widening disparity as age increased. Near equal
representation was evident in the 0 to 4 years age group (AIHW
2018). There were an estimated 483 672 cases of injury during
2014–15. Rates of injury among Indigenous people (3593 cases per
100 000) were almost twice those of non-Indigenous people (1922
cases per 100 000) in 2014–15 (AIHW 2018). Major external cause
groups for injury cases are shown in Table 33.3
.
13 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018). Trends in Hospitalised Injury,
Australia 1999–00 to 2014–15. Injury research and statistics series No. 110. Cat. no.
INJACT190. Canberra: AIHW.
Table 33.2 Hospitalised injury cases by age and sex, Australia,
1999–2000 to 2014–15
Source: AIHW
. Trends in Hospitalised Injury, Australia 1999–00 to 2014–15, Table 2.1. Injury research and
statistics series No. 110. Cat. no. INJACT190. Canberra: AIHW.
13
14


14 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2018). Risk
Management. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Table 33.3 Major external cause groups for injury cases, by sex,
Australia 2014–15
*Other external causes of accidental injury include (as examples)
categories such as exposure to electrical current, contact with
venomous animals and plants and exposure to forces of nature.
Source: AIHW (2018). Trends in Hospitalised Injury, Australia 1999–00 to 2014–15, p. 10, Table 2.5. Injury
research and statistics series No. 110. Cat. no. INJACT190. Canberra: AIHW.
The age-standardised rate of injury increased from 1999–2000 to
2014–15 by an average of 1% per year. The rate of injury was 1715
cases per 100 000 population at the beginning of the period; by the
end, the rate was 1966 per 100 000. Increases in age-standardised
rates across the period were found for injuries due to falls (2%
increase per year) and intentional self-harm (0.4% increase per
year). Significant decreases occurred in the rate of hospitalised
cases due to poisoning by pharmaceuticals (4% per year) and by
other substances (4% per year), and drowning and near-drowning
(1% decrease per year—3.5% per year for boys 0–4 and 2.8% for
girls 0–4). No significant trends were observed for transport-related
injuries, assaults and thermal injuries such as burns.
Rates of injury for Indigenous males and females increased
consistently over the period, but slowed a little in more recent years
(e.g. 2.2% increase in 2014–15). After a noticeable decrease (2%)


in the 2012–13 period, a clear spike in incidence (3.3% and 4.99%
increase) in the following 2 years was identified for non-Indigenous
Australians. There were increases in rates of poisoning by
pharmaceuticals, falls, intentional self-harm and assault during this
time.
The ability of people to protect themselves from injury is affected by
such factors as age and development, lifestyle, mobility and health
status, sensory–perceptual alterations, cognitive awareness, ability
to communicate, safety awareness and environmental factors.
Nurses need to assess each of these factors when they plan care or
teach people how to protect themselves.
Age and development
Through assessment and familiarity of the environment, people learn
to protect themselves from injury. For example, children walking to
school are taught to stop before crossing the street and wait for
oncoming traffic. Across Australia there are designated school
crossings, with reduced speed limits and traffic lights often
monitored by trained traffic monitors. Children are made aware of
‘stranger danger’ and the need to report to both their school
teachers and parents if they are approached by strangers while
walking unaccompanied.
In the home, children also learn to avoid potential hazards. For the
very young, learning and being taught about their environment is


essential for their life and social skills development.
In contemporary Australian society, another source of potential
danger for children is the easy access to online media and social
networking sites. As most children are exposed to, and adept at
using, technology, which is available to them at very young ages, the
online environment is becoming the preferred method of interacting
and communication, ensuring children’s protection from cyber
danger is becoming more important.
Social networking sites and communication apps are a source of the
phenomenon ‘cyberbullying’ (Whittaker & Kowalski ). Waasdorp and
Bradshaw  argue that cyberbullying has some correlation with
traditional bullying but it occurs in a more public domain, often by an
unknown perpetrator, and is consistent with increased internalisation
of psychological distress. Jadambaa, Thomas and Scott
 provide
an overview of the effects of cyberbullying among children and
adolescents from the perspective of being bullied and bullying
others. The Australian government has established the eSafety
Commissioner (<www.esafety.gov.au>), which provides information
and support relating to cyberbullying. Another government strategy
for managing online safety may be found at
<www.australia.gov.au/information-and-services/public-safety-
and-law/online-safety>.
15 Whittaker, E. & Kowalski, R. M. (2014). Cyberbullying via social media. Journal of School
Violence, 14, 11–29.
15
16
17


16 Waasdorp, T. E. & Bradshaw, C. P. (2015). The overlap between cyberbullying and

17 Jadambaa, A., Thomas, H. J. & Scott, J. G. (2019). Prevalence of traditional bullying and
cyberbullying among children and adolescents in Australia: A systematic review and meta-
analysis. Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry, 53(9), 878–888.
Nurses, in particular school nurses, have unique opportunities to
detect the existence of bullying and report to the relevant authorities,
which in the case of children will be the schools and parents (Byrne,
Vessey & Pfeifer
). The authors further argue that incidents of
bullying should be treated and reported as a public health issue.

and interventions for school nurses working with victims, student, and families. The Journal of
School Nursing, 34(1), 38–50.
The Australian government has an online resource, Stay Smart
Online (Attorney-General’s Department
), which has important
information about protecting children of all ages from internet
dangers. Children and their parents/carers need this information,
which will enable them to recognise potential sources of danger as
well as give them the skills and knowledge to best manage these
situations.

The AIHW
 has published the National Framework for Protecting
Australia’s Children 2009–2020. The paper draws together the
available data sources and provides consistent definitions and

indicators for reporting on children who are subject to abuse in its
various forms.

Older adults can have difficulty with movement and diminished
sensory acuity that contributes to the likelihood of injury. Specific
age-related potential hazards and preventive measures are
discussed later in this chapter. Box 33.3
 summarises selected
hazards for each age group.

33.3 Selected safety hazards
throughout the lifespan*
Developing fetus: exposure to maternal smoking, alcohol
consumption, addictive drugs, x-rays (first trimester),
environmental risks. Newborns and infants: falling,
suffocation in bassinet, choking from aspirated milk or

electric shock, poisonings, harm from other people and
animals.
Toddlers: physical trauma from falling, banging into

harm from other people and animals.
Preschoolers: injury from traffic, playground equipment
and other objects; choking, suffocation, airway or ear
canal obstruction with foreign objects; poisoning,
drowning, fire and burns; harm from other people and
animals.
Adolescents: vehicular (motor vehicle, motor bikes,
bicycles) accidents, recreational accidents, firearms and
other weapons, substance abuse.
Older adults: falling, burns, pedestrian and vehicular
accidents, harm from other people and animals.

Lifespan considerations
Older adults
The Department of Health  publishes resources that
focus on managing cognitive impairment in the older
person.
21 Department of Health (2015a). Tackling Dementia. Retrieved from
