The information included in the fact sheets covers topics
such as:
– tackling dementia
– new dementia and cognition and dementia, and severe
behaviour supplements
– supporting people with dementia across the health
system
– improving acute services for people with dementia
– improved support for people with younger-onset
dementia.
In Australia, dementia was the second leading cause of
death in 2017 (AIHW
). Because of this, Australia’s
health ministers have included dementia as the ninth
National Health Priority Area, underpinned by the National
Framework for Action on Dementia 2015–2019
(Department of Health ).
22 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019). National Health
Performance Framework. Retrieved from <http://meteor.aihw.gov.au>.
23 Department of Health (2015b). National Framework for Action on Dementia
2015–2019. Retrieved from <https://agedcare.health.gov.au>.
Nurses should assess people for potential personal
causes of falls: hypotension, unsteady gait, altered mental
responsiveness (such as from medications), poor vision,
foot pathology, cognitive changes and fear.
22
23


In the home or community setting, assess for potential
environmental causes of falls:
– lighting: inadequate amount, inaccessible or
inconvenient switches
– floors: presence of electrical cords, loose rugs, clutter,
slippery surfaces
– stairs: absent or unsteady railings, uneven step height
or surface
– furniture: unsteady base, lack of armrests, cabinets too
high or too low
– bathroom: inappropriate toilet height, slippery floors or
tub, absence of grab bars
– animals—pets, vermin etc.
Social factors
Social factors that place people at risk include unsafe work
environments, living in neighbourhoods with high crime rates, access
to guns and ammunition, insufficient income to buy safety equipment
(house alarms, car alarms) or to make necessary household repairs,
and access to any illicit drugs that may be contaminated with
harmful additives. The Australian Crime Commission (ACC) reports


that the illicit drug posing the greatest risk to the Australian
community is methamphetamine (street names ice, speed) (ACC
2015 in AIHW
). The AIHW (2019) reports that the death rate from
methamphetamine and other stimulants was four times higher in
2017 compared to 1999 data.
24 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2014). Australia’s health series No. 14.
Cat. no. AUS 178. Canberra: AIHW.
The Intergovernmental Committee on Drugs released a Draft
National Drug Strategy 2016–2025 for wide consultation. The draft
report focuses on a nationally agreed harm minimisation approach to
manage alcohol, tobacco and other drug use.
Risk-taking behaviours also contribute to motor vehicle accidents
(e.g. speeding, driving while under the influence of drugs and
alcohol).
Mobility and health status
People with impaired mobility due to paralysis, muscle weakness
and poor balance or coordination are prone to injury from falls or as
a result of prolonged bed rest. People with spinal cord injury or
lower-body paralysis may be unable to move when they perceive
discomfort. Individuals weakened by illness or surgery are not
always fully aware of their condition or their capacity and capability
24


for mobility and will require assistance from nurses to minimise risk
of injury.
Sensory–perceptual alterations
Accurate sensory perception of environmental stimuli is vital to
safety. People with impaired touch perception, hearing, taste, smell
and vision are highly susceptible to injury. A person who does not
see well may trip over a toy or not see an electric cord or other
hazards. Deaf people do not hear a siren in traffic, nor will they hear
alarms in hospitals. People with impaired smell may not smell
burning food or a gas leak. Loss of sensation leads to tissue injury;
for example, diabetics being unable to feel their toes, leaving them
susceptible to injury.
Cognitive awareness
Cognitive awareness is the ability to perceive environmental stimuli
and body reactions and to respond appropriately through thought
and action. People with impaired awareness include people who are
sleep deprived; unconscious or semi-conscious people; disoriented
people, people experiencing sensory hallucinations; and people
whose judgment is altered by disease or medications such as
narcotics, tranquillisers, hypnotics and sedatives. These individuals’


clinical and psychological conditions need to be observed and
monitored closely and any variations noted and responded to.
Emotional state
Labile emotional states can alter people’s ability to perceive or see
environmental hazards, increasing the potential for injury. Stressful
situations can reduce a person’s level of concentration, cause errors
of judgment and negatively impact on situational awareness. People
who use illicit substances may also present with altered sensory
perceptual states that require close monitoring and observation by
nursing staff. People with significant mood disturbances may think
and react to environmental stimuli more slowly than usual and
respond inappropriately with the potential to injure themselves and
others.
Ability to communicate
People with a diminished ability to receive and convey information
are at risk of injury. They include people with aphasia, people
speaking a language different from the nurse’s and those with poor
literacy skills. For example, the person unable to read and interpret
the sign ‘No smoking—oxygen in use’ could expose themself and
others to harm. Communication is not only the ability to transmit and
receive information, it also requires that the information has the


same meaning for both the transmitter and receiver. Nurses,
therefore, have to ensure that any information communicated to
people is understood correctly by the person and/or carer (see also
Chapter 27
).
Safety awareness
People in unfamiliar environments will need specific safety
information, such as information about equipment, summoning
assistance (call bell placement) and fire exits. Nurses need to be
able to communicate this information to people from all backgrounds
and ensure that people from non-English-speaking backgrounds
receive this information in a language they can understand.
People need information about water safety, car safety, fire
prevention, ways to prevent the ingestion of harmful substances and
other preventive measures related to specific age-related hazards.
People should also be informed and shown how to access the
relevant information relating to maintaining their safety and the
safety of their families and loved ones by using the internet or other
media. In particular, older people or those with a disability receiving
community-based care should be shown how to access emergency
services by dialling 000 or how to use a medical alert device which
when pressed contacts the relevant emergency services.
Communication and internet technologies are now available so that
people can contact their local emergency services and check for
potential environmental disasters such as bushfires.


Environmental factors
Depending on the person’s situation, the nurse may need to assess
the environment in the health care facility or the person’s home,
workplace or community.
In Australia, environmental assessments by nurses working in all
health care settings are an essential component of admitting the
person to the service. Individual personal safety is affected by the
health care setting, and nurses have a responsibility to ensure that
the health care environment is safe for the person and the
caregivers, including themselves and other health professionals.
This applies in the health care facility, the community setting and the
person’s home.
The Australian government provides a nationally coordinated
approach to managing disasters. In 2006, the Australian Health
Ministers Advisory Committee (AHMAC) established the Australian
Health Protection Principal Committee (AHPPC) to advise the
AHMAC on the country’s preparedness to deal with health
emergencies, to identify and address any deficits and to coordinate
a national response to significant events (Department of Health and
Ageing ). A National Incident Room has been established to ensure
a nationally consistent and coordinated approach to any national
health emergency.
25


25 Department of Health and Ageing (2013). National Incident Room. Retrieved from
<www.health.gov.au>.
Australia has a robust health care system with measures to provide
a comprehensive and effective health response to disasters, such as
mass casualty events including bioterrorist attacks, natural
disasters, bombing or communicable disease outbreaks. In
November 2011, the AHPPC released the National Health
Emergency Response Arrangements. The National Health
Emergency Response Arrangements direct how the Australian
health sector (incorporating state and territory health authorities and
relevant Commonwealth agencies) would work cooperatively and
collaboratively to contribute to the response to, and recovery from,
emergencies of national consequence (Department of Health and
Ageing , p. 3).
26 Department of Health and Ageing (2011). National Health Emergency Response
Arrangements. Retrieved from <www.health.gov.au>.
Every year in Australia, metropolitan and regional communities face
devastating losses caused by disasters ranging from tropical
cyclones to floods and bushfires. These disasters have significant
personal, community, economic and environmental impact. The peak
operational Commonwealth body for emergency management is
Emergency Management Australia (EMA), which comes under the
jurisdiction of the federal Attorney-General’s Department (Attorney-
General’s Department
; EMA ).
27 Attorney-General’s Department (2013). Emergency Management. Retrieved from
<www.ag.gov.au>.
26
27
28


28 Emergency Management Australia (EMA) (2013). Retrieved from <www.ag.gov.au>.
In 2009, the Council of Australian Governments (COAG) agreed to
adopt a whole-of-nation resilience-based approach to disaster
management. This initiative recognises that a national, coordinated
and cooperative effort is needed to enhance Australia’s capacity to
withstand and recover from emergencies and disasters.
EMA assists states and territories in enhancing their emergency
management capabilities through development of national
strategies, production of best-practice manuals and provision of
training courses. During disasters, EMA coordinates the provision of
Commonwealth technical and material assistance to states and
territories through the National Emergency Management
Coordination Centre (NEMCC) in Canberra. This assistance is
usually provided at no cost to the states or territories. EMA is led by
a director-general and comprises numerous functional units. There
are no emergency medicine specialists or other medical specialists
on staff or in a representative capacity. Nevertheless, EMA has
many advisory groups, one of which, the Commonwealth Advisory
Panel of Experts, has particular importance to emergency medicine.
This is a group of professionals from many fields who advise EMA
on standards, education training packages and so on.
The states and territories do not have to comply with
Commonwealth directives that are not part of the Constitution. There
is, however, a good working relationship in disaster management
between the Commonwealth and the states. Except for the


Australian Defence Force, the Commonwealth government does not
have on-ground resources of its own.
Police, fire, ambulance and state emergency services are all
controlled by the particular state or territory. The primary role of the
Commonwealth is coordination of resources and dealing with issues
relating to international responses. Box 33.4
 lists the peak
emergency management bodies in the states and territories. Each
health care organisation will have its own disaster management plan
that is linked to the state/territory disaster plan. An example of this is
the organisational responses to fire alarms being activated.

Terrorism
Terrorism—domestic and international—is defined as ‘the unlawful
use of violence and intimidation especially against civilians, in the
pursuit of political aims’ (Oxford Dictionary
). In Australia, the media
reports on acts of domestic and international terrorism regularly.
29


Health professionals including paramedics and emergency room
staff now deal with the consequences of such violence. More
information may be found at <http://tacmedaustralia.com.au>.
29 Oxford Dictionary (2016). Retrieved from <https://en.oxforddictionaries.com>.
Safety considerations
Home
A safe home requires well-maintained flooring and carpets, a non-
skid bathtub or shower surface, functioning smoke alarms that are
strategically placed and knowledge of fire escape routes. Outdoor
areas need to be safely secured and maintained. In Australia,
legislation requires that all backyard swimming pools be fenced and
fitted with child safety locks and gates. Kidsafe  is the home of the
Child Accident Prevention Foundation of Australia and a member of
Safe Kids Worldwide. Its interactive website contains useful
resources to help locate state and territory offices.
30 Kidsafe (2017). Parents’ Guide to Kidsafe Homes. Retrieved from
<https://kidsafe.com.au>.
Workplace
In the health care workplace, equipment, furniture, trolleys, slippery
floors, people movement and chemicals all pose potential risks.
30


Worker fatigue, noise and air pollution, or working at great heights or
in subterranean areas may also create occupational hazards. The
work environment of the nurse may also be unsafe from
environmental hazards, faulty equipment and unsafe work systems.
All health care workers need to remain risk-aware in their work
environment, which may include increased patient acuity, high
workloads, unsafe systems of work and practice, and minimal
staffing levels/skill mix. Nurses therefore have a responsibility to
always report an unsafe working environment.
The principles of workplace health and safety are embedded in state
and territory legislation. Health care workers in Australia are given
information about their rights and responsibilities, as well as the
employer’s rights and responsibilities, as part of employment
induction. All health care organisations must develop policy and
procedure frameworks that support safe practice, and these must
be made available to staff. As well as being directed to these policies
and procedures at induction, employees must be informed of any
changes to the legislation or to the regulations. For example,
knowledge of manual handling principles and practices is essential
for nurses working in all areas of the health and aged care sectors.
This is a mandatory competency and is a part of the organisational
risk and quality management strategy. Workplace incidents are
investigated by the organisation, recorded in a state-monitored
database and possibly investigated by a regulatory agency.
Community


Adequate street lighting, safe water and sanitation, and regulation of
food hygiene all contribute to a healthy community with minimised
risks. The federal government in Australia has established regulatory
agencies to monitor these community services, and the state and
territory departments of health are also involved in auditing and
monitoring community-based services. A safe and secure
community strives to be free of excess noise, crime, traffic
congestion, dilapidated housing or unprotected creeks and landfill,
and these are the responsibility of the different levels of government
and services.
Health care organisations
Safety in health care organisations is also closely monitored by the
federal government through its agencies. Data are available via
agency websites. The ACSQHC produces reports relating to safety
and quality management in hospitals and aged care settings
(ACSQHC 2018).
The hospital environment is complex and is where the majority of
nurses work. Nurses may be directly or indirectly involved in patient
errors. Studies by Keers et al.
 and Hinno, Partanen and
Vehvilainen-Julkunen  suggest that hospital errors occur because of
workforce fatigue, human error and system flaws. Singer and
Vogus
 argue that a fundamental cause of hospital errors is a weak
organisational culture of safety. For example, medication errors
occur as a result of poor health care delivery systems rather than
because of incompetent health professionals (Mahmood, Chaudbury
31
32
33


& Valente ). Analysing the administration of a single medication can
involve ‘30−40 steps’, and with each step comes a potential for error
to occur (Sears, O’Brien-Pallas & Stevens , p. 351). Because
nurses administer most medications, they are involved in the
majority of medication errors. Nurses also pick up 86% of
medication errors made at the prescribing and/or dispensing stage
of medication administration (Sears et al. 2013, p. 351).
31 Keers, R. N., Williams, S. D., Cooke, J. & Ashcroft, D. M (2013). Prevalence and nature of
medication errors in health care settings: A systematic review of direct observational
evidence. The Annals of Pharmacotherapy, 37, 237–256.
32 Hinno S., Partanen, P. & Vehvilainen-Julkunen, K. (2011). Nurse activities, nurse staffing
and adverse patient outcomes as perceived by hospital nurses. Journal of Clinical Nursing,
21, 1584−1593.
33 Singer, S. J. & Vogus, T. J. (2013). Reducing hospital errors: Interventions that build safety
culture. Annual Review of Public Health, 34, 373−396.
34 Mahmood, A., Chaudbury, H. & Valente, M. (2011). Nurses’ perceptions of how physical
environments affect medication errors in acute care settings. Applied Nursing Research, 24,
229−237.
35 Sears, K., O’Brien-Pallas, L. & Stevens, B. (2013). The relationship between the nursing
work environment and the occurrence of reported paediatric medication administration errors:
A Pan Canadian Study. Journal of Paediatric Nursing, 28, 351−356.
34
35


Nursing management
Assessing
Assessing people at risk of accidents and injury involves (a) noting
any indicators in the nursing history and physical examination, (b)
using specifically developed risk assessment tools and (c) evaluating
the person’s home/living environment.
Nursing history and physical examination
The nursing history and physical examination provide valuable
information about the person’s risks of harm. Data include age and
developmental level; general health status; mobility status; of
physiological or perceptual deficits or sensory impairments; cognitive
impairment or emotional disturbance; substance use; indications of
abuse or neglect; and an accident and injury history. A safety history
also needs to include the person’s awareness of hazards, knowledge
of safety precautions both at home and at work and any perceived
threats to safety (see Figures 33.1
 and 33.2
).
Figure 33.1


Safety of a child in the home is in your hands.
Source: © Jupiterimages/liquidlibrary/Thinkstock.com.
Figure 33.2


The picture shows how easy it is for young children to be burnt in
the home.
Risk assessment tools
Risk assessment tools are available to determine people at risk both
of specific kinds of injury such as falls, and of the general safety of
the home and health care setting. In general, these tools direct the
nurse to appraise the factors affecting safety. The tools summarise
specific data contained in the person’s nursing history and physical
examination. Risk factors for falls are discussed later in this chapter
(see ‘Falls
’ on pages 733–735).
National patient safety goals
Australia has national quality standards which were implemented in
July 2012 (see Box 33.5
). The Australian Health Service Safety
and Quality Accreditation Scheme delivers national coordination of
accreditation processes and builds on the strength of the current
accreditation arrangements (ACSQHC ).
36 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2013). Retrieved
from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
36


BO X
33.5 Examples of clinical safety
initiatives
Improve the accuracy of patient
identification
Accuracy in patient identification, especially when
administering blood products and medications, is an
important nursing function. Health care organisations are
required to have a defined, robust patient identification
system of matching patients to procedures that includes at
least three appropriate patient identifiers. The World Health
Organization (WHO) supports the use of safety checklists,
with the Surgical Safety Checklist an example (see Figure
33.3
) (WHO
).

from <www.who.int>.

Communication tools that are used widely in health care
organisations include the ISBAR tool and the OSSIE Guide to
Clinical Handover (ACSQHC ). Figure 33.4
 is a pictorial
example of the ISBAR tool. ISBAR is an acronym that stands
for a structured communication tool used in clinical
handovers.

Improve the safe use of medications
The APINCHS acronym (ASCQHC ) assists Australian
health care workers to identify high-risk medications. This
alerts clinicians to certain groups of medications that have a
higher potential for harm:

Antimicrobial stewardship
Antimicrobial stewardship is a measure to ensure safe
and appropriate prescribing of antimicrobials (antibiotics),
with the goal of decreasing antimicrobial resistance and
minimising patient harm.
Comply with the national standards for antimicrobial
stewardship from the ACSQHC .
41 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC)
(2017d). Antimicrobial Stewardship Initiative. Retrieved from
<www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
Comply with the facility guidelines for surveillance,
reporting and prescribing standards associated with health
care infections and antimicrobial therapy.
Early-warning alerts: MEWS and
METS
In response to the need to prevent patient deterioration
through early intervention, there have been a number of
tools developed to assist clinicians to identify early signs
of deterioration and summon appropriate clinical support
in a timely manner. A MEWS tool is a Modified Early
Warning Score. This tool uses physiological data collected
by the nurse to highlight signs of deterioration, prompting
41


the nurse to seek clinical review or perform further
assessment.
A MET or MER call is a Medical Emergency Team or
Medical Emergency Response. Designed to reduce the
hierarchical communication barriers in health care
organisations, MET or MER calls are emergency calls that
can be initiated by any clinician, with any level of
expertise, who has witnessed a patient deterioration,
determined by a number of physiological parameters. This
ensures appropriate and skilled support is made available
to the patient and the clinician in a timely manner. The
MET or MERS criteria contain an important safety feature
called the ‘worried criteria’. This allows for a clinician to
summon the medical response team even if they are
unable to identify a single defining sign of deterioration but
feel that the patient is acutely unwell and needs review.
In August 2008, Australian health ministers endorsed the Australian
Charter of Health Care Rights, which summarises the basic rights of
people and consumers when accessing health care services
throughout Australia. These rights involve access, safety, respect,
communication, participation, privacy and comment (ACSQHC ).
42 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2008).
Australian Charter of Health Care Rights. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
The Australian Charter of Health Care Rights links to the Australian
Patient Safety Foundation (APSF), which is a non-profit independent
42


organisation dedicated to the advancement of patient safety. The
APSF provides leadership in the reduction of harm to patients in all
health care environments. The National Performance Framework for
health care in Australia clearly links health status and determinants
of health with health system performance (see Figure 33.5
).
Figure 33.5


National Health Performance Framework 2009 (updated 2019).
Source: AIHW (2019). National Health Performance Framework. Retrieved from <http://meteor.aihw.gov.au/
content/index.phtml/itemId/392569>.
The National Health Performance Framework was developed in
2009 and is made up of three domains: health status, determinants
of health and health system performance. Since 2009, the AIHW
has continued to review the health-related indicators supporting the
framework, ensuring that it reflects the contemporary health status
of Australians.
Through its subsidiary Patient Safety International (PSI), the APSF
provides a software tool, the Advanced Incident Management
System (AIMS), to capture information from a wide variety of
sources to enable deconstruction and classification of incidents from
near-misses to sentinel events in a consistent way, so that
subsequent, detailed analysis is possible. The AIMS reporting
system enables anonymity when reporting critical incidents—only the
organisation is identified.


Planning
When planning care to prevent accidents and injury, the nurse
considers all factors affecting the person’s safety, specifies desired
outcomes and selects nursing activities to meet these outcomes.
The major goal for people with safety risks is to prevent accidents
and injury to both person and nurse. To meet this goal, people often
need to change their health behaviour and may need to modify the
environment.
Desired outcomes associated with preventing injury depend on the
individual person’s clinical physical and mental condition.
Nursing interventions to meet desired outcomes are largely directed
towards helping the person and family to accomplish the following:
Identify environmental hazards in the home and community.
Demonstrate safe practices that comply with Australian safety
standards. The work health and safety legislation applies in all
practice areas across Australia.
Experience a decrease in the frequency or severity of injury.
Demonstrate safe child-rearing practices or lifestyle practices.
Once a plan has been developed, it is implemented and evaluated
as shown in ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and
interventions’.


Implementing
Promoting safety across the lifespan
Measures to ensure the safety of people of all ages focus on (a)
observation or prediction of potentially harmful situations so that
harm can be avoided, and (b) education that empowers people to
protect themselves and their families from injury. Safety measures
covering the lifespan from infancy to elders are listed in ‘Patient
education’.
Newborns and infants
Accidents are a leading cause of death during infancy, especially
during the first year of life. Infants are completely dependent on
others for care and they are oblivious to such dangers as falling or
ingesting harmful substances. Parents need to learn the amount of
observation necessary to maintain infant safety. They also need help
to identify and remove common hazards in and around the home
and make available first aid information that includes
cardiopulmonary resuscitation and interventions for airway
obstruction. Common accidents during infancy include burns,
suffocation or choking, car accidents, falls and poisoning. Education
and support of parents can make them more knowledgeable and
better prepared to protect their children from accidents and injuries.


Toddlers
Toddlers are curious and like to feel and taste everything. They are
fascinated by potential dangers, such as pools and busy roads, so
they need constant supervision and protection (see Figure 33.6
).
Parents may prevent many accidents by ‘toddler-proofing’ the home
or other settings where the child will be. This practice extends to the
use of approved car restraints and removing or securing all items
that can pose a safety hazard to the child in any setting. It may be
necessary to inspect for and remove sources of lead from the
environment. Lead poisoning (plumbism) is a risk for children
exposed to lead paint chips, fumes from leaded petrol or any
‘leaded’ substances. The most common cause of lead poisoning in
Australia is the dust from old lead paint or ceiling dust disturbed
during renovations of homes built pre-1970. Go to the KidSafe
website for more information about safety for children in Australia
<https://kidsafe.com.au>. You can also access your state or
territory’s websites and information through this link.
Figure 33.6


Keep your driveway safe.
Source: Kidsafe Victoria <www.kidsafevic.com.au/road-safety/driveway_safety>.
All children from toddlers to through to adolescents need to be
educated about driveway safety and taught not to walk around large
vehicles (e.g. buses) where there is no clear view of cyclists or
oncoming traffic.
School-age children


The AIHW’s report, A Picture of Australia’s Children (AIHW
),
remains the most recent comprehensive overview, providing
information on how Australia is performing according to key
indicators of child health, development and wellbeing. Death rates
for children have decreased since 1986. Drinking and smoking rates
for children are also decreasing and the majority of children are
achieving minimum standards for reading and numeracy. There is
still a proportion (25%) of children who are developmentally at risk at
the school entry age. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children
and children from low socioeconomic groups have lower
achievement rates across most indicators (AIHW 2012).
43 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2012). A Picture of Australia’s Children.
Cat. no. PHE 167. Canberra: AIHW. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Adolescents and young adults
Obtaining a driver’s licence is an important event in the life of an
adolescent. Adolescents may use driving as an outlet for stress, as
a way to assert independence or as a way to impress peers. When
setting limits on motor vehicle use, parents or guardians need to
assess the adolescent’s understanding of responsibility, common
sense and ability to resist negative peer pressure. The age of the
adolescent alone does not determine readiness to handle this
responsibility.
Adolescents are at risk of sports injuries because their coordination
skills are not fully developed. However, sports activities are
43


important to the adolescent’s self-esteem and overall development.
In addition to providing beneficial exercise, sports activities enhance
social and personal development. They help the adolescent
experience competition, teamwork and conflict resolution. Deaths
from suicide and accidents are still high in the adolescent age group,
as reported in Trends in Hospitalised Injury, Australia 1999–00 to
2014–15 (AIHW 2018).
Illicit drug use is a complex issue which can contribute to illness,
injury, social and family disruptions, workplace concerns, violence
and crime, community safety issues and fatality (Ministerial Council
on Drug Strategy ). According to the 2016 National Drug Strategy
Household Survey (NDSHS), around 3.1 million people in Australia
aged 14 and over were estimated to have used illicit drugs in the
previous 12 months and 37.1% of Australians aged 14 and over
were estimated to have done so in their lifetime (AIHW
). Both
nationally and internationally, the proportion of people using illicit
drugs has remained relatively stable over the last 10 years—around
15% of adults in Australia, and around 5% of the global adult
population (AIHW 2016; United Nations Office of Drugs and
Crime ).
44 Ministerial Council on Drug Strategy (2011). The National Drug Strategy 2016. Canberra:
Commonwealth of Australia.
45 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2016). National Drug Strategy
Household Survey. Detailed report 2016. Drug statistics series No. 31. Cat. no. PHE 214.
Canberra: AIHW.
44
45
46


46 United Nations Office of Drugs and Crime (2015). World Drug Report. Vienna: United
Nations.
Analysis of the 2017 Australian Secondary Students’ Alcohol and
Drug Survey suggests that an estimated 19% of 12–17-year-olds
had used an illicit drug, up from 16% in 2011. Among secondary
students, misuse of tranquillisers (misuse of a specific
pharmaceutical) (17%) was the most common behaviour of concern
reported to have occurred in their lifetime, followed by
marijuana/cannabis use (15%) (Department of Health ).
47 Department of Health (2017). 2017 Australian Secondary Students’ Alcohol and Drug
Survey. Retrieved from <www.health.gov.au>.
Middle-aged adults
Changing physiological factors, as well as concern over personal
and work-related responsibilities, may contribute to the injury rate of
middle-aged people. Motor vehicle accidents are the most common
cause of accidental death in this age group. Decreased reaction
times and visual acuity may make the middle-aged adult more prone
to accidents. Other unintentional causes of death for middle-aged
adults include falls, fires, burns, poisonings and drownings. Unlike in
the adolescent and young adult age group, the rates of suicide in
females 45–54 years were similar for Indigenous and non-
Indigenous groups (AIHW 2016). Work-related injuries continue to
be a significant safety hazard during the middle years. For further
information, see the Safe Work Australia website
<www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/sites/SWA>.
47


Older adults
Injury prevention is a major concern for older adults. Because vision
is limited, reflexes are slowed and bones are brittle, climbing stairs,
driving a car and even walking require caution. Driving, particularly
night driving, requires caution because accommodation of the eye to
light is impaired and peripheral vision is diminished. Older adults
need to learn to turn their head before changing lanes or crossing a
street and should not rely on side vision. Driving in fog or other
hazardous conditions should be avoided.
Fires are a hazard for an older adult with a failing memory. The older
adult may forget that the iron or the stove has been left on or may
not extinguish a cigarette completely. Because of reduced sensitivity
to pain and heat, care must be taken to prevent burns when the
person bathes or uses heating devices. Taps may be fitted with
temperature control devices to minimise the risk of this occurring.
Older adults at risk of wandering due to organic brain syndromes
need to wear identification devices. They can also be registered with
the local Alzheimer’s Association’s Wanderer’s Alert Program.
Dementia Australia is an excellent resource for advice and support
services. (See <www.dementia.org.au>.)
Because older adults who take analgesics or sedatives may become
lethargic or confused, they should be monitored regularly and
closely. Other measures to induce sleep should be used whenever
possible. Nurses can help elderly adults make the home


environment safe by doing an environmental assessment and
identifying and correcting specific hazards; for example, additional
hand rails can be installed on staircases. The nurse teaches the
importance of taking only prescribed medications and contacting a
health professional at the first indication of medication intolerance.
Clinical consideration
Older adults have trouble seeing the edges of
stairs. Painting white stripes on the edges of the
steps will help increase contrast and may
prevent falls in the person’s home.
Studies from the RADAR (Researched Abuse, Diversion and
Addiction-Related Surveillance) program show an increase in
accidental deaths from opioid use in older people (West & Dart
).
Pillans et al.
 report that an increase in the use of opioids among
older Australians seems to be one of the key factors in the increase
in accidental opioid-induced deaths in this age group. The incidence
of suicide in older adults in Australia, while increasing, is still under-
reported and therefore goes unnoticed, making it difficult to identify
the causes for this.
48 West, N. A. & Dart, R. C. (2015). Prescription opioid exposures and adverse outcomes
among older adults. Pharmacoepidemiology and Drug Safety, 25(5), 539–544.
48
49


49 Pillans, P., Page, C. B., Ilango, S., Kashchuk, A. & Isbister, G. K. (2017). Self-poisoning by
older Australians: A cohort study. The Medical Journal of Australia, 206(4), 164–169.
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
People at risk of harm
Home environmental assessment
History Mrs H has an active, inquisitive toddler, Amy. The
community nurse’s assessment of the home environment
reveals cleaning products in unlocked cupboards, including
bleach-based products accessible to the toddler. It was
apparent that many products had been decanted into
containers which were not labelled correctly or had no labels
at all. Mrs H was receiving home-based nursing care for
wound management and diabetes management.
History Mr P suffered a stroke resulting in left-sided
weakness. As a result, his gait is unsteady. The community
nurse has noticed that his home has several throw rugs and
furniture that can obstruct his mobility.
Touhy and Jett
 indicate some important facts regarding suicide of
the older adult in the US: (a) white men are the most likely to
commit suicide; (b) uncontrollable pain, loss of a loved one and
major life changes can be contributing factors; (c) major depression
and social isolation increase the risk of suicide; and (d) older people
50


do not tend to disclose suicidal intent ahead of attempting to end
their life.
50 Touhy, T. & Jett, K. (2013). Ebersole and Hess’ Gerontological Nursing & Healthy Aging
(4th ed.). St Louis: Mosby.
A study by Koo, Kolves and de Leo  supports the findings above,
commenting that suicide in older Australians remains a public health
issue. The study concluded that risk factors such as psychosocial,
environmental and general aspects of health in later life must also
be considered when assessing for potential to suicide. Nurses need
to be aware of the symptoms and risk factors for suicide. They
should direct the person to the appropriate professional or agency
for treatment and counselling.
51 Koo, Y. W., Kolves, K. & de Leo, D. (2017). Suicide in older adults: A comparison with
middle-aged adults using the Queensland Suicide Register. International Psychogeriatrics,
29(3), 419–430.
Patient education
Safety measures throughout the lifespan
Newborns and infants
Use a government safety-standards-approved infant/child
car seat at all times. Check the temperature of the infant’s
bath water and formula prior to using.
Investigate the infant’s cot for compliance with national
safety regulations: slats no more than 6 cm apart, lead-
51


free paint, height of cot sides, tight fit of mattress to cot.
Use a playpen with sides made of small-size netting.
Never leave playpen sides down.
Provide large soft toys with no small detachable or sharp-
edged parts.
Use guard gates on stairs and screens on windows.
Supervise the infant in swings and highchairs.
Cover electric outlets. Coil cords out of reach.
Place plants, household cleaners and wastepaper baskets
out of reach. Lock away potential poisons, such as
medicines, paint and petrol.
Toddlers
Continue to use approved car seats at all times. Place
children in back seat when travelling in a car, appropriately
restrained.
Keep objects with sharp edges (such as furniture and
knives) out of children’s reach.
Place hot saucepans on back burners with handles turned
inwards.
Keep cleaning solutions, insecticides and medicines in
locked cupboards.
Keep windows and balconies screened.
Supervise toddlers in the bath.
Fence pools and supervise toddlers at all times when in or
near pools. Cover outlets with safety covers or plugs.


Preschoolers
Teach children not to put small objects in the mouth, nose
and ears.
Always supervise preschoolers crossing streets and begin
safety teaching about obeying traffic signals and looking
both ways.
Teach children to play in ‘safe’ areas
Teach preschoolers the dangers of playing with matches
and playing near fire and heating appliances.
Teach children to avoid strangers and keep parents
informed of their whereabouts.
Teach preschoolers not to walk in front of swings and not
to push others off playground equipment.
School-age children
Teach children safety rules for recreational and sports
activities: never swim alone, always wear a lifejacket when
in a boat and wear a protective helmet and knee and
elbow pads when needed.
Supervise contact sports and activities in which children
aim at a target.
Teach children to obey all traffic and safety rules for
bicycling, skateboarding and roller skating.
Teach children to use light-coloured or reflective clothing
when walking or cycling at night.


Teach children safe ways to use the stove, garden tools
and other equipment.
Supervise children when they use saws, electric
appliances, tools and other potentially dangerous
equipment.
Teach children to avoid excavations, quarries, vacant
buildings and playing around heavy machinery.
Teach children the health hazards of smoking. If you
smoke, stop.
Teach children the effects of drugs and alcohol on
judgment and coordination.
Adolescents
Set firm limits on car use; namely, never to drive after
drinking or using drugs and never to ride with a driver who
has done so. Encourage adolescents to call home for a lift
if they have been drinking, assuring them they can do so
without a reprimand.
Advise adolescents to always wear a safety helmet when
riding motorcycles, scooters and other sports vehicles.
Teach safety rules for water sports.
Encourage adolescents to use proper equipment when
participating in sports. Encourage adolescents to swim,
jog and go boating in groups so they can obtain help in
case of an accident.
Teach safety measures for use of power tools.


Inform the adolescent of the dangers of drugs, alcohol
and unprotected sex. Include teaching about personal
safety and self-defence.
Be alert to changes in the adolescent’s mood and
behaviour. Listen to and maintain open communication
with the adolescent. Monitor adolescents’ use of online
environments and be aware of the potential for
cyberbullying and other negative online activities.
Set a good example of behaviour that the adolescent can
follow.
Young adults
Reinforce motor vehicle safety: drive defensively, use
‘designated drivers’ if alcohol is consumed, routinely check
brakes and tyres, seatbelts must be used by all
passengers.
Discuss evaluating the potential for workplace injuries or
death when making decisions about a career or
occupation. Encourage the young adult to participate
actively in programs that reduce occupational hazards. All
workplaces in Australia must provide a work, health and
safety induction program for new employees.
Discuss avoiding excessive sun radiation by limiting
exposure, using sun-blocking agents and wearing
protective clothing. Explain the skin changes that may
indicate a cancerous condition.


Encourage young adults who are struggling with the
pressures, responsibilities and expectations of adulthood
to seek counselling.
Advise young people about the dangers of binge drinking
and taking illicit substances—encourage harm
minimisation rather than prohibition.
Middle-aged adults
Reinforce motor vehicle safety: seatbelts to be used at all
times and driving within the designated speed limit,
especially at night. Test visual acuity periodically.
Ensure that stairways in premises are well lit and
uncluttered.
Equip bathrooms with hand grasps and non-skid
bathmats.
Test smoke detectors and fire alarms regularly.
Keep all machines and tools in good working condition at
work and at home. Follow safety precautions when using
machinery.
Reinforce safety measures taught earlier in life, such as
the hazards of excessive sun exposure.
Older adults
Encourage the person to have vision and hearing tests
annually.
Assist the person to have a home hazard appraisal.


Encourage the person to keep as active as possible.
Preventive measures
Ensure glasses are functional.
Ensure appropriate lighting.
Mark doorways and edges of steps as needed.
Keep environment tidy and uncluttered.
Set safe limits to activities.
Remove unsafe objects.
Wear shoes or well-fitted slippers with non-skid soles.
Use ambulatory devices as necessary (cane, crutches,
walking frame, braces, wheelchair).
Provide assistance with ambulation as needed.
Monitor gait and balance.
Adapt living arrangements to one floor if necessary.
Encourage exercise and activity as tolerated to maintain
muscle strength, joint flexibility and balance.
Ensure uncluttered environment with securely fastened
rugs.
Encourage person to request assistance.
Keep bed in the low position.
Install grab bars in bathroom.
Provide raised toilet seat.
Instruct person to rise slowly from a lying to sitting to
standing position and to stand in place for several
seconds before walking.
Provide a bedside commode as needed.


Assist with voiding on a frequent and scheduled basis.
Encourage person to summon help.
Monitor activity tolerance.
Attach side rails to the bed.
Keep rails in place when the bed is in the lowest position.
Monitor orientation and alertness status.
Encourage annual or more frequent review of all
medications prescribed.
Safety problems across the lifespan
Domestic violence is increasing at an alarming rate and involves
individuals of all ages. It includes child abuse, intimate partner abuse
and older adult abuse, and affects the health and safety of families
and the community. The AIHW estimates that 2.2 million Australians
have experienced violence (including sexual violence) from their
partner (AIHW 2019). In 2013, the Australian Bureau of Statistics
published a directory Defining the Data Challenge for Family,
Domestic and Sexual Violence, Australia 2013. The directory
contributes to the National Plan to Reduce Violence Against Women
and their Children 2010−2022.
The report indicates the complexities inherent in defining domestic
violence, noting that any definition would have to include behaviours
and relationships. The impacts of family and domestic violence can
have profound psychological, financial and social consequences for


those directly involved, with flow-on effects to the community and
social structures (ABS ).
52 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2013). Defining the Data Challenge for Family,
Domestic and Sexual Violence, Australia 2013. Cat. no. 4529.0. 2014. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au>.
Promoting safety in the health care setting
All states and territories in Australia now require potential health care
employees to have police checks done as part of the employment
process. This applies to university students going on clinical
placements as part of their studies. In the aged care sector, police
checks are required for health care workers and volunteers.
Inherent in the roles and functions of all health care professionals is
the promotion of safety and wellbeing to patients through the
provision of safe, quality care which can be measured. The
ACSQHC is the peak body for overseeing safety and quality in the
health care workplace.
Preventing specific hazards in
communities and health care facilities
Implementing measures to prevent specific hazards or injuries such
as burns, fires, falls, poisoning, suffocation, electrocution and so on
are critical aspects of community nursing care. Teaching people
about safety is another important aspect. Nurses working in inpatient
52


settings usually have opportunities to educate their patients while
providing care and should take advantage of these opportunities.
Scalds and burns
A scald
 is a burn from a hot liquid or vapour such as steam. A
burn
 results from excessive exposure to thermal, chemical,
electric or radioactive agents.
Common home hazards causing scalds include the following:
saucepan handles that protrude over the edge of a stove
electric appliances used to heat liquids or oils, especially those
with dangling cords that are within reach of crawling infants and
young children
excessively hot bath water.
In health care organisations, the risk of scalds and burns is greater
for people whose skin sensitivity to temperature is impaired. Scalds
can occur from overly hot bath water, hot-water bottles or hot packs,
and burns can occur from therapeutic applications of heat (see
Chapter 37
). It is important for the nurse to assess how well
individuals can protect themselves and what special precautions, if
any, need to be taken. The use of hot- water bottles in the aged care
setting is banned.
Fires


Fires continue to be a constant risk in both health care settings and
homes. A fire in a health care organisation usually results from
malfunctioning electrical equipment or combustion of anaesthetic
gases. Home fires most frequently result from careless disposal of
burning cigarettes or matches, from fat or oil catching fire or from
faulty electric wiring.
Health care/community/aged care facilities
In these facilities, fire is particularly hazardous when people are
incapacitated and unable to leave the building without assistance. All
health and aged care facilities in Australia have an emergency
evacuation plan to be implemented in times of fire. Staff who are
designated and trained as floor wardens have the responsibility of
working with emergency services to evacuate buildings. This
emergency training is a mandatory competency for all clinical and
non-clinical staff and is embedded in a health care/aged care
facility’s risk management strategy. Staff must know how to:
protect and evacuate people who are in immediate danger
report the fire
contain the fire
extinguish the fire.
Extinguishing the fire requires knowledge of three categories of fire,
classified according to the type of material that is burning:
Class A: paper, wood, upholstery, rags, ordinary rubbish
Class B: flammable liquids and gases


Class C: electrical.
The right type of extinguisher must be used to fight the fire.
Extinguishers have picture symbols showing the type of fire for
which they are to be used. Directions for use are also attached.
Home fire safety
Nursing interventions focus on teaching fire safety to people living in
their own homes. Preventive measures include the following:
Keep emergency numbers near the telephone or stored for
speed dialling.
Be sure the smoke alarms are operable and appropriately
located.
Teach people to change the batteries in their smoke alarms twice
a year at the changeover of daylight saving.
Have a family ‘fire drill’ plan. Every member needs to know the
plan for the nearest exit from different locations of the home.
People living in regional areas, especially in densely vegetated
areas, need to have a fire evacuation plan to be implemented
during bushfires.
Keep fire extinguishers available and accessible and in working
order.
Falls
People of any age can fall, but infants and older adults are
particularly prone to falling and causing serious injury to themselves.


Falls are the leading cause of injuries among older adults. Most falls
occur in the home and are a major threat to the independence of
older adults. Fear of falling is common in older adults, even in those
who have not experienced a fall. This fear is of particular concern for
those who live alone and who anticipate being helpless and unable
to summon help after a fall. For these individuals, the nurse should
encourage daily or more frequent contact with a friend or family
member, installation of a personal emergency response system and
measures to maintain a physical environment that prevents falls.
Risk factors and associated preventive measures are shown in
Table 33.4
. See also the ACSQHC website, which provides the
latest research and information relating to falls prevention.
Table 33.4 Risk factors and preventive measures for falls
Clinical consideration
Falls can cause fractures and soft tissue injury
and reduce self-confidence, leading to fear of
falling. This fear prompts decreased activity
levels and decreased muscle strength, which
increase the risk of falling.
Older people, because of physiological and psychological processes
associated with the ageing process, tend to be at a greater risk of


falling than younger adults. There are a number of validated risk
assessment tools available to nurses and to other health
professionals that may be used to assess a person’s risk of falling.
These risk assessment tools may be used in a variety of health care
environments (Matarese et al.
) and appropriate assessment tools
and questioning techniques, along with an assessment of the
person’s environment, can help the nurse recommend safety
measures to the person and family.
53 Matarese, M., Ivziku, D., Bartolozzi, F., Piredda, M. & De Marinis, M. G. (2014).
Systematic review of fall risk screening tools for older patients in acute hospitals. Journal of
Advanced Nursing, 71(6), 1198–1209.
The Department of Health and Ageing released Natframe, an
assessment framework designed to provide for initial:
assessment of those entering care and for continuing evaluation
reassessment and planning of care throughout their residence
(Department of Health and Ageing , updated 2018).
54 Department of Health and Ageing (2012a). Natframe. Retrieved from
<http://webarchive.nla.gov.au>.
Natframe was designed to help communicate and deliver high-
quality care for older people. It provides for initial assessment of
those entering care and for continuing evaluation, reassessment and
planning of care throughout their residency (Department of Health
and Ageing 2012a).
53
54


Prevention of falls in health care organisations is an ongoing
concern. Health care environments are designed with many safety
features to reduce the risk of falls, such as railings along corridors;
buzzers at each bedside; safety bars in toilet areas; locks on beds,
wheelchairs and trolleys; side rails on beds; night-lights; and so on.
In addition, nurses can implement measures to decrease the
incidence of falls (see the following ‘Practice guidelines’).
Clinical consideration
When a person falls, the nurse’s first duty is to
the person. First, assess for injuries. Then notify
the doctor.
Practice guidelines
Prevention of falls in health/residential care facilities
On admission, orient people to their surroundings and
explain the call system.
Carefully assess the person’s ability to ambulate and
transfer. Provide walking aids and assistance as required.
Closely supervise the people at risk of falls, especially at
night.
Encourage the person to use the buzzer to request
assistance. Ensure that the buzzer is within easy reach.


Place bedside tables and other tables near the bed or
chair so that people do not overreach and consequently
lose their balance.
Always keep hospital beds in the low position and wheels
locked when not providing care so that individuals can
move in or out of bed easily.
Encourage individuals to use grab bars mounted in toilet
and bathing areas and railings along corridors.
Make sure non-skid bath mats are available in tubs and
showers.
Encourage the person to wear non-skid footwear.
Keep the environment tidy; especially keep light cords
from underfoot and furniture out of the way.
Use individualised interventions (e.g. alarm sensitive to a
person’s position) rather than side rails for confused
people.
Although it may seem that raising the side rails on a bed is an
effective method of preventing falls, rails should not be raised
routinely for this purpose. Research has shown that people with
memory impairment, altered mobility, nocturia and other sleep
disorders are prone to becoming entrapped in side rails and may, in
fact, be more likely to fall trying to get out of bed by going around or
over the raised rails (Morse, Merry & Bloswick ).
55 Morse, J., Merry, A. & Bloswick, D. (2017). Research approaches to the prevention and
protection of patient falls. In: H. Hsiao (Ed.), Fall Prevention and Protection: Principles,
Guidelines and Practices. Boca Raton: Taylor & Francis.
55


Electronic devices are available to detect that people are attempting
to move or get out of bed. A bed or chair safety monitoring
device
 has a position-sensitive switch that triggers an audio alarm
when the person attempts to get out of the bed or chair. Skill
33.1
 describes how to use these devices.
Home care considerations
Using a bed or chair exit safety monitoring device
If the device is used in the home, instruct caregivers to
do the following:
Test the monitoring device every 12 to 24 hours to
ensure that it is working.
Check the volume of the alarm to ascertain they
can hear it.
Use of the device does not take the place of proper
supervision of people at risk of falling. Assessment of
the reasons for falling, especially among older adults,
can lead to effective prevention.


Promoting safety in the community
Nurses play an important role in educating the community about
safety. Nursing is one of the most trusted professions and you will
often be called upon for advice about lifespan safety in the general
community. Nurses are commonly asked for advice or information
on how to manage accidental poisoning, keeping toddlers safe from
choking and first aid considerations such as managing a choking
episode.
Poisoning
Children/toddlers generally ingest toxic substances accidentally, but
deliberate overdose is increasing in the adolescent age group (see
Box 33.6
). Statistically, in Australia, approximately 50 children per
week present with toxicology- related symptoms. Seventy per cent
of these presentations are due to inappropriate ingestion of
medications (see Box 33.7
). Similar statistics come from New
Zealand presentations of children under 5 years of age (Parkinson et
al.
).
56 Parkinson, S., Cadogan, M., Armstrong, J. & Nickson, C. (2015a). Toxicological
emergencies. In K. Curtis & C. Ramsden (Eds), Emergency and Trauma Care. Sydney:
Elsevier Australia.
BO X
56


33.6 Ingesting poisons
When a child swallows poison:
Never try to induce vomiting.
Pick up the product container and take it with you to the
phone. The Poisons Information Centre will want to know
what ingredients are in the product.
Read and follow label directions on all products before
using them.
Do not keep poisonous plants in the home and avoid
planting poisonous plants in the yard. Check the
identification of poisonous plants with the Department of
Agriculture in your state, the CSIRO or the Poisons
Information Centre.
Display the telephone number of the Poisons Information
Centre 13 11 26 in a prominent place near or on all
telephones in the home so that it is available to
babysitters, family and friends.
For more information about what to do when a child swallows
poison, see the Poisoning factsheet from Kidsafe .
57 Kidsafe (2019). Poisoning. Retrieved from <www.kidsafevic.com.au/>.
BO X
57


33.7 Management of a toddler/child
who has ingested unidentified
tablets/pills
A minimum observation period of 12 hours is
recommended for a toddler/child who is suspected of
ingesting unidentified tablets.
Nurses should ensure they have access to sufficient
resources when the child shows signs of toxicity.
Assessment for IV insertion is made on the level of clinical
and emotional distress.
Blood glucose levels need to be checked on admission to
eliminate hypoglycaemia.
The ISBAR tool should be used to hand over the child’s
clinical condition to other staff.
There must be regular observations of vital signs and level
of consciousness to detect any changes in the clinical
condition (frequency of observations is determined by the
child’s clinical condition and/or clinical policies/guidelines).
Cardiac monitoring may be indicated by observed
changes in the child’s clinical condition.
Discharge to occur once the child is symptom free and
during the day.
Source: Adapted from S. Parkinson, M. Cadogan, J. Armstrong & C. Nickson (2015a). Toxicological
emergencies. In K. Curtis & C. Ramsden (Eds), Emergency and Trauma Care (p. 743). Sydney:


Elsevier Australia.
Table 33.5
 shows potentially lethal medications if ingested by
toddlers. Nurses must have a good knowledge of pharmacology if
they are to deal with this sort of emergency. Note: it is important to
treat the child and not the poison.
Table 33.5 Potentially lethal medications if two tablets are
ingested by a 10 kg toddler
Source: Adapted from S. Parkinson, M. Cadogan, J. Armstrong & C. Nickson (2015a). Toxicological emergencies.
In K. Curtis & C. Ramsden (Eds), Emergency and Trauma Care (pp. 725−744). Sydney: Elsevier Australia.
Poisoning, whether deliberate or accidental, is the leading cause of
death in people under 40 years of age. Over all groups, the most
commonly ingested substances are:
alcohol and toxic alcohols—toxic alcohols include methanol,
glycol and isopropyl alcohol
analgesics—aspirin, paracetamol
anticonvulsants
antidepressants
antipsychotics
cardiac drugs
calcium channel blockers
digoxin
colchicine
lithium carbonate
herbicides


glyphosate—intentional ingestion can be life threatening
insecticides
organophosphates and carbamates—intentional ingestion is
potentially life threatening and there is the potential for cross-
contamination between the person and treating health
professionals.
Adequate resuscitation of people who have ingested these
substances is often compromised/delayed because of beliefs that
staff may be ‘poisoned’ following exposure, and also because of the
implementation of HAZMAT precautions in the pre-hospital period,
which delays transport to emergency departments, and/or refusal
into emergency departments (Parkinson et al. 2015a) (see Box
33.8
).

33.8 Risk assessment approach to
managing poisonings in hospital
settings
A risk assessment approach should be adopted when treating
an individual presenting with poisoning.
Steps for constructing a risk assessment are:
agent(s) or medications


dose or doses
time since ingestion
clinical symptoms on presentation and from history
other individual clinical factors (weight and other
comorbidities). Weight is especially important when
treating children.
Resuscitation steps for managing
poisonings
Airway
Breathing
Circulation
Control seizures
Correct hypoglycaemia
Correct hyperthermia
Consider possible resuscitation antidotes
Investigations for poisonings
Screening—toxicology screening: blood pictures,
pathophysiology
Specific investigations
12 lead ECG
Decontamination following poisonings


Enhanced elimination
– Multiple dose activated charcoal
Carbamazepine
Dapsone
Phenobarbitone
Theophylline
Quinine
Haemodialysis and haemofiltration for
treating overdoses of:
Lithium
Metformin lactic acidosis
Potassium
Salicylates
Theophylline
Toxic alcohols
Valproic acid
The purpose of enhanced elimination is to reduce the severity
and duration of the ingested agent. Enhanced elimination
techniques are useful only if they can reduce mortality, further
complications and length of stay (Parkinson et al. 2015a).


Urinary alkinisation
Phenobarbitone
Salicylate
Charcoal haemoperfusion
Theophylline
Antidotes
Antidotes are the drugs used to correct the effects of
poisoning and, contrary to popular beliefs and in fiction,
not all poisons have a corresponding antidote. Antidotes,
as with all medications, have specific indications and
contraindications
Routes of administration
Appropriate therapeutic endpoints
Monitoring requirements
The potential for adverse effects (Parkinson et al. 2015a,
p. 731)
Antidotes are administered when the potential therapeutic
benefits are determined to outweigh the potential adverse
events, costs and resource requirements (Parkinson et al.
2015a, p. 731).


Iron overload is common in children receiving blood transfusions for
cancers or blood disorders. Iron directly corrodes the gastric
mucosa and in large doses acts as a cellular toxin on the liver, heart
and central nervous system. In clinically poisoned people including
children, initial presentation is vomiting and diarrhoea, which then
progresses to increasing acidosis, shock and multi-organ failure
(Parkinson et al. 2015a).
See Box 33.9
 for management of an acute poisoning episode.
BO X
33.9 Managing an acute poisoning
episode
Check the person’s airway, breathing and circulation.
Do a complete physical assessment and history noting
that poisoning from certain classes of medication,
especially anticholinergics, opioids and
sympathomimetics, result in a suite of symptoms known
as toxidromes that show as delirium, hyperthermia, ileus,
mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention and warm dry
skin, especially the anticholinergic class of drugs.
Take blood for laboratory tests to check for electrolyte
imbalance, liver and renal impairment.


Unless a specific antidote is available, management is
supportive in the majority of cases because less than 1% of
poisonings are fatal. This could be higher in children.
Use single-dose activated charcoal
This is the preferred treatment in the majority of poisonings
because it prevents gut absorption of the drug, but it may be
contraindicated with some medications which require specific
therapies (Juurlink ).
58 Juurlink, D. N. (2015). Activated charcoal for acute overdose: A reappraisal.
British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, 81(3), 482–487.
Monitoring People who are clinically unstable require
ongoing monitoring and treatment to correct hypoxia and
acidosis and maintain adequate circulation. Even when
people appear to be responding to treatment, their
condition may deteriorate rapidly.
Resuscitation is always the first priority and cardiac arrest
treatment should follow usual advanced life support
guidelines.
People who have attempted suicide should have a
psychiatric assessment and appropriate ongoing care.
People with a history of illicit substance use should be
referred to the drug and alcohol team for assessment and
care.
All interventions need to be evaluated and the outcomes
documented in the person’s record.
58
