. General management of poisoned patients. In J. E. Tintinalli, S.
Stapczynski, O. J. Ma, D. M. Yealy, G. D. Meckler & D. M. Cline (Eds), Tintinalli’s Emergency
Medicine: A Comprehensive Study Guide (8th ed.). New York: McGraw-Hill.
59 Greene, S. (2018). General management of poisoned patients. In J. E. Tintinalli, S. Stapczynski, O.
J. Ma, D. M. Yealy, G. D. Meckler & D. M. Cline (Eds), Tintinalli’s Emergency Medicine: A
Comprehensive Study Guide (8th ed.). New York: McGraw-Hill.
Envenomation
Australia is home to a large number of deadly land- and marine-
based creatures. The increasing urbanisation of the country has
meant that a large number of land-based venomous creatures are
finding their way into metropolitan backyards. Venom is the
poisonous secretion of an animal and is released following a bite or
sting from snakes, spiders and scorpions (Parkinson et al.
, p.
747). All people are at risk from being bitten by a snake, but the
most vulnerable are toddlers and young children, and adults working
in gardens. If bitten by a snake, the appropriate first aid treatment
for bites and stings is as follows.
60 Parkinson, S., Nickson, C., Armstrong, J. & Cadogan, M. (2015b). Envenomation. In K.
Curtis & C. Ramsden (Eds), Emergency and Trauma Care. Sydney: Elsevier Australia.
Pre-hospital treatment
Apply a pressure immobilisation bandage. This delays the
lymphatic spread of venom proximally from the bite site. It is
used for bites from funnel web spiders and the blue-ringed
59
60


octopus. The principles of the pressure immobilisation bandage
are:
– Apply a firm broad bandage (preferably elasticised) directly
over the bite site and extend it proximally over the whole of the
affected limb.
– Use firm pressure to occlude lymphatic flow but preserve blood
flow, as for supporting a sprained ankle.
– Check for distal pulse to ensure adequate blood flow.
– Include fingers and toes in the bandage to reduce limb
movement.
– Splint the limb to further restrict movement.
– Immobilise the limb and person.
– Do not elevate the limb.
Hospital treatment
Resuscitation
Risk assessment of possible physiological outcomes
Determine if the person is envenomed. Regular assessment
observation for at least 12 hours, including history and physical
assessments, vital signs, including consciousness levels,
laboratory investigations
If envenomed:
– determine the type of monovalent anti-venom required
– determine geographical area (type of snake, spider common to
the area)


– determine clinical and laboratory features
– utilise Snake Venom Detection Kit (SVDK)
– administer the dose of monovalent anti-venom required (for
children this is calculated per kg/body weight)
– supply supportive treatment (Parkinson et al. 2015b, pp.
747−762).
Lifespan considerations
Management of acute poisoning from
medication ingestion
Acute poisoning from medication ingestion occurs frequently
either by accident (children accessing medications or other
toxic products; elderly people overmedicating due to memory
loss) or by deliberate self-poisonings (self-harm or suicide).
A child presenting after swallowing an unknown tablet/pill
presents a complex clinical scenario to treating clinicians (see
Boxes 33.7
 and 33.8
). On admission, every effort
should be made to identify the tablet/pill swallowed by the
child. If this is not possible, the child should be observed for a
minimum of 8 hours and not discharged overnight. The
administration of activated charcoal should only occur if there
is evidence that a lethal dose has been ingested and this only


after a clinical toxicologist has been consulted (Poisons
Information Centre Australia 13 11 26; New Zealand
0800 764 766).
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Carbon monoxide
 (CO) is an odourless, colourless, tasteless
gas that is very toxic. Exposure to CO can cause symptoms
including headaches, dizziness, weakness, nausea, vomiting or loss
of muscle control. Prolonged exposure to CO can lead to
unconsciousness, brain damage or death. Learning the steps to
prevent CO exposure is particularly important because all petrol-
powered vehicles, lawn mowers, kerosene stoves, barbecues and
burning wood emit CO. Incomplete or faulty combustion of any fuel,
including natural gas used in furnaces, also produces CO. CO
detectors are available for the home.
Suffocation or choking
Suffocation, or asphyxiation
, is lack of oxygen due to interrupted
breathing. Suffocation occurs when the air source is cut off for any
reason. One common reason for choking is that food or a foreign
object has become lodged in the throat. Guidelines for managing
choking or suffocation have been developed by the Australian
Resuscitation Council (ARC) (ARC ). Airway obstruction may be
partial or complete and may occur in the conscious or unconscious
61


person. For the ARC flowchart for management of airway
obstruction caused by a foreign body, see Figure 33.7
.
61 Australian Resuscitation Council (ARC) (2016a). Guideline 4-Airway. Retrieved from
<www.resus.org.au>.
Figure 33.7


Management of foreign body airway obstruction (choking).
Source: Adapted from Australian Resuscitation Council
. ANZCOR Foreign Body Airway Obstruction (Choking)
Flowchart, <www.resus.org.au/>.
62 Australian Resuscitation Council (2016b). ANZCOR Foreign Body Airway Obstruction
(Choking) Flowchart. Retrieved from <www.resus.org.au>.
Some common causes of airway obstruction are:
relaxation of airway muscles in the unconscious person
inhaling of a foreign body—fish bones, for example, in adults or
small objects such as coins in infants or young children
any trauma to the airway including a sharp blow to the larynx
anaphylactic reactions.
The signs and symptoms will depend on the cause and severity. This
may be sudden or gradual in onset and may result in complete
obstruction very quickly. Therefore, the person must be observed
closely and continuously.
The conscious person who presents with an airway obstruction will
show signs of extreme agitation, make gasping sounds, cough
62


continuously and may lose their voice, ending with the universal sign
for choking—clutching the neck with thumb and fingers.
In the unconscious person, all muscles are relaxed and if left lying
on their back, the person’s tongue will fall against the back wall of
the throat preventing air from entering the lungs. In the unconscious
person, care of the airway takes precedence over any other injury,
including the possibility of spinal injury. Individuals should be turned
to the side and the mouth opened and turned slightly downwards to
allow any obvious foreign materials to drain out using gravity.
Dentures, if loose, can be removed but well-fitted dentures may be
left in. If the airway is blocked with fluid (blood or vomit) the person
should be turned to the side with the head and neck well supported
(see Box 33.10
).
BO X
33.10 Management of airway
obstruction
Signs and symptoms of airway
obstruction
Partial obstruction


Breathing is laboured.
Breathing may be noisy.
Some air escaping from the mouth may be felt.
Complete obstruction
There may be some attempts at breathing.
There is no sound of breathing.
No air is escaping from the nose or mouth.
For unresponsive adults and children, the airway may be
opened using the chin lift manoeuvre.
Chin lift manoeuvre
Head tilt/chin lift: One hand is placed on the forehead or the
top of the head. The other hand is used to provide the chin
lift. The head not the neck is tilted backwards. Excessive
force is not to be applied, especially in cases where a spinal
injury is suspected. The chin lift may be used in conjunction
with the backward head tilt. In this, the person’s chin is held
up by the nurse’s/rescuer’s thumb and fingers in order to
open the mouth and to pull the tongue and soft tissues
forward and away from the back of the throat (see Figure
33.8
).
Figure 33.8


Chin lift and backward head tilt.
Source: © St John Ambulance Australia Inc.
Children and infants
An infant is defined as being up to 1 year of age and a child is
1 year to 8 years of age (ARC 2016a).
Children are treated as adults when maintaining an open
airway, but there are some points that need to be
remembered when dealing with children or infants:
Upper airways of children are easily obstructed because
of their narrow nasal passages, entrance to the vocal
cords and the trachea.
The trachea is soft and pliable and may be distorted by
excessive backward head tilt or jaw thrust. The head
should be kept neutral. Maximum head tilt should not be
used in children or infants.
The lower jaw should be supported at the point of the chin
and the mouth kept open and no pressure on the soft
neck tissues.
If the airways are not clear using these manoeuvres, the
child’s head may be tilted very slightly with a light
movement.
Back blows


An ineffective cough indicates a severe obstruction. If the
victim is conscious, call an ambulance then administer five
sharp back blows with the heel of one hand in the middle of
the back between the shoulder blades (Figure 33.9
).
Check to see if each back blow has relieved the airway
obstruction. The aim is to relieve the obstruction with each
back blow rather than to give all five blows. An infant may be
placed in a head-downwards supine position prior to
delivering the back blows, which will not be as an intense as
for an adult. It is important that you do not cause further
injury to a child or infant (up to 1 year of age) when delivering
back blows or chest thrusts.
Figure 33.9


Alternating back blows and chest thrusts.
Source: © St John Ambulance Australia Inc.
Chest thrusts
If back blows are unsuccessful, perform up to five chest
thrusts. Check to see if each thrust has relieved the airway
obstruction. The aim is for each chest thrust to relieve the
obstruction rather than to give all five thrusts. To perform
chest thrusts, identify the same compression point as for
CPR and give up to five chest thrusts. An infant should be
placed in a head-downwards supine position across the
rescuer’s thigh. If the obstruction is not relieved, continue
alternating five back blows with five chest thrusts.
An airway obstruction causes the diaphragm muscle to work
harder to achieve adequate ventilations. The abdomen will
continue to move out but there will be a loss of the natural
rise of the chest (paradoxical movement) and an in-drawing
of the spaces between the ribs and above the collar bones
during respiration.
Assessing and documenting the effectiveness of the back
blows and chest thrusts is an important nursing function. It is
important to document this event, including the time the
resuscitation procedures have taken, for the paramedics if
such a situation occurs outside a health care facility, as this
forms an integral part of the person’s medical history and
could influence ongoing diagnosis and treatment.


Other causes of airway obstruction are drowning, gas or smoke
inhalation, accidental coverage of the nose and mouth by a piece of
plastic, accidental strangulation by the shoulder harness of a
seatbelt and being trapped in a confined space (e.g. a discarded
refrigerator). If a person does not receive immediate relief from
suffocation, the interrupted breathing leads to respiratory and
cardiac arrest and death. Any obstruction to the air passages must
be immediately removed and life-support measures instituted when
an arrest occurs.
Excessive noise
Excessive noise is a health hazard that can cause hearing loss,
depending on (a) the overall level of noise, (b) the frequency range
of the noise and (c) the duration of exposure and individual
susceptibility.
Sound levels above 120 decibels (units of loudness) are painful and
may cause hearing damage even if a person is exposed for only a
short period. Exposure to 85 to 95 decibels for several hours a day
can lead to progressive or permanent hearing loss. Noise levels
below 85 decibels usually do not affect hearing.
When ill or injured, people are frequently sensitive to noises that
normally would not disturb them. Loud voices, the clatter of dishes
and even a nearby television can disturb people. Physiological
effects of noise include (a) increased heart and respiratory rates, (b)


increased muscular activity, (c) nausea and (d) hearing loss, if the
noise is sufficiently loud.
Noise can be minimised in several ways. Acoustic tiles on ceilings,
walls and floors as well as curtains and carpeting absorb sound.
Background music can mask noise and have a calming effect on
some people. It is important for nurses to minimise noise in the
hospital setting and to encourage people to protect their hearing as
much as possible.
Electrical hazards
All electrical equipment must be properly grounded. The electric plug
of grounded equipment has three prongs. The two short prongs
transmit the power to the equipment. The third, longer prong is the
grounding device, which carries short circuits or stray electric current
to the ground. Grounding prongs offer a path of least resistance to
stray electric currents. All electrical equipment must comply with
Australian standards for electrical safety.
Faulty equipment, such as equipment with a frayed cord, presents a
danger of electric shock or may start a fire. For example, an electric
spark near certain anaesthetic gases or a high concentration of
oxygen can cause a serious fire. Actions to reduce electrical hazards
are described in ‘Patient education’.
When major electrical injury (macro-shock) does occur, the person
may sustain both superficial and deep burns, muscle contractions


and cardiac and respiratory arrest, necessitating cardiopulmonary
resuscitation and life support. Electric shock
 occurs when a
current travels through the body to the ground rather than through
electric wiring or from static electricity that builds up on the body.
Using machines in good repair, wearing shoes with rubber soles,
standing on a non-conductive floor and using non-conductive gloves
can prevent macro-shock. However, even with such precautions the
rescuer must know that the person is not to be touched until the
electricity is turned off or the person has been removed from contact
with the electric current; otherwise the rescuer may also receive an
electrical injury.
Firearms
In Australia, following the Port Arthur shootings in 1996, possession
of firearms is regulated by a federal Act of Parliament (Attorney-
General’s Department
). The legislation is monitored by state and
territory police forces, with each state and territory maintaining a
firearms registry.
63 Attorney-General’s Department (2016b). Firearms Regulations. Retrieved from
<www.ag.gov.au>.
Parents who bring a handgun into the home must accept full
responsibility for teaching safety rules to any children who have
knowledge of the presence of firearms. The following basic firearm
safety rules must be implemented for any gun:
63


Store all guns in sturdy locked cabinets without glass and make
sure the keys are inaccessible to children.
Store the bullets in a different location from the guns.
Tell children never to touch a gun or stay in a friend’s house
where a gun is accessible.
Teach children never to point the barrel of a gun at anyone.
Ensure the firearm is unloaded and the action is open when
handing it to someone else.
Don’t handle firearms while affected by alcohol or drugs of any
kind, including pharmaceuticals.
When cleaning or dry firing a firearm, remove all ammunition to
another room and double-check the firearm prior to cleaning it.
Have firearms that are used regularly inspected by a qualified
gunsmith at least every 2 years.
Radiation
Radiation injury can occur from overexposure to radioactive
materials used in diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. People
being examined using radiography or fluoroscopy generally receive
minimal exposure and few precautions are necessary. Nurses need
to protect themselves, however, from radiation when some people
are receiving radiation therapy. Exposure to radiation can be
minimised by (a) limiting the time near the source, (b) providing as
much distance as possible from the source and (c) using shielding
devices such as lead aprons when near the source. Nurses need to
become familiar with organisation protocols related to radiation
therapy.


Patient education
Reducing electrical hazards
Check cords for fraying or other signs of damage before
using an appliance. Do not use if damage is apparent.
Avoid overloading outlets and fuse boxes with too many
appliances.
It is now mandatory for all new dwellings to have safety
trip switches installed. These switches cut off power when
a fault occurs or in times of high demand (the use of
multiple pieces of electrical equipment).
Use only grounded outlets and plugs.
Always pull a plug from the wall outlet by firmly grasping
the plug and pulling it straight out. Pulling a plug by its
cord can damage the cord and plug unit.
Never use electric appliances near sinks, bathtubs,
showers or other wet areas, because water readily
conducts electricity.
Keep electric cords and appliances out of the reach of
young children.
Place protective covers over wall outlets to protect young
children.
Have all non-insulated wiring in the home altered to meet
safety standards.
Carefully read instructions before operating electrical
equipment. People who do not understand how to operate
the equipment should seek advice.


Always disconnect appliances before cleaning or repairing
them.
Unplug any appliance that has given a tingling sensation
or shock and have an electrician evaluate it for stray
current.
Keep electric cords coiled or taped to the ground away
from areas of traffic to prevent others from damaging the
cords or tripping over them.
Bioterrorism attack
No one knows when a bioterrorism attack will occur. Thus, it is
important that health care personnel and facilities plan and prepare
for the unknown. The EMA website (EMA 2013) provides information
for managing pre-hospital disasters. The agency is the key access
point for emergency management information from the Australian
government, including disaster planning and national emergency
management of health, community and residential aged care
organisations.
Terrorism attacks
All emergency departments now have policies, procedures and
protocols for managing mass casualty events resulting from terrorist
attacks and other sources of multiple trauma.
Procedure- and equipment-related accidents


Risk assessment in the health care setting must include risks related
to procedures and equipment. Whether giving a medication or
assisting a person out of bed, nurses need to follow safeguards to
prevent errors or accidents. Most health care organisations establish
protocols that are designed to prevent accidents. When in doubt
about a course of action, the nurse should consult the appropriate
written guidelines before proceeding. As part of all purchasing
agreements, all Australian health care and aged care organisations
will ensure onsite training for staff in the use of new equipment and
procedures and protocols prior to the equipment being introduced
into practice. In highly specialised areas of clinical practice, nurses
need to demonstrate competencies in the use of specialist
equipment. It becomes a mandatory competency and is embedded
in the individual nurse’s performance management program, which
is an integral component of risk management.
When an accident or error does occur, all health, community and
aged care facilities are required to report the incident so that it can
be investigated and recorded and remedial action can be taken.
There may be different reporting mechanisms for each state and
territory Department of Health, so you need to know the correct
procedure in your organisation.
The nurse completes the report immediately after taking whatever
action is required to safeguard the person and notifies the charge
nurse or nurse in charge of the shift. For additional information
about incident reports, see Chapter 4
.


Safety interventions in inpatient facilities
Restraining people
Formal guidelines around use of restraint were initially confined to
the care of people experiencing a mental illness who were gravely
agitated. They covered restraint of the person themself or restraint
by secluding or preventing free movement of the person.
The United Nation’s  principles for the protection of people with
mental illness and the improvement of mental health care (Principle
11, para. 11) state that:
64 United Nations (1991). The Protection of Persons with Mental Illness and the Improvement
of Mental Health Care. Retrieved from <www.un.org/documents>.
Physical restraint or involuntary seclusion of a patient shall not be employed except in
accordance with the officially approved procedures of the mental health facility and only
when it is the only means available to prevent immediate or imminent harm to the patient
or others. It shall not be prolonged beyond the period which is strictly necessary for this
purpose. All instances of physical restraint or involuntary seclusion, the reasons for them
and their nature and extent shall be recorded in the patient’s medical record. A patient who
is restrained or secluded shall be kept under humane conditions and be under the care
and close and regular supervision of qualified members of the staff. A personal
representative, if any and if relevant, shall be given prompt notice of any physical restraint
or involuntary seclusion of the patient.
Although this quotation refers to people with a mental health diagnosis, the principles can
be applied more generally (see Box 33.11
).
64


BO X
33.11 General principles on the use of
restraints in the Australian health care
sector
The ACSQHC (2017e) guideline Action 5.24: Preventing Falls
and Harm from Falls has a section on the use of restraints
which highlights the following:
All health care and aged care facilities should have clear
policies and guidelines on the use of restraints in line with
state and territory legislation and guidelines.
The focus of caring for people with behavioural issues
(potential for restraint) should be about responding to the
behaviour rather than trying to control the behaviour.
All alternatives to restraint must be considered first and
trialled for all people with cognitive impairment, including
delirium.
If all alternatives have proven to be inadequate, the
rationale for using restraints must be documented and a
specified time frame for the restraint period agreed to by
the health care team.
If medications are to be used specifically for restraint, the
minimal dose should be administered and the person
observed and monitored to ensure their safety. Chemical


restraint must not be used as a substitute for quality care,
nor in cases of staff shortages. All observations and
outcomes must be documented accurately in the patient
record.
Organisational protocols must be followed when using
restraints.
Any restraint should be agreed to by the health care team
and by the person’s family and/or carers (p. 64).
Alternatives to restraints
Increase surveillance and observation of the person.
Provide companionship.
Provide physical and diversional activities for the person.
Ensure the person is comfortable and routines are
individualised.
Use low beds.
Explore different care and routine options with the person,
family and carers, and incorporate these into the person’s
care plan.
While some of these alternatives may not be possible
because of workload issues, there should be evidence that
some of these alternative measures have been tried.
Staff should also be provided with education and information
about the use of alternative strategies to restraints because
this can reduce the need to use restraints as well as minimise
risk of injury to people when restraints are used (p. 65).


When the use of alternatives to restraint is ineffective, the
temporary application of restraints is used to:
minimise or prevent harm to the person
prevent harm to other people and staff
result in positive health outcomes for the person (p. 65).
Minimum standards of documentation for restraint use are:
date and time of the application
name and designation of the person ordering the restraint
type of restraint
reasons for the restraint
alternatives considered and trialled, and why they were
ineffective
discussion with the person, family, carers or others with
the legal authority to make decisions for the person
(advance care directives)
any restrictions on the circumstances in which the
restraint may be applied
the intervals at which the person must be observed (e.g.
hourly, half hourly)
any special measures necessary to ensure the person’s
treatment is continued during the period of restraint
the duration of the restraint (p. 66).
Source: ACSQHC (2017). Action 5.24: Preventing Falls and Harm from Falls. Retrieved from
<www.safetyandquality.gov.au/standards/nsqhs-standards/comprehensive-care-standard/
minimising-patient-harm/action-524>.


The Australian Department of Health and Ageing  publication
Decision-making Tool: Supporting a Restraint Free Environment in
Residential Aged Care (updated 2019) provides guidelines for a
restraint-free environment and recommends that the ‘use of restraint
must always be the last resort after exhausting all reasonable
management options’ (p. 5). The broad principles underpinning the
decision-making tool (see Figure 33.10
) are:
65 Department of Health and Ageing (2012b). Decision-making Tool: Supporting a Restraint
Free Environment in Residential Aged Care. Retrieved from <https://agedcare.health.gov.au>.
Figure 33.10
65


Decision-making tool.
Source: Department of Health and Ageing (2012b). Decision-making Tool: Supporting a Restraint Free
Environment in Residential Aged Care, p. 18. Canberra: Department of Health and Ageing.
person centred
driven by information
organised for safety.
These principles comply with the Australian Safety and Quality
Framework for Health Care.
The guidelines recommend that when considering restraint, nurses
and other health care workers need to:
determine the clinical and psychological status of the person


complete a comprehensive assessment noting and reporting
physical and psychological changes
consult with health team members and family and carers of the
person
document the assessment of the person
ask for the person’s medications to be reviewed
document decision-making process to restrain the person
obtain consent for a restraint order from the person’s legal
guardian (guardianship board, enduring power of attorney
holder).
This may differ in states and territories.
Family members and/or legal guardians cannot request a person to
be restrained. This is a clinical decision made by appropriately
qualified health professionals who are legally accountable and
responsible for the outcomes of such a decision. Therefore, the
decision-making process must be well documented. (See Box
33.12
. See also Figure 33.10
 for the decision-making tool.)
BO X
33.12 What constitutes restraint?
Restraint
 is any aversive practice, device or action that
interferes with a person’s ability to make a decision or
restricts their free movement.


Physical restraint
The intentional restriction of a person’s voluntary movement
or behaviour by the use of a device, removal of mobility aids
or physical force for behavioural purposes is physical
restraint
. Physical restraint devices include but are not
limited to lap belts, tabletops, Posey restraints or similar
products, bed rails and chairs that are difficult to get out of
such as beanbags, water chairs and deep chairs.
Chemical restraint
The intentional use of medication to control a person’s
behaviour when no medically identified condition is being
treated, where the treatment is not necessary for the
condition or amounts to over-treatment of the condition is
chemical restraint
. Chemical restraint includes the use of
medication when the behaviour to be affected by the
medication does not appear to have a medical cause and
part of the intended pharmacological effect of the drug is to
sedate the person for convenience or disciplinary purposes.
Examples of pharmacological agents used as chemical
restraint are antipsychotic, antidepressant, antimanic,
anxiolytic and hypnotic drugs.
Aversive treatment
practices/punishment


An aversive practice is one that uses unpleasant physical,
sensory or verbal stimuli (any voice tone, command or threat
used to limit a person’s mobility) in an attempt to reduce
undesired behaviour. Aversive treatment also refers to any
withholding of basic human rights or needs (e.g. food,
warmth, clothing or positive social interaction), a person’s
goods/belongings or favoured activity for the purpose of
behaviour management or control.
Environmental restraint
Limiting a person to a particular environment (e.g. confining a
person to their bedroom) or excluding a person from an area
to which they want to go (e.g. restricting access to an outside
courtyard or sitting room or preventing a person from leaving
the building) is also a form of restraint.
Source: Department of Health and Ageing (2012b). Decision-making Tool: Supporting a Restraint
Free Environment in Residential Aged Care. Canberra: Department of Health and Ageing.
Standards require that a doctor’s order for restraints states the
reason and time period. The use of an ‘as necessary’ (prn) order for
restraints is prohibited. In all cases, restraints should be used only
after every other possible way of ensuring safety has been
unsuccessful and documented.
When behavioural changes in an individual trigger concerns for their
safety, the first thing to do is a comprehensive assessment which
considers:


context: the geographical and physical location of the person
needs: the needs of the person, their family, friends, carers
time frame: the assessment should be over a period of time so
that patterns of behaviour and the person’s needs for care are
identified (Department of Health and Ageing 2012b).
The assessment should include:
temperature, pulse and respiration rate
blood pressure
urinalysis
evidence of unexplained weight loss
hunger and thirst
dehydration
constipation
infection (chest, ear, systemic, urinary tract)
changes in mobility
pain
deterioration in hearing, vision
change in eating, sleeping or toilet habits
unattended ailments—dental, pressure sores
the need for a review of medications (Department of Health and
Ageing 2012b, p. 14).
Changes to mental status and cognitive functioning may be reversed
by appropriate treatments. These changes may be due to
depression, medications, withdrawal from alcohol and illicit drug use.
Therefore, when assessing a person for restraint it is important to


consider context because an acute environment is very different
from a residential care environment or community (Department of
Health and Ageing 2012b, p. 10).
Individuals have the right to be free from restraints that are not
medically necessary. As a result, there must be justification that the
use of restraints will protect the person and also that less restrictive
measures were attempted and found not effective; that is, the
expected benefits have been weighed against the potential harm of
any form of restraint (Department of Health and Ageing 2012b).
Restraints cannot be used for staff convenience or punishment of
the person (see Box 33.12
). Restrained people often become
more restless and anxious as a result of the loss of self-control.
Nurses must document that the need for the restraint was made
clear to both the person and the family.
Given that the above conditions are met and restraints are needed
in the person’s best interests, it is important for the nurse to be able
to correctly apply restraints without endangering the person’s safety.
Precautions must be rigorously observed in the care of the person
who is restrained (Department of Health and Ageing 2012b). See
also Figure 33.10
.
Types of restraints
There are several kinds of restraints. Among the most common for
adults are jacket restraints, belt restraints, mitt or hand restraints
and limb restraints. Geri chairs, wheelchairs with lap trays and bed
rails can also be considered restraints. Restraints for infants and


children include mummy restraints, elbow restraints and bassinet
restraints (see ‘Lifespan considerations
’).
Lifespan considerations
Restraints
Infants
Elbow restraints (see Figure 33.11
) are used to prevent
infants or small children from flexing their elbows to touch or
reach their face or head, especially after surgery. Ready-
made elbow restraints are available commercially.
Figure 33.11


Infant with elbow restraints.
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.
A mummy restraint (see Figure 33.12
) is a special folding
of a blanket or sheet around the infant to prevent movement
during a procedure such as gastric washing, eye irrigation or
collection of a blood specimen.
Figure 33.12


Making a mummy restraint.
Obtain a blanket or sheet large enough so that the
distance between opposite corners is about twice the
length of the infant’s body. Lay the blanket or sheet on a
flat, dry surface.
Fold down one corner and place the baby on it in the
supine position.
Fold the right side of the blanket over the infant’s body,
leaving the left arm free (see Figure 33.12A
). The right
arm is in a natural position at the side.
Fold the excess blanket at the bottom up under the infant
(see Figure 33.12B
, 2).
With the left arm in a natural position at the baby’s side,
fold the left side of the blanket over the infant, including
the arm, and tuck the blanket under the infant’s body (see
Figure 33.12B
, 3).
Remain with the infant who is in a mummy restraint until
the specific procedure is completed.
Children
A cot tent is simply a device placed over the top of a cot to
prevent active young children from climbing out of the cot. At
the same time, it allows them freedom to move about in the
cot. The cot tent is not attached to the movable parts of the
cot so the caregiver can have access to the child without
removing the dome or net.


Place the tent over the sides and ends of the cot.
Secure the ties to the springs or frame of the cot. The cot
sides can then be freely lowered without removing the net.
Test with your hand that the tent will stretch if the child
stands against it in the cot.
For further information, see Parents’ Guide to Kidsafe Homes
(Kidsafe 2017) and Safe Sleeping (Clinical Nursing Guideline)
(The Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne ).
66 The Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne (2016). Safe Sleeping (Clinical Nursing
Guideline). Retrieved from <www.rch.org.au>.
When evaluating if a device is a restraint or not, you need to
determine the intended use (e.g. physical restriction), its involuntary
application and/or the need for the restraint. For example, if all of
the bed’s side rails are up and restrict the person’s freedom to leave
the bed and the person did not voluntarily request all rails to be up,
they are a restraint. If, however, one side rail is up to assist the
person to get in and out of the bed, it is not a restraint. Also, if the
person can release or remove a device, it would not be considered a
restraint.
There are several types of vest restraints, but all are essentially
sleeveless jackets or vests with straps (tails) that can be tied to the
bed frame under the mattress. These body restraints are used to
ensure the safety of confused or sedated people in beds or
wheelchairs.
66


Belt or safety strap body restraints (see Figure 33.13
) are used
to ensure the safety of all individuals who are being moved on
stretchers or in wheelchairs. Some wheelchairs have a soft, padded
safety bar that attaches to side brackets that are installed under the
arm rests. To prevent the person from slumping forward, the nurse
then attaches a shoulder ‘Y’ strap to the bar and over the person’s
shoulders to the rear handles. Other safety belt models have a
three-loop design. One loop surrounds the person’s waist and
attaches to the rear handles. If such restraints are unavailable, the
nurse can place a folded towel or small sheet around the person’s
waist and fasten it at the back of the wheelchair. Belt restraints may
also be used for certain people confined to bed or to chairs.
Figure 33.13


A belt restraint.
A mitt or hand restraint (see Figure 33.14
) is used to prevent
confused people from using their hands or fingers to scratch and
injure themselves. For example, a confused person may need to be
prevented from pulling at intravenous tubing or a head bandage
following brain surgery. Hand or mitt restraints allow the person to be
ambulatory and/or to move the arm freely rather than be confined to
a bed or a chair. Mittens need to be removed on a regular basis to
permit the person to wash and exercise the hands. The nurse also
needs to take off the mitten to check the circulation to the hand.
Figure 33.14


A mitt restraint.
Limb restraints (see Figure 33.15
), which are generally made of
cloth, may be used to immobilise a limb, primarily for therapeutic
reasons (e.g. to maintain an intravenous infusion).
Figure 33.15


A limb restraint.
See Skill 33.2
 for applying restraints.


Consent issues
Any decision to restrain a person in a health care or aged setting
has significant ethical and legal responsibilities. The use of restraint
should only be a temporary solution to any behavioural changes or
circumstances.
Before a person is restrained, there needs to be consultation
between the health care team and the person’s family, guardian or
legal representative prior to any decision about restraint. Legal
requirements for restraint where a person is not mentally competent
will vary between states and territories, and family members must
have the legal capacity to act for their relative in these situations
through the mechanisms of an enduring power of attorney, advance
care directive or guardianship orders. These may be different in
different states and territories.
Nurses should note that family members and legal representatives
do not have legal power to require a person to be restrained. This is
a clinical decision made by appropriately qualified health
professionals, and these health professionals are legally accountable
for the decision to restrain a person and for the subsequent
consequences of this decision. Therefore, the clinical decision-
making process must be well documented.
Evaluating
To prevent injury, the nurse’s role is largely educative and desired
outcomes reflect the person’s acquisition of knowledge of hazards,


behaviours that incorporate safety practices and skills to perform in
the event of certain emergencies. The nurse needs to individualise
these for people. Examples of desired outcomes include the person
being able to do the following:
describe methods to prevent specific hazards (e.g. falls,
suffocation, choking, fires, drowning, electric shock)
report use of home safety measures (e.g. fire safety measures,
smoke detector maintenance, fall prevention strategies, burn
prevention measures, poison prevention measures, safe storage
of hazardous materials, firearm safety precautions, electrocution
prevention, water safety precautions, bicycle safety, motor
vehicle safety)
alter home physical environment to reduce the risk of injury
describe emergency procedures for poisoning and fire
describe age-specific risks, work safety risks or community
safety risks
demonstrate correct use of child safety seats
demonstrate correct administration of cardiopulmonary
resuscitation
Home care considerations
Applying restraints
Restraints may be necessary for people in
wheelchairs or in the home. Safety guidelines apply


in all cases. Assess the knowledge and skill of all
caregivers in the use of restraints and educate as
indicated.
Use means other than restraints as much as
possible and stay with the person.
Pad bony prominences, such as wrists and ankles,
if needed before applying a restraint over them.
Tie restraints with knots that will not tighten when
pulled and to parts of the wheelchair that do not
move and will release quickly in case of emergency.
Assess restrained limbs for signs of impaired blood
circulation.
Always stay with a person whose restraint is
temporarily removed.
Lifespan considerations
Safety
Some of the changes due to ageing that place the older adult
at higher risk of safety concerns are:
decrease in hearing and sight
decrease in response of reflexes
increasing fragility of bones and decreasing flexibility of
joints and muscles


decrease in temperature regulation, increasing the risk of
hypothermia and hyperthermia
decrease in kidney function, which increases risk of
toxicity from medications.
A home environment that was safe when they were younger
may need modifications for older adults to decrease the risk
of injury. A plan and telephone numbers of those to call
should be available for emergency situations. In Australia,
there are also emergency alert devices available for the older
adult in which programmed emergency telephone numbers
can be inserted and activated by the individual in an
emergency.
Case study
Mr Moore is a 72-year-old widower who is recovering from a
fall in which he fractured his hip and underwent surgical repair
1 week ago. He will be staying with his son for 2 weeks after
he is discharged from the hospital, but he is eager to return
to his own home. Once he is home, his son will visit nightly
after work, he will receive Meals on Wheels once a day and a
home health care worker will visit weekly to assist him with
hygiene care until he is more independent. Mr Moore’s wife
died 3 years ago but he has remained independent and
continued his social functions. He lives in a small single-level


house with his dog and cat and he enjoys gardening. Prior to
fracturing his hip, he walked his dog daily. You will be his
home health care nurse.
Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. While hospitalised, Mr Moore experienced some mild
confusion during the night but his nurses decided not


to restrain him. What are the best reasons for avoiding
the use of restraints for people such as Mr Moore?
2.
 Which of Mr Moore’s physical fundamentals of
care might be impacted while he is in hospital? What
continuing issues might he experience upon his
discharge and why?
3. What are some of the more obvious factors that may
affect Mr Moore’s safety as he returns home?
4. What do you need to assess in regard to Mr Moore’s
safety and what suggestions can you make for
enhancing his safety?
5. What strengths do you note about Mr Moore that may
protect him from injury when he returns home?
6.
What psychosocial, relational and physical
fundamentals of care are relevant to Mr Moore’s
situation at home? Using the Fundamentals of Care
Framework, think about how you might help to address
these needs.


SKILL
33.1 Using a bed or chair exit
safety monitoring device
Purposes
To alert the nurse that the person is attempting
to get out of bed.
To help decrease the risk of falls.
Assessment
Assess
Mobility status.
Judgment about ability to get out of bed safely.
Proximity of the person’s room to nurses’ station.
Position of side rails.
Functioning status of buzzer.
Planning
Determine the appropriate location for the device. If
the device will be applied to a thigh, ensure that the
location has intact skin.


Delegation
Risk factors for falls may be observed and recorded
by people other than the nurse. The Registered
Nurse is responsible for assessing the person and
confirming that there is a risk of the person falling
when getting out of a chair or bed unassisted. The
Registered Nurse develops a plan of care that
includes a variety of interventions that will protect
the person. If indicated, use of a safety monitoring
device may be delegated to care workers/Assistants
in Nursing who have been trained in their application
and monitoring.
Equipment
Alarm and control device
Sensor
Connection to nurse call system
Implementation
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain to person and
family the purpose and procedure of using a
safety monitoring device. Explain that the
device does not limit mobility in any manner;
rather, it alerts the staff when the person is


about to get out of bed. Explain that the
nurse must be called when the person needs
to get out of bed.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for the person’s privacy.
4. Test the battery device and alarm sound.
Rationale: testing ensures that the device is
functioning properly prior to use.
5. Apply the sensor pad or leg band.
Place the leg band according to the
manufacturer’s recommendation. 1 Place
the person’s leg in a straight, horizontal
position. Rationale: the alarm device is
position sensitive; that is, when it
approaches a near-vertical position (such
as in walking, crawling or kneeling as the
person attempts to get out of bed), the
audio alarm will be triggered.


1 Placing the leg band alarm
Source: Courtesy of Alert Care, Mill Valley CA.
For the bed or chair device, the sensor is
usually placed under the buttocks area. 2


2 Placement of a bed exit monitoring
device
Source: Posey Company, Arcadia, California.
For a bed or chair device, set the time
delay for determining the person’s
movement patterns from 1 to 12 seconds.
Connect the sensor pad to the control unit
and the nurse call system.
6. Educate the person to call the nurse when
the person wants or needs to get up and
assist as required. Check for understanding.
When assisting the person to get up,
deactivate the alarm.
Assist the person back to bed and
reattach the alarm device.
7. Ensure the person’s safety with additional
safety precautions.
Place buzzer within the person’s reach, lift
side rails per organisation policy and lower
the bed to its lowest position. The alarm
device is not a substitute for other
precautionary measures.


Place ambulation monitoring stickers on
the person’s door, chart and medical
record.
8. Document the type of alarm used, where it
was placed and its effectiveness in the patient
record using forms or checklists
supplemented by narrative notes when
appropriate. Record all additional safety
precautions and interventions discussed and
employed.
Evaluation
If the alarm is too sensitive to person movement
that is not an attempt to move from bed or chair,
reassess and modify alarm controls accordingly.
Conduct appropriate follow-up relating to
effectiveness of safety precautions.
Report any difficulties using the device or any
falls to the person’s doctor.


SKILL
33.2 Applying restraints
Purposes
To promote safety and prevent injury.
To allow a medical or surgical treatment to
proceed without person interference (e.g. to
prevent movements that would disrupt therapy to
a limb connected to tubes or appliance).
Assessment
Assess
The behaviour indicating the possible need for a
restraint.
Underlying cause for assessed behaviour.
What other protective measures may be
implemented before applying a restraint.
Status of skin to which restraint is to be applied.
Circulatory status distal to restraints and of
extremities.
Effectiveness of other available safety
precautions.


Planning
Review organisation policy for restraints and seek
consultation as appropriate before independently
deciding to apply a restraint. All other possible
interventions that are less restrictive must have
been tried. The doctor must be notified prior to using
a restraint, unless there is a danger to self or others.
In that case the doctor must be notified within the
prescribed time frame as per the organisation
protocol.
Delegation
The Registered Nurse must make the determination
that restraints are appropriate in specific situations,
select the proper type of restraints, evaluate the
effectiveness of the restraints and assess for
potential complications from their use. Application of
ordered restraints and their temporary removal for
skin assessment and care may be delegated to
assistants in nursing who have been trained in their
use.
Equipment
Appropriate type and size of restraint
Implementation
Performance


1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain to the person
and family what you are going to do, why it is
necessary and how they can cooperate.
Discuss how the results will be used in
planning further care or treatments. Allow
time for the person to express feelings about
being restrained. Provide needed emotional
reassurance that the restraints will be used
only when absolutely necessary and that
there will be close contact with the person in
case assistance is required.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe
appropriate infection control procedures.
3. Provide for a person’s privacy if indicated.
4. Apply the selected restraint.
Belt restraint (safety belt)
Determine that the safety belt is in good
order. If a Velcro safety belt is to be used,
make sure that both pieces of Velcro are
intact.
If the belt has a long portion and a shorter
portion, place the long portion of the belt
behind (under) the bedridden person and
secure it to the movable part of the bed
frame. The long, attached portion will then
move up when the head of the bed is


elevated and will not tighten around the
person. Place the shorter portion of the
belt around the person’s waist, over the
gown. There should be a finger’s width
between the belt and the person.
or
Attach the belt around the person’s waist
and fasten it at the back of the chair.
or
If the belt is attached to a stretcher,
secure the belt firmly over the person’s
hips or abdomen. Belt restraints must be
applied to all people on stretchers even
when the side rails are up.
Jacket restraint
Place vest on the person, with opening at
the front or the back, depending on the
type.
Pull the tie on the end of the vest flap
across the chest and place it through the
slit in the opposite side of the chest.
Repeat for the other tie.
Mitt restraint


Apply the commercial thumbless mitt (see
Figure 33.14
) to the hand to be
restrained. Make sure the fingers can be
slightly flexed and are not caught under
the hand.
Follow the manufacturer’s directions for
securing the mitt.
If a mitt is to be worn for several days,
remove it at regular intervals as per
organisation protocol. Wash and exercise
the person’s hand, then reapply the mitt.
Check organisation practices about
recommended intervals for removal.
Assess the person’s circulation to the
hands shortly after the mitt is applied and
at regular intervals. Individual complaints
of numbness, discomfort or inability to
move the fingers could indicate impaired
circulation to the hand.
5. Adjust the plan of care as required, for
example to include releasing the restraint,
providing skin care, range-of-motion
exercises and attending to the person’s
physical needs by providing fluids, nutrition
and toileting.
6. Record on the person’s chart the
behaviour(s) indicating the need for the


restraint, all other interventions implemented
in an attempt to avoid the use of restraints
and their outcomes and the time the doctor
was notified of the need for restraint. Also
record:
the type of restraint applied, the time it
was applied and the goal for its application
the person’s response to the restraint
the times that the restraints were removed
and skin care given
any other assessments and interventions
explanations given to the person and
significant others.
Evaluation
Perform a detailed follow-up of the need for the
restraints and the person’s response. Relate
these findings to previous data if available.
Evaluate circulatory status of restrained limbs.
Evaluate skin status beneath restraints.
Remove the restraints as soon as they are no
longer needed and document.
Report significant deviations from normal to the
doctor.


Chapter 33 Review


Chapter highlights
Injuries are a major cause of death among individuals of all ages
in Australia.
Nurses need to be aware of what constitutes a safe environment
for specific individuals and for groups of people in the home,
community and workplace.
Hazards to safety occur at all ages and vary according to the age
and development of the individual.
Nursing assessment of safety includes assessing factors that
can affect safety; for example, age, lifestyle, mobility, sensory
alterations, level of awareness, emotional state and
environmental factors.
Nurses assess people at risk of injury through methods such as
nursing history and physical examination, risk assessment tools
and home hazard appraisal.
Nurses need to sustain a heightened awareness of and alertness
to circumstances or patterns that may indicate potential
bioterrorism. Early detection and management is needed to help
stop a bioterrorism attack.
When planning to meet safety needs of people, nurses need to
consider physical factors in the environment and the
psychological and physiological state of the individual. People
often need to change their health behaviour and may need to
modify the environment.
Measures to ensure the safety of people of all ages focus on (a)
observation or prediction of situations that are potentially


harmful, and (b) patient education that empowers people to
safeguard themselves and their families from injury. Education is
a major health protection strategy in preventing accidents.
Nurses must be familiar with the fire procedures in the health
care organisation where they practice. In the event of a fire, the
nurse must (a) protect people from injury, (b) report, (c) contain
and (d) put out the fire.
Falls are a common cause of injury among older adults.
Prevention of falls in health care agencies is a continuous
concern.
Side rails do not protect hospitalised people from falls. It is more
likely the person will fall trying to get around or over the side rail.
Seizure precautions are safety measures taken by the nurse to
protect people from injury should they have a seizure.
Major reasons for poisoning in children are inadequate
supervision and improper storage of household toxic substances.
Suffocation can occur when foreign objects are swallowed or
inhaled, cutting off the person’s oxygen supply.
Prolonged exposure to excessive noise can produce hearing
loss.
Faulty electric equipment and improper grounding pose health
hazards in the hospital and the home. Accidents can be
prevented by using grounded outlets and plugs, putting
protective covers over outlets, keeping appliances in good repair
and making sure that electric wiring and circuits meet safety
standards.
Firearms pose a risk to individuals of all ages. Adults must take
full responsibility for following safety procedures when keeping


firearms in the home, including storage of ammunition in a
separate location.
In hospitals, radioactive substances are used for both diagnostic
and treatment purposes; organisation policy should be followed
to safeguard people and staff from unsafe exposure.
The use of any restraint must always be the last resort after
exhausting all reasonable alternative management options.
Because restraints restrict a person’s basic freedom to move,
careful assessment and accurate, complete documentation are
important when restraints are used.
Concept check
1. Place the following nursing priorities in correct sequence if a
fire occurs in a health setting.
1. Report the fire.
2. Extinguish the fire.
3. Protect the people.
4. Contain the fire.
2. What is the leading cause of deaths in young and middle-
aged adults?
1. Car crashes.
2. Drowning and firearms.
3. Falls.
4. Suicide and homicide.


3. Because a hospitalised older female who walks with a walking
frame is receiving diuretics, which result in frequent trips to
the bathroom at night, the nurse should perform which of the
following?
1. Leave the bathroom light on.
2. Withhold the person’s diuretic medication.
3. Provide a bedside commode.
4. Keep the side rails up.
4. A 75-year-old person hospitalised with a cerebral vascular
accident (stroke) becomes disoriented at times and tries to
get out of bed but is unable to ambulate without help. What is
the most appropriate safety measure?
1. Restrain the person in bed.
2. Ask a family member to stay with the person.
3. Check the person every 15 minutes.
4. Use a bed exit safety monitoring device.
5. A person is being admitted to hospital because of a seizure
that occurred at his home. The person has no previous
history of seizures. In planning the person’s nursing care,
which of the following measures is most essential at the time
of admission? Select all that apply.
1. Place a padded tongue depressor at the head of the
bed.
2. Pad the bed with blankets.
3. Inform the person about the importance of wearing a
medical identification tag.


4. Teach the person about epilepsy.
5. Test oral suction equipment.
6. Which of the following nursing interventions is the highest in
priority for a person at risk of falls in a hospital setting?
1. Keep all the side rails up.
2. Review prescribed medications.
3. Complete the ‘get up and go’ test.
4. Place the bed in the lowest position.
7. Medication errors can place the person at significant risk.
Which of the following practices will help decrease the
possibility of errors? Select all that apply.
1. Hire only competent nurses.
2. Improve the nurse’s ability to multi-task.
3. Establish a reporting system for ‘near-misses’.
4. Communicate effectively.
5. Create a culture of trust.
8. When planning to teach health care topics to a group of male
adolescents, the nurse should consider which of the following
topics a priority?
1. Sports contribute to an adolescent’s self-esteem.
2. Sunbathing and tanning beds can be dangerous.
3. A driver’s education course is mandatory for safety.
9. The nurse, at handover report, learns that one of the people
in his care has bilateral soft wrist restraints. The person is


confused, has tried to get out of bed and has pulled out the
IV line, which was subsequently reinserted. Which of the
following actions by the nurse is appropriate? Select all that
apply.
1. Document the behaviour(s) that require continued use
of the restraints.
2. Ensure that the restraints are tied to the side rails.
3. Provide range-of-motion exercises when the restraints
are removed.
4. Orient the person.
5. Assess the tightness of the restraints.

providing hygiene care.
Apply the nursing process to common problems related to
hygiene care of the skin, feet, nails, mouth, hair, eyes, ears and
nose.
Identify the purposes of bathing.


Describe various types of baths.
Explain specific ways in which nurses help hospitalised people
with hygiene.
Describe steps for identified hygiene care procedures.
Identify steps in removing contact lenses.
Describe steps for removing, cleaning and inserting hearing aids.
Identify safety and comfort measures underlying bed-making
procedures.

Hygiene is an array of personal activities which
support good health and wellbeing. Personal
hygiene is the self-care by which people attend
to such functions as bathing, toileting, general
body hygiene and grooming. Hygiene is a highly


personal matter determined by individual values
and practices. It involves care of the skin, hair,
nails, teeth, oral and nasal cavities, eyes, ears
and perineal–genital areas.
It is important for nurses to know exactly how
much assistance a person needs for hygiene
care to promote independence and autonomy
and ensure safe completion of cares. In addition
to daily hygiene care, people may require help
after urinating or defecating, after vomiting and
whenever they become soiled—for example,
from wound drainage, from profuse perspiration
or after surgical procedures. Table 34.1
 lists
factors that influence hygiene practices.
Table 34.1 Factors influencing hygiene
practices


Skin
The skin is the largest organ of the body. It serves five major
functions:
1. It protects underlying tissues from injury by preventing the
passage of micro-organisms. The skin and mucous
membranes are considered the body’s first line of defence.
The normal skin of a healthy person has transient and
resident micro-organisms that are not usually harmful. (See
Chapter 37
.)
2. It regulates the body temperature. Cooling of the body occurs
through the heat loss processes of evaporation of
perspiration and by radiation and conduction of heat from the
body when the blood vessels of the skin are vasodilated.
Body heat is conserved through lack of perspiration and
vasoconstriction of the blood vessels. See Chapter 30
.
3. It secretes sebum
, an oily substance that (a) softens and
lubricates the hair and skin, (b) prevents the hair from
becoming brittle and (c) decreases water loss from the skin
when the external humidity is low. Fat is a poor conductor of
heat, and sebum (d) lessens the amount of heat lost from the
skin, and (e) has a bactericidal
 (bacteria-killing) action.
4. It transmits sensations through nerve receptors, which are
sensitive to pain, temperature, touch and pressure.


5. It produces and absorbs vitamin D in conjunction with
ultraviolet rays from the sun, which activate a vitamin D
precursor present in the skin.
Sudoriferous (sweat) glands
 are on all body surfaces except
the lips and parts of the genitals. The body has from 2 to 5 million
sweat glands, which are all present at birth. They are most
numerous on the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet.
Sweat glands are classified as apocrine and eccrine. The apocrine
glands
, located largely in the axillae and anogenital areas, begin
to function at puberty under the influence of androgens. Although
they produce sweat almost constantly, apocrine glands are of little
use in thermoregulation. The secretion of these glands is odourless,
but when decomposed or contacted by bacteria on the skin, it takes
on a musky, unpleasant odour. The eccrine glands
 are important
physiologically. They are more numerous than the apocrine glands
and are found chiefly on the palms of the hands, the soles of the
feet and the forehead. The sweat they produce cools the body
through evaporation. Sweat is made up of water, sodium, potassium,
chloride, glucose, urea and lactate.


Nursing management
Assessing
Assessment of the person’s skin and hygiene practices includes (a)
a nursing health history to determine the person’s skin care
practices, self-care abilities and past or current skin problems, (b)
physical assessment of the skin and (c) identification of people at
risk of developing skin impairments (e.g. those with dry, cracked or
fragile skin or people at risk of developing pressure areas).
Nursing history
Understanding and respecting people’s skin care practices is
important in the provision of safe care, as well as improving
individual experiences (Geller et al. ). Perception about the
importance of disguising natural body odours by bathing frequently
and using deodorant or perfumes may differ between people from
different cultures. In Australia, for many people this may be
considered usual practice, but some people from other countries
where water or other resources are scarce may bathe less often
than people from countries where these are more accessible.
1


1 Geller, G., Branyon, E., Forbes, L., Rushton, C. H., Beach, M. C., Carrese, J. & Sugarman,
J. (2015). Health care professionals’ perceptions and experiences of respect and dignity in the
intensive care unit. Narrative Inquiry in Bioethics, 5(1A), 27A–42A.
Assessment of the person’s self-care abilities determines the
amount of nursing assistance and the type of hygiene activity (e.g.
bed, bath or shower) best suited for the person. Important
considerations include the person’s balance (for bathtub and
shower), ability to sit unsupported (in the bathtub or bed), activity
tolerance, coordination, adequate muscle strength, appropriate joint
range of motion, presence of pain, postoperative timeline, vision and
preferences. Cognition and motivation are also essential. People
whose cognitive function is impaired or whose illness alters energy
levels and motivation will usually need more assistance. It is
important for the nurse to determine the person’s functional level
and to maintain and promote as much independence as possible.
This also enables the nurse to identify the person’s potential for
growth, rehabilitation and discharge readiness or requirements.
There are several models of functional levels of self-care.
The presence of past or current skin problems alerts the nurse to
specific nursing interventions or referrals the person may require.
Many skin care conditions have implications for hygiene care. The
person may provide descriptions of these problems during the
nursing health history or the nurse may observe some during the
physical examination that follows. Common skin problems and
implications for nursing interventions are shown in Table 34.2
.
Questions to elicit data about the person’s skin care practices, self-


care abilities and skin problems are shown in the ‘Assessment
interview
’.
Table 34.2 Common skin problems
Assessment interview
Skin hygiene
Skin care practices
What are your usual showering or bathing times?
What hygiene products do you routinely use (e.g. bath
oils, powder, facial cleansing creams, body lotions or
creams, deodorants, antiperspirants)?
What hygiene or cosmetic products do you avoid because
of the skin problems they create (e.g. skin dryness or
allergic reactions)?
Self-care abilities
Do you have any problems managing your hygiene
practices (e.g. baths and facial care)? If so, what are

How can a nurse best assist you?


Skin problems
Do you have any tendency towards skin dryness,
itchiness, rashes, bruising, excessive perspiration or lack
of perspiration? Have you had skin or scalp lesions in the
past?
Do you have any allergies or sensitivities? If so, what?
Positive responses to any of these require further exploration
in terms of duration (When did it start?); frequency (How
often have you had this?); description of lesion or rash; any
associated signs, such as fever or nausea; aggravating
factors (e.g. season of the year, stress, occupation,
medication, food, recent travel, housing, washing powders,
hygiene products, personal contact); alleviating factors (e.g.
medications, lotions, home remedies); and any family history
of the problem.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: Communicating for safety
The intent of this standard is to ‘ensure timely, purpose-driven
and effective communication and documentation that supports
continuous, coordinated and safe care for patients’ (Australian
Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC) , p. 49).
2


2 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Taking a person-centred care approach, the
nurse facilitates communication with people
requiring hygiene assistance. Techniques such
as active listening and open-ended questioning
assist in ensuring personal preferences and
cultural requirements are met. Timely,
structured, verbal clinical handover between
colleagues at point of care and within the
multidisciplinary team should be undertaken.
Accurate documentation of care supports
ongoing adherence to patient needs and
ensures safe, evidence-based practice is
promoted.
Physical assessment
Physical assessment of the skin, which involves inspection and
palpation, is described in Chapter 31
. When assisting with bathing
and other hygiene care, the nurse often can collect data about the
person’s skin including colour, uniformity of colour, texture, turgor,
temperature, intactness and lesions.


Diagnosing
In this chapter, we discuss assessment and diagnoses for people
who have problems performing hygiene care. This may be where
there is an alteration to health status that impacts on independent
bathing, showering, dressing or toileting.
Difficulties encountered by the person in performing bathing
activities include the inability to wash the body or body parts, to
obtain or get to a water source and to regulate or react to water
temperature and flow. Difficulties in dressing and grooming include
inability to obtain, put on, take off, fasten or replace articles of
clothing; and to maintain appearance at a satisfactory level. Toileting
problems may involve difficulties getting to the toilet or commode or
sitting on and rising from it. In addition, the person may experience
problems manipulating clothing for toileting, carrying out proper toilet
hygiene or flushing the toilet or emptying the commode. The
reasons (aetiologies or related factors) for these problems are
varied (see Box 34.1
).
BO X
34.1 Aetiologies of self-care deficits
Fatigue.
Pain or discomfort.
Perceptual or cognitive impairment.


Inability to perceive body part or spatial relationship.
Neuromuscular or musculoskeletal impairment.
Medically imposed or postoperative restrictions.
Therapeutic procedure restraining mobility (e.g.
intravenous infusion, cast).
Severe anxiety, depression, inertia
Environmental barriers.
Clinical examples are shown in ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses,
outcomes and interventions
’.
Planning
In planning care, the nurse and the person and, if appropriate, the
family set outcomes for each identified nursing diagnosis. The nurse
then performs nursing interventions and activities to assist the
person in achieving these outcomes.
The specific, detailed nursing activities undertaken by the nurse may
include assisting dependent people with bathing, skin care and
perineal care; instructing people/families about appropriate hygiene
practices and alternative methods for dressing; and demonstrating
use of assistive equipment and adaptive activities. Although the
nursing interventions discussed in this chapter focus on hygiene
measures, the aetiology of the nursing diagnoses established may
point to other interventions that promote circulation, promote self-


esteem, restore nutritional status, correct fluid deficits or excesses,
or prevent problems associated with immobility. Nursing strategies to
manage these aetiologies are provided in other chapters.
Planning to assist a person with personal hygiene includes
consideration of the person’s personal preferences, health and
limitations; the best time to give the care; and the equipment,
facilities and personnel available. A person’s personal preferences—
about when and how to bathe, for example—should be followed as
long as they are compatible with the person’s health and the
resources and equipment available. Another consideration for the
nurse is to assess the person’s comfort level with the gender of the
caregiver. Hygiene care, particularly bathing, can be embarrassing
and stressful to individuals. Modesty needs vary from person to
person and may have origins in cultural practices. Nurses must
respect a person’s modesty, whether male or female, and provide
adequate privacy and sensitivity. Nurses need to provide whatever
assistance the person requires, either directly or by delegating this
task to other nursing personnel.
Planning for home care
To provide for continuity of care, it is important that the nurse
assesses the person’s and family’s abilities for care and discusses
the need for referrals and home health services to assist with
hygiene needs after discharge (see ‘Home care considerations’). In
addition, the nurse needs to determine the person’s learning needs.

Maintaining independence with hygiene needs
History Stan Bailey, 75 years old, suffered a ‘stroke’ 2 weeks
ago, resulting in paralysis of his left side.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: Comprehensive care
The intent of this standard is to ‘ensure that people receive
comprehensive care – that is, coordinated delivery of the total
health care required or requested by a patient. This care is
aligned with the patient’s expressed goals of care and health
care needs, considers the impact of the patient’s health issues
on their life and wellbeing, and is clinically appropriate’. It also
‘ensures that risks of harm for patients during health care are
prevented and managed. Clinicians identify patients at risk of
specific harm during health care by applying the screening and
assessment processes required in this standard’ (ACSQHC
2017 p. 36).
By direct or indirect supervision, the Registered
Nurse (RN) facilitates comprehensive care with
people requiring hygiene assistance. When
hygiene care is delegated to another staff
member (e.g. an Assistant in Nursing or


Enrolled Nurse), the RN undertakes a
comprehensive assessment to ensure an
evidence-based care plan is provided. A person-
centred approach is promoted to develop a plan
that meets the personal requirements of
patients. The RN evaluates that care practices
have been undertaken in accordance with the
plan. Based on this evaluation the RN, in
collaboration with the multidisciplinary health
care team, reviews and adjusts the plan as
required and ensures accurate documentation
of care is completed to enable the team to work
collaboratively to meet patient needs.
Implementing
The nurse applies the general guidelines for skin care while providing
one of the various types of baths available. Skill 34.1
 describes
how to bathe an adult, child or young person.
Home care considerations


Hygiene
The person and the environment
Self-care abilities for hygiene: assess the person’s
ability to bathe, to regulate and turn water taps, to
dress and undress, to stand or sit safety in a wet
area, to groom and to use the toilet.
Self-care aids required: determine if there is a need
for a bathtub/shower seat (see Figure 34.1
), a
hand shower, a non-skid surface or mat in the
bathtub or shower, hand rails on the sides of the
bathtub or toilet (see Figure 34.2
) or a raised
toilet seat.
Figure 34.1

Figure 34.2
