Source: © J. E. Gaulton.


Facilities: check for the presence of laundry
facilities and running water.
Mechanical barriers: note furniture obstructing
access to the bathroom and toilet, or a doorway too
narrow for a wheelchair.
Family
Caregiver availability, skills and responses:
determine whether individuals are available, willing
and able to assist with bathing, dressing and
toileting if required.
Education needs: assess whether the caregiver
needs instruction in how to assist the person during
hygiene activities.
Family role changes and coping: assess effects of
person’s illness on financial status, parenting,
spousal roles, sexuality and social roles.
Community
Explore resources that will provide assistance with
bathing, laundry and foot care (e.g. home help,
home nurses, podiatrist).
Consult a social worker as needed to coordinate
placement of a person unable to remain in the
home or to identify community resources that will
help the person stay safely in the home.
Consider a consult with (a) a physiotherapist to
assess, develop and improve the person’s motor


function, (b) a home health nurse to provide follow-
up for care, teaching and support and (c) an
occupational therapist to assess and develop
abilities to perform activities of daily living.
Lifespan considerations
Bathing
Infants
Sponge baths are suggested for the newborn because
daily tub baths are not considered necessary. After the
bath, the infant should be immediately dried and wrapped.
Parents need to be advised that the infant’s ability to
regulate body temperature has not yet fully developed and
newborns’ bodies lose heat readily.
Children
Encourage a child’s participation appropriate for
developmental level.
Closely supervise children in the bathtub. Do not leave
them unattended.


Adolescents
Provide privacy and offer assistance as requested.
Adolescents place high value on personal privacy and
independence.
Older adults
Changes of ageing can decrease the protective function
of the skin in older adults. These changes include fragile
skin, less oil and moisture and a decrease in elasticity.
To minimise skin dryness in older adults, avoid excessive
use of soap. The ideal time to moisturise the skin is
immediately after bathing.
Avoid powder because it causes moisture loss, is a
hazardous inhalant and may be a slip hazard on tiled
flooring.
Protect vulnerable older adults and children from injury
related to hot water burns.
Skin dryness (xerosis) and itching (pruritis) may cause
irritation, pain, social isolation and decreased quality of
life.
General guidelines for skin care
1. An intact, healthy skin is the body’s first line of defence.
Nurses need to ensure that all skin care measures prevent


injury and irritation. Harsh rubbing or use of rough towels and
washcloths can cause tissue damage, particularly when the
skin is irritated or when circulation or sensation is diminished.
Bottom bedsheets must be kept taut and free from wrinkles
to reduce friction and abrasion to the skin. Top bed linens are
arranged to prevent undue pressure on the toes. When
necessary, bed cradles are used to keep bedclothes off the
feet.
2. The degree to which the skin protects the underlying
tissues from injury depends on the general health of the
cells, the amount of subcutaneous tissue and the
dryness of the skin. Skin that is poorly nourished and dry is
less easily protected and more vulnerable to injury and
infection. When the skin is dry, lotions or creams can be
applied, and when very dry, bathing may be limited to once or
twice a week because frequent bathing removes the natural
oils of the skin and may further exacerbate dryness.
3. Moisture in contact with the skin for more than a short
time can result in increased bacterial growth, irritation
and skin breakdown. After a bath, the skin is dried carefully.
Particular attention is paid to areas such as the axillae, the
groin, beneath the breasts and between the toes, where the
potential for irritation is greatest. A non-irritating dusting
powder tends to reduce moisture and can be applied to these
areas after they are dried. People who are incontinent of
urine or faeces or who perspire excessively are provided with
immediate skin care to prevent skin irritation.


4. Body odours are caused by resident skin bacteria acting
on body secretions. Cleanliness is the best deodorant.
Commercial deodorants and antiperspirants can be applied
only after the skin is cleaned and dried. Deodorants diminish
odours, whereas antiperspirants reduce the amount of
perspiration. Neither is applied immediately after shaving
because of the possibility of skin irritation, nor are they used
on skin that is already irritated.
5. Skin sensitivity to irritation and injury varies between
individuals and in accordance with their health. Generally
speaking, skin sensitivity is greater in infants, very young
children and older people. A person’s nutritional status also
affects sensitivity, as does insufficient fluid intake. Emaciated
and obese people tend to experience more skin irritation and
injury. Even in healthy people, skin sensitivity is highly
variable. Some people’s skin is sensitive to chemicals in skin
care agents and cosmetics. Hypoallergenic cosmetics and
soaps or soap substitutes are available. The nurse needs to
ascertain if the person has any sensitivities and what agents
are appropriate to use.
6. Agents used for skin care have selective actions and
purposes. Commonly used agents are described in Table
34.3
.
Table 34.3 Agents commonly used on the skin
Bathing


Bathing removes accumulated oil, perspiration, dead skin cells and
some bacteria. Excessive bathing, however, can interfere with the
intended lubricating effect of the sebum, causing dryness of the
skin, especially for older adults, who produce less sebum.
In addition to cleaning the skin, bathing also stimulates circulation. A
warm or hot bath dilates superficial arterioles, bringing more blood
and nourishment to the skin.
Bathing also produces a sense of wellbeing and social acceptance. It
is refreshing and relaxing and frequently improves morale. Some
people take a morning shower for its refreshing, stimulating effect.
Others prefer an evening bath because it is relaxing. These effects
are more evident when a person is ill. For example, it is not
uncommon for people who have had a restless or sleepless night to
feel relaxed, comfortable and sleepy after a morning bath.
Real-world practice
Many people have the support of their family, including
extended family members, throughout their hospital
stay. Family members may want to assist but may not
know how to do so. The nurse can facilitate the
person’s recovery by teaching family members how to
provide certain basic care functions. Appropriate tasks
to delegate to family members, after their expression


of wanting to assist and proper instruction, can include
mouth care, range of motion, skin care and assisting
with meals. For the person who will be hospitalised for
an extended period, the family can be asked to bring in
music that the person likes, pictures of family
members, a favourite pillow or blanket from home or
even a stuffed animal.
—Marie Lasater RN Barnes-Jewish Hospital, St Louis, MO
Attending to hygiene needs offers an excellent opportunity for the
nurse to undertake a thorough assessment. The nurse can observe
the condition of the skin and physical conditions such as sacral
oedema or rashes. While assisting a person with a bath, the nurse
can also assess the person’s psychosocial needs, such as
orientation to time and ability to cope with the illness. Learning
needs, such as a need to learn foot care for the person with
diabetes, can also be assessed.
Categories
There are two categories of baths: cleaning and therapeutic.
Cleaning baths
 are given chiefly for hygiene purposes and
include different types:
Complete bed bath. The nurse washes the entire body of a
dependent person in bed.


Self-help bed bath. People confined to bed are able to bathe
themselves with help from the nurse for washing the back and
perhaps the feet.
Partial bath (face, hands and back). Only the parts of the
person’s body that might cause discomfort or odour, if neglected,
are washed: the face, hands, axillae, perineal area and back.
Omitted are the arms, chest, abdomen, legs and feet. Some
ambulatory people prefer to take a partial bath at the sink with a
face washer and warm water. The nurse can assist them by
washing their backs.
Disposable wet wipes. This bath is a commercially prepared
product (not available in all organisations) with 10 to 12 pre-
soaked disposable washcloths that contain a no-rinse cleanser
solution. The package is warmed in a microwave. The warming
time is about 1 minute, but the nurse needs to determine how
long it takes to attain a desirable temperature. Each area of the
body is cleaned with a different cloth and then air dried. Because
the body is not rubbed dry, the emollient in the solution remains
on the skin.
Hot towel sponge. Where the aforementioned commercially
prepared product is not available, the nurse may prepare the
bath by diluting a commercial no-rinse cleanser solution with hot
water and adding this solution to rolled towels and washcloths
contained inside a large plastic bag that sits within a washbowl.
The cloths will be impregnated with the solution and stay hot until
used.
Bath. Baths are often preferred to bed baths because it is easier
to wash and rinse in a bathtub. Baths can also be used


therapeutically. The amount of assistance the nurse offers
depends on the person’s abilities and safety considerations.
There are specially designed bathtubs for dependent people.
These bathtubs greatly reduce the work of the nurse in lifting
people in and out of the bathtub and offer greater benefits than a
sponge bath in bed.
Shower. Many ambulatory people are able to use shower
facilities and require minimal or no assistance from the nurse.
People in need of more assistance or in circumstances whereby
mobility is limited may require a shower chair. The wheels on the
shower chair allow people to be transported from their room to
the shower. The shower chair also has a commode seat to
facilitate cleansing of the perineal area during the shower
process (see Figure 34.3
).
Figure 34.3


A shower chair.
The water for a bath should feel comfortably warm. People vary in
their sensitivity to heat; generally, the temperature should be 43°C to
46°C. Most people will verify a suitable temperature. Those with
decreased circulation or cognitive problems will not be able to verify
or react appropriately to excessive water temperatures. Therefore,
the nurse must check the water temperature to avoid injury to the
person with water that is too hot. The water for a bed bath should be
changed when it becomes dirty or cool.
Therapeutic baths
 are given for physical effects, such as to
soothe irritated skin or to treat an area (e.g. the perineum).
Medications may be placed in the water. A therapeutic bath is
generally taken in a bathtub one-third or one-half full. The person
remains in the bath for a designated time, often 20 to 30 minutes. If
the person’s back, chest and arms are to be treated, these areas
need to be immersed in the solution. The bath temperature is
generally included in the order; 37.7°C to 46°C may be ordered for
adults and 40.5°C is usually ordered for infants. Skill 34.1
provides guidelines for bathing.
An individualised approach focusing on therapeutic and comforting
outcomes of bathing is especially important for people with
dementia. Given Australia’s ageing population, the prevalence of
dementia is expected to increase from 447 115 in 2019 to
approximately 1 million by 2058 (Dementia Australia ). This statistic
has implications for nursing care. For example, people with dementia
3


may be more likely to become agitated before or during hygiene
activities (Bidewell & Chang ; Rasin & Barrick ). See Box 34.2
 for
possible strategies that can reduce the stress of the bathing
experience for both the person with dementia and the caregiver.
3 Dementia Australia (2019). Dementia Statistics. Retrieved from <www.dementia.org.au>.
4 Bidewell, J. W. & Chang, E. (2010). Managing dementia agitation in residential aged care.
Dementia, 10(3), 299–315.
5 Rasin, J. & Barrick, A. L. (2004). Bathing patients with dementia: Concentrating on the
patient’s needs rather than merely the task. American Journal of Nursing, 104(3), 30–33.
BO X
34.2 General guidelines for bathing
people with dementia
Lack of privacy
Washing and dressing are intimate, private activities. Many
people have never undressed in front of others and may be
embarrassed or humiliated by their need for assistance. They
may feel particularly embarrassed if they are incontinent and
may refuse to bathe or change their clothes in an attempt to
disguise the problem.
What to try:
4
5


Close curtains, blinds or doors to create a feeling of
privacy.
Cover mirrors if people don’t recognise themselves.
A great deal of reassurance and patience will be needed.
Environment
The room may be too hot or cold or produce feelings of
claustrophobia, causing the person with dementia to feel
uncomfortable. They may not be used to bathing or
showering daily.
What to try:
Make sure the bathroom is comfortably warm.
Provide adequate lighting in the bathroom, especially
during evening hours.
It may be helpful to play soft music in the background to
create a calming and relaxing atmosphere.
Choose the best time of day for bathing and try to be
consistent with the person’s bathing routine before the
onset of dementia.
Consider the time of day when the person is most relaxed
and the type of bathing, such as bath, shower or sponge
bath, that they are used to.
It is important that you do not impose your own values
about how often the person should bathe.


Task is too confusing or complicated
Getting undressed, having a wash and brushing teeth can be
very complex tasks because of the many steps involved.
Some people with dementia may have a changed sense of
perception of hot and cold water caused by damage to the
region of the brain that regulates the ‘internal thermostat’.
They may feel a different sensation from water.
What to try:
Break down the tasks into simple steps, gently explaining
each step. Use simple, respectful language.
Try offering limited choices; for example, ‘Would you like
to have a bath or a shower?’ or ‘Would you like to have
your bath now or before bed?’.
Let the person feel the water before getting into the bath.
Sometimes gently pouring water over their hands
reassures them that the water isn’t too hot. Saying ‘the
water feels nice’ or ‘this feels good’ can also be reassuring
and calming.
Source: Alzheimer’s Australia . Caring for Someone with Dementia. Hygiene Factsheet 17. Retrieved
from <www.fightdementia.org.au/support-and-services/families-and-friends/personal-care/hygiene>.
6 Alzheimer’s Australia (2012). Caring for Someone with Dementia. Hygiene Factsheet 17. Retrieved
from <www.fightdementia.org.au>.
Providing personal hygiene to people with dementia is often an
ongoing challenge. Being sensitive to the rhythm of their behaviour
6


and looking for cues can often offset problems related to this.
People with dementia, whether they are at home or in a health care
facility, often have certain times of the day when they may be more
agitated—these are times to avoid doing things that will increase
their fear and agitation. It is sometimes helpful to wait and attempt
the hygiene care again at a later time when the person is less
agitated.
In addition, collaboration between the nurse and the AIN or other
caregiver is a critical element to implementing the individualised
person-focused approach for cognitively impaired people who exhibit
aggressive behaviour during bathing. The nurse, after observing a
difficult bathing situation, should discuss with the AIN or other
caregiver possible alternative strategies or methods they might
implement for this person. More than one intervention may be
required (e.g. reassurance, simple explanations, distraction
techniques, moving slowly). It is important for the nurse to
subsequently evaluate the person’s response to the new
intervention(s).
Home care considerations
Hygiene
Suggest that at home the following is provided:


Purchase of a bath seat that fits in the bathtub or
shower.
Installation of a hand-held shower hose for use with
a bath seat.
Use of a non-skid surface on the bathtub or
shower, such as a suction mat or anti-slip bathroom
strips.
Installation of hand bars on both sides of the
bathtub or shower to facilitate transfers in and out
of the bathtub or shower.
Careful monitoring of bathwater temperature.
Apply lotion and oil after a bath, not during,
because these solutions can make a bathtub
surface slippery. Avoid spilling excess product on
tiled surfaces as this will make the tiles slippery.
Clean up any spills of lotion, oils or powder as soon
as possible.
Perineal–genital care
Perineal–genital care is also referred to as perineal care or pericare.
Perineal care as part of the bed bath is embarrassing for many
people. Most people who require a bed bath from the nurse can
clean their own genital areas with minimal assistance. The nurse


may need to hand a moistened washcloth and soap to the person,
rinse the washcloth and provide a towel.
Because some people are unfamiliar with terminology for the
genitals and perineum, it may be difficult for nurses to explain what
is expected. Some people, however, understand what is meant if the
nurse simply says, ‘I’ll give you a washcloth to finish your bath’.
Some older people may be familiar with the term private parts.
Nurses should wear gloves while providing this care for the comfort
of the person involved and to protect themselves from infection.
Skill 34.2
 explains how to provide perineal–genital care.
Clinical consideration
Always wash or wipe from ‘clean to dirty’. For a
female, cleanse the perineal area from ‘front to
back’ (urethra to vaginal opening to anus). For a
male, cleanse the urinary meatus by moving in
a circular motion from the centre of the urethral
opening around the glans.
Education


People often need information about dry skin, skin rashes and acne
(see also ‘Patient education
’).
Patient education
Skin problems and care
Dry skin
Health care settings are often dry environments, exposing
people to low humidity, airconditioning or heating, which
may cause dry skin in some people.
Use cleansing creams to clean the skin rather than soap,
which causes drying and, in some cases, allergic
reactions.
Use bath oils, but take precautions to prevent falls caused
by slippery bathtub surfaces.
Thoroughly rinse soap or cleansing lotion, if used, from
the skin.
Bathe less frequently when environmental temperature
and humidity are low.
Increase fluid intake to prevent skin dehydration.
Use moisturising or emollient creams that contain
sorbolene or other lipid-free and non-alkaline products to
retain skin moisture.
Skin rashes


Keep the area clean by washing it with a mild, low-irritant
soap. Rinse the skin well and pat it dry.
To relieve itching, try a tepid bath. Some over-the-counter
preparations may help but should be used with full
knowledge of the product.
Avoid scratching the rash to prevent inflammation,
infection and further skin lesions.
Avoid unnecessary layers of clothing which may cause
perspiration and aggravate a rash.
Evaluating
Using data collected during care, the nurse judges whether desired
outcomes have been achieved. If the outcomes are not achieved,
the nurse explores reasons why. For example:
Did the nurse overestimate the person’s functional abilities
(physical, mental, emotional) for self-care?
Were provided instructions not clear?
Were appropriate assistive devices or supplies not available to
the person?
Did the person’s condition change?
Were required analgesics provided before hygiene care?
What currently prescribed medications and therapies could affect
the person’s abilities or tissue integrity?


Is the person’s fluid and food intake adequate or appropriate to
maintain skin and mucous membrane moisture and integrity?


SKILL
34.1 Bathing an adult, child or
young person
Purposes
To remove transient micro-organisms, body
secretions and excretions and dead skin cells.
To stimulate circulation to the skin.
To promote a sense of wellbeing and improve
social acceptance.
To produce relaxation and comfort.
To prevent and eliminate unpleasant body
odours.
Assessment
Assess
Condition of the skin (colour; texture and turgor;
presence of pigmented spots or scars;
temperature; lesions; excoriations; abrasions;
bruises; reddened, blistered or open skin over


pressure points such as sacrum, coccyx,
scapula, trochanter or heel).
Presence of pain and need for adjunctive
measures (e.g. analgesia) before the bath.
Range of motion of the joints.
Requirement of more staff to assist with
mobilisation, if needed.
Any other aspect of health that may affect the
person’s bathing process (e.g. mobility, strength,
cognition).
Planning
Delegation
The RN may delegate the skill of bathing to the
Assistant in Nursing (AIN) or another caregiver.
However, the RN remains responsible for
assessment and care. The RN needs to do the
following:
Inform the AIN of the type of bath appropriate for
the person and precautions, if any, specific to the
needs of the person.
Remind the AIN to notify the nurse of any
concerns or changes (e.g. redness over bony
prominences, skin breakdown, rash) so the
nurse can assess, intervene if needed and
document.


Instruct the AIN to encourage the person to
perform as much self-care as appropriate in
order to promote independence and self-esteem.
Obtain a complete report about the bathing
experience from the AIN.
Equipment
Basin or sink with warm water (between 43°C
and 46°C)
Soap and soap dish or disposable wet wipes if
available
Linens: bath blanket, two bath towels, washcloth,
clean gown or pyjamas or clothes as needed,
additional bed linen and towels, if required
Gloves, if appropriate (e.g. presence of body
fluids or open lesions)
Personal hygiene articles (e.g. deodorant,
powder, lotions)
Shaving equipment
Table or trolley for bathing equipment
Linen carrier
Implementation
Preparation
Before bathing determine: (a) the purpose and type
of bath the person needs; (b) self-care ability of the
person; (c) any movement or positioning precautions


specific to the person; (d) other care the person
may be receiving, such as physiotherapy or x-rays,
in order to coordinate all aspects of health care and
prevent unnecessary fatigue; (e) the comfort level of
the person with being bathed by someone else; and
(f) necessary bath equipment and linens.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can participate. Discuss the
plan for bathing and explain any unfamiliar
procedures.
2. Perform hand hygiene by thoroughly washing
hands and keep a supply gloves handy for
contact with bodily fluids. Observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures as
necessary.
3. Provide for privacy by drawing the curtains
around the bed or closing the door to the
room. Some organisations provide signs
indicating the need for privacy. Rationale:
hygiene is a personal matter.
4. Prepare the person and the environment.
Invite a family member or significant other
to participate if desired after consent has


been given by the person.
Close windows and doors to ensure the
room is a comfortable temperature.
Rationale: air currents increase loss of
heat from the body by convection.
Offer the person a bedpan or urinal or ask
whether the person wishes to use the
toilet or commode. Rationale: warm
water and activity can stimulate the need
to void. The person will be more
comfortable after voiding and voiding
before cleaning the perineum is advisable.
Encourage the person to perform as much
personal self-care as possible. Rationale:
this promotes independence, exercise and
self-esteem.
During the bath, assess each area of the
skin carefully.
For a bed bath
5. Prepare the bed and position the person
appropriately.
Position the bed at a comfortable working
height. Lower the side rail on the side
close to you. Keep the other side rail up.
Assist the person to move near you.
Rationale: this avoids undue reaching


and straining and promotes good body
mechanics.
Place a bath blanket or towels (depending
on what resources are available) over the
top sheet. Remove the top sheet from
under the bath blanket by starting at the
person’s shoulders and moving linen down
toward the person’s feet. 1 Ask the person
to grasp and hold the top of the bath
blanket while pulling linen to the foot of the
bed. Rationale: the bath blanket provides
comfort, warmth and privacy. Note: if the
bed linen is to be reused, place it over the
bedside chair. If it is to be changed, place
it directly in the linen carrier, not on the
floor.


1 Remove top sheet from under the bath
blanket
Remove gown while keeping the person
covered with the bath blanket. Place gown
in linen carrier.
6. Wash the face. Rationale: begin the bath at
the cleanest area and work downwards
towards the feet.
Place towel under person’s head.
Using a washcloth, clean the eyes with
water only. Using the other hand, dry eyes


well using a separate corner of the
washcloth for each eye. Rationale: using
separate corners prevents transmitting
micro-organisms from one eye to the
other. Wipe from the inner to the outer
canthus. 2 Rationale: this prevents
secretions from entering the nasolacrimal
ducts.


2 Using a separate corner of the
washcloth for each eye, wipe from the
inner to the outer canthus
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.


Ask whether the person wants soap to be
used on the face. Rationale: soap has a
drying effect and the face, which is
exposed to the air more than other body
parts, tends to be drier. The person may
have their own supply of products they
prefer to use on their face.
Using the washcloth in dominant hand,
wash and rinse the person’s face, ears
and neck. Dry using non-dominant hand
and a clean towel.
Remove the towel from under the
person’s head.
7. Wash the arms and hands. (Optional) Place a
towel on the bed and put a washbasin on it.
Place the person’s hands in the basin.
Rationale: many people enjoy immersing
their hands in the basin and washing
themselves. Soaking loosens dirt under the
nails. Assist the person as needed to wash,
rinse and dry the hands, paying particular
attention to the spaces between the fingers.
(Omit the arms for a partial bath.)
Place a towel lengthwise under the arm
away from you. Rationale: it protects the
bed from becoming wet.


Using the washcloth, wash and rinse the
arm by elevating the person’s arm and
supporting the wrist and elbow. Dry arm
well with a towel. Use long, firm strokes
from wrist to shoulder, 3 including the
axillary area. Rationale: firm strokes from
distal to proximal areas promote
circulation by increasing venous blood
return. In people with exceptionally fragile
skin, gently patting with a dry towel may
be more appropriate to avoid the risk of
skin damage.


3 Washing the far arm using long, firm
strokes from wrist to shoulder area
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Apply deodorant or powder, depending on
patient preference.
Repeat for hand and arm nearest you.
Exercise caution if an intravenous infusion
is present and check its flow after moving
the arm.
8. Wash the chest and abdomen. (Omit the
chest and abdomen for a partial bath).
Place the bath towel lengthwise over the
chest. Fold the bath blanket down to the
pubic area. Rationale: this keeps the
person warm while preventing
unnecessary exposure of the chest.
Lift the bath towel off the chest and bathe
the chest and abdomen with the
washcloth using long, firm strokes. 4 Give
special attention to the skin under the
breasts and any other skin folds,
particularly if the person is overweight,
diaphoretic or shows signs of skin
irritation. Rinse. Dry well with towel.


4 Washing the chest and abdomen
Source: Patrick Watson.
Replace the bath blanket when the areas
have been dried.
9. Wash the legs and feet. (Omit legs and feet
for a partial bath.)
Expose the leg furthest from you by
folding the bath blanket towards the other
leg, being careful to keep the perineum


covered. Rationale: covering the
perineum promotes privacy and maintains
the person’s dignity.
Lift leg and place the bath towel
lengthwise under the leg. Using the
washcloth, wash and rinse the leg using
long, firm strokes from the ankle to the
knee to the thigh. 5 Dry with towel.
Rationale: washing from the distal to
proximal areas promotes circulation by
stimulating venous blood flow.
Reverse the coverings and repeat for the
other leg.
Wash the feet by placing them in the
basin of water placed on a towel on the
bed. 6
Dry each foot. Pay particular attention to
the spaces between the toes. If preferred,
wash one foot after that leg before
washing the other leg.


5 Washing far leg
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Obtain fresh, warm bathwater now or
when necessary. Rationale: water may
become dirty or cold. Lower the bed and
raise the bed rail if needed when refilling
basin. Rationale: this ensures the safety
of the person.


6 Soaking a foot in a basin
10. Wash the back and then the perineum.
Instruct the person to use the bed rail on
the other side of the bed and assist the
person into a prone or side-lying position
facing away from you. Rationale: using
the bed rail assists the person to roll
further, prevents falling and assists in


making the person feel secure. Place the
bath towel lengthwise alongside the back
and buttocks while keeping the person
covered with the bath blanket as much as
possible. Rationale: this provides warmth
and prevents undue exposure and
protects the linen below the patient from
becoming wet.
7 Washing the back
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Using the washcloth, wash the person’s
back, moving from the shoulders to the
buttocks and upper thighs, paying


attention to the gluteal folds. 7 Dry well
using a towel.
(Optional) Perform a back massage now
or after completion of bath. (See Skill
48.1.)
While in this position, bed linen may be
changed if required. (See Skill 34.10
.)
Assist the person to the supine position
and determine whether they can wash the
perineal area independently. If they cannot
do so, drape the person’s torso and pelvic
region and, using the washcloth, wash the
perineal area. Dry well using a towel.
Discard towel by placing directly into the
linen carrier.
11. Assist with grooming aids such as powder,
lotion or deodorant.
Use powder sparingly. Release as little as
possible into the atmosphere. Rationale:
this will avoid irritation of the respiratory
tract by powder inhalation. Excessive
powder can cause caking, which leads to
skin irritation. If used in the bathroom,
powder on the floor can cause a person to
slip and fall.
Help the person put on a clean gown or
pyjamas; ensure the back of the gown or


pyjamas and linen are wrinkle free.
Rationale: wrinkles in linen or bedclothes
are uncomfortable to lie on and may
cause pressure areas in those with frail
skin.
Assist with care for hair, mouth and nails.
Some people prefer or need mouth care
prior to their bath.
For a bath or shower
12. Prepare the person and the bathtub.
Fill the bathtub about one-half full of water
at 43°C to 46°C. Rationale: sufficient
water is needed to cover the perineal
area.
Cover all intravenous catheters, plaster
casts or wound dressings with plastic
coverings and instruct the person to
prevent wetting these areas if possible.
Put a rubber bath mat on the floor of the
bathtub if safety strips are not present.
Rationale: to prevent slippage of the
person during the bath or shower.
13. Assist the person into the shower or bathtub.
Assist the person taking a standing
shower with the initial adjustment of the
water temperature and water flow


pressure, as needed. Rationale: some
people may need to sit on a chair in the
shower because of weakness or fatigue.
Hot water or steamy environments can
cause older adults to feel faint or become
short of breath.
Explain how the person can signal for
help, leave the person for 2 to 5 minutes
and place an ‘occupied’ sign on the door.
For safety reasons, do not leave a person
with decreased cognition or who may be
at risk (e.g. history of seizures, syncope).
14. Assist with washing and getting out of the
bathtub as necessary.
Using a washcloth, wash the person’s
back, lower legs and feet, if necessary.
Assist the person out of the bathtub. If the
person is unsteady, place a bath towel
over their shoulders and drain the bathtub
of water before they attempt to get out of
it. Rationale: draining the water first
lessens the likelihood of a fall. The towel
prevents chilling.
15. Assist the person to dry themself and assist
with follow-up care.
Follow step 11.


Assist the person back to their bed.
16. Clean the bathtub or shower area in
accordance with organisation practice,
discard the used linen in the linen carrier and
place the ‘unoccupied’ sign on the door.
17. Document:
type of bath given (i.e. complete, partial or
self-help)—this is usually recorded on a
care plan
skin assessment, such as excoriation,
erythema, exudates, rashes, drainage or
skin breakdown
nursing interventions related to skin
integrity
ability of the person to assist or cooperate
with bathing
the person’s response to bathing
educational needs regarding hygiene
information or teaching shared with the
person or the family.
Variation: bathing using a hydraulic bathtub
chair
If the person requires considerable assistance
getting into a bathtub, a hydraulic bath chair may be
required. A hydraulic lifting machine, or hoist, often
used in long-term care or rehabilitation settings, can


facilitate the transfer of a person who is unable to
manoeuvre in and out of a bathtub. The lifting
machine also helps eliminate strain on the nurse’s
back.
Bring the person to the bathroom in a wheelchair
or shower chair.
Fill the bath and check the water temperature
with a bath thermometer, if available, to avoid
thermal injury to the person.
Lower the hydraulic chair lift to its lowest point,
outside the bathtub. 8
8 Lower the hoist to its lowest point, outside the
bath


Transfer the person to the chair lift and secure
the seatbelt.
Raise the chair lift above the bath.
Support the person’s legs as the chair is moved
over the bathtub to avoid injury to the legs.
Position the legs down into the water and slowly
lower the chair lift into the bath.
Assist in bathing, as required.
Reverse the procedure when taking the person
out of the bath.
Assist the person to dry themselves or dry the
person and transport them to their room.
Evaluation
Note the person’s tolerance of the procedure
(e.g. respiratory rate and effort, pulse rate,
behaviours of acceptance or resistance,
statements regarding comfort).
Conduct appropriate follow-up, such as:
condition and integrity of skin (dryness,
turgor, redness, lesions)
condition of wound dressings etc.)
assessment of strength
percentage of bath done without assistance
Relate to prior assessment data, if available.


SKILL
34.2 Providing perineal–genital
care
Purposes
To remove normal perineal secretions and
odours.
To protect the skin around the perineal area.
To promote comfort.
Assessment
Assess for the presence of
Irritation, excoriation, inflammation, swelling.
Excessive discharge.
Odour; pain or discomfort.
Urinary or faecal incontinence.
Recent rectal or perineal surgery.
Indwelling catheter.
Determine
Perineal–genital hygiene practices.


Self-care abilities.
Planning
Delegation
Perineal–genital care can be delegated to the AIN or
other caregivers. If the person has recently had
perineal, rectal or genital surgery, the nurse needs
to assess if it is appropriate for the AIN or other
caregiver to perform this care.
Equipment
Perineal–genital care provided in conjunction with
the bed bath:
Bath towel
Bath blanket
Gloves
Bath basin with water at 43°C to 46°C (or
disposable wet wipes, if available)
Soap (or disposable wet wipes, if available)
Washcloth
Special perineal–genital care:
Bath towel
Bath blanket
Gloves


Cotton balls or gauze swabs
Solution bottle, jug or container filled with warm
water or a prescribed solution
Bedpan to receive rinse water
Moisture-resistant bag or receptacle for used
swabs
Perineal pad
Implementation
Preparation
Determine whether the person is experiencing
any discomfort in the perineal–genital area.
Obtain and prepare the necessary equipment
and supplies.
Perineal care always requires the use of gloves.
Determine if the person wishes to defecate or
urinate before the hygiene care.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can cooperate, being
particularly sensitive to any embarrassment
felt by the person.


2. Perform hand hygiene (hand wash) and
observe other appropriate infection-control
procedures (e.g. gloves).
3. Provide for privacy by drawing the curtains
around the bed or closing the door to the
room. Some organisations provide signs
indicating the need for privacy. Rationale:
hygiene is a personal matter.
4. Prepare the person:
Fold the top bed linen to the foot of the
bed and fold the gown up to expose the
genital area.
Place a bath towel under the person’s
hips. Rationale: the bath towel prevents
the bed from becoming soiled.
5. Position and drape the person.
Put on gloves; wash and dry the upper
inner thighs.
For females
Position the female in a back-lying
position with the knees flexed and
spread well apart. The person may
have limited rage of movement or find
this position uncomfortable, in which
case, pillows may be used for extra
support for the hips and knees.


Cover her body and legs with the bath
blanket positioned so a corner is at her
head, the opposite corner at her feet
and the other two on the sides. Drape
the legs by tucking the bottom corners
of the bath blanket under the inner
sides of the legs. 1 Rationale:
minimum exposure lessens
embarrassment and helps to provide
warmth. Bring the middle portion of the
base of the blanket up over the pubic
area.
Put on gloves, wash and dry the upper
inner thighs.
Note excessive discharge, unusual
odours or secretions from the orifices.
For males
Position the male person in a supine
position with knees slightly flexed and
hips slightly externally rotated.


1 Draping the woman for perineal–
genital care
Put on gloves; wash and dry the upper
inner thighs.
6. Inspect the perineal area.
Note particular areas of inflammation,
excoriation or swelling, especially between


the buttocks, between the labia in females
and the scrotal folds in males.
7. Wash and dry the perineal–genital area.
For females
Clean the labia majora. Then spread the
labia to wash the folds between the labia
majora and the labia minora. 2


2 Female genitals
Rationale: secretions that tend to collect
around the labia minora facilitate bacterial
growth and odour.
Use separate quarters of the washcloth
for each stroke and wipe from the pubis to


the rectum. For menstruating women and
people with indwelling catheters, use
disposable wipes, using a new wipe for
each stroke. Rationale: using separate
quarters of the washcloth or new wipes
prevents the transmission of micro-
organisms from one area to the other.
Wipe from the area of least contamination
(the pubis) to that of greatest (the
rectum).
Rinse the area well. You may place the
woman on a bedpan and use a periwash
or solution bottle to pour warm water over
the area. Dry the perineum thoroughly,
paying attention to the folds between the
labia. Rationale: moisture supports the
growth of many micro-organisms.
For males
Wash and dry the penis
If the man is uncircumcised, retract the
prepuce (foreskin) to expose the glans
penis (the tip of the penis) for cleaning.
Replace the foreskin after cleaning the
glans penis. 3 Rationale: retracting the
foreskin is necessary to remove the
smegma (thick, cheesy secretion) that
collects under the foreskin and facilitates


bacterial growth. Replacing the foreskin
prevents constriction of the penis, which
may cause oedema.
3 Male genitals
Wash and dry the scrotum. The posterior
folds of the scrotum may need to be
cleaned when the buttocks are cleaned
(see step 9). Rationale: the scrotum
tends to be more soiled than the penis
because of its proximity to the rectum;
thus it is usually cleaned after the penis.


8. Inspect perineal orifices for intactness.
Inspect particularly around the urethra in
people with indwelling catheters.
Rationale: a catheter may cause
excoriation and pressure areas around the
urethra.
9. Clean between the buttocks.
Assist the person to turn onto the side
facing away from you.
Pay particular attention to the anal area
and posterior folds of the scrotum in
males. Clean the anus with toilet tissue

Dry the area well.
For post-delivery or menstruating females,
apply a perineal pad as needed.
10. Remove gloves and wash hands well.
11. Document any unusual findings such as
redness, excoriation, skin breakdown, odour,

of tenderness.
Evaluation
Relate current assessments to previous
assessments.


Conduct appropriate follow-up such as
prescribed ointment for excoriation.
Report any deviation from normal to the doctor.


Feet
The feet are essential for ambulation and merit attention even when
people are confined to bed. Each foot contains 26 bones, 107
ligaments and 19 muscles. These structures function together for
both standing and walking.
Developmental variations
The average person takes 5000–7500 steps per day. Each step
places 2 to 3 times the force of the body weight on the feet. This
repetitive use leads to normal changes associated with ageing.
These include wider and longer feet, mild settling of the arches and
loss of natural padding on the bottom of the heels. The cartilage
around the joints also deteriorates, producing loss of normal range
of motion of the foot and ankle (Tomassoni, Traini & Amenta ). All
older adults should know about foot care. However, some older
individuals require special attention for their feet. For example,
reduced blood supply and accompanying arteriosclerosis can make
a foot prone to ulcers and infection.
7 Tomassoni, D., Traini, E. & Amenta F. (2014). Gender and age related differences in foot
morphology. Maturitas, 79, 421–427.
7


Clinical consideration
People with diabetes are at high risk of lower
extremity amputations (LEA). Routine foot
assessment and education in proper foot care
can significantly reduce the risk of LEA.


Nursing management
Assessing
Assessment of the feet includes a nursing health history, physical
assessment of the feet and identifying people at risk of foot
problems.
Nursing health history
The nurse determines the person’s history of (a) normal nail and
foot care practices, (b) type of footwear worn, (c) self-care abilities,
(d) presence of risk factors for foot problems, (e) any foot
discomfort and (f) any perceived problems with foot mobility. To
obtain such data, the nurse asks the questions provided in the
‘Assessment interview
’.
Physical assessment
Each foot and toe is inspected for shape, size and presence of
lesions, and is palpated to assess areas of tenderness, oedema and
circulatory status. Normally, the toes are straight and flat. Table
34.4
 lists physical assessment methods for the feet. Common
foot problems include calluses, corns, unpleasant odours, plantar


warts, fissures between the toes and fungal infections such as
athlete’s foot.
Table 34.4 Assessment of the feet
A callus
 is a localised, thickened, hardened portion of epidermis,
resulting from repetitive friction from footwear. Most calluses are
painless and flat and are found on the bottom or side of the foot
over a bony prominence. They can be softened by soaking the foot
in warm water with Epsom salts and abraded with pumice stones or
similar abrasives. Creams help to keep the skin soft and prevent the
formation of calluses.
Assessment interview
Foot hygiene
Foot care practices
How often do you wash your feet and cut your toenails?
What hygiene products do you usually use on your feet
(e.g. soap, foot powder or deodorant, lotion or cream)?
What type of shoes and socks do you wear?
How often do you change your socks or put on clean
socks?
Do you ever go barefoot? If so, when, where and how
often?


Self-care abilities
Do you have any problems managing your foot care? If
so, what are these?
What assistance do you need to care for your feet?
Can you reach your feet to dry between your toes?
Do you have any vision problems that may prevent you
from clearly seeing your feet?
Foot problems and risk factors
Do you have any foot odour or discomfort? If so, where?
When does this occur? What do you do to relieve the
discomfort?
Have you noticed any problems with foot mobility (e.g.
joint stiffness)?
Do you have diabetes, any circulatory problems with feet
(e.g. swelling, changes in skin colour, arthritis) or any
instances of prolonged exposure to chemicals or water?
A corn
 is a keratosis caused by friction and pressure from a
shoe. It commonly occurs on the fourth or fifth toe, usually on a
bony prominence such as a joint. Corns are usually conical (circular
and raised). The base is the surface of the corn. The apex is in
deeper tissues, sometimes even attached to bone. Corns are
generally removed surgically. They are prevented from re-forming by


relieving the pressure on the area (i.e. wearing comfortable shoes)
and massaging the tissue to promote circulation. The use of oval
corn pads should be avoided because they increase pressure and
decrease circulation.
Unpleasant foot odours occur as a result of perspiration and its
interaction with micro-organisms. Regular and frequent washing and
thorough drying of the feet and wearing clean hosiery help to
minimise odour. Foot powders and deodorants also help to manage
this problem.
Plantar warts
 appear on the sole of the foot. These warts are
caused by the human papilloma virus. They are moderately
contagious. The warts are frequently painful and often make walking
difficult. Current treatments include debridement, freezing with solid
carbon dioxide and topical applications such as salicylic acid
(Webber & Hoffman ).
8 Webber, C. A. & Hoffman, K. M. (2013). How to treat recalcitrant plantar warts. Podiatry
Today, 26(7).
Fissures
, or deep grooves, frequently occur between the toes as
a result of dryness and cracking of the skin. The treatment of choice
is good foot hygiene and application of an antiseptic to prevent
infection. Often a small piece of gauze is inserted between the toes
in applying the antiseptic and left in place to assist healing by
allowing air to reach the area.
8


Athlete’s foot, or tinea pedis
 (ringworm of the foot), is caused by
a fungus. The symptoms are scaling and cracking of the skin,
particularly between the toes. Sometimes small blisters form,
containing a thin fluid. In severe cases, the lesions may also appear
on other parts of the body, particularly the hands. Treatments
usually involve the application of commercial antifungal ointments or
powders. Prevention is important. Common preventive measures
are keeping the feet well ventilated, drying the feet well after
bathing, wearing clean socks or stockings, and not going barefoot in
public showers.
An ingrown toenail
, the growing inwards of the nail into the soft
tissues around it, most often results from improper nail trimming.
Pressure applied to the area from footwear or touch causes
localised pain. Treatment involves frequent, hot antiseptic soaks and
surgical removal of the portion of nail embedded in the skin.
Preventing recurrence involves appropriate instruction and
adherence to proper nail-trimming techniques.
Identifying people at risk
Due to reduced peripheral circulation to the feet, people with
diabetes or peripheral vascular disease are particularly prone to
infection if skin breakage occurs. Many foot problems can be
prevented by teaching simple foot care guidelines.
Diagnosing


Assessment and diagnoses related to people with foot or foot care
problems include:
Self-care deficit: hygiene (foot care) related to:
a. visual impairment
b. impaired hand coordination
c. inability to reach the feet
d. other related or contributing factors (see Box 34.1
).
Risk of impaired skin integrity related to:
a. altered tissue perfusion: peripheral (associated with
oedema, inadequate arterial circulation)
b. ageing
c. poorly fitting shoes.
Risk of infection related to:
a. impaired skin integrity (ingrown toenail, corn, trauma)
b. deficient nail or foot care.
Deficient knowledge (diabetes foot care) related to:
a. lack of teaching/learning activities about diabetes foot care
b. newly established medical diagnosis (diabetes) and
necessary foot hygiene practices.
Examples are provided in ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes
and interventions’.


Planning
Planning involves (a) identifying nursing interventions that will help
the person maintain or restore healthy foot care practices, and (b)
establishing desired outcomes for each individual. Interventions may
include teaching about correct nail and foot care, proper footwear
and ways to prevent potential foot problems (e.g. infection, injury
and decreased circulation). For people with self-care difficulties, the
nurse plans a schedule for soaking the person’s feet and assisting
with regular cleaning and trimming of nails (if not contraindicated).
Foot and nail care is often provided when hygiene needs are
attended to. The frequency of foot care is determined together by
the nurse and the individual and is based on objective assessment
data and the person’s specific problems. For some people, the feet
need to be bathed daily; for those whose feet perspire excessively,
bathing more than once a day may be necessary.
Implementing
Skill 34.3
 describes how to provide foot care. See also the
discussion of nails. During these procedures, the nurse can teach
the appropriate methods for foot care; that is, methods designed to
prevent foot tissue injury and infection.


IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
Assisting people with foot care
History Mrs Maria Camporeale is an 83-year-old widow who
lives alone. She receives home support services twice a week
and Meals on Wheels service daily. Mrs Camporeale has
pronounced hand tremors and obvious cataracts and
manages to shower once a week with her daughter’s help.
History Jim Wakefield, 64 years old, was recently diagnosed
with type 2 diabetes mellitus. States he has heard of
‘diabetes’ and is worried because a friend of his father had
diabetes and, after cutting his foot, had his leg amputated.
Evaluating
Examples of desired outcomes for foot hygiene include the person
being able to:
participate in self-care (foot hygiene) to optimal level of capacity
(specify)
describe hygiene and other interventions (e.g. proper footwear)
to maintain skin integrity, prevent infection and maintain


peripheral tissue perfusion
demonstrate optimal foot hygiene, as evidenced by:
a. intact, pink, smooth, soft, hydrated and warm skin
b. intact cuticles and skin surrounding nails
c. correct foot care and nail care practices.
Clinical consideration
People with diabetes often have extremely dry
skin. Encourage them to use a non-perfumed
lotion and to avoid putting lotion between the
toes. Creams and lotions are available
specifically for dry skin associated with diabetes.
Advise to not soak their feet in water because it
may increase the risk of foot problems.


SKILL
34.3 Providing foot care
Purposes
To maintain the skin integrity of the feet.
To prevent foot infections.
To prevent foot odours.
To assess or monitor foot problems.
Assessment
Determine
History of any problems with foot discomfort, foot
odour, foot mobility, circulatory problems (e.g.
swelling, changes in skin colour and/or
temperature and pain), structural problems (e.g.
bunion, hammer toe or overlapping digits).
Usual foot care practices (e.g. frequency of
washing feet and cutting nails, foot hygiene
products used, how often socks are changed,
whether the person ever goes barefoot, whether
the person sees a podiatrist).


Assess
Skin surfaces for cleanliness, odour, dryness and
intactness.
Each foot and toe for shape, size, presence of
lesions (e.g. corn, callus, wart or rash) and areas
of tenderness, ankle oedema.
Skin temperatures of both feet to assess
circulatory status.
Pedal pulses (dorsalis pedis and posterior tibialis)
and capillary refill times.
Self-care abilities (e.g. any problems managing
foot care).
Planning
Delegation
Foot care for the healthy person (i.e. without
diabetes) can be delegated to the assistant in
nursing (AIN) or other caregivers. Remind these
caregivers to notify the RN of anything that looks out
of the ordinary. Review with the AIN or other
caregiver the organisation policy about cutting or
trimming nails.
Equipment
Washbasin containing warm water
Pillow
Moisture-resistant disposable pad


Towels
Soap
Washcloth
Toenail cleaning and trimming equipment, if
organisation policy permits
Lotion or foot powder
Implementation
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can cooperate.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for privacy by drawing the curtains
around the bed or closing the door to the
room. Some organisations provide signs
indicating the need for privacy. Rationale:
hygiene is a personal matter.
4. Prepare the person and equipment.
Fill the washbasin with warm water at
about 40°C to 43°C. Rationale: warm
water promotes circulation, softens skin,
comforts and refreshes.


Assist the ambulatory person to a sitting
position in a chair or the person confined
to bed to a supine or semi-Fowler’s
position.
For a person in bed, place a pillow under
the knees. Rationale: this provides
support and prevents muscle fatigue.
Place the washbasin on the moisture-
resistant pad on the foot of the bed for a
person in bed or on the floor in front of the
chair for an ambulatory person.
For a person in bed, pad the rim of the
washbasin with a towel. Rationale: the
towel prevents undue pressure on the skin
and protects the linen below from
becoming wet.
5. Wash the foot and soak it.
Place one of the person’s feet in the basin
and wash it with soap, paying particular
attention to the interdigital areas.
Prolonged soaking is generally not
recommended for the person with
diabetes or individuals with peripheral
vascular disease. Rationale: prolonged
soaking may remove natural skin oils, thus
drying the skin and making it more
susceptible to cracking and infection.


Rinse the foot well to remove soap.
Rationale: soap irritates the skin if not
completely removed.
Rub callused areas of the foot with the
washcloth. Rationale: this helps remove
dead skin layers.
If the nails are brittle or thick and require
trimming, replace the water and allow the
foot to soak for 10 to 20 minutes.
Rationale: soaking softens the nails and
loosens debris under them.
Clean the nails as required with an orange
stick. Rationale: this removes excess
debris that harbours micro-organisms.
Remove the foot from the basin and place
it on the towel.
6. Dry the foot thoroughly and apply lotion or
foot powder.
Blot the foot gently with the towel to dry it
thoroughly, particularly between the toes.
Rationale: harsh rubbing can damage the
skin. Thorough drying reduces the risk of
infection.
Apply lotion or cream to the foot but not
between the toes. Rationale: this
lubricates dry skin and keeps the area
between the toes dry.


or
Apply a foot powder containing a non-
irritating deodorant if the feet tend to
perspire excessively. Rationale: foot
powders have greater absorbent
properties than regular bath powders;
some also contain menthol, which makes
the feet feel cool.
7. If organisation policy permits, trim the nails of
the first foot while the second foot is soaking.
See the discussion on nails for the
appropriate method to trim nails. Note that
in many organisations, toenail trimming
requires a doctor’s order or is
contraindicated for people with diabetes
mellitus, toe infections and peripheral
vascular disease, unless performed by a
podiatrist, general practitioner or
advanced practice provider such as a
Nurse Practitioner.
8. Document any foot problems observed.
Foot care is not generally recorded unless
problems are noted.
Record any signs of inflammation,
infection, breaks in the skin, corns,
troublesome calluses, bunions and


pressure areas. This is of particular
importance for people with peripheral
vascular disease and diabetes.
Evaluation
Inspect nails and skin after the soak.
Compare to prior assessment data.
Report any abnormalities to the doctor.


Nails
Nails grow throughout life and change very little until people are
aged. At that time, the nails tend to be tougher, more brittle and in
some cases thicker. The nails of an older person normally grow
more slowly than those of a younger person and may be
discoloured, ridged and grooved.


Nursing management
Assessing
During the nursing health history, the nurse explores the person’s
usual nail care practices, self-care abilities and any problems
associated with them (see ‘Assessment interview
’). Physical
assessment involves inspection of the nails (e.g. nail shape and
texture, nail bed colour and tissues surrounding the nails).
Assessment interview
Nail hygiene
Do you have any problems managing your nail care? If
so, what are these?
Have you had any problems associated with your nails
(e.g. inflammation of the tissue surrounding the nail,
injury, prolonged exposure to water or chemicals,
circulatory problems)?


Diagnosing
Problems relating to nails include:
Self-care deficit: grooming related to:
a. impaired vision
b. impaired hand coordination.
Risk of infection around the nail bed related to:
a. impaired skin integrity of cuticles
b. altered peripheral circulation.
Planning
The nurse identifies measures that will assist the person to develop
or maintain healthy nail care practices. A schedule of nail care needs
is to be established.
Implementing
To provide nail care, the nurse needs a nail cutter or sharp scissors,
a nail file, an orange stick to push back the cuticle, hand lotion or
mineral oil to lubricate any dry tissue around the nails and a basin of
water to soak the nails if they are particularly thick or hard. Check


the organisation’s policy regarding nail care. Often podiatrists must
be consulted for people with diabetes.
One hand or foot is soaked, if needed, and dried; then the nail is cut
or filed straight across beyond the end of the finger or toe (see
Figure 34.4
). Avoid trimming or digging into nails at the lateral
corners. This predisposes the person to ingrown toenails. People
who have diabetes or circulatory problems should have their nails
filed rather than cut; inadvertent injury to tissues can occur if
scissors are used (Diabetes Australia ). After the initial cut or filing,
the nail is filed to round the corners and the nurse cleans under the
nail. The nurse then gently pushes back the cuticle, taking care not
to rip or cause injury. The next finger or toe is cared for in the same
manner. Any abnormalities, such as an infected cuticle or
inflammation of the tissue around the nail, are recorded and
reported.
9 Diabetes Australia (2015). Living with Diabetes, Preventing Complications—Foot Care.
Retrieved from <www.diabetesaustralia.com.au>.
Figure 34.4
9


Fingernails are trimmed straight across.
Evaluating


Examples of desired outcomes for nail hygiene include the person
being able to:
demonstrate healthy nail care practices, as shown by:
a. clean, short nails with smooth edges
b. intact cuticles and hydrated surrounding skin
describe factors contributing to the nail problem
describe preventive interventions for the specific nail problem
demonstrate nail care as instructed.
In addition, the person should have pink nail beds and quick return
of nail bed colour after the blanch test (pressure applied to the nail
bed).


Mouth
Each tooth has three parts: the crown, the root and the pulp cavity
(see Figure 34.5
). The crown is the exposed part of the tooth,
which is outside the gum. It is covered with a hard substance called
enamel. The ivory-coloured internal part of the crown below the
enamel is the dentin. The root of a tooth is embedded in the jaw and
covered by a bony tissue called cementum. The pulp cavity in the
centre of the tooth contains the blood vessels and nerves.
Figure 34.5


The anatomical parts of a tooth.
Developmental variations


Teeth usually appear 5 to 8 months after birth. By the time children
are 2 years old, they usually have all 20 of their temporary teeth
(see Figure 34.6
). At about age 6 or 7, children start losing their
deciduous teeth and these are gradually replaced by the 33
permanent teeth (see Figure 34.7
). By age 25, most people have
all of their permanent teeth.
Figure 34.6


Temporary teeth and their times of eruption (stated in months).
Figure 34.7


Permanent teeth and their times of eruption (stated in years).
In Australia, tooth decay in young children with deciduous (baby)
teeth has been reported as occurring in 42% of 5-year-olds. In
children with permanent teeth, tooth decay can be as high as 61%
for 9-year-olds and 58% for teenagers. Tooth decay is often due to
inadequate dietary intake or dental care as a result of the cost of
dental insurance and care (Chrisopoulos & Harford ).
10 Chrisopoulos, S. & Harford, J. E. (2013). Oral Health and Dental Care in Australia: Key
Facts and Figures 2012. Cat. no. DEN 224. Canberra: AIHW.
Teeth are normally off-white and turn yellowish in colour as a part of
the ageing process. With age, the enamel thins and the yellow-grey
colour of the inner portion of the teeth begins to show. In addition,
coffee drinking and cigarette smoking can stain the teeth.
Loss of teeth in adults occurs mainly because of periodontal
disease
 (gum disease) and cavities (dental caries
), although
the latter are more common in younger adults. Lack of fluoridated
water and preventive dentistry during developmental years may
cause tooth and gum problems in older adults. In Australia,
complete edentulism (loss of teeth) in older adults has decreased
and rates of periodontal disease and tooth decay have increased
(Bernoth & Winkler
).
10
11


11 Bernoth, M. & Winkler, D. (2017). Healthy Ageing and Aged Care. South Melbourne, Vic:
Oxford University Press.


Nursing management
Assessing
Assessment of the mouth and hygiene practices includes (a) a
nursing health history, (b) physical assessment of the mouth and (c)
identification of people at risk of developing oral problems.
Nursing history
During the nursing health history, the nurse obtains data about the
person’s oral hygiene practices, including dental visits, self-care
abilities and past or current mouth problems. Data about oral
hygiene helps the nurse determine learning needs and incorporate
the person’s needs and preferences in the plan of care. Assessment
of the self-care abilities determines the amount and type of nursing
assistance to provide. People whose hand coordination or vision is
impaired, whose cognitive function is impaired, whose illness alters
energy levels and motivation, or whose therapy imposes restrictions
on activities will need assistance from the nurse. Information about
past or current problems alerts the nurse to specific interventions
required or referrals that may be necessary. Questions to elicit this
information are shown in the ‘Assessment interview
’.


Assessment interview
Oral hygiene
Oral hygiene practices
What are your usual mouth care and/or denture care
practices?
What oral hygiene products do you routinely use (e.g.
mouthwash, type of toothpaste and toothbrush, dental
floss, denture cleaner)?
When was your last dental examination and how often do
you see your dentist?
Self-care abilities
Do you have any problems managing your mouth care?
Past or current mouth problems
Have you had or do you have any problems such as
bleeding, swollen or reddened gums, ulcerations, lumps or
tooth pain?
Do your dentures fit well? Do they cause you any pain?


Physical assessment
For information about mouth assessment, see Chapter 31
.
Dental caries (cavities) and periodontal disease are the two
problems that most frequently affect the teeth. Both problems are
commonly associated with plaque and tartar deposits. Plaque
 is
an invisible soft film that adheres to the enamel surface of teeth; it
consists of bacteria, molecules of saliva and remnants of epithelial
cells and leukocytes. When plaque is unchecked, tartar (dental
calculus) is formed. Tartar
 is a visible, hard deposit of plaque and
dead bacteria that forms at the gum lines. Tartar build-up can alter
the fibres that attach the teeth to the gum and eventually disrupt
bone tissue. Periodontal disease is characterised by gingivitis
(red, swollen gingiva), bleeding, receding gum lines and the
formation of pockets between the teeth and gums. In advanced
periodontal disease (pyorrhoea
), the teeth are loose and pus is
evident when the gums are pressed. Table 34.5
 lists additional
problems of the mouth.
Table 34.5 Common problems of the mouth
Identifying individuals at risk
A lack of knowledge or the inability to maintain oral hygiene
predisposes some people to oral problems. These include those
people who are seriously ill, confused, unconscious, fatigued,
dehydrated or who have a decrease in motivation for self-care. In
addition, people with nasogastric tubes or receiving oxygen are likely


to develop dry oral mucous membranes, especially if they breathe
through their mouths. People who have had oral or jaw surgery must
have meticulous oral hygiene care to prevent the development of
infections.
Healthy-appearing individuals, too, may be at risk. High-risk
variables such as inadequate nutrition, lack of money and/or
insurance for dental care, excessive intake of refined sugars in
either foods or drinks and family history of periodontal disease also
need to be identified. Some older people may also be at risk; for
example, those who choose salty and enamel-eroding sugary foods
because of a decline in their number of taste buds. Decreased saliva
production in older adults, which produces a dry mouth and thinning
of the oral mucosa, is another factor.
A dry mouth can be aggravated by poor fluid intake, heavy smoking,
alcohol use, high salt intake, anxiety and many medications.
Medications that can cause dryness of the mouth include diuretics,
excessive laxative use, neuroleptics (used for psychosis and
schizophrenia) and anxiolytics (used for anxiety disorders). Some
chemotherapeutic agents used to treat cancer also cause oral
dryness and lesions. A common side effect of the anticonvulsant
drug phenytoin (Dilantin) is gingival hyperplasia, an overgrowth of
gum tissue around the teeth. Optimal oral hygiene (e.g. brushing
with a soft toothbrush and flossing) is needed.
Culturally competent care


Biocultural variation in teeth
In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children
have approximately twice as much tooth decay as non-
Indigenous children. Periodontal decay and disease is more
likely to be untreated in the Indigenous population, possibly
due to less access to dental care and fluoridated water,
particularly in regional and remote settings. In 2014–15, the
proportion of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children
aged 4–14 years who had teeth or gum problems was 34%
compared with 39% in 2008. Indigenous children living in
remote areas were more likely to have had teeth or gum
problems (37%) than children in non-remote areas (25%)
(Australian Bureau of Statistics ).
12 Australian Bureau of Statistics (2016). 2014–15 National Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander Social Survey. Canberra: ABS.
People who are receiving or have received radiation treatments to
the head and neck may have permanent damage to teeth, jaw
structure or salivary glands. Damage to the salivary glands results in
a very dry mouth and can often be treated by providing a thick liquid
called artificial saliva. Some people prefer to sip on liquids to moisten
their mouth.
Diagnosing
12


Problems related to oral hygiene and the oral cavity include having a
deficit in self-care and abnormal presentations.
Clinical consideration
People in long-term care settings are at high
risk of oral health problems. Aspiration
pneumonia can be caused by foreign material,
such as food debris, moving into the bronchial
tree and lung alveoli. Proper oral hygiene and
regular mouth care reduce the risk of aspiration
pneumonia (Müller
). The nurse must assess
the individual’s oral health and teach the AIN or
other caregiver about the importance of regular
and routine oral hygiene.
13 Müller, F. (2015). Oral hygiene reduces the mortality from
aspiration pneumonia in frail elders. Journal of Dental Research,
94(3 Suppl), 14S–16S. Doi: 10.1177/0022034514552494.
Impaired oral mucous membrane refers to, for example, a coated
tongue; dry mouth; halitosis; gingivitis; oral pain, discomfort,
erythema, oral lesions or ulcers; and dry mouth. These may be the
result of ineffective oral hygiene, physical injury or drying effect (e.g.
13


mouth breathing, oxygen therapy, dehydration), mechanical trauma
(e.g. oral surgery, braces or ill-fitting dentures), chemical trauma
(e.g. side effects of medications or recreational drug use) or
radiation therapy.
Clinical examples are shown in the ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses,
outcomes and interventions’.
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
Assisting people with mouth care
History Elena Psyridis, 77 years old, suffered a
cerebrovascular accident. Elena is unconscious and breathing
through the mouth with supplemental oxygen via a face
mask. She is receiving 2500 mL of fluid daily via intravenous
therapy located in her right forearm.
Planning
In planning care, the nurse and, if appropriate, the person and/or
family set outcomes for each nursing problem identified during
assessment. The nurse then performs nursing interventions and
activities to achieve these outcomes.


During the planning phase, the nurse also identifies interventions
that will help the person achieve these goals. Specific, detailed
nursing activities taken by the nurse may include the following:
Monitor every shift for dryness of the oral mucosa.
Monitor for signs and symptoms of glossitis (inflammation of the
tongue) and stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth).
Prioritise and assist dependent people with oral care.
Provide special oral hygiene for people who are debilitated or
unconscious, or have lesions of the mucous membranes or other
oral tissues.
Teach about good oral hygiene practices to prevent tooth decay.
Implementing
Good oral hygiene includes daily stimulation of the gums,
mechanical brushing and flossing of the teeth and flushing of the
mouth. The nurse is often in a position to help people maintain oral
hygiene by helping or teaching them to clean the teeth and oral
cavity, by inspecting whether individuals (especially children) have
done so or by actually providing mouth care to people who are ill or
incapacitated.
Promoting oral health through the lifespan


A major role of the nurse in promoting oral health is to teach people
about specific oral hygienic measures.
Infants and toddlers
Most dentists recommend that dental hygiene should begin when
the first tooth erupts and be practised after each feeding. Cleaning
can be accomplished by using a wet washcloth or small gauze
moistened with water.
The nurse should give parents the following instructions to promote
and maintain dental health:
Brush the child’s teeth with a soft toothbrush. Use only a
toothbrush moistened with water at first and introduce a fluoride
toothpaste at about 18 months of age.
Give a fluoride supplement daily or as recommended by the
doctor or dentist, unless the drinking water is fluoridated. In
Australia, 89% of the population have regular access to
fluoridated drinking water (National Health and Medical Research
Council ).
14 National Health and Medical Research Council (2017). Information Paper—Water
Fluoridation: Dental and Other Human Health Outcomes. Report prepared by the Clinical
Trials Centre at University of Sydney. Canberra: NHMRC.
Seek professional dental attention for any problems such as
pain, unusual discolouring of the teeth, chipping or signs of
infection such as redness and swelling (Australian Dental
Association ).
14
15


15 Australian Dental Association (2016a). Your Dental Health—Babies. Retrieved from
<www.ada.org.au>.
Preschoolers and school-age children
Deciduous teeth guide the entrance of permanent teeth and dental
care is essential to keep these teeth in good repair. Abnormally
placed or lost deciduous teeth can cause misalignment of
permanent teeth. Fluoride remains important at this stage to prevent
dental caries. Preschoolers need to be taught to brush their teeth
after eating and to limit their intake of refined sugars. Regular dental
check-ups are required during these years when permanent teeth
appear.
Adolescents and adults
Proper diet and tooth and mouth care should be evaluated and
reinforced to adolescents and adults. Specific measures to prevent
tooth decay and periodontal disease are listed in ‘Patient
education
’.
Patient education
Measures to prevent tooth decay
Brush the teeth thoroughly after meals and at bedtime. If
the teeth cannot be brushed after meals, vigorous rinsing
of the mouth with water is recommended.
Floss the teeth daily.


Ensure an adequate intake of nutrients, particularly
calcium, phosphorus, vitamins A, C and D and fluoride.
Avoid sweet foods and drinks between meals.
Eat coarse, fibrous foods (cleansing foods), such as fresh
fruits and raw vegetables.
Have a check-up by a dentist every 6 months.
Older adults
Age-related changes place older adults at risk of dental cavities and
periodontal disease. Older adults who are frail and have self-care
deficits are at an increased risk because they cannot maintain their
oral hygiene practices and/or may not be able to visit the dentist on
a routine basis. Excessive collection of bacteria in the mouth due to
poor oral hygiene increases the risk of pneumonia and
arteriosclerosis (Göstemeyer, Baker & Schwendicke ).
16 Göstemeyer, G., Baker, S. & Schwendicke, R. (2019). Barriers and facilitators for
provision of oral health care in dependent older people: A systematic review. Clinical Oral
Investigations, 23(3), 979–993. Doi: 10.1007/s00784-019-02812-4.
Brushing and flossing the teeth
Thorough brushing of the teeth with a fluoride toothpaste is
important in preventing tooth decay. The mechanical action of
brushing removes food particles that can harbour and incubate
bacteria. It also stimulates circulation in the gums, thus maintaining
16


their healthy firmness. Flossing teeth after brushing assists in
removing food particles and plaque and contributes to tooth and
gum health.
Caring for artificial dentures
Some people have artificial teeth in the form of a plate—a complete
set of teeth for one jaw. A person may have a lower denture or an
upper denture or both. When only a few artificial teeth are needed,
the individual may have a partial denture that is held in place by
clasps around existing teeth. A partial denture may be fixed or
removable. An implant-retained denture is a fixed denture that
replaces one or more single teeth and is held in place by implants
fixed in the jaw (Australian Dental Association ). Artificial teeth are
fitted to the individual and usually will not fit another person. People
who wear dentures or other types of oral prostheses should be
encouraged to use them. Ill-fitting dentures or other oral prostheses
can cause discomfort and chewing difficulties and often contribute to
poor enjoyment of food and malnutrition. Those who do not wear
their prostheses are prone to shrinkage of the gums, which results in
further tooth loss.
17 Australian Dental Association (2016b). Your Dental Health—Older Adults 651. Dentures.
Retrieved from <www.ada.org.au>.
Like natural teeth, artificial dentures collect micro-organisms and
food. They need to be cleaned at least once a day. Dentures are
removed from the mouth, scrubbed with a toothbrush, rinsed and
reinserted. Some people use a denture cream, sodium bicarbonate
17


or natural soap (rinsing well) for cleaning teeth and others use
commercial cleaning compounds for plates.
Assisting with oral care
When providing mouth care for partially or totally dependent people,
the nurse should wear gloves and protective eyewear to guard
against infections. Other required equipment includes a curved basin
that fits snugly under the person’s chin (e.g. a kidney basin) to
receive the rinse water and a towel to protect the person and the
bedclothes. See Skill 34.4
.
Large cottonwool swabs are often used in health care facilities to
clean the mouths of dependent people (see Figure 34.8
). These
swabs are convenient and effective in removing most excess debris
from the teeth and mouth but should be used infrequently and for
short periods (i.e. less than 3 days) as they do not remove plaque
that is at the base of the teeth.
Figure 34.8


Example of a cottonwool swab used to clean the mouth of a
dependent person.
Source: School of Nursing and Midwifery, University of South Australia.
Most people prefer privacy when they take out their artificial teeth to
clean them. Many do not like to be seen without their teeth or may
feel uncomfortable without them in place; one of the first requests of
many people postoperatively is ‘May I have my teeth in, please?’
The ‘Variation’ section in Skill 34.4
 describes how to clean
artificial dentures.


People with special oral hygiene needs
For the person who is debilitated or unconscious, or who has
excessive dryness, sores or irritations of the mouth, it may be
necessary to clean the oral mucosa and tongue in addition to the
teeth. Organisation practices differ in regard to special mouth care
and the frequency with which it is provided. Depending on the health
of the person’s mouth, special care may be needed every 2 to 8
hours.
Mouth care for unconscious or debilitated people is important
because their mouths tend to become dry and consequently
predisposed to tooth decay and infections. Saliva has antiviral,
antibacterial and antifungal effects (Tiwari ). Dry mouth—called
xerostomia
—occurs when the supply of saliva is reduced (Delli et
al.
; Olver
). This condition can be caused by side effects of
certain medications (e.g. antihistamines, antidepressants,
antihypertensives), oxygen therapy, tachypnoea and NBM status
where the person cannot take fluids by mouth (Bereznicki ; Olver
2006).
19 Tiwari, M. (2011). Science behind human saliva. Journal of Natural Science, Biology and
Medicine, 2(1), 53–58.
20 Delli, K., Spijkervet, F. K. L., Kroese, F. G. M., Bootsma, H. & Vissink, A. (2014). Saliva:
Secretion and functions. Monographs in Oral Science, 24, 109–125.
21 Olver, I. N. (2006). Xerostomia: A common adverse effect of drugs and radiation.
Australian Prescriber, 29, 97–98.
19
20
21
22


22 Bereznicki, L. (2011). Xerostomia. Australian Pharmacist, 30(12), 1022–1025.
For individuals with special oral hygiene needs, the nurse needs to
