focus on removal of plaque and micro-organisms as well as comfort.
If possible, a soft-bristled toothbrush should be used as it provides
the best means of plaque removal. If the person cannot tolerate the
use of a toothbrush, the nurse can use a cottonwool swab (see
Figure 34.8
) to provide oral hygiene to dependent people for
short periods of time.
Skill 34.5
 focuses on oral care for the unconscious person but
may be adapted for conscious people who are seriously ill or have
mouth problems.
Lifespan considerations
Oral hygiene
Infants
Most dentists recommend that dental hygiene should
begin when the first tooth erupts and be practised after
each feeding. Cleaning can be accomplished by using a
wet washcloth or small gauze moistened with water.
Children


Beginning when the first teeth appear, brush the child’s
teeth with a soft toothbrush. Use only a toothbrush
moistened with water. Introduce a fluoride toothpaste at
about 18 months of age.
Frequent snacking of products containing sugar, including
sugary drinks, increases the child’s risk of developing
cavities.
Older adults
Oral care is often difficult for certain older adults to
perform due to problems with vision, dexterity or cognitive
problems related to dementia.
Most long-term health care facilities have dentists that
visit on a regular basis to see people with special needs.
Dryness of the oral mucosa is a common occurrence in
older adults. As this can lead to tooth decay, advise
individuals to discuss it with their dentist or doctor.
Decay of the tooth root is common among older adults.
When the gums recede, the tooth root is more vulnerable
to decay.
Promoting good oral hygiene can have a positive effect on
older adults’ ability to eat and can prevent respiratory
infections.


Evaluating
Using data collected during care—status of oral mucosa, lips,
tongue, teeth and so on—the nurse judges whether desired
outcomes have been achieved.
If outcomes are not achieved, the nurse and individual need to
explore the reasons before modifying the care plan. Examples of
questions to consider are as follows:
Did the nurse overestimate the person’s functional abilities?
Is the person’s hand coordination or cognitive function impaired?
Did the person’s condition change?
Has there been a change in the person’s energy level and/or
motivation?


SKILL
34.4 Brushing and flossing the
teeth
Purposes
To remove food particles from around and
between the teeth.
To remove dental plaque.
To promote the person’s feelings of wellbeing.
To prevent sores and infection of the oral tissues.
To decrease the risk of respiratory infections.
Assessment
Determine the extent of the person’s self-care
abilities.
Inspect lips, gums, oral mucosa and tongue for
deviations from normal.
Identify presence of oral problems such as tooth
caries, halitosis, gingivitis and loose or broken
teeth.


Check if the person has bridgework or wears
dentures. If the person has dentures, ask if any
tenderness or soreness is present and, if so, the
location of the area(s) for ongoing assessment.
Planning
Delegation
Oral care, brushing and flossing of teeth and
denture care can be delegated to the AIN or other
caregiver. After performing the above assessment,
the RN should instruct the AIN as to the type of oral
care and amount of assistance needed by the
person. Remind the AIN to report changes in the
person’s oral mucosa, denture fit or self-care ability.
Equipment
Brushing and flossing
Towel
Disposable gloves
Protective eyewear
Curved basin (emesis basin)
Toothbrush (soft bristle)
Cup of tepid water
Toothpaste
Dental floss, at least two pieces 45 cm in length


Cleaning artificial dentures
Disposable gloves
Protective eyewear
Tissue or piece of gauze
Denture container
Clean washcloth
Toothbrush or stiff-bristled brush
Toothpaste or denture cleaner
Cup of tepid water or mouthwash (depending on
patient preference)
Curved basin (emesis basin)
Towel
Implementation
Preparation
Assemble all the necessary equipment.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain what you are
going to do, why it is necessary and how they
can participate.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures
Rationale: wearing gloves while providing
mouth care prevents the nurse from acquiring


infections. Gloves also prevent transmission
of micro-organisms to the person.
3. Offer privacy to the person. Rationale:
hygiene is a personal matter.
4. Prepare the person.
Assist the person to a sitting position in
bed, if health permits. If not, assist the
person to a side-lying position with the
head turned so liquid may be prevented
from draining down the throat.
5. Prepare the equipment.
Place the towel under the person’s chin.
Put on disposable gloves and eyewear
Use a soft toothbrush (a small one for a
child) and the person’s choice of
toothpaste.
For the person who must remain in bed,
place or hold the curved basin under the
person’s chin, fitting the small curve
around the chin or neck.
Inspect the mouth and teeth.
6. Brush the teeth.
Hand the toothbrush to the person or
brush the teeth as follows:
a. Hold the brush against the teeth
with the bristles at a 45 degree


angle. The tips of the outer bristles
should rest against and penetrate
under the gingival sulcus. 1 The
brush will clean under the sulcus of
two or three teeth at one time.
Rationale: this sulcular technique
removes plaque and cleans under
the gingival margins.
1 The sulcular technique: place the
bristles at a 45 degree angle with
the tips of the outer bristles under
the gingival margins


b. Move the bristles up and down
gently in short strokes from the
sulcus to the crowns of the teeth. 2
2 Brushing from the sulcus to the
crown of the teeth
c. Repeat until all outer and inner
surfaces of the teeth and sulci of
the gums are cleaned.
d. Clean the biting surfaces by moving
the brush back and forth over them
in short strokes. 3


3 Brushing the biting surfaces
e. Brush the tongue gently with the
toothbrush. Rationale: brushing
removes bacteria and freshens
breath. A coated tongue may be
caused by poor oral hygiene and
low fluid intake. Brushing gently and
carefully helps prevent gagging or
vomiting.


Hand the person the water cup or
mouthwash to rinse the mouth vigorously.
Then ask the person to spit the water and
excess toothpaste into the basin.
Rationale: vigorous rinsing loosens food
particles and washes out already loosened
particles.
Repeat the preceding steps until the
mouth is free of toothpaste and food
particles.
Remove the curved basin and help the
person wipe the mouth.
7. Floss the teeth.
Assist the person to floss independently or
floss the teeth of an alert and cooperative
person as follows. Waxed floss is less
likely to fray than unwaxed floss; particles
between the teeth attach more readily to
unwaxed floss than to waxed floss.
a. Wrap one end of the floss around
the third finger of each hand. 4


4 Stretching the floss between the
third finger of each hand.
b. To floss the upper teeth, use your
thumb and index finger to stretch
the floss. Move the floss up and
down between the teeth. When the
floss reaches the gum line, gently
slide the floss into the space
between the gum and the tooth.
Gently move the floss in a side-to-
side motion to avoid traumatising


the gum (Australian Dental
Association ).
18 Australian Dental Association (2016c).
Flossing—Adults 31–64. Retrieved from
<www.ada.org.au>.
c. To floss the lower teeth, use your
index fingers to stretch the floss. 5
Give the person tepid water or mouthwash
to rinse the mouth and a curved basin in
which to spit the water.
Assist the person in wiping their mouth.
8. Remove and dispose of equipment
appropriately.
Remove and clean the curved basin.
18


5 Flossing the lower teeth by using the
index fingers to stretch the floss
Source: Al Dodge, Pearson Education/PH College.
Remove and discard the gloves, face
mask and eyewear.
Wash hands thoroughly.
9. Document assessment of the teeth, tongue,
gums and oral mucosa. Include any problems
such as sores or inflammation, bleeding and


swelling of the gums. Brushing and flossing
teeth are not usually recorded.
Variation: artificial dentures
1. Remove the dentures.
Put on gloves. Rationale: wearing gloves
decreases the likelihood of spreading
infection.
If the person cannot remove the dentures,
take the tissue or gauze, grasp the upper
plate at the front teeth with your thumb
and second finger and move the denture
up and down slightly. 6 Rationale: the
slight movement breaks the suction that
holds the plate on the roof of the mouth.


6 Removing the top dentures by first
breaking the suction
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.


Lower the upper plate, move it out of the
mouth and place it in the denture
container.
Lift the lower plate, turning it so that the
left side, for example, is slightly lower than
the right, to remove the plate from the
mouth without stretching the lips. Place
the lower plate in the denture container.
Remove a partial denture by exerting
equal pressure on the border of each side
of the denture, not on the clasps, which
can bend or break.
2. Clean the dentures.
Take the denture container to a sink. Take
care not to drop the dentures as damage
to them will directly affect the person’s
ability to eat. Place a washcloth in the
bowl of the sink to prevent damage if the
dentures are dropped.
Using a toothbrush or special stiff-bristled
brush, scrub the dentures with the
cleaning agent and tepid water.
Rinse the dentures with tepid running
water. Rationale: rinsing removes the
cleaning agent and food particles.
If the dentures are stained, soak them in a
commercial cleaner at a time convenient


to the person’s eating habits. Inspect the
dentures and the mouth.
Observe the dentures for any rough,
sharp or worn areas that could irritate the
tongue or mucous membranes of the
mouth, lips and gums.
Inspect the mouth for any redness,
irritated areas or indications of infection.
Assess the fit of the dentures. People who
have dentures should see a dentist at
least once a year to check the fit and the
presence of any irritation to the soft
tissues of the mouth. Give the person a
sip of tepid water or mouthwash, to rinse
the mouth before reinserting the dentures,
and a curved basin in which to spit the
water. Rationale: vigorous rinsing of the
mouth washes out already loosened food
particles.
3. Return the dentures to the mouth.
If the person cannot insert the dentures
independently, insert the plates one at a
time. Hold each plate at a slight angle
while inserting it, to avoid injuring the lips.
7


7 Inserting the dentures at a slight angle
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.
4. Assist the person as needed.


Wipe the person’s hands and mouth with
the towel.
If the person does not want to or cannot
wear the dentures, store them in a
denture container with water. Label the
container with the person’s name and
identification number.
5. Remove and discard gloves.
6. Wash hands well.
7. Document all assessments and include any
problems such as an irritated area on the
mucous membrane.


SKILL
34.5 Providing special oral care
for the unconscious person
Purposes
To maintain the intactness and health of the lips,
tongue and mucous membranes of the mouth.
To prevent oral or respiratory infections.
To clean and moisten the membranes of the
mouth and lips.
Assessment
Inspect lips, gums, oral mucosa and tongue for
deviations from normal.
Identify presence of oral problems such as tooth
caries, halitosis, gingivitis and loose or broken
teeth.
Assess for gag reflex, when appropriate.
Planning


Delegation
Special oral care may be delegated to the AIN;
however, the RN needs to assess for the gag reflex.
Dependent on this assessment, the RN needs to
inform the AIN of the correct positioning of the
person and how to use the oral suction catheter, if
needed. Remind the AIN to report changes in the
person’s oral mucosa.
Equipment
Brushing and flossing
Towel
Curved basin (emesis basin)
Disposable clean gloves and protective eyewear
Toothbrush
Cup of tepid water
Toothpaste or denture cleaner
Tissue or piece of gauze to remove dentures
(optional)
Denture container as needed
Mouthwash
Suction catheter with suction apparatus when
aspiration is a concern
Large cottonwool swabs and cleaning solution for
cleaning the mucous membranes
Water-soluble lip moisturiser


Implementation
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain to the person
and the family what you are going to do and
why it is necessary. This is important even
with the unconscious person.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures (e.g.
disposable gloves, protective eyewear).
3. Provide for privacy by drawing the curtains
around the bed or closing the door to the
room. Rationale: hygiene is a personal
matter.
4. Prepare the person.
Position the unconscious person in a side-
lying position, with the head of the bed
lowered. Rationale: in this position, the
saliva automatically runs out by gravity
rather than being aspirated into the lungs.
This position is chosen for the
unconscious person receiving mouth care.
If the person’s head cannot be lowered,
turn it to one side. Rationale: the fluid will
readily run out of the mouth or pool in the


side of the mouth, where it can be
suctioned.
Place the towel under the chin.
Place the curved basin against the chin
and lower cheek to receive the fluid from
the mouth. 1
1 Position of person and placement of
curved basin when providing special
mouth care


Put on gloves, face mask and eyewear.
5. Clean the teeth and rinse the mouth.
If the person has natural teeth, brush the
teeth as described in Skill 34.4
. Brush
gently and carefully to avoid injuring the
gums. If the person has artificial teeth,
clean them as described in the ‘Variation’
component of Skill 34.4
.
Soak the large cottonwool swabs in water
and use to gently remove toothpaste from
inside the mouth. Rationale: excessive
fluids introduced into the mouth may flow
down the person’s throat and be aspirated
into the lungs.
Watch carefully to make sure that all the
rinsing solution has run out of the mouth
into the basin. If not, suction the fluid from
the mouth. Rationale: fluid remaining in
the mouth may be aspirated into the
lungs.
6. Repeat rinsing until the mouth is free of
toothpaste, if used.
Inspect and clean the oral tissues.
If the tissues appear dry or unclean, clean
them with the cottonwool swabs or gauze


and cleaning solution following
organisation policy.
Picking up a moistened cottonwool swab,
wipe the mucous membrane of one
cheek. Discard the swab in a waste
container; use a fresh one to clean the
next area. Rationale: using separate
applicators for each area of the mouth
prevents the transfer of micro-organisms
from one area to another.
Clean all mouth tissues using separate
applicators: the cheeks, roof of the mouth,
base of the mouth and tongue.
Rinse the person’s mouth as described in
step 5.
Remove and discard gloves and eyewear.
Wash hands thoroughly.
7. Ensure comfort.
Remove the basin and dry around the
person’s mouth with the towel. Replace
artificial dentures, if indicated.
Lubricate the lips with water-soluble
moisturiser. Rationale: lubrication
prevents cracking and subsequent
infection.


8. Document assessment of the teeth, tongue,
gums and oral mucosa. Include any problems
such as sores or inflammation and swelling of
the gums.
Evaluation
Consider the person’s medical diagnosis and
treatment (e.g. chemotherapy, oxygen) and the
necessary nursing interventions related to oral
hygiene.
Conduct an ongoing assessment, if appropriate,
of the oral mucosa, gums, tongue and lips.
Report deviations from normal to the doctor.
Conduct appropriate follow-up such as a referral
to a dentist for dental caries or poorly fitting
dentures.


Hair
Each person has particular ways of caring for hair. Becoming familiar
with hair care needs and practices that may be different from our
own is an important aspect of providing competent nursing care to
all individuals. People who feel ill may not groom their hair as before;
this may have a significant impact on a person’s general wellbeing,
appearance and self-esteem (Mackie ). A dirty scalp and hair are
itchy and uncomfortable and can have an odour. The hair may also
reflect state of health (e.g. excessive coarseness and dryness may
be associated with endocrine disorders such as hypothyroidism).
23 Mackie, S. (2009). Renal nursing basics: Oral hygiene and hair care. Journal of Renal
Nursing, 1(2), 77–79. Doi: 10.12968/jorn.2009.1.2.77.
Home care considerations
Oral hygiene
Assess the oral hygiene practices and attitude
towards oral hygiene of family members and the
individual.
Remind adults to replace their toothbrush every 3
to 4 months
23


The person with a nasogastric tube or who is
receiving oxygen is likely to develop dry oral
mucous membranes, especially if the person
breathes through the mouth. More frequent oral
hygiene will be needed.
Developmental variations
Newborns may have lanugo
 (the fine hair on the body of the
fetus, also referred to as down or woolly hair) over their shoulders,
back and sacrum. This generally disappears and the hair distribution
on the eyebrows, head and eyelashes of young children
subsequently becomes noticeable. Some newborns have hair on
their scalps; others are free of hair at birth but grow hair over the
scalp during the first year of life.
Pubic hair usually appears in early puberty, followed in about 6
months by the growth of axillary hair. Boys develop facial hair in later
puberty.
In adolescence, the sebaceous glands increase in activity as a result
of increased hormone levels. As a result, hair follicle openings
enlarge to accommodate the increased amount of sebum, which can
make the adolescent’s hair more oily.


In older adults, the hair is generally thinner, grows more slowly and
loses its colour as a result of ageing tissues and diminishing
circulation. Men may lose scalp hair and may become completely
bald. This phenomenon may occur even when a man is relatively
young. The older person’s hair also tends to be drier. With age,
axillary and pubic hair becomes finer and scanter, in contrast to the
eyebrows, which become bristly and coarse. Many women develop
hair on their faces.


Nursing management
Assessing
Assessment of the hair, hair care practices and potential problems
includes a nursing health history and physical assessment.
Nursing history
During the nursing history the nurse elicits data about usual hair
care, self-care abilities, history of hair or scalp problems and
conditions known to affect the hair. Chemotherapeutic agents,
radiation of the head, stress and some medical conditions may
cause alopecia
 (hair loss). Hypothyroidism may cause the hair to
be thin, dry and/or brittle. Use of some hair dyes and curling or
straightening preparations can cause the hair to become dry and
brittle. Questions to elicit these data are shown in the accompanying
‘Assessment interview
’.
Assessment interview
Hair care


Hair care practices
What are your usual hair care practices?
What hair care products do you routinely use?
Self-care abilities
Do you have any problems managing your hair?
Past or current hair problems
Have you had any of the following conditions or therapies:
recent chemotherapy, hypothyroidism, radiation of the
head, unexplained loss of hair, growth of excessive body
hair?
Physical assessment
Physical assessment of the hair is discussed in Chapter 31
.
Problems include dandruff, hair loss, pediculosis and scabies.
Dandruff


Often accompanied by itching, dandruff
 appears as a diffuse
scaling of the scalp. In severe cases it involves the auditory canals
and the eyebrows. Dandruff can usually be treated effectively with a
commercial shampoo. In severe or persistent cases, the person
may need the advice of a doctor.
Hair loss
Hair loss and growth are continual processes. Some permanent
thinning of hair normally occurs with ageing. Baldness, common in
men, is thought to be hereditary.
Pediculosis (lice)
Lice are parasitic insects that infest mammals. Infestation with lice is
called pediculosis
 or, more commonly, ‘nits’.
Pediculus capitis is found on the scalp and tends to stay hidden in
the hairs; similarly, Pediculus pubis stays in pubic hair. Pediculus
corporis tends to cling to clothing, so that when a person undresses,
the lice may not be evident on the body; these lice suck blood from
the person and lay their eggs on the clothing. The nurse can suspect
their presence in the clothing if (a) the person habitually scratches,
(b) there are scratches on the skin and (c) there are haemorrhagic
spots on the skin where the lice have attached.
Head and pubic lice lay their eggs on the hairs; the eggs look like
oval particles, similar to dandruff, clinging to the hair. Bites and


pustular eruptions may also be noticed at the hair lines and behind
the ears. Lice are very small, greyish white and difficult to see. The
crab louse in the pubic area has red legs. Lice may be contracted
from infested clothes and direct contact with an infested person.
Commercial head lice shampoos are available, and fine-toothed ‘nit’
combs are available to treat the lice and remove eggs. Transmission
is from head-to-head contact and it is suggested that the hair care
items and bedding of the person who has the lice infestation be
washed with hot water (Watkins ).
24 Watkins, J. (2015). Looking at the diagnosis and treatment of head lice. British Journal of
School Nursing, 10(2), 90–92.
Scabies
Scabies
 is a contagious skin infestation by the itch mite. The
characteristic lesion is the burrow produced by the female mite as it
penetrates into the upper layers of the skin. Burrows are short,
wavy, brown or black, thread-like lesions most commonly observed
between the fingers, in the creases of the wrists and elbows,
beneath breast tissue and in the groin area. The mites cause
intense itching that is more pronounced at night as the increased
warmth of the skin has a stimulating effect on the parasites.
Treatment involves thorough cleansing of the body with soap and
water to remove scales and debris from crusts and then an
application of a scabicide lotion. All bed linens and clothing should be
washed in very hot or boiling water (Engelman et al.
).
24
25


25 Engelman, D., Kiang, K., Chosidow, O. et al. (2013). Toward the global control of human
scabies: Introducing the International Alliance for the Control of Scabies. PLOS Neglected
Tropical Diseases, 7(8), e2167. Doi: 10.1371/journal.pntd.0002167.
Diagnosing
Nursing diagnoses related to hair hygiene and hair and scalp
problems include Deficit in grooming, Impaired skin integrity and
Risk of infection. Examples of these nursing diagnoses with
contributing factors include:
Deficit in grooming related to:
a. activity intolerance
b. imposed immobility (bed rest)
c. pain in upper extremities
d. altered level of consciousness
e. lack of motivation associated with depression.
Impaired skin integrity related to:
a. scalp laceration
b. insect bite.
Risk of infection related to:
a. scalp laceration
b. insect bite.


Planning
In planning care, the nurse and, if appropriate, the person and/or
family set outcomes for each nursing diagnosis. The nurse then
performs nursing interventions and activities to achieve these
outcomes. ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and
interventions
’ provides suggested outcomes and interventions
for hair grooming.
The specific, detailed nursing activities undertaken by the nurse to
assist the person should take into account the person’s personal
preferences, health and energy resources as well as the time,
equipment and personnel available. Often, people like to receive hair
care after a bath, before receiving visitors and before going to bed.
Nursing interventions may include instruction in alternative methods
for hair care including facilitating the assistance of a barber or
hairdresser or recommending aerosol dry shampoos, as necessary.
Implementing
Hair needs to be brushed or combed daily and washed, as needed,
to keep it clean. Nurses may need to provide hair care for people
who cannot meet their own self-care needs.
Brushing and combing hair


To be healthy, hair needs to be brushed daily. Brushing has three
major functions: (1) it stimulates the circulation of blood in the scalp;
(2) it distributes the oil along the hair shaft; and (3) it helps to
arrange the hair.
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
Assisting people with hair care
History Josh, 24 years old, was hit by a car while riding his
bicycle on Christmas Day. He sustained a fractured right (R)
clavicle and left (L) femur. His left (L) hand is bruised and
very swollen and he is finding it difficult to use. He was
admitted to the ward overnight. Josh is right-handed.
Clinical consideration
Excessively matted or tangled hair may be
infested with lice, or dry brushing may be painful
or uncomfortable for the person.
Long hair may present a problem for people confined to bed
because it may become matted. It should be combed and brushed


at least once a day to prevent this. A brush with stiff bristles
provides the best stimulation to blood circulation in the scalp;
however, the bristles should not be so sharp that they injure the
scalp. A comb with dull, even teeth is advisable as a comb with
sharp teeth might injure the scalp and combs that are too fine can
pull and break the hair. Some people prefer to have their hair tied
neatly back or plaited until other assistance is available or until they
feel better and can look after it themselves. Plaiting also prevents
tangling and matting for those confined to bed.
Keeping the scalp and hair clean and oiled remain important and
necessary. Skill 34.6
 describes how to provide hair care.
Shampooing the hair
Hair should be washed as often as needed to keep it clean. There
are several ways to shampoo hair, depending on the health, strength
and age of the person. The person who is well enough to take a
shower can shampoo while in the shower. The person who is unable
to shower may be given a shampoo while sitting on a chair in front of
a sink. The person confined to lying flat on their back in bed but who
can move to a stretcher can be given a shampoo on a stretcher
wheeled to a sink. The person who must remain in bed can be given
a shampoo with water brought to the bedside. A commercial
product, similar to the hot towel sponge, called a ‘head bath’ is
another approach but this may not be available in all health care
facilities. It consists of a specially designed cap (like a shower cap)


placed over the hair and scalp. The cap contains shampoo and
conditioner and gently massaging the cap cleans the hair and scalp.
Shampoo basins to catch the water and direct it to the washbasin or
other receptacle are usually made of plastic. A bucket or large
washbasin can be used as a receptacle for the shampoo water. If
possible, the receptacle should be large enough to hold all shampoo
water so that it does not have to be emptied during the shampoo.
Water used for the shampoo should be 40.5°C for an adult or child
to be comfortable and not injure the scalp. The person may have
their own supply of their preferred shampoo. If the shampoo is being
performed to destroy lice, a medicated shampoo should be used.
Dry shampoo, an aerosol of a powdered shampoo, can used to
reduce hair greasiness and odours without the need for water. It will
remove some of the dirt, odour and oil. The main disadvantage is
that it dries the hair and scalp.
How often a person needs a shampoo is highly individual, depending
largely on the person’s activities and the amount of sebum secreted
by the scalp. Oily hair tends to look stringy and dirty and it feels
unclean to the person. Skill 34.7
 explains how to provide a
shampoo for a person confined to bed.
Lifespan considerations
Hair care


Infants
Shampoo an infant’s hair daily to prevent seborrhoea.
Children
Monitor school-age children for head lice (pediculosis).
Older adults
Ensure adequate warmth for older adults when
shampooing their hair because they are susceptible to the
cold.
Beard and moustache care
Beards and moustaches also require daily care to keep them clean.
Food particles tend to collect in beards and moustaches, so they
need washing and combing periodically. Some people may also
request a beard or moustache trim to maintain a well-groomed
appearance.


Clinical consideration
A beard or moustache should not be shaved off
without consent.
Men often shave or are shaved after a bath. Frequently men supply
their own electric or safety razors. See Box 34.3
 for the steps
involved in shaving facial hair with a safety razor. If a person is
taking an anticoagulant (e.g. warfarin, dabigatran, rivaroxaban,
apixaban, heparin), an electric shaver should be used.
BO X
34.3 Using a safety razor to shave
facial hair
Wear gloves in case facial nicks occur and you come in
contact with blood.
Apply shaving cream or soap and warm water to soften
the bristles and make the skin more pliable.
Hold the skin taut, particularly around creases, to prevent
cutting the skin.
Hold the razor so that the blade is at a 45 degree angle to
the skin and shave in short, firm strokes in the direction of


hair growth (see Figure 34.9
).
Figure 34.9
Shaving in the direction of hair growth.


After shaving the entire area, wipe the face with a wet
washcloth to remove any remaining shaving cream and
hair.
Dry the face well, then apply aftershave lotion or powder
as the person prefers.
Rinse the razor frequently to free up clogged hairs
between the blades.
To prevent irritating the skin, pat on the lotion with the
fingers and avoid rubbing the face.
Evaluating
Using data collected during care, the nurse judges whether desired
outcomes have been achieved. Examples of outcomes that are
measurable or observable include the person being able to:
perform hair grooming with assistance (specify)
exhibit clean, well-groomed, resilient hair with a healthy sheen
reduce or get rid of scalp lesions or infestations
describe factors, interventions and preventive measures for a
specific hair problem (e.g. dandruff).


SKILL
34.6 Providing hair care
Purposes
To stimulate the blood circulation to the scalp.
To distribute hair oils and provide a healthy
sheen.
To increase comfort and self-esteem.
To assess or monitor hair or scalp problems (e.g.
matted hair or dandruff).
Assessment
Determine
History of the following conditions or therapies:
recent chemotherapy, hypothyroidism, radiation
of the head, unexplained hair loss and growth of
excessive body hair.
Usual hair care practices and routinely used hair
care products (e.g. hairspray, shampoo,
conditioners, hair oil preparation, hair dye, curling
or straightening preparations).


Whether wetting the hair will make it difficult to
comb.
Assess
Condition of the hair and scalp. Is the hair
straight or curly? Is the hair matted or tangled?
Is the scalp dry?
Have there been injuries or surgical procedures
to the scalp resulting in broken skin, dried blood,
debris or suture lines?
Evenness of hair growth over the scalp, in
particular, any patchy loss of hair; hair texture,
oiliness, thickness or thinness; presence of
lesions, infections or infestations on the scalp;
presence of hirsutism.
Self-care abilities (e.g. any problems managing
hair care).
Planning
Delegation
Brushing and combing hair, shampooing hair and
shaving facial hair can be delegated to the AIN or
other caregiver unless the person has a condition in
which the procedure would be contraindicated (e.g.
cervical spinal injury or trauma).
Equipment


Clean brush and comb
A wide-toothed comb is usually used for many
people because finer combs pull the hair into
knots and may also break the hair
Towel
Hair oil preparation, if appropriate
Implementation
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can cooperate.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for privacy by drawing the curtains
around the bed or closing the door to the
room. Some organisations provide signs
indicating the need for privacy. Rationale:
hygiene is a personal matter.
4. Position and prepare the person
appropriately.
Assist the person who can sit to move to a
chair. Rationale: hair is more easily
brushed and combed when the person is
in a sitting position. If health permits,


assist a person confined to a bed to a
sitting position by raising the head of the
bed. Otherwise, assist the person to
alternate side-lying positions and do one
side of the head at a time.
If the person remains in bed, place a
clean towel over the pillow and the
person’s shoulders. Place it over the
sitting person’s shoulders. Rationale: the
towel collects any removed hair, dirt and
scaly material.
Remove any pins, elastics, ribbons or
large debris in the hair.
5. Remove any mats or tangles gradually.
Mats can usually be pulled apart with
fingers or worked out with repeated
brushings.
If the hair is very tangled, use a hair oil or
small amounts of conditioner on the
strands to help loosen the tangles and
decrease discomfort.
Comb out tangles in a small section of
hair. Stabilise the hair with one hand and
comb towards the ends of the hair with
the other hand. Rationale: this avoids
scalp trauma.


6. Brush and comb the hair.
For short hair, brush and comb one side at
a time. Divide long hair into two sections
by parting it down the middle from the
front to the back. If the hair is very thick,
divide each section into front and back
subsections or into several layers.
7. Arrange the hair as neatly and attractively as
possible, according to the individual’s
preferences.
Plaiting long hair helps prevent tangles.
8. Document assessments and special nursing
interventions. Daily combing and brushing of
the hair are not normally recorded.
Evaluation
Conduct ongoing assessments for problems
such as dandruff, alopecia, pediculosis, scalp
lesions or excessive dryness or matting.
Evaluate effectiveness of medication (e.g. for
treating pediculosis), if appropriate.


SKILL
34.7 Shampooing the hair of a
person confined to bed
Purposes
To stimulate the blood circulation to the scalp
through massage.
To clean the hair and increase the sense of
wellbeing.
Assessment
Determine routinely used hair care products.
Assess for any scalp problems and activity
tolerance of the person.
Planning
Delegation
Brushing and combing hair, shampooing hair and
shaving facial hair can be delegated to the AIN or
other caregiver unless the person has a condition in


which the procedure would be contraindicated (e.g.
cervical spinal injury or trauma).
Equipment
Comb and brush
Plastic sheet or pad
Two bath towels
Shampoo basin, if available
Washcloth or pad
Bath blanket
Receptacle for the shampoo water
Jug of water
Bath thermometer
Shampoo
Hair dryer
Implementation
Preparation
Determine whether a doctor’s order is needed
before a shampoo can be given. Rationale: after
facial or cranial surgery, shampooing and wetting
of the hair may require the doctor to review the
incision first.
Determine the type of shampoo to be used (e.g.
medicated shampoo).
Determine the best time of day for the shampoo.
Discuss this with the person requiring the care. A


person who must remain in bed may find the
shampoo tiring. Choose a time when the person
is rested and can rest after the procedure.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain what you are
going to do, why it is necessary, if
appropriate, and how they can cooperate.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures as
needed.
3. Provide for privacy by drawing the curtains
around the bed or closing the door to the
room. Some organisations provide signs
indicating the need for privacy. Rationale:
hygiene is a personal matter.
4. Position and prepare the person
appropriately.
Assist the person to the side of the bed
from which you will work.
Remove pins, hair ties, debris or ribbons
from the hair and brush and comb it to
remove any tangles.
5. Arrange the equipment.


Put the plastic sheet or pad on the bed
under the head. Rationale: the plastic
keeps the bedding dry.
Remove the pillow from under the head
and place it under the shoulders unless
there is some underlying condition (e.g.
neck surgery, arthritis of the neck).
Rationale: this hyperextends the neck.
Tuck a bath towel around the shoulders.
Rationale: this keeps the shoulders dry.
Place the shampoo basin under the head,
1 putting a folded washcloth or pad where
the neck rests on the edge of the basin. If
the person is on a stretcher, the neck can
rest on the edge of the sink with the
washcloth as padding. Rationale: padding
supports the muscles of the neck and
prevents undue strain and discomfort.


1 Shampooing the hair of a person
confined to bed. Note the shampoo basin
and the receptacle below
Fanfold the top bedding down to the waist
and cover the upper part of the person
with the bath blanket. Rationale: the
folded bedding will stay dry and the bath
blanket, which can be discarded after the
shampoo, will keep the person warm.
Place the receiving receptacle on a table
or chair at the bedside. Put the spout of
the shampoo basin over the receptacle.
6. Protect the eyes.
Place a damp washcloth over the eyes.
Rationale: the washcloth protects the
eyes from soapy water. A damp washcloth
will not slip.
7. Shampoo the hair.
Wet the hair thoroughly with the water.
Apply shampoo to the scalp. Make a good
lather with the shampoo while massaging
the scalp with the pads of your fingertips.
Massage all areas of the scalp
systematically; for example, starting at the
front and working towards the back of the


head. Rationale: massaging stimulates
the blood circulation in the scalp. The
pads of the fingers are used so that the
fingernails will not scratch the scalp.
Rinse the hair briefly and apply shampoo
again, if needed.
Make a good lather and massage the
scalp as before.
Rinse the hair thoroughly this time to
remove all shampoo. Rationale: shampoo
remaining in the hair may dry and irritate
the hair and scalp.
Squeeze as much water as possible out of
the hair with your hands.
8. Dry the hair thoroughly.
Rub the hair with a heavy towel.
Dry the hair with the dryer. Set the
temperature at ‘warm’.
Continually move the dryer to prevent
burning the scalp.
9. Ensure comfort.
Assist the person confined to bed to a
comfortable position.
Arrange the hair using a clean brush and
comb.


10. Document the shampoo and any
assessments.
Evaluation
Conduct ongoing assessments such as any scalp
problems or intolerance to the procedure. Report
any problems noted to the nurse in charge.


Eyes
Normally eyes require no special hygiene because lacrimal fluid
continually washes the eyes and the eyelids, and lashes prevent the
entrance of foreign particles. Special interventions are needed,
however, for unconscious individuals and for people recovering from
eye surgery or having eye injuries, irritations or infections. In
unconscious people, the blink reflex may be absent and excessive
drainage may accumulate along eyelid margins. In individuals with
eye trauma or eye infections, excessive discharge or drainage is
common. Excessive secretions on the lashes need to be removed
before they dry on the lashes as crusts. People who wear glasses,
contact lenses or an artificial eye also may require instruction from
and care by the nurse.


Nursing management
Assessing
Assessment of the eyes includes a nursing health history and
physical assessment.
Nursing health history
During the nursing history, the nurse obtains data about the person’s
glasses or contact lenses, recent examination by an ophthalmologist
and any history of eye problems and related treatments. The nurse
also obtains data about medical conditions that may affect eye
health (e.g. diabetes). Questions to elicit these data are shown in
the ‘Assessment interview
’.
Assessment interview
Eyes
For individuals who wear glasses


When do you use your glasses? (e.g. do you wear
glasses for reading, distance or both?)
What is your vision like with and without the glasses?
For individuals who wear contact
lenses
How often do you wear lenses? Daily? On special
occasions?
How long do you wear your lenses in a given day,
including sleep time?
Do you have any problems with the lenses (e.g. cleaning,
insertion, removal, damage)?
Do you carry an emergency identification label to alert
others to remove the lenses and ensure appropriate care
in an emergency? (If not, advise the person to acquire
one.)
What are your insertion and removal procedures?
What are your cleaning and storage procedures?
Have you had any problems with either or both eyes or
eyelids, such as excessive tearing, burning, redness,
sensitivity to light, swelling or feelings of dryness?
Are you using any eye drops or ointments? (These
medications can combine chemically with soft lenses and
cause lens damage and eye irritation.)


For all
When did you last have your eyesight tested?
Are you currently taking any eye medication? If so,
provide name, dosage and frequency.
Do you have any of the following eye problems: difficulty
reading or seeing objects, blurring of vision, tearing, spots
or floaters, photophobia (sensitivity to light), burning,
itching, pain, double vision, flashing lights or halos around
lights?
Physical assessment
In physical assessment, all external eye structures are inspected for
signs of inflammation, excessive drainage, encrustations or other
obvious abnormalities. Inspection of the external eye structures is
discussed in Chapter 31
.
Diagnosing
People may not have an adequate knowledge base with which to
manage their eye health. Eye problems may include risk of injury or
infection due to:


a. improper contact lens hygiene
b. impaired vision associated with cataracts
c. accumulation of secretions on eyelids
d. prolonged wearing of contact lenses
e. absence of blink reflex associated with unconsciousness.
Planning
In planning care, the nurse identifies nursing activities that will assist
to maintain the integrity of the eye structures or a prosthesis, and
prevent eye injury and infection.
Implementing
Nursing activities may include teaching about how to insert, clean
and remove contact lenses or a prosthesis and ways to protect the
eyes from injury and strain.
Eye care
Dried secretions that have accumulated on the lashes need to be
softened and wiped away. Soften dried secretions by placing a
sterile cotton ball or gauze swab moistened with tepid sterile water
or normal saline over the lid margins. Wipe the loosened secretions
from the inner canthus of the eye to the outer canthus to prevent


the particles and fluid from draining into the lacrimal sac and
nasolacrimal duct.
If the person is unconscious and lacks a blink reflex or cannot close
the eyelids completely, drying and irritation of the cornea must be
prevented. Lubricating eye drops may be ordered. Box 34.4
 gives
suggestions for providing eye care for the person who is in a
comatose state.
BO X
34.4 Eye care for the person in a
comatose state
When the corneal reflex is impaired in a person in a
comatose state, eye care is essential to keep moist the areas
of the cornea that are exposed to air.
Administer moist compresses to cover the eyes every 2 to
4 hours.
Clean the eyes with saline solution and cotton balls or
gauze swab. Wipe from the inner to outer canthus. This
prevents debris from being washed into the nasolacrimal
duct.
Use a new swab for each wipe. This prevents extending
infection in one eye to the other eye.


Instil ophthalmic ointment or artificial tears into the lower
lids as ordered. This keeps the eyes moist.
If the corneal reflex is absent, keep the eyes moist with
artificial tears and protect the eye with a protective shield.
These should be ordered by a doctor.
Monitor the eyes for redness, exudate or ulceration.
Glasses care
It is essential that the nurse exercise caution when cleaning glasses
to prevent breaking or scratching the lenses. Glass lenses can be
cleaned with warm water and dried with a soft tissue that will not
scratch the lenses. Commercial cleaning wipes may also be used if
available. Plastic lenses are easily scratched and may require
special cleaning solutions and drying tissues. When not being worn,
all glasses should be placed in a case, with the person’s name
clearly marked, and stored in the bedside table drawer.
Contact lens care
Contact lenses, thin curved discs of hard or soft plastic, fit on the
cornea of the eye directly over the pupil. They float on the tear layer
of the eye. For some people, contact lenses offer several
advantages over glasses: (a) they cannot be seen and thus have
cosmetic value; (b) they are highly effective in correcting some
astigmatisms; (c) they are safer than glasses for some physical


activities; (d) they do not fog, as glasses do; and (e) they provide
better vision in many cases.
Contact lenses have two main categories—soft and hard—with a
number of different variations and options in each category.
Most people normally care for their own contact lenses. In general,
each lens manufacturer provides detailed cleaning instructions.
Depending on the type of lens and cleaning method used, warm tap
water, normal saline or special rinsing or soaking solutions may be
used.
All users should have a special container for their lenses. Some
contain a solution so that the lenses are stored wet; in others, the
lenses are dry. Each lens container has a slot or cup with a label
indicating whether it is for the right or left lens. It is essential that the
correct lens be stored in the appropriate slot so that it will be placed
in the correct eye.
Removing contact lenses
Seek medical advice regarding removing lenses so as not to cause
damage to the eye. This should only be undertaken by nurses with
experience in this practice area. To avoid lens mix-ups, the nurse
places the first lens in its designated cup in the storage base before
removing the second lens (see Figure 34.10
).
Figure 34.10


Storing lenses. Place the first lens in its designated cup in the
storage case before removing the second lens. This avoids mixing
up two potentially different lenses.
Source: © Karen Roach/Fotolia.com.
Inserting contact lenses
Seriously ill people whose contact lenses have been removed will not
need them reinserted until they become more active in their care


and require the lenses to see properly. Contact lenses need to be
lubricated in a sterile, non-irritating wetting solution before they are
inserted. The wetting solution helps the lens glide over the cornea,
thus reducing the risk of injury. Most people, when well, will reinsert
the lenses independently.
Artificial eyes
Artificial eyes are usually made of glass or plastic. Some are
permanently implanted; others are removed regularly for cleaning.
Most people who wear a removable artificial eye follow their own
care regimen. Even for an unconscious person, daily removal and
cleaning are not necessary.
Removing an artificial eye should only be undertaken by nurses with
experience in this practice area.
General eye care
General principles for eye care include:
Avoid home remedies for eye problems. Eye irritations or injuries
at any age should be treated medically and immediately.
If dirt or dust gets into the eyes, rinse them copiously with clean,
tepid water as an emergency treatment.
Take measures to guard against eyestrain and to protect vision,
such as maintaining adequate lighting for reading and obtaining
shatterproof lenses for glasses.


Schedule regular eye examinations, particularly after age 40, to
detect problems such as cataracts and glaucoma.
Evaluating
Using data collected during care, the nurse judges whether desired
outcomes have been achieved. Examples of desired outcomes to
evaluate the effectiveness of nursing interventions follow:
conjunctiva and sclera free of inflammation
eyelids free of secretions
no tearing
no eye discomfort
demonstrates appropriate methods of caring for contact lenses
describes interventions to prevent eye injury and infection.


Ears
Normal ears require minimal hygiene. People who have excessive
cerumen
 (earwax) and dependent people who have hearing aids
may require assistance from the nurse. Hearing aids are usually
removed before surgery.
Clinical consideration
Cerumen impaction is a relatively common
cause of hearing loss in adults (Adobamen &
Ogisi ), but there is no association between
hearing aid use and cerumen impaction
(Manchaiah, Arthur & Williams ).
26 Adobamen, P. R. & Ogisi, F. O. (2012). Hearing loss due to
wax impaction. Nigerian Quarterly Journal of Hospital Medicine,
22(2), 117–120.
27 Manchaiah, V., Arthur, J. & Williams, H. (2015). Does hearing
aid use increase the likelihood of cerumen impaction? Journal of
Audiology and Otology, 19(3), 168–171.
26
27


Cleaning the ears
The auricles of the ear are cleaned during the bed bath. The nurse
or person may remove excessive cerumen that is visible or that
causes discomfort or hearing difficulty. Visible cerumen may be
loosened and removed by retracting the auricle up and back. If this
measure is ineffective, irrigation by experienced nurses or a medical
officer is necessary. People need to be advised never to use bobby
pins, toothpicks or cotton-tipped applicators to remove cerumen.
Bobby pins and toothpicks can injure the ear canal and rupture the
tympanic membrane; cotton-tipped applicators can cause wax to
become impacted within the canal.
Care of hearing aids
A hearing aid is a battery-powered, sound-amplifying device used by
people with hearing impairments. It consists of a microphone that
picks up sound and converts it to electric energy, an amplifier that
magnifies the electric energy electronically, a receiver that converts
the amplified energy back to sound energy and an earmould that
directs the sound into the ear. There are four types of digital hearing
aids to provide different hearing solutions:
1. behind-the-ear (BTE) (see Figure 34.11
)
Figure 34.11


A: A behind-the-ear hearing aid. B: A behind-the-ear hearing
aid attached to glasses.
Source: B: SPL Creative/Getty Images Australia Pty Ltd.
2. receiver-in-the-ear (RITE, RIC)
3. invisible styles (IIC)
4. canal styles (CIC, ITC, ITE). See Figure 34.12
.
Figure 34.12


A: An in-the-ear hearing aid. B: Small hearing aid in ear
canal. C: Large hearing aid in ear canal.


Sources: B: © Yuli/Fotolia.com; C: SPL Creative/Getty Images Australia Pty Ltd.
For correct functioning, hearing aids require appropriate handling
during insertion and removal, regular cleaning of the earmould and
replacement of dead batteries. With proper care, hearing aids
generally last 5 to 10 years. Earmoulds generally need readjustment
every 2 to 3 years. Skill 34.8
 describes how to remove, clean and
insert a hearing aid.
Home care considerations
Hearing aids
People who need a hearing aid may not wear one
because they view the hearing aid as a stigma of
old age.
It is important for the person who has just
purchased a hearing aid to know that it often takes
weeks or even months to adjust to the hearing aid.
At first, the sounds may seem shrill as the person
starts hearing high-frequency sounds that had been
forgotten.
Emphasise the importance of maintaining the
hearing aid; that is, having it cleaned and checked
regularly.


SKILL
34.8 Removing, cleaning and
inserting a hearing aid
Purposes
To maintain proper hearing aid function.
Assessment
Determine if the person has experienced any
problems with the hearing aid and hearing aid
practices. Assess for the presence of
inflammation, excessive wax, drainage or
discomfort in the external ear.
Planning
Delegation
A nurse can delegate the task of caring for a hearing
aid to the AIN or other caregiver. It is important,
however, for the nurse to first determine that the
AIN knows the correct way to care for a hearing aid.


Inform the AIN to report the presence of ear
inflammation, discomfort, excess wax or drainage to
the RN.
Equipment
Hearing aid
Clean dry cloth
Manufacturer tools to clean difficult to reach
parts
New battery (if needed)
Implementation
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain what you are
going to do, why it is necessary and how they
can cooperate.
2. Acquaint yourself with the hearing aid
manufacturer’s cleaning instructions. These
can differ greatly between appliances.
3. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures.
4. Provide for privacy by drawing the curtains
around the bed or closing the door to the
room. Some organisations provide signs


indicating the need for privacy. Rationale:
hygiene is a personal matter.
5. Remove the hearing aid.
If the hearing aid is not to be used for
several days, remove the battery.
Rationale: removal prevents corrosion of
the hearing aid in the event of battery
leakage.
Store the hearing aid in a safe place and
label with the person’s name. Avoid
exposure to heat and moisture.
Rationale: proper storage prevents loss
or damage.
Wipe the hearing aid with a clean dry
cloth.
Using the manufacturer’s tools, remove
debris (e.g. earwax).
6. Insert the hearing aid.
Determine if the earmould is for the left or
the right ear.
Check that the battery is inserted in the
hearing aid. Turn off the hearing aid and
make sure the volume is turned all the
way down. Rationale: a volume that is too
loud on insertion is distressing.
Check that the ear mould fits snugly by
asking if it feels secure and comfortable.


Adjust the other components of a behind-
the-ear hearing aid.
Turn the hearing aid on and adjust the
volume according to the person’s needs.
Whistling emitted from the hearing aid
when turning it on indicates an incorrect
fit. Gently move and wiggle the earmould
until it fits snugly and ceases whistling.
7. Document pertinent data.
The removal and the insertion of a hearing
aid are not normally recorded.
Report and record any problems the
person has with the hearing aid.
Evaluation
Speak in a normal conversational tone and
observe the person’s behaviours.
Compare the person’s hearing ability with
previous assessments.
Report to the doctor any deviations from normal
for this person.


Nose
Nurses usually need not provide special care for the nose, because
people can ordinarily clear nasal secretions by blowing gently into a
soft tissue. When the external nares are encrusted with dried
secretions, they should be cleaned with a cotton-tipped applicator or
moistened with warmed saline or water. The applicator should not be
inserted beyond the length of the cotton tip; inserting it further may
cause injury to the mucosa.


Supporting a hygienic
environment
When people are confined to bed for long periods when ill, the bed
becomes an important element in their life. A place that is clean,
safe and comfortable contributes to the person’s ability to rest and
sleep, and to a sense of wellbeing. Basic furniture in a health care
facility includes the bed, bedside table, overway table, one or more
chairs and a storage space for clothing. Most bed units also have a
call bell, light fixtures, electric outlets and hygienic equipment in the
bedside table. Three types of equipment often installed in an acute
care facility are a suction outlet for several kinds of suction, an
oxygen outlet for most oxygen equipment and a
sphygmomanometer to measure blood pressure. Many long-term
care facilities also permit people to have personal furniture, such as
a television, a chair and lamps, at the bedside. In the home, a
person often has personal and medical equipment.
Environment
When providing a comfortable environment, it is important to
consider the person’s age, severity of illness and level of activity.


Room temperature
The very young, the very old and the acutely ill frequently need a
room temperature higher than normal. A room temperature between
20°C and 23°C is comfortable for most people. In cases where
temperatures cannot be adjusted, extra blankets are to be provided
for those who may have difficulty regulating their own body
temperature.
Ventilation
Good ventilation is important to remove unpleasant odours and stale
air. Odours caused by urine, draining wounds or vomitus, for
example, can be offensive to people. Nurses should consider their
personal hygiene also as body odour, perfume and smoking can also
be offensive to people when unwell. Room deodorisers can help
eliminate odours. However, good hygiene practices are the best way
to prevent offensive body and breath odours. Smoking is not allowed
inside any Australian hospitals and most will have a perimeter
around buildings that also disallow this practice.
Noise
When unwell, people can be sensitive to noise such as clanging of
metal equipment, call bells, equipment alarms, loud talking and
laughter. Nurses should try to manage noise in health care settings.


Hospital beds
Most hospital beds have electric motors to operate the movable
joints. Common bed positions are shown in Table 34.6
.
Table 34.6 Commonly used bed positions
Hospital beds are usually narrower than a standard bed so that the
nurse can reach the person from either side of the bed without
undue stretching. Some beds can be extended in length to
accommodate very tall people. Long-term care facilities for walking
people usually have low beds to facilitate movement in and out of
bed. Most hospital beds have ‘high’ and ‘low’ positions that can be
adjusted electrically. The high position permits the nurse to reach the
person without undue stretching or stooping. The low position allows
the person to step easily to the floor. Hospital staff must remember
to return the bed position from high to low after completing care to
ensure the safety of the person.
Mattresses
Mattresses are usually covered with a water-repellent material that
resists soiling and can be cleaned easily. Many special mattresses
are also used in hospitals to relieve pressure on the body’s bony
prominences, such as the heels and sacrum. They are particularly
helpful when people are confined to bed for a long time. For
additional information about mattresses, see Chapter 37
.


Side rails
Side rails, or split rails, are used on both hospital beds and
stretchers. Devices to raise and lower side rails differ between
manufacturers. When side rails are being used, it is important that
the nurse never leaves the bedside while the rail is lowered. Some
side rails have two positions: up and down. Others have three: high,
intermediate and low.
Legislation may prohibit the use of bed rails in some Australian
states unless specifically ordered by a medical officer and/or
undertaken in consultation with the person’s relatives. Organisations
should have a clear policy on this issue to guide staff in the careful
use of this type of restraint (Staunton & Chiarelli , pp. 176–177).
Alternatives to side rails do exist and can include low-height beds,
mats placed at the side of the beds, motion sensors and bed alarms
(see Chapter 33
).
28 Staunton, P. & Chiarella, M. (2013). Law for Nurses and Midwives (7th ed.). Chatswood,
NSW: Elsevier Churchill Livingstone Australia.
Footboard or footboot
These are used to support the immobilised person’s foot in a normal
right angle to the legs to prevent plantar flexion contractures (see
Chapter 47
).
28


Bed cradles
A bed cradle is a device designed to keep the top bedclothes off the
feet, legs and even abdomen. The bedclothes are arranged over the
device and may be pinned in place. There are several types of bed
cradles.
Intravenous poles
Intravenous poles (rods, stands, standards), usually made of metal,
support intravenous (IV) infusion containers and pumps while fluid is
being administered to a person. These poles can be freestanding on
wheels on the floor beside the bed or attached to hospital beds,
depending on the person’s mobility requirements. Some hospital
units have overhead hanging rods on a track for IVs.
Clinical consideration
Side rail entrapment, injuries and deaths do
occur. When side rails are used, the nurse must
assess the person’s physical and mental status
and closely monitor high-risk (frail, elderly or
confused) people.


Making beds
Nurses need to be able to prepare hospital beds in different ways for
specific purposes. In most instances, beds are made after the
person receives certain care and when beds are unoccupied. At
times, however, nurses need to make an occupied bed or prepare a
bed for a person who is having surgery (an anaesthetic,
postoperative or surgical bed). Regardless of what type of bed
equipment is available, whether the bed is occupied or unoccupied,
or the purpose for which the bed is being prepared, certain practice
guidelines pertain to all bed making.
Unoccupied bed
An unoccupied bed can be either closed or open. Generally, the top
covers of an open bed are folded back (thus the term open bed) to
make it easier for a person to get in. Open and closed beds are
made the same way, except that the top sheet, blanket and
bedspread of a closed bed are drawn up to the top of the bed and
under the pillows.
Practice guidelines
Bed making


To avoid unnecessary trips to the linen supply area,
gather all linen before starting to strip a bed.
Wash hands thoroughly after handling used bed linen.
Linens that have been soiled with secretions and
excretions harbour micro-organisms that can be
transmitted to others directly or by the nurse’s hands or
uniform.
When removing the linen from the bed, fold it in on itself
to prevent the spread of micro-organisms.
Hold soiled linen away from uniform.
Linen, fresh or lightly soiled, for one person is never (even
momentarily) placed on another bed or on another
person’s tray table, as this may cause cross-
contamination.
Place soiled linen directly in a portable linen carrier or
tucked into a pillow case at the end of the bed before it is
gathered up for disposal.
Do not shake soiled linen in the air because shaking can
disseminate secretions and excretions and the micro-
organisms they contain.
When stripping and making a bed, conserve time and
energy by stripping and making up one side as much as
possible before working on the other side.
Check the bed linen after meal times for food particles or
soiling.
Bed linen must be changed as soon as possible on becoming wet or
soiled or if the person is sweating profusely. The frequency of


routine linen changes may differ between organisations, so check
the policy at each clinical organisation. Unfitted sheets, blankets and
bedspreads are mitred at the corners of the bed. The purpose of
mitring is to secure the bedclothes while the bed is occupied. Figure
34.13
 shows how to mitre the corner of a bed. Skill 34.9
explains how to change an unoccupied bed.
Figure 34.13


Mitring the corner of a bed.
Changing an occupied bed
Some people may be too weak to get out of bed. The nature of their
illness may contraindicate their sitting out of bed or they may be
restricted in bed by the presence of traction or other therapies.
When changing an occupied bed, the nurse works quickly and


disturbs the person as little as possible to conserve the person’s
energy, using the following guidelines:
Maintain the person in good body alignment. Never move or
position a person in a manner that is contraindicated by the
person’s health. Obtain assistance, if necessary, to ensure
safety.
Move the person gently and smoothly. Rough handling or
grabbing can cause the person discomfort and abrade the skin.
Explain what you plan to do throughout the procedure before you
do it. Use terms that the person can understand.
Use the bed-making time, like the bed bath time, to assess and
meet the person’s needs.
Skill 34.10
 explains how to change an occupied bed.
Case study
It is the fourth day for a person you are caring for following
abdominal surgery. She is progressing well, is ambulating
several times each day, has been providing for her own
hygiene needs and is planning on going home tomorrow.
During your early morning assessment, you note that her hair
is oily and matted and she has an unpleasant body odour.
Her dentures in a container at the bedside are in need of
cleaning. You check her abdominal incision and verify that
there is no drainage, redness or signs of infection. You


inquire about her ability to take care of her own hygiene and
personal needs and offer to assist her with her shower. She
replies that she had a shower yesterday, doesn’t feel that she
needs another one today and requests to omit her personal
care for the day.
Fundamentals of care framework in
context


1. You are considering Ineffective or deficient attendance
to hygiene needs as an appropriate nursing diagnosis
for this person. You review the defining characteristics
and related factors and discover what?
2. What else should you ask her?
3. Why is it important that you obtain the assessments
you have already completed along with the above
questions you asked?
4. What approaches might you use if you feel that she
does need her hair shampooed and needs to have her
personal care attended to?
5.

 What advantages do performing showers
and personal hygiene for people offer to the nurse?
Consider the Fundamentals of Care Framework,
particularly the Relationship and Integration of Care
dimensions, when crafting your answer.
6. What considerations need to be made for her
upcoming discharge home?


SKILL
34.9 Changing an unoccupied
bed
Purposes
To provide a clean, neat environment.
To provide a smooth, wrinkle-free bed
foundation, thus minimising sources of skin
irritation.
Assessment
Assess the person’s health status to determine
that the person can safely get out of bed. In
some hospitals it is necessary to have a written
order if the person has been in bed continuously.
Assess the blood pressure, pulse and
respirations if indicated.
Note all the tubes and equipment connected to
the person. Rationale: this may influence the
need for additional linens or waterproof pads.


Planning
Delegation
Bed making may be delegated to the AIN but all
RNs are responsible for this activity and must be
able to perform it effectively. If appropriate, inform
the AIN of the proper disposal method of linens that
are soiled. Ask the AIN to inform you immediately if
any tubes or dressings become dislodged or
removed. Stress the importance of the call bell being
readily available while the person is out of bed.
Equipment
Two flat sheets or one fitted and one flat sheet
Cloth drawsheet (optional)
One blanket
One bedspread
Waterproof pads (optional)
Pillowcase(s) for the head pillow(s)
Plastic laundry bag or portable linen carrier
Implementation
Preparation
Determine what linens the person may already
have in the room to avoid stockpiling of
unnecessary extra linens.


Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain what you are
going to do, why it is necessary and how they
can cooperate.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for privacy.
4. Place the fresh linen on the individual’s chair
or overway table; do not use another person’s
bed. Rationale: this prevents cross-
contamination (the movement of micro-
organisms from one person to another) via
soiled linen.
5. Assist the person out of bed.
Make sure that this is an appropriate and
convenient time for the person to be out
of bed.
Assist the person to a comfortable chair or
to the shower, if indicated and appropriate.
6. Raise the bed to a comfortable working
height. This is usually hip height of the
shortest person making the bed.
7. Strip the bed.
Check bed linens for any items belonging
to the person and remove the call bell or


any drainage tubes or other items from
the bed linen.
Loosen all bedding systematically, starting
at the head of the bed on the far side and
moving around the bed up to the head of
the bed on the near side. Rationale:
moving around the bed systematically
prevents stretching and reaching and
possible muscle strain.
Remove the pillowcases if soiled and
place the pillows on the bedside chair or
on the foot of the bed.
Fold reusable linens, such as the
bedspread on the bed, into quarters. First,
fold the linen in half by bringing the top
edge even with the bottom edge and then
grasp it at the centre of the middle fold
and bottom edges. 1 Rationale: Folding
linens saves time and energy when
reapplying the linens on the bed and
keeps them clean.


1 Folding reusable linens into quarters
when removing them from the bed
Remove the waterproof pad and discard it
if soiled.
Roll all soiled linen inside the bottom
sheet, hold it away from your uniform and
place it directly in the linen carrier, not on
the floor. 2 Rationale: these actions are


essential to prevent the transmission of
micro-organisms to the nurse and others.
2 Rolling soiled linen inside the bottom
sheet and holding away from the body
Grasp the mattress securely, using the
lugs if present, and move the mattress up


to the head of the bed, if needed.
8. Apply the bottom sheet and drawsheet.
Place the folded bottom sheet with its
centre fold on the centre of the bed. Make
sure the sheet is hem side down for a
smooth foundation. Spread the sheet out
over the mattress and allow a sufficient
amount of sheet at the top to tuck under
the mattress. 3 Rationale: the top of the
sheet needs to be well tucked under to
remain securely in place, especially when
the head of the bed is elevated. Place the
sheet along the edge of the mattress at
the foot of the bed and do not tuck it in
(unless it is a contour or fitted sheet).


3 Placing bottom sheet on bed
Mitre the sheet at the top corner on the
near side (see Figure 34.13
) and tuck
the sheet under the mattress, working
from the head of the bed to the foot.
If a waterproof drawsheet is used, place it
over the bottom sheet so that the
centrefold is at the centreline of the bed
and the top and bottom edges extend
from the middle of the back to the area of
the mid-thigh or knee. Fanfold the
uppermost half of the folded drawsheet at
the centre or far edge of the bed and tuck
in the near edge. 4

Source: Patrick Watson.
Lay the cloth drawsheet over the
waterproof sheet in the same manner.
Optional: before moving to the other side
of the bed, place the top linens on the bed
hem side up, unfold them, tuck them in
and mitre the bottom corners. Rationale:
completing one entire side of the bed at a
time saves time and energy.
9. Move to the other side and secure the bottom
linens.
Tuck in the bottom sheet under the head
of the mattress, pull the sheet firmly and
mitre the corner of the sheet.
Pull the remainder of the sheet firmly so
that there are no wrinkles. Rationale:
wrinkles can cause discomfort for the
person and breakdown of skin.
Tuck the sheet in at the side.
Complete this same process for the
drawsheet(s).
10. Apply or complete the top sheet, blanket and
spread.


Place the top sheet, hem side up, on the
bed so that its centrefold is at the centre
of the bed and the top edge is even with
the top edge of the mattress.
Unfold the sheet over the bed.
Optional: make a vertical or a horizontal
toe pleat in the sheet to provide additional
room for the feet.
a. Vertical toe pleat: make a fold in the
sheet 5 to 10 cm perpendicular to
the foot of the bed. 5
a. Horizontal toe pleat: make a fold in
the sheet 5 to 10 cm across the
bed near the foot. 6
Follow the same procedure for the blanket
and the spread, but place the top edges
about 15 cm from the head of the bed to
allow a cuff of sheet to be folded over
them.
Tuck in the sheet, blanket and spread at
the foot of the bed and mitre the corner,
using all three layers of linen. Leave the
sides of the top sheet, blanket and spread
hanging freely unless toe pleats were

Fold the top of the top sheet down over
the spread, providing a cuff. 7 Rationale:
the cuff of sheet makes it easier for the

5 A vertical toe pleat


6 A horizontal toe pleat


7 Making a cuff of the top linens
Source: Patrick Watson.
Move to the other side of the bed and
secure the top bedding in the same
manner.
11. Put clean pillowcases on the pillows as
required.
Grasp the closed end of the pillowcase at
the centre with one hand.
Gather up the sides of the pillowcase and
place them over the hand grasping the


case. Then grasp the centre of one short
side of the pillow through the pillowcase. 8
8 Method for putting a clean pillowcase on
a pillow


With the free hand, pull the pillowcase
over the pillow.
Adjust the pillowcase so that the pillow fits
into the corners of the case and the
seams are straight. Rationale: a smoothly
fitting pillowcase is more comfortable than
a wrinkled one.
Place the pillow/s neatly at the head of the
bed.
12. Provide for comfort and safety.
Attach the call bell cord so that the person
can conveniently reach it. Some cords
have clamps that attach to the sheet or
pillowcase.
If the bed is currently being used, either
fold back the top covers at one side or
fanfold them down to the centre of the
bed. Rationale: this makes it easier for
the person to get into the bed.
Place the bedside table and the overway
table so that they are available and within

Leave the bed in the high position if the

13. Document and report pertinent data.
Bed making is not normally recorded.
Record any nursing assessments, such as
the person’s physical status and pulse and
respiratory rates before and after being
out of bed, as indicated.
Variation: surgical bed
While the person is in the operating room, the bed is
prepared for the postoperative phase. In some
organisations, the person is brought back to the unit
on a stretcher and transferred to the bed in the
room. In other organisations, the bed is brought to
the surgery suite and the person is transferred
there. In the latter situation, the bed needs to be
made with clean linens as soon as the person goes
to surgery so that it can be taken to the operating
room when needed.
Strip the bed
Place and leave the pillows on the bedside chair.
Rationale: pillows are left on a chair to facilitate
transferring the person into the bed.
Apply the bottom linens as for an unoccupied
bed. Place a blanket on the foundation of the bed
if this is organisation practice. Rationale: a
blanket provides additional warmth.


Place the top covers (sheet, blanket and
bedspread) on the bed as you would for an
unoccupied bed. Do not tuck them in, mitre the
corners, or make a toe pleat.
Make a cuff at the top of the bed as you would
for an unoccupied bed. Fold the top linens up
from the bottom.
On the side of the bed where the person will be
transferred, fold up the two outer corners of the
top linens so they meet in the middle of the bed
forming a triangle. 9
9 Fold up the two outer corners of the top linens,
forming a triangle


Pick up the apex of the triangle and fanfold the
top linens lengthwise to the other side of the bed
to facilitate the transfer into the bed. 10
10 Surgical bed. The linens are horizontally
fanfolded to the other side of the bed to facilitate
transfer of the person into the bed
Leave the bed in high position with the side rails
down. Rationale: the high position facilitates the
transfer.
Lock the wheels of the bed if the bed is not to be
moved. Rationale: locking the wheels keeps the
bed from rolling when the person is transferred


from the stretcher to the bed and promotes
safety.
Evaluation
Make sure the call bell is accessible to the
person.
Relate parameters of activity (e.g. blood
pressure, pulse and respirations) to previous
assessment data, particularly if the person has
been on bed rest for an extended period of time
or if it is the first time that the person is getting
out of bed after surgery.

bed
Purposes
To conserve the energy.
To promote comfort.
To provide a clean, neat environment.
To provide a smooth, wrinkle-free bed
foundation, thus minimising sources of skin
irritation.
Assessment
Note specific orders or precautions for moving
and positioning.
Determine presence of incontinence or excessive
drainage from other sources indicating the need
for protective waterproof pads.
Assess skin condition and need for special
mattress (e.g. egg crate), footboard or heel
protectors.

Equipment
Two flat sheets or one fitted and one flat sheet
Cloth drawsheet (optional)

One bedspread

(optional)
Pillowcase(s) for the head pillow(s)
Plastic laundry bag or portable linen carrier
Implementation
Performance
1. Explain what you are going to do, why it is
necessary and how the person can
cooperate.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures. Put
on disposable gloves if linen is soiled with
body fluids.
3. Provide for privacy.
4. Remove the top bedding.
Remove any equipment attached to the
bed linen, such as a call bell.


Loosen all the top linen at the foot of the
bed and remove the spread and the
blanket.
Leave the top sheet over the person (the
top sheet can remain over the person if it
is being changed and if it will provide

blanket as follows:
Spread the blanket over the top sheet.
a. Ask the person to hold the top edge
of the blanket.
b. Reaching under the blanket from
the side, grasp the top edge of the
sheet and draw it down to the foot
of the bed, leaving the blanket in
place. 1

blanket
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
c. Remove the sheet from the bed
and place it in the soiled linen
carrier.
5. Change the bottom sheet and drawsheet.
Assist the person to turn on the side

linen is. Encourage the person to pull
themself over by holding onto the opposite
side rail.
Raise the side rail nearest the person.
Rationale: this protects the person from

Loosen the foundation of the linen on the

Fanfold the drawsheet and the bottom
sheet at the centre of the bed, 2 as close

Rationale: doing this leaves the near half
of the bed free to be changed.

person as possible

and vertically fanfold the half to be used

Tuck the sheet under the near half of the

Chapter 34 Review


Chapter highlights
Hygiene practices are influenced by numerous factors, including
culture, religion, environment, developmental level, health,
motivation and energy, and personal preferences.
The major functions of the skin are to protect underlying tissues,
to help regulate body temperature, to secrete sebum, to transmit
sensations through nerve receptors for sensory perception and
to produce and absorb vitamin D in conjunction with ultraviolet
rays from the sun.
When planning hygiene care, the nurse must take the
preferences of the people being cared for into consideration.
Nurses provide perineal–genital care for individuals who are
unable to do so for themselves.
Nurses can often teach people how to prevent foot problems.
Oral hygiene should include daily dental flossing and mechanical
brushing of the teeth. Dentures require daily brushing.
Regular dental check-ups and fluoride supplements are
recommended to maintain healthy teeth.
Nurses provide special oral care to people who are unconscious
or debilitated.
Hair care includes daily combing and brushing and regular
shampooing.
Nurses may need to assist dependent people with their artificial
eyes, glasses and contact lenses.
People with a hearing aid may require nursing assistance with
the device.


Changing bed linen is a part of maintaining hygiene.
It is important to keep beds clean and comfortable.
