Diagnostic and laboratory tests (commonly
called lab tests) are tools that provide
information about the person. Tests may be
used as basic screening as part of a wellness
check. Frequently tests are used to help confirm


a diagnosis, monitor an illness and provide
valuable information about the person’s
response to treatment. Nurses require
knowledge of the most common lab and
diagnostic tests because one primary role of the
nurse is to teach the person and family or
significant other how to prepare for the test and
the care that may be required following the test.
Diagnostic and laboratory tests are like any
other medical procedure in that the person
should be informed about the indication for the
testing, what to expect during the test, potential
adverse outcomes and available alternatives.
Nurses must also know the implications of the
test results in order to provide the most
appropriate nursing care for the person.


Diagnostic testing phases
Diagnostic testing occurs in many environments, including hospitals,
clinics, doctors’ offices and community laboratory testing centres.
Diagnostic testing may also occur in places such as the home,
workplace, shopping malls and mobile units. The more complex
diagnostic tests are performed at diagnostic centres specifically built
for those tests.
Diagnostic testing involves three phases: pre-test, intra-test and
post-test.
Pre-test
The major focus of the pre-test phase is preparation for the person
undergoing the test. A thorough assessment and data collection
(e.g. biological, psychological, sociological, cultural and spiritual)
assist the nurse in determining communication and teaching
strategies. Prior to radiological studies it is important to ask females
if pregnancy is possible. Where a contrast medium (dye) is used, it
is important to know of any allergies or previous reactions to
contrast. It is also important to ascertain whether the person has
kidney disease as contrast may further impair renal function. Special


precautions may be necessary or the test may need to be
postponed.
The nurse also needs to know what equipment and supplies are
needed for the specific test. Common questions include the
following: What type of sample will be needed and how will it be
collected? Does the person need to stop oral intake for a certain
number of hours prior to the test? Does the test include
administration of contrast media and, if so, is it injected or
swallowed? Are fluids restricted or forced? Are medications given or
withheld? How long is the test? Is a consent form required? Answers
to these types of questions can help avoid costly mistakes and
reduce inconvenience to all involved. Most facilities have information
about the tests available to the health care team. The laboratory at
the facility can also act as a resource for information.
Intra-test
This phase focuses on specimen collection and performing or
assisting with certain diagnostic testing. The nurse uses standard
precautions and sterile technique as appropriate. During the
procedure the nurse provides emotional and physical support while
monitoring the person as needed (e.g. vital signs, pulse oximetry,
ECG). The nurse ensures correct labelling, storage and
transportation of the specimen to avoid invalid test results.


Post-test
The focus of this phase is on nursing care of the person and follow-
up activities and observations. As appropriate, the nurse compares
the previous and current test results and modifies nursing
interventions as needed. The nurse also reports the results to
appropriate health team members.
Patient Education
Educating and preparing for diagnostic testing
Prior to the test, the person undergoing the test is given an
explanation of the purpose of the test, which should include:
why the test has been ordered for them
what the test involves
potential adverse effects
any practical and available alternatives to the test
timing of result availability
possible or expected outcomes of the test, including
follow-up and further tests or treatment.
A good understanding of these aspects of the test is required
for the person to be able to consent to the test.
Following an explanation of the test, time should be
allowed for the person and their family to voice questions


or concerns that they may have about the test. An
interpreter should be provided if required.
It is important to ensure that the person does not have
any allergies to any of the medications or substances that
may be used for the test (e.g. contrast) and that the
person is physically able to comply with any requirements
for the test (e.g. the ability to lie flat after a femoral
angiogram).
It is often useful to have written information about the test
to give to the person so that the person and their family
can read it at their leisure and refer to it later, particularly
if preparation is required for the test. The written
information should be an adjunct to a verbal explanation
rather than the only source of information.
Any education given to the person and their responses or
concerns should be documented and followed up as
needed with the relevant health care worker who is
responsible for ordering or conducting the test.


Blood tests
Blood tests are the most commonly used diagnostic tests and can
provide valuable information about the haematological system and
many other body systems. A venipuncture
 (puncture of a vein
for collection of a blood specimen) can be performed by various
members of the health care team. Often, a phlebotomist
, a
person from a laboratory who performs venipuncture, collects the
blood specimen for the tests ordered by the doctor or specialist. In
some institutions, nurses may draw blood samples. The nurse needs
to know the guidelines for drawing blood samples for the facility and
the relevant statutory authority that regulates nursing practice.
Full blood count
Specimens of venous blood are taken for a full blood count
(FBC)
, also known as a complete blood picture (CBP)
, full
blood examination (FBE)
 or complete blood examination (CBE),
which includes haemoglobin and haematocrit measurements,
erythrocyte (RBC) count, leukocyte or white blood cell (WBC) count,
red blood cell (RBC) indices
 and a differential white cell count.
The FBC is a basic screening test and one of the most frequently
ordered blood tests (see Table 35.1
).

Haemoglobin
 is the main intracellular protein of erythrocytes. It
carries oxygen to and removes carbon dioxide from red blood cells.
The haemoglobin test is a measure of the total amount of
haemoglobin in the blood. The haematocrit
 measures the
percentage of red blood cells in the total blood volume. Normal
values for both haemoglobin and haematocrit vary, with males
having higher levels than females. Haemoglobin and haematocrit
increase with dehydration as the blood becomes more concentrated
and decrease with hypervolaemia and resulting haemodilution.
Haemoglobin and haematocrit are often ordered together. Both the
haemoglobin and haematocrit are related to the red cell count
(RCC)
, which is the number of RBCs in a given volume of blood.
It also varies by gender and age. Low RCCs are indicative of
anaemia. People with chronic hypoxia may develop higher than
normal counts, a condition known as polycythaemia
. RCC
indices may be performed as part of the FBC to evaluate the size,
weight and haemoglobin concentration of RBCs.


Culturally Competent Care
Population screening and barriers to participation among
minority populations and Indigenous people
Australia has one of the highest rates of colorectal cancer
(CRC) in the world. Death due to CRC is thought to be largely
preventable with early detection, leading to the adoption of
the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program (NBCSP).
Australians receive a screening invitation, free screening test
kit and other program information through the post around
the time of their 50th birthday. Participation rates in CRC
screening have been shown to be lower for Indigenous and
non-English-speaking populations, potentially resulting in a
missed opportunity for early diagnosis and removal of curable
lesions. A study of enablers of CRC screening by Ward,
Coffey and Meyer
 found that language was a significant
barrier to participation for people from culturally and
linguistically diverse (CALD) backgrounds, despite available
translation on the NBCSP website.
13 Ward, P. R., Coffey, C. & Meyer, S. (2015). Trust, choice and obligation: A
qualitative study of enablers of colorectal cancer screening in South Australia.
Sociology of Health & Illness, 37(7), 988–1006. Doi: 10.1111/1467-9566.12280.
Cultural and religious beliefs also had a role in non-
participation. While most Anglo-Saxon Australians saw CRC
as treatable, many people from CALD backgrounds saw
cancer as unpreventable and avoided screening because of
fear of cancer diagnosis. Others, particularly those from a
13


Vietnamese background, expressed the belief that health and
disease and life and death were in God’s hands, and
therefore were not preventable (Ward, Coffey & Meyer
2015). For Indigenous Australians, mistrust of the
government-run NBCSP, which was attributed to perceived
historical and discriminatory practices in health care, led to
non-participation. Indigenous Australians living in regional and
remote communities relying on postal services for receipt and
return of the tests had concerns about their privacy and
embarrassment linked to the ‘shame’ of cancer and handling
faeces (Ward, Coffey & Javanparast et al.
). Even with the
best of intentions and efforts made to provide information in
different languages, cultural context for individuals and
groups is an important predictor of participation in health
care.
14 Ward, P. R., Coffey, C., Javanparast, S., Wilson, C. & Meyer, S. B. (2015).
Institutional (mis)trust in colorectal cancer screening: A qualitative study with Greek,
Iranian, Anglo-Australian and Indigenous groups. Health Expectations, 18(6), 2915–
2927.
Culturally Competent Care
Biocultural considerations
Disorders involving haemoglobin are among the most
common genetic disorders worldwide. Sickle cell disease, an
abnormality of RBCs causing anaemia, is common among
African, Mediterranean and Middle Eastern ethnicities.
14


Another inherited disorder affecting haemoglobin production
and causing anaemia is thalassaemia, common among
Asian, Filipino, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and African
ethnic populations.
The leukocyte
 or white cell count (WCC)
 determines the
number of circulating WBCs per cubic millimetre of whole blood.
High WBC counts are often seen in the presence of a bacterial
infection; by contrast, WCCs may be low if a viral infection is
present. In the WCC differential, leukocytes are identified by type
and the percentage of each type is determined. This information is
useful in diagnosing certain disorders that have characteristic
patterns of distribution (see Figure 35.1
).
Figure 35.1


Composition of blood.
Serum electrolytes
Serum electrolytes are often routinely ordered for any person
admitted to a hospital as a screening test for electrolyte and acid–
base imbalances. Serum electrolytes also are routinely assessed for
people at risk in the community; for example, people who are being
treated with a diuretic for hypertension or heart failure. The most
commonly ordered serum tests are for sodium, potassium, chloride
and bicarbonate ions. Normal values of commonly measured
electrolytes are shown in Box 35.1
.


BO X
35.1

Venous blood

Blood levels of two metabolically produced substances, urea and
creatinine, are routinely used to evaluate renal function. The
kidneys, through filtration and tubular secretion, normally eliminate
both. Urea, the end product of protein metabolism, is measured as
blood urea nitrogen (BUN)
. Creatinine
 is produced in
relatively constant quantities by the muscles and is excreted by the
kidneys. Thus, the amount of creatinine in the blood relates to renal
excretory function. Although serum creatinine concentration is often
used in assessing overall kidney function, the estimated
glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
 is a better measure. It is
especially important to know what a person’s renal function is like
prior to giving drugs that are renally cleared to prevent toxicity.


Drug monitoring
Therapeutic drug monitoring is often conducted when a person is
taking a medication with a narrow therapeutic range (e.g. digoxin,
theophylline, aminoglycosides). This monitoring includes drawing
blood samples for peak and trough levels to determine if the blood
serum levels of a specific drug are at a therapeutic level and not a
subtherapeutic or toxic level. The peak level
 indicates the highest
concentration of the drug in the blood serum and the trough level
represents the lowest concentration. Ideally, a person’s peak and
trough levels fall within the therapeutic range.
Arterial blood gases
Measurement of arterial blood gases
 is another important
diagnostic procedure (see Chapter 53)
. Specialty nurses, medical
technicians and respiratory therapists normally take specimens of
arterial blood from the radial, brachial or femoral arteries. Because
of the relatively great pressure of the blood in these arteries, it is
important to prevent haemorrhaging by applying pressure to the
puncture site for about 5 to 10 minutes after removing the needle.
Blood chemistry


A number of other tests may be performed on blood serum (the
liquid portion of the blood). These are often referred to as blood
chemistry
. In addition to serum electrolytes, common chemistry
examinations include determining certain enzymes that may be
present (including lactic dehydrogenase (LDH), creatine kinase (CK),
aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase
(ALT)), serum glucose, hormones such as thyroid hormone and
other substances such as cholesterol and triglycerides. These tests
provide valuable diagnostic cues. For example, cardiac markers
(e.g. CK, troponin T and troponin I) are released into the blood
during a myocardial infarction (MI or heart attack). Elevated levels of
these markers in the venous blood can help differentiate between an
MI and chest pain from a different cause, such as angina, and chest
pain with non-cardiac origins. Levels of CK can be increased in
conditions causing damage to skeletal muscle (e.g. intense exercise,
intramuscular injection, rhabdomyolysis) and therefore lack
specificity in the diagnosis of MI. CKMB, an isoenzyme of CK, is
specific to cardiac injury. CK is still used for monitoring the extent of
MI and early reinfarction, but has largely been superseded in
detecting MI by cardiac troponin T, troponin I and high sensitivity
troponin (hsTnT) as these tests are more sensitive and specific, and
can detect myocardial damage within 2 to 3 hours of symptom onset
(RCPA 2019).
A common lab test is the glycosylated haemoglobin or haemoglobin
A  HbA
, which is a measurement of blood glucose that is
bound to haemoglobin. Haemoglobin A  is a reflection of how well
blood glucose levels have been controlled during the prior 3 to 4
1C
1C
1C


months. The normal range is 4.0% to 5.5%. An elevated HbA
reflects hyperglycaemia in diabetics.
The first specific blood test to detect and guide treatment for heart
failure is the B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP)
 test. Increases in
volume and pressure in the left ventricle result in release of pro-B-
type natriuretic peptide (proBNP) from the cardiac myocytes.
ProBNP is cleaved into BNP and its N-terminal pro-B-type
natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP)
 fragment. BNP and NT-proBNP
are most useful in the emergency department in ruling out heart
failure as a cause of dyspnoea.
C-reactive protein (CRP)
 and erythrocyte sedimentation rate
(ESR)
 are tests that detect inflammation. While they are not
specific enough to diagnose a particular disease, they serve as a
general marker for presence of infection and inflammation. ESR
increases with age, does not exclude active disease and should not
be used to screen asymptomatic patients for the presence of
disease (RCPA 2019).
See Table 35.2
 for normal values of common blood chemistry
tests.

<www.rcpa.edu.au>.
1C


Metabolic screening
Newborns are routinely screened for congenital metabolic conditions
such as phenylketonuria (PKU), hypothyroidism and cystic fibrosis.
Other conditions that are frequently screened include sickle cell
disease and galactosaemia. Screening involves collecting peripheral
venous blood (via a heel stick) on a prepared blotting paper and
sending the specimen to the state laboratory for analysis.
Discovered abnormalities allow the provider and parents to plan
early care (e.g. special diets for children with PKU) that can prevent
long-term complications.
Capillary blood glucose
A capillary blood specimen is often taken to measure blood glucose
when frequent tests are required or when a venipuncture cannot be
performed. This technique is less painful than a venipuncture and
easily performed. Hence, people can perform this technique on
themselves.
The development of home glucose test kits and reagent strips has
simplified the testing of blood glucose and greatly facilitated the
management of home care by people with diabetes. A number of
manufacturers have developed blood glucose meters (glucometers)
or monitors.


Capillary blood specimens are commonly obtained from the lateral
aspect or side of the finger in adults. This site avoids the nerve
endings and calloused areas at the fingertip. The earlobe may be
used if the person is in shock or the fingers are oedematous. Some
newer monitors allow for obtaining specimens from less sensitive
areas on the arms, legs or abdomen.
Technology in Practice
Advances in technology have resulted in people having
greater choices for a glucose meter that meets their needs.
Considerations in purchasing a glucose monitor may include
cost of the meter and test strips, data storage size and
capability, ability to mark or flag an event for a reading (such
as exercising before the reading) that may help to guide
therapy, accuracy and size. Physical disability or impairment
may also guide the selection of an appropriate meter. For
example, a person with vision impairment may prefer a meter
with a backlight, increased text size and colour.
Skill 35.1
 describes how to obtain a capillary blood specimen and
measure blood glucose using a portable meter.
Real-world practice
Consider the Registered Nurse Standards for Practice
(Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia ) and how
15


they apply to the student and faculty exemplar below.
