of pathogenic micro-organisms to prevent
their spread to others.
Crush the inner ampoule containing the
medium for organism growth at the
bottom of the tube. Rationale: this
ensures that the swab with the specimen
is surrounded by culture medium.
Twist the cap to secure.


If a specimen is required from another
site, repeat the steps. Specify the exact
site (e.g. inferior drain site or lower aspect
of incision) on the label of each container.
Be sure to put each swab in the
appropriately labelled tube.
9. Dress the wound.
Apply any ordered medication to the
wound.
Cover the wound with a sterile wound
dressing. See Table 37.4
 on pages
937–938 for selecting a wound dressing.
10. Arrange for the specimen to be transported to
the laboratory immediately. Be sure to include
the completed requisition and transport in an
appropriate biohazard bag.
11. Document all relevant information.
Record on the person’s chart the taking of
the specimen and source.
Include the date and time; the appearance
of the wound; the colour, consistency,
amount and odour of any drainage; the
type of culture collected; and any
discomfort experienced by the individual.
Variation: obtaining a specimen for anaerobic culture


Insert a sterile 10 mL syringe (without needle)
into the wound and aspirate 1 to 5 mL of
drainage into the syringe.
Attach the needle to the syringe and expel all air
from the syringe and needle.
Immediately inject the drainage into the
anaerobic culture tube and cap the tube tightly.
or
Use an anaerobic culture swab system in which
the swab is immediately placed into a tube filled
with an oxygen-free gas or gel environment.
Label the tube or syringe appropriately.
Send the tube or syringe of drainage to the
laboratory immediately. Do not refrigerate the
specimen.


Chapter 37 Review


Chapter highlights
Maintaining skin integrity is an important independent function of
nursing.
Wounds are described as intentional or unintentional, closed or
open, and clean, clean contaminated, contaminated or dirty
(infected). Wounds are also classified by depth as
superficial/partial thickness or full thickness. In addition, wounds
are classified according to how they are acquired, as incisions,
contusions, abrasions, punctures, lacerations and penetrating
wounds.
A pressure injury is any lesion caused by unrelieved pressure
that results in damage to underlying tissues. Pressure injuries
usually occur over bony prominences.
Two other factors that act in conjunction with pressure to produce
a pressure injury are friction and shearing forces.
Several factors increase the risk of the development of pressure
injuries: immobility and inactivity, inadequate nutrition, faecal and
urinary incontinence, decreased mental status, diminished
sensation, excessive body heat and advanced age.
Several risk assessment tools are available to identify people at
risk of pressure injury development. They include scoring
systems to evaluate a person’s degree of risk.
There are four stages of pressure injuries, which vary according
to the degree of tissue damage.
There are two types of wound healing, which are distinguished by
the amount of tissue loss: primary intention healing and


secondary intention healing.
The wound-healing process has three phases: inflammatory,
proliferative and maturation.
Major types of wound exudate are serous, purulent and
sanguineous (haemorrhagic). Exudate can be a combination of
two or three of these types (e.g. serosanguineous). The process
of pus formation is referred to as suppuration.
The main complications of wound healing are haemorrhage,
infection, dehiscence and evisceration, each of which is
identifiable by specific clinical signs and symptoms.
Factors affecting wound healing include developmental stage,
nutritional status, lifestyle, medications, underlying disease
processes and the presence of infection.
Meticulous skin assessment of common pressure injury sites by
the nurse is an important ongoing assessment activity for
individuals at risk, paying particular attention to those individuals
with darkly pigmented skin.
When a pressure injury is present, the nurse describes the injury
in terms of location, size, depth, stage, colour, status of wound
bed and surrounding skin, and specific signs of infection, if
present.
Wound assessment is an ongoing process to evaluate healing.
The nurse assesses wounds by visual inspection, palpation,
measurements and the sense of smell. Essential data for
assessing wounds include wound appearance, size, exudate,
swelling, pain and the presence of tubes and drains.
Laboratory data that may be used to assess the progress of
wound healing include leukocyte count, haemoglobin, blood


coagulation studies, serum protein analysis and wound cultures.
Nurses are usually responsible for obtaining specimens of wound
drainage for culture.
The nursing diagnoses Risk of impaired skin integrity, Impaired
skin integrity and Impaired tissue integrity apply to people at risk
of developing and to those with pressure injuries.
Nursing diagnoses related to people with wounds may include
Risk of infection and Pain.
Major goals for people at risk of developing pressure injuries are
to maintain skin integrity and to avoid potential associated risks.
Nursing interventions to prevent the formation of pressure
injuries include conducting ongoing assessment of risk factors
and skin status, providing skin care to maintain skin integrity,
ensuring adequate nutrition, implementing measures to avoid
skin trauma, providing supportive devices and education.
Treatment for pressure injuries varies according to the stage of
the injury and organisation protocol.
Major nursing responsibilities related to wound care include
assisting the person in obtaining sufficient nutrition and fluids,
preventing wound infections and proper positioning.
Wound care may involve cleaning/irrigating, protecting,
filling/hydrating and covering wounds; applying heat and cold;
and applying bandages and binders.
Various dressing materials are available to protect wounds,
absorb exudate and keep the wound bed moist, thus facilitating
healing.
Synthetic dressings have been developed for use with specific
types of wounds. These include transparent adhesive films,


impregnated non-adherent dressings, hydrocolloids, hydrogels,
polyurethane foams, clear acrylic dressings and alginates. The
nurse must be aware of the specific purposes of each and their
indications for use.
The type of dressing used depends on (a) location, size and type
of wound; (b) amount of exudate; (c) whether or not the wound
requires debridement, is infected or has sinus tracts; and (d)
such considerations as frequency of dressing change, ease or
difficulty of dressing applications and cost.
The RYB colour code of wounds can assist nurses to provide
appropriate nursing interventions for wounds that heal by
secondary intention. In this scheme, the nurse protects red,
cleanses yellow and debrides black.
Heat and cold produce specific local physiological and systemic
responses that account for their therapeutic effects.
Various parts of the body differ in tolerance to heat and cold. The
physiological tolerance of individuals also varies. Specific
conditions such as neurosensory and circulatory impairments
necessitate precautions when applying heat or cold.
When applying heat or cold, individuals and nurses need to be
aware of the effects of thermal receptor adaptation and the
rebound phenomenon.
Concept check

score of 17. The appropriate nursing action is:

within normal limits.
2. Implement a turning schedule; the person is at
increased risk of skin breakdown.
3. Apply a transparent wound barrier to major pressure
sites; the person is at moderate risk of skin
breakdown.
4. Request an order for a special low-air-loss bed; the
person is at very high risk of skin breakdown.

2. Dry gauze.
3. Hydrocolloid.
4. No dressing is indicated.

postoperative phase of recovery from surgery.
Evaluate the effectiveness of perioperative nursing interventions.

The frequency of elective surgery performed
each year in Australia has been rising for
decades, reflecting improvements in surgical
techniques to meet the needs of an ageing
population (Australian Institute of Health and
Welfare (AIHW) ). For the period 2017–18, the
number of cases slowed nationally, increasing
by only 0.9% from previous years. There were in
excess of 2.3 million surgical cases performed in
Australian hospitals in 2017–18. Of these
procedures, 66% were performed in private
hospitals and 34% in public hospitals (AIHW
2019a). Outpatient procedures do not require
an overnight hospital stay: the person goes to
the outpatient site on the day of the surgery, has
the procedure and leaves the same day.
1 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2019a).
Admitted Patient Care 2017–18. Cat. no. HSE 225.
Canberra: AIHW. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
1


There is a social gradient associated with
access to surgery; the rate of private elective
surgery being highest among people from the
most advantaged socioeconomic group (more
than 70 per 1000 people) and decreasing for
the most disadvantaged group (35.6 per 1000
people). Previous health data found that the
most advantaged socioeconomic group also has
the shortest overall median waiting time for
surgery (24 days). However, in 2017–18,
Indigenous Australians had a higher median
waiting time but were less likely than non-
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians
to wait over 365 days for surgery (AIHW ).
2 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2019b).
Elective Surgery Waiting Times 2017–18. Health services
series no. 64. Cat. no. HSE 222. Canberra: AIHW.
Surgery is a unique experience because it
involves a planned physical alteration to the
body. People are in need of emotional support
when they experience fear associated with loss
of personal control which can be related to the
type of anaesthesia, unknown consequences of
the surgery, potentially altered body image and
the prospect of pain. For the many people who
2


have surgery as a treatment for cancer, there is
the potential for cure as well as the prospect of
unsuccessful excision of the tumour.
The most common types of surgery in Australia
in 2017–18 originated almost exclusively from
five diagnostic groups: musculoskeletal,
gynaecological, gastrointestinal, dermatological
and ophthalmic surgery. Excision of skin lesion
was the most common elective surgical
procedure (AIHW 2019a).
The pace of physical recovery following surgery
is generally determined by the rate of tissue
healing and the need for adjunctive therapy, and
is very context specific. For example, women
who have their ovaries removed during a
hysterectomy will experience the sudden onset
of symptoms associated with surgically induced
menopause. Hormonal replacement therapy
(HRT) is used as an adjunctive treatment.
However, only limited research exists that
assesses the risks and benefits of using HRT in
women who have experienced a surgical
menopause. For men having a prostatectomy,
adjunctive therapy to treat erectile dysfunction,
incontinence or bladder neck contractures is
3


commonly offered (Kovell & Terlecki ;
O’Shaughnessy & Laws ).
3 Kovell, R. C. & Terlecki, R. P. (2015). Management
strategies for post-prostatectomy bladder neck
contractures. Current Urology Reports, 16(65). Doi:
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11934-015-0536-4.
4 O’Shaughnessy, P. K. & Laws, T. A. (2010). Australian
men’s long term experiences following prostatectomy: A
qualitative descriptive study. Contemporary Nurse, 34(1),
98–109.
Long-term psychological support is essential for
those who have had surgery for cancer and
their family (Carlson et al. ; O’Shaughnessy,
Laws & Esterman ). Nearly two-thirds of people
with cancer experience long-term psychological
distress, with an estimated one-third having
clinically significant problems with anxiety. The
incidence of suffering in this group is wide
ranging and a prominent aspect of their
experience (Sharpe et al. ). The need for long-
term follow-up of people following their surgery
has been highlighted in the development of
3
4
5
6
7


case management frameworks for all tumours
(Department of Health, Victoria ).

P., Dirske, D. & Speca, M. (2014). Tailoring mind-body
therapies to individual needs: Patients’ program
preferences and psychological traits as moderators of the
effects of mindfulness-based cancer recovery and
supportive-expressive therapy in distressed breast cancer
survivors. Journal of the National Cancer Institute,
Monographs, 2014(50), 308–314.

(2013). The prostate cancer journey: Results of an online

E1.

The perioperative workforce
Perioperative nursing is practised in hospital-based inpatient and
outpatient clinics (surgical/laser/endoscopy suites), doctors’ office-
based surgical suites and freestanding day surgery units
(outpatient). Perioperative nurses are specialists with a long history
of working collaboratively and autonomously with other health
professionals (anaesthetist, surgeon, surgeon’s assistant and
radiographer). Emerging economic forces and social change are
shifting traditional health provider roles and relationships.
Technicians are increasingly managing medical devices (robotic
devices, perfusions apparatus, anaesthetic) once overseen by the
perioperative nurse. However, the role of the perioperative nurse is
also expanding with nurse specialists now administering sedation for
minor procedures and medical investigations. Australian
anaesthetists have resisted the accreditation and registration of
nurse anaesthetists of the kind that have existed in the United
States and many European countries for several decades.


Standards and guidelines
Perioperative nursing is the delivery of nursing care through a
nursing process framework. The nurse’s role involves person-
centred assessment to identify risk factors and determine the
person’s suitability for surgery, provide psychological support,
educate the person on what to expect along the surgical pathway,
promote safety and provide pain relief.
The Australian College of Operating Room Nurses (ACORN),
founded in 1977, is a professional body that has made itself
responsible for formulating national standards of care and clinical
guidelines for operating room nurses with the aim to provide safe
and high-quality perioperative care (ACORN ).
9 Australian College of Operating Room Nurses (ACORN) (2018). Standards for
Perioperative Nursing in Australia (15th ed.). Adelaide: ACORN.
Safety factors
Elective surgery is a relatively safe pathway, with only 5.4% of
people having surgery recorded as having an adverse event; this
figure is 40% lower than for all hospital separations (AIHW
).
However, the perioperative journey is inherently risky and, as such,
9
10


the promotion of safety along all phases of the perioperative
pathway is a key mission for all surgical teams. For example, within
the intraoperative phase, three formalised safety stages exist: ‘sign
in’ (before induction of anaesthesia), ‘time out’ (before skin incision)
and ‘sign out’ (before patient leaves the operating room) (Hamlin et
al.
). The aim is to improve communication and reinforce safety
practices. There are many useful guides on reducing risks to
individuals, such as the ACORN Position Statement on Surgical
Safety (ACORN 2018).
10 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2008). Elective Surgery in Australia:
New Measures of Access. Cat. no. HSE 57. Canberra: AIHW.
11 Hamlin, L., Davies, M., Richardson-Tench, M. & Sutherland-Fraser, S. (2016).
Perioperative Nursing: An Introduction (2nd ed.). Chatswood: Elsevier.
Patient safety competency framework
7 Preventing, minimising and responding to
adverse events
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must
demonstrate the capacity to prevent, minimise
and respond to adverse events by practising
within legal and ethical frameworks, relevant
guidelines, policies and evidence-based
resources in relation to patient safety (Levett-
Jones et al.
).
11
12

T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.


Types of surgery
Surgical procedures are commonly grouped according to (a)
purpose, (b) degree of urgency and (c) degree of risk.
Purpose
Surgical procedures may be categorised according to their purpose
(see Table 38.1
).
Table 38.1 Purposes of surgical procedures
Degree of urgency
Surgery is classified by its urgency and necessity to preserve the
person’s life, body part or body function. Emergency surgery
 is
performed immediately to preserve function or the life of the person.
Surgery to control internal haemorrhage or repair a displaced
fracture are examples of emergency surgery. Elective surgery
 is
performed when surgical intervention is the preferred treatment for a
condition that is not imminently life threatening (but may ultimately
threaten life or wellbeing) or to improve the person’s quality of life.
Examples of elective surgeries include hip replacement surgery,


cataract surgery and plastic surgery procedures such as breast
reduction surgery.
Degree of risk
Surgery is also classified as major or minor according to the degree
of risk to the person. The physical status classification in Box
38.1
 is a measure of the overall severity of systemic disease and
has long been used to assess perioperative risk.
BO X
38.1 American Society of
Anesthesiologists’ physical status
classification
Class
I. A normal healthy person.
II. A person with mild systemic disease.
III. A person with severe systemic disease.
IV. A person with severe systemic disease being a
constant threat to life.


V. A moribund person—not expected to survive without
the surgery.
VI. A person declared brain dead/potential organ donor.
Source: Sankar et al.
. Reliability of the American Society of Anesthesiologists’ physical status scale
in clinical practice. British Journal of Anaesthesia, 113(3), 424–432.
13 Sankar, A., Johnson, S. R., Beattie, W. S., Tait, G. & Wijeysundera, D. N. (2014). Reliability of the
American Society of Anesthesiologists’ physical status scale in clinical practice. British Journal of
Anaesthesia, 113(3), 424–432.
The degree of risk involved in a surgical procedure is affected by the
person’s age, general health, presence of comorbidities, medication
use and mental status.
Age
Neonates/infants and older adults are greater surgical risks than
children and adults. Age and developmental status affect a child’s
ability to cope with the physiological and psychological stresses of
surgery. Neonates and infants have a higher metabolic rate than
adults and a different physiological make-up. These differences
cause a substantially different response to a surgical procedure. For
example, the blood volume in an infant is small and fluid reserves
are limited. This increases the risk of volume depletion during
surgery resulting in inadequate oxygenation of body tissues.
Because of the infant’s relatively large body surface area and
immature temperature regulatory mechanisms, the risk of
hypothermia during surgery is significant (Derieg ). Other organ
13
14


systems, such as the kidneys, liver and immune system, also have
not achieved maturity in infants, affecting their ability to metabolise
and eliminate drugs and resist infection.
14 Derieg, S. (2017). An overview of perioperative care for paediatric patients. ACORN, 30(3),
23–29.
Toddlers and older children are better able to withstand surgery
physiologically but they often fear separation from their parents,
strangers, bodily injury/mutilation and death. The child’s
developmental level and age-appropriate communication are
important in implementing the paediatric plan of care. The parent–
child relationship, the parents’ coping abilities and the preoperative
teaching and support will affect how well the child is able to deal with
these surgical fears and the level of anxiety experienced (Panella ).
15 Panella, J. J. (2016). Preoperative care of children: Strategies from a child life perspective.
AORN Journal, 104(1), 11–22.
The older adult (65 years and older) often has fewer physiological
reserves to meet the extra demands caused by surgery. The
physiological deficits of ageing increase the surgical risk for the older
adult. For example, because of a lower percentage of body water,
decreased kidney function and a decreased thirst response, older
adults are at greater risk of fluid and electrolyte imbalances
(Colburn, Mohanty & Burton ). Many older adults demonstrate
changes in liver and kidney function, both of which can affect
response to an anaesthetic and other medications that may be
administered during the perioperative period. The older adult may be
15
16


poorly nourished, which can impair healing. Declines in sensory
function (hearing in particular) or the presence of dementia make it
more difficult to understand directions and teaching. In addition, the
older adult is more likely to have a chronic disease, such as
cardiovascular disease, chronic lung disease or diabetes, that
affects healing and responses to medication and surgery (Neuman
et al.
).
16 Colburn, J. L., Mohanty, M. S. & Burton, J. R. (2017). Surgical guidelines for perioperative
management of older adults: What geriatricians need to know. Journal of the American
Geriatrics Society, 65(6), 1339–1346.
17 Neuman, M. D., Silber, J. H., Magaziner, J. S., Passarella, M. A., Mehta, S. & Werner, R.
M. (2014). Survival and functional outcomes after hip fracture among nursing home residents.
JAMA, 174(8), 1273–1280.
There is little data to indicate the true incidence and extent of
complications and mortality in older Australians having surgery.
However, there is evidence to suggest that adults older than 75
years have a higher 30-day mortality than younger age groups (Ou
et al.
).
18 Ou, L., Chen, J., Assareh, H., Hollis, S., Hillman, K. & Flabouris, A. (2014). Trends and
variations in the rates of hospital complications, failure-to-rescue and 30-day mortality in
surgical patients in New South Wales, Australia, 2002–2009. PLoS ONE, 9(5), e96164.
General health
Surgery is least risky when the person is in good general health with
minimal comorbidities. Any infection or pathophysiology increases
17
18


the risk of adverse outcomes. Of particular concern are upper
respiratory tract infections, which together with a general
anaesthetic can adversely affect respiratory function. Where there is
a high risk of infection, prophylactic antibiotics may be administered
parenterally within 1 hour of surgery and continued for 24 to 72
hours after surgery. This practice allows time for drugs to reach
therapeutic levels in the tissues but does not permit bacterial
resistance to develop. Common health problems that increase
surgical risk and may lead to the decision to postpone or cancel
surgery are listed in Box 38.2
.
BO X
38.2 Health problems that increase
surgical risk
Malnutrition can lead to delayed wound healing, infection
and reduced energy. Protein and vitamins are needed for
wound healing; vitamin K is essential for blood clotting.
Obesity leads to hypertension, impaired cardiac function
and impaired ventilation. Obese people are also more
likely to have delayed wound healing and wound infection
because adipose tissue impedes blood circulation and the
delivery of nutrients, antibodies and enzymes required for
wound healing.
Cardiovascular conditions such as angina pectoris, recent
myocardial infarction, hypertension and heart failure


reduce contractility and increase the risk of arrhythmias.
Well-controlled cardiac problems generally pose minimal
operative risk.
Coagulation disorders may lead to severe bleeding,
haemorrhage and subsequent hypovolaemic shock.
Upper respiratory tract infections or chronic obstructive
lung diseases such as emphysema adversely affect
pulmonary function, especially when exacerbated by the
effects of general anaesthesia. They also predispose the
person to postoperative atelectasis and lung infections.
Renal disease impairs regulation of the body’s fluids and
electrolytes and excretion of drugs and other toxins.
Type 1 and type 2 diabetes predisposes the person to
wound infection and delayed healing.
Liver disease (e.g. cirrhosis) impairs the liver’s abilities to
detoxify medications used during surgery, produce the
prothrombin necessary for blood clotting and metabolise
nutrients essential for healing.
Neurological disease such as epilepsy may result in
seizures during surgery or recovery.
Nutritional status
Adequate nutrition is required for normal tissue repair. Surgery
increases the body’s need for nutrients due to the tissue healing and


prevention of infection required during the postoperative period
(Steenhagen ). Obesity and malnutrition increase surgical risk.
19 Steenhagen, E. (2015). Enhanced recovery after surgery. Nutrition in Clinical Practice,
31(1), 18–29.
Obesity contributes to postoperative complications such as
pneumonia, wound infections and wound separation (Fencl, Walsh &
Vocke ). Both obese and underweight people are vulnerable to
pressure injury due to positioning required for surgery. The
perioperative nurse provides padding and other measures to protect
the person’s skin over pressure points during surgery.
20 Fencl, J. L., Walsh, A. & Vocke, D. (2015). The bariatric patient: An overview of
perioperative care. AORN Journal, 102(2), 116–131.
Many vitamins and minerals are essential in wound healing (see
Table 38.2
). A malnourished person is at risk for delayed wound
healing, wound infection and fluid and electrolyte alterations. If a
person has serious malnutrition, the surgery may be postponed to
improve the nutritional status. In this instance, if the surgery cannot
be delayed, or if the surgery will impact on postoperative nutritional
intake (e.g. laryngectomy), parenteral or enteral nutrition may be
initiated.
Table 38.2 Vitamins and minerals essential to wound healing
Medications
19
20


The regular use of certain medications can increase surgical risk.
Consider these examples:
Anticoagulants increase blood coagulation time.
Tranquillisers may interact with anaesthetics, increasing the risk
of respiratory depression.
Corticosteroids may interfere with wound healing and increase
the risk of infection.
Diuretics may affect blood pressure and fluid and electrolyte
balance.
People can be unaware of the potential adverse interactions of
medications and may fail to report the use of medications for
conditions unrelated to the indication for surgery. The astute nurse
interviewer should question the person and family about the use of
commonly prescribed medications, over-the-counter preparations
and any herbal remedies for specific conditions mentioned during
the nursing history. Having identified medications that may affect
surgical risk or anaesthetic risk, the Registered Nurse needs to refer
these details to the anaesthetist. Some medications will need to be
continued to prevent the occurrence of symptoms from underlying
diseases and conditions.
Mental status
Disorders that affect cognitive function, such as mental illness,
dementia or developmental delay affect the person’s ability to
understand and cope with the stresses of surgery. These people


also may require medication such as anticonvulsants or
antipsychotic drugs that can interact with anaesthetic and analgesic
medications used during and after surgery. Mental illness is
prevalent across the globe and represents 13% of the global disease
burden (World Health Organization (WHO)
); however, not all
people seek medical help. Accurate assessment of the mental
health status of an individual assists in confirming the person’s ability
to give an informed consent to treatment. Consent is not valid if a
person cannot make an informed decision regarding treatment and
treatment options (Forrester & Griffiths ).
21 World Health Organization (2012). Global Burden of Mental Disorders and the Need for a
Comprehensive, Coordinated Response from Health and Social Sectors at the Country Level.
Secretariat Report A65/10. Retrieved from <http://apps.who.int>.
22 Forrester, K. & Griffiths, D. (2015). Essentials of Law for Health Professionals (4th ed.).
Chatswood, NSW: Mosby Elsevier.
People with dementia may have difficulty understanding proposed
surgical procedures and may respond unpredictably to anaesthesia
(Chen et al.
). Manifestations of dementia such as confusion,
disorientation and agitation also may be aggravated by the change
of environment in the hospital, interfering with the person’s ability to
cooperate with pre- and postoperative care.
23 Chen, P. L., Yang, C. W., Tseng, Y. K., Sun, W. Z., Wang, J. L., Oyang, Y. J. & Fuh, J. L.
(2014). Risk of dementia after anaesthesia and surgery. The British Journal of Psychiatry,
204(3), 188–193.
21
22
23


Extreme anxiety also increases surgical risk and interferes with the
person’s ability to process information and respond appropriately to
instructions. In some instances, professional counselling is indicated
prior to surgery. It is also important to determine whether a person
has coping skills and support systems in place to help them.


The surgical pathway
The surgical pathway has three distinct phases: preoperative,
intraoperative and postoperative. Together the three phases are
referred to as the perioperative period
. The nursing activities
associated with each phase include assessment of the person,
identifying potential or actual health problems, and planning specific
care based on the individual’s needs. Each phase is associated with
a set of activities and nursing theory that reflects specific knowledge
and skills required at different stages along the clinical pathway
common to all people requiring surgery.
The preoperative phase
 begins when the decision to have
surgery is made. The preoperative period is used to assess the
person’s suitability for surgery, identify potential risk factors, educate
the person on avoiding complications of surgery and anaesthesia,
and plan to meet the person’s needs for a safe and sustained
recovery upon discharge.
The intraoperative phase
 begins when the nurse who has
prepared the person for surgery hands over the person’s details to
the operation room/anaesthetic nurse. The nursing activities related
to this phase include a variety of checks and procedures designed to
create and maintain a safe therapeutic environment for the person
and the health care personnel. These activities include interventions
that provide for the person’s safety by maintaining an aseptic


environment, ensuring proper functioning of equipment and
providing the surgical team with the instruments and supplies
needed during the procedure. The intraoperative phase involves
administering an anaesthetic, performing the procedure and closure
of any wounds on completion of the procedure. Transition to the
postoperative period is marked by wound closure and reversal of the
anaesthetic.
The postoperative phase
 begins with the handover of the person
by operating room staff to staff in the post-anaesthesia care unit
(PACU) (also referred to as the post-anaesthetic room or recovery
room). The effects of anaesthesia and surgery are monitored by the
nurse who also coaches the person towards a return to preoperative
body function or better. In the immediate postoperative period,
nurses focus on assessing the person’s airway, characteristics of
breathing and circulatory parameters. This stage then progresses to
the prevention of complications following the effects of the
anaesthesia and surgery, including the alleviation of pain and
nausea. In the day surgery context, PACU nurses are involved in
teaching and providing support to the person and their support
people and planning for home care.


Preoperative phase
Preoperative consent
Prior to any surgical procedure, informed consent is required from
the person having surgery or from their legal guardian. Informed
consent requires that the person has been informed and involved in
decisions affecting their health. The surgeon is responsible for
obtaining the informed consent by providing the following information
to the person or legal guardian:
the nature of and the reason for the surgery
all available options and the risks associated with each option
the risks of the surgical procedure and its potential outcomes
name and qualifications of the surgeon performing the procedure
the right to refuse consent or later withdraw consent.
The surgeon documents the informed consent conversation with the
person or legal guardian in the preoperative progress notes.
The surgical consent form, provided by the organisation, protects
the person from incorrect/unwanted procedures and the surgeon
and the organisation from litigation related to unauthorised surgeries


or uninformed people. This consent form becomes part of the
person’s medical record and goes to the operating room with them.
Although the surgeon maintains legal responsibility for ensuring that
the person is giving informed consent, the nurse may witness the
person’s signature on the health organisation’s consent form. In
doing so, the nurse ensures that the consent form is signed and
serves as a witness to the signature but not to the fact that the
person is informed. If the nurse assesses that the person does not
understand the procedure to be performed, the surgeon is contacted
and requested to speak with the person before surgery can proceed.
Informed consent is only possible when the person understands the
provided information; that is, speaks the language and is conscious,
mentally competent and not sedated. Generally, informed consent
may not be given by a minor unless the minor is considered to be
Gillick competent (Morgan 2018 ). Specific guidelines regarding
consent for minors vary between the states and territories. Nurses
must be aware of their responsibilities regarding consent and of the
particular hospital’s policies (see Chapter 4
).
24 Morgan, D. (2018). Ethical considerations with regard to adolescent consent in the
perioperative setting: Talking points for anaesthetic practitioners. Journal of Perioperative
Practice, 28(7–8), 184–187.
24


Nursing management
Assessing
Preoperative assessment includes collecting and reviewing the
person’s physical, psychological and social data to determine the
needs of the individual throughout the three perioperative phases.
The perioperative nurse collects the data by interviewing the person
in the pre-surgical care unit or by telephone prior to the day of
surgery. When data cannot be collected directly, the perioperative
nurse uses other data sources such as the nursing admission
assessment. Although forms vary considerably between
organisations, Box 38.3
 summarises essential preoperative
information that should be included.
BO X
38.3 Preoperative assessment data
Current health status. Essential information includes
general health status and the presence of any chronic
diseases, such as diabetes or asthma, that may affect the
person’s response to surgery or anaesthesia. Note any
physical limitations that may affect the person’s mobility or


ability to communicate after surgery, as well as any
prostheses such as hearing aids or contact lenses.
Allergies. Include allergies to prescription and non-
prescription drugs, food allergies and allergies to tape,
latex, soaps or antiseptic agents. Some food allergies
may indicate a potential reaction to drugs or substances
used during surgery or diagnostic procedures; for
example, an allergy to seafood alerts the nurse to a
potential allergy to iodine-based dyes or soaps commonly
used in hospitals.
Medications. List all current medications (prescribed and
over the counter). It may be vital to maintain a therapeutic
serum level of some medications (e.g. anticonvulsants)
throughout the surgical experience; others, such as
anticoagulants or aspirin, increase the risks of surgery
and an anaesthetic, and need to be discontinued several
days prior to surgery. It is important to include in the list
any herbal remedies the person currently takes as many
complementary medicines may interact with anaesthetic
medication or surgical haemostasis.
Previous surgeries. Previous surgical experiences may
influence the person’s physical and psychological
responses to surgery or may reveal unexpected
responses to the anaesthetic.
Mental status. The person’s mental status and ability to
understand and respond appropriately can affect the
entire perioperative experience. Note any developmental


disabilities, history of mental illness, history of dementia or
anxiety related to the procedure.
Understanding of the surgical procedure and the
anaesthetic. The person should have a good
understanding of the planned procedure and what to
expect during and after surgery as well as the expected
outcome of the procedure.
Smoking. Smokers may have more difficulty clearing
respiratory secretions after surgery, increasing the risk of
postoperative complications such as pneumonia and
atelectasis as well as delayed wound healing.
Alcohol and other substances. Use of substances that
affect the central nervous system, liver or other body
systems can affect the person’s response to the
anaesthetic and surgery and postoperative recovery.
Coping. Individuals with a healthy self-concept who have
successfully employed appropriate coping mechanisms in
the past may be better able to manage the stressors
associated with surgery.
Social resources. Determine the availability of family or
other caregivers as well as the person’s social support
network. These resources are important to the person’s
recovery, particularly for the person undergoing same-day
or short-stay surgery.
Cultural and spiritual considerations. Immigration
patterns have contributed to a significant shift in the size
and composition of the Australian population. Cultural
competence is a requirement of the Nursing and


Midwifery Board of Australia’s  code of conduct and is
expected of all perioperative nurses. Culture and
spirituality influence the person’s response to surgery;
respecting cultural and spiritual beliefs and practices can
reduce preoperative anxiety and improve recovery.
25 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (2018). Code of Conduct for
Nurses. Retrieved from <www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Howe, Condon and Goodchild  designed a study to explore
and describe problems that arise when Indigenous
Australians undergo general anaesthesia. Aside from a range
of common health problems (diabetes mellitus, renal disease
and rheumatic heart disease), some difficulties in maintaining
cultural safety were identified. This study has been more
recently complemented by Cheng, Blum and Spain  who
explored communication between Indigenous Australians and
anaesthetists in the perioperative setting. Communication
difficulties were more commonly reported in Indigenous
groups; the most common difficulty was apparent shyness or
fear, in turn leading to a reluctance or difficulty in
communicating effectively. The results suggest that the
treatment involves diagnosis and management of diverse
preoperative medical problems and that better management
may be achieved by ensuring the nurse acts in culturally safe
ways and by adding Aboriginal interpreters and health
workers to the anaesthetic team (Howe et al. 1998, p. 86).
26 Howe, P. W., Condon, J. R. & Goodchild, C. S. (1998). Anaesthesia for Aboriginal
Australians. Anaesthetic Intensive Care, 26(1) (Feb), 86–91.
25
26
27


27 Cheng, W. Y. C., Blum, P. & Spain, B. (2004). Barriers to effective perioperative
communication in Indigenous Australians: An audit of progress since 1996.
Anaesthesia and Intensive Care, 32(4), 542–547.
Table 38.3
 lists routine preoperative screening tests.
Table 38.3 Routine preoperative screening tests
Planning
The overall goal in the preoperative period is to ensure that the
person is mentally, emotionally and physically prepared for surgery.
Examples of nursing activities to meet this goal are discussed in the
‘Implementing’ section that follows.
Planning should involve the person, their family and/or significant
others. Preoperative care planning and teaching interventions are
usually done on an outpatient basis either in person or via a
telephone interview by the perioperative nurse.
Planning for home care
For the perioperative person, discharge planning begins before
admission for the planned procedure. Early planning to meet the
discharge needs of the person is particularly important for outpatient


procedures, as generally they are discharged within hours after the
procedure is performed.
Discharge planning incorporates an assessment of the person’s and
significant others’ abilities and resources for care, their financial
resources and the need for referrals and home health services.
However, the extent of discharge planning and home care will vary
significantly depending on the type of surgery.
Implementing
The major nursing activity to ensure that the person is prepared for
surgery is preoperative teaching.
Preoperative education
Preoperative teaching is a vital part of nursing care. Studies have
shown that preoperative teaching reduces anxiety and the incidence
of postoperative complications and increases an individual’s
satisfaction with their surgical experience (Alanazi ; Lee & Lee ).
Good preoperative teaching also facilitates a person’s successful
and early return to work and other activities of daily living. However,
to maximise effectiveness, this education must be individualised
(Bisbey et al.
). Hovsepian, McGah and O’Brien  found that in
addition to the importance of individualised education, preoperative
teaching allowed the nurse to establish and promote health literacy.
28
29
30
31


28 Alanazi, A. A. (2014). Reducing anxiety in preoperative patients: A systematic review.
British Journal of Nursing, 23(7), 387–393.
29 Lee C. K. & Lee, I. F. K. (2013). Preoperative patient teaching: The practice and
perceptions among surgical ward nurses. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 22(17), 2551–2561.
30 Bisbey, C. C., Ristau, T. A., Johnson, M. D., Streed, M. M., Bursiek, A. A. & Grubbs, P. L.
(2017). The power of education: Preoperative class reduces anxiety and improves
confidence. MedSurg Nursing, 26(5), 324. Retrieved from <https://link.gale.com>.
31 Hovsepian, J., McGah, C. & O’Brien, C. (2017). Postoperative instructions preoperatively:
Evaluating the effectiveness of a teaching model on patient satisfaction regarding instructions
for home care. Journal of Perianaesthesia Nursing, 32(3), 231–237.
Five dimensions of preoperative teaching have been identified as
important to people having surgery:
1. Information, including what will happen to them,
outlining when and what the person will experience
(expected sensations and level of discomfort). The nurse
must listen carefully and attentively to the person to identify
specific concerns and fears. Typical questions include, ‘What
will happen during surgery?’, ‘How will I feel after the
operation?’, ‘What will the surgeon find?’, ‘How long will I be in
the hospital?’.
2. Psychosocial support to reduce anxiety. The nurse
provides support by actively listening and providing accurate
information. It is important to rectify any misperceptions the
person may have.
3. The roles of the person and support people in
preoperative preparation, the surgical procedure and


during the postoperative phase. Understanding their role
during the perioperative experience increases the individual’s
sense of control and reduces anxiety. This includes what will
be expected of the person, desired behaviours, self-care
activities and what the person can do to facilitate recovery.
4. Skills training. This includes activities such as moving and
mobilisation, deep breathing, coughing and splinting incisions
with the hands or a pillow.
5. Pain relief education. Implementation of an intentional and
structured education program outlining the nature of expected
pain, nursing interventions that will be used to manage pain
and the expectations on the patient in identifying and
participating in pain management (e.g. use of PCA) must be
implemented.
If the person is scheduled for outpatient surgery, preoperative
teaching is often provided before the day of surgery using some
combination of DVDs and verbal and written instructions. The person
may have an appointment with the outpatient perioperative nurse
(usually scheduled to coincide with preoperative diagnostic testing)
to discuss preoperative concerns and implement the teaching plan.
Written instructions are always provided to reinforce verbal teaching.
Teaching is further reinforced on admission on the day of surgery
and before discharge from the post-anaesthetic unit. Preoperative
instructions are summarised in Box 38.4
.
BO X


38.4 Preoperative instructions
Preoperative regimen
Explain the need for preoperative tests (e.g. laboratory, x-
ray, ECG).
Discuss surgically specific preparations (e.g. bowel
preparation), if required.
Discuss skin preparation, including operative area and
preoperative bath or shower.
Discuss preoperative medications, if ordered.
Explain individual therapies such as venous
thromboembolism (VTE) prevention, intravenous therapy,
the insertion of a urinary catheter or nasogastric tube, and
the use of a spirometer.
Discuss the preoperative visit by the anaesthetist.
Explain the need to restrict food at least 6 hours and clear
fluids 2 hours before surgery.
Provide a general timetable for perioperative events,
including the time of surgery.
Discuss the need to remove jewellery, make-up and all
prostheses (e.g. glasses, hearing aids, complete or partial
dentures, wig) immediately before surgery.
Inform the person about the preoperative holding area
and give the location of the waiting room for support
people.
Teach deep-breathing and coughing exercises, leg
exercises, ways to turn and move (see Skill 38.1
) and


splinting techniques.
Complete the preoperative checklist.
Postoperative regimen
Discuss the post-anaesthesia recovery room patient
routine.
Review the type and frequency of assessment activities.
Discuss pain management.
Explain usual activity restrictions and precautions related
to getting up for the first time post surgery.
Describe possible dietary alterations.
Discuss postoperative dressings and drains.
Provide an explanation and tour of the intensive care unit
if person is to be transferred there post surgery.
The surgical outpatient
Review all instructions in the preoperative and
postoperative regimen.
Confirm place and time of surgery, including when to
arrive and where to register.
Discuss appropriate attire (e.g. people having hand
surgery should wear a garment with large sleeve openings
to fit over a bulky dressing; all people need to leave
valuables at home).


Explain the need for a responsible adult to drive or
accompany the person home.
Discuss discharge criteria and how long the person should
expect to stay post surgery.
Discuss medications, including any specific preoperative
medications and the person’s current medication regimen.
Communicate by telephone the evening before surgery to
confirm time of surgery and arrival time.
Communicate by telephone within 48 hours
postoperatively to evaluate surgical outcomes and identify
any problems or complications.
When the person is a child, addressing the fears and anxieties of
both the child and the family is vital. Parents need to know what to
expect and to be able to express their concerns. Parents should be
considered members of the perioperative team and allowed to
participate in providing as much care as possible.
Skill 38.1
 provides guidelines for teaching the person about
mobility restriction, leg exercises, deep breathing and coughing.
Real-world practice
When teaching preoperative routines and expected
behaviours, the nurse tries to incorporate all of the


senses. Include a description of the expected
experiences people are likely to have throughout the
perioperative phase, as well as what they might expect
to feel, hear, smell and taste from the time they are
called to the OR until they return to their room.
Discuss the bright lights, masks and hair coverings
that hospital personnel wear, operating room tables
that feel hard and air that is cooler. The environment
may smell of antiseptic solutions, noises will seem loud
and monitor equipment beeps continuously. In the
PACU/recovery room, nurses will be calling out their
name, asking them to take deep breaths and checking
to see if they are uncomfortable. Their mouth may feel
dry and perhaps taste as if they’ve lost their
toothbrush for a week. Dressings can feel tight, their
throat may be sore and their vision blurred. By
describing sensory experiences, people can have
better outcomes, decreased pain and anxiety levels
and feel more satisfied because they know what to
expect.
—Mary Catherine Rawls, RN, MS, BC Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center, Lebanon, NH
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SIS, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
The preoperative patient


History Mr Taylor, 62 years old, has disabling osteoarthritis
and is scheduled for a total knee replacement tomorrow. This
is his first surgical experience and he is asking many
questions about what to expect before and after surgery. He
says, ‘The more I know, the less anxious I feel’.
Lifespan considerations
Preoperative teaching
Children
Parents need to know what to expect and to be able to
express their concerns.
Separation from parents often is the child’s greatest fear;
the time of separation should be minimised and parents
allowed to interact with the child both immediately
preceding and following the surgery, once it is safe to
facilitate this.
Teaching/communicating with children (both timing and
content) should be geared to the child’s developmental
level and cognitive abilities and use age-appropriate
language. Play is an effective teaching tool with children
(e.g. the child can put a bandage on an incision on a doll).
Older adults


Assess hearing ability to ensure the older adult hears the
necessary information.
Assess short-term memory. Presenting one focused idea
at a time and repeating or reinforcing information may be
necessary.
Older adults are at greater risk for postoperative
complications, such as pneumonia. Reinforce moving and
deep-breathing and coughing exercises.
Assess potential postoperative needs at this time.
Arrangements can be made preoperatively to obtain
necessary items. Examples are medical equipment, such
as walkers, raised toilet seats and bed trapezes; Meals on
Wheels; and help with transportation.
If the older adult will need to be in extended care for a
period of time after surgery, this is the time to initiate
these plans.
Assess the person for risk of pressure injury development
and be extra attentive to the use of proper paddings and
support devices to prevent injury during positioning and
transfers in the operating room. Risks are:
– older age
– poor nutritional status
– history of diabetes or cardiovascular problems
– history of taking steroids, which cause increased
bruising and skin breakdown.


Home care considerations
Postoperative instructions
Adults want information about activities they normally
perform in advance of their recovering at home. This is
important information for all people undergoing
surgery, particularly for those having the surgery as an
outpatient. Discuss the following areas:
Food. Eat small portions at first because
anaesthetic medications and analgesics slow
gastric emptying.
Elimination. Constipation occurs frequently as a
result of decreased gastrointestinal mobility due to
factors such as anaesthesia, decreased activity
and opiates. Discuss strategies to prevent
constipation.
Sexual activity. Intimacy such as gentle hugging
and kissing is non-harmful to the healing process.
The resumption of sexual intercourse will depend
on wound healing and level of soreness or
tenderness. It is recommended most people wait
until approximately 2 to 4 weeks following minor
surgery. The person should discuss
recommendations with the surgeon with regards to


the resumption of intercourse following
gynaecological procedures.
Wound care. Discuss wound strength and care,
including the signs and symptoms of infection and
when to notify the surgeon.
Lifting. Be specific about weight limits, if
appropriate. Relate the weight limit to everyday
items (e.g. a litre of milk weighs approximately 1
kg).
Pain. Provide information about the person’s
analgesic regimen. Ask the person to describe their
daily activities and discuss ways to avoid or reduce
painful activities.
Bathing. Check with the surgeon with regards to
preferences for keeping the wound dry. There is no
evidence that water on a closed wound is harmful
or interferes with wound healing. If allowed, inform
the person to shower, letting the warm water wash
over the incision and gently pat the incision dry.
Activities. Advise the person that they will tire
easily and to plan short activities with frequent rest
breaks.
Physical preparation


Preoperative preparation includes the following areas: nutrition and
fluids, elimination, hygiene, medications, rest, care of valuables and
prostheses, special orders and surgical skin preparation. In most
organisations a preoperative checklist is used on the day of surgery.
The nurse completes the checklist following appropriate
documentation protocols. It is essential that all pertinent records
(laboratory records, x-ray films, consents) be available for
perioperative personnel for referral and that all physical preparation
is completed to meet legal and safety requirements.
Nutrition and fluids
Adequate hydration and nutrition promote healing. Nurses need to
identify and record any signs of malnutrition or fluid imbalance. If the
person is receiving intravenous fluids or a measured fluid intake,
nurses must ensure that the fluid intake and output is accurately
measured and recorded.
The order ‘NBM from midnight’ has been a long-standing tradition
because it was believed that anaesthetic agents suppress
gastrointestinal functioning, thus creating an increased risk of
vomiting and aspiration during the administration of a general
anaesthetic. Re-evaluation and research does not support this
tradition and, as a result, the American Society of Anesthesiologists
(ASA) has revised its guidelines for preoperative fasting in the
healthy person undergoing elective procedures. According to
Kyrtatos et al.
, the revised guidelines allow for:
32


32 Kyrtatos, P. G., Constandinou, N., Loizides, S. & Mumtaz, T. (2014). Improved patient
education facilitates adherence to preoperative fasting guidelines. Journal of Perioperative
Practice, 24(10), 228–231.
the consumption of clear liquids up to 2 hours before elective
surgery requiring general anaesthesia, regional anaesthesia or
sedation analgesia
a light breakfast (e.g. tea and toast) 6 hours before the
procedure
a heavier meal 8 hours before surgery.
Elimination
Enemas before surgery are no longer routine, but cleansing enemas
may be ordered if bowel surgery is planned. The enemas help
prevent postoperative constipation and intraoperative contamination
of the surgical area by faecal matter. After surgery involving the
intestines, a degree of paralysis occurs along the small intestine,
which may take up to 72 hours to resolve. This is known as paralytic
ileus and is discussed in further detail in Chapter 52
.
Prior to surgery, an in-and-out catheterisation or insertion of an
indwelling urinary catheter may be required to ensure that the
bladder remains empty. This helps prevent inadvertent injury to the
bladder, particularly during pelvic surgery. If the person does not
have a catheter, it is important to empty the bladder prior to
receiving preoperative medications.


Hygiene
In some settings, people are asked to bathe or shower the evening
before or the morning of surgery (or both). The purpose of hygienic
measures is to reduce the risk of wound infection by reducing the
amount of normal flora on the person’s skin. The bath includes a
shampoo whenever possible.
The person’s nails should be trimmed and free of polish, and all
cosmetics should be removed so that the nail beds, skin and lips are
visible when circulation is assessed during the perioperative phases.
Intraoperatively, the person will be required to wear a surgical cap.
The surgical cap contains the person’s hair and any micro-
organisms on the hair and scalp.
Before going into the operating room, the person should remove all
hair pins and clips as they may cause pressure or accidental
damage to the scalp when the person is unconscious. The person
also removes personal clothing and puts on an operating room
gown.
Medications
Occasionally, the anaesthetist may request that routinely taken
medications be withheld on the day of surgery. In most settings,
preoperative medications are given to the person prior to going to
the operating room. They include the following:


sedatives and anxiolytics such as benzodiazepines to reduce
anxiety and ease anaesthetic induction
opiate analgesics such as morphine sulfate to provide sedation
and reduce the required amount of anaesthetic
anticholinergics such as atropine, scopolamine and
glycopyrrolate to reduce oral and pulmonary secretions and
prevent laryngospasm.
histamine-receptor antihistamines such as ranitidine to reduce
gastric fluid volume and gastric acidity.
Preoperative medications must be given at a scheduled time or ‘on
call’; that is, when a member of the operating suite team notifies the
nurse to give the medication.
Rest and sleep
Nurses should employ suitable strategies to support sleep on the
night before surgery. This may include administering prescribed
sedatives, minimising environmental distractions and assisting the
person to follow their own sleep rituals where possible. Adequate
rest helps the person manage the stress of surgery and helps
healing.
Valuables
Valuables such as jewellery and money should be sent home with
the person’s next of kin. If valuables cannot be sent home, they
need to be labelled and placed in a locked storage area according to


the organisation’s policy. Removing jewellery includes any body-
piercing jewellery; there is a risk of injury from burns if an
electrosurgical unit is used (Burlingame ; Smith ). If a person
wishes to keep a wedding band on, the nurse can tape it in place,
but wedding bands must be removed if there is danger of the fingers
swelling after surgery. Situations warranting removal include surgery
to an arm, cast application or a mastectomy that involves removal of
the lymph nodes (mastectomies may cause oedema of the arm and
hand).
33 Burlingame, B. (2017). Jewellery removal when using electrosurgical devices. AORN
Journal, 105(1), 110–116.
34 Smith, F. D. (2016). Caring for surgical patients with piercings. AORN Journal, 103(6),
583–596.
Culturally competent care
Body piercing
Body art (i.e. tattooing and piercing) has been practised from
ancient times to the present. Body piercing is considered one
of the oldest forms of body art. The reasons for modern body
piercing include making a fashion statement, observing a rite
of passage and creatively expressing oneself through highly
visible piercing of the ears, nose, eyebrow and navel.
Piercings of the tongue, nipples and genitals are of a more
sexual expression or function. Understanding the cultural and
social meanings of body piercing helps provide culturally
sensitive and safe care (Smith 2016).
33
34


The nurse needs to ensure that this jewellery is removed in
addition to the more traditional jewellery. The risks of failing to
remove body-piercing jewellery include alternate site burns
when using electrosurgery, pressure injuries from the
jewellery, dislocation and aspiration of the jewellery during
tracheal intubation and possible inability to insert a urinary
catheter because of genitalia piercings (Dunn ).
35 Dunn, D. (2016). Body art and the perioperative process. AORN Journal, 104(4),
326–340.
The perioperative nurse may need to help the person remove
the jewellery. It is important that the jewellery not be
damaged or the person harmed (physically or
psychologically) when removing the jewellery. Certain tools
may need to be available for removal of the jewellery.
Sources: Based F. D. Smith (2016). Caring for surgical patients with piercings, AORN Journal, 103(6),
583–596; and D. Dunn (2016). Body art and the perioperative process. AORN Journal, 104(4), 326–
340.
Prostheses
All prostheses (artificial body parts, contact lenses, artificial eyes
and artificial limbs) and eyeglasses, wigs and false eyelashes must
be removed before surgery. Hearing aids are often left in place and
the operating room personnel notified. It is increasingly common for
dentures to remain in situ to allow for effective airway management
during induction of anaesthesia. The nurse should follow local policy
in this practice. In some hospitals, dentures are placed in a locked
35


storage area; in others they are placed in labelled containers and
kept at the person’s bedside. Partial dentures can become dislodged
and obstruct an unconscious person’s breathing.
The nurse also checks for the presence of chewing gum or loose
teeth. Loose teeth are a common problem with 5- or 6-year-olds
undergoing tonsillectomy and can become dislodged and/or
aspirated during anaesthesia.
Special orders
The nurse checks the surgeon’s orders for special requirements
(e.g. the insertion of a nasogastric tube prior to surgery, the
administration of medications, such as insulin, or the application of
anti-embolic stockings). For the technique of inserting a nasogastric
tube, see Skill 49.1
.
Skin preparation
In most organisations, skin preparation is carried out during the
intraoperative phase. The surgical site is cleansed with an
antimicrobial to remove normal skin flora and reduce the resident
microbial count to subpathogenic levels.
Safety protocols
The US Joint Commission on Accreditation of Health Care
Organizations (JCAHO) established, effective July 2004, the


Universal Protocol for Preventing Wrong Site, Wrong Procedure,
Wrong Person Surgery (Gillespie et al.
; JCAHO
). This protocol
involves three steps.
36 Gillespie, B., Harbeck, E., Lavin, J., Gardiner, T., Withers, T. & Marshall, A. (2019). The
impact of improved surgical safety checklist participation on OR efficiencies: A pretest-post
test analysis. ACORN, 32(1), 9–18.
37 Joint Commission on Accreditation of Health Care Organizations (JCAHO) (2003).
Universal Protocol for Preventing Wrong Site, Wrong Procedure, Wrong Person Surgery.
Retrieved from <www.acep.org>.
The protocol requires verification of an individual’s identification (ID)
at the time surgery is scheduled, during admission and whenever
the person is transferred to another caregiver.
The second step involves marking of the operative site in an
unambiguous manner. The facility chooses its own surgical site
method (e.g. the person’s initials, surgeon’s initials, the word ‘YES’).
An ‘X’ is considered ambiguous and cannot be used for marking the
site. The mark must be permanent and visible after the person has
been prepped and draped for surgery.
The third step is called ‘time out’. Before surgery begins the surgical
team takes a time out to conduct a final verification of the correct
person, procedure and site. Any questions or concerns must be
resolved before the procedure can begin.
Transfusion errors are often attributed to incomplete ID of those
receiving blood products. Recipient ID in operating rooms is often
36
37


difficult because the person having surgery may be covered in
surgical drapes; additional ID checks are required (Laws &
Goudas ).
38 Laws, T. A. & Goudas, L. (2013). Transfusion errors in the operating room: A systematic
review. Australian College of Operating Room Nurses, Spring, 26(3), 10-18.
In November 2009, Australian health ministers unanimously
endorsed the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Surgical Safety
Checklist (WHO
) as the best strategy for improving surgical safety
in Australia. All versions of the checklist should have been
implemented in all jurisdictions by 1 July 2011. This supersedes the
Correct Patient, Correct Procedure, Correct Site Protocol (C3
Protocol).
39 World Health Organization (2008). Surgical Safety Checklist. Retrieved from
<www.who.int>.
Vital signs
Complete a preoperative assessment and documentation of vital
signs for baseline data. Report any abnormal findings, such as
elevated blood pressure or elevated temperature.
Anti-embolic stockings
Anti-embolic stockings are firm elastic hose that compress the veins
of the legs and thereby facilitate the return of venous blood to the
heart. They also improve arterial circulation to the feet and prevent
38
39


oedema of the legs and feet; stockings are applied for several days
or more.
There are several types of stockings. One type extends from the
foot to the knee and another from the foot to mid-thigh. These
stockings usually have a partial foot that exposes the heel or toes so
that extremity circulation can be assessed. Elastic stockings usually
come in small, medium and large sizes. Skill 38.2
 details the
steps required to apply anti-embolic stockings.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: Communicating for Safety
‘The intention of this standard is to ensure there is a timely,
purpose-driven and structured communication that supports
continuous, coordinated and safe care for consumers.’
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC)
, p. 26)
40 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health
Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved by
focusing on effective transfer of information at
all points, not just clinical handover.
Organisations need to support continuity and
coordination of care by maintaining an
40


organisation-wide consumer identification
system, robust clinical handover, consumer–
procedure matching and communicating
changes to consumer care.
In the perioperative environment,
communicating for safety is fundamental to safe
and effective care. Key elements include
consent, patient identification and procedure
matching, surgical site identification and
marking, and transfer of care between ward,
anaesthesia, surgery, PACU and ward. Systems
such as preoperative checklists, anaesthesia
‘check-in’ at transfer of care and ‘time out’
before commencing surgery support safety and
ensure the preservation of reliable, effective
transfer of information pertaining to the person’s
care.
Lifespan considerations
Anti-embolic stockings
Children
Anti-embolic stockings are infrequently used on children.


Older adults
Anti-embolic stockings are highly elasticised and the older
adult may need assistance with application. People with
arthritis may need to have another person put the
stockings on for them.
Many older adults have altered circulation and wear anti-
embolic stockings. It is important to check for wrinkles in
the stockings and to see if the stocking has rolled down or
twisted. If so, this should be corrected immediately
because the stockings must be evenly distributed over the
limb to promote rather than hinder circulation. Wrinkled or
bunched stockings that impair circulation also increase the
risk of damage to the skin and underlying tissues.
Stockings should be removed at least once each shift so
that a thorough assessment can be made of the legs and
feet. Redness and skin breakdown on the heels can occur
quickly and go undetected if the person is not assessed
on a regular basis.
Home care considerations
Anti-embolic stockings
Teach the person or caregiver how to apply the
anti-embolic stockings.


Stress the importance of correcting wrinkles or
rolling down of the stockings and explain the
rationale.
Ask the person or caregiver to remove the
stockings daily and inspect the skin on the legs.
Provide instructions about:
Laundering the stockings including using two pairs
of stockings to allow for one pair to be worn while
the other is being laundered.
Replacing the stockings when they lose their
elasticity.
Sequential compression devices
People undergoing surgery may benefit from a sequential
compression device (SCD) to promote venous return from the legs.
The SCD has circumferential sleeves that inflate and deflate around
the legs to promote venous flow. SCDs are discussed in Chapter
54
 (see Skill 54.1
).
Evaluating


The goals established during the planning phase are evaluated
according to specific desired outcomes, also established in that
phase.


SKILL
38.1 Teaching moving, leg
exercises, deep breathing and
coughing
Purposes
Moving
To promote venous return.
To enhance lung expansion and mobilise
secretions.
To stimulate gastrointestinal motility.
To facilitate early ambulation.
Leg exercises
To promote venous return, thereby preventing
thrombophlebitis and thrombus formation.
Deep breathing and coughing
To enhance lung expansion and mobilise
secretions, thereby preventing atelectasis and
pneumonia.


Assessment
Assess
Vital signs.
Discomfort.
Temperature and colour of feet and legs.
Breath sounds.
Presence of dyspnoea or cough.
Learning needs of the person.
Anxiety level of the person.
The individual’s experience with previous surgery
and anaesthesia.
Planning
Before commencing patient teaching on moving, leg
exercises, deep-breathing exercises and coughing,
the nurse should determine a number of important
points. These include (a) the type of surgery, (b) the
time of the surgery, (c) the name of the surgeon or
treating team, (d) the preoperative orders and (e)
the stipulated practices of the organisation for
preoperative care. The nurse should also confirm
that a member of the surgical team has completed
the medical history and physical examination and
that the person has signed the consent form.
Delegation


Assessment of the learning needs of the person and
their support people and determining the teaching
content and appropriate strategies for teaching
requires application of professional knowledge and
critical thinking. Preoperative teaching is conducted
by the nurse and is not delegated to Assistants in
Nursing (AINs). The AIN, however, can reinforce
teaching, assist the person with the exercises and
report to the nurse if the person is unable to perform
the exercises.
Equipment
Pillow
Teaching materials (e.g. DVD, written materials)
if available at the organisation
Implementation
Preparation
Ensure that potential distracters (e.g. pain, TV,
visitors) to teaching are not present. Family and/or
significant others should be included in the teaching
plan, if appropriate.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using the
organisation’s protocol. Explain to the person


what you are going to teach and the
importance of the person’s participation in the
exercises they are going to be taught.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for privacy.
4. Show the person ways to turn in bed and to
get out of bed.
Instruct a person having a right abdominal
incision or a right-sided chest incision to
turn to the left side of the bed and sit up
as follows:
a. Flex the knees.
b. Splint the wound by holding the left
arm and hand or a small pillow
against the incision.
c. Turn to the left while pushing with
the right foot and grasping a partial
side rail on the left side of the bed
with the right hand.
d. Come to a sitting position on the
side of the bed by using the right
arm and hand to push down
against the mattress and swing the
feet over the edge of the bed.
Teach a person with a left abdominal or
left-sided chest incision to perform the


same procedure but splint with the right
arm and turn to the right.
For people undergoing orthopaedic
surgery (e.g. hip surgery), explain the use
of special aids, such as a trapeze, to
assist with movement.
5. Teach the person the following three leg
exercises:
Alternate dorsiflexion and plantar flexion of
the feet. Rationale: this exercise is
sometimes referred to as calf pumping,
because it alternately contracts and
relaxes the calf muscles, including the
gastrocnemius muscles. 1


1 Leg muscles: anterior and posterior
views
Flex and extend the knees and press the
backs of the knees into the bed while
dorsiflexing the feet. 2 Instruct those who
cannot raise their legs to do isometric
exercises that contract and relax the
muscles.


2 Flexing and extending the knees
Raise and lower the legs alternately from
the surface of the bed. Flex the knee of
the stable leg and extend the knee of the
moving leg. 3 Rationale: this exercise
contracts and relaxes the quadriceps
muscles.
3 Raising and lowering the legs
6. Demonstrate deep-breathing (diaphragmatic)
exercises as follows:
Place your hands palms down on the
border of your rib cage and inhale slowly
and evenly through the nose until the
greatest chest expansion is achieved. 4


4 Demonstrating deep breathing
Hold your breath for 2 to 3 seconds.
Then exhale slowly through the mouth.
Continue exhalation until maximum chest
contraction has been achieved.
7. Help the person perform deep-breathing
exercises.
Ask the person to assume a sitting
position.


Place the palms of your hands on the
border of the person’s rib cage to assess
respiratory depth.
Ask the person to perform deep breathing,
as described in step 6.
8. Instruct the person to cough voluntarily after
five deep inhalations.
Ask the person to inhale deeply, hold the
breath for a few seconds and then cough
once or twice.
Ensure that the person coughs deeply and
does not just clear the throat.
9. If the incision will be painful when the person
coughs, demonstrate techniques to splint the
abdomen.
Show the person how to support the
incision by placing the palms of the hands
on either side of the incision site or directly
over the incision site, holding the palm of
one hand over the other. Rationale:
coughing uses the abdominal and other
accessory respiratory muscles. Splinting
the incision may reduce pain while
coughing if the incision is near any of
these muscles.


Show the person how to splint the
abdomen with interlocked hands or a
firmly rolled pillow held against the
person’s abdomen. 5
5 Splinting abdomen while coughing
10. Inform the person about the expected
frequency of these exercises.


Instruct the person to start the exercises
as soon after surgery as possible.
Encourage them to carry out deep
breathing and coughing at least every 2
hours, taking a minimum of five breaths at
each session. Note, however, that the
number of breaths and frequency of deep
breathing varies with the person’s
condition. People who are susceptible to
pulmonary problems may need deep-
breathing exercises every hour. People
with chronic respiratory disease may need
special breathing exercises (e.g. pursed-
lip breathing, abdominal breathing,
exercises using various kinds of incentive
spirometers). See Chapter 53
.
11. Document the teaching and all assessments.
Some organisations may have a preoperative
teaching flow sheet. Check organisation
policy.
Evaluation
Document the outcome of the teaching plan, such
as:


The person demonstrated an ability to perform
moving, leg exercises, deep breathing and
coughing exercises.
The person was able to recount key information
discussed by the nurse.


SKILL
38.2 Applying anti-embolic
stockings
Purposes
To facilitate venous return from the lower
extremities.
To prevent venous stasis and venous
thrombosis.
To reduce peripheral oedema.
Assessment
Assess both lower extremities for
Rates, volumes and rhythms of posterior tibial
and dorsalis pedis pulses.
Skin colour (note pallor, cyanosis or other
pigmentation).
Skin temperature.
Presence of distended veins or oedema.
Skin condition (e.g. thickened, shiny, taut).


Planning
Before applying anti-embolic stockings, determine
any potential or present circulatory problems and the
surgeon’s orders involving the lower extremities.
Delegation
AINs frequently remove and apply anti-embolic
stockings as part of morning and evening hygiene
care. The nurse should stress the importance of
removing and reapplying the stockings and reporting
any changes in the person’s skin to the nurse.
Equipment
Tape measure
Clean anti-embolic stockings of appropriate size
and type.
Implementation
Preparation
Take measurements as needed to obtain the
appropriate-size stockings.
Measure the length of both legs from the heel to
the gluteal fold (for thigh-length stockings) or
from the heel to the popliteal space (for knee-
length stockings).


Measure the circumference of each calf and
each thigh at the widest point.
Compare the measurements with the size chart
to obtain stockings of correct size. Obtain two
sizes if there is a significant difference.
Rationale: stockings that are too large do not
place adequate pressure on the legs to facilitate
venous return and may bunch, increasing the
risk of pressure and skin irritation. Stockings that
are too small may impede blood flow to the feet
and cause discomfort.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using the
organisation’s protocol. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can cooperate.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for privacy.
4. Select an appropriate time to apply the
stockings.
Apply stockings in the morning, if possible,
before the person rises. Rationale: in
sitting and standing positions, the veins
can become distended so that oedema


occurs; the stockings should be applied
before this happens.
Assist the person who has been
ambulating to lie down and elevate the
legs for 15 to 30 minutes before applying
the stockings. Rationale: this facilitates
venous return and reduces swelling.
5. Prepare the person.
Assist them to a recumbent position in
bed.
Wash and dry the legs as needed.
6. Apply the stockings.
Reach inside the stocking from the top
and, grasping the heel, turn the upper
portion of the stocking inside out so the
foot portion is inside the stocking leg.
Rationale: firm elastic stockings are
easier to fit over the foot and calf when
inverted in this manner rather than
bunching up the stocking.
Ask the person to point their toes, then
position the stocking on the person’s foot.
With the heel of the stocking down and
stretching each side of the stocking, ease
the stocking over the toes taking care to
place the toe and heel portions of the


stocking appropriately. 1 Rationale:
pointing the toes makes application easier.
1 Applying the inverted stocking over the
toes
Source: Elena Dorfman.
Grasp the loose portion of the stocking at
the ankle and gently pull the stocking over
the leg, turning it right side out in the
process. 2


2 Pulling the stocking snugly over the leg
Source: Elena Dorfman.
Inspect the person’s leg and stocking,
smoothing any folds or creases. Ensure
that the stocking is not rolled down or
bunched at the top or ankle. Rationale:
folds and creases can cause skin irritation
under the stocking; bunching of the
stocking can further impair venous return.
Remove the stockings for 30 minutes
every 8 hours, inspecting the legs and
skin while the stockings are off.


Soiled stockings may be laundered by
hand with warm water and mild soap.
Hang to dry.
7. Document the procedure. Record the
procedure, your assessment data and when
the stockings are removed and reapplied.
Evaluation
Remove anti-embolism stockings one to three
times a day for 30 minutes for skin care and
inspection.
Note the appearance of the legs and skin
