around the drain site outward, using
separate swabs for each wipe 2C.
Support and hold the drain erect while
cleaning around it. Clean as many times
as necessary to remove the drainage.
Dry the surrounding skin with dry gauze
swabs as required. Do not dry the incision
or wound itself. Moisture facilitates wound
healing.
8. Apply dressings to the drain site and the
incision.
Place a pre-cut
 gauze
snugly around the drain 3, or open a
 gauze to
 fold it lengthwise to
 and place the
gauze around the drain
so that the ends overlap. Rationale: this
dressing absorbs the drainage and helps
prevent it from excoriating the skin. Using
pre-cut gauze or folding it as described,
10?cm × 10?cm
10?cm × 10?cm
10?cm × 20?cm
5?cm × 20?cm
5?cm × 20?cm


instead of cutting the gauze, prevents any
threads from coming loose and getting
into the wound, where they could cause
inflammation and provide a site for
infection.
3 Pre-cut gauze in place around a drain
Apply the sterile dressings one at a time
over the drain and the incision. Place the
bulk of the dressings over the drain area
and below the drain, depending on the
person’s usual position. Rationale: layers
of dressings are placed for best
absorption of drainage, which flows by
gravity.


Apply the final surgipad, remove gloves
and dispose of them. Secure the dressing
with tape or ties.
9. Document the procedure and all nursing
assessments.
Evaluation
Conduct appropriate follow-up, such as amount
of granulation tissue or degree of healing;
amount of drainage and its colour, consistency
and odour; presence of inflammation; and
degree of discomfort associated with the incision
or drain site.
Compare with previous findings, if available.
Report significant deviations from normal to the
doctor.


Chapter 38 Review


Chapter highlights
Surgery is a unique experience that creates stress and
precipitates physical, and possibly psychological, changes.
The perioperative period includes three phases: preoperative,
intraoperative and postoperative.
Surgical procedures are categorised by degree of urgency,
purpose and degree of risk.
Factors such as age, general health, nutritional status,
medication use and mental status contribute to the level of risk to
the person during surgery.
The surgical team is required to ensure the person agrees to
surgery in writing, via informed consent and signing of a consent
form.
Nursing history and physical assessment data are important
sources for planning preoperative and postoperative care.
The overall goal of nursing care during the preoperative phase is
to prepare the person mentally and physically for surgery.
Preoperative teaching includes situational information and
psychosocial support, the role of the person throughout the
perioperative period, expected sensations and discomfort, and
training for the postoperative period.
Preoperative teaching should include moving, leg exercises and
coughing and deep-breathing exercises. Many aspects of
preoperative teaching are intended to prevent postoperative
complications.


Physical preparation includes the following areas: nutrition and
fluids, elimination, hygiene, rest, medications, care of valuables
and prostheses, special orders and surgical skin preparation.
Anti-embolic stockings or sequential compression devices may
be ordered for some people to facilitate venous return.
A preoperative checklist provides a guide to and documentation
of a person’s preparation before surgery.
Maintaining the person’s safety is the overall goal of nursing care
during the intraoperative phase.
Anaesthetic may be general or regional. Regional anaesthesia
includes topical, local, nerve block, intravenous block, spinal
anaesthetic (subarachnoid block) and epidural.
Surgical skin preparation should be carried out as close to the
time of surgery as possible and is commonly performed during
the intraoperative phase.
Positioning of the person during surgery is important to reduce
the risk of tissue and nerve damage.
Immediate post-anaesthetic care focuses on assessment and
monitoring parameters to prevent complications from
anaesthesia or surgery.
Initial and ongoing assessment of the postoperative person
includes level of consciousness, vital signs, oxygen saturation,
skin colour and temperature, comfort, fluid balance, dressings,
drains and tubes.
The overall goals of nursing care during the postoperative period
are to promote comfort and healing, restore the highest possible
level of wellness and prevent associated risks such as infection
or respiratory and cardiovascular complications.


Ongoing postoperative nursing interventions include: (a)
managing pain; (b) appropriate positioning; (c) encouraging
incentive spirometry and deep-breathing and coughing exercises;
(d) promoting leg exercises and early ambulation; (e) maintaining
adequate hydration and nutritional status; (f) promoting urinary
elimination; (g) continuing gastrointestinal suction; and (h)
providing wound care.
Surgical aseptic technique (sterile technique) is used when
changing dressings on surgical wounds to promote healing and
reduce the risk of infection.
Penrose drains and Hemovac drainage systems are examples of
drains that may be placed in or near surgical wounds to promote
drainage of excess haemoserous or purulent exudate.
Sutures, wire clips or staples are used to approximate skin and
underlying tissues after surgery. These are generally removed 7
to 10 days after surgery.
Concept check
1. Which of the following tests is the best resource for
determining the status of a person’s preoperative liver
function?
1. Serum potassium.
2. Urea and electrolytes
3. Alanine amino transferase (ALT), aspirate amino
transferase (AST), bilirubin.
4. Serum albumin.


2. A woman who is undergoing a mastectomy expresses
sadness about losing her breast. Based on this information,
the nurse would consider exploring which areas of
psychological support with the patient?
1. Changes to body image and sexual identity.
2. Anticipatory grief.
3. Fear and anxiety about impending surgery and
anaesthesia.
4. Concerns about coping strategies.
3. Which of the following statements by the person indicates
that they have understood the nurse’s preoperative teaching
regarding gall bladder surgery?
1. ‘I cannot eat or drink anything after midnight.’
2. ‘I’m not going to cough after surgery because it might
open my incision.’
3. ‘I might have a stroke if I stop taking my anticoagulant.’
4. ‘The nurse showed me how to contract and relax my
calf muscles.’
4. The nurse assesses a postoperative person who has a rapid,
weak pulse; urine output less than 30 mL/hr; and decreased
blood pressure. The person’s skin is cool and clammy. What
complication should the nurse suspect?
1. Thrombophlebitis.
2. Hypovolaemic shock.
3. Aspiration pneumonia.
4. Wound dehiscence.


5. The person is most likely to require the greatest amount of
analgesia for pain during which of the following time periods?
1. Immediately after surgery.
2. 4 hours after surgery.
3. 12 to 36 hours after surgery.
4. 48 to 60 hours after surgery.
6. A person who has had abdominal surgery is holding a pillow
against his abdomen during deep breathing and coughing.
What term does the nurse use to describe this technique?

7. A semi-conscious person in the post-anaesthetic care unit
(PACU) is experiencing dyspnoea (difficulty breathing). Which
of the following immediate actions should the nurse perform
first?
1. Place a pillow under the person’s head.
2. Remove the oropharyngeal airway.
3. Apply oxygen by mask.
4. Reposition the person to keep the tongue forwards.
8. The person’s postop orders state ‘diet as tolerated’. The
person has been NBM. The nurse will advance the person’s
diet to clear liquids based on which of the following
assessments? Select all that apply.
1. No complaints of nausea or vomiting.
2. Pain level is maintained at a rating of 2–3/10.
3. States passing flatus.
4. Ambulates with minimal assistance.


5. Expresses feeling ‘hungry’.
9. The overall goal of nursing care during the intraoperative
phase is the person’s                .
10. The nurse plans to remove the person’s sutures. Which of the
following actions demonstrate appropriate standards of care?
Select all that apply.
1. Use clean technique.
2. Grasp the suture at the knot with a pair of forceps.
3. Place the curved tip of the suture scissors under the
suture as close to the skin as possible.
4. Pull the suture material that is visible beneath the skin
during removal.
5. Remove alternate sutures first.
Focus on critical thinking
1. Australian law recognises that children become increasingly
competent at making informed decisions as they move
towards adulthood. How would a nurse determine the validity
of a consent signed by a person younger than 18 years of
age?
2. Perioperative nurses play a vital role in identifying people
experiencing problems using a screening questionnaire. What
factors determine the role of the nurse in determining health
problems most likely to result in an adverse surgical


outcome? When is it appropriate to notify the surgeon and/or
anaesthetists of a potential problem?
3. Fasting policies vary depending on the type of surgery and
anaesthesia. Identify the basic principles that determine when
and for how long. Determine how these principles can be
used to challenge lengthy and inappropriate fasting orders.

Unit 9 Promoting psychosocial
health
Vital to the art of providing effective and
appropriate nursing care is the nurse’s ability to
convey understanding, sensitivity and
compassion to the person who has a negative
self-concept or who confronts a stressful life
event. The nurse recognises the impact of low
self-esteem, loss or other stressors on the
individual as well as on the family and support
people. By providing a supportive environment
in which to express feelings, by listening
attentively and offering comfort, the nurse helps
those affected to develop a healthy self-image
or cope with stress and to transcend the
experience of loss.

Learning outcomes
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Discuss the components of the sensory-perception process.
Describe factors influencing sensory function.
Identify clinical signs and symptoms of sensory overload and
deprivation.
Describe essential components in assessing a person’s sensory-
perception function.
Discuss factors that place a person at risk of sensory alterations.


Develop nursing diagnoses and outcome criteria for individuals
with impaired sensory function.
Discuss nursing interventions to promote and maintain sensory
function.
Identify strategies to promote a therapeutic environment for the
individual with acute confusion/delirium.

An individual’s senses are essential for growth,
development and survival. Sensory stimuli give
meaning to events in the environment. Any
alteration in a person’s sensory function can
affect their ability to function within the
environment. For example, many people have
impaired sensory functions that put them at risk
in the health care setting; nurses can help them
find ways to function safely in this often
confusing environment.


Components of the sensory
experience
The sensory process involves two components: reception and
perception. Sensory reception
 is the process of receiving stimuli
or data. These stimuli are either external or internal to the body.
External stimuli are visual
 (sight), auditory
 (hearing),
olfactory
 (smell), tactile
 (touch) and gustatory
 (taste).
Gustatory stimuli can be internal as well. Other types of internal
stimuli are kinaesthetic or visceral. Kinaesthetic
 refers to
awareness of the position and movement of body parts. For
example, a person walking is aware of which leg is forward. A
related sense is stereognosis
, the ability to perceive and
understand an object through touch by its size, shape and texture.
For example, a person holding a tennis ball is aware of its size,
round shape and soft surface without seeing it. Visceral
 refers to
any large organ within the body. Visceral organs may produce stimuli
that make a person aware of them (e.g. a full stomach). Sensory
perception
 involves the conscious organisation and translation of
the data or stimuli into meaningful information.
For an individual to be aware of the surroundings, four aspects of
the sensory process must be present: a stimulus, a receptor,
impulse conduction and perception.


1. Stimulus. This is an agent or act that stimulates a nerve
receptor.
2. Receptor. A nerve cell acts as a receptor by converting the
stimulus to a nerve impulse. Most receptors are specific; that
is, they are sensitive to only one type of stimulus, such as
visual, auditory or tactile.
3. Impulse conduction. The impulse travels along nerve
pathways to the spinal cord or directly to the brain (see
Figure 39.1
). For example, auditory impulses travel to the
organ of Corti in the inner ear. From there the impulses travel
along the eighth cranial nerve to the temporal lobe of the
brain.
Figure 39.1


The nerve impulses run along the ascending sensory tracts to
reach the reticular activating system (RAS); then certain


impulses reach the cerebral cortex where they are perceived.
Source: E. N. Marieb & K. Hoehn (2019). Human Anatomy and Physiology: Global Edition (11th ed.).
Essex: Pearson Education Limited. Copyright © 2019 by Pearson Education, Inc. Reproduced with
permission.
4. Perception. Perception, or awareness and interpretation of
stimuli, takes place in the brain, where specialised brain cells
interpret the nature and the quality of the sensory stimuli. The
level of consciousness affects the perception of the stimuli.
Arousal mechanism
For the person to receive and interpret stimuli, the brain must be
alert. The reticular activating system (RAS) in the brain stem is
thought to mediate the arousal mechanism. There are two
components of the reticular activating system: (1) the reticular
excitatory area (REA); and (2) the reticular inhibitory area (RIA). The
REA is responsible for stimulus arousal and wakefulness.
People have their own zone of optimum arousal—the level at which
the person feels comfortable. Sensoristasis
 is the term used to
describe when a person is in optimal arousal. Beyond this comfort
zone, people must adapt to the increased or decreased sensory
stimuli. An absence of stimuli from the RAS to the cerebrum results
in the brain becoming inactive or useless.


The brain has the capacity to adapt to sensory stimuli. For example,
a person living in a city may not notice traffic noise that someone
from a regional area finds loud and disturbing. Not all sensory stimuli
are acted upon; some are stored by the memory to be used at a
later date. Cognition is cerebral functioning. It involves such
processes as conscious thought, reality orientation, problem solving,
judgment and comprehension.
Awareness
 is the ability to perceive internal and external stimuli
and to respond appropriately through thought and action. There are
several states of awareness (see Table 39.1
). The normal, alert
person can assimilate many kinds of information at one time.

Factors affecting sensory function
A number of factors affect sensory reception and perception,
including a person’s developmental stage, culture, level of stress,
medications and illness, and lifestyle and personality.
Developmental stage
Perception of sensation is critical to the intellectual, social and
physical development of infants and children. Infants learn to
recognise their mother’s or caregiver’s face and establish bonding
essential to later emotional development. Young children respond to
music by singing and dancing as they begin to interact with their
peers in groups. As children grow, they learn to interpret visual and
auditory signals when preparing to cross the street. Adults have
many learned responses to sensory stimuli. The sudden loss or
impairment of any sense, therefore, has a profound effect on a
person of any age.
Normal physiological changes in older adults put them at higher risk
of altered sensory function. The diminishing of sensory perception
that may come with chronic disease or ageing is generally gradual.
About 50% of the Australian population aged 60 years have a
hearing loss, with this increasing to 70% for those over 70 years and


80% for those over 80 years (Hearing Australia ). Additionally, with
the ageing population, 1 in every 4 Australians is projected to have
hearing loss by 2050 (Better Hearing Australia ). In Australia, men
have a higher incidence of hearing loss than women and, in general,
Indigenous Australians have a significantly higher incidence of
hearing impairment than non-Indigenous Australians because of the
high incidence in the younger age groups of otitis media (Australian
Institute of Health and Welfare ). For those with significant hearing
loss, the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) (2019)
provides funding to help individuals access hearing supports, such
as Auslan (Australian Sign Language) resources.

Vision loss is also a normal physiological change in older adults.
Presbyopia is an age-related eye condition where a person needs
glasses for reading. The most common causes of vision loss in
Australia are age-related macular degeneration, cataracts,
glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy and uncorrected or under-corrected
refractive error (Vision 2020 Australia ). Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander people are 3 times more likely than non-Indigenous
1
2
3
4

Australians to report complete or partial blindness, with the most
common cause of blindness being cataracts (Vision 2020 Australia ).
Diabetes is a leading cause of vision loss and, sadly, almost all vision
loss from diabetes is preventable (Vision 2020 Australia ). Nurses
can help by ensuring people with diabetes undertake regular eye
screening. Vision Australia  helps people access the National
Disability Insurance Scheme, offers individual emotional and
practical support and resources, such as access to occupational
therapists, mobility specialists, adaptive technology specialists and
orthoptists, to enable people to continue to live meaningful and
independent lives.

Culture
An individual’s culture often determines the amount of stimulation
that a person considers usual or ‘normal’. For example, a child
reared in an extended family environment with aunts, uncles and
6
7
8


grandparents who share responsibilities for the care of all the
children may be accustomed to more stimulation than a child reared
in an Australian suburb of scattered nuclear family homes. In
addition, the normal amount of stimulation associated with ethnic
origin, religious affiliation and income level, for example, affects the
amount of stimulation an individual desires and believes to be
meaningful. A sudden change in cultural surroundings experienced
by immigrants or visitors to Australia, especially where there are
differences in language, dress and cultural behaviours, may also
result in sensory overload or cultural shock (Wali & Renzaho ).
9 Wali, N. & Renzaho, A. (2018). ‘Our riches are our family’, the changing family dynamics
and social capital for new migrant families in Australia. PLoS ONE, 13(12), e0209421.
Cultural deprivation
, or cultural care deprivation
, is a lack
of culturally assistive, supportive or facilitative acts. It is important
that nurses be sensitive to what stimulation is culturally acceptable
to each individual. For example, in some cultures, touching is
comforting, whereas in others, it is offensive. Some people find the
presence of cultural or religious symbols reassuring and their
absence a source of anxiety. Nurses should encourage individuals
who want to have culturally related symbols present to follow
practices with which they are comfortable, provided that these
practices do not endanger health (see Chapter 19
).
Stress
9


During times of increased stress, people may find their senses
already overloaded and thus seek to decrease sensory stimulation.
For example, a person dealing with physical illness, pain,
hospitalisation and diagnostic tests may wish to have only close
support people visit. In addition, the person may need the nurse’s
help to decrease unnecessary stimuli (e.g. noise) as much as
possible. On the other hand, the person may seek sensory
stimulation during times of low stress.
Medications and illness
Certain medications can alter an individual’s awareness of
environmental stimuli. Narcotics and sedatives, for example, can
decrease awareness of stimuli. Some antidepressants can alter
perceptions of stimuli. Anyone taking several medications
concurrently may show alterations in sensory function; older adults
are especially at risk and need to be monitored carefully. Certain
medications, if taken over a long period of time, become ototoxic,
injuring the auditory nerve and causing hearing loss that may be
irreversible. Some of these medications are aspirin, frusemide
(Lasix), the aminoglycosides and certain drugs given for cancer
chemotherapy.
Certain diseases, such as atherosclerosis, restrict blood flow to the
receptor organs and the brain, thereby decreasing awareness and
slowing responses. Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, poor diet and
smoking can all lead to vision impairment. Uncorrected refractory


errors, cataracts and diabetic retinopathy are prevalent causes of
vision impairment in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
communities (Vision 2020 Australia 2019b). Some central nervous
system diseases, such as multiple sclerosis and motor neurone
disease, cause varying degrees of paralysis and sensory loss.
Lifestyle and personality
Lifestyle influences the quality and quantity of stimulation to which
an individual is accustomed. A person who is employed in a large
company may be accustomed to many diverse stimuli, whereas
someone who is self-employed and works in the home is exposed to
fewer, less diverse stimuli. People’s personalities also differ in terms
of the quantity and quality of stimuli with which they are comfortable.
Some people delight in constantly changing stimuli and excitement,
whereas others prefer a more structured life with few changes.


Sensory alterations
People become accustomed to certain sensory stimuli and, when
these change markedly, the individual may experience discomfort.
For example, when a person enters a hospital, they usually
experience stimuli that differ in quantity and quality from those to
which they are accustomed. These changes may cause the person
to become confused and disoriented (see Table 39.1
).
Nurses are aware of the behaviours that often result from different
stimuli. They now pay more attention to colour, sound, privacy and
social interaction for individuals so that the stimuli more closely
resemble those in the home environment. Factors that contribute to
alterations in behaviour include sensory deprivation, sensory
overload and sensory impairments.
Sensory deprivation
Sensory deprivation
 is generally thought of as a decrease in or
lack of meaningful stimuli. When a person experiences sensory
deprivation, the balance in the RAS is disturbed. The RAS is unable
to maintain normal stimulation to the cerebral cortex. Because of
this reduced stimulation, a person becomes more acutely aware of
the remaining stimuli and often perceives these in a distorted


manner. Thus, the person often experiences alterations in
perception, cognition and emotion. The ‘Clinical manifestations
’
box lists clinical signs of sensory deprivation.
Clinical manifestations
Sensory deprivation
Excessive yawning, drowsiness, sleeping.
Decreased attention span, difficulty concentrating,
decreased problem solving.
Impaired memory.
Periodic disorientation, general confusion or nocturnal
confusion.
Preoccupation with somatic complaints, such as
palpitations.
Hallucinations or delusions.
Crying, annoyance over small matters, depression.
Apathy, emotional lability.
Sensory overload
Sensory overload
 generally occurs when a person is unable to
process or manage the amount or intensity of sensory stimuli. Three
factors contribute to sensory overload:


1. increased quantity or quality of internal stimuli, such as pain,
dyspnoea, anxiety
2. increased quantity or quality of external stimuli, such as a
noisy health care setting, intrusive diagnostic tests, contact
with many strangers
3. inability to disregard stimuli selectively, perhaps as a result of
nervous system alterations or medications that stimulate the
arousal mechanism.
Sensory overload can prevent the brain from ignoring or responding
to specific stimuli. Because of the many stimuli, the individual has
difficulty perceiving the environment in a way that makes sense. As
a result, the individual’s thoughts race in many directions and
restlessness occurs. The person usually feels overwhelmed and
does not feel in control. It is important for nurses to remember that
sights and sounds that are familiar to them often represent overload
to people who are not familiar with being in hospital. People who
have sensory overload may appear fatigued. They often cannot
internalise new information and experience cognitive overload as a
result of everything that is happening to them. Such factors as pain,
lack of sleep and worry can also contribute to sensory overload
(Delaney et al.
). See the ‘Clinical manifestations
’ box for
common signs of sensory overload.
10 Delaney, L., Currie, M., Huang, H.-C., Lopez, V. & Van Haren, F. (2018). ‘They can rest at
home’: An observational study of patients’ quality of sleep in an Australian hospital. BMC
Health Services Research, 18, 524. Doi: 10.1186/s12913-018-3201-z.
10


Sensory impairments
A sensory impairment
 is compromised reception, perception, or
both, of one or more of the senses. Blindness and deafness are
sensory impairments. When only one sense is affected, other
senses may become more acute to compensate for the loss.
However, sudden loss of eyesight can result in disorientation.
When the loss of sensory function is gradual, individuals often
develop behaviours to compensate for the loss; sometimes these
behaviours are unconscious. For example, a person with gradual
hearing loss in the right ear may unconsciously turn the left ear
towards a speaker. However, sudden loss of one of the senses can
result in disorientation, and compensatory behaviour often takes
days or weeks to develop.
Individuals with sensory impairments are at risk of both sensory
deprivation and sensory overload. For example, people who are
sight impaired may be unable to read, watch television or recognise
nurses by sight, which could lead to sensory deprivation. On the
other hand, sight-impaired people often have highly structured home
environments, and the diversity and unfamiliarity of the hospital
environment can create sensory overload. At the same time,
impaired vision often results in an inability to move around readily or
socialise with others.


Clinical manifestations
Sensory overload
Fatigue, sleeplessness.
Irritability, anxiety, restlessness.
Periodic or general disorientation.
Reduced problem-solving ability and task performance.
Increased muscle tension.
Scattered attention and racing thoughts.


Nursing management
Assessing
Nursing assessment of sensory-perceptual functioning includes six
components: (1) nursing history; (2) mental status examination; (3)
physical examination; (4) identification of people at risk; (5) the
individual’s environment; and (6) social support network.
Nursing history
During the nursing history the nurse assesses present sensory
perceptions, usual functioning, sensory impairments and potential
problems. In some instances, significant others can provide data the
person cannot provide. For example, support people may reveal
signs of recent changes in hearing ability, such as inattention to
others, recent mood swings, difficulty following clear instructions,
frequent requests to have something repeated and unusually loud
radio or television volumes. Data obtained in the assessment phase
are organised, validated and documented so that actual and
potential problems can be identified and treatment protocols can be
implemented. Examples of interview questions to elicit data about
the person’s sensory-perceptual functioning are shown in the
accompanying ‘Assessment interview’.


Mental status examination
Mental status is critical to any evaluation of the sensory-perceptual
process. Usually data on mental status, including level of
consciousness, orientation, memory and attention span, can be
obtained during the nursing history (see Chapter 31
). It is
important to note that sensory alterations can cause changes in
cognitive functioning (Lafreniere & Parham
).
11 Lafreniere, D. & Parham, K. (2019). Sensory health and healthy aging: Hearing and smell.
In P. Coll (Ed.), Healthy Aging: A Complete Guide to Clinical Management (eBook) (pp. 145–
158). Switzerland: Springer Nature.
Physical examination
Physical assessment determines whether the senses are impaired.
During the physical examination, the nurse assesses vision and
hearing, and the olfactory, gustatory, tactile and kinaesthetic senses.
The examination should reveal the person’s specific vision and
hearing abilities; perception of heat, cold, light touch and pain in the
limbs; and awareness of the position of the body parts. Specific
sensory tests include the following:
visual acuity, using a Snellen chart or other reading material such
as a newspaper; and visual fields
hearing acuity, by observing the person’s conversation with
others and by performing the whisper test and the Weber and
Rinne tuning fork tests
11


olfactory sense, by identifying specific aromas
gustatory sense, by identifying four tastes such as lemon, salt,
coffee and sugar
tactile sense, by testing light touch, sharp and dull sensation,
two-point discrimination, hot and cold sensation, vibration sense,
position sense and stereognosis.
These sensory tests are described in detail in Chapter 31
. The
nurse should also determine whether sensory adaptive devices that
the person uses, such as glasses or hearing aids, function properly.
Assessment interview
Sensory-perceptual functioning
Visual
How would you rate your vision (excellent, good, fair or
poor)?
Do you wear glasses or contact lenses?
Describe any recent changes in your vision.
Do you have any difficulty seeing near or far objects?
Do you have any difficulty seeing at night? Have you ever
experienced blurred vision, double vision, spots moving in
front of your eyes, blind spots, light sensitivity, flashing
lights or halos around objects?


When did you last visit an eye doctor or an optometrist for
eye screening?
Auditory
How would you rate your hearing (excellent, good, fair or
poor)?
Do you wear a hearing aid?
Describe any recent changes in your hearing.
Can you locate the direction of sounds and distinguish
various voices?
Do you experience any dizziness or vertigo? Do you
experience any ringing, buzzing, humming, crackling
noises or fullness in the ears?
Gustatory
Have you experienced any changes in taste (e.g. difficulty
in differentiating sweet, sour, salty and bitter tastes)?
Do you enjoy the taste of foods as you did previously?
Olfactory
Have you experienced any changes in smell?
Do things (foods, flowers, perfumes and so on) smell the
same as previously?


Can you distinguish foods by their odours and tell when
something is burning?
Have you experienced any changes in appetite? (Changes
in appetite may be related to an impaired sense of smell.)
Tactile
Are you experiencing any pain or discomfort?
Have you experienced any decrease in your ability to
perceive heat, cold or pain in your limbs?
Do you have any numbness or tingling in your
extremities?
Kinaesthetic
Have you noticed any difficulty in perceiving the position of
parts of your body?
People at risk of sensory deprivation or
overload
People at risk of sensory-perceptual alterations need to be identified
to ensure that preventive measures can be initiated. Box 39.1
describes people at risk.


BO X
39.1 People at risk of sensory
deprivation and overload
Sensory deprivation
People who:
are confined in a non-stimulating or monotonous
environment in the home or health care facility
have impaired vision or hearing
have mobility restrictions such as quadriplegia or
paraplegia, are confined to bed rest, have splinting or
traction restrictions
are unable to process stimuli (e.g. people who have brain
damage or who are taking medications that affect the
central nervous system)
have emotional disorders (e.g. depression) and withdraw
within themselves
have limited social contact with family and friends (e.g.
individuals from a different culture).
Sensory overload
People who:


have pain or discomfort
are acutely ill and have been admitted to hospital
are being closely monitored in an intensive care unit (ICU)
(see Figure 39.2
) and have invasive tubes such as IVs,
catheters or nasogastric or endotracheal tubes
Figure 39.2
A person in an intensive care unit may experience
sensory overload.


have decreased cognitive ability (e.g. head injury).
Environment
The nurse assesses the individual’s environment for quantity, quality
and type of stimuli. The individual’s environment may produce
insufficient stimuli, placing them at risk of sensory deprivation, or
excessive stimuli, placing them at risk of sensory overload. Non-
stimulating environments include those that (a) severely restrict
physical activity, and (b) limit social contact with family and friends.
Because appropriate or meaningful stimuli decrease the incidence of
sensory deprivation, the nurse must consider the person’s health
care environment for the presence of the following stimuli:
radio or other auditory device (e.g. iPod, tablet, smartphone),
television
clock or calendar
reading material (or toys for children)
number and compatibility of roommates
number of visitors.
To assess a health care environment that produces excessive
stimuli, the nurse considers, for example, bright lights, noise,
therapeutic measures and frequency of assessments and
procedures. In the person’s home, the nurse may also note the


presence of smart devices, pets, bright colours, adequate lighting
and so on.
Clinical consideration
Are you aware of the noise level around you or
the noise level you create while providing
nursing care? The World Health Organization
(Berglund, Lindvall & Schwela ) recommends a
standard of 30 decibels (dB) for rest and sleep.
However, sounds in critical care units often
exceed 70 dB at least six times every hour,
thereby suggesting sensory overload (Delaney
et al.
).
12 Berglund, B., Lindvall, T. & Schwela, D. (Eds) (1999).
Guidelines for Community Noise. Geneva: World Health
Organization.
13 Delaney, L., Parke, J., Robinson, R., Da Fonte, N. & Lopez, V.
(2014). What hath night to do with sleep; noise levels in ICU—
Preliminary findings. Australian Critical Care, 27(1), 52.
Social support network
12
13


The degree of isolation a person feels is significantly influenced by
the quality and quantity of support from family members and friends.
The nurse assesses: (a) whether the person lives alone; (b) who
visits and when; and (c) any signs indicating social deprivation, such
as withdrawal from contact with others to avoid embarrassment or
dependence on others, negative self-image, reports of lack of
meaningful communication with others and absence of opportunities
to discuss fears or concerns that facilitate coping mechanisms.
Diagnosing
There are a number of potential problems that are applicable to a
person with a sensory perception alteration:
Altered sensory perception: visual, auditory, kinaesthetic, touch,
taste or smell
Acute confusion
Chronic confusion
Impaired memory.
Clinical consideration
It is easy to confuse the problems altered
sensory perception and altered thought
processes. Altered sensory perception refers to


sensory input—the person’s ability to accurately
interpret stimuli. In contrast, when a person’s
cognitive abilities (because of mental illnesses)
interfere with the ability to interpret stimuli
accurately, the problem is probably altered
thought processes.
Sensory-perception problem as the
aetiology
Depending on the data obtained, alterations in sensory-perception
function may affect other areas of human functioning and indicate
other diagnoses. In these instances, the sensory-perception problem
becomes the aetiology.
Examples of nursing diagnoses for which sensory-perception
alterations are the aetiology include the following:
Risk of injury related to sensory-perception alteration (specify).
For example:
a. vision impairment (e.g. decreased depth perception)
b. reduced tactile sensation secondary to neurological or
circulatory alterations
c. decreased sense of smell
d. hearing impairment
e. decreased kinaesthetic sense.


Unable to maintain a safe home environment related to sensory-
perception alteration (declining visual abilities).
Risk of impaired skin integrity related to sensory-perception
alteration (altered tactile sensation).
Impaired verbal communication related to sensory-perception
alteration (specify). For example:
a. altered level of consciousness
b. hearing impairment
c. sensory overload
d. sensory deprivation.
Unable to perform activities of daily living: bathing/hygiene
related to sensory-perception alteration (specify). For example:
a. vision impairment
b. diminished kinaesthetic sense
c. inability to perceive body part or spatial relationship.
Social isolation related to sensory-perception alteration (specify).
For example:
a. impaired vision
b. impaired hearing.
Planning
Planning includes goals associated with the care of individuals
independent of setting and those specific to the home environment.


Planning independent of setting
The overall outcome criteria (or goals) for individuals with sensory-
perception alterations are to:
prevent injury
maintain the function of existing senses
develop an effective communication mechanism
prevent sensory overload or deprivation
reduce social isolation
perform activities of daily living independently and safely.
Appropriate nursing interventions may include:
cognitive stimulation activities (i.e. crosswords, puzzles)
communication enhancement strategies for hearing impairment
(i.e. correctly fitted hearing aid device)
communication enhancement strategies for vision impairment
(i.e. correct prescription eye glasses)
nutrition/diet management (i.e. healthy diet, avoid alcohol or only
drink in moderation)
environmental management (i.e. keeping the floor clear of
objects)
fall prevention strategies (i.e. installing handrails and using bath
mats)
promotion of good body mechanics (i.e. bring objects close to
centre of body when lifting)


peripheral sensation management strategies (i.e. splints,
massage, wearing shoes)
emotional support strategies (i.e. promote family involvement
and support groups)
safety strategies (i.e. check the temperature of water with elbow,
not hand or foot, before immersing limb/body).
See ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and
interventions
’.
Planning for home care
To provide for continuity of care, the nurse must consider the
person’s needs for assistance with care in the home or residential
and community care options. Some people with severe alterations in
sensory-perception functioning may be discharged to an assisted
living facility that provides the specific support the person requires.
Discharge planning incorporates a reassessment of the person’s
abilities for self-care, the availability and skills of support people,
financial resources and the need for referrals and home help
services. See ‘Home care assessment
’ for sensory-perception
alterations and confusion. A major aspect of discharge planning
involves the instructional needs of the person and family. The next
section provides strategies to support visual and auditory function
and maintain a safe environment for people.

INTERVENTIO NS
People with sensory-perception alteration
History Tony Manfredi, a 52-year-old lawyer, has multiple
sclerosis. Muscle strength and tactile sensation have declined
during the past 2 years. He uses a motorised wheelchair to
move about. He reports loss of sensation in his lower limbs
and fingers and inability to discern temperature differences.
His wife assists with bathing and grooming.
History Joan Lambert, an 84-year-old widow, lives alone in
her unit. She can hear words spoken clearly and close to the
left ear but cannot hear any sounds with the right ear. She
says she spends her time listening to the television and radio
(at a loud volume). She tends to speak loudly and shouts
when talking with others and nods and smiles when others
speak. Her daughter, who visits, says she refuses to wear a
hearing aid. (Mrs Lambert says it doesn’t help and is
uncomfortable.) Her daughter has recently noted that her
mother has become withdrawn, appears absorbed in her own
thoughts and talks and laughs to herself.
Implementing


Nurses can assist individuals with sensory alterations by promoting
healthy sensory function, adjusting environmental stimuli and helping
people to manage acute sensory impairments.
Promoting healthy sensory function
Early detection of sensory problems is one step towards preventing
serious problems. The arousal mechanism for sensation is normally
present at birth; however, it is undifferentiated. The special senses
are also present at birth, although some changes in function occur
during the growth process.
Early screening to detect problems in vision and hearing functions is
essential. Universally, all infants should be screened for hearing loss
by 1 month of age, preferably before hospital discharge. In Australia,
a free Healthy Hearing program exists where all newborn babies are
screened as soon as possible after birth to identify babies with a
hearing loss. If there are any concerns with this first screening, a
second screening will be done. If, on the second screening, concern
still exists, a ‘refer result’ will be made to an audiologist for further
testing. Infants identified with a hearing loss should get follow-up
evaluation before 3 months; those who are deaf or hard of hearing
should be enrolled in an intervention program by 6 months of age
(Queensland Health ). In addition, children with chronic ear
infections and people who live or work in an environment where
there is a high noise level should receive routine auditory testing.
Women who are considering pregnancy should be advised of the
importance of testing for syphilis and rubella, which can cause
14


hearing impairments in newborns. Periodic vision screening of all
newborns and children is recommended to detect congenital
blindness, strabismus and refractive errors. A child’s visual acuity
develops during early childhood. Children often have 6/6 or ‘20/20’
vision by 6 years of age (Ball et al. 2019 ).
14 Queensland Health (2018). Healthy Hearing Program. Retrieved from
<www.childrens.health.qld.gov.au>.
15 Ball, J. W., Bindler, R. C., Cowen, K. J. & Shaw, M. (2019). Child Health Nursing (3rd ed.).
Upper Saddle River, NJ: Pearson Prentice Hall.
Home care assessment
Sensory-perception alterations
Individual and environment
Self-care abilities: ability to care for self while
adapting to sensory impairment.
Safety: physical safety of the person’s environment
including lighting, noise, access, lack of clutter or
obstructions, use of stairs, assistive devices with
respect to sensory impairment, such as flashing fire
alarms or telephones for hearing impaired.
Level of knowledge: assistive devices available;
ways to maximise use of other senses; local,
regional or national organisations that may provide
15


education, training, support or other assistance,
such as the Australian Braille Authority, Guide Dogs
Australia, Deaf Australia, Vision Australia.
Resources: availability of family, friends;
community assistance such as senior citizen
centres; transportation; religious or cultural
organisations.
Healthy sensory function can be promoted with environmental stimuli
that provide appropriate sensory input. This input should vary and be
neither excessive nor too limited. As many senses as possible
should be stimulated. Various colours, sounds, textures, smells and
body positions can provide various sensations. Nurses can teach
parents to stimulate infants and children and teach family members
to stimulate an older person and others in the home with sensory
deficits. Social activities often help stimulate the mind and the
senses.
Nurses should also teach people at risk of sensory loss how to
prevent or reduce the loss and should teach general health
measures, such as getting regular eye examinations and controlling
chronic diseases such as diabetes (see ‘Patient education
’).
Patient education
Preventing sensory alterations


Preventive/educative strategies
Explain the importance of childhood immunisations to
prevent diseases capable of causing hearing loss (e.g.
rubella, mumps and measles).
Avoid giving infants and toddlers toys with long, pointed
handles and keep pointed instruments (e.g. scissors and
screwdrivers) out of reach. Supervise young children
when they use scissors and ensure they do not run with a
pointed object in their hand.
Avoid allowing children under 2 years old to watch
computer screens, such as tablets and smartphones, and
restrict children 2–5 years old to less than 1 hour of
screen time a day. Excessive screen time can affect
eyesight.
Teach school-age children and adolescents the proper use
of sports equipment (e.g. hockey sticks) and power tools.
Wear protective eyewear when using power tools, riding
motorcycles, spraying chemicals and so on; wear dark
glasses with UV protection to avoid damage from
ultraviolet rays; never look directly into the sun.
Wear ear protectors/plugs when working in an
environment with high noise levels or brief loud impulse
noises (e.g. blasting and farm machinery).
Monitoring strategies


Have regular health examinations.
Have regular eye and hearing examinations as
recommended by the doctor to screen for eye/hearing
problems. For people aged 40 and over, a medical eye
examination is generally recommended every 3 to 5
years, or every 1 to 2 years if there is a family history of
glaucoma.
Therapeutic strategies
Seek early medical attention if signs suggesting vision
impairment arise; for example, failure to react to light,
photophobia, halo effect, reduced eye contact from an
infant, persistent eye redness, discharge or increased
tearing, growths on or near the eye, pupil asymmetry or
other irregularity, or any pain or discomfort.
Seek early medical attention if signs suggesting hearing
impairment arise; for example, earaches or ear infections;
changes in the ability to hear; any experience of dizziness,
vertigo, humming or ringing noises.
Adjusting environmental stimuli
The person functions best when the environment is somewhat
similar to that of the individual’s ordinary daily life. Sometimes


nurses need to take steps to adjust the person’s environment to
prevent either sensory overload or sensory deprivation.
Preventing sensory overload
For people who are at risk of overstimulation, nurses should reduce
the number and type of environmental stimuli. The nurse can
counteract sensory overload by blocking stimuli and by helping the
person organise the stimuli and alter responses to the stimuli.
Dark glasses with UV protection can partially block light rays and a
window shade or curtain can reduce visual stimulation. Earplugs
reduce auditory stimuli, as do soft background music and
earphones. The odour from a draining wound can be minimised by
keeping the dressing dry and clean and applying a liquid deodorant
on a gauze near the wound.
Another method of blocking stimuli is to reduce novelty and surprise,
and provide rest intervals free of interruptions. Sometimes the
number of visitors and the length of visits must be restricted. Also, if
the nurse carries out several nursing measures together, the person
can have a scheduled quiet period before the next activity.
By explaining sounds in the environment, the nurse can help the
person organise them mentally: lift doors opening and closing; the
sound of the call buzzer; a beep from an IV alarm. By associating
the stimuli with a meaning, they are often less confusing and more
easily ignored. People can also learn through practice and feedback


to alter their responses to the stimuli. People can employ relaxation
techniques to reduce anxiety and stress despite continual sensory
stimulation (see Chapter 43
). Box 39.2
 provides nursing
interventions for people with sensory overload.
BO X
39.2 Preventing sensory overload
Minimise unnecessary light, noise and distraction. Provide
dark glasses and earplugs as needed.
Control pain as indicated at the level desired by the
person, on a scale of 0 to 10.
Introduce yourself by name and address the person in
your care by name.
Provide orienting cues, such as clocks, calendars,
equipment and furniture in the room.
Provide a private room.
Limit visitors.
Plan care to allow for uninterrupted periods for rest or
sleep.
Schedule a routine of care so the person knows when and
what to expect (post the schedule for the person
wherever possible).
Speak in a low tone of voice and in an unhurried manner.
Provide new information gradually so that the meaning
can be processed. When providing information, ask the


person to repeat it so that there are no
misunderstandings.
Describe any tests and procedures to the person
beforehand.
Reduce noxious odours. Empty a commode or bedpan
immediately after use, keep wounds clean and covered,
use a room deodoriser when indicated and provide good
ventilation.
Take time to discuss the person’s problems and to correct
misinterpretations.
Assist the person with stress-reducing techniques.
Preventing sensory deprivation
For people who are at risk of sensory deprivation, nurses can
increase environmental stimuli in a number of ways. For example,
newspapers, books, music and television can stimulate the visual
and auditory senses. Providing objects that are pleasant to touch,
such as a pet to stroke, can provide tactile and interactive
stimulation. Clocks that differentiate night from day by colour can
help orient a person to time. The olfactory sense can be stimulated
by the presence of fresh flowers or plants.
Arrangements should also be made for people to visit and talk with
the person regularly. Many church and community groups provide
visitors to people who are confined to their homes or who reside in


nursing homes. Box 39.3
 provides nursing interventions to
prevent sensory deprivation.
BO X
39.3 Preventing sensory deprivation
Encourage the person to use eyeglasses and hearing
aids.
Address the person by name and use touch while
speaking if this is not culturally offensive.
Communicate frequently with the person and maintain
meaningful interactions (e.g. discuss current events).
Provide a telephone, radio and/or TV, clock and calendar.
Provide murals, pictures, sculptures and wall hangings.
Many libraries will lend artwork free of charge or a local
school may provide art projects developed by its students.
Have family and friends bring freshly cut flowers and
plants.
Consider having a resident pet such as fish, a cat or a
bird or make arrangements for pets to visit on a regular
basis.
Include different-textured objects to feel such as a
sheepskin pillow, silk scarf, soft blanket or other inanimate
objects.
Increase tactile stimulation through physical care
measures such as back massages, hair care and foot
soaks.


Encourage social interaction through activity groups or
visits by family and friends.
Encourage the use of crossword puzzles or games to
stimulate mental function.
Encourage environment changes such as a walk through
a shopping centre or, for an immobilised person, sitting
near a window where they can watch outside activities.
Encourage the use of self-stimulation techniques such as
singing, humming, whistling or reciting.
Managing acute sensory impairments
When assisting people who have a sensory impairment, the nurse
needs to (a) encourage the use of sensory aids to support residual
sensory function, (b) promote the use of other senses, (c)
communicate effectively and (d) ensure safety for the person.
Sensory aids
Many sensory aids are available for people who have vision and
hearing impairments. Examples are listed in Box 39.4
. Sensory
aids can be used in the health care setting as well as in the home. In
all situations, the assistance of support people needs to be enlisted
whenever possible to help the person deal with the impairment.


BO X
39.4 Sensory aids for vision and
hearing impairments
Vision
Glasses of the correct prescription, clean and in good
repair.
Adequate room lighting, including night-lights.
Sunglasses or blinds on windows to reduce glare.
Bright contrasting colours in the environment.
Magnifying glass.
Phone with large numbers; teach how to use the ‘speak
aloud’ function on mobile phones.
Clock and wristwatch with large numbers.
Colour code or texture code on stoves, medicine
containers and so on.
Coloured or raised rims on dishes.
Reading material with large print.
Braille or audio books.
Seeing-eye dog.
Hearing


Hearing aid in good order.
Lip reading.
Sign language (Auslan).
Amplified telephones; select the vibrate option on mobile
phones if keeping next to body.
Telecommunication device for the deaf (TDD).
SMS, instant messenger.
Amplified, flashing telephone ringers and doorbells.
Flashing alarm clocks.
Flashing smoke detectors.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Comprehensive Care
The intent of this standard is to ‘ensure that patients receive
comprehensive care—that is, coordinated delivery of the total
health care required or requested by a patient’ (Australian
Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
, p. 38).
16 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved by
ensuring the development of comprehensive
care plans which include screening, assessment
16


and risk identification processes. Cognitive
impairment is a common condition experienced
by many people in a hospital environment and
can be minimised if sensory-overload-reduction
strategies are put in place by the health care
team caring for the person.
Nurses care for individuals who are exposed to
activities and environments that may create
sensory overload; for example, intensive care
units. It is essential for nurses to promote an
environment that allows the person to have at
least 6 hours of uninterrupted sleep by
implementing noise-reduction strategies,
clustering care if possible and collaboratively
working with other members of the health care
team.
Promoting the use of other senses
When one sense is lost, the nurse can teach the person to use other
senses to supplement the loss. This stimulation is similar to that
provided to prevent sensory deprivation, discussed earlier. However,
the type of stimulation needs to be adapted in accordance with the
person’s specific deficit. For example, for the vision-impaired person,
stimulation of hearing, taste, smell and touch can be encouraged. A


radio, CDs of music or books, clocks that chime, music boxes and
wind chimes can be used for auditory stimulation. Diets that include
a variety of flavours, temperatures and textures can be planned to
stimulate the taste buds. Taking sips of water between foods and
eating foods separately can emphasise the taste sensation. Fresh
flowers, scented candles (safely used), room fragrances, brewing
coffee and baking can stimulate the sense of smell. People can also
be encouraged to remember pleasant or familiar odours such as the
perfume of frangipanis. Measures such as providing a hug,
massage, hair brushing, grooming, different textures in clothing and
upholstery fabrics, and pets can be used to stimulate touch
receptors.
Communicating effectively
Communication with people who have sensory impairments should
convey respect, enhance the person’s self-esteem and ensure the
exchange of correct information. A person with a hearing impairment
has to concentrate more than other people and therefore tires more
readily. Fatigue compounded by an illness can further reduce the
person’s ability to hear. A person with a vision impairment is unable
to observe most non-verbal cues during communication and relies
largely on the spoken word and tone of voice. Guidelines for
communicating with people who are vision or hearing impaired are
shown in Box 39.5
.
BO X


39.5 Communicating with people who
have a vision or hearing deficit
Vision impairment
Always announce your presence when entering the
person’s room and identify yourself by name.
Stay in the person’s field of vision if they have a partial
vision loss.
Speak in a warm and pleasant tone of voice. Some people
tend to speak louder than necessary when talking to a
blind person.
Always explain what you are about to do before touching
the person.
Explain the sounds in the environment.
Indicate when the conversation has ended and when you
are leaving the room.
Hearing impairment
Before initiating conversation, convey your presence by
moving to a position where you can be seen or by gently
touching the person.
Decrease background noises (e.g. television) before
speaking.


Talk at a moderate rate and in a normal tone of voice.
Shouting does not make your voice more distinct and in
some instances makes understanding more difficult.
Address the person directly. Do not turn away in the
middle of a remark or story. Make sure the person can
see your face easily and that it is well lit.
Avoid talking when you have something in your mouth,
such as chewing gum. Avoid covering your mouth with
your hand.
Keep your voice at about the same volume throughout
each sentence, without dropping the voice at the end of
each sentence.
Always speak as clearly and accurately as possible.
Articulate consonants with particular care.
Do not ‘overarticulate’; mouthing or overdoing articulation
is just as troublesome as mumbling. Pantomime or write
ideas or use sign language or finger spelling as
appropriate.
Use longer phrases, which tend to be easier to
understand than short ones. For example, ‘Would you like
a drink of water?’ presents much less difficulty than
‘Would you like a drink?’. Word choice is important: ‘Six
eggs’ and ‘sixteen eggs’ may be confused, but ‘half a
dozen’ is clear.
Pronounce every name with care. Make a reference to
the name for easier understanding; for example, ‘Joan,
the girl from the office’ or ‘Myer, the big department store’.


Change to a new subject at a slower rate, making sure
that the person follows the change to the new subject. A
key word or two at the beginning of a new topic is a good
indicator.
Ensuring safety of the person
Nurses must implement safety precautions in health care settings
for people with sensory impairments. Examples of precautions
include keeping the bed in the lowest position and placing the buzzer
within reach.
Impaired vision
For people with vision impairments, nurses need to do the following
in a health care setting:
Orientate the person to the arrangement of room furnishings and
maintain an uncluttered environment.
Keep pathways clear and do not rearrange furniture without
orienting the person. Ensure that housekeeping personnel are
informed about this.
Organise self-care articles within the person’s reach and
orientate them to their location.
Keep the buzzer within easy reach and place the bed in the low
position.


Assist with ambulation by standing at the person’s side, walking
about half a metre ahead and allowing the person to grasp your
arm. Confirm whether the person prefers grasping your arm with
the dominant or non-dominant hand.
Research has established an association between vision impairment
and greater disability in activities of daily living (e.g. bathing,
dressing, eating) and instrumental tasks (e.g. shopping,
housekeeping) (Hochberg et al.
). Studies have also shown that
vision impairment increases the risk of depression among older
adults living in the community (Petch ). Explanations for this
relationship vary. One explanation is that vision loss leads to
increased disability, which leads to depression. Another explanation
states that loss of vision causes fear—a fear of losing one’s
autonomy and becoming dependent on another or others. Vision
loss also affects how a person obtains information (e.g. reading the
newspaper). In addition, reading is often a leisure activity and its
loss can affect a person’s quality of life. It is important for the nurse
to be aware of and assess for signs of depression and intervene as
appropriate if an older adult is experiencing depression as a result of
a vision impairment.
17 Hochberg, C., Maul, E., Chan, E., Van Landingham, S., Ferrucci, L., Friedman, D. &
Ramulu, P. (2012). Association of vision loss in glaucoma and age-related macular
degeneration with IADL disability. Investigative Ophthalmology and Visual Science, 53(6),
3201-3206.
18 Petch, I. (2016). Visual Impairment, Depression and Access to Psychological Therapies.
London: Thomas Pocklington Trust.
17
18


Drug capsule
Travoprost (Travatan)
Person taking medication for
glaucoma
Travoprost belongs to a class of medicines known as
‘prostaglandins’ and decreases pressure in the eye to
treat glaucoma.
Nursing responsibilities
Assess eye for inflammation, exudate and pain.
Note iris colour.
Person and family teaching
Use once daily or as directed—usually one drop in each
eye.
Wash hands first. Shake bottle. Release one drop into the
pocket formed between the eye and eyelid. Do not let the
tip of the dropper touch any part of the eye.
Close eye and do not rub. A slight burning sensation may
be felt immediately after using eye drops. If it persists or
is very uncomfortable see your doctor.


Travoprost may be used with other eye products to lower
intraocular pressure. If using more than one medication,
administer 5 minutes apart.
Inform of risk of darkening of the iris, eyelashes or skin
around the eye.
Do not administer while wearing contact lenses. Remove
contact lens and wait 15 minutes after instilling eye drops
before reinserting contact lens.
Discard the bottle of eye drops 4 weeks after it has been
opened.
Note: prior to administering any medication, review all
aspects with a current drug handbook or other reliable
source.

from <www.nps.org.au/medicine-finder/travatan-eye-drops>.

Research note
Health is more than just the physical!
N. Wali & A. Renzaho (2018). ‘Our riches are our family’, the changing family dynamics and social
capital for new migrant families in Australia. PLoS ONE, 13(12), e0209421.
Australia is home to many migrants. The purpose of this
study was to explore how seven migrant communities, living
in the greater western Sydney area, transitioned to life in
19


Australia. The methodology was an exploratory qualitative
design involving migrants from Afghanistan, Sub-Saharan
African countries, Bangladesh, Burma, Nepal and India.
Purposive sampling was done by country of origin and a total
of 14 focus groups were conducted with 164 participants. The
major themes that emerged from the data were: changing
gender roles and women’s empowerment; sending money
home; culture shock and increased intercultural conflict;
change in lifestyle from collective to individual culture; and
role of extended community in mitigating culture shock. The
theme ‘culture shock and increased intercultural conflict’
referred to people feeling pressured to fit in; this
subsequently led to conflicts within the home and society.
Furthermore, new migrants often had a limited social circle
due to language and cultural barriers and this resulted in
loneliness and social isolation.
Implications Nurses caring for new migrants in our health
care system need to be cognisant of the various challenges
these individuals and families face. Some may be
experiencing sensory overload due to having to learn a new
language, dress differently and interact with people in a new
way, especially females. Alternatively, others may be
experiencing sensory deprivation from loneliness and social
isolation. Informing new migrants of support groups and
culturally appropriate social networks may ease their
loneliness and improve their health.


Impaired hearing
People with hearing impairments who are unable to hear the alarms
of IV pumps and cardiac monitors need to be assessed frequently.
They can be taught to use their visual sense to identify kinks in the
IV tubing or a loose ECG lead and so on. For home safety, people
with impaired hearing need to obtain devices that either amplify
sounds or respond with flashing lights to sounds such as a doorbell
or smoke detector, a baby crying or a burglar alarm. The sounds of
doorbells and alarm clocks may be amplified or changed to a lower
frequency or buzzer-like sound. These devices can be obtained from
hearing aid dealers, telephone companies and electrical stores.
Culturally competent care
Vision impairment and older Australian adults
The most common vision diseases affecting older adults are
age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, cataracts and
diabetic retinopathy. Together with uncorrected refractive
error, they account for nearly 90% of the vision problems in
older Australians (Vision 2020 Australia 2019a).
Approximately 60% of vision-impaired people in Australia
are over 65 years old (Tong et al.
).
20 Tong, B., Duff, G., Mullen, G. & O’Neill, M. (2015). A Snapshot of Blindness
and Low Vision Services in Australia. Sydney: Vision 2020 Australia, National
Disability Services, Australian Blindness Forum.
20


The risk of eye disease triples for each decade over the
age of 40 (Tong et al. 2015).
Limited authoritative data exists on the eye health of older
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people (National
Trachoma Surveillance and Reporting Unit (NTSRU)
).
21 National Trachoma Surveillance and Reporting Unit (NTSRU) (2019).
Australian Trachoma Surveillance Report 2018. Retrieved from
<www1.health.gov.au>.
Trichiasis is prevalent in older Indigenous adults; this is
often as a result of untreated eye infections, such as
trachoma, when they were children (NTSRU 2019).
Diabetic retinopathy is more prevalent among older
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people because of
the high rate of diabetes mellitus type 2 (Vision 2020
Australia 2019b).
The number of Australians with vision problems will
increase in the future due to the ageing of the population;
this will be a global phenomenon. Because of this, the
focus for blindness, low vision and rehabilitation services
are aimed at people over 65 years (Tong et al. 2015).
Older Australians between 70 and 79 years have a 1 in 16
chance of being affected by blindness; between 80 and
89 years, there is a 1 in 10 chance (Tong et al. 2015).
ANATO M Y & PHYSIO LO G Y REVIEW
Glaucoma
21


Glaucoma is a group of diseases of the eye caused by
increased intraocular pressure that can lead to optic nerve
damage and eventual vision loss (see Figure D). Review
Figure A for the normal anatomy of the eye.
A clear liquid, the aqueous humour, circulates inside the front
portion of the eye, nourishing the lens and cornea. To
maintain a normal level of pressure in the eye, the body
constantly produces a small amount of aqueous humour and
an equal amount flows out of the eye through a drainage
system at the junction of the iris and the cornea (Marieb &
Hoehn ). It is at this angle that the fluid passes through a
trabecular meshwork, drains into the Canal of Schlemm and
enters into the bloodstream in the back of the eye.
22 Marieb, E. N. & Hoehn, K. (2019). Human Anatomy and Physiology: Global
Edition (11th ed.). Essex: Pearson Education Limited.
In acute open-angle glaucoma, the anterior chamber angle
remains open but drainage of the aqueous humour through
the Canal of Schlemm is impaired. This causes a slow rise of
the intraocular pressure. The eye’s drainage angle becomes
less efficient as a person ages and the risk of developing
chronic open-angle glaucoma increases. The cause is
unknown.
In acute closed-angle glaucoma, the drainage angle narrows
and closes or becomes blocked by the iris. The intraocular
pressure can rise quickly and cause an acute attack.
22

5. The increasing fluid pressure pushes against which

An important consequence of a decline in hearing as a person ages
is difficulty understanding speech. Factors that influence this
difficulty are the environment, rate of speech and presence of an
accent. Environments that are noisy and reverberant (echoing,
hollow sounds) cause difficulty for older listeners. Older adults with a
hearing loss have difficulty understanding fast speech. A person who
speaks with an accent can also affect speech understanding by the
older person. People who have English as their second language
may vary their pronunciation of syllables and/or words, making it
challenging for the older adult.
Impaired olfactory sense
People with an impaired sense of smell need to be taught about the
dangers of cleaning with chemicals such as ammonia. Because a
gas leak can go undetected, it is important to keep gas stoves and
heaters in good working order in any homes of people ‘at risk’.
Strong chemicals such as ammonia used in confined spaces such
as a bathroom may affect the person before they are smelled. Food
poisoning is a concern with people who have difficulty detecting
spoiled meat, fish or dairy products. These people need to carefully


inspect food for freshness (check its colour and texture) and check
expiration dates on food packages.
Research note
Caring for children with autism
K. Churruca, L. Ellis, J. Long, C. Pomare, L. Wiles, G. Arnolda, . . . J. Braithwaite
. The quality of care
for Australian children with autism spectrum disorders. Journal of Autism and Developmental
Disorders, 49(3). Doi: 10.1007/s10803-019-04195-7.
24 Churruca, K., Ellis, L., Long, J., Pomare, C., Wiles, L., Arnolda, G., . . . Braithwaite, J. (2019). The
quality of care for Australian children with autism spectrum disorders. Journal of Autism and
Developmental Disorders, 49(3). Doi: 10.1007/s10803-019-04195-7.
The purpose of this study was to determine the quality of
care provided to children diagnosed with autism spectrum
disorders (ASD) in Australia and to highlight the need for
improved standardised diagnostic criteria. The study involved
retrospectively auditing the charts of 228 children diagnosed
with ASD during the years 2012 and 2013 and assessing
them using a validated set of clinical indicators. The clinical
indicators being assessed were grouped under the categories
of assessment, diagnosis and management. The findings of
the study suggested that Australian children with ASD
received good-quality care from general practitioners and
paediatricians and that the indicators were largely adhered to.
The study also found that potential areas for improvement
could include increasing adherence to diagnosis indicators
24


and improving care integration in the context of clinical
documentation by different care providers.
Implications It is likely that a large percentage of nurses will
care for both children and adults diagnosed with ASD in the
clinical environment due to its high prevalence. It is important
to recognise that children with ASD may present in various
ways, and that they can potentially overreact or underreact to
sensory stimulus such as sound, touch, sight, taste and
smell. The ability to recognise certain sensory reactions may
contribute to the early diagnosis of ASD, which has been
shown to improve the quality of care provided.
Impaired tactile sense
People with an impaired sense of touch may not be aware of hot
temperatures, which can cause burns, or pressure on bony
prominences, which can produce pressure injuries. People with
decreased sensation to temperature should have the temperature
adjusted on their hot water system and test water temperature with
a thermometer before showering or bathing. People with decreased
sensation to pressure must change their position frequently.
The confused person
Confusion can occur in people of all ages but it is most commonly
seen in older people. Confusion often presents with subtle


symptoms, but an attempt should be made to differentiate between
acute confusion (delirium)
 and chronic confusion (dementia).
Delirium is often called acute confusion; it has an abrupt onset and a
cause which, when treated, reverses the confusion. Dementia is
often called chronic confusion with symptoms that are gradual and
irreversible (e.g. Alzheimer’s disease). It is important to differentiate
between the two (see Table 39.2
).
Table 39.2 Differentiating between delirium and dementia
Acute confusion or delirium is a common and serious problem in
older hospitalised adults. There are numerous reasons for the older
adult being at risk of delirium when hospitalised. They often have
other chronic medical problems (e.g. dementia, chronic obstructive
pulmonary disease, hypertension, stroke) that place them at risk.
Many older people take numerous medications, with anticholinergics,
narcotics and sedatives often increasing the risk of delirium. Under-
treating pain can also contribute to the risk. Many older adults have
a vision or hearing loss. All these risks, plus the unfamiliar
surroundings and routine of a hospital, possible sleep deprivation,
stress and sensory overload, compound the older adult’s risk of
developing delirium. People who are confused often know something
is wrong and want help. Box 39.6
 lists nursing interventions to
help promote a therapeutic environment for the person with acute
confusion/delirium (see also Figure 39.3
).
BO X


39.6 Promoting a therapeutic
environment for a person with acute
confusion/delirium
Wear a readable ID badge.
Address the person by name and introduce yourself
frequently: ‘Good morning, Mr Richards. I am Sue Smith.
I will be your nurse today.’
Identify time and place as indicated: ‘Today is 5 December
and it is 8 o’clock in the morning.’
Ask the person ‘Where are you?’ and orientate them to
place (e.g. hospital ward) if indicated.
Place a calendar and clock in the person’s room. Mark
holidays with ribbons, pins or other means.
Speak clearly and calmly, allowing time for your words to
be processed and for the person to give a response.
Encourage family to visit frequently, except if this activity
causes the person to become hyperactive.
Provide clear, concise explanations of each treatment
procedure or task.
Eliminate unnecessary noise.
Reinforce reality by interpreting unfamiliar sounds, sights
and smells; correct any misconceptions of events or
situations.
Schedule activities (e.g. meals, bath, activity and rest
periods, treatments) at the same time each day to provide


a sense of security. If possible, assign the same
caregivers.
Provide adequate sleep.
Keep eye glasses and hearing aid within reach.
Ensure adequate pain management.
Keep familiar items in the person’s environment (e.g.
photographs) and keep the environment uncluttered. A
disorganised, cluttered environment increases confusion.
Keep room well lit during waking hours.
Figure 39.3


Promoting orientation to time and date is essential for people who
are confused or have memory loss.

5 Clinical reasoning
Nursing students must develop the skills to
notice deviations from normal and subtle
changes in a patient’s condition that signal the
need for further investigation, immediate clinical
review or rapid response (Levett-Jones et al.
).
