T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Clinical consideration
Sleep deprivation is known to cause both
adverse physiological and psychological effects,
such as decreased immune function and
cardiovascular health, and endocrine instability
as well as neurocognitive changes (Delaney ;
Wang & Greenberg ). Nurses are ideally
placed to undertake interventions to promote an
environment conducive to sleeping, and thereby
facilitating recovery for the person.
25
26
27


26 Delaney, L. (2016). The role of sleep in patient recovery.
Australian Nursing and Midwifery Journal, 23(7), 26–29.
27 Wang, J. & Greenberg, H. (2013). Sleep and the ICU. Open
Critical Care Medical Journal, 6(S1: M6), 80–87.
Evaluating
Using the measurable desired outcomes developed during the
planning stage as a guide, the nurse collects data needed to judge
whether goals and outcomes have been achieved for the person.
Examples of outcomes and related indicators are shown in the
earlier ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and interventions’
and in the following ‘Nursing care plan’. If outcomes are not
achieved, the nurse needs to explore the reasons for this, together
with the person and significant others, before modifying the care
plan.
Lifespan considerations
Sensory perception
Children


Newborns should be screened for hearing loss prior to
hospital discharge. Universal screening of all newborns is
recommended in Australia and New Zealand, with most areas
now offering established screening programs. If a hearing
loss is detected early, treatment can begin early and
complications such as speech loss can be prevented. If an
infant is found to have a hearing loss, the aim is to
commence treatment before 6 months of age. Children with a
severe hearing impairment can be fitted with cochlear
implants by 12 months of age (Queensland Health 2018).
Older adults
Normal changes of ageing often result in varying degrees of
impairments in sensory perception of the senses—hearing,
vision, smell, taste and touch. Diseases and conditions that
are more common in older adults and which also alter
sensory perception are diabetes, strokes and neurological
disorders such as Parkinson’s disease. Nursing interventions
need to be very specific and individualised and may be
directed to either increase or decrease sensory stimuli.
The goals of nursing care should be focused on maintaining
safety and communication with people who have these
impairments. Individuals with dementia may have problems
that fit more appropriately under ‘altered thought processes’
but the goals should be similar—to maximise their potential,
maintain their quality of life and dignity and at the same time
be aware of safety and communication issues.


Culturally competent care
Traditional Chinese medicine
Australia is comprised of different cultures which influence
our traditional beliefs about health care. According to the
2016 Census data (Australian Bureau of Statistics ),
Australia is home to approximately 1.2 million people of
Chinese ancestry.
28 Australian Bureau of Statistics (2018). ABS Chinese New Year Insights.
Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) is based on the belief
that there are two main forces within the body: the yang
(positive, hot, dry, light) and the yin (negative, wet, cold,
heavy). These two forces need to be in equilibrium in order
for there to be optimal health. TCM practitioners believe that
illness is present when there is an imbalance between these
two forces or energies. To re-establish the balance, a number
of TCM techniques and herbal remedies can be used. These
include diet, exercise, acupressure, acupuncture, meditation
and herbal therapies.
Among the Chinese people who practise traditional beliefs,
confusion and memory impairment of an older adult may be
treated with herbal therapies such as Ginkgo biloba, sage,
lemon balm and ginseng. Ginkgo biloba is native to China and
many people, especially the older population, believe that it
28


improves mental performance and alertness and prevents
cognitive impairment.
People living in Australia may seek out TCM alongside
Western medicine. Health care professionals need to honour
traditional beliefs while providing Western medical care.
There is a Chinese Medicine Board of Australia which
regulates Chinese medicine practitioners.
Source: Based on A. Franke et al.
. The use of Ginkgo biloba in healthy elderly. Age, 36(1), 435–
444.
29 Franke, A., Heinrich, I., Lieb, K. & Fellgiebel, A. (2014). The use of Ginkgo biloba in healthy elderly.
Age, 36(1), 435–444. Doi: 10.1007/s11357-013-9550-y.

Mrs Schaffert is a 51-year-old woman who is being cared for
in the intensive care unit following a motor vehicle accident in
which she suffered extensive traumatic injuries. Mrs Schaffert
is connected to several monitoring devices, is intubated and
ventilated to assist her with breathing and is receiving various
pain and other medications.
1. Identify factors that place Mrs Schaffert at risk of the
development of sensory deprivation or overload.
29


2. What assessment findings would alert you to Mrs
Schaffert experiencing sensory overload as opposed
to sensory deprivation?
3. How can you intervene to help Mrs Schaffert during
this stressful event?
4. How might the care of a person in the home setting
differ from the care of Mrs Schaffert who is receiving
care in an intensive care unit?
CO NCEPT M AP
Sensory-perception alteration


Chapter 39 Review


Chapter highlights
The sensory experience consists of two components: sensory
reception and sensory perception.
Sensory stimuli can be either external or internal. Visual,
auditory, olfactory, tactile and gustatory stimuli orient a person to
the external environment. Kinaesthetic and visceral stimuli orient
the person to the internal environment. Kinaesthetic stimuli make
the person aware of the position and movement of body parts.
Sensory perception involves the awareness and interpretation of
stimuli into meaningful information. This process occurs in the
cerebral cortex.
The reticular activating system (RAS), with its many ascending
and descending connections to other areas of the brain, monitors
and regulates incoming stimuli. The RAS maintains, enhances or
inhibits cortical arousal.
The normal, alert person can assimilate many kinds of
information at one time and respond appropriately through
thought and action.
Sensory deprivation occurs when a person receives decreased
sensory input or monotonous or meaningless sensory input.
Sensory overload occurs when a person experiences excessive
sensory input and is unable to process or manage the stimuli.
The person feels overwhelmed and not in control.
Responses to both sensory deprivation and sensory overload
include perceptual changes (e.g. mild distortions or
hallucinations), cognitive changes (e.g. decreased concentration


and problem-solving ability) and affective changes (e.g. apathy,
anxiety, anger, depression and rapid mood swings).
People at risk of sensory deprivation include: (a) those who are
confined to home or are institutionalised; (b) those on bed rest or
isolation precautions; (c) those with sensory deficits; (d) those
who come from a different culture; (e) those with certain affective
disorders or alterations of the nervous system; and (f) those on
certain medications that affect the central nervous system.
People at risk of sensory overload include: (a) those in pain; (b)
those in intensive care units; (c) those with invasive and
uncomfortable monitoring or treatment equipment; and (d) those
with alterations of the nervous system.
Factors affecting sensory stimulation include developmental
stage, culture, stress, medications, illness, and lifestyle and
personality.
Assessment for sensory-perception alterations includes: (a) a
nursing history to identify sensory impairments; (b) physical
examination; (c) mental status; (d) identification of people at risk;
(e) immediate environment; and (f) presence of clinical signs of
sensory deprivation or overload.
Nursing diagnoses related to a person’s sensory-perception
impairments are: Sensory perception alterations—visual,
auditory, gustatory, olfactory, tactile, kinaesthetic; Acute
confusion; Chronic confusion; Impaired memory; Social isolation;
Impaired verbal communication; Risk of impaired skin integrity;
Unable to perform self-care activities; Unable to maintain a safe
home environment; and Risk of injury.


Goals for people with sensory-perception alterations include: (a)
maintaining or promoting the function of existing senses; (b)
maintaining or improving communication; (c) preventing injury;
(d) avoiding sensory deprivation or overload; (e) reducing social
isolation; and (f) maintaining or restoring ability to function safely
in the environment and to perform self-care.
Interventions to prevent or modify sensory deprivation, sensory
overload and sensory impairments include promoting healthy
sensory function, adjusting environmental stimuli and managing
sensory impairments.
People with sensory impairments need instruction about sensory
aids available to support residual sensory function, ways to
promote the use of other senses and methods to ensure safety
from bodily harm.
Nurses and support people need to devise and implement
effective communication mechanisms for people who have vision
and hearing impairments.
People with acute confusion/delirium need care that is directed to
promoting their orientation to time, place, person and situation.

Self-concept  is one’s mental image of
oneself. A positive self-concept is essential to a
person’s mental and physical health. Individuals
with a positive self-concept are better able to
develop and maintain interpersonal relationships
and resist psychological and physical illness. An
individual possessing a strong self-concept
should be better able to accept or adapt to
changes that may occur over the lifespan. How
one views oneself affects one’s interaction with
others.
Nurses have a responsibility to assess people
for a negative self-concept and to identify the
possible causes in order to help them develop a
more positive view of themselves. Individuals
who have a poor self-concept may express
feelings of worthlessness, self-dislike or even
self-hatred. They may feel sad or hopeless and


may state they lack energy to perform even the
simplest of tasks.


Self-concept
Self-concept involves all of the self-perceptions—appearance,
values and beliefs—that influence behaviour and are referred to
when using the words I or me. Self-concept is a complex idea that
influences the following:
how one thinks, talks and acts
how one sees and treats another person
choices one makes
the ability to give and receive love
the ability to take action and to change things
the ability to cope with life’s stressors.
There are four dimensions of self-concept:
1. Self-knowledge: the knowledge that one has about oneself,
including insights into one’s abilities, nature and limitations.
2. Self-expectation: what one expects of oneself; may be a
realistic or unrealistic expectation.
3. Social self: how a person is perceived by others and society.
4. Social evaluation: the appraisal of oneself in relation to
others, events or situations.
People who value ‘how I perceive me’ above ‘how others perceive
me’ can be termed me-centred. They try hard to live up to their own


expectations and compete only with themselves, not others. In
contrast, strongly other-centred people have a high need for
approval from others and try hard to live up to the expectations of
others, comparing, competing and evaluating themselves in relation
to others. They tend not to deal with their personal shortcomings,
are unable to assert themselves and fear disapproval. A positive
self-concept, therefore, is me-centred and is formed with minimal
reference to others’ opinions.
Assessing and promoting a positive self-concept is not limited to the
person seeking health care. A nurse’s own self- concept is also
important. Nurses who understand the different dimensions of
themselves and work towards improving their emotional
intelligence (EI or EQ)
 are better able to understand the needs,
desires, feelings and conflicts of the person seeking health care. EQ
is defined as incorporating five components: self-awareness, self-
regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills (see Figure 40.1
)
(Goleman ). Possessing EQ is a paramount attribute of a nurse as it
enables the nurse to understand the emotions of others while self-
regulating their own feelings (Shahbazi et al. ). Using these
components, the nurse is better equipped to create a therapeutic
relationship with the person while maintaining professional
boundaries (Al-Metyazidy, El-Ghafar & Weheida ). Having high
levels of EQ also assists the nurse in dealing with stressful events
and aids in preventing burnout (Beydler ).

training on emotional intelligence of nursing students: An experimental study. Journal of

3 Al-Metyazidy, H. A., El-Ghafar, S. & Weheida, S. M. (2019). The effect of emotional

Figure 40.1


Emotional intelligence consists of five components.
Self-awareness
 refers to the relationship between your own
perception of yourself and others’ perceptions of you. Self-


awareness is an essential attribute of the nurse as it assists the
nurse to develop rapport with the people they care for and work
with. It also encourages the nurse to identify potential stressors that
may impede their practice (Rasheed, Younas & Sundus ). Becoming
more self-aware is a process that requires time and energy and is
never complete. Heightened self-awareness is developed by the
nurse reflecting on their own beliefs, attitudes, motivations,
strengths and limitations to foster behavioural and affective change
(Rasheed ). In addition to using individual reflective exercises, the
nurse gains insight into the self through working with other nurses
who serve as mentors and by acting on the feedback obtained
during regular performance reviews.
5 Rasheed, S. P., Younas, A. & Sundus, A. (2019). Self-awareness in nursing: A scoping
review. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(5–6), 762–774. Doi: 10.1111/jocn.14708.
6 Rasheed, S. P. (2015). Self-awareness as a therapeutic tool for nurse/client relationship.
International Journal of Caring Sciences, 8(1), 211–216. Retrieved from <https://search-
proquest-com.elibrary.jcu.edu.au>.
Once the nurse has developed a clear understanding and
awareness of the self, the nurse can respect others and avoid
projecting their own beliefs onto them. While in the caregiver role,
the self-aware nurse is able to suspend judgment and focus on the
needs of the person, even if they differ from those of the nurse.
When conflicts arise, the nurse can analyse their reactions through
introspection and by asking:
5
6


‘What is there in me that produces this kind of reaction in the
person?’
‘Why do I react this way (fear, anger, anxiety, annoyance,
worry)?’
‘Can I change the way I respond to this situation to affect the
person’s reaction in a helpful way?’.


Formation of self-concept
A person is not born with a self-concept; rather, it develops as a
result of social interactions with others. Chapter 21
 discusses the
development of self-concept, including Erikson’s stages of
development, Piaget’s cognitive developmental stages and
Havighurst’s developmental tasks.
According to Erikson , throughout life people face developmental
tasks associated with eight psychosocial stages that provide a
theoretical framework. The success with which a person copes with
these developmental tasks largely determines the development of
self-concept. Difficulty in coping results in self-concept problems at
the time and often later in life. Table 40.1
 lists examples of
behaviours indicating successful and unsuccessful resolution of
these developmental tasks.
7 Erikson, E. H. (1963). Childhood and Society (2nd ed.). New York: Norton.
Table 40.1 Examples of behaviours associated with Erikson’s
stages of psychosocial development
There are three broad steps in the development of one’s self-
concept:
7


1. The infant learns that the physical self is separate and
different from the environment.
2. The child internalises others’ attitudes towards self.
3. The child and adult internalise the standards of society.
The term global self
 refers to the collective beliefs and images
one holds about oneself. It is the most complete description that
individuals can give of themselves at any one time. It is also a
person’s frame of reference for experiencing and viewing the world.
Some of these beliefs and images represent statements of fact; for
example, ‘I am a woman’, ‘I am a father’, ‘I am short’. Others refer
to less tangible aspects of the self; for instance, ‘I am competent’, ‘I
am shy’.
Each separate image and belief one holds about oneself has a
bearing on self-concept. However, self-concept is not simply a sum
of its parts. The various images and beliefs people hold about
themselves are not given equal weight and prominence. Each
person’s self-concept is like a piece of art. At the centre of the art
are the beliefs and images that are most vital to the person’s
identity. They constitute core self-concept
; for example, ‘I am
very smart/of average intelligence’; ‘I am single/in a relationship’.
Images and beliefs that are less important to the person are on the
periphery. For example, ‘I am left-/right-handed’; ‘I am athletic/non-
athletic’.
People are thought to base their self-concept on how they perceive
and evaluate themselves in these areas:


vocational performance
intellectual functioning
personal appearance and physical attractiveness
sexual attractiveness and performance
being liked by others
ability to cope with and resolve problems
independence
particular talents.
Self-concept in these areas also extends to the choices people
make and perceptions they have about their health. People with a
strong positive self-concept about their appearance are likely to
value healthy behaviours and take actions to maintain the health of
their skin, hair and body tone, for example. People with negative
self-concepts may be less proactive about health promotion and
illness-prevention activities.
Maintaining and evaluating one’s self-concept is an ongoing process.
Events or situations may change the level of self- concept over time.
Having a basic self-concept includes how we see ourselves and how
we are seen by others. There is also the ideal self
, which is how
we should be or would prefer to be. The ideal self is the individual’s
perception of how one should behave based on certain personal
standards, aspirations, goals and values. Sometimes this ideal self is
realistic; sometimes it is not. When the perceived self is close to
ideal self, people do not wish to be much different from what they
believe they already are. A discrepancy between ideal self and


perceived self can be an incentive to self-improvement. However,
when the discrepancy is great, low self-esteem can result.
Nurses, like other adults, view themselves based on both internal
and external inputs acquired over many years. The ability to
appraise one’s own strengths, the desire to follow in the steps of role
models and the feedback received from colleagues and people
receiving care from the nurse are some of the influences on the
nurse’s self-concept.


Components of self-concept
There are four components of self-concept: personal identity, body
image, role performance and self-esteem (see Figure 40.2
).
Figure 40.2


A person’s self-concept is influenced by four components.


Personal identity
Personal identity
 is the conscious sense of individuality and
uniqueness that is continually evolving throughout life. People often
view their identity in terms of name, gender, age, race, ethnicity,
culture, occupation, roles, talents and other situational
characteristics (e.g. marital status and education).
Personal identity also includes one’s beliefs, values, personality and
character. For instance, is the person outgoing, friendly, reserved,
generous or selfish? Personal identity therefore encompasses both
the tangible and the factual, such as name and gender, and the
intangible, such as values and beliefs. Identity is what distinguishes
self from others.
A person with a strong sense of identity has integrated body image,
role performance and self-esteem into a complete self-concept. This
sense of identity provides a person with a feeling of continuity and a
unity of personality. Furthermore, the individual sees themself as a
unique person.
Body image
The image of physical self, or body image
, is how a person
perceives the size, appearance and functioning of the body and its
parts. Body image has both cognitive and affective aspects. The


cognitive is the knowledge of the material body; the affective
includes the sensations of the body, such as pain, pleasure, fatigue
and physical movement. Body image is the sum of these attitudes,
conscious and unconscious, that a person has towards their body.
Body image includes clothing, make-up, hairstyle, jewellery and
other things intimately connected to the person (see Figure 40.3
).
It also includes body prostheses, such as artificial limbs and
dentures, as well as aids or devices required for functioning, such as
wheelchairs, walking sticks and glasses. Past as well as present
perceptions and how the body has evolved over time are all part of
one’s body image.
Figure 40.3


Body image is the sum of a person’s conscious and unconscious
attitudes about their body.
Source: Photographee.eu. Shutterstock.
A person’s body image develops partly from others’ attitudes and
responses to that person’s body and partly from the individual’s own


exploration of the body. For example, body image develops in
infancy as parents or caregivers respond to the child with smiles and
touching, and as the child explores its own body sensations during
breastfeeding, thumb sucking and bathing. Cultural and societal
factors are widely accepted influential factors of a person’s body
image. This is of particular concern during adolescence when
internal views of oneself are strongly influenced by external
influences, such as media and social media images portraying
unrealistic thin body shapes as the ‘ideal’, as well as peer pressure
and evaluation. Increased awareness and internalisation of the ‘thin
ideal’ can negatively influence body image and satisfaction levels
(Kenny et al. ; Cribb & Haase ). This can lead to increased anxiety
and lower self-esteem (Yu & Jung ). In contrast, if a person’s body
image closely resembles their perceived body ideal, the individual is
more likely to think positively about the physical and non-physical
components of the self.
8 Kenny, U., O’Malley-Keighran, M., Molcho, M. & Kelly, C. (2017). Peer influences on
adolescent body image: Friends or foes? Journal of Adolescent Research, 32(6), 768–799.
Doi: 10.1177/0743558416665478.
9 Cribb, V. & Haase, A. (2016). Girls feeling good at school: School gender environment,
internalization and awareness of socio-cultural attitudes associations with self-esteem in
adolescent girls. Journal of Adolescence, 46, 107–114. Doi:
10.1016/j.adolescence.2015.10.019.
10 Yu, U. & Jung, J. (2018). Effects of self-discrepancy and self-schema on young women’s
body image and self-esteem after media image exposure. Family and Consumer Sciences
Research Journal, 47(2), 142–160. Doi: 10.1111/fcsr.12284.
8
9
10


Another aspect of body image is understanding that different parts
of the body have different values for different people. For example,
large breasts may be highly important to one woman and
unimportant to another, or the occurrence of grey hair may be
traumatic to one person and barely noticed by another.
The individual who has a body image disturbance may hide or not
look at or touch a body part that is significantly changed in structure
by illness or trauma. Some individuals may also express feelings of
helplessness, hopelessness, powerlessness and vulnerability and
may exhibit self-destructive behaviour such as over- or under-eating
or self-harm.
Role performance
Throughout life people undergo numerous role changes. A role
 is
a set of expectations about how the person occupying a specific
position behaves. Role performance
 relates what a person in a
particular role does to the behaviours expected of that role. Role
mastery
 means that the person’s behaviours meet social
expectations. Expectations, or standards of behaviour of a role, are
set by society, a cultural group or a smaller group to which a person
belongs. Each person usually has several roles. For example, a 40-
year-old man may be a partner, parent, brother, son, employee,
friend and volunteer. Some roles are assumed for only limited
periods, such as being a health care recipient or student. Role
development
 involves socialisation into a particular role. For


example, nursing students are socialised into nursing through
exposure to a variety of learning experiences such as lectures,
tutorials, simulation and clinical experience placements.
To act appropriately, people need to know who they are in relation to
others and what society expects of the positions they hold. Role
ambiguity
 occurs when expectations are unclear and people do
not know what to do or how to do it and are unable to predict the
reactions of others to their behaviour. Failure to master a role
creates frustration and feelings of inadequacy, often with consequent
lowered self-esteem.
Clinical consideration
Having a clear understanding of each member’s
role in the multidisciplinary team reduces role
ambiguity and can improve health care delivery.
Self-concept is also affected by role strain and role conflicts. People
undergoing role strain
 are frustrated because they feel or are
made to feel inadequate or unsuited to a role. Role strain can be
associated with gender role stereotypes. For example, women in
occupations traditionally held by men might be treated as having
less knowledge and competence than men in the same roles.


Role conflicts
 arise from opposing or incompatible expectations.
In an interpersonal conflict, people have different expectations about
a particular role. For example, a grandparent may have different
expectations from the mother about how she should care for her
children. In an inter-role conflict, one person’s or group’s role
expectations differ from the expectations of another person or
group. For example, a woman who has little flexibility in her full-time
job schedule has a role conflict if her husband expects her to handle
all child care problems. In a person–role conflict, role expectations
violate the beliefs or values of the role occupant. For example, a
nurse in a family planning clinic may be expected to advise couples
about birth control methods that are inconsistent with the nurse’s
belief system regarding prevention or management of unwanted
pregnancy. Role conflict can lead to tension, a decrease in self-
esteem and embarrassment if needs for achievement,
independence and recognition are unmet.
Self-esteem
Self-esteem
 is one’s judgment of one’s own worth; that is, how
one’s standards and performances compare with others and with
one’s ideal self. If a person’s self-esteem does not match the ideal
self, low self-concept results.
There are two types of self-esteem: global and specific. Global self-
esteem
 is how much one likes oneself as a whole. Specific self-
esteem
 is how much one approves of a certain part of oneself.


Global self-esteem is influenced by specific self- esteem. For
example, if a man values his looks, how he looks will strongly affect
his global self-esteem. By contrast, if a man places little value on his
cooking skills, how well or badly he cooks will have little influence on
his global self-esteem.
Self-esteem is derived from self and others. In infancy, self-esteem
is related to the caregiver’s evaluations and acceptances. Later, the
child’s self-esteem is affected by competition with others. As an
adult, a person who has high self-esteem has feelings of
significance, of competence, of the ability to cope with life and of
control over one’s destiny.
The foundation for self-esteem is established during early life
experiences, usually within the family structure. However, an adult’s
level of overall self-esteem may change markedly from day to day
and moment to moment. Severe stress—for example, stress related
to prolonged illness or unemployment—can substantially lower a
person’s self-esteem. In health care, people who believe that their
condition is viewed negatively by society may have lower self-
esteem (Kobosko et al.
; Schibalski et al.
). People frequently
focus on their negative aspects and spend less time on their positive
aspects. It is important that both strengths and weaknesses be
identified.

& Skarzynski, H. (2018). Self-esteem in the deaf who have become cochlear implant users
as adults. PloS ONE, 13(9), e0203680–e0203680. Doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0203680.

12


12 Schibalski, J. V., Müller, M., Ajdacic-Gross, V., ... Rüsch, N. (2017). Stigma-related stress,
shame and avoidant coping reactions among members of the general population with elevated
symptom levels. Comprehensive Psychiatry, 74, 224–230. Doi:
10.1016/j.comppsych.2017.02.001.


Factors that affect self-concept
Many factors affect a person’s self-concept. Major factors are stage
of development, family and culture, stressors, resources, history of
success and failure, and illness.
Stage of development
As an individual develops, the conditions that affect the self-concept
change. For example, an infant requires a supportive, caring
environment, while a child requires freedom to explore and learn.
Older adults’ self-concept is based on their experiences in
progressing through life’s stages.
Family and culture
A young child’s values are largely influenced by the family and
culture. In contrast, an adolescent’s self-concept is challenged and
modified due to biological and cognitive development as well as
social interactions (Tatlow-Golden & Guerin ). During late
adolescence, the teenager is faced with multiple societal and
relational transitions including moving from secondary schooling to
tertiary education or work and moving out of the family home to
13


independent living (Crocetti et al.
). These changes can result in the
teenager experiencing a confused sense of self (Crocetti et al.
2016). This can be challenging for the teenager and parents alike
due to the change in role expectations (see Figure 40.4
). For
example, a teenager may realise that his parents expect he will not
drink alcohol and that he will attend religious services each Saturday
evening. At the same time, his peers drink beer and encourage him
to spend Saturday evenings with them.
13 Tatlow-Golden, M. & Guerin, S. (2017). Who I am: The meaning of early adolescents’ most
valued activities and relationships, and implications for self-concept research. The Journal of
Early Adolescence, 37(2), 236–266. Doi: 10.1177/0272431615599064.
14 Crocetti, E., Rubini, M., Branje, S., Koot, H. M. & Meeus, W. (2016). Self-concept clarity in
adolescents and parents: A six-wave longitudinal and multi-informant study on development
and intergenerational transmission. Journal of Personality, 84(5), 580–593. Doi:
10.1111/jopy.12181.

14


A teenager is often pulled in opposite directions by family and peer
expectations.

Stressors
Stressors can strengthen the self-concept as an individual copes
successfully with problems. On the other hand, overwhelming
stressors can cause maladaptive responses including substance
abuse, withdrawal and anxiety. The ability of a person to handle
stressors will largely depend on personal resources.
Real-world practice
Some tips on how to stay positive and develop in your
role as a newly graduated Registered Nurse without
being overwhelmed by the responsibility of caring for
others follow:
Keep realistic expectations of yourself—you will not
know everything and you never will! Colleagues will
appreciate this insight and are more likely to share
their knowledge and skills. Overconfidence can lead
to unsafe practice.
There are no silly questions! Don’t be afraid to
clarify or ask questions (or consult policy and
procedures) until you are satisfied that the person’s
safety and best interests are being served.


Be aware of your own limitations. Every nurse is
learning something regardless of how experienced
they are, so it is important to be honest with your
colleagues when you are unsure about a condition
and/or how to perform a procedure.
It is important to develop prioritisation skills and
learn to delegate or hand over tasks when needed
because nursing is an unpredictable and dynamic
role.
When beginning practice, graduate nurses are at
risk of letting the immense responsibility
overburden them. Make sure you take your breaks
and leave work on time.
Develop a ritual to help yourself turn off from work
when your shift is over (shower and change out of
uniform).
Your first year of practice is a huge learning curve. You
get to choose the kind of nurse you want to be. Keep
the person as the central point of care. Challenge
yourself and seek out learning opportunities. You will
discover that what you once saw as a daunting
responsibility of caring for another has transformed to
becoming a rewarding and honoured responsibility.
—Elspeth Wood RN, BHlthScN, MNSt, GCert EdTT, GCRM Townsville, Queensland


Resources
An individual’s resources are internal and external. Examples of
internal resources include confidence and values, whereas external
resources include support network, sufficient finances and
organisations. Generally, the greater the number of resources a
person has and uses, the more positive the effect on the self-
concept.
Research note
Understanding the potential impact of disability on self-
concept and body image
C. N. Shpigelman & N. HaGani
. The impact of disability type and visibility on self-concept and body
image: Implications for mental health nursing. Journal of Psychiatric and Mental Health Nursing,
26(3–4), 77–86. Doi: 10.1111/jpm.12513.
15 Shpigelman, C. N. &. HaGani, N. (2019). The impact of disability type and visibility on self-concept
and body image: Implications for mental health nursing. Journal of Psychiatric and Mental Health
Nursing, 26(3–4), 77–86. Doi: 10.1111/jpm.12513.
Researchers in this study compared how self-concept and
body image were perceived by individuals who were living
with a visible disability (i.e. a physical impairment) and those
who had less visible disabilities (i.e. a mental illness). A cross-
sectional survey was deployed to 119 participants who
voluntarily identified as having either a visible
 or
15
(n = 62)


invisible disability
. The results of the survey were
then analysed using inferential statistics. Poorer body image
and lower levels of self-concept were found in the participants
who reported an invisible disability. In contrast, participants
who reported a visible disability were found to have higher
levels of self-concept and better body image. The degree of
disability was also associated with the level of self-concept,
with participants who reported mild or moderate levels of
disability being more likely to indicate they had a positive self-
concept.
Implications This study highlights the importance of nurses
being aware of the impacts a physical or psychiatric disability
can have on an individual’s body image and self-concept. By
having a heightened awareness of the potential stigma
people living with invisible disabilities may face, the nurse can
employ interventions to limit this risk and enhance the
development of a more positive self-concept.
History of success and failure
Usually people who have a history of failures come to see
themselves as ‘failures’, whereas people with a history of successes
will have a more positive self-concept. Likewise, people with a
positive self-concept tend to find contentment in their level of
(n = 57)


success, while a negative self-concept can lead to viewing one’s life
situation as negative.
Illness, trauma and disability
Illness, trauma and disability can also affect an individual’s self-
concept. People respond to stressors such as illness or trauma and
alterations in function related to ageing or disability in a variety of
ways. Acceptance, denial, withdrawal and depression are common
reactions. For example, a woman who has a mastectomy may see
herself as less attractive and the loss may affect how she acts and
values herself. Nonetheless, it is important to note that the same
woman may choose to view the mastectomy as a life-saving
operation and not let the loss of her breast tissue define who she is
as a person.
It is sometimes difficult to determine the direction of the relationship
between self-concept and health. Some research has shown that
people with a positive self-concept may enhance their health
because they are more likely to follow the health care plan. Other
research shows that health conditions, including psychosocial
situations such as loss and grieving, have an impact on self-concept
(Thomas et al.
; Ward Khan et al.
; Türk & Yilmaz
). Thus, self-
concept and health- related behaviours are intertwined.

related self-concept questionnaire. American Journal of Health Promotion, 33(3), 452–456.

Nursing management
Assessing
A thorough assessment includes a psychosocial assessment of the
person and their family or support person because this provides
clues to actual or potential problems. The nurse assessing self-
concept focuses on the four components: (1) personal identity; (2)
body image; (3) role performance; and (4) self-esteem.
Before conducting a psychosocial assessment, the nurse must
establish trust and a working relationship with the person. Guidelines
for conducting a psychosocial assessment include the following:
Create a quiet, private environment.
Minimise interruptions.
Maintain appropriate eye contact.
Sit at eye level with the person.
Demonstrate an interest in the person’s concerns.
Indicate acceptance of the person by not criticising, frowning or
demonstrating shock.
Ask open-ended questions to encourage the person to talk rather
than close-ended questions that tend to block free sharing.
Avoid asking more personal questions than are actually needed.


Minimise writing detailed notes during the interview because this
can create feelings of concern that confidential material is being
‘recorded’ as well as interfere with your ability to focus on what
the person is saying.
Determine whether the family can provide additional information.
Maintain confidentiality.
Be aware of your own biases, assumptions and discomforts that
could influence the assessment.
Consider how the person’s behaviour is influenced by culture.
It is also important that the nurse identify any stressors that may
affect aspects of self-concept. See Box 40.1
 for examples of
stressors that may place a person at risk of problems with self-
concept.
BO X
40.1 Stressors affecting self-concept
Identity stressors
Change in physical appearance (e.g. surgical scarring).
Declining physical, mental or sensory abilities.
Inability to achieve goals.
Relationship concerns.
Sexuality concerns.
Unrealistic ideal self.


Body image stressors
Loss of body parts (e.g. amputation, mastectomy,
hysterectomy).
Loss of body functions (e.g. resulting from stroke, spinal
cord injury, neuromuscular disease, arthritis, declining
mental or sensory abilities).
Disfigurement (e.g. through severe burns, amputation,
colostomy, tracheostomy).
Unrealistic body ideal (e.g. a muscular configuration that
cannot be achieved).
Self-esteem stressors
Lack of positive feedback from significant others.
Repeated failures.
Unrealistic expectations.
Abusive relationship.
Loss of financial security.
Role stressors
Loss of parent, spouse, child, close friend or family
member.
Change or loss of job or other significant role.
Divorce.
Illness.


Ambiguous or conflicting role expectations.
Inability to meet role expectations.
Patient safety competency framework
1 Person-centred care
Nursing students must demonstrate empathy by
seeking to understand the person’s
perspectives, views and feelings (Levett-Jones
et al.
).
19 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.

Clinical consideration
The degree to which a stressor is perceived to
affect self-concept varies from person to
person. For example, some people may
19


respond to repeated failures by trying harder,
whereas others may give up.
Culturally competent care
Assessing self-concept
It is the nurse’s responsibility to use therapeutic
communication and to remain sensitive to the effect that
cultural influences will have on the person’s self-concept. This
responsibility can be described as providing culturally safe
care (see Chapter 19
 for further details). The person’s
cultural background is not only assessed directly but is also
considered as a factor in the areas of self-perception, role
relationships, major stressors and coping strategies. In the
area of behaviours that may suggest low self- esteem,
nurses need to ask themselves the following question: is this
really a behaviour that would suggest a low self-esteem or is
it part of the cultural behaviour(s) of the person? In addition,
consider if the person is experiencing cultural dissonance, a
situation in which there are conflicting beliefs and attitudes
between the person’s culture and the current culture in which
they are living.
When stressors are identified, the nurse needs to determine how the
person perceives the stressor. A positive, growth- oriented
perception of stressful events reinforces self-worth; a negative,
hopeless, defeatist perception leads to decreased self-esteem. The


nurse should also identify the individual’s coping style and determine
whether this style is effective by asking the person questions such
as these:
When you have a problem or face a stressful situation, how do
you usually deal with it?
Do these methods work? Why?
Personal identity
When assessing self-concept, the information obtained should first
be about the person’s personal identity as this information assists
the nurse to gain a sense of who the person believes they are. See
the accompanying ‘Assessment interview
’ for examples of
questions to ask.
Assessment interview
Personal identity
How would you describe your personal characteristics?
How do you see yourself as a person?
How do others describe you as a person?
What do you like about yourself?
What are your personal strengths, talents and abilities?
What do you do well?
What would you change about yourself if you could?


Does it bother you a great deal if you think someone
doesn’t like you?
Body image
If there are indications of a body image disturbance, the nurse must
assess the person carefully for possible functional or physical
problems. The disturbance may be a result of a present abnormality
or malfunction or an anticipated one. See the accompanying
‘Assessment interview
’ for examples of questions to ask about
body image. In addition to the stated responses about the problem,
it is important for the nurse to observe for signs of a potential body
image disturbance; for example, observing for erratic eating
behaviours or excessive exercising in a teenager with a suspected
eating disorder.
Assessment interview
Body image
How do you feel about your appearance?
Is there any part of your body you would like to change?
Why?
Are you comfortable discussing your surgery?
Do you feel different or inferior to others?


What changes in your body do you expect following your
surgery?
How have significant others in your life reacted to changes
in your body?
Role performance
The nurse assesses the person’s satisfaction and dissatisfaction
associated with role responsibilities and relationships including family
roles, work roles, student roles and social roles. Family roles are
especially important to people because family relationships are
particularly close. Relationships can be supportive and growth
producing; or, at the opposite extreme, they can be highly stressful if
there is violence or abuse. Assessment of family role relationships
may begin with structural aspects such as the number in the family
group, ages and residence location. To obtain data related to the
person’s family relationships and satisfaction or dissatisfaction with
work roles and social roles, the nurse might ask some of the
questions shown in the accompanying ‘Assessment interview
’.
Keep in mind, however, that questions need to be tailored to the
individual and their culture, age and current situation.
Assessment interview
Role performance


Family relationships
Tell me about your family.
What is home like?
How is your relationship with your
spouse/partner/significant other (if appropriate) going?
What are your relationships like with your other relatives?
How are important decisions made in your family?
What are your responsibilities in the family?
How well do you feel you accomplish what is expected of
you?
What about your role or responsibilities would you like
changed?
Are you proud of your family members?
Do you feel your family members are proud of you?
Work roles and social roles
Do you like your work?
How do you get along at work?
What about your work would you like to change if you
could?
How do you spend your free time?
Are you involved in any community groups?
Are you most comfortable alone, with one other person or
in a group?
Who is most important to you?


Who do you seek out for help?
Self-esteem
A nurse can ask the following questions to determine a person’s
self-esteem:
Are you satisfied with your life?
How do you feel about yourself?
Are you accomplishing what you want?
What goals in life are important to you?
It is important for the nurse to determine the person’s cultural
background first, in order not to misinterpret specific behaviours. An
example of the impact of culture can be seen by considering
Australia’s colonisation and how this continues to affect Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander peoples today, particularly when dealing
with government organisations such as hospitals. To minimise
feelings of mistrust and disempowerment among Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander people, the nurse must strive to create a
culturally safe environment (Australian Commission on Safety and
Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC)
).
20 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC) (2017a). National
Safety and Quality Health Service Standards: User Guide for Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander Health. Sydney: ACSQHC. Retrieved from <www.safetyandquality.gov.au>.
20


The following behaviours might reflect low self-esteem or may be
misinterpreted due to the person’s cultural background:
avoids eye contact
stoops in posture and moves slowly
is poorly groomed and has an unkempt appearance
is hesitant or halting in speech
is overly critical of self (e.g. ‘I’m no good’, ‘I’m ugly’ or ‘People
don’t like me’)
may be overly critical of others
is unable to accept positive remarks about self
apologises frequently
verbalises feelings of hopelessness, helplessness and
powerlessness, such as, ‘I really don’t care what happens’, ‘I’ll do
whatever anyone wants’, ‘Whatever is destined will happen’.
It is important for the nurse to determine the influence of culture on
the communication style of the person before determining a problem
with self-esteem.
Diagnosing
Nursing diagnoses that specifically relate to disturbances in self-
concept include the following:
Disturbed body image
Ineffective role performance


Low or poor self-esteem
Altered personal identity
Anxiety related to changed physical appearance (e.g.
amputation, mastectomy)
Poor or ineffective coping with role change related to death of
spouse
Grieving related to change in physical appearance or identity
A sense of hopelessness
A sense of powerlessness
Role conflict/strain
Readiness for enhanced self-concept
Altered sleep pattern
Perceived or actual social isolation
Spiritual distress
Disturbed thought processes.
Planning
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
Individuals with self- concept and role problems
History Frank Sawyers had a permanent colostomy formed 7
days ago following a bowel resection for cancer of the
sigmoid colon. When the nurse was changing the colostomy


appliance, Frank said, ‘I am really repulsed by this’. He avoids
looking at the stoma by putting his arm over his eyes.
The nurse develops plans in collaboration with the person and their
support people when possible, according to the person’s state of
health, level of anxiety, resources, coping mechanisms and
sociocultural background. The nurse who has little experience in
intervening with individuals with altered self-concept may wish to
consult with a more experienced nurse to develop an effective plan
of care. The nurse works with the person in setting goals to enhance
their self-concept.
The goals established will vary according to the diagnoses and
defining characteristics related to each individual. Examples of
desired outcomes, interventions and activities are shown in
‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and interventions
’.
Specific nursing orders associated with each of these activities can
be selected to meet the individual needs of the person.
Implementing
Nursing interventions to promote a positive self-concept include
helping a person to identify areas of strength. In addition, for people
who have an altered self-concept, nurses need to establish a
therapeutic relationship with the person and assist them with
behavioural changes to improve their self-worth.


Identifying areas of strength
Healthy people often perceive their problems and weaknesses more
easily than their assets and strengths. People with low self-esteem
tend to focus even more on their limitations and may experience
more difficulty identifying personal strengths. When a person has
difficulty identifying personality strengths and assets, the nurse
provides the person with a set of guidelines or a framework for
identifying such strengths (see Box 40.2
).
BO X
40.2 Framework for identifying
personality strengths
Note the individual’s past, present and anticipated future
participation in:
education, training and related areas (including self-
education)
work (paid and voluntary)
other roles/commitments (e.g. home duties, club
membership)
relaxation activities such as hobbies, sports and outdoor
activities.
In addition, determine the individual’s:


health status, including healthy aspects of body function
and good health maintenance practices
relationship strengths, including the ability to make people
feel comfortable, the capacity to enjoy being with people,
being aware of people’s needs and feelings, and being
able to listen
emotional strengths, including the capacity to give and
receive warmth, affection and love; the ability to ‘take’
anger and to feel and express a wide range of emotions;
and the capacity for empathy
spiritual strengths such as religious faith, participation in
spiritual activities (i.e. attending church, synagogue,
mosque) or related activities
sense of humour and the ability to laugh at oneself
special aptitudes such as sales or mechanical ability, a
‘green thumb’, ability to recognise and enjoy beauty, ability
to solve problems, a liking for adventure, having
perseverance and the drive needed to get things done.
Nurses can employ the following specific strategies to reinforce
strengths:
Stress positive thinking rather than self-negation.
Notice and verbally reinforce personal strengths.
Encourage the setting of realistic and attainable goals.
Acknowledge goals that have been attained.
Provide honest, positive feedback.


Enhancing self-esteem
Nurses assisting people who have an altered self-concept must
establish a therapeutic relationship. To do this the nurse must have
self-awareness and effective communication skills. The following
nursing techniques may help individuals analyse the problem and
enhance their self-concept:
Encourage the person to appraise the situation and express their
feelings.
Encourage the person to ask questions.
Provide accurate information.
Become aware of distortions, inappropriate or unrealistic
standards and faulty labels in the person’s speech.
Explore the person’s positive qualities and strengths.
Encourage the person to express positive self-evaluation more
than negative self-evaluation.
Avoid criticism.
Teach individuals to substitute negative self-talk (‘I can’t walk to
the shops anymore’) with positive self-talk (‘I can walk half a
block each morning’). Negative self-talk reinforces a negative
self-concept.
Certain strategies vary depending on the age of the person (see
‘Lifespan considerations
’).


Lifespan considerations
Enhancing self-esteem
Children
Children build strong self-esteem if they develop five basic
attitudes: (1) security and trust; (2) identity; (3) belonging;
(4) purpose; and (5) personal competence.
Security and trust are developed early in life; infants
should not be left ‘to cry it out’, for example, but should
learn that they can rely on their parents to meet their
needs promptly and consistently. With older children, trust
and security are strengthened when adults spend time
with them: listening, playing, reading or just being there.
Both emotional and physical contact, such as a hug,
convey warmth and caring.
Identity is developed when children are allowed to explore
and experiment with the world around them and to
express themselves as unique individuals in that world.
They should be given opportunities to ‘practise’ who they
are. Preschoolers, for example, love to dress themselves
and should be allowed to wear outlandish outfits (within
limits of weather and safety) if they choose. Teenagers
who try new hair colours and styles, some of which may
‘offend’ their parents, are engaging in a crucial
developmental step.


Belonging is essential for all humans and having a sense
that others in your social network care about you, want
you there and benefit by your contribution is important to
healthy self-esteem. Children gain this sense of belonging
by being included in activities, by being praised for their
efforts and achievements and by being valued by parents,
siblings, caregivers and other adults. Parents should
make an effort to ‘catch their children doing well’ and
praise them for it (e.g. ‘I like the way you share with your
brother’). Children also need to hear that they are valued
just for being themselves (e.g. ‘I like doing things with you.
Remember when we went to the park? Wasn’t that fun?’).
Purpose and belonging are closely related. Children need
opportunities to participate in the family and their
community in order to discover what they can best
contribute based on their strengths and skills. For
example, a mother may state, ‘Our 4-year-old, Leo, is our
actor. He is wonderful with costumes and can make any of
us smile when he starts his routine’. Leo may never
become an actor, but he knows he makes a significant
contribution to his family’s wellbeing. He brings them joy.
Personal competence grows as children identify and refine
their skill sets. Children develop competence as they
confront and solve problems, face challenges, expand
their thinking and are asked to do more than they think
they can do. Adults must, however, provide children with
support, guidance, appropriate assistance and
constructive feedback (including praise) in order to


prevent the child from being overwhelmed. Too much
frustration or uncertainty can lead to giving up, avoidance,
lying, bullying and other antisocial behaviours. If adults
help children to accomplish goals that are important to
them, children are more likely to develop a sense of
personal competence and independence.
Key ingredients for helping children develop high self-
esteem are love, acceptance, firmness, consistency and
the establishment of expectations. Such qualities provide
children with a safe, loving, supportive and predictable
world in which to live.
Adolescents
Provide increasing levels of responsibility. Adolescents
need to experience successes and failures and the
consequences of their own behaviour.
Encourage discussion about issues including problems
and mistakes.
Show appreciation for effort and contributions. Emphasise
the process, not only the result.
Ask for their opinions and suggestions.
Encourage participation in decision making in areas that
affect the adolescent. Show confidence in the teen’s
judgments.
Avoid comparison with or ridicule or punishment in front of
others.
Assist in the creation of realistic goals and standards.


Adolescents often engage in volunteer activities in their
schools or communities, helping them to identify their
strengths and find meaning in their activities. Knowing that
they have a purpose and make a difference assists the
adolescent to develop a strong self-esteem.
Adults
Explore the meaning of self-esteem and how their self-
esteem has influenced past behaviours and actions (and
can influence present and future plans and decisions).
Assist the person in assessing the internal and external
forces contributing to or retarding their self-esteem.
Act in ways that demonstrate belief that the person can
cope with the realities and demands of life and is worthy
of experiencing joy and happiness.
Avoid comparisons with other people.
Discourage statements about the self that are negative.
Encourage the use of affirmations to enhance self-
esteem: statements such as ‘I like myself’ or ‘I am a
valuable person’.
Encourage associations with positive, supportive people.
Make positive statements about the person’s past
successes (major or minor).
Assist the person to make a list of their positive qualities
and to review this list often.
Suggest the person do things for others. Making a
positive contribution enhances positive feelings of self-
worth.


Older adults
Older adults who become increasingly dependent can
develop low self-esteem. Old age is frequently accompanied
by changes such as reduced income, decline in physical
health and loss of friends and family members. In addition to
those actions listed above for use with adults, nurses can use
the following techniques to help older adults enhance their
self-esteem:
Encourage people to participate in planning their own
care.
Listen carefully to their concerns.
Assist people to identify and use their own strengths.
Encourage them to participate in activities in which they
can be successful.
Communicate that the older adult is valued. Use the
person’s name.
Encourage older adults to stay connected with their
memories. Reminiscing by writing or recording an
autobiography or storytelling are excellent ways to achieve
this connection.
Encourage creative activities to tap their resources.
Examples are music, art, storytelling, quilting and
photography.
Work with the older adult to establish small, incremental
goals—achieving smaller targets can help bolster self-
esteem.


Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Communicating for Safety
The intention of this standard is to ‘ensure there is timely,
purpose-driven and effective communication and
documentation that support continuous, coordinated and safe
care for patients’ (ACSQHC
, p. 48).
21 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) (2017b). National Safety and Quality Health
Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved by
ensuring effective communication at clinical
handover, including the communication of critical
information and adhering to documentation
protocols.
People who are hospitalised experience
significant strain on their self-concept. For
example, a parent will experience role strain due
to their inability to complete normal caregiver
duties; or a woman who has undergone a
mastectomy will likely experience an altered
body image. Nurses need to be mindful of these
potential self-concept disturbances and assist
the person where possible. It is imperative that
21


other health professionals are also alerted to
these concerns via clinical handover,
documentation and other referral tools so that
appropriate strategies are implemented.
Evaluating
To determine whether individualised outcomes have been achieved,
the nurse uses data collected during interactions with the person
and significant others (see ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses,
outcomes and interventions
’). If outcomes are not achieved,
the nurse should explore the reasons why by considering questions
such as the following:
Have old situations recurred, triggering feelings or behaviours
associated with low self-esteem?
Have new stressful situations occurred with which the person
feels unable to cope, resulting in continuing or recurrent low self-
esteem?
Are new or additional roles causing increased stress in adapting?
Are significant others supporting the person adequately in
attempts to improve self-esteem?
Did the person follow through on referrals to appropriate
agencies? Did the agencies provide the expected services?


Were the individual’s expectations too high in relation to the time
needed for successful resolution of self-esteem problems?
The nurse, individual and significant others need to understand that
to change beliefs, feelings and behaviours affecting self-esteem
requires time and ongoing effort. Unlike many physical problems
(e.g. wounds) where healing can be quickly observed, improving
one’s self-concept can be a continuing concern and is not so easily
evaluated. New crises can cause people to doubt themselves and
revert to former feelings of inadequacy. However, individuals can
also learn from each new situation and gain new strategies to
enhance their self-concept.
Case study
Trevor is an 18-year-old male university student who was
involved in a motor vehicle accident 5 days ago, suffering a
traumatic amputation of his left lower leg. Trevor’s mother
has remained with him since the crash and is very supportive.
His father is grief-stricken and having difficulty dealing with
Trevor’s condition because Trevor was captain of his local
rugby team and had aspirations of becoming a professional
footballer. Trevor will soon be placed into a rehabilitation
program and undergo fitting of a leg prosthesis. Despite
these important steps towards recovery, Trevor is no longer
his optimistic self. Instead, he appears sombre and is
monosyllabic in conversation. He does not look at his leg


when dressings are being changed and he refuses to discuss
his upcoming rehabilitation.
Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. Trevor’s self-concept has changed due to the physical
changes from the amputation. What other factors may
have affected his self-concept?


2. In addition to Trevor’s amputation, what other factors
may influence his self-esteem? What factors are likely
to affect Trevor’s adaptation to his amputation and
rehabilitation?
3. What strategies could you use to assist Trevor and his
family to adapt to his amputation?
4. How would your interventions differ for a person with
the same condition who is 70 years old?
5. What other groups of people, in addition to those with
amputations, are at risk of the development of altered
self-esteem or body image?
6.
 Which of the psychosocial elements of the
Fundamentals of Care Framework are most relevant
to this case and why?


Chapter 40 Review


Chapter highlights
A positive self-concept is essential to a person’s physical and
psychological wellbeing.
A person’s self-perception can differ from the person’s
perception of how others see them and from the ideal self; that
is, how the person would like to be.
Interactions with significant others create the conditions that
influence self-concept throughout life.
Nurses who develop a positive self-concept incorporating the
components of emotional intelligence are more likely to help
people meet their health care needs.
When individuals are able to conceptualise the self, they begin a
lifelong process of deciding whether, and to what extent, they are
valuable and worthy.
Individuals who grow up in families whose members value each
other are likely to feel good about themselves.
Factors affecting self-concept include development, family and
culture, stressors, resources, history of success and failure, and
illness.
The nurse assesses four areas of self-concept: personal identity,
body image, role performance and self-esteem.
Because a positive self-concept is basic to health, one of the
nurse’s major responsibilities is to assist the person whose self-
concept is disturbed to develop a more positive and realistic
image of themself.


A therapeutic relationship is essential for the effective
assessment of an individual’s self-concept, for providing help and
support and for motivating personal behaviour change.
Concept check

All humans are sexual beings. Regardless of
gender, age, race, socioeconomic status,
religious beliefs, physical and mental health, or
other demographic factors, we express our
sexuality in a variety of ways throughout our
lives.
Sexuality
 is an individually expressed and
highly personal phenomenon whose meaning
evolves from life experiences. Physiological,
psychosocial and cultural factors influence a
person’s sexuality and lead to the wide range of
attitudes and behaviours seen in humans. There
are no normal, universal sexual behaviours.
Satisfying or ‘normal’ sexual expression can
generally be described as whatever behaviours
give pleasure and satisfaction to those adults


involved, without threat of coercion or injury to
self or others.


Development of sexuality
The development of sexuality begins with conception and continues
throughout the lifespan. Table 41.1
 outlines characteristics of
sexual development throughout the lifespan, with nursing
interventions and teaching guidelines for each developmental stage.
Table 41.1 Sexual development throughout life
Birth to 12 years
The ability of the human body to experience a sexual response is
present before birth. As evidenced by ultrasound, males have
erections several months before birth. Male infants continue to
experience erections after birth. As females have vaginal lubrication
at birth, it is assumed that lubrication also occurs prior to birth.
When babies find their fingers and toes, they also find their genitals.
They seem to experience a pleasurable sensation from the touch
but one would not call this a sexual experience. By the age of 3,
more purposeful masturbation begins and the orgasmic response is
quite common, although males do not ejaculate until after puberty.
By age 2½ or 3, children know what gender they are and have
beginning awareness of genital differences between males and
females.


Around age 9 or 10, the first physical changes of puberty begin—the
development of breast buds in girls and the growth of pubic hair. As
the adrenal glands mature, they produce more testosterone and
oestrogen, which contributes to the first experiences of sexual
attraction to another person. Girls need to be taught about
menstruation
 (monthly uterine bleeding) and related self-care.
Adolescence
During early adolescence (12 to 18 years), primary and secondary
sex characteristics continue to develop, necessitating more
information about body changes. For boys, the testes and scrotum
increase in size, the skin over the scrotum becomes darker, pubic
hair grows and axillary sweating begins. Development of the genitals
to adult size takes about 5 to 6 years. For girls, the pelvis and hips
broaden, the breast tissue develops (see Chapter 31
), pubic hair
grows, axillary sweating begins and vaginal secretions become milky
and change from alkaline to acidic.
Adolescents’ sexual experimentation is currently occurring at ages
younger than in previous decades. According to the Sixth National
Survey of Australian Secondary Students and Sexual Health
(NSASSSH) conducted in 2018, 89% of the students surveyed had
engaged in some form of sexual activity; however, only 47% of them
had engaged in sexual intercourse (Fisher et al. ). The increase in
‘sexting’, where sexual images and messages are sent through
electronic means (e.g. text messaging), is often cited in the media
1


as the cause for this increased sexual activity among teenagers. To
date, this belief is unproven; however, a recent meta-analysis found
the mean prevalence of adolescents receiving and sending a sext
was 14.8% and 27.4% respectively (Madigan et al. ). In Australia,
the sixth NSASSSH found that one-third of the surveyed students
had engaged in sexting in the previous 2 months (Fisher et al.
2019).
1 Fisher, C. M., Waling, A., Kerr, L., ... Lucke, J. (2019). Sixth National Survey of Australian
Secondary Students and Sexual Health 2018. Bundoora, Vic.: Australian Research Centre in
Sex, Health and Society, La Trobe University. Retrieved from <www.latrobe.edu.au>.
2 Madigan, S., Ly, A., Rash, C. L., Van Ouytsel, J. & Temple, J. R. (2018). Prevalence of
multiple forms of sexting behavior among youth: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
JAMA Pediatrics, 172(4), 327–335. Doi: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2017.5314.
Teenage girls may have irregular menstruation initially, which can
lead to embarrassment. They can be taught to be aware of subtle
signs of impending menstruation, such as tender breasts, bloating or
the appearance of pimples. Girls should also be counselled
regarding the variety of feminine hygiene products available (e.g.
sanitary pads and tampons) so that they can make informed
choices. Parents and nurses should advise teenage girls to wash
their hands thoroughly before inserting a tampon, to change
tampons frequently, to avoid super absorbent tampons, to alternate
them with sanitary pads and to use pads at night. These measures
will help to decrease infection, including the risk of ‘toxic shock
syndrome’, a rare yet potentially life-threatening bacterial infection.
2


Dysmenorrhoea
 (painful menstruation) is prevalent among
adolescent females. Cramping, lower abdominal pain radiating to the
back and upper thighs, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and headaches
may occur. Dysmenorrhoea results from powerful uterine
contractions which cause ischaemia and, in turn, cramping pain. The
symptoms of dysmenorrhoea can be treated with bed rest,
administration of analgesics such as paracetamol, application of
heat to the abdomen, certain exercises such as abdominal muscle
strengthening and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications, such
as ibuprofen.
All adolescents want to know about sexual behaviours but are often
uneasy about discussing these concerns with their parents. Nurses,
schools and families need to provide accurate information. During
the nursing assessment, teenagers should be asked directly what
they know about sex, contraception and reproduction. Sometimes a
lot of the teenager’s information is based on popular myths (see
Table 41.2
). The nurse should discuss factual information about
sex, sexual actions and their consequences, the individual’s right to
make a decision regarding ways to express oneself sexually and the
responsibilities of each person with respect to sexual activity.
Table 41.2 Common sexual misconceptions
Sexually transmissible infections (STIs) are the most common
bacterial infections among adolescents. Currently, the rates of
diagnosis of STIs in Australia are increasing. For example, between
2012 and 2016, the rate of gonorrhoea notifications increased by


43% in females and 72% in males (Department of Health ). STI
rates are substantially higher in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
young people (Department of Health ). In 2017, almost one-third
(31%) of gonorrhoea notifications in Indigenous Australians occurred
in teens aged 15 to 19 years, compared to a 6% incidence in the
same age group of non-Indigenous Australians (Kirby Institute ).
Teens need education about these diseases, preventive measures
and early treatment. ‘Clinical manifestations’ lists the common types
and symptoms of STIs for which teenagers should seek medical
care.
3 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018). Census of Population and Housing: Reflecting
Australia—Stories from the Census, 2016: Same Sex Couples in Australia, 2016. Cat no.
2071.0. Canberra: ABS. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
4 Department of Health (2018). Fourth National Sexually Transmissible Infections Strategy
2018–2022. Retrieved from <www1.health.gov.au>.
5 Kirby Institute (2018). HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexually Transmissible Infections in Australia:
Annual Surveillance Report 2018. Sydney: Kirby Institute, University of New South Wales.
Retrieved from <https://kirby.unsw.edu.au>.
The nurse should also inform teens about the various methods of
contraception—abstinence; contraceptive pills, injections and
implants; diaphragms; vaginal rings; intrauterine devices and
condoms—to prevent an unplanned pregnancy. Importantly, the
nurse must recommend the use of condoms to minimise the risk of
STIs. Different contraceptive methods are discussed later in this
chapter.
3
4
5


Young and middle adulthood
In young adulthood, many people begin to form intimate
relationships with long-term implications. These relationships may
take the form of dating, cohabitation or marriage. Note, however,
that some people do not form intimate relationships until late
adulthood and that some never form these types of relationships.
Young adult men and women are often concerned about normal
sexual response, for both themselves and their partners. In
heterosexual relationships, problems may arise because of basic
differences in male and female expectations and responses. Same-
sex couples often fare better in this respect. Couples need to
communicate their needs to one another early in the relationship so
that a successful intimate partnership can develop and grow. Any
changes to these sexual needs must also be communicated to the
other partner.
Clinical manifestations
Sexually transmissible infections
During middle adulthood, both men and women experience
decreased hormone production, causing the climacteric, which is
called menopause in women. These events often affect the
individual’s sexual self-concept, body image and sexual identity. See
Chapter 23
 for further information on menopause.


Older adulthood
Older adults may define sexuality far more broadly and include in
their definition such things as touching, hugging, romantic gestures
(e.g. giving or receiving flowers), comfort, warmth, dressing up, joy,
spirituality and beauty. Interest in sexual activity is not lost as people
age. For men, however, more time is needed to achieve an erection
and to ejaculate, more direct genital stimulation is required to
achieve an erection, the volume of ejaculated fluid decreases and
the intensity of contractions with orgasm may decrease. The
refractory period after orgasm is longer.
Older women remain capable of multiple orgasms and may, in fact,
experience an increase in sexual desire after menopause. However,
the phases of the sexual response cycle may take longer to occur.
Vaginal lubrication and elasticity decrease with menopause and
reduced oestrogen levels. Vaginal dryness can contribute to the
possibility of pain during sexual activity and intercourse
(dyspareunia).
Other factors that can be potential barriers to older adults’ sexual
activity include a concern for lack of privacy, especially for those
individuals living with family or in a residential aged care facility. Pain
during intercourse can also result from conditions that may impair
mobility (e.g. arthritis). These potential barriers can be misread as
the older adult being uninterested in having an active sex life. The
nurse can assist the older adult who is interested in maintaining their


sexual activity with suggestions about more comfortable positioning
and provide information about the products that are available to
assist older adults with enhancing their sexual experiences. These
range from simple lubricants to surgically implanted devices that
enable penile erections.


Sexual health
Sexual health is an individual and constantly changing phenomenon
falling within the wide range of human sexual thoughts, feelings,
needs and desires. For most people, sexual health is not considered
until its absence or an impairment is noticed. A person’s degree of
sexual health is best determined by that individual, sometimes with
the assistance of a qualified professional. The World Health
Organization (WHO ) defines sexual health
 as ‘a state of
physical, emotional, mental and social wellbeing in relation to
sexuality; it is not merely the absence of disease, dysfunction or
infirmity. Sexual health requires a positive and respectful approach
to sexuality and sexual relationships, as well as the possibility of
having pleasurable and safe sexual experiences, free of coercion,
discrimination and violence. For sexual health to be attained and
maintained, the sexual rights of all persons must be respected,
protected and fulfilled’ (p. 3). This definition recognises the
biological, psychological and sociocultural dimensions of sexuality.
Characteristics of sexual health are listed in Box 41.1
.
6 World Health Organization (WHO) (2010). Developing Sexual Health Programmes: A
Framework for Action. Geneva: Author. Retrieved from <https://apps.who.int>.
BO X
6


41.1 Characteristics of sexual health
Knowledge about sexuality and sexual behaviour.
Ability to express one’s full sexual potential, excluding all
forms of sexual coercion, exploitation and abuse.
Ability to make autonomous decisions about one’s sexual
life within a context of personal and social ethics.
Experience of sexual pleasure as a source of physical,
psychological, cognitive and spiritual wellbeing.
Capability to express sexuality through communication,
touch, emotional expression and love.
Right to make free and responsible reproductive choices.
Ability to access sexual health care for the prevention and
treatment of all sexual concerns, problems and disorders.
Source: Based on World Association for Sexual Health . Declaration of Sexual Rights. Retrieved
from <www.worldsexology.org/wp-
content/uploads/2013/08/declaration_of_sexual_rights_sep03_2014.pdf>.
7 World Association for Sexual Health (2014). Declaration of Sexual Rights. Retrieved from
<www.worldsexology.org>.
Components of sexual health
Five critical components of sexual health are sexual self-concept,
body image, gender identity, gender expression, and freedoms and
7


responsibilities.
One’s sexual self-concept
 (how one values oneself as a sexual
being) determines with whom one will have sex, the gender and
kinds of people a person is attracted to and the values about when,
where, with whom and how one expresses sexuality. A positive
sexual self-concept enables people to form intimate relationships
throughout life. A negative sexual self-concept may impede the
formation of relationships.
Body image
, a central part of one’s sense of self, is constantly
changing. Pregnancy, ageing, trauma, disease and therapies can
alter an individual’s appearance and function, which can affect body
image. How a person feels about their body is related to one’s
sexuality. People who feel good about their bodies are likely to be
comfortable with and enjoy sexual activity. People who have a poor
body image may respond negatively to sexual arousal. A major
influence on body image for women is the media focus on physical
attractiveness. Likewise, many men worry about penis size. The
