myth that ‘larger is better’, particularly if it is erect and has staying
power, is pervasive in Australia and many other parts of the world.
People’s body image can suffer when they perceive that they have
not met these unrealistic expectations.
Gender identity
 is a person’s self-image or internal sense of their
gender. Rather than being based on one’s apparent biological sex,
gender identity is influenced by a series of developmental events
and sociocultural norms. While most people identify as a male or


female, for some individuals, their gender does not fit such binary
classifications. Such individuals may identify as being non-binary
,
or genderqueer
. A non-binary person does not exclusively
identify as male or female. Instead, they may identify as fitting
somewhere in between male and female, identify as both male and
female at the same time, as different genders at different times or
as having no gender at all (agendered).
Gender expression
 is the outward expression of a person’s
sense of maleness or femaleness, including their physical
appearance, behaviours, pronouns and clothing choice. Physical
structure, variations in the internal sense of what is male or female,
family values and sociocultural values all influence gender
expression. For example, in Australia, boys are given reinforcement
for behaving in a ‘masculine’ way (e.g. blue clothing, playing with toy
trucks) and girls receive reinforcement for exhibiting ‘feminine’
behaviours (e.g. pink clothing, playing with dolls) from an early age.
Such reinforcement influences the formation of one’s gender
expression; however, it can also cause confusion and be detrimental
to a young person’s mental wellbeing if they feel their true gender is
being denied.
Androgyny
, or flexibility in gender roles, is the belief that most
characteristics and behaviours are human qualities that should not
be limited to one specific gender or the other. Being androgynous
does not mean being sexually neutral or imply anything about one’s
sexual orientation. Rather, it describes the degree of flexibility a
person has regarding gender-stereotypical behaviours.


Sexual health includes both freedoms and responsibilities. Sexually
healthy people engage in activities that are freely chosen, including
both self-pleasuring and shared-pleasuring activities. Sexually
healthy individuals have freedom of their sexual thoughts, feelings
and fantasies; yet, they also have the responsibility to make
appropriate decisions and safe practices to ensure the safety and
wellbeing of themselves and others (WHO ).
8 World Health Organization (WHO) (2019a). Sexual and Reproductive Health. Retrieved
from <www.who.int>.
8


Varieties of sexuality
There is a tremendous range of variation in how people experience
and express their sexuality. There are also many differences in the
priority people place on sexuality in their lives. Sexual varieties
include sexual orientation, gender identity, erotic preferences and
sexual lifestyles.
Sexual orientation
Sexual orientation
 refers to the patterns of one’s romantic,
sexual and emotional attraction to others. The origins of sexual
orientation are not well understood. Some biological theories
describe sexual orientation in terms of the genetic composition of
the individual. Psychological theories stress the role of early learning
experiences and cognitive processes. Other theories acknowledge
the confluence of genetics and the environment in the development
of sexual orientation.
Sexual orientation lies along a continuum with a wide range between
the two extremes of exclusively heterosexual attraction and
exclusively homosexual attraction. Other types of sexual orientation
include:


bisexuality, where the person is romantically and sexually
attracted to males and females
pansexuality or omnisexuality, where the person’s romantic and
sexual attraction to others is not restricted by gender and
biological sex
asexuality, where the person has little or no sexual attraction to
others
questioning, where the person is in the process of discovering
their sexuality and/or gender identity.
In Australia, up to 11% of the population identify as LGBTIQA+
(lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, intersex, queer or questioning,
asexual and other gender and sexual diversities) (Australian Human
Rights Commission ). Possibly due to growing acceptance of the
LGBTIQA+ community, the number of same-sex couples living
together in Australia has more than quadrupled between 1996 and
2016 (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2018). Importantly, the Sex
Discrimination Act 1984 was amended in 2013 to make it against the
law to discriminate on the basis on an individual’s sexual orientation,
gender identity or intersex status (Australian Human Rights
Commission 2014).
9 Australian Human Rights Commission (2014). Face the Facts: Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual,
Trans and Intersex People. Retrieved from <www.humanrights.gov.au>.
Queer
9


Queer
 is an umbrella term used to describe a range of gender
identities and sexual orientations. It is consequently used to describe
the full range of LGBTIQA+ identities and may be preferred by some
individuals who feel labels such as gay, lesbian or bisexual are too
limiting. While the word ‘queer’ was originally associated with
negative connotations (e.g. ‘strange’ or ‘peculiar’), the term is now
used positively as a sign of empowerment and acceptance.
Gender diversity
Until recently, Western culture was deeply committed to the idea that
there were only two genders. However, over the past decade, there
has been a growing awareness of the diverse range of genders that
go beyond the expression of male and female. Gender diversity is
the extent to which an individual’s gender identity or expression
differs from cultural norms (American Psychological Association ).
Nurses have a key role in promoting an inclusive and safe place for
people who are gender diverse and seeking health care. Nurses
need to be aware that people who identify as gender diverse are not
‘attention seeking’; rather, they are being their authentic selves.
10 American Psychological Association (2015). Key Terms and Concepts in Understanding
Gender Diversity and Sexual Orientation Among Students. Retrieved from <www.apa.org>.
Intersex
10


An estimated 1.7% of children born in Australia are believed to be
intersex
 (Australian Human Rights Commission 2014). According
to the Australian Human Rights Commission , ‘intersex refers to
people who are born with genetic, hormonal or physical sex
characteristics that are not typically “male” or “female”. Intersex
people have a diversity of bodies and identities’ (p. 5). For example,
individuals with an intersex condition may have chromosomal
anomalies or contradictions to their gonadal gender, internal organs
and external genital appearance, and as such do not fit the medical
norms for gender identity. At birth, the gender of such an infant may
be ambiguous as they may have some parts that are usually
associated with males and some parts usually associated with
females. However, intersex anatomy may also not be apparent at
birth. Sometimes it remains undetected until puberty, until the
person is identified as an infertile adult or until the person dies and is
autopsied. For more information, visit the Intersex Human Rights
Australia website (see ‘Web links
’ at the end of this chapter).
11 Australian Human Rights Commission (2015). Resilient Individuals: Sexual Orientation,
Gender Identity and Intersex Rights—National Consultation Report 2015. Retrieved from
<www.humanrights.gov.au>.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard Partnering with Consumers
The intention of this standard is ‘to create an organisation in
which there are mutually beneficial outcomes by having:
consumers as partners in planning, design, delivery,
11


measurement and evaluation of systems and services; [and]
patients are partners in their own care, to the extent that they
choose’ (Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in
Health Care
, p. 14).
12 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved through
the nurse actively involving the consumer in
determining their own care. This includes
recognising and acknowledging the individualism
of each consumer.
In accordance with this standard is the
recognition of sexual orientation and gender
diversity in the Australian population. Such
diversity is acknowledged via the inclusion of an
I or X category (indeterminate, intersex or
unspecified) for gender classification on medical
charts. The I or X descriptor can be used for the
individual who does not wish to identify
exclusively as male or female.
Transgender
12


The WHO
 defines transgender
 as ‘an umbrella term that
describes a diverse range of people whose internal sense of gender
is different than that which they are assigned at birth’. Transgender
therefore refers to gender identity and expression rather than sexual
orientation.
13 World Health Organization (WHO) (2019b). WHO/Europe Brief—Transgender Health in the
Context of ICD-11. Retrieved from <www.euro.who.int>.
Most transgender (commonly abbreviated to trans) people report
that they have felt gender dysphoria since early childhood. Gender
dysphoria
 refers to the distress experienced by a person
because of incongruity between their gender identity and their
gender assigned at birth. Trans people often suffer for many years
and try to hide the situation from family and friends for fear of being
stigmatised and discriminated against. Despite changing views
towards transgender people over the past decade in Australia, an
alarming 64.8% of trans men and women have reported being
harassed or discriminated against (Hyde et al.
). Understandably,
such events can affect an individual’s mental health and wellbeing
(see Chapter 45
 for additional information).
14 Hyde, Z., Doherty, M., Tilley, P. J. M., McCaul, K. A., Rooney, R. & Jancey. J. (2014). The
First Australian National Trans Mental Health Study: Summary of Results. Perth: Curtin
University. Retrieved from <www.beyondblue.org.au>.
Cross-dressers
13
14


Cross-dressers
 are typically males who cross-dress to express
the feminine side of their personality. In most instances, cross-
dressers are not interested in permanently altering their bodies
through surgical means, especially as the majority of them are
comfortable with their original birth identity and behaviour in their
public and professional lives.
Cross-dressing is a conscious choice and may occur at home or in
public settings. The frequency of the activity ranges from rarely to
often. It is not unusual for cross-dressers to have a female name to
go with the female personality and wardrobe. Cross-dressing occurs
more frequently in cultures where males are expected to be strong,
independent and unemotional protectors.
Clinical consideration
The incorrect use of a pronoun can be offensive
to someone who identifies as gender diverse.
Misgendering can be limited through calling the
health care recipient by their name rather than
he, she/him or her. Asking the person what
pronoun they would prefer is also acceptable.
Erotic preferences


Over a lifetime, sexual fantasies and single-partner sex are the most
common sexual outlets experienced by people. Masturbation
 is
self-stimulation of the genital organs. Masturbation is normal and is
the way we discover our erotic feelings and learn about our sexual
response. Mutual masturbation can provide sexual pleasuring and
intimacy without hurrying to genital interaction before both partners
are ready. Masturbation shared with a partner is a safe alternative to
unprotected genital sex.
Male-to-female or female-to-female oral–genital sex
 is known as
cunnilingus. This involves kissing, licking or sucking of the female
genitals including the mons pubis, vulva, clitoris, labia and vagina.
Fellatio is oral stimulation of the penis by licking and sucking. Sixty-
nine is simultaneous oral–genital stimulation by two people.
Preconceptions and myths are a major deterrent for those who have
not tried oral sex. However, like most sexual practices, oral–genital
sex is not completely free of the potential for STI transmission and
safe sex practices must be used.
Anal stimulation
 can be a source of sexual pleasure because
the anus has a rich nerve supply. Stimulation may be applied with
fingers, mouth or sex toys such as vibrators. The anus is
surrounded by strong muscles and the rectum contains no natural
lubrication. Thus, inserting a finger or penis in the rectum requires
relaxation and water-soluble lubricant.
A common form of sexual activity for heterosexual couples is
genital intercourse
. Penile–vaginal intercourse (coitus) can be


both physically and emotionally satisfying. There are varieties of
positions for this kind of intercourse; the most common is lying face
to face (with female or male on top). Side-lying, standing, sitting and
rear-entry positions are also used. Side-lying, female-on-top and
rear-entry positions can often facilitate clitoral stimulation, either by
penile or manual contact. The choice of intercourse positions and
activities depends on physical comfort and beliefs, values and
attitudes about different practices.
During intercourse, the man moves the penis back and forth along
the vaginal walls by rhythmic thrusting movements of his hips. At the
same time, the woman may move her own body to match the
partner’s hip movements. Movements continue until orgasm is
achieved by one or both partners. Simultaneous orgasm can be
difficult to achieve. After coitus, caressing, hugging and kissing can
increase the shared intimacy.
The other form of genital intercourse is anal intercourse, during
which the penis is inserted into the anus and rectum of the partner.
Anal intercourse is commonly practised by gay men but
heterosexual couples also engage in this type of intercourse.
Positions for anal intercourse are similar to those for penile–vaginal
intercourse, with minor differences due to the position of the anus.
Current safe sex practices dictate the use of a condom in both
forms of intercourse to prevent the transmission of disease.
Because anorectal tissue is not self-lubricating, a water-based
lubricant must be used on the condom. As normal bacterial flora


from the bowel can produce infection in other parts of the body, the
used condom should be removed and another applied before
inserting the penis into other body orifices.
There are many other varieties of sexuality that are beyond the
scope of this chapter. These include several or many partners,
swinging, group sex, fetishism, sexual sadism and sexual
masochism.


Factors influencing sexuality
Many factors influence a person’s sexuality. Discussed here are
family, culture, religion and personal expectations and ethics.
Family
For the majority of us, the family is the earliest and most enduring
social relationship. Families are the fabric of our day-to-day lives and
shape the quality of our lives by influencing our outlooks on life, our
motivations, our strategies for achievement and our styles for coping
with adversity. It is within our families that we develop our gender
identity, body image, sexual self-concept and capacity for intimacy.
Through family interactions, we learn about relationships and gender
roles and our expectations of others and ourselves.
From earliest beginnings, children observe their parents and model
themselves after these role models. If parents are able to share
affection with one another and other family members, children will
most likely become adults who are able to give and receive
affection. If parents seldom hug, hold hands or kiss each other, their
children may become adults who are very uncomfortable with
romantic touch. If family gender-role behaviour is very rigid,
arguments and hurt feelings will abound if a person from this system


is partnered with a person who grew up in an androgynous family
system. Family messages about sex range from ‘sex is so shameful
it shouldn’t be talked about’ to ‘sex is a joyful part of adult
relationships’. The following are some common sexual messages
children get from their families:
Sex is dirty.
Premarital sex is sinful.
Good girls don’t do it.
Masturbation is wrong.
Men should be the sexual experts.
Sex is for procreating.
Bodies, including genitals, are beautiful.
Sex should be fun for both women and men.
Sexual thoughts and feelings are natural.
Masturbation is a common, pleasurable activity.
Culture
Sexuality is often regulated by the individual’s culture. For example,
culture influences the sexual nature of dress, rules about marriage,
expectations of role behaviour, gender expression and social
responsibilities, and specific sex practices. Societal attitudes vary
widely. Attitudes about childhood sexual play with self or children of
the same gender or other gender may be restrictive or permissive.
Premarital sex, extramarital sex and homosexuality may be
unacceptable or tolerated. Polygamy (several marriage partners) or


monogamy (one marriage partner) may be the norm. Nurses need
to be aware of their own cultural beliefs around sexuality and sexual
health and be able to recognise that their perspectives may be quite
different from others’ perspectives. Being aware of these differences
helps to create a more inclusive environment and allows the nurse to
become more sensitive to the person’s health care needs.
Cultural norms can also influence how somebody’s sexual
attractiveness is perceived by others. For example, in some
cultures, legs are erotic and breasts are not. Body weight may also
be a determinant of sexual attractiveness. There is a great deal of
pressure in Australian culture for men to be muscular and women to
be thin. Yet, women who would be considered obese in Australia are
found highly attractive in other cultures. The degree of acceptable
public nudity also changes according to culture, ranging from
women’s entire bodies and faces being covered in Islamic societies
to nudism being accepted in some European cultures.
Female circumcision, also known as female genital mutilation,
female ritual cutting (FRC) or female genital cutting (FGC), is a
dangerous practice influenced by cultural beliefs and practised in
parts of Africa. Some of the cultural beliefs behind the practice
include the following: female genitals are offensive to men; if not
removed, the clitoris will become the size of a penis; the labia get in
the way of intercourse; the cutting enhances fertility; and it prepares
the woman for childbirth. Removal of the clitoris may or may not be
accompanied by removal of the labia and closure of the vaginal
entrance except for a small opening. Long-term medical


complications include urinary incontinence, chronic urinary tract
infections, vaginal scarring, pain syndromes, infertility and sexual
dysfunctions. FGC is illegal in several African and European
countries, as well as Australia and the United States. In 1997, the
WHO, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the United
Nations Children’s Emergency Fund (UNICEF) unanimously
recommended that all forms of female circumcision be abolished
(WHO
).
15 World Health Organization (WHO) (2018). Fact Sheet—Female Genital Mutilation.
Retrieved from <www.who.int>.
Male circumcision is controversial. Approximately 10–20% of male
infants undergo circumcision in Australia (Royal Australasian College
of Physicians (RACP)
). Reasons for male circumcision include
religious/cultural beliefs, that it can reduce the rate of urinary tract
infections, it can reduce the transmission of HIV and other STIs in
adults who live in countries with a high prevalence of these
infections, it reduces cervical cancer in women due to reduction of
HPV transmission and it reduces phimosis-related penile cancer
(RACP 2010). A violation of ethical rights, such as ignoring the
child’s right to choose, and procedural and psychological
complications are all risks associated with the procedure (RACP
2010). Currently, there is no clear consensus on whether the
benefits of infant male circumcision outweigh the risks associated
with the procedure and the RACP (2010) advocates that parental
choice should be respected regardless of the decision made.
15
16


16 Royal Australasian College of Physicians (RACP) (2010). Circumcision of Infant Males.
Sydney: RACP. Retrieved from<www.ccyp.vic.gov.au>.
Religion
Religion influences sexual expression. It provides guidelines for
sexual behaviour and acceptable circumstances for the behaviour,
as well as prohibited sexual behaviour and the consequences of
breaking the sexual rules. The guidelines or rules may be detailed
and rigid or broad and flexible. For example, some religions view
forms of sexual expression other than male–female intercourse as
unnatural and hold virginity before marriage to be the rule.
Many religious values conflict with the more flexible values of society
that have developed during the past few decades (often labelled the
‘sexual revolution’), such as the acceptance of premarital sex,
unwed parenthood, LGBTIQA+ communities and abortion. These
conflicts create marked anxiety and potential sexual dysfunctions in
some individuals. See Chapter 42
 for additional information about
religious values.
Personal expectations and ethics
Although ethics is integral to religion, ethical thought and ethical
approaches to sexuality can be viewed separately from religion.


Cultures have developed written or unwritten codes of conduct
based on ethical principles. Personal expectations concerning sexual
behaviour come from these cultural norms. What one person or
culture views as bizarre, perverted or wrong may be completely
natural and right to another. Examples include values regarding
masturbation, oral or anal intercourse and cross-dressing. Many
people accept a variety of sexual expressions if they are performed
by consenting adults, are practised in private and are not harmful.
Couples need to explore and communicate clearly about various
types of acceptable sexual expression to prevent domination of
sexual decision making by one member of the couple. To assess a
few of your personal values, complete the statements in Box
41.2
.
BO X
41.2 Assessing personal sexual
values
Sex is for ...
I believe sexual satisfaction is ...
When I think of my parents having sex, I ...
My beliefs about casual sex are ...
My beliefs about sexual experimentation are ...
Masturbation is ...
My beliefs about oral sex are ...


Research note
Engaging migrant and refugee young people with sexual
health care
J. R. Botfield, C. E. Newman & A. B. Zwi
. Engaging migrant and refugee young people with sexual
health care: Does generation matter more than culture? Sexuality Research and Social Policy, 15(4),
398–408. Doi: 10.1007/s13178-018-0320-6.
17 Botfield, J. R., Newman, C. E. & Zwi, A. B. (2018). Engaging migrant and refugee young people
with sexual health care: Does generation matter more than culture? Sexuality Research and Social
Policy, 15(4), 398–408. Doi: 10.1007/s13178-018-0320-6.
This study explored the challenges and opportunities for
engaging young people from migrant and refugee
backgrounds with sexual and reproductive health care in
Sydney. Three rounds of interviews were conducted with 27
young people (16–24 years) who self-identified as coming
from a migrant or refugee background. A thematic analysis
was then used on the data. Despite being from diverse
cultural and linguistic backgrounds, commonalities existed in
their conversations about sexual health. The study found that
the majority of participants came from a cultural background
where sex was a taboo topic. Consequently, most participants
could not openly discuss their sexual health issues with their
parents or other family members. Rather than seeking advice
about sexual health from a health professional, the
participants instead gained information from internet
searching and discussing their queries with close friends.
17


Many of the participants also felt ‘older people’ were
judgmental when it came to discussing sexual health issues.
A key factor to whether a young person decided to access a
sexual health service was the health professional’s
demeanour and the service’s ‘youth friendliness’.
Implications Currently, migrant and refugee young people
may not be fully benefitting from the options for sexual health
care that are available in Australia. Nurses can help to create
a more inclusive environment by adopting a welcoming, non-
judgmental and friendly attitude to young people who decide
to access sexual health care services.


Sexual response cycle
Commonly occurring phases of the human sexual response follow a
similar sequence in both females and males regardless of sexual
orientation (see Figure 41.1
). It does not matter if the motive for
being sexually active is true love or passionate lust. Table 41.3
provides a summary of the physiological changes associated with
each of the phases of the cycle.
Figure 41.1


Phases of the sexual response cycle.
Table 41.3 Physiological changes associated with the sexual
response cycle


The response cycle starts in the brain, with conscious sexual desires
called the desire phase
. Sexually arousing stimuli, often called
erotic stimuli, may be real or symbolic. Sight, hearing, smell, touch
and imagination (sexual fantasy) can all invoke sexual arousal.
Sexual desire fluctuates within each person and varies from person
to person. If people suppress or block out conscious sexual desires,
they may not experience any physiological response. Although
psychological issues are the more common causes of lack of sexual
desire, medications, drugs and hormone imbalances can also
interfere.
The excitement phase
 involves two primary physiological
changes. Vasocongestion is an increase in the blood flow to various
body parts resulting in erection of the penis and clitoris, and swelling
of the labia, testes and breasts. Vasocongestion stimulates sensory
receptors within these body parts that in turn transmit messages to
the conscious brain where they are usually interpreted as
pleasurable sensations. When stimulation is continued,
vasocongestion increases until it either is released by orgasm or
fades away. Likewise, myotonia, an increase of tension in muscles,
may increase until released by orgasm, or it may also simply fade
away.
The orgasmic phase
 is the involuntary climax of sexual tension,
accompanied by physiological and psychological release. This phase
is considered the measurable peak of the sexual experience.
Although the entire body is involved, the major focus of the orgasm
is felt in the pelvic region. Male orgasms usually last 10 to 30


seconds while female orgasms last 10 to 50 seconds. Men usually
have an ejaculation and expel semen as part of their orgasm. Before
puberty and in later years, males experience orgasms without
ejaculation.
The resolution phase
, the period of return to the unaroused
state, may last 10 to 15 minutes after orgasm, or longer if there is
no orgasm. This phase in females is quite varied as some women
experience multiple successive orgasms followed by a longer period
of resolution.


Altered sexual function
The ability to engage in sexual behaviour is of great importance to
most people. Many individuals experience transient problems with
their ability to respond to sexual stimulation or to maintain the
response. A smaller percentage of people experience problems that
are lifelong in duration. The problems may be generalised to all
sexual interactions and settings, or they may be situational,
occurring in a specific setting or with specific types of sexual activity.
It is often difficult to sort out the multiple factors contributing to an
individual’s or a couple’s sexual problems. Generally, a number of
past and current factors are involved. When assessing sexual
function it is useful to adopt a biopsychosocial approach to the
assessment (see Figure 41.2
).
Figure 41.2


Understanding sexual function using a biopsychosocial approach.
Past and current factors
Sociocultural factors interfering in sexual function include a very
restrictive upbringing accompanied by inadequate sex education.
Rigid gender-role socialisation may inhibit exploration of sexual
activities, positions, toys and other lovemaking behaviours. If
people’s religious affiliations believe that sex is only for procreation,
there may be great difficulty in celebrating the pleasure and fun of a
loving sexual relationship. Another factor may be parental
punishment for normally exploring one’s genitals or for normal


childhood sex play. In our current culture, the pressures of family
and work often leave couples with too little time and not enough
energy to enjoy sex.
Psychological factors may include negative feelings, such as guilt,
anxiety or fear, which interfere with the ability to experience pleasure
and joy. Some people experience guilt regarding the choice of
partner, when they simply enjoy sex or when they participate in what
they label ‘unusual’ sexual activities. People who have been sexually
abused at any time of their lives may experience overwhelming
anxiety when faced with the decision to engage in sex. Fears may
include pregnancy, STIs or pain. Because vulnerability and intimacy
are inherent in most sexual relationships, fear such as these may
lead to an avoidance of sex. Fear of failure in sexual performance
often becomes a vicious cycle; that is, fear of failure creates actual
failure, which in turn produces more fear. Spectatoring is the
detached appraisal of sexual performance or the body during a
sexual act: ‘Am I going to lose my erection?’, ‘Am I going to have an
orgasm this time?’, ‘My stomach is too flabby’, ‘When did his thighs
get that fat?’. Depressed people lose interest in sexual activity and
often experience a complete loss of sexual desire and fulfilment.
Cognitive factors include the internalisation of negative expectations
and beliefs. Those with low self-esteem may not understand how
another person could value and love them and also find them
sexually attractive. For those who have not yet accepted their sexual
orientation or gender identity, this cognitive conflict may interfere
with sexual relationships.


Sexual problems may also be symptomatic of
interpersonal/relationship problems. Conflict and anger with one’s
partner are not conducive to positive sexual interaction. Some
people lose the physical attraction to another or feel more attracted
to someone else.
Lack of intimacy and feeling like a sex object inhibit the feeling of
communion and connection that is an important part of making love.
Another factor is expecting one’s partner to read one’s mind about
sexual needs. Failure to communicate may result in one or both
partners not knowing how to please the other. Unless the partners
experiment, sex may, in time, become boring. Disagreements about
sexual frequency and/or sexual activities may lead to further
relationship conflict.
Physiological factors can interfere with people’s expression of
sexuality. Physical changes brought on by illness, injury or surgery
may inhibit full sexual expression. Illnesses and diseases including
heart disease, diabetes mellitus, neuromuscular disorders,
hypothyroidism, arthritis, cancer and mental disorders can have an
impact on sexual functioning (Faubion & Rullo ).
18 Faubion, S. & Rullo, J. (2015). Sexual dysfunction in women: A practical approach.
American Family Physician, 92(4), 281–288.
Some surgeries (e.g. a laparotomy or cardiac surgery) may delay
the individual’s return to sexual activity. Other surgeries (e.g. a
hysterectomy or mastectomy) may also alter the individual’s body
image, which can impede the person’s willingness to resume sexual
18


activity with their significant other. Physical disability such as those
resulting from a spinal cord injury or prostatectomy can negatively
affect sexual functioning. The presence of an STI in one partner
may induce fear of transmission in the other, resulting in abstinence
of sexual contact.
Many prescription medications have side effects that affect sexual
functioning. Most frequently, the impact is negative, but sometimes
there is a positive impact. Table 41.4
 provides an overview of the
effects of medications on sexual function. For example, anti-
depressants may slow ejaculation. This slowing may be a problem
for the man who finds himself suddenly feeling unable to ejaculate. If
the man is suffering from rapid ejaculation, however, the
antidepressant may ‘cure’ this problem. Some street drugs such as
marijuana, amphetamines and cocaine enhance sexual functioning.
Others, such as opioids and anabolic steroids, interfere with sexual
functioning.
Table 41.4 Effects of medications on sexual function
Nurses and the person taking the medication must familiarise
themselves with the specific medication prescribed or used because
effects vary in each category of drug.
Sexual desire disorders
*


For most people, sexual desire varies from day to day as well as
over the years. Some people, however, report a deficiency in or
absence of sexual fantasies and persistently low interest or a total
lack of interest in sexual activity. These people suffer from
hypoactive sexual desire disorder
. If both individuals in a
relationship are similarly uninterested in sex, there really is no
problem (O’Sullivan & Vannier
). More typically, there is a disparity
of sexual needs and the person with the greater desire becomes
dissatisfied with the sexual relationship. The key issue in the
relationship is not frequency but rather the dovetailing of partners’
needs.
19 O’Sullivan, L. F. & Vannier, S. A. (2016). Women’s sexual desire and desire disorders from
a developmental perspective. Current Sexual Health Reports, 8, 47–56. Doi: 10.1007/s11930-
016-0070-5.
Sexual aversion disorder
 is a severe distaste for sexual activity
or the thought of sexual activity, which then leads to a phobic
avoidance of sex. It occurs in both women and men. Intense
emotional dread of an impending sexual interaction can also trigger
the physiological symptoms of anxiety: sweating, increased heart
rate and extreme muscle tension. The person then stops the sexual
interaction or prevents it from even beginning. The cause of sexual
aversion disorder is usually some type of psychological trauma such
as rape. The severe trauma can lead to a phobic response to sexual
activity (Wohl & Kirschen ).
20 Wohl, A. & Kirschen, G. W. (2018). Betrayal of the body: Group approaches to hypo-
sexuality for adult female sufferers of childhood sexual abuse. Journal of Child Sexual Abuse,
19
20


27(2), 154–160. Doi: 10.1080/10538712.2018.1435597.
Sexual arousal disorders
Sexual arousal refers to the physiological responses and subjective
sense of excitement experienced during sexual activity. Lack of
lubrication and failure to attain or maintain an erection are the major
disorders of the arousal phase. In female sexual arousal
disorder
, the lack of vaginal lubrication causes discomfort or pain
during sexual intercourse. The diagnosis of male erectile
disorder
 is usually made when the man has erection problems
during 25% or more of his sexual interactions. Some men cannot
attain a full erection and others lose their erection prior to orgasm.
The term commonly applied to this condition, impotency, implies that
the man is feeble, inadequate and incompetent. The accurate term
is erectile dysfunction (ED), which is objectively descriptive and non-
judgmental. The incidence of ED is somewhere between 32% and
80%, depending on the age group studied, with older men reporting
increased rates of ED (Colson et al.
). Arousal disorder may also
be diagnosed even when lubrication and erection are adequate if
individuals report a persistent or recurring lack of subjective sexual
excitement or pleasure.
21 Colson, M. H., Cuzin, B., Faix, A., Grellet, L. & Huyghes, E. (2018). Current epidemiology
of erectile dysfunction, an update. Sexologies, 27(1), e7–e13. Doi:
10.1016/j.sexol.2018.01.018.
21


Orgasmic disorders
The term commonly applied in the past to women who did not
experience orgasm, frigid, implied that the woman was totally
incapable of responding sexually. The more accurate and objective
term is female orgasmic disorder
, which simply means that the
sexual response stops before orgasm occurs. Symptoms of this
disorder include infrequent or absent orgasms or a decrease in the
intensity of the orgasm in at least 75% of interactions over a period
of 6 months or more (Faubion & Rullo 2015). Compounding this
difficulty is the associated anxiety. In the preoccupation with orgasm,
the real goal of being sexual—mutual pleasuring and intimacy—is
lost and the interchange becomes one of anxiety, frustration and
anger (Faubion & Rullo 2015).
Drug capsule
Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitor sildenafil
citrate (Viagra); tadalafil (Cialis); vardenafil (Levitra or
Staxyn)
The person taking medication for
erectile dysfunction (ED)
In erectile dysfunction (ED), the sexually stimulated penis
does not achieve or maintain an erection, often due to


restricted blood flow to the penis. These medications inhibit
the breakdown of the enzymes and products that allow
muscle relaxation which, in turn, facilitates adequate blood
flow to the penis. Thus, the medications do not enhance
sexual desire or cure the ED but allow the stimulated penis to
obtain and sustain an erection.
Nursing responsibilities
ED medications are contraindicated for men with
uncontrolled high or low blood pressure, stroke, renal or
liver problems, vision loss or bleeding disorders.
Men with an anatomically deformed penis should consult
with their doctor prior to taking these medications.
Medications come in different dose strengths and may
require adjustment.
Person prescribed the medication
and family teaching
General safety in using these medications is the same as
for engaging in sexual activity overall. The risk of adverse
outcomes of sexual activity after taking these medications
is not increased.
Explain that men who take medications that are nitrates—
those that are prescribed (e.g. nitroglycerine) or those


that are recreational (e.g. amyl nitrate ‘poppers’)—should
not take these medications.
The person should take the medication about 1 hour prior
to sexual activity (up to 4 hours prior) and not more than
once per day.
Teach the person side effects to immediately report to the
doctor: loss of vision or an erection that lasts more than 4
hours. In the case of the latter, the man may wish to first
try taking a shower, refraining from sexual activity or
emptying his bladder prior to seeking medical assistance.
Other common side effects may include headache,
muscle pain, flushing or stuffy nose.
These medications do not prevent pregnancy or STIs.
Note: prior to administering any medication, review all
aspects with a current drug handbook or other reliable
source; you may find the online MIMS or Australian
Medicines Handbook helpful for this revision.
Some men suffer from male orgasmic disorder
. Men with this
disorder can maintain an erection for long periods (an hour or more)
but have extreme difficulty ejaculating, referred to as retarded
ejaculation. In heterosexual intercourse, the difficulty may be limited
to the inability to ejaculate in the vagina. Some men ejaculate after
self-stimulation or manual or oral stimulation by the partner, whereas
others have great difficulty ejaculating with any type of stimulation.
This disorder is much less common than rapid ejaculation.


Rapid ejaculation is one of the most common sexual dysfunctions
among men. There are many definitions, with descriptions ranging
from ejaculating before being touched, ejaculating before
penetration, ejaculating with one internal thrust, to ejaculating within
a minute or two of penetration. A more helpful description is the
absence of voluntary control of ejaculation. The problem is best self-
defined as when a man is concerned about his ejaculatory control or
the couple agrees that ejaculation is too rapid for mutual
satisfaction.
Sexual pain disorders
Both women and men can experience dyspareunia
, pain during
or immediately after intercourse. It is associated with many
physiological causes, especially those that inhibit lubrication. Thus,
skin irritations, vaginal infections, oestrogen deficiencies and use of
medications that dry vaginal secretions can cause women to
experience discomfort with intercourse.
Pelvic disorders, such as infections, lesions, endometriosis, scar
tissue or tumours, can result in painful intercourse. Similarly, in
males, infection or inflammation of the glans penis or other
genitourinary organs can cause pain with intercourse. Also, some
contraceptive foams, creams, sponges or latex products can irritate
either the vagina or penis.


Vaginismus
 is the involuntary spasm of the outer one-third of the
vaginal muscles, making penetration of the vagina painful and
sometimes impossible. The woman often experiences desire,
excitement and orgasm with stimulation of the external sexual
structures. Attempts at intercourse, however, elicit the involuntary
spasm. She may have similar difficulty undergoing pelvic exams and
inserting tampons or a diaphragm.
Vulvodynia
 is constant, unremitting burning that is localised to
the vulva with an acute onset. The girl or woman can have problems
in sitting, standing and sleeping related to the intensity of pain.
Vestibulitis
 causes severe pain only on touch or attempted
vaginal entry. Half of the women with vestibulitis report lifelong
dyspareunia. Women with either of these disorders report a negative
impact on their sexual functioning and partner relationship, as well
as their self-esteem and mental health. Partners of women with
either disorder are also at risk of sexual dissatisfaction and distress
(Bois et al.
).
22 Bois, K., Bergeron, S., Rosen, N., Mayrand, M., Brassard, A. & Sadikaj, G. (2016).
Intimacy, sexual satisfaction, and sexual distress in vulvodynia couples: An observational
study. Health Psychology, 35(6), 531–540. Doi: 10.1037/hea0000289.
Problems with satisfaction
Some people experience sexual desire, arousal and orgasm and yet
feel dissatisfied with their sexual relationships. These sexual
22


problems are more commonly related to the emotional tone of the
relationship than to the physiological response. Because giving and
receiving pleasure in a mutually intimate relationship are the primary
goals of sex for most people, dissatisfaction problems
 may be
more disturbing than other types of sexual dysfunctions.
At times, satisfaction problems may be situational. For example, one
partner may choose an inconvenient time, or a partner may feel
anxious and therefore cannot experience much pleasure or joy.
Some people describe their problems as related to lack of
extragenital satisfaction. These people describe how much they miss
and continue to need all the touching and caressing of their earlier
lovemaking experiences. Unfortunately, people who have been
relating sexually for a long time often become genitally focused and
neglect the rest of the body. One or both partners may feel touch-
starved, long for more extragenital loving and become dissatisfied
with sex.
Satisfaction problems are often related to relationship difficulties.
The inability to communicate effectively in other relationship areas
frequently results in sexual frustration. Partners who are angry with
each other and make love without resolving the conflict may feel
unhappy about the relationship despite having experienced arousal
and orgasm. Couples who define their relationship in terms of rigid,
unequal power and gender roles may have difficulty negotiating and
compromising about sexual issues. Not infrequently, the person with
the least amount of power feels helpless and dissatisfied with the
sexual interchanges.


Lack of intimacy or a feeling of connectedness is understandably
related to satisfaction problems. If one has sex with a stranger, the
body may function well, but there is often a sense of something
missing after the sexual experience. Making love to one person
while feeling more attracted to or in love with another person can
result in feelings of emptiness or disconnection. Even couples in a
committed relationship may complain of lack of intimacy.
Dissatisfaction issues include lack of romance, love, tenderness and
nurturance. Fulfilment of sexuality, then, depends on the ability to
relate to a partner in an intimate and mutually pleasing manner that
is compatible with values and chosen lifestyle.


Nursing management
Assessing
Because sexuality and sexual functioning are aspects of health and
wellbeing, they are a part of nursing care and need to be assessed.
Individuals are often hesitant to introduce the topic of sex with their
nurse or doctor. They may be too embarrassed; they may think that
they should not have sexual problems in our liberated times; or they
may think that they are too old or too young to have these problems.
When health care professionals do not introduce the topic, these
individuals are unrecognised and unserved.
Information about a person’s sexual health status should always be
an integral part of a nursing assessment. The amount and kind of
data collected will depend on the context of the assessment; that is,
the individual’s reason for seeking health care and how the person’s
sexuality interacts with other problems.
Generally, the nurse conducts a sexual history on the following
categories of people:
those receiving care for pregnancy, infertility, contraception or an
STI


those whose illness or therapy will affect sexual functioning (e.g.
people with diabetes, gynaecological problems or heart disease)
those currently experiencing a sexual problem.
Nursing history
Including a sexual history as part of the general nursing history is
important for some people and not important for others. It is critical,
however, to introduce the topic of sexuality to all people in order to
give them permission to bring up any concerns or problems. All
nursing histories should at least include a question such as: ‘Have
there been any changes in your sexual functioning that might be
related to your illness or the medications you take?’. Nurses might
also facilitate communication by saying, ‘As a nurse, I’m concerned
about all aspects of your health. People often have questions about
sexual matters, both when they are well and when they are ill. When
I take your history, sexual concerns are included to help plan a
comprehensive treatment approach’.
It is critical that nurses not make assumptions about people because
such assumptions interfere with accurate history taking. If you
assume that all people do all things, you will be more open to
individuals than if you make assumptions about who is, and who is
not, sexually active and how. Likewise, imposing personal values on
others is detrimental to the therapeutic relationship and can lead to
the nurse obtaining inaccurate information.


Interviewing a person regarding sexual health may be uncomfortable
for some nurses (and for the person). Nurses must be aware of their
own feelings and beliefs so that they can prepare approaches for
gathering data and creating the nursing care plan. The nurse sets
aside personal values about sexual practices and uses a culturally
safe, non-judgmental, non-threatening and reassuring approach. It is
extremely important to create an atmosphere that facilitates open
communication and comfort for the person. Remind the person that
all personal health information is handled in a confidential manner.
Also see Chapter 5
 for a review of values clarification and
Chapter 12
 for more information on the health history.
The accompanying ‘Assessment interview
’ provides questions
that nurses may ask as part of the health history. These questions
typically are asked in the assessment process after rapport with the
individual has been established.
Patient safety competency framework
1 Person-centred care
Nursing students must be able to demonstrate
an ability to provide holistic care that takes into
account the person’s current situation, previous
experiences and life history (Levett-Jones et
al.
).
23


23 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Assessment interview
Sexual health history
Are you currently sexually active? With men, women or
both?
With one or more than one partner?
Describe the positive and negative aspects of your sexual
functioning.
Do you have difficulty with sexual desire? Arousal?
Orgasm? Satisfaction?
Do you experience any pain with sexual interaction?
If there are problems, how have they influenced how you
feel about yourself? How have they affected your partner?
How have they affected the relationship?
Do you expect your sexual functioning to be altered
because of your illness?
What are your partner’s concerns about your future
sexual functioning?
Do you have any other questions or concerns that I have
not addressed?


Physical examination
Physical examination of the female genitals and reproductive tract
and the male genitals is part of a routine physical examination in
some health services. Check your local health service for its current
policy. See Chapter 31
 for details of the examination. If the
individual has not been examined in the past year or if data from the
recent nursing history indicate a need, the nurse performs a physical
examination. Nursing history data indicating the need for a physical
examination include the following:
suspicion of infertility, pregnancy or an STI
reports of discharge, presence of a lump or sore, or change in
colour, size and shape of a genital organ
changes in urinary function
need for an HPV test
request for birth control.
Identifying people at risk
People at risk of altered sexual patterns include those experiencing
the following:
altered body structure or function due to disability, trauma,
surgery, anatomical abnormalities of the genitals or a variety of
diseases


physical, psychosocial, emotional or sexual abuse; sexual assault
disfiguring conditions, such as burns, skin conditions, birthmarks,
scars (e.g. mastectomy) and stomas (e.g. colostomy)
specific medication regimens that are known to cause sexual
problems (see Table 41.4
)
temporary or long-term impaired physical ability to perform
grooming and maintain sexual attractiveness
value conflicts between personal beliefs and religious doctrine
loss of a partner
lack of knowledge or misinformation about sexual functioning and
expression.
Diagnosing
Nursing diagnoses relating specifically to sexuality include:
Ineffective sexuality pattern
Sexual dysfunction.
Examples of clinical applications of these diagnoses are shown in
the table ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and
interventions’.
Sexual problems can also be the aetiology of other diagnoses,
including the following:


Deficient knowledge (e.g. about conception, STIs, contraception
or normal sexual changes over the lifespan) related to
misinformation and sexual myths.
Pain related to inadequate vaginal lubrication or the effects of
genital surgery.
Anxiety related to loss of sexual desire or functioning.
Fear related to history of sexual abuse or dyspareunia.
Disturbed body image (e.g. mastectomy) related to perceived
sexual rejection by spouse.
Planning
Overall goals to meet the individual’s sexual needs include the
following:
Maintain, restore or improve sexual health.
Increase knowledge of sexuality and sexual health.
Prevent the occurrence or spread of STIs.
Prevent unwanted pregnancy.
Increase satisfaction with the level of sexual functioning.
Improve sexual self-concept.
Examples of specific desired outcomes related to some of these
goals are provided in ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and
interventions’. Nursing interventions to promote sexual health and
function focus largely on the nurse’s teaching role. For example, the
nurse encourages the person to learn about normal sexual function,


the effects of medications on sexual function, preventing STIs and
performing breast self-examination. In addition to teaching, nurses
can do the following to help the person maintain a healthy sexual
self-concept:
Provide privacy during intimate body care.
Involve the person’s partner in physical care.
Give attention to the person’s appearance and dress.
Give the person privacy to meet their sexual needs alone or with
a partner within physically safe limits.
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
People with sexuality problems
History Chloe Fisher, 55 years old, reports vaginal burning
and pain whenever she and her husband have intercourse.
Her last period was 14 months ago. She says her husband is
concerned about her lack of libido.
Remember that the person’s comfort in discussing sex-related topics
and being examined is culturally influenced. Culture and age often
interact in determining some sexual practices, as previously
discussed, and will affect a person’s ability to openly discuss their
sexual practices with the nurse.


Implementing
The interventions the nurse selects are based on the data obtained
from the person and the identified nursing diagnoses. Many
interventions are directed at providing information about sexual
health and counselling for altered sexual function.
Nurses require six basic skills to help people in the area of sexuality:
1. self-knowledge and comfort with their own sexuality
2. acceptance of sexuality as an important area for nursing
intervention and a willingness to work with people who
express their sexuality in a variety of ways
3. knowledge of sexual growth and development throughout the
life cycle
4. knowledge of basic sexuality, including how certain health
problems and treatments may affect sexuality and sexual
function, and which interventions facilitate sexual expression
and functioning
5. therapeutic communication skills
6. ability to recognise the need for all individuals and their family
members to have the topic of sexuality introduced not only in
written or audiovisual materials but also in a verbal
discussion.


Clinical consideration
As a result of culture, age, gender and personal
characteristics, not every nurse will be
comfortable discussing sex with every individual.
However, it is the nurse’s responsibility to
ensure that someone introduces the topic with
the person.
Providing sexual health teaching
Providing education for sexual health is an important component of
nursing implementation. Many sexual problems exist because of
sexual ignorance; many others can be prevented with effective
sexual health teaching. Examples of important areas of teaching are
sex education, self-examination, education regarding screening
programs and responsible sexual behaviour.
Sex education
Nurses can assist people to understand their anatomy and how their
body functions. For example, understanding the anatomy of the
genitals may help women learn how their body responds to sexual
stimulation. Both men and women need to learn the kind of
stimulation that is pleasing and causes arousal. The importance of


open communication between partners should also be encouraged.
Women may also benefit from learning pelvic floor muscle (Kegel)
exercises. These exercises involve contraction and relaxation of the
pubococcygeal muscle, the muscle that contracts when a person
prevents urine flow. The benefits of pelvic floor exercises include
increased pelvic floor muscle tone, increased vaginal lubrication
during sexual arousal, increased sensation during intercourse,
increased genital sensitivity, stronger gripping of the base of the
penis, earlier postpartum recovery of the pelvic floor muscle and
increased flexibility of episiotomy scars (Basgol & Oskay ; Kao et
al.
). The steps to perform pelvic floor exercises are discussed in
Chapter 51
 as these exercises are also used in continence
training.
24 Basgol, S. & Oskay, U. (2016). Examining the effectiveness of home-based pelvic floor
muscle training in treating sexual dysfunction in women. International Journal of Caring
Sciences, 9(1), 135–143. Retrieved from <http://search.proquest.com>.
25 Kao, H., Hayter, M., Hinchliff, S., Tsai, C. & Hsu, M. (2015). Experience of pelvic floor
muscle exercises among women in Taiwan: A qualitative study of improvement in urinary
incontinence and sexuality. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 24(13–14), 1985–1994. Doi:
10.1111/jocn.12783.
Details about physiological changes that occur during major
developmental crises should be provided as part of general health
care. For example, the nurse needs to discuss the effects of
puberty, pregnancy, menopause and the male climacteric on sexual
function. When the person experiences illness or surgery that may
alter sexual function, the nurse needs to discuss effects of treatment
(e.g. medications) and any changes that need to be undertaken to
24
25


ensure safe sex (e.g. position changes or a safe time to resume
sexual intercourse after a myocardial infarction (heart attack)).
Parents often need assistance to learn ways to answer questions
and what information to provide for their children, starting in the
preschool years. Parents need to be the primary educators of
children at an early age; however, peers, teachers, media and toys
also teach about sexual issues.
Although there is an increasing awareness today of sexuality and
sexual functioning, some people still hold certain myths and
misconceptions about sexuality. Many of these are handed down in
families and are part of the beliefs in a particular culture. It is
essential that nurses learn about the beliefs that people hold and
provide up-to-date information. The Australian government
healthdirect website provides a wealth of information on various
aspects of sexuality (see ‘Web links
’ at the end of this chapter).
Teaching self-examination
Monthly breast self-examination (BSE) for women can play an
important role in the early detection of breast cancer, resulting in a
greater chance of cure and less complex treatment. Women need to
be assured that most lumps and physical changes discovered are
not cancerous, but it is essential that all lumps and physical changes
or other detected abnormalities be checked by the woman’s doctor
for accurate diagnosis. All nursing history assessments need to


include the woman’s understanding and practice of BSE. Self-
examination involves both inspection and palpation.
For BSE, a regular time is best—such as 1 week following
menstruation, when breast tenderness and fullness caused by fluid
retention has usually subsided, or on the same day of the month for
postmenopausal women. People who examine themselves regularly
become familiar with the shape and texture of their breasts. The
steps of BSE are very similar to those used when the nurse
performs breast examination (see Skill 31.14
 in Chapter 31
).
For specific techniques of BSE, see ‘Patient education
’.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend testicular self-
examination (TSE) as a preventive screening activity for men.
Studies have found that there is no increase in the detection of
testicular cancer in men who perform monthly testicular self-exams;
hence, this practice is no longer routinely recommended (Royal
Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP)
).
26 Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) (2018). Guidelines for
Preventive Activities in General Practice (9th ed.). East Melbourne: RACGP. Retrieved from
<www.racgp.org.au>.
Education regarding screening programs
When teaching BSE, the nurse should also remind women aged
between 50 and 74 years of the BreastScreen Australia program for
early breast cancer detection. With this program, free mammogram
screening every 2 years is available to Australian women who are in
26


this age category (Department of Health ). Mammograms may also
be indicated for women who are between 40 and 49 years of age or
over 75 after discussion with the woman’s general practitioner.
Mammograms for women who are younger than 40 are not normally
recommended due to denser breast tissue; however, ultrasounds
may be recommended for younger women who detect a change in
their breast or have a familial history of breast cancer. An increase in
the frequency of mammography, ultrasound screening and/or
magnetic resonance imaging may also be required for women who
are at a high risk of developing breast cancer (RACGP 2018).
27 Department of Health (2015). BreastScreen Australia. Retrieved from <www.
cancerscreening.gov.au>.
Responsible sexual behaviour
Responsible sexual behaviour involves the prevention of STIs, the
prevention of unwanted pregnancy and the avoidance of sexual
harassment or abuse.
STI prevention
The prevention of STIs is an essential part of sexual health teaching.
Increases in these diseases are due to two factors: (1) changing
sexual morals that have permitted increased sexual activity; and (2)
an increase in the number of sexual partners. Because the term
sexually transmissible infection elicits feelings of guilt, shame and
fear, people frequently do not seek medical help as early as they
27


should. People need education about these diseases, preventive
measures and early treatment. An example of a preventive measure
is Gardasil, which is a vaccination used to prevent HPV. This
vaccination is available as part of the National Immunisation
Program and is free to adolescents (Cancer Council ). HPV is
linked to an increased risk of women developing some forms of
cervical cancer; hence, it is hoped that cervical cancer rates will
decrease in Australia in coming years.
28 Cancer Council (2019). Cervical Cancer. Retrieved from <www.cancer.org.au>.
Patient education
Breast self-examination
Look
While standing in front of the mirror with shoulders back and
hands on hips:
Check for changes in size, shape and colour of both
breasts.
Note if there is any dimpling, puckering or bulging of skin.
Be aware of whether the nipple has changed position or if
it has inverted.
Monitor for redness, soreness, rashes or swelling.
Repeat this inspection while the arms are raised in the air.
28


Press
Apply minimal pressure with the thumb and forefinger to each
nipple and check for discharge (milky, yellow fluid or blood).
Feel
Feel your breast while lying down, sitting, standing or in the
shower:
Use a method which you become familiar with and record
your observations on a monthly basis.
When checking the left breast use your right hand (right
breast use your left hand) and work gently on the top
layer and then a little firmer as you press deeper into the
tissue with your middle three fingers feeling down to the
ribcage.
Be sure to check all over your breast with a sequence you
can remember; from the armpit to your cleavage and from
the top of the collarbone to top of your stomach, all the
time feeling for irregular lumps, lumpiness or thickening,
particularly in one breast only.
Source: Adapted from Breast Cancer Care Western Australia
. Being Breast Aware. Retrieved from
<www.breastcancer.org.au/about-breast-cancer/being-breast-aware.aspx>.
29 Breast Cancer Care Western Australia (2013). Being Breast Aware. Retrieved from
<www.breastcancer.org.au>.
While many STIs can be treated quickly and effectively, others may
have serious consequences. For example, women may develop
29


pelvic inflammatory disease resulting in damage to the reproductive
structures and possible infertility if an STI is left untreated.
Clinical consideration
The National Cervical Screening Program
recommendations have recently changed. From
1 December 2017, biennial routine Pap test
screening for women was replaced with HPV
testing every 5 years for all women (regardless
of vaccination status) between the ages of 25
(or 2 years after the woman first becomes
sexually active) and 74. The procedure for
sample collection is the same as a Pap smear.
Nurses have a key role promoting these
important preventive changes.
The ‘Clinical manifestations
’ feature earlier in this chapter lists
common signs of STIs for which people should seek medical care.
Methods for decreasing exposure to STIs are described in ‘Patient
education
’.
Prevention of unwanted pregnancies


Prevention of unwanted pregnancies must be addressed not only
with adolescents but also with couples who are not wanting children
or are planning the time of births, wanting to space children or limit
family size. Nurses need to be familiar with various contraceptive
methods and their advantages, disadvantages, contraindications,
effectiveness, safety and cost (see Figure 41.3
). The various
methods are outlined in Box 41.3
. It is beyond the scope of this
text to discuss contraceptives in detail. The Family Planning
Associations in each state can provide you with the most up-to-date
information on contraception.
Figure 41.3


Methods of contraception.
BO X


41.3 Methods of contraception
Abstinence.
Mechanical barriers: vaginal diaphragm, dental dam,
female and male condom. (Note: there are three types of
condom materials: latex, lambskin and polyurethane. All
are equally effective at preventing pregnancy. Latex
condoms are the least expensive. Lambskin pore size
does not protect against STIs as well as the others.
Polyurethane condoms are recommended if contact with
latex should be avoided. Polyurethane is the material used
in female condoms.)
Intrauterine devices (IUDs).
Intrauterine systems (IUSs). Similar to an IUD; however, it
releases progesterone (rather than copper) to prevent
pregnancy.
Hormonal: oral contraceptives (combined contraceptive
pill or progesterone-only ‘mini’ contraceptive pill);
contraceptive implants and injections; vaginal rings.
Emergency contraception: ‘morning after pill’.
Surgical sterilisation: tubal ligation, tubal occlusion and
vasectomy.
Natural family planning (identification of the days of the
month when conception is most likely to occur and
abstaining during that time).


Counselling for altered sexual function
One technique nurses can use to help people with altered sexual
function is the PLISSIT model, developed by Annon  for this
purpose. The model involves four progressive levels represented by
the acronym PLISSIT:
30 Annon, J. (1974). The Behavioural Treatment of Sexual Problems. Vol. 1. Brief Therapy.
New York: Harper & Row.
Patient education
Preventing transmission of STIs and HIV
Be vaccinated against HPV with Gardasil.
Limit the number of sexual partners.
Use condoms in non-monogamous or casual relationships
that have the potential for STI transmission.
Follow safe-sex practices during oral sex, including the
use of a latex dental dam during cunnilingus to prevent
STI transmission.
Talk openly with sexual partners about how to have ‘safer
sex’ and be honest about any history of an STI.
Abstain from high-risk sexual activity with a partner known
to have or suspected of having an STI.
Report to a health care facility for examination whenever
in doubt about possible exposure or when signs of an STI
are evident.
30


When an STI is diagnosed, notify all partners and
encourage them to seek treatment.
At each level, the nurse provides additional guidance and
information to the person and therefore requires more specialised
and specific knowledge and skill. All Registered Nurses should be
able to function at the first three levels. At the levels of limited
information, specific suggestions and intensive therapy, the nurse
can also refer the person to a health care provider more skilled to
assist the individual with the particular issues identified during the
first level.
Permission giving
People may feel that they need permission to be sexual beings, to
ask questions, to show affection and to express themselves
sexually. Giving permission means that the nurse by attitude or word
lets the person know that sexual thoughts, fantasies and behaviours
between informed consenting adults are allowed. Giving permission
begins when the nurse acknowledges the individual’s spoken and
unspoken sexual concerns and conveys the attitude that sexual
concerns and needs are important to health and recovery.
For example, the nurse might ask a person recuperating from a
myocardial infarction the following questions:
Now that you’re recuperating and you’ve had some time to sort out your feelings, have you
thought about how your heart attack might alter your sex life?


Have you and your partner discussed how you both feel about it?
Limited information
People need accurate but concise information. The nurse might
explain what is normal; how some medical conditions, treatments,
injuries or surgeries may affect sexuality and sexual functioning; or
how ageing may affect sexuality and functioning.
Continuing with the prior example, the nurse shares information and
informs the person about how the myocardial infarction may affect
the person’s sex life, including the following:
Your heart attack will not change your sexual responsiveness. Most people can resume
intercourse in 4 to 6 weeks, but this should be confirmed by your doctor. If you can climb a
flight of stairs without having chest pain you should be able to resume having sex because
it takes about the same amount of energy.
Many heart attack survivors fear sexual intercourse because of the physical exertion
associated with it. However, your prescribed program of progressive physical activity will
also increase your tolerance for sexual activity.
Many people recuperating from surgery, illnesses or diseases (e.g.
post-spinal surgery) need instruction about safe sexual activities and
the effects that therapy may have on sexual functioning. The
following topics need to be considered:
when sexual activity is safe
specific sexual activities that are unsafe and why


adaptations needed for resuming a satisfactory sexual life
the side effects of prescribed medications on sexual functioning
and the need to notify the doctor for possible dose or medication
adjustment should problems develop.
Specific suggestions
At this level, the nurse requires specialised knowledge and skill
about how sexuality and functioning may be affected by a disease
process or therapy and what interventions might be effective. The
nurse offers suggestions to help the person adapt sexual activity to
promote optimal functioning, such as what measures might be used
to alleviate vaginal dryness, safe and unsafe positions for
intercourse that consider the person’s physical condition and
postoperative orders/restrictions; and ways to handle stoma
appliances, urinary catheters, casts or other devices (e.g.
prostheses) during sexual activity. Similarly, nurses who work on a
cardiac unit need specialised knowledge about sexual readjustment
during cardiac rehabilitation and nurses working with people with
spinal cord injuries need information about the sexual consequences
of spinal injuries at various levels.
Using the prior example of the person recuperating from a
myocardial infarction, the nurse may offer the following suggestion:
Many people express concern about the stress of certain positions for intercourse but you
may use whatever position is comfortable for you and your partner, or try side-lying or
partner-on-top positions.


Intensive therapy
At this level of intervention, nurses must have specialised
preparation and knowledge of sexual and gender identity disorders.
Prior to referring the person for intensive therapy with a sex
counsellor or therapist, it is important that the nurse validates the
person’s concerns and seeks permission for the referral. Referrals
should be to reputable practitioners such as those who are members
of professional organisations such as the Australian Society of Sex
Educators, Researchers and Therapists (ASSERT).
Sex counselling helps people incorporate their sexual knowledge into
satisfying lifestyles and socially responsible behaviour. Sex therapy
is a highly specialised, in-depth treatment to help the individual
resolve serious sexual problems.
Dealing with inappropriate sexual
behaviour
Nurses, both male and female, may encounter a variety of sexually
inappropriate behaviours for a number of reasons. The behaviour
may be either aggressive or non-aggressive. Individuals may act out
sexually by:
exposing themselves
asking the nurse to provide intimate physical care, such as
bathing genital areas, when they are capable of doing this


themselves
touching or grabbing the nurse’s genitals or buttocks
making blatant sexual statements to the nurse
offering the nurse sex
whistling; making comments about the nurse’s attractiveness or
desirability
making sexual comments to another person in the same room or
to visitors about the ‘sexy’ nurse or what they would like to do
sexually with the nurse.
Possible reasons for this inappropriate behaviour are:
fear or anxiety over future ability to function sexually
unmet needs for intimacy and sexual closeness because of
hospitalisation, injury, illness, treatment, lack of a partner or lack
of privacy
misinterpretation of the nurse’s behaviour as sexual or
provocative
need for reassurance that they are still sexual beings and are still
sexually attractive
need for attention
confusion: neurological impairment or trauma can lead the
person to use profane sexual language, engage in masturbation,
expose themselves or inappropriately touch or grab at the nurse
need to control: the person may be experiencing loss of control
over their lives because of hospitalisation, injury or illness
need for power


belief that flirtatious behaviour is expected due to the stereotype
of nurses as sexy, available and experienced.
Before implementing any nursing interventions, the nurse should first
ensure that the behaviour is inappropriate and not an attempt to
communicate a physical need. For example, the person may expose
themself if they are febrile, pull at the penis if a catheter is
uncomfortable or irritating, or reach for the nurse if unable to
communicate verbally. Nursing strategies to deal with inappropriate
sexual behaviour are listed in Box 41.4
.
BO X
41.4 Nursing strategies for
inappropriate sexual behaviour
Communicate that the behaviour is not acceptable by
saying, for example, ‘I do not like the things you are
saying’, or ‘I see you are not dressed. I will be back in 10
minutes and will help you with breakfast when you get
your clothes on’.
Tell the person how the behaviour makes you feel: ‘When
you act like that towards me, I am very uncomfortable. It
embarrasses me and makes it hard for me to give you the
kind of nursing care you need’.
Identify the behaviour you expect: ‘Please call me by my
name, not “honey”’; or ‘I expect you to keep yourself


covered when I am in the room. If you are feeling hot or
something is uncomfortable, let me know and I will try to
make you more comfortable’.
Set firm limits. Take the person’s hand and move it away,
use direct eye contact and say, ‘Don’t do that!’.
Try to refocus the individual from the inappropriate
behaviour to their real concerns and fears; offer to
discuss sexuality concerns: ‘All morning you have been
making very personal sexual comments about yourself.
Sometimes people talk like that when they are concerned
about the sexual part of their life and how their illness will
affect them. Are there things that you have questions
about or would like to talk about?’.
Report the incident to your educator, nurse unit manager
or clinical nurse specialist. Discuss the incident, your
feelings and possible interventions.
Assign a nurse who will confront the behaviour and relate
to the person in a consistent manner.
Clarify the consequences of continued inappropriate
behaviour (avoidance, withdrawal of services, no
opportunity to help resolve underlying concerns of
person).
Evaluating


The goals established during the planning phase are evaluated
according to specific desired outcomes also established during that
phase. If any outcomes have not been achieved, the nurse should
explore the reasons with questions such as the following:
Were risk factors correctly identified?
Did the individual convey all significant fears and concerns about
sexuality?
Was the person more comfortable following discussions about
sexual matters?
Did the person understand the nurse’s teaching?
Was the health teaching compatible with the person’s culture and
religious values?
Was the person ready to deal with sexuality problems?
Case study
Mr Curry is a 50-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus
who suffered a myocardial infarction 6 weeks ago. He is
doing well and is in a cardiac rehabilitation program. His
diabetes is controlled with diet and his only medications
consist of a daily aspirin and an antihypertensive medication.
During a routine check-up you inquire how he is feeling and
whether he is doing well on his medications. Reluctantly, he
admits that he is having some sexual problems. You
encourage further discussion of the matter by displaying
interest and explaining that it is okay for him to share his


concerns with you. Mr Curry states that he is having some
difficulty achieving erections but is more concerned that he
will have another heart attack if he engages in sexual
activities.
Fundamentals of care framework in
context


1.
 Discuss why Mr Curry may be reluctant to
discuss his sexual concerns. Using the Fundamentals
of Care Framework, what strategies would you use to
establish a therapeutic relationship with Mr Curry to
help him overcome his reluctance to discuss his sexual
concerns?
2. What factors influence nurses’ abilities to discuss
sexual concerns with individuals?
3. What is the relationship between health and sexual
function?
4. How can you best intervene to help Mr Curry?


Chapter 41 Review


Chapter highlights
Sexuality is important in developing self-identity, interpersonal
relationships, intimacy and love.
There is a tremendous range of variation in how people express
their sexuality including sexual orientation, gender identity, erotic
preferences and sexual lifestyles.
Factors that affect sexuality include developmental level, family,
culture, religious values, personal expectations and ethics,
disease processes, medications and relationship problems.
Sexual problems include desire disorders, arousal disorders,
orgasmic disorders, problems with satisfaction and sexual pain
disorders.
Assessing risk of or actual sexual problems is part of the initial
nursing assessment. Further assessment is carried out when
individuals or their significant other present cues that problems
exist or when individuals have an illness that could cause sexual
problems.
Nurses assess attitudes towards sexuality, including factors that
affect attitudes and behaviours.
Before assisting individuals with sexual problems, nurses must
acquire accurate information about sexuality, identify and accept
their own sexual values and behaviours as well as those of
others and be comfortable acquiring and disseminating
information about sexuality.
Nursing diagnoses for the person with sexual problems are
related to many contributing factors, including altered body


structure or function, lack of knowledge or misinformation about
sexual matters, physical or psychological abuse, value conflicts
and loss or lack of a partner.
Nursing interventions focus largely on teaching the person about
sexual function and sexuality, responsible sexual behaviour that
includes the prevention of STIs and unwanted pregnancies.
Counselling individuals with altered sexual functions can be
facilitated by using the PLISSIT model: permission giving (P),
