limited information (LI) and specific suggestions (SS). Intensive
therapy (IT) requires intervention by clinical nurse specialists or
sex therapists.

1. They assume that health care providers know little
about sexual functioning.
2. Most people have few, if any, questions or problems.
3. Females prefer to discuss problems with female health
care providers.
4. They are too embarrassed to introduce the topic of
sex.
2. A nurse is caring for a trans person. Appropriate care is
based on the knowledge that which of the following is most
representative of this person?


1. Gonadal gender, internal organs and external genitals
are contradictory.

3. Sexual attraction is to individuals of both genders.

4. Masturbation is a way people learn about their sexual
response.

Which of the following should be included in the teaching?
1. ‘Your partner will be pleased because your sexual

2. ‘You may find that your desire for sex will decrease
while on this medication.’
3. ‘Retrograde ejaculation is a common problem when

4. ‘Your skin will probably become supersensitive to touch

3. Antihypertensives (blood pressure medications).
4. Antihistamines.

This communication is most representative of which

1. Permission giving (P).


2. Limited information (LI).
3. Specific suggestions (SS).
4. Intensive therapy (IT).
9. A 75-year-old male reports decreased frequency of sexual

1. Sexual dysfunction.
2. Disturbed body image.
3. Sedentary lifestyle.
4. Readiness for enhanced knowledge.

Chapter 42 Spirituality
Kristin Wicking
Learning outcomes
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Describe the interconnection of spirituality and religion concepts
as they relate to health and spiritually sensitive nursing care.
Compare and contrast spiritual needs, spiritual distress and
spiritual health.
Describe the spiritual development of the individual across the
lifespan.
Describe the influence on health care of a person’s spiritual and
religious beliefs and practices regarding healing, holy days,


sacred texts, diet, dress, prayer, meditation, birth and death.
Describe methods to assess the spiritual and religious
preferences, strengths, concerns and/or distress of people.
Plan and implement appropriate and spiritually sensitive nursing
care to support and promote spiritual health.
Describe nursing interventions to support the spiritual and
religious beliefs and practices of people.
Identify desired outcomes for evaluating a person’s spiritual
health.
Describe strategies that can increase a nurse’s own spiritual
awareness.

Nurses provide holistic care—they care not only
for the physical body and mind but also for the
person’s spirit. Meeting the person’s spiritual
needs can help reduce suffering, provide
comfort and reassurance, and aid in physical
and mental healing. Earlier in this text, spiritual
health was defined as ‘the ability to develop
one’s inner nature to its fullest potential,
including the ability to discover and articulate
one’s basic purpose in life, to learn how to
experience love, joy, peace and fulfilment and


how to help ourselves and others achieve their
fullest potential’ (Pender, Murdaugh &
Parsons ). Consider this definition carefully for it
alludes to notions of what provides meaning and
purpose to a person’s life. During periods of
illness or when confronting death, these
moments are often the impetus for significant
self-reflection and reassessment. As Dossey,
Keegan and Guzzetta  (p. 48) state, ‘Spirituality
permeates life, shapes our life journey and is
vital to the process of discovering purpose,
meaning and inner strength’. The person’s
relationships with significant others and a higher
power are often examined during times of
illness, when one is feeling vulnerable and less
resilient. During such times, spirituality can
serve as an important coping mechanism for the
person and their family. Nurses have a vital role
as providers of sensitive and compassionate
care, and in assessing the spiritual needs of the
people to whom they provide such care.
1 Pender, N. J., Murdaugh, C. L. & Parsons, M. A. (2019).
Health Promotion in Nursing Practice (8th ed.). Upper
Saddle River, NJ: Prentice Hall.
1
2


2 Dossey, B. M., Keegan, L. & Guzzetta, C. E. (2005).
Pocket Guide for Holistic Nursing. Boston: Jones and
Bartlett Publishers.
We cannot claim to provide holistic care for
people without nurturing their spirit, a fact that is
emphasised by noting that the ‘words healing,
whole and holy derive from the same root: old
Saxon hal, meaning whole. This suggests that,
by its nature, healing is a spiritual process that
attends to the wholeness of a person’ (Dossey
et al. 2005, p. 50), thus making spirituality the
very foundation of holistic nursing. To implement
spiritual care, nurses need to be skilled in
establishing trusting relationships. Such spiritual
caregiving skill requires that the nurse possess
a healthy spiritual self-awareness. This personal
spirituality inevitably influences nursing care, as
the nurse becomes attuned to the spiritual
needs of the person and recognises that such
needs are intertwined with the person’s
physical, social and psychological dimensions.
In addition to spiritual self-awareness, nurses
need to be cognisant of the diverse spiritual
beliefs and practices that people possess.
Because such beliefs and practices are


personal coping resources, understanding how
they help or hinder a person’s health is vital. A
person’s experience with, and expression of,
what they perceive to constitute spiritual matters
may invoke issues they have previously never
discussed or even considered. Conversely,
some people may feel very comfortable
discussing spiritual matters and have a very
clear sense of their own spirituality.
Thus, each person needs to be approached in a
manner that very clearly indicates that spiritual
matters can be discussed in an open and non-
judgmental fashion. If the person expresses the
need for assistance to discuss spiritual issues,
or needs help to relieve spiritual distress, nurses
need to be able to provide spiritually sensitive
care in ways that promote spiritual and
emotional health, help with coping and
adjustment, or assist the person to face a more
peaceful death.


Spirituality and religion contrasted
Spirituality, faith and religion are separate entities, yet the words are
often used interchangeably. The word spiritual derives from the Latin
word spiritus, which means ‘to blow’ or ‘to breathe’, and has come to
connote that which gives life or essence to being human. Pesut  (p.
98) has argued that ‘spirituality is increasingly being defined by the
universal search for meaning, connectedness, energy and
transcendence’. To be human is to be a spiritual being; it is, after all,
what sets us apart from all other beings on the planet. Over recent
years, many definitions and applications of spirituality have been
proposed within the nursing and health care literature (Nahardani et
al. ; Hurlbut & Ditmyer ; Sessanna, Finnell & Jezewski ), as
researchers endeavour to describe this dimension of nursing in a
more rigorous and balanced way. Such is the difficulty in defining
and describing spirituality
 that Sessanna et al. (2007, p. 256)
conclude that it is an ‘intricate, enigmatic, abstract and ambiguous
concept’. Puchalski et al.  (p. 644) reported a definition developed
through international consensus during conferences held in
subsequent years between 2009 and 2013:

Nursing Philosophy, 9, 98–109.
4 Nahardani, S. Z., Ahmadi, F., Bigdeli, S. & Soltani Arabshahi, K. (2019). Spirituality in
medical education: A concept analysis. Medicine, Health Care, and Philosophy, 22(2), 179–
189. Doi: 10.1007/s11019-018-9867-5.
3
4
5
6
7


5 Hurlbut, J. & Ditmyer, M. (2016). Defining the meaning of spirituality through a qualitative
case study of sheltered homeless women. Nursing for Women’s Health, 20(1), 52–62. Doi:
10.1016/j.nwh.2015.12.004.
6 Sessanna, L., Finnell, D. & Jezewski, M. A. (2007). Spirituality in nursing and health-related
literature: A concept analysis. Journal of Holistic Nursing, 25(4), 252–262.
7 Puchalski, C. M., Vitillo, R., Hull, S. K. & Reller, N. (2014). Improving the spiritual dimension
of whole person care: Reaching national and international consensus. Journal of Palliative
Medicine, 17(6) 642–656. Doi: 10.1089/jpm.2014.9427.
Spirituality is the dynamic dimension of human life that relates to the way persons
(individual and community) experience, express and/or seek meaning, purpose and
transcendence, and the way they connect to the moment, to self, to others, to nature, to
the significant, and/or to the sacred.
For Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, the
concept of spirituality ‘derives from a philosophy that establishes the
holistic notion of the interconnectedness of the elements of the earth
and the universe, animate and inanimate, whereby people, the
plants and animals, landforms and celestial bodies are interrelated’
(Grieves , p. 7). Other aspects of spirituality within Australian
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures are discussed later in
this chapter.
8 Grieves, V. (2009). Aboriginal Spirituality: Aboriginal Philosophy, the Basis of Aboriginal
Social and Emotional Wellbeing. Discussion paper No. 9. Darwin: Cooperative Centre for
Aboriginal Health.
Although many people express their spirituality through religious
practices, belonging to a religion does not necessarily make one
8


‘spiritual’. Religion
 is typically an organised system of beliefs and
practices. It offers means for accessing and expressing spirituality
and provides support for believers in responding to life’s ultimate
questions and challenges. According to Vardey  (p. xv), the
organised religions offer (a) a sense of community bound by
common beliefs, (b) the collective study of scripture (the Torah,
Bible, Koran or others), (c) the performance of ritual, (d) the use of
disciplines and practices, commandments and sacraments and (e)
ways of taking care of the person’s spirit such as fasting, prayer and
meditation. Many traditional religious practices and rituals are related
to such life events as birth, transition from childhood to adulthood,
marriage, illness and death (see Figure 42.1
). Religious rules of
conduct, typically influenced concurrently by culture, may also apply
to matters of daily life such as dress, food, social interaction,
menstruation, child rearing and sexual relationships.
9 Vardey, L. (1996). God in All Worlds. Toronto: Vintage Canada.
Figure 42.1
9


Hospital chaplains minister to people and their families.
Source: © Fabiàn Cevallos/Contributor/Getty Images.
Religious development
 of an individual refers to the acceptance
of specific beliefs, values, rules of conduct and rituals. Religious
development may or may not parallel spiritual development. For
example, a person may follow certain religious practices and yet not
internalise the symbolic meaning behind the practices. Often,
religious development underpins and enhances spirituality by
providing a system of belief that can suggest areas of growth to the
believer. For example, the daily prayers of Muslims bring the


believers into direct relationship with the profound questions of life
several times per day.
An agnostic
 is a person who doubts the existence of God or a
supreme being or believes the existence of God has not been
proven. An atheist
 is a person without belief in a God.
Monotheism
 is the belief in the existence of one God, while
polytheism
 is the belief in more than one God.
Table 42.1
 describes the religious affiliation of Australians for four
recent Census periods. Over the past two decades, the
Western/traditional religions such as Catholicism, Anglicanism and
Presbyterianism have decreased, whereas religions such as
Buddhism, Hinduism and Islam have increased. This change reflects
the immigration patterns in Australia over this period. Indigenous
Australians report similar patterns of religious affiliation as non-
Indigenous Australians, with approximately 1% reporting affiliation
with Australian Indigenous traditional religions (Australian Bureau of
Statistics (ABS)
). Although conflict between their Christian spiritual
beliefs and their Indigenous spiritual traditions can occur, many
Indigenous Australians embrace the two belief systems concurrently
(Skye ).

The most recent national Census (2016) contained an altered format
for the religion question, with the option for ‘no religion’ being moved
to the top of the options available to select (ABS ). Previously, the
option for ‘no religion’ was potentially difficult to find as it was located
at the bottom of the list. The ‘no religion’ option has been chosen by
a steadily increasing proportion (3.9% per year) of the Australian
population, particularly since 1971, which was the last time the
religion question’s wording and instructions were changed (ABS
2014). In 1911, only 0.4% selected ‘no religion’, while in 2011, 22%
reported ‘no religion’ (ABS 2014). In 2016, this rate further increased
to 30.1% (ABS ). The role that religion previously played in
transmitting values, stipulating allowed and prohibited behaviours,
providing practical examples of how to embody ethical principles into

may or may not be substituted by other organisations or belief

If that crucial role remains unfilled, and no alternative spiritual
framework is adopted, nurses may find people increasingly
presenting with more spiritual distress as they attempt to reframe
and make sense of the role of illness and death in their lives.
Similarly, nurses themselves may be more poorly equipped to cope
with the secondary trauma to which they are repeatedly exposed
when caring for seriously ill and dying people, as higher scores on
religious indices have been correlated with lower rates of anxiety for
nursing students (Fabbris et al.
).

Spiritual needs
Just as everybody has a spiritual dimension, all people have needs
that reflect their spirituality. These needs are often accentuated by
an illness or other health (or life) crisis. People who have well-
defined spiritual beliefs may find that their beliefs are challenged by
their health situation or they may cling to their beliefs more firmly
and appreciatively. Those who have no defined beliefs may suddenly
come face to face with challenging questions such as ‘Why me?’ and
other existential issues such as the meaning and purpose of life.
Nurses need to be sensitive to indications of the person’s spiritual
needs and respond appropriately, as will be discussed later.
Examples of spiritual needs are listed in Box 42.1
.
BO X
42.1 Examples of spiritual needs
Needs related to the self:
need for meaning and purpose
need to express creativity
need for hope
need to transcend life challenges
need for personal dignity
need for gratitude


need for vision
need to prepare for and accept death.
Needs related to others:
need to forgive others
need to cope with loss of loved ones.
Needs related to the Ultimate Other:
need to be certain there is a God or Ultimate Power in the
universe
need to believe that God is loving and personally present
need to worship.
Needs between and within groups:
need to contribute to or improve one’s community
need to be respected and valued
need to know what and when to give and take.

. Spiritual Care: Nursing Theory, Research and Practice. Upper Saddle River,
NJ: Prentice Hall.

Spiritual wellbeing
Spiritual health
, or spiritual wellbeing
, is manifested by a
feeling of being ‘generally alive, purposeful and fulfilled’ (Ellison , p.
332). According to Pilch , spiritual wellness is ‘a way of living, a
lifestyle that views and lives life as purposeful and pleasurable, that
seeks out life-sustaining and life-enriching options to be chosen
freely at every opportunity and that sinks its roots deeply into
spiritual values and/or specific religious beliefs’ (p. 31). Spiritual
health, as defined by the Nursing Outcomes Classification project
(Moorhead, Johnson & Maas , p. 519), is the ‘connectedness with
self, others, higher power, all life, nature and the universe that
transcends and empowers the self’. Indicators of spiritual health are
shown in Box 42.2
.

Classification. St Louis, MO: Mosby.
People nurture or enhance their spirituality in many ways. Some
focus on development of the inner self; others focus on the


expression of their spiritual energy with others or the outer world.
Relating to one’s inner self or soul may be achieved by conducting
an inner dialogue with a higher power or with oneself through prayer
or meditation, by analysing dreams, by communing with nature or by
experiencing the inspiration of art (e.g. drama, music, dance). The
expression of a person’s spiritual energy to others is manifested in
loving relationships with and service to others, joy and laughter,
participation in religious services and associated fellowship
gatherings and activities, and expression of compassion, empathy,
forgiveness and hope. Nurses who attend to their own spirituality are
better able to work with people who have spiritual needs (Taylor
).
Therefore, it is important to become aware of, and comfortable with,
one’s own spirituality.
21 Taylor, E. J. (2005). What have we learned from spiritual care research? Journal of
Christian Nursing, 22(1), 22–28.
21


Spiritual distress
Spiritual distress
 refers to a challenge to the spiritual wellbeing
or to the belief system that provides strength, hope and meaning to
life. Some factors that may be associated with or contribute to a
person’s spiritual distress include physiological problems, treatment-
related concerns and situational concerns. Physiological problems
include having a medical diagnosis of a terminal or debilitating
disease, experiencing pain, experiencing the loss of a body part or
function, or experiencing a miscarriage or stillbirth. Treatment-
related factors include recommendation for blood transfusions,
abortion, surgery, dietary restrictions, amputation of a body part or
undergoing a course of chemotherapy. Situational factors include the
death or illness of a significant other, inability to practise one’s
spiritual rituals or feelings of embarrassment when practising them.


Related concepts
Because spirituality is a reflection of an inner experience that is
expressed individually, it includes as many representations as there
are human beings. Concepts related to spirituality include religion
(as discussed above), faith, hope, transcendence and forgiveness.
Faith
Faith
 is to believe in or be committed to something or someone.
Faith is present in both religious and non-religious people. Faith
gives life meaning, providing the individual with strength in times of
difficulty. For the person who is ill, faith—whether in a higher
authority (e.g. God, Allah, Jehovah), in oneself, in the health care
team or in a combination of all—provides strength and hope.
Hope
Hope
 is a concept that incorporates spirituality. Stephenson
suggested this definition: ‘a process of anticipation that involves the
interaction of thinking, acting, feeling and relating and is directed
toward a future fulfilment that is personally meaningful’ (p. 1459). In
22


the absence of hope, the person gives up, loses the will to go on
with their life, and illness is likely to progress more rapidly.
22 Stephenson, C. (1991). The concept of hope revisited for nursing. Journal of Advances in
Nursing, 16, 1456–1461.
Transcendence
The term transcendence
 is often used interchangeably with self-
transcendence, which Coward  defined as ‘the capacity to reach
out beyond oneself, to extend oneself beyond personal concerns
and to take on broader life perspectives, activities and purposes’ (p.
162). Transcendence is also thought to involve a person’s
recognition that there is something other or greater than the self and
a seeking and valuing of that greater other, whether it is an ultimate
being, a force or a value.
23 Coward, D. D. (1990). The lived experience of self-transcendence in women with
advanced breast cancer. Nursing Science Quarterly, 3(4), 162–169.
Forgiveness
The concept of forgiveness is receiving increased attention among
health care professionals. For many people illness or disability brings
a sense of shame or guilt. The health problem is interpreted as a
punishment for past sins’. The person facing imminent death may
23


seek forgiveness from others, such as from family and friends, as
well as from God. Nurses can play a pivotal role in assisting people
they care for to understand the process of forgiveness and, if
required or requested, to facilitate a process according to the
person’s wishes.


Spiritual development
Just as individuals develop physically, cognitively and morally, they
also develop spiritually. Several theologians have identified specific
linear stages through which individuals may progress while maturing
spiritually. Westerhoff
, for example, described faith as a way of
behaving that evolves from a faith guided by parents and others
during infancy and childhood to an owned faith that is internalised in
adulthood and serves as a directive for action. Table 42.2
describes some of the aspects of spiritual development
 and
healthy religious behaviours during different life stages.
24 Westerhoff, J. (2012). Will Our Children Have Faith? (3rd rev. ed.) New York: Morehouse
Publishing.
Table 42.2 Stages of spiritual development

. Stages of Faith Development: The Psychology of Human Development

Development and the Quest for Meaning (rev. ed.). San Francisco, CA: Harper & Row.

Spiritual self-awareness for the
nurse
Nurses cannot hear, never mind respond to, a person’s spiritual
need unless they hear and respond to their own need. Indeed, the
notion that effective healers are ‘wounded healers’ has long existed.
A nurse’s spiritual needs, pains or ‘woundedness’ can affect how
they care for people. Nurses who are unaware of, afraid of, or
misunderstand their spiritual needs will be very limited in their ability
to accurately identify and explore a person’s spiritual needs. When
people realise that the nurse does not understand them, they can
become quiet, change the topic, give superficial responses to
queries or may retreat in other ways.
Nurses do not need to have shared the same experience as the
person they are caring for, but to be compassionate they do need to
recognise how they have shared similar emotions. Recognising and
addressing the fears that are inevitable responses to caring for
people (e.g. our own fear of dying) are essential requisites to
providing appropriate spiritual care. Beckman et al.
 offer a variety
of strategies for nurses who wish to increase their spiritual
awareness; here are a few:
26 Beckman, S., Boxley-Harges, S., Bruick-Sorge, C. & Salmon, B. (2007). Five strategies
that heighten nurses’ awareness of spirituality to impact client care. Holistic Nursing Practice,
26


21, 135-139.
Write a self-epitaph. Sum up in a couple lines what is significant
about your life or how you would like to be remembered.
List significant values. Write down the possessions, people,
activities, roles, personal attributes and so forth that you prize
the most.
Conduct a spiritual self-assessment. Consider what gives you
strength and hope. What makes you joyful or despairing? How
do you explain or relate to suffering? What is your sense of
purpose or mission in life? What nurtures your spirit?


Spiritual practices affecting
nursing care
People frequently identify religious practices such as prayer as
important strategies for coping with illness (Hamilton et al.
; Rayo et
al.
). The most common practices affecting the nursing care of
people include holy days, sacred writings, sacred symbols, prayer,
meditation and those practices associated with diet, nutrition,
healing, dress, birth and death.
27 Hamilton, J. B., Kweon, L., Brock, L. B. & Moore, A. D. (2019). The use of prayer during
life-threatening illness: A connectedness to god, inner-self, and others. Journal of Religion and
Health. Advance online publication. Doi: 10.1007/s10943-019-00809-7.
28 Rao, A., Hickman, L. D., Jane, P. L. & Sibbritt, D. (2016). Prevalence and characteristics of
Australian women who use prayer or spiritual healing. A nationally representative cross-
sectional study. Complementary Therapies in Medicine, 27, 35–42. Doi:
10.1016/j.ctim.2016.05.005.
It is possible for nurses to unethically impose their own personal
spiritual beliefs on others in their care whose circumstances
inherently leave them vulnerable. Observing guidelines for ethical
conduct in spiritual caregiving is essential. The following guidelines
for nurses were offered by Winslow and Winslow
:
29 Winslow, G. R. & Winslow, B. W. (2003). Examining the ethics of praying with patients.
Holistic Nursing Practice, 17(4), 170–177.
27
28
29


First seek a basic understanding of the person’s spiritual needs,
resources and preferences (i.e. assess).
Follow the person’s expressed wishes regarding spiritual care.
Do not prescribe or urge people to adopt certain spiritual beliefs
or practices and do not pressure them to relinquish such beliefs
or practices.
Strive to understand personal spirituality and how it influences
caregiving.
Provide spiritual care in a way that is consonant with personal
beliefs.
Clinical consideration
While some people are eager for nurses’ overt
offers of ‘spiritual care’, others may be uncertain
or opposed to such offers. People often confuse
religiosity with spirituality; this may contribute to
their uncertainty about receiving spiritual care
from nurses. Observing and using their
language for spirituality (e.g. ‘being at peace’ or
‘faith’), as well as large measures of sensitivity
and respect, will help nurses to converse
therapeutically with people to provide spiritual
care.


Holy days
A holy day
 is a day set aside for special religious observance and
all the world religions observe certain holy days. Examples of holy
days are Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur (Jewish), Good Friday
(Christian) and the month-long Ramadan (Islam). Similarly,
Buddhists observe the birthday of the Buddha and Hindus observe
Mahashivarathri, a celebration of Lord Shiva.
Many religions require fasting, extended prayer and reflection or
ritual observances on sacred (or high holy) days. Believers who are
seriously ill are often exempted from such requirements.
Many hospitals and health organisations facilitate ritual observances
for patients and staff on holy days. Because many religions follow
calendars other than the Gregorian calendar, a multifaith calendar
can be used to identify the holy days of the various religious groups.
The concept of the Sabbath is common to both Christians and Jews
in response to the biblical commandment ‘Remember the Sabbath
day to keep it holy’. Most Christians observe the Sabbath on
Sunday, whereas Jews and sabbatarian Christians (e.g. Seventh-
day Adventists) observe Saturday as their Sabbath. People who are
devout in their religious practices may want to avoid any special
treatments or other intrusions on their own religion’s nominated day
of rest and reflection.


Muslims follow the practice of prayer five times a day and a Muslim
in your care may need assistance to maintain this commitment. In
addition, Muslims traditionally gather on Friday at noon to worship
and learn about their faith. Hindus and Buddhists practise meditation
and the nurse can support this practice by creating a quiet time for
them to meditate.
Sacred writings
Each religion has sacred and authoritative scriptures that provide
guidance for its adherents’ beliefs and behaviours; in addition,
sacred writings frequently tell instructive stories of the religion’s
leaders, kings and heroes. In most religions, these scriptures are
thought to be the word of the Supreme Being as written down by
prophets or other human representatives. Christians rely on the
Bible, Jews on the Torah and Talmud, Muslims on the Koran, Hindus
have several holy texts, or Vedas, and Buddhists value the teachings
of the Tripitakas. Scriptures generally set forth religious law in the
form of admonitions and rules for living (e.g. the Ten
Commandments). This religious law may be interpreted in various
ways by subgroups of a religion’s adherents and may affect a
person’s willingness to accept treatment suggestions; for example,
blood transfusions are in conflict with the religious admonitions of
Jehovah’s Witnesses.
People often gain strength and hope from reading religious writings
when they are ill or in crisis. Examples of scriptural stories that may


give comfort are Job’s suffering, in both the Jewish and Christian
scriptures, and Jesus’ healing of people who were physically or
mentally ill, in the New Testament of the Bible.
While the Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander sacred
stories have historically been passed on only through their oral
storytelling tradition and spiritual art, the increasing use of Dadirri as
a research methodology is beginning to capture the Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander perspective on various topics in writing, thus
preserving some of this literary treasure in a written format as well
(West et al.
).
30 West, R., Stewart, L., Foster, K. & Usher, K. (2012). Through a critical lens: Indigenist
research and the Dadirri method. Qualitative Health Research, 22(11), 1582–1590. Doi:
10.1177/1049732312457596.
Sacred symbols
Sacred symbols include jewellery, medals, amulets, icons, totems or
body ornamentation (e.g. tattoos) that carry religious or spiritual
significance. They may be worn to pronounce one’s faith, to remind
the practitioner of the faith, to provide spiritual protection or to be a
source of comfort or strength. People may wear religious medals at
all times and they may wish to wear them when they are undergoing
diagnostic studies, medical treatment or surgery. People who are
Roman Catholic may carry a rosary for prayer; a person who is
Muslim or Hindu may carry a mala or string of prayer beads.
30


People may have religious icons or statues in their home, car or
place of work as a personal reminder of their faith or as part of a
personal place of worship or meditation. Hospitalised persons or
long-term care residents may wish to have their spiritual icons or
statues with them as a source of comfort. Traditional healers in
Indigenous Australian communities, known as Ngangkari, address
spiritual imbalances by using specialised techniques such as
‘massage, coaxing, and using special powerful sacred tools’
(Dudgeon & Walker
, p. 290) (see Figure 42.2
). There are also
sacred symbols associated with the Dreaming (Indigenous creation
theology), such as the rainbow serpent (Dudgeon & Bray ). A study
of 14 Indigenous Australian women experiencing gynaecological
cancer (Gall et al.
) found that 79% of them reported using at least
one form of traditional and complementary medicine in the past 12
months, including a strong sense of spirituality and faith, with one
participant reporting: ‘I do believe in something up there . . . [I] go
out to the bush and sit under the stars and just pray’ (p. 90).

strategies, and practice. Journal of Social and Political Psychology, 3(1), 276–297. Doi:
10.5964/jspp.v3i1.126.
32 Dudgeon, P. & Bray, A. (2018). Indigenous healing practices in Australia. Women &
Therapy, 41(1–2), 97–113. Doi: 10.1080/02703149.2017.1324191.
33 Gall, A., Anderson, K., Diaz, A. Matthews, V., Adams, J., Taylor, T. & Garvey, G. (2019).
Exploring traditional and complementary medicine use by Indigenous Australian women

Practice, 36, 88–93. Doi: 10.1016/j.ctcp.2019.06.005.
