Research note
Understanding the effect of music on the spirituality of
patients


W. de Andrade Alvarenga, A. C. Leite, M. S. Oliveira, L. C. Nascimento, F. M. Silva-Rodrigues, M. D.
Nunes & E. C. de Carvalho
. The effect of music on the spirituality of patients: A systematic review.
Journal of Holistic Nursing, 36(2), 192–204. Doi: 10.1177/ 0898010117710855.
34 de Andrade Alvarenga, W., Leite, A. C., Oliveira, M. S., Nascimento, L. C., Silva-Rodrigues, F. M.,
Nunes, M. D. & de Carvalho, E. C. (2018). The effect of music on the spirituality of patients: A
systematic review. Journal of Holistic Nursing, 36(2), 192–204. Doi: 10.1177/0898010117710855.
A systematically conducted literature review located and
analysed seven studies that investigated the effect of music
on spirituality, finding mixed results. The review included
studies conducted in any setting with any type of patient
population, as long as they investigated music as an
intervention and also used a quantifiable outcome measure
for spirituality. Outcome measures used in the studies
included: the Reed Spiritual Perspective Scale; the Index of
Core Spiritual Experience (Inspirit Scale); the Functional
Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy—Spiritual Well-Being
Scale (FACIT-SP); and the Spiritual Well-Being Questionnaire.
A variety of musical interventions were used across the
seven studies, delivered to individuals, to groups or to both.
Some interventions consisted of passive listening to singing
or musical instruments, live or recorded, while other
interventions were comprised of active participation by the
study participants, who sang along or played musical
instruments with the music therapist or, in one study, even
made a music video together. Music genres were mostly not
reported, although one study did list a variety of genres: pop,
rock, rap, country and rhythm and blues.
34


The music intervention was most often compared to standard
care or other audio stimuli such as audiobooks. In three of
the studies, total instrument scales and/or specific sub-scales
(such as peace or faith) showed an improvement in scores
after the music intervention for the pre/post comparisons or
showed a higher score in the music group than in the
standard care group. However, four of the studies showed no
difference in the outcome measures after the music
intervention or for the music group over the comparator
group. The review concluded that the effect of music on
improving measures of spirituality is inconclusive to date.
Implications Further research is warranted to explore the
potential benefits of this non-invasive modality to improve
spiritual wellbeing. In the meantime, nurses can be guided by
the wishes of health care recipients.
Sacred songs or chants
Many formal religions use sound as a central feature in communal
worship services by singing together, particular sacred songs or
hymns, or chanting and reciting prayers together. In Indigenous
Australian culture, special songs and chants are not only
expressions of spirituality, but they can also be used in healing
ceremonies by a traditional healer or by older men or women who
have inherited a specific healing song, thus giving them ownership of


it. It is incorrect and ineffective to sing a healing song that one does
not own (Maher
).
35 Maher, P. (1999). A review of ‘traditional’ Aboriginal health beliefs. Australian Journal of
Rural Health, 7, 229–236.
Prayer and meditation
Prayer is a spiritual practice; for many, it is also a religious practice.
An encyclopaedia of religion defines prayer
 simply as ‘human
communication with divine and spiritual entities’ (Gill , p. 489).
Some argue that because prayer requires a belief in a divine or
spiritual entity not all people pray, while others consider prayer a
universal phenomenon that does not require such belief. Ulanov and
Ulanov , for example, proposed that everyone prays: ‘People pray
whether or not they call it prayer. We pray every time we ask for
help, understanding, or strength, in or out of religion . . . who and
what we are speak out of us . . . To pray is to listen to and hear this
self who is speaking’ (p. 1). Prayer is intention plus love, often
communicated with ‘the Absolute’, according to Dossey ; that is,
prayer is a loving wish or thought for oneself or another and not an
invocation of positive or negative forms of magic.
36 Gill, S. D. (1987). Prayer. In M. Eliade (Ed.), The Encyclopedia of Religion (pp. 489–492).
New York: Macmillan.
37 Ulanov, A. & Ulanov, B. (1983). Primary Speech: A Psychology of Prayer. Atlanta: John
Knox Press (Classic).
35
36
37
38


38 Dossey, L. (1999). Healing and the nonlocal mind: Interview by Bonnie Horrigan.
Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine, 5(6), 85–93.
There are different types of prayer experience. Paloma and Gallup
categorised prayer experiences as follows:
39 Paloma, M. M. & Gallup, G. H. Jr (1991). Varieties of Prayer: A Survey Report.
Philadelphia: Trinity Press International.
ritual (e.g. the ‘Hail Mary’ or memorised prayers that can be
repeated)
petitionary (e.g. ‘God, help me!’ or intercessory prayers when
one is requesting something of the divine)
colloquial (i.e. conversational prayers)
meditational (e.g. moments of silence focused on nothing, on a
meaningful phrase or on a certain aspect of the divine).
While meditational and colloquial prayer experiences have been
found to be associated with spiritual wellbeing and quality of life in
healthy adults, ritual and petitionary prayer experiences may be
most comforting and appropriate for those who are ill.
Some religions have prescribed prayers that are printed in a prayer
book, such as the Anglican Book of Common Prayer or the Catholic
Missal. Some religious prayers are attributed to the source of faith;
for example, the ‘Lord’s Prayer’ for Christians is attributed to Jesus
and the first sutra for Muslims is attributed to Mohammed.
39


Some religions require daily prayers or dictate specific times for
prayer and worship: the five daily prayers, or Salat, of Muslims
(performed while facing east towards Mecca at dawn, noon, mid-
afternoon, sunset and evening), the daily Kaddish of the Jews or the
seven canonical prayers of Roman Catholics. People who are ill may
want to continue or increase their prayer practices. They may need
uninterrupted quiet time during which they have their prayer books,
rosaries, malas or other icons available to them.
Meditation
 is the act of focusing one’s thoughts or engaging in
self-reflection or contemplation. Some people believe that through
deep meditation one can influence or control physical and
psychological functioning and the course of illness.
Beliefs affecting diet and nutrition
Many religions have proscriptions regarding diet. There may be rules
about which foods and beverages are allowed and which are
prohibited. For example, Orthodox Jews are not permitted to eat
shellfish or pork, and Muslims avoid drinking alcoholic beverages or
eating pork. Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of the Latter-
day Saints (Mormons) are not allowed to drink caffeinated or
alcoholic beverages. Older Catholics may choose not to eat meat on
Fridays because it was proscribed in years past. Buddhists and
Hindus are generally vegetarian, not wanting to take life to support
life. Religious law may also dictate how food is prepared; for
example, many Jewish people require kosher
 food, which is food


prepared according to Jewish law, and many Muslims will only eat
meat prepared/slaughtered according to halal
 preparation
standards.
Some solemn religious observances are marked by fasting (an
abstinence from food for a specified period of time). Some religions
also restrict beverages; others allow drinking of water or other
sustaining beverages on fast days. Examples of religions that
observe fasting include Islam, Judaism and Catholicism. During the
month of Ramadan, devout Muslims eat no food and avoid
beverages during daylight hours; the fast is broken after sunset.
Members of Jewish synagogues fast on Yom Kippur and devout
Catholics may fast on Good Friday. Most religions lift the fasting
requirements for seriously ill believers for whom fasting may be a
detriment to health (e.g. people with diabetes). Some religions may
exempt pregnant and breastfeeding women or menstruating women
from fasting requirements. The beliefs of some Indigenous
Australians restrict certain foods during mourning, pregnancy,
lactation and menstruation (Maher 1999).
It is important that health care providers prescribe diet plans with an
awareness of the person’s dietary and fasting beliefs.
Beliefs related to healing
People may have religious beliefs that attribute illness to a spiritual
disruption. Healing for such people may appear to be unrelated to


current treatment practices. The nurse needs to assess the person’s
beliefs and, if possible, include some aspects of healing that are part
of the person’s belief system in the planning of care. Indigenous
Australians’ beliefs vary widely across the different cultural
subgroups, but most include a belief in at least a partial spiritual
causation for serious illnesses and for sudden, unexpected,
premature death (Maher 1999) (see Figure 42.3
). Retribution for
disturbing a sacred site or for neglecting a duty to the social group
or to the land is viewed as the true underlying causes for
illness/death, but the illness may also be believed to have been set
in motion by the use of sorcery as a proximate cause (Maher 1999).
Traditional healers have powers such as spirit travel, the ability to
communicate with the spirit world, to manipulate the patient’s spirit
and to protect people against attack from spirits via counter-sorcery
(Maher 1999). Strong spiritual support is a key function for
traditional healers (Maher 1999).
Figure 42.3


Some Indigenous Australians believe in partial spiritual causation for
illnesses and unexpected deaths.
Source: Penny Tweedie/Contributor/Getty Images.
Beliefs related to dress
Many religions have laws or traditions that dictate dress. For
example, Orthodox and Conservative Jewish men believe that it is
important to have their heads covered at all times and therefore
wear yarmulkes. Orthodox Jewish women cover their hair with a wig


or scarf as a sign of respect to God. Many Muslim women also
cover their hair in accordance with their particular ethnic or national
background. Mormons may wear temple undergarments in
compliance with religious law.
Some religions require that women dress in a conservative manner,
which may include wearing sleeves and modestly cut tops and skirts
that cover the knees. Some religions, for example Islam, may
require that the body (torso, arms and legs) be covered. Hindu
women accustomed to wearing saris prefer to cover all of the body
except arms and feet. The shorter length of hospital gowns may
make women wishing to comply with religious dress codes feel
uneasy and uncomfortable. People may be especially disconcerted
when undergoing diagnostic tests or treatments, such as
mammography, that require body parts to be bared.
Beliefs related to birth
For all religions the birth of a child is an important event giving cause
for celebration. Many religions have specific ritual ceremonies that
consecrate the new child to God. When a Muslim child is born,
someone recites the call to prayer in the infant’s ear. On the seventh
day after birth, the child is named and hair is shaved from the head
(Khademi et al.
).
40 Khademi, G., Abbasi, M. A., Bahreini, A. & Saeidi, M. (2016). Customs and desirable after
childbirth, in Islam. International Journal of Pediatrics, 4(1), 1297–1303. Retrieved from
40


<www.doaj.org>.
In the Christian faith, baptism and christening ceremonies may take
place after the birth of a child to confirm that the ‘infant [was] born
into a Christian family as part of the organism of the church’
(Frankiel , p. 556). Christian parents of seriously ill infants may
want baptism performed at birth by the nurse or doctor if a chaplain
or member of the clergy is not present.
41 Frankiel, S. S. (1993). Christianity: A way of salvation. In H. Byron Earhart (Ed.), Religious
Traditions of the World (pp. 484–601). New York: Harper San Francisco.
In the Jewish religion, the ritual circumcision conducted on male
children on the eighth day after birth is an expression of the religious
bond between the prophet Abraham, his descendants and their God.
Following the ritual circumcision by the trained person, called a
mohel, the child is named. Girls are named in the synagogue on the
Sabbath after their birth (DeVito ).
42 DeVito, J. (2019). Understanding the orthodox Jewish family during childbirth. Nursing
Forum, 54(2), 220–226. Doi: 10.1111/nuf.12320.
When nurses are aware of the religious needs of families and their
infants, they can assist families in fulfilling their religious obligations.
This is especially important when the newborn infant is seriously ill or
in danger of dying, because some people believe that if religious
obligations are not fulfilled the infant will not be accepted into the
community of the faithful after death.
41
42


Beliefs related to death
Spiritual and religious beliefs play a significant role in the believer’s
approach to death just as they do in other major life events. Many
believe that the person who dies transcends this life for a better
place or state of being.
Some religions have special rituals surrounding dying and death that
must be observed by the faithful. Observance of these rituals
provides comfort to the dying person and the person’s loved ones.
Some rituals are carried out while the person is still alive and can
include special prayers, singing or chants, and reading of sacred
scriptures. Roman Catholic priests perform the Sacrament of the
Anointing of the Sick (previously referred to as the Last Rites), which
traditionally only happened when people were very ill or near death.
However, it is now recommended that this sacrament be performed
at an earlier stage in a person’s illness. Muslims who are dying want
their body or head turned towards Mecca (Fouché ).
43 Fouché, N. (2019). A contemporary review of understanding the religious and cultural
diversity of patients dying or who have died in the intensive care unit. A South African
perspective. International Journal of Africa Nursing Sciences, 10, 61–67. Doi:
10.1016/j.ijans.2019.01.003.
Jews have a tradition of burial within 24 hours following death,
except on the Sabbath, and they ‘sit Shiva’ (gather to pay respects),
draping any mirrors in black to ensure that guests are focused on
memory of the deceased rather than on themselves. Tibetan
43


Buddhists read the Tibetan Book of the Dead within 7 days of the
death to release the soul of the deceased from the Bardos, or
nether worlds. Hindus cremate the body within 24 hours to release
the soul from any earthly attachment.
In the case of a terminal illness, the person and their family should
be asked about observances or rituals that follow death. It is
important for nurses to take a person-centred and culturally
sensitive approach and attempt to understand individual needs.
Some religions require that the body of the deceased be touched
only by members of that faith. In both the Muslim and Jewish
religions, believers may require that a ritual bath be done after death
by a family member or by a ritual burial society (Fouché 2019).
Religious symbols or objects should be treated with respect and kept
with the body. The nurse can support the family of the deceased by
providing an environment conducive to the performance of their
traditional death rituals.
Some traditions specific to Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander culture were thoroughly explored in a descriptive qualitative
study that used open-ended questions to interview patients, carers,
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health workers and other health
care professionals in the Northern Territory regarding Indigenous
cultural practices associated with a deceased person’s hair, clothing,
possessions and name as part of a larger study of palliative care
services (McGrath & Phillips ). It is important to give clothing that
the deceased person was wearing back to the family or to the
Jungai (a person within that network of kinship and community
44


relationships who had decision-making responsibility for and power
over the individual who had died) either for inclusion in the smoking
ceremony that is part of the death ritual in some locations, or for
burying, or as a memento. Similarly, the hair of the deceased is
considered to have spirit power and samples should be kept and can
only be given to the family or the Jungai, and not be touched by
merely anyone. The possessions of the deceased are meant to be
distributed to others, in part to prevent the spirit from remaining in
the house, but also in gratitude and compensation to family
members who have provided care during the terminal phase. Again,
this distribution may be handled by a Jungai. The name of the
deceased person is not to be written or spoken aloud, especially to
the immediate family members. The purpose of this practice is to
ensure that the deceased person’s spirit is not called back to the
world.
44 McGrath, P. & Phillips, E. (2008). Australian finding on Aboriginal cultural practices
associated with clothing, hair, possessions and use of name of deceased persons.
International Journal of Nursing Practice, 14, 57–66.
Research Note
The role of spirituality in palliative care and emotional
wellbeing
J. Penman
. Finding paradise within: How spirituality protects palliative care clients and caregivers
from depression. Journal of Holistic Nursing, 36(3), 243–254. Doi: 10.1177/0898010117714665.
45 Penman, J. (2018). Finding paradise within: How spirituality protects palliative care clients and
caregivers from depression. Journal of Holistic Nursing, 36(3), 243–254. Doi:
45


10.1177/0898010117714665.
Penman (2018) used van Manen’s phenomenology to explore
how four palliative care patients and 10 caregivers of
palliative care in South Australia managed depression, and
found that patient’s spirituality was a critical element in both
preventing and overcoming depression. The sample
consisted of seven Caucasians and seven Asians, nine of
whom were Catholic and five were Protestant, with an
average age of 59 years old. The researcher identified three
distinct themes, aligned with the conceptualisation of
spirituality being about connection with self, with others and
with the divine.
The first theme, ‘Finding paradise within’, was the term used
by one participant to describe the experience many reported,
of finding peace and meaning in life despite a terminal
prognosis and transcending their current circumstances to
feel connected to their own values and destiny. Participants’
comments included: ‘My spiritual beliefs helped me cope’ and
‘My spirituality makes me powerful as it gives me strength
and courage to persevere in life’.
A second theme, titled ‘It’s like building community’,
encompassed the key role that the support, visits and
prayers of friends, family and members of patients’ religious
or spiritual community played in staving off depression and
helping them feel connected to others. One participant
commented: ‘Friends distract you for a while, we talk, then
cry, then talk some more. We draw on happy memories and


imagine a time when there will be no more death and
sickness’.
A final theme of ‘God/religious matters’ more explicitly related
to patients’ sense of connection, support and strength in their
relationship to God or a supreme being, nature or humanity
as a whole—something bigger than themselves and their own
current situation. Participating in religious rituals, either alone
or with others, was prominent in this theme. As one
participant noted: ‘Experiencing God living in us even in bad
times helps . . . and being there at the right time when
needed by father’.
Implications Depression is prevalent in the palliative care
population, for both patients and their caregivers, and
spirituality is an effective and desired strategy to offset it.
Nurses should be educated to comfortably initiate
conversations about spiritual matters, to assess for spiritual
strengths and to then assist patients to access and enact
their spiritual beliefs to achieve transcendence and remain
connected to their conceptualisation of a divine deity, their
religious practices and their fellow worshippers, friends and
family members.


Spiritual health and the nursing
process
The nursing process, which includes assessing, diagnosing,
planning, implementing and evaluating, can be applied to the area of
spiritual health.
Clinical consideration
Before sharing personal beliefs or practices, a
nurse must consider questions such as the
following:
For what purpose am I sharing my beliefs or
practices? By doing so, am I meeting my
needs or those of the people for whom I am
caring?
Is my spiritual care reflecting a spiritual
assessment?
Am I preying on a vulnerable person?
Am I offering my beliefs or practices in a
manner that allows the person to feel
comfortable about refusing?


Does my spiritual care detract from or
enhance a therapeutic relationship?


Nursing management
Assessing
Data about a person’s spiritual beliefs are obtained from their
general history (religious preferences or orientation); through a
nursing history; and by clinical observations of the person’s
behaviour, verbalisations, mood and so on. Nurses should never
assume that a person follows all the practices of their stated religion.
Nor should they assume that all people will express their spirituality
through an organised religion as some may have profound spiritual
beliefs that are not affiliated with any specific recognised religion.
Nursing history
Each person admitted to a health care facility should be assessed
for spiritual beliefs and practices using a two-tier approach. All
individuals can be asked a general question or two; for example,
‘What spiritual beliefs or practices are important to you now while
you live with illness?’, ‘How would you like your health care team to
support you spiritually?’. A more thorough spiritual assessment is
then conducted on people who manifest some type of unhealthy
spiritual need or are at risk of spiritual distress. This assessment can


be further streamlined to hone in on the individual’s particular
spiritual concern.
Although the nurse will continually be assessing, the initial spiritual
assessment is best taken at the end of the assessment process or
following the psychosocial assessment, after the nurse has
developed a relationship with the individual and/or their support
person. A nurse who has demonstrated sensitivity and personal
warmth, thus earning respect and building rapport, will be more
successful during a spiritual assessment.
The questions provided in the ‘Assessment interview’ below may be
suitable. Remembering an acronym such as FICA can also help the
nurse to ask appropriate questions:
F (faith or beliefs)—for example: What spiritual beliefs are most
important to you?
I (implications or influence)—for example: How do your spiritual
beliefs or faith affect the way you cope now?
C (community)—for example: Is there a group of like-minded
believers with which you regularly meet?
A (address)—for example: How would you like your health care
team to support you spiritually? (Dameron ; Massey, Fitchett &
Roberts ).
46 Dameron, C. M. (2005). Spiritual assessment made easy ... with acronyms! Journal of
Christian Nursing, 22(1), 14–16.
46
47


47 Massey, K., Fitchett, G. & Roberts, P. A. (2004). In K. L. Mauk & N. K. Schmidt (Eds),
Spiritual Care in Nursing Practice. Assessment and Diagnosis in Spiritual Care (pp. 209–242).
Philadelphia: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
Assessment interview
Spirituality/religiosity
Are any particular religious practices important to you? If
so, could you please tell me about them?
How will being sick interfere with your religious practices?
How is your faith helpful to you? In what ways is it
important to you right now?
In what ways can I support your spiritual health or
practices? For example, would you like me to read your
prayer book to you?
Would you like a visit from your spiritual counsellor or the
hospital chaplain?
What are your hopes and your sources of strength right
now? What comforts you during hard times?
Clinical assessment
Cues to spiritual and religious preferences, strengths, concerns or
distress may be revealed by one or more of the following:


1. Environment. Does the person have a Bible, Torah, Koran,
other prayer book, devotional literature, religious medals, a
rosary, a cross, a Star of David or religious get-well cards in
the room? Does a church send flowers or Sunday bulletins?
2. Behaviour. Does the person pray before meals or at other
times or read religious literature? Does the person verbalise
experiencing nightmares and/or sleep disturbances, or
express anger at religious representatives or at a deity?
3. Verbalisation. Does the person mention God or a higher
power, prayer, faith, the church, synagogue, mosque, temple,
a spiritual or religious leader or religious topics? Has the
person requested a visit from the clergy? Have they
expressed a fear of death, concern with the meaning of life,
inner conflict about religious or spiritual beliefs, concern about
a relationship with the deity, questions about the meaning of
existence or the meaning of suffering, or about the moral or
ethical implications of therapy?
4. Affect and attitude. Does the person appear lonely,
depressed, angry, anxious, agitated, apathetic or
preoccupied?
5. Interpersonal relationships. Who visits? How does the
person respond to visitors? Does a minister come? How does
the person relate to others, including nursing personnel?
Patient safety competency framework
3 Cultural competence


Nursing students must be able to demonstrate
cultural empathy by seeking to understand the
person’s cultural and spiritual values, needs,
practices and perspectives (Levett-Jones et
al.
).
48 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Diagnosing
In diagnosing spiritual health, the nurse may find that a spiritual
problem exists that is caused by other factors or, alternatively, the
nurse may find that altered spirituality itself becomes the cause for
other related problems, such as loss of hope or withdrawal from a
faith community. Examples of some ways of expressing a nursing
diagnosis are given below, but the nurse always needs to tailor the
wording of a spiritual diagnosis in terms that are relevant and
understandable to the entire caregiving team and to the person
under their care.
Spiritual distress (where the person’s spiritual belief system and
wellbeing are threatened).
48


Impaired religiosity (where the person’s ability to engage in
religious beliefs or practices is impaired).
Readiness for enhanced religiosity (where the person is willing to
newly engage with, or increase their participation in, religious
practices of a particular faith).
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Comprehensive Care
The intention of this standard is to ‘ensure that patients receive
comprehensive care—that is, coordinated delivery of the total
health care required or requested by a patient; and, to ensure
that risks of harm for patients during health care are prevented
and managed’ (Australian Commission on Safety and Quality
in Health Care
, p. 38).
49 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved by
providing care that is aligned with the person’s
goals, needs and preferences. That is, care
provision is much broader than focusing only on
the treatment of disease or symptomology.
The right to retain, embrace and practise their
spiritual beliefs during their challenging illness
experiences is a sacred right of all people under
49


our care and one that must be supported by
holistic nursing care and by organisational
infrastructure/policies/human and material
resources. Both individual bedside nurses and
all layers of management need to be open and
responsive to identified problems in providing
appropriate spiritual care to create and enact
reasonable solutions that will improve the ability
to provide spiritual care for future nurse–person
encounters. Examples the nurse can implement
include flexibility in routine care to accommodate
spiritual practices; adequate staffing to allow
time to be fully present with people under our
care; privacy through provision of curtains at the
least, and private rooms when possible;
provision of a chapel or other reserved quiet
place for praying/meditation on site; and
adequate space and flexibility for visitors from a
faith community to pray with the person under
our care.
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
Individuals with spiritual distress


History Marilyn Eckhardt, 72 years old, is crying, fingering
her rosary and voicing concern that she has not seen her
priest for confession since being admitted to the hospital. She
states that she is afraid to die without confessing her sins.
She also states that she does not want to see the hospital
chaplain but rather her own priest, whose parish is about 45
km away. The hospital record indicates that Ms Eckhardt is
Catholic.
Spiritual distress may affect other areas of functioning and indicate
other diagnoses. In these instances, spiritual distress becomes the
aetiology. Examples include the following:
Fear related to apprehension about the soul’s future after death
and unpreparedness for death
Chronic or situational low self-esteem related to failure to live
within the precepts of one’s faith
Disturbed sleep pattern related to spiritual distress
Ineffective coping related to feelings of abandonment by God
and loss of religious faith
Decisional conflict related to conflict between treatment plan and
religious beliefs.
Planning


In the planning phase, the nurse identifies interventions to help the
person achieve the overall goal of maintaining or restoring spiritual
wellbeing so that spiritual strength, serenity and satisfaction are
realised. (See ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and
interventions’.)
Planning in relation to spiritual (and/or religious) needs should be
designed to do one or more of the following:
Help the individual to draw on and use inner resources more
effectively to meet the present situation.
Help the individual find meaning in existence and the present
situation.
Promote a sense of hope.
Provide spiritual resources otherwise unavailable.
Help the individual to maintain or establish a dynamic, personal
relationship with a supreme being in the face of unpleasant
circumstances.
Help the individual to fulfil religious obligations.
Implementing
Numerous nursing actions are available to help people meet their
spiritual needs. Spiritual care includes actions as diverse as
recognising and validating inner resources of an individual, such as
coping methods, humour, motivation, self-determination, positive
attitude and optimism. It can also include assisting the person to


leave a legacy by storytelling and/or recording life stories for family
and friends and encouraging creative expression through art, music
and writing. Such activities help to preserve the person’s imagination
and serve to regenerate the body, mind and spirit. Fostering ways
for people to keep in touch with nature and maintain a sense of
wonder are also forms of spiritual care. Recognising the seasons,
the emergence of flowers in spring, the phases of the moon, the
migrations of birds and the unchanging stars provides examples of
orderliness in the universe, even in the midst of chaos and loss. A
person with a good measure of spiritual health will find hope,
meaning, purpose and value in existence. Although nursing
therapeutics that enhance spiritual health are diverse, some of the
most common and most desired include (a) providing presence, (b)
supporting religious practices, (c) assisting people with prayer and
(d) referring them for spiritual counselling (Taylor & Mamier
).
50 Taylor, E. J. & Mamier, I. (2005). Spiritual care nursing: What cancer patients and family
caregivers want. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 49(3), 260–267.
Providing presence
Presencing
 is the act of being present or there with a person.
Pettigrew
 identified four distinguishing features of presencing:
51 Pettigrew, J. (1990). Intensive nursing care: The ministry of presence. Critical Care
Nursing Clinics of North America, 2, 503–508.
1. giving of self in the present moment
2. being available with all of the self
50
51


3. listening, with full awareness of the privilege of doing so
4. being there in a way that is meaningful to another person.
Presencing is a ‘gift of self’ given by the nurse who maintains an
attitude of attentiveness towards the person. Thus, nurses who
listen attentively yet fail to give of self (i.e. inwardly ‘make room’)
diminish their effectiveness. There are multiple levels of presencing.
Osterman and Schwartz-Barcott
 identified four ways of being
present for people:
52 Osterman, P. & Schwartz-Barcott, D. (1996). Presence: Four ways of being there. Nursing
Forum, 31(2), 23–30.
1. presence (when a nurse is physically present but not focused
on the person)
2. partial presence (when a nurse is physically present and
attending to some task on the person’s behalf but not relating
to them on any but the most superficial level)
3. full presence (when a nurse is mentally, emotionally and
physically present; intentionally focusing on the person)
4. transcendent presence (when a nurse is physically, mentally,
emotionally and spiritually present for a person; involves a
transpersonal and transforming experience).
Presencing is often the best and sometimes the only intervention to
support a person who suffers under circumstances that medical
interventions cannot address. When they are helpless, powerless
and vulnerable, a nurse’s presencing can be most beneficial. Rather
than worrying about saying or doing ‘the right thing’, nurses should
52


focus on being fully present. Taylor (2002, p. 100) offers some
strategies for nurses to achieve effective presencing:
being aware of ways they may attempt to avoid spiritual pain and
suffering in order to overcome such avoidance when they
observe individuals experiencing spiritual discomfort
centring before entering into the presence of people
using eye contact and touch appropriately
gaining permission from the person to be present
limiting expectations of the individual
recognising that presencing does not require long periods of time
with a person (even a knowing look can be helpful)
avoiding over-involvement by maintaining appropriate
boundaries.
Supporting religious practices
During the assessment of the person, the nurse will have obtained
specific information about the person’s religious preference and
practices. Nurses need to consider specific religious practices that
will affect nursing care, such as the person’s beliefs about birth,
death, dress, diet, prayer, sacred symbols, sacred writings and holy
days as discussed earlier in this chapter. See ‘Practice guidelines’ for
ways the nurse can help individuals to continue their usual spiritual
(or religious) practices. Box 42.3
 provides health-related
information about specific religions.


BO X
42.3 Health-related information about
specific religions: a sampler
Anglican, Catholic: appreciate receiving Eucharist (Holy
Communion), a ritual of ingesting bread and wine (or grape
juice) led by clergy or trained lay ministers to commemorate
the death of Jesus. Forehead may be marked by priest with
ashes on Ash Wednesday (40 days before Easter); no need
to wash off. Lenten season (Ash Wednesday to Easter) may
involve some degree of abstention from food.
Buddhist: may be vegetarian. Facilitate meditation (may
desire incense, visual focal point, use breathing or chanting,
etc.).
Catholic: Sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick is
appropriate for anyone who is ill. Be aware that some may
think that the rite means they are dying as it was traditionally
previously reserved for such situations.
Christian Scientist: typically oppose Western medical
interventions, relying instead on lay and professional Christian
Science practitioners.
Hindu: most eat no beef; many are vegetarian. Cleanliness
highly valued. Many food preferences (e.g. foods fresh or
cooked in oil).


Jehovah’s Witness: abstain from most blood products; need
to discuss alternative treatments such as blood conservation
strategies, autologous techniques, haematopoietic agents,
non-blood volume expanders and so on; contact the local
Jehovah’s Witness hospital liaison committee.
Jewish: Some observe kosher diet to varying degrees (e.g.
avoid pork and shellfish, do not mix dairy and meat). Sabbath
observance varies (e.g. Orthodox Jews avoid travelling in
vehicles, writing, turning on electric appliances and lights).
Latter-day Saints (Mormon): avoid alcohol, caffeine. May
prefer to wear temple undergarments. Arrange for priestly
blessing if requested.
Muslim: respect modesty, avoid nakedness. Provide same-
gender nurse if possible. Support prayers five times daily
(may need to assist with ritual washing and positioning
beforehand). Allow for family and imam (religious leader) to
follow Islamic guidelines for burial when the person dies. Eat
no pork. Children, pregnant women, older adults and the sick
are exempt from daytime fasting during month of Ramadan.
Seventh-day Adventist: avoid unnecessary treatments on
Saturday (Sabbath). Sabbath begins Friday sundown and
ends Saturday sundown. Adventists prefer restful, spirit-
nurturing, family activities on Sabbaths. Likely to be
vegetarian and abstain from caffeinated beverages. Do not
drink alcohol.


Assisting people with prayer
Prayer involves a sense of love and connection, as well as a
reaching out. It can have a positive effect on health and wellbeing.
Prayer offers a means for talking to someone, a mechanism for
expressing care and a sense of serenity and connection with
something greater than themselves.
A person may choose to participate in private prayer or want group
prayer with family, friends or clergy. In such situations the nurse’s
major responsibility is to ensure a quiet environment and privacy.
Nursing care may need to be adjusted to accommodate periods for
prayer.
Illness can interfere with some people’s ability to pray. Feelings such
as anxiety, fear, guilt, grief, despair and isolation can produce
barriers to relationships in general and to the relationship the person
has with the Divine. In these instances, the person may ask the
nurse to pray with them. Prayers should only be done when there is
mutual agreement between the person and those praying with them.
Nurses who are unaccustomed to praying aloud or in public may find
it helpful to have a formal prayer or a scriptural passage readily
available. Because prayer can evoke deep feelings, the nurse may
need to spend time with the person following a prayer to enable
them to express these feelings.


Practice guidelines
Supporting religious practices
Create a trusting relationship with the person so that any
religious concerns or practices can be openly discussed
and addressed.
If unsure of the person’s religious needs, ask how nurses
can assist in having these needs met. Avoid relying on
personal assumptions when providing care.
Do not discuss your own personal spiritual beliefs with a
person in your care unless they request it. Be sure to
assess whether such self-disclosure on the part of the
nurse actually contributes to the therapeutic relationship.
Inform the person and family caregivers about spiritual
support available at your organisation (e.g. chapel or
meditation room, chaplain services).
Allow time and privacy for, and provide comfort measures
prior to, private worship, prayer, meditation, reading or
other spiritual activities.
Respect and ensure safety of the person’s religious
articles (e.g. icons, amulets, clothing, jewellery).
If desired by the person, facilitate clergy or spiritual care
specialist visitation. Collaborate with a chaplain (if
available).
Prepare their environment for spiritual rituals or clergy
visitations as needed (e.g. have chair near bedside for
clergy, create private space).


Make arrangements with dietitian so that dietary needs
can be met. If the organisation cannot accommodate the
person’s needs, ask the family to bring food.
Acquaint yourself with the religions, spiritual practices and
cultures commonly found in either the geographical area
or specialty area in which you are working.
Remember there can be a difference between
facilitating/supporting a person’s religious practices and
participating in it yourself.
Ask another nurse to assist you if a particular religious
practice makes you uncomfortable.
All spiritual interventions must be done within organisation
guidelines.
Lifespan considerations
Spiritual development
Children
The development of spirituality in children parallels their
cognitive and psychosocial development. As children mature,
they are increasingly capable of understanding spiritual
matters, stating spiritual beliefs and incorporating spirituality
into their lives.
A developing spirituality includes:


a sense of wholeness, having internal resources and
identity
being attached to others and being a part of a greater,
even transcendent, world
having a sense of meaning and purpose in one’s life
being able to express hope, even in the face of fear,
uncertainty and serious illness.
Nurses can help ill children and their parents identify and
express these qualities. This can be done by actively
listening, by offering opportunities to practise religious rituals
and by providing materials for nonverbal expression (e.g.
painting, play, music).
Older adults
Many older adults frequently use and highly value religious
coping strategies such as prayer. Spiritual wellbeing can
influence mental health and the incidence of comorbidities
among older adults (Harrington ). It is therefore important to
address the spiritual issues of older adults. Older adults may
be especially concerned about living a purposeful life, about
maintaining loving relationships to avoid social isolation and
about preparing for a good death. Nursing care for older
adults that attends to such spiritual issues includes:
53 Harrington, A. (2016). The importance of spiritual assessment when caring for
older adults. Ageing and Society, 36(1), 1–16. Doi: 10.1017/S0144686X14001007.
53


Supporting meaning-making activities (e.g. conducting a
life review or reminiscence therapy; allowing them to
weave together the strands of a life lived; encouraging the
person to become dedicated to some social, political,
religious or artistic cause; supporting them to leave a
legacy or do an altruistic deed). Such activities provide
older adults with a sense of purpose for their life and
assist them to make sense of the life that they have lived.
Allowing open discussions about suffering and dying,
encouraging disclosure by asking open-ended questions
and providing responses that are respectful and
compassionate. Do not avoid discomforting topics and
questions that older adults raise by imposing positivity,
giving ‘pat’ answers and otherwise minimising or avoiding
their spiritual pain.
As appropriate, supporting older adults to reframe the
‘losses’ of ageing as ‘liberations’. For example, older
adults possess great wisdom and are in a season of life
that promotes spiritual growth.
Older adults with dementia present special circumstances for
spiritual caregiving. Allowing older adults with dementia to tell
their stories allows them to maintain some identity (amid a
disease that threatens the very sense of self) and allows the
nurse a window into their world. Older adults with dementia
can also worship and express their hope and creativity
through various art forms (e.g. movement, painting, music). It
is also possible for them to experience the compassion of


others when they feel their caring touch or hear their soothing
voice.
Referring people for spiritual counselling
There are times when more complex spiritual care is best referred to
other members of the health care team. Referrals can be made for
hospitalised individuals and their families through the hospital
chaplain’s office if one is available. Nurses in home and community
health settings can identify spiritual resources by checking
directories of community service agencies, telephone directories or
religious directories that describe available spiritual counsellors and
the services provided through the religious community. Many
Australians’ spiritual beliefs are not expressed through an organised
religion, and sensitive assessment will be needed to ascertain
whether certain people or objects not traditionally seen as spiritual
may in fact have great personal spiritual significance for these
people.
Referrals may be necessary when the nurse makes a diagnosis of
spiritual distress. In this situation the nurse and religious counsellor
can work together to meet the person’s needs. One situation the
nurse may encounter is refusal of necessary medical intervention
because of religious tenets. In this case the nurse encourages the
person, doctor and spiritual advisor to discuss the conflict and
consider alternative methods of therapy. The nurse’s major role is to


provide information needed to make an informed decision and to
support that decision.
Evaluating
Using the measurable desired outcomes developed during the
planning stage, the nurse collects data needed to judge whether
goals and outcomes have been achieved. See the ‘Nursing care
plan
’ and ‘Concept map
’.
NURSING  CARE PLAN
Spiritual distress
CO NCEPT M AP
Spiritual distress


Case study


Terry is a 52-year-old male with quadriplegia following a car
crash 5 years ago. He has been admitted to hospital with
pneumonia and is feeling very discouraged. While you are
caring for Terry, he comments, ‘I might as well die right now
because I’m not going to get well. My parents were
Methodist, but I guess I’m being punished because I’m not
very religious’.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. Terry stated that he was ‘not very religious’. Does that
mean that he is not spiritual? Explain.
2. What data suggests Terry may be experiencing
spiritual distress?
3. How might illness and/or a chronic condition affect
one’s spiritual beliefs? Religious beliefs?
4. How might a spiritual assessment be of benefit to both
you and Terry?
5.
 Which elements of the Integration dimension of
the Fundamentals of Care Framework could help you
to support Terry with his spiritual/religious distress?


Chapter 42 Review


Chapter highlights
To implement spiritual care, nurses need to be skilled in
establishing a trusting and therapeutic relationship.
All people have a right to receive care that respects their
individual spiritual and religious values.
Nurses must follow ethical guidelines for providing spiritual care
and not impose their own personal beliefs or practices on those
for whom they are caring.
Nurses need to be aware of their own spiritual beliefs in order to
be comfortable assisting others.
The spiritual needs of people and their support persons often
come into focus at a time of illness. Spiritual beliefs can help
people accept illness and plan for what lies ahead.
Spiritual distress refers to a disturbance in or a challenge to a
person’s belief or value system that provides strength, hope and
meaning to life. Possible factors in spiritual distress include
physiological problems, treatment-related concerns and
situational concerns. Spiritual distress may be reflected in a
number of behaviours, including depression, anxiety,
verbalisations of unworthiness and fear of death.
Nurses can support people’s religious practices if they
understand needs related to holy days, sacred writings, sacred
symbols, prayer and meditation, dietary practices, dress
requirements or prohibitions, healing, birth rituals and death
rituals.


Spiritual assessment should collect information not only about
spiritual beliefs and practices affecting health but also about how
the person desires spiritual care from the health care team.
Nursing interventions that promote spiritual health include
offering one’s presence, supporting the person’s religious
practices, praying with them and referring them to a religious
counsellor.
Concept check
1. When planning care for an older adult residing in your
residential aged care facility who is searching to make life
meaningful, which nursing action would be most beneficial?
1. Assess for depression.
2. Diagnose and document that the person has ‘spiritual
distress’.
3. Keep the person busy with social activities.
4. Explore with the person their desired legacy.
2. A patient’s wife asks the nurse to pray for her. What would be
the best initial response for a nurse who believes in prayer?
1. ‘May I call the chaplain to come and pray with you?’
2. ‘I know your faith is important to you. It is to me, too.’
3. ‘What should I pray for?’
4. ‘Isn’t it wonderful that we have a God with whom we
can share our concerns?’


3. A person is experiencing severe pain that cannot be
controlled by analgesics. An appropriate intervention is full
presencing. Full presencing involves which of the following?
1. Physical presence.
2. Physical presence with mental awareness of the
person.
3. Physical, mental and emotional presence.
4. Physical, mental, emotional and spiritual presence.
4. A dying individual states, ‘Part of what makes dying hard is
that I don’t know for sure where I’m going. Nurse, what do
you believe happens in the hereafter?’. Which ethical
guideline should guide your response?
1. Never share personal spiritual beliefs.
2. Share all spiritual beliefs, favouring none.
3. Share only your beliefs.
4. First assess their beliefs.
5. Research evidence that supports providing spiritual care to
older adults suggests that:
1. Older adults are not very religious but are very
spiritual.
2. Older adults who are more religious have more illness.
3. Spiritual health and mental health are correlated.
4. Increased spiritual wellbeing is found among older
adults with depression.


6. Which of the following is an appropriate spiritual screening or
assessment question?
1. ‘Tell me more about your religion.’
2. ‘How can we support your spiritual beliefs and
practices?’
3. ‘How has your prayer experience been affected by
your illness?’
4. ‘What do you see as the purpose or mission of your
life?’
Focus on critical thinking
1. Consider how you might provide assistance to someone who
requests to talk about their spiritual distress. What strategies
could you use to provide spiritually sensitive care?
2. Discuss how you would respond to a request from a person
to pray with them, remembering that prayers may be lengthy;
emotion-filled; spontaneous; contain petitions, pleadings and
requests; and include long periods of silence. By contrast,
they may be quite structured, brief and even be read from a
prayer book. What personal experience have you had that
might affect your response to this request?
3. Discuss with another student your own spiritual practices.
Consider how these needs could be met if you were in
hospital.


Chapter 43 Stress and coping
Nichole Harvey
Learning outcomes
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Differentiate between the concepts of stress as a stimulus, as a
response and as a transaction.
Describe the three stages of Selye’s general adaptation
syndrome.
Identify physiological, psychological, behavioural and cognitive
indicators of stress.
Differentiate four levels of anxiety.
Identify behaviours related to specific ego defence mechanisms.


Discuss types of coping and coping strategies.
Identify essential aspects of assessing a person’s stress and
coping patterns.
Identify nursing diagnoses related to stress.
Describe interventions to help individuals minimise and manage
stress.
Differentiate between culturally safe, person-centred care for the
person experiencing harmful stress, and that which is unsafe and
not person centred.
