Everyone experiences loss, grieving and death
at some time during their life. People may suffer
the loss of valued relationships through life
changes, such as moving from one city to
another, separation, divorce or the death of a
parent, spouse or friend. People may grieve
changing life roles as grown children leave
home or they retire from their lifelong work. The
loss of valued material objects through theft or
natural disaster can evoke feelings of grief and
loss. When people’s lives are affected by civil or


national strife, they may grieve the loss of
valued ideals such as safety, freedom or
democracy.
In the clinical setting, the nurse encounters
people who may be experiencing grief related to
declining health, loss of a body part, terminal
illness or the impending death of self or a
significant other. The nurse may also work with
individuals in community settings who are
grieving losses related to a personal crisis (e.g.
divorce, separation) or a natural disaster, such
as a bushfire or a cyclone. Therefore, it is
important for the nurse to understand the
significance of loss and develop the ability to
assist people as they work through the grieving
process.
Nurses may interact with individuals who are
dying and their families or caregivers in a variety
of situations. Nurses must recognise the various
influences on the dying process—legal, ethical,
religious and spiritual, cultural, biological,
personal—and be prepared to provide sensitive,
skilled and supportive care to all those affected.


Loss and grief
Loss
 is an actual or potential situation in which something that is
valued is changed or is no longer available. People can experience
the loss of body image, body function, a significant other, a sense of
wellbeing, a job, personal possessions or beliefs. Illness and
hospitalisation often produce losses.
Death is a fundamental loss, both for the dying person and for those
who survive. Although death is inevitable, it can stimulate people to
grow in their understanding of themselves and others. Death can be
viewed as the dying person’s final opportunity to experience life in
ways that bring significance and fulfilment. People experiencing loss
often search for the meaning of the event, and it is generally
accepted that finding meaning is needed in order for healing to
occur. However, people can be well adjusted without searching for
meaning, and even those who find meaning may not see it as an
end point but rather an ongoing process.
Types and sources of loss
There are two general types of loss: actual and perceived. An actual
loss
 can be recognised by others. A perceived loss
 is
experienced by one person but cannot be verified by others.


Psychological losses are often perceived losses in that they are not
directly verifiable. For example, a woman who leaves her
employment to care for her children at home may perceive a loss of
independence and freedom.
Loss can be viewed as situational or developmental. The loss of
one’s job, the death of a child or the loss of functional ability due to
an illness or injury are situational losses. Losses that occur in the
process of normal development, such as occur in the transition from
childhood to adolescence, the departure of grown children from the
home, retirement from a career and the death of aged parents are
developmental losses that can to some extent be anticipated and
prepared for.
There are many sources of loss: (a) loss of an aspect of oneself—a
body part, a physiological function or a psychological attribute; (b)
loss of an object external to oneself; (c) separation from an
accustomed environment; and (d) loss of a loved or valued person.
Aspect of self
The loss of an aspect of ‘self’ changes a person’s body image, even
though the loss may not be obvious. A face scarred from a burn is
generally obvious to people; loss of part of the stomach or loss of
ability to feel emotion may not be as obvious. The degree to which
these losses affect a person largely depends on the individual’s
perception of their body image.


The loss of body function resulting in disability can provoke a
profound sense of loss for the affected person. This sense of loss
may be particularly acute when the change in body function is the
result of an accident rather than a gradual decline or when the
resulting disability significantly impacts on the person’s life, such as
no longer being able to work or engage in physical activity. With such
loss, the person’s body image and self-concept are also tested.
During old age, changes occur in physical and mental capabilities.
Again, the self-image is vulnerable. Old age is the stage in life when
people may experience many losses including those related to
employment, usual activities, independence, health, friends and
family. Consequently, the older adult may have difficulty adapting to
loss due to the convergence of such factors (Perng & Renz ).
1 Perng, A. & Renz, S. (2018). Identifying and treating complicated grief in older adults. The
Journal for Nurse Practitioners, 14(4), 289–295. Doi: 10.1016/j.nurpra.2017.12.001.
External objects
Loss of external objects includes (a) loss of inanimate objects that
have importance to the person, such as the loss of money or the
burning down of a family’s house, and (b) loss of animate (live)
objects such as pets that provide love and companionship.
Familiar environment
1


Separation from an environment and people who provide security
can result in a sense of loss. The 5-year-old is likely to feel loss
when first leaving the home environment to attend school, as can
the university student who moves away from home for the first time.
Loved ones
The loss of a loved one or valued person through illness, divorce,
separation or death can be very disturbing. Illnesses, such as
Alzheimer’s or dementia, which may involve personality changes,
may instil a sense of loss of that person in friends and family.
The death of a loved one is a permanent and complete loss. In
contemporary Australian society, people may be uncomfortable
talking about death and being around people who are dying. The use
of extraordinary measures to prolong and preserve life is often
considered.
Grief, bereavement and mourning
Grief
 is the total response to the emotional experience related to
loss. Grief is manifested in thoughts, feelings and behaviours
associated with overwhelming distress or sorrow. Bereavement
 is
the subjective response experienced by the surviving loved ones
after the death of a person with whom they have shared a significant
relationship. Mourning
 is the behavioural process through which


grief is eventually resolved or altered, and is often influenced by
culture, spiritual beliefs and customs. Grief and mourning are
experienced not only by the person who faces the death of a loved
one but also by the person who suffers other kinds of losses.
Grieving permits the individual to cope with the loss gradually and to
accept it as part of reality, thus facilitating mental and physical
health. Grief is also a social process and is best shared and carried
out with the support of others.
Working through one’s grief is important because bereavement may
have potentially devastating effects on health. Among the symptoms
that can accompany grief are anxiety, depression, weight loss or
gain, difficulties in swallowing, vomiting, fatigue, headaches,
dizziness, fainting, blurred vision, skin rashes, excessive sweating,
menstrual disturbances, palpitations, chest pain and dyspnoea. The
bereaved may also experience alterations in libido, concentration,
patterns of eating, sleeping, activity and communication.
Although bereavement can threaten health, a positive resolution of
the grieving process can enrich the individual with new insights,
values, challenges, openness and sensitivity. For some, the pain of
loss, though diminished, recurs for the rest of their lives.
Types of grief responses
A normal grief reaction may be abbreviated or anticipatory.
Abbreviated grief is brief but genuinely felt. This grief can occur
when the lost object is not significantly important to the grieving


person or may have been replaced immediately by another, equally
esteemed object. Anticipatory grief
 is experienced in advance of
the event, such as the wife who grieves before her ailing husband
dies. A young girl may grieve in advance of an operation that will
leave a scar on her body. Because many of the normal symptoms of
grief will have already been expressed in anticipation, the reaction
when the loss actually occurs is sometimes quite abbreviated.
Disenfranchised grief occurs when a person is unable to
acknowledge the loss to other people. Situations in which this type of
grief may occur often relate to a socially unacceptable loss that
cannot be spoken about, such as suicide, abortion or giving a child
up for adoption. Other examples include the loss of relationships
that are socially unsanctioned and may not be known to other
people (such as an extramarital relationship).
Unhealthy grief—that is, complicated grief
—exists when the
strategies to cope with the loss are maladaptive. Complicated grief
can be defined as:
A clinically significant deviation from the (cultural) norm in either (a) the time course or
intensity of specific or general symptoms of grief and/or (b) the level of impairment in
social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. (Stroebe, Schut & van den
Bout , p. 3)
2 Stroebe, M., Schut, H. & van den Bout, J. (2013). Introduction. In M. Stroebe, H. Schut &
J. van den Bout (Eds), Complicated Grief: Scientific Foundations for Health Care
Professionals. New York: Routledge.
2


Many factors can contribute to complicated grief, including a prior
traumatic loss, family or cultural barriers to the emotional expression
of grief, sudden death, a history of depression, loss of a child, a
strained relationship between the survivor and the deceased, death-
associated feelings of guilt, age of the survivor, socioeconomic
factors and a lack of social support (Mason & Tofthagen ; Tofthagen
et al. ).
3 Mason, T. M. & Tofthagen, C. S. (2019). Complicated grief of immediate family caregivers: A
concept analysis. Advances in Nursing Science, 42(3), 255–265. Doi:
10.1097/ANS.0000000000000243.
4 Tofthagen, C. S., Kip, K., Witt, A. & McMillan, S. C. (2017). Complicated grief: Risk factors,
interventions, and resources for oncology nurses. Clinical Journal of Oncology Nursing, 21(3),
331–337. Doi: 10.1188/17.CJON.331-337.
Real-World practice
I first experienced the concept of death when I was 11
—I remember being woken early in the morning to be
told that my great-grandmother had passed away. This
event was followed by further experiences of death
and dying throughout my teenage years before I
embarked upon my nursing journey. Thinking about
those who I was surrounded by at this time showed
me that there are many ways in which people cope
with grief and the death and dying process. This is
important to remember as nurses play a significant
3
4


role throughout the death and dying process. Being
aware of the different types of grief is essential to
ensure that care is tailored to each specific person and
their family. No two people are alike in their grief
process; there is no specific pathway to follow.
I have cared for many people throughout the death
and dying process. As a nurse, this can be an
extremely challenging and overwhelming period. The
valuable communication tools we are taught at the
beginning of our nursing journeys are the most
powerful and beneficial sources to use during this time.
Discussing issues on death and dying is not easy.
Active listening, paraphrasing and asking open-ended
questions are powerful in helping us to assess people’s
wishes, beliefs and stages of grief. Also, never
overestimate the power of silence.
I am very fortunate to be part of a wonderful and
supportive nursing team. As a novice nurse, I had
many wonderful mentors who have imparted invaluable
knowledge when showing dignity, care and respect to
people and their families. I hope that your nursing
journey is as supportive as mine. You are never alone
in the journey of caring for somebody who is dying.
—Alison Boisen RN, BNSc, PGCertNSc(IntCare), MAdvNPrac Townsville, Queensland


Complicated grief may take several different forms. Absent grief is
the absence of grieving in the person who has experienced a major
bereavement. The person may appear emotionally numb or
detached from the loss as though nothing has happened.
Unresolved or chronic grief is extended in length and severity. The
same signs are expressed as with normal grief but the bereaved
may also have difficulty expressing the grief, may deny the loss or
may grieve beyond the expected time. With inhibited grief, many of
the normal symptoms of grief are suppressed and other effects,
including somatic, are experienced instead. Delayed grief occurs
when feelings are purposely or subconsciously suppressed until a
much later time. A survivor who appears to be using dangerous
activities (e.g. excessive sedation, alcohol consumption or illicit
drugs) as a method to lessen the pain of grieving may be
experiencing exaggerated grief.
Complicated grief after a death may be inferred from the following
data or observations:
The person fails to grieve; for example, a husband does not cry
at or fails to attend his wife’s funeral.
The person avoids visiting the grave and refuses to participate in
memorial services, even though these practices are a part of
their culture.
The person becomes recurrently symptomatic on the anniversary
of a loss or during holidays.
The person develops persistent guilt and lowered self-esteem.


Even after a prolonged period, the person continues to search
for the individual they have lost. Some may consider suicide to
effect reunion.
A relatively minor event triggers symptoms of grief.
Even after a period of time, the person is unable to discuss the
deceased with composure; for example, their voice cracks and
quivers and eyes become moist.
After the normal period of grief, the person experiences physical
symptoms similar to those of the individual who died.
The person’s relationships with friends and relatives worsen
following the death.
Many factors contribute to unresolved grief after a death:
ambivalence (intense feelings, both positive and negative)
towards the deceased; a perceived need to be brave and in
control; fear of losing control in front of others
endurance of multiple losses, such as the loss of an entire family,
which the bereaved finds too overwhelming to contemplate
extremely high emotional value invested in the deceased; failure
to grieve in this instance helps the bereaved avoid the reality of
the loss
uncertainty about the loss—for example, when a loved one is
missing
lack of support systems.
Stages of grieving


Many authors have described stages or phases of grieving, perhaps
the most well known of them being Kübler-Ross , who described five
stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance (see
Table 44.1
). Engel  identified six stages of grieving: shock and
disbelief, developing awareness, restitution, resolving the loss,
idealisation and outcome (see Table 44.2
). Sanders  described
five phases of bereavement: shock, awareness of loss,
conservation/withdrawal, healing and renewal (see Table 44.3
).
5 Kübler-Ross, E. (1969). On Death and Dying. New York: Macmillan.
6 Engel, G. L. (1964). Grief and grieving. American Journal of Nursing, 64(9), 93–98.
7 Sanders, C. M. (1998). Grief: The Mourning After: Dealing with Adult Bereavement (2nd
ed.). New York: John Wiley & Sons.
Table 44.1 Individual responses and nursing implications in
Kübler-Ross’s stages of grieving

Table 44.2 Engel’s stages of grieving

Table 44.3 Sanders’ phases of bereavement
