John Wiley & Sons. Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
5
6
7


Martocchio  described five clusters of grief: shock and disbelief;
yearning and protest; anguish, disorganisation and despair;
identification in bereavement; and reorganisation and restitution—
and maintained that there is no single correct way, nor a correct
timetable, by which a person progresses through the grief process.
Whether a person can succeed in integrating the loss and how this
is accomplished are related to that person’s individual development
and personal make-up. In addition, individuals responding to the
very same loss cannot be expected to follow the same pattern or
schedule in resolving their grief, even while they support each other.
8 Martocchio, B. C. (1985). Grief and bereavement: Healing through hurt. Nursing Clinics of
North America, 20, 327–341.
Rando ( ;
;
) has written extensively on the subject of grief and
describes three categories of responses: avoidance, confrontation
and accommodation. Avoidance is similar to Kübler-Ross’s phases
of denial, anger and bargaining and Engel’s phase of shock and
disbelief. Confrontation is the most upsetting phase for the grieving
person facing the loss. Accommodation is the phase in which the
person begins to resume more usual activities, feels better and
places the loss in perspective.
9 Rando, T. A. (1991). How to Go on Living When Someone You Love Dies. New York:
Bantam.
10 Rando, T. A. (1993). Treatment of Complicated Mourning. Champaign, IL: Research Press.
11 Rando, T. A. (2000). Clinical Dimensions of Anticipatory Mourning: Theory and Practice in
Working with the Dying, Their Loved Ones and Their Caregivers. Champaign, IL: Research
8
9 10 11


Press.
Manifestations of grief
The nurse assesses the grieving person or family members following
a loss to determine the phase or stage of grieving. Physiologically,
the body responds to a current or anticipated loss with a stress
reaction. The nurse can assess the clinical signs of this response.
See Chapter 43
.
Manifestations of grief that would be considered normal include
verbalisation of the loss, crying, sleep disturbance, loss of appetite
(anorexia) and difficulty concentrating. Complicated grieving may be
characterised by an extended time of denial, depression, severe
physiological symptoms or suicidal thoughts.
Factors influencing the loss and
grief responses
A number of factors affect a person’s response to a loss or death.
These factors include age, significance of the loss, cultural
background, spiritual beliefs, gender, socioeconomic status, support
systems and the cause of the loss or death. Nurses can learn
general concepts about the influence of these factors on the grieving
experience, but the grouping of these factors and their significance
will vary from individual to individual.


Age
Age affects a person’s understanding of and reaction to loss. With
familiarity, people usually increase their understanding and
acceptance of life, loss and death.
People do not usually experience the loss of loved ones at regular
intervals. As a result, preparation for these experiences is difficult.
Coping with other types of losses, such as the loss of a pet, the loss
of a colleague and the loss of a job, can help people anticipate the
more severe loss of death of loved ones by teaching them
successful coping strategies.
Childhood
Children differ from adults not only in their understanding of loss and
death but also in how they are affected by the loss of others. The
loss of a parent or other significant person can threaten the child’s
ability to develop and regression sometimes results. Assisting the
child with the grief experience includes helping the child regain the
normal continuity and pace of emotional development.
Some adults may assume that children do not have the same need
as an adult to grieve the loss of others. In situations of crisis and
loss, children are sometimes pushed aside or protected from the
pain. They can feel afraid, abandoned and lonely. Careful work with
bereaved children is especially necessary because experiencing a


loss in childhood can have serious effects later in life (see Figure
44.1
).
Figure 44.1


Children experience the same emotions of grief as adults.
Source: © Michael Ireland/Fotolia.com.
Early and middle adulthood
As people grow, they come to experience loss as part of normal
development. By middle age, for example, the loss of a parent
through death seems a more normal occurrence compared with the
death of a younger person. Coping with the death of an aged parent
has even been viewed as an essential developmental task of the
middle-aged adult. However, even though the death of a parent is
anticipated for middle-aged adults, it is not necessarily an easier loss
to cope with.
The middle-aged adult can experience losses other than death. For
example, losses resulting from impaired health or body function and
losses of various role functions can be difficult for the middle-aged
adult. How the middle-aged adult responds to such losses is
influenced by previous experiences with loss, the person’s sense of
self-esteem and the strength and availability of support.
Late adulthood
Losses experienced by older adults include loss of health, mobility,
independence and work role. Limited income and the need to
change one’s living accommodations can also lead to feelings of loss
and grieving.


For older adults, the loss through death of a long-time mate is
profound. Although individuals differ in their ability to deal with such
a loss, research suggests that health problems for widows and
widowers increase following the death of their spouse (Milic et al.
;
Shin, Kim & Park ). Because the majority of deaths occur among
elderly people and because the number of older adults is increasing
in Australia, nurses will need to be especially alert to the potential
problems of older grieving adults.
12 Milic, J., Saavedra Perez, H., Zuurbier, L. A., Boelen, P. A., Rietjens, J. A., Hofman, A. &
Tiemeier, H. (2019). The longitudinal and cross-sectional associations of grief and
complicated grief with sleep quality in older adults. Behavioral Sleep Medicine, 17(1), 31–40.
Doi: 10.1080/15402002.2016.1276016.
13 Shin, S. H., Kim, G. & Park, S. (2018). Widowhood status as a risk factor for cognitive
decline among older adults. The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, 26(7), 778–787.
Doi: 10.1016/j.jagp.2018.03.013.
Significance of the loss
The significance of a loss depends on the perceptions of the
individual experiencing the loss. One person may experience a great
sense of loss over a divorce; another may find it only mildly
disrupting. A number of factors affect the significance of the loss:
importance of the lost person, object or function
degree of change required because of the loss
the person’s beliefs and values.
12
13


For older people who have already encountered many losses, an
anticipated loss such as their own death may not be viewed as
highly negative and they may be indifferent about it instead of
reactive. More than fearing death, some may fear loss of control or
becoming a burden.
Cultural background
Culture influences an individual’s reaction to loss. How grief is
expressed is often determined by the customs of the culture. Unless
an extended family structure exists, grief is handled by the nuclear
family. The death of a family member in a typical nuclear family
leaves a great void because the same few individuals fill most of the
roles. In cultures where several generations and extended family
members either reside in the same household or are physically
close, the impact of a family member’s death may be softened
because the roles of the deceased are quickly filled by other
relatives.
Some people adopt the belief that grief is a private matter to be
endured internally, resulting in a repression of feelings. Therefore,
individuals who have been socialised to ‘be strong’ and ‘make the
best of the situation’ may not express deep feelings or personal
concerns when they experience a serious loss.
Some cultural groups value social support and the expression of
loss. In some groups, expressions of grief through wailing, crying,
physical prostration and other outward demonstrations are


acceptable and encouraged. Other groups may frown on this
demonstration as a loss of control, favouring a more quiet and stoic
expression of grief. In cultural groups where strong kinship ties are
maintained, physical and emotional support and assistance are
provided by family members.
Spiritual beliefs
Spiritual beliefs and practices greatly influence both a person’s
reaction to loss and their subsequent behaviours. Most religious
groups have practices related to dying and these are often important
to the individual and support people. To provide support at a time of
death, nurses need to understand the individual’s particular beliefs
and practices.
Gender
Gender roles into which many people are socialised in Australia may
affect their reactions at times of loss. Men are frequently expected
to ‘be strong’ and show very little emotion during grief, whereas it is
acceptable for women to show grief by crying. For example, when a
male is confronted with a loss of his significant other, he is more
likely to repress his own emotions in order to comfort others (e.g.
children) in their grieving.
Socioeconomic status


The socioeconomic status of an individual often affects the support
system available to them at the time of a loss. A pension plan, a
funeral plan or life insurance, for example, can offer a widowed or
disabled person a choice of ways to deal with a loss. In contrast, a
person who is confronted with both severe loss and economic
hardship may be at greater risk of developing complicated grief or
other maladaptive behaviours (West & Ramcharan ).
14 West, R. & Ramcharan, P. (2019). The emerging role of financial counsellors in supporting
older persons in financial hardship and with management of consumer-directed care
packages within Australia. Australian Journal of Social Issues, 54(1), 32–51. Doi:
10.1002/ajs4.55.
Support system
The people closest to the grieving individual are often the first to
recognise and provide needed emotional, physical and functional
assistance. However, because many people are uncomfortable or
inexperienced in dealing with losses, the usual support people may
instead withdraw from the grieving individual. In addition, support
may be available when the loss is first recognised but as the support
people return to their usual activities, the need for ongoing support
may be unmet. Sometimes, the grieving individual may be unable or
unready to accept support when it is offered.
Cause of loss or death
14


Individual and societal views on the cause of a loss or death may
significantly influence the grief response. Some diseases are
considered ‘clean’, such as cardiovascular disorders, and engender
compassion, whereas others (e.g. a death that results from a drug
overdose) may be viewed as less unfortunate. A loss or death that is
beyond the control of those involved may be more acceptable than
one that is preventable, such as a drink-driving accident. Injuries or
deaths occurring during respected activities, such as ‘in the line of
duty’, are considered honourable, whereas those occurring during
illicit activities may be considered the individual’s ‘just reward’.


Nursing management
Assessing
Nursing assessment of a person experiencing a loss includes three
major components: (1) nursing history; (2) assessment of personal
coping resources; and (3) physical assessment. During routine
health assessments, the nurse poses questions regarding previous
and current losses to the person. If the person reports a current or
recent loss, the nurse needs to explore the nature and significance
of this loss. The nurse may also need to ask probing questions to
identify possible loss-related stresses as people do not always
associate physical ailments with emotional responses such as grief.
Assessment interview
Loss and grieving
Previous losses
Have you ever lost someone or something very important
to you?


Have you or your family ever moved to a new home or
location?
What was it like for you when you first started school?
Moved away from home? Got a job? Retired?
Are you physically able to do all the things you used to
do?
Has anyone important or close to you died?
Do you think there will be any losses in your life in the
near future?
If there has been previous grieving:
Tell me about (the loss). What was losing
like for you?
Did you have trouble sleeping? Eating? Concentrating?
What kinds of things did you do to make yourself feel
better when something like that happened?
Did you observe any spiritual or cultural practices when
you had a loss like that?
Who did you turn to if you were very upset about (the
loss)?
How long did it take you to feel more like yourself again
and go back to your usual activities?
If there is a current loss:
What have you been told about (the loss)? Is there
anything else you would like to know or don’t understand?


What changes do you think this (illness, surgery, problem)
will cause in your life? What do you think it will be like
without (the lost object)?
Have you ever experienced a loss like this before?
Can you think of anything good that might come out of
this?
What kind of help do you think you will need? Who is
going to be helping you with this loss?
Are there any people or organisations in your community
that might be able to help?
Current grieving
Are you having trouble sleeping? Eating? Concentrating?
Do you have any pain or other new physical problems?
What are you doing to help you deal with this loss?
Are you taking any drugs or medications to help you cope
with this loss?
Where the person reports a significant loss, the nurse needs to
explore how the person usually copes with loss and what resources
are available to assist them to cope during this period. Data
regarding general health status; other personal stressors; cultural
and spiritual traditions, rituals and beliefs related to loss and
grieving; and the person’s support network are needed to determine
an appropriate plan of care (see the ‘Assessment interview
’). In
assessing the individual’s response to a current loss, the nurse may


identify complicated grief which is best treated by a health care
professional who is an expert in assisting such people (e.g. a
psychologist or counsellor). If the nursing assessment reveals
severe physical or psychological signs and symptoms, the person
should be referred to other members of the health care team where
appropriate.
Patient safety competency framework
1 Person-centred care
Nursing students must demonstrate empathy by
seeking to understand the person’s
perspectives, views and feelings (Levett-Jones
et al.
).
15 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Diagnosing
Nursing diagnoses relating specifically to grieving include the
following:
15


Grieving: a normal complex process that includes emotional,
physical, spiritual, social and intellectual responses and
behaviours by which individuals, families and communities
incorporate an actual, anticipated or perceived loss into their
daily lives.
Complicated grieving/Risk of complicated grieving: a
disorder that occurs after the death of a significant other in which
the experience of distress accompanying bereavement fails to
follow normative expectations and manifests in functional
impairment.
Other nursing diagnoses may include:
Interrupted family processes if the loss has had such an impact
on the individual and family that usual effective roles and
interactions are negatively affected.
Risk-prone health behaviour if the individual has great difficulty
placing the loss in an appropriate perspective to their other life
activities.
Risk of loneliness related to the loss of relationships with others.
Examples of clinical applications of some of these diagnoses are
shown in the following ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and
interventions’.
Planning


The overall goals for people who are grieving the loss of body
function or a body part are to adjust to the changed ability and to
redirect both physical and emotional energy into rehabilitation. The
goals for people who are grieving the loss of a loved one are: to
remember the person without feeling intense pain, to redirect
emotional energy into one’s own life and to adjust to the actual or
impending loss.
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
People who are grieving
HISTORY Marion Williams’ son Billy, age 15, has cystic
fibrosis. Mother and son are waiting for an appropriate donor
for a heart–lung transplant. She says, ‘We’ve been called to
the transplant unit twice but things didn’t work out. Billy gets
his hopes all geared up and then he’s deflated. I can’t eat or
sleep worrying. I don’t know what I’ll do if he doesn’t get that
transplant. He’s all I’ve got since my husband left us six years
ago’.
History Sebastian Peter’s partner died 14 months ago of a
ruptured aortic aneurysm at age 59. He lives alone, has no
children and refuses to see friends. He reports frequent
headaches, an inability to concentrate at work, little interest in
food and early morning insomnia. These symptoms increase
at the time of his partner’s birthday and at Christmas. He


says, ‘I still can’t find it in myself to visit his grave. There are
times when I’d just like to die and be with him’.
Examples of nursing outcomes and interventions are shown in the
following ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and
interventions’.
Planning for home care
Individuals who have sustained or anticipate a loss may require
ongoing nursing care to assist them in adapting to the loss. The
determination of how much and what type of home care follow-up is
needed is based primarily on the nurse’s knowledge of the person’s
current abilities and care needs and how the person and their family
have coped with previous losses. The ‘Home care assessment’
describes data to gather for home care or follow-up assessment.
Home care assessment
Grieving
Individual
Knowledge: the individual’s understanding of the
implications of the loss.


Self-care abilities: skill in caring for self based on
any physical abilities that may have been altered by
the loss.
Current coping: stage in the grieving or
bereavement process.
Current manifestations of the grief response:
adaptive or maladaptive signs and symptoms;
cultural or spiritually based behaviours.
Role expectations: the individual’s perception of
the need to return to work or family roles.
Family
Knowledge: various family members’ perception of
the loss.
Support people’s availability and skills:
sensitivity to the health care recipient’s emotional
and physical needs; ability to provide an accepting
environment.
Role expectations: family perception of the health
care recipient’s need to return to work or family
roles.
Community
Resources: availability and familiarity with possible
sources of assistance such as grief support groups,
religious or spiritual centres, counselling services,
physical care providers.


Implementing
The skills most relevant to situations of loss and grief are attentive
listening, silence, open and closed questioning, paraphrasing,
clarifying and reflecting feelings, and summarising. Less helpful to
people are responses that give advice and evaluation, those that
interpret and analyse, and those that give unwarranted reassurance.
To ensure effective communication, the nurse must make an
accurate assessment of what is appropriate for the person.
Communication with grieving people needs to be relevant to their
stage of grief. Whether the person is angry or depressed affects
how the person hears messages and how the nurse interprets the
individual’s statements. In addition to using effective communication
skills, the nurse implements a plan to provide the person and their
family education and to help the person work through the stages of
grief.
Facilitating grief work
Explore and respect the individual’s and family’s ethnic, cultural,
religious and personal values in their expressions of grief.
Tell the individual or family what to expect in the grief process,
such as that certain thoughts and feelings are normal


(acceptable) and that labile emotions, feelings of sadness, guilt,
anger, fear and loneliness will stabilise or lessen over time.
Knowing what to expect may lessen the intensity of some
reactions.
Encourage the individual to express and share grief with support
people. Sharing feelings reinforces relationships and facilitates
the grief process.
Teach family members to encourage the individual’s expression
of grief, not to push the person to move on or enforce their own
expectations of appropriate reactions. If the health care recipient
is a child, encourage family members to be truthful and to allow
the child to participate in the grieving activities of others.
Encourage the individual to resume normal activities on a
schedule that promotes physical and psychological health. Some
people may try to return to normal activities too quickly. However,
a prolonged delay in return may indicate complicated grieving.
Providing emotional support
Use silence and personal presence along with techniques of
therapeutic communication. These techniques enhance
exploration of feelings and let the person know that the nurse
acknowledges their feelings.
Acknowledge the grief of the individual’s family and significant
others. Family support people are part of the grieving person’s
world.
Offer choices that promote autonomy. People need to have a
sense of some control over their own lives at a time when much


control may not be possible.
Provide appropriate information regarding how to access
community resources: clergy, support groups and counselling
services.
Nurses should ensure that they are familiar with the range of
community support services in their region. Geographical isolation in
some areas of Australia may mean that some families are unable to
travel to support group meetings or make face-to-face contact. In
many instances, strategies have been implemented to offer support
services through other means such as tele- and video-conferencing
(see the ‘Web links
’ at the end of the chapter).
Examples of nursing actions appropriate for individuals in various
stages of the grief process are shown in the ‘Concept map’ at the
end of the chapter.
Evaluating
Evaluating the effectiveness of nursing care of the grieving person is
difficult because of the long-term nature of the life transition. Criteria
for evaluation must be based on goals set by the person and their
family.
Person-centred goals and related desired outcomes for a grieving
individual will depend on the characteristics of the loss and the
person. Examples of person-centred goals and related outcomes


are shown in the earlier ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes
and interventions’.
If outcomes are not achieved, the nurse needs to explore why the
plan was unsuccessful. Such exploration begins with reassessing the
person and their experience of loss in case the initial nursing
diagnoses were inappropriate. Examples of questions guiding the
exploration include:
Do the person’s grieving behaviours indicate abnormal grieving or
another nursing diagnosis?
Is the expected outcome unrealistic for the given timeframe?
Does the person have additional stressors previously not
considered that are affecting their grief resolution?
Have nursing strategies been implemented consistently,
compassionately and genuinely?


Dying and death
The concept of death is developed over time as the person grows,
experiences various losses and thinks about concrete and abstract
concepts. In general, humans move from a childhood belief in death
as a temporary state, to adulthood in which death is accepted as
very real but also very frightening, to older adulthood in which death
may be viewed as more desirable than living with a poor quality of
life. Table 44.4
 describes some of the specific beliefs common to
different age groups. The nurse’s knowledge of these developmental
stages helps in understanding some of the individual’s responses to
a life-threatening situation.
Table 44.4 Development of the concept of death
Responses to dying and death
The reaction of any person to another person’s impending or real
death, or to the potential reality of their own death, depends on all
the factors regarding loss and the development of the concept of
death. In spite of the individual variations in a person’s views about
the cause of death, spiritual beliefs, availability of support systems
or any other factor, responses tend to cluster in the phases
described by theorists (see Tables 44.1
 to 44.3
).


Both the person who is dying and the family members grieve as they
recognise the loss. Defining characteristics for the nursing diagnosis
of Grieving include denial, guilt, anger, despair, feelings of
worthlessness, crying and inability to concentrate. They may extend
to thoughts of suicide, delusions and hallucinations. Fear, the feeling
of disruption that is related to an identifiable source (in this case
someone’s death), may also be present. Many of the characteristics
seen in a fearful person are similar to those of grieving and include
crying, immobility, increased pulse and respirations, dry mouth,
anorexia, difficulty sleeping and nightmares. Hopelessness occurs
when the person perceives no solutions to a problem—when the
death becomes inevitable and the person is unable to see how to
move beyond the death. The nurse may observe apathy, pessimism
and indecision. A person who does perceive a solution to the
problem but does not believe that it is possible to implement the
solution may be said to experience Powerlessness. This loss of
control may be manifested by anger, violence, depression or passive
behaviours.
Research note
Exploring parent–health care provider relationships
when a child dies
A. E. Butler, B. Copnell & H. Hall
. The impact of the social and physical environments on parent–
healthcare provider relationships when a child dies in PICU: Findings from a grounded theory study.
Intensive & Critical Care Nursing, 50, 28–35. Doi: 10.1016/j.iccn.2017.12.008.
16


16 Butler, A. E., Copnell, B. & Hall, H. (2019). The impact of the social and physical environments on
parent–healthcare provider relationships when a child dies in PICU: Findings from a grounded theory
study. Intensive & Critical Care Nursing, 50, 28–35. Doi: 10.1016/j.iccn.2017.12.008.
This study explores the influence of the paediatric intensive
care unit (PICU) environment on the development of parent–
health care provider (HCP) relationships when a child is
dying. This qualitative study used semi-structured interviews
to collect data from 26 bereaved parents. The data was then
analysed using grounded theory methods such as open
coding, constant comparative analysis and memo writing. The
findings identified that the physical and social environment of
the PICU influenced the quality of the parent–HCP
relationship. Physical factors of the PICU environment such
as prohibiting parents bringing their child’s personal items
(e.g. toys, blankets) into the unit and lacking facilities for
parental self-care activities (e.g. kitchen, laundry and
bathroom facilities) can hinder the formation of a collaborative
parent–HCP relationship. Social factors such as restricting
parental presence or not allowing parents to assist in care
can also create a negative experience for the parents.
Implications Clinician attitudes and restrictive clinical
environments can result in the parent of a dying child feeling
excluded from their child’s care. Nurses can assist parents
come to terms with their dying child’s impending death by
creating an open and flexible environment where the parents
feel welcome and are able to participate in their child’s care.


Caregivers, both professionals and support people, also respond to
the impending death. The nursing diagnosis Risk of caregiver role
strain may be applied to this group. The ongoing responsibilities for
providing physical, economic, psychological and social support to a
dying person can create extreme stress for the provider. Often the
length of time between a terminal diagnosis and when death will
occur is unknown and the people supporting the dying person
become fatigued and depressed. They may also become frustrated
or angry due to the loss of time and resources for personal activities
or the provision of attention to other people. Within a family that
usually functions effectively, death of a member may result in
Interrupted family processes. In this situation, the family may be
unable to meet the physical, emotional or spiritual needs of the
members and may have difficulty communicating and problem
solving.
Professional caregivers, including nurses, may experience role strain
due to repeated interactions with dying individuals and their families.
Although most nurses who work in oncology, palliative care,
intensive care, emergency or other areas where death is a common
event have chosen such assignments, there can still be a sense of
failure when people die. Just as there must be support systems for
grieving individuals, there must also be support systems for grieving
health care professionals.
Some people may think of death as the worst occurrence in life and
do their best to avoid thinking or talking about death—especially
their own. Nurses are not immune to such attitudes. They need to


take time to analyse their own feelings about death and dying before
they can effectively help others with a terminal illness. Nurses who
are uncomfortable with individuals who are dying tend to impede
attempts to discuss dying and death in these ways:
changing the subject (e.g. ‘Let’s think of something more
cheerful’ or ‘You shouldn’t say things like that’)
offering false reassurance (e.g. ‘You are doing very well’)
denying what is happening (e.g. ‘You don’t really mean that’ or
‘You’re going to live until you’re a hundred’)
being fatalistic (e.g. ‘Everyone dies sooner or later’ or ‘What’s
meant to be, will be’)
blocking discussion (e.g. ‘I don’t think things are really that bad’)
and conveying an attitude that stops further discussion of the
subject
being aloof and distant or avoiding the person
‘managing’ the individual’s care and making them feel
increasingly dependent and powerless.
Looking critically at each of these points will allow nurses to develop
individual strategies that can be used as bridges to overcome such
potential barriers.
Caring for the dying and the bereaved is one of the nurse’s most
complex and challenging responsibilities, bringing into play all the
skills needed for holistic physiological and psychosocial care.


Definitions and signs of death
In 1977, the Australian Law Reform Commission recognised the
need for a statutory definition of death to be introduced into
Australian law. Its recommendation was death should be defined as
(a) irreversible cessation of all function of the brain of the person, or
(b) irreversible cessation of circulation of blood in the body of the
person (Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society
(ANZICS)
). While each Australian state and territory law’s
definition of death is slightly different, they are all based on the
above recommendation.
17 Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society (ANZICS) (2013a). The ANZICS
Statement on Death and Organ Donation (Edition 3.2). Melbourne: ANZICS. Retrieved from
<www.anzics.com.au>.
With circulatory death
, death can be determined when all the
following signs are evident:
immobility
apnoea
absent skin perfusion
absence of circulation (evidenced by absent arterial pulse for a
minimum of 2 minutes) (ANZICS ).
18 Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society (ANZICS) (2015). Circulatory
Death Determination. Retrieved from <www.anzics.com.au>.
17
18


Another definition of death is brain death
. In Australia, unlike
some other countries, brain death is defined as the cessation of
circulation to the brain resulting in the entire brain (including the
brainstem) dying (ANZICS ). The determination of brain death is
complex and multiple testing must be conducted by two medical
practitioners who are qualified to determine brain death. Prior to the
conduction of these tests, a number of other causes (such as drugs,
hypothermia, hypo/hyperglycaemia and deranged electrolyte levels)
for deep coma must be excluded. If brain death is determined by the
two medical practitioners, there may be an option for the family to
donate the person’s organs.
19 Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society (ANZICS) (2013b). Brain Death
Determination Statement. Retrieved from <www.anzics.com.au>.
Death-related religious and
cultural practices
Various cultural and religious traditions and practices associated with
death, dying and the grieving process help people cope with these
experiences. Nurses are often present through the dying process
and at the moment of death. Knowledge of the person’s religious
and cultural heritage helps nurses provide individualised care to the
person and their family, even though they may not participate in the
rituals associated with death. In a clinical setting, this display of
19


respect may require the nurse to be flexible and innovative to
accommodate the cultural needs of the person and their family.
In many cultures, people prefer a peaceful death at home rather
than in the hospital. Members of some ethnic groups may request
that health professionals not reveal the prognosis to individuals who
are dying. They believe the person’s last days should be free of
worry. People in other cultures prefer that a family member
(preferably a male in some cultures) be told the diagnosis so that
the individual can be tactfully informed by a family member in
gradual stages or not be told at all. Nurses also need to determine
who to call and when, as the impending death draws near.
Beliefs and attitudes about death, its cause and the soul also vary
between cultures. Unnatural deaths, or ‘bad deaths’, are sometimes
distinguished from ‘good deaths’. In addition, the death of a person
who has behaved well in life may be considered less threatening
based on the belief that the person will be reincarnated into a good
life.
Beliefs about preparation of the body, autopsy, organ donation,
cremation and prolonging life are closely aligned to the person’s
religion. Autopsy, for example, may be prohibited, opposed or
discouraged by Hindus, Muslims, Jehovah’s Witnesses and
Orthodox Jews unless under specific circumstances (Fouché ;
Chakraborty et al.
). Some religions prohibit the removal of body
parts or dictate that all body parts be given appropriate burial. For
example, organ donation is prohibited in Shintoism and for Romani
20
21


people (Organ and Tissue Authority ). Nonetheless, most religions
practised in Australia support organ donation, with some religions
such as Buddhism encouraging it as an act of mercy (Organ and
Tissue Authority 2019). Cremation is discouraged, opposed or
prohibited by the Church of the Latter-day Saints, Eastern Orthodox
and Islamic faiths. Hindus, in contrast, prefer cremation and cast the
ashes in a holy river. Additionally, Christianity encompasses many
different religions whose beliefs vary quite significantly.
20 Fouché, N. (2019). A contemporary review of understanding the religious and cultural
diversity of patients dying or who have died in the intensive care unit. A South African
perspective. International Journal of Africa Nursing Sciences, 10, 61–67. Doi:
10.1016/j.ijans.2019.01.003.
21 Chakraborty, R., El-Jawahri, A. R., Litzow, M. R., Syrjala, K. L., Parnes, A. D. & Hashmi,
S. K. (2017). A systematic review of religious beliefs about major end-of-life issues in the five
major world religions. Palliative & Supportive Care, 15(5), 609–622. Doi:
10.1017/S147895151600106.
22 Organ and Tissue Authority (2019). Organ Donation and Religion. Retrieved from
<www.donatelife.gov.au>.
Nurses also need to be knowledgeable about the person’s death-
related rituals, such as last rites, chanting at the bedside and other
practices, and special procedures for washing, dressing, positioning,
shrouding and attending the dead. For example, certain cultures
retain their native customs in which family members of the same sex
wash and prepare the body for burial and cremation. Muslims also
customarily turn the body towards Mecca. In several religions, the
body cannot be left unattended until burial and people may be hired
to sit with the body if family members do not perform this duty.
22


Nurses need to ask family members about their preference and
verify who will carry out these activities. Burial clothes and other
cultural or religious items are often important symbols for the
funeral.
Death and dying in indigenous Australian
cultures
In Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures, death
may be regarded as more significant than birth and marriage as it
completes the life–death–life cycle (South Australian Department for
Health and Ageing ) (see Figure 44.2
). Therefore, death and
dying are major topics that the nurse must discuss with the
individual, their family and the community. It is not expected that the
nurse will fully understand the beliefs, but there is an expectation of
respect and facilitation which will form the individualised holistic care
plan for the person.
23 South Australian Department for Health and Ageing (2013). SA Health Aboriginal Culture
and History Handbook. Retrieved from <www.sahealth.sa.gov.au>.
Figure 44.2
23


In the traditional Indigenous Tiwi ceremony connected with death,
the Ilaninga, carved and painted poles are displayed on the site
where the funeral dances take place, near the house of the dead
person.
Source: Bill Tompkins/Contributor/Getty Images.
The specific traditional practices will vary greatly depending on the
community to which the person belongs. However, there are some
practices that are common to many communities. These may
include:


When returning the person’s belongings, it is very important that
any item belonging to the person is accounted for. This practice
is a spiritual acknowledgment rather than an economic one, as it
is believed there may be severe repercussions if some parts or
belongings are left behind. All ‘parts’ of the person will include all
body parts, hair, clothing or possessions. The nurse needs to
remain vigilant and ensure that all belongings are kept together
and returned to the family.
If a person dies at home, the house may be marked and
abandoned for some time by its residents. If the person dies in
hospital, a selected family member will be required to escort the
body home. These practices can impact on the family’s financial
situation and the ability to maintain contact with health providers
or government agencies and, as such, require inclusion in the
care planning for the person. It has been a tradition to ‘smoke’
the room where an Indigenous person has died. While this may
not be common practice in some areas, if it is a belief of the
family, hospital procedures and protocols are adapted to facilitate
the ritual.
Wailing and self-mutilation (known as ‘sorry cuts’) continue to be
grief practices in some communities. These practices may cause
distress to staff and other health care recipients. This custom
may necessitate adjusting bed allocations or the use of a private
room to enable the family to express their grief.
Not calling the deceased by their name is another important
custom the nurse must follow. It is believed that using the
deceased person’s name can call back their spirit. To avoid
disrespecting this custom, the nurse can refer to the deceased


by choosing phrases such as ‘your father’ or ‘your son’)
(Queensland Health ).
24 Queensland Health (2015). Sad News, Sorry Business: Guidelines for Caring for
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People Through Death and Dying. Brisbane:
Queensland Government. Retrieved from <www.health.qld.gov.au>.
24


Nursing management
Assessing
To gather a complete database that allows accurate analysis and
identification of appropriate nursing diagnoses for individuals who
are dying and their families, the nurse first needs to recognise the
states of awareness manifested by the person and family members.
In cases of terminal illness, the state of awareness shared by the
dying person and the family affects the nurse’s ability to
communicate freely with individuals and other health care team
members and to assist in the grieving process. Three types of
awareness that have been described are closed awareness, mutual
pretence and open awareness (Glaser & Strauss ).
25 Glaser, B. & Strauss, A. (1965). Awareness of Dying. Chicago: Aldine.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: Comprehensive care
The intention of this standard is to ‘ensure that patients receive
comprehensive care—that is, coordinated delivery of the total
25


health care required or requested by a patient; and, to ensure
that risks of harm for patients during health care are prevented
and managed’ (Australian Commission on Safety and Quality
in Health Care
, p. 38).
26 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved by
clinicians identifying people at risk of specific
harm during health care by applying the
screening and assessment processes outlined
in this standard. These processes include using
systems to identify people at the end of life, to
provide safe and high-quality care and to use
systems to recognise and meet the nutrition and
hydration needs of patients.
Providing quality end-of-life care is complex.
There are certain legal requirements that the
nurse should review when caring for a terminally
ill person, including whether an advance health
directive (AHD)
 and an acute resuscitation
plan (ARP)
 are in place. An AHD (sometimes
known as a ‘living will’) is a document that
outlines the person’s wishes and requests
regarding their future health care for a variety of
medical conditions, including the decision to
26


prolong life via interventions such as
resuscitation and mechanical ventilation. This
document comes into effect once the person no
longer has the cognitive capacity to consent to
treatment (Queensland Health ). Many people
who are terminally ill or are undergoing major
surgery elect to have an AHD prepared while
they are still well in case of a complication or
deterioration. If the person has an AHD, a copy
will be stored in their medical record. The ARP
is a form outlining the interventions that should
be included and/or withheld in the event of a
respiratory or cardiac arrest. This form
acknowledges the person’s autonomy to refuse
life-sustaining measures and is completed
collaboratively with the treating doctor and the
person. A copy of the ARP is stored in the
person’s medical record, normally close to the
front for easy access.
27 Queensland Health (2018). Advance Health Directive.
Retrieved from <www.qld.gov.au>.
Clinical consideration
27


Victoria was the first state in Australia to pass
voluntary assisted dying laws. From June 2019,
Victorian citizens who meet strict eligibility
criteria, including being in the advanced stages
of a terminal illness or neurodegenerative
disease, have the legal option to plan and time
their death under the Voluntary Assisted Dying
Act 2017. Western Australia is currently seeking
public consultation regarding the introduction of
a similar law. Nurses need to be remain abreast
of such changes to legislation.
In closed awareness
, the individual is not made aware of
impending death. The family may choose this path because they do
not completely understand why the person is ill or they believe that
they will recover. The doctor may believe it is best not to
communicate a diagnosis or prognosis to the individual. Nursing staff
are confronted with an ethical problem in this situation. See Chapter
5
 for further information on ethical dilemmas.
With mutual pretence
, the individual, family and health
professionals know that the prognosis is terminal but do not talk
about it and make an effort not to raise the subject. Sometimes the
person refrains from discussing death to protect the family from
distress. The person may also sense discomfort on the part of the
health care professional and therefore may not bring up the subject.


Mutual pretence permits the person a degree of privacy and dignity,
but it places a heavy burden on them because there is no one in
whom they can confide.
With open awareness
, the individual and others know about the
impending death and feel comfortable discussing it, even though it is
difficult. This awareness gives them an opportunity to finalise affairs
and even participate in planning funeral arrangements.
Not all people are comfortable with open awareness. Some believe
that terminally ill individuals have a perception of the nature of their
condition even if they are not directly informed. Others believe that
individuals remain unaware of their condition until the end. It is
difficult, however, to distinguish what people know from what they
are willing to accept or acknowledge.
Nursing care and support for the dying person and their family
include making an accurate assessment of the physiological signs of
approaching death. In addition to signs related to the person’s
specific disease, certain other physical signs are indicative of
impending death. The four main characteristic changes are loss of
muscle tone, slowing of the circulation, changes in respirations and
sensory impairment. ‘Clinical manifestations
’ lists indications of
impending clinical death.
Various consciousness levels may exist just before death. Some
people are alert, whereas others are drowsy, stuporous or
unconscious. Hearing is thought to be the last sense lost.


As death approaches, the nurse assists the significant others to
prepare. Depending in part on knowledge of the person’s state of
awareness, the nurse asks questions that help identify ways to
provide support during the period before and after death. In
particular, the nurse needs to know what the family expects to
happen when the person dies so that accurate information can be
given at the appropriate depth. See the following ‘Assessment
interview
’ for sample interview questions. When the family
members know what to expect, they may be better able to support
the dying person and others who are grieving. In addition, they may
be able to make certain decisions about events surrounding the
death such as whether they will want to view the body after death.
Clinical manifestations
Impending clinical death
Loss of muscle tone
Relaxation of the facial muscles (e.g. the jaw may sag).
Difficulty speaking.
Difficulty swallowing and gradual loss of the gag reflex.
Decreased activity of the gastrointestinal tract, with
subsequent nausea, accumulation of flatus, abdominal
distension and retention of faeces, especially if narcotics
or tranquillisers are being administered.
Possible urinary and rectal incontinence due to decreased
sphincter control.


Diminished body movement.
Slowing of the circulation
Diminished sensation.
Mottling and cyanosis of the extremities.
Cold skin, first in the feet and later in the hands, ears and
nose (the person, however, may feel warm if there is a
fever).
Slower and weaker pulse.
Decreased blood pressure.
Changes in respirations
Cheyne–Stokes respirations
 (rhythmic waxing and
waning of respirations from very deep breathing to very
shallow breathing with periods of temporary apnoea).
Noisy breathing, referred to as the ‘death rattle’, due to
collecting of mucus in the throat.
Mouth breathing, dry oral mucous membranes.
Sensory impairment
Blurred vision.
Impaired senses of taste and smell.


Diagnosing
A range of nursing diagnoses, addressing both physiological and
psychosocial needs, can be applied to the dying person, depending
on the assessment data. Diagnoses that may be particularly
appropriate for them are Fear, Hopelessness and Powerlessness. In
addition, Risk of caregiver role strain and Interrupted family
processes are not uncommon diagnoses for caregivers and family
members.
Examples of the clinical applications of some of these nursing
diagnoses are shown in ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes
and interventions’.
Assessment interview
The family of the dying person
Ask the spouse, partner or significant others:
Have you ever been close to someone who was dying?
What have you been told about what may happen when
death occurs?
Do you have questions about what may happen at the
time of death?
How do you think you would like to say goodbye?
How are you taking care of yourself during this time?


Who can you turn to for help at this time?
Is there anyone you would like us to contact now or when
the death occurs?
Planning
Major goals for individuals who are dying are (a) maintaining
physiological and psychological comfort, and (b) achieving a dignified
and peaceful death, which includes maintaining personal control and
accepting declining health status. When planning care with these
individuals, the Dying Person’s Bill of Rights (see Box 44.1
) can
be a useful guide.
BO X
44.1 The Dying Person’s Bill of Rights
I have the right to be treated as a living human being until I
die.
I have the right to maintain a sense of hopefulness, however
changing its focus may be.
I have the right to be cared for by those who can maintain a
sense of hopefulness, however changing its focus might be.


I have the right to express my feelings and emotions about
my approaching death in my own way.
I have the right to participate in decisions concerning my
care.
I have the right to expect continuing medical and nursing
attention even though ‘cure’ goals must be changed to
‘comfort’ goals.
I have the right not to die alone.
I have the right to be free from pain.
I have the right to have my questions answered honestly.
I have the right not to be deceived.
I have the right to have help from and for my family in
accepting my death.
I have the right to die in peace and with dignity.
I have the right to retain my individuality and not be judged
for my decisions which may be contrary to the beliefs of
others.
I have the right to discuss and enlarge my religious and/or
spiritual experiences, whatever these may mean to others.
I have the right to expect that the sanctity of the human body
will be respected after death.


I have the right to be cared for by caring, sensitive,
knowledgeable people who will attempt to understand my
needs and will be able to gain some satisfaction in helping me
face my death.
Source: A. J. Barbus
. The Dying Person’s Bill of Rights. Created at the workshop ‘The terminally ill
patient and the helping person’. Lansing, MI: South Western Michigan Inservice Education Council.
28 Barbus, A. J. (1975). The Dying Person’s Bill of Rights. Created at the workshop ‘The terminally ill
patient and the helping person’. Lansing, MI: South Western Michigan Inservice Education Council.
Examples of clinical applications of nursing outcomes and
interventions are shown in ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses,
outcomes and interventions
’.
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
People who are dying
History John Yee, age 63, has metastatic carcinoma of the
bowel. He has noticed a rapid deterioration in energy in the
past week and feels bloated and nauseated. He has become
increasingly jaundiced and says, ‘I know I haven’t long to live.
Nothing I do will help. Why can’t they just give me a big dose
of morphine and get it over with?’.
28


Planning for home care
People facing death may need help accepting that they have to
depend on others. Some people who are dying require only minimal
care; others need continuous attention and services. People need
help, well in advance of death, in planning for the period of
dependence. They need to consider what will happen and how and
where they would like to die.
A major factor in determining whether a person will die in a health
care facility or at home is the availability of willing and able
caregivers. If the dying person wishes to be at home and family or
others can provide care to maintain symptom control, the nurse
should facilitate a referral to community-based hospice services.
Community palliative care nurses will then conduct a full assessment
of the home and care providers’ skills.
Implementing
The major nursing responsibility for individuals who are dying is to
assist them to a peaceful death. More specific responsibilities are
the following:
to minimise loneliness, fear and depression
to maintain the individual’s sense of security, self-confidence,
dignity and self-worth
to help the individual adapt to losses


to provide physical comfort.
Helping people die with dignity
Nurses need to ensure that the person is treated with dignity; that is,
with honour and respect. People who are dying often feel they have
lost control over their lives and over life itself. Helping them die with
dignity involves maintaining their humanity, consistent with their
values, beliefs and culture. By introducing options available to the
individual and significant others, nurses can restore and support
feelings of control. Some choices that individuals can make are the
location of care (e.g. hospital, home or hospice facility), times of
appointments with health professionals, activity schedule, use of
health resources and times of visits from relatives and friends.
People want to be able to manage the events preceding death so
they can die peacefully. Nurses can help individuals to determine
their own physical, psychological and social priorities. Dying people
often strive for self-fulfilment more than self-preservation and may
need to find meaning in continuing to live while suffering. Part of the
nurse’s challenge, then, is to support the ‘will’ and ‘hopes’ of the
individual.
Although it is natural for people to be uncomfortable discussing
death, steps can be taken to make such discussions easier for both
the nurse and the dying person. Strategies include the following:


Identify your personal feelings about death and how they may
influence your interactions with people. Acknowledge your
personal fears about death and discuss them with a friend and/or
colleague.
Focus on the individual’s needs. Their fears and beliefs may be
different from the nurse’s. It is also important that the nurse
avoids imposing personal fears and beliefs on the individual or
their family.
Talk to the person or their family about how they usually cope
with stress. People will use their usual coping strategies for
dealing with impending death. For example, if they are usually
quiet and reflective, they are likely to become more quiet and
withdrawn when facing terminal illness.
Establish a therapeutic relationship that shows concern for and
commitment to the person. Communication strategies that let
them know you are available to talk about death include the
following:
Describe what you see; for example, ‘You seem sad. Would you
like to talk about what’s happening to you?’.
Clarify your concern; for example, ‘I’d like to have a better
understanding of how you feel and how I may help you’.
Acknowledge the individual’s struggle; for example, ‘It must be
difficult to feel so uncomfortable. I would like to help you be more
comfortable’.
Provide a caring touch. Holding the person’s hand can encourage
them to verbalise feelings.
Determine what the individual knows about their illness and
prognosis.


Respond with honesty and directness to the individual’s
questions about death.
Make time to be available to the individual to provide support,
listen and respond.
Hospice and palliative care
The present-day hospice movement was founded in the 1960s.
Hospice care
 focuses on support and care of the dying person
and family, with the goal of facilitating a peaceful and dignified death.
Hospice care is based on holistic concepts, emphasises care to
improve quality of life rather than cure, supports the dying person
and their family through the dying process and supports the family
through bereavement. Assessing the needs of the person’s family is
just as important as caring for the person who is receiving hospice
care. The condition of the person usually deteriorates and attention
needs to be focused on the caregivers to ensure that they are
receiving support and resources as these changes occur. If the
hospice team meets regularly, these needs can be discussed and
interventions initiated. Physical needs are usually apparent, but
emotional and behavioural signs are often more subtle. A good
assessment and ongoing evaluation can help indicate when
modifications or changes are needed.
The principles of hospice care can be carried out in a variety of
settings including in the home and hospital. Services focus on
symptom control and pain management.


Palliative care
 is described by the World Health Organization
as ‘an approach that improves the quality of life of individuals and
their families facing the problems associated with life-threatening
illness, through the prevention and relief of suffering by means of
early identification and impeccable assessment and treatment of
pain and other problems—physical, psychosocial and spiritual’.
Palliative care may differ from hospice care in that the person is not
necessarily believed to be imminently dying. Both hospice and
palliative care can include end-of-life care
; that is, the care
provided in the final weeks before death.
29 World Health Organization (2019). WHO Definition of Palliative Care. Retrieved from
<www.who.int>.
In 2010, the National Palliative Care Strategy was developed to
guide palliative care policy development and service delivery across
Australia. Updated in 2018, the initiatives contained in this strategy
reflect the growing demand for quality, evidence-based end-of-life
care in Australia (see Box 44.2
). Accordingly, there is the need for
competent palliative care nurses or, at the very least, nurses with a
sound working knowledge of the principles of palliative care.
BO X
44.2 Guiding principles of palliative
care provision in Australia
29


Palliative care is person-centred care.
Death is recognised as a part of life.
Carers are valued and receive the support and information
they need.
Care is accessible.
Everyone has a role to play in palliative care.
Care is high quality and evidence based.
Source: Department of Health
. The National Palliative Care Strategy 2018. Retrieved from
<www.health.gov.au/resources/publications/the-national-palliative-care-strategy-2018>.
30 Department of Health (2019). The National Palliative Care Strategy 2018. Retrieved from
<www.health.gov.au>.
Dying at home
Home may be interpreted differently by individuals; however, the
context referred to in this case will be the residence or dwelling of an
individual rather than a residential or aged care facility. Many people
wish to die ‘at home’; however, about half of Australian deaths
continue to occur in people who were hospitalised (Australian
Institute of Health and Welfare ). The hospital environment, with its
constant noise and activity, remains a challenge for the nurse to
provide quality end-of-life care (Beckstrand et al.
).
30
31
32


31 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2017). Deaths in Australian Hospitals 2014–15.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
32 Beckstrand, R. L., Isaacson, R. F., Macintosh, J. L. B., Luthy, K. E. & Eden, L. (2019).
NICU nurses’ suggestions for improving end-of-life care obstacles. Journal of Neonatal
Nursing, 25(1), 32–36. Doi: 10.1016/j.jnn.2018.08.004.
Importantly, dying at home raises specific issues that may not be
experienced when a person dies in a hospital or residential aged
care facility. The death may be sudden and unexpected, such as a
myocardial infarction, SIDS (sudden infant death syndrome) or
suicide; or the deceased may have been receiving palliative care for
an end-stage illness. In all cases, where and how the individual dies
will impact on all other aspects associated with the care of the body
and the reactions and subsequent care of the family, friends and
significant others. Some of the issues that may need to be
considered are:
If the death was unexpected or sudden, the element of shock will
need to be taken into account when caring for the deceased’s
family and friends.
How long can the deceased’s body remain in the home? This
question may be raised when cultural customs and rituals
associated with death need to be considered.
Depending on the circumstances of death, who will collect the
body from the home—police, ambulance or funeral director—and
how will this affect the family?
Who was with the deceased when they died or who found the
deceased after they had died? This raises implications for


debriefing and appropriate counselling services to become
involved.
If the deceased was receiving palliative care, are there still
Schedule 8 medications on the premises? If so, who should
dispose of them and how?
If the cause of death cannot be unequivocally determined, there
may need to be a coroner’s inquiry and associated autopsy,
increasing the distress of family and friends of the deceased.
Meeting the physiological needs of the
dying person
The physiological needs of people who are dying are related to a
slowing of body processes and to homeostatic imbalances.
Interventions include providing personal hygiene measures;
controlling pain; relieving respiratory difficulties; assisting with
movement, nutrition, hydration and elimination; and providing
measures related to sensory changes (also see Table 44.5
).
Table 44.5 Physiological needs of dying people
Pain control is essential to enable people who are dying to maintain
some quality in their life and their daily activities, including eating,
moving and sleeping. Often opioid analgesics are used to control the
pain associated with terminal illness including morphine and fentanyl.
When prescribing the analgesia, the doctor should discuss with the
person and family any observed pain patterns (e.g. waking in the


night), how well controlled their pain is and whether they experience
any side effects from the medication. Doctors often prescribe
dosage ranges for opioid medications. When deciding how much
medication to administer, it is imperative that the nurse conducts a
pain assessment with the person (where possible) to appropriately
titrate the amount and frequency of administered medication to
maximise the comfort experienced by the person. A variety of routes
for analgesia may be prescribed including oral, transdermal, rectal,
subcutaneous injection/infusion or intravenous injection/infusion.
Individuals on opioid analgesics also require implementation of a
protocol to treat opioid-induced constipation. See Chapter 49
 for
more on pain management.
Providing spiritual support
Spiritual support is of great importance in dealing with death.
Although not all people identify with a specific religious faith or belief,
most have a need for meaning in their lives, particularly as they
experience a terminal illness.
The nurse has a responsibility to ensure that the person’s spiritual
needs are attended to, either through direct intervention or by
arranging access to individuals who can provide spiritual care. By
honouring the person’s spiritual beliefs, the nurse treats the person
holistically, improving the quality of the person’s end-of-life care
(O’Brien et al.
). In order to provide such spiritual care, the nurse
needs to be aware of their own comfort with spiritual issues and be
clear about their own ability to interact supportively with the person
33


who is dying. This awareness includes not imposing one’s own
religious or spiritual beliefs on the dying person. Communication
skills are paramount in helping the person articulate their needs and
in developing a sense of caring and trust.
33 O’Brien, M. R., Kinloch, K., Groves, K. E. & Jack, B. A. (2019). Meeting patients’ spiritual
needs during end-of-life care: A qualitative study of nurses’ and healthcare professionals’
perceptions of spiritual care training. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(1–2), 182–189. Doi:
10.1111/jocn.14648.
Specific interventions may include facilitating expressions of feeling,
prayer, meditation, reading and supporting discussions with the
appropriate clergy or a spiritual advisor. It is important for nurses to
establish an effective interdisciplinary relationship with spiritual
support specialists. For a further discussion of spiritual issues, see
Chapter 42
.
Supporting the family
Employing therapeutic communication is one of the most important
aspects of providing support to the family members of a dying
person. When nothing can reverse the inevitable dying process, the
nurse can provide an empathetic and caring presence to assist the
family to express their fears and grief. The nurse also serves as a
teacher, explaining what is happening and what the family can
expect. Due to the stress of moving through the grieving process,
family members may not absorb what they are told so may need to
have information repeated several times. During such interactions,
the nurse must display a calm and patient demeanour.


Family members should be encouraged to participate in the physical
care of the dying person as much as they wish to and are able. The
nurse can suggest the family assist with bathing, speak or read to
the person and hold their hand. The nurse must not, however, have
specific expectations of family members’ participation. Those who
feel unable to care for or be with the dying person also require
support from the nurse and from other family members. They should
be shown to an appropriate waiting area if they wish to remain
nearby.
Sometimes it seems as if the dying person is ‘holding on’, possibly
out of concern for the family not being ‘ready’ for the impending
death. In such circumstances, it may be therapeutic, for both the
dying person and their family, for family members to verbally give
permission to the person to ‘let go’ - to die when they are ready. This
act is a painful process and the nurse must be prepared to
encourage and support the family through saying their last
goodbyes.
After the person dies, family members are encouraged to view the
body because this viewing can help to facilitate the grieving process
(Rodgers, Calmes & Grotts ). The family may also wish to clip a
lock of hair as a remembrance or token of their loved one. It is
acceptable to include children in such events if they are willing
participants.
34 Rodgers, D., Calmes, B. & Grotts, J. (2016). Nursing care at the time of death: A bathing
and honouring practice. Oncology Nursing Forum, 43(3), 363–371. Doi: 10.1188/16.ONF.363-
371.
34


Post-mortem care
Rigor mortis
 is the stiffening of the body that occurs about 2 to 4
hours after death. It results from a lack of adenosine triphosphate
(ATP), resulting in muscle contraction that in turn immobilises the
joints. Rigor mortis starts in the involuntary muscles (heart, bladder
and so on), then progresses to the head, neck and trunk, and finally
reaches the extremities.
Because the deceased person’s family often wants to view the body
and because it is important that the deceased appear natural and
comfortable, nurses need to position the body, place dentures in the
mouth and close the eyes and mouth before rigor mortis sets in.
Rigor mortis usually leaves the body about 96 hours after death.
Algor mortis
 is the gradual decrease of the body’s temperature
after death. When blood circulation terminates and the
hypothalamus ceases to function, body temperature falls about 1°C
per hour until it reaches room temperature. Simultaneously, the skin
loses its elasticity and can easily be broken when removing
dressings and adhesive tape.
After blood circulation has ceased, the red blood cells break down,
releasing haemoglobin, which discolours the surrounding tissues.
This discolouration, referred to as livor mortis
, appears in the
lowermost or dependent areas of the body.


Tissues after death become soft and eventually liquefied by bacterial
fermentation: the hotter the temperature, the more rapid the
change. Therefore, bodies are often stored in cool places to delay
this process. Embalming prevents the process through injection of
chemicals into the body to destroy the bacteria.
Nurses are responsible for care of a body after death. Post-mortem
care should be carried out according to the policy of the hospital or
organisation. Because care of the body may be influenced by
religious beliefs or cultural customs, the nurse should check the
deceased’s religion and cultural background and make every
attempt to comply with these customs. If the deceased’s family or
friends wish to view the body, it is important to make the
environment as clean and pleasant as possible and to make the
body appear natural and comfortable. The removal of equipment,
soiled linen and supplies from the bedside can assist with this
appearance. Some agencies require that all tubes in the body
remain in place; in other agencies, tubes may be cut to within 2.5
cm of the skin and taped in place; in others, all tubes may be
removed. It is important to remember that the family’s perception of
the person’s death is strongly influenced by all aspects of care
including providing quality after-death care (Rodgers et al. 2016).
Normally, the body is placed in a supine position with the arms either
at the sides with palms down or across the abdomen. One pillow is
placed under the head and shoulders to prevent blood from
discolouring the face by settling in it. The eyelids are closed and held
in place for a few seconds so they remain closed. Dentures are


usually inserted to help give the face a natural appearance. The
mouth is then closed.
Soiled areas of the body are washed; however, a complete bath may
not be necessary as the body will be washed by the mortician (also
referred to as an undertaker), a person trained in care of the dead.
A continence pad or disposable underpad is placed under the
buttocks to take up any faeces and urine released because of
relaxation of the sphincter muscles. A clean gown is placed on the
person and their hair is brushed and combed. All jewellery is
removed, except a wedding ring in some instances, which is taped
to the finger. The top bed linens are adjusted neatly to cover the
person to the shoulders. Soft lighting and chairs are provided for the
family.
In the hospital, after the body has been viewed by the family, the
deceased’s wrist identification tag is left on and additional
identification tags are applied. The body is wrapped in a shroud
,
a large piece of plastic or cotton material used to enclose a body
after death. Identification is then applied to the outside of the
shroud. The body is taken to the morgue if arrangements have not
been made to have a funeral director pick it up from the hospital
room. Nurses have a duty to handle the deceased with dignity and
to label the corpse appropriately. Mishandling can cause emotional
distress to survivors and mislabelling can create legal problems if the
body is misidentified.


Evaluating
To evaluate the achievement of the goals of the dying person, the
nurse collects data in accordance with the desired outcomes
established in the planning phase. Evaluation activities may include
the following:
listening to the individual’s reports of feeling in control of the
environment surrounding death, such as control over pain relief,
visitation of family and support people, or treatment plans
observing the individual’s relationship with significant others
listening to the individual’s thoughts and feelings related to
hopelessness or powerlessness.
Examples of desired outcomes for people who are dying are shown
in ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and interventions’. Some
of the special needs of older adults and their families during death
and dying are found in ‘Lifespan considerations
’.
Lifespan considerations
Responses to death
Children


Children’s response to death or loss depends on the
messages they get from adults and others around them
as well as their understanding of death. When adults are
able to cope effectively with a death, they are more likely
to be able to support children through the process.
As children develop, they will ‘reprocess’ their grieving
about a loss or death. Preschoolers who have lost a
parent, for example, often reconceptualise their
understanding of that loss when they reach school age
and adolescence and have greater cognitive and
emotional skills. The same process occurs with parents
who have lost a child to death; as the years pass and the
child ‘would have been in first grade’, for example, parents
must cope with the added dimensions of the loss.
Older adults
The older adult who is dying often has a need to know that
their life has had meaning. An excellent way to assure them
of their legacy is to encourage the older adult to make
audiovisual recordings of their life stories. Recording such
anecdotes gives the person a sense of self-worth and
provides a lasting testament for their family and friends.
Involving other family members such as their children or
grandchildren in making these recordings can also improve
intrafamily communication and support during this difficult
time.


Caregivers of the older adult who is dying need ongoing
support and education throughout this period. As the older
adult progressively deteriorates, caregivers may need to be
educated on:
ways to feed the person when swallowing becomes
difficult
ways to transfer and reposition the person safely
ways to communicate if verbalisation becomes difficult
non-pharmacological methods of pain control
comfort measures, such as frequent oral care and
frequent repositioning.
Case study
Mrs Govinda, 75, was admitted to the hospital after repeated
episodes of pneumonia. Despite aggressive antibiotic therapy,
her condition rapidly deteriorated and she died unexpectedly
1 week after being admitted to the hospital. Mrs Govinda’s
eldest son, who lived nearby and frequently cared for his
mother, arranged for the funeral and visited with relatives. He
misses his mother and cries occasionally but managed to
return to work the following week. The youngest son had
difficulty attending the funeral, has been unable to sleep or
eat, cannot concentrate at work and is having trouble
accepting that his mother is deceased. The middle son did
not weep at the funeral and had little to say to his brothers or


other relatives. He returned home to another state but has
remained distant. He is back at work but feels very fatigued
and apathetic.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. Using the case study, describe the phase of
bereavement being experienced by each of the three
surviving sons.
2. What factors may have affected how each of the
brothers reacted to the death of their mother?
3. What cues, other than physical signs, might have
indicated that Mrs Govinda was dying, even though
her death was unexpected?
4.
 With the diagnosis of pneumonia, a respiratory
infection, what physiological (palliative) needs might
she have had? Using the Fundamentals of Care
Framework, determine what fundamental physical,
psychosocial and relational needs might also be
relevant.
5. How might your own feelings about death impact on
the care you provide to the dying person?
CO NCEPT M AP
The grieving person


Chapter 44 Review


Chapter highlights
Nurses help people deal with all kinds of losses, including loss of
body image, loss of a loved one, loss of a sense of wellbeing and
loss of a job.
Loss, especially loss of a loved one or a body part/function, can
be viewed as either a situational or a developmental loss and
may also be an actual or a perceived loss (both of which can be
anticipatory).
Grieving is a normal, subjective emotional response to loss; it is
essential for mental and physical health. Grieving allows the
bereaved person to cope with loss gradually and to accept it as
part of reality.
Knowledge of different stages or phases of grieving and factors
that influence the loss reaction can help the nurse understand
the responses and needs of people.
How an individual deals with loss is closely related to the
individual’s stage of development, personal resources and social
support system.
Caring for the dying and the bereaved is one of the nurse’s most
complex and challenging responsibilities.
Nurses’ attitudes about death and dying directly affect their ability
to provide care.
Nurses must consider the entire family as requiring care in
situations involving loss, especially death.
People who are dying require open communication, physical help
and emotional and spiritual support to ensure a peaceful and


dignified death. The dying person needs to maintain a sense of
control in managing the events preceding death.
Concept check
1. Which of the following may be considered normal or ‘healthy’
types of grief? Select all that apply.
1. Abbreviated grief.
2. Anticipatory grief.
3. Disenfranchised grief.
4. Complicated grief.
5. Unresolved grief.
6. Inhibited grief.
2. An individual’s family tells the nurse that their culture does not
permit a dead person to be left alone before burial. Hospital
policy states that after 6 p.m., when mortuaries are closed,
bodies are to be stored in the hospital morgue refrigerator
until the next day. How would the nurse best manage this
situation?
1. Gently explain the policy to the family and then
implement it.
2. Inquire of the nursing supervisor how an exception to
the policy could be made.
3. Call the dying person’s doctor for advice.
4. Move the deceased to an empty room and assign an
aide to stay with the body.


3. The shift changed while the nursing staff were waiting for the
adult children of a deceased person to arrive. The oncoming
nurse has never met the family. Which of the following
greetings is most appropriate?
1. ‘I’m very sorry for your loss.’
2. ‘I’ll take you in to view the body.’
3. ‘I didn’t know your father, but I am sure he was a
wonderful person.’
4. ‘How long will you want to stay with your father?’
4. At which age does a child begin to accept that they will

1. Less than 5 years old.
2. 5–9 years old.
3. 9–12 years old.
4. 12–18 years old.
5. An 82-year-old man has been told by his doctor that it is no

1. ‘I told the doctor I would stop driving, but I am not
going to yet.’
2. ‘I always knew this day would come, but I hoped it
wouldn’t be now.’

4. ‘Well, at least I have friends and family who can take

6. When asked to sign the permission form for surgical removal
of a large but non-cancerous lesion on her face, Mary begins

response?
1. ‘Tell me what it means to you to have this surgery.’

removed.’
3. ‘I cry when I am happy or relieved sometimes too.’

2. Family members’ understanding of the extent of their

3. Psychological support resources available from friends
or other sources.
4. Family members’ grief responses and coping
behaviours.
