Throughout Australia and the world, all nurses
encounter people with mental health problems.
The increased number of people with emotional
and psychological disorders places a large
responsibility of care on nurses, some of whom
do not have the necessary specialised
education and understanding regarding each
individual’s nursing needs. Drawing from data


from the 2007 National Survey of Mental Health
and Wellbeing, the Australian Institute of Health
and Welfare  tells us that an estimated 45% of
Australians between the ages of 16 and 85
experienced a mental disorder some time in
their life and that an estimated 20% had
experienced a common mental disorder in the
previous 12 months. Because mental illness is
so prevalent in the community, knowledge and
skills relating to mental health care are
necessary and useful across all areas of nursing
and midwifery practice.
1 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2016). Mental
Health Services—In Brief 2016. Retrieved from
<www.aihw.gov.au>.
1


Holistic mental health care
Despite the fact that many nurses may not practise within a
specialised mental health setting, it is highly likely that they will
provide nursing care for someone who is experiencing a mental
health issue. Mental health problems are very common and nurses
will encounter people with mental illness in ‘generalist’ environments
such as the emergency department, surgical and medical wards,
intensive and critical care units, maternity, outpatients, day surgery,
baby health clinics, GP surgeries, paediatrics, community health,
sexual health clinics and x-ray departments.
At times, it may not be the actual person seeking assistance who
has the mental health issue; rather, it may be someone such as their
sibling, partner, uncle, mother, daughter or son. As a nurse, it is
beholden on you to provide the best care you can to each person no
matter what condition they present with.
Providing effective and safe nursing care for a person who has a
mental illness therefore involves working closely with family
members and significant others. Working collaboratively increases
early recognition of signs and symptoms, enhances treatment
compliance and increases necessary support. Nurses provide
holistic care, which means it should be person centred and needs to
be provided in the safest and best way possible in a manner that
projects unconditional positive regard. This means the nurse accepts


the person requiring assistance unconditionally and non-
judgmentally.
Valuing lived experience
Mental health nursing is based on the premise of person-centred
care located within a social model of health. This philosophy views
the person as the best authority on their own illness, which makes
them ‘experts by experience’ and recognises them as being capable
of fulfilling their own potential for growth. The person is seen as
someone of worth and their lived experience is valued and regarded
within a context of equality and collegiality. Mental health nursing
incorporates working with the person, not making decisions for or
about the person without their involvement. Nothing about me,
without me! Achieving one’s full potential requires favourable
conditions, and being treated with respect, fairness and empathic
understanding from nurses contributes much to positive growth. This
concept is integral to personal recovery and is discussed in greater
detail later in this chapter.
Because of the widespread nature of mental health issues, nurses
need to be aware of mental health trends across Australia.


Mental health and mental illness
Our understanding of definitions of wellness and illness is dynamic,
moving from being diagnosis-focused in the mid-twentieth century to
the current person-focused definition of mental illnesses, and
moving from an ‘absence of disease’ model to one that stresses
positive psychological function for mental health.
It is difficult to define mental health and mental illness as there is not
a singularly accepted definition. There are many reasons for this.
Humans express themselves individually and uniquely and change
constantly. Mental illness, as an expression, is also culturally
determined, and what might be deemed as mental illness in one
culture, might not be viewed that way in another. A defined clinical
pathway for a person who has a mental illness is not the norm; two
people who have schizophrenia will present and be treated
differently, but two people with appendicitis will have a much more
homogeneous clinical pathway. In the struggle to make sense of
mental health and mental illness, various attempts have been made
to conceptualise it. These usually come from different ontologies and
include the medical model, which emphasises the processes of
diagnosis and treatment and is based on traditional reductionist
models of science (Blaney ). Then there are the psychoanalytical or
psychodynamic approach (Wampold & Imel ), biogenetic
explanations (Haslam & Kvaale ) and cognitive behavioural
perspectives (Funder ). Other positions on what constitutes mental
2
3
4
5


health and mental illness are the legal framework, the lived
experience perspective and sociological stances such as social
causation, social reaction (labelling theory), holism and the social
model of disability.
2 Blaney, P. H. (2015). Medical model of mental disorders. The Encyclopedia of Clinical
Psychology, 1–6.
3 Wampold, B. E. & Imel, Z. E. (2015). The Great Psychotherapy Debate: The Evidence for
What Makes Psychotherapy Work (2nd ed.). New York: Routledge.
4 Haslam, N. & Kvaale, E. P. (2015). Biogenetic explanations of mental disorder: The mixed
blessings model. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 24(5), 399–404. Doi:
10.1177/0963721415588082.
5 Funder, D. C. (2015). The Personality Puzzle (7th international student ed.). New York: WW
Norton & Co.
Defining mental health
Despite an absence of a specific universal definition, mental health is
a positive concept—a state in which the person is individually and
socially responsible, self-directive, displays self-awareness,
possesses resilience and good functioning, and is generally
accepted within a group. Thus, the mentally healthy person:
has the ability to accept their strengths and limitations realistically
perceives reality accurately and has the capacity to feel in control
of self and their environment


exhibits self-determination and autonomy and is confident and
sure of their role and direction in life.
The Dual Continua Model of Mental Health (Tudor ) shows how
mental health and mental ill health belong to two interconnected but
separate continua (see Figure 45.1
). It may seem
counterintuitive, but mental illness and mental wellbeing can be
experienced by a single individual at the same time.
6 Tudor, K. (1996). Mental Health Promotion: Paradigms and Practice. London: Routledge.
Figure 45.1
6


Dual Continua Model of Mental Health (adapted).
Source: K. Tudor (1996). Mental Health Promotion: Paradigms and Practice. London: Routledge.
There are a number of factors that impact on mental health:
genetics, childhood nurturing and life circumstances. Genetics are
completely out of the control of the individual and refer to the genes


that have been inherited. Nurturing during childhood refers to
parent/carer/adult–child interactions, sibling interactions and early
communication patterns. Positive childhood nurturing refers to the
child feeling loved, secure and accepted. Life circumstances can
also have a profound influence on our mental health. These social
determinants of health are the conditions in which people are ‘born,
grow, work, live, and age, and the wider set of forces and systems
shaping the conditions of daily life. These forces and systems
include economic policies and systems, development agendas,
social norms, social policies and political systems’ (see Figure
45.2
) (World Health Organization (WHO) ).
8 World Health Organization (WHO) (2019a). Social Determinants of Health. Retrieved from
<www.who.int>.
Figure 45.2
8


Factors contributing to the mental health–mental illness continuum.
Source: K. L. Fontaine . Mental Health Nursing (6th ed.). Upper Saddle River, NJ: Pearson.
9 Fontaine, K. L. (2009). Mental Health Nursing (6th ed.). Upper Saddle River, NJ: Pearson.
Mental health is generally identified by indicators rather than a
specific statement about a state of health. To conceptualise mental
health, authors often compare mental health with mental illness. This
is an attempt to distinguish the ‘normal’ from the ‘abnormal’. In the
absence of a universal definition, Table 45.1
 offers a set of
indicators for both mental health and mental illness.
9


Table 45.1 Indicators and influencing factors for mental health
and mental illness
Source: Adapted from G. Bauldoff, P. Gubrud, M.-A. Carno et al.
. LeMone & Burke’s Medical–Surgical Nursing:
Critical Thinking for Person-Centred Care (4th Australian edition), p. 1856. Frenchs Forest: Pearson.
10 Bauldoff, G., Gubrud, P., Carno, M.-A. et al. (2019). LeMone & Burke’s Medical–Surgical
Nursing: Critical Thinking for Person-Centred Care (4th Australian edition). Frenchs Forest:
Pearson.
Considerations that are related to mental health or mental illness are
not scientifically precise. Mental illness has largely been defined by a
white, male, middle class, Western biomedical model. The specific
causes of mental illness remain unknown. Western biomedicine and
psychiatry have their roots in historical and cultural notions of self,
society, the individual and normality versus abnormality. This makes
treatment and management of mental illness both complicated and
challenging.
Contemporary mental health practice is interdisciplinary and
synthesises knowledge and understanding from various theoretical
models and conceptual approaches. Despite mental health teams
being interdisciplinary, treatment and management approaches
remain heavily dominated by medical models and medical discourse.
This is because psychiatrists are specialist medical practitioners
trained in ways that: (1) identify sick individuals (diagnosis); (2)
predict the future course of their illness (prognosis); (3) speculate
about the cause (aetiology); and (4) prescribe a response to the
10


condition, either to cure it or ameliorate its symptoms (medication)
(Elder, Evans & Nizette ).
11 Elder, R., Evans, K. & Nizette, D. (Eds) (2013). Psychiatric and Mental Health Nursing (3rd
ed.). Sydney: Elsevier.
Diagnosis of a mental illness
Diagnosing a mental illness sits within the medical model and
involves assessment against set criteria. There are two types of
diagnostic criteria widely used: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual
of Mental Disorders (DSM)
 and International Classification of
Diseases (ICD)
. The current DSM is DSM-5. This version was
published in May 2013. The authors of DSM-5 took into
consideration how gender, race and ethnicity may affect diagnosis
(American Psychiatric Association (APA)
). The other set of
diagnostic criteria is the ICD. The ICD is the global standard to
report and categorise diseases, health-related conditions and
external causes of disease and injury in order to compile useful
health information related to deaths and illness (mortality and
morbidity). The current version is ICD 11. This version was published
June 2018 and can be accessed from <www.who.int/
classifications/icd/en/>.
12 American Psychiatric Association (2013). Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental
Disorders (DSM-5). Retrieved from <www.psychiatry.org/psychiatrists>.
11
12


As a result of these powerful determinants, psychiatrists think of
‘illness’ when they encounter variations in conduct or when they
have to assess someone who is ‘different’. This is because they are
informed by a biomedical paradigm—their clinical ‘lens’. Given that
psychiatrists are in powerful and dominant positions within mental
health settings (they are often the directors of services at local,
state, territory and national levels), medical opinion remains at the
fore of any debate about mental health. The concept of illness and
its associated language, the symptoms, the therapies and the
people who have the illness, who are invariably known as ‘patients’,
clients or ‘consumers’, legitimise and perpetuate the prevailing public
perceptions and attitudes. Nurses need to be mindful and consider
other paradigms of practice when working with people who have a
mental illness.
One of the places where discourse about mental health occurs is at
the Australian College of Mental Health Nurses (ACMHN)
. This
college is the peak professional body for mental health nurses in
Australia and is the only organisation that specifically represents the
specialised interests of mental health nurses in Australia. Every year,
the ACMHN hosts an international conference during which issues
related to clinical practice, service delivery, mental health nursing
education and workforce, and research about mental health, mental
illness and mental health care are presented, discussed and
debated.
Mental Health Australia (MHA) (formerly known as the Mental Health
Council of Australia) is also an important resource for all matters


pertaining to mental health. The MHA was established in November
1997 as the peak, national non-government organisation
representing and promoting the interests of the Australian mental
health sector. This organisation is committed to achieving better
mental health for all Australians (visit <www.mhaustralia.org>).
Stigma and mental illness
Stigma
 is still the single most difficult issue facing people who
have a mental illness. Sensationalist headlines and negative
portrayal of mental illness in the media lead to a perpetuation of
stigma.
Research shows that the relationship that exists between mental
health issues and dangerous acts is modest (Van Dorn, Volavka &
Johnson ). However, some DSM-5 psychiatric disorders, such as
substance misuse, are significantly associated with the violence
typology (Harford et al.
). The general belief that people who have
a mental illness are dangerous persists. This negative belief can
lead to destructive stereotypes. People with a mental illness are, in
fact, quite often themselves victims of violent acts. They are often
fearful and are among the most vulnerable members of society. The
media, who are often the main source of information about mental
health for many people, have promulgated negative stereotypes,
portraying people with mental illness as violent, murderous and
13
14


unpredictable, and have a focus on illness rather than wellness
(Atanasova et al.
; Srivastava et al.
).
13 Van Dorn, R., Volavka, J. & Johnson, N. (2012). Mental disorder and violence: Is there a
relationship beyond substance use? Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology, 47(3),
487-503. Doi: 10.1007/s00127-011-0356-x.
14 Harford, T. C., Chen, C., Kerridge, B. T. & Grant, B. F. (2018). Self- and other-directed
forms of violence and their relationship with lifetimes DSM 5 psychiatric disorders: Results
from the National Epidemiological Survey on Alcohol Related Conditions-III (NESARC-III).
Psychiatry Research, 262, 384–392. Doi: 10.1016/j.psychres.2017.09.012.
15 Atanasova, D., Koteyko, N., Brown, B. & Crawford, P. (2019). Mental health and the media:
From illness to wellbeing. Sociology Compass, 13(5), 1–12. Doi: 10.1111/soc4.12678.
16 Srivastava, K., Chaudhury, S., Bhat, P. S. & Mujawar, S. (2018). Media and mental health.
Industrial Psychiatry Journal, 27(1), 1–5. Doi: 10.4103/ipj.ipj_73_18.
The 10th of October is World Mental Health Day. The day is
celebrated as the initiative of the World Federation of Mental Health,
and the WHO supports this initiative through raising awareness on
mental health issues.
Most people who have a mental illness do not need hospital care. If
they do, admissions to mental health inpatient units are as brief as
possible as least restrictive care is now best practice. Effective
medication, mostly developed in the 1950s, as well as community-
based psychosocial interventions, make isolation and confinement—
a common occurrence in the past—a practice now considered not
recovery focused (see Figure 45.3
). The attitudes of nurses,
family, friends and the community play a critical part in determining a
15
16


person’s quality of life and their recovery journey. Many people with
a mental illness face isolation and discrimination. This experience is
not the case for people who have a physical illness; people with
diseases such as cancer, diabetes and heart disease are often met
with empathy and support. Conversely, people who have a mental
illness are often on the receiving end of jokes, name calling,
innuendos and scaremongering.
Figure 45.3


Isolation and confinement in asylums was a common treatment for
mental illness.
Source: © Jerry Cooke/Photo Researchers/Getty Images.


Box 45.1
 lists some important myths and facts about mental
illness.
BO X
45.1 Facts: mental illness basics
Mental illness is real
Knowledge of mental illness is incomplete, but we can say
one thing for certain: mental illness is not laziness; attention
seeking; bad diet; mental, physical or spiritual weakness; or a
failure of character. Mental illness is illness, as real as cancer,
diabetes and heart disease.
Anyone can develop a mental illness
There is no immunity to mental illness. Not everyone
develops a mental illness during their lives, but anyone could.
At least 45% of us will experience a
mental illness during our lives
And that’s just anxiety, mood disorders and substance
addictions in people aged 16–85. Add in young people,
schizophrenia, eating disorders, personality disorders and
more, and the figure is likely far higher.


At least 20% of adults are affected by
mental illness every year
Anxiety disorders are the most common, followed by
depression. A significant number of Australians are also
affected by personality disorders, eating disorders, psychotic
illnesses such as schizophrenia and more. Some people have
more than one diagnosis and far too many Australians go
undiagnosed.
Four million Australians are affected
by complex mental illness
At least 690 000 Australians live with complex mental illness
(CMI), but an experience such as CMI affects the lives of
many people around the person with symptoms. For each
person with CMI, it is likely that five other people—families,
friends, partners, colleagues and more—are affected. That
makes 4 million Australians affected.
Some Australians are more likely to
be affected than others
Indigenous Australians experience much higher rates of
psychological distress than the general population and lower
access to mental health services. LGBTIQA+ people


experience very high rates of depression and psychological
distress and are the most at-risk group in Australia for
suicide. Mental illness is not more common in regional and
remote areas than in cities, but rates of suicide are much
higher, services are harder to access and stigma can be
higher. One in 7 children aged 4–17 have experienced a
mental illness and over a quarter of Australians aged 16–24
are experiencing a mental illness at any given time. Many
people who live with mental illness first experience symptoms
during adolescence.
The causes of mental illness are
complex
There is not one simple, obvious thing, such as a virus or
bacteria, that causes mental illness, which makes the causes
hard to work out. For some mental illnesses, such as
schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, it is possible to inherit a
predisposition—a greater likelihood that someone will develop
the disorder. For others, there seems to be no genetic link at
all. But a predisposition does not mean a person will develop
a mental illness. Likelihood of developing a mental illness is
influenced by a complex combination of genetic, neurological,
developmental, environmental, socioeconomic, cultural, life
experience and other factors.


There is no link between mental
illness and creativity
Experiencing mental illness does not make people more
creative and being creative does not make people more likely
to experience a mental illness. Likewise, getting treatment for
mental illness does not reduce creativity, although some
medicines have side effects.
Source: Adapted from SANE Australia
. Facts About Mental Illness. Retrieved from
<www.sane.org>. Reproduced with permission of SANE Australia, the national mental health charity.
43 SANE Australia (2019a). Facts About Mental Illness. Retrieved from <www.sane.org>.
Stigma and the role of the nurse
Nurses should discuss mental illness openly. When nurses think and
talk about mental illness in matter-of-fact ways, as they do for other
illnesses or conditions, this helps educate the community and can
assist to overcome attitudes based on misconceptions and negative
stereotypes. Open and honest discussion based on fact assists with
addressing discrimination.
As the ‘Examples of stigmatising reporting’ section below
demonstrates, the community receives a distorted portrayal of
people with mental illness. Sensationalist reporting exacerbates the
already discriminatory attitudes and stigmatising responses that the
43


community in general has towards people with mental health
problems.
It is common for individuals to accept and actually internalise
negative stereotypes (self-stigma), which then negatively impacts on
recovery. Nurses therefore need to advocate for people with mental
illnesses and at every instance dispel myths and challenge
discrimination.
Mental health nurses play an important part in preventing mental
illness by promoting mental health. This starts early by nurturing
healthy attitudes and coping mechanisms throughout early childhood
and adult life. Nurses can also assist people by learning appropriate
and effective ways to deal with trauma. All nurses, no matter what
their discipline area, should provide high-quality support and
treatment that enables people with a mental illness to participate
fully in all aspects of their life (recovery-focused trauma-informed
care). Even when nurses are not on duty, they can advocate for
mental health by encouraging and assisting friends and relatives to
seek care and obtain health care and treatment. The nurse can then
encourage engagement and adherence with the treatment regimen,
which should be established collaboratively, just as they would with a
person who has a physical condition.
Nurses contribute to knowledge by conducting mental health
research which assists the community to understand mental health
issues. Research can lead to better interventions and education to
ensure nursing practice is evidence-based.


Clinical consideration
Equality and respect incorporate tolerance,
active listening, empathy, compassion, safety,
trust, diversity and cultural competence. Nurses
should develop these virtues and practise them
every day.
Examples of stigmatising reporting
The way in which media both informs and misinforms the public
about mental illness has a direct effect on attitudes about people
with mental illness. Research has shown that exposure to negative
media stories has a direct effect on attitudes about people with
mental illness, which is not altered by subsequent exposure to
positive stories.
Research note
Mental health nursing placement: a comparative study of
non-traditional and traditional placement
C. Patterson, D. Perlman, E. K. Taylor, L. Moxham, R. Brighton & J. Rath
. Mental health nursing
placement: A comparative study of non-traditional and traditional placement. Nurse Education in
Practice, 33, 4–9. Doi: 10.1016/j.nepr.2018.08.010.

Professional placement experiences have been considered
as an approach to improving nursing attitudes towards mental
health nursing and selection of mental health nursing as a
career. Mental health nursing placements are now occurring
in less traditional settings; however, published research of
these placements remains scarce. The aim of this non-
experimental comparative study was to investigate the impact
of nursing student participation in a non-traditional placement
compared to participation in traditional placement. Particular
focus was on the attitudes of nursing students towards
mental health nursing and career preferences. Participants of
the intervention group attended the non- traditional placement
 Participants of the comparison group attended
traditional placement settings
 including
placements in inpatient and community mental health. The
study utilised The Preplacement Survey. Results showed
significant differences in scores of the non-traditional
placement Recovery Camp cohort related to reduced anxiety,
reduced negative attitudes and increased preparedness for
mental health. These correlated with a comparatively
increased desire to pursue a future career in mental health;
albeit, not a statistically significant increase.

setting, is highly dependent on the training and ability of

nurses to deliver effective service, the findings of the study
are important.
Examples of media portrayal regarding mocking mental illness,
misuse of medical terminology, demeaning language, victimising
language and sensationalist reporting can be found at
<www.sane.org/news/841-examples-of-stigmatising-reporting-
about-mental-illness-and-suicide>.


The role of the mental health
nurse
The role of the mental health nurse is multifaceted and continually
developing and evolving. Skills that mental health nurses have, and
the roles that they perform, vary according to the context of their
practice and their level of education and experience. Mental health
nurses provide nursing care for people whose lives are affected by
mental illness (see Figure 45.4
). The provision of care includes
the promotion of mental health, the prevention of mental illness and
the minimisation of issues associated with mental illness on
individuals, their families and on the community.
Figure 45.4


Mental health nurses provide specialised nursing care for people
whose lives are affected by mental illness.
The ACMHN describes mental health nursing as a specialised field
of nursing which focuses on meeting the mental health needs of the
person in partnership with family, significant others and the
community in any setting. The ACMHN has Standards of Practice
(2010) for mental health nurses (see Box 45.2
). These do not
replace professional standards from the Nursing and Midwifery


Board of Australia but provide practical benchmarks to guide and
measure how care is provided. There are nine standards.
BO X
45.2 Australian college of mental
health nurses Standards of Practice
in Mental Health Nursing
Standard 1
The mental health nurse acknowledges diversity in culture,
values and belief systems and ensures his/her practice is
non-discriminatory and promotes dignity and self-
determination.
Standard 2
The mental health nurse establishes collaborative
partnerships that facilitate and support people with mental
health issues to participate in all aspects of their care.
Standard 3
The mental health nurse develops a therapeutic relationship
that is respectful of the individual’s choices, experiences and


circumstances. This involves building on strengths, holding
hope and enhancing resilience to promote recovery.
Standard 4
The mental health nurse collaboratively plans and provides
ethically based care consistent with the mental, physical,
spiritual, emotional, social and cultural needs of the individual.
Standard 5
The mental health nurse values the contributions of other
agencies and stakeholders in the collaborative provision of
holistic, evidence-based care and in ensuring comprehensive
service provision for people with mental health issues.
Standard 6
The mental health nurse actively pursues opportunities to
reduce stigma and promotes social inclusion and community
participation for all people with mental health issues.
Standard 7
The mental health nurse demonstrates evidence-based
practice and actively promotes practice innovation through
lifelong education, research, professional development,
clinical supervision and reflective practice.


Standard 8
The mental health nurse’s practice incorporates and reflects
common law requirements, relevant statutes and the nursing
profession’s code of conduct and ethics. The mental health
nurse integrates international, national, local and state
policies and guidelines with professional standards and
competencies.
Standard 9
The mental health nurse holds specialist qualifications and
demonstrates advanced specialist knowledge, skills and
practice, integrating all the Standards competently and
modelling leadership in the practice setting.
Source: ACMHN . Standards of Practice in Mental Health
Nursing. Retrieved from <www.acmhn.org/publications/
standards-of-practice>. Copyright © 2010 Australian
College of Mental Health Nurses. All rights reserved.
17 Australian College of Mental Health Nurses (ACMHN) (2010). Standards of
Practice in Mental Health Nursing. Retrieved from <www.acmhn.org>.
Mental health nursing has long been recognised as a specialist area
and for many years had a separate registration or specialist
endorsement. In Australia, when nursing education was hospital-
based, students could enter directly into a 3-year hospital-based
psychiatric nursing course, graduating with specialised certification in
17


psychiatric nursing, which also had general nursing content (e.g.
anatomy and physiology). Today pre- registration programs prepare
the nurse at a ‘beginning level’ for all health settings, with many
students have only limited mental health theory and placements.
Specialist mental health nurse skills are now predominantly at
postgraduate level and include qualifications such as a graduate
certificate (Grad Cert), graduate diploma (Grad Dip), master’s,
professional doctorate or Doctor of Philosophy (PhD).


Mental health nursing in practice
Nurses are often described as the eyes and ears of the
interdisciplinary team. Nurses interact with people 24 hours a day,
observe activities of daily living (ADLs) and social functioning,
assess effects of medication and other treatments, and work closely
with the person in a therapeutic manner. This places nurses in an
excellent position, in collaboration with the person, to ascertain
individual needs with regard to the provision of nursing care. This
involves:
planning, implementing and evaluating interactions that assist the
person to achieve the highest possible quality of life using a
‘recovery’ focus
monitoring the responses of the person to treatment and
interventions
establishing and maintaining the therapeutic relationship.
The relationship or therapeutic alliance between the person and the
nurse is associated with therapeutic outcomes (Murphy & Hutton ).
This illustrates the central role that mental health nurses play in the
recovery of a person with mental illness. The essence of mental
health nursing is not in the tasks (the psychomotor skills) but in the
relationships nurses develop with the person and their significant
others; not in the illness (the diagnosis) but in the individual’s
response to it and how it affects their life. It is founded on a
18


therapeutic relationship
, which is based on empathy and trust,
with the person involved and their family (Peplau ).
18 Murphy, R. & Hutton, P. (2018). Practitioner review: Therapist variability, patient-reported
therapeutic alliance, and clinical outcomes in adolescents undergoing mental health treatment
—A systematic review and meta-analysis. The Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry,
59(1), 5–19. Doi: 10.1111/jcpp.12767.
19 Peplau, H. E. (1952). Interpersonal Relations in Nursing. New York: G. P. Putnam and
Sons.
Specialties within mental health
nursing
Mental health nurses have the ability to subspecialise even further
within the discipline. The following briefly outlines some of these
subspecialties. An area of growing concern is asylum seeker and
refugee mental health (Hodes, Anagnostopoulos & Skokauskas ).
Australian immigration detention centres employ specialist mental
health nurses due to asylum seekers’ mental health issues,
particularly issues related to trauma from the countries from which
they have fled and issues related to detention.
20 Hodes, M., Anagnostopoulos, D. & Skokauskas, N. (2018). Challenges and opportunities
in refugee mental health: Clinical, service and research considerations. European Child &
Adolescent Psychiatry, 27(4), 385–388. Doi: 10.1007/s00787-018-1115-2.
19
20


Acute inpatient units
The current function of acute inpatient units
 means that mental
health nurses who work in these settings provide care to people who
are acutely unwell and often exhibit complex and challenging
behaviour. Within many Australian inpatient facilities, there are
mental health high-dependency units (MHHDU) which can be
equated to critical care or intensive care units in general hospitals.
MHHDUs are for people who require close care, who are often in
states of acute distress, who pose a risk of absconding and who
need to be nursed away from other individuals. They are also for
people who pose a risk to themselves and/or others. In these units,
staff–patient ratios are high and close and intensive observation
occurs.
Acute care/assertive assessment/crisis
assessment teams
Mental health nurses who work on acute care/assertive or crisis
assessment teams work with people who have high acuity.
Sometimes these teams are also known as mobile assertive
outreach response teams. These nurses are often considered the
gatekeepers to mental health services and have expertise in
observation, assessment, negotiation, psychopharmacology and de-
escalation. Nurses in these teams offer a range of short-term
interventions such as comprehensive assessment and clinical care
that lead to initial recovery planning, including relapse prevention


and implementation for community consumers presenting with acute
mental health needs.
These variously named teams aim to reduce inpatient admissions
and provide rapid access to services. Their role is to assess
everyone for whom acute admission is considered and, whenever
feasible, to provide intensive home treatment instead. In New South
Wales, for example, there is also a Mental Health Line
(1800 011 511) where mental health nurses on these teams provide
telephone counselling. It takes special expertise to be able to
conduct an accurate assessment if you are not seeing the person
face to face. The role of mental health nurses in this setting is also
to liaise with other services and agencies and offer referral options.
Community care coordinators
The continued focus on integration, coupled with increasing
demands for primary care, compels the ongoing need for community
mental health care coordinators. Previously known as case
managers, this term is used less as people are not ‘cases’ that need
to be ‘managed’. Community care coordinators work in community
settings, providing continuing care for individuals in their homes.
These nurses often have large client loads and undertake duties
such as medication administration, management and monitoring,
and assisting with accommodation and employment options, as well
as linking individuals with therapeutic leisure and recreation-based
activities. Community mental health nurses
 also provide family


support and work with the broader community in mental health
promotion, advocacy and education.
Forensic mental health nurses
Forensic mental health
 nurses work with people who have had
contact with the criminal justice system or with individuals who have
generally demonstrated antisocial behaviour associated with their
mental illness. Such individuals usually receive treatment under the
auspices of a Mental Health Act
 (see the ‘Mental health
legislation’ section); therefore, a sound knowledge of mental health
legislation is required. Nurses in this specialty may be required to
conduct a forensic mental health assessment of the person in their
care. This comprehensive and systematised evaluation provides
relevant clinical and scientific data to a legal decision maker or the
litigants involved in civil or criminal proceedings. Forensic mental
health care can be provided in correctional facilities, health care
facilities and/or in the community.
Consultation liaison
This area of mental health care is rapidly expanding as a result of
the number of people within generalist care settings who also have a
mental illness. The theoretical base of this specialty is the result of
an integration of biological, psychological and sociological
perspectives. The consultation liaison (CL) nurse
 provides a
service to people who are admitted to a general hospital with a non-
psychiatric condition. The CL nurse provides direct consultation with


the person or indirect consultation through support, education and
advice for health colleagues. Importantly, CL nurses have high-level
assessment and interpersonal skills, coupled with a broad
knowledge of nursing practice that enables them to exclude physical
causes.
Peer workers
Although not a nursing role, the need to develop a national
professional peer workforce and encourage support structures and
professional development for the peer workforce is a key priority for
the National Mental Health Commission (National Mental Health
Commission ). Nurses need to work alongside these ‘experts by
experience’ and value the important contribution they provide to
mental health care.
21 National Mental Health Commission (2014). Mental Health Peer Work Development and
Promotion. Retrieved from <www.mentalhealthcommission.gov.au>.
21


Mental health legislation
While there is similar intent in all mental health legislation across
Australian states and territories (see Box 45.3
), differences
create major challenges. Mental health nurses need to understand
and implement different Mental Health Acts as they move about the
country. Subtle legal differences and definitions also complicate
individuals’ compliance when embarking on or continuing with their
own journey of recovery, particularly if they also wish to travel.

Definitions about mental health and mental illness differ between
jurisdictions. As the various legislative definitions indicate, what is
not a mental illness is just as important as what is a mental illness.
This distinction is indicative of the complexity of defining a mental
illness; in fact, some mental health legislation does not actually
define mental illness.


Mental state assessment (MSA)
Gathering sound data and undertaking a comprehensive
assessment is vital. It is this information that provides the platform
with which to establish a beginning path of action to work with each
person. Probably the most common of these mental health
assessment processes is the mental state assessment (MSA).
The MSA is a key diagnostic instrument that is important because in
mental health there are no laboratory examinations (e.g. blood tests)
or investigations (e.g. x-rays) that provide scientific evidence for
psychopathology. Mental health nursing derives its practice from
sound and objective clinical observations that take place between
the person and the nurse. During this interaction, the person’s
thoughts, language and communication (verbal and non-verbal) are
closely investigated. A mental state assessment (MSA)
therefore is a systematic clinical assessment that provides a picture
of what a nurse discerns during an interaction or interview with a
person. The components of an MSA are presented in the ‘Practice
guidelines
’.
All nurses need to use their skills to conduct an MSA in a variety of
areas within the broader general health care setting. In fact, some of
the elements of an MSA are probably already being applied by you.
When you first meet someone, when you decide who it is that you
will sit next to in class or on the bus or train, when you catch up with


an old friend after a time apart you ‘check out’ (assess) what they
are wearing, how they are behaving, what sort of things they are
talking about, how their mood
 seems. In doing this you are
actually conducting an evaluation. All are elements of an MSA.
The MSA is more formal and systematic. It forms part of a
complete, holistic (bio-psycho-social-cultural-spiritual) assessment
that is undertaken while cognisant of the context of the person’s
presentation and history. A full mental health assessment includes
information about why a person is being seen, significant mental
health or medical history, medications the person is taking, drug or
alcohol use, family history, work and leisure habits, spirituality,
developmental history, the person’s social situation and current level
of functioning, including sleep, self-care, diet and sexual health.
The reason that the person presents for mental health care is often
related to the impact that symptoms are having on their daily level of
functioning. Individuals often seek help because things are ‘out of
control’ and/or they are in distress. This distress can include
experiencing phenomenon such as auditory hallucinations, where
the voices have become overwhelming and derogatory, or
depression, where the person’s mood is so low they no longer want
to be alive. There are other reasons such as anxiety
, where the
person worries excessively about life events or issues.


Clinical consideration
The MSA is a snapshot of the person at that
time. An MSA is highly contextual because an
individual’s mental state is constantly subject to
change. The initial MSA provides baseline data
which can be compared with subsequent
improvement or deterioration.
Health practitioners, however, are often focused on the need for a
diagnosis. While diagnosis is important in many ways, people
generally just want their life to improve. Their focus may be different
from those whose work is embedded within the medical model. It is
the needs of the individual that should be the focus of all nursing
care, not the diagnosis that they have been assigned. Diagnoses are
apt to change and nurses need to look beyond them.
The process of undertaking an assessment is in itself an
intervention. It provides an opportunity for the nurse to form a
therapeutic relationship and engage with the person and their
significant others in a meaningful way. There are many different
assessment tools used in practice settings.
When a nurse is conducting an MSA, it is beholden on them as
health professionals to help the person express their thoughts and


feelings in a safe, supportive environment. A conversational
approach is more likely to make the person feel less anxious about
their circumstances, leading to greater rapport, resulting in better
information being obtained. This approach leads to a more
meaningful understanding of why the person needs help. Nurses
should use open-ended questions and probe responses. Nurses
need to be conscious of their own non-verbal responses, facial
expressions and posture. Validating feelings is always helpful and,
where possible, the nurse should sit with the person and/or their
significant others. Be aware that, as a health professional, there is a
power imbalance. It is not up to the person to put you at ease; it’s
your job to put them at ease.
The MSA cannot be rushed so do not be tempted to do so. Often,
people who have a mental illness feel anxious, are afraid and feel
vulnerable. They are likely to have experienced stigma and fear that
nurses too will judge them negatively. The more patience and
respect the nurse shows, the faster the nurse will build rapport and
gather information. The information will also be more accurate as a
result of the trust that is formed.


Types of mental illness
The brevity of this chapter does not allow for an in-depth discussion of all the various types of mental
illness. Broadly speaking, mental illness falls into two large groups—psychotic disorders and non-
psychotic disorders.
Psychotic disorders
A psychotic disorder includes a number of mental illnesses. When someone is out of touch with reality
and is experiencing a psychosis
, this is known as a psychotic episode. A person with psychosis
‘loses touch with reality’. This means that they may have disorganised thoughts, experience
hallucinations (these can be in any of the five senses) and/or delusions. As a result of these symptoms,
it can be difficult to interact with others. The psychotic episode may be a one off or part of an ongoing
illness.
As a result of the lack of contact with reality, there is a distortion in the person’s reasoning and thinking
(cognition
). A psychotic episode can occur as a result of a number of reasons; for example,
schizophrenia, a drug-induced state, in affective illnesses such as depression or mania, and where
there is an established physically defined brain disease, including brain tumours or even epilepsy.
There is no specific examination that can ‘test’ for psychosis. The mental health nurse needs to
recognise the behavioural and cognitive patterns and make a sound clinical judgment; hence the
importance of conducting a thorough MSA.

General: alertness and cooperation
Attention: WORLD backwards (i.e. any five-letter word backwards) and serial sevens
Language: naming and repetition
Calculation: division and subtraction
Abstraction: proverbs and similarities
Insight and judgment
Awareness of illness.
Ask the person:
Do you consider that you are ill in any way?
What has brought you to the hospital?
Do you have a physical or a mental illness?
Are you suffering from a mental health problem? What is it?
Correct labelling of abnormality:
You described several symptoms, namely . . .
What is your explanation of these experiences?


Willingness to engage with treatment:
How do you feel about being in hospital . . . coming to the clinic . . .?
How do you feel about taking medication?
Has the medication been helpful? Have any other treatments been helpful?
Do you think that medication helps you to remain well?
Impulse control
Can the person control their urges of anger, laughter, self-harm?
One of the difficulties with psychosis in its early stages is that it can be mistaken for something else.
People who take illicit drugs, misuse alcohol or have a delirium can display behaviours that appear
psychotic.
A psychotic episode is a frightening and confusing event for the individual and for their carers and
friends. Approximately 3 in every 100 people will experience a psychosis at some time. A psychotic
episode usually first occurs between the ages of 15 and 35 years. Sometimes a psychotic episode has
a rapid onset (a few days); but often the onset of a psychotic episode is more gradual, over a period of
weeks or months. When the onset is more gradual, individuals and their families will often report that
things ‘haven’t been quite right’ for some time. A psychotic episode always requires treatment and
studies have shown that the earlier that treatment is obtained, the better the outcome for the individual
(Correll, Galling & Pawar
).
22 Correll, C. U., Galling, B. & Pawar, A. (2018). Comparison of early intervention services vs treatment as usual for early-phase psychosis.
JAMA Psychiatry, 75(6), 555–565. Doi: 10.1001/jamapsychiatry. 2018.0623.
Symptoms of psychotic disorders
The main distinguishing feature of a psychotic disorder is the loss of contact with reality. Two of the key
symptoms that a nurse might observe in a person who is experiencing a psychotic disorder are
delusions and hallucinations.
Delusions
Delusions
 are fixed false beliefs that are not a normal part of the person’s cultural or spiritual
environment. These beliefs cannot be altered by logic. A person who has a delusion is convinced that
what they think is true. A nurse who tries to dispel the delusion, argues with the person or tries to use
logic to prove to the person that their beliefs aren’t true runs the risk of becoming incorporated into the
delusion. Delusions are often complex and can be difficult to comprehend, especially when they
incorporate very unusual beliefs. Such beliefs can be very distressing and cause the person to act in
ways they would not normally act. There are many different types of delusions, including:
22


Delusions of reference: beliefs that the behaviour of others, events, objects or information on
television, in radio songs or in newspapers contains messages that are specifically meant for them.
For example, the person might believe that car number plates have special messages.
Delusions of grandeur: beliefs of having great importance or having extraordinary powers or
abilities. For example, the person believes they are ‘The President of the World’.
Somatic delusions: despite medical evidence to the contrary, people with these delusions believe
that something is happening to their body, that they have a disease or that part of their body is
missing or has been changed in some way. For example, a person believes they have no stomach
even though it can be seen on x-ray.
Delusions of persecution/paranoia: the person believes they are being followed, harassed,
cheated, poisoned or drugged, conspired against, spied on, attacked or obstructed in the pursuit of
their goals. For example, the person might believe that their every move is being traced and
recorded by government spies.
Hallucinations
A hallucination
 is an alteration in sensory perception. It occurs when a person experiences a
sensation that is not objectively present. A person can experience hallucinations in any of the five
senses—auditory, visual, olfactory, gustatory and tactile.
Lifespan considerations
Mental health is contingent on many variables. Culture, education, work and gender are
examples, but another important factor is lifespan considerations. A person’s age has a
significant effect on their mental health and needs to be taken into consideration when
undertaking a mental health assessment (MSA) and deciding on appropriate forms of
intervention (including medications). The score for an MSA or mini mental status examination
must be interpreted according to each person’s age and educational status. ‘Normal’ limits will
alter according to the stages of the lifespan. For example:
Children
Introduce yourself in a way that the child can relate to.
Speak clearly and quietly and use language that the child will understand.
Use examples that are age appropriate. Allow a parent, guardian or support person to be
present.
Adults 18–24 years: median score = 29
Older adults over 80 years: median score = 25
Educational level: left school in year 4: median score = 22;
year 8 = 26; year 12 = 29.


Take your time; silence is acceptable and enables the child to think about what they want to
say.
Remember that a child will see you as an authority figure.
Find a private place to talk to the child.
Seek constant clarifications that you are being understood.
Be patient.
Don’t be confrontational, the child will be nervous.
Adults
Use language appropriate to their educational level.
Seek constant clarifications that you are being understood.
Be patient. Sit at eye level and look at the person to whom you are speaking; use the
acronym SOLER:
Be genuine and don’t be judgmental.
Older adults
When introducing yourself, seek confirmation as to how the person wants to be addressed.
Older people sometimes prefer to be more formal (e.g. Mr or Mrs).
Allow extra time for the person to answer questions.
Use questioning techniques that consider sensory loss (hearing, vision).
Use language the person understands.
Accept answers that are age appropriate.
Be patient.
Auditory: a common type of hallucination is auditory; that is, hearing ‘voices’ or ‘sounds’. The voices
and/or sounds that the person hears are real to the person and should never be dismissed or
treated as a joke. The actual voices/sounds—that is, the words or noises the person hears—can be
frightening, threatening or critical. The voices may comment on what the person is doing, tell them
they are wrong or should be doing something else, or that they are worthless. Alternatively, the
voices may say nice things, be comforting, kind or neutral.
Sometimes voices command a person to do something. These are command hallucinations and,
depending on what the voices are commanding the person to do, can pose a threat to the safety of
the person or others. It is very important that the nurse establishes what it is these particular voices
are commanding. Refer back to the MSA and note that when assessing perceptual disturbances,
nurses are encouraged to ascertain the content of the voices. Yet other voices may repeat the
person’s thoughts. Sometimes the person may hear two or more voices having a conversation about
them or several voices at once shouting or yelling at them. Auditory hallucinations can also take the
S = sit squarely, O = open posture, L = lean forward, E = eye contact, R = relax


form of music, humming or any manner of things, and they can be frightening, hard to distinguish
from ‘real’ voices or noises and are often tiring for the person to live with.
Visual: the person sees people or things that cannot be seen by others. Visual hallucinations are
not illusions. An accurate assessment (MSA) will ascertain the difference. An illusion
 is a
distortion of sensory perception and, therefore, reality. It is a misinterpretation of a true sensation
and is shared by most people. A desert oasis is an example of an illusion.
Olfactory: if a person experiences olfactory hallucinations, they smell things that others cannot.
These smells may be good or offensive and because smell and taste are linked, gustatory
hallucinations can have an effect on what the person does or does not eat.
Gustatory: if a person experiences gustatory hallucinations, food may taste as if it is bad,
contaminated or poisoned. If this is the case, the nurse has to be very skilful in ensuring the
person’s nutritional input is adequate.
Tactile: with this type of hallucination, sensations are experienced that have not actually occurred or
are sensed differently from the way they usually are. For example, the person may feel as though
spiders, bugs or ants are crawling over their skin (common with ‘ice’ users) or that they are being
touched by someone.
Types of psychotic disorders
Drug-induced psychosis
Using drugs or withdrawing from certain drugs can precipitate psychotic symptoms. It is common to see
a person who has a drug-induced psychosis present with delusions and hallucinations. Sometimes
these symptoms wane within a few days as the effects of the substances wear off, and the person may
not experience another episode unless they continue to use drugs. If someone has an underlying
vulnerability to a psychotic disorder such as schizophrenia, the psychotic episode can last much longer
and may be triggered by the substance use. Drugs such as amphetamines are often linked to psychotic
episodes. Research has shown a complex connection between cannabis and schizophrenia (Gilman,
Sobolewski & Evins ).
23 Gilman, J. M., Sobolewski, S. M. & Evins, A. E. (2018). Cannabis use as an independent risk factor for, or component cause of,
schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders. In M. T. Compton & M. W. Manseau (Eds), The Complex Connection Between Cannabis and
Schizophrenia (pp. 221–246). London: Elsevier.
Organic psychosis
The importance of a physical health assessment cannot be underestimated. A physical injury or an
illness that affects the brain can be the cause of an organic psychosis. Such conditions include brain
tumours and infections, Alzheimer’s disease, cardiovascular accident and some vitamin deficiencies.
Treating the underlying physical problem is paramount.
Brief reactive psychosis
23


A traumatic or very stressful event in someone’s life, such as the death of a loved one, a physical or
sexual assault or a natural disaster can cause a psychotic episode. During a brief reactive psychosis,
the symptoms can be severe and appear quickly. Symptoms often abate rapidly as well.
Delusional disorder
In delusional disorder, the main sign is a strong belief in something that others do not believe to be true.
Refer to delusions, above, for examples. People who have a delusional disorder may not experience
any other symptoms of mental illness. If the delusions do not affect their lives per se, they can usually
continue to manage their responsibilities and their behaviour may not be very different from the way it
usually is.
Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia
 is a mental illness that affects roughly 1 in 100 people. Signs of this disorder are
often hallucinations, delusions and thought disorder (see Figure 45.5
). The onset of schizophrenia
may be rapid, with acute symptoms developing very quickly, or more slowly, over months or even years.
For some people, it is a lifelong condition. First onset is usually in adolescence, but it can also occur for
the first time in older people. Schizophrenia refers to a change in a person’s mental function. A person
who has schizophrenia does not have a ‘split personality’, which is a common misperception. They may,
however, experience changes to their own personality as a result of disturbed perceptions and thoughts.
Figure 45.5
The person with schizophrenia can experience hallucinations and delusions.
Source: Triangle Images/Photodisc/Getty Images.


Schizophrenia normally has three phases:
1. prodromal phase: early warning signs are present; something is ‘not quite right’
2. acute phase: symptoms of a psychosis are observed, such as hallucinations and/or delusions
and/or thought disorder
3. recovery phase: people return to their day-to-day lives with the help of treatment.
Bipolar affective disorder
Bipolar affective disorder
 aptly describes the recurrent episodes of ‘up and down’ mood swings,
which range from elation and excitement to sadness and depression. When people experience such
extremes in mood it can be difficult for them to manage day-to-day responsibilities such as work,
finances and family commitments. As with other types of mental illness (e.g. schizophrenia), there are
different types of bipolar disorder. Episodes of mania (see ‘Clinical manifestations’) and episodes of
depression (see Box 45.4
) can last for a short time (days) or for a longer time (months).
BO X
45.4 Symptoms of depression
Sadness or depressed mood.
Lack of energy.
Amotivation.
Changes in sleep patterns—sleeping more or less than usual.
Changes in appetite—eating more or less than usual.
Feelings of hopelessness and helplessness.
Less interest in and less enjoyment from usually enjoyed activities.
Feelings of worthlessness and guilt.
Depressive delusions.
People who have bipolar disorder can experience psychotic episodes. The symptoms experienced
usually match the person’s current mood. If a person is depressed, they might hear voices that tell
them that they are horrible or no good or direct the person to hurt themselves. But a person who is in a
manic phase might believe that they are very special and can do remarkable things (delusions of
grandeur).
Some famous people said to live/have lived with bipolar disorder include Mel Gibson, Mark Twain, Kurt
Cobain, Virginia Woolf, Catherine Zeta-Jones, Vivien Leigh, Edgar Allan Poe, Marilyn Monroe, Nina
Simone, Jean-Claude Van Damme, Sidney Sheldon, Sinéad O’Connor and Richard Dreyfuss.
Psychotic depression (uni-polar)


People who experience psychotic depression can have many of the same symptoms that people with
bipolar disorder experience when they are depressed. People who have uni-polar psychotic depression
do not experience periods of mania. When people are experiencing a psychotic depression, they too
tend to experience symptoms that match their mood. For example, the person who is very depressed
might look in the mirror and visualise themself as something horrible or hear voices telling them how
worthless they are and that they should kill themselves.
Clinical manifestations
Mania
Look for changes such as:
A happy, elated mood or an irritated, angry mood.
Increased activity levels and energy.
Difficulty getting to sleep/decreased sleep/less need for sleep.
Talking louder and faster or more than usual.
More thoughts and faster/more rapid thinking than usual.
Overly ambitious plans and reckless behaviour, such as spending too much money or
engaging in careless activities or potentially dangerous behaviour.
Grandiose delusions.
Non-psychotic disorders
Throughout life, most people have experienced feelings of sadness, depression, tension or fear. For
some, these feelings can become so overwhelming that they have difficulty coping with ADLs. The
processes of going to work, enjoying leisure time and maintaining relationships can become so intense
that they are unable to carry them out. Nurses who tell a person to ‘Get on with it’, ‘It could be worse’ or
‘Pull your socks up’ show a lack of understanding of the illness and display a lack of empathy.
Such all-consuming feelings are not often evident to others. For the person who is experiencing them
though, they can cause considerable distress and anguish. Such mental illnesses are labelled non-
psychotic illnesses. They are a common experience for many people and the following list demonstrates
how widespread and prevalent these illnesses are. It is highly likely that someone with one of these
illnesses will require care within the general nursing setting. As with all mental illnesses, nurses and
students can also have these illnesses:
phobias
anxiety disorders
obsessive compulsive disorder
adjustment disorder


post-traumatic stress disorder
eating disorders
impulse control
 disorders
mood disorders
sexual disorders
sleep disorders
sexual dysfunctions
somatoform disorders
substance disorders
personality disorders
borderline personality disorders.
Types of non-psychotic disorders
Most non-psychotic illnesses are treated effectively, usually with a combination of medication and
psychotherapy. Psychotherapy helps the person understand their illness and assists them to gain
insight into what exacerbates their symptoms. Developing an understanding of the illness also assists
with management and recovery.
Depression
The most common type of non-psychotic disorder is depression. Depression is so commonplace that
the WHO predicts that in 2020 it will be the second main contributor to the world’s disease burden
(WHO
).
24 World Health Organization (WHO) (2016). Depression Fact Sheet. Retrieved from <www.who.int>.
A depressed mood, which is a common experience, can result from something that has been
experienced—a loss, relationship difficulties, trauma—or an event to which we can attribute feeling
down. Sometimes, though, we experience feelings of depression for no apparent reason at all. Such
feelings are normal and are not cause for concern. However, ‘feeling down’ can be an illness.
Indications that a person may have a depressive illness include that a low mood becomes very severe
and lasts for 2 weeks or more, and the mood interferes with the person’s ability to function (see ‘Clinical
manifestations’).
Depression affects nearly all physical and psychological functions. A person with depression may have
difficulty getting out of bed, not care for their ADLs, have difficulty coping at work, find it hard to
concentrate and suffer with memory
 loss. Many famous people are said to have or have had
depression: Tchaikovsky, Winston Churchill, Robin Williams, Billy Joel, Buzz Aldrin, Drew Carey, Vincent
Van Gogh, Rodney Dangerfield, Sheryl Crow and Rosie O’Donnell, to name but a few.
Clinical manifestations
24


Mania
Look for changes such as:
Lowered energy levels.
Indifference and apathy.
Feelings of despondency and dejection.
Reduced motivation.
Reduced libido.
Lowered pain tolerance.
New aches and pains.
Weight changes or changes to appetite.
Reduced ability to control emotions (crying, labile, anger outbursts).
Poor memory and concentration.
Changes in sleep patterns.
Reduced capacity to enjoy life—nothing is pleasurable.
Having one or two symptoms is not necessarily indicative of a depressive illness. Another sign of a
depressive illness is that the person may have suicidal thoughts (ideation). Such thoughts need to be
explored by the nurse so that risk and safety can be assessed.


Suicide
Every year thousands of people lose their lives to suicide. Suicide is
from a Latin word suicidium, from sui caedere, ‘to kill oneself’.
Suicide is the act of a human being intentionally causing their own
death (see Figure 45.6
).
Figure 45.6


Thomas Chatterton, an English Romantic poet thought to have killed
himself in 1770 with arsenic.
Source: Henry Wallis/The Bridgeman Art Library/Getty Images.
Personal reasons for each individual suicide will never be known and
not every person leaves a suicide note, so reasons are not always
disclosed. What is known though is that everyone who knew the
person or their family is left feeling empty, guilty and often angry.
Most people are left wondering ‘Why?’. It is thought that people who
suicide may not actually want to die but want the pain or distress
they are feeling to stop. This pain can be physical pain, but it is often
emotional pain. See Box 45.5
for suicide triggers.
BO X
45.5 Suicide triggers
There is no one cause of suicide. Potential suicide triggers
include:
pressure at work/school/university
bullying
stress
recent suicide of friend or relative
a sense of failure
unemployment, particularly long term
family conflict
experiencing discrimination


loneliness
isolation
having been abused as a child or incest
trauma (e.g. rape)
loss of
– independence (mobility, continence, vision, no longer
able to drive etc.)
– a loved one, spouse, girl/boyfriend, child
– reputation
– status
– ‘face’
depression.
Suicide statistics
Many Australians take their own lives each year, with suicide being a
prominent public health concern. In 2017, preliminary data showed a
total of 3128 deaths by suicide in Australia (Mindframe ). This
incidence equates to an average of 8.57 deaths by suicide each day
in Australia. The WHO
 states that suicide results in almost
800 000 deaths per year globally, which equates to approximately
one suicide every 40 seconds. Despite these alarming statistics,
25
26


suicide remains largely hidden. Suicide kills more Australians than
road accidents and is on the rise. Facts surrounding suicide are not
widely known because of stigma, prejudice and ignorance. Public
discussion around suicide and greater community awareness may
help save lives. More detailed information on suicide statistics in
Australia can be obtained from Mindframe (see <https://
mindframe.org.au/suicide/data-statistics>.
25 Mindframe (2019). Suicide Data and Statistics. Retrieved from
<www.mindframe.org.au>.
26 World Health Organization (WHO) (2019b). Suicide Data. Retrieved from <www.who.int>.
There are now websites, YouTube channels and Facebook sites
dedicated to suicide prevention. One such site, Suicide Prevention
Australia (SPA), holds as its vision ‘A world without suicide’ (SPA ).
27 Suicide Prevention Australia (SPA) (2018). Suicide Prevention Australia. Retrieved from
<www.suicidepreventionaust.org>.
Suicide statistics for indigenous
Australians
In Australia, the proportion of Indigenous Australians who die by
suicide is increasing. Cultural dislocation, personal trauma,
disadvantage, racism, alienation and exclusion are all acknowledged
as contributing to the heightened risk of mental health problems,
substance misuse and suicide. Suicide among Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander people is significantly higher than the non-Indigenous
27


Australian population. Estimates suggest that in some years, the
suicide rate for Indigenous Australians in specific communities is as
much as 40% higher than that for the Australian population as a
whole. Over the past 30 years, suicide by Indigenous Australians
has increased, with young Indigenous males being the most at risk
(Creative Spirits ).
28 Creative Spirits (2019). Aboriginal Suicide Rates. Retrieved from
<www.creativespirits.info>.
In 2016, 162 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people died as a
result of suicide. The standardised death rate for Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander Australians was 23.8 deaths per 100 000
people, compared to 11.4 deaths per 100 000 for non-Indigenous
Australians. Suicide deaths also accounted for a greater proportion
of all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander deaths (5.5%) compared
to deaths of non-Indigenous Australians (1.7%) (Australian Bureau
of Statistics ). See Figure 45.7
.

harm in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People. Cat. no. 3303.0. Canberra: ABS.
Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
