Suicide prevention
The Suicide Prevention Hub is an online resource to support sharing
and learning of evaluated suicide prevention initiatives. It is
important that nurses use evidence-based resources. These
resources can be accessed at
<www.suicidepreventionhub.org.au>.
A National Suicide Prevention Program was established in order to
fund initiatives to reduce the incidence of suicide and self-harm and
promote mental health and resilience in Australian populations. In
response to the growing concern about suicide in Indigenous
populations, the federal government released its first ever National
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Suicide Prevention Strategy
(see
<www.health.gov.au/internet/main/publishing.nsf/Content/mental-
pub-atsi-suicide-prevention-strategy>).
World Suicide Prevention day is the 10th of September every year.
Suicide warning signs


Culturally competent care
Cultural awareness in Indigenous communities
Nurses need to consider cultural differences when working
with Indigenous people and communities. The following are
some suggestions:
Interconnectedness:
spiritual
physical
emotional
social
environmental
cultural.
Focus on promoting protective factors rather than suicide
prevention (e.g. cultural determinants of health).
Approaches to verbal and non-verbal communication can
include:
use of non-confrontational language
being a respectful listener
asking for clarification when uncertain.
It is helpful to employ Indigenous health workers where
possible and workers who are culturally sensitive in suicide
prevention activities. Consider engaging a cultural
consultant/broker to help understand the variances between
different Indigenous communities.


Source: Department of Health and Ageing
. Living Is for Everyone. Retrieved from
<www.livingisforeveryone.com.au/Indigenous.html>.
30 Department of Health and Ageing (2014). Living Is for Everyone. Retrieved from
<www.livingisforeveryone.com.au>.
People believe that someone who talks about suicide won’t do it.
Wrong! Suicide threats should always be taken seriously. People
who have previously attempted suicide are more likely to try again
and those who have a history of deliberate self-harm are also at
higher risk. See Box 45.6
for advice on how to help a suicidal
person.
BO X
45.6 How to help
1. Ask
If you think someone might be suicidal, ask them
directly, ‘Are you thinking about suicide?’. Don’t be
afraid to do this—it shows you care and will actually
decrease their risk because it shows someone is
willing to talk about it. Make sure you ask directly and
unambiguously.
2. Listen and stay with them
If they say ‘yes’ they are suicidal, listen to them and
allow them to express how they are feeling. Don’t
leave them alone. Stay with them or get someone else
reliable to stay with them.
30


3. Get help
Get appropriate help. Call a crisis line such as Lifeline
13 11 14 or 000 if life is in danger. If you can get in
straight away, visit a GP or psychologist. Even if the
danger is not immediate, they may need longer-term
support for the issues that led to them feeling this way.
Source: Lifeline
. Preventing Suicide: 3 Steps to Prevent Suicide. Retrieved from
<www.lifeline.org.au/Get-Help/Facts—Information/Preventing-Suicide/Preventing-Suicide>.
31 Lifeline (2016). Preventing Suicide: 3 Steps to Prevent Suicide. Retrieved from
<www.lifeline.org.au>.
Predicting suicide is difficult, but some warning signs could be:
giving away possessions
sudden and striking personality changes
loss of interest in previously pleasurable activities
problem behaviour and substance misuse
apathy in dress and appearance, or a sudden change in weight
withdrawal from friends and social activities
increased ‘accident proneness’ and self-harming behaviours.
31


Treatments in mental health
Treatments for mental illnesses are as varied and diverse as the
illnesses themselves but largely fall into two categories: physical
treatments and psychological therapies.
Physical treatments
There are a number of physical treatments. The most common is
medication.
Medications
In addition to other treatments, mental health nurses administer,
monitor and evaluate drug therapy. Medications are used widely and
fall broadly into a number of categories: antidepressants, anxiolytics,
antipsychotics and mood stabilisers (see Figure 45.8
). If a person
takes medication, it is important they know why they are taking it,
they can manage the side effects of the drug and that they take it as
prescribed. The mental health nurse needs to engage with the
person and provide psycho-education, with the aim of increasing
medication understanding.
Figure 45.8


Types of medications: A: an antidepressant; B: an antipsychotic.
Sources: © Scott Camazine/Alamy Stock Photo; Chris Gallagher/Photo Researchers/Getty Images.


Mild brain stimulation (MBS)
This procedure takes about 20 minutes. A small series of very weak
currents is applied to the brain while the person remains awake and
alert.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS)
A magnetic field is applied via a coil held near the head to stimulate
relevant parts of the brain. Although relatively new in psychiatry, it
has been a diagnostic tool used by neurologists for many years.
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
ECT is a treatment with a controversial past. It is considered useful
for someone who has severe depression or life-threatening mania.
Electrodes are placed on the person’s temples, bilaterally or
unilaterally, and an electric current is applied through the brain. The
person, who is under anaesthesia, does not feel this impulse,
although a convulsion is induced. These days, this convulsion is
barely visible, unlike early days. Media portrayal of the individual
thrashing about has contributed to societal apprehension and fear of
ECT. ECT is known to have some short-term side effects. In
contemporary psychiatry practice, it is considered a safe form of
treatment.


Psychological therapies
Psychological therapies play a major role in someone’s personal
recovery. The most important of these is the development and
maintenance of a therapeutic relationship between each person and
their care manager. The importance of this relationship cannot be
underestimated and has been the subject of many research papers.
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
The aim of CBT is for the therapist to work with a person in order for
them to see the links between mood and thinking. The objective is
therefore to get the person to think in ways that are more positive.
Interpersonal therapy (IPT)
IPT aims to help the person identify current life factors that
contribute to being unwell. IPT is founded upon the assumption that
a person’s vulnerabilities lead them to an illness. IPT aims to
facilitate strengthening the vulnerable parts of the individual’s
personality.
Narrative therapy (NT)
The main emphasis of NT is the person’s strengths. Narrative
therapists listen closely to the person’s life story and help the
individual recognise times when they have positively problem solved.


These efficacious situations are learned from and are built upon,
ready to be used in future situations.
All therapies and treatments work best when the person involved is
accepting of and actively seeking treatment. It is often difficult to
know whether someone needs mental health treatment. See Box
45.7
for the SANE checklist; this checklist can help you determine
whether someone should seek mental health assistance.
Psychological therapies will not work if the person does not trust the
therapist. This situation again demonstrates the importance of
developing and maintaining a therapeutic relationship.
BO X
45.7 SANE checklist for when to seek
assistance
Are you worried about someone whose behaviour has
changed? Has someone you know become confused, says
odd things, avoids people, has changes in their mood,
worries people are ‘out to get them’ or has developed strange
ideas that are not shared by others? It is important they seek
help so that reasons for this change can be assessed. The
SANE helpline is 1800 187 263.
Checklist


Encourage someone to see a health specialist as soon as
possible if the person:
withdraws completely from family, friends and others
sleeps poorly; for example, sleeps during the day and
stays awake all night
becomes very preoccupied with a particular topic; for
example, death, politics or religion
uncharacteristically neglects responsibilities, personal
hygiene or appearance; eats poorly
deteriorates in performance at school or work
has difficulty concentrating, following conversation or
remembering things
panics, becomes anxious or depressed, or talks about
suicide
has extreme changes in mood for no real reason
hears voices that no-one else can hear
believes, without reason, that others are plotting against
or spying on them, and feels fearful or angry about this
believes they are being harmed or influenced to do things
against their will; for example, by television, the internet,
aliens or the devil
believes they have special powers or influence when this
is not so
believes their thoughts are being interfered with or that
they can influence the thoughts of others
spends extravagant and unrealistic sums of money.


How to get help
Encourage the person to see a doctor.
Offer to go with them as a support.
Ask for a longer appointment so there is sufficient time to
explain concerns.
Suggest you write some notes together to help explain
things to the doctor.
If the person is reluctant to seek help, visit the doctor
yourself to ask for advice.
Source: SANE Australia
. Is Someone You Know Unwell? Retrieved from <www.sane.org/mental-
health-and-illness/facts-and-guides/is-someone-you-know-unwell>. Reproduced with permission
from SANE Australia, the national mental health charity.
44 SANE Australia (2019b). Is Someone You Know Unwell? Retrieved from <www.sane.org>.
44


Mental health care models
Despite many approaches to mental health care, mental health
service provision in Australia is still largely based on the medical
model. The medical model is increasingly being challenged as more
people with a lived experience of mental illness gain a legitimately
stronger voice. The ongoing reform in mental health policies enables
people accessing mental health services to actively contribute to
their own care. The consumer voice is strengthened further when
nurses advocate for them. Nurses appreciate that a balanced
understanding of mental health involves a recognition that is broader
than only medical or clinical knowledge and that treatment for mental
illness is not just about the administration of medicine.
Traditional models of mental health service delivery were not
focused on recovery; rather, they focused on containing and
controlling the individual. Asylums are an example of this type of
control.
Mental health services should be delivered with the focus on
‘recovery’. Recovery is embedded in the very personal and unique
journey of the individual. Research has shown that people with a
mental illness can and do recover. Recovery is not synonymous with
cure; nor does it necessarily mean a return to a pre-illness state.


Recovery model
The concept of recovery
 is a recognised and accepted paradigm
that has significant implications for consumers, carers, mental health
professionals and mental health services. Recovery, as it is
conceptualised in mental health, is the journey towards a new and
valued sense of identity. This includes a role and purpose outside
the parameters of mental illness. The role of a mental health service
is to facilitate the process of recovery rather than determine its
direction. As such, recovery plans within mental health services
should always be formulated collaboratively.
Clinical consideration
The recovery plan should be completed by the
mental health nurse and the person together.
Goals and objectives are mutually agreed and
should not be documented in clinical language
or in a way that demonstrates the person was
not involved. A recovery plan is a dynamic
document, changing as the journey proceeds.
Remember the saying, Nothing about me,
without me.


The recovery model in relationship to mental illness is a
comparatively recent concept. The main impetus for the
development of a recovery model of care came from the collective
voice of the people receiving care. The Australian government is
committed to the notion of recovery and encourages a recovery
model of care in the Roadmap for National Mental Health Reform
2012–2022 (Council of Australian Governments (COAG)
). The
roadmap outlines the direction governments take during this period
and sets out the ongoing reform necessary to achieve:
32 Council of Australian Governments (COAG) (2012). Roadmap for National Mental Health
Reform 2012-2022. Retrieved from <www.coag.gov.au>.
A society that values and promotes the importance of good mental health and wellbeing,
maximises opportunities to prevent and reduce the impact of mental health issues and
mental illness and supports people with mental health issues and mental illness, their
families and carers to live full and rewarding lives. (COAG 2012, p. 6)
The roadmap has six goal-oriented and action-focused principles for
reform:
The roadmap includes a robust accountability framework where
governments report their progress on the implementation of the plan
to COAG.
Principles of recovery
The recovery model is an expression of a contemporary approach to
empower each individual and is collaborative in nature. Mental health
32


clinicians, including nurses, are sometimes uncomfortable with this
sharing of control and authority.
The personal recovery journey for a person with mental illness is, as
suggested earlier in the chapter, an individual journey. Although very
personal, there are principles of personal recovery that can be
considered for everyone.
The principles need to be fully understood and appreciated. Each
person’s perspective may be different, but they should nevertheless
be complementary. The personal recovery approach aims to support
people to move beyond mere survival and existence, and to carry
out activities and develop relationships that are meaningful.
Hope
: this principle is the foundation of recovery. It is the
belief that things do not have to remain the same and that they
can change for the better. Hope is about concentrating on a
person’s strengths and not on the things they are currently
unable to do. Hope focuses on the future, not the past, nor even
the present per se. Building hope means enabling the person to
celebrate even the smallest success rather than expecting and
insisting on rapid change. Hope invigorates the personal recovery
journey and forms the foundations for healing and emotional
wellbeing. Hope is important for everyone and does not apply
only to people who have a mental illness. For example, people
who have been diagnosed with cancer need hope. It is important
for the person to hold on to hope, but it is equally important for
others to have hope for the person involved. The positive impact


that the hope of others can have on a person with mental illness
cannot be underestimated. What do we have if we have no
hope?
Active sense of self
: for people living with mental illness, their
sense of self can become lost and identity can revolve around
the illness. This is commonly seen in self-stigma, where the
person internalises all of the negative stereotypes that society
holds. It is important that mental health nurses do not perpetuate
this and further contribute to low self-esteem. Nurses need to be
aware of language and avoid referring to people by their
diagnosis, such as ‘the schizophrenic’ or ‘the depressive’. This
form of language, or labelling, is easy to fall into the habit of
using, and sometimes you will hear it in clinical practice, but what
it does is place the emphasis on the illness/disease and not on
the person. It is fundamentally disrespectful and very
disempowering to use judgmental and labelling language and it
can help to further undermine an already fragile sense of self.
Language like this cannot be condoned in the modern person-
centred care environment and we need to challenge our peers
when we hear them use it.
Clinical consideration
Mental health nurses should be the holders of
hope. When a person has little or no hope, offer
to hold their hope in your own hands. Tell them


you will care for it and nurture it and, when they
are ready, you will hand it back.
A mental illness does not define who the person is—it is only one
part of the whole person. Having a positive self-image comes from
being treated as a whole person instead of only a part—this
contributes to the sense of self. Personal recovery extends the
person beyond merely functioning and is the development of
meaningful existence and a sense of purpose. Everyone needs a
reason to get up in the morning, and our sense of purpose is
developed through things such as relationships, leisure activities and
work. Renowned psychiatrist Victor Frankl’s (see Figure 45.9
)
premise is that ‘man’s search for meaning’ is life’s primary motivator.
Figure 45.9


Victor Frankl.
Source: Katharina Vesely/Imagno/Getty Images.
Positive regard: everyone deserves equality and respect. People
who are living with a mental illness struggle every day with
stereotypes perpetuated in the media. They are the most
stigmatised and discriminated group in society.
Connectedness
: personal recovery
 is a social process
and positive outcomes correlate closely with the strength of
people’s social networks. Strong social networks are considered
a protective factor. For personal recovery to happen, people


need to be involved with other people and connected to others.
Few humans really enjoy being alone: we are in fact ‘herd’
animals. There are times, though, when we all enjoy solitude.
Humans are social creatures and desire the company of others.
Humans need company (interpersonal relationships) to be
mentally healthy. To make connections, social roles must be
established, which can be hard for the person who has a mental
illness. Society is not very accepting of ‘differentness
’ and, as
has already been discussed, members of the wider community
often subscribe to myths and stereotypes about mental illness
that are simply untrue.
When fostering social connectedness, issues regarding community
integration and full community participation need to be considered.
Community integration is drawn from the larger disability and civil
rights movements and is founded on the belief that all people have a
right to full community participation and full community membership.
This integration includes jobs, relationships with non-mentally ill
peers and appropriate and affordable housing.
Autonomy: the person who is actually living with a mental illness
is the one who holds the key to their personal recovery. Mental
health nurses need to ensure that people with mental illness are
recognised as individuals who are self-determining. Self-
determination theory is something that a good mental health
nurses will understand and apply. All people need to be
recognised as being able to make their own choices, take


personal responsibility and live with the consequences of their
decisions.
During the personal recovery journey, it is important that people are
empowered to ‘own’ their illness and take an active role in the
process (see Box 45.8
). Empowerment
 is vital for helping
people understand and change the learned helplessness that many
people experience as a result of long-term interactions with a mental
health system. The importance of people participating in their own
health care has long been recognised as an essential element of
effective service provision. This right is included in the WHO’s
Declaration of Alma Ata  and within the principles in the Roadmap
for National Mental Health Reform 2012–2022. Empowerment is
also incorporated in the National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards Partnering with Consumers standard. These important
documents highlight the need for the provision of care to be focused
on the needs of the individual rather than the service.
34 World Health Organization (WHO) (1978). Declaration of Alma Ata. International
Conference on Primary Health Care. WHO: Alma-Ata, USSR, 6–12 September.
BO X
45.8 Assisting recovery
People who are recovering have described specific ways
others have helped them. These include:
34


Ventilation: being able to converse with others; share
concerns.
Reality testing: having people assist in maintaining clear
distinctions between reality and psychotic distortions.
Material support: helping with financial, housing and
transportation problems.
Social approval and integration: receiving reassurance
when people accept them and provide a sense of
belonging.
Constancy: associating with people they knew before
hospitalisation, connecting current identity with pre-
hospital identity and giving roots to existence.
Motivation: receiving encouragement to achieve higher
levels of occupational and social functioning.
Modelling: observing the behaviour of others and
incorporating it into their own behaviour.
Symptom monitoring: having others alert them to
manifestations of symptoms.
Problem solving: discussing problems and getting
concrete feedback.
Empathic understanding: being understood by people
important to them.
Reciprocal relating: becoming an equal partner, able to
share and be of assistance to others.
Insight:
acquiring more complete and accurate
understanding of themselves.

. Carers Matter. Retrieved from <www.health.qld.gov.au/mhcarer/
recovery.asp>.

Patient safety competency framework

Nursing students must be able to engage the
person (and significant others) as an integral
member of the health care team (Levett-Jones
et al.
).

NSQHS standard partnering with consumers
The intention of this standard is ‘to create an organisation in
which there are mutually beneficial outcomes by having:
consumers as partners in planning, design, delivery,
measurement and evaluation of systems and services;
35
36


patients are partners in their own care, to the extent that they

Health Care
, p. 14).
37 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health

Implementing this standard is achieved by
creating a health service that is responsive to
the needs and inputs of the person and/or their
carer. In addition, the clinician works with the
person to improve the quality and safety of their
care. Care is individualised to maximise the
person’s recovery.
37


Mental health care policy
All governments have invested in mental health reform in recent
years. Fiscal investment is significantly less than that spent on
physical illnesses over the same period, despite the fact that mental
illness affects 1 in 5 people.
The Roadmap for National Mental Health Reform 2012–2022 seeks
to improve mental health and facilitate recovery from illness by
confirming the shared intents and goals of Commonwealth, state
and territory governments to develop better mental health services
and support across all relevant government portfolios, including
mental health, health, education, early childhood, child protection,
youth, employment and workplace relations, housing and
homelessness, police and the justice system (COAG 2012). COAG
recognises that its vision can only be achieved through close
cooperation throughout the sector, in particular with consumers and
carers, and that policy should be guided by and respond to people’s
lived experience. Recent efforts at improving the care system have,
in turn, served to focus greater national attention on ensuring better
coordinated care. This change has particularly engendered a greater
consideration of the best means for building greater workforce
capacity. Much attention has been placed on national initiatives, and
individual state and territory governments have also implemented
their own suite of specific mental health action plans and initiatives.


Mental health is, and should remain for many years to come, a
National Health Priority Area.
The 66th World Health Assembly (see Figure 45.10
), consisting
of Ministers of Health of 194 member states, adopted the WHO’s
Comprehensive Mental Health Action Plan 2013–2020 on 27 May
2013 (WHO
). The member states emphasised the importance of
mental health, stating their commitment to implementing the action
plan and achieving the specific targets in the plan by year 2020.
39 World Health Organization (WHO) (2013). WHO’s Comprehensive Mental Health Action
Plan 2013-2020. Retrieved from <http://apps.who.int>.
Figure 45.10
39


WHO Assembly.
Source: © WHO/Pierre Albouy.


Recovery vs rehabilitation
The difference between recovery and rehabilitation can be subtle:
Rehabilitation refers to the services and technologies that are made available to disabled
persons so that they may learn to adapt to their world. Recovery refers to the lived or real-
life experience of persons as they accept and overcome the challenge of the disability.
(Deegan
)
40 Deegan, P. E. (1988). Recovery: The lived experience of rehabilitation. Psychosocial
Rehabilitation Journal, 11, 11–19.
The aim of rehabilitation is the restoration of function and the
minimisation of disability. Rehabilitation does this through the
development of strengths, restoration of hope, environmental
modifications, enhancement of vocational potential and the
facilitation of social and community integration.
Recovery therefore forms the basis on which rehabilitation services
can be developed, but rehabilitation services should not be
considered the only vehicle for recovery. Rather, rehabilitation
services are just one component in a framework that ensures hope,
respect and pathways to community participation within a
comprehensive service system that collectively works towards the
individualised goal of recovery.
40


Case study
Jess Neumann is 34 years old and was recently involuntarily
admitted into an acute inpatient unit under the Mental Health
Act. The admission was precipitated by the fact that Jess
decided not to take any more medication. Jess gradually
became unwell. Upon admission, staff noticed apparent
alterations to his perception and thought processes. Jess
didn’t think an admission was necessary and informed the
staff in very clear terms: ‘I feel great!!’.
Jess was observed responding to unseen stimuli and
constantly asked staff about matters of safety. Jess insisted
locks be fitted to the bedroom and also wanted a CCTV
camera installed, which he said he would pay for, so that he
could monitor the front door. Jess was so concerned that
someone would ‘get’ him that he said he had to sit in the
nurses’ station all night. Jess refused to sleep at all as he
needed to be vigilant at all times. Jess was worried that
people wanted his ideas as business plans because these
were of international significance and were going to make him
extremely rich. Rather than have anyone get their hands on
this important information, he would take it to his grave. Jess
could clearly describe a suicide plan and he had the means to
carry it out.
Jess was diagnosed with schizophrenia. This medical label
was given to him using a set of well-recognised mental health


diagnostic criteria. Jess has had a community care
coordinator for some years and has been provided with
psycho-education. His community care coordinator described
him as having poor insight. Jess continues to believe it is
everyone else who has an illness, not him, and that he
certainly does not need treatment.
>


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. What do you think has happened so that Jess was
admitted involuntarily?
2. Jess has a psychotic illness. What would lead you to
believe this from the information provided in the case
study?
3. What makes Jess’s care coordinator think that he has
poor insight?
4. Is Jess at risk of self-harm? On what basis have you
come to this conclusion and how high do you perceive
the level of risk to be?
5. What set of diagnostic criteria was most likely used in
order to give Jess his medical diagnosis?
6.
What are some of the aspects of this case study
that might make it difficult for you to develop a
relationship with Jess? Using the Fundamentals of
Care Framework, how might you work to overcome
this?


Chapter 45 Review


Chapter highlights
Mental illness accounts for an estimated 11% of the disease
burden worldwide and continues to increase.
In Australia, mental disorders are the third leading cause of
overall disease burden.
Mental illness represents the largest single cause of disability,
accounting for almost 25% of the burden of non-fatal disease.
All nurses need skills and knowledge to provide safe and
effective care for this large and vulnerable group of people.
People who have a mental illness receive care that is no less
evidence-based than that provided to people who have a physical
illness.
Nurses should show respect and be non-judgmental; nurses
should demonstrate unconditional positive regard and always act
professionally.
Concept check
1. Which of the following two main criteria are used to diagnose
mental illness?
1. DSN and ICD.
2. DSM and ICC.
3. DSM and ICD.
4. DMM and ICD.


2. Which of the following is the current version of the American
Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual?
1. DSM-5-TR.
2. DSM-5.
3. DSM-V-R.
4. DSM-TR-V.

processes. What is an appropriate nursing response?
1. To explore his delusions with him.
2. To redirect his attention back to the here and now.
3. To point out gently the way in which his thinking is
altered so he can gain insight into his illness.
4. To ensure you speak loudly enough so that Jess can
hear you above the voices in his head.
4. Which of the following best describes schizophrenia?
1. A non-reactive set of depressive symptoms caused by
smoking cannabis.
2. A common disorder in young males.
3. A psychotic disorder.
4. A genetic disorder.

schizophrenia?
1. Delusions and spatial disruption.
2. Positive and negative symptoms.
3. Mood swings.

schizophrenia?

2. It develops during menopause.
3. It is a result of trauma.
4. It is the result of the mother’s mental illness.

schizophrenia?
1. Little eye contact.
2. Loss of appetite.

9. Which of the following is not an example of a perceptual
disturbance?

2. Seeing things.
3. Hearing voices.

10. Jess is described as having poor insight. This concept means
that he:
1. Will not engage in case management.
2. Does not have a fully developed understanding of his
illness.

are labelled as eccentric?

Chapter 46 Disability
Virginia Howie, Katrina Lane-Krebs, Nathan J. Wilson
Learning outcomes
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Understand the complexity of defining disability.
Recognise the effects of social exclusion on the health of people
with disability, including from a historical perspective.
Appreciate the right to self-determination, autonomy and
inclusion for people with disability as a human rights issue.
Appreciate the importance of dignity, respect and person-centred
care for people with disability.


Understand the role of the nurse as well as the caregiver as
advocates when caring for a person with disability.
Identify the barriers and enablers for people with a range of
disabilities when accessing health care, including poor attitudes
by health care professionals.
Recognise that health care for people with intellectual disability is
complex due to the diversity of this population group.
Understand the role of governments in developing policy and
legislation that reduce barriers and promote access and
inclusion.

Australia is one of the wealthiest countries in the
world, yet people with disability (PWD) struggle
to access the very things that people without
disability take for granted, such as employment,
housing, education, recreation, sports, goods
and services, and health care. PWD are more
likely to belong to the lower socioeconomic
group; have low participation rates in the
workforce and education; and experience high
rates of psychological distress, violence and
discrimination, resulting in poor health outcomes
(Australian Institute of Health & Welfare
(AIHW) ). This is a socially constructed disparity
and a human rights issue. Although
governments around the world recognise these
inequities, change, including health care
services, is slow. Globally, people with
disabilities have the same health care needs as
those without disability; however, they are twice
as likely to find health care services and skills
inadequate, three times more likely to be denied
health care and four times more likely to be
1


treated badly in the health care system (World
Health Organization (WHO) ). Compared to the
general population, PWD are more likely to have
comorbid conditions and higher rates of
premature death, experience secondary (e.g.
pressure injuries) and age-related conditions
(e.g. premature ageing) and engage in health
risk behaviours (e.g. poor diet, physical
inactivity) (WHO 2019a).
1 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW)
(2019a). People with Disability in Australia: Web Report.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
2 World Health Organization (2019a). Disabilities.
Retrieved from <www.who.int>.
Health services must not discriminate on the
grounds of disability and are required to provide
the same services to PWD as to those without
disability (Federal Register of Legislation ).
However, service disparities and poor attitudes
by staff, including nurses, result in inequitable
access to quality health care. One of the key
issues affecting nurse attitudes is nurses’
general lack of knowledge and confidence
2
3


about disability issues due to an inadequate
amount of disability content in undergraduate
nursing programs in Australia.
3 Federal Register of Legislation (2018). Disability
Discrimination Act 1992. Canberra: Australian Government.
Retrieved from <www.legislation.gov.au>.
Nurses represent the largest group of the health
care workforce (Department of Health ) and
therefore are in a strong position to advocate for
PWD in their care, although this is not without its
challenges. Disability is the result of some type
of functional impairment that may require
support from multiple services and health care
systems across the lifespan. Therefore, nurses
are likely to encounter PWD many times
throughout their nursing career. It is important
that nurses have a solid understanding of the
challenges faced by PWD when accessing
health care in order to optimise positive health
outcomes. This chapter explores social
exclusion/inclusion and is designed to stimulate
your thinking about attitudes to one of the most
marginalised groups in society. Social
inclusion
 is the act of making all members of
society feel valued and important by promoting
4


equal opportunities throughout the community.
PWD want to be part of mainstream society and
have full access to services, just like everyone
else.
4 Department of Health (2014). Health Workforce Australia
2014: Australia’s Future Health Workforce—Nurses
Overview. Commonwealth of Australia. Retrieved from
<www1.health.gov.au>.


What is disability?
Disability may be evident from birth (i.e. lifelong) or occur any time in
a person’s life (i.e. acquired) as a permanent or temporary condition.
Disabilities can also be ‘invisible’, such as a mental health condition,
intellectual disability (ID) or chronic pain. Disability is a complex,
evolving concept that is challenging to define and varies according to
the context of the source. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS ,
p. 1) defines disability as ‘a limitation, restriction or impairment which
restricts everyday activities and has lasted, or is likely to last, for at
least six months’. The AIHW  offers a binary approach: those with
severe or profound core activity limitation and those without severe
or profound core activity limitation. A more comprehensive definition
can be found in the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (DDA) (Section
4):
5 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2019). Disability, Ageing and Carers, Australia:
Summary of Findings, 2018. Cat. no. 4430.0. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
6 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2018). Australia’s Health 2018. Retrieved
from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
total or partial loss of the person’s bodily or mental functions
total or partial loss of a part of the body
the presence in the body of organisms causing disease or illness
the presence in the body of organisms capable of causing
disease or illness
5
6


the malfunction, malformation or disfigurement of a part of the
person’s body
a disorder or malfunction that results in the person learning
differently from a person without the disorder or malfunction
a disorder, illness or disease that affects a person’s thought
processes, perception of reality, emotions or judgment or that
results in disturbed behaviour.
The DDA categorises disability into six broad areas: physical,
intellectual, psychiatric, sensory, neurological and intellectual
disabilities. The focus in this chapter is more concerned with
physical, sensory and intellectual disability, since the other topics are
well covered in other chapters.
Adopting a more socially constructed approach, the WHO (2019a,
para. 1) defines disability using the International Classification of
Functioning as ‘an umbrella term for impairments, activity limitations
and participation restrictions’, and is the interaction between
individuals with a health condition (e.g. Down syndrome) and
personal and environmental factors (e.g. negative attitudes,
inaccessible transport). This chapter aligns with the WHO definition
and approaches disability in terms of identifying barriers to and
promoting opportunities for full participation in life.
Box 46.1
 offers a brief insight into disability in Australia.
BO X


46.1 Australian bureau of statistics
figures for disability in Australia
In 2018, there were 4.4 million Australians with disability
(17.7% of the population), down from 18.3% in 2015.
The prevalence of disability increased with age—1 in 9
(11.6%) people aged 0–64 years and 1 in 2 (49.6%)
people aged 65 years and over had disability.
Disability prevalence was similar for males (17.6%) and
females (17.8%).
5.7% of all Australians had a profound or severe disability.
Almost one-quarter (23.2%) of all PWD reported a mental
or behavioural disorder as their main condition, up from
21.5% in 2015.
37.9% of those aged 15–64 years said their main source
of personal income was a government pension or
allowance, down from 41.9% in 2015.
One in 10 (9.6%) aged 15 years and over had
experienced discrimination in the previous 12 months
because of their disability, up from 8.6% in 2015.
Labour force participation for those aged 15–64 years has
remained stable since 2015 at 53.4%, in contrast to an
increase in the participation rate for people without
disability (84.1%).
Source: ABS (2019). Disability, Ageing and Carers, Australia: Summary of Findings, 2018. Cat. no.
4430.0. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/Latestproducts/4430.0>.


It is important to understand the need for respectful language when
referring to PWD.


Respectful disability language
When communicating with, or about, PWD, it is important to use
inclusive and non-discriminatory language. The person always
comes first; for example, ‘person with disability’, ‘person with vison
impairment’, ‘person with intellectual disability’ or ‘person who uses a
wheelchair’. The following ‘Practice guidelines’ seek to promote
inclusive practice.
Clinical consideration
Do not make assumptions about lack of ability.
Many PWD work in a variety of professions and
contexts, participate in sport and contribute to
community life, as well as have families.
Practice guidelines
Inclusive practice
Do not use inappropriate terminology (e.g. ‘blind person’,
intellectually disabled person’ or ‘wheelchair-bound’


person).
Do not compare people with disability to the term ‘normal’,
as being ‘normal’ is a questionable concept. Make the
comparison using the same language (e.g. ‘compared to
people without disability’).
Avoid adopting a sympathetic (values-based) stance (i.e.
pitying a person who uses a wheelchair). Remember that
the wheelchair is a way of getting about as it increases
mobility and access to community life. Similarly, people
are not ‘suffering’ because they use a wheelchair.
Avoid language that ‘talks down’ to the person with a
disability (e.g. adults with intellectual disability dislike being
spoken to as though they are children or as if they are
deaf). People with hearing impairment dislike over-
exaggeration of the mouth when being spoken to as lip
movements become distorted, making lip-reading more
difficult.
Avoid language that has negative connotations, such as
‘handicapped’, ‘crippled’, ‘mentally retarded’ or ‘invalid’.
Clinical consideration
Often PWD do not see themselves as disabled.
Instead, they will see themselves as part of the


world’s diversity. PWD wish to be accepted for
who they are, not their disability.


Historical context of disability in
Australia
Social stigma and disability
PWD were once viewed as horrible or grotesque, burdens on
society, childlike, ‘special’ or victims in need of pity. Furthermore,
they were often seen as ‘objects’ of charity, medical treatment and
social protection instead of as people with rights who were capable
of making informed decisions about their lives (United Nations (UN)
General Assembly ). Indeed, parents were often encouraged to
hand over their ‘defective’ child to custodian institutions. The
institutionalised model of care was often a communal approach
offering dormitory style accommodation, shared clothing, separation
of the sexes, heavy reliance on physical and chemical restraints,
and strict rules and regulations that stripped inmates of any dignity
and respect. In the 1970–80s, the process of de-institutionalisation
began in response to society’s recognition that institutionalised care
was discriminatory and an abuse of human rights. Human rights
are ‘rights inherent to all human beings, regardless of race, sex,
nationality, ethnicity, language, religion or any other status . . .
Everyone is entitled to these rights, without discrimination’ (UN n.d. ,
para. 1).
7
8


7 United Nations (UN) General Assembly (2007). Convention on the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities: Resolution Adopted by the General Assembly. [A/RES/61/106.] Retrieved from
<www.un.org>.
8 United Nations (UN) (n.d.). Human Rights. Retrieved from <www.un.org>.
Disability discrimination
Discrimination is defined as ‘when a person, or a group of people, is
treated less favourably than another person or group because of
their background or certain characteristics’ (Australian Human Rights
Commission (AHRC) , para. 1). This is known as direct
discrimination
 and includes acts such as refusing an individual’s
entry to a restaurant because they have an assistance animal.
Indirect discrimination
 occurs through systemic approaches or
policy that may apply to everyone but that may effectively
disadvantage those with a disability (AHRC 2019a); for example, a
health care policy that does not include reasonable adjustments.
Reasonable adjustments
 refer to administrative, environmental
or procedural alterations that accommodate a person’s disability
(AHRC ). Unreasonable adjustments are referred to as
unjustifiable hardship
, where the alteration or adjustment would
seem unreasonable due to costs, practicality, complexity or degree
of disruption (AHRC 2019b). Businesses and organisations must
make reasonable adjustments in order to meet obligations to PWD
under the DDA. Reasonable adjustments vary according to the
context, such as employers providing an accessible and inclusive
9
10


workplace; for example, a desk at a suitable height to allow access
for a person who uses a wheelchair (see Figure 46.1
).
9 Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) (2019a). Discrimination. Retrieved from
<www.humanrights.gov.au>.
10 Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) (2019b). Disability Rights. Retrieved from
<www.humanrights.gov.au>.
Figure 46.1
An example of an accessible reception desk.
Source: © Peter Noyce PLBS/Alamy Stock Photo.


However, if the situation reaches a point where there is unjustifiable
hardship, such as the cost to reconstruct a doorway to allow
wheelchair access, the employer is under no obligation to make
significant changes to the building.
Clinical consideration
In the context of health care provision, health
care providers and health care workers have a
duty to make reasonable adjustments in a
variety of ways. For example, health service
providers can make reasonable adjustments for
bariatric patents by providing bariatric
equipment; nurses can make reasonable
adjustments for people with communication
disability by allowing more time during nurse–
patient interactions.
Discrimination due to disability affects mental health, self- esteem
and self-worth, impacting on a person’s desire to fully participate in
society, which results in social isolation. Social isolation
 is being
separated from other people and the environment and is a
significant barrier for PWD, as identified in the Shut Out report
(Department of Social Services 2009). According to the ABS , the
sources of discrimination were identified as service, hospitality and
11


teaching staff, including health care staff, bus drivers, retail staff,
taxi drivers or sales assistance. As a result, one-third of PWD
avoided situations (e.g. work, educational and medical facilities,
shops, banks, restaurants, public transport, recreational areas and
other public places or social situations) because of their disability
(ABS 2018). In relation to health care, when PWD are treated poorly
by health care staff, they are less likely to return for follow-up care
or further treatment and will avoid accessing services in the future.
This results in missed opportunities to receive health information,
resulting in poor health literacy and poor health outcomes.
11 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018). Disability Discrimination in Australia.
Disability, Ageing and Carers, Australia: Summary of Findings, 2015. Cat. no. 4430.0.
Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Governments around the world have an obligation to develop policy
and legislation to improve access and equity for PWD in the areas of
public life where disability discrimination can occur. Discrimination is
against the law and is a human rights issue.
Australian human rights
commission
The Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) was established
by an act of Federal Parliament in 1986 to promote and protect
human rights in Australia and internationally. Operating as a human


rights watchdog, it serves to conciliate discrimination complaints
against individuals or groups. The AHRC also holds public inquiries,
develops educational resources for schools and workplaces,
provides legal advice to courts, makes submissions to parliaments
and governments and develops research into human rights issues.
The AHRC is guided by the DDA.
Disability discrimination act 1992
(Cth) (DDA)
In the 1990s, the Federal government determined the need for a
national approach to anti-discrimination law in order to standardise
legislation across states and territories in response to international
commitments on the rights of PWD, as well as enable regulation of
discriminatory practices. The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth)
(DDA) serves to provide protection against discrimination based on
disability for everyone in Australia (AHRC 2019a). This provision
includes protecting family members, carers, interpreters, co-workers
or associates of the person with disability who may be subject to
disability discrimination by association; for example, a support
worker being excluded from accompanying the person to a concert
or event. Section 8 of the DDA states that discrimination is also
unlawful where it occurs because a person with a disability: uses a
palliative, therapeutic or assistive device; is accompanied by a carer,
interpreter, reader or assistant; or is accompanied by a trained
assistance animal. The areas of life covered by the DDA are


employment; education; access; provision of goods, services and
facilities; accommodation; buying land; activities of clubs and
associations; sport; and administration of Commonwealth
government laws and programs (AHRC 2019b).
United nations (UN) convention on
the rights of persons with
disabilities (CRPD)
In the 1970s, there was global shift in attitudes and understanding
about disability from one of welfare to one of human rights. In 1971,
the UN proclaimed the Declaration of Rights of Mentally Retarded
Persons. This was followed by the Declaration of Rights of Disabled
Persons in 1975. In 1981, the UN declared the International Day of
Disabled Persons with a plan of action promoting equal opportunities
and full participation in society for PWD, targeting a number of
social, economic, civil and political rights (AHRC ).
12 Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) (2019c). Timeline. Retrieved from
<www.humanrights.gov.au>.
In 2006, the UN held a Convention on the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities (CRPD), the purpose of which was to ‘promote, protect
and ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights and
fundamental freedoms by all persons with disabilities, and to
12


promote respect for their inherent dignity’ (UN General Assembly
2007, p. 4). The UN directed that governments adopt a social model
of disability, meaning that barriers which make life more difficult with
for PWD are removed (e.g. barriers to public transport, inaccessible
toilets). Focal areas of concern of the CRPD were: respect for
inherent dignity, autonomy
 (a person’s right to self-
determination
) and independence; non-discrimination; full
participation and inclusion in society; respecting disability as part of
human diversity; equality of opportunity; accessibility; equality
between men and women; and respect for children with disabilities
(UN General Assembly 2007, p. 1). One way in which the Australian
government responded to the CRPD was through the introduction of
the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).
National disability insurance
scheme (NDIS)
In 2007 and 2008 respectively, two important things occurred: 1) the
Federal government initiated a senate inquiry into the funding of
disability services and supports; and 2) Australia was among the first
nations to sign the CRPD. This impetus was carried through by the
newly elected Federal government when a new, individualised
insurance model was proposed by leading disability advocates Bruce
Bonyhady and Helen Sykes (Department of Parliamentary
Services ). One part of the government’s response was to ask
PWD and their carers their views on disability supports across
13


Australia; the resulting Shut Out report highlighted systemic
disadvantage across all age ranges (Department of Social
Services ). While PWD were once shut in (institutionalised), the
report revealed they now felt shut out of mainstream services.
13 Department of Parliamentary Services (2018). The National Disability Insurance Scheme:
A Chronology. Parliament of Australia. Retrieved from <www.aph.gov.au>.
14 Department of Social Services (2009). Shut Out: The Experiences of People with
Disabilities and Their Families in Australia. Canberra: Australian Government. Retrieved from
<www.dss.gov.au>.
By 2011, the Federal government committed to the idea of an NDIS,
heralding one of the biggest social reforms since the introduction of
Medicare in 1984 and representing a paradigm shift in the way that
PWD accessed services and supports. For the first time at a
national level, people with a disability and their families accessed
individualised funding that was based upon support needs.
Moreover, PWD and their families had more choice and control over
who and how services were provided, rather than service provision
based on service provider vacancies and who had the greatest
need. The NDIS began to roll out over several trial sites in 2013 in
Tasmania, New South Wales, South Australia and Victoria, with
national implementation completed by June 2019.
Most state governments have now closed their state-based disability
departments and very few, if any, state-run disability services
remain. The disability sector has been transformed and now consists
of thousands of different private and non- government providers
14


across different service categories. Specialist services can include
assistive technology, early childhood intervention services, life skills
development, specialist accommodation, community living support,
community participation support and respite care (AIHW
). For
nurses, this represents both a challenge and an opportunity as,
unlike almost all other health professions, nursing currently lacks a
named presence within therapy supports. Instead, nursing was
belatedly listed in the core supports category in late 2019, in a
capacity-building role where nurses are able to train others in health-
specific procedures such as gastrostomy feeding or catheter care. It
is desired that into the future, PWD will not be denied access to
nursing knowledge and skills through the NDIS.
15 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019b). Supporting People with
Disability. Australia’s Welfare 2019. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Nevertheless, the early years of NDIS have not been without
challenges. Problems reported are long waiting times for plan
approval, inadequate funding, inconsistency between participants
with similar needs, lack of background knowledge of planners and
insufficient funding for disability service providers (Committee for
Economic Development of Australia ). Although the NDIS offers an
opportunity to elevate the position of PWD in society so that they no
longer feel ‘shut in’, further work is required to overcome feelings of
being ‘shut out’.
16 Committee for Economic Development of Australia (2019). The Challenges and
Opportunities of the NDIS. Retrieved from <www.ceda.com.au>.
15
16


Inclusion in the community
According to the ABS , most PWD now live in the community;
however, barriers to participating in meaningful activities endure.
Business and organisations often overlook the needs of PWD, and
although this may be unintentional, it is discriminatory and against
the law.
17 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2016a). Community Profiles. Retrieved from
<www.abs.gov.au>.
What are the challenges and
barriers?
Optimising inclusion to enhance quality of life (QoL) remains the
ultimate goal of any health promotion, illness prevention and other
supportive interventions. Enhancing health and wellbeing for any
sector of the community will increase the overall health status of the
community (Hinton et al.
). It is only through consideration of the
barriers faced by PWD that inequities can be addressed. Facilitating
inclusion requires consideration of physical, social and behavioural
characteristics of the individual and their connection with the
environment. In planning access, it is important to consider how
17
18


PWD might access environments, goods and services and lifestyle
events. Table 46.1
 offers four different ways of access.
18 Hinton, C., Kraus, L., Richards, A., Fox, M. & Campbell, V. (2017). The guide to preventive
services and disability inclusion. American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 53(6), 898–903.
Doi: 10.1016/j.amepre.2017.06.025.
Table 46.1 Categories of access and inclusion
PWD may experience barriers in navigating the built environment
and participating in lifestyle activities. These are examined in the
context of physical, cognitive, emotional and behavioural, or social
and cultural domains as follows:
The physical domain is a general classification linked to
ergonomic or physiological function. It relates to impairment in
mobility, balance, agility or dexterity (Australian Network on
Disability ).
19 Australian Network on Disability (2019a). What Is Disability? Retrieved from
<www.and.org.au>.
The cognitive domain relates to understanding concepts. While
there may be some crossover into the concept of emotional
disability, not all people with cognitive or intellectual disability (ID)
will necessarily demonstrate emotional limitations. Cognitive
disability or ID is more connected to learning challenges where
the primary cause relates to cognition.
The emotional and behavioural domain relates to several mental
health conditions which may include elements of disruptive,
19


developmental or anxiety-related behaviours; for example, social
anxiety or autism (Ogundele ).
20 Ogundele, M. (2018). Behavioural and emotional disorders in childhood: A brief
overview for paediatricians. World Journal of Clinical Pediatrics, 7(1), 9–26. Doi:
10.5409/wjcp.v7.i1.9.
The social and cultural domains are interrelated. The concept of
culture is commonly associated with race, ethnicity and
geographical location. However, in the definitive sense, the term
culture also refers to a group of individuals who share common
behaviours and characteristics (Dorrian et. al.
), such as PWD.
Social barriers are based on a social construction of ‘difference
and otherness’, usually stemming from a perspective of fear
associated with lack of knowledge and understanding of disability.
This results in projecting characteristics onto PWD. Such fears
and knowledge deficits of society at large create stereotyping,
labelling and stigmatisation of PWD.
21 Dorrian, J., Thorsteinsson, E., Di Benedetto, M., Lane-Krebs, K., Hutchinson, A. &
Sherman, K. (2017). Health Psychology in Australia. Cambridge: Cambridge University
Press.
Key areas that support inclusion in the community in line with the
DDA involve access to the built environment, transport, sports and
goods and services. Following on, access to the health care
environment is also worthy of our attention.
Access to the built environment
20
21


The built environment is a term that relates to human constructions,
ranging from public buildings, housing, educational and recreational
facilities (e.g. aquatic and sporting complexes) to open spaces such
as parks. The built environment also includes supporting
infrastructures such as transport and utilities (State of the
Environment
).
22 State of the Environment (2011). 10 Built Environment: Australia State of the Environment
Report. Retrieved from <https://soe.environment.gov.au>.
The DDA makes it against the law for public places to be
inaccessible to PWD (31AHRC 2019b). Any place that is open to the
public should be accessible to all people, including those with
disability. The DDA offers a series of disability standards and
guidelines that incorporate technical codes to regulate building
design. As a result, individuals with mobility impairments have
experienced improvements in user-friendly infrastructure through
new building codes to include structures such as ramps, access to
lifts, doorway widths to accommodate wheelchairs, hoists and
sloping entries into public facilities such as swimming pools.
Examples of infrastructure considerations include undercover drop-
off and pick-up areas, parking bays to accommodate wheelchair
access, accessible toileting facilities and accessible public transport
options.
Sensory impairment
 such as vision or hearing loss creates
unique challenges to navigating built environments. Wayfinding
strategies play an important role for people with sensory impairment.
Wayfinding
 is defined as ‘The process or activity of ascertaining
22


one’s position and planning and following a route’ (Oxford
Dictionary ). Tactile ground surface indicators (TGSIs) assist in
orientating people with sensory impairment to the direction of travel
or as a warning, such as those placed at the top of stairs or
escalators (see Figure 46.2A
). Directories with strong colour
contrast and voice activated screens, as well as braille
 (patterns
of raised dots that are felt with the fingertips by people who are
vision impaired as an alternative to written text) and tactile access
signage for directions, promote independence for people with
sensory impairments when navigating public places (see Figure
46.2B
). Strong lighting and flooring that reduce glare is also a
useful strategy.
23 Oxford Dictionary (2019). Retrieved from <www.oxforddictionairies.com>.
Figure 46.2
23


A: Wayfinding: tactile ground surface indicators (TGSIs) with strong
colour contrast; B: wayfinding signage.
Sources: A: © 2checkingout/Shutterstock; B: © Bill45/Shutterstock.
Other features are hearing loops (induction loops), where wireless
signals can be received using ‘T’ (telecoil) settings on hearing
devices. These loops help those with hearing issues by reducing
background noise and acoustic distortions. Other examples include
GPS devices and wayfinding applications for smartphones (Ko &
Kim
).
24 Ko, E. & Kim, E. (2017). A vision-based wayfinding system for visually impaired people
using situational awareness and activity-based instructions. Sensors, 17(8), 1882. Doi:
10.3390/s17081882.
Facilitating access for emotional and behavioural impairment can be
assisted by reducing sensory overload. Providing low-stimulation
environments (e.g. removing fluorescent lighting, playing soothing
music, halting loudspeaker announcements and creating soundproof
zones) meets the needs of individuals with specific disabilities, such
as autism. Several larger shopping centres and supermarkets have
introduced the ‘quiet hour’ for PWD, whose behaviours are triggered
by fluorescent lighting and noise factors in shopping centres.
Providing rest areas, where behaviours such as self-soothing (e.g.
stimming
, a repetitive mannerism such as rocking, pacing,
making noises) can be practised during times of high arousal,
anxiety or frustration can help maintain the dignity of the individual.
24


Access to transport
Transport and mobility are identified in the CRPD (UN General
Assembly 2007) as fundamental human rights for full participation in
society. Accessing transport is an added challenge for PWD, as
many are unable to afford private vehicles or costly modifications to
vehicles (e.g. hand controls, wheelchair access or hoists).
Individuals with vision impairment or ID are usually unable to drive a
car or independently manage their own transport. Many PWD rely
on public transport to access health services, employment,
education, lifestyle and social activities. Travelling on public transport
during peak hours can be difficult, with limited access for
wheelchairs or mobility devices. The time allowances at regulated
stops for PWD to embark and exit public transport remain
challenging to manage, despite the provision of access ramps and
assisted-boarding staff. Added to these barriers can be social
attitudes to disability when service providers are not wanting to
accept customers who have a disability. Inclusive practices such as
voice prompting of approaching stations promotes confidence in the
use of public transport.
Access to sports
Participation in sporting activities that include social interaction is
essential for mental and physical wellbeing. Australia is renowned as
a sporting nation, and it is not surprising that developing sporting


activities that are inclusive of PWD is where Australia sets the
standard. Increased opportunities in sports are evolving to transition
more PWD from non-participation to various levels of inclusion and
engagement. Participation in sport has many illness prevention and
health promotion advantages, as optimising physical health will have
flow-on effects spanning all biopsychosocial domains.
Structured and competitive sports activities have been developed
that incorporate technical advances to accommodate people with
hearing, vision, cognitive and mobility impairments, thereby enabling
continued participation across multiple stages of the lifespan.
Programs directed at early childhood include Little Athletics and
AUSTSWIM. During the school-age years, education departments
have created alternative pathways for PWD by modifying the
curriculum in physical education, as set down in the Disability
Standards for Education 2005 (Department of Education, Skills and
Employment
).
25 Department of Education, Skills and Employment (2018). Disability Standards for
Education 2005. Retrieved from <www.education.gov.au>.
Following the introduction of the NDIS, many PWD include sporting
activities as part of their therapy packages. Indeed, this inclusion
makes maintaining and increasing functional ranges more enjoyable
and can also include social engagement, therefore blending the
physical (biological/medical) and social domains. Examples of
nationwide sporting organisations that specifically target PWD
include, but are not limited to, Sailability, Disability Surfers’
Association, Sporting Wheelies, Riding for the Disabled, Special
25


Olympics, Paralympics and AFL Kickability. Most of these non-
government organisations are manned by qualified coaches and
volunteers.
Performance and elite athletes who also live with disability are well
respected as national sporting heroes alongside their able-bodied
peers. Elite athletes with disability are highly skilled performance
competitors who represent Australia at Commonwealth- and
Olympic-standard events (see Figure 46.3
). Para-athletics first
commenced in 1960 (Paralympics Australia ); therefore, the
concept is not new. However, increased government support and
funding over recent years has enhanced development, training and
competition. Often, para-athletics is mistakenly thought to relate to
paraplegic competitors. Paralympics
 means ‘parallel with the
Olympics’ (being held at the same time and same venues as the
Olympic Games). The Australian Institute of Sport supports and
develops para-athletes to achieve ‘podium success’ in a parallel
fashion to able-bodied athletes (Paralympics Australia 2019).
26 Paralympics Australia (2019). About Us. Retrieved from <www.paralympic.org.au>.
Figure 46.3
26


Paralympian Dylan Alcott.
Source: © Mark Davidson/Alamy Stock Photo.


Access to health care services
The AIHW
 reports that unmet needs by PWD concerning health
services relate to no services available in regional and remote areas,
the service being unaffordable or lack of awareness of the existence
or the process to access the service. These concerns mainly relate
to medical expenses, geographical location and health care
professionals’ attitudes.
27 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2017a). Access to Health Services by
Australians with Disability. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
Medical expenses. PWD encounter financial barriers to
maintaining an optimised QoL, including costs associated with
health care such as medications, physiotherapy, occupational
therapy and psychology interventions, as well as travel to access
services. Statistics indicate that 1 in 4 PWD were not able to
access a required health service due to cost factors (AIHW
2017a).
Problems also arise related to the general shortage of health
professionals in Australia, with this shortage being more
pronounced in regional and remote areas, leaving these areas in
crisis (Dew et al. 2013). A lack of health services places
significant pressure on existing services, impacting on waiting
times and sometimes causing the need to travel further
distances to access services. Travel costs place further pressure
on the financial situation of PWD and their families, as NDIS
funding for travel is limited. For people without NDIS packages,
27


funding is available through subsidised patient travel and
accommodation support schemes, relevant to the different states
and territories (Queensland Government
).
28 Queensland Government (2019a). The Patient Travel Subsidy Scheme. Retrieved
from <www.qld.gov.au>.
Geographical location. Some PWD may relocate to regional and
remote areas for financial reasons; for example, to seek more
affordable living, which may then be at the cost of access to
specialist health services (Dorrian et al. 2017, p. 289). Travel to
services can be exhausting and adds financial, physical,
psychological and social burden to PWD and their families. For
example, if the PWD is a parent, leaving other family members
(e.g. children and partner, who may also be the carer for PWD,
have work and other family obligations) adds to disruption,
complexity and cost. Sometimes, an entire family may need to
travel so one member can attend services; therefore, the cost of
accommodating and transporting other family members is an
‘out-of-pocket’ expense. The need to access specialist services is
an ongoing process for the PWD, not a ‘one-off’ event, and may
well continue across many stages of the lifespan.
Lengthy delays in accessing services, particularly for children,
with reports of an average of 127 days waiting time for initial
service, makes this a priority for improvement for the NDIS (SBS
News Australia ). While on a waiting list, ‘ageing out of service’
may occur. By the time a physical appointment with a therapist
occurs, the PWD may have ‘aged out’ of the eligibility guidelines
(e.g. early intervention programs are only available until the child
28
29


reaches school age) (Dew et al.
). Subsequently, the PWD on a
waiting list has an extended period without receiving any
intervention, thereby worsening their situation.
29 SBS News Australia (2019). Disability Steward Wants Waiting Times Halved.
Retrieved from <www.sbs.com.au>.
30 Dew, A., Bulkeley, K., Veitch, C., .?.?. Griffiths, S. (2013). Addressing the barriers to
accessing therapy services in rural and remote areas. Disability and Rehabilitation,
35(18), 1564–1570. Doi: 10.3109/09638288.2012.720346.
Health care professionals’ attitudes. Health care professionals
across all disciplines are known for disability discrimination,
through conscious or unconscious bias, that can lead to negative
health outcomes. Unconscious bias
 is when we are biased
towards the world around us based on our upbringing and
experiences, where it is easier to accept what we know, while
difference is harder to accommodate (Queensland
Government
). In addition, institutional disability discrimination
occurs within organisations through processes and service
provision that are not inclusive of PWD, as a result of lack of
understanding of the needs of PWD at leadership level.
31 Queensland Government (2019b). Unconscious Bias. Retrieved from
<www.forgov.qld.gov.au>.
According to the ACT Council of Social Service , 1 in 6
Australians with disability aged between 15 and 64 years had
experienced discrimination by a health professional in the past 12
months. Poor attitudes of health care workers are often a result
of inadequate education and training in disability care, leading to
30
31
32


fear and lack of confidence and understanding of disability needs
(Pelleboer-Gunnink et al.
).
32 ACT Council of Social Service (2017). Factsheet: Disability and Access to Health
Services. Retrieved from <www.actcoss.org.au>.
33 Pelleboer-Gunnink, H., Van Oorsouw, W., Van Weeghel, J. & Embregts, P. (2017).
Mainstream health professionals’ stigmatising attitudes towards people with intellectual
disabilities: A systematic review. Journal of Intellectual Disability Research, 61(5), 411–
434. Doi: 10.1111/jir.12353.
Real-world practice
The story
John, a male with Down syndrome, was admitted to
the Intensive Care Unit for regular neurological
observations for a suspected stroke. At afternoon
clinical handover, the morning nurse reported that John
was non-compliant because he refused to eat lunch.
The afternoon nurse began her shift by introducing
herself and asking John some questions about his
home situation in order to build a rapport. This
approach gained the trust of John, who then explained
that he did not want to eat because he felt sick and
was worried that he would vomit everywhere and make
the morning nurse cross with him.
Clinical reflection
33


The morning nurse failed to gain an adequate
assessment of the situation because of a poor attitude
towards the person with intellectual disability. By taking
a little more time to develop a therapeutic relationship
with John, the afternoon nurse was able to correctly
ascertain the reason for refusing to eat, and
subsequently was able to advocate for John by liaising
with the medical officer for some anti-emetic
medication to relieve the nausea.
—Virginia Howie RN, MCN (Cardiac), PGCTE, PhD (Candidate)
Clinical consideration
Poor attitudes by nurses and health care staff
can lead to reduced communication interactions,
negative hospital experiences and neglect (at
worst), with associated poorer health outcomes.
Such experiences lead to feelings of frustration
and helplessness, for both the individual and
their support network, which lead to reluctance
to engage in services at a later time. This
experience can therefore perpetuate a cycle of
missed opportunities for information sharing,


impacting on health literacy and widening health
disparities.


Disability and Australia’s first
nations peoples
Almost a quarter of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people live
with a disability—almost twice the rate of the non-Indigenous
disability population (ABS ). Physical disability is the most common
type of disability (14.8%), with ID being more common (7%) in
children aged 0–14 years (ABS 2017a). Sensory and speech
disability are similar to reported non-Indigenous rates (ABS 2017a).
Indigenous people with disability experience multiple barriers to
accessing appropriate services through a range of contexts. Not
only are Indigenous Australians subject to disability bias and
prejudice, they are also disadvantaged by systemic, community and
individual racial discrimination associated with their heritage
(Department of Social Services 2009). In addition, cultural
understanding is lacking in disability services and, similarly, deficits in
knowledge and understanding of disability needs are apparent in
mainstream services.
34 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2017a). Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People
with Disability. Cat. no. 4430.0.55.005. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Geographical location may also affect access to services, with
associated costs for Indigenous Australians living with disability.
While 43% of Indigenous Australians living with disability live in
34


metropolitan areas (compared to 30% living in regional and remote
areas), the statistics may reflect that some people relocate to cities
to be closer to services related to their disability (ABS 2017a).
Research note
Do Australian aboriginal and torres strait islander people
with neurocognitive disability (NCD) have equitable
access to the NDIS scheme?
C. Townsend, M. McIntyre, A. Lakhani, C. Wright, P. White, J. Bishara & J. Cullen
. Inclusion of
marginalised Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples with neurocognitive disability in the
National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS). Disability and the Global South, 5(2), 1531–1552.
35 Townsend, C., McIntyre, M., Lakhani, A., Wright, C., White, P., Bishara, J. & Cullen, J. (2018).
Inclusion of marginalised Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples with neurocognitive disability
in the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS). Disability and the Global South, 5(2), 1531–
1552. Retrieved from <www.dgsjournal.org>.
The purpose of this study was to report on the
implementation of the Guddi Protocol, a culturally informed
screening protocol that identifies neurocognitive disability
(NCD) in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. The
study was conducted over two locations in far north
Queensland and north Queensland and involved 76
Indigenous adult participants. Culturally respectful interviews
were conducted and quantitative and qualitative data
collected to determine the level of NCD. Quantitative data
was analysed using IBM SPSS software. Qualitative data was
thematically analysed. Results indicated high levels of NCD
35


and a number of factors associated with disability: 1)
intergenerational trauma; 2) disadvantage, marginalisation
and exclusion in the social context; and 3) failure to identify
disability.
Implications Unless brain injury, acquired by either traumatic
or non-traumatic injury, in Australian Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander people is correctly identified, this marginalised
group will continue to be effectively excluded from the NDIS.
Having considered the background of disability in Australia, we will
now examine more specific areas within the disability experience in
more detail in order to get a sense of the types of disparities
encountered in the community, as well as in the health care setting.
Strategies for overcoming barriers are offered. First, we must
consider the role of the carer, as caregivers are integral to the
person’s interaction with the world around them. In the health care
environment, carers are essential to maximising nurse–patient
interactions and the health care experience for PWD.


Role of carers
Generally speaking, carers can be unpaid or paid workers.
According to the ABS  unpaid carers are individuals who provide
informal care and who are primarily family and friends. Paid carers
are those who work in disability services. Over-reliance on family
carers and paid carers for care in hospital and the provision of
information and communication has been reported in the literature.
However, caregivers are integral to the wellbeing of PWD as carers
have insider knowledge of the individual’s personal history, needs,
wants and behaviours. Nurses need to find a balance in carer
involvement so that carers are rested during intense care needs.
Finding this balance is reliant on the nurse gaining an appreciation of
the complex role of a carer. Family members tend to stay longer,
often over the 24-hour period, to minimise fear and anxiety and
ensure adequate care and safety, whereas visits by paid carers are
dependent on the service provider and working hours (Webber,
Bowers & Bigby ).
36 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2016b). A Profile of Carers in Australia, 2015. Cat.
no. 4430.0. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
37 Webber, R., Bowers, B. & Bigby, C. (2010). Hospital experiences of older people with
intellectual disability: Response of group home staff and family members. Journal of
Intellectual & Developmental Disability, 35(3), 155–164. Doi: 10.3109/13668250.2010.491071.
36
37


The burden of the caregiver role may also impact on the physical
health and emotional wellbeing of the carer. Given that the average
age of carers is 55 years (ABS 2016b), the nurse needs to be
mindful that the carer’s physical capacity to provide the same level
of care may be progressively reduced with advancing age. This
capacity may be further impacted by the increasingly complex care
needs of the PWD due to the coexistence of associated chronic
conditions (Walker & Hutchinson ). Additionally, succession
planning for infirmity and death is a major concern for ageing
parents. These areas require consideration during the discharge
planning period.
38 Walker, R. & Hutchinson, C. (2018). Planning for the future among older parents of adult
offspring with intellectual disability living at home and in the community: A systematic review
of qualitative studies. Journal of Intellectual & Developmental Disability, 43(4), 453–462.
https://doi.org/10.3109/13668250.2017.1310823.
38


Role of the nurse in caring for a
person with disability
While nurses frequently meet and care for PWD in their everyday
roles, a very small minority of the Australian nursing workforce have
a primary role where they work with people with ID. Historically,
these nurses have worked within a range of residential and other
segregated services, such as day programs. Their need in the lives
