of people with ID started to be questioned in the 1980s, alongside
the move towards closing all large residential services for people
with ID (Wilson, Wiese et al.
). Despite the likelihood that the
closure of many large residential settings would lead to the end of
nurses who specialise in the care of people with ID, the health
issues facing people with ID have meant that many nurses still
specialise in these roles (Wilson, Wiese et al. 2019). With the advent
of the NDIS, the state-based health systems around Australia
appear to be acknowledging the need for better insight into and
specific roles for health professionals to cater to the needs of people
with ID. These include, for example, nurses working as part of
assessment teams in paediatric hospitals and nurses with specific
dual diagnosis expertise working within mental health teams. As
nurses, wherever they work, will encounter high numbers of PWD
and their carers, it is important that they gain a solid understanding
of the difficulties faced by PWD so that they can advocate for them,
particularly when communication is a challenge.
39


39 Wilson, N. J., Wiese, M., Lewis, P., Jaques, H. & O’Reilly, K. (2019). Nurses working in
intellectual disability-specific settings talk about the uniqueness of their role: A qualitative
study. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 75(4), 812–822. https://doi.org.10.1111/jan.13898.


Communication disability
Communication disability
 is defined as having limitations in
expressing thoughts, needs or emotions due to impaired physical,
psychological, developmental or sensory functions (ABS ). The
2016 Census revealed that 1.2 million Australians identified as living
with communication disability (ABS 2016a). A person living with a
communication limitation may be non-verbal (e.g. autism), have
difficulty speaking (e.g. cerebral palsy), have complications
formulating thoughts (developmental language disorder, some
mental health conditions), have difficulty finding or selecting the
correct words (dysphasia
), have difficulties with reading and
writing (dyslexia
) or experience sensory impairment (hearing or
vision). Common challenges in communication are concerned with
pain, toileting, positioning, breathing, suctioning and feelings.
Difficulties in communication may be exacerbated if English is a
second language or the PWD’s carer is absent. In order to
overcome the challenges of communication, a number of assistive
devices and communication strategies have been developed.
40 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2017b). Australians Living with Communication
Disability. Disability, Ageing and Carers, Australia: Summary of Findings, 2015. Cat. no.
4430.0. Retrieved from <www.abs.gov.au>.
Communication tools
40


Education by improving the health literacy of general public remains
an easily implemented intervention to reduce the fear factor of
society and increase the potential for inclusion in the community for
PWD. A main component of raising health literacy is to promote the
tools utilised by those with communication disability. Such
approaches are required to quell misconceptions that those with
communication disabilities must also lack intelligence. The public
gaze on and legacy of academic super-normatives, such as the late
Professor Stephen Hawking (1942–2018), have certainly raised
awareness of these misconceptions. Professor Hawking (see Figure
46.4
) was a theoretical physicist and cosmologist whose work was
regarded as being on a par with Einstein. He was diagnosed with
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or motor neurone disease, at age 21
and was given 2 years to live. However, defying medical prognosis,
he went on to make significant contributions to the world of science.
As his disease progressed and muscular dexterity deteriorated,
communication became a challenge. By the time of his death, he
was utilising a speech-generating device (SGD) or speech output
communication tool generated through a computer. Initially, he used
a clicker with thumb control, but as his condition deteriorated, an
infrared switch mounted on his glasses traced movements in his
cheek muscles that generated speech. Predictive text similar to that
used in smartphones improved the speed of communication. A
speech synthesiser that spoke in complete sentences out loud
completed the process.
Figure 46.4


The late Stephen Hawking using a speech-generating device (SGD).
Source: © The World in HDR/Shutterstock.


Physical disability
Physical disability
 relates to conditions that reduce an
individual’s mobility, endurance, stamina, agility or dexterity. There is
a wide range of factors associated with physical disabilities, including
missing or deformed body structures due to congenital abnormality,
trauma or surgical amputation. Examples of congenital abnormalities
include hand and foot abnormalities (symbrachydactyly
, club
foot/talipes equinovarus
) and neuromuscular conditions such as
muscular dystrophy
, which causes a progressive weakening of
muscles (Muscular Dystrophy Foundation ). Neurological conditions
such as cerebral palsy and traumatic brain injury may affect the
person’s coordination of movement and posture (Cerebral Palsy
Alliance ).
41 Muscular Dystrophy Foundation (2016). About Muscular Dystrophy. Retrieved from
<https://mdaustralia.org.au>.
42 Cerebral Palsy Alliance (2018). What Is Cerebral Palsy. Retrieved from <https://
cerebralpalsy.org.au>.
Practice guidelines
Communication tools
Nurses must be aware of the variety of more common and
affordable communication tools that they are likely to
41
42


encounter when caring for someone with a communication
disability. Some examples are communication boards, spelling
cards and simple electronic assistive devices. Eye
pointing
 is the controlled and intentional use of eye gaze
to direct another person’s visual attention to an object for
communication purposes, sometimes using an eye gaze
board (see Figure 46.5
). For example, the person may
point their eyes to the left for ‘Yes’ and to the right for ‘No’.
Nurses must also be aware of the use of signing and
behaviour changes (discussed later in this chapter) as a way
of communication for a person with communication disability.
The individual’s communication preference must be
established and documented during the initial nursing
assessment. This may include liaising with the person’s family
or carer.
Figure 46.5


Hand-held writing tablet—letter selection is achieved by
looking at the letter and blinking, then looking at the block,
which is the same colour as the selected letter.
Source: © <www.makersmakingchange.com/project/laser-cut-eye-gaze-board/>.
The impact of physical conditions can range from mild to severe.
The severity of a condition relates to the impacts it has on the
individual’s capacity to self-care and participate in meaningful
activities and is reflective of their QoL.


Assistive devices/robotic
technologies/technological
advances
The goal of assistive devices is to promote independence and
functioning, thereby increasing dignity and QoL for PWD. Assistive
devices can range from wheelchairs and prosthetics to pill
organisers and memory aids. Scientific and biomedical advances
also serve to promote independence and inclusion (e.g. surgically
inserted drivers to deliver medications for muscle spasticity).
Areas gaining increased attention include the role of artificial
intelligence (AI), human–machine learning and virtual reality (VR).
Systems using algorithms to enable computer software to identify
objects and sounds are increasing. Coding algorithms can also be
used to identify environments and predict actions. Examples of
predictive software include personal diagnostic devices such as a
smartphone or a wearable device to indicate the likelihood of a
seizure episode based on real-time biodata from the PWD. The
software alerts first response warnings to the PWD, aiming to
prevent a medical emergency or, alternatively, it alerts medical
facilities and/or ambulance services. AI and chatbot technologies are
combining to create virtual assistants. For example, Google Home
is popular household technological device that offers a wide range of
inclusivity for PWD, particularly for those who are unable to use a
®


keyboard. Other AI systems include voice recognition software that
changes voice to text. This type of software is useful for people with
hand dexterity issues (e.g. stroke, cerebral palsy, amputation or
limb/digit malformations), processing disabilities such as dyslexia or
vision impairment and blindness.
VR options can extend to disability environments by providing
entertainment experiences to those who are physically challenged
(e.g. a roller coaster ride), increasing the potential for psychosocial
enhancement. VR delivery of physical therapy is also receiving more
interest, with the development of software packages that link VR
with therapeutic exercises.
Biomedicine continues to make significant breakthroughs such as
nerve grafts and transplants for cranial nerve palsies associated with
visual abnormalities. Exoskeleton applications for spinal cord injuries
and cerebral palsy, as well as soft robotic exo-sheaths for hand
rehabilitation, are more recent scientific contributions to improving
muscle control (see Figure 46.6
).
Figure 46.6


Example of a brain-controlled exoskeleton that allows a paralysed
woman to walk.
Source: © dpa picture alliance/Alamy Stock Photo.
Clinical consideration
Due to the wide variety and evolving
technologies in assistive devices, nurses are not
expected to have expert knowledge in this area.


However, when nurses encounter such
technologies when caring for a PWD, they must
endeavour to bridge their knowledge gap in
order to maximise the patient experience and
promote positive health outcomes.
It is evident that from small modification to major biomedical
breakthroughs, assistive devices contribute to biopsychosocial QoL
experiences for PWD, their families and significant others.


Sensory impairment
Sensory impairment is a disability of the senses, involving sight,
hearing, smell, touch and/or taste. Our focus here is on the two
more common sensory disabilities: vision and hearing. Vision and
hearing disabilities can vary in degree and extent, so it is not
possible to generalise about interacting with people experiencing
vision- and hearing-related impairments. Once again, care must be
tailored to the individual. This section discusses access and inclusion
in the community for the person with a sensory impairment. See
Chapter 39
 for more details on how to communicate with people
with sensory impairment in health care settings.
Vision impairment
There are approximately 20 000 Australians who are totally blind and
over 1 million Australians living with vision impairment (AHRC
2019b). Over 28% of people living with moderate to severe vision
impairment are in their working years, which impacts on their ability
to gain employment and support themselves and their families
(WHO
). In order to address low rates of employment, employers
and organisations must find ways to remove barriers affecting
workplace access for motivated and qualified people who are vision
impaired. Employers have a responsibility to address reasonable
43


adjustments in the workplace so that the person with vision
impairment can do their job effectively (AHRC 2019b); for example,
improving lighting, removing clutter, providing screen-reading
software, providing written information in accessible formats
(Microsoft Word format, audio) or allowing assistance animals in the
work environment.
43 World Health Organization (2019b). Ten Facts About Blindness and Visual Impairment.
Retrieved from <www.who.int>.
Assistance animals
Specially trained guide dogs allow independence in the community
and home life, improving QoL for people with low vision or who are
blind. The first Seeing Eye Dogs training school was established in
Victoria in 1960, merging with Vision Australia in 2008 (Seeing Eye
Dogs Vision Australia ). Vision Australia Seeing Eye Dogs is a
national provider of world-class bred and trained dogs that meets
the accreditation standards of the International Guide Dog
Federation. The traditional ‘guide dog’ has since evolved to a
broader concept, that of an assistance animal (not only dogs), that
provides support to people with a range of disabilities, including
‘invisible’ disabilities, as described in the introduction; for example,
people who experience episodic crises such as seizures, elevated
blood pressure or blood sugars; people who experience mental
health conditions such as anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder or
suicidal ideation; as well as people who have a hearing impairment
(see Figure 46.7
).
44


44 Seeing Eye Dogs Vision Australia (2019). Who We Are. Vision Australia. Retrieved from
<https://sed.visionaustralia.org>.
Figure 46.7
Assistance animals.
Source: Boris Djuranovic. Shutterstock.
Assistance animals are working animals, not pets. Patting or talking
to a working animal is distracting and can place the handler at risk of
harm. Legislation ensures that assistance animals meet
accreditation standards such as hygiene and behaviour that are
appropriate for an animal in a public place According to the AHRC


(2019a), common areas where discrimination involving assistance
animals occurs include cafes, restaurants, shopping centres and
other recreational areas; health and medical services; travel; and
accommodation. The main issues of concern are refusal of entry or
manner of treatment; refusal of travel or manner of travel on
airlines/in airports; and refusal of service or manner of service in
residential accommodation or the provision of medical/health
services.
Clinical consideration
Section 8 of the DDA states that discrimination
is unlawful when it occurs because a person
with a disability is accompanied by a guide or
hearing dog or other trained assistant animal.
This includes guide dogs in the clinical
environment.
Accessible information and
communications technology (ICT)
Written information needs to be presented in an accessible format
with clear concise language, strong colour contrast (black on white,
yellow on blue), a sans serif font (Arial, Calibri), left aligned (for


consistent spacing), with no whole words in upper case (can look like
a rectangle) and have a large font size (minimum 12 to 14 point
font) (Vision Australia ). It is also a requirement that information in
alternative formats be available on request and according to the
individual’s preferred communication needs, such as via the internet,
by email, SMS, audio recording, large print text, captioning of any
visual information (YouTube or films) or braille.
45 Vision Australia (2019). Print Accessibility. Retrieved from <www.visionaustralia.org>.
Clinical consideration
When developing patient education materials,
nurses must take into account the formatting
considerations above so that people with vision
impairment have equitable access to relevant
health information that supports their health
literacy.
Documents on the internet must also be available in Microsoft Word
format so that screen-reading technologies can increase the size of
the text. PDF format is not considered accessible as text becomes
blurred and distorted when the text size is enlarged. Additionally,
there is a lack of support for PDF in mobile environments.
45


Accessing online information can be challenging for individuals with
sight impairment. In the first instance, disability law requires that
websites must be accessible and designed in accordance with set
standards. Detailed guidance on how to design accessible websites
and mobile devices is available in the Web Content Accessibility
Guidelines (WCAG), technical standards developed by the World
Wide Web Consortium (W3C) in 2008 (W3C ). The WCAG
guidelines were developed to make Web content more accessible to
people with disabilities, including visual, auditory, physical, speech,
cognitive, language, learning, intellectual and neurological disabilities
(W3C 2018).
46 World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) (2018). Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
(WCAG) 2.1. Retrieved from <www.w3.org>.
There is a range of accessibility tools and devices that are designed
to meet the needs of vision impaired individuals when they are
accessing information. These tools can be accessed on the Vision
Australia website (<www.visionaustralia.org>) and are free for
governments, commercial organisations, educational institutions and
digital agencies.
Screen-reader software offers alternatives to text through non-visual
platforms using text to speech, braille and magnifier options (see
Figure 46.8
). Operating the software usually requires the use of
only four to six keys on the keyboard. Most available screen-reader
software allows choice in the tone of voice, speed of the voice
narration, accent and language. Magnifiers increase the size of the
46


text and the size of the pointer on the screen, allowing more choice
for those with low vision.
Figure 46.8
Screen-reader software for people with low vision.
Source: © dpa picture alliance/Alamy Stock Photo.
Although barriers to accessing information are still apparent for
people with vision impairment, advances in technology serve to
promote independence, self-esteem and being valued in society.


Similarly, improving the experience of people with hearing
impairment is the focus of further technological research.
Auditory impairment
There are over 1 million Australians who have a hearing impairment,
with approximately 30 000 residents being totally deaf (AHRC
2019b). A variety of communication techniques are available to
people who have a hearing impairment or who are deaf, such as
audio loops at public meetings, skilled sign language interpreters
(AUSLAN) and adapted telephones called a telephone typewriter
(TTY) that can be offered through a national relay service or can be
purchased individually. Captioning also serves to connect people with
hearing impairment with the community. Closed captioning
 is a
text version of a spoken part in a movie or television and requires
teletext equipment to see the text, whereas open captioning
appears on screen without the need for special equipment to see the
text. Subtitles or written transcripts of video and audio content also
service to improve access to communication for people who are
hearing impaired.


Intellectual disability
Approximately 3% of the Australian population have intellectual
disability (ID). Individuals with ID have endured the effects of social
stigma in the past, although societal attitudes are gradually
changing. Social stigma
 is societal disapproval of a person that
sets them apart from another group and results in stereotyping,
prejudice and discrimination. People with ID have poorer health
status than the general population and face considerable barriers to
accessing the community and health care. Intellectual disability
is ‘characterised by significant limitations both in intellectual
functioning (reasoning, learning, problem solving) and in adaptive
behaviour, which covers a range of everyday social and practical
skills. This disability originates before the age of 18’ (American
Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities ).
Intellectual functioning can also be measured using IQ, where a
score of 70 or below indicates a limitation in intellectual functioning.
Assessment of adaptive behaviour, such as understanding
concepts, social skills and activities of daily living, serves to assist
with a diagnosis of ID.
47 American Association on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (2019). Intellectual
Disability. Retrieved from <https://aaidd.org>.
The causes of ID occur during the developmental period—before
(e.g. genetic conditions), during (e.g. hypoxia) or after birth (e.g.
47


measles)—although sometimes the cause is unknown (Centers for
Disease Control and Prevention ). Genetic conditions are the most
common and can affect other organs in the body. Therefore, it is
important to be aware of coexisting conditions associated with each
syndrome so that appropriate diagnosis is not missed. Down
syndrome is the most common genetic cause (approximately 1:700).
People with Down syndrome are more likely to have congenital heart
defects, vision impairment, hearing impairment, anxiety and
depression, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, epilepsy and
hypothyroidism, and have an increased risk of infections due to a
compromised immune system (Queensland Centre for Intellectual
and Developmental Disability ).
48 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2019). Disability and Health. Retrieved from
<www.cdc.gov>.
49 Queensland Centre for Intellectual and Developmental Disability (2012). Comprehensive
Health Assessment Program (CHAP), Version 11-Syndrome-specific List for General
Practitioners. Retrieved from <https://qcidd.centre.uq.edu.au>.
Autism spectrum disorder
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
 is defined as ‘a range of
conditions that affect communication, social interaction and
behaviour’ (Ministry of Health , p. 1). According to the AIHW
,
there are an estimated 1 in 150 Australians living with autism. Of
those diagnosed with autism, 83% were aged under 25 and were
48
49
50
51


four times more likely to be male. Increasing awareness and higher
levels of diagnosis have contributed to the increased prevalence of
autism (AIHW 2017b). Diagnosis is based on symptoms evident
from childhood that can range from mild to severe. People with
autism face barriers to education and employment because of their
condition. These barriers are thought to increase if the person with
autism also has an ID. About 27% of people with autism also have
ID (AIHW 2017b). No two people with ASD are alike and all have
characteristics that are unique to the individual.
50 Ministry of Health (2017). Engaging with People with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
Wellington: New Zealand Government. Retrieved from <www.health.govt.nz>.
51 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2017b). Autism in Australia. Cat. no.:
WEB 187. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
People with ASD may require assistance or supervision with self-
care (73%), interpersonal interactions (91%), education (90%),
domestic life (80%) and employment (91%) (AIHW 2017b). A person
with ASD may have difficulty with the following:
understanding verbal or non-verbal communication
understanding social behaviour, which affects their ability to
interact with others and maintain relationships
adapting to change of routine or the environment, which may
result in unusual behaviour such as flapping, spinning or
repetitive behaviour
hypersensitivity to sound, flashing lights or varying textures that
result in the unusual behaviour (Ministry of Health 2017).


How do i communicate with a person with
ASD?
Across the autism spectrum there will be variations according to the
individual’s personality and accompanying support systems. The tips
in the following ‘Practice guidelines’ are a guide only and may not
apply to all people with ASD.
Practice guidelines
How do I communicate with a person with ASD?
The following tips are a guide only and may not apply to all
people with ASD. Across the autism spectrum there will be
variations according to the individual’s personality and
accompanying support systems.
Presume intelligence in the first instance.
Inform the person well in advance of any likely treatments
or procedures. Offer written information and include
support people (family, carers) if present.
Try to keep to routine.
Avoid triggers such as alarms on machines, flashing
lights, extra noise, different textures.
Consider offering a single room to avoid triggers.
Keep distractions to a minimum.
Do not insist on making eye contact. People with ASD can
find this uncomfortable.


Keep communication short and avoid conversations with
more than one person talking.
Use clear and concise language as some people with ASD
may have literal comprehension.
Consider using communication boards with images,
objects and symbols.
Recognise an individual’s strengths and interests and offer
support in these areas.
Source: Ministry of Health (2017). Engaging with People with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Wellington:
New Zealand Government. Retrieved from <www.health.govt.nz/our-work/making-services-better-
users/community-engagement-people-disabilities/engaging-people-particular-impairments/
engaging-people-autism-spectrum-disorder>.
It is important to remember that people with ASD will have patterns
of behaviour that are normal for them. Anxiety and compulsions are
common. Talking to the person’s carers will identify usual behaviours
when they are calm and what to expect when they are
uncomfortable or fearful (Centre for Developmental Disability Health
(CDDH)
).
52 Centre for Developmental Disability Health (CDDH) (2016a). Information for Health
Professionals: Understanding Behaviour Change for People with Intellectual Disability or
Autism Spectrum Disorders. Retrieved from <www.cddh.monashhealth.org>.
Inequitable access to health care
52


People with ID face a range of health inequalities that stand in stark
contrast to the general population. One of the key issues
underpinning these inequalities is nurses’ general lack of knowledge
about ID, as most undergraduate nursing programs in Australia have
little content about ID and health (Trollor et al.
). When compared
to the population without ID, people with ID have greater rates of
both physical and mental health problems, are disengaged from
preventive health care initiatives, present at hospitals and are
admitted at twice the rate and face a greater risk of a potentially
avoidable death (Troller et al.
). Although some of the reasons for
this health inequity are related to modifiable factors, such as
sedentary behaviour and obesity, many are associated with greater
rates of non-modifiable factors.
53 Trollor, J., Eagleson, C., Turner, B., Salomon, C., Cashin, A., Iacono, T., Goddard, L. &
Lennox, N. (2016). Intellectual disability health content within nursing curriculum: An audit of
what our future nurses are taught. Nurse Education Today, 45, 72–79. http://dx.doi.org/
10.1016/j.nedt.2016.06.011.
54 Trollor, J., Srasuebkul, P., Xu, H. & Howlett, S. (2017). Cause of death and potentially
avoidable deaths in Australian adults with intellectual disability using retrospective linked data.
British Medical Journal Open, 7(2), 1–9. http://dx.doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2016-013489.
Co-existing, non-modifiable,
chronic health conditions
53
54


People with ID have high rates of chronic health conditions such as
epilepsy, dysphagia, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD),
poorer oral health (Wilson, Lin et al.
) and higher rates of both
obesity and being underweight (Wilson & Charnock ). It is vital that
nurses have some insight into these health disparities. For example,
people with ID who have severe dysphagia and GORD are at major
risk of silent aspiration. Contemporary treatment is often
gastrostomy insertion, resulting in the person becoming nil by mouth
as all nutrition is provided by a gastrostomy tube. While the provision
of nutrition via a gastrostomy instead of the mouth avoids many of
the risks of developing aspiration complications, it does not entirely
eliminate the risk of aspiration as the people will still produce saliva,
which can silently leak into the trachea. Aspiration pneumonia is one
of the leading causes of hospitalisation and mortality of people with
ID (O’Leary, Cooper & Hughes-McCormack ).
55 Wilson, N. J., Lin, Z., Villarosa, A. & George, A. (2019). Oral health status and reported oral
health problems in people with intellectual disability: A literature review. Journal of Intellectual
and Developmental Disability, 44(3), 292–304. Doi: 10.3109/13668250.2017.1409596.
56 Wilson, N. J. & Charnock, D. (2017). Developmental and intellectual disability. In E. Chang
& A. Johnson (Eds), Living with Chronic Illness and Disability: Principles for Nursing Practice
(3rd ed., pp. 129–145). Sydney: Elsevier.
57 O’Leary, L., Cooper, S.A. & Hughes-McCormack, L. (2018). Early death and causes of
death of people with intellectual disabilities: A systematic review. Journal of Applied Research
in Intellectual Disabilities, 31(3), 325–342. Doi: 10.1111/jar.12417.
55
56
57


Morbidity and mortality
In addition to having greater health problems compared to the
general population, people with ID also experience earlier mortality
(Trollor et al. 2017). A literature review about mortality and ID found
that, on average, people with ID die 20 years earlier than the
general population, representing a major inequality gap (O’Leary et
al. 2018). The leading causes of death in people with ID are
respiratory and congenital circulatory disease. In addition, the more
profound the ID, in the presence of any comorbidity, the earlier the
mortality. Perhaps the most alarming statistic is from a recent
Australian data linkage study reporting that people with ID were also
more likely to die from a potentially preventable death, mainly
caused by infection and diseases of the circulatory system (Trollor et
al. 2017).
Health workers’ negative attitudes towards people with a disability
have been noted as a significant part of the problem associated with
potentially preventable deaths. For instance, negative attitudes have
been reported to influence access to diagnostic procedures or
treatments (Iacono et al.
). Other underlying issues are a lack of
knowledge about ID and autism, limited insight into how to interact
or modify one’s communication style and overlooking the possibility
that an individual’s behaviour might have a physical, as opposed to
behavioural, origin.
58


58 Iacono, T., Bigby, C., Unsworth, C., Douglas, J. & Fitzpatrick, P. (2014). A systematic
review of hospital experiences of people with intellectual disability. BMC Health Services
Research, 14(1), 327–342. Doi: 10.1186/s12913-014-0505-5.
Diagnostic overshadowing
One of the key reasons that people with ID are more likely to die a
potentially preventable death is an inability to tell others how they
are feeling. What this means is that an individual’s struggle to
verbally communicate physical symptoms, such as pain, will often
present itself as a form of unusual behavioural communication. This
could be through either becoming totally withdrawn or presenting
with behaviour that challenges the nurses and other health
professionals. Diagnostic overshadowing
 occurs when a nurse,
or other health professional, attributes the unusual behaviour to the
person’s ID rather than the possibility that it could be due to a
physical cause (Mason & Scior
). The following ‘Real-world practice’
demonstrates the dire consequences of diagnostic overshadowing.
59 Mason, J. & Scior, K. (2004). ‘Diagnostic overshadowing’ amongst clinicians working with
people with intellectual disabilities in the UK. Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual
Disabilities, 17(2), 85–90. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1360-2322.2004.00184.x.
Real-world practice
59


What happens when health care
professionals have a poor attitude
towards PWD?
The story
Michelle was a 28-year-old woman with a mild intellectual
disability who was found by her mother sitting on the floor,
screaming, rocking back and forth and holding her ears.
Michelle’s mother took her to the emergency department as
she was worried about Michelle’s behaviour. Michelle was
deemed okay to return home after she received some
painkillers for her headache. However, her mother advocated
that her behaviour was not normal and refused to leave.
Security was subsequently called and the pair were bundled
into a taxi and sent home, where Michelle died the next day
from meningitis, a complication resulting from an ear
infection. The discharge medical notes stated that Michelle
was having a temper tantrum related to having an intellectual
disability.
Clinical reflection
Assuming that the behaviour was ‘normal’ and not listening to
the parent’s concerns were fundamental errors in


assessment. Sadly, this case is not isolated. According to
Troller et al. (2017), potentially avoidable deaths for people
with ID are twice the rate of those seen in the general
population, and this increased rate has been somewhat
attributed to poor staff attitudes. Problems arise because of
communication difficulties and time constraints in a busy
health care environment.
Adapted from the ABC’s 7:30 Report, Wednesday 8 Feb 2017. Presenter, Leigh Sales.
Nurses who are keen to learn about ID, who adopt positive attitudes
about disability and who work closely with caregivers are less likely
to misinterpret a person with ID’s behaviour.
Communicating with the person
with ID
Communication is a challenge for most people with ID and can lead
to frustration for the individual, their support network and the nurse.
Clinical consideration
Difficulties with comprehension related to
intellectual disability.


May be complicated by hearing or vision
impairments.
May be complicated by physical disability
involving muscles of speech.
Some people with ID have receptive
communication difficulties (receiving and
understanding information).
Some people with ID have expressive
communication difficulties (verbal language,
non-verbal cues, gestures and facial
expressions).
Some people with ID have both receptive
and expressive communication difficulties.
If staff perceive communication is too
difficult, this barrier puts the person at risk of
adverse health outcomes.
Facilitating appropriate communication is a
sign of respect and assists the person with
ID to maintain autonomy and independence.
Involve carers and family to determine
communication preferences and behaviours.
Allow more time during therapeutic
interactions.


Supported decision making and
capacity to consent
Consent to treatment is a legal and ethical obligation in health care
and can be complicated by communication difficulties. Supported
decision making
 is a principle tenet of the CRPD that recognises
that people with ID are entitled to make decisions about themselves
the same as everyone else. Supported decision making can be
informal or formal, the latter pertaining to legalities concerning
enduring powers of attorney and the Office of the Public Advocate.
Informal decision support is made by families, significant others,
paid carers or advocates and is based on knowing the person well
(Bigby, Whiteside & Douglas ).
60 Bigby, C., Whiteside, M. & Douglas, J. (2017). Providing support for decision making to
adults with intellectual disability: Perspectives of family members and workers in disability
support services. Journal of Intellectual & Developmental Disability, 44(4). https://doi.org/
10.3109/13668250.2017.1378873.
Common misconceptions are that people with ID do not have the
capacity to consent and that other people can consent on their
behalf. Capacity to consent
 is when a person has the ability to
understand and use information to make a decision and then
consent to treatment based on the information provided. However, it
is important that nurses assume capacity in the first instance.
Capacity and competence are used interchangeably and concern a
person’s ability to consent to an intervention, procedure or treatment
60


(University of Hertfordshire ). Consent, in its basic form, may
include asking permission to perform a nursing intervention such as
taking a person’s blood pressure. In this instance, if the person does
not understand the procedure, they may feel assaulted; this puts
both the person and nurse at risk of harm. Conversely, if treatment
is denied because of assumptions that the person lacks capacity,
this is considered neglect (University of Hertfordshire 2018).
Consent can also be demonstrated through behaviour; for example,
a person who is non-verbal puts their arm out when the nurse asks if
it is okay to take their blood pressure. Consent, from a legal
perspective, is central to the four ethical principles of respecting the
person’s right to self-determination (autonomy), doing no harm (non-
maleficence), promoting good (beneficence) and equitable treatment
(justice).
61 University of Hertfordshire (2018). Intellectual Disability and Health: Consent and
Intellectual Disability—The Basics. Retrieved from <www.intellectualdisability.info>.
In Australia, each state and territory provides its own laws on
guardianship, for which nurses must be cognisant. It is appropriate
for a substitute decision maker who is authorised by law to assist in
the decision-making process if a person does not have the capacity
to consent. Capacity to consent about a specific decision is
determined by a multidisciplinary team and concerns a person’s
inability to make wise decisions (Office of the Public Advocate ).
62 Office of the Public Advocate (2019). Supported Decision Making. Retrieved from
<www.publicadvocate.vic.gov.au>.
61
62


Other strategies that nurses may employ to promote or enable
decision making are building a rapport and developing trust through
therapeutic relationships, so that information is more likely to be
shared. Again, involving families and carers serves to reinforce
knowledge gained, particularly when memories may be challenged.
Allowing time to assimilate information and ask questions that may
involve the support of a carer facilitates the decision-making
process. If information is not understood, keep trying and say it in a
different way (CDDH ).
63 Centre for Developmental Disability Health (CDDH) (2016b). CDDH Fact Sheet: Working
with People with Intellectual Disabilities in Health Care Settings. Retrieved from
<www.cddh.monashhealth.org>.
Capacity relates to understanding. Understanding is reliant on
cognitive ability, effective communication and information that is
tailored to the individual. When participating in the information
sharing, a nurse must facilitate opportunities for learning by offering
information in a variety of forms. For example, written information
should be presented in Easy English with use of images and
diagrams, be sequenced with simple layout and design, be simple
and concise and use minimal punctuation (Scope Australia ). Audio
recordings and online resources are also useful for people whose
literacy levels are limited. Communication and information-sharing
may be more difficult when combined with behaviours associated
with ID.
64 Scope Australia (2019). Accessible Information. Retrieved from
<www.scopeaust.org.au>.
63
64


Behavioural considerations
Over 50% of people with ID experience anxiety (Agency for Clinical
Innovation (ACI)
), which often manifests in a behavioural manner.
Situations that may trigger a change in behaviour are disruption of
routine, unfamiliar surroundings, poor communication, poor
interactions with staff, constipation, pain, other manifestations of
presenting problem and previous poor hospital experience. Often
behaviours are related to personal needs. Sometimes a person with
ID is unable to verbally communicate these needs due to their
disability and behaviour is the only way of communication. However,
the danger here is that health professionals can make assumptions
that the behaviour is normal and miss important cues (ACI 2018).
Tapping into carer knowledge is essential in determining the meaning
of the behaviour in order to respond appropriately.
65 Agency for Clinical Innovation (ACI) (2018). Intellectual Disability Resources: Education
and Training. Retrieved from <www.aci.health.nsw.gov.au>.
Challenging behaviours
Challenging behaviour is defined as ‘behaviour of such intensity,
frequency or duration as to threaten the QoL and/or the physical
safety of the individual or others and is likely to lead to responses
that are restrictive, aversive or result in exclusion’ (Royal College of
Psychiatrists , p. 13). This type of behaviour relates to the
interaction of the person with the environment and can manifest as
65
66


aggression, self-injury (such as head banging), withdrawal or
disruptive and destructive behaviour (National Institute of Health and
Care Excellence (NICE)
). Other presentations may include sexual
abuse, arson or violence, which often lead to contact with the
criminal justice system. Behaviours are usually self-seeking in terms
of attention seeking, avoidance of demands, avoidance of
communicating with others or sensory stimulation (NICE 2015). A
background of severe ID, communication difficulties, autism,
sensory impairments and/or mental health conditions contributes to
the problem.
66 Royal College of Psychiatrists (2007). Challenging Behaviour: A Unified Approach. College
Report CR144. Retrieved from <www.rcpsych.ac.uk>.
67 National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) (2015). Challenging Behaviour and
Learning Disabilities: Prevention and Interventions for People with Learning Disabilities Whose
Behaviour Challenges. Retrieved from <www.nice.org.uk>.
Strategies to reduce unwanted behaviour are aimed at reinforcing
positive behaviour through reward systems that are tailored to the
individual, rather than restrictive practices such as restraint and
seclusion, which often serve the person well in terms of attention
seeking. Other strategies may include the use of noise-eliminating
headsets or music delivered through headsets which screen
unwanted noise, offering a single room and, of course, liaising with
carers to determine the best approach.
Pain assessment
67


Pain often presents as behavioural changes in people who cannot
verbalise or who have communication difficulties. Pain should also
be considered if there is self-injurious behaviour (e.g. head banging,
self-slapping), which often manifests as a response to pain. Other
clues may be loss of appetite, sleep disturbance, withdrawal and/or
depression, rocking or any unusual behaviour. Pain assessment
tools that include behavioural elements such as the FLACC pain
scale (Chapter 49
) are useful assessment tools for determining
levels of pain, together with baseline assessments (Dillane &
Doody ). However, a number of alternative pain assessment tools
may soon be available that offer different solutions to pain
management. The painHS test is a revolutionary new Australian
discovery that identifies chronic pain by colour biomarkers to
determine severity through a simple on the spot blood test. It is ideal
for people with ID who have trouble expressing their level of pain.
The Dementia Training Institute’s PainChek is currently available as
an app for smartphones. It uses facial recognition technology for
pain assessment and monitoring in people with cognitive impairment.
68 Dillane, I. & Doody, O. (2019). Nursing people with intellectual disability and dementia
experiencing pain: An integrative review. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 28(1), 2472–2485. Doi:
10.1111/jocn.14834.
Clinical consideration
Pain in people with ID is often unrecognised
and undertreated.
68


Health professionals often mistake self-
injurious behaviour as insensitivity to pain.
If pain is not identified, the person is at risk
of increasing stress as well as misdiagnosis
and adverse clinical events.
Pain assessment may require a combination
of approaches by using pain rating scales,
physical assessment and observation of
behaviours.
Typical indicators of pain such as
tachycardia, elevated blood pressure,
grimacing or crying may be absent in people
with ID who have central nervous damage
associated with ID.
Presence of caregivers can be a significant
support for a person with ID in pain.
Polypharmacy
As a direct consequence of being diagnosed with a greater number
of chronic illnesses, many people with ID are prescribed multiple
medications (Wilson et al.
). This is referred to as polypharmacy
(see Chapter 36
). Although a person with ID who is prescribed
multiple medications may need them all, effective collaboration
between the nurse, general practitioner, psychiatrist, pharmacist and
69


direct caregivers is required to eliminate any unnecessary
medications, thereby reducing of drug-to-drug interactions.
Furthermore, nurses, along with other members of the health care
team, need to be vigilant about monitoring for unwanted side effects
that may be the result of polypharmacy or the use of certain
medications. For example, psychotropic medications, medicines
prescribed for mental illness, pose a major challenge for people with
ID due to risks such as overmedication (National Health Service ).
69 Wilson, N. J., Riches, V. C., Riches, T., Durvasula, S. Rodrigues, R. & Pinto, S. (2020).
Complex support needs profile of an adult cohort with intellectual disability transitioning from
state-based service provision to NDIS-funded residential support. Journal of Intellectual and
Developmental Disability.
70 National Health Service (2017). Stopping Over-medication of People (STOMP) with a
Learning Disability, Autism or Both. London: NHS. Retrieved from <www.england.nhs.uk>.
Patient safety competency framework
4 Teamwork and collaborative practice
Nursing students must develop the skills to
engage the person (and significant others) as
an integral member of the health care team
(Levett-Jones et al.
).
71 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
70
71


Lifespan considerations
Children
From birth, the primary lifespan consideration is obtaining an
accurate diagnosis of any congenital disorders that might be
the cause of the child having ID and/or autism. While there
are many causes that are not genetic in origin, it is critical to
determine if there is a genetic cause as this can immediately
alert the multidisciplinary team of any syndrome-specific
health risks to screen. If the person has, for example, an
endocrine problem, establishing what will be a long-term
relationship with an endocrinology team is vital. Once the
diagnostic causes have been explored, the primary issue for
parents and the child becomes one of function and early
intervention for any problems identified. The NDIS has a
diverse range of funded possibilities from early intervention
therapists. For babies and young children, many of these are
based on speech, occupational and physical therapies. For
nurses, clear roles within the therapeutic and rehabilitation
domains are not yet mandated. Therefore, most nurse
interactions with babies and children with ID and autism will
be within the paediatric health services system.


Challenges in transition from child to
adult
One of the major problems facing adolescents as they
transition into adult services is the shift from services that are
family focused to services that are individual, or adult,
focused. Transition from paediatric to adult health services
can be traumatic for individuals and families, so transition
planning takes precedence during the older adolescent years.
As it stands, there are few, if any, rigorously tested and widely
adopted transition models across Australia. This means that
some adults with ID and autism may fall through the cracks
and start to experience health inequities in terms of access
and outcomes.
Premature ageing
The health literature shows that for many people with ID,
premature ageing is a critical issue. In fact, literature about
retirement and people with lifelong disabilities suggests that
many people start to experience ageing issues from their
mid-40s (Wilson et al.
). Underlying health problems are one
of the major push factors for entering retirement involuntarily
(Denton, Plenderleith & Chowan ). This is in part due to
factors such as congenital disorders, decades of taking a
range of medications for underlying chronic illnesses,
72
73


potentially modifiable lifestyle choices and a greater risk of
age-related issues.
72 Wilson, N. J., Stancliffe, R. J., Bigby, C., Balandin, S. & Craig, D. (2010). The
potential for active mentoring to support a positive transition into retirement for older
adults with a lifelong disability. Journal of Intellectual & Developmental Disability,
35(3), 211–214. Doi: 10.3109/13668250.2010.481784.
73 Denton, M., Plenderleith, J. & Chowan, J. (2013). Health and disability as
determinants for involuntary retirement of people with disabilities. Canadian Journal
on Aging, 32(2), 159–172. Doi: 10.1017/S0714980813000202.


Other considerations in disability
care
Disability, sexuality and health
PWD have emotional responses and psychologically desire love,
affection and companionship in the same way as able- bodied men
and women (Sigelman et al.
, p. 475). While some disabilities may
reduce the person’s functional ability to engage in sexual
intercourse, most PWD are physiologically capable of engaging in
intimate behaviours including sexual intercourse. Therefore, many
PWD are capable of procreation and parenting. Nonetheless, there
remains an unfounded assumption that PWD are asexual or sexless
and not interested in intimacy or sexual relationships. As a result of
this misnomer, sexual health education is often not offered (East &
Orchard ) or what is offered is not fit for purpose (Frawley &
Wilson ). The failure to provide appropriate sexual health education
places the PWD at risk of sexually transmissible infections and
unwanted pregnancy (see Chapter 41
 for more information).
74 Sigelman, C., De George, L., Cunial, K. & Rider, E. (2019). Lifespan Human Development.
South Melbourne: Cengage
74
75
76


75 East, L. & Orchard, T. (2014). Somebody else’s job: Experiences of sex education among
health professionals, parents, and adolescents with physical disabilities in Southwestern
Ontario. Sexuality and Disability, 32(3), 335–350. Doi: 10.1007/s11195-013-9289-5.
76 Frawley, P. & Wilson, N. (2016). Young people with intellectual disability talking about
sexuality education and information. Sexuality and Disability, 34(4), 469–484. Doi:
10.1007/s11195-016-9460-x.
Furthermore, PWD may face some obstacles when attempting to
form relational partnerships. For example, fewer opportunities for
engaging in lifestyle activities for PWD reduce the potential to meet
a serious, life or marriage partner who is accepting of their situation
(Nguyen, Liamputtong & Monfries ). In contrast, sometimes the
absence of seeking an intimate relationship more readily links with
the PWD’s self- image as they may feel unable to attract a partner
(Parker & Yau ; Bremer, Cockburn & Ruth ).
77 Nguyen, T., Liamputtong, P. & Monfries, M. (2016). Reproductive and sexual health of
people with physical disabilities: A metasynthesis. Sexuality and Disability, 34(1), 3–26. Doi:
10.1007/s11195-015-9425-5.
78 Parker, M. & Yau, M. (2011). Sexuality, identity and women with spinal cord injury. Journal
of Sex and Disability, 30, 15–27. Doi: 10.1007/s11195-011-9222-8.
79 Bremer, K., Cockburn, L. & Ruth, A. (2010). Reproductive health experiences among
women with physical disabilities in the Northeast Region of Cameroon, International Journal of
Gynecology and Obstetrics, 108, 211–213. Doi: 10.1016/j.ijgo.2009.10.008.
PWD are also at risk of sexual assault and abuse. According to the
AHRC , 1 in 4 people who report sexual assault are PWD and 9 in
10 women with ID have been sexually abused. These figures are
alarming, triggering the emergence of a number of organisations
77
78
79
80


that offer counselling services specific to PWD. Prevention programs
are also available on relationships training for PWD that guide PWD
on how to form healthy relationships and strategies to reduce
behaviours that put the person at risk of abuse.
80 Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) (2014). Face the Facts: Disability Rights.
Sydney: AHRC. Retrieved from <www.humanrights.gov.au>.
Allow time
Allowing more time is a reasonable and achievable adjustment and
provides the dignity and respect that PWD deserve. For example,
PWD with mobility issues may require more time to move between
locations within school, work or recreational or lifestyle environments
due to mobility, sensory, psychosocial or cognitive impairments.
Additional time may be required for the person to change
positioning; for example, standing to greet an incomer to a
conversation or raising a height elevational mobility device to allow
the PWD to be at the same eye level in a standing group.
Cognitive functioning and language disabilities (e.g. stammering or
slurring) may require extra time for the person to formulate their
thoughts and speak or utilise a communication device to transform
text to speech. Allowing time to perform social introductions, such as
shaking hands even if the person has a prosthetic hand or a
deformity, promotes openness and acceptance (Australian Network
on Disability ). If the traditional handshake is not physically
81


possible, other social conventions may be useful, such as body
language, eye contact, smiling and active listening. In the health
care setting, allowing more time must be factored into time
management practices, both from a workload allocation perspective
and at a nurse–patient interaction level (Hemsley, Balandin &
Worrall ).
81 Australian Network on Disability (2019b). Disability Etiquette. Retrieved from
<www.and.org.au/pages/etiquette.html>.
82 Hemsley, B., Balandin, S. & Worrall, L. (2012). Nursing the patient with complex
communication needs: Time as a barrier and a facilitator to successful communication in
hospital. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 68(1), 116–126. Doi: 10.1111/j.1365-
2648.2011.05722.x.
82


Nursing research in disability care
Research note
Audit of intellectual disability content in the national
curricula in Australia
J. Trollor, C. Eagleson, B. Turner, C. Salomon, A. Cashin, T. Iacono, L. Goddard & N. Lennox (2016).
Intellectual disability health content within nursing curriculum: An audit of what our future nurses are
taught. Nurse Education Today, 45, 72–79. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2016.06.011.
The purpose of this study was to report on the nature of ID
content within the Australian nursing degree curricula. One of
the barriers to equitable health care for people with ID is
inadequate education of health professionals. A two-phase
national audit of nursing curriculum content was conducted in
2016 using an interview and online survey. Course
coordinators from 31 universities completed the Phase 1
interview on course structure. The results of Phase 1
demonstrated 52% of universities did not offer ID content.
Phase 2 involved an online survey of the academics from the
15 universities that identified as teaching ID content. The
results of this phase revealed an average of 3.6 hours per
unit of study was dedicated to teaching ID content.
Implications Despite the disparity in health care needs for
people with ID, there is considerable variability in the teaching


of ID key content in nursing. Upskilling in this area is vital to
improving nurse confidence and positive patient outcomes for
people with ID.
Nursing research is vital as a means to not only inform and evaluate
our practice, but also as a means to build the evidence base for the
profession itself. For example, a review of nursing research in the
field of acquired disability, specifically neurorehabilitation nursing,
highlighted a summary of the role of the rehabilitation nurse as well
as an overview of nursing interventions and the characteristics that
define rehabilitation nursing practice (Thorn ). By contrast, an
international review of nursing research in the field of ID shows a
lack of evidence, in the form of intervention studies and evaluations,
for the work that these nurses do in addition to limited use of robust
research designs (Griffiths, Bennett & Smith ). In the Australian
context, a recent review shows an almost total absence of
scholarship in the area (Wilson, Lewis et al.
). Exactly why it is that
nursing research in the ID field remains so limited in breadth and
poor in quality remains open to conjecture; nevertheless, this gap
also acts as an opportunity for nurses to engage with disability
research and fill this space. In particular, the NDIS represents the
policy-specific turning point for nurses to argue for its relevance;
building an evidence base is the only way forward. The most
pressing challenge, however, is the lack of adequate educational
preparation of nurses within undergraduate nursing programs across
the world and the limited evidence for nursing interventions. In the
Australian context, the Professional Association of Nurses in
Developmental Disability Australia (PANDDA) Inc. has embarked on
83
84
85


a number of funded initiatives to increase the amount and rigour of
research in this field.
83 Thorn, S. (2000). Neurological rehabilitation nursing: A review of the research. Journal of
Advanced Nursing, 31(5), 1029–1038. https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1365-2648.2000.01393.x.
84 Griffiths, P., Bennett, J. & Smith, E. (2007). The research base for Learning Disability
Nursing: A rapid scoping review. London: Kings College London.
85 Wilson, N. J., Lewis, P., O’Reilly, K., .?.?. & Goddard, L. (2019). Reframing the role, identity
and standards for practice for registered nurses working in the specialty area of intellectual
and developmental disability in Australia: The NDIS and beyond. Collegian, 26(1), 132–139.
Doi: 10.1016/j.colegn.2018.06.002.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: partnering with consumers
The intention of this standard is ‘to create an organisation in
which there are mutually valuable outcomes by having:
consumers as partners in planning, design, delivery,
measurement and evaluation of systems and services; [and]
patients as partners in their own care, to the extent that they
choose’ (Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in
Health Care
, p. 14).
86 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
86


Implementing this standard is achieved by
ensuring PWD, their families, carers and
disability advocate groups have input in decision
making at all levels of health care service
provision. Consumer partnerships with PWD,
carers and families are integral to person-
centred care to ensure the best possible health
outcomes.
The three key levels of partnership are at an:
1. Individual level: nursing care is provided
in a respectful manner that optimises
supported decision making by involving
the person, carer and family members
and encouraging autonomy and self-
management.
2. Service level: partnerships may involve
quality improvement design by planning,
implementing and evaluating change at
organisational and/or unit level; for
example, consultation with a local
advocacy group to improve wayfinding
signage in a hospital.
3. Health service organisation level:
partnerships concerned with governance,
policy and planning at board and
committee level that may involve key


areas such as quality improvement,
patient safety, facility design, ethics and
research.

Intellectual disability and adjusting to hospital

Applying critical thinking
1. What past experiences may have led Sandy to
become fearful of hospitals?
2. Can you think of any other strategies you could use to
develop rapport with Sandy?
3. What would you do if you witnessed another staff
member attempting to perform interventions without
first explaining them to Sandy?
Case study


Michael is a 6-year-old boy who lives with cerebral palsy. He
is a happy and outgoing member of his Year 3 primary school
class. Michael has difficulties with his posture and balance
and uses a posterior walker (see Figure 46.9
) to mobilise.
He is very interested in astronauts, spaceships and
astronomy. The local museum will be hosting a space travel
and exploration exhibit for the next 3 months. According to
the brochure, the exhibit will include many interactive features
and activities. Michael is looking forward to visiting with his
classmates. The school curriculum has an assessment task
to be completed during the planned two visits to the museum.
The class will be travelling from its primary school on a public
bus to the museum and spending the day at the venue. The
excursion includes a lunch provided at the café on site.

Chapter 46 Review


Chapter highlights
This chapter adopts the socially constructed approach to
disability that considers the interaction between people with
disability and the attitudinal and environmental barriers that
hinder full participation in society on equal basis with others.
Appreciation of the long history of societal attitudes to disability
offers a deeper understanding of the disparities experienced by
people with disability.
Disability discrimination occurs when a person is treated less
favourably because of their disability. It can be direct
discrimination or indirect discrimination.
Health care providers and health care professionals must make
reasonable adjustments to accommodate a person’s disability so
that they may have equitable access to health care.
The introduction of the National Disability Insurance Scheme
(NDIS) offers more choice and control for individuals so that they
may participate more fully in community life.
Barriers to full inclusion in society have a detrimental effect on
health, wellbeing and quality of life.
Recognition of the complexity of disability and the need for
individualised, person-centred care addresses the need for
independence, self-determination, dignity and respect.
Nurses must be aware of the adverse effects of stigmatisation by
health professionals on health outcomes and must advocate for
people with disability while in their care.


Understanding the role of carers facilitates communication,
thereby reducing the risk of negative health outcomes associated
with poor communication.
Awareness of assistive technologies, resources and social
supports for people with a range of disabilities enables nurses to
promote autonomy and independence for people with disability.
People with autism spectrum disorder may have difficulty with
communication, social behaviour and adapting to change. Nurses
need to be cognisant of triggers and preventive measures in
order to be supportive and help minimise anxietal behaviour.
People with intellectual disability are a diverse group and have
poorer health outcomes than the general population. Problems
arise because of lack of knowledge, staff attitudes,
communication difficulties and time constraints in a busy health
care environment.
Supported decision making can be informal or formal. Assume
capacity in the first instance during the process of informed
consent.
Behaviour is often a way of communication when the ability to
communicate is compromised. Liaising with carers helps to
determine the meaning of the behaviour so that appropriate
responses are facilitated.
A comprehensive approach to care incorporating lifespan
considerations across a range of settings involving the
multidisciplinary team as well as carers and families is required.
Concept check


1. The nurse is aware of the need to use respectful, inclusive
language when caring for a person with disability. Which of
the following responses is false?
1. People with disability do not see themselves as
disabled; they see themselves as part of the world’s
diversity.
2. Accept the person in a wheelchair as an individual first
before acknowledging the disability.
3. When communicating with or about disability, the
person always comes last (e.g. ‘disabled person’).
4. Avoid language that talks down to the person (e.g.
speaking childish language to a person with intellectual
disability).
2. Which of the following statements is false? The National
Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) is concerned with:
1. A new way of providing individualised support for
eligible people with permanent and significant disability.
2. Providing a flexible whole-of-life approach to support
PWD so that they can pursue goals and aspirations
and participate in daily life.
3. Providing an institutional, inflexible approach to long-
term support.
4. Raising community awareness and encouraging
greater inclusion and access to mainstream services
and community activities.


3. The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (DDA) provides
protection for everyone in Australia against discrimination
based on disability. Which of the following statements is
false?
1. The DDA serves to protect family members, carers,
interpreters, co-workers or associates of the person
with disability who may experience disability
discrimination by association.
2. It is against the law to refuse a person with an
assistance animal entry to a restaurant.
3. The areas of life covered by the DDA include
employment, education, access and provision of
goods, services and facilities.
4. Access to the built environment only concerns
buildings and does not include infrastructure such as a
disability parking.
4. Reasonable adjustments are considerations that help to make
a PWD feel more included. Which of the following is the best
response? Reasonable adjustments refer to:
1. An alteration to a building requiring a large expenditure
to allow for bariatric wheelchair access.
2. The administrative, environmental or procedural
alterations that accommodate a person’s disability.
3. Allowing nursing staff to take sick leave because a
person with ID and challenging behaviours is
exhausting work.
4. None of these.


5. Negative staff attitudes contribute to poor hospital
experiences for people with intellectual disability. Which one of
the following statements does NOT demonstrate disability
discrimination?
1. Medical staff decide that a woman is not suitable for an
operation because she has intellectual disability and
would not comprehend the benefits.
2. As people with intellectual disability take more time in
communication, the nurse prioritises other health care
recipients first.
3. Talk to the carer first about a new procedure before
talking to the person with intellectual disability, as it is
unlikely that the person will understand.
4. Take time to establish a rapport with the person with
intellectual disability as well as the carer in order to
gain trust.
Focus on critical thinking
1. Did you ever think that people with disability should accept
their position in life and accept that they cannot access the
environment the same as everyone else? Did you think that
there was not much that could be done to improve their
situation? Do you think it is the responsibility of governments,
the whole of community or the individual with disability to
make change?


2. What type of reasonable adjustment could you make in the
health care environment? Could you allow more time for a
person with physical disability to perform their activities of
daily living? Could you allow more time to talk to the person
with ID so that you can build a rapport? Could you present
information to a person with vision impairment in an
accessible format?
3. What is your understanding of disability discrimination? Does
it include the person’s family, friends and associates? Have
you considered that because PWD find it difficult to get a job
because of discrimination, this puts them in the lower
socioeconomic group that affects their ability to access quality
housing, services and goods? Does it concern you that this
would make them feel unworthy and have low self-esteem?
4. Have you ever engaged with a PWD in the health care
environment? If so, was it a positive experience? If not, how
could it have been done better now that you have read this
chapter?

Unit 10 Promoting physiological
health
The human body consists of a complex network
of intricate and interacting systems. Drawing on
a comprehensive knowledge base, nurses are
cognisant of a host of factors that influence
physical health as they provide care to support
optimal physiological function. Efforts to restore,
maintain or improve function include measures
that address a person’s individual need for
nourishment, comfort and physical activity.
