b. 1 to 2 hours after taking an antihypertension
medication.
Get out of a hot bath very slowly because high
temperatures can lead to venous pooling.
Use a rocking chair to improve circulation in the lower
extremities. Even mild leg conditioning can strengthen
muscle tone and enhance circulation.
Refrain from any strenuous activity that results in holding
the breath and bearing down. This Valsalva manoeuvre
slows the heart rate, leading to subsequent lowering of
blood pressure.
Some people experience postural (orthostatic) hypotension on
assuming a vertical position from a lying position and may need
information about ways to control this problem (see ‘Patient
education’). The person may exhibit some or all of the following
symptoms: pallor, diaphoresis, nausea, tachycardia and dizziness. If


any of these are present, the person should be assisted to a supine
position in bed and closely assessed.
Using mechanical aids for walking
Mechanical aids for ambulation include walking sticks, walking
frames and crutches.
Walking sticks
Two types of walking sticks are used today: the standard straight-
legged walking stick and the quad walking stick, which has four feet
and provides the most support (see Figure 47.26
). Walking stick
tips should have rubber caps to improve traction and prevent
slipping. The standard walking stick is 91 cm long; some aluminium
walking sticks can be adjusted from 56 to 97 cm. The length should
permit the elbow to be slightly flexed. The person using the aid may
use either one or two walking sticks, depending on how much
support they require.
Figure 47.26


A quad walking stick.
Source: 2574523. Shutterstock.
Lifespan considerations
Assisting the person to ambulate
Children
Children and adolescents who have suffered a sports
injury (e.g. sprained ankle) may want to be more active
than they should be. A cast, splint or boot may be put in
place to limit activity and assist in healing. Teach the child
the importance of appropriate activity and the use of
assistive devices (e.g. crutches) if necessary. Help them
focus on what they can do rather than what they cannot
do.
Older adults
Inquire how the person ambulated previously and modify
assistance accordingly.
Take into account a decrease in speed, strength,
resistance to fatigue, reaction time and coordination due
to a decrease in nerve conduction.
Be cautious when using a transfer belt with someone who
has osteoporosis. Too much pressure from the belt can
increase the risk of vertebral compression fractures.


If assistive devices such as a walker or walking stick are
used, make sure the person is supervised in the beginning
to learn the proper method of using them. Crutches may
be much more difficult for older people due to decreased
upper body strength.
Be alert to signs of activity intolerance, especially in older
people with cardiac and lung problems.
Set small goals and increase slowly to build endurance,
strength and flexibility.
Be aware of any fall risks older people may have, such as
the following:
– effects of medications
– neurological disorders
– environmental hazards
– orthostatic hypotension.
In older people, the body’s responses return to normal
more slowly. For instance, an increase in heart rate from
exercise may stay elevated for hours before returning to
normal.
Home care considerations
Assisting the person to ambulate


When making a home visit, assess carefully for
safety issues for ambulation. Educate the person
and their family or carers about falls prevention
strategies.
There are several measures that an older person
can take to help prevent a fall. Simple, everyday
measures around the home include:
using non-slip mats in the bathroom
mopping up spills to avoid wet floors
getting help lifting or moving items that are
heavy or difficult to lift
removing clutter and ensuring that all areas of
the home are properly lit (Department of
Health ).
42 Department of Health (2017). Fall Prevention. Retrieved from
<www.healthdirect.gov.au>.
Walking frames
Walking frames are mechanical devices for ambulatory people who
need more support than a walking stick provides. Walking frames
come in many different shapes and sizes, with devices suited to
individual needs. The standard type is made of polished aluminium.
It has four legs with rubber tips and plastic hand grips (see Figure
47.27A
). Many walking frames have adjustable legs.
42


Figure 47.27
A: standard walking frame. B: two-wheeled walking frame.
Sources: A: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia. B: Gts. Shutterstock.
Standard walking frames need to be picked up to be used. The
person therefore requires enough strength in their hands and wrists,
elbow extensors and shoulder depressors to do this. The person
using the walking frame also needs the ability to bear at least partial
weight on both legs.


Four-wheeled and two-wheeled models of walking frames do not
need to be picked up to be moved but are less stable than the
standard walking frame (see Figure 47.27B
). They are used by
people who are too weak or unstable to pick up and move the
walking frames with each step. Some wheelie walkers have a seat at
the back so the person can sit down to rest when desired and a
basket in the front for carrying their belongings. An adaptation of the
standard and four-wheeled walking frame is one that has two tips
and two wheels. This type provides more stability than the four-
wheeled model yet still permits the person to keep the walking frame
in contact with the ground at all times. The person tilts the walking
frame towards the body, lifting the tips while the wheels remain on
the ground, and then pushes the walking frame forward.
Patient education
Using walking sticks
Hold the walking stick with the hand on the stronger side
of the body to provide maximum support and appropriate
body alignment when walking.
Position the tip of a standard walking stick (and the
nearest tip of other walking sticks) about 15 cm to the
side and 15 cm in front of the near foot, so that the elbow
is slightly flexed.
When maximum support is required


Move the walking stick forward about 30 cm, or a distance
that is comfortable, while the body weight is borne by both
legs (see Figure 47.28A
).
Then move the affected (weak) leg forward to the walking
stick while the weight is borne by the walking stick and
stronger leg (see Figure 47.28B
).
Next, move the unaffected (stronger) leg forward ahead
of the walking stick and weak leg while the weight is borne
by the walking stick and weak leg (see Figure 47.28C
).
Repeat the steps. This pattern of moving provides at least
two points of support on the floor at all times.
Figure 47.28


Steps involved in using a walking stick to provide maximum
support.
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.
As the person becomes stronger and
requires less support


Move the walking stick and weak leg forward at the same
time, while the weight is borne by the stronger leg (see
Figure 47.29A
).
Move the stronger leg forward, while the weight is borne
by the walking stick and the weak leg (see Figure
47.29B
).
Figure 47.29


Steps involved in using a walking stick when less than
maximum support is required.
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.
The nurse may need to adjust the height of the walker so that the
hand bar is just below the person’s waist and so that their elbows
are slightly flexed. This position helps the person assume a more
normal stance. A walker that is too low causes the person to stoop;
one that is too high makes the person stretch and reach.
Crutches
Crutches may be a temporary need for some people and a
permanent one for others. Sometimes people become discouraged
when they attempt crutch walking. The person who is confined to
bed is often unaware of weakness which becomes apparent when
they try to stand or walk. The person then realises that they can no
longer take balance for granted when they have to cope with the
weight of a heavy cast or a paralysed limb. Frequently, progress
may be slower than they had anticipated. Encouragement from the
nurse and realistic goal setting undertaken collaboratively are
especially important.
There are several kinds of crutches. The most frequently used are
the underarm crutch, or axillary crutch with hand bars, and the
Lofstrand crutch, which extends only to the forearm (see Figure
47.30
). On the Lofstrand crutch, the metal cuff around the
forearm and the metal bar stabilise the wrists and thus make walking


safer and easier. The platform, or elbow extensor, crutch also has a
cuff for the upper arm (see Figure 47.30
). All crutches require
suction tips, usually made of rubber, which help to prevent slipping
on a floor surface.
Figure 47.30


Types of crutches: axillary, Lofstrand and platform.
In crutch walking, the person’s weight is borne by the muscles of the
shoulder girdle and the upper extremities. Before beginning crutch
walking, exercises that strengthen the upper arms and hands are
recommended.
Measuring a person for crutches
Patient education
Using walking frames
When maximum support is required
Move the walking frame ahead about 15 cm while your
body weight is borne by both legs.
Then move the right foot up to the walking frame while
your body weight is borne by the left leg and both arms.
Next, move the left foot up to the right foot while your
body weight is borne by the right leg and both arms.
If one leg is weaker than the other
Move the walking frame and the weak leg ahead together
about 15 cm while your weight is borne by the stronger
leg.


Then move the stronger leg ahead while your weight is
borne by the affected leg and both arms.
When nurses measure a person for axillary crutches, it is most
important to obtain the correct length for the crutches and the
correct placement of the hand piece. There are two methods of
measuring crutch length:
1. The person lies in a supine position and the nurse measures
from the anterior fold of the axilla to the heel of the foot and
adds 2.5 cm.
2. The person then stands erect and positions the crutch as
shown in Figure 47.31
. The nurse makes sure the
shoulder rest of the crutch is at least three finger widths; that
is, 2.5 to 5 cm below the axilla.
Figure 47.31


The standing position for measuring the correct length for
crutches.
To determine the correct placement of the hand bar:
1. The person stands upright and supports the body weight by
the hand grips of the crutches.
2. The nurse measures the angle of elbow flexion. It should be
about 30 degrees. A goniometer may be used to verify the


correct angle.
Crutch gaits
The crutch gait is the gait a person assumes on crutches by
alternating body weight on one or both legs and the crutches. Five
standard crutch gaits are the four-point gait, three-point gait, two-
point gait, swing-to gait and swing-through gait. The gait used
depends on the following individual factors: (a) the ability to take
steps; (b) the ability to bear weight and keep balance in a standing
position on both legs or only one; and (c) the ability to hold the body
erect.
People who are using crutches also need instruction about how to
get into and out of chairs and go up and down stairs safely. All of
these crutch skills are best taught before the person is discharged
and preferably before they have surgery.
Crutch stance (tripod position)
Before crutch walking is attempted, the person needs to learn about
posture and balance. The proper standing position with crutches is
called the tripod (triangle) position
 (see Figure 47.32
). The
crutches are placed about 15 cm in front of the feet and out laterally
about 15 cm creating a wide base of support. The feet are slightly
apart. A tall person requires a wider base than a shorter person.
Hips and knees are extended, the back is straight and the head is
held straight and high. There should be no hunch to the shoulders


and thus no weight borne by the axillae. The elbows are extended
sufficiently to allow weight bearing on the hands. If the person is
unsteady, the nurse places a walking belt around their waist and
grasps the belt from above, not from below. A fall can be prevented
more effectively if the belt is held from above.
Figure 47.32
The tripod position.
Four-point alternate gait
This is the most elementary and safest gait, providing at least three
points of support at all times, but it requires coordination. This gait
can be used when walking in crowds because it does not require
much space. To use this gait, the person needs to be able to bear


weight on both legs (see Figure 47.33
, reading from bottom to
top). The nurse asks the person to:
1. Move the right crutch ahead a suitable distance, such as 10
to 15 cm.
2. Move the left front foot forward, preferably to the level of the
left crutch.
3. Move the left crutch forward.
4. Move the right foot forward.
Figure 47.33


The four-point crutch gait
Patient education
Using crutches
Follow the plan of exercises developed to strengthen arm
muscles before beginning crutch walking.
Have a health care professional establish the correct
length for the crutches and the correct placement of the
handpieces. Crutches that are too long force the
shoulders upward and make it difficult to push the body
off the ground. Crutches that are too short make you
hunch over and develop an improper body stance.
The weight of the body should be borne by the arms
rather than the axillae (armpits). Continual pressure on
the axillae can injure the radial nerve and eventually cause
crutch palsy, a weakness of the muscles of the forearm,
wrist and hand.
Maintain an erect posture as much as possible to prevent
strain on muscles and joints and to maintain balance.
Each step taken with crutches should be a comfortable
distance. It is wise to start with a small rather than a large
step.
Inspect the crutch tips regularly and replace them if worn.
Keep the crutch tips dry and clean to maintain their
surface friction. If the tips become wet, dry them before
use.


Wear a shoe with a low heel that grips the floor. Rubber
soles decrease the chances of slipping. Adjust shoelaces
so they cannot come untied or reach the floor where they
might catch on the crutches. Consider shoes with
alternative forms of closure (e.g. Velcro), especially if it is
difficult to bend to tie laces. Slip-on shoes are acceptable
only if they are snug and the heel does not come loose
when the foot is bent.
Three-point gait
To use this gait, the person must be able to bear the entire body
weight on the unaffected leg. The two crutches and the unaffected
leg bear weight alternately (see Figure 47.34
, reading from
bottom to top). The nurse asks the person to:
1. Move both crutches and the weaker leg forward.
2. Move the stronger leg forward.
Figure 47.34


The three-point crutch gait.
Two-point alternate gait
This gait is faster than the four-point gait. It requires more balance
because only two points support the body at one time; it also
requires at least partial weight bearing on each foot. In this gait, arm
movements with the crutches are similar to the arm movements
during normal walking (see Figure 47.35
, reading from bottom to
top). The nurse asks the person to:
1. Move the left crutch and the right foot forward together.
2. Move the right crutch and the left foot ahead together.
Figure 47.35


The two-point alternate crutch gait.
Swing-to gait
The swing gaits are used by someone who has paralysis of the legs
and hips. Prolonged use of these gaits results in atrophy of the
unused muscles. The swing-to gait is the easier of these two gaits.
The nurse asks the person to:
1. Move both crutches ahead together.
2. Lift body weight by the arms and swing to the crutches (see
Figure 47.36
).
Figure 47.36


The swing-to crutch gait.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Swing-through gait
This gait requires considerable skill, strength and coordination. The
nurse asks the person to:


1. Move both crutches forward together.
2. Lift body weight by the arms and swing through and beyond
the crutch (see Figure 47.37
).
Figure 47.37
The swing-through crutch gait.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.


Getting into a chair
Chairs that have armrests and are secure or braced against a wall
are essential for someone who is using crutches. For this procedure,
the nurse instructs the person to:
1. Stand with the back of the unaffected leg centred against the
chair. The chair provides support during the next steps.
2. Transfer the crutches to the hand on the affected side and
hold the crutches by the hand bars. The person grasps the
arm of the chair with the hand on the unaffected side (see
Figure 47.38
). This allows them to support their body
weight on the arms and the unaffected leg.
3. Lean forward, flex the knees and hips and lower into the
chair.
Figure 47.38


A person using crutches getting into a chair.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Getting out of a chair


For this procedure, the nurse instructs the person to:
1. Move forward to the edge of the chair and place the
unaffected leg slightly under or at the edge of the chair. This
position helps them stand up from the chair and achieve
balance, since the unaffected leg is supported against the
edge of the chair.
2. Grasp the crutches by the hand bars in the hand on the
affected side and grasp the arm of the chair by the hand on
the unaffected side. The body weight is placed on the
crutches and the hand on the armrest to support the
unaffected leg when they rise to stand.
3. Push down on the crutches and the chair armrest while
elevating the body out of the chair.
4. Assume the tripod position before moving.
Going up stairs
For this procedure, the nurse stands behind the person and slightly
to the affected side if needed. The nurse instructs them to:
1. Assume the tripod position at the bottom of the stairs.
2. Transfer the body weight to the crutches and move the
unaffected leg onto the step (see Figure 47.39
).
3. Transfer the body weight to the unaffected leg on the step
and move the crutches and affected leg up to the step. The
affected leg is always supported by the crutches.


4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the person reaches the top of the
stairs.
Figure 47.39


Climbing stairs: placing weight on the crutches while first moving the
unaffected leg onto a step.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Going down stairs
For this procedure, the nurse stands one step below the person on
the affected side if needed. The nurse instructs the person to:
1. Assume the tripod position at the top of the stairs.
2. Shift the body weight to the unaffected leg and move the
crutches and affected leg down onto the next step (see
Figure 47.40
).
3. Transfer the body weight to the crutches and move the
unaffected leg to that step. The affected leg is always
supported by the crutches.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the person reaches the bottom of
the stairs.
Figure 47.40


Descending stairs: moving the crutches and affected leg to the next
step.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
Evaluating
The goals established during the planning phase are evaluated
according to specific desired outcomes, also established in that
phase. Examples of these are shown in the accompanying ‘Nursing
care plan’.
If outcomes are not achieved, all people involved need to explore
the reasons before modifying the care plan. For example, the
following questions may be considered if a person who is
immobilised fails to maintain muscle mass and tone and joint
mobility:
Has their physical or mental condition changed motivation to
perform the required exercise?
Were appropriate range-of-motion exercises implemented?
Were they encouraged to participate in self-care activities as
much as possible?
Were they encouraged to make as many decisions as possible
when developing a daily activity plan and to express concerns?
Did the nurse provide appropriate supervision and monitoring?
Was the person’s diet adequate to provide appropriate
nourishment for energy requirements?


NURSING  CARE PLAN
Risk of disuse syndrome
Applying critical thinking
1. What assessment findings alert you to the fact that Mr
Chan is developing problems associated with his
current state of decreased mobility?
2. Mr Chan may benefit from using a walker to assist with
ambulation at home. What teaching should be done in
regard to use of a walker?
3. The care plan does not address one of Mr Chan’s risk
factors—obesity. Would you add this to the plan?
4. What assumptions has the nurse made in assigning
the desired outcome of ‘Immobility consequences:
psychocognitive’?
5. How are the choices of outcomes influenced by the
cause of his nursing diagnosis (a chronic illness)?
CO NCEPT M AP
The person at risk of disuse syndrome


SKILL
47.1 Person-assisted bed slide:
one nurse
Implementation
1. Refer to risk assessment tools (see Chapter
32
). Prepare area and remove clutter and
obstructions.
2. Explain the procedure and the role the person
will play.
3. Adjust the bed height to between mid-thigh
and hip height.
4. Ask or assist the person to fold their arms
across the chest.
5. Tuck two slide sheets under the person’s
shoulders and hips.
6. Ask or assist the person to roll to the side to
pull the slide sheets into position.
7. Ask the person to sit or assist them to bend
the knee/s.
8. The nurse should stand at the foot of the bed
and place their hands over the person’s


ankles to secure them during the manoeuvre.
9. Ask the person to tuck their chin onto their
chest and extend their legs while the nurse
holds the feet against the mattress. This will
assist the person to push themself up in bed.


SKILL
47.2 Person-assisted bed slide:
two nurses
Implementation
1. Refer to risk assessment tools (see Chapter
32
). Prepare area and remove clutter and
obstructions.
2. Explain to the person and staff the procedure
and their role/s. Nominate a transfer leader.
3. Adjust the bed height to between mid-thigh
and hip height.
4. Place the person’s arm across their chest.
Tuck two slide sheets (on top of each other)
under the length of the person’s body.
5. Place one leg over the other. Roll the person
onto the other side. Position slide sheets over
mattress. Roll the person back to a supine
position.
6. Handlers should stand at the top end of the
bed corners (or kneel on the mattress with


one knee if possible) and gather the ends of
the top slide sheet with palms down.
7. In a controlled manner and with arms
straight, both lifters should lunge backwards
on the command ‘1, 2, 3, . . . move!’,
transferring their weight from their front foot
to their back foot, moving the person towards
the bed head.
8. Pull out the bottom slide sheet feet end first
and then tuck the remaining slide sheet under
the person and pull out the sheet from
beneath them. Position the person
comfortably and safely.


SKILL
47.3 Person-assisted lateral
shift and roll: two nurses
Implementation
1. Refer to risk assessment tools (see Chapter
32
). Prepare area and remove clutter and
obstructions.
2. Ensure there is the correct number of staff.
Explain the procedure to the person and their
role.
3. Adjust the bed to between mid-thigh and hip
height.
4. Fold the person’s arms across their chest.
5. Tuck the slide sheets under the person’s
shoulders and hips with the fold facing the
direction of the roll.
6. Cross the person’s leg over the other leg. If
rolling to the left, cross right over left.
7. Roll the person to the side and place the slide
sheets into position. Roll the person back to a
supine position. ❶


❶ Using slide sheets, the nurses pull the
sheet with the person on it to the edge of the
bed
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
8. The nurse on the opposite side of the roll
direction rolls up the slide sheets with palms
down and arms straight, adopting a
forward/rearward stance, while the nurse to
which the person will roll towards gathers the
slide sheets in both hands (palms up) firmly
against the person, adopting a parallel
stance.


9. In a controlled movement, the nurse on the
opposite side of the roll transfers their weight
onto the back foot, while the nurse on the
other side gently pushes the person, thereby
transferring them to the side of the bed.
10. The nurse on the opposite side of the roll
direction then gathers the slide sheets in both
hands, steps in closer, lowers themself and
pushes against the person’s buttock and
shoulder with the slide sheet in the hands
(semi-prone) with the other nurse’s hands
placed over the person’s thigh and shoulder,
thereby rolling them over onto the side. ❷


❷ The nurse on the left uses the far edge of
the sheet to roll the person towards them; the
nurse on the right remains behind the person
and assists with turning
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.


SKILL
47.4 Logrolling: two to four
nurses
Implementation
1. Refer to risk assessment tools (see Chapter
32
). Prepare area and remove clutter and
obstructions.
2. Ensure there is the correct number of staff.
Explain the procedure and the person’s role.
Depending on the person’s abilities/condition,
two or four people may be required.
3. Adjust the bed height to between mid-thigh
and hip height. Place a pillow between the
person’s legs.
4. The handler at the head should support the
person’s head while the pillow is repositioned
towards the direction of the roll.
5. Place the person’s arms across the chest.
6. Roll the bed sheet tightly against the person
on the opposite side of the transfer direction.


7. The handler that rolled the sheets gives them
to the two handlers on the side to which the
person is to be rolled.
8. The handler nearest the foot of the bed on
the side of the direction of the roll grasps the
sheet (palms down) at the person’s ankle and
mid-thigh. The second handler grasps the
sheet (palms down) at the person’s hip and
shoulder.
The handler at the person’s head supports
the head with one hand on each side of the
person’s head. All stand with a parallel stance
with natural spinal alignment.
9. The handler on the opposite side places the
hands (palms down) at the person’s hips and
shoulders in a forward/rearward stance.
10. On the command ‘1, 2, 3 . . . move!’, the
person is rolled to the side in a slow
controlled manner, keeping the person’s body
in a straight line at all times.


SKILL
47.5 Person-assisted bed to
chair slide: one or two nurses
Implementation
1. Refer to risk assessment tools (see Chapter
32
). Prepare area and remove clutter and
obstructions.
2. Explain the procedure to the person and to
the staff and their role/s. Nominate a transfer
leader.
3. Adjust the bed slightly higher than the chair.
4. Tuck the transfer board under the person’s
hips. Ask or assist the person to roll towards
the nurse. Pull the transfer board into place.
5. The nurse should place one hand under the
furthest knee and the other hand under the
person near shoulder. Ask them to tuck their
chin onto their chest and sit them up in a
pivoting movement around the hips.
6. Ask the person to place their hands on the
bed to support themself. Locate the chair


(with the closest arm rest removed) alongside
the bed on the person’s strongest side. ❶
❶ The wheelchair is placed parallel to the bed
as close to the bed as possible. Note that
placement of the nurse’s feet mirrors that of
the person’s feet
7. Remove the slide sheet. Place the person in
a position of comfort and safety. A slide board


could also be placed between the bed and the
chair.
8. Assist the person to sit. ❷
❷ Using a transfer (walking) belt
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.


SKILL
47.6 Bed to chair (4-point
frame): two nurses
Implementation
1. Refer to risk assessment tools (see Chapter
32
). Prepare the area and remove clutter
and obstructions.
2. Ensure there is the correct number of staff
and that hoist capacity is not exceeded.
Nominate a leader and explain the procedure
to the person and their role in the procedure.
3. Position the person in a side-lying posture to
fit the sling by raising their knee to 90
degrees and then roll them to opposite side.
Roll up leg section of the sling and tuck under
the person.
4. Roll the person to the supine position, raise
their other knee and roll them to opposite
side. Pull out their leg section and position the
sling.


5. Position hoist (legs apart and brake
disengaged) over the person. Lower boom
and attach sling to frame with the head end
attached first. Raise the person’s knees and
feed the leg sections of the sling under their
thighs and attach to frame.
6. Raise the boom gently, ensuring the head is
supported.
7. Position the person over the chair (brakes on
if present) and slowly lower them.
8. Detach sling from frame and remove hoist.
Pull leg straps to the side, tilt the person
forward and remove sling.
9. Reposition the person in a position that is
comfortable and safe.


SKILL
47.7 Assisting the person to sit
on the side of the bed
Purpose
To help a person assume a sitting position on the
edge of the bed before walking, moving to a chair or
wheelchair, eating or performing other activities.
Implementation
Preparation
Determine:
Assistive devices that will be required.
Encumbrances to movement such as an IV or a
heavy cast on one leg.
Medications the person is receiving, because
certain medications may hamper movement or
alertness.
Assistance required from other health care
personnel.


Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
agency protocol. Explain what you are going
to do, why it is necessary and how they can
cooperate. Discuss how the results will be
used in planning further care or treatment.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Ensure privacy.
4. Position yourself and the person appropriately
before performing the move.
Assist them to a lateral position facing
you.
Raise the head of the bed slowly to its
highest position. Rationale: this
decreases the distance that the person
needs to move to sit up on the side of the
bed.
Position the person’s feet and lower legs
at the edge of the bed. Rationale: this
enables the person’s feet to move easily
off the bed during the movement, and the
person is aided by gravity into a sitting
position.
Stand beside the person’s hips and face
the far corner of the bottom of the bed
(the angle in which movement will occur).


Assume a broad stance, placing the foot
nearest the patient forward. Lean your
trunk forward from the hips. Flex your
hips, knees and ankles. ❶
1 Assisting a person to a sitting position
on the edge of the bed
5. Move the person to a sitting position.
Place one arm around their shoulders and
the other arm beneath both of the
person’s thighs near the knees.


Rationale: supporting the person’s
shoulders prevents them from falling
backward during the movement.
Supporting the person’s thighs reduces
friction of the thighs against the bed
surface during the move and increases
the force of the movement.
Tighten your gluteal, abdominal, leg and
arm muscles.
Lift the thighs slightly. Rationale: this
reduces the friction of the person’s thighs
and the nurse’s arm against the bed
surface.
Pivot on the balls of your feet in the
desired direction facing the foot of the bed
while pulling the person’s feet and legs off
the bed (Figure 1B
). Rationale:
pivoting prevents twisting of the nurse’s
spine. The weight of the legs swinging
downward increases downward movement
of the lower body and helps make the
person’s upper body vertical.
Keep supporting the person until they are
well balanced and comfortable. Rationale:
this movement may cause some people to
faint.
Assess vital signs (e.g. pulse, respirations
and blood pressure) as indicated by the


person’s health status.
Variation: teaching a person how to sit
on the side of the bed independently
Someone who has had recent abdominal
surgery or is weak may have too much
abdominal pain or too little strength to sit
straight up in bed. This person can be taught
to assume a dangle position without
assistance. Instruct them to:
Roll to the side and lift the far leg over the
near leg.
Grasp the mattress edge with the lower
arm and push the fist of the upper arm
into the mattress. ❷


2 Moving to a sitting position
independently
Push up with the arms as the heels and
legs slide over the mattress edge.
Maintain the sitting position by pushing
both fists into the mattress behind and to
the sides of the buttocks.
6. Document all relevant information. Record:
ability of the person to assist in moving
and turning


response of the person to moving and
turning (e.g. anxiety, discomfort,
dizziness).
Evaluation
Check the skin integrity of the pressure areas
from the previous position. Relate findings to
previous assessment data if available. Conduct
follow-up assessment for previous and/or new
skin breakdown areas.
Check for proper alignment after the position
change. Do a visual check and ask the person
for a comfort assessment.
Determine that all required safety precautions
(e.g. side rails) are in place.
Determine the person’s tolerance of the activity
(e.g. vital signs before and after dangling),
particularly the first time they change position.
Report significant changes.


SKILL
47.8 Assisting the person to
ambulate
Purpose
To provide a safe condition for the person to walk
with whatever support is needed.
Assessment
Assess
Length of time in bed and time up previously.
Baseline vital signs.
Range of motion of joints needed for ambulating
(e.g. hips, knees, ankles).
Muscle strength of lower extremities.
Need for ambulation aids (e.g. walking stick,
walker, crutches).
The person’s intake of medication (e.g. narcotics,
sedatives, tranquillisers and antihistamines) may
cause drowsiness, dizziness, weakness and


orthostatic hypotension, and seriously hinder the
person’s ability to walk safely.
Presence of joint inflammation, fractures, muscle
weakness or other conditions that impair physical
mobility.
Ability to understand directions.
Level of comfort.
Planning
Implement pain-relief measures so that they are
effective when the transfer begins.
The amount of assistance needed while ambulating
will depend on the person’s condition; for example
age, health status, length of inactivity and emotional
readiness. Review any previous experiences with
ambulation and the success of such efforts. Plan the
length of the walk with the patient, in light of the
Nurse Practitioner’s or doctor’s orders. Be prepared
to shorten the walk according to the person’s activity
tolerance.
Delegation
Ambulation of a person is frequently delegated to
staff other than the nurse. However, the nurse
should conduct the initial assessment of the
person’s abilities in order to direct other personnel in


providing appropriate assistance. Any unusual
events that arise from assisting the person to
ambulate must be validated and interpreted by the
nurse.
Equipment
Transfer belt if the person is known to be
unsteady.
Wheelchair for following the person, or chairs
along the route if they need to rest.
Implementation
Preparation
Be certain that others are available to assist you if
needed. Also, plan the route of ambulation that has
the fewest hazards.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using the
organisation’s protocol. Explain how you are
going to assist, why ambulation is necessary
and how they can cooperate. Discuss how
this activity relates to the overall plan of care.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe
appropriate infection-control procedures.


3. Ensure that the person is appropriately
dressed to walk and has shoes or slippers
with non-skid soles.
4. Prepare the person for ambulation.
Apply elastic (anti-emboli) stockings as
required.
Assist the person to sit on the edge of the
bed.
Assess carefully for signs and symptoms
of orthostatic hypotension (dizziness, light-
headedness or a sudden increase in heart
rate) prior to leaving the bedside.
Assist the person to stand by the side of
the bed until they feel secure.
5. Ensure the person is safe while they are
being assisted to ambulate.
Encourage the person to ambulate
independently if they are able, but walk
beside their weak side, if appropriate.
Remain physically close in case
assistance is needed at any point.
Use a transfer or walking belt if they are
slightly weak and unstable. Make sure the
belt is pulled snugly around the person’s
waist and fastened securely. Grasp the
belt at the back and walk behind and
slightly to one side of the person. ❶


❶ Using a transfer (walking) belt to
support the person
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.
If it is the person’s first time out of bed
following surgery, injury or an extended
period of immobility, or if the person is
quite weak or unstable, have an assistant
follow you and the person with a
wheelchair in the event that it is needed
quickly.
If the person is moderately weak and
unstable, walk on their weaker side and
interlock your forearm with the person’s


closest forearm. Encourage them to press
their forearm against your hip or waist for
stability if desired. In addition, have the
person wear a transfer or walking belt.
Rationale: you can quickly grab the belt
and prevent a fall if the person feels faint.
If the person is very weak and unstable,
place your near arm around their waist
and with your other arm support their near
arm at the elbow. Walk on the person’s
stronger side. Again, have them wear a
transfer or walking belt in case of an
emergency. Encourage the person to
assume a normal walking stance and gait
as much as possible.
6. Protect the person who begins to fall while
ambulating.
If someone begins to experience the signs
and symptoms of orthostatic hypotension or
extreme weakness, quickly assist them into a
nearby wheelchair or other chair and help
them to lower their head between their knees.
Stay with the person. Rationale: a person
who faints while in this position could fall
head first out of the chair.
When the weakness subsides, assist the
person back to bed.


If a chair is not close by, assist them to a
horizontal position on the floor before
fainting occurs. ❷
❷ Lowering a fainting person to the floor
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.
a. Assume a broad stance with one
foot in front of the other. Rationale:
a broad stance widens your base of
support. Placing one foot behind
the other allows you to rock
backward and use the femoral
muscles when supporting the
person’s weight and lowering the


centre of gravity (see the next
step), thus preventing back strain.
b. Bring the person backward so that
your body supports them.
Rationale: people who faint or start
to fall usually pitch slightly forward
because of the momentum of
ambulating. Bringing the person’s
weight backward against your body
allows gradual movement to the
floor without injury to them.
c. Allow the person to slide down your
leg and lower them gently to the
floor, making sure their head does
not hit any objects.
Variation: two nurses
After the person stands, assume a
position with one nurse at either side.
Grasp the inferior aspect of the person’s
upper arm with your nearest hand and
their lower arm or hand with your other
hand. ❸ Rationale: this provides a secure
grip for each nurse.
Optional: place a walking belt around the
person’s waist. Each nurse grasps the
side handle with their near hand and the


lower aspect of the person’s upper arm
with the other hand.
Walk in unison with the person using a
smooth, even gait, at the same speed and
with steps the same size. ❸ Rationale:
this provides a greater feeling of security.


❸ Two nurses supporting an ambulatory
person
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.


If the person starts to fall and cannot
regain strength or balance, slip your arms
under their axillae, grasp their hands and
lower them gently to the floor or to a
nearby chair. ❹ Rationale: placing the
nurse’s arms under the person’s axillae
evenly balances the person’s weight
between the two nurses, preventing injury
to both the nurses and the person.
❹ Two nurses lowering a fainting person
to the floor


Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.
7. Document distance and duration of
ambulation in the person’s file using forms or
checklists supplemented by narrative notes
when appropriate. Include description of the
person’s gait (including body alignment) when
walking, pace, activity tolerance when walking
(e.g. pulse rate, facial colour, any shortness
of breath, feelings of dizziness or weakness),
degree of support required and respiratory
rate and blood pressure after initial
ambulation to compare with baseline data.
Evaluation
Establish a plan for continued ambulation based
on expected or normal ability for the person.


Chapter 47 Review


Chapter highlights
The ability to move freely, easily and purposefully in the
environment is essential for people to meet their basic needs.
Exercise and activity are essential components for maintaining
and regaining health and wellness.
Research on exercise has demonstrated it to be an excellent
strategy for preventing and treating some cardiovascular and
pulmonary diseases, mood disorders, diseases of ageing,
diabetes and immune diseases.
Purposeful coordinated movement of the body relies on the
integrated functioning of the musculoskeletal system, the
nervous system and the vestibular apparatus of the inner ear.
Body movement involves four basic elements: body alignment,
joint mobility, balance and coordinated movement.
People maintain alignment and balance when the line of gravity
passes through the centre of gravity and the base of support.
The broader the base of support and the lower the centre of
gravity, the greater the stability and balance achieved.
Exercise is physical activity performed to maintain muscle tone
and joint mobility, to enhance physiological functioning of body
systems and to improve physical fitness. Activity tolerance is the
type and amount of exercise or daily living activities an individual
can perform without experiencing adverse effects. Functional
strength is the ability to do work.
Exercise is classified as isotonic, isometric or isokinetic and as
either aerobic or anaerobic.


Many factors influence body alignment and activity. These
include growth and development, physical health, mental health,
personal values and attitudes, medications and prescribed
limitations to movement.
Immobility affects almost every body organ and system
adversely; complications also include psychosocial problems.
Exercise, by contrast, provides many benefits to the same body
organs and systems and can be used to prevent and treat many
disease processes.
Problems of immobility include disuse osteoporosis and atrophy;
contractures; diminished cardiac reserve; orthostatic
hypotension; venous stasis, oedema and thrombus formation;
decreased respiratory movement and pooling of secretions;
decreased metabolic rate and negative nitrogen balance; urinary
stasis, retention, infection and calculi; constipation; and varying
emotional reactions.
Complete bed rest is almost never required and is usually
dangerous due to the hazards of immobility. A risk–benefit
assessment and ongoing assessment of rationale for complete
bed rest is essential.
The nurse has responsibilities (a) to determine causes of
immobility and address these whenever possible (with the
person) with the goal of getting them moving as much and as
soon as possible, (b) to prevent the complications of immobility
and reduce the severity of any problems resulting from immobility
and (c) to partner with the person and appropriate support
people to design individualised exercise programs that promote
wellness.


Assessment relative to a person’s activity and exercise includes
a nursing history and physical examination of body alignment,
gait, joint appearance and movement, capabilities and limitations
for movement, muscle mass and strength, activity tolerance and
problems related to immobility.
An activity and exercise history includes daily activity level,
activity tolerance, type and frequency of exercise and factors
affecting mobility.
Body mechanics is the efficient, coordinated and safe use of the
body to move objects and carry out the activities of daily living.
Nurses must use good body mechanics in their daily work and
especially when moving and turning people in bed and assisting
people to make transfers. Proper body mechanics do not ensure
protection from injury, however, and nurses and caregivers are
encouraged to avoid manual lifting. At the very least, they should
avoid solo lifting, repositioning and transferring.
Positioning a person in good body alignment and changing the
position regularly and systematically are essential aspects of
nursing practice.
Before positioning someone who is dependent, the nurse should
plan a systematic 24-hour schedule for position changes,
including positions that provide for full extension of the neck, hips
and knees. The nurse also uses appropriate supportive devices
to maintain alignment and prevent strain on the person’s muscles
and joints.
Before moving, turning or transferring someone, the nurse must
consider the person’s health status and degree of exertion
permitted, physical ability to assist, ability to comprehend


instruction, degree of discomfort, their weight and whether to use
assistive devices or another caregiver to assist.
Assistance from others or the use of mechanical lifting aids is
essential for most adults or even adolescents.
Safety measures must always be employed when the nurse uses
a wheelchair or trolley to undertake a move or transfer.
Ambulating techniques that facilitate normal walking gait yet
provide needed supports are most effective. The nurse can
assist people to prepare for ambulation by helping them become
as independent as possible while in bed.
Pre-ambulatory exercises that strengthen the muscles for
walking are essential for someone who has been immobilised for
a prolonged period.
Specific instructions about appropriate use of walking sticks,
walking frames and crutches are required prior to use.
Concept check
1. To increase stability during a transfer, the nurse increases the
base of support by performing which of the following?
1. Leaning slightly backward.
2. Spacing the feet further apart.
3. Tensing the abdominal muscles.
4. Bending the knees.
2. Isotonic exercises such as walking are intended to achieve
which of the following? Select all that apply.


1. Increase muscle tone and improve circulation.
2. Increase blood pressure.
3. Increase muscle mass and strength.
4. Decrease heart rate and cardiac output.
5. Maintain joint range of motion.
3. Five minutes after a person’s first postoperative exercise, the
person’s vital signs have not yet returned to baseline. An
appropriate nursing diagnosis might be:
1. Activity intolerance.
2. Risk of activity intolerance.
3. Impaired physical mobility.
4. Risk of disuse syndrome.
4. Which of the following statements regarding a person with
one weak leg using crutches on stairs indicates a need for
increased teaching?
1. ‘Going up, the strong leg goes first, then the weaker
leg with both crutches.’
2. ‘Going down, the weaker leg goes first with both
crutches, then the strong leg.’
3. ‘The weaker leg always goes first with both crutches.’
4. ‘A walking stick or single crutch may be used instead of
both crutches if held on the weaker side.’
5. Which of the following drugs seem to be implicated most
frequently as contributing to falls and fractures in older
people?


1. Sinemet.
2. Benzodiazepines.
3. Elavil.
4. Lasix.
6. When assessing gait, nurses should look for and encourage
which of the following?
1. The spine rotates, initiating locomotion.
2. Gaze is slightly downward.
3. Toes strike the ground before the heel.
4. Arm on the same side as the swing-through foot
moves forward at the same time.
7. Performance of activities of daily living (ADLs) and active
range of motion (ROM) exercises can be accomplished
simultaneously as illustrated by which of the following? Select
all that apply.
1. Elbow flexion with eating and bathing.
2. Elbow extension with shaving and eating.
3. Wrist hyperextension with writing.
4. Thumb ROM with eating and writing.
5. Hip flexion with walking.
8. Because the person weighs 115 kg, the nurse should provide
assistive personnel with instructions that reflect an awareness
of workplace injury. Which of the following is most
appropriate?


1. ‘Using proper body mechanics will prevent you from
injuring yourself.’
2. ‘You are physically fit and at lesser risk of injury when
transferring the person.’
3. ‘Use the mechanical lift and another person to transfer
from the bed to the chair.’
4. ‘Use the back belt to avoid hurting your back.’
9. The person is ambulating for the first time after surgery. They
tell the nurse, ‘I feel faint’. The best action by the nurse
includes which of the following?
1. Find another nurse for help.
2. Return the person to their room as quickly as possible.
3. Tell the person to take rapid, shallow breaths.
4. Assist the person to a nearby chair.
10. The nurse is performing an assessment of a person who is
immobilised. Which of the following assessments causes the
nurse to take action?
1. Heart rate 86 BPM.
2. Reddened area on sacrum.
3. Non-productive cough.
4. Urine output of 50 mL/hour.
Focus on critical thinking


1. What health promotion activities can nurses engage in to
ensure better outcomes?
2. What are the underlying determinants of good physiological
health?
3. Physical inactivity contributes to so many preventable chronic
diseases. Why do you think it is so difficult to get people
physically active?


Chapter 48 Sleep
Tracy Flenady, Rachelle Cole, Trish Channell
Learning outcomes
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Explain the functions and the physiology of sleep.
Identify the characteristics of the sleep states: NREM and REM
sleep.
Describe variations in sleep patterns throughout the lifespan.
Identify factors that affect sleep.
Describe common sleep disorders.
Identify the components of a sleep pattern assessment.


Develop nursing diagnoses, outcomes and nursing interventions
related to sleep problems.
Describe interventions that promote normal sleep.
Key terms
biological rhythms

Sleep is a basic human need; it is a universal
biological process common to all people.
Humans spend about one-third of their lives
asleep. We require sleep for many reasons: to
cope with daily stresses, to prevent fatigue, to
conserve energy, to restore the mind and body
and to enjoy life more fully. Sleep enhances
daytime functioning. It is integral for optimal
health and wellbeing, impacting on the
cognitive, physiological, psychological, physical
and emotional aspects of our life (Hirshkowitz et
al. ).
1 Hirshkowitz, M., Whiton, K., Albert, S. M., .?.?. Ware, J. C.
(2015). National Sleep Foundation’s updated sleep
duration recommendations: Final report. Sleep Health, 1(4),
1233–1243. Doi: 10.1016/j.sleh.2015.10.004.
Sleep is an important factor in a person’s quality
of life. Despite this, a report prepared for the
Sleep Health Foundation stated that an
estimated 7.4 million Australian adults did not
get the sleep they require, resulting in adverse
1
2


effects on health (Sleep Health Foundation ).
Furthermore, many members of the general
public and health professionals are unaware of
the consequences of chronic sleep loss (e.g.
increased risk of hypertension, diabetes,
obesity, depression, heart attack and stroke). A
recent national sleep study was conducted by
the University of Sydney ; results to date have
shown that more than 50% of participants
indicated that they felt tired during the day at
least a few days per week, with more females
than males reporting this. According to a report
by Boccabella and Malouf , women experience
more daytime sleepiness and are predisposed
to having sleep disorders.

Road accidents carry a huge cost to the
community, not only in direct medical costs. It is
estimated that fatigue contributes to 20–30% of
all road deaths (Centre for Road Accident
Research and Road Safety—Queensland
(CARRS-Q) ). Driving while sleep impaired is
similar to driving with a blood alcohol reading of
greater than 0.05 and can be as high as 0.15
after 21 hours without sleep. This can lead to
death or work-related accidents (Sleep Health
Foundation 2019; CARRS-Q 2018).
5 Centre for Road Accident Research and Road Safety—

Factsheet. Retrieved from <www.carrsq.qut.edu.au>.
Austroads  publishes a standard for assessing
fitness to drive that incorporates a discussion of
the relevance of sleep disorders to driving,
guidelines for assessment and management,
advice to patients and medical standards for

6 Austroads (2016). Assessing Fitness to Drive for
Commercial and Private Vehicle Drivers. Sydney:

5
6


Physiology of sleep
Historically, sleep was considered a state of unconsciousness. More
recently, sleep
 has come to be considered an altered state of
consciousness in which the individual’s perception of and reaction to
the environment are decreased. Sleep is characterised by minimal
physical activity, variable levels of consciousness, changes in the
body’s physiological processes and decreased responsiveness to
external stimuli. Some environmental stimuli, such as a smoke
detector alarm, will usually wake a sleeper, whereas many other
noises will not. It appears that individuals respond to meaningful
stimuli while sleeping and selectively disregard non-meaningful
stimuli. For example, a mother may respond to her baby’s crying but
not to the crying of another baby.
The cyclical nature of sleep is thought to be controlled by centres
located in the lower part of the brain. Neurons within the reticular
formation, located in the brain stem, integrate sensory information
from the peripheral nervous system and relay the information to the
cerebral cortex (see the following ‘Anatomy & physiology
review
’). The upper part of the reticular formation consists of a
network of ascending nerve fibres called the reticular activating
system (RAS), which is involved with the sleep–wake cycle. An intact
cerebral cortex and reticular formation are necessary for the
regulation of sleep and waking states.


Neurotransmitters, located within neurons in the brain, affect the
sleep–wake cycles. For example, serotonin is thought to lessen the
response to sensory stimulation and gamma-aminobutyric acid
(GABA) to shut off the activity in the neurons of the reticular
activating system. Another key factor to sleep is exposure to
darkness. Darkness and preparing for sleep cause a decrease in
stimulation of the RAS. During this time, the pineal gland in the brain
begins to actively secrete the natural hormone melatonin and the
person feels less alert. During sleep, the growth hormone is
secreted and cortisol is inhibited.
With the beginning of daylight, melatonin is at its lowest level in the
body and the stimulating hormone, cortisol, is at its highest.
Wakefulness is also associated with high levels of acetylcholine,
dopamine and noradrenaline. Acetylcholine is released in the
reticular formation, dopamine in the midbrain and noradrenaline in
the pons. These neurotransmitters are localised within the reticular
formation and influence cerebral cortical arousal.
Circadian rhythms
Biological rhythms
 exist in plants, animals and humans. In
humans, these are controlled from within the body and synchronised
with environmental factors, such as light and darkness. The most
familiar biological rhythm is the circadian rhythm. The term circadian
is from the Latin circa dies, meaning ‘about a day’. Although sleep
and waking cycles are the best known of the circadian rhythms,


body temperature, blood pressure and many other physiological
functions also follow a circadian pattern (Tranah et al. ).
7 Tranah, G. J., Blackwell, T., Ancoli-Israel, S., .?.?. Stone, K. L. (2010). Circadian activity
rhythms and mortality: The study of osteoporotic fractures. Journal of the American Geriatric
Society, 58, 282–290. Doi: 10.1111/j.1532-5415.2009.02674.x.
Sleep is a complex biological rhythm. When a person’s biological
clock coincides with the sleep–wake cycles, the person is said to be
in circadian synchronisation; that is, the person is awake when the
body temperature is highest and asleep when the body temperature
is lowest. Circadian regularity begins to develop by the sixth week of
life, and by 3 to 6 months most infants have a regular sleep–wake
cycle.
Types of sleep
Sleep architecture
 refers to the basic organisation of normal
sleep. There are two types of sleep: NREM
 (non-rapid-eye-
movement) sleep
 and REM
 (rapid-eye-movement) sleep
.
During sleep, NREM and REM sleep alternate in cycles. Irregular
cycling and/or absent sleep stages are associated with sleep
disorders. Abbott and Videnovic ( ) report that sleep disruption is an
early symptom of neurodegenerative disease.
8 Abbott, S. M. & Videnovic, A. (2016). Chronic sleep disturbance and neural injury: Links to
neurodegenerative disease. Nature and Science of Sleep, 8, 55–61. Doi:
10.2147/NSS.S78947.
7
8


NREM sleep
NREM sleep occurs when activity in the RAS is inhibited. About 75%
to 80% of sleep during a night is NREM sleep. NREM sleep is
divided into three stages, each associated with distinct brain activity
and physiology. Stage 1 is the stage of very light sleep and lasts only
a few minutes. During this stage, the person feels drowsy and
relaxed, the eyes roll from side to side and the heart and respiratory
rates drop slightly. The sleeper can be readily woken and may deny
that they were sleeping.
ANATO M Y & PHYSIO LO G Y REVIEW
Reticular activating system
Nerve impulses from the senses reach the reticular activating
system (RAS), which is in the reticular formation (located in
the brain stem) with projections to the hypothalamus and
cerebral cortex. The nerve fibres in the RAS relay impulses to
the cerebral cortex for perception by the person.
Questions
1. How would you describe activity of the RAS in
preparation for and during sleep?
2. What happens physiologically when your alarm clock
wakes you in the morning?


3. What areas of the brain are affected by head trauma
or stroke and affect an individual’s level of alertness?


Stage 2 is the stage of light sleep during which body processes
continue to slow down. The eyes are generally still, the heart and
respiratory rates decrease slightly and body temperature falls. Stage
2 lasts only about 10 to 15 minutes but constitutes 44% to 55% of
total sleep. An individual in stage 2 requires more intense stimuli
than in stage 1 to wake.
Stage 3 is the deepest stage of sleep, differing only in the
percentage of delta waves recorded during a 30-second period.
During deep sleep or delta sleep, the sleeper’s heart and respiratory
rates drop 20% to 30% below those exhibited during waking hours.
The sleeper is difficult to arouse. The person is not disturbed by
sensory stimuli, the skeletal muscles are very relaxed, reflexes are
diminished and snoring is most likely to occur. This stage is essential
for restoring energy and releasing important growth hormones. See
Box 48.1
.
BO X
48.1 Physiological changes during
NREM sleep
Arterial blood pressure falls.
Pulse rate decreases.
Peripheral blood vessels dilate.
Cardiac output decreases.


Skeletal muscles relax.
Basal metabolic rate decreases 10% to 30%.
Growth hormone levels peak.
Intracranial pressure decreases.
Clinical consideration
In a sleep-deprived person, the loss of NREM
sleep causes apathy, depression, irritability,
confusion, disorientation, hallucinations,
impaired memory and paranoia (Mehta et al. ).
9 Mehta, R., Singh, A., Bókkon, I. & Nath Mallick, B. (2016). REM
sleep and its loss-associated epigenetic regulation with reference
to noradrenaline in particular. Current Neuropharmacology, 14(1),
28–40. Doi: 10.2174/1570159X13666150 414185737.
REM sleep
REM sleep usually recurs about every 90 minutes and lasts 5 to 30
minutes. Most dreams take place during REM sleep but usually will
9


not be remembered unless the person arouses briefly at the end of
the REM period.
During REM sleep, the brain is highly active and brain metabolism
may increase as much as 20%. For example, during REM sleep,
levels of acetylcholine and dopamine increase, with the highest
levels of acetylcholine release occurring during REM sleep. Because
both of these neurotransmitters are associated with cortical
activation, it makes sense that their levels would be high during
dreaming sleep. This type of sleep is also called paradoxical sleep
because electroencephalogram (EEG) activity resembles that of
wakefulness. Distinctive eye movements occur, voluntary muscle
tone is dramatically decreased and deep tendon reflexes are absent.
In this phase, the sleeper may be difficult to arouse or may wake
spontaneously, gastric secretions increase and heart and respiratory
rates often are irregular. It is thought that the regions of the brain
that are used in learning, thinking and organising information are
stimulated during REM sleep.
Sleep cycles
During a sleep cycle, people typically pass through NREM and REM
sleep, the complete cycle usually lasting about 90 to 110 minutes in
adults. In the first sleep cycle, a sleeper usually passes through all
of the first two stages of NREM sleep in a total of about 20 to 30
minutes. Stage 3 lasts about 50 to 60 minutes. After stage 3 NREM,
the sleep passes back through stages 2 and 1 over about 20


minutes. Thereafter, the first REM stage occurs, lasting about 10
minutes, completing the first sleep cycle. It is not unusual for the
first REM period to be very brief or even skipped entirely. The
healthy adult sleeper usually experiences four to six cycles of sleep
during 7 to 8 hours (see Figure 48.1
). The sleeper who is woken
during any stage must begin anew at stage 1 NREM sleep and
proceed through all the stages to REM sleep.
Figure 48.1
Time spent in REM and non-REM stages of sleep in an adult.
The duration of NREM stages and REM sleep varies throughout the
sleep period. During the early part of the night, the deep sleep
periods are longer. As the night progresses, the sleeper spends less
time in stage 3 of NREM sleep. REM sleep increases and dreams


tend to lengthen. Before sleep ends, periods of near wakefulness
occur and stages 1 and 2 NREM sleep and REM sleep dominate.


Functions of sleep
The effects of sleep on the body are not completely understood.
Sleep exerts physiological effects on both the nervous system and
other body structures. Sleep in some way restores normal levels of
activity and normal balance between parts of the nervous system.
Sleep is also necessary for protein synthesis, which allows repair
processes to occur.
The role of sleep in psychological wellbeing is best noticed by the
deterioration in mental functioning related to sleep loss. People who
receive inadequate amounts of sleep tend to become emotionally
irritable, have poor concentration and experience difficulty making
decisions.


Normal sleep patterns and
requirements
Although it used to be believed that maintaining a regular sleep–
wake rhythm is more important than the number of hours actually
slept, recent research has shown that sleep deprivation is
associated with significant cognitive and health problems. Although
re-establishing the sleep–wake rhythm (e.g. after the disruption of
surgery) is an important aspect of nursing, it is not appropriate to
curtail or decrease daytime napping in hospitalised people.
Newborns 0–3 months
Newborns are recommended to sleep 14 to 17 hours a day on an
irregular schedule, with periods of 1 to 3 hours spent awake. Unlike
older children and adults, newborns enter REM sleep (called active
sleep during the newborn period) immediately. Rapid eye
movements are observable through closed lids and the body
movements and irregular respirations may be observed. NREM
sleep (also called quiet sleep during the newborn period) is
characterised by regular respirations, closed eyes and the absence
of body and eye movements. Newborns spend nearly 50% of their
time in each of these states and the sleep cycle is about 50 minutes.


It is best to put newborns to bed when they are sleepy but not
asleep. Newborns can be encouraged to sleep less during the day
by exposing them to light and by playing more with them during the
day hours. As evening approaches, the environment can be less
bright and quieter with less activity (Ohayon et al.
; Hirshkowitz et
al. 2015).
10 Ohayon, M., Wickwire, E. M. Hirshkowitz, M., .?.?. Vitiello, M. V. (2017). National Sleep
Foundation’s sleep quality recommendations: First report. Sleep Health, 3(1): 6–19.
Infants 4–11 months
At first, infants wake every 3 or 4 hours, eat and then go back to
sleep. Periods of wakefulness gradually increase during the first
months. By 6 months, most infants sleep through the night (from
midnight to 5 a.m.) and begin to establish a pattern of daytime naps.
At the end of the first year, an infant usually takes two naps per day
and should get about 12 to 15 hours of sleep in 24 hours (Ohayon et
al. 2017; Hirshkowitz et al. 2015).
About half of the infant’s sleep time is spent in light sleep. During
light sleep, the infant exhibits a great deal of activity, such as
movement, gurgles and coughing. Parents need to make sure that
infants are truly awake before picking them up for feeding and
changing. Putting infants to bed when they are drowsy but not
asleep helps them to become ‘self-soothers’. This means that they
fall asleep independently and, if they do wake at night, they can put
10


themselves back to sleep. Infants who become used to parental
assistance at bedtime may become ‘signallers’ and cry for their
parents to help them return to sleep at night (Hirshkowitz et al.
2015).
Research note
Are there barriers to following the SIDS and Kids Safe
Sleeping Program recommendations for infants?
E. R. Colson, L. K. McCabe, K. Fox, S. Levenson, T. Colton, G. Lister & M. J. Corwin (2005). Barriers to
following the back-to-sleep recommendations: Insights from focus groups with inner-city caregivers.
Ambulatory Pediatrics, 5(6), 349–354; Queensland Health (2008). Sleep Baby in Their Own Safe
Sleeping Environment Next to the Parent’s Bed for the First Six to Twelve Months of Life. Retrieved
from <www.sidsandkids.org/wp-content/uploads/Safe-Infant-Sleeping-Policy-Statement-and-
Guidelines.pdf>.
Research has shown that placing infants to sleep in the
supine position decreases the risk of sudden infant death
syndrome (SIDS). The SIDS and Kids Safe Sleeping Program
educational initiative has resulted in many more caregivers
placing their infants in the supine position for sleep. The
campaign promotes five key messages:
1. Put baby on back to sleep from birth.
2. Sleep baby with face uncovered.
3. Avoid exposing baby to cigarette smoke.
4. Provide an environment for sleeping for baby that is
safe (cot, mattress, bedding).


5. Put baby to sleep in his/her own safe environment
beside parent’s bed until 6 to 12 months of age
(Queensland Health ).
11 Queensland Health (2008). Sleep Baby in Their Own Safe Sleeping
Environment Next to the Parent’s Bed for the First Six to Twelve Months of
Life. Retrieved from <www.sidsandkids.org>.
The rate of SIDS deaths in Australia has remained relatively
unchanged since 2003. In 2010, the rate of SIDS was
reported as 27 deaths per 100 000 live births, with most
occurring between 29 and 364 days of age; of those, 72%
were males (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare
(AIHW)
). In 2015, SIDS was reported as the cause of death
in 5% of infants (AIHW
). The incidence of SIDS among
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander infants remains higher
than among non-Indigenous Australians, with a rate of
approximately 60 per 100 000 live births (Australian Health
Ministers’ Advisory Council ). A longitudinal birth study
involving 159 mothers from an Aboriginal community in
Australia found that while the cohort instinctively slept their
babies in a supine position, other risk-prevention strategies
such as maintaining a cigarette-free environment and
providing a safe sleeping environment still needed work
(Queensland Health ; Knight et al.
). Three infants from
within the study cohort died during the first 18 months, with
their deaths identified as SIDS related. Of the deaths, all
three mothers smoked ante- and postnatally, all three babies
had been placed on their back but were found face down and
11
12
13
14
15
16


two of the three babies were found by the coroner to have
been sleeping in unsafe bedding (one on a sofa, the other co-
sleeping on a mattress on the floor).
12 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2012). A Picture of Australia’s
Children 2012. Cat. no. PHE 167. Canberra: AIHW.
13 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2015). Leading Causes of
Death. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
14 Australian Health Ministers’ Advisory Council (2012). Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander Health Performance Framework 2012 Report. Canberra: AHMAC.
15 Queensland Health (2019). Safe Sleeping Fact Sheet. Retrieved from
<http://conditions.health.qld.gov.au>.
16 Knight, J., Webster, V., Kemp, L. & Comino, E. (2013). Sudden infant death
syndrome in an urban Aboriginal community. Journal of Paediatrics and Child
Health, 49, 1025–1031. Doi: 10.1111/jpc.12306.
In the US, researchers (Colson et al.
) wanted to determine
new barriers and more information about previously identified
barriers that interfere with adherence to the Back-to-Sleep
recommendations (which are very similar to the Australian
SIDS and Kids advice) among inner-city caregivers, primarily
African Americans. They conducted a qualitative research
study using focus groups.
17 Colson, E. R., McCabe, L. K., Fox, K., Levenson, S., Colton, T., Lister, G. &
Corwin, M. J. (2005). Barriers to following the back-to-sleep recommendations:
Insights from focus groups with inner-city caregivers. Ambulatory Pediatrics, 5(6),
349–354.
17


Four themes were identified:
1. Safety. All were concerned about the safety of their
infants while they slept, which prompted some of the
participants to bring their infants into their beds for
closer observation. Many believed that the infant would
choke if placed in the supine position.
2. Comfort. Many of the participants made their decision
about the position of the infant based on their
perception of whether the baby seemed comfortable.
Some felt that the infant looked more comfortable on
its side or stomach and the baby slept longer in that
position. Some felt that the infant seemed more
comfortable close to them and had the infant sleep in
bed with them.
3. Advice. Participants trusted the advice of older female
family members with previous child-rearing experience.
They also trusted their own instincts and their previous
experience. Some did not trust health care providers
as a reliable source of advice, especially about the
care of infants. They recommended that advice from
health professionals be delivered in a certain way:
‘Don’t tell us . . . Tell us why’.
4. Knowledge. Some of the participants believed that
SIDS could only happen if the infant slept in a cot
(SIDS is sometimes called crib or cot death) and, as a
result, did not place their infant in a cot. Some doubted
the existence of SIDS and others referred to religious


beliefs (e.g. ‘It’s an act of God . . . there is no way to
really stop it’).
Implications The generalisability of this US study is limited
because the data were collected in only two cities. However,
the study did identify barriers to following the Back-to-Sleep
recommendations. Nurses should work with caregivers to
identify their knowledge about SIDS and implement effective
teaching strategies that will enhance the trust and knowledge
of the caregiver.
Toddlers 1–2 years
Between 11 and 14 hours of sleep per day is recommended for
children 1 to 2 years of age (Hirshkowitz et al. 2015). Most still need
an afternoon nap, but the need for mid-morning naps gradually
decreases. The toddler may exhibit a great deal of resistance to
going to bed and may wake during the night. Night-time fears and
nightmares are also common. A security object such as a blanket or
stuffed animal may help. Parents need assurance that, if the child
has had adequate attention from them during the day, maintaining a
daily sleep schedule and consistent bedtime routine will promote
good sleep habits for the entire family.


Preschoolers 3–5 years
The National Sleep Foundation considered the health and wellbeing,
as well as cognitive, emotional and physical health, of preschoolers
before recommending they have 10 to 13 hours of sleep per day.
Also considered was published evidence that preschoolers who
sleep less than 9 hours per night have a greater probability of being
obese than those sleeping 10 hours or more (Hirshkowitz et al.
2015). Sleep needs fluctuate in relation to activity and growth spurts.
Many children of this age dislike bedtime and resist by requesting
another story, game or TV program. The 3- to 5-year-old may
become restless and irritable if sleep requirements are not met.
Parents can help children who resist bedtime by maintaining a
regular and consistent sleep schedule. It also helps to have a
relaxing bedtime routine that ends in the child’s room. Preschool
children wake frequently at night and they may be afraid of the dark
or experience night terrors or nightmares. Often limiting or
eliminating TV will reduce the number of nightmares.
School-age children 6–13 years
Research indicating associations between short sleep in school-age
children (6 to 13 years of age) and lower cognitive functioning and
poorer academic performance was a major factor when the National
Sleep Foundation formed its recommendations of between 9 and 11


hours of sleep per day for school-age children (Hirshkowitz et al.
2015). However, most receive less because of increasing demands
(e.g. homework, sports, social activities). They may also be
spending more time at the computer and watching TV. Some may
be drinking caffeinated beverages. All of these activities can lead to
difficulty falling asleep and fewer hours of sleep. Nurses are ideally
positioned to be able to educate parents and school-age children
about healthy sleep habits. A regular and consistent sleep schedule
and bedtime routine need to be continued.
Teenagers 14–17 years
The National Sleep Foundation recommends 8 to 10 hours of sleep
per night for teenagers. There is evidence that less than this amount
on a regular basis could potentially result in decreased alertness, car
accidents, depressed mood, obesity, poor health and low academic
performance (Hirshkowitz et al. 2015). Few teenagers actually get
the required amount of sleep and, interestingly, while more than half
of the teens knew they were not getting enough sleep, 90% of the
parents believed their teen was getting enough sleep. Nurses can
support parents to recognise signs and symptoms that indicate their
teen is not getting enough sleep. See ‘Clinical manifestations
’.
As children reach adolescence, their circadian rhythms tend to shift.
Research in the 1990s found that later sleep and wake patterns
among adolescents are biologically determined; the natural tendency
for teenagers is to stay up late at night and wake up later in the


morning (Marczyk Organek et al.
). Some schools, however, start
at 8 a.m., which is in conflict with adolescents’ sleep patterns and
needs and contributes to their sleep deprivation (see Figure
48.2
). As a result, some schools are reviewing early start times.
During adolescence, boys begin to experience nocturnal
emissions
 (orgasm and emission of semen during sleep), known
as ‘wet dreams’, several times each month. Boys need to be
informed about this normal development to prevent embarrassment
and fear.
18 Marczyk Organek, K., Taylor, D., Petrie, T., Martin, S., Greenleaf, C., Deitch, J. & Ruiz, J.
(2015). Adolescent sleep disparities: Sex and racial/ethnic differences. Sleep Health, 36–39.
Doi: 10.1016/j.sleh.2014.12.003.
Figure 48.2
18


Many adolescents do not get enough sleep.
Source: Patrick Watson.
Clinical consideration
Children who have a TV and/or computer in
their bedroom are more likely to get less sleep.


Adults 18–64 years
Most healthy adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night (Hirshkowitz
et al. 2015). However, there is individual variation as some adults
may be able to function well (e.g. without sleepiness or drowsiness)
with 6 hours of sleep; others may need 10 hours to function
optimally. Signs that may indicate that a person is not getting
enough sleep include falling asleep or becoming drowsy during a
task that is not fatiguing (e.g. listening to a boring or monotonous
presentation), not being able to concentrate or remember
information, and being unreasonably irritable with others.
In a guide to sleep disorders for Australian health care practitioners
(Cunnington, Junge & Fernando ; Rajaratnam, Howard &
Grunstein ), it is reported that some adults are particularly
vulnerable to not getting enough sleep: students, shift workers,
travellers and people suffering from acute stress, depression or
chronic pain. Adults working long hours or multiple jobs may find
their sleep less refreshing. Also, the sleep habits of children have an
impact on the adults caring for them. Parents and caregivers whose
children get the least amount of sleep are twice as likely to say they
sleep less than 6 hours a night (Hirshkowitz et al. 2015). Parents of
infants lose the most sleep—nearly an hour on a typical night.
Women may experience more disrupted sleep during pregnancy,
menses and the peri-menopausal period. Sleep deprivation is a
widespread issue in the adult population, affecting 45- to 54-year-
olds, especially due to the work commitments this cohort maintains.
19
20


Insufficient sleep for this age group manifests as reduced
multitasking ability, weight regulation issues, reduced job safety,
diminished mental health, irregular blood pressure and poor
cardiovascular health.
19 Cunnington, D., Junge, M. & Fernando, A. (2013). Insomnia: Prevalence, consequences
and effective treatment. The Medical Journal of Australia (Supplement), 199(8), S36–S40.
20 Rajaratnam, S., Howard, M. & Grunstein, R. (2013). Sleep loss and circadian disruption in
shift work: Health burden and management. The Medical Journal of Australia (Supplement),
199(8), S11–S15.
Clinical manifestations
Sleep deprivation and sleep problems in adolescence
The adolescent
Has difficulty waking in the morning for school.
Falls asleep in class or during quiet times of the day.
Increases the use of caffeinated beverages such as
coffee or cola.
Feels tired, making it difficult to initiate or persist in
projects such as school assignments.
Is irritable and anxious, and gets angry easily on days
when they get less sleep.
Is involved in many extracurricular activities, has a job and
stays up late doing homework every night, cutting into
sleep time.
Sleeps extra-long periods on the weekend.


Source: National Sleep Foundation
. Parents of Teens: Recognise the Signs and Symptoms of
Sleep Deprivation and Sleep Problems. Retrieved from <https://sleepfoundation.org/sites/default/
files/teensigns.pdf>. Used with permission of the National Sleep Foundation. For further information,
please visit <www.sleepfoundation.org>.
21 National Sleep Foundation (n.d.). Parents of Teens: Recognise the Signs and Symptoms of Sleep
Deprivation and Sleep Problems. Retrieved from <https://sleepfoundation.org>.
Nurses should discuss the importance of obtaining sufficient sleep
and tips on how to promote sleep that results in the person waking
up feeling restored or refreshed. See the ‘Patient education
’ box
later in this chapter.
Older adults and over
A hallmark change with age is a tendency towards earlier bedtime
