Pain quality
Descriptive adjectives help people communicate the quality of pain. A headache
may be described as ‘unbearable’ or an abdominal pain as ‘piercing like a knife’.


The astute clinician can glean subtle clinical clues from the quality of the pain
described; thus, it is important to record the description verbatim. Some of the
commonly used pain descriptors are listed in Table 49.4
. Note that the term
‘unbearable’ is listed as an affective term and ‘piercing’ is a sensory term. Both
pains are real physical conditions signalling an underlying condition, but the
affective description ‘unbearable’ suggests that there is a coexisting emotional
distress that needs to be addressed as well. Pain described as burning or shock-
like tends to be neuropathic in origin and may be responsive to anticonvulsants
(e.g. gabapentin), with or without an opioid (e.g. morphine).
Table 49.4 Commonly used pain descriptors
Pattern
The pattern of pain includes time of onset, duration and recurrence or intervals
without pain. The nurse therefore aims to identify when the pain began; how long
the pain lasts; whether it recurs and, if so, the length of the interval without pain;
and when the pain last occurred. Attention to the pattern of pain helps the nurse
anticipate and meet the needs of the person as well as recognise patterns of
significant concern (e.g. chest pain only on exertion).
Precipitating factors
Certain activities sometimes precede pain. For example, physical exertion may
precede chest pain or abdominal pain may occur after eating. These observations
can help prevent pain and determine its cause. Environmental factors such as
extreme cold or heat and extremes of humidity can affect some types of pain. For
example, people with rheumatic conditions have worse pain on cold, damp days
or just before a large storm. Physical and emotional stressors can also precipitate
pain. Strong emotions can trigger a migraine headache or an episode of chest
pain. Extreme physical exertion can trigger muscle spasms in the neck, shoulders
or back.


Alleviating factors
Nurses should encourage people to describe anything they have done to alleviate
the pain (e.g. home remedies such as herbal teas, medications, rest, applications
of heat or cold, prayer or distractions such as TV). It is important to explore and
understand the effect any of these measures had on the pain, whether or not
relief was obtained or whether the pain became worse.
Associated symptoms
Also included in the clinical appraisal of pain are associated symptoms such as
nausea, vomiting, dizziness and diarrhoea. These symptoms may relate to
the onset of the pain or they may result from the presence of the pain.
Effect on ADLs
Understanding how ADLs are affected by pain assists the nurse to understand
the person’s perspective on the pain’s severity. The nurse encourages the person
to describe how the pain has affected the following aspects of life:
sleep
appetite
concentration
work/school
interpersonal relationships
marital relations/sex
home activities
driving/walking
leisure activities
emotional status (mood, irritability, depression, anxiety).
A rating scale of none, a little or a great deal, or another suitable scale can be
used to determine the degree of alteration.


Coping resources
Each individual will exhibit personal ways of coping with pain. Strategies may
relate to earlier pain experiences or the specific meaning of the pain; some may
reflect religious or cultural influences. Nurses can encourage and support the
person’s use of methods known to have helped in modifying pain unless they are
specifically contraindicated. Strategies may include seeking quiet and solitude,
learning about their condition, pursuing interesting or exciting activities (for
distraction), prayer (or other meaningful rituals) or social support (from family,
friends, support groups etc.).
Affective responses
Affective responses vary according to the situation, the degree and duration of
pain, the interpretation of it and many other factors. The nurse should endeavour
to explore the person’s feelings of anxiety, fear, exhaustion, depression or a
sense of failure. People with chronic pain have a significantly higher incidence of
anxiety, depression and thoughts of suicide than the general population (Velley &
Mohit
). Therefore, it may be necessary to assess the person’s mental health,
including risk of suicide. In such situations, the nurse needs to ask the person,
‘Do you ever feel so bad that you want to die? Have you considered harming
yourself or others recently?’. The findings from a meta-analysis research found
that individuals with ongoing physical pain have increased suicidal ideation and an
increased risk of dying by suicide (Campbell et al. 2015). For those who express
suicidal intent, nurses need to be familiar with state regulations, organisational
policies and available resources to guide practice in this area.
44 Velley, A. M. & Mohit, S. (2018). Epidemiology of pain and relation to psychiatric disorders. Progress in
Neuro-Psychopharmacology and Biological Psychiatry, 87, 159–167.
Observation of behavioural and physiological
responses
44


There are wide variations in non-verbal responses to pain. For people who are
very young, aphasic, confused or disoriented, non-verbal expressions may be the
only means of communicating pain. Facial expression is often the first indication
of pain and it may be the only one. Clenched teeth, tightly shut eyes, open
sombre eyes, biting of the lower lip and other facial grimaces may be indicative of
pain. Vocalisations such as moaning and groaning, or crying and screaming, are
sometimes associated with pain.
Immobilisation of the body or a part of the body may also indicate pain. The
person with chest pain often holds the left arm across the chest. A person with
abdominal pain may tense the abdominal wall muscles to minimise pain to the
inflamed organs and may assume a position of comfort, with the knees and hips
flexed.
Body movement can also indicate pain—for example, people may move
reluctantly or may toss and turn in bed. Involuntary movements such as a
reflexive jerking away from a needle inserted through the skin indicate pain. An
adult may be able to control this reflex; however, a child may be unable or
unwilling to do so. Rhythmic limb movements or rubbing an area may indicate
pain. An adult or child may assume a fetal position and rock back and forth when
experiencing abdominal pain. During labour, a woman may massage her
abdomen rhythmically with her hands.
Behavioural changes such as confusion and restlessness may be indicators of
pain in both cognitively intact and cognitively impaired older people. Older adults
with chronic pain may become hostile or aggressive.
It is important to note that behavioural responses are not reliable indicators of the
presence or severity of pain. When pain is chronic, there are rarely overt
behavioural responses because the individual develops personal coping styles for
dealing with pain, discomfort or suffering.
Physiological responses vary with the origin and duration of the pain. Early in the
onset of acute pain the sympathetic nervous system is stimulated, resulting in


increased blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, pallor, diaphoresis and
pupil dilation. The body does not sustain the increased sympathetic function over
a prolonged period and therefore the sympathetic nervous system adapts,
making the physiological responses less evident or even absent. Physiological
responses are most likely to be absent in people with chronic pain because of
autonomic nervous system adaptation. Thus, measures of physiological
responses (e.g. pulse, blood pressure) are poor indicators of the presence,
absence or severity of pain and should not be used.
Research note
What are nurses’ knowledge and attitudes regarding paediatric pain
management in an Australian paediatric hospital?
D. Peirce, V. Corkish, M. Lane & S. Wilson (
). Nurses’ knowledge and attitudes regarding pediatric pain management in
Western Australia. Pain Management Nursing, 19(6), 707–717.
45 Peirce, D., Corkish,V., Lane, M. & Wilson, S. (2018). Nurses’ knowledge and attitudes regarding pediatric pain
management in Western Australia. Pain Management Nursing, 19(6), 707–717.
It is well recognised that managing pain is an important aspect of nursing
care and nursing knowledge. In fact, pain has been nominated as the fifth
vital sign. However, pain in children is complex and research has reported
that children consistently describe experiencing moderate to severe pain
when in hospital. These reports indicate that pain management for children
is not completely understood or well managed by clinicians.
The study was conducted in a major teaching hospital in Western Australia
and used a cross-sectional descriptive study design. There were 261
nurses who participated in the study from a possible cohort of 590 eligible
participants. The participants answered 64 questions around nurses’
attitudes about the physiology, sociology and psychology of pain in
children.
The study found that outdated beliefs and knowledge deficits in nurses
contributed to poor pain management and that even when nurses
45


understood the most recent evidence-based knowledge, it did not always
translate into changed practice.
Implications Competent nurses undertake regular and ongoing education
so they can reflect on and examine their practice to ensure it is aligned
with current knowledge. Ongoing education and reflective practice are
skills that enable nurses to make sound clinical decisions.
Daily pain diary
For people who experience chronic pain, a daily diary may help the person and
the nurse identify pain patterns and factors that exacerbate or mediate the pain
experience. In home care the family or other caregiver can be taught to complete
the diary with the family member who is unable to do it alone. Diary entries should
be made three times a day at the same time each day to note time of day and
day-to-day variability. The record can include the following:
time of onset of pain
activity or situation
physical pain character (quality) and intensity level (0–10)
emotions experienced and intensity level (0–10)
use of analgesics or other relief measures.
Recorded data can provide the basis for developing or modifying the plan of care.
For this tool to be effective, it is important that the nurse explores the value and
use of the diary in achieving effective pain control with the person and family.
Reviewing the diary at each visit gives the opportunity for sharing observations
and questions, as well as the provision of hints. The person may want to add a
column to the diary; for example, for the temperature if it is believed that the pain
changes substantially with the weather. Confirming the person’s ability to use the
diary is essential to the potential success of this strategy.


Diagnosing
The nursing diagnosis is the judgment made after conducting a systematic
assessment, collecting both subjective and objective cues. The nursing diagnosis
can be an actual diagnosis or a risk diagnosis (see Chapter 13
).
Examples of nursing risk diagnoses include:
Risk of hopelessness related to feelings of continual pain.
Risk of anxiety related to past experiences of poor control of pain and to
anticipation of pain.
Risk of ineffective coping related to prolonged continuous back pain,
ineffective pain management and inadequate support systems.
Risk of ineffective health maintenance related to chronic pain and fatigue.
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND INTERVENTIO NS
People experiencing pain
History Mary Anderson, 75, fell and broke her right hip while shopping.
She had surgery yesterday to repair the fracture. She rates her pain in the
surgical site as 6 on a 0–10 scale and states the pain goes up to 9 when
she is repositioned in bed. Morphine 10 mg 4 hourly prn is ordered. She
received a dose 5 hours ago. She states, ‘I try to hold out as long as I can
before asking for a pain killer’.
Examples of actual diagnosis include:
Ineffective airway clearance secondary to postoperative incisional abdominal
pain, evidenced by weak cough.
Deficient knowledge (pain control measures) related to lack of exposure to
information resources, evidenced by acknowledgment of poor pain


management.
Impaired physical mobility related to arthritic pain in knee and ankle joints,
evidenced by reduced physical activity and/or the need for mobility aids.
Insomnia related to increased pain perception at night, evidenced by disturbed
sleep patterns.
Clinical examples of related nursing assessment, diagnoses, planning,
implementation and evaluation are shown in the following ‘Identifying nursing
diagnoses, outcomes and interventions
’, and in the ‘Nursing care plan
’
and ‘Concept map
’ at the end of this chapter.
Planning
The established goals for the individual should be personalised and will vary
according to the diagnosis and its defining characteristics. Specific nursing
interventions can be selected to meet the individual needs of the person.
Planning independent of setting
When planning, nurses need to choose pain relief measures appropriate for the
person, based on the assessment data and input from the individual or support
people. Nursing interventions may include a variety of pharmacological and non-
pharmacological interventions. Developing a plan that incorporates a wide range
of strategies is usually most effective. Whether in acute care or home care, it is
important for everyone involved in pain management to understand the plan of
care. The plan should be documented in the person’s record; in home care, a
copy needs to be made available to the person, support people and caregivers.
Involvement of the person and support people is essential in pain management.
When the person’s pattern and level of pain can be anticipated or is already
known, regular or scheduled administration of analgesics can provide a steady
serum level. With acute pain, this may be possible in the first 24 to 48 hours


following surgery when the person is likely to have pain requiring opioid
analgesics. Frequency of administration can be adjusted to prevent pain from
recurring. When persistent, continuous pain exists, analgesics should be given
around the clock (ATC), with additional as-needed (prn) doses available (Pasero &
McCaffery 2011). Non-pharmacological interventions should also be regularly
scheduled. The additional advantage of scheduling measures is that the person
spends less time in pain and does not experience as much anxiety or fear of the
pain recurring or the helplessness of not knowing what to do when pain flares.
Planning for home care
In preparation for discharge, the nurse needs to determine the person’s and
family’s needs, strengths and resources. The ‘Home care assessment
’ below
describes the specific assessment data required when establishing a discharge
plan. Using the assessment data, the nurse tailors a teaching plan for the person
and family.
Home care assessment
Pain
Individual
Level of knowledge: pharmacological and non-pharmacological
pain relief measures selected; adverse effects and measures to
counteract these effects; warning signs to report.
Self-care abilities for analgesic administration: ability to use
analgesics appropriately (e.g. to prepare correct dosages of
analgesics and adhere to scheduled administration); physical
dexterity to take pills or to administer intravenous medications
and to store medications safely; and ability to obtain
prescriptions or over-the-counter medications at the pharmacy.


Family
Caregiver availability, skills and willingness: primary and
secondary people able and willing to assist with pain
management; shopping if the person has restricted activity;
ability to comprehend selected therapies (e.g. infusion pumps,
imagery, massage, positioning and relaxation techniques) and
perform them or assist the person with them as needed.
Family role changes and coping: effect on financial status,
parenting and spousal roles, sexuality, social roles.
Community
Resources: availability of and familiarity with resources, such as
supplies, home health aid or financial assistance.
Implementing
Pain management is the alleviation of pain or a reduction in pain to a level of
comfort that is acceptable to the person. It includes two basic types of nursing
interventions: pharmacological and non-pharmacological. Nursing management of
pain consists of both independent and collaborative nursing actions. In general,
non-invasive measures may be performed as an independent nursing function,
whereas administration of analgesic medication generally requires a medical order
from a doctor. However, because many analgesics are ordered to be
administered on an as-needed (prn) basis, the decision to administer the
prescribed medication is frequently the nurse’s, often requiring judgment as to the
dose and the time of administration. Professional nursing judgment remains a key
factor in relieving pain by determining which medication in what dosage would
best meet the person’s comfort needs (Schug et al.
).
46


46 Schug, S. A., Palmer, G. M., Scott, D. A., Halliwell, R., Trinca, J.; APM: SE Working Group of the Australian
and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists and Faculty of Pain Medicine (2015). Acute Pain Management:
Scientific Evidence (4th ed.). Melbourne: ANZCA & FPM.
Generally speaking, a combination of strategies is best for the person in pain.
Sometimes strategies need to be tried and changed until the person obtains
effective pain relief. See the ‘Practice guidelines’ for individualising care for people
with pain.
Barriers to pain management
Misconceptions and biases can affect pain management. These may involve
attitudes of the nurse or the person, as well as knowledge deficits. Individuals
respond to pain experiences based on their culture, personal experiences and the
meaning the pain has for them. For many people, pain is expected and accepted
as a normal aspect of illness. People and families may lack knowledge of the
adverse effects of pain and may have misinformation regarding the use of
analgesics. People may not report pain because they expect nothing can be
done, they think it is not severe enough or they feel it would distract or prejudice
the health care provider. Other common misconceptions are shown in Table
49.5
. Another barrier to effective pain management is the fear of becoming
addicted, especially when long-term opioid use is prescribed. This fear is often
held by both nurses and individuals. It is important that all individuals know the
difference between tolerance, dependence and addiction (see Box 49.4
).
Pseudo-addiction is a condition that results from the undertreatment of pain
where the person may become focused on obtaining medications, ‘clock watch’
and may otherwise seem inappropriately ‘drug seeking’. Even behaviours such as
illicit drug use and deception can occur in the person’s efforts to obtain pain relief.
Pseudo-addiction can be distinguished from true addiction in that the motivation
for engaging in aberrant drug-related behaviours is to alleviate unrelieved pain as
opposed to seeking euphoria (Greene & Chambers ).
47 Greene, M. S. & Chambers, R. A. (2015). Pseudoaddiction: Fact or fiction? An investigation of the medical
literature. Current Addiction Reports, 2(4), 310–317. Doi: 10.1007/s40429-015-0074-7.
47


Table 49.5 Common misconceptions about pain
BO X
49.4 Definitions
The Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists and Faculty of
Pain Medicine (2015) recognises the following definitions and recommends
their use.
Addiction
A disease characterised by aberrant drug-seeking and drug-taking
behaviours that may include cravings, compulsive drug use and loss of
control over drug use, despite the risk of physical, social and psychological
harm.
Physical dependence
Physical dependence is a physiological adaptation to a drug whereby
abrupt continuation or reversal of that drug, or sudden reduction in its
dose, leads to a withdrawal (abstinence) syndrome.
Tolerance
Tolerance is the decrease in the effect of a drug over time so that
progressive increase in the dose of that drug is required to achieve the
same effect.
Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists and Faculty of Pain Medicine (2015). Acute Pain
Management: Scientific Evidence (4th ed.). Retrieved from <http://fpm.anzca.edu.au/resources/publications>.
Key strategies in pain management


Key strategies to reduce pain include acknowledging and accepting the person’s
pain, assisting support people, reducing misconceptions about pain, reducing fear
and anxiety and preventing pain.
Acknowledging and accepting individual’s pain
According to the professional standards of conduct, nurses have a duty to ask
people about their pain and to believe their reports of discomfort. Challenging the
person’s report of discomfort undermines the environment of trust that is an
essential component in the therapeutic relationship. Consider these four ways of
communicating this belief:
1. Acknowledge the possibility of the pain. ‘Many people with your condition
are bothered by leg pain. Are you experiencing any leg discomfort? What
does it feel like? How concerned/upset are you about it?’
2. Listen attentively to what the person says about the pain, restating your
understanding of the reported discomfort. Adding an empathetic statement
such as ‘I’m sorry you are hurting, it must be very upsetting. I want to help
you feel better’ lets the person know you believe the pain is real and intend
to help.
3. Convey that you need to ask about the pain because, despite some
similarities, everybody’s experience is unique. For example, ‘Many people
with your condition report having some discomforts. Do you have any pain
or other discomforts now?’.
4. Attend to the person’s needs promptly. It is unconscionable to believe the
person’s report of pain and then do nothing. After determining the person
has pain, discuss options and plan actions for providing relief.
Clinical consideration
What if you are fooled by a person’s self-report of pain?
Evidence suggests 5% of people reporting pain may be
dishonest and seeking some secondary gain. By believing


everyone, you will not short change the 95% of people who
so desperately need to have help controlling their pain,
providing them with competent, compassionate and
appropriate nursing care based on the best available
information.
Assisting support people
Support people often need assistance to respond in a helpful manner to the
person experiencing pain. Nurses can help by giving them accurate information
about the pain and providing opportunities for them to discuss their emotional
reactions, which may include anger, fear, frustration and feelings of inadequacy.
Teaching the support people about the disease and medications (including
warning signs to report) and non-drug pain-relieving techniques they can help with
(e.g. massage, application of ice, coached relaxation techniques) may diminish
their feelings of helplessness and strengthen their relationship. Support people
also may need the nurse’s understanding, reassurance and perhaps access to
resources that will help them cope as they add the caregiver role to an already
stressful life circumstance.
Reducing misconceptions about pain
Reducing a person’s misconceptions about the pain and its treatment will
encourage and increase the likelihood of optimal pain relief. The nurse should
explain to the person that pain is a highly individual experience and that it is only
the person who really experiences the pain, although others can understand and
empathise. Misconceptions are also dealt with when the nurse and person
discuss the context of pain control as part of the healing process. For example, a
person may refuse pain medicine out of concern for addiction, explaining that the
pain is more tolerable as long as they remain totally still. This misconception
overstates the risk of addiction (estimated at less than 5% of people without a
history of substance abuse when treated for acute pain) while underestimating


the risks associated with immobility (atelectasis, muscle atrophy, pressure ulcers,
infections etc.).
Practice guidelines
Individualising care for people with pain
Establish a trusting relationship. Convey your concern and
acknowledge that you believe that the person is experiencing pain. A
trusting relationship promotes expression of the person’s thoughts and
feelings and enhances effectiveness of planned pain therapies.
Consider the person’s ability and willingness to participate actively in
pain relief measures. Individuals who are excessively fatigued, sedated
or have altered levels of consciousness are less able to participate
actively. For example, a person with an altered level of consciousness
or altered thought processes cannot safely or effectively use patient-
controlled analgesia. In contrast, a fatigued person may express a
willingness to use pain relief measures that require little effort, such as
listening to music or performing relaxation techniques.
Use a variety of pain relief measures. It is thought that using more than
one measure has an additive, if not synergistic, effect in relieving pain.
Two types of relief measures that should be part of any pain treatment
plan are active (relief strategies that are self-initiated) and passive
(relief strategies that require the assistance of others). Establishing
rapport and individual education are necessary components of all
therapeutic encounters and may be implicit or explicit in the care plan.
Because a person’s pain may vary throughout a 24-hour period,
different types of pain relief or pre-emptive interventions may be
scheduled (e.g. medication 1 hour before dressing change, relaxation
techniques with pleasant imagery after bedtime medication).
Provide measures to relieve pain before it becomes severe. For
example, providing an analgesic before the onset of pain is preferable
to waiting for the person to complain of pain, when a larger dose may
be required.


Use pain-relieving measures that the person believes are effective. It
has been recognised that individuals are the authorities on their own
pain. Thus, incorporating the person’s preferred methods of relieving
their pain into the treatment plan should be seriously considered.
The selection of pain relief measures should be aligned with the
person’s report of the severity of the pain. If a person reports mild pain,
an analgesic such as paracetamol may be indicated, whereas a person
who reports severe pain often requires a more potent relief measure.
Telling a person to ignore the pain (e.g. through distraction techniques)
when they are reporting severe pain is an example of a misalignment of
the pain severity and intervention selected.
If a pain relief measure is ineffective, encourage the person to try it
again before abandoning it. Medications may need repeated doses to
saturate plasma proteins before sufficient ‘free drug’ is available to
work on the intended target. Non-pharmacological measures often
require practice before they are effective.
Maintain an unbiased attitude (open mind) about what may relieve the
pain. New ways to relieve pain are continually being developed. It is not
always possible to explain the effectiveness of particular pain relief
measures; however, using approaches the person believes will work
should be considered.
Keep trying. Do not ignore a person because pain persists despite
failed attempts to alleviate the discomfort. In these circumstances,
reassess the pain and consider other relief measures.
Prevent harm to the person. Pain therapy should not increase
discomfort or harm the person. Some pain relief measures may have
adverse untoward effects, such as fatigue, but they should not disable
the person.
Educate the person and caregivers about pain. Individuals and support
people need to be informed about the possible causes of pain,
precipitating and alleviating factors and alternatives to drug therapy.
Misconceptions also need to be corrected.


Culturally competent care
People in pain
Nurses are in a position of power as they decide whether to believe the
person’s subjective report of pain. It is, therefore, important to develop an
effective, positive relationship with the person, a relationship that
incorporates caring behaviours.
Respect people as individuals by recognising that they can hold
different beliefs about pain and inquiring about their beliefs and ways of
coping with pain.
Respect the person’s response to pain by recognising that individuals
have the right to respond to pain in the way they learned is appropriate,
that expressions of pain vary widely and no expression is good or bad.
Never stereotype a person on the basis of culture. Expressions of pain
vary between and within cultures.
Source: Adapted from M. M. Andrews, J. S. Boyle & J. Collins (2019). Transcultural Concepts in Nursing Care (8th ed.).
Philadelphia: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
Patient education
Monitoring pain in the home setting
Teach the person to keep a pain diary to monitor pain onset, activity
before pain, pain intensity, use of analgesics or other relief measures
and so on.
Educate the person on the importance of contacting a health care
professional if planned pain control measures are ineffective.
Pain control
Teach the use of preferred and selected non-pharmacological
techniques such as relaxation, guided imagery, distraction, music


therapy, massage and so on.
Discuss the actions, side effects, dosages and frequency of
administration of prescribed analgesics.
Suggest ways to handle side effects of medications.
Provide accurate information about tolerance, physical dependence
and addiction if opioid analgesics are prescribed and these topics are of
concern.
Use appropriate techniques to communicate to the person the
importance of using pain control measures before the pain becomes
severe.
Inform the person of the effects of untreated pain.
Ensure the person or caregiver can demonstrate appropriate skills to
administer analgesics (e.g. skin patches, injections, infusion pumps or
patient-controlled analgesia). If a home infusion pump is being used,
caregivers need to be able to:
− Demonstrate stopping and starting the pump.
− Change the medication cartridge and tubing.
− Adjust the delivery dose.
− Demonstrate site care.
− Identify signs indicating the need to change an injection site.
− Describe care of the pump and insertion site when the person is
ambulatory, bathing, sleeping or travelling.
− Perform problem solving for pumps when alarms are activated.
− Change the battery.
Resources
Provide appropriate information about how to access community
resources, home care agencies and associations that offer self-help
groups and educational materials.


Reducing fear and anxiety
It is important to help relieve strong emotions capable of amplifying pain (e.g.
anxiety, anger and fear). When people have no opportunity to talk about their pain
and associated fears, their perceptions and reactions to the pain can be
intensified. Often these emotions are related to uncertainty about the future,
feeling mistreated in the past or having unmet expectations. By providing
accurate information, the nurse can also reduce many of the person’s fears or
anxiety, while clarifying expectations can minimise frustration and anger.
Specifically, individual education about the range of pain that is considered normal
for the condition as well as the types of discomforts that signal a potential for
problems will help alleviate this fear and uncertainty.
Preventing pain
A preventive approach to pain management involves the provision of measures to
treat the pain before it occurs or before it becomes severe. Pre-emptive
analgesia
 is the administration of analgesics prior to an invasive or operative
procedure in order to treat pain before it occurs. For example, treating people
preoperatively with local infiltration of an anaesthetic or parenteral administration
of an opioid can reduce postoperative pain. Nurses can also use a pre-emptive
approach by providing an analgesic ATC and supplementing with prn doses prior
to painful procedures (e.g. dressing changes, physical therapy). This strategy
prevents the wind-up and sensitisation described earlier that spreads, intensifies
and prolongs pain.

48 Veal, F., Williams, M., Bereznicki, I., Cummings, E., Thompson, A., Peterson, G. & Winzenberg, T. (2018). Barriers to
optimal pain management in aged care facilities: An Australian qualitative study. Pain Management Nursing, 19(2), 177–
185.
Previous research noted that residents of aged care facilities had a high
incidence of pain, reported to be as high as 80%. Difficulties exist when
residents are no longer able to articulate that they have pain and this can
be compounded by a wide range of factors including staff workload, staff
knowledge and attitude, as well as stoicism of this age group.
Semi-structured interviews were conducted of 23 staff from five different
aged care facilities. The researchers identified that there was a wide range
of barriers to effective pain management in aged care facilities. These
barriers included a lack of policy and protocol around pain assessment as
well as a lack of formalised education. The research also noted that when
staff were familiar with residents and knew their behaviours, they could
assess pain more easily. Frequent changes in staff impacted on the quality
of pain management. Communication between different levels of health
care professionals, residents and family members was also identified as a
barrier.
Implications Effective management of pain is complex and requires a
wide range of approaches to be successful. Some of these strategies
include modifying staffing arrangements; ensuring staff are educated;
building relationships between staff, residents and family members; and
establishing standardised protocols for pain assessment and management.
Clinical consideration
Educate the person that at times treatment may need to
balance the demands of providing pain reduction with
functional improvement. Too much pain medicine might
impair alertness or gait; too much pain impairs alertness and


ability to move. Therefore, a person may have to tolerate
mild pain in order to do what is necessary to maximise
functioning and recovery (e.g. cough, deep breathing and
walk). Focus on reducing any anxiety that the person may be
feeling subsequent to this discussion.
Pharmacological pain management
Pharmacological pain management involves the use of opioids (narcotics), non-
opioids/non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and co-analgesic drugs
(see Box 49.5
). The principles of modern analgesic use are built on a
foundation established by the World Health Organization (WHO) three-step
approach to treating cancer pain (see Figure 49.9
). This approach focuses on
aligning the proper analgesic with the intensity of pain. It has evolved into what is
currently termed ‘rational polypharmacy’, which demands that health
professionals be aware of all ingredients of medications that alleviate pain and
use combinations to reduce the need for high doses of any one medication and to
maximise pain control with a minimum of side effects or toxicity. These multidrug
strategies, combined with multimodal therapy (use of non-drug approaches such
as heat/relaxation), ‘may permit opioid dose reduction and improve individual
outcomes’ (Schug et al. 2015).

Practice guidelines
Strategies for holding colleagues accountable for believing
individuals and managing pain
What do we do if the health care team does not respond positively to the
person’s report of pain?
Speak up! Inappropriate professional behaviour will persist if not
challenged. If necessary, file an ‘incident’ or a ‘variance’ report for
persistent patterns or egregious violations of standards of care. These
types of behaviours (ignoring reports of pain, failing to treat or
mistreating people with pain) are not only unethical but legally
indefensible as the expected level of care is not delivered.
Clarify that the sensation of pain is subjective and that professionals
have a duty to believe people’s reports of their symptoms.
Cite recommendations from evidence-based clinical practice guidelines
(e.g. Australian Pain Society or the Australian and New Zealand
College of Anaesthetists), Joint Commission on Accreditation of Health
Care Organizations standards, organisation-specific documents (e.g.
mission statement, patient bill of rights, practice standards) or relevant
research/quality reports. As necessary, distribute or post with key
passages highlighted.
Involve key committees, managers and administrators in studying and
addressing the problem from a cost, quality, competency and
credentialing perspective.
Real-world practice
The story


My patient this evening was a 35-year-old woman who was in the
surgical high-dependency unit (HDU) after emergency abdominal
surgery to relieve a small bowel obstruction that had been caused
by extensive abdominal and pelvic adhesions. She had previously
undergone surgery for a ruptured appendix as well as multiple
gynaecology surgical procedures for severe endometriosis. When I
commenced my shift, the person was experiencing nausea and
severe abdominal pain that was not relieved by the intravenous (IV)
patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) infusion of morphine. On
examination, I noted that her abdomen was extremely distended
and ‘tense’ on palpation and bowel sounds were absent. She had
been given an IV anti-emetic just 15 minutes prior. She rated her
pain as 7 out of 10 and she was visibly upset and was reluctant to
move due to the pain.
I consulted with the clinical Registered Nurse (RN) responsible for
her care and she administered an additional bolus dose of IV
morphine as per the PCA order. While waiting for the additional
morphine to take effect, the RN suggested we also implement some
alternative therapies. We applied a warm pack to her lower back
and then used a very gentle massage technique known as
effleurage on her abdomen. These additional measures seemed to
have a positive effect as she became more relaxed, verbalised
reduction in pain level and allowed us to assist her to move to a
lateral position in bed.
Student reflection
What I learned from this experience is that medication alone cannot
always ease the person’s pain. Where I previously may have felt
that medications were the panacea to all individual complaints, this
experience reinforced the need to treat the entire person.
This is probably the first time I realised that pain medications are
not always 100% effective. Also, I don’t know why, but it seems I


always think the person is overstating their pain or making up
symptoms in order to receive pain medication. Maybe this is the
result of watching too much television! The RN brought me back to
reality in this instance by asking if I had ever experienced pain
severe enough to make me vomit. With this perspective, I could
now somewhat relate to what the person must be experiencing.
Clinical facilitator reflection
James made two important discoveries. One is that pain is
personal, complex and multidimensional. Because it is so complex,
we should not be surprised when a pain medication alone cannot
relieve its intensity. It is also important to recognise what
conclusions we formulate when a person’s pain is not relieved with
medication. Can you think of other factors that might be contributing
to this person’s experience of pain? Are there other pain relief
interventions you as a nurse could institute?
—Student: James Wright Clinical Facilitator: Debbie Jones RN
World Health Organization (WHO): three-step approach
For people with mild pain (1–3 on a 0–10 scale), step 1 of the analgesic ladder,
non-opioid analgesics (with or without a co-analgesic) is the appropriate starting
point. If the person has mild pain that persists or increases despite using full
doses of step 1 medications, or if the pain is moderate (4–6 on a 0–10 scale),
then a step 2 regimen is appropriate. At the second step, a weak opioid (e.g.
codeine, tramadol) or a combination of opioid and non-opioid medicine (e.g.
paracetamol and codeine) is provided with or without co-analgesic medications. If
the person has moderate pain that persists or increases despite using full doses
of step 2 medications, or if the pain is severe (7–10 on a 0–10 scale), then a step
3 regimen is medically indicated. At the third step, opiates (e.g. morphine,


pethidine and fentanyl) are administered and titrated in ATC scheduled doses until
the pain is relieved or dose-limiting respiratory depression occurs.
Clinical consideration
Combining opioid and non-opioid analgesics is frequently
overlooked. Each has different side effects, mechanisms of
action and toxicity profile. Alternating the two or giving them
at the same time creates no danger and often produces a
synergistic effect rather than a merely additive effect.
Non-opioids/NSAIDs
Non-opioids include paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
(NSAIDs)
 such as ibuprofen or aspirin. NSAIDs have anti-inflammatory,
analgesic and antipyretic effects whereas paracetamol has only analgesic and
antipyretic effects. The anti-inflammatory action relieves pain by interfering with
the cyclo-oxygenase (COX) chemical cascade that is activated by damaged
tissue. The COX chemical reactions produce prostaglandins and other
inflammatory chemicals that cause a firing of nociceptive fibres. The COX-1
specific isoforms are found in platelets, the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, kidneys and
most other tissue, and are believed to be the cause of the well-known side effects
of NSAIDs (GI bleed, diminished renal blood flow, inhibited clotting etc.).
Individual drugs in this category vary little in their analgesic potency but do vary in
their anti-inflammatory properties, metabolism, excretion and side effects. These
drugs have a ceiling effect and a narrow therapeutic index. The ceiling effect
means that once the maximum analgesic benefit is achieved, more drug will not
produce more analgesia; however, more toxicity may occur. The narrow
therapeutic index indicates that there’s not much margin for safety between the
dose that produces a desired effect and the dose that may produce a toxic, even


lethal, effect. The most common side effect of non-opioid analgesics is
gastrointestinal, such as heartburn or indigestion. These effects can become toxic
or lethal when silent GI bleeding occurs. Given the interference with platelet
aggregation, a small stomach ulcer can bleed a lot, making it a potentially life-
threatening condition. People should be advised to take NSAIDs with food and a
full glass of water. Routine monitoring by a health professional is indicated if these
preparations are taken daily for more than a couple of weeks.
Paracetamol (Panadol), on the other hand, has a different mechanism of action
and side effect/toxicity profile. It does not affect platelet function and rarely
causes GI distress, ulcers or kidney, skin or cardiovascular problems.
Hepatotoxicity, and possible renal toxicity, does occur with high doses or with
long-term use (Pasero & McCaffery 2011). Generally, 25 grams of paracetamol is
considered a lethal dose, with 10–15 grams causing measurable liver damage. It
is recommended that otherwise young and healthy people limit their paracetamol
consumption to less than 4 grams per day, with susceptible individuals (e.g. older
adults, those with a history of alcoholism, dehydration or liver disease) limiting
their consumption to 2.4 grams per day or less. Given that paracetamol is so well
tolerated, it is often a hidden ingredient in over-the-counter (OTC) remedies (e.g.
pain, fever, allergy, cough and cold preparations), so people must be instructed to
read the ingredient list of all OTC medicines they take. Box 49.6
 provides
consumption parameters for medications that contain paracetamol. Table 49.6
lists common misconceptions about non-opioids.

Opioids
There are two primary types of opioids available in Australia:
1. Full agonists. These pure opioid drugs bind tightly to mu receptor sites,
producing maximum pain inhibition, an agonist effect. A full agonist
analgesic
 includes morphine (e.g. Kapanol, MS Contin), oxycodone
(e.g. Endone, Oxycontin) and hydromorphone (e.g. Dilaudid). There is no
ceiling on the level of analgesia from these drugs; their dose can be
steadily increased to relieve pain. There is also no maximum daily dose
limit unless they are in compound with a non-opioid analgesic drug such as
paracetamol, which has a daily maximum limit of 2400 to 4000 mg.
2. Partial agonists. Partial agonists have a ceiling effect in contrast to a full
agonist. These drugs such as buprenorphine (Temgesic) block the mu
receptors or are neutral at that receptor but bind at a kappa receptor site.
This drug has good analgesic potency and is emerging as an alternative to
methadone for opioid maintenance/narcotic treatment programs. The
safety and favourable side effect profile make it an increasingly popular
choice.
Opioid analgesics for moderate pain
These include drugs that are weak opioids (e.g. codeine, tramadol), mixed
agonist–antagonist drugs or combination opioids with non-opioid (NSAIDs)
analgesics compounds. These medicines are generally two to four times more
potent than non-opioids alone and have some of the risks of both drug classes.
Since 2018, in Australia, all these drugs have been controlled substances and
must be ordered by a doctor adhering to applicable federal and state laws. These
drugs also have a ceiling effect and a maximum daily dose limit. There are
advantages to giving combination drugs, such as lowering the amount of any one
medicine needed in a 24-hour period, thus reducing the potential for side effects


or toxicity; however, nurses need to be familiar with each medication and be
aware of daily dose limits of the ingredients as well as the potential to receive
duplicate medications for different clinical indications (e.g. if giving a combined
paracetamol/ibuprofen medication for headache, avoid giving paracetamol for
back pain). These opioids have a narrow therapeutic index. Codeine at doses of
30 to 60 mg produces dose-limiting gastrointestinal distress in many people.
Propoxyphene produces a by-product that irritates nerves and muscles and
tramadol lowers seizure threshold. The mixed agonist–antagonist drugs have
some properties of naloxone (Narcan) and thus in individuals who have been on
opioids for a period of time these drugs can cause a serious withdrawal reaction.
Therefore, mixed agonist–antagonist medications may be the first opioid tried but
the person is not switched from another opioid to these preparations.
Opioid analgesics for severe pain
Pure agonist opioid analgesics include opium derivatives, such as morphine,
hydromorphone, oxycodone, fentanyl and methadone (American Pain Society ).
Opioid is the pharmacological class of pain relievers, many of which are
‘scheduled’ as a controlled substance (narcotic) due to the potential for misuse.
Pure agonist opioids relieve pain primarily by binding to mu receptors in the
peripheral and central nervous systems. In addition to pain reduction, changes in
mood may make the person feel more comfortable even though the pain persists.
As the most potent class of pain relievers, these drugs are indicated for severe
pain or when other medications have failed to control moderately severe or worse
pain. Among this class, meperidine has been identified as a medication to avoid
because of its short half-life, toxic metabolite and potential to induce seizures with
repeated doses.
50 American Pain Society (2016). Principles of Analgesic Use (7th ed.). Glenview, IL: Author.
Opioid side effects
When administering any analgesic, the nurse must review side effects. Side
effects of the opioids typically include respiratory depression, sedation,
50


nausea/vomiting, urinary retention, blurred vision, sexual dysfunction and
constipation. The most concerning adverse effect of opioids is respiratory
depression (e.g. 8 per minute or less), which usually occurs early in therapy
among opioid-naïve people; with dose escalation; or in people with drug–drug or
drug–disease interactions. Clinically, the person will appear overly sedated and
respirations will be slow and deep with periods of apnoea. The nurse needs to
assess an individual’s level of alertness and respiratory rate for baseline data
before administering narcotics. See the sedation rating scale in Box 49.7
.
Often people will manifest an increase in sedation before they manifest a
decrease in respiratory rate and depth. Early recognition of an increasing level of
sedation or respiratory depression will enable the nurse to implement appropriate
measures promptly (e.g. pulse oximetry monitoring, obtaining an order to
decrease the opioid dosage). Box 49.8
 provides suggested measures to
prevent and treat side effects of opioid analgesics.

49.8 Common opioid side effects, preventive
and treatment measures
Constipation
Increase fluid intake (e.g. 6 to 8 glasses daily).
Increase fibre and bulk-forming agents to the diet (e.g. fresh fruits and
vegetables). Increasing exercise is often ineffective in controlling this
type of constipation.
Administer daily stool softeners combined with a mild laxative (e.g.
Senokot) as a first line of prevention against constipation for individuals
on opioid maintenance therapy.
Stimulants (bisacodyl), osmotic laxatives (lactulose, sorbitol and
polyethylene glycol), enemas (tap water and sodium phosphate) and
even prokinetic agents (metoclopramide) may be needed for refractory
cases of constipation.
Nausea and vomiting
Inform the person that tolerance to this emetic effect generally
develops after several days of opiate therapy.
Provide an anti-emetic: the 5HT antagonist ondansetron (Zofran),
phenothiazines (Phenergan) or the GI stimulant metoclopramide
(Maxalon).
Change the dose or analgesic agent as indicated.
Sedation
Explain to the person that tolerance usually develops over 3 to 5 days.
Consider the administration of a stimulant (e.g. Dexedrine or Ritalin) or
an alternative route of administration (e.g. epidural) for people with


persistent pain and sedation.
Observe the person for evidence of respiratory depression that may
occur with sedation.
Respiratory depression
Administer an opioid antagonist, such as naloxone hydrochloride
(Narcan), cautiously by diluting 1 ampoule in 10 mL of saline and then
administering 1 mL per minute until the respirations are at or greater
than 10/min. Make provisions for repeat administration, continuous
infusion or a longer acting version of a reversal agent as the half-life of
naloxone is considerably shorter than most opioids being reversed.
Stop, change or slow the administration of opioids until respirations are
restored.
Pruritus
Apply cool packs, lotion and diversional activity.
Administer an antihistamine (e.g. diphenhydramine hydrochloride
(Benadryl)).
Inform the person that tolerance also develops to pruritus within a few
days.
Urinary retention
May need to catheterise the person or change or lower the analgesic
dose.
Drug Capsule
Narcotic analgesic oxycodone (Endone, OxyContin)


The person with pain
Opioids relieve moderate to severe pain by inhibiting the release of
substance P in both central and peripheral nerves, reducing the perception
of pain, producing sedation and decreasing the emotional stress of pain.
Oxycodone is a semisynthetic derivative of codeine. It is a Schedule 8
controlled substance. It is often administered as a combination drug with
paracetamol or aspirin.
Nursing responsibilities
Assess pain prior to and 60 minutes after administration.
Assess bowel function to prevent constipation.
Keep track of the total amount of paracetamol and/or aspirin the
person is receiving when taking a combination drug. The maximum
daily dose of paracetamol is 4000 mg (unless the person is at risk of
liver problems).
Individual and family education
Take with food to decrease GI upset.
Avoid crushing or chewing long-acting tablets such as OxyContin.
Avoid alcohol or other CNS depressants.
Explain that the medication may cause dizziness and instruct to make
position changes slowly.
Instruct that constipation is a common side effect. Discuss preventive
measures.
Take only as prescribed.
Note: prior to administering any medication, review all aspects with a
current drug handbook or other reliable source.
Older people are particularly sensitive to the analgesic properties of opioids and
may require less medication, or medication administered at less frequent


intervals, than younger people. This sensitivity may be related to reduced or
delayed excretion of the drug in older adults. As such, the clinical pearl of ‘start
low (25–50% dose reduction) and go (titrate) slow’ is often followed in the older
population.
Clinical consideration
Constipation is a common adverse effect of opioid use, so
unless contraindicated, all people receiving opioids should
also receive prophylactic stimulant laxative therapy. Stool
softeners are not useful alone but are effective when
combined with a stimulant laxative (e.g. Senokot). If the
person remains constipated, a regimen of cathartic laxatives
(e.g. bisacodyl) followed by more aggressive forms of
treatment (e.g. osmotic laxatives, enema, manual
disimpaction) may be necessary.
Clinical consideration
Assessing sedation and respiratory status is critical during
the first 12 to 24 hours after starting opioid therapy. The most
critical period is during the peak effect of the first dose (15
minutes if administered IV; first hour after IM, oral or rectal
route). An exception is with opioids administered via the
spinal route. Respiratory depression may increase over time
with epidural infusions and with intrathecal analgesia;
respiratory depression may manifest 24 hours after the spinal
injection even after the analgesic effect has worn off. In
general, the longer the person receives opioids, the wider the
safety margin as the person develops a tolerance to the
sedative and respiratory depressive effects of the drug.


Equianalgesic dosing
The term equianalgesia
 refers to the relative potency of various opioid
analgesics compared with a standard dose of parenteral morphine. This tool helps
professionals individualise the analgesic regimen by guiding the adjustment of
medication, dose, time interval and route of administration. An equianalgesic
chart can be used to help provide doses of approximately equal ability to relieve
pain. The two basic techniques for calculating doses based on equianalgesic
equivalents are ratio and cross-multiplication methods. For example, with the ratio
technique, it is known that the oral:IV morphine ratio is 3:1, meaning IV morphine
is 3 times more potent than oral morphine. Thus, a person who has required 100
mg of IV morphine per day will require 300 mg of oral morphine per day to control
the same level of pain. If a different person who had an opioid requirement of 40
mg IV morphine per day were to be switched to oral Dilaudid, the equianalgesia
chart informs us that 10 mg IV morphine is equivalent to 7.5 mg hydromorphone
(Dilaudid). Using the cross-multiplication technique (X represents unknown dose),
the following steps are calculated:
Cross-multiply:
Thus 30 mg oral hydromorphone per day would provide equivalent analgesia to
40 mg of parenteral morphine per day. The hydromorphone dose is then divided
based on the duration of action of the available preparations (Dilaudid every 4
hours).
10 mg IV morphine = 7.5 mg oral hydromorphone
40 mg IV morphine = X mg hydromorphone
