Clinical consideration
Many health care professionals underestimate the
effectiveness of ordinary aspirin and paracetamol. The
ordinary dose of aspirin or paracetamol relieves as much pain
as 1.5 mg of parenteral morphine.
Co-analgesics
A co-analgesic
 agent (formerly known as an adjuvant) is a medication that is
not classified as a pain medication. However, co-analgesics have properties that
may reduce pain alone or in combination with other analgesics, relieve other
discomforts, potentiate the effect of pain medications or reduce the pain
medication’s side effects. Examples of co-analgesics that relieve pain are
antidepressants (increase pain relief, improve mood and improve sleep),
anticonvulsants (stabilise nerve membranes, reducing excitability and
spontaneous firing) and local anaesthetics (block the transmission of pain
signals). Anxiolytics, sedatives and antispasmodics are examples of medicines
that relieve other discomforts; however, they do not alleviate pain and thus should
be used in addition to rather than instead of analgesics. Examples of medications
used to reduce the side effects of analgesics include stimulants, laxatives and
anti-emetics.
Co-analgesics appear to be particularly beneficial for the management of
neuropathic pain. Tricyclic antidepressant drugs seem to be particularly useful for
central neuropathic pain, which often manifests as pain with a burning, unusual or
stinging quality. Anticonvulsant drugs such as gabapentin seem particularly useful
for peripheral neuropathic conditions that often present with a stabbing, shooting
or electrical-shock quality. Local anaesthetics such as the Lignocaine patch also
alleviate neuropathic as well as other types of pain and are particularly useful for
people with the skin sensitivity known as allodynia. There is a growing scientific


and clinical basis for the use of these medications in relieving pain, especially for
persistent pain that is not relieved by the analgesic classes of medication alone.
Administration of placebos
A placebo
 is ‘any sham medication or procedure designed to be void of any
known therapeutic value’ (Arnstein et al.
, p. 226). An example would be a sugar
pill or an injection of saline. In contrast, the placebo effect is ‘the positive
response some patients/participants experience after receiving a placebo’
(Arnstein et al. 2011, p. 226). Some professionals try to justify the use of
placebos to elicit the desirable placebo effect or in a misguided attempt to
determine if the patient’s pain is ‘real’. The use of placebos, outside the context of
an approved research study, is deceptive and represents fraudulent and unethical
treatment. Nursing and other professional organisations adamantly oppose the
use of placebos without consent.
51 Arnstein, P. M., Broglio, K., Wuhrman, E. & Kean, M. B. (2011). Use of placebos in pain management. Pain
Management Nursing, 12(4), 225–229. Doi: 10.1016/j.pmn. 2010.10.033.
Routes for opiate delivery
Opioids have traditionally been administered by oral, subcutaneous, intramuscular
and intravenous routes. In addition, newer methods of delivering opiates have
been developed to circumvent potential obstacles that occur with these traditional
routes. Examples are transnasal, transmucosal and transdermal drug therapy,
continuous subcutaneous infusions and intraspinal infusion.
Oral
Oral administration of opiates remains the preferred route of delivery because of
ease of administration. Given that the duration of action of most opiates is
approximately 4 hours, people with chronic pain have had to wake during the
night to medicate themselves for pain. To circumvent this problem, long-acting or
51


sustained-release forms of morphine with a duration of 8 or more hours have
been developed. An example of long-acting morphine is MS Contin. Individuals
receiving long-acting morphine may also need prn ‘rescue’ doses of immediate-
release analgesics such as short-acting oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate (Actiq)
for acute breakthrough pain. As a transmucosal agent, it immediately enters the
bloodstream and begins to work. Another method of oral opiate delivery is high-
concentration liquid morphine. This formulation enables people who can swallow
only small amounts to continue taking the drug orally.
Nasal
Transnasal administration has the advantage of rapid action of the medication
because of direct absorption through the vascular nasal mucosa. A commonly
used agent in the US is a mixed agonist–antagonist butorphanol for acute
migraine headaches. Note: this medication is not available in Australia. Treating
migraine headaches via the nasal route of administration is particularly beneficial
because of the nausea, vomiting and gastroparesis that occur with that condition,
making oral medications relatively contraindicated.
Transdermal
Transdermal drug therapy is advantageous in that it delivers a relatively stable
plasma drug level and is non-invasive. Fentanyl (Durogesic) is an opioid currently
available as a skin patch with various dosages. It provides drug delivery for up to
72 hours. The transdermal route is distinguished from the topical route in that the
effects of the medications are systemic after the medication is absorbed, whereas
topical medications placed on the skin (e.g. Lignocaine or capsaicin) work locally
at the point they are placed on the body. Applications of heat (e.g. hot packs)
must not be used with the fentanyl patch as increased absorption may result.
Rectal


Several non-opiate and opiate medicines are now available in suppository form.
The rectal route is particularly useful for individuals who have dysphagia (difficulty
swallowing) or nausea and vomiting. It is best to use commercially available rectal
preparations or have them compounded by a licensed compound pharmacist.
Subcutaneous
Although the subcutaneous (SC) route has been used extensively to deliver
opioids, another technique uses subcutaneous catheters and infusion pumps to
provide continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSCI) of narcotics. CSCI is
particularly helpful for people (a) whose pain is poorly controlled by oral
medications, (b) who are experiencing dysphagia or gastrointestinal obstruction or
(c) who have a need for prolonged use of parenteral narcotics. CSCI involves the
use of a small, light, battery-operated pump that administers the drug through a
23- or 25-gauge butterfly needle. The needle can be inserted into the anterior
chest, the subclavicular region, the abdominal wall, the outer aspects of the upper
arms or the thighs. Individual mobility is maintained with the application of a
shoulder bag or holster to hold the pump. The frequency of site change ranges
from 3 to 7 days.
Because family caregivers must operate the pump and also change and care for
the injection site, the nurse needs to provide appropriate instruction. Caregivers
need to understand their use and operation, including being able to:
Describe the basic parts and symbols of the system.
Identify ways to determine whether the pump is working.
Change the battery.
Change the medication.
Demonstrate stopping and starting the pump.
Demonstrate tubing care, site care and changing of the injection site.
Identify signs indicating the need to change an injection site.
Describe general care of the pump when the person is ambulatory, bathing,
sleeping or travelling.
Identify actions to take to solve problems when the alarm signals.


Intramuscular
The intramuscular (IM) route should be avoided if possible because of variable
absorption, unpredictable onset of action and peak effect, as well as the tissue
damage that may result, even if properly administered. Regardless of precautions
taken, there is pain involved with administration and may lead to nerve damage
with persistent neuropathic pain (Schug et al. 2015).
Intravenous
The intravenous (IV) route provides rapid and effective pain relief with few side
effects. However, just as the onset of pain relief occurs in 5 to 10 minutes, so can
adverse effects such as respiratory depression. IV analgesics should be
administered slowly to decrease adverse events. Caution is needed to prevent
the introduction of air or bacteria into the tubing and to prevent introducing
medications that are incompatible with other medications dissolved in the IV
solution.
Intraspinal
Another method of delivery is the infusion of opiates into the epidural or
intrathecal (subarachnoid) space (see Figure 49.10
). Analgesics administered
via the intraspinal route are delivered adjacent to the opiate receptors in the
dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Two commonly used medications are morphine
sulfate and fentanyl. All medicines administered via the intraspinal route need to
be sterile and preservative-free (preservatives are neurotoxic). The major benefit
of intraspinal drug therapy is superior analgesia with less medication used. The
epidural space is most commonly used because the dura mater acts as a
protective barrier against infection, including meningitis, and there is less risk of
developing a ‘spinal headache’. Intraspinal catheters are not in constant contact
with blood and thus an infusion can be stopped and restarted later without
concern that the catheter is no longer patent.
Figure 49.10


Placement of the intraspinal catheter in the epidural space.
Intrathecal administration delivers medication directly into the cerebrospinal fluid
(CSF) that bathes and nourishes the spinal cord. Medicines quickly and efficiently
bind to the opioid receptor sites in the dorsal horn when administered in this way,
speeding the onset and peak effect while prolonging the duration of action of the
analgesic. An example of how the route of administration affects the relative
potency of opiates is as follows: a person who needs 300 mg of oral morphine per
day to control pain will need 100 mg of parenteral morphine, 10 mg of epidural


morphine and only 1 mg of intrathecal morphine in a 24-hour period. Very little
drug is absorbed by blood vessels into the systemic circulation. In fact, the drug
must circulate through the CSF to be excreted. As a result, there may be a
delayed onset (24 hours after the administration) of respiratory depression, as
medication that has left the spinal opioid sites travels through the brain to be
eliminated.
In contrast, the epidural space is separated from the spinal cord by the dura
mater, which acts as a barrier to drug diffusion. In addition, it is filled with fatty
tissue and an extensive venous system. With this diffusion delay, some
medications (especially fat-soluble medications such as fentanyl) from the
epidural space enter the systemic circulation via the venous plexus. Thus, a
higher dose of opiate is required to create the desired effect, which can produce
side effects of itching, urinary retention and/or respiratory depression. Often, a
mixture of an opioid (e.g. fentanyl) and a local anaesthetic (e.g. bupivacaine) are
combined to lower the dose of opioid needed. As a result, there may be an
increase in fall risk for some people who develop muscular weakness in their legs
or orthostatic hypotension in response to the local anaesthetic.
Intraspinal analgesia can be administered by three modes of operation:
1. Bolus. A single or repeated bolus dose may be provided. When people
have spinal anaesthesia (e.g. during a caesarean section), a bolus of 1 mg
intrathecal morphine can provide significant pain control for up to 24 hours.
For shorter-acting medications, an epidural catheter may be intact and
accessed by a qualified health professional (e.g. anaesthetist) to
administer bolus doses on an as-needed basis. Check your organisation’s
policy regarding who can provide bolus doses, how they are documented
and the post-bolus monitoring procedures.
2. Continuous infusion administered by pump. The pump may be external
(for acute or chronic pain) or surgically implanted (for chronic pain) to
provide a continuous infusion of pain relievers into the epidural or
intrathecal space.


3. Continuous plus intermittent bolus. With this mode of operation, the
person receives a continuous infusion with bolus ‘rescue’ doses
administered for breakthrough pain. Often a pump with patient-controlled
epidural analgesia (PCEA) capabilities is used for this mode of operation.
This is similar to patient-controlled analgesia (detailed later) in which a
basal rate may or may not be used to meet the person’s anticipated
analgesic need, with the person’s ability to request an incremental dose at
set intervals by pressing a button. PCEA is often used to manage acute
postoperative pain, chronic pain and intractable cancer pain. The ‘walking
epidurals’ used for women in labour are typically PCEA devices that are
programmed in the bolus mode without a continuous infusion (basal rate)
set.
The anaesthetist inserts a needle into the intrathecal or epidural space (typically
in the lumbar region) and threads a catheter through the needle to the desired
level. The catheter is connected to tubing that is then positioned along the spine
and over the person’s shoulder for the nurse to access. The entire catheter and
tubing are taped securely to prevent dislodgment. Often an occlusive, transparent
dressing is placed over the insertion site for easy identification of catheter
displacement or local inflammation. Temporary catheters, used for short-term
acute pain management, are usually placed at the lumbar or thoracic vertebral
level and often removed after 2 to 4 days. Permanent catheters, for people with
chronic pain, may be tunnelled subcutaneously through the skin and exit at the
person’s side or be connected to a pump implanted in the abdomen. Tunnelling of
the catheter reduces the risk of infection and displacement of the catheter. After
the catheter is inserted, the nurse is responsible for monitoring the infusion and
assessing the person as per organisation policy. Nursing care of people with
intraspinal infusions is summarised in Table 49.7
.
Table 49.7 Nursing interventions for individuals receiving analgesics
through an epidural catheter
Misconceptions exist about the risks of spinal analgesia. This is in part due to the
importance of the technique of the professional inserting the catheter. In general,


people receiving epidural analgesia do not need to be monitored in an intensive
care setting but they do need vigilant assessment of their pain, their neurological
and respiratory status and the insertion site frequently during the course of
therapy (Pasero & McCaffery 2011).
Clinical consideration
As a precaution, have naloxone (Narcan), sodium chloride
0.9% diluent and injection equipment on hand for each
person receiving an opioid-containing epidural infusion.
Continuous local anaesthetics
Continuous subcutaneous administration of long-acting local anaesthetics into or
near the surgical site is a technique being used to provide postoperative pain
control. This technique has been used for a variety of surgical procedures,
including knee arthroplasty, abdominal hysterectomy, hernia repair and
mastectomy. Nursing interventions for the person with infusion of a continuous
local anaesthetic include:
Conduct pain assessment and documentation every 2 to 4 hours while the
person is awake.
Check the dressing every shift for intactness. The dressing is not usually
changed in order to avoid dislodging the catheter. Contact the doctor if the
dressing becomes loose.
Check the site of the catheter. It should be clean and dry.
Assess the person for signs of local anaesthetic toxicity (e.g. cardiac
arrhythmias; dizziness; ringing in the ears; a metallic taste; tingling or
numbness of the lips, gums or tongue) or neurological deficit distal to the
catheter insertion site.


Notify the doctor of signs of local anaesthetic toxicity or neurological deficit. If
detected early, prompt treatment can be initiated and serious complications
avoided.
Real-world practice
Mrs Black was an end-stage renal disease patient who had been on
haemodialysis for many years. She was also dealing with
neuropathic pain stemming from her diabetes. After receiving a new
diagnosis of colon cancer with spinal metastasis, spinal cord
compression and increased nerve pain in both legs, Mrs Black and
her family wanted pain relief as her life neared its end. The evening
nurse initiated a morphine PCA at 2 mg per hour basal rate with
injections of 1 mg when Mrs Black had jolts of nerve pain. She
would push the button before turning, since it precipitated the jolts
of pain. Mrs Black and her family had decided on a Not for
Resuscitation (NFR) status and comfort care.
As Mrs Black became more sedated due to the dialysis being
terminated, she was unable to push the button on her PCA. Her
daughters decided that they should push the button for their mother
when she had jolts of pain during turning throughout the night.
When I arrived on duty the next morning, I introduced myself to Mrs
Black and her family. I told them that my goal for the day was to get
her comfortable and that because of hospital policy only she should
push the button on the PCA. I explained that we could titrate the
morphine basal rate, which would deliver more constant pain relief,
and that the doctor would like to add Ativan in combination with the
morphine to help the nerve pain and the jolts of pain. By the end of
my shift, we had the morphine running at 5 mg per hour and used
the Ativan twice, especially before turning. When the family noticed


any signs of moaning or agitation, they would notify the nurse for a
dose of Ativan. Mrs Black was comfortable and we achieved our
goal.
With her family at her side, Mrs Black died the next day in comfort
due to combination drug therapy.
—Ann M. Ohmann RN
Patient-controlled analgesia
Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)
 is an interactive method of pain
management that permits people to treat their pain by self-administering doses of
analgesics. The IV route is the most common in an acute care setting.
Subcutaneous and epidural routes may also be used. The PCA mode of therapy
minimises the roller-coaster effect of peaks of sedation and valleys of pain that
occur with the traditional method of prn dosing. With the parenteral routes, the
person administers a predetermined dose of an opioid by an electronic infusion
pump. This allows the person to maintain a more constant level of relief yet need
less medication for pain relief. Patient-controlled analgesics can be used
effectively for people with acute pain related to a surgical incision, traumatic injury
or labour and delivery, and for chronic pain as with cancer.
The prescriber orders the analgesic dose, route, dose and lock-out intervals.
Whether in an acute hospital setting, an outpatient clinic or with home care, the
nurse is responsible for the initial instruction regarding use of the PCA and for the
ongoing monitoring of the therapy. Two Registered Nurses must double check the
initial settings and also any changes in dose or medication. The person’s pain,
ability to understand and use of the device must be assessed at regular intervals
and analgesic use is documented in the person’s record.


Patient-controlled analgesia pumps are designed with built-in safety mechanisms
to prevent overdosage, abusive use and narcotic theft. The most significant
adverse effects are respiratory depression and hypotension; however, they occur
rarely. Although PCA pumps vary in design, they all have similar protective
features. The line of the PCA pump, a syringe-type pump, is usually introduced
into the injection port of a primary IV fluid line (see Figure 49.11
). When the
individual wants a dose of analgesic, they can push a button attached to the
infusion pump and the pre-set dose is delivered (see Figure 49.12
). A
programmable lockout interval (typically 5 to 15 minutes) follows the dose, during
which an additional dose cannot be given even if the person activates the button.
It is also possible to program the maximum dose that can be delivered over a
period of hours (usually 4 hours). Many pumps are capable of delivering a basal
rate (continuous infusion), with or without additional PCA doses available. The
person prescribed a PCA must be able to understand how to use the PCA and be
physically able to push the button independently (D’Arcy 2011).
Figure 49.11


PCA line introduced into the injection port of a primary line.
Figure 49.12


The older child is able to regulate the PCA pump.
Source: Beau Lark/Corbis/VCG/Getty Images.
Lifespan considerations PCA pump
Children
Include the parents in teaching.
Assess the child’s ability to use the control button.
Older adults
Carefully monitor for drug side effects.
Use cautiously for individuals with impaired pulmonary or renal function.


Assess the person’s cognitive and physical ability to use the control
button.
Home care considerations
PCA pump
Monitor for signs and symptoms of over-sedation such as
excessive drowsiness, slowed respiratory rate or change in
mental state.
Do not adjust settings without consulting with the medical
practitioner who is responsible for the medication order.
Tape to the back of the pump the following emergency contact
numbers: emergency medical services, doctor, home care
organisation and pump manufacturer.
Non-pharmacological pain management
Non-pharmacological pain management consists of a variety of physical,
cognitive–behavioural and lifestyle pain management strategies that target the
body, mind, spirit and social interactions (see Table 49.8
). Physical modalities
include cutaneous stimulation, ice or heat, immobilisation or therapeutic
exercises, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) and acupuncture.
Mind–body (cognitive–behavioural) interventions include distracting activities,
relaxation techniques, imagery, meditation, biofeedback, hypnosis, cognitive
reframing, emotional counselling and spiritually directed approaches such as
therapeutic touch or Reiki. Lifestyle management approaches include symptom
monitoring, stress management, exercise, nutrition, pacing activities, disability


management and other approaches needed by many people with persistent pain
that has drastically changed their life. For further information on selected mind–
body interventions and acupuncture, see Chapter 20
. This discussion is limited
to selected physical and cognitive–behavioural interventions.
Table 49.8 Non-pharmacological interventions for pain control
Physical interventions
The goals of physical intervention include providing comfort, altering physiological
responses to reduce pain perception and optimising functioning.
Cutaneous stimulation
Cutaneous stimulation can provide effective temporary pain relief. It distracts the
person and focuses attention on the tactile stimuli, away from the painful
sensations, thus reducing pain perception. Cutaneous stimulation is also believed
to interfere with the transmission and perception of pain by stimulating the large-
diameter A-beta sensory nerve fibres that activate the descending mechanisms
that can reduce the intensity of pain, activate the endorphin system of pain
control and thus diminish conscious awareness of pain. Selected cutaneous
stimulation techniques include the following:
massage
application of heat or cold
acupressure
contralateral stimulation.
Cutaneous stimulation can be applied directly to the painful area, proximal to the
pain or distal to the pain (along the nerve path or dermatome) and contralateral
(exact location, opposite side of the body) to the pain. Cutaneous stimulation is
contraindicated in areas of skin breakdown or impaired neurological functioning.


Massage
Massage is a comfort measure that can aid relaxation, decrease muscle tension
and may ease anxiety because the physical contact communicates caring. It can
also decrease pain intensity by increasing superficial circulation to the area.
Massage can involve the back and neck, hands and arms, or feet. The use of
ointments or liniments may provide localised pain relief with joint or muscle pain.
Massage is contraindicated in areas of skin breakdown, suspected clots or
infections. See Skill 49.1
.
Patient education
Self-management of pain
Choose a time to provide education for the person about pain
management when the pain is controlled so that the person is able to
focus on the teaching. Teaching the person about self-management of
pain can include the following:
Demonstrate the operation of the PCA pump and explain that the
person can safely push the button without fear of overmedicating.
Sometimes it helps people who are reluctant to repeatedly push the
button to know that they must dose themselves (i.e. push the button) 5
to 10 times to receive the same amount of medication (10 mg
morphine equivalent) they would receive in a standard ‘shot’.
Describe the use of the pain scale and encourage the person to
discuss this with you to confirm they are able to demonstrate
understanding.
Explore a variety of non-drug pain relief techniques that the person
considers may be applicable and encourage their use to promote pain
relief and optimise functioning.
Explain the rationale for needing to notify staff when they need to
mobilise (e.g. for bathroom use) if applicable to optimise their safety.


Heat and cold applications
A warm bath, heating pads, ice bags, ice massage, hot or cold compresses and
warm or cold sitz baths in general relieve pain and promote healing of injured
tissues (see Chapter 37
). Cold works best when applied within the first 24
hours of injury or condition, while heat is primarily used to treat the chronic phase
of an injury or condition, usually 48 hours after acute injury.
Acupressure
Acupressure developed from the ancient Chinese healing system of acupuncture.
The therapist applies finger pressure to points that correspond to many of the
points used in acupuncture (see Chapter 20
).
Contralateral stimulation
Contralateral stimulation can be accomplished by stimulating the skin in an area
opposite to the painful area (e.g. stimulating the left knee if the pain is in the right
knee). The contralateral area may be scratched for itching, massaged for cramps
or treated with cold packs or analgesic ointments. This method is particularly
useful when the painful area cannot be touched because it is hypersensitive,
when it is inaccessible by a cast or bandages, or when the pain is felt in a missing
part (phantom pain). The nurse should explain that nerves are crossed in the
spinal cord and that is why these techniques may work contralaterally.
Immobilisation/bracing
Immobilising or restricting the movement of a painful body part (e.g. arthritic joint,
traumatised limb) may help to manage episodes of acute pain. Splints or
supportive devices should hold joints in the position of optimal function and should
be removed regularly in accordance with organisation protocol to provide range-
of-motion (ROM) exercises. Prolonged immobilisation can result in joint
contracture, muscle atrophy and cardiovascular problems. Therefore, people


should be encouraged to participate in self-care activities and remain as active as
possible with frequent ROM exercises.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)
 is a method of applying
low-voltage electrical stimulation directly over identified pain areas, at an
acupressure point, along peripheral nerve areas that innervate the pain area or
along the spinal column. The TENS unit consists of a portable, battery-operated
device with lead wire and electrode pads that are applied to the chosen area of
skin. Cutaneous stimulation from the TENS unit is thought to activate large-
diameter fibres that modulate the transmission of the nociceptive impulse in the
peripheral and central nervous system (closing the pain ‘gate’), resulting in pain
relief. This stimulation may also cause a release of endorphins from the CNS
centres. The use of TENS is contraindicated for people with pacemakers or
arrhythmias, or in areas of skin breakdown. It is generally not used on the head
or over the chest.
Cognitive–behavioural interventions
The goals of cognitive–behavioural interventions include providing comfort,
altering psychological responses to reduce pain perception and optimising
functioning. Selected cognitive–behavioural interventions include distraction,
eliciting the relaxation response, re-patterning thinking and facilitating coping with
emotions.
Distraction
Distraction draws the person’s attention away from the pain and lessens the
perception of pain. In some instances, distraction can make a person completely
unaware of pain. Distraction makes the person unaware of the pain only for the
amount of time and to the extent that the distracting activity holds their ‘undivided’
attention. For example, a person recovering from surgery may feel no pain while


watching a football game on television yet feel pain again during commercials or
when the game is over. Different types of distractions are shown in Box 49.9
.
Using multiple forms of distraction simultaneously adds value to the activity. For
example, listening to music can be distracting; however, the value can be added
by tapping to the music, singing along or playing along on a musical instrument.
Play therapy can be a distraction for children.
BO X
49.9 Types of distraction
Visual distraction
Reading or watching TV.
Watching a football game.
Guided imagery.
Auditory distraction
Humour.
Listening to music.
Tactile distraction
Slow, rhythmic breathing.
Massage.
Holding or stroking a pet or toy.
Intellectual distraction
Crossword puzzles.


Card games (e.g. bridge).
Hobbies (e.g. stamp collecting, writing a story).
Eliciting the relaxation response
Stress increases pain, in part by increasing muscle tension, activating the
sympathetic nervous system and putting the person at risk of stress-related types
of pain (e.g. tension headaches). The relaxation response decreases and
counteracts the harmful effects of stress, including the effect it has on physical,
cognitive and emotional functioning. Eliciting this response requires more than
simply helping a person to relax; rather, it involves a structured technique
designed to focus the mind and relax muscle groups. Basic techniques with
helpful scripts are available for common techniques including progressive
relaxation, breath-focus relaxation and meditation. The nurse can coach the
person, urge self-directed meditation or provide an audio recording to help elicit
the relaxation response. Many people can achieve the desired state after a few
attempts, but mastery of this skill requires daily practice over a few weeks. In
general, relaxation techniques by themselves do not have remarkable pain-
relieving properties; however, they can reduce pain that may have been
exacerbated by stress. Some people may become more consciously aware of
their pain while practising relaxation techniques before they have learned mastery
of controlling ‘mind chatter’ and remaining mentally focused.
Once the person has mastered the basic skills for eliciting the relaxation
response, techniques of imagery or self-hypnosis can be used. Both imagery and
hypnosis begin with attaining a deep state of relaxation and are capable of
altering the experience of pain; for example, having the person replace the pain
with a feeling of pleasant numbness. Additional post-hypnotic suggestions can
then be made, linking these pleasant numb sensations to coping efforts used
during the day (e.g. ‘Every time you stop to take a slow, deep, diaphragmatic
breath, you will feel this pleasant numbness instead of pain’).


There is evidence to suggest that music therapy is useful for providing relaxation
(Warth et al.
); with smartphones and portable music devices, people can listen
to their favourite music as a helpful distraction from pain.
53 Warth, M., Keßler, J., Hillecke, T. K. & Bardenheuer, H. J. (2015). Music therapy in palliative care: A
randomized controlled trial to evaluate effects on relaxation. Deutsches Ärzteblatt International, 112(46), 788–
794.
Re-patterning unhelpful thinking
Some people harbour strong self-doubts, unrealistic expectations (e.g. ‘I just want
someone to make the pain go away’), rumination (e.g. ‘I keep thinking about my
pain and the person who did this to me’), helplessness (e.g. ‘I can’t do anything’)
and magnification (e.g. ‘My life is ruined, I’ll never be a good parent because of
my pain’). These cognitive patterns have been identified as important contributors
to treatment failures, the intensification of pain, disability and depression. Nurses
can help by challenging the truthfulness and helpfulness of these thoughts and
replacing them with realistic and confidence-building ones that are particularly
powerful predictors of more effective coping, better clinical outcomes and
improved quality of life.
Facilitating coping
Nurses can help by intervening with people who are anxious or sad, or express
overly pessimistic or helpless points of view. Awareness of the person’s
misperceptions or unrealistic expectations also helps the professional avoid a
common cause of therapeutic failure. Therapeutic communication with an
emphasis on listening, providing encouragement, teaching self-management
skills, sharing vicarious experiences and persuading people to act on their own
behalf are strategies that enhance coping. Helping individuals to better
communicate with the professional staff, family members and friends can also
promote coping. Counselling from trained professionals may be indicated for
those people with severe emotional distress but must be offered to them in a
53


sensitive way that does not convey the notion that pain is ‘in their head’. Chronic
pain support groups can be effective for many people.
Selected spiritual interventions
The spiritual dimension encompasses a person’s innermost concerns and values,
including the ascribed purpose, meaning and driving force in their life. It may
include rituals that help the individual become part of a community or feel a bond
with the universe that is not necessarily religious in nature. For those who express
their spirituality in a religious context, it is appropriate to offer prayer, intercessory
prayer (being prayed for by others) or access to meaningful rituals. For some
people, a caring presence, attentive listening and facilitating the process of
acceptance can help reduce spiritual distress whereas others benefit from
manipulation of energy patterns (e.g. therapeutic touch).
Through improved spiritual insights, individuals with pain can find meaning in what
seems incomprehensible and learn to cope with the intolerable. This process
often begins by making peace with their past, being spiritually aware in the
present and making a commitment to go forward with life despite the pain
(Corbett, Lovell & Siddall ). By shifting awareness from within to external sources
of power, pain sufferers can transcend the limits of their pain to find new energy
and a renewed sense of purpose.
54 Corbett, M., Lovell, M. & Siddall, P. J. (2017). The role of spiritual factors in people living with chronic pain: A
qualitative investigation. Journal for the Study of Spirituality, 7(2), 142–153. Doi:
10.1080/20440243.2017.1370908.
Non-pharmacological invasive therapies
A nerve block
 is a chemical interruption of a nerve pathway, effected by
injecting a local anaesthetic into the nerve. Nerve blocks are widely used during
dental work. The injected drug blocks nerve pathways from the painful tooth, thus
stopping the transmission of pain impulses to the brain. Nerve blocks are often
used to relieve the pain of whiplash injury, lower back disorders, bursitis and
54


cancer. With the intention of quieting ‘pain generators’ (irritable nerves that cause
the pain), a combination of a long-acting local anaesthetic and a steroid is injected
adjacent to the problem nerve (e.g. lumbar epidural steroid injections, joint
injections). The local anaesthetic should provide relief for several hours before the
effect of the steroid begins a day or two later. Often a series of three injections is
scheduled weeks or months apart. Each subsequent injection should result in a
longer duration of pain relief. No more than three injections per year are
recommended because of the mineral-robbing effect steroids have on bones in
the area.
Evaluating
The goals established in the planning phase are evaluated according to specific
desired outcomes, also established in that phase (see the ‘Identifying nursing
diagnoses, outcomes and interventions
’ box earlier in this chapter). To
assist in the evaluation process, flow sheet records or an individual diary may be
helpful. A weekly log or diary can be structured in a similar fashion for the
individual person. For example, columns including day, time, onset of pain, activity
before pain, pain relief measure and duration of pain can be devised to help the
person and nurse determine the effectiveness of pain relief strategies.
If outcomes are not achieved, the nurse and person need to explore the reasons
before modifying the care plan. The nurse might consider the following questions:
Is adequate analgesic being given? Would the person benefit from a change in
dose or in the time interval between doses?
Were the person’s beliefs, expectations and values about pain therapy
considered?
Did the person understate the pain experience for some reason?
Were appropriate instructions provided to allay misconceptions about pain
management?


Did the person and support people understand the instructions about pain
management techniques?
Is the person receiving adequate support for both physical pain and emotional
distress?
Has the person’s physical condition changed, necessitating modifications in
interventions?
Should selected intervention strategies be re-evaluated?
See the ‘Nursing care plan
’ and the ‘Concept map
’.
Home care considerations
Pain management
Explain the benefits of keeping a pain diary to monitor pain
onset, activity before pain, pain intensity, use of analgesics or
other relief measures and effectiveness of each measure.
Encourage the person to contact a health care professional if
planned pain control measures are ineffective.
Teach the use of preferred and selected non-pharmacological
techniques such as relaxation, guided imagery, distraction, music
therapy and massage.
Ensure that the person understands the benefits of using pain
control measures before the pain becomes severe.
Inform the person of the effects of untreated pain.
Provide appropriate information about how to access community
resources, home care agencies and associations that offer self-
help groups and educational materials.


Clinical consideration
The statement ‘Please tell me how I can best help you control
your pain’ sends subtle messages that are an important part
of treatment planning and evaluation of care. First, it
reinforces that ownership and responsibility for controlling
pain remains with the person. Second, it acknowledges that
the person may be the best judge of what is needed,
respecting the cultural meaning of pain and acceptable ways
of expressing/controlling pain. Third, it establishes the nurse’s
role in helping the person be more comfortable and in control
of their condition.
Lifespan considerations
Pain management
Infants
Giving an infant, particularly a very low birth weight infant, a water and
sucrose solution administered through a dummy provides some
evidence of pain reduction during procedures that may be painful but
should not be a substitute for anaesthetic or analgesic medications.
Children
Distract the child with toys, books or pictures.
Hold the child (or ask the parent to hold) to console and promote
comfort.
Explore misconceptions about pain and correct in understandable
‘concrete’ terms. Be aware of how your explanations may be


misunderstood. For example, telling a child it won’t hurt during surgery
because they will be ‘put to sleep’ will be very upsetting to a child who
knows of an animal that was ‘put to sleep’.
Children can use their imagination during guided imagery. Ask the child
to imagine a ‘pain switch’ (even give it a colour) and to visualise turning
the switch off in the area where there is pain. A ‘magic glove’ or ‘magic
blanket’ is an imaginary object that the child applies on areas of the
body (e.g. hand, thigh, back, hip) to lessen discomfort.
Older adults
Encourage the person to use pain control measures that have worked
in the past for them.
Spend time with the person and listen actively.
Clarify misconceptions. Encourage independence whenever possible.
Carefully review the treatment plan to avoid drug–drug, food–drug or
disease–drug interactions.
NURSING  CARE PLAN
Acute pain
Applying critical thinking
1. Is there any other assessment data you would want to gather to
help plan Mr C’s pain management?
2. Mr C does not have a PCA. What nursing interventions are
important?
3. What kind of data would you gather prior to having a discussion with
the doctor about options for improving pain control in this person?


Case Study
Mrs Jones underwent abdominal surgery approximately 6 hours ago. She
has a 15 cm midline incision that is covered with a dry and intact surgical
dressing. When assessing Mrs Jones, you note that she is perspiring, lying
in a rigid position, holding her abdomen and grimacing. Her blood pressure
is 150/90, heart rate 100 and respiratory rate 32. When asked to rate her
pain on a scale of 0 to 10, Mrs Jones rates her pain as 5 as long as she
remains perfectly still. There is a sharp area of pain at her incision;
however, the most troublesome pain is crampy and dull, like she was
‘kicked in the stomach’ with severe exacerbations that come in
unpredictable waves.
Fundamentals of care framework in context

49.1 Providing a back massage
Effleurage
 is a type of massage consisting of
long, slow, gliding strokes. A systematic review of 25
trials (Furlan et al.
) assessed the efficacy of
massage therapy for acute lower back pain. Results
from this review found massage to be better than
inactive controls for pain in the short term, but had
no impact on improving function. When combined
with exercise and education, massage provides
effective short-term relief.
52 Furlan, A. D., Giraldo, M., Baskwill, A., Irvin, E. & Imamura, M.
(2015). Massage for low-back pain. Cochrane Database of Systematic
Reviews, 9. Doi: 10.1002/14651858.CD001929.pub3.
Purposes
To relieve muscle tension.
To decrease pain intensity.
To promote physical and mental relaxation.
Assessment
52


Assess
Behaviours indicating potential need for a back
massage, such as a complaint of stiffness,
muscle tension in the back or shoulders, or
difficulty sleeping related to tenseness or anxiety.
Whether the person is willing to have a massage
—some individuals may not enjoy a massage.
Contraindications for back massage (e.g.
impaired skin integrity, back surgery, vertebral or
rib fracture).
Planning
Ensure that you have the full amount of time
available for the massage. Although the actual
technique may require only about 5 minutes, the
entire process should be conducted in a calm and
unhurried manner.
Delegation
The nurse can delegate this skill to an Assistant in
Nursing or carer; however, the nurse should first
assess for any contraindications and confirm that
the person is willing to accept this treatment.
Equipment
Lotion
Towel for excess lotion


Implementation
Preparation
Determine (a) previous assessments of the skin, (b)
special lotions to be used and (c) positions
contraindicated for the person. Arrange for a quiet
environment with no interruptions to promote
maximum effect of the back massage.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can cooperate. Encourage the
person to give you feedback as to the amount
of pressure you are using during the back
rub.
2. Perform hand hygiene.
3. Provide for individual privacy.
4. Prepare the person.
Assist the person to move to the near side
of the bed within your reach and adjust
the bed to a comfortable working height to
prevent back strain.
Establish which position the person
prefers. The prone position is
recommended for a back rub. The side-


lying position can be used if a person
cannot assume the prone position.
Expose the back from the shoulders to the
inferior sacral area. Cover the remainder
of the body to prevent chilling and
minimise exposure.
5. Massage the back.
Pour a small amount of lotion onto the
palms of your hands and hold it for a
minute. The lotion bottle can also be
placed in a bath basin filled with warm
water. Rationale: back rub preparations
tend to feel uncomfortably cold to people.
Warming the solution facilitates personal
comfort.
Using your palm, begin in the sacral area
using smooth, circular strokes. Move your
hands up the centre of the back and then
over both scapulae. Massage in a circular
motion over the scapulae.
Move your hands down the sides of the
back.
Massage the areas over the right and left
iliac crests. 1
Apply firm, continuous pressure without
breaking contact with the person’s skin.


Repeat above for 3 to 5 minutes,
obtaining more lotion as necessary.
While massaging the back, assess for skin
redness and areas of decreased
circulation.
Pat dry any excess lotion with a towel.
6. Document that a back rub was performed
and the person’s response. Record any
unusual findings.


1 One suggested pattern for a back massage
Evaluation
Compare the person’s current response to their
previous response. Is there a positive outcome such


as increased relaxation and decrease in pain and
anxiety because of the back massage?


Chapter 49 Review


Chapter highlights
Pain is ‘whatever the person says it is, and exists whenever he
says it does’. It is a subjective sensation to which no two people
respond in the same way. It can directly impair health and
prolong recovery from surgery, disease and trauma.
Types of pain may be described in terms of location, duration,
intensity and aetiology.
Pain threshold is generally similar in all people but pain tolerance
and response vary considerably.
The physiological processes related to pain perception are
described as nociception. Four processes are involved in
nociception: transduction, transmission, perception and
modulation.
For nociceptive pain to be perceived, nociceptors must be
stimulated. Three types of pain stimuli are mechanical, thermal
and chemical.
According to the gate control theory, peripheral nerve fibres
carrying pain to the spinal cord can have their input modified at
the spinal cord level before transmission to the brain. This theory
is the basis of many pain intervention strategies.
Numerous factors influence a person’s perception of and reaction
to pain: ethnic and cultural values, developmental stage,
environment and support people, past pain experiences and
meaning of pain.
Pain is subjective and the most reliable indicator of the presence
or intensity of pain is the person’s self-report. Pain assessment is


the fifth vital sign. Assessment of a person who is experiencing
pain should include a comprehensive pain history.
Although the actual nursing diagnosis given to people suffering
pain is Acute pain or Chronic pain, the pain itself may be the
aetiology of many other risk diagnoses.
Overall individual goals include preventing, modifying or
eliminating pain so that the person is able to partly or completely
resume usual daily activities and to cope more effectively with
the pain experience.
When planning, nurses need to choose pain relief measures
appropriate for the person based on assessment data.
Key strategies to reduce pain include acknowledging and
accepting the person’s pain, assisting support people, reducing
misconceptions about pain, reducing fear and anxiety, and
preventing pain.
Pain management includes two basic types of nursing
interventions: pharmacological and non-pharmacological.
Key strategies to reduce pain include acknowledging and
accepting the person’s pain, assisting support people, reducing
misconceptions about pain, reducing fear and anxiety, and
preventing pain.
Pharmacological interventions, ordered by the doctor or nurse
practitioner, include the use of opioids, non-opioids such as
NSAIDs and co-analgesic drugs.
The World Health Organization recommends a three-step ladder
approach to manage chronic cancer pain. This model establishes
the pharmacological foundation upon which other types of pain
are managed.


Placebos should never be used to determine whether or not
someone is in pain. Deceptive use of placebos is unethical.
Analgesic medication can be delivered through a variety of routes
and methods to meet the specific needs of the person. These
routes include oral, transmucosal, nasal, rectal, transdermal,
topical, subcutaneous, intramuscular, intravenous, intraspinal and
continuous local anaesthetics.
Patient-controlled analgesia enables the person to exercise
control and treat the pain by self-administering doses of
analgesics.
Physical modalities of non-pharmacological pain interventions
include such cutaneous stimulation as hot and cold applications,
massage, acupressure and contralateral stimulation;
immobilisation/bracing; and transcutaneous electrical nerve
stimulation (TENS).
Cognitive-behavioural interventions include distraction
techniques, eliciting the relaxation response, re-patterning
unhelpful thinking, facilitating coping and selected spiritual
interventions.
Evaluation of the person’s pain therapy includes the response of
the person, the changes in the pain and the person’s perceptions
of the effectiveness of the therapy. Ongoing verbal or written
feedback from the person and family is integral to this process.

Nutrition
 is the sum of all the interactions
between an organism and the food it consumes.
In other words, nutrition is what a person eats
and how the body uses it. Nutrients
 are
organic and inorganic substances found in
foods that are required for body functioning.
Adequate food intake consists of a balance of
nutrients: water, carbohydrates, proteins, fats,
vitamins and minerals. Foods differ greatly in
their nutritive value
 (the nutrient content of a
specified amount of food) and no one food
provides all essential nutrients. Nutrients have
three major functions: providing energy for body
processes and movement, providing structural
material for body tissues and regulating body
processes.


Essential nutrients
The body’s most basic nutrient need is water. Because every cell
requires a continuous supply of fuel, the most important nutritional
need, after water, is for nutrients that provide fuel, or energy. The
energy-providing nutrients are carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
Hunger compels people to eat enough  energy-providing nutrients to
satisfy their energy needs. Carbohydrates, fats and protein are
referred to as macronutrients
, because they are needed in large
amounts (e.g. hundreds of grams) to provide energy.
Micronutrients
, vitamins and minerals, are those required in
small amounts (e.g. milligrams or micrograms) to metabolise the
energy-providing nutrients.
Carbohydrates
Carbohydrates
 are composed of the elements carbon (C),
hydrogen (H) and oxygen (O) and include simple sugars, starches
and fibre. Carbohydrates are essential for the provision of energy to
cells, in particular the brain, which needs glucose for its metabolism.
Carbohydrate (from mainly low energy density and/or low glycaemic
index foods) should make up approximately 45−65% of total energy
intake. The type of carbohydrate influences energy intake, digestion


and metabolism, and is considered critical in relation to their health
effects.
Natural sources of carbohydrates supply vital nutrients (such as
protein, vitamins and minerals) and other phytochemical compounds
(e.g. flavonoids, lignans, ellagic acid, monoterpenes) which are not
found in processed foods. Processed carbohydrate-rich foods (e.g.
lollies, potato chips, sweet biscuits and cakes) are relatively low in
nutrients in relation to the large amount of energy they provide.
These types of foods are sometimes referred to as ‘energy dense’
foods or ‘empty calories’. It is important that a majority of our
carbohydrate intake comes from natural and unprocessed foods
which are more  nutrient-dense and likely to contain more dietary
fibre.
Types of carbohydrates
Sugars
Sugars, the simplest of all carbohydrates, are water soluble and are
produced naturally by both plants and animals. Sugars may be
monosaccharides
 (single molecules) such as glucose, fructose
and galactose, disaccharides
 (double molecules) such as
sucrose, maltose, trehalose and lactose, or sugar alcohols such as
sorbitol, maltitol and lactitol. Of the three monosaccharides, glucose
is by far the most abundant simple sugar.


Most sugars are produced naturally by plants, especially fruits,
sugar cane and sugar beets. However, other sugars are from an
animal source. For example, lactose, a combination of glucose and
galactose, is found in animal milk. Processed or refined sugars (e.g.
glucose, maltose, dextrose, raw sugar, cane sugar and molasses)
have been extracted and concentrated from natural sources. These
refined sugars are added to a wide range of manufactured foods for
preservation, flavour enhancement, bulk or texture. While there is no
physiological difference between naturally occurring and refined
sugars, foods with high added sugar content usually have lower
nutritive value and are considered energy dense (National Health
and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) ). To promote energy
balance and the intake of essential nutrients from more nutrient-
dense foods, the intake of these ‘added’ or refined sugars should be
limited (
 total energy intake).
1 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) (2006). Nutrient Reference
Values for Australia and New Zealand. Canberra: Department of Health and Ageing.
Dietary fibre
Dietary fibre refers to the edible parts of plants/plant extracts that
are resistant to digestion and absorption in the small intestine, and
which pass into the large intestine where they are completely or
partially fermented. Adequate dietary fibre promotes laxation,
reduces blood cholesterol and modulates blood glucose) and is
associated with weight loss, reduced risk of chronic diseases such
as heart disease, some cancers and diabetes (NHMRC ).
1
≤10%
2


2 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) (2013a). Australian Dietary
Guidelines. Australian Guide to Healthy Eating (Poster). Canberra: Department of Health and
Ageing. Retrieved from <www.eatforhealth.gov.au>.
Most Australians do not meet current recommendations for dietary
fibre intake—adults: females 25 g/day; males 30 g/day; children and
adolescents 14−22 g/day relative to age (NHMRC 2013a). Dietary
fibre should be obtained through a wide variety of foods including
fruits, vegetables, breads, cereals and legumes. Fibre supplements
should only be taken on recommendation by a medical practitioner
or dietitian. A person’s nutritional status may be negatively affected
by fibre supplements due to altered absorption of iron, zinc and
calcium.
Carbohydrate digestion
Major enzymes involved in carbohydrate digestion include ptyalin
(salivary amylase), pancreatic amylase and the disaccharidases:
maltase, sucrase and lactase. Enzymes
 are biological catalysts
that speed up chemical reactions. The desired end products of
carbohydrate digestion are monosaccharides. Some simple sugars
(glucose, fructose and galactose) are already monosaccharides and
require no digestion. Except for sugar alcohols (which are poorly
absorbed and partly fermented), and lactose (which is fermented in
the large bowel) all sugars are absorbed from the small intestine in
healthy people.
Carbohydrate metabolism


Carbohydrate metabolism is a major source of body energy. One
gram of carbohydrate provides approximately 17 kilojoules of
energy. After the body breaks carbohydrates down into glucose,
some glucose continues to circulate in the blood to maintain blood
levels and to provide a readily available source of energy. The
remainder is either used as energy or stored. Insulin, a hormone
secreted by the pancreas, enhances the transport of glucose into
cells and is essential for the maintenance of blood glucose levels
within normal range.
Storage and conversion
Carbohydrates are stored either as glycogen or as fat. Glycogen
is a large polymer (compound molecule) of glucose. The process of
glycogen formation is called glycogenesis
. Almost all body cells
are capable of storing glycogen; however, most is stored in the liver
and skeletal muscles where it is available for conversion back into
glucose. Glucose that cannot be stored as glycogen is converted to
fat.
Glycaemic index (GI)
All carbohydrate foods differ in relation to their digestion and
absorption and their resultant impact on blood glucose levels. The
rate of digestion of carbohydrates varies with health status, race and
gender. The glycaemic index (GI)
 is based on a physiological
classification of foods containing carbohydrates. Foods containing
carbohydrate are ranked on a scale from 0 to 100. This ranking


relates to the speed at which sugars are broken down and
absorbed. The factors that affect the GI of a food include particle
size of grains (larger grains will have a lower GI), the ratio of
amylase to amylopectin (higher ratios, e.g. beans,
basmati/Doongara rice, will have a lower GI), degree of starch
gelatinisation (greater gelatinisation means higher GI) and the
presence of soluble fibres, fat, protein and organic acids.
Foods with a high GI are those that are rapidly digested and
absorbed and elicit an insulin response that results in increased
glycogen synthesis or glycogenesis; if there is inadequate secretion
of insulin, this may lead to hyperglycaemia. Low-GI foods are slowly
digested and absorbed. They produce more gradual rises in blood
sugar and insulin levels and have proven benefits for health.
Although research related to GI and diabetes risk and/or
management is equivocal, low-GI diets have been found to be
associated with improved glucose control and lipid levels in people
with diabetes (type 1 and type 2), and reduced insulin levels and
insulin resistance. Low-GI diets may also assist in weight loss and
weight maintenance because they assist in appetite control and
hunger delay.
The GI symbol
The GI symbol was introduced in Australia in 2002 and was updated
in 2009 (see Figure 50.1
). Foods undergo testing in accredited
laboratories and must meet strict nutrient criteria for their category
before being marked with the GI symbol. If a food does not have a


GI symbol near the nutrition panel, this does not mean it is not a
low-GI food; it may be that it has not yet been tested and/or
marketers have chosen not to include the symbol in their packaging.
See the Glycaemic Index Foundation website for more official
information <www.gisymbol.com>.
Figure 50.1
GI symbol.
Source: ©  and  The University of Sydney. Used under licence.
®
™


Proteins
Amino acids, organic molecules made up primarily of carbon,
hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, combine to form proteins
. Every
cell in the body contains some protein, and about three-quarters of
body solids are proteins.
Amino acids are categorised as essential (indispensable) or non-
essential (dispensable). Essential amino acids
 are those that
cannot be manufactured in the body and must be supplied as part of
the protein ingested in the diet. The nine essential amino acids—
histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine,
tryptophan, threonine and valine—are necessary for tissue growth
and maintenance. A tenth amino acid, arginine, appears to have a
role in the immune system.
Non-essential amino acids
 are those that the body can
manufacture. The body takes amino acids derived from the diet and
reconstructs new ones from their basic elements. Non-essential
amino acids include alanine, aspartic acid, cystine, glutamic acid,
glycine, hydroxyproline, proline, serine and tyrosine.
The nutritional quality of proteins is related to their digestibility and
how well their essential amino acid content matches body
requirements. Complete
, or ‘high-quality’, proteins
 contain
all of the essential amino acids plus many non- essential ones. Most


animal proteins, including meats, poultry, fish, dairy products and
eggs, are complete proteins.
Incomplete
, or ‘lower-quality’, proteins
 lack one or more
essential amino acids (most commonly lysine, methionine or
tryptophan) and are usually derived from vegetables. If, however, an
appropriate mixture of plant proteins is provided in the diet, a
balanced ratio of essential amino acids can be achieved. For
example, a combination of corn (low in tryptophan and lysine) and
beans (low in methionine) is a complete protein. Such combinations
of two or more vegetables are called complementary mixtures of
proteins. Another way to take full advantage of vegetable proteins is
to eat them with a small amount of animal protein. Pasta with
cheese, rice with pork, noodles with tuna and cereal with milk are
just a few examples of combining vegetable and animal proteins to
enhance their nutritional quality. The complementariness of proteins
is one of the key reasons for recommending a varied diet (see Box
50.7
 Australian Dietary Guidelines on page 1325).
Protein digestion
Digestion of protein foods begins in the mouth and then continues in
the stomach where the enzyme pepsin is secreted and activated by
hydrochloric acid to break protein down into smaller units. However,
most protein is digested in the small intestine. The pancreas
secretes the proteolytic enzymes trypsin, chymotrypsin and
carboxypeptidase; glands in the intestinal wall secrete


aminopeptidase and dipeptidase. These enzymes break protein
down into smaller molecules and eventually into amino acids.
Storage
Amino acids are absorbed by active transport through the small
intestine into the portal blood circulation. The liver uses some amino
acids to synthesise specific proteins (e.g. liver cells and the plasma
proteins albumin, globulin and fibrinogen). Plasma proteins are a
storage medium that can rapidly be converted back into amino
acids.
Other amino acids are transported to tissues and cells throughout
the body where they are used to make protein for cell structures. In
a sense, protein is stored as body tissue. The body cannot actually
store excess amino acids for future use. However, a limited amount
is available in the ‘metabolic pool’ that exists because of the
constant breakdown and build-up of the protein in body tissues.
Protein metabolism
One gram of protein provides approximately 17 kilojoules of energy;
however, little dietary protein is used for energy needs in weight-
stable people. Protein metabolism includes three activities:
anabolism
 (building tissue), catabolism
 (breaking down
tissue) and nitrogen balance
.


Nitrogen balance
Because nitrogen is the element that distinguishes protein from lipids
and carbohydrates, nitrogen balance reflects the status of protein
nutrition in the body. Nitrogen balance is a measure of the degree of
protein anabolism and catabolism; it is the net result of intake and
loss of nitrogen. When nitrogen intake equals nitrogen output, a
state of nitrogen balance exists. A positive protein balance is
required when a body is growing or recovering from illness or injury
(i.e. dietary protein requirements are greater). Strength/weight
training and hormones (insulin, human growth hormone and
testosterone) stimulate positive protein balance. A negative protein
balance may occur when dietary protein intake is inadequate and/or
protein needs are greater (e.g. fasting, burns, infection, illness)
and/or when protein losses are greater (e.g. renal disease).
Lipids (dietary fat)
Lipids
 are organic substances that are greasy and insoluble in
water but soluble in alcohol or ether. Fats
 are lipids that are solid
at room temperature; oils
 are lipids that are liquid at room
temperature. In common use, the terms fats and lipids are used
interchangeably. Lipids have the same elements (carbon, hydrogen
and oxygen) as carbohydrates but they contain a higher proportion
of hydrogen.


Fatty acids
, made up of carbon chains and hydrogen, are the
basic structural units of most lipids. Fatty acids are described
according to the relative number of hydrogen atoms they contain.
Saturated fatty acids
 are those in which all carbon atoms are
filled to capacity (i.e. saturated) with hydrogen; an example is butyric
acid, found in butter. Although saturated fatty acids have
physiological and structural functions, they can be synthesised in the
body and are therefore not required in our diet. An unsaturated
fatty acid
 is one that could accommodate more hydrogen atoms
than it currently does. It has at least two carbon atoms that are not
attached to a hydrogen atom; instead, there is a double bond
between the two carbon atoms. Fatty acids with one double bond
are called monounsaturated fatty acids
. An example is oleic
acid, which is found in foods such as olive, canola and peanut oils.
Monounsaturated fatty acids are also synthesised in the body and
are not required in our diet. Fatty acids with more than one double
bond (or many carbons not bonded to a hydrogen atom) are
polyunsaturated fatty acids
. An example of a polyunsaturated
fatty acid is linoleic acid, found in sunflower, safflower and corn oil.
Linoleic acid is one of several n-6 (omega 6) polyunsaturated fats
which, if consumed in high amounts, are associated with lower
serum total and LDL (low density lipoprotein) cholesterol levels,
increased HDL (high density lipoprotein) cholesterol and reduced
triglyceride levels. Omega 3 fatty acids are also polyunsaturated
fatty acids with double bonds in the n-3 position. These fatty acids
cannot be synthesised in the body and it is necessary to obtain them
from foods such as legumes, canola oils and margarines, linseed
oils and products, and walnuts, leafy vegetables and oily fish.


Based on their chemical structure, lipids are classified as simple or
compound. Glycerides
, the simple lipids, are the most common
form of lipids. They consist of a glycerol molecule with up to three
fatty acids attached. Triglycerides
 (which have three fatty acids)
account for more than 90% of the lipids in food and in the body.
Triglycerides may contain saturated or unsaturated fatty acids.
Saturated triglycerides are found in animal products, such as butter,
and are usually solid at room temperature. Unsaturated triglycerides
are usually liquid at room temperature and are found in plant
products, such as olive oil and corn oil.
Cholesterol
 is a fat-like substance that is both produced by the
body and also found in foods of animal origin. Most of the body’s
cholesterol is synthesised in the liver; however, some is absorbed
from the diet (e.g. from milk, egg yolk and organ meats). Cholesterol
is necessary to create bile acids and to synthesise steroid
hormones. Along with phospholipids, large quantities of cholesterol
are present in cell membranes as well as other cell structures.
Lipid digestion
Although chemical digestion of lipids begins in the stomach, they are
digested mainly in the small intestine, primarily by bile, pancreatic
lipase and enteric lipase. The end products of lipid digestion are
glycerol, fatty acids and cholesterol. These are immediately
reassembled inside the intestinal cells into triglycerides and
cholesterol esters (cholesterol with a fatty acid attached to it), which
are not water soluble. For these reassembled products to be


transported and used, the small intestine and the liver must convert
them into soluble compounds called lipoproteins. Lipoproteins
are made up of various lipids and a protein.
Lipid metabolism
Converting fat into usable energy occurs through the use of the
enzyme hormone-sensitive lipase that breaks down triglycerides in
adipose cells, releasing glycerol and fatty acids into the blood. One
gram of fat provides approximately 38 kilojoules of energy. Fasting
people will obtain most of their energy from fat metabolism, but
some amount of carbohydrate or protein must also be used because
the brain, nerves and red blood cells are dependent upon glucose.
Lipids are necessary for energy provision and the absorption of fat-
soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
Micronutrients
Many essential micronutrients have been identified; however, the
extent of their role and their interaction with other nutrients are not
completely understood. Micronutrients are required in relatively small
amounts (micrograms rather than grams) and include water-soluble
and fat-soluble vitamins and minerals.
A vitamin
 is an essential organic compound that cannot be
manufactured by the body and is needed to catalyse metabolic


processes. Thus, when vitamins are lacking in the diet, metabolic
deficits result. Water-soluble vitamins
 include vitamin C and the
B-complex vitamins:





 pantothenic acid and biotin.
The body cannot store water-soluble vitamins; thus, people must
obtain a daily supply in the diet. Water-soluble vitamins can be
affected by food processing, cooking, storage and preparation. For
example, thiamine (a vitamin essential to energy metabolism) is lost
in cell juices from frozen food as it defrosts, leaches into soaking
and cooking water and is destroyed by heat. Similarly, the vitamin C
content of foods is reduced by prolonged heating, boiling and the
use of copper and iron cooking pots. In many
manufactured/processed foods, such vitamin losses are restored by
fortifying foods with additional vitamins to account for losses that
occur with food processing (e.g. bread may be fortified with thiamine
and orange juice may be fortified with vitamin C).
Fat-soluble vitamins
 include A, D, E and K. The body can store
these vitamins, although there is a limit to the amounts of vitamins E
and K the body can store. Therefore, a daily supply of fat-soluble
vitamins is not absolutely necessary. Vitamin content is highest in
fresh foods that are consumed as soon as possible after harvest.
Vitamin D is different from all other vitamins, as it can be
synthesised by the body in the presence of sunlight. This exposure
to sunlight is the major source of vitamin D in Australia and New
Zealand. Therefore, vitamin D deficiency will most likely occur as a
result of limited exposure to sunlight (UVB radiation), rather than
B1 (thiamine), B2 (riboflavin),
B3 (niacin or nicotinic acid), B6 (pyridoxine),
B9 (folic acid), B12 (cobalamin),


limited intake of vitamin D rich foods. Individuals who are
housebound or in residential care, naturally dark-skinned individuals
and those who remain covered up (with clothing) when outdoors
(either for cultural reasons or for protection from the weather) are at
risk of vitamin D deficiency.
Minerals
 are found in organic compounds as inorganic
compounds and free ions. Macrominerals
 are those that people
require daily in amounts over 100 mg. They include calcium,
phosphorus, sodium, potassium and magnesium. Microminerals
are those that people require daily in amounts less than 100 mg.
They include iron, zinc, manganese, iodine, fluoride, copper,
chromium, molybdenum and selenium.
Common problems associated with the mineral nutrients are iron
deficiency resulting in anaemia, osteoporosis resulting from loss of
bone calcium and dental caries because of low natural levels of
fluoride in some water supplies. Additional information about major
minerals associated with the body’s fluid and electrolyte balance is
given in Chapter 55
.


Energy balance
Energy balance is the relationship between the energy derived from food
and the energy used by the body. The body obtains energy in the form of
kilojoules from carbohydrates, protein, fat and alcohol. The body uses
energy for voluntary activities such as walking and talking and for
involuntary activities such as breathing and secreting enzymes. A person’s
energy balance is determined by comparing energy intake with energy
output.
Energy intake
Energy is provided in the food and fluids we consume, and the amount of
energy that nutrients or foods supply to the body is measured in kilojoules
(kJ) or megajoules
 A kilojoule (kJ)
 is the amount
of work energy required when a force of 1 newton (N) moves 1 kilogram of
weight 1 metre distance. The terms calorie
 and kilocalorie
 are
imperial measures commonly used in magazines and US or Canadian
textbooks. One calorie/kilocalorie is equal to 4.18 kilojoules.
Energy intake is essential to maintaining basic human functions. This
includes respiratory, circulatory, hormonal and neurological processes,
thermal regulation and cell and tissue synthesis. Vitamins, minerals and
water provide essential nutrients but have no energy value and do not
contribute to our daily energy intake. Energy is released from food
components by oxidation, and the average amount of energy released is
(1 MJ = 1000 kJ).


17 kJ for carbohydrates, 17 kJ for protein, 38 kJ for fat and 29 kJ for
alcohol
Food composition tables and food labels provide information on the
nutrient content of foods. You can calculate how much energy is in a
particular food by multiplying the macronutrient (protein, carbohydrate and
fats) energy value by the amount of the nutrient in the food. For example,
1 cup of white rice (cooked) provides approximately 992 kJ.
The macronutrient content of 1 cup of rice includes 53.3 grams of
carbohydrate, 4.4 grams of protein and 0.3 grams of fat. The total energy
content can be calculated:
Many mobile phone apps and computerised dietary analysis programs
may also be used to calculate total daily energy intakes. Apps allow people
to monitor their dietary intakes and patterns and can assist in weight loss
or weight management. Apps may also be valuable education tools to
assist people in managing nutrition-related diseases or conditions. The
quality of information provided in nutrition/diet apps is a concern of
consumers in the rapidly growing app market. When using apps, users
should be aware that many apps lack evidence of their effectiveness.
Choosing an app that includes an Australian and New Zealand nutrient
database will help users to obtain more accurate data regarding their food
and nutrient intakes. Computer programs for nutritional analysis and
monitoring are also available; however, these are relatively costly and time
consuming and their use requires training and expertise in understanding
food composition.
