Digestive system


Energy expenditure
Energy expenditure is the amount of energy we expend to maintain basic
human functions. Metabolism
 refers to all biochemical and
physiological processes by which the body grows and maintains itself.
Metabolic rate is normally expressed in terms of the rate of heat liberated
during these chemical reactions. The basal metabolic rate (BMR)
 is
the rate at which the body metabolises food to maintain the energy
requirements of a person who is awake and at rest. The energy in food
maintains the BMR of the body and provides energy for activities such as
running and walking.
BMR is affected by several factors, including body size, gender, body fat
levels, alterations in hormone and nervous system controls, infection and
illness, fasting and some drugs. Body surface area impacts on BMR, so
people who are thin and tall will have a higher BMR than those who are
thin and short. Body weight also increases BMR, so people who are
overweight will have a higher BMR than a person of healthy weight.
However, as body fat has a lower metabolic rate than lean tissue, people
with high body fat percentage will have a lower BMR than people with
greater muscle mass or lean body mass. Males generally have a higher
BMR than females due to their greater muscle mass and lower body fat
levels. Metabolic rate is controlled by nervous and hormone systems and
thyroid hormones have a key role in controlling metabolic rate. Infection
and illness increase BMR, fasting reduces BMR and drugs such as
caffeine and nicotine increase BMR slightly. Energy requirements for each
individual varies with age, gender, body size and activity levels. Factorial
estimates are the most convenient method for determining energy


requirements; however, due to the wide variability in the behavioural,
physiological and metabolic components of energy requirements of
individuals, these should be used with caution. Estimates of energy needs
are based on the time allocated to routinely perform activities and an
understanding of the energy cost of these activities. The nutrient
reference values for Australia and New Zealand include tables and
methodology for estimating energy requirements.


Body weight and body mass
standards
Maintaining a healthy body weight requires a balance between the
expenditure of energy and the intake of energy. If energy
expenditure is greater than energy intake over a period of time, body
weight will decrease, and when energy intake frequently exceeds
energy expenditure over a period of time, body weight will increase.
Adipose tissue is the main energy store in the body and is generally
found either under the skin (subcutaneous) or around internal
organs (visceral). The amount of visceral fat is strongly influenced
by heredity and is more easily broken down and used as energy
under stressful situations. Because it is served by the portal blood
system, excess visceral fat can contribute to insulin resistance and
atherosclerosis. The distribution of excess body fat provides the
general distinguishing characteristics of males and females, with
males more commonly accumulating excess visceral fat around the
abdomen (android or ‘apple’ body shape) and females more
commonly accumulating excess fat around the hips, bottom and
thighs (gynoid or ‘pear’ shape). These relative distributions of body
fat strongly influence the risk of developing lifestyle diseases such as
hypertension, coronary heart disease and type 2 diabetes, and this
is why men generally have a higher risk than women of developing
these diseases.


Body weight and body composition are used as measures of healthy
body weight. Epidemiological research shows that there is a strong
association between body mass index (BMI) and excess morbidity
and mortality from conditions such as hypertension, dyslipidaemia,
diabetes mellitus, coronary heart disease, some cancers, gall
bladder disease and osteoarthritis. However, BMI alone is not an
adequate measure of body weight and relative health risk, nor is it
appropriate for some population groups. Waist circumference
measures and BMI are the most frequently used measures of
healthy body weight and health risk. It is important to understand the
limitations of using BMI in different population groups and the
correct method for measuring waist circumference.
The body mass index (BMI)
 is an indicator of changes in body
fat stores and whether a person’s weight is appropriate for height. It
may provide a useful estimate of malnutrition. BMI must be used
with caution in people who have fluid retention (e.g. ascites or
oedema), athletes, older adults, children, adolescents and some
ethnic and Indigenous groups (Asian and Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander). To calculate BMI:
1. Measure the person’s height in metres, e.g. 1.7 m
2. Measure the person’s weight in kilograms, e.g. 72 kg
3. Calculate the BMI using the following formula:
BMI = Weight in kilograms
(Height in metres)2 =
72
(1.7 × 1.7) = 24.9


For children and adolescents (aged 2 to 17 years), BMI calculations
are sex specific, age adjusted and compared with growth reference
charts (Cole & Lobstein ). Unlike adult BMI cut-off points, child and
adolescent BMI cut-off points (percentiles) do not relate to morbidity.
3 Cole, T. J. & Lobstein, T. (2012). Extended international (IOTF) body mass index cut-offs for
thinness, overweight and obesity. Pediatric Obesity, 7(4), 284–294.
In adults, waist circumference is used to measure excess abdominal
fat and is a better predictor of relative health risk than BMI (see Box
50.1
). Measures of waist circumference should be taken midway
between the lower rib and top of the pelvic bone (iliac crest) while
the individual is standing in a relaxed position and on the end of
exhalation. No tissue should be compressed beneath the tape. The
umbilicus should not be used as the measurement site as an
individual’s umbilicus may sit above or below this level depending on
the body shape and size.

Other measures of health risk and body fatness include skinfold
thicknesses, waist-to-hip ratio, hip circumference, bioelectrical
impedance, underwater weighing and dual-energy x-ray
absorptiometry (DEXA). Skinfold testing requires trained and skilled
personnel to take averaged readings of skinfold measures at various
body sites including biceps, triceps, subscapular and suprailiac.
Measures taken at each site are combined to provide a sum of
skinfolds and can be compared with standardised tables.
Bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) is used by some modern
weight scales and is considered one of the most accurate methods
of body fat determination. The speed with which an electrical signal
passes through the body is influenced by the amount of water in the
4
5


body. The more muscle, the more water the body can hold and the
easier it is for current to pass through it. The more fat mass, the
more resistance to current. Height, age, gender and weight, or other
physical characteristics such as body type, physical activity level and
ethnicity, are used with the impedance data to determine percentage
of body fat.


Factors affecting nutrition
Individual eating habits are influenced by a range of factors,
including developmental considerations, gender, ethnicity and
culture, beliefs about food, personal preferences, religious practices,
lifestyle, economics, health and nutrition literacy, medications and
therapy, health, alcohol consumption, advertising and psychological
factors. One or more of these factors may be a source of conflict for
people who are hospitalised or living in residential care and are
unable to consume their usual diet.
Growth and development
People in rapid periods of growth such as pregnancy, infancy and
adolescence have increased needs for nutrients.
Pregnancy
Poor nutritional status and/or unhealthy lifestyle behaviours prior to
pregnancy increase the risk of developing nutrient deficiencies, birth
defects and pregnancy complications. Maternal underweight is
associated with an increased risk of premature birth and low infant
birth weight, and maternal overweight is associated with a higher
frequency of premature birth, higher Caesarean section rates and


increased risk of neural tube defects. A healthy diet and regular
physical activity may reduce the risk of negative pregnancy
outcomes associated with underweight and overweight. Many
women mistakenly believe that during pregnancy you need to ‘eat
for two’; however, the additional energy requirements of pregnancy
are relatively small and are usually offset by the decrease in physical
activity that occurs as pregnancy progresses.
Food safety is critical during pregnancy when contraction of a food-
borne infection may result in serious consequences for the mother
and her unborn child. The vomiting and diarrhoea associated with
such infections may result in maternal exhaustion and dehydration,
and a Listeria infection can lead to miscarriage, stillbirth or
premature birth. (See Food Standards Australia New Zealand at
<www.foodstandards.gov.au> for more information on Listeria and
pregnancy.)
Infants
Infancy is considered a critical period for nutrition due to the rapid
growth and development that occurs between birth and 1 year of
age (body weight doubles between birth and 6 months and trebles
by 1 year, and body length increases 50%). Infants’ nutritional needs
are affected by their small body size and physiological immaturity,
which limit the amount of food/fluid that can be consumed at one
time. Infants also have a high resting metabolic rate (RMR) relative
to their body weight, which increases their need for water, energy
and nutrients.


Children and adolescents
Children and adolescents are vulnerable to the development of
micronutrient deficiencies, protein-energy malnutrition,  nutrition-
related chronic diseases (type 2 diabetes) and behavioural problems
including poor eating patterns and eating disorders. Studies of
Australian children and adolescents suggest that their dietary intakes
and behaviours are often suboptimal and that many are missing out
on the nutrients that are critical for normal growth and development
and the maintenance of health and wellbeing.
Older adults
As we live longer, our nutritional needs change and are affected by
many biological factors (decreases in lean body mass, mobility,
nutrient absorption, alterations in sense of smell, taste and sight),
social factors (bereavement, social inactivity, independent/dependent
living, residential living) and environmental factors (access to
food/shops and finances). Older adults generally need a nutrient-
dense diet and consideration must be made for dietary changes in
relation to their risk of coronary heart disease, osteoporosis, type 2
diabetes and hypertension. The Australian government has
legislated to provide standards around the provision of nutrition in
aged care and health care facilities. The standards outline
requirements for people in residential care, including food, nutrition
and hydration; developing positive social food environments;
malnutrition screening and treatment strategies; food preparation;
and assisted feeding (Bartl & Bunney ).
6


6 Bartl, R. & Bunney, C. (2015). Best Practice Food and Nutrition Manual for Aged Care
Homes, Edition 2. Gosford, NSW: Central Coast Local Health District. Retrieved from
<www.cclhd.health.nsw.gov.au>.
Gender
Nutrient requirements are different for men and women because of
body composition and reproductive functions. The larger muscle
mass of men translates into a greater need for energy intake and a
slightly greater need for proteins. Because of menstruation, pre-
menopausal women require more dietary iron than men. Pregnant
women have increased nutrient needs and lactating women have
increased energy, nutrient and fluid needs.
Ethnicity and culture
Ethnicity often determines food preferences. With more than 30% of
Australians born overseas and approximately 2.5% of our population
identifying as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander (Australian Bureau
of Statistics (ABS) ), it is important to appreciate the cultural
diversity within Australia and how traditions and cultural background
may influence dietary intake and behaviours. Traditional diets may
not be available or supported by current lifestyles and food systems,
and hospitals and residential care facilities may not support culturally
diverse diets.
7


7 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2013a). 2011 Census QuickStats Retrieved from
<www.censusdata.abs.gov.au>.
A ‘good food, bad food’ approach should not be used; rather, it
should be appreciated that variations of intake are acceptable under
different circumstances. It is important to understand that food
preferences may differ as much between individuals of the same
cultural background as between cultures, and the only ‘universally’
accepted guidelines are to (a) eat a wide variety of foods to ensure
adequate intake of nutrients, and (b) eat moderately to maintain
correct body weight. When providing dietary recommendations for
different ethnic or Indigenous groups, it is important first to
recognise or identify (with the person) where differences in
traditional versus contemporary food choices/behaviours exist and
provide guidance in choosing foods that are most like traditional
foods rather than convenience and processed foods.
Beliefs about food
Beliefs about the effects of foods on health and wellbeing can affect
food choices. Many people acquire their beliefs about food from
television, magazines, the internet, social media and other media.
Food fads that involve non-traditional food practices are relatively
common. A fad
 is a widespread but short-lived interest or practice
followed with considerable zeal. It may be based on either the belief
that certain foods have special powers or the notion that certain


foods are harmful. Examples of some dietary fads and myths are
given in Box 50.2
. Dietary fads may appeal to the individual
seeking to lose weight or obtain a miracle cure for a disease, the
person who desires superior health or one who wants to delay
ageing. Some fad diets are harmless but others are potentially
dangerous (Collins ). Many fad diets are based on the elimination of
at least one or more food groups (e.g. grain foods) or nutrients (e.g.
carbohydrates) and, as such, place an individual at risk of nutrient
deficiencies with a possibly greater risk of nutrition-related
diseases/conditions. To provide appropriate support and guidance
and/or suggestions for a more nutritious diet, nutrition information
must be considered critically and a sound knowledge and
understanding of facts developed, personal choices and decisions
must be appreciated, and the advice must be based on objective
and credible evidence.
8 Collins, C. (2014). Food facts and furphies. Australasian Science, 35(1), 16–17.
BO X
50.2 Examples of dietary fads and
myths
Elimination/avoidance of carbohydrate-rich foods (e.g.
ketogenic diet, Dukan diet).
Lectin-free diet—avoiding legumes and wholegrains that
contain lectins.
8


Paleo eating—based on eating foods similar to what might
have been eaten during the Palaeolithic period (2.5 million
to 10 000 years ago). Diet is generally high in protein and
fat and low in carbohydrate.
Acidic foods such as meat, chicken, fish, eggs, dairy and
grains will make blood more acidic and more at risk of
illness and disease.
Honey is healthier than sugar, more readily digested and a
cure for the common cold.
Eating grapefruit melts body fat.
Raw eggs, rare lean beef and oysters increase sexual
potency or fertility.
Organic foods are always healthier than non-organic
foods.
Stomach enzymes cannot work on carbohydrates and
proteins at the same time and therefore these foods
should not be eaten together.
Personal preferences
People develop likes and dislikes based on associations with a
typical food. A child who loves to visit his grandparents may love
pickled onions because they are served in the grandparents’ home.
Another child who dislikes a very strict aunt grows up to dislike the


chicken casserole she often prepares. People may carry such
preferences into adulthood.
Individual likes and dislikes are also related to familiarity. Children
often say they dislike a food before they sample it and it is important
that children are encouraged to at least try each new food presented
to them. Parents should provide opportunities for their children to
explore and taste a wide variety of foods and model these
behaviours for their children (i.e. parents themselves should also
explore and taste a wide variety of foods). Food preferences can
become very pronounced during illness and significantly impact on
the appetite of a person who is unwell. This is an important
consideration when providing care to patients during hospitalisation.
Religious practices
Australia has a multicultural and multi-religious population and it is
important to appreciate how religious practice also affects diet.
People who identify as Catholics may avoid meat on certain days
and some Protestant faiths prohibit meat, tea, coffee or alcohol.
Both Orthodox Judaism and Islam prohibit pork and people who
identify as Muslims consume only halal (‘lawful’) foods. People who
identify as Orthodox Jews observe kosher customs and eat certain
foods only if they are inspected by a Rabbi and prepared according
to dietary laws. The nurse must plan care with consideration of such
religious dietary practices and in consultation with the person.


Lifestyle
Certain lifestyles are linked to food-related behaviours. People who
are always in a hurry may buy convenience grocery items or eat
restaurant meals more often than less busy people. People who
spend many hours at home may spend more time preparing meals
‘from scratch’. Individual differences also influence lifestyle patterns
(e.g. cooking skills, concern about health). Some people work at
different times, such as evening or night shifts. They may need to
adapt their eating habits to this and make changes to medication
schedules if they are related to food intake.
Economics
What, how much and how often a person eats are frequently
affected by socioeconomic status. Social disadvantage or exclusion
(e.g. refugees, the homeless and those living on government
allowances) influences food intake and behaviours and may impact
nutrition status and chronic disease risk. People with limited income
may not be able to afford meat, fresh fruit and vegetables, or they
may live in areas with unsupportive food environments (close
proximity to take-away food outlets/convenience stores) which
prompt more frequent consumption of foods with low nutritive value
(Darmon & Drewnowski ).
9


9 Darmon, N. & Drewnowski, A. (2015). Contribution of food prices and diet cost to
socioeconomic disparities in diet quality and health: A systematic review and analysis.
Nutrition Reviews, 73(10), 643–660.
People with higher incomes may spend relatively high amounts of
their food budget on foods prepared outside the home (restaurants,
take-away food outlets) and also consume excessive amounts of
foods with low nutritive value and/or foods high in protein and fat.
Not all people have the financial resources and/or knowledge for
extensive food preparation, and many may not have storage
facilities (cupboards, refrigerators, freezers) or cooking facilities. In
some low-income areas and regional areas, food costs at
supermarkets or small grocery stores can be significantly higher
than at similar stores further away or in cities. All these factors may
impact food choices and overall nutritional intake. Appropriate
nutrition advice and education is dependent on an appreciation of
the impact of lifestyles and nutrition environments on food
consumption, and consideration of a range of individual
characteristics.
Health and nutrition literacy
Health literacy is defined as ‘the degree to which individuals have the
capacity to obtain, process and understand basic health information
and services needed to make appropriate health decisions’ (Ratzan
& Parker
). In our contemporary societies, our decisions and
actions around health are made across a range of settings (home,
10


work, school, online etc.) and occur when we are both sick and well.
The amount of health information available to us has undergone
significant expansion in line with the use of the internet for multiple
purposes. While making access to information much easier for most,
the abundance of information and varying degrees of authenticity in
the information being provided have resulted in much confusion and
declining trust in health information that is provided online. In
addition, much of the information available may not be easily
understood due to inability to speak the language it is published in,
low education levels and a lack of standards ensuring health
information is written so it can be understood by laypeople and those
with limited education. Studies conducted in the past decade have
found that people with higher education and higher health literacy
levels have higher- quality diets, but health literacy skills are context
dependent, and any person may experience low health literacy at
various times and in different contexts. For health professionals, it is
necessary to be aware of the need to provide options for patients to
access health and dietary information from different mediums (e.g.
paper based and/or online) and that the information provided is
relevant and comprehensible. In a practical sense, this means not
assuming a person’s health and nutrition literacy is equivalent to
their education or employment, using simple plain language when
speaking with patients and assessing understanding of information
provided by using teach-back techniques. In many situations, in is
prudent to ensure that nutrition and dietary information is also
provided to a spouse, partner, carer or parent in addition to the
patient.


10 Ratzan, S. C. & Parker, R. M. (2000). Introduction. In C. R. Selden, M. Zorn, S. C. Ratzan,
R. M. Parker (Eds), National Library of Medicine Current Bibliographies in Medicine: Health
Literacy. Bethesda, MD: National Institutes of Health, US Department of Health and Human
Services.
Medications and therapy
The effects of drugs on nutrition vary considerably. They may alter
appetite, disturb taste perception or interfere with nutrient absorption
or excretion. The nutritional effects of specific drugs (including over-
the-counter (OTC) medications) must be considered, and the
nursing assessment and history should include questions about all
medications and supplements (prescribed and OTC) the person is
taking. Conversely, nutrients can affect drug utilisation. Some
nutrients can decrease drug absorption; others enhance absorption.
Older adults are at particular risk of drug–food interactions due to
the number of medications they may take, age-related physiological
changes affecting medication actions (e.g. decrease in lean-to-fat
ratio, decrease in renal or hepatic function) and disease-restricted
diets..
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: comprehensive care
The intention of this standard is to ‘ensure that patients receive
comprehensive care—that is, coordinated delivery of the total


health care required or requested by a patient. This care is
aligned with the patient’s expressed goals of care and
healthcare needs, considers the impact of the patient’s health
issues on their life and wellbeing, and is clinically appropriate’
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC)
, p. 38).
11 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health
Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
This standard will assist the clinician to identify
patients at risk of poor nutrition and develop an
effective nutritional plan which is respectful of
the person’s individual preferences and cultural
and lifespan issues. The standard recognises
that patients with poor nutrition are at greater
risk of pressure injuries, infection and mortality.
Poor nutrition has also been recognised as a
significant factor in extended lengths of stay in
health care facilities. This standard includes
ensuring ‘that patients at risk of poor nutrition
are identified and that strategies are put in place
to reduce these risks’ (ACSQHC 2017, p. 39).
Chemotherapies and radiation may also adversely affect eating
patterns and nutrition. Normal cells of the bone marrow and the
gastrointestinal mucosa are naturally very active and particularly
11


susceptible to antineoplastic agents. Oral ulcers, intestinal bleeding
or diarrhoea resulting from the toxicity of antineoplastic agents used
in chemotherapy can seriously diminish a person’s nutritional status.
The effects of radiotherapy depend on the area that is treated. For
example, radiotherapy of the head and neck may cause decreased
salivation, taste distortions and swallowing difficulties; radiotherapy
of the abdomen and pelvis may cause malabsorption, nausea,
vomiting and diarrhoea. Many people undergoing this therapy feel
profound fatigue and anorexia (loss of appetite).
Culturally competent care
Selected variations in nutritional practices and
preferences between different cultures
Indigenous Australians
Traditional
The diet included a wide variety of animal and plant-based
foods, depending on season and location.
Most foods were eaten raw and some were roasted or
baked.
Hunting, growing or collecting food required significant
energy expenditure and skill.
Diets were high in protein, carbohydrate, fibre and overall
nutrient content.


Babies were breastfed until 3 years of age.
Highly prized foods included those with a high fat content
such as witchetty grubs, organ meats, fatty insects and
honey.
Traditional foods and dietary intakes are strongly
associated with health.
Contemporary
Most indigenous Australians are lactose intolerant.
Diets are commonly high in energy density, fat and refined
sugar.
Foods with high fat and sugar content have replaced
traditional food choices.
Breastfeeding rates are lower than in the non-Indigenous
population.
Arab heritage
Many spices and herbs are used, such as cinnamon,
allspice, cloves, mint, ginger and garlic.
Meats are often skewer roasted or slow simmered; most
common are lamb and chicken.
Bread is served at every meal.
Do not eat pork or its derivatives, meat and poultry that
have not been slaughtered according to the Zibah
method, animals that can live on both land and water,


vicious sea animals, sea mammals and carnivorous
animals. All meats must be cooked well done.
Food is eaten (and people are fed) with the right hand.
Beverages are drunk after the meal, not during.
Fast during daylight hours during the month of Ramadan
(may fall at a slightly different time each year on non-
Muslim calendars).
Chinese heritage
Foods are served at meals in a specific order.
Each region in China has its own traditional diet.
Traditional Chinese may not want ice in their drinks.
Foods are chosen to balance yin and yang in order to
avoid indigestion.
Health
An individual’s health status greatly affects eating habits and
nutritional status. Lack of teeth, ill-fitting dentures or a sore mouth
makes chewing food difficult. Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia
)
due to a painfully inflamed throat or a stricture of the oesophagus
can prevent a person from obtaining adequate nourishment. Disease
processes and surgery of the gastrointestinal tract can affect
digestion, absorption, metabolism and excretion of essential
nutrients. Gastrointestinal and other diseases also create nausea,


vomiting and diarrhoea, all of which adversely affect a person’s
appetite and nutritional status. Gallstones, which can block the flow
of bile, are a common cause of impaired lipid digestion. Metabolic
processes can be impaired by diseases of the liver. Diseases of the
pancreas can affect glucose metabolism or fat digestion.
Lactose intolerance
Lactose intolerance is more common in Indigenous Australians and
people from Asia and southern Europe than in other groups in
Australia. Approximately 1 in 20 Australians is affected by lactose
intolerance, about 5% of all Caucasians and 75% of non-
Caucasians. Lactose intolerance, a shortage of the enzyme lactase
which is needed to break down the sugar in milk (lactose), rarely
occurs in infants and most commonly manifests in children after the
age of 5 years. Temporary lactose intolerance may also occur with
malnutrition or after gastrointestinal surgery or infection.
The malabsorption of milk and milk products that occurs with lactose
intolerance may cause abdominal pain, bloating, flatulence and
persistent diarrhoea. Most people with lactose intolerance do not
need to eliminate dairy foods from their diet completely and may
tolerate cheese and yoghurt (which are low in lactose) and small
quantities of milk. To reduce the risk of nutritional deficiencies, it is
important that people with self-perceived lactose intolerance obtain
professional diagnosis from their doctor or dietitian. Additional fact
sheets and information are available from Dairy Australia .
12


12 Dairy Australia (2011). Lactose Intolerance Fact Sheet. Retrieved from <www.dairy
australia.com.au>.
Alcohol consumption
Alcohol is a depressant drug. When consumed in low amounts it
may offer some protective health effects, but when consumed in
high amounts (i.e. above recommendations) it increases the risk of
cardiovascular disease, liver cirrhosis and some cancers. Australian
guidelines for alcohol consumption recommend that healthy men
and women drink no more than two standard drinks on any day to
reduce lifetime risk of harm from alcohol-related disease or injury,
and no more than four standard drinks should be consumed on a
single occasion (see also Box 50.3
). The guidelines also
recommend that for ‘women who are pregnant, planning a
pregnancy or breastfeeding, not drinking alcohol is the safest option’
and, for young people, ‘the safest option is to delay the initiation of
drinking for as long as possible’ (NHMRC ).
13 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) (2009). Australian Guidelines to
Reduce Health Risks from Drinking Alcohol. Canberra: Department of Health and Ageing.
Retrieved from <www.nhmrc.gov.au>.
BO X
13


50.3 Australians and their alcohol
consumption
The proportion of people aged 14 years or older who drink
alcohol daily has declined (from 6.5% in 2013 to 5.9% in
2016).
Males are more likely than females to drink daily.
Adults aged 70 years or older are the most likely age
group to drink daily.
Approximately 20% of Australian adults consume alcohol
at levels that put them at risk of harm over their lifetime.
26% of Australian adults exceed the recommendations for
single occasion drinking at least once per month.
Males are more likely than females to consume alcohol at
levels that put them at risk of harm and/or exceed
recommendations for single-occasion drinking. More
adolescents are delaying drinking, with the average age
for trying alcohol for the first time increasing to 16.1 years
in 2016, compared to 14.7 years in 2001.
People living in remote and very remote areas are more
likely than people living in major cities to drink at risky
levels.

juices or other beverages added to the drink. This can contribute a

Drinking alcohol can lead to weight gain through the addition of
kilojoules to the regular diet plus the effect of alcohol on fat
metabolism. Excessive alcohol use contributes to nutritional
deficiencies by replacing food in a person’s diet, suppressing
appetite, affecting intestinal mucosa and absorption of nutrients, and
impairing the storage of nutrients and increasing nutrient catabolism
and excretion.
Although some studies have found low levels (i.e. drinking within the
guidelines) of alcohol consumption associated with reduced risk of
cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, there are other
significant adverse health outcomes from excessive and/or frequent
alcohol consumption (Matsumoto et al.
). Additionally, any
15


cardiovascular benefits gained from alcohol can also be gained from
exercise and dietary changes.
15 Matsumoto, C., Miedema, M. D., Ofman, P., Gaziano, J. M. & Sesso, H. D. (2014). An
expanding knowledge of the mechanisms and effects of alcohol consumption on
cardiovascular disease. Journal of Cardiopulmonary Rehabilitation and Prevention, 34(3),
159–171.
Advertising
Food producers and marketers are very persuasive and many
strategies are used to influence television viewers’ or radio listeners’
choices. Advertising is thought to influence people’s food choices
and eating patterns to a certain extent. Take-away (fast) foods,
alcoholic beverages, coffee, convenience foods (frozen or packaged
and easy to prepare foods), soft drinks and confectionary are more
heavily advertised than products such as bread, vegetables and
fruits. Television commercials promote energy-dense, nutrient-poor
foods (take-away and fast foods, snack foods, chocolate and
confectionary, soft drinks and sugared cereals) over fresh, healthy
foods. In Australia, the marketing of food and beverages is governed
by the Australian Association of National Advertisers’ (AANA) Food
and Beverages Advertising Code (AANA ). The code and
accompanying Practice Note provide guidance for developing and
maintaining high levels of social responsibility in advertising and
marketing of foods and beverages in Australia. The code includes
regulations that prohibit untruthful, dishonest or misleading
16


advertising or marketing of foods and beverages, exploiting
children’s imaginations, urging parents to buy particular products or
undermining parent roles in guiding food choices.
16 Australian Association of National Advertisers (2019). AANA Food and Beverages
Advertising Code. Retrieved from <www.aana.com.au>.
Psychological factors
Although some people overeat when stressed, depressed or lonely,
others eat very little under the same conditions. Disordered eating
behaviours and weight loss can indicate severe stress or
depression, and although these behaviours (which may include
purging, binge eating and/or strict and excessive dieting) are most
commonly associated with females, a recent study of Australians
showed that disordered eating behaviours occur across all ages, in
males and females, and most commonly in people who are
overweight (Hay, Girosi & Mond ).
17 Hay, P., Girosi, F. & Mond, J. (2015). Prevalence and sociodemographic correlates of
DSM-5 eating disorders in the Australian population. Journal of Eating Disorders, 3(1), 1.
Anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa are severe
psychophysiological conditions where individuals exhibit severe
disordered eating behaviours. Although these conditions are
relatively uncommon in the Australian population (
 of the
female population aged over 15 years and rare in men), anorexia
17
< 0.5%


nervosa has the highest death rate of all mental illnesses. Early
recognition and treatment of anorexia nervosa and other eating
disorders is considered critical to reducing the severity and impact of
the conditions.


Nutritional variations throughout
the life cycle
Nutritional requirements vary throughout the life cycle. Guidelines
follow for the major developmental stages.
Infancy (neonate to 12 months)
The neonate’s fluid and nutritional needs are met by breast milk or
formula. Fluid needs of infants are proportionately greater than
those of adults because of a higher metabolic rate, immature
kidneys and greater water losses through the skin and the lungs.
The latter is largely due to a more rapid respiratory rate. Therefore,
fluid balance is a critical factor. Under normal environmental
conditions, infants do not need additional water; however, neonates
in very warm environments may require additional fluids.
The total daily nutritional requirement of the newborn is about 80 to
100 mL of breast milk or formula per kilogram of body weight. The
newborn infant’s stomach capacity is about 90 mL and feedings are
required every 2½ to 4 hours.


The newborn infant is usually fed ‘on demand’. Demand feeding
means that the child is fed when hungry. This method tends to
decrease the problem of overfeeding or underfeeding the infant. The
newborn that is hungry usually cries and exhibits tension in the
entire body. Parents should be warned that infant bottles should
never be propped up for feeding. There is a real danger that
aspiration or choking could result.
Infants demonstrate satisfaction by slowing their sucking activity or
by falling asleep. Once satisfaction has been demonstrated, infants
should not be coaxed into finishing the feeding. This could lead to
discomfort or overfeeding. When feeding is completed, healthy
infants (up to 6 months of age) should be placed in a supine position
for sleep to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).
Regurgitation
, or spitting up, during or after a feed is a common
occurrence during the first year. Although this may be of concern to
parents, it does not usually result in nutritional deficiency.
Demonstration of adequate weight gain should reassure parents that
the infant is receiving adequate nutrition.
Current Australian Infant Feeding Guidelines (NHMRC ) include
recommendations for exclusive breastfeeding until the infant is
around 6 months of age and introducing appropriate solid food and
continue breastfeeding until 12 months of age and beyond. In
recognition for some of the difficulties encountered in maintaining
breastfeeding for up to 12 months, these guidelines also state that
any breastfeeding is beneficial to the mother and infant, and
18


mothers should be provided with appropriate support and
information to assist in their decisions to feed their infant. If an infant
is not breastfed, it is important that formula feeds are prepared,
stored and used correctly (NHMRC 2012).
18 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) (2012). Infant Feeding
Guidelines. Canberra: Department of Health and Ageing.
Complementary feeding (the introduction of solid foods) should
commence when an infant is around 6 months of age to ensure
provision of essential nutrients and development of the gut
microbiome. It is at this age that infants are able to sit up and have
decreased sucking and tongue protrusion reflexes (extrusion reflex).
At about 6 months of age, infants’ iron stores become depleted and
it is necessary to provide foods with supplemental iron to prevent
iron deficiency anaemia
. Iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) is a
form of anaemia
 (decrease in red blood cells) caused by
inadequate supply of iron for synthesis of haemoglobin. Prolonged
IDA in early life results in impaired neurological development
(Berglund & Domellof
). Breast milk and cow’s milk are low in iron;
thus, iron-fortified cereals or formulas are recommended for infants
from 6 months of age and may be continued until the child reaches
18 months. Iron-containing solid foods should be the first foods
provided to the infant (e.g. iron-fortified rice cereals, pureed meat
and poultry, cooked plain tofu and legumes/beans).
19 Berglund, S. & Domellof, M. (2014). Meeting iron needs for infants and children. Current
Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care, 17(3), 267–272.
19


Zinc is another mineral essential for normal growth and
development, immune response and cognitive function. Infants are
born with a storage of zinc which progressively declines until about 4
months of age. In addition, the zinc concentration in breastmilk
declines in the first 6 months. While iron fortified foods are important
for supplemental iron supplies, there is also a need to introduce
pureed meats and vegetables such as peas, beans and lentils to
assist in meeting zinc requirements.
Solid foods (strained or pureed to start with) should be introduced at
around 6 months (but not before 4 months) while breastfeeding (or
formula feeding) continues. Foods should be introduced one at a
time, usually with only one new food introduced every 2 to 3 days to
ensure that the infant tolerates the food and demonstrates no
allergy to it. In Australia, food allergy affects approximately 10% of
infants, with the most common food triggers for infants being egg,
cow’s milk, peanut, tree nuts, sesame, soy, fish, shellfish and wheat.
Most infants or children with allergies to cow’s milk, soy, wheat or
egg will outgrow their allergy but reactions to the other foods are
more likely to affect the individual throughout their lifetime. Food
allergy reactions can be mild, moderate or severe (anaphylaxis). It is
important that food allergy is diagnosed correctly and, if a positive
diagnosis is made, strict avoidance of the responsible food/s is
necessary. The Australian Society of Clinical Immunology and
Allergy (ASCIA) has released guidelines for infant feeding and
allergy prevention (ASCIA ) and food allergy information for
patients, consumers and carers (ASCIA ). Current guidelines
highlight the need to give all infants allergenic solid foods during their
20
21


first year of life. Introducing foods slowly and one at a time is
important for monitoring a child’s reaction.
20 Australian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy (ASCIA) (2016). ASCIA Guidelines:
Infant Feeding and Allergy Prevention. Balgowlah, NSW: ASCIA. Retrieved from
<www.allergy.org.au>.
21 Australian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy (ASCIA) (2019). Food Allergy
Information for Patients, Consumers and Carers. Balgowlah, NSW: ASCIA. Retrieved from
<www.allergy.org.au>.
With the eruption of teeth at about 7 to 9 months, the infant is ready
to chew and can begin to experience different textures of food. At
this time, the infant enjoys finger foods, such as skinless fruit (cut
into small pieces to prevent choking), dry cereal or toast. Nuts and
other hard foods should be avoided to reduce the risk of choking.
Sugar, honey and salt should not be added to infant foods. All juices
and sugar-sweetened drinks, and nutrient-poor convenience and
snack type foods, should be avoided. By the age of 12 months the
infant should be eating most foods that adults eat and consistent
with the Australian Dietary Guidelines (NHMRC ). Weaning from
breast milk or formula to cow’s milk can commence at around 12
months or thereafter, when desired by the mother. By the age of 12
months, most infants can be completely fed on table food, and milk
intake is about 600 mL per day. Care must be taken when
introducing foods to infants, and some foods are not recommended
for infants in Australia (see Table 50.1
).
22 National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) (2013b). Australian Dietary
Guidelines. Summary. Canberra: Department of Health and Ageing. Retrieved from
22


<www.nhmrc.gov.au>.
Table 50.1 Foods to be avoided during infancy
Weaning from the breast or bottle to the cup takes place gradually
and is usually achieved by 12 to 24 months of age. Some infants
have difficulty giving up the bottle, particularly at naptime or bedtime.
Parents should be warned that putting a child to bed with a bottle
can lead to bottle mouth syndrome
. The term describes decay
of the teeth caused by constant contact with liquid from the bottle.
Infants should not be put to bed with a bottle or the bottle should be
taken away before they fall asleep. Some dentists advocate
brushing or cleaning the infant’s teeth to prevent bottle mouth
syndrome, especially for the infant who requires a bottle only at
naptime or bedtime. Dental advice should be sought for those living
in areas where household water supply is not fluoridated.
Toddler
Because of a maturing gastrointestinal tract, toddlers can eat most
foods and adjust to three meals each day. Toddlers’ fine motor skills
are sufficiently well developed for them to learn how to feed
themselves. Before the age of 20 months, most toddlers require
help with glasses and cups because their wrist control is limited. By
the age of 3 years, when most deciduous teeth have emerged, the
toddler is able to bite and chew adult table food.


Developing independence may be exhibited through the toddler’s
refusal of certain foods. Meals should be short because of the
toddler’s brief attention span and environmental distractions. Often
toddlers display their liking of rituals by eating foods in a certain
order, cutting foods a specific way or accompanying certain foods
with a particular drink.
The toddler is less likely to have fluid imbalances than the infant.
The toddler’s gastrointestinal function is more mature and the
percentage of fluid body weight is lower. A healthy toddler weighing
15 kg needs about 1250 mL of fluid per 24 hours.
During the toddler stage, the energy intake requirement is 3600 to
7200 kJ per day. From 12 months to 2 years of age, the toddler may
be eating some prepared toddler foods, but mainly table foods.
Teach parents to read labels carefully and be aware that table foods
offer more variety and are less expensive and more nutritious than
prepared toddler foods. The need for adequate iron, calcium and
vitamins C and A, which are common toddler deficiencies, should
also be considered.
Preschooler
The preschooler eats adult foods. Parents should become informed
about the diet of their child in kindergarten and preschool settings so
that they can be sure of meeting the child’s total nutritional needs.
Children at this age are very active and may rush through meals to


return to playing. The 4-year-old still requires parents’ help in cutting
meat and may spill milk when pouring from a large container.
Parents also need to teach preschoolers how to use utensils and
should provide them with the opportunity to practise (e.g. buttering
bread, cutting softer foods). However, 4- and 5-year-olds often use
their fingers to pick up food. Appropriate table manners may be
marginal at best but should be encouraged. Active children often
require snacks between meals. Cheese, fruits, yoghurt raw
vegetables and milk are good choices. Children at this age may
enjoy helping in the kitchen and perhaps growing some vegetables
and herbs, and both girls and boys should be encouraged to do so.
The preschooler is even less susceptible than the toddler to fluid
imbalances. The average 5-year-old weighing 20 kg requires at least
75 mL of liquid per kilogram of body weight per day or 1500 mL
every 24 hours.
School-age child
Nutrition continues to be a high priority for growing children. School-
age children should be encouraged to eat a wide variety of nutritious
foods in sufficient quantities to allow them to grow and develop
normally. Children should eat three meals per day as well as one or
two nutritious snacks between meals. Breakfast is particularly
important to help a child to meet their nutritional requirements and
sustain the prolonged physical and mental effort required at school.
Children who skip breakfast can become inattentive and restless by


late morning and have decreased problem-solving ability.
Undernourished children become fatigued easily and face a greater
risk of infection, resulting in frequent absences from school.
The average healthy 8-year-old weighing 30 kg requires about 1750
mL of fluid per day. Meal times should be social times enjoyed by all
and parents should refrain from discussing a child’s poor eating
habits during these times. Parents should be aware that children
learn many of their food habits by observing their parents. Eating a
balanced diet should be the norm for both parent and child (see Box
50.4
).

children and adolescents
Sixty-nine per cent of children aged 5−11 years and 54% of
children aged 12−17 years consume two or more serves of
fruit per day; 28% of children aged 5−11 years and 36% of
children aged 12−17 years consume three or more serves of
vegetables per day.

23


Dietary problems may arise as children enter school and begin
seeking independence in food choices. The children may trade their
food, not eat lunch at all or buy sweets or junk food with their lunch
money. Parents should discuss with the child the foods that they
should eat and continue to role model healthy eating behaviours and
provide a balanced diet in the home setting.
Poor eating habits may result in obesity. In Australia, 24.9% of
children aged 5−17 years are classified overweight or obese (17%
overweight; 8.1% obese) (AIHW
). Obesity in school-age children
tends to result in adult obesity and all the related health risks.
Obesity
 is a complex disease with no single cause and is
associated with physical and psychosocial problems. Obese children
may be ridiculed and discriminated against by peers. Such behaviour
reinforces low self-esteem. The goal of treatment for overweight
children is to reduce weight gain not lose weight, allowing their
weight to increase more slowly than their height as they continue to
grow. Counselling and teaching parents should include the following:
24 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2019). Overweight and Obesity: An
Interactive Insight. Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
reviewing the child’s eating habits, including snacks (see Box
50.5
)
reviewing parent/family eating behaviours
altering meal content
using rewards other than food
promoting an active lifestyle and regular exercise.
24


BO X
50.5 Promoting children’s healthy
eating
The following suggestions may help parents meet the child’s
nutritional needs, promote effective parent–child interactions
and promote healthy eating behaviours:
Parents should acknowledge and appreciate their role in
modelling the food behaviours of their children.
Meal times should be pleasant times—avoid tensions at
the table and discussions of bad behaviour.
Turn off the TV and computer at meal times; avoid playing
with toys at the dining table.
Offer a variety of simple, attractive and different-coloured
foods in small portions and avoid meals that combine
foods into one dish, such as a stew.
Do not use food as a reward or punish a child who does
not eat.
Schedule meals, sleep and snack times that will allow for
optimum appetite and behaviour.
Eat a healthy breakfast every day.
Avoid the routine use of sweet desserts.
Save discretionary foods such as sweet biscuits, cakes,
desserts, ice-cream, confectionary, pastries and sugar-
sweetened drinks for special occasions.


Adolescent
The adolescent’s need for nutrients and energy intake increases,
particularly during growth spurts. Adolescents should be encouraged
to eat a wide variety of nutritious foods in sufficient quantities to
meet their increased need for protein, calcium, vitamin D, iron and B
vitamins. Calcium intake (1000 to 1300 mg/day) is particularly
important during the adolescent years when 40% of total bone mass
development occurs (Zhou et al.
). Ensuring adequate calcium
intake helps reduce the risk of developing osteoporosis (a decrease
in bone density) in later life. Adolescents with marginal calcium
intakes may also have greater requirements for vitamin D (which is
important for the absorption of calcium), particularly during winter
months or when sun exposure is reduced (e.g. extended
hospitalisation).
25 Zhou, W., Langsetmo, L., Berger, C., ... Anastassiades, T. (2013). Longitudinal changes in
calcium and vitamin D intakes and relationship to bone mineral density in a prospective
population-based study: The Canadian Multicentre Osteoporosis Study (CaMos). Journal of
Musculoskeletal and Neuronal Interactions, 13(4), 470–479.
Teenagers have active lifestyles and irregular eating patterns. They
tend to diet or snack frequently, often eating energy-dense foods
such as lollies, soft drinks, ice-cream and fast foods. Parents and all
health practitioners can promote better lifelong eating habits by
25


encouraging teenagers to eat mostly healthy snacks, such as fruits
and cheese, and limiting the amount of ‘junk food’ available in the
home. The teenager’s food choices relate to physical, social and
emotional factors and impulses and may not be influenced by
teaching.
Common problems related to nutrition and self-esteem among
adolescents include obesity, anorexia nervosa and bulimia. Obesity
is a common problem of the preadolescent period and continues to
be a problem in the adolescent period. Many obese adolescents
may have body dissatisfaction and feel self-conscious and socially
unacceptable. Depression is not unusual among obese adolescents.
Treatment of obesity in this age group requires professional
consultation and includes education on nutrition as well as
assessment of physical conditions associated with obesity, and
psychosocial problems that may produce overeating.
With much social pressure to be slim, some adolescents severely
limit their food intake to a level significantly below that required to
meet the demands of normal growth. In some instances, the
adolescent may develop an eating disorder, such as anorexia or
bulimia. Anorexia nervosa and bulimia are severe
psychophysiological conditions which may occur in adolescent girls
and boys. They are considered to be disorders related to the need
for control. Anorexia nervosa
 is characterised by a prolonged
inability or refusal to eat, rapid weight loss and emaciation in people
who continue to believe they are fat. People who suffer from
anorexia nervosa may also exhibit disordered eating behaviours and


may induce vomiting and use laxatives and diuretics to remain thin.
Bulimia nervosa
 is an uncontrollable compulsion to consume
enormous amounts of food (binge) and then expel it by self-induced
vomiting or by taking laxatives (purge). These illnesses are most
effectively treated in the early stages by psychotherapy.
Hospitalisation may be necessary when the effects of starvation
become life threatening.
In Australia, almost half of teenagers aged 12–17 years have
reported trying alcohol (Guerin & White ). However, the average
age of initiation of drinking alcohol is increasing (i.e. in 2013, the
average age of teenagers first trying alcohol was around 15.5 years,
whereas in 2016, the average age was 16.1 years) and the
proportion of teenagers abstaining from alcohol is also increasing
(72% in 2013 compared to 82% in 2016) (AIHW 2017). Alcohol
intake by Australian adolescents is often considered a normal part of
adolescent development; however, the widespread use and social
acceptance of this drug may mask the serious consequences of
adolescent alcohol intake and, in particular, under-age drinking and
high-risk consumption (‘binge drinking’ and excessive daily intake).
26 Guerin, N. & White, V. (2018). Australian Secondary School Students’ Use of Tobacco,
Alcohol, and Over-the-Counter and Illicit Substances 2017. Victoria: Centre for Behavioural
Research in Cancer.
Young adult
26


The nutritional habits established during young adulthood often lay
the foundation for the patterns maintained throughout a person’s life.
Young adult females need to maintain adequate iron intake. A
substantial number of women do not ingest sufficient dietary iron
each day. To prevent iron deficiency anaemia, menstruating females
should ingest 18 mg of iron daily. To meet these requirements,
young females should eat a varied diet and include a range of iron-
rich foods, such as red meat and organ meats (liver and kidneys),
eggs, fish, poultry, leafy vegetables and dried fruits, in their daily diet
(see ‘Major food sources of iron’ in Table 50.3
 on pages 1321–
1322). They should also be encouraged to consume a source of
vitamin C (citrus fruits/juice, dark green leafy vegetables, tomatoes,
capsicum, melon or strawberries) to enhance the absorption of iron
in foods.
Calcium is needed in young adulthood to maintain bones and help
decrease the chances of developing osteoporosis in later life. Along
with calcium, the person must have adequate vitamin D, necessary
for the calcium to enter the bloodstream. Vitamin D is made in the
skin on exposure to the sun and after regular sun exposure the body
can produce and store adequate vitamin for 6 months. If the person
does not get sufficient sun exposure (15 minutes three times each
week), supplements may be indicated. Most young adults living in
Australia are not at risk of vitamin D deficiency. However, some
dark-skinned people, veiled women and individuals who cover up to
reduce exposure to weather may have limited sun exposure and
may develop a mild deficiency (NHMRC 2006).


Obesity may occur during the young adult years as the active teen
becomes the sedentary adult but does not decrease energy intake.
The overweight or obese young adult is at risk of hypertension and
premature development of cardiovascular disease and type 2
diabetes.
Hypertension and obesity are two of more than 40 risk factors that
have been identified in the development of cardiovascular disease
(CVD). Preventing these risk factors and lowering the risk of CVD
are critical. Low-fat and/or low-cholesterol diets play a significant role
in both the prevention and treatment of CVD.
Middle-aged adult
The middle-aged adult should aim to consume a diet that aligns with
the Australian Dietary Guidelines (NHMRC 2013b) and prevents
weight gain by being physically active and eating according to
energy needs. Post-menopausal women need to ingest sufficient
calcium and vitamin D to reduce the risk of osteoporosis, and
antioxidants such as vitamins A, C and E may be helpful in reducing
the risks of heart disease in women. Although iron supplements are
no longer needed, the amount in a multivitamin is not harmful and
may be beneficial for post-menopausal women taking oestrogen
supplements (Toxqui & Vaquero ).
27 Toxqui, L. & Vaquero, M. P. (2015). Chronic iron deficiency as an emerging risk factor for
osteoporosis: A hypothesis. Nutrients, 7(4), 2324–2344.
27


Middle-aged adults who gain weight may not be aware of some
common facts about this age period. Decreased metabolic activity
and decreased physical activity mean a decrease in energy needs.
All adults should be educated about the risks of being overweight,
including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and associated
problems with mobility and psychosocial wellness.
During late middle age, gastric juice secretions and free acid
gradually decline. As a result, some individuals may complain of
‘heartburn’ (acid indigestion) or an increase in belching. They may
determine that certain foods disagree with them.
Older adults
The older adult requires the same basic nutrition as the younger
adult. However, total energy intake requirements are reduced due to
a decrease in metabolic rate and physical activity that commonly
occurs with ageing.
Some older adults may need more carbohydrates for fibre and bulk,
but most nutrient requirements remain relatively unchanged. Tooth
loss, impaired sense of taste and smell and decreased saliva and
gastric juice secretion may affect a person’s eating habits and
nutritional status.
Loss of appetite is a common problem in older adults and places
them at risk of reduced food and nutrient intake, weight loss and


nutrition deficiencies. Detecting loss of appetite before weight loss or
deficiencies occur can help prevent a decline in health. The
Simplified Nutritional Appetite Questionnaire (SNAQ) (Wilson et al.
)
(see Box 50.6
) is a brief and simple questionnaire that can be
used to identify appetite loss.
28 Wilson, M., Thomas, D., Rubenstein, L. et al. (2005). Appetite assessment: Simple
appetite questionnaire predicts weight loss in community-dwelling adults and nursing home
residents. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 82, 1074–1081.

Psychosocial factors may also contribute to nutritional problems.
Older adults who live alone may not want to cook for themselves or
eat alone and may adopt poor dietary habits. Lack of transportation,
limited mobility, poor access to stores and inability to prepare food
may also affect nutritional status. Loss of spouse, anxiety,
depression, dependence on others and lowered income all affect
eating habits (see Table 50.2
). Guidelines for the inclusion of
high-nutrient foods that are compatible with the nutritional needs of
older adults are summarised in ‘Patient education’ and in the
‘Nutritional reference values’ in Table 50.3
. Also see ‘Lifespan
considerations
’.
Table 50.2 Problems associated with nutrition in older adults
Table 50.3 Nutritional reference values


Standards for a healthy diet
Various daily food guides have been developed to help healthy
people meet the daily requirements of essential nutrients and to
facilitate meal planning. Food selection guides translate scientific
knowledge of food composition, reference intakes and dietary
guidelines into practical food selection advice. They emphasise the
general types and amounts of foods that make up a ‘healthy’ diet
and the need for variety, balance and moderation. These guides are
simple to use, but they do not provide examples of standard serving
sizes, which differ between different foods and different food
manufacturers.
The Australian Dietary Guidelines (NHMRC 2013b) and the
Australian Guide to Healthy Eating (NMHRC 2013a) provide advice
about the amounts and kinds of foods that we need to eat for health
and wellbeing. The recommendations provided in these guides are
based on scientific evidence and are intended for people of all ages
and backgrounds in the general healthy population (including those
with nutrition-related risk factors such as overweight).
Patient education
Nutrition for older adults


Reduce total energy intake. Energy needs generally
decrease in older adults often because of decreased
activity. Older adults need to consume nutrient-dense
foods and avoid foods that are high in energy but have
few nutrients.
Limit saturated fat and total fat consumption. Use lean
cuts of meat and always remove fat from meat before
cooking. (But be sure that intake of meat is sufficient
because older adults often consume inadequate amounts
of these foods.) Grill, boil or bake foods instead of frying
them. Use reduced-fat or low-fat milk and cheese; limit
intake of saturated fats.
Reduce consumption of energy-dense, nutrient-free
foods. Use fruit or puddings made with low-fat milk in
place of pastry, biscuits and rich desserts.
Reduce sodium consumption for people who have
hypertension or other cardiac problems. Avoid canned
soups, sauces and mustard. Avoid salted, smoked, cured
and pickled meats (e.g. ham and bacon), poultry and fish.
Do not add salt when cooking foods or at the table.
Ensure adequate calcium intake (at least 1300 mg) to
prevent bone loss. Milk, cheese, yoghurt, cream soups,
puddings and frozen milk products are good sources. See
the ‘Major food sources of calcium’ in Table 50.3
.
Ensure adequate vitamin D intake. Vitamin D is
essential to maintain calcium homeostasis. Include some
milk, margarines, fatty fish and eggs. If milk cannot be


tolerated because of a lactose deficiency, vitamin D
supplements may be required.
Ensure adequate iron intake. Iron intake in older adults
may be compromised by such factors as increased
incidence of gastrointestinal disturbance, chronic
diarrhoea, regular aspirin use and possible reduction in
meat consumption. See ‘Major food sources of iron’ in
Table 50.3
.
Consume fibre-rich foods to prevent constipation and
minimise use of laxatives. See the ‘Fibre-rich foods’ in
Table 50.3
. Because fibre-rich foods provide bulk and a
feeling of fullness, they help people control their appetite
and lose weight.
Lifespan considerations
Nutrition
Children
Children learn eating habits from their parents. It is the
parents’ responsibility to be good nutritional role models,
both in terms of what they eat and how they incorporate
food into their lifestyle.
During the preschool and early school-age years children
learn lifelong eating habits. It is the parents’ responsibility


to provide the child with adequate amounts of nutritious
foods in an environment that is relaxed and comfortable
for eating. It is the child’s responsibility to decide what and
how much of the nutritious foods to eat. Parents should
be aware that eating can become a source of conflict if
the parent tries to tell the child what and how much to eat,
or if the child tries to tell the parent what foods should be
eaten. Children’s access to ‘junk food’ should be limited,
but completely forbidding a food also creates conflict.
Vegetarian diets can be appropriate for children and
adolescents; however, it is important that energy needs
are met and growth is monitored. Attention should be paid
to ensure adequate intake of specific nutrients (protein,
essential fatty acids, iron, zinc, calcium, vitamins B  and
D) and supplementation considered for those who avoid
all animal products (Amit
). Compared with non-
vegetarians, adolescents who are vegetarians have
healthier diets and are likely to have a healthier body
weight (Burkholder et al.
; Grant et al.
). However,
adolescents who adopt this type of eating in order to lose
weight should be monitored as they may become overly
restrictive of their intakes and be at risk of nutrient
deficiencies and eating disorders.

30 Burkholder, N., Siapco, G., Tabrizi, S. H. & Sabate, J. (2014). Comparison of
food intake of vegetarian and non-vegetarian adolescents (1024.12). The
FASEB Journal, 28(1 Suppl), 1024–1012.

17(1), 107–115.
Older adults
Most older adults take several medications as a result of
having an increase in the number of chronic illnesses.
Considerations for potential problems include:
Some foods interact adversely or decrease the
effectiveness of certain medications, such as foods high in
vitamin K and the anticoagulant Coumadin. Older adults
should not change their diet significantly without consulting
their doctor because drug dosage may have been based
on the older adults’ previous dietary intake.
Some medications increase appetite, such as
glucocorticoids.
Some medications decrease appetite by their actions or
by causing an unpleasant taste.
Certain tablets should not be crushed to be given by
mouth or by gastric tubes, such as enteric-coated or slow-
release medications.
Conditions such as neuromuscular disorders and dementia
can make it difficult for older adults to eat or to be fed. Safety
should always be a priority concern, with attention paid to
prevent aspiration. All health care personnel and family


caregivers should be taught proper techniques to reduce this
risk. Effective techniques include:
Use the chin-tuck method when feeding people with
dysphagia. Having them flex the head towards the chest
when swallowing decreases the risk of aspiration into the
lungs.
Use foods of prescribed consistency. Some older adults
can swallow foods with thicker consistency more easily
than thin liquids.
Try to focus on food preferences—the family can help
provide this information.
Maintain meal times as positive social occasions with
conversations and extra attention to having a pleasant
environment.
Economic factors may influence older adults’ nutritional status
if they cannot afford food, especially if a prescribed diet
requires expensive supplements. Inexpensive or convenience
foods such as canned soups are often high in fat and sodium.
The Australian Guide to Healthy Eating generally represents a ‘food
plate’ that shows the types of foods you should eat from each of the
five food groups each day. The amounts (or number of serves)
recommended are based on nutrient requirements for different age
groups and genders and height and activity levels. The Australian
Guide to Healthy Eating is a food selection guide which aims to


provide practical advice on how to implement the Australian Dietary
Guidelines.
The Eat for Health Program
Dietary intake is key modifiable behaviour and considered one of the
most important contributors to health and wellbeing. The Eat for
Health Program provides a range of practical information and
resources which aim to assist Australians to develop dietary intake
behaviours that promote health and wellbeing. The Australian
Dietary Guidelines and the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating are
key resources included in the Eat for Health Program.
Australian Dietary Guidelines
The Australian Dietary Guidelines (see Figure 50.3
) provide
information for health professionals and the general population about
healthy food choices (see Box 50.7
). The guidelines are
considered valuable companion documents to the Nutrient
Reference Values for Australia and New Zealand (NHMRC 2006).
These publications are available as free downloads from the
Australian government NHMRC website at
<www.eatforhealth.gov.au/guidelines> and <www.nrv.gov.au>.

50.7 Australian Dietary Guidelines
Guideline 1
To achieve and maintain a healthy weight, be physically
active and choose amounts of nutritious food and drinks
to meet your energy needs.
Children and adolescents should eat sufficient nutritious
foods to grow and develop normally. They should be
physically active every day and their growth should be
checked regularly.
Older people should eat nutritious foods and keep
physically active to help maintain muscle strength and a
healthy weight.
Guideline 2
Enjoy a wide variety of nutritious foods from the five food
groups every day:
plenty of vegetables of different types and colours, and
legumes/beans


fruit
grain (cereal) foods, mostly wholegrain and/or high-cereal-
fibre varieties, such as breads, cereals, rice, pasta,
noodles, polenta, couscous, oats, quinoa and barley
lean meats and poultry, fish, eggs, tofu, nuts and seeds,
and legumes/beans
milk, yoghurt, cheese and/or their alternatives, mostly
reduced fat
drink plenty of water.
Guideline 3
Limit intake of foods containing saturated fat, added salt,
added sugars and alcohol.
Limit intake of foods high in saturated fat such as many
biscuits, cakes, pastries, pies, processed meats,
commercial burgers, pizza, fried foods, potato chips,
crisps and other savoury snacks.
Replace high-fat foods that contain predominately
saturated fats such as butter, cream, cooking margarine,
coconut and palm oil with foods that contain
predominately polyunsaturated and monounsaturated fats
such as oils, spreads, nut butters/pastes and avocado.
Low-fat diets are not suitable for children under the age of
2 years.
Limit intake of foods and drinks containing added salt.
Read labels to choose lower sodium options among
similar foods.


Do not add salt to foods in cooking or at the table.
Limit intake of foods and drinks containing added sugars
such as confectionary, sugar-sweetened soft drinks and
cordials, fruit drinks, vitamin waters, energy and sports
drinks.
If you choose to drink alcohol, limit intake. For women
who are pregnant, planning a pregnancy or breastfeeding,
not drinking alcohol is the safest option.
Guideline 4
Encourage, support and promote breastfeeding.
Guideline 5
Care for your food: prepare and store it safely.
Source: NHMRC (2013b). Australian Dietary Guidelines. Canberra: Department of Health and
Ageing.
Australian Guide to Healthy Eating
The Australian Guide to Healthy Eating is a food modelling tool
designed to support education and promotion of good health and
wellbeing of Australians, which includes those with common health
risks such as overweight (NHMRC 2013a). This guide provides
visual representation of the proportion of the five food groups (grain


(cereal) foods, mostly wholegrain and/or high- cereal-fibre varieties;
vegetables and legumes/beans; fruit; milk, yoghurt, cheese and/or
alternatives, mostly reduced fat; and lean meat and poultry, fish,
eggs, tofu, nuts and seeds, legumes/beans) recommended each
day (see Figure 50.4
). The Eat for Health website provides
resources to assist people to understand the recommended serving
sizes of each of the different food groups and to develop meal plans.
For more information regarding the various tools and resources
available within the Eat for Health Program, see
<www.eatforhealth.gov.au>.

Nutrient reference values for
Australia and New Zealand
Nutrient reference values (NRVs) (including recommended dietary
intakes) quantify the levels of intake of essential nutrients
considered, on the basis of available scientific knowledge, to be
adequate to meet the known nutritional needs of practically all
healthy people for prevention of deficiency states. For each nutrient,


values are set for the estimated average requirement (EAR) for
people in different age and gender groups as well as for pregnancy
and lactation.
The recommended dietary intake (RDI) is also derived from the EAR
and includes consideration for variation in absorption and
metabolism of nutrients within age and gender groups. If evidence is
limited, an adequate intake (AI) figure is provided. An upper level of
intake (UL) is set for some nutrients where regular and excessive
consumption could lead to adverse effects.
The publication on NRVs (NHMRC 2006) also provides guidance for
some nutrients in relation to reduction of chronic disease risk and
are used by professionals to:
assess the likelihood of inadequate intake of individuals or groups
plan meals and/or menus
develop and assess new food products
set food policy and legislation as in the development of food
choice guides or food labelling.
Food labelling
Australian food labels provide useful information to help make
choices about the foods you consume and make comparisons
between different food products. Food labelling laws are governed
by the food standards code, which is administered by Food


Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ). The food standards
code stipulates that all foods produced or imported into Australia and
New Zealand (including those foods with nutrition claims) have a
nutrition information panel. The few exceptions include very small
packages and foods such as herbs and spices, tea, coffee, foods
sold unpackaged (if a claim is not made) and foods made and
packaged at the point of sale. Information regarding ‘truth in
labelling’ can be found at <www.foodstandards.gov.au/consumer/
labelling/truth/Pages/default.aspx>.
Information on a food label includes:
product name
brand name
ingredient list
nutrition information panel
use-by date
manufacturer details
product weight
possibly a nutrition claim.
Patient education
Reducing intake of dietary fat
Cook meat by grilling, baking or microwaving rather than
frying.
Substitute plain popcorn or pretzels for snacks such as
potato chips and corn chips.


Read nutrient information panels on food labels. Some
biscuits/crackers, for example, are high in fat; others are
not.
Limit desserts high in fat, such as confectionary, ice-
cream, cake and sweet biscuits.
Use skim or reduced-fat milk instead of whole milk.
Limit the use of butter and margarine on breads.
Remove fat from meat and skin from chicken BEFORE
cooking.
Eat less meat; eat more fish.
Limit intake of salad dressings and sauces.
Eat plant sources of protein (e.g. kidney, cannellini and
navy beans).
Use nuts as a source of protein but take care to limit
intake as they are high in fat.
The nutrition information panel must include the amounts of energy,
protein, total fat, saturated fat, total carbohydrate, sugar and sodium
(salt) in the food. Information on the fibre or calcium content may
also be included if the food is a good source of these nutrients or if
the product has made a nutrient claim about them. Nutrient
reference values underpin the nutrient information provided on food
labels (see Figure 50.5
).

Vegetarian diets
People may become vegetarians for economic, health, religious,
ethical or ecological reasons. There are three main types of
vegetarian diets: those who consume only plant foods (vegan);
those who avoid meat, seafood and eggs but include dairy and plant
foods (lacto-vegetarian); and those who avoid meat and seafood but
include milk, eggs and dairy products (lacto-ovo vegetarian). Some
people eat fish and poultry but not beef, lamb or pork; others eat
only fresh fruit, juices and nuts; and still others eat plant foods and
dairy products but not eggs. See the ‘Types of vegetarian diets’ in
Table 50.3
.
Vegetarian diets can be nutritionally sound if they include a wide
variety of foods, are balanced and are well planned. Consideration
must be given to foods that provide protein, iron, zinc, vitamin B
and calcium (Dietitians Association of Australia (DAA)
). Because
the proteins found in plant foods are incomplete proteins,
vegetarians must eat complementary protein foods to obtain all the
essential amino acids. A plant protein can be complemented by
combining it with a different plant protein. The combination produces
a complete protein (see Box 50.8
). Complementary foods need
not be consumed at the same meal but can be taken in over the
course of a day to help meet amino acid needs. Obtaining complete
proteins is especially important for growing children and pregnant
and lactating women, whose protein needs are high. Generally,
legumes (starchy beans, peas, lentils) have complementary
12
32


relationships with grains, nuts and seeds. Diets such as the fruitarian
diet do not provide sufficient amounts of essential nutrients and are
not recommended for long-term use.
32 Dietitians Association of Australia (DAA) (2010). Vegetarian Diets. Retrieved from
<www.daa.asn.au>.

(e.g. cheese) = complete protein.


Foods of animal origin are the best source of vitamin B . Therefore,
vegans need to obtain this vitamin from other sources: brewer’s
yeast, foods fortified with vitamin B  or a vitamin supplement.
Because iron from plant sources is not absorbed as efficiently as
iron from meat, vegans should eat iron-rich foods (e.g. green leafy
vegetables, wholegrains, raisins and molasses) and iron-enriched
foods. They should eat a food rich in vitamin C at each meal to
enhance iron absorption. Calcium deficiency is a concern only for
strict vegetarians. It can be prevented by including in the diet
calcium-fortified soybean milk and tofu (soybean curd) and leafy
green vegetables.

Altered Nutrition
Malnutrition
 is defined as ‘a state of nutrition in which a
deficiency or excess (or imbalance) of energy, protein and other
nutrients causes measurable adverse effects on tissue/body form
(body shape, size and composition)’ (Elia ). In practice this includes
both undernutrition and overnutrition. Overnutrition
 refers to a
total energy intake in excess of daily energy requirements, resulting
in storage of energy in the form of adipose tissue. As the amount of
stored fat increases, the individual becomes overweight or obese. A
person is said to be underweight when their BMI is less than
 normal/acceptable weight when their BMI is between
18.5 and
 overweight
 when their BMI is between 25
and
 and obese
 when their BMI is
(World Health Organization ).

Maidenhead.

Report of a WHO Consultation. World Health Organization.
Excess body weight increases the stress on body organs and
predisposes people to chronic health problems such as hypertension
and diabetes mellitus (see Box 50.9
). Obesity that interferes with
mobility or breathing is referred to as morbid obesity. Obese people

may also manifest undernourishment in important nutrients (e.g.
