Nutrition


SKILL
50.1 Inserting a nasogastric
tube
Purposes
To administer tube feedings and medications to
people unable to eat by mouth or swallow a
sufficient diet without aspirating food or fluids into
the lungs.
To establish a means for suctioning stomach
contents to prevent gastric distension, nausea
and vomiting.
To remove stomach contents for laboratory
analysis.
To lavage (wash) the stomach in case of
poisoning or overdose of medications.
Assessment
Assess
Check for history of nasal surgery or deviated
septum. Assess patency of nares.


Determine presence of gag reflex.
Assess mental status or ability to cooperate with
procedure.
Planning
Before inserting a nasogastric tube, determine the
size of tube to be inserted and whether the tube is
to be attached to suction.
Delegation
Insertion of a nasogastric tube is an invasive
procedure requiring application of knowledge (e.g.
anatomy and physiology, risk factors) and problem
solving. In some organisations, only health care
providers with advanced training are permitted to
insert nasogastric tubes that require use of a stylet.
Delegation of this skill to unqualified personnel is not
appropriate.
Equipment
Large- or small-bore tube (non-latex preferred)
Non-allergenic adhesive tape, 2.5 cm wide or
nasal tube tape
Clean gloves
Water-soluble lubricant
Facial tissues
Glass of water and drinking straw


20 to 50 mL syringe with an adapter
Basin
pH test strip or metre
Bilirubin dipstick
Stethoscope
Disposable pad or towel
Clamp or plug (optional)
Anti-reflux valve for air vent if Salem sump tube
is used
Suction apparatus
Safety pin and elastic band
Implementation
Preparation
Assist the person to a high Fowler’s position if their
health condition permits and support the head on a
pillow. Rationale: it is often easier to swallow in this
position and gravity helps the passage of the tube.
Place a towel or disposable pad across the chest.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the insertion, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity. Explain to
the person what you are going to do, why it is
necessary and how they can cooperate. The
passage of a gastric tube is unpleasant


because the gag reflex is activated during
insertion. Establish a method for the person
to indicate distress and a desire for you to
pause the insertion. Raising a finger or hand
is often used for this.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures (e.g.
clean gloves).
3. Provide for the person’s privacy.
4. Assess the person’s nares.
Ask the person to hyperextend the head
and, using a torch, observe the intactness
of the tissues of the nostrils, including any
irritations or abrasions.
Examine the nares for any obstructions or
deformities by asking the person to
breathe through one nostril while
occluding the other.
Select the nostril that has the greater
airflow.
5. Prepare the tube.
If a small-bore tube is being used, ensure
stylet or guidewire is secured in position.
Rationale: an improperly positioned stylet
or guidewire can traumatise the
nasopharynx, oesophagus and stomach.


6. Determine how far to insert the tube.
Use the tube to mark off the distance from
the tip of the person’s nose to the tip of
the earlobe and then from the tip of the
earlobe to the tip of the xiphoid. 1
Rationale: this length approximates the
distance from the nares to the stomach.
This distance varies between individuals.
Mark this length with adhesive tape if the
tube does not have markings.


1 Measuring the appropriate length to insert a
nasogastric tube
7. Insert the tube.
Put on gloves.
Lubricate the tip of the tube well with
water-soluble lubricant or water to ease
insertion. Rationale: a water-soluble
lubricant dissolves if the tube accidentally


enters the lungs. An oil-based lubricant,
such as petroleum jelly, will not dissolve
and could cause respiratory complications
if it enters the lungs.
Insert the tube, with its natural curve
towards the person, into the selected
nostril. Ask the person to hyperextend the
neck and gently advance the tube towards
the nasopharynx. Rationale:
hyperextension of the neck reduces the
curvature of the nasopharyngeal junction.
Direct the tube along the floor of the
nostril and towards the ear on that side.
Rationale: directing the tube along the
floor avoids the projections (turbinates)
along the lateral wall.
Slight pressure and a twisting motion are
sometimes required to pass the tube into
the nasopharynx and some people’s eyes
may water at this point. Rationale: tears
are a natural body response. Provide the
person with tissues as needed.
If the tube meets resistance, withdraw it,
relubricate it and insert it in the other
nostril. If resistance is encountered in the
other nostril you may need to consult with
medical personnel before proceeding.
Rationale: the tube should never be


forced against resistance because of the
danger of injury.
Once the tube reaches the oropharynx
(throat), the person will feel the tube in the
throat and may gag and retch. Ask the
person to tilt the head forward and
encourage the person to drink and
swallow. Rationale: tilting the head
forward facilitates passage of the tube into
the posterior pharynx and oesophagus
rather than into the larynx; swallowing
moves the epiglottis over the opening to
the larynx. 2


2 Swallowing closes the epiglottis


If the person gags, stop passing the tube
momentarily. Have the person rest, take a
few breaths and take sips of water to calm
the gag reflex.
In cooperation with the person, pass the
tube 5 to 10 cm with each swallow, until
the indicated length is inserted.
If the person continues to gag and the
tube does not advance with each swallow,
withdraw it slightly and inspect the throat
by looking through the mouth. Rationale:
the tube may be coiled in the throat. If so,
withdraw it until it is straight and try again
to insert it.
Ascertain correct placement of the tube.
Aspirate stomach contents and check the
pH, which should be acidic.
Rationale: testing pH is a reliable way to
determine location of a feeding tube.
Gastric contents are commonly pH 1 to 5;
6 or greater would indicate the contents
are from lower in the intestinal tract or in
the respiratory tract. Some researchers
suggest that a pH of greater than 5 should
be followed by further confirmation of tube
location (Gilbertson ).
51 Gilbertson, H. (2015). Use of pH cutoff level for enteral
nutrition. Diet and Nutrition in Critical Care, 1369–1381.
51


Aspirate can also be tested for bilirubin.
Bilirubin levels in the lungs should be
almost zero while levels in the stomach
will be approximately 1.5 mg/dL and in the
intestine over 10 mg/dL.
Almost all nasogastric tubes are
radiopaque and position can be confirmed
by x-ray. Check agency policy. If a small-
bore tube is used, leave the stylet or
guidewire in place until correct position is
verified by x-ray. If the stylet has been
removed, never reinsert it while the tube is
in place. Rationale: the stylet is sharp
and could pierce the tube and injure the
person or cut off the tube end.
Place a stethoscope over the person’s
epigastrium and inject 10 to 30 mL of air
into the tube while listening for a
whooshing sound. Although still one of the
methods used, do not use this method as
the primary method for determining
placement of the feeding tube because it
does not guarantee tube position.
If the signs indicate placement in the
lungs, remove the tube and begin again.
If the signs do not indicate placement in
the lungs or stomach, advance the tube 5
cm and repeat the tests.


Note: feeding via a nasogastric tube
should never be commenced without
confirmation of tube placement.
8. Secure the tube by taping it to the bridge of
the person’s nose.
If the person has oily skin, wipe the nose
first with alcohol to de-fat the skin.
If using tape, cut 7.5 cm of tape and split
it lengthwise at one end, leaving a 2.5 cm
tab at the end.
Place the tape or nasal tube tape over the
bridge of the person’s nose and bring the
split ends either under and around the
tubing, or under the tubing and back up
over the nose. 3 Rationale: taping in this
manner prevents the tube from pressing
against and irritating the edge of the
nostril.


3 Taping a nasogastric tube to the bridge
of the nose
9. Once correct position has been determined,
attach the tube to a suction source or feeding
apparatus as ordered, or clamp the end of
the tubing.
10. Secure the tube to the person’s gown.


Loop an elastic band around the end of
the tubing and attach the elastic band to
the gown with a safety pin.
or
Attach a piece of adhesive tape to the
tube and pin the tape to the gown.
Rationale: the tube is attached to prevent
it from dangling and pulling.
If a Salem sump tube is used, attach the
anti-reflux valve to the vent port (if used)
and position the port above the person’s
stomach area so gastric contents do not
flow into the vent lumen.
11. Document relevant information: the insertion
of the tube, the means by which correct
placement was determined and the person’s
responses (e.g. discomfort or abdominal
distension).
12. Establish a plan for providing daily
nasogastric tube care.
Inspect the nostril for discharge and
irritation.
Clean the nostril and tube with moistened,
cotton-tipped applicators.
Apply water-soluble lubricant to the nostril
if it appears dry or encrusted.
Change the adhesive tape as required.


Give frequent mouth care. Due to the
presence of the tube, the person may
breathe through the mouth.
13. If suction is applied, ensure that the patency
of both the nasogastric and suction tubes is
maintained.
Irrigations of the tube may be required at
regular intervals. In some organisations,
irrigations must be ordered by the doctor.
If a Salem sump tube is used, follow
organisation policies for irrigating the vent
lumen with air to maintain patency of the
suctioning lumen. Often, a sucking sound
can be heard from the vent port if it is
patent.
Keep accurate records of the person’s
fluid intake and output and record the
amount and characteristics of the
drainage.
14. Document the type of tube inserted, date and
time of tube insertion, type of suction used,
colour and amount of gastric contents and
the person’s tolerance of the procedure.
Evaluation


Conduct appropriate follow-up, such as degree of
the person’s comfort, tolerance of the nasogastric
tube, correct placement of nasogastric tube in
stomach, the person’s understanding of restrictions,
colour and amount of gastric contents if attached to
suction, or stomach contents aspirated.


SKILL
50.2 Removing a nasogastric
tube
Assessment
Assess
For the presence of bowel sounds.
For the absence of nausea or vomiting when
tube is clamped.
Planning
Equipment
Disposable pad or towel
Tissues
Clean gloves
50 mL syringe (optional)
Plastic rubbish bag
Implementation


Preparation
Confirm the doctor’s order to remove the tube.
Assist the person to a sitting position if health
permits.
Place the disposable pad or towel across the
person’s chest to collect any spillage of
secretions from the tube.
Provide tissues to the person to wipe the nose
and mouth after tube removal.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the removal, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
agency protocol. Explain to the person what
you are going to do, why it is necessary and
how they can cooperate. Discuss how the
results will be used in planning further care or
treatments.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures (e.g.
clean gloves).
3. Provide for the person’s privacy.
4. Detach the tube.
Disconnect the nasogastric tube from the
suction apparatus, if present.
Unpin the tube from the person’s gown.
Remove the adhesive tape securing the
tube to the nose.


5. Remove the nasogastric tube.
Put on clean gloves.
(Optional) Instil 50 mL of air into the tube.
Rationale: this clears the tube of any
contents such as feeding or gastric
drainage.
Ask the person to take a deep breath and
to hold it. Rationale: this closes the
glottis, thereby preventing accidental
aspiration of any gastric contents.
Pinch the tube with the gloved hand.
Rationale: pinching the tube prevents any
contents inside the tube from draining into
the person’s throat.
Smoothly withdraw the tube.
Place the tube in the plastic bag.
Rationale: placing the tube immediately
into the bag prevents the transference of
micro-organisms from the tube to other
articles or people.
Observe the intactness of the tube.
6. Ensure the person’s comfort.
Provide mouth care if desired.
Assist the person as required to blow the
nose. Rationale: excessive secretions
may have accumulated in the nasal
passages.


7. Dispose of the equipment appropriately.
Place the pad, bag with tube and gloves in
the receptacle designated by the
organisation. Rationale: correct disposal
prevents the transmission of micro-
organisms.
8. Document all relevant information.
Record the removal of the tube, the
amount and appearance of any drainage if
connected to suction and any relevant
assessments of the person.
Evaluation
Perform a follow-up examination, such as
presence of bowel sounds, absence of nausea or
vomiting when tube is removed and intactness of
tissues of the nares.
Relate findings to previous assessment data if
available.
Report significant deviations from normal to the
doctor.


SKILL
50.3 Administering a tube
feeding
Purposes
To restore or maintain nutritional status.
To administer medications.
Assessment
Assess
For any clinical signs of malnutrition or
dehydration.
For allergies to any food in the feeding. If the
person is lactose intolerant, check the tube
feeding formula. Notify the doctor if any
incompatibilities exist.
For the presence of bowel sounds.
For any problems that suggest lack of tolerance
of previous feedings (e.g. delayed gastric
emptying, abdominal distension, diarrhoea,
cramping or constipation).


C L I N I C A L  C O N S I D E R A T I O N
Do not add coloured food dye to
tube feedings. Previously, blue
dye was often added to assist in
recognition of aspiration.
However, some cases have
been reported of adverse
reactions to the dye, including
toxicity and death.
Planning
Before commencing a tube feeding, determine the
type, amount and frequency of feedings and
tolerance of previous feedings.
Delegation
Administering a tube feeding requires application of
knowledge and problem solving and must be carried
out by appropriately trained and skilled personnel.
Equipment
Correct type and amount of feeding solution
60 mL catheter-tip syringe
Emesis basin


Clean gloves
pH test strip or metre
Large syringe or calibrated plastic feeding bag
with label and tubing that can be attached to the
feeding tube or pre-filled bottle with a drip
chamber, tubing and a flow-regulator clamp
Measuring container from which to pour the
feeding (if using open system)
Water (60 mL unless otherwise specified) at
room temperature
Feeding pump as required
Implementation
Preparation
Assist the person to a Fowler’s position (at least 30
degrees elevation) in bed or a sitting position in a
chair, the normal position for eating. If a sitting
position is contraindicated, a slightly elevated right
side-lying position is acceptable. Rationale: these
positions enhance the gravitational flow of the
solution and prevent aspiration of fluid into the lungs.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the feeding, introduce self
and verify the person’s identity. Explain to the
person what you are going to do, why it is


necessary and how they can cooperate.
Inform the person that the feeding should not
cause any discomfort but may cause a feeling
of fullness.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe
appropriate infection-control procedures (e.g.
clean gloves).
3. Provide privacy for this procedure if the
person desires it. Tube feedings are
embarrassing to some people.
4. Assess tube placement.
Attach the syringe to the open end of the
tube and aspirate. Check the pH.
Allow 1 hour to elapse before testing the
pH if the person has received a
medication.
Use a pH metre rather than pH paper if
the person is receiving a continuous
feeding. Follow organisation policy if the
pH is 6 or greater.
5. Assess residual feeding contents.
If the tube is placed in the stomach,
aspirate all contents and measure the
amount before administering the feeding.
Rationale: this is done to evaluate
absorption of the last feeding; that is,
whether undigested formula from a


previous feeding remains. If the tube is in
the small intestine, residual contents
cannot be aspirated.
If 100 mL (or more than half the last
feeding) is withdrawn, check with the
nurse in charge or refer to organisation
policy before proceeding. The precise
amount is usually determined by the
doctor’s order or by organisation policy.
Rationale: at some organisations, a
feeding is delayed when the specified
amount or more of formula remains in the
stomach.
or
Re-instil the gastric contents into the
stomach if this is the organisation policy or
doctor’s order. Rationale: removal of the
contents could disturb the person’s
electrolyte balance.
If the person is on a continuous feeding,
check the gastric residual every 4 to 6
hours or according to organisation policy.
6. Administer the feeding.
Before administering feeding:
Check the expiration date of the feeding.
Warm the feeding to room temperature.
Rationale: an excessively cold feeding


may cause abdominal cramps.
When an open system is used, clean the
top of the feeding container with alcohol
before opening it. Rationale: this
minimises the risk of contaminants
entering the feeding syringe or feeding
bag.
Feeding bag (open system)
Hang the labelled bag from an infusion
pole about 30 cm above the tube’s
point of insertion into the person.
Clamp the tubing and add the formula
to the bag.
Open the clamp, run the formula
through the tubing and re-clamp the
tube. Rationale: the formula will
displace the air in the tubing, thus
preventing the instillation of excess air
into the person’s stomach or intestine.
Attach the bag to the feeding tube ❶
and regulate the drip by adjusting the
clamp to the drop factor on the bag
(e.g. 20 drops/mL) if not placed on a
pump.


❶ Using a calibrated plastic bag to
administer a tube feeding
Syringe (open system)


Remove the plunger from the syringe
and connect the syringe to a pinched
or clamped nasogastric tube.
Rationale: pinching or clamping the
tube prevents excess air from entering
the stomach and causing distension.
Add the feeding to the syringe barrel.
❷
❷ Using the barrel of a syringe to
administer a tube feeding


Permit the feeding to flow in slowly at
the prescribed rate. Raise or lower the
syringe to adjust the flow as needed.
Pinch or clamp the tubing to stop the
flow for a minute if the person
experiences discomfort. Rationale:
quickly administered feedings can
cause flatus, cramps and/or vomiting.
Pre-filled bottle with drip chamber
(closed system)
Remove the screw-on cap from the
container and attach the administration
set with the drip chamber and tubing.
❸


❸ Feeding set with spike and tubing
Note: the port on the cap can only be
accessed using this special safety screw
spike to prevent accidental connection
using intravenous tubing.
Source: Courtesy Covidien.
Close the clamp on the tubing.
Hang the container on an intravenous
pole about 30 cm above the tube’s
insertion point into the person.
Rationale: at this height, the formula


should run at a safe rate into the
stomach or intestine.
Squeeze the drip chamber to fill it to
one-third to one-half of its capacity.
Open the tubing clamp, run the
formula through the tubing and re-
clamp the tube. Rationale: the formula
will displace the air in the tubing, thus
preventing the instillation of excess air.
Attach the feeding set tubing to the
feeding tube and regulate the drip rate
to deliver the feeding over the desired
length of time or attach to a feeding
pump.
7. If another bottle is not to be immediately
hung, flush the feeding tube before all of the
formula has run through the contamination.
Instil 50 to 100 mL of water through the
feeding tube or medication port.
Rationale: water flushes the lumen of the
tube, preventing future blockage by sticky
formula.
Be sure to add the water before the
feeding solution has drained from the neck
of a syringe or from the tubing of an
administration set. Rationale: adding the
water before the syringe or tubing is


empty prevents the instillation of air into
the stomach or intestine and thus
prevents unnecessary distension.
8. Clamp the feeding tube.
Clamp the feeding tube before all of the
water is instilled. Rationale: clamping
prevents leakage and air from entering the
tube if done before water is instilled.
9. Ensure the person’s comfort and safety.
Secure the tubing to the person’s gown.
Rationale: this minimises pulling of the
tube, thus preventing discomfort and
dislodgment.
Ask the person to remain sitting upright in
Fowler’s position or in a slightly elevated
right lateral position for at least 30
minutes. Rationale: these positions
facilitate digestion and movement of the
feeding from the stomach along the
alimentary tract and prevent the potential
aspiration of the feeding into the lungs.
Check the organisation’s policy on the
frequency of changing the nasogastric
tube and the use of smaller lumen tubes if
a large-bore tube is in place. Rationale:
these measures prevent irritation and


erosion of the pharyngeal and
oesophageal mucous membranes.
10. Dispose of equipment appropriately.
If the equipment is to be reused, wash it
thoroughly with soap and water so that it
is ready for reuse.
Change the equipment every 24 hours or
according to organisation policy.
11. Document all relevant information.
Document the feeding, including amount
and kind of solution taken, duration of the
feeding and assessments of the person.
Record the volume of the feeding and
water administered on the person’s intake
and output record.
12. Monitor the person for possible problems.
Carefully assess person’s receiving tube
feedings for problems.
To prevent dehydration, give the person
supplemental water in addition to the
prescribed tube feeding as ordered.
Variation: continuous drip feeding


Clamp the tubing at least every 4 to 6 hours, or
as indicated by organisation protocol or the
manufacturer, and aspirate and measure the
gastric contents. Then flush the tubing with 30 to
50 mL of water. Rationale: this determines
adequate absorption and verifies correct
placement of the tube. If placement of a small-
bore tube is questionable, a repeat x-ray should
be done.
Determine organisation policy regarding
withholding a feeding. Many organisations
withhold the feeding if more than 75 to 100 mL of
feeding is aspirated.
To prevent spoilage or bacterial contamination,
do not allow the feeding solution to hang longer
than 4 to 8 hours. Check organisation policy or
manufacturer’s recommendations regarding time
limits.
Follow organisation policy regarding how
frequently to change the feeding bag and tubing.
Changing the feeding bag and tubing every 24
hours reduces the risk of contamination.
Evaluation
Perform a follow-up examination of the following:
Tolerance of feeding (e.g. nausea, cramping)


Bowel sounds
Regurgitation and feelings of fullness after
feedings
Weight gain or loss
Faecal elimination pattern (e.g. diarrhoea,
flatulence, constipation)
Skin turgor
Urine output and specific gravity
Glucose and acetone in urine.
Relate findings to previous assessment data if
available. Report significant deviations from
normal to the doctor.


SKILL
50.4 Administering a
gastrostomy or jejunostomy
feeding
Purposes
See Skill 50.3
.
Assessment
See Skill 50.3
.
Planning
Before commencing a gastrostomy or jejunostomy
feeding, determine the type and amount of feeding
to be instilled, frequency of feedings and any
pertinent information about previous feedings (e.g.
the position in which the person best tolerates the
feeding).


Delegation
See Skill 50.3
.
Equipment
Correct amount of feeding solution
Graduated container and tubing with clamp to
hold the feeding
60 mL catheter-tip syringe
For a tube that remains in place
Mild soap and water
Clean gloves
Petrolatum, zinc oxide ointment or other skin
protectant
10 cm × 10 cm gauze squares
For tube insertion
Clean gloves
Moisture-proof bag
Water-soluble lubricant
Feeding tube (if needed)
Implementation
Preparation
See Skill 50.3
.


Performance
1. Prior to performing the feeding, introduce self
and verify the person’s identity. Explain to the
person what you are going to do, why it is
necessary and how they can cooperate.
Discuss how the results will be used in
planning further care or treatments.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe other
appropriate infection-control procedures (e.g.
clean gloves).
3. Provide for the person’s privacy.
4. Assess and prepare the person.
See Skill 50.3
.
5. Insert a feeding tube, if one is not already in
place.
Wearing gloves, remove the dressing.
Then discard the dressing and gloves in
the moisture-proof bag.
Apply new clean gloves.
Lubricate the end of the tube and insert it
into the stoma opening 10 to 15 cm.
6. Check the location and patency of a tube that
is already in place.
Determine correct placement of the tube
by aspirating secretions and checking the
pH.


Follow organisation policy for amount of
residual formula. This may include
withholding the feeding, rechecking in 3 to
4 hours, or notifying the doctor if a large
residual remains.
For continuous feedings, check the
residual every 4 to 6 hours and hold
feedings according to organisation policy.
Remove the syringe plunger. Pour 15 to
30 mL of water into the syringe, remove
the tube clamp and allow the water to flow
into the tube. Rationale: this determines
the patency of the tube. If water flows
freely, the tube is patent.
If the water does not flow freely, notify the
nurse in charge and/or the doctor.
7. Administer the feeding.
Hold the barrel of the syringe 7 to 15 cm
above the stoma opening.
Slowly pour the solution into the syringe
and allow it to flow through the tube by
gravity.
Just before all the formula has run
through and the syringe is empty, add 30
mL of water. Rationale: water flushes the
tube and preserves its patency.


If the tube is to remain in place, hold it
upright, remove the syringe and then
clamp or plug the tube to prevent leakage.
If a catheter was inserted for the feeding,
remove it.
8. Ensure the person’s comfort and safety.
After the feeding, ask the person to
remain in the sitting position or a slightly
elevated right lateral position for at least
30 minutes. Rationale: this minimises the
risk of aspiration.
Assess status of peristomal skin.
Rationale: gastric or jejunal drainage
contains digestive enzymes that can
irritate the skin. Document any redness
and broken skin areas.
Check orders about cleaning the
peristomal skin, applying a skin protectant
and applying appropriate dressings.
Generally, the peristomal skin is washed
with mild soap and water at least once
daily. The tube may be rotated between
thumb and forefinger to release any
sticking and promote tract formation.
Petrolatum, zinc oxide ointment or other
skin protectant may be applied around the
stoma and precut 10 cm × 10 cm gauze


squares may be placed around the tube.
Additional gauze squares are then used to
cover the site and the tube is coiled over
them.
Observe for common complications of
enteral feedings: aspiration,
hyperglycaemia, abdominal distension,
diarrhoea and faecal impaction. Report
findings to the doctor. Often, a change in
formula or rate of administration can
correct problems.
When appropriate, teach the person how
to administer feedings and when to notify
the doctor concerning problems.
9. Document all assessments and interventions.
Evaluation
See Skill 50.3
.


Chapter 50 Review


Chapter highlights
Essential nutrients are grouped into categories: carbohydrates,
proteins, lipids, water, vitamins and minerals.
Nutrients serve three basic purposes: forming body structures
(such as bones and blood), providing energy and helping to
regulate the body’s biochemical reactions.
The amount of energy that nutrients or foods supply to the body
is their energy value. The amount of energy required to maintain
basic body functions is referred to as the resting energy
expenditure (REE). The basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the rate at
which the body metabolises food to maintain the energy and
requirements of a person who is awake and at rest.
A person’s state of energy balance can be determined by
comparing total energy intake with total energy expenditure.
The glycaemic index (GI) is an important aspect of healthy
nutrition. In particular, when the GI of overall diet is low, the risk
of coronary heart disease and diabetes is reduced and weight
loss and weight management are more sustainable.
Ideal body weight (IBW) is the optimal weight recommended for
optimal health.
Body mass index (BMI), waist circumference and per cent body
fat are indicators of changes in body fat stores. They indicate
whether a person’s weight is appropriate and may provide a
useful estimate of nutrition status and health risk.
Factors influencing a person’s nutrition include development,
gender, ethnicity and culture, beliefs about foods, personal


preferences, religious practices, lifestyle, economics, medications
and therapy, health, alcohol consumption, advertising and
psychological factors.
Nutritional needs vary considerably according to age, growth and
energy requirements. Adolescents have high energy
requirements due to their rapid growth; a varied diet plentiful in
dairy foods, meats, green and yellow vegetables and fresh fruits
is required. Middle-aged adults and older adults often need to
reduce their total energy intake because of decreases in
metabolic rate and activity levels.
Various daily food guides have been developed to help healthy
people meet the daily requirements of essential nutrients and to
facilitate meal planning. These include the Dietary Guidelines for
Australians and the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating.
Both inadequate and excessive intakes of nutrients result in
malnutrition. The effects of malnutrition can be general or
specific, depending on which nutrients and what level of
deficiency or excess are involved.
Assessment of nutritional status may involve all or some of the
following: nursing history data, nutritional screening, physical
examination, calculation of the percentage of weight loss, a
dietary history, anthropometric measurements and laboratory
data.
Nursing diagnoses for people with nutritional problems may be
broadly stated as Imbalanced nutrition: less than body
requirements or More than body requirements. Because
nutritional problems may affect many other areas of human


functioning, the nutritional problem may be the aetiology of other
diagnoses, such as Activity intolerance and Low self-esteem.
Major goals for people with or at risk of nutritional problems
include the following: maintain or restore optimal nutritional
status, decrease or regain specified weight, promote healthy
nutritional practices and prevent complications associated with
malnutrition.
Assisting and supporting people with therapeutic diets is a
function shared by the nurse and the dietitian. The nurse
reinforces the dietitian’s instructions, assists the person to make
beneficial changes and documents the person’s response to
planned changes.
Because many hospitalised people have poor appetites, a major
responsibility of the nurse is to provide nursing interventions that
stimulate their appetites.
Whenever possible, the nurse should help incapacitated people
to feed themselves; a number of self-feeding aids help those who
have difficulty handling regular utensils.
The nurse can refer people to various community programs that
help special subgroups of the population meet their nutritional
needs.
Enteral feedings, administered through nasogastric,
nasointestinal, gastrostomy or jejunostomy tubes, are provided
when the person is unable to ingest foods or the upper
gastrointestinal tract is impaired.
A nasogastric or nasointestinal tube is used to provide enteral
nutrition for short-term use. A gastrostomy or jejunostomy tube


can be used to supply nutrients via the enteral route for long-
term use.
The two most accurate methods of confirming gastrointestinal
tube placement are radiographs and pH testing of aspirate.
Aseptic technique is required during tube feedings.
Parenteral nutrition (PN), provided when the gastrointestinal tract
is non-functional (e.g. absorptive capacity impaired), is given
intravenously into a large central vein (e.g. the superior vena
cava).
Concept check
1. An adult reports eating, on average, the following each day: 3
cups dairy foods, 2 cups fruit, 2 cups vegetables, 2 serves of
breads and cereals and 150 g meat. The nurse would counsel
the person to:
1. Maintain the diet; the servings are adequate.
2. Increase the number of servings of dairy foods.
3. Decrease the number of servings of vegetables.
4. Increase the number of servings of breads and
cereals.
2. Which of the following are allowed on a full fluids diet? Select
all that apply.
1. Scrambled eggs.
2. Chocolate pudding.
3. Tomato juice.


4. Hard lollies/confectionary.
5. Mashed potatoes.
6. Creamed rice.
7. Rolled oats.
8. Fruit smoothies.
3. Which of the following is the best indication of proper
placement of a nasogastric tube in the stomach?
1. Person is unable to speak.
2. Person gags during insertion.
3. pH of the aspirate is less than 5.
4. Fluid is easily instilled into the tube.
4. What is the proper technique with gravity tube feeding?

insertion point into the person.
2. Nurse administers the next feeding only if there is less
than 25 mL of residual volume from the previous
feeding.
3. Place the person in the left lateral position.
4. Feeding is administered directly from the refrigerator.

Chapter 51 Urinary elimination

Learning outcomes
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Describe the process of urination, from urine formation through
to micturition.
Identify factors that influence urinary elimination, with
consideration of people with disabilities.
Identify common causes of selected urinary problems.
Describe nursing assessment of urinary function, including
subjective and objective data.


Identify normal and abnormal characteristics and constituents of
urine.
Develop nursing diagnoses, desired outcomes and interventions
related to urinary elimination.
Describe ways to prevent urinary tract infection.
Explain the care of people with indwelling urinary catheters or
urinary diversions.

Elimination from the urinary tract is usually taken
for granted. Only when a problem arises do
most people become aware of their urinary
habits and any associated symptoms.
A person’s urinary habits depend on social
culture, personal habits and physical abilities or
disabilities. In Australia, most people are


accustomed to privacy and clean surroundings
while they urinate.
Personal habits regarding urination are affected
by the social propriety of leaving to urinate, the
availability of a private, clean facility and initial
bladder training. Urinary elimination is essential
to health and voiding can be postponed for only
so long before the urge normally becomes too
great to control.


Physiology of urinary elimination
Urinary elimination depends on effective functioning of the upper
urinary tract (kidneys and ureters) and the lower urinary tract
(urinary bladder, urethra and pelvic floor) (see Figure 51.1
).
Figure 51.1


Anatomical structures of the urinary tract.
Kidneys
The paired kidneys are usually situated on either side of the spinal
column, behind the peritoneal cavity. The right kidney is slightly lower
than the left due to the position of the liver. They are the primary
regulators of fluid and acid–base balance in the body. The functional
units of the kidneys, the nephrons, filter the blood and remove
metabolic wastes. In the average adult, 1200 mL of blood (21% of
the cardiac output) passes through the kidneys every minute. Each
kidney contains approximately 1 million nephrons. Each nephron has
a glomerulus
, a tuft of capillaries surrounded by Bowman’s
capsule (see Figure 51.2
). The endothelium of glomerular
capillaries is porous, allowing fluid and solutes to readily move
across this membrane into the capsule. Plasma proteins and blood
cells, however, are too large to cross the membrane normally.


Glomerular filtrate is similar in composition to plasma, and is made
up of water, electrolytes, glucose, amino acids and metabolic
wastes.
Figure 51.2


The nephrons of the kidney are composed of six parts: the
glomerulus, Bowman’s capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of
Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct.
From the Bowman’s capsule the filtrate moves into the tubule of the
nephron (see Figure 51.3
). In the proximal convoluted tubule,
most of the water and electrolytes are reabsorbed. Solutes such as
glucose are reabsorbed in the loop of Henle, but in the same area
other substances are secreted into the filtrate, concentrating the
urine. In the distal convoluted tubule, additional water and sodium
are reabsorbed under the control of hormones such as antidiuretic
hormone (ADH) and aldosterone. This controlled reabsorption allows
fine regulation of fluid and electrolyte balance in the body. When fluid
intake is low or the concentration of solutes in the blood is high, ADH
is released from the anterior pituitary, more water is re-absorbed in
the distal tubule and less urine is excreted. By contrast, when fluid
intake is high or the blood solute concentration is low, ADH is
suppressed. Without ADH, the distal tubule becomes impermeable
to water and more urine is excreted. Aldosterone also affects the
tubule. When aldosterone is released from the adrenal cortex,
sodium and water are reabsorbed in greater quantities, increasing
the blood volume and decreasing urinary output.


Figure 51.3


Anatomy of a kidney.
Source: ducu59us. Shutterstock.
Ureters
Once the urine is formed in the kidneys, it moves through the
collecting ducts into the calyces of the renal pelvis and from there
into the ureters. Calyces are spaces where urine collects before
moving to the kidneys.
The ureters are from 25 to 30 cm long in the adult and about 1.25
cm in diameter. The upper end of each ureter is funnel-shaped as it
enters the kidney. The lower ends of the ureters enter the bladder at
the posterior corners of the floor of the bladder (see Figure 51.1
).
At the junction between the ureter and the bladder, a flap-like fold of
mucous membrane acts as a valve to prevent reflux
 (backflow)
of urine up the ureters.
Bladder
The urinary bladder (vesicle) is a hollow, muscular organ that serves
as a reservoir for urine and as the organ of excretion. When empty,
it lies behind the symphysis pubis. In men, the bladder lies in front of


the rectum and above the prostate gland (see Figure 51.4
); in
women, it lies in front of the uterus and vagina (see Figure 51.5
).
The wall of the bladder is made up of: (a) an inner mucous layer; (b)
a connective tissue layer; (c) three layers of smooth muscle fibre,
some of which extend lengthwise, some obliquely and some more or
less circularly; and (d) an outer serous layer. The smooth muscle
layers are collectively called the detrusor muscle. The detrusor
muscle
 allows the bladder to expand as it fills with urine and to
contract during voiding or elimination (see ‘Anatomy & physiology
review
’). The trigone
 at the base of the bladder is a triangular
area marked by the ureter openings at the posterior corners and the
opening of the urethra at the anterior inferior corner (see Figure
51.1
).
Figure 51.4


The male urogenital system.
Figure 51.5


The female urogenital system.
The bladder is capable of considerable distension because of rugae
(folds) in the mucous membrane lining and because of the elasticity
of its walls. When full, the dome of the bladder may extend above
the symphysis pubis; in extreme situations, it may extend as high as
the umbilicus. Normal bladder capacity is between 300 and 400 mL
of urine during the day and up to 800 mL at night (Continence
Foundation of Australia ). Bladder capacity in infants and children
1


increases through toddlerhood and kidneys reach near-adult
functional levels at about 16–24 months of age (Mills & Woodring ).
1 Continence Foundation of Australia (2019). Bladder Training. Retrieved from
<www.continence.org.au>.
2 Mills, D. A. & Woodring, B. C. (2012). Growth and development of the toddler. In N. L. Potts
& B. L. Medleco (Eds), Pediatric Nursing Caring for Children and Their Families (3rd ed., pp.
273–305). New York: Delmar Cengage Learning.
Urethra
The urethra extends from the bladder to the urinary meatus
(opening). In the adult woman, the urethra lies directly behind the
symphysis pubis, anterior to the vagina, and is between 3 and 4 cm
long (see Figure 51.5
). The urethra serves only as a passageway
for the elimination of urine. The urinary meatus is located between
the labia minora, in front of the vagina and below the clitoris. The
male urethra is approximately 20 cm long and serves as a
passageway for semen as well as urine (see Figure 51.4
). The
urethral orifice or meatus is located at the distal end of the penis.
In both men and women, the urethra has a mucous membrane lining
that is continuous with the bladder and the ureters. Thus, an
infection of the urethra can extend through the urinary tract to the
kidneys. Women are particularly prone to urinary tract infections
(UTIs) because of their short urethra and the proximity of the urinary
meatus to the vagina and anus.
2


Pelvic floor
The vagina and the urethra and rectum pass through the pelvic floor,
which consists of sheets of muscles and ligaments that provide
support to the viscera of the pelvis. They extend from the symphysis
pubis to the coccyx forming a sling. Specific sphincter muscles
contribute to the continence mechanism (see the ‘Anatomy &
physiology review
’). The internal sphincter muscle situated in
the proximal urethra and the bladder neck is composed of smooth
muscle under involuntary control. It provides active tension designed
to close the urethral lumen. The external sphincter muscle is
composed of skeletal muscle under voluntary control, allowing the
individual to choose when urine is eliminated.
ANATO M Y & PHYSIO LO G Y REVIEW
Female and male urinary bladders and urethras
The pelvic floor muscles are under voluntary control and are
important in controlling urination (continence). These muscles
can become weakened by pregnancy and childbirth, chronic
constipation, a decrease in oestrogen (menopause), being
overweight, ageing and lack of general fitness. High-impact
athletic activity can also predispose females to incontinence
(Dias et al. ). The ability to voluntarily control these muscles
can be impeded by neurological and spinal cord damage
(Chermansky & Moalli ).
3
4


3 Dias, N., Peng, Y., Khavari, R., ... Zhang, Y. (2017). Pelvic floor dynamics during
high-impact athletic activities: A computational modeling study. Clinical
Biomechanics, 41, 20–27.
4 Chermansky & Moalli (2016). Role of pelvic floor in lower urinary tract function.
Autonomic Neuroscience: Basic and Clinical, 200, 43–48.
Review the figures and find the pelvic floor muscles.


Questions
1. Do you think pelvic floor muscles can be
strengthened? Provide your rationale.
2. Why would urinary function be affected by neurological
damage?
Refer to page 1378 for the ‘Patient education
’ box about
pelvic floor exercises.
Urination
Urination
, micturition
 and voiding
 all refer to the process
of emptying the urinary bladder. Urine collects in the bladder until
pressure stimulates special sensory nerve endings in the bladder
wall called stretch receptors. This occurs when the adult bladder
contains between 250 and 450 mL of urine. It should be noted that


the adult bladder can hold as much as 800 mL of urine. In children,
a considerably smaller volume, 50 to 200 mL, stimulates these
nerves.
The stretch receptors transmit impulses to the spinal cord,
specifically to the voiding reflex centre located at the level of the
second to fourth sacral vertebrae, causing the internal sphincter to
relax and stimulating the urge to void. If the time and place are
appropriate for urination, the conscious portion of the brain relaxes
the external urethral sphincter muscle and urination takes place. If
the time and place are inappropriate, the micturition reflex usually
subsides until the bladder becomes more filled and the reflex is
stimulated again.
Voluntary control of urination is possible only if the nerves supplying
the bladder and urethra, the neural tracts of the cord and brain and
the motor area of the cerebrum are all intact. The individual must be
able to sense that the bladder is full. Injury to any of these parts of
the nervous system—for example, by a cerebral haemorrhage or
spinal cord injury above the level of the sacral region—results in
intermittent involuntary emptying of the bladder. Older adults whose
cognition is impaired may not be aware of the need to urinate or
able to respond to this urge by seeking toilet facilities.


Factors affecting voiding
Numerous factors affect the volume and characteristics of the urine
produced and the manner in which it is excreted.
Developmental factors
Infants
Minimum urine output for infants and children should be between 1
and 2 mL/kg/hour (King & Mandleco ). An infant may urinate as
often as 20 times a day. The urine of the neonate is colourless and
odourless and has a specific gravity of 1.008. Because newborns
and infants have immature kidneys, they are unable to concentrate
urine very effectively.
5 King, P. & Mandleco, B. L. (2012). Growth and development of the newborn. In N. L. Potts &
B. L. Medleco (Eds), Pediatric Nursing Caring for Children and Their Families (3rd ed., pp.
191–225). New York: Delmar Cengage Learning.
Infants are born without urinary control. Most will develop this
between the ages of 2 and 5 years. Control during the daytime
normally precedes night-time control. As infants have repetitive
contact with urine and faeces, they are especially susceptible to
dermatitis in the nappy area. The best possible way to prevent this is
5


to change the nappy as soon as it becomes wet or is soiled, and to
clean the skin with a soap-free solution and water. The skin also
benefits from periods of drying in the air (but not heat) without a
barrier of occlusion. A protective layer of pH-friendly moisturiser can
protect the skin from further irritation and encourage healing
(Hockenberry & Wilson) .
6 Hockenberry, M. & Wilson, D. (2014). Wong’s Nursing Care of Infants and Children (10th
ed.). St Louis: Mosby.
Preschoolers
The preschooler is able to take responsibility for independent
toileting. Parents need to realise that accidents do occur and the
child should never be punished or chastised for this. Children often
forget to wash their hands or flush the toilet and need instruction in
wiping themselves. Girls should be taught to wipe from front to back
to prevent contamination of the urinary tract by faeces.
School-age children
The school-age child’s elimination system reaches maturity during
this period. The kidneys double in size between ages 5 and 10
years. During this period, the child urinates six to eight times a day.
Enuresis
, which is defined as the involuntary passing of urine
when control should be established (5 years of age), can be a
problem for some school-age children. About 10% of all 6-year-olds
experience difficulty controlling the bladder. Nocturnal enuresis
,
6


or bed-wetting, is the involuntary passing of urine at night. Diurnal
enuresis
 occurs during the daytime. Enuresis can also be defined
as primary and secondary. Primary enuresis is bed-wetting in
children who have never been dry for extended periods; secondary
enuresis is considered to be bed-wetting that occurs after the
establishment of urinary continence (McCord ). Bed-wetting affects
at least 15% of 5-year-olds (and 2% of young adults). Enuresis can
cause serious psychological issues. It is often associated with stress
and considerable embarrassment and can cause children to become
socially and emotionally ostracised. Although no clear cause for
enuresis has been determined, some predictive factors have been
noted, such as family history and slower development in toddlerhood
(McCord 2014; Huang et al. ). If a child or caregiver expresses
concern about bed-wetting, further assessment and advice from the
health care team should be sought.
7 McCord, S. (2014). Health problems of middle childhood. In M. J. Hockenberry & D. Wilson
(Eds), Wong’s Nursing Care of Infants and Children (10th ed.). St Louis, MO: Mosby.
8 Huang, T., Shu, X., Huang, Y. S. & Cheuk, D. K. L (2011). Complementary and
miscellaneous interventions for nocturnal enuresis in children. Cochrane Database of
Systematic Reviews, Issue 12, Art No: CD005230. John Wiley and Sons.
Older adults
The excretory function of the kidney diminishes with age, but usually
not significantly below normal levels unless a disease process
intervenes. Blood flow can be reduced by arteriosclerosis (see
Chapter 30)
, impairing renal function. With age, the number of
7
8


functioning nephrons decreases to some degree, impairing the
kidney’s filtering abilities. Conditions that alter normal fluid intake and
output, such as diabetes insipidus or pre- or postoperative fasting,
can compromise the kidney’s ability to filter, maintain acid–base
balance and maintain electrolyte balance in older adults. It also
takes a much longer time for these processes to return to normal
functioning. The decrease in kidney function also places the older
adult at higher risk of toxicity from medications if excretion rates are
longer.
The more noticeable changes with age are those related to the
bladder. The capacity of the bladder and its ability to completely
empty diminish with age. Also, as we age we produce less
antidiuretic hormone, which normally suppresses some production of
urine during the night. This explains the need for older adults to rise
during the night to void (nocturnal frequency
) and the retention
of residual urine, predisposing the older adult to bladder infections.
Complaints of urinary urgency and urinary frequency are common.
They can be related to UTIs or, in men, these changes are often due
to nerve impairment related to an enlarged prostate gland or post
surgery. In women, they may be due to weakened muscles
supporting the bladder or weakness of the urethral sphincter.
Clinical consideration
The older adult who experiences problems with
urinary elimination, including incontinence, is at


greater risk of experiencing a fall. This is a
factor that all nurses should consider when
caring for the older adult in any health care
facility. Preventive falls strategies should be
implemented, including scheduled toileting when
required.
See Table 51.1
 for a summary of the developmental changes
affecting urinary output, and the ‘Lifespan considerations’ feature.
Table 51.1 Changes in urinary elimination through the lifespan
9 Atkinson, S. & Russell, D. (2015). Gender dysphoria. Australian Family Physician, 44(11),
792–796.
Psychosocial factors
For many people, a set of conditions helps stimulate the micturition
reflex. These conditions include privacy, normal position, sufficient
time and, occasionally, running water. Circumstances that do not
allow for the person’s accustomed conditions may produce anxiety
and muscle tension. As a result, the person is unable to relax
abdominal and perineal muscles and the external urethral sphincter
and voiding is inhibited. People also may voluntarily suppress
urination because of perceived time pressures; for example, nurses


often ignore the urge to void until they are able to take a break. This
behaviour can increase the risk of urinary tract infections.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Comprehensive Care
The intention of this standard is to ensure that patients receive
comprehensive health care that meets their individual needs
and considers the impact of their health issues on their life and
wellbeing. It also aims to ensure that risks of harm for patients
during health care are prevented and managed through
targeted strategies (Australian Commission on Safety and
Quality in Health Care 2017, p. 38
).
10 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard to reduce the risk of
falls is achieved by implementing multifactorial,
best practice falls prevention systems, providing
equipment and devices to promote safe mobility
and working in partnership with consumers to
provide information about falls and appropriate
services.
Older individuals experiencing incontinence are
at greater risk of falls due to reduced mobility,
poor eyesight and urgency. All individuals
10


require screening for risk of falls on admission
to hospital. Those at risk should be provided
with a well-lit environment, free of clutter, in a
position close to a toilet, commode or urinal and
with appropriate mobility devices. Scheduled
toileting should also be considered in the care
plan.
Lifespan considerations
Factors affecting voiding
Infants and children
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common infections in
children and can involve the kidneys, bladder or both.
Children usually recover quickly from acute episodes.
When UTIs are frequent, the child should be evaluated by
a doctor (Jadresic ).
11 Jadresic, L. (2013). Urinary tract infections in children. Pediatrics and Child
Health, 24(7), 280–292.
Teaching correct perineal hygiene can reduce infection.
Girls should learn to wipe from front to back and wear
11


cotton underwear.
Children should be taught to go to the toilet as soon as
the sensation to void is felt.
Adults
Sex reassignment surgery involves changes to the urethra.
This can result in long-term issues such as stress
incontinence, overactive bladder and reduced blood flow
(Combaz & Kuhn ).
12 Combaz, N. & Kuhn, A. (2017). Long-term urogynecological complications after
sex reassignment surgery in transsexual patients: A retrospective study of 44
patients and diagnostic algorithm proposal. American Journal of Urology Research,
2(2), 38–43. Retrieved from <www.scireslit.com>.
The older adult
Changes related to ageing cause specific problems in urinary
elimination in the older adult. Many conditions can be treated
and interventions can be used to either resolve or decrease
the problem. Some of the following conditions are causative
factors in problems with urinary elimination:
Older adults, especially women, are susceptible to urinary
tract infection, which can lead to incontinence, confusion
and falls.
Many older men have enlarged prostate glands, which
can inhibit complete emptying of the bladder, resulting in
urinary retention and overflow dribbling of urine.
12


Women past menopause have decreased oestrogen,
which results in a decrease in perineal tone and support of
bladder, vagina and supporting tissues. This often results
in stress incontinence or leakage on exertion and can
even increase the incidence of urinary tract infections.
An overactive bladder or urge incontinence results in a
sudden and often uncontrollable urge to void. It is
associated with nerve damage as a result of diabetes,
stroke, injury or surgery.
Functional incontinence is associated with impaired
mobility due to increased stiffness and pain in joints,
previous joint surgery and neuromuscular problems, which
often make it difficult to get to the bathroom.
Cognitive impairment, such as in dementia, often prevents
the person from understanding the need to urinate and
the actions needed to perform the activity.
Interventions that may improve these conditions include:
Adequate fluid intake and good toileting hygiene to reduce
the risk of UTIs.
Prevention of constipation, straining at stool and faecal
impaction will reduce the pressure on the bladder.
Kegel or pelvic floor exercises to improve support of
bladder and other pelvic organs (see page 1376).
Medications or surgery to relieve obstructions in men and
strengthen support in the urogenital area in women.
Bladder or behavioural training for better bladder control
(see ‘Practice guidelines: Maintaining normal voiding


habits
’, page 1375).
Providing safe, easy access to the bathroom or bedside
commode. Make sure well-fitting, non-skid footwear is
available, the room is well lit, the environment is safe and
the proper assistive devices are within reach (such as
walkers, walking sticks).
Habit training, such as taking the person to the bathroom
at a regular, scheduled time. This can often work very well
with cognitively impaired people. These include regular
timed intervals and tracking the person’s individual pattern
for 72 hours, culminating in the development of an
individualised plan for that person (Ostaszkiewicz 2017).
Fluid and food intake
The healthy body maintains a balance between the amount of fluid
ingested and the amount of fluid eliminated. When the amount of
fluid intake increases, therefore, the output normally increases.
Certain fluids, such as alcohol, increase fluid output by inhibiting the
production of antidiuretic hormone. Fluids that contain caffeine (e.g.
coffee, tea and some fizzy drinks) also increase urine production. By
contrast, food and fluids high in sodium can cause fluid retention
because water is retained to maintain the normal concentration of
electrolytes.


Some foods and fluids can change the colour of urine. For example,
beetroot can cause urine to appear red. Other foods such as
asparagus can alter the usual odour of urine.
Medications
Many medications, particularly those affecting the autonomic
nervous system, interfere with the normal urination process and may
cause retention (see Box 51.1
) or urinary incontinence (see Box
51.2
). Diuretics
 are a group of drugs that promote the
formation and excretion of urine. They are prescribed to reduce the
volume of extracellular fluid in the treatment of many disorders,
including congestive cardiac failure, hypertension and oedema. The
diuretic drugs available in Australia and New Zealand are classified
by their chemical structure and activity into groups: aldosterone
antagonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, hyperosmotic agents,
loop diuretics, potassium-sparing diuretics and thiazides (Australian
Medicines Handbook ). Some medications may alter the colour or
smell of the urine.
13 Australian Medicines Handbook (2019). Diuretics. Retrieved from <https://amhonline-amh-
net-au>.
BO X
13


51.1 Medications that may cause
urinary retention
Urinary retention can result when medications listed below
interfere with nerve signals to the prostate and bladder:
antihistamines and decongestants
anticholinergic and antispasmodic medications
tricyclic antidepressants
nifedipine (Procardia) for hypertension
carbamazepine (Tegretol) for seizures, epilepsy
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
amphetamines
opioid analgesics.
Source: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.
 Urinary Retention.
Retrieved from <www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/urinary-
retention#sec3>.
14 National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (2019). Urinary Retention.
Retrieved from <www.niddk.nih.gov>.
BO X
51.2 Medications that may cause or
aggravate urinary incontinence
14


Diuretics
Muscle relaxants and sedatives
Narcotics
Antihistamines
Alpha-adrenergic antagonists
Source: Harvard Health Publishing
. Medications that can cause urinary incontinence. From Better
Bladder and Bowel Control. Retrieved from <www.health.harvard.edu/bladder-and-bowel/
medications-that-can-cause-urinary-incontinence>.
15 Harvard Health Publishing (2014). Medications that can cause urinary incontinence. From Better
Bladder and Bowel Control. Retrieved from <www.health.harvard.edu>.
Muscle tone
Good muscle tone is important to maintain the stretch and
contractility of the detrusor muscle so the bladder can fill adequately
and empty completely. A person who requires an indwelling catheter
(see page 1382) for a long period may develop poor bladder muscle
tone because continuous drainage of urine prevents the bladder
from filling and emptying normally.
Pathological conditions
15


Some diseases and pathologies can affect the formation and
excretion of urine. Diseases that primarily affect renal function are
generally classified into pre-renal, renal and post-renal in origin (see
Box 51.3
). Alterations in renal function that occur at the pre-renal
level decrease circulating blood flow to and through the kidneys.
Subsequently, there is decreased renal perfusion to renal tissue. As
a result, oliguria can occur. Oliguria is a diminished capacity to form
and pass urine and is considered in the next part of this chapter.
Decreased renal perfusion can also lead to anuria, although this is
less common. Anuria is also considered in the next part of this
chapter and refers to an absence of urine production or a urine
production of less than 100 mL per day.
BO X
51.3 Conditions that affect renal
function
Pre-renal
Decreased intravascular volume: dehydration,
haemorrhage, burns, shock.
Altered peripheral vascular resistance: sepsis,
anaphylactic (allergic) reactions.
Cardiac pump failure: heart failure, myocardial infarction,
hypertensive heart disease, valvular disease, pericardial
tamponade.


Renal
Nephrotoxic agents (e.g. gentamycin).
Transfusion reactions.
Diseases of the glomeruli (e.g. glomerulonephritis).
Renal neoplasms.
Systemic diseases (e.g. diabetes mellitus).
Hereditary diseases (e.g. polycystic kidney disease).
Infections.
Post-renal
Ureter bladder or urethral obstruction: calculi, blood clots,
tumours, stricture.
Prostatic hypertrophy or tumour.
Neurogenic bladder (lack of bladder control related to
nerve, brain or spinal cord problems) (see page 1366).
Pelvic tumours.
Source: J. Crisp, C. Taylor, C. Douglas & G. Rebeiro
. Potter and Perry’s Fundamentals of Nursing
(5th ed.). Chatswood, NSW: Elsevier.
16 Crisp, J., Taylor, C., Douglas, C. & Rebeiro G. (2016). Potter and Perry’s Fundamentals of Nursing
(5th ed.). Chatswood, NSW: Elsevier.
Alterations at the renal level are caused by factors that damage or
injure the glomerulus or renal tubule. Such injury then interferes with
the filtering, reabsorbitive and secretory functions of the kidney.
Alterations at the post-renal level result from obstruction to the
16


urinary collecting system. This can occur from the calyces, being the
drainage system within the kidney, to the urethral meatus. At the
post-renal level, urine is formed by the urinary system, but the
problem is that it cannot be eliminated by normal means. A urinary
stone (calculus) may obstruct a ureter, blocking urine flow from the
kidney to the bladder. Hypertrophy of the prostate gland, a common
condition affecting older men, may obstruct the urethra, impairing
urination and bladder emptying.
Surgical and diagnostic
procedures
Some surgical and diagnostic procedures affect the passage of urine
and the amount and characteristics of urine produced. The urethra
may swell following a cystoscopy (inserting a tube with a lens into
urethra, allowing visualisation of the bladder), and surgical
procedures on any part of the urinary tract may result in some
postoperative bleeding; as a result, the urine may be red or pink
tinged for a time. People who have had sex reassignment surgery, in
particular, are at risk of developing long-term urination disorders,
such as stress urinary incontinence and overactive bladder (Combaz
& Kuhn 2017).
Spinal anaesthetics can affect the passage of urine because they
decrease the person’s awareness of the need to void. Surgery on


structures adjacent to the urinary tract (e.g. the uterus) can also
affect voiding because of swelling in the lower abdomen.


Altered urine production
Although people’s patterns of urination are highly individual, most
people void about five to six times a day. People usually void when
they first wake in the morning, before they go to bed and around
meal times. Table 51.2
 shows the average urinary output per day
at different ages.
Table 51.2 Average daily urine output by age
Polyuria
Polyuria
 (or diuresis
) refers to the production of abnormally
large amounts of urine by the kidneys, often several litres more than
the person’s usual daily output. Polyuria can follow excessive fluid
intake, caused by polydipsia
 (excessive thirst), or may be
associated with diseases such as diabetes mellitus, diabetes
insipidus and chronic nephritis. Polyuria can cause excessive fluid
loss, leading to intense thirst, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance and
weight loss.
Oliguria and anuria


The terms oliguria and anuria, as previously mentioned, are used to
describe decreased urinary output. Oliguria
 is low urine output,
usually less than 500 mL a day or 30 mL an hour for an adult.
Although oliguria may occur because of abnormal fluid losses or a
lack of fluid intake, it often indicates impaired blood flow to the
kidneys or impending acute kidney injury (AKI)
 and should be
promptly reported to the doctor. Restoring renal blood flow and
urinary output promptly can prevent AKI and its complications.
Anuria
 refers to a lack of urine production which can be caused
by medications, toxins, muscle trauma, injury or disease.
Should the kidneys become unable to adequately function, some
mechanism of filtering the blood is necessary to prevent illness and
death. This filtering is done through the use of renal dialysis
, a
technique by which fluids and molecules pass through a semi-
permeable membrane according to the rules of osmosis. The two
most common methods of dialysis are haemodialysis and peritoneal
dialysis. In haemodialysis, the person’s blood flows through vascular
catheters, passes by the dialysis solution in an external machine and
then returns to the person. In peritoneal dialysis, the dialysis solution
is instilled into the abdominal cavity through a catheter, allowed to
rest there while the fluid and molecules exchange and then removed
through the catheter. Both haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis
must be performed at frequent intervals until the person’s kidneys
can resume the filtering function, which for some people may never
be possible.


Altered urinary elimination
Despite normal urine production, a number of factors or conditions
can affect urinary elimination. Frequency, nocturia, urgency and
dysuria often are manifestations of underlying conditions such as a
urinary tract infection. Enuresis, incontinence, retention and
neurogenic bladder may be either a manifestation of or the primary
problem affecting urinary elimination. Selected factors associated
with altered patterns of urine elimination are identified in Table
51.3
.
Table 51.3 Selected factors associated with altered urinary
elimination
Frequency and nocturia
Urinary frequency
 is voiding at frequent intervals; that is, more
than four to six times per day. An increased intake of fluid causes
some increase in the frequency of voiding. Conditions such as
urinary tract infection, enlarged prostate, stress and pregnancy can
cause frequent voiding of small quantities (50 to 100 mL) of urine.
Total fluid intake and output may be normal.


Nocturia
 is a condition where a person wakes up more than once
during the night to void.
Urgency
Urgency
 is the sudden strong desire to void. There may or may
not be a great deal of urine in the bladder, but the person feels a
need to void immediately. Urgency accompanies psychological
stress and irritation of the trigone and urethra. It is also common in
people who have poor external sphincter control and unstable
bladder contractions. It is not a normal finding.
Dysuria
Dysuria
 means voiding that is either painful or difficult. It can
accompany a stricture (decrease in calibre) of the urethra, urinary
infections and injury to the bladder and urethra. Often, a person will
say they have to push to void or that burning accompanies or follows
voiding. The burning may be described as severe, like a hot poker,
or more subdued, like a sunburn. Often, urinary hesitancy
 (a
delay and difficulty in initiating voiding) is associated with dysuria.
Enuresis


Enuresis is involuntary urination in children beyond the age when
voluntary bladder control is normally acquired, usually by 5 years of
age. Nocturnal enuresis often is irregular in occurrence and affects
boys more often than girls. Diurnal (daytime) enuresis may be
persistent and pathological in origin. It affects women and girls more
frequently.
Urinary incontinence
Urinary incontinence
, or involuntary urination, is a symptom, not
a disease. It can have a significant impact on the person’s life,
creating physical problems such as skin breakdown and possibly
leading to psychosocial problems such as embarrassment, isolation
and social withdrawal. Common causes of incontinence include
pregnancy, menopause, obesity, urinary tract infections,
constipation, certain surgeries (prostatectomy, hysterectomy),
restricted mobility, select medications and some health conditions
(diabetes, stroke) (Continence Foundation of Australia ). Urinary
incontinence can be broken into two categories: acute and chronic.
17 Continence Foundation of Australia (2016a). Who’s at Risk? Retrieved from
<www.continence.org.au>.
Acute
Many factors can contribute to acute or reversible incontinence,
including polyuria, exposure to irritants, infection, urinary retention,
17


use of pharmaceuticals, stool impaction or constipation, atrophic
urethritis (urethra vulvar tissue thinning during menopause) or
vaginitis (inflammation of the vagina), restricted mobility or dexterity,
psychological conditions and delirium, or acute confused state.
Some of these factors are readily reversible, with a lessening of
symptoms if not complete resolution of urinary incontinence.
Chronic
Urinary incontinence can be categorised according to five main
types: stress, urge, mixed, nocturnal and ‘other’ (see Table 51.4
).
Table 51.4 Types of urinary incontinence
Diverse populations within Australia may have comorbidities and risk
factors which increase their risk of urinary incontinence. Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Islander people experience obesity, diabetes and
dementia at a higher rate than non-Indigenous people. Female
migrants from Africa, the Middle East and Asia may have undergone
female genital mutilation or suffer from obstetric fistulas which
increase the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections and leakage.
People who have undergone gender reassignment may report
urgency, urge incontinence or stress incontinence (AIHW
).
18 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2013). Incontinence in Australia. Cat. no.
DIS 61. Canberra: AIHW.
Although incontinence is experienced in some older adults, it is not a
normal consequence of ageing and can often be treated.
18


The preliminary assessment and identification of the symptom of
urinary incontinence is truly within the scope of nursing practice. All
people should be asked about their voiding patterns. Older adults
who are incontinent while in their home or who manage to contain or
conceal their incontinence from others may not consider themselves
incontinent. Therefore, if asked if they are incontinent, they may
deny it. Newman  suggests asking questions such as, ‘Do you
experience a loss of urine when you sneeze, cough, or laugh?’ or
‘Do you sometimes experience urine leakage on the way to the
bathroom?’. If incontinence is described, a thorough history and
assessment is indicated. Treatment may include surgery, medication
or behavioural therapies. Nursing management of incontinence
includes implementing individualised bladder programs, containment
of urine and meticulous skin care.
19 Newman, D. K. (2009). Talking to patients about bladder control problems. The Nurse
Practitioner, 34(12), 33–45.
Urinary retention
When emptying of the bladder is impaired, urine accumulates and
the bladder becomes overdistended, a condition known as urinary
retention
. Overdistension of the bladder causes poor contractility
of the detrusor muscle, further impairing urination. Common causes
of urinary retention include prostatic hypertrophy (enlargement),
surgery and some medications (see Box 51.1
).
19


People with urinary retention may experience overflow voiding or
incontinence, eliminating 25 to 50 mL of urine at frequent intervals.
The bladder is firm and distended on palpation and may be
displaced to one side of midline.
Neurogenic bladder
Impaired neurological function (e.g. due to disability) can interfere
with the normal mechanisms of urine elimination, resulting in a
neurogenic bladder
. The person with a neurogenic bladder does
not perceive bladder fullness and is unable to control the urinary
sphincters. The bladder may become flaccid and distended, or
spastic, with frequent involuntary urination.


Nursing management
Assessing
A complete assessment of a person’s urinary function includes the
following:
nursing history
physical assessment of the genitourinary system, hydration
status and examination of the urine as well as consideration of
any disabilities (refer to Table 51.4
)
recording a fluid balance chart or bladder chart
relating the data obtained to the results of any diagnostic tests
and procedures.
Nursing history
The nurse determines the person’s normal voiding pattern and
frequency, appearance of the urine and any recent changes, any
past or current problems with urination, the presence of a stoma and
factors influencing the elimination pattern.
Examples of interview questions to elicit this information are shown
in the ‘Assessment interview’. The number of questions asked


depends on the individual and the responses to the first three
categories.
Physical assessment
Physical assessment of the urinary tract usually includes percussion
of the kidneys to detect areas of tenderness. Palpation and
percussion of the bladder are also performed. If the person’s history
or current problems indicate a need for it, the urethral meatus of
both male and female people is inspected for swelling, discharge
and inflammation. If urine retention is suspected, the nurse should
use a bladder scanner to determine bladder volume. A bladder
scanner is a non-invasive portable ultrasound device used at the
bedside to provide a visual image of the urine remaining in the
bladder.
Assessment interview
Urinary elimination
Voiding pattern
How many times do you urinate during a 24-hour period?
Has this pattern changed recently?
Do you need to get out of bed to void at night? How
often?


Description of urine and any changes
How would you describe your urine in terms of colour,
clarity (clear, transparent or cloudy) and odour (faint or
strong)?
Urinary elimination problems
What problems have you had or do you now have with
passing your urine?
Passage of small amounts of urine?
Voiding at intervals that are more frequent?
Trouble getting to the bathroom in time or feeling an
urgent need to void?
Painful voiding?
Difficulty starting urine stream?
Frequent dribbling of urine or feeling of bladder fullness
associated with voiding small amounts of urine?
Reduced force of stream?
Accidental leakage of urine? If so, when does this occur
(e.g. when coughing, laughing or sneezing; at night;
during the day)?
Past urinary tract illness such as infection of the kidney,
bladder or urethra; urinary calculi; surgery of kidney,
ureters or bladder?


Factors influencing urinary elimination
Medications. Do you take any medications that could
increase urinary output or cause retention of urine? Note
specific medication and dosage.
Fluid intake. What amount and kind of fluid do you take
each day (e.g. six glasses of water, two cups of coffee,
three fizzy drinks with or without caffeine)?
Environmental factors. Do you have any problems with
toileting (mobility, removing clothing, toilet seat too low,
facility without grab bar)?
Stress. Are you experiencing any major stress? If so,
what are the stressors? Do you think these affect your
urinary pattern?
Disease or disability. Have you had or do you have any
illnesses or disability that may affect urinary function, such
as hypertension, heart disease, neurological disease,
cancer, prostatic enlargement, neurological disease or
injury, or diabetes?
Diagnostic procedures and surgery. Have you recently
had a cystoscopy or anaesthetic?
Because problems with urination can affect the elimination of wastes
from the body, it is important that the nurse assess the skin for
colour, texture and tissue turgor as well as the presence of oedema.
If incontinence, dribbling or dysuria is noted in the history, the skin of


the perineum should be inspected for irritation, because contact with
urine can lead to erosion or ulceration of the skin.
Assessing urine
Normal urine consists of 96% water and 4% solutes. Organic solutes
include urea, ammonia, creatinine and uric acid. Urea is the chief
organic solute. Inorganic solutes include sodium, chloride,
potassium, sulphate, magnesium and phosphorus. Sodium chloride
is the most abundant inorganic salt. Variations in colour can occur.
Characteristics of normal and abnormal urine are shown in Table
51.5
.
Table 51.5 Characteristics of normal and abnormal urine
20 Joanna Briggs Institute (2013). Urine Specimen Ward Testing. JBI Clinical Information
Service Evidence Summary. Retrieved from <http://joannabriggs.org>.
Measuring urinary output
Normally, the kidneys produce urine at a rate of approximately 60
mL per hour or about 1500 mL per day. Urine output is affected by
many factors, including fluid intake, body fluid losses through other
routes such as perspiration and breathing or diarrhoea, and the
cardiovascular and renal status of the individual.
Urine outputs below 30 mL per hour in people aged over 14 years or
less than 1–2 mL/kg/hr in children may indicate low blood volume or


kidney malfunction and must be reported. To measure fluid output
the nurse follows these steps:
1. Perform hand hygiene and don personal protective equipment
(PPE) (non-sterile gloves, eye protection and plastic apron)
as per organisation policy to prevent contact with micro-
organisms or blood in urine.
2. Ask the person to void in a clean urinal, bedpan, commode or
a collection device.
3. Tell the person to keep urine separate from faeces and to
avoid putting toilet paper in the urine collection container.
4. Pour the voided urine into a calibrated container.
5. Place the container on a flat surface. Measure at eye level
and read the amount in the container. Containers usually
have a measuring scale on the inside.
6. Record the amount on the fluid balance chart, usually located
at the person’s bedside.
7. Clean and/or dispose of the urine collection and measuring
containers as per organisation policy.
8. Remove gloves and perform hand hygiene.
9. Calculate and document the total output at the end of each
shift and at the end of 24 hours on the person’s fluid balance
chart.
Many people can measure and record their own urine output when
the procedure is explained to them.


When measuring urine from a person who has a urinary catheter,
the nurse follows these steps:
1. Perform hand hygiene and don PPE (non-sterile gloves, eye
wear, plastic apron) as per organisation policy.
2. Take the calibrated container to the bedside.
3. Place a disposable absorbent underpad (such as a bluey or
Chux) on the ground beneath the catheter bag to protect the
environment from urine spills.
4. Place the container under the urine collection bag so that the
