spout of the bag is above the container but not touching it.
The calibrated container is not sterile but the inside of the
collection bag is sterile (see Figure 51.6
).
5. Open the spout and permit the urine to flow into the
container.
6. Close the spout then proceed as described in the previous
list.
Figure 51.6


Urine being measured from a urine collection bag.
Source: Sian Bradfield, Pearson Australia.


Measuring residual urine
Residual urine
 (urine remaining in the bladder following the
voiding) is normally 50 to 100 mL. However, a bladder outlet
obstruction (e.g. enlargement of the prostate gland) or loss of
bladder muscle tone may interfere with complete emptying of the
bladder during urination. Manifestations of urine retention may
include abdominal distension, discomfort or frequent voiding of small
amounts (e.g. less than 100 mL in an adult). Urinary stasis and
urinary tract infection are possible consequences of incomplete
bladder emptying. Residual urine is measured to assess the amount
of retained urine after voiding and determine the need for
interventions (e.g. medications to promote detrusor muscle
contraction or catheterisation).
To measure residual urine, the nurse bladder scans or catheterises
using an in/out technique after the person has voided. Bladder
scanning is the preferred assessment because it is non-invasive.
The amount of urine voided and the amount obtained by
catheterisation or bladder scan are measured and recorded. An
intermittent catheter regimen may be implemented or an indwelling
catheter may be inserted if the residual urine exceeds a specified
amount.
Diagnostic tests
Blood levels of two metabolically produced substances, urea and
creatinine, are routinely used to evaluate renal function; both are


normally eliminated by the kidneys through filtration and tubular
secretion. Urea, the end product of protein metabolism, is measured
as blood urea nitrogen (BUN)
. Creatinine is produced in
relatively constant quantities by the muscles. The creatinine
clearance
 test uses 24-hour urine and serum creatinine levels to
determine the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), a sensitive indicator
of renal function. Other tests related to urinary functions are
described in Chapter 35
. These include collecting urine
specimens for a routine urinalysis, collecting a clean catch or
midstream urine specimen for urine culture and timed urine
specimens for a variety of tests. Skill 51.1
 describes urinalysis.
Urine samples in infants and children
Often urine specimens are required in infants and small children.
However, due to their developmental stage, infants and children are
unable to provide a sample of urine voluntarily. Options can include
urine from a potty, or some samples can be taken directly from the
disposable nappy for protein, blood, glucose, ketones and urea.
Organisation policy will provide guidance on the parameters for this
within your workplace. Please note that if a sterile sample of urine is
required and the child looks unwell, the child may need suprapubic
collection or an in/out catheter procedure.
Diagnosing


The nursing diagnosis is the judgment made after conducting a
systematic assessment, collecting both subjective and objective
cues. The nursing diagnosis can be an actual diagnosis or a risk
diagnosis (see Chapter 13)
.
Examples of nursing risk diagnoses include:
Risk of infection related to catheterisation
Risk of decreased skin integrity related to skin maceration
Risk of social isolation related to incontinence
Risk of caregiver strain related to ongoing care
Risk of fluid deficiency/overload related to impaired renal
functioning
Risk of falls related to urgency.
Examples of actual diagnoses include:
Disturbed body image related to diversion stoma, as evidenced
by embarrassment, vocalising anger/contempt for the stoma and
urostomy bag
Deficient knowledge related to new self-care procedure, as
evidenced by acknowledgment of lack of education or practice
regarding new device/procedure.
Clinical examples of assessment data clusters and related nursing
diagnoses, outcomes and interventions are shown in the following
‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and interventions’ and in
the ‘Nursing care plan’ and ‘Concept map’ at the end of this chapter.


Planning
The goals established will vary according to the diagnosis and
defining characteristics. The goals should be SMART—specific,
measurable, achievable, relevant and timed (Queensland
Government
). Examples of overall goals that can be adapted to
SMART for a person with urinary elimination problems may include
the following:
21 Queensland Government (2019). Set SMART Performance Goals. Retrieved from
<www.forgov.qld.gov.au>.
Maintain or restore an acceptable voiding pattern.
Regain baseline or regular urine output.
Prevent associated risks such as infection, skin breakdown, fluid
and electrolyte imbalance and lowered self-esteem.
Perform toilet activities independently with or without assistive
devices.
Contain urine with the appropriate device, catheter, urostomy
appliance or absorbent product.
Put in place falls prevention strategies for the person who
experiences urinary elimination problems.
Appropriate preventive and corrective nursing interventions that
relate to these must be identified. Specific nursing activities
associated with each of these interventions can be selected to meet
the person’s individual needs.
21


Planning for home care
To provide for continuity of care, the nurse needs to consider the
person’s needs for teaching and assistance with care in the home.
Discharge planning includes assessment of the person’s and family’s
resources and abilities for self-care, available financial resources,
the need for education, including falls prevention (if the person is at
risk of falls due to their incontinence) and the need for referrals and
home health services. The ‘Home care assessment’ outlines an
assessment of home care capabilities related to urinary elimination
problems and needs. The ‘Patient education
’ box addresses the
learning needs of the person and the person’s family.
Implementing
Maintaining normal urinary elimination
Most interventions to maintain normal urinary elimination are
independent nursing functions. These include promoting adequate
fluid intake, maintaining normal voiding habits and assisting with
toileting.


Research note Reframing continence
care in care dependence
J. Ostaszkiewicz, J. (2017). Reframing continence care in care-dependence. Geriatric Nursing, 38(6),
520–526.
In this article, Ostaszkiewicz provides a Dignity in Continence
Care Framework that supports nurses who care for people
with continence care needs. The author situates the
framework around two main concepts: dignity and care.
Therapeutic communication is a key component of the
framework and is something that nursing students must learn
and master. The author writes that when communicating with
people with continence issues, the nurse must aim to ‘build
the care-dependent person’s resilience, and enhance their
physiological and psychological wellbeing’ (Ostaszkiewicz ,
p. 523). This requires having a good understanding of the
physiological causes of incontinence, as well as using
therapeutic communication to help protect the person’s
dignity in every encounter. People with incontinence are well
aware of the stigma associated with their condition and often
try to conceal and manage the condition along with their
feelings of shame and discomfort. To address this, nurses
must understand the psychosocial issues that they face and
demonstrate ‘warmth, compassion and humanity’ in their
communications. This may involve using humour, when
appropriate.
22


22 Ostaszkiewicz, J. (2017). Reframing continence care in care dependence.
Geriatric Nursing, 38(6), 520–526.
Implications Nursing students should look for opportunities
to learn and practise therapeutic communication. Role-playing
with peers is a good way to learn how to communicate
effectively in a safe, non-threatening environment. It also
provides an opportunity to play the role of the patient and to
understand the challenges faced by a person with continence
issues.
Promoting fluid intake
Increasing fluid intake increases urine production, which in turn
stimulates the micturition reflex. A normal daily intake averaging
1500–2000 mL (eight glasses) of measurable fluids is adequate for
most adults.
Many unwell people have increased fluid requirements, necessitating
a higher daily fluid intake. For example, people who are perspiring
excessively (have diaphoresis) or who are experiencing abnormal
fluid losses through vomiting, gastric suction, diarrhoea or wound
drainage require fluid to replace these losses in addition to their
normal daily intake requirements.
Patient safety competency framework


2 Therapeutic communication
Therapeutic communication is central to
providing safe and responsive nursing practice.
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must
demonstrate therapeutic communication by
using verbal and non-verbal communication
skills to convey respect and empathy and to
encourage the person to express their feelings
and needs (Levett-Jones et al.
).
23 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
People who are at risk of urinary tract infection or urinary calculi
(stones) should consume a greater volume of fluid daily. Diluted
urine and frequent urination reduce the risk of urinary tract infection
as well as stone formation.
Drug capsule
Anticholinergic agents
23


The person with medications for urge
urinary incontinence
Anticholinergic agents reduce urgency and frequency by
blocking muscarinic receptors in the detrusor muscle of the
bladder, thereby inhibiting contractions and increasing storage
capacity. (Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors mediate
functions within the central and peripheral nervous system
such as the regulation of cardiovascular, respiratory and
bladder function (Saternos et al.
).) Anticholinergic agents
are useful in relieving symptoms associated with voiding in
people with neurogenic bladder and reflex neurogenic bladder
and urge urinary incontinence. Oxybutynin (Ditropan XL) is an
example of an anticholinergic drug that treats urge
incontinence by reducing muscle spasms in the bladder and
urinary tract.
24 Saternos, H. C., Almarghalani, D. A., Gibson, H. M., Meqdad, M. A., Antypas, R.
B., Lingireddy, A. & AbouAlaiwi, W. A. (2018). Distribution and function of the
muscarinic receptor subtypes in the cardiovascular system. Physiological
Genomics, 50(1), 1–9. Doi:10.1152/physiolgenomics.00062.2017.
Nursing responsibilities
Monitor for constipation, dry mouth, urinary retention,
blurred vision and mental confusion in the older adult;
symptoms may be dose related.
24


Monitor and keep doctor informed of expected responses
to therapy (e.g. effect on urinary frequency, urge
incontinence, nocturia and bladder emptying).
Start with small doses for a person over the age of 75.
Try using intermittently.
Person and family teaching
Check for allergies.
Explain the reason for taking the medication and assess
for adherence issues.
Explain when and how the medication should be taken
(discuss any diet, medication or activity restrictions).
Explain the side effects and the importance of reporting
them to the health care provider.
Provide strategies for managing expected side effects.
Note: prior to administering any medication, review all
aspects with a current drug handbook or other reliable
source.
Home care assessment
Urinary Elimination
The person and the environment


Self-care abilities: ability to consume adequate
fluids, adhere to drug regimens, perceive bladder
fullness, ambulate and get to the toilet, manipulate
clothing for toileting and to perform hygiene
measures after toileting.
Current level of knowledge: medications, fluid
and dietary intake modifications to promote normal
patterns of urinary elimination, bladder training
methods and specific techniques to promote
voiding care for indwelling catheter or stoma (if
appropriate).
Assistive devices required: ambulatory aids such
as walker, walking stick or wheelchair; safety
devices such as grab bars; toileting aids such as
raised toilet seat, urinal, commode or bedpan;
presence of a urinary catheter.
Physical layout of the toileting facilities:
presence of mobility aids; toilet at correct height to
enable older adults to get up after voiding.
Home environment factors that interfere with
toileting: distance to the bathroom from living
areas or bedrooms; barriers such as stairways,
scatter rugs, clutter or narrow doorways that
interfere with bathroom access; lighting (including
night lighting). Falls prevention strategies are
important.
Urinary elimination problems: type of
incontinence and precipitating factors;


manifestations of urinary tract infection such as
dysuria, frequency, urgency; evidence of prostatic
hypertrophy and effect on urination; ability to
perform self-catheterisation and care for other
urinary elimination devices such as indwelling
catheter, urinary diversion stoma or external urinary
sheath connected to a urinary drainage system.
Family
Caregiver availability, skills and responses:
ability and willingness to assume responsibilities for
care, including assisting with toileting, intermittent
catheterisation, indwelling catheter care, urinary
drainage devices or stoma care; ready access to
laundry facilities; access to and willingness to use
respite or relief caregivers.
Family role changes and coping: effect on
spousal and family roles, sleep/rest patterns,
sexuality and social interactions.
Financial resources: ability to purchase protective
pads and garments, supplies for catheterisation or
stoma care.
Community
Environment: access to public toilets.
Current knowledge of and experience with
community resources: medical and assistive
equipment and supply companies, home health


agencies, local pharmacies, available financial
assistance, support and educational organisations.
Increased fluid intake may be contraindicated for some individuals
such as people with kidney failure or heart failure. For these people,
a fluid restriction may be necessary to prevent fluid overload and
oedema.
Patient education
Urinary elimination in the home setting
Facilitating urinary elimination self-
care
Teach the person and family to maintain easy access to
toilet facilities, including removing scatter rugs, ensuring
that halls and doorways are free from clutter, keeping pets
secure.
Suggest graduated lighting for night-time voiding: a dim
night-light in the bedroom and hallway and utilise well
fitting, non-slip footwear.
Advise the person and family to install grab bars and
elevated toilet seats as needed. People using elevated
toilet seats or commodes need to be able to place their


feet on a commode foot plate or a small stool in order to
ensure best positioning for bladder and bowel emptying.
Provide for instruction in safe transfer techniques.
Suggest clothing that is easily removed for toileting, such
as elastic waist pants or Velcro closures.
Promoting urinary elimination
Unless the person has a diagnosis of urge incontinence
and is undergoing bladder retraining, educate the person
on the importance of responding to the urge to void as
soon as possible; avoid voluntary urinary retention.
Educate the person to empty the bladder completely at
each voiding.
Emphasise the importance of drinking eight to 10 glasses
of water daily.
Educate the female person about pelvic muscle exercises
to strengthen perineal muscles (see ‘Pelvic floor
exercises’, p. 1376).
Inform the person that smoking can increase the risk of
developing bladder cancer and provide information on
smoking cessation programs (Cancer Council ) if
indicated.
25 Cancer Council (2019). Bladder Cancer. Retrieved from
<www.cancer.org.au>.
Educate the person to promptly report any of the following
to the doctor: pain or burning on urination, changes in
25


urine colour or clarity, malodorous urine or changes in
voiding patterns (e.g. nocturia, frequency, dribbling).
Hygiene
Educate the person to maintain perineal–genital
cleanliness, washing with soap and water daily and
cleansing the anal and perineal area after defecating.
Educate girls and women to wipe from front to back (from
the urinary meatus towards the anus) after voiding and to
discard toilet paper after each wipe.
Provide information about products to protect the skin,
clothing and furniture for a person who is incontinent.
Emphasise the importance of cleaning and drying the
perineal area after incontinence episodes. Educate in the
use of protective skin barrier products as needed.
Moisture, combined with unrelieved pressure on a bony
prominence, could result in a pressure injury.
Educate people with an indwelling catheter and their
family about care measures such as frequency of catheter
change, cleaning the urinary meatus, managing and
emptying the collection device, maintaining a closed
system and bladder irrigation or flushing if ordered.
For a person with a surgically created urinary diversion
(ileal conduit or vesicostomy), teach about care of the
stoma, drainage devices and surrounding skin. For
continent diversions (a surgically created internal
pseudobladder), a stomal therapy nurse (STN) (a nurse


with education and expertise in this area) should teach the
person how to perform intermittent catheterisation of the
pouch via the stoma to drain urine.
For a person with an indwelling urinary catheter or urinary
diversion, emphasise the importance of maintaining a
generous fluid intake and of promptly reporting changes in
urinary output, signs of urinary retention such as
abdominal pain and manifestations of urinary tract
infection such as malodorous urine, abdominal discomfort,
fever or confusion.
Medications
Emphasise the importance of taking medications as
prescribed. Educate the person to take the full course of
antibiotics ordered to treat a urinary tract infection, even
though symptoms are relieved.
Educate the person and family about any expected
changes in urine colour or odour associated with
prescribed medications.
For people with urinary retention, emphasise the need to
contact the doctor before taking any medication (even
over-the-counter medications such as antihistamines) that
may exacerbate symptoms.
For people taking medications that may damage the
kidneys (e.g. aminoglycoside antibiotics), stress the
importance of maintaining a generous fluid intake while
taking the medication.


Suggest measures to reduce anticipated side effects of
prescribed medications, such as increasing intake of
potassium-rich foods by eating dark leafy greens or
bananas, when taking a potassium-depleting diuretic
medication.
Dietary alterations
Teach the person about dietary changes to promote
urinary function, such as consuming cranberry juice and
foods that acidify the urine to reduce the risk of repeated
urinary tract infections or formation of calcium-based
urinary calculi (stones). See ‘Dietary measures’ on page
1383.
Encourage people with stress or urge incontinence to limit
their intake of caffeine, alcohol, citrus juices and artificial
sweeteners because these are bladder irritants that may
increase incontinence. Also, teach individuals to limit their
evening fluid intake to reduce the risk of night-time
incontinence episodes.
Measures specific to urinary
problems
Provide instructions for a person with specific urinary
problems or treatments such as:


− timed urine specimens (see Chapter 35
)
− urinary incontinence
− urinary retention
− indwelling catheters.
Referrals
Make appropriate referrals to home health agencies,
community health organisations or social services for
assistance with resources such as grab bars and raised
toilet seats, providing wheelchair access to bathrooms,
obtaining toileting aids such as commodes, urinals or
bedpans, and services such as home health aides for
assistance with activities of daily living.
Community organisations and other
resources
Provide information about resources available, through
government schemes, for durable medical equipment
such as commodes or raised toilet seats, possible
financial assistance and medical supplies such as
drainage bags, incontinence briefs or protective pads.
Additional resources such as websites are included at the
end of the chapter.


Maintaining normal voiding habits
Prescribed medical therapies often interfere with a person’s normal
voiding habits. When a person’s urinary elimination pattern is
adequate, the nurse should help the person to adhere to normal
voiding habits as much as possible (see ‘Practice guidelines
’).
Assisting with toileting
People who are weakened by a disease process or impaired
physically may require assistance with toileting. The nurse should
assist these people to the bathroom and remain with them if they
are at risk of falling. The bathroom should contain an easily
accessible buzzer to summon help if needed. A person may also
need to be encouraged to use handrails placed near the toilet.
For people unable to use bathroom facilities, the nurse should
provide urinary equipment close to the bedside (e.g. urinal, bedpan,
commode) and provides the necessary assistance to use them.
Positioning is also very important. Refer to ‘Practice guidelines’.
Preventing urinary tract infections
The rate of urinary tract infection (UTI) is greater in women than
men because of the short urethra and its proximity to the anal and
vaginal areas. It is estimated that 60% of women will experience a
UTI in their lifetime, with the risk increasing with age (Kline &
Bowdish ). UTIs are commonly acquired in the health care setting.
26


They are referred to as nosocomial or hospital-acquired urinary tract
infections and are usually related to use of indwelling catheterisation.
Most UTIs are caused by bacteria common to the intestinal
environment (e.g. Escherichia coli). These gastrointestinal bacteria
can colonise the perineal area and move into the urethra, especially
when there is urethral trauma, irritation or manipulation. Women are
particularly at risk because they have a short urethra and bacteria
can easily make its way to the bladder.
26 Kline, K. & Bowdish, D. (2016). Infection in an aging population. Current Opinion in
Microbiology, 29, 63–67.
Practice guidelines
Maintaining normal voiding habits
Positioning
Assist the person to a normal position for voiding:
standing for the male and, for the female, squatting or
sitting safely on the toilet, leaning slightly forward with
lower back straight and feet flat on the floor or small stool
(see Figure 51.7
). These positions enhance movement
of urine through the tract by gravity. Women should sit on
the toilet and not ‘hover’ over, with feet on the floor and
knees spread apart wide (Women’s Health Queensland
Wide ).
27 Women’s Health Queensland Wide (2014). Urinary Incontinence. Retrieved
from <www.womhealth.org.au>.
27


If the person is unable to ambulate to the toilet, use a
bedside commode for females and a urinal for males
standing at the bedside wherever possible.
If necessary, encourage the person to push over the pubic
area with the hands or to lean forward to increase intra-
abdominal pressure and external pressure on the bladder.
Figure 51.7
Good sitting position for bladder emptying.
Source: Medical Aids Subsidy Scheme (MASS) Continence Project.
 Good Sitting Position for
Bladder Emptying, Figure 6, p. 141. Brisbane: Queensland Health. © State of Queensland
(Queensland Health). Reproduced with permission.
28


28 Medical Aids Subsidy Scheme (MASS) Continence Project (2010). Good Sitting
Position for Bladder Emptying. Brisbane: Queensland Health. Retrieved from
<www.continencexchange.org.au>.
Relaxation
Provide privacy for the person. Many people cannot void
in the presence of another person.
Allow the person sufficient time to void.
Suggest the person read or listen to music.
Provide sensory stimuli that may help the person relax.
Pour warm water over the perineum of a female or have
the person sit in a warm bath to promote muscle
relaxation.
Turn on running water within hearing distance of the
person to stimulate the voiding reflex and to mask the
sound of voiding for people who find this embarrassing.
Provide ordered analgesics and emotional support to
relieve physical and emotional discomfort to decrease
muscle tension.
Timing
Assist a person who has the urge to void immediately.
Delays only increase the difficulty in starting to void and
the desire to void may pass.
Offer toileting assistance to a person at usual times of
voiding; for example, on waking, before or after meals and
at bedtime.


For a person who is confined to bed
Ensure privacy.
Once the urinary collection device is obtained, the nurse
needs to educate the person about the urinary device
(bedpan or urinal) and establish their confidence in how it
collects the urine. Pans and urinals are not always made
from plastic. Many organisations now have disposable
receptacles made from paper pulp. The paper pulp
bedpans sit inside plastic holders. Once the person is
aware of the device, confidence needs to be established
in their positioning. For a full explanation of positioning a
person on a bedpan, refer to p. 1419.
In terms of promoting urination, it is important to elevate
the head of the person’s bed to Fowler’s position, place a
small pillow or rolled towel at the small of the back to
increase physical support and comfort, and have the
person flex their hips and knees. This position simulates
the normal voiding position as closely as possible.
The following guidelines are useful for preventing urinary infections:
Drink sufficient water every day to flush bacteria out of the
urinary system.
Practise frequent voiding (every 2 to 4 hours) to flush bacteria
out of the urethra and prevent organisms from ascending into the
bladder. Void immediately after intercourse.


Avoid use of harsh soaps, bubble bath, powder or sprays in the
perineal area. These substances can be irritating to the urethra
and encourage inflammation and bacterial infection.
Avoid tight-fitting pants or other clothing that creates irritation to
the urethra and prevents ventilation of the perineal area.
Wear cotton underclothes. Accumulation of perineal moisture
facilitates bacterial growth and cotton enhances ventilation of the
perineal area.
Girls and women should always wipe the perineal area from front
to back in order to prevent introduction of gastrointestinal
bacteria into the urethra.
If recurrent urinary infections are a problem, take showers rather
than baths. Bacteria present in bathwater can readily enter the
urethra.
For sexually active women who experience recurrent urinary
infections, nurses need to instruct how to prevent a recurrence,
such as washing the genital area of self and partner before sex
and urinating after sex (Allen ).
29 Allen, C. (2016). Recurrent urinary tract infections. Australian Pharmacist, 35(2), 36–
39.
Managing urinary incontinence
It is important to remember that urinary incontinence is not a normal
part of ageing and often is treatable. Incontinence in itself is
considered a disability. It is also noted as a leading cause of carer
strain. Independent nursing interventions for a person with urinary
incontinence include: (a) a behaviour-oriented continence training
29


program that may consist of bladder training, habit training,
prompted voiding, pelvic muscle exercises and positive
reinforcement; (b) meticulous skin care; and (c) for males,
application of an external drainage device (condom-type catheter
device).
Clinical consideration
For males, there is no difference in urine flow
and post-void residual urine volume in the
standing and sitting positions.
Continence (bladder) training
A continence training program requires the involvement of the
doctor, nurse, the person and support people. A person must be
alert and physically able or have caregivers who can assist with
implementation of the plan of care in order to follow a program. A
bladder-training program may include the following:
Education of the person and support people.
Bladder training
 requires the person to postpone voiding,
resist or inhibit the sensation of urgency and void according to a
timetable rather than according to the urge to void. The goals are
to gradually lengthen the intervals between urination to correct


the person’s frequent urination, to stabilise the bladder and to
diminish urgency. This form of training may be used for a person
who has bladder instability and urge incontinence. Delayed
voiding provides larger voided volumes and longer intervals
between voiding. Initially, voiding may be encouraged every 2 to
3 hours except during sleep and then every 4 to 6 hours. A vital
component of bladder training is inhibiting the urge-to-void
sensation. To do this, the nurse educates the person to practise
deep, slow breathing until the urge diminishes or disappears.
This is performed every time the person has a premature urge to
void.
Habit training
, also referred to as timed voiding or scheduled
toileting, attempts to keep a person dry by having them void at
regular intervals. With habit training, there is no attempt to
motivate the person to delay voiding if the urge occurs. This
approach can be effective in children who are experiencing
urinary dysfunction. Biofeedback therapy in which the child is
taught to relax the pelvic floor can also decrease incidents of
wetting (Zeng et al.
).
30 Zeng, F., Chen, H. Q., Qi, L., Zhang, X. Y. & Li, Y. (2012). Comparative study of pelvic
floor biofeedback training and tolterodine for treatment of detrusor after-contraction in
posturination dribbling in children. The Journal of International Medical Research, 40(6),
2305–2310.
Prompted voiding
 supplements habit training by encouraging
the person to try to use the toilet (prompting) and reminding the
person when to void.
Pelvic floor exercises
30


Pelvic floor exercises, or Kegel exercises, help to strengthen pelvic
floor muscles and can reduce or eliminate episodes of incontinence.
The person can identify the perineal muscles by stopping urination
midstream or by tightening the anal sphincter as if to hold a bowel
movement.
The following technique is sometimes used to teach pelvic floor
exercises. Ask the person to think of the perineal muscles as an
elevator. When the person relaxes, the elevator is on the first floor.
To perform the exercise, contract the perineal muscles, bringing the
elevator to the second, third and fourth floors. Keep the elevator on
the fourth floor for a few seconds and then gradually relax the area.
When the exercise is properly performed, contraction of the muscles
of the buttocks and thighs is avoided. Pelvic floor exercises can be
performed anytime, anywhere, sitting or standing—even when
voiding. Specific instructions for the person performing these are
summarised in ‘Patient education
’ below.
Maintaining skin integrity
Skin that is continually moist becomes macerated (softened). Urine
that accumulates on the skin is converted to ammonia, which is very
irritating to the skin. Because both skin irritation and maceration
predispose the person to skin breakdown and ulceration, the
incontinent person requires meticulous skin care. To maintain skin
integrity, the nurse washes the person’s perineal area with mild soap
and water or a commercially prepared no-rinse pH neutral cleanser
after episodes of incontinence, rinses it thoroughly if soap and water


used, dries it gently and thoroughly and provides clean, dry clothing
or bed linen. The nurse applies barrier ointments or creams to
protect the skin from contact with urine. If it is necessary to use
incontinence pads for ongoing protection, the nurse should use
products that absorb wetness and leave a dry surface in contact
with the skin.
Specially designed incontinence bed linen may be used for
incontinent people. These sheets are double layered with a quilted
upper nylon or polyester surface and an absorbent viscose rayon
layer below. The rayon soaker layer generally has a waterproof
backing on its underside. Fluid (e.g. urine) passes through the upper
quilted layer and is absorbed and dispersed by the viscose rayon,
leaving the quilted surface dry to the touch. This absorbent bed linen
helps maintain skin integrity; it does not stick to the skin when wet,
decreases the risk of pressure injuries and reduces odour. It is
important to avoid using rubber-backed sheets or a plastic layer as
these are non-absorbent and can increase the risk of the incontinent
person sustaining broken skin integrity. Some incontinence bed linen
that is placed over a mattress and designed to reduce the incidence
of pressure injuries may in fact counteract the effect of the mattress,
so it must be used with caution or not at all.
Practice guidelines
Bladder training
Determine the person’s voiding pattern and encourage
voiding at those times, or establish a regular voiding


schedule and help the person to maintain it, whether the
person feels the urge or not (e.g. on waking, every 1 or 2
hours during the day and evening, before retiring at night,
every 4 hours at night). The stretching–relaxing sequence
of such a schedule tends to increase bladder muscle tone
and promote more voluntary control. Encourage the
person to inhibit the urge-to-void sensation when a
premature urge to void is experienced. Educate the
person to practise slow, deep breathing until the urge
diminishes or disappears.
When the person finds that voiding can be controlled, the
intervals between voiding can be lengthened slightly
without loss of continence.
Regulate fluid intake, particularly during evening hours, to
help reduce the need to void during the night.
Encourage fluids between the hours of 0600 and 1800.
Avoid excessive consumption of citrus juices, fizzy drinks
(especially those containing artificial sweeteners), alcohol
and drinks containing caffeine because these irritate the
bladder, increasing the risk of incontinence.
Schedule diuretic medication early in the morning.
Explain to people that adequate fluid intake is required to
ensure adequate urine production that stimulates the
micturition reflex.
Apply protector pads to keep the bed linen dry and
provide specially made absorbent protective underwear to
contain the urine and decrease the person’s
embarrassment. When possible, avoid using incontinence


pads, which may be demeaning and also suggest that
incontinence is permissible.
Assist the person with an exercise program to increase
the general muscle tone and a pelvic floor muscle
exercise program aimed at strengthening the pelvic floor
muscles.
Provide positive reinforcements to encourage continence.
Praise people for attempting to toilet and for maintaining
continence.
Research note Patients with
concurrent dementia and urinary
incontinence
M. Barrie
. Dealing with patients with concurrent dementia and urinary incontinence. Journal of
Community Nursing, 30(3), 37–46.
31 Barrie, M. (2016). Dealing with patients with concurrent dementia and urinary incontinence.
Journal of Community Nursing, 30(3), 37–46.
Dementia affects a person’s ability to undertake activities of
daily living, especially in regard to toileting. People with
dementia may not know or forget to go to the toilet, or they
may not know where the toilet is located. Because of this,
nurses must be ‘proactive in their continence promotion’
(Barrie 2016, p. 37) and must devise a continence plan that
addresses both physical and cognitive needs. It is also
31


imperative to include family or carers in the plan. Barrie
(2016) provided a case study to illustrate different strategies
that can be applied for people with dementia living in the
community.
The case involved Max, a 78-year-old male who was
experiencing urinary stress incontinence, an overactive
bladder, urgency and nocturia. His medical history included
prostatectomy, type 2 diabetes, arthritis and poor eyesight.
His wife, Ruby, described his memory as ‘muddled’ and
worsening. She reported he would forget to drink or ask for
sweet beverages that should not be part of his diet due to his
diabetes. She admitted she was struggling to care for him
because he would often disregard her suggestions. His
incontinence issue was stressful for her and she had asked
for some respite assistance.
The plan devised for Max included a toileting regimen. Ruby
was educated on bladder retraining and was instructed to
have Max go to the toilet every 3–4 hours. Pelvic floor
exercises were ruled out due to his cognitive challenges, as
were any type of catheterisation because there was a risk he
would remove the catheter. Loose clothing and incontinence
pads were ordered. Irritability can worsen incontinence
symptoms so Ruby was instructed to play his music to help
keep him calm, as needed. His medications were reviewed
and diet and fluid changes were recommended to prevent
constipation, because some of his medications caused
constipation. Follow-up visits indicated the plan was working


well and Ruby was coping better with her husband’s
incontinence.
Implications Managing an incontinent patient with dementia
is complex and a plan must be developed to suit both
physical and cognitive needs. Barrie (2016) suggested other
patient-focused strategies nurses should consider when
developing a continence plan for dementia patients. For
example, to address the issue of identifying where the toilet is
located, keeping the bathroom door open or placing a photo
of a toilet on the door is advised. Instructing caregivers to be
aware of signs that a person requires toileting, such as
restlessness, is important, as is the carer providing prompt
assistance as needed. Recommend clothing that is
comfortable and has elastic waistbands or Velcro strips for
easy removal. Simple steps such as these will help to
facilitate continence care in people with dementia.
Patient education
Correct positioning when doing pelvic floor muscle
education
Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels)
First, sit or lie in a comfortable, relaxed position.
If in a chair:
− Sit supported but away from the back of the chair.


− Have legs comfortably apart with feet firmly on the
ground.
− Ensure lower back is straight, not slumped.
− Ensure shoulders are relaxed.
− Feel the perineal area in contact with the seat.
− Maintain normal breathing.
Verbal cues helpful for correct pelvic
floor muscle contraction
For females
Gently and slowly lift/draw in/tense around the bladder
opening and vagina.
For males
Gently and slowly tighten muscles as if trying to stop the
flow of urine. Feel the testicles rise and the base of the
penis move closer to the abdomen.
For both
Hold the contraction up to the maximum time
recommended while continuing to breathe normally.
Suggest the following to the person:


− Contract (up to 10 seconds) and relax for 10 seconds
and repeat this contraction/relaxation combination 8–10
times. Perform the exercise 4–5 times daily.
− Develop a schedule that will help remind you to do these
exercises; for example, before getting out of bed in the
morning, when working at the kitchen sink or at scheduled
times (e.g. 0700, 1200, 1800 hours).
To control episodes of stress incontinence, perform a
pelvic floor muscle contraction when initiating any activity
that increases intra-abdominal pressure, such as
coughing, laughing, sneezing or lifting.
Signs of incorrect technique
Signs of incorrect technique include the person:
− taking a breath while starting the contraction
− holding their breath
− lifting their shoulders; moving their trunk, spine or pelvis
− tensing their buttocks
− pulling their knees or legs apart.
Applying external urinary sheaths


The application of an external urinary or penile sheath, also known
as a uridome, connected to a urinary drainage system can be used
for incontinence. Use of an external urinary sheath is preferable to
insertion of an indwelling urinary catheter because the risk of urinary
tract infection is minimal.
Types and methods of applying external urinary sheaths vary. Most
of these devices are self-adhesive as they incorporate inner
adhesive sections, which secure the sheath to the penis. The nurse
needs to follow the manufacturer’s instructions when applying the
urinary sheath. First the nurse determines when the person
experiences incontinence. Some people may require a urinary
sheath at night only, others continuously. Skill 51.2
 describes how
to apply and remove an external urinary sheath.
Clinical consideration
Never underestimate the importance of
checking the urinary sheath after application.
While some people may be able to verbalise
that the appliance is too tight, others may not.
For example, the quadriplegic person may not
have any sensation to determine if the
application is too tight. Additionally, other people
may not have the ability to verbalise or
recognise problems with the application, as is
the case with some neurological conditions.


Managing urinary retention
Interventions that assist the person to maintain a normal voiding
pattern, discussed earlier, also apply when dealing with urinary
retention. If these actions are unsuccessful, the doctor may order a
cholinergic drug to stimulate bladder contraction and facilitate
voiding. People who have a flaccid
 bladder (weak, soft and lax
bladder muscles) may use manual pressure on the bladder to
promote bladder emptying. This is known as Credé’s manoeuvre
or Credé’s method. It is not advised without a doctor’s order and is
used only for people who have lost and are not expected to regain
voluntary bladder control. When all measures fail to initiate voiding,
urinary catheterisation may be necessary to empty the bladder
completely. An indwelling catheter, also referred to in this chapter as
an indwelling urinary catheter, may be inserted until the underlying
cause is treated. Alternatively, intermittent straight catheterisation
(every 3 to 4 hours) may be performed because the risk of urinary
tract infection may be less than with an indwelling catheter.
Urinary catheterisation
Urinary catheterisation is the introduction of a catheter into the
urinary bladder. This is usually performed only when absolutely
necessary because the danger exists of introducing micro-
organisms into the bladder. People who have lowered immune
resistance are at the greatest risk. Once an infection is introduced


into the bladder, it can ascend the ureters and eventually involve the
kidneys. The hazard of infection remains after the catheter is in
place because normal defence mechanisms such as intermittent
flushing of micro-organisms from the urethra through voiding are
bypassed. Thus, strict aseptic non-touch technique is used for
catheterisation.
Clinical consideration
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are one of the
most common hospital-acquired infections,
accounting for approximately 20% to 40% of all
hospital-acquired infections. It is estimated that
80% of these are associated with the use of
urinary catheters (Rahman ). The risk is high
because bacteria can travel up the catheter
tubing and enter the bladder, or the tubing can
be obstructed and urine can stagnate in the
bladder (Carter, Reitmeier & Goodloe ).
33 Rahman, M. A. (2016). Urinary Catheter (Short Term):
Antibiotic Policies. JBI Evidence Summaries. Retrieved from
<http://connect.jbiconnectplus.org>.
34 Carter, N., Reitmeier, L. & Goodloe, L. (2014). An evidence-
based approach to the prevention of catheter-associated urinary
tract infections. Urologic Nursing, 34(5), 238–245.
33
34


Because of the significance and risk of urinary
tract infections, appropriate hygiene
management for the person is essential, as well
as vigilant hand washing and use of PPE by the
nurse.
Another hazard is trauma with urethral catheterisation, particularly in
the male person, whose urethra is longer and more tortuous. It is
important to insert a catheter along the normal contour of the
urethra. Damage to the urethra can occur if the catheter is forced
through strictures or at an incorrect angle. In males, the urethra is
normally curved, but it can be straightened by elevating the penis to
a position perpendicular to the body.
The technology in the manufacturing of catheters is changing in line
with evidence. They are increasingly more commonly made of latex
or silicone rather than the traditional rubber, plastic or polyvinyl
chloride (PVC). Catheters are usually coated with silver alloy or
antibiotics to help reduce the incidence of catheter-associated
infections; however, this does not guarantee an infection will not
develop (Singha, Locklin & Handa ). Catheters are sized by the
diameter of the lumen using the French (Fr) scale: the larger the
number, the larger the lumen. Either intermittent catheters, inserted
to drain the bladder and then immediately removed, or indwelling
urinary catheters, which remain in the bladder to drain urine, may be
used. See Table 51.6
 for categorisation of urinary catheters.
35


Suprapubic catheters, which are inserted surgically through the
abdominal wall, are discussed later in the chapter.
35 Singha, P., Locklin, J. & Handa, H. (2017). A review of the recent advances in antimicrobial
coatings for urinary catheters. Acta Biomaterialia, 50, 20–40. Doi:
10.1016/j.actbio.2016.11.070.
Table 51.6 Categorisation of urinary catheters
36 NHS Choices (2015). Urinary Catheterisation—Treatment Options. Retrieved from
<www.nhs.uk>.
37 Continence Product Advisor (2016). Products. Retrieved from
<www.continenceproductadvisor.org>.
The intermittent (straight) catheter is a single-lumen tube with a
small eye or opening about 1¼ cm from the insertion tip (see Figure
51.8
). The Coudé catheter is a variation of the straight catheter. It
is more rigid than other straight catheters and has a tapered, curved
tip (see Figure 51.9
). This catheter is often used for men with
benign prostatic hypertrophy (BPH) (prostate gland enlargement)
because the tip is shaped in such a way that it can more easily
move past the enlarged prostate gland; thus, it is more easily
controlled and less traumatic on insertion.
Figure 51.8


Intermittent urinary catheters. Left: Red rubber (latex) Robinson
catheter; Right: straight PVC catheter.
Source: Courtesy Covidien.
Figure 51.9


A Coudé catheter.
There are four different techniques for intermittent catheterisation:
(1) sterile non-touch (used in operating theatres and for diagnostic
purposes); (2) aseptic; (3) no touch; and (4) clean (used in the
home setting by patients or carers). This type of catheterisation has
a lower rate of infection and is therefore preferred in some situations
to the use of an indwelling urinary catheter. Education and training
are required to ensure the catheter is inserted properly to avoid
trauma and risk of infection (Chu ). As a nurse, you will be required
38


to gain competency in this skill and to teach patients and carers
proper technique.
38 Chu, W. H. (2016). Urinary Catheter (Intermittent): Management. JBI Evidence
Summaries. Retrieved from <http://connect.jbiconnectplus.org>.
Clinical consideration
Some organisations may have policies in place
that do not permit Registered Nurses to
undertake male catheterisations because of the
risk of a person having an enlarged prostate, or
BPH. Hence, it is advised that prior to
undertaking this procedure the nurse should
examine the organisation policies.
The indwelling urinary catheter, often referred to as a Foley catheter,
is a double-lumen catheter. The larger lumen drains urine from the
bladder. A second, smaller lumen is used to inflate a balloon near
the tip of the catheter to hold the catheter in place within the bladder
(see Figure 51.10
). Indwelling urinary catheters for long-term use
have a protective hydrogel/silver coating that is less irritating, with an
extended, reliable wear time of approximately 6 weeks. The surgical
latex-type catheters are made for short-term use, as in 1 day to 1
week, and should be avoided for long-term use. People who require


continuous or intermittent bladder irrigation may have a three-way
catheter (see Figure 51.11
).
Figure 51.10
An indwelling urinary catheter with the balloon inflated.
Figure 51.11


A three-way catheter often used for continuous bladder irrigation.
Source: Courtesy Covidien.


The three-way catheter has a third lumen through which sterile
irrigating fluid can flow into the bladder. The fluid then exits the
bladder through the drainage lumen, along with the urine. This type
of catheter is needed when continuous bladder irrigation is required
to help prevent blood clot retention following urological surgery.
The balloons of indwelling urinary catheters are sized by the volume
of fluid used to inflate them. The two commonly used sizes are 10
mL and 30 mL balloons. The size of the balloon is indicated on the
catheter along with the diameter; for example, ‘#18 Fr—10 mL’. Box
51.4
provides guidelines for catheter selection.
BO X
51.4 Clinical decision making in
catheter selection
Select the type of material in accordance with the
estimated length of the catheterisation period and allergy
status. Antimicrobial-impregnated or hydrogel/silver-
coated catheters may also be used in catheters for
shorter term to reduce the risk of infection if this is
deemed to be likely.
‒ Use a rubber or silicone-covered catheter for periods of
2 or 3 weeks. Latex may be used for people with no
known latex allergy. However, because of these allergies,
latex is being phased out of health care products.


‒ Use silicone catheters for long-term use (e.g. 2 to 3
months) because they create less encrustation at the
urethral meatus.
‒ Use PVC catheters for 4- to 6-week periods. They
soften at body temperature and conform to the urethra.
Determine appropriate catheter length by the person’s
age and gender. For adult females, use a 25 cm catheter;
for adult male, use a 40–45 cm catheter.
Determine appropriate catheter size by the size of the
urethral canal. French units (Fr) are used to measure and
describe the catheter diameter. Fr = 0.33 mm. Use sizes
such as 8–10 Fr for children, 14–16 Fr for adults. Men
frequently require a larger size than women; for example,
18 Fr.
Consider the retention balloon size. The catheter is held in
place in the bladder by a small balloon containing a sterile
water or normal saline solution. For adults, the balloon
usually holds 10 mL. However, a 30 mL balloon may be
used to achieve haemostasis of the prostatic area
following a prostatectomy. Purpose-specific catheters
should be used with children. These may have variable
balloon sizes or no balloons.
Indwelling urinary catheters usually are connected to a closed
gravity drainage system. This system consists of the catheter,
drainage tubing and a collecting bag for the urine. A closed system


cannot be opened anywhere along the system, from catheter to
collecting bag. Closed systems reduce the risk of micro-organisms
entering the system and infecting the urinary tract. Urinary drainage
systems typically depend on the force of gravity to drain urine from
the bladder to the collecting bag.
Skill 51.3
 describes catheterisation of females and males using
intermittent and indwelling urinary catheters.
Evaluation
Conduct appropriate follow-up, such as notifying the doctor of the
catheterisation results. Perform a detailed follow-up based on
findings that deviated from expected or normal for the person.
Relate findings to previous assessment data if available. Teach the
person how to care for the indwelling catheter, to drink more fluids
and other appropriate instructions.
Nursing interventions for people with
indwelling urinary catheters
Nursing care of the person with an indwelling catheter and
continuous drainage is largely directed towards preventing infection
of the urinary tract and encouraging urinary flow through the
drainage system. It includes accurately recording the fluid intake and
output, changing the indwelling urinary catheter and tubing if


indicated, maintaining the patency of the drainage system by
checking for kinks in the tubing, preventing contamination of the
drainage system, vigilant hand washing and teaching these
measures to the person.
Fluids
The person with an indwelling urinary catheter should maintain an
optimal fluid intake. Some people may have conditions that may
require them to be on fluid restriction. Large amounts of fluid ensure
a large urine output, which keeps the bladder flushed out and
decreases the likelihood of urinary stasis and subsequent infection.
Large volumes of urine also minimise the risk of sediment or other
particles obstructing the drainage tubing.
Dietary measures
Acidifying the urine of people with an indwelling urinary catheter may
reduce the risk of urinary tract infection and calculus formation.
Foods such as eggs, cheese, meat and poultry, whole grains,
cranberries, plums, prunes and tomatoes tend to increase the
acidity of urine. Conversely, most fruits and vegetables, legumes
and milk and milk products result in alkaline urine.
Perineal care
Good personal hygiene around the meatal area on a regular basis is
recommended. Individual organisation practices regarding catheter


care vary. The nurse should check organisation policy in this regard.
Changing the catheter and tubing
Routine changing of the catheter and tubing is not recommended.
Collection of sediment in the catheter or tubing or impaired urine
drainage are indicators for changing the catheter and/or drainage
system. When this occurs, the catheter and/or drainage system are
removed and discarded and a new sterile catheter and/or a
closed/sealed drainage system is inserted. At times, the drainage
system may be changed but the catheter remains in situ. Sealed
drainage systems are considered better at preventing bacteruria
(Joanna Briggs Institute ).
41 Joanna Briggs Institute (2010b). Management of short term indwelling urethral catheters to
prevent urinary tract infections. Best Practice Evidence Based Practice Information Sheets for
Health Professionals, 14(12).
Guidelines to prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infections are
given in the ‘Practice guidelines’. Ongoing assessment of people
with indwelling urinary catheters is a high priority (see Box 51.5
).
BO X
51.5 Ongoing assessment of people
with indwelling urinary catheters
41


Assess the person’s catheter care understanding and
technique. Provide additional education and guidance if
necessary.
Empower the person or their family members to ask that
any person who touches the catheter wash their hands
and uses appropriate PPE.
Ensure that there are no obstructions in the drainage.
Check that there are no kinks in the tubing, the person is
not lying on the tubing and the tubing is not clogged.
Check that there is no tension on the catheter or tubing,
that the catheter is securely attached to the thigh or
abdomen and that the tubing is fastened appropriately to
the bedclothes.
Ensure that gravity drainage is maintained by keeping the
drainage bag below the level of the bladder. Make sure
there are no loops in the tubing below its entry to the
drainage receptacle and that the drainage bag is below
the level of the person’s bladder but never on the floor.
Ensure that the drainage system is well sealed or closed.
Check that there are no leaks at the connection sites in
open systems.
Ensure the drainage bag is emptied in the toilet following
standard precautions at least once a shift or when the
volume reaches 500–750 mL.
Observe the flow of the urine at least every 2 or 3 hours
and note colour, odour and any abnormal constituents.
Conduct a daily dipstick urinalysis as per institution
protocol. If urinalysis has protein, leukocytes or nitrites


present, a sterile specimen of urine should be collected
for micro-culture sensitivity. This is dependent on
organisation policy.
Removing indwelling catheters
Indwelling urinary catheters are removed after their purpose has
been achieved, usually on the order of the doctor. If the catheter has
been in place for a short time (e.g. a few days), the person usually
has little difficulty regaining normal urinary elimination patterns.
Swelling of the urethra, however, may initially interfere with voiding,
so the nurse should regularly assess the person for urinary retention
until voiding is re-established.
Clinical consideration
It is not uncommon for a person with an
indwelling catheter to report that they have a
sensation to void. If a person reports this, never
ignore it. Simple things such as a twisted or
kinked catheter, a blocked catheter or the
catheter being caught between a bed rail can be
causative factors.


Practice guidelines
Discharge activities and exercise
Preventing catheter-associated
urinary infections
Have an established infection-control program.
Catheterise people only when necessary using aseptic
technique, sterile equipment and trained personnel.
Maintain a sterile sealed-drainage system.
Ensure the drainage bag is not in contact with the floor
while the person is in bed or while mobilising.
Check the catheter tubing on a regular basis for kinking so
that free drainage of urine occurs.
Do not disconnect the catheter and drainage tubing unless
absolutely necessary.
Remove the catheter as soon as possible.
Follow and reinforce vigilant and effective hand washing
technique.
Provide routine perineal and meatal hygiene, including
cleansing with soap and water after defecation.
Prevent contamination of the catheter with faeces in the
incontinent person.
People who have had an indwelling urinary catheter for a prolonged
period may require bladder retraining to regain bladder muscle tone.
With an indwelling urinary catheter in place, the bladder muscle does


not stretch and contract regularly as it does when the bladder fills
and empties by voiding. A few days before removal, the catheter
may be clamped for specified periods of time (e.g. 2 to 4 hours),
then released to allow the bladder to empty. This allows the bladder
to distend and stimulates its musculature. A tap or flip flow valve can
be added to the indwelling urinary catheter at insertion. The drainage
system is attached to the end of the valve. The person is educated
by qualified clinical staff or a continence nurse advisor about turning
the outflow off at regular intervals several days prior to the removal
of the indwelling catheter. This will allow the bladder to fill and
distend so as to stimulate the nerve receptors once again. However,
prior to any indwelling catheter removal, the nurse should check the
organisation policy regarding bladder-training procedures.
To remove an indwelling urinary catheter, the nurse follows these
steps:
1. Ascertain that a doctor’s order is in place for the catheter to
be removed.
2. Obtain a receptacle for the catheter (e.g. a disposable basin);
a clean, disposable towel; clean gloves; and a sterile syringe
to deflate the balloon. The syringe should be large enough to
withdraw all the solution in the catheter balloon. The size of
the balloon is indicated on the label at the end of the catheter.
(The volume of solution inserted into the balloon should be
recorded in the person’s record.)
3. Explain the procedure to the person. Provide privacy and ask
the person to assume a supine position as for a


catheterisation.
4. Optional: obtain a sterile specimen before removing the
catheter. Check organisation policy.
5. Perform hand hygiene. Remove the tape or catheter-securing
device attaching the catheter to the person, put on gloves
and then place the towel between the legs of the female
person or over the thighs of the male.
6. Insert the syringe into the injection port of the catheter and
withdraw the fluid from the balloon. If not all the fluid can be
removed, report this to a senior nurse or medical officer
before proceeding.
7. Do not pull the catheter while the balloon is inflated; doing so
may injure the urethra.
8. After all the fluid is withdrawn from the balloon, gently
withdraw the catheter and place it in the waste receptacle.
9. Dry the perineal area with a towel.
10. Remove gloves and perform hand hygiene.
Lifespan considerations
Catheterisation
Infants and children
Adapt the size of the catheter for the infant or child
based on the child’s age or weight. A guide to size
selection in infants and children is in Table 51.7
.
Table 51.7 Catheter size selection


42 The Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne (2017). Clinical Guidelines
(Nursing): Indwelling Urinary Catheter—Insertion and Ongoing Care:
Catheter Size. Retrieved from <www.rch.org.au>.
The amount required for inflation of catheter balloons
in children is dependent on the manufacturer’s
predetermined capacity of the balloon. This information
usually can be found at the distal end of the catheter.
Balloons in children can be inflated with less volume
than recommended by the manufacturer but NEVER
more. Prior testing of the balloon is not required as it
can alter the diameter of the catheter, which can make
insertion in infants difficult.
Before inserting the catheter:
Establish rapport and try to gain the confidence of
the infant or child prior to the procedure.
Seek consent from the parent and or significant
other prior to insertion.
Explain the procedure in simple terms to the child
and consider an appropriate explanation to the
parent and or significant other.
If parents and/or significant other are not present
during the procedure, always have a second
person present. Be mindful of embarrassment that
a teenager may experience during the insertion of
a catheter.
If dealing with an infant or child, ask the family
member and/or other staff to assist in supporting
the infant or child during catheterisation.


Careful attention needs to be paid to the securing
of a catheter in infants and small children. Follow
organisation policy for this.
Consider distraction techniques.
Transgender
People undergoing gender-confirming surgery with
urethral lengthening may require a smaller catheter
size. Consult the person’s doctor prior to insertion
(Tollinche et al.
).
43 Tollinche, L. E., Walters, C. B., Radix, A., ... Yeoh, C. (2018). The
perioperative care of the transgender patient. Anesthesia and Analgesia,
127(2), 359–366. Doi: 10.1213/ANE.0000000000003371.
Older adult
When catheterising the older adult, be very attentive to
problems of limited movement, especially in the hips.
Arthritis or previous hip or knee surgery may limit the
person’s movement and cause discomfort. Modify the
position (e.g. side-lying) as needed to perform the
procedure safely and comfortably. For women, obtain
the assistance of another nurse to flex and hold the
person’s knees and hips as necessary or place her in
a modified Sims’ position.
11. Measure the urine in the drainage bag and record the
removal of the catheter. Include in the recording: (a) the time
43


the catheter was removed; (b) the amount, colour and clarity
of the urine; (c) the intactness of the catheter; and (d)
instructions given to the person and how well the person
tolerated the procedure.
12. Provide the person with either a urinal (men), bedpan,
commode or urine collection device to be used with each
subsequent unassisted void.
13. Following removal of the catheter, determine the time of the
first voiding and the amount voided during the first 8 hours.
Compare this output with the person’s intake. If the person
does not void, notify the doctor.
14. Observe for dysfunctional voiding behaviour (e.g. < 100 mL
per void), which might indicate urinary retention. If this
occurs, assess post-void residuals using a bladder scanner if
available. Generally, post-void residuals greater than 200 mL
will require straight catheterisation as needed.
Clinical consideration
After an indwelling catheter has been removed,
some people may report that they are
experiencing difficulty in gaining back the desire
to void. Some simple strategies include
encouraging the person to go to the toilet—sit in
a relaxed, leaning-forward position with the
lower back straight and turn on the water tap.
The nurse should monitor the time the catheter


was removed, the person’s first void and the
consecutive voids in the following 8 hours. The
nurse should also be alert for urinary retention.
Clean intermittent self-catheterisation
Clean intermittent self-catheterisation (CISC) is performed by many
people who have some form of neurogenic bladder dysfunction,
such as that caused by spinal cord injury. Clean or medical aseptic
technique is used. Intermittent self-catheterisation:
enables the person to retain independence and gain control of
the bladder
Home care considerations
Catheterisation
For intermittent catheterisation, educate the person
to:
Follow instructions for clean technique.
Wash hands well with warm water and soap
prior to and following the handling equipment or
performing catheterisation.
Monitor for signs and symptoms of urinary tract
infection, including burning, urgency, abdominal


pain and cloudy urine; in older people, confusion
may be an early sign.
Ensure adequate oral intake of fluids.
After each catheterisation, assess the urine for
colour, odour, clarity and the presence of blood.
Wash rubber catheters thoroughly with soap
and water after use, dry and store in a clean
place.
For indwelling urinary catheters, educate the
person to:
Never pull on the catheter.
Secure the catheter tubing to the leg using a
catheter-securing device.
Ensure that there are no kinks or twists in the
tubing.
Keep the urine drainage bag below the level of
the bladder (see Figure 51.12
). A leg bag
may substitute for a hanging bag for those who
are upright.
Empty the drainage bag regularly.
Take a shower rather than a tub bath. Sitting in
a tub allows bacteria easier access into the
urinary tract.
Monitor for signs and symptoms of urinary tract
infection, including burning, urgency, abdominal
pain, cloudy urine; in older adults, confusion
may be an early sign.
Ensure adequate oral intake of fluids.


People who have indwelling catheters for
lengthy periods of time need to have the
catheter and bag changed at regular intervals.
Follow organisation policy in this regard.
Many people who live with indwelling catheters
also have sex lives. The person may have been
instructed to remove the catheter prior to sexual
intimacy. If this is not practical, men may be told
to tape the catheter to the shaft of the penis to
allow for an erection; to reduce friction (and
prevent infection), use a condom with a water-
based lubricant. The person should also empty
their bladder prior to sex and protect their
bed/surfaces with a towel (Continence
Foundation of Australia ).
44 Continence Foundation of Australia (2016b). Common
Questions. Retrieved from <www.continence.org.au>.
Figure 51.12
44


Positioning the collecting bag and tubing when
sitting in a chair.


reduces incidence of urinary tract infection
protects the upper urinary tract from reflux
allows normal sexual relations without incontinence
reduces the use of aids and appliances
frees the person from embarrassing dribbling.
The procedure for self-catheterisation is similar to that used by the
nurse to catheterise a person. Essential steps are outlined in the
‘Patient education’ feature. Because the procedure requires physical
and mental preparation, individual assessment is important. The
person should have:
sufficient manual dexterity to manipulate a catheter
sufficient cognitive understanding
motivation and acceptance of the procedure
for women, reasonable agility to access the urethra
bladder capacity greater than 100 mL.
Before teaching CISC, the nurse should establish the person’s
individual voiding patterns, the volume voided, fluid intake and
residual amounts. CISC is easier for males to learn because of the
visibility of the urinary meatus. Initially females need to learn with the
aid of a mirror but eventually should perform the procedure by using
only the sense of touch (as described in ‘Patient education
’).
Urinary irrigations


An irrigation
 is a flushing or washing-out with a specified
solution. Bladder irrigation is carried out on a doctor’s order, usually
to wash out the bladder and sometimes to apply a medication to the
bladder lining. Catheter irrigations may be performed to maintain or
restore the patency of a catheter; for example, to remove pus or
blood clots blocking the catheter.
The closed method is the preferred technique for catheter or bladder
irrigation because it is associated with a lower risk of urinary tract
infection. Closed catheter irrigations may be either continuous or
intermittent. This method is most often used for people who have
had genitourinary surgery. The continuous irrigation helps prevent
blood clots occluding the catheter. A three-way, or triple lumen,
catheter (see Figure 51.11
) is generally used for closed
irrigations. The irrigating solution flows into the bladder through the
irrigation port of the catheter and out through the urinary drainage
lumen of the catheter.
Patient education
Clean intermittent self-catheterisation
Perform as often as needed. At first, catheterisation may
be necessary every 2 to 3 hours, increasing to 4 hours.
Attempt to void before catheterisation; insert the catheter
to remove residual urine if unable to void or if amount
voided is insufficient (e.g. less than 100 mL).
Assemble all needed supplies ahead of time. Good
lighting is essential, especially for women.


If a woman is wearing a tampon, it should be removed
before catheterising. A tampon can inhibit catheterisation.
Wash your hands.
Clean the urinary meatus with either a towelette or soapy
washcloth, then rinse with a wet washcloth. Women
should clean the area from front to back.
Assume a position that is comfortable and that facilitates
passage of the catheter, such as a semi-reclining position
in bed or sitting on a chair or the toilet. Men may prefer to
stand over the toilet; women may prefer to stand with one
foot on a stool while positioned over the toilet or
commode.
Apply lubricant to the catheter tip (2.5 cm for women; 5–
15 cm for men).
Insert the catheter until urine flows through.
a. If a woman, locate the meatus using a mirror or
other aid, or use the ‘touch’ technique as follows:
‒ Place the index finger of your non-dominant hand
on your clitoris.
‒ Place the third and fourth fingers at the vagina.
‒ Locate the meatus between the index and third
fingers.
‒ Direct the catheter through the meatus and then
upward and forward.
b. If a man, hold the penis with a slight upward
tension at a 60- to 90-degree angle to insert the


catheter. Return the penis to its natural position
when urine starts to flow.
Hold the catheter in place until all urine is drained.
Withdraw the catheter slowly to ensure complete drainage
of urine.
Wash the catheter with soap and water; store in a clean
container. Replace the catheter when it becomes difficult
to clean, or too soft or hard to insert easily.
Contact your care provider if your urine becomes cloudy
or contains sediment; if you have bleeding, difficulty or
pain when passing the catheter; or if you have a fever.
Drink sufficient fluid a day to ensure adequate bladder
filling and flushing. To keep your urine acidic and reduce
the risk of bladder infections, drink cranberry and prune
juices.
Research note What guides practice
in the nursing care of people with
problems of urinary elimination?
When do you insert a urinary catheter? What type of urinary
catheter is best for this person? Do you clamp the catheter
prior to discontinuing an indwelling catheter? Is cranberry
juice effective in preventing urinary tract infections? Which


management strategy is most effective for urge urinary
incontinence? How often should the urostomy appliance be
changed? These are some of the questions faced daily by the
nurse clinician when caring for people experiencing problems
with urinary elimination.
To find the answers, nurses must search for the most current
peer-reviewed research on these topics. A review of the
literature may reveal there is a lack of evidence from
randomised or quasi- randomised controlled studies, whereby
no conclusions can be made regarding the use of specific
products, techniques or interventions that support current
practice. Studies that do exist may be small and consistently
identify the need for larger, randomised controlled studies.
Implications Nurses at the bedside are aptly positioned to
complete needed research trials to document evidence and
person outcomes.
Occasionally, an open irrigation may be necessary to restore
catheter patency. The risk of injecting micro-organisms into the
urinary tract is greater with open irrigations because the connection
between the indwelling catheter and the drainage tubing is broken.
Strict precautions to maintain the sterility of the drainage tubing
connector and interior of the indwelling catheter must be taken to
minimise this risk. The open method of catheter or bladder irrigation
is performed with double-lumen indwelling urinary catheters. It may
be necessary for people who develop blood clots and mucus
fragments that occlude the catheter and when it is undesirable to


change the catheter. Techniques for bladder irrigation are outlined in
Skill 51.4
.
Suprapubic catheter care
A suprapubic catheter
 is inserted surgically through the
abdominal wall above the symphysis pubis into the urinary bladder
(see Figure 51.13
). The doctor inserts the catheter using local
anaesthetic or during bladder or vaginal surgery. The catheter may
be secured in place with sutures (if a retention balloon is not used)
and then attached to a closed drainage system. The suprapubic
catheter may be placed for temporary bladder drainage until the
person is able to resume normal voiding (e.g. after urethral, bladder
or vaginal surgery) or it may become a permanent device (e.g.
urethral or pelvic trauma).
Figure 51.13


A suprapubic catheter in place.


Care of people with a suprapubic catheter includes regular
assessments of the person’s urine, fluid intake and comfort;
maintenance of a patent drainage system; skin care around the
insertion site; and periodic clamping of the catheter prior to removing
it if it is not a permanent appliance. If the catheter is temporary,
orders generally include leaving the catheter open to drainage for 48
to 72 hours, then clamping the catheter for 3- to 4-hour periods
during the day until the person can void satisfactory amounts.
Satisfactory voiding is determined by measuring the person’s
residual urine after voiding.
A particular challenge with suprapubic catheters can be poor
drainage because of obstruction of the catheter tip. The tip may
become blocked by the wall of the bladder or sediments and clots.
Should blockage occur, the person may experience discomfort due
to bladder distension. Two simple strategies the nurse can employ to
promote drainage are: (1) maintain gravity drainage by ensuring that
the catheter tube is not kinked; and (2) encourage the person to turn
from side to side to promote drainage. The nurse must carefully
monitor the urine output to ensure that drainage is occurring.
Care of the catheter insertion site involves sterile technique.
Dressings around the newly placed suprapubic catheter are changed
whenever they are soiled with drainage to prevent bacterial growth
around the insertion site and reduce the potential for infection.
Organisation policy may indicate the use of some antiseptic
solutions when cleaning around the catheter site as well as
protective dressings being applied after cleansing. For catheters that


have been in place for an extended period, no dressing may be
needed and the healed insertion tract enables removal and
replacement of the catheter as needed. Securing the catheter tube
to the abdomen helps to reduce tension at the insertion site. The
nurse assesses the insertion area at regular intervals. If abdominal
hair invades the insertion site, it may be carefully shaved. Any
redness or discharge at the skin around the insertion site must be
reported.
Urinary diversions
A urinary diversion is the elimination of urine via a surgically created
diversion or pathway other than the urethra. There are two
categories of diversions: incontinent and continent.
Incontinent diversions
With incontinent diversions, people have no control over the
passage of urine and require the use of an external stoma appliance
to contain the urine. Urinary diversions may or may not involve the
removal of the bladder (cystectomy). Examples of incontinent
diversions include ureterostomy, nephrostomy, vesicostomy and ileal
conduits. A ureterostomy
 is when one or both of the ureters may
be brought directly to the side of the abdomen to form small stomas.
This procedure, however, has some disadvantages in that the
stomas provide direct access for micro-organisms from the skin to
the kidneys, the small stomas are difficult to fit with an appliance to
collect the urine and they may narrow, impairing urine drainage. A
nephrostomy
 involves the insertion of a drainage tube into the


kidney for the purpose of draining urine into a closed system
collection device (see Figure 51.14
). A vesicostomy
 may be
formed when the bladder is left intact but voiding through the urethra
is not possible (e.g. due to an obstruction or a neurogenic bladder).
The ureters remain connected to the bladder and the bladder wall is
surgically attached to an opening in the skin below the navel,
forming an incontinent stoma.
Figure 51.14


A nephrostomy.
The most common urinary diversion or urostomy is the ileal
conduit
 (see Figure 51.15
). In this procedure, a segment of
the ileum is removed but the blood supply is maintained. The divided


ileum is re-anastomosed. The ileal conduit is used to create an
everted stoma (mouth) on the abdomen as the lumen of the ileum is
larger than the urethra and strictures are less likely to occur. A
urostomy stoma is usually created to protrude from the abdomen by
1–3 cm so that a urostomy appliance can be securely fitted and
leakage prevented. The ureters are surgically implanted into the
internal ileal conduit and urine drains externally via the stoma. The
mucous membrane lining of the ileum also provides some protection
from ascending infection. Urine drains continuously from the ileal
pouch and the person must wear a urostomy appliance at all times
to collect the urine. A urostomy appliance will contain a non-return
valve to prevent backflow of urine around the peristomal skin and will
have a tap outlet for easier draining. Some urostomates (people with
a urinary stoma) will connect their appliance to a straight drainage
device at night to prevent having to get up to empty the appliance.
Figure 51.15


An incontinent urinary diversion (ileal conduit).
Continent diversions
A portion of ileum or colon is used to create an internal urinary
reservoir or pouch. The ureters are inserted into the pouch which
fills with urine. A flap valve opening is created in the portion of ileum
that connects to the abdomen in order to provide a continent
mechanism.


A neobladder replaces a diseased or damaged bladder with a piece
of ileum or colon, thus surgically creating a new bladder. This
neobladder is then sutured to the functional urethral sphincter or an
artificial sphincter is inserted to ensure continence. People with a
neobladder can control voiding. See Figure 51.16
.
Figure 51.16


A neobladder.
Ureteric stents may be present following surgery for a continent or
incontinent urinary diversion and these will protrude from the stoma.
They remain in place for 10 to 14 days postoperatively to maintain
