patency of the ureters at the anastomotic sites. They will be


removed by either the surgeon or the stomal therapy nurse,
depending on organisation policy. Nurses must observe the flow of
urine from the stents and report immediately any obstruction to flow.
When caring for people with a urinary diversion, the nurse must
accurately assess fluid intake and output; note any changes in urine
colour, odour or clarity (mucus shreds from the intestinal conduit are
commonly seen in the urine of people with an ileal diversion); and
frequently assess the condition of the stoma and surrounding skin.
People with an ileal conduit must wear a well-fitting urostomy
appliance at all times to prevent leakage and peristomal skin
ulceration. Stomal therapy nurses are able to provide preoperative
and postoperative counselling to facilitate recovery and
rehabilitation. They provide advice on how to care for the stoma and
appliances and the management of any skin problems. People with
urinary diversions may experience problems associated with
alterations in their body image and sexuality and may require
assistance in coping. Most people are able to resume their normal
activities and lifestyle.
Individuals with a stoma obtain their appliances at no cost from state
ostomy associations which distribute appliances on behalf of the
Commonwealth Stoma Appliance Scheme. The steps for changing a
urostomy appliance are similar to those described in the procedure
for changing a bowel diversion appliance (see Chapter 52)
.
Evaluating


Using the overall goals and desired outcomes identified in the
planning stage, the nurse collects data to evaluate the effectiveness
of nursing activities. Examples of desired outcomes for the identified
goals are listed in the ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, interventions
and outcomes’ box earlier in this chapter.
If the desired outcomes are not achieved, explore the reasons
before modifying the care plan. For example, if the outcome
‘Remains dry between voiding and at night’ is not met, examples of
questions that need to be considered include:
What is the person’s perception of the problem?
Does the person understand and comply with the health care
instructions provided? If not, ask what issues are preventing
them from following health care instructions.
Is access to toilet facilities a problem?
Can the person manipulate clothing for toileting? Are there
adjustments that can be made to allow easier disrobing?
Are scheduled toileting times appropriate?
Is there adequate transition lighting for night-time toileting?
Are mobility aids such as a walking frame, an elevated toilet seat
or a grab bar needed? If currently used, are they appropriate or
adequate?
Is the person performing pelvic floor muscle exercises
appropriately as scheduled?
Is the person’s fluid intake adequate? Does the timing of fluid
intake need to be adjusted (e.g. restricted after dinner)?


Is the person restricting caffeine, citrus juice, fizzy drinks and
artificial sweetener intake?
Is the person taking a diuretic? If so, when is the medication
taken? Do the times need to be adjusted (e.g. taking second
dose no later than 4 p.m.)?
Should continence aids such as an external urinary sheath or
absorbent pads be considered or used?
NURSING  CARE PLAN
Urinary elimination
Applying critical thinking
1. Considering Baker’s history and assessment data,
what other physical conditions could explain his
symptoms?
2. The doctor has recommended surgery. What
assumptions will the nurse need to validate in helping
prepare Mr and Mrs Baker for this surgery?
3. It does not appear that other alternatives have been
considered. Why might this be so?
4. Incontinence can lead people to limit social
interactions. What would be an appropriate response if
Baker states that he will stay home until he has his
surgery?


CO NCEPT M AP
Urinary elimination


SKILL
51.1 Dipstick urinalysis
Purposes
To provide a fast and accurate method of
screening urine samples for a variety of
conditions.
To reduce the amount of unnecessary urine
samples that traditionally would have been
processed in a laboratory (Joanna Briggs
Institute 2013).
Assessment
Assess person for indicators for urine testing and
the most appropriate method of collection. Urinalysis
is often a routine procedure attended by nurses on
admission to a health care facility to identify
causative factors for illness and underlying
conditions. Urinalysis machines are available in
some health care facilities but dipstick urinalysis is
still performed and is a required nursing skill. Note:
do not test first morning urine specimen if


specifically monitoring for glucose as it can be
inaccurate (Joanna Briggs Institute 2013).
Planning
Explain to the person the reasons for testing and the
method for collection and gain consent. The method
of collection for urinalysis can be a purposeful
specimen or can also be a sterile procedure
collected from an indwelling catheter. Regardless of
the approach for collection, it is important to have a
fresh specimen to ensure an accurate reading. For
this reason, it is not recommended to use urine from
collection bags for urinalysis unless using a specific
collection bag in a paediatric person. Only a small
volume of urine is required; usually less than 1 mL
will suffice. If a purposive specimen is to be
achieved, privacy must be ensured for the person
and a clean, dry, leak-proof container should be
supplied to obtain the specimen. If the person is
immobile, the urine can be collected in a pan or
urinal. (The person should also be provided with a
disposable plastic bag for toilet paper as the used
paper should not be placed in the pan, as it will soak
up the urine as well contaminate it.)
Equipment


Specimen container (clearly marked with patient
identifiers)
Pan or urinal as required
Disposable gloves
PPE as required by organisation policy
Urinalysis testing strips
Implementation
Preparation
Check the expiry date on the urinalysis testing
strips and ascertain the amount of time required
to be exposed to urine before reading can occur.
In addition, find out from product information the
maximum length of time before the reading
becomes invalid (overexposed).
Performance
1. Perform hand hygiene and put on disposable
gloves and other appropriate PPE.
2. Place test strip into urine specimen for length
of time designated by manufacturer and
remove. Usually the time frame is that which
is sufficient to moisten the strip. If the
specimen cannot be tested immediately, it
may be refrigerated for up to 2 hours before
testing (Joanna Briggs Institute 2013).


3. Wait for the manufacturer’s designated time
frame for reaction before reading the result in
comparison with the colour chart (usually on
the side of the test strip bottle). 1 Ensure the
test is read within the reaction curve time
frame, otherwise the reading may be
inaccurate.
4. The colour, smell and density of the urine
should also be noted and recorded.
5. Discard all specimens and test strip into the
appropriate waste receptacle.
6. Ensure testing area is cleaned with general
purpose detergent.
7. Remove gloves. Perform hand hygiene.
8. Document findings, verifying that the identity
of the patient and the sample match.


1 Test by matching strip against markers on bottle
Evaluation
Report any abnormal results to the treating
health care provider/doctor.
Develop a plan for follow-up based on the
abnormal findings.


In some situations, this may include collecting a
further urine specimen for laboratory analysis or a
follow-up ward urinalysis.


SKILL
51.2 Applying an external
urinary sheath
Purposes
To collect urine and control urinary incontinence.
To permit the person’s physical activity while
controlling urinary incontinence.
To prevent skin irritation as a result of urine
incontinence.
Assessment
Review the person’s record to determine a
pattern to voiding and other pertinent data.
Perform hand hygiene and don clean gloves
before examining the person’s penis for swelling
or skin erosion that would contraindicate use of
the urinary sheath. During this time determine
the size of the external urinary sheath required to
suit the person. Disposable measure guides are
provided by manufacturers of these devices.


Determine if the person requires trimming of
pubic hair in preparation for application. If so,
explain and seek the person’s permission prior to
conducting any trimming.
Planning
Determine if the person has had an external urinary
sheath previously and any difficulties with it. Check
for possible latex, rubber or adhesive allergies.
Perform any procedures that are best completed
without the urinary sheath in place; for example,
weighing the person would be easier without the
tubing and bag.
Equipment
Leg drainage bag with tubing or urinary drainage
bag with tubing
External urinary sheath of correct size
Drape (e.g. sheet or bath blanket)
Clean gloves
Basin of warm water and soap
Washcloth and towel
Elastic tape or Velcro strap to secure drainage
tubing to leg
Scissors and/or razor


Implementation
Preparation
Assemble the leg drainage bag or urinary
drainage bag for attachment to the urinary
sheath.
Roll the sheath outward onto itself to facilitate
easier application. 1 On some models, an inner
flap will be exposed. This flap is applied around
the urinary meatus to prevent the reflux of urine.
Position the person in either a supine or a sitting
position.


1 Before application, roll the urinary sheath
outward onto itself
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how he can cooperate.
2. Perform hand hygiene, don personal
protective equipment, such as non-sterile


gloves, and observe appropriate infection-
control procedures.
3. Provide for privacy.
Drape the person appropriately with the bath
blanket, exposing only the penis.
4. Inspect and clean the penis.
Trim hair at the base of penis if necessary.
In some cases, shaving may be
necessary.
Clean the genital area and dry it
thoroughly. Rationale: this minimises skin
irritation and excoriation after the external
urinary sheath is applied.
5. Apply and secure the urinary sheath.
Roll the urinary sheath smoothly over the
penis, leaving 2.5 cm between the end of
the penis and the rubber or plastic
connecting tube. 2 Rationale: this space
prevents irritation of the tip of the penis
and provides for full drainage of urine
(Joanna Briggs Institute ).
32 Joanna Briggs Institute (2010a). Urinary
Sheaths/Condoms. Retrieved from
<http://connect.jbiconnectplus.org>.
Secure the urinary sheath, which should
have an adhesive section inside the
proximal end that adheres to the skin of
32


the base of the penis. Do not use tape
around the base of the penis over the
urinary sheath, as it can stop blood flow.
6. Securely attach the urinary drainage system.
Make sure that the tip of the penis is not
touching the urinary sheath and that the
sheath is not twisted. Rationale: a twisted
urinary sheath could obstruct the flow of
urine (Joanna Briggs Institute 2010a).
Attach the urinary drainage system to the
external urinary sheath.
Remove the gloves and perform hand
hygiene.
If the person is to remain in bed, attach
the urinary drainage bag to the bed frame.
If the person is ambulatory, attach the bag
to the person’s leg. 3 Rationale: attaching
the drainage bag to the leg helps control
the movement of the tubing and prevents
twisting of the thin material of the urinary
sheath at the tip of the penis.
7. Teach the person about the drainage system.
Educate the person to keep the drainage
bag below the level of the external urinary
sheath and to avoid loops or kinks in the
tubing.


8. Inspect the penis for swelling and colour
changes 30 minutes following the application
of the urinary sheath and every 4 hours.
Rationale: an allergy to the sheath may
develop (Joanna Briggs Institute 2010a).
Assess the penis for swelling and
discolouration, which indicates that the
urinary sheath is too tight.
Assess urine flow if the person has
voided. Normally, some urine is present in
the tube if the flow is not obstructed.
9. Change the urinary sheath daily and provide
skin care.
Apply clean gloves and remove the
external urinary sheath.
Wash the penis with soapy water, rinse
and dry it thoroughly.
Assess the foreskin for signs of irritation,
swelling and discolouration.
Reapply a new urinary sheath.
10. Document in the person’s record using forms
or checklists supplemented by narrative notes
when appropriate. Record the application of
the urinary sheath, the time and pertinent
observations, such as irritated areas on the
penis.


2 The urinary sheath rolled over the penis


3 Urinary drainage leg bag
Evaluation
Perform a detailed follow-up based on findings
that deviated from expected or normal for the
person. Relate findings to previous assessment
data if available.
Report significant deviations from normal to the
doctor or an experienced Registered Nurse.


SKILL
51.3 Performing urinary
catheterisation
Purposes
To relieve discomfort due to bladder distension or
to provide gradual decompression of a distended
bladder.
To assess the amount of residual urine if the
bladder empties incompletely.
To obtain a sterile urine specimen.
To empty the bladder completely prior to surgery.
To facilitate accurate measurement of urinary
output for critically ill or postoperative patients
whose output needs to be monitored.
To provide for intermittent or continuous bladder
drainage and/or irrigation.
To prevent urine from contacting an incision after
perineal surgery.
To manage incontinence when other measures
have failed.


Assessment
Determine the most appropriate method of
catheterisation based on the purpose and any
criteria specified in the order, such as total
amount of urine to be removed or size of
catheter to be used.
Use a non-balloon catheter if only a spot urine
specimen is needed, if amount of residual urine
is being measured or if temporary
decompression/emptying of the bladder is
required.
Use an indwelling catheter if the bladder must
remain empty or continuous urine
measurement/collection is needed.
Assess the person’s overall condition. Determine
if the person is able to cooperate and hold still
during the procedure and if the person can be
positioned supine with head relatively flat.
Children will require additional staff to hold in
appropriate position. Parents are able to stay if
desired, and age-appropriate distraction therapy
should be implemented when possible.
Determine when the person last voided or was
last catheterised.
Percuss the bladder to check for fullness or
distension.


When possible, complete a bladder scan to
assess the amount of urine present in the
bladder before performing a urethral
catheterisation.
Planning
Allow adequate time to perform the catheterisation.
Although the entire procedure can require as little as
15 minutes for skilled nurses, several sources of
difficulty could result in a much longer time.
Equipment
Sterile catheter of appropriate size (an extra
catheter should also be at hand)
Indwelling catheterisation kit or individual sterile
items: 1


1 A selection of items required for insertion of an
indwelling urinary catheter (sterile gloves, urinary
drainage bag, lubrication, ‘bluey’)
− 1–2 pair sterile gloves
− Sterile waterproof drape(s)
− Cleaning solution (normal saline) or as per
organisation policy
− Cleansing swabs


− Forceps
− Water-soluble lubricant
− Specimen container
− Syringe pre-filled with sterile water or normal
saline in amount specified by catheter
manufacturer for use with indwelling catheter
Urinary collection bag and tubing
2% xylocaine gel for numbing (if organisation
policy permits)
Supplies for performing perineal cleansing (liquid
soap, wash bowl with warm water and washcloth)
Bath blanket or sheet for draping the person
Adequate lighting (obtain a flashlight or lamp if
necessary)
For intermittent urinary catheterisation, you will need
all of the above except the pre-filled syringe and
urinary collection bag, plus:
Red rubber or Robinson catheter (Figure
51.8
) and a urine drainage basin.
Implementation


Preparation
Note: the following instructions are for both
indwelling and intermittent catheterisation. The steps
are very similar, with the main difference being
inflation of the balloon and use of a bag with
indwelling catheterisation versus one-time
catheterising to remove urine.
If using a catheterisation kit, read the label carefully
to be sure all necessary items are included.
Performance
1. Confirm patient identification, confirm the
catheterisation has been ordered by the
appropriate clinician. Rationale: ensures the
right patient is undergoing the right procedure
at the right time.
2. Explain the procedure to the patient and gain
consent. Provide patient education on
catheterisation as appropriate. Rationale:
ensures the patient has a good understanding
of the procedure and gives informed consent.
This may need further reinforcement at the
end of the procedure if the patient is to be
discharged home with catheter. Rationale:
ensures safe catheter management in the
home.


3. Check current medications and any known
allergies (e.g. latex or lignocaine), previous
urology history and previous reactions to
catheterisation, as well as the patient’s
ethical, religious and cultural beliefs.
Rationale: prevents adverse reactions and
preserves the patient’s dignity.
4.
Ensure a good light source is available, to
maximise visibility, and an appropriate
buddy clinician is available to assist with
the procedure. Rationale: reduces the
risk of infection.
Ensure a chaperone is available if
required. Rationale: maintains patient
safety.
5.
Undertake the procedure on the patient’s
bed or in a clinical setting, utilising screens
or curtains to promote and maintain
dignity and privacy.
Optional: some clinicians prefer to insert
lignocaine gel prior to step 6 to reduce
catheter insertion discomfort. Before
inserting the lignocaine, clean the urethral
meatus and ensure hand hygiene is
performed before and after this step. See
step 11 for more details.


6.
Apply manual handling principles and set
the bed at a suitable height for the
procedure to ensure accessibility and to
maintain dignity and comfort.
Position the patient in the supine position.
For females, position so the knees are
slightly flexed and the feet a little apart.
Place a waterproof sheet under the
buttocks. Ensure the patient is not
exposed and maintain warmth.
Perform hand hygiene using alcohol gel or
soap and water. Rationale: reduces the
risk of infection.
If an existing catheter is being replaced,
do the following before step 7:
‒ don non-sterile gloves, eye protection
and gown/apron
‒ deflate the balloon passively with a 10
mL syringe
‒ with the dominant hand, remove the
catheter
‒ discard the used catheter
‒ remove non-sterile gloves and perform
hand hygiene
‒ remove PPE and perform hand hygiene.


7.
With the assistance of the buddy clinician,
to reduce the risk of infection, clean and
prepare the trolley and assemble the
aseptic field. Add any additional sterile
equipment required to the aseptic field
(e.g. catheter, drainage device, sterile
water and syringe if not included in
catheter pack).
Open sterile gloves onto the sterile
surface, maintaining the sterility of the
gloves.
Don eye protection and apron/gown.
Perform hand hygiene for aseptic
procedures (30–60 seconds) and don
sterile gloves.
Fill syringe with 5–10 mL of sterile water.
Remove the catheter from the plastic
sleeve, ensuring to maintain sterility of the
catheter at all times.
If lignocaine was not inserted at step 2,
attach nozzle to lignocaine syringe.
Lubricate catheter tip and place into an
empty tray. This is the drainage tray.
Rationale: a small amount of anaesthetic
gel allows adequate lubrication to insert
the catheter nozzle into the meatus prior
to insertion.


8. Buddy clinician removes the cover that is
maintaining patient privacy to maximise
visibility.
9. Cleanse the meatus with the cleansing
solution as required by the organisation.
Male: with the non-dominant hand and
using a gauze square, hold the patient’s
penis. Retract foreskin if uncircumcised.
Using the dominant hand, clean urethral
meatus and glans penis, using one
downward stroke (e.g. towards tip of the
penis) per gauze square.
Female: with the non-dominant hand, use
the gauze squares to separate the labia
minora, exposing the urethral meatus.
Using the dominant hand, clean the labia
minora and urethral orifice with gauze
soaked with 0.9% sodium chloride,
performing one downward stroke per
square.
10. Apply the fenestrated drape to create a sterile
field.
11. If lignocaine was not inserted earlier, hold the
penis at a right angle to the body and insert
the lignocaine nozzle into urethral meatus.
Inject the lignocaine gel into the urethra,
ensuring a firm seal around the meatus.


Compress the penis and hold for 3–5
minutes. Warn the patient about the risk of
stinging from anaesthetic gel. Rationale: a
small amount of anaesthetic gel allows
adequate lubrication to insert the catheter
nozzle into the meatus prior to insertion; use
of a local anaesthetic minimises the
discomfort experienced by the patient.
12. Pick up catheter with the dominant hand and
ensure that the drainage end of the catheter
is in the tray. Place drainage tray on the
fenestrated drape between the patient’s legs.
Male: hold the penis at a 90 degree angle,
then gently insert catheter into urethral
meatus. When resistance is felt, lower the
penis and continue inserting until the start
of the Y junction of catheter. When urine
flows, inflate the balloon with sterile water
in accordance with the manufacturer’s
recommendations and with clinical
discretion (e.g. consider spinal cord
injury).
Female: use the non-dominant hand and
gauze square to separate the labia minor
and expose the urethral meatus. Use the
dominant hand to gently insert 5–7 cm of
the catheter into the urethral meatus.
When urine flows into the tray, advance


the catheter 2–3 cm, then inflate balloon
with sterile water in accordance with the
manufacturer’s recommendations and with
clinical discretion (e.g. consider spinal
cord injury).
Troubleshooting
Males: if resistance is felt at the external
sphincter:
‒ Consider second tube of lubricant
‒ Apply gentle steady pressure on the
catheter
‒ Ask the patient to take a deep breath
‒ Ask the patient to cough or bear down
‒ Ask the patient to try to pass urine
‒ Gently rotate the catheter.
Females: if the catheter has been
incorrectly inserted into the vagina, keep
initial catheter in situ until the second
catheter is correctly in place in the
urethra.
13. Gently inflate the balloon according to the
manufacturer’s instruction. Rationale:
reduces the risk of urethral, prostatic and
bladder neck trauma.


14. Never inflate the balloon until urine flows
freely and stop if pain is felt. Rationale: pain
could indicate bladder spasm or incorrect
placement.
15. Withdraw the catheter slightly until resistance
is felt. Rationale: ensures correct catheter
placement.
16. Attach the catheter to a compatible valve or
drainage system.
17. Support the catheter by using a specifically
designed support strap or tape. Rationale:
ensures patient comfort and to reduce the
risk of urethral and bladder neck trauma.
18. Ensure that the catheter does not become
taut when the patient is mobilising.
Rationale: movement-induced trauma can
lead to UTIs and tissue necrosis.
19. Ensure that the glans penis is clean and dry
and reposition the foreskin in uncircumcised
males. Rationale: prevents paraphimosis. If
the area is left wet skin irritation may occur.
20. Remove gloves and perform hand hygiene
using alcohol gel or soap and water.
21. Ensure the patient is comfortable.
22. Dispose of equipment and gloves in a
biohazard bag utilised in the clinical area.
Rationale: prevents environmental
contamination.


23. Dispose of clinical waste bag into appropriate
waste system. Rationale: prevents
environmental contamination.
24. Perform hand hygiene using alcohol gel or
soap and water. Rationale: reduces risk of
cross-infection from micro-organisms.
25. Complete documentation. At a minimum, the
following information should be included:
how consent was obtained and whom it
was obtained from
indication for catheterisation
catheter option used (in/out, IDC, SPC)
size and type of catheter
time and date of insertion
balloon volume in
total urine volume drained on insertion
(refer to the fluid balance chart)
any abnormalities observed during or after
catheter insertion (e.g. pain, bleeding)
any clinical misadventures during insertion
(e.g. false passage, haematuria,
blockage)
presence of UTI signs and symptoms
colour of urine, sediment or abnormality
whether a urine specimen for culture was
collected
post-procedure tests that are clinically
relevant


follow-up actions (e.g. review of catheter,
catheter removal).
Sources: Adapted from White, Brinson &
Glentworth ; NSW Health .
39 White, T., Brinson, L. & Glentworth, J. (2013). Catheterisation Clinical
Guidelines. Australian and New Zealand Urological Nurses Society Inc.
Retrieved from <https://anzuns.org>.
40 NSW Health (2015). Adult Urethral Catheterisation for Acute Care
Settings. Retrieved from <www1.health.nsw.gov.au>.
39
40


SKILL
51.4 Performing bladder
irrigation
Purposes
To maintain the patency of a urinary catheter and
tubing (closed continuous irrigation).
To free a blockage in a urinary catheter or tubing
(open intermittent irrigation).
Assessment
Determine the person’s current urinary drainage
system. Review the person’s record for recent
intake and output and any difficulties the person
has been experiencing with the system. Review
the results of previous irrigations.
Assess the person for any discomfort, bladder
spasms or distended bladder.
Planning


Before irrigating a catheter or bladder, check: (a) the
reason for the irrigation; (b) the order authorising the
continuous or intermittent irrigation (in most
organisations, a doctor’s order is required); (c) the
type of sterile solution, the amount and strength to
be used and the rate (if continuous); and (d) the
type of catheter in place. If these are not specified
on the person’s chart, check the organisation policy.
Equipment
Clean gloves (2 pairs)
Indwelling urinary catheter in place
Drainage tubing and bag (if not in place)
Drainage tubing clamp
Antiseptic swabs
Sterile receptacle
Sterile irrigating solution warmed or at room
temperature. (Label the irrigant clearly with the
words bladder irrigation, including the information
about any medications that have been added to
the original solution and the date, time and
nurse’s initials.)
Infusion tubing
IV pole
Implementation
Performance


1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can cooperate. Gain permission
to proceed. The irrigation should not be
painful or uncomfortable. Discuss how the
results will be used in planning further care or
treatments.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for person privacy.
4. Put on clean gloves.
5. Empty, measure and record the amount and
appearance of urine present in the drainage
bag. Discard urine and gloves. Rationale:
emptying the drainage bag allows more
accurate measurement of urinary output after
the irrigation is in place or completed.
Assessing the character of the urine provides
baseline data for later comparison.
6. Prepare the equipment.
Perform hand hygiene.
Connect the irrigation infusion tubing to
the irrigating solution and flush the tubing
with solution, keeping the tip sterile.
Rationale: flushing the tubing removes air


and prevents it from being instilled into the
bladder.
Apply clean gloves and cleanse the port
with antiseptic swabs.
Connect the irrigation tubing to the input
port of the three-way catheter.
Connect the drainage bag and tubing to
the urinary drainage port if not already in
place.
Remove the gloves and perform hand
hygiene.
7. Irrigate the bladder.
a. For closed continuous irrigation, open
the flow clamp on the urinary drainage
tubing (if present). 1
Rationale: this allows the irrigating
solution to flow out of the bladder
continuously.
Open the regulating clamp on the
irrigating tubing and adjust the flow
rate as prescribed by the doctor or
to 40 to 60 drops per minute if not
specified.
Assess the drainage for amount,
colour and clarity. The amount of
drainage should equal the amount


of irrigant entering the bladder plus
expected urine output.


1 A continuous bladder irrigation (CBI)
set-up
b. For closed intermittent irrigation,
determine whether the solution is to
remain in the bladder for a specified
time.
If the solution is to remain in the
bladder (a bladder irrigation or
instillation), apply the flow clamp to
the urinary drainage tubing.
Rationale: closing the flow clamp
allows the solution to be retained in
the bladder and in contact with
bladder walls.
If the solution is being instilled to
irrigate the catheter, open the flow
clamp on the urinary drainage
tubing. Rationale: irrigating
solution will flow through the urinary
drainage port and tubing, removing
mucus shreds or clots.
Open the flow clamp on the
irrigating tubing, allowing the


specified amount of solution to
infuse. Clamp the tubing.
After the specified period the
solution is to be retained, open the
drainage tubing flow clamp and
allow the bladder to empty.
Assess the drainage for amount,
colour and clarity. The amount of
drainage should equal the amount
of irrigant entering the bladder plus
expected urine output.
8. Assess the person and the urinary output.
Assess the person’s comfort.
Empty the drainage bag and measure the
contents. Subtract the amount of irrigant
instilled from the total volume of drainage
to obtain the volume of urine output.
9. Document the procedure and results in the
person’s record using forms or checklists
supplemented by narrative notes when
appropriate.
Note any abnormal constituents such as blood clots,
pus or mucus shreds.


Variation: open irrigation using a two-way
indwelling catheter

Perform hand hygiene.
Using aseptic non-touch technique, open

Rationale: aseptic technique is vital to

Chapter 51 Review


Chapter highlights
Urinary elimination depends on normal functioning of the urinary,
cardiovascular and nervous systems.
Urine is formed in the nephron, the functional unit of the kidney,
through a process of filtration, reabsorption and secretion.
Hormones such as antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and aldosterone
affect the reabsorption of sodium and water, thus affecting the
amount of urine formed.
The normal process of urination is stimulated when sufficient
urine collects in the bladder to stimulate stretch receptors.
Impulses from stretch receptors are transmitted to the spinal
cord and the brain, causing relaxation of the internal sphincter
(unconscious control) and, if appropriate, relaxation of the
external sphincter (conscious control).
In the adult, urination generally occurs after 250 to 450 mL of
urine has collected in the bladder.
Many factors influence a person’s urinary elimination, including
growth and development, fluid intake, stress, activity,
medications and various diseases and disability.
Alterations in urine production and elimination include polyuria,
oliguria, anuria, frequency, nocturia, urgency, dysuria, enuresis,
haematuria, incontinence and retention. Each may have various
influencing and associated factors that need to be identified.
Assessment of a person’s urinary function includes: (a) a nursing
history that identifies voiding patterns, recent changes, past and
current problems with urination and factors influencing the


elimination pattern; (b) a physical assessment of the
genitourinary system; (c) inspection of the urine for amount,
colour, clarity and odour; and, if indicated, (d) testing of urine for
specific gravity, pH and the presence of glucose, ketone bodies,
protein and occult blood.
Many nursing diagnoses may apply to people with altered urinary
elimination patterns; for example, Functional incontinence,
Urinary retention and related diagnoses such as Risk of infection.
Incontinence can be physically and emotionally distressing to
people because it is considered socially unacceptable.
Bladder training can often reduce episodes of incontinence.
People with urinary retention not only experience discomfort but
also are at risk of urinary tract infection.
The most common cause of urinary tract infection is an invasive
procedure such as catheterisation and cystoscopic examination.
Women in particular are prone to ascending urinary tract
infections because of their short urethras.
Goals for the person with problems with urinary elimination
include maintaining or restoring normal elimination patterns and
preventing associated risks such as skin breakdown.
In planning for home care, the nurse considers the person’s
needs for teaching and assistance or assistive devices in the
home.
Nursing interventions related to urinary elimination are generally
directed towards facilitating the normal functioning of the urinary
system or towards assisting the person with particular problems.
Interventions include (a) assisting the person to maintain an
appropriate fluid intake, (b) assisting the person to maintain


normal voiding patterns, (c) monitoring the person’s daily fluid
intake and output and (d) maintaining cleanliness of the genital
area.
Urinary catheterisation is frequently required for people with
urinary retention but is only performed when all other measures
to facilitate voiding fail. Sterile technique is essential to prevent
ascending urinary infections.
Care of people with indwelling catheters is directed towards
preventing infection of the urinary tract and encouraging urinary
flow through the drainage system.
People with urinary retention may be taught to perform clean
intermittent self-catheterisation to enhance their independence,
reduce the risk of infection and eliminate incontinence.
Bladder or catheter irrigations may be used to apply medication
to bladder walls or maintain catheter patency.
When the urinary bladder is removed, a urinary diversion is
formed to allow urine to be eliminated from the body. The ileal
conduit or ileal loop is the most common diversion and requires
that the person wear a urine collection device continually over the
stoma.

Nurses are frequently involved in assisting
people with elimination problems. These
problems can be embarrassing to the individual
and can cause considerable discomfort. Some
older adults may become preoccupied with their
bowels. People who have had a bowel
movement once a day for 75 years can view
missing one day as a serious problem.
Elimination of the waste products of digestion
is the passage of faecal material that remains in
the colon following the digestion and absorption
of nutrients and fluids which are required for
maintenance of metabolic health. The excreted
waste products are referred to as faeces
 or
stool
.


The digestive system
The digestive system comprises the gastrointestinal tract (also
referred to as the alimentary canal) and the accessory organs of
digestion, which include the salivary glands, liver, pancreas and gall
bladder. The functions of the digestive system are ingestion,
mastication, deglutition, digestion, absorption and elimination
.
The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is one long hollow tube divided into
various sections: mouth, oropharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small
intestine, large intestine and anus. Basically, the structure of the
gastrointestinal tract is composed of four layers or tunics: the
mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa and serosa. The internal
mucosa is the absorptive and secretory layer. Goblet cells in the
mucosa secrete mucus for lubrication throughout most of the GI
tract. The mucosa is comprised of simple columnar epithelium which
is supported by a thin layer of connective tissue known as the lamina
propria. The muscularis mucosa surrounds the lamina propria, and it
is this segment that is responsible for the many folds in mucosa of
the GI tract. The submucosa covers the mucosa and is a highly
vascular connective tissue layer. Absorbed molecules pass into the
submucosa and are taken up by the blood vessels. The muscularis
externa has inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of smooth
muscle, and their combined activity is responsible for segmental and
peristaltic contractions. However, there are some modifications to
this structure in the stomach where the muscularis is comprised of


three rather than two layers: the longitudinal layer, the circular layer
and the oblique layer. The outer serosa layer is comprised of
connective tissue covered with a layer of squamous epithelium which
is referred to as the visceral peritoneum.
Upper gastrointestinal tract
In addition to the secretions produced by the GI tract, the digestive
accessory organs produce other secretions required for digestion.
Food is ingested via the mouth, and mastication, or the mechanical
act of chewing, involves the teeth, tongue and jaws. Approximately
1000 to 1200 mL of saliva is secreted by the salivary glands each
day. Saliva lubricates the oral and pharynx mucosa, cleanses the
teeth, moistens and binds food into a bolus for easier swallowing
and dissolves some food particles, which enhances taste. Saliva has
a slightly alkaline pH (6.0−7.0) and contains amylase (ptyalin), which
converts simple starches to disaccharides.
Deglutition, or swallowing, is under voluntary and involuntary control.
Mastication and the addition of saliva secretions results in a wet
bolus which the tongue moves towards the oropharynx. Sequential
contractions of the constrictor muscles in the pharynx facilitate the
movement of the bolus into the oesophagus. Peristalsis in the
oesophagus moves the bolus down the oesophagus and through the
cardiac sphincter into the stomach.


The stomach is a J-shaped pouch which is divided into four sections:
the cardia, fundus, body and pyloris. The gastric rugae, or thick
longitudinal mucosal folds, line the stomach and increase the
surface area during gastric distension on eating. The digestive
functions of the stomach include the partial digestion of protein and
fats; and some absorption occurs, primarily water, alcohol and
aspirin. Approximately 2−3 L of gastric secretions, which contain
water, salts, enzymes and hydrochloric acid, are produced daily by
the different cells in the gastric glands. These cells are the goblet
cells, which secrete mucus; the chief cells, which secrete
pepsinogen; the parietal cells, which secrete hydrochloric acid; G
cells, which secrete the hormone gastrin; and the argentaffin cells,
which secrete serotonin and histamine. In addition, the intrinsic
factor is secreted by the gastric mucosa and is required for the
absorption of vitamin B  in the intestine. The gastric secretions have
an acidic pH that ranges from 1.0−3.5. The gastric secretions
denature the food bolus in the stomach and convert it to a thick fluid
called chyme
. Peristalsis propels the chyme through the pyloris
into the C-shaped duodenum and beyond.
Small intestine
The small intestine is approximately 3 m long and is 2.5 cm in
diameter. It is divided into three segments: the duodenum is 25 cm
in length, the jejunum measures 1 m and the ileum 2 m.
Approximately 700−1200 mL of highly alkaline pancreatic juice (pH
8.0) and 500−700 mL of bile (pH 7.8) enter the duodenum daily via
the ampulla of Vater and aid digestive processes. These secretions
12


combine with the 2−3 L of small intestinal secretions to maintain the
soft chyme consistency.
Rapid absorption of nutrients, water and electrolytes occurs in the
small intestine. Absorption across the mucosal surface is rapid; it is
facilitated by the increased surface area that results from the
multiple folds in the mucosa and submucosa, called the plicae
circularis, and by microscopic finger-like projections called microvilli.
Digestion is further aided by the brush border enzymes produced by
the microvilli. Segmentation (churning contractions) mixes the
chyme and increases exposure to the intestinal mucosal surface,
while peristalsis (wave-like movement) moves it towards the
ileocaecal (ileocolic) valve, which is located at the junction of the
terminal ileum and caecum. Approximately 450 mL to as much as
1500 mL of chyme passes into the large intestine daily, and all but
about 100 mL is reabsorbed in the proximal half of the colon.
Large intestine
The large intestine or colon measures 1.5 m in length and is 6.5 cm
in diameter. It extends from the ileocaecal valve to the anus and is
divided into seven sections: the caecum; ascending, transverse,
descending and sigmoid colons; rectum; and anus (see Figure
52.1
).
Figure 52.1


A large intestine.
Source: B. F. Fremgen & S. S. Frucht . Medical Terminology: A Living Language (5th ed.), Figure 8.6, p. 263.
Reproduced with permission of Pearson Education, Inc., Upper Saddle River, NJ.
1 Fremgen, B. F. & Frucht, S. S. (2012). Medical Terminology: A Living Language (5th ed.),
Upper Saddle River, NJ: Pearson Education, Inc.
The large intestine is lined with mucous membrane. The muscle
fibres are both circular and longitudinal, permitting the intestine to
enlarge and contract in both width and length. There are three
longitudinal bands of muscles, or taeniae coli, which are shorter than
the colon and therefore cause the large intestine to form pouches,
or haustra
.
The colon’s main functions are the absorption of water and the few
remaining nutrients not absorbed by the small intestine, the mucoid
protection of the intestinal wall and faecal elimination. The contents
of the colon normally represent foods ingested over the previous 4
days, although most of the waste products are excreted within 48
hours of ingestion
. However, the transit time from ingestion to
evacuation differs between individuals.
The colon also serves a protective function in that it secretes mucus.
This mucus contains large amounts of bicarbonate ions. The mucus
secretion is stimulated by excitation of parasympathetic nerves.
During extreme stimulation—for example, as a result of emotions—
large amounts of mucus are secreted, resulting in the passage of
stringy mucus with little or no faeces. Mucus serves to protect the
wall of the large intestine from trauma by the acids formed in the
1


faeces, and it serves as an adherent for holding the faecal material
together. Mucus also protects the intestinal wall from bacterial
activity.
The colon acts to transport along its lumen the products of digestion,
which are eventually eliminated through the anal canal. These
products are flatus and faeces. Flatus
 is largely air and the by-
products of the digestion of carbohydrates. Three types of
movements occur in the large intestine: haustral churning, colon
peristalsis and mass peristalsis. Haustral churning
 involves
movement of the chyme back and forth within the haustra. In
addition to mixing the contents, this action aids in the absorption of
water and moves the contents forward to the next haustra.
Peristalsis
 is produced by the circular and longitudinal muscle
fibres of the intestinal walls; it propels the intestinal contents
forward. Peristaltic waves occur at a rate of 3 to 12 per minute on
average in the large intestine, compared with 17 to 18 per minute in
the small intestine. Mass peristalsis
, the third type of colonic
movement, involves a wave of powerful muscular contraction that
moves the contents of the colon over large areas. Usually mass
peristalsis occurs after eating; it is stimulated by the gastrocolic
reflex (presence of food in the stomach and small intestine). In
adults, mass peristaltic waves occur 2 to 3 times a day.
Rectum and anal canal
The rectum in the adult is usually 20 cm long; the most distal
portion, 2.5 to 3 cm in length, forms the anal canal. In the rectum


are folds that extend vertically. Each of the vertical folds contains a
vein and an artery. It is believed that these folds help retain faeces
within the rectum. When the veins become distended, as can occur
with repeated pressure, a condition known as haemorrhoids
occurs (see Figure 52.2
).
Figure 52.2


Internal and external haemorrhoids.


The anal canal is bounded by an internal and an external sphincter
muscle (see Figure 52.3
). The internal sphincter is under
involuntary control and the external sphincter normally is voluntarily
controlled. The internal sphincter muscle is innervated by the
autonomic nervous system; the external sphincter is innervated by
the somatic nervous system.
Figure 52.3


The rectum, anal canal and anal sphincters. A: Open, B: Closed.


Physiology of defecation
Defecation
 is the expulsion of faeces from the anus and rectum.
It is also called a bowel movement. The frequency of defecation is
highly individual, varying from several times per day to two or three
times per week. The amount defecated also varies from person to
person subject to the amount of food and dietary fibre ingested.
When peristaltic waves move the faeces into the sigmoid colon and
the rectum, the sensory nerves in the rectum are stimulated and the
individual becomes aware of the need to defecate. Stimulation of the
peripheral afferent nerve fibres in the rectum prompts the recto–anal
inhibitory reflex and the internal anal sphincter relaxes, allowing
faeces to move into the anal canal.
Stimulation of the stretch receptors in the rectum, proximal anal
canal and pelvic floor triggers the conscious awareness of a need to
defecate. Nerve receptors in the anal canal can differentiate
between the contents of the rectum; that is, the presence of formed
or liquid stool or flatus. It is because of this that individuals know
when they can safely pass flatus rather than stool.
Clinical consideration


Individuals with culturally diverse backgrounds
and children may use very different terms for a
bowel movement. The nurse may need to try
several common words before finding one the
person understands.
When a need to defecate is identified, and provided the time and
place is appropriate, an individual will squat on a toilet or commode.
Once seated, the external anal sphincter is relaxed voluntarily.
Expulsion of the faeces is assisted by straining and the Valsalva
manoeuvre (holding the breath while straining), which prompts
voluntary contraction of the abdominal muscles and the diaphragm.
Intra-abdominal pressure is increased and contraction of the
muscles of the pelvic floor and straightening of the anorectal angle
occurs, which facilitates the movement of the faeces through the
anal canal. Normal defecation is supported by thigh flexion, which
increases the pressure within the abdomen, and a squatting position
with legs comfortably apart and feet supported on the ground, which
increases the downward pressure on the rectum and straightens the
anorectal angle. The lower back should be straight and not slumped.
The anorectal angle is situated at the junction of the rectum and the
anal canal, and it is created by the sling effect of the relaxed
puborectalis muscle against the rectum. In the relaxed state, the
angle measures approximately 90 degrees and it forms a ‘flap
valve’, but during straining or defecation, the angle straightens and
can be measured at 135 degrees by defecating proctography, also


known as defecography (see image at <www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/
pmc/articles/PMC3228983/bin/jnm-17-416-g002.jpg>), a test
performed to see what happens to the pelvic floor during a bowel
movement (Schawkat et al. ). Following evacuation, the normal
anorectal angle is resumed, rectal pressures drop and the internal
anal sphincter closes the anal canal. The person who needs to use a
bedpan for defecation is at a disadvantage as they cannot avail
themselves of a good sitting position and must rely principally on the
Valsalva manoeuvre and straining to increase intra-abdominal
pressure to aid evacuation.
2 Schawkat, K., Heinrich, H., Parker, H., ... Reiner, C. (2018). How to define pathologic pelvic
floor descent in MR defecography during defecation? Abdominal Radiology, 43(12), 3233–
3240.
If the defecation reflex is ignored, or if defecation is consciously
inhibited by contracting the external sphincter muscle, the urge to
defecate normally disappears for a few hours before occurring
again. Repeated inhibition of the urge to defecate can result in
expansion of the rectum to accommodate accumulated faeces and
eventual loss of sensitivity to the need to defecate. Constipation and
faecal impaction can result. Faecal impaction and persistent rectal
distension alter the anorectal angle and result in increased rectal
pressures, which in turn stimulate internal anal sphincter relaxation
and leakage of stool. This is why people with frequent passing of
small liquid stools or encopresis (faecal incontinence) need to be
assessed for faecal impaction with overflow.
2


Faeces
Normal faeces are made up of about 75% water and 25% solid
materials such as undigested foods (cellulose, fats, proteins),
inorganic salts, bacteria (especially Escherichia coli) and epithelial
cells shed from the gastrointestinal tract. Faeces should be soft but
formed. If the faeces are propelled very quickly along the large
intestine, there is reduced time for most of the water in the chyme to
be reabsorbed and the faeces will be more fluid. Normal soft-formed
faecal consistency is dependent upon an adequate fluid intake;
faeces that contain less water will be hard and difficult to expel.
Faeces are normally brown, chiefly due to the presence of
stercobilin and urobilin, which are derived from bilirubin (a red
pigment in bile). Another factor that affects faecal colour is the
action of bacteria such as E. coli or Staphylococci, which are
normally present in the large intestine. The action of micro-
organisms on the chyme is also responsible for the odour of faeces.
Table 52.1
 lists the characteristics of faeces including normal and
abnormal, while Box 52.1
 lists the characteristics for the definition
of normal bowel functioning.
Table 52.1 Characteristics of faeces
BO X


52.1 Definitions of normal bowel
functioning
1. Soft, well-formed bowel movements.
2. Easily passed without pain.
3. Defecates 1–3 times a day to 3 times a week.
4. Able to control first urge to allow time to get to toilet.
5. Able to pass a motion within a minute of sitting on the
toilet.
6. Completely empties bowel in one sitting.
Source: Adapted from Continence Foundation of Australia . About Your Bowel. Retrieved from
<www.continence.org.au/pages/about-your-bowel.html>.
3 Continence Foundation of Australia (2016). About Your Bowel. Retrieved from
<www.continence.org.au>.
An adult usually forms 7 to 10 L of flatus (gas) in the large intestine
every 24 hours. The gases include carbon dioxide, methane,
hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. Some air is swallowed with food and
fluids taken by mouth, other gases are formed as a result of the
action of bacteria on the chyme in the large intestine and other gas
diffuses from the blood into the gastrointestinal tract.
3


Factors that affect defecation
Defecation patterns vary at different stages of life. Diet, fluid intake
and intolerances, activity, psychological factors such as anxiety and
depression, disability, certain medications, gastrointestinal infection
and disease processes can also affect defecation.
Development
Newborns and infants, toddlers, school-age children and
adolescents and older adults are groups within which members have
similarities in elimination patterns.
Newborns and infants
Meconium
 is the first faecal material passed by the newborn,
normally within 24 hours after birth. It is black, tarry, odourless and
sticky. Transitional stools, which follow for about a week, are
generally loose and greenish-yellow in colour, and contain mucus.
Newborns and infants pass stool frequently, often after each
feeding. Because the intestine is immature, water is not well
absorbed and the stool is soft, liquid and frequent. When the


intestine matures, bacterial flora increases in number. After solid
foods are introduced, the stool becomes less frequent and firmer.
Infants who are breastfed have light yellow to golden faeces; infants
who are taking formula will have dark yellow or tan stool which is
more formed. It should be noted that from 8 weeks of age,
breastfed babies’ bowel motion frequency can be highly variable—
babies may pass a motion after every feed or once every 10 days.
Caregivers can be encouraged to seek advice from health
professionals if they have any concerns (Amir & Bearzatto ).
4 Amir, L. H. & Bearzatto, A. (2016). Overcoming challenges faced by breastfeeding mothers.
Australian Family Physician, 45(8), 552–556.
Toddlers
Some control of defecation starts around 18 months to 2 years of
age. By this time, children have learned to walk and the nervous and
muscular systems are sufficiently well developed to permit bowel
control. A desire to control daytime bowel movements and to use
the toilet generally starts when the child becomes aware of (a) the
discomfort caused by a soiled nappy, and (b) the sensation that
indicates the need for a bowel movement. Daytime control is
typically attained by age 2½ after a process of toilet training.
Clinical consideration
4


Nurses may often find it difficult to describe
what the stool actually looks like. The Bristol
Stool Form Scale is useful in that it not only
categorises stools into different types, it also
gives a description of the type. A ‘normal’ stool
consistency may be defined as Type 3 or 4 on
the Bristol Stool Form Scale (see Figure
52.4
).
Bristol stool form scale
Figure 52.4


Bristol Stool Form Scale.
Source: Reproduced with the kind permission of Dr K. W. Heaton, Reader in
Medicine at the University of Bristol. © 2001 Norgine Pty Ltd.
School-age children and adolescents
School-age children and adolescents have bowel habits similar to
those of adults. Patterns of defecation vary in frequency, quantity
and consistency, although most children defecate at least every 2–3
days (Mitsuhashi et al. ). Constipation is a common condition in
children, with some school-age children delaying defecation because
of an activity such as play or unfamiliar surroundings which, if
prolonged, may lead to a cycle of withholding and passage of hard
5


stool. Passage of hard stool can be painful, which can lead to
apprehension, retention and further painful defecation (The Royal
Children’s Hospital (RCH) 2017).
5 Mitsuhashi, S. G., Ballou, S., Jiang, Z., ... Lembo, A. (2018). Characterizing normal bowel
frequency and consistency in a representative sample of adults in the United States
(NHANES). American Journal of Gastroenterology, 113(1), 115–123.
Older adults
Constipation is also a common bowel management problem in the
older person. This is due in part to reduced activity levels,
inadequate amounts of fluid and fibre intake, and muscle weakness.
Many older people believe that ‘regularity’ means a bowel movement
every day. Those who do not meet this criterion often seek over-the-
counter preparations to relieve what they believe to be constipation.
Older people should be advised that normal patterns of bowel
elimination vary considerably. For some, a normal pattern may be
every second day; for others, twice a day. Adequate roughage in the
diet, adequate exercise and 6 to 8 glasses of fluid daily are essential
preventive measures for constipation. Clear fluids are recommended
instead of tea or coffee (Joanna Briggs Institute ).
6 Joanna Briggs Institute (2008). Management of constipation in older adults. Best Practice,
12(7), 1–4. Retrieved from <http://joannabriggs.org>.
Responding to the gastrocolic reflex
 (increased peristalsis of the
colon after food has entered the stomach) is also an important
consideration. For example, toileting is recommended 30–40
6


minutes after meals, when the gastrocolic and duodenocolic reflexes
are strongest (Mann ). The older person should be warned that
consistent use of laxatives inhibits natural defecation reflexes and
may cause, rather than cure, constipation due to nerve damage.
7 Mann, E. (2016). Evidence summary: Management of constipation: Hospitalized patients. In
The Joanna Briggs Institute, Aged Care Practice Manual, 161–164. Retrieved from
<http://connect.jbiconnectplus.org>.
Diet
Sufficient bulk (cellulose or fibre) in the diet is necessary to provide
faecal volume. Bland diets and diets consisting of mainly processed
foods are low in natural fibre and therefore lack the bulk that creates
sufficient faecal volume in the rectum to stimulate the reflex for
defecation. Low-residue foods, such as rice, eggs and lean meats,
move more slowly through the intestinal tract. Increasing fluid intake
with a diet that contains substantially more portions of fresh fruit,
vegetables, legumes, seeds and whole grains will increase the rate
of peristaltic function.
Certain foods are difficult or impossible for some people to digest.
This inability results in digestive upsets and, in some instances, the
passage of watery stools. Irregular eating can also impair regular
defecation. Individuals who eat at the same times every day usually
have a regularly timed, physiological response to the food intake and
a regular pattern of peristaltic activity in the colon.
7


Spicy foods can produce diarrhoea and flatus in some individuals.
Excessive sugar can also cause diarrhoea. Other foods that may
influence bowel elimination include the following:
gas-producing foods: cabbage, onions, cauliflower, broccoli,
brussels sprouts, wheat and bran, carbonated drinks
laxative-producing foods: bran, prunes, figs, chocolate, spices.
Dietary fibre
Fibre absorbs water and makes stools bulkier. Natural fibre that is
contained in the foods we eat is classed as insoluble fibre and
soluble fibre. Insoluble fibre adds bulk to the stool, increases the
peristaltic action and enhances elimination regularity. Sources of
insoluble fibre are found in whole grains, seeds, nuts, wheat, corn
and rice cereals, unprocessed bran, fibrous vegetables, pumpkin,
peas, cabbage, cauliflower, broccoli and fruits such as pears and
apples with skin intact. Soluble fibre attracts water and turns into a
gel during digestion, which in turn slows down digestion. Sources of
natural soluble fibre are found in psyllium husks, oats, barley, rye
legumes, most vegetables, bananas and oranges. Some people
may require fibre supplements, also known as bulking agents, that
are soluble. Examples include:
Metamucil™
natural psyllium husks (available at health food stores); this
product can also be used with children
guar gum (Benefibre™).


Be cautious when administering bulking agents to the frail, immobile
or elderly, or people who have faecal impaction, as these
supplements can decrease peristalsis and increase the risk of
impaction (Schuster, Kosar & Kamrul ).
8 Schuster, B., Kosar, L. & Kamrul, R. (2015). Constipation in older adults: Stepwise approach
to keep things moving. Canadian Family Physician, 61(2), 152–158.
Fluid
Even when fluid intake is inadequate or output (e.g. urine or
vomitus) is excessive for some reason, the body continues to
reabsorb fluid from the chyme as it passes along the colon. The
chyme becomes drier than normal, resulting in hard faeces. In
addition, reduced fluid intake slows the chyme’s passage along the
intestines, further increasing the reabsorption of fluid from the
chyme. Healthy faecal elimination usually requires a daily fluid intake
of 1500 to 2000 mL for an adult. Children have varying fluid
requirements dependent on age, weight and condition. If chyme
moves abnormally quickly through the large intestine, however, there
is less time for fluid to be absorbed through the intestinal mucosa
and into the blood; as a result, the faeces are soft or even watery.
Physical activity
Physical activity stimulates peristalsis, thus facilitating the movement
of chyme along the colon. Weak abdominal and pelvic muscles are
8


often ineffective in increasing the intra-abdominal pressure during
defecation or in controlling defecation. Weak muscles can result
from lack of exercise, disability, immobility or impaired neurological
functioning. People confined to bed may experience constipation.
Psychological factors
Some people who are anxious, angry or frightened experience
increased peristaltic activity and subsequent nausea or diarrhoea. In
contrast, people who are depressed may experience slowed
intestinal motility, resulting in constipation. How a person responds to
these emotional states is the result of individual differences in the
response of the enteric nervous system to vagal stimulation from the
brain. Constipation is a common problem in children, particularly
around the time of toilet training or after a painful or frightening
bowel movement, such as doing a hard or painful poo (RCH ).
Healthy bowel habits and encouraging regular, timed ‘sitting’ on the
toilet is recommended for children (RCH 2017).
9 The Royal Children’s Hospital (RCH) (2017). Clinical Practice Guideline on Constipation.
Melbourne. Retrieved from <www.rch.org.au>. BIB>
Defecation habits
9


Early bowel training may establish the habit of defecating at a
regular time. Many people defecate after breakfast, when the
gastrocolic reflex causes a mass peristaltic wave in the large
intestine. If a person ignores this urge to defecate, water continues
to be reabsorbed, making the faeces hard and difficult to expel.
When the normal defecation reflexes are inhibited or ignored, these
conditioned reflexes tend to be progressively weakened and
ultimately lost. Adults may ignore these reflexes because of the
pressures of time or work, or unfamiliar or unhygienic toilets.
Hospitalised individuals may suppress the urge because of
embarrassment about using a bedpan, lack of privacy or defecation
being too uncomfortable due to surgery or disease processes.
Medications
Many drugs have side effects that can interfere with normal
elimination. Some cause diarrhoea; others, such as large doses of
certain tranquillisers and repeated administration of pain medications
such as morphine and codeine, cause constipation because they
decrease gastrointestinal activity through their action on the central
nervous system. Iron tablets, which have an astringent effect, act
more locally on the bowel mucosa to cause constipation.
Some medications directly affect elimination. Laxatives
 (also
referred to as aperients
) are medications that stimulate bowel
activity and so assist faecal elimination. Other medications soften


stool, facilitating defecation. Certain medications suppress peristaltic
activity and may be used to treat diarrhoea.
Medications also affect the appearance of the faeces. Any drug that
causes gastrointestinal bleeding (e.g. aspirin products) can cause
the stool to be red or black. Iron salts lead to black stool because of
the oxidation of the iron; antibiotics may cause a grey-green
discolouration; and antacids can cause a whitish discolouration or
white specks in the stool.
Diagnostic procedures
Before certain diagnostic procedures, such as visualisation of the
colon (colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy), the person is fasted. The
person may also be given a cleansing enema or oral bowel cleansing
solutions such as polyethylene glycol-electrolyte (CoLyte™,
GoLYTELY™) or sodium picosulfate (Picolax™) prior to the
examination. Normal defecation following these procedures usually
will not occur until eating resumes. In paediatrics, an inpatient may
be given ColonLYTELY™ or Glycoprep™ to clear the bowel; for an
outpatient, Movicol™ is commonly used (RCH 2017). These
products may also be used to treat faecal impaction.
Anaesthesia and surgery


General anaesthetics cause the normal colonic movements to cease
or slow by blocking parasympathetic stimulation to the muscles of
the colon. People who have regional or spinal anaesthesia are less
likely to experience this problem.
Surgery that involves direct handling of the intestines can cause
temporary cessation of intestinal movement. This condition, called
paralytic ileus, usually lasts 24 to 48 hours. Monitoring the individual
post surgery for return of bowel sounds and function is important.
The nurse should listen for bowel sounds that reflect intestinal
motility, assess for vomiting and abdominal distension and question
the person as to whether they have passed flatus or have had a
bowel motion.
Pathological conditions
Spinal cord injuries and head injuries can decrease the sensory
stimulation for defecation. A disability or impaired mobility may limit
the person’s ability to respond to the urge to defecate and the
person may experience constipation. Or a person may experience
faecal incontinence because of poorly functioning anal sphincters.
Clinical consideration


A person who has experienced abdominal
surgery and has an absence of bowel sounds
(thus is not passing flatus), has a distended
abdomen and is experiencing nausea or
vomiting may have a paralytic ileus. Food
should be withheld and the person should be
reviewed immediately by a doctor to determine
if management is necessary to rest the gut.
Pain
A person who experiences discomfort when defecating (e.g.
following haemorrhoid surgery or from prolonged withholding in
children) often suppresses the urge to defecate to avoid the pain.
The person can experience constipation as a result. People taking
narcotic analgesics for pain may also experience constipation as a
side effect of the medication.
Pregnancy
Pregnancy can cause a change in bowel movements. This is
particularly apparent as the pregnancy advances and the size of the
fetus increases, with pressure being exerted on the rectum.
Additionally, during pregnancy, especially during the third trimester, a


slowing of peristalsis and an increase in water absorption in the large
bowel may lead to constipation. Straining with constipation, together
with a change in hormones, can lead to the development of
haemorrhoids.


Faecal elimination problems
Four common problems are related to faecal elimination:
constipation, diarrhoea, encopresis (faecal incontinence) and
flatulence.
Constipation
Constipation
 may be defined as fewer than three bowel
movements per week. This infers the passage of dry, hard stool or
the passage of no stool. It occurs when the movement of faeces
through the large intestine is slow, thus allowing time for additional
reabsorption of fluid from the large intestine. Associated difficulty in
evacuation of stool and increased effort or straining of the voluntary
muscles of defecation results. The person may also have a feeling
of incomplete stool evacuation after defecation. Box 52.2
 lists the
frequent defining characteristics of constipation.
BO X
52.2 Sample defining characteristics
of constipation


Decreased frequency of defecation.
Hard, dry, formed stools.
Straining at stool; painful defecation.
Reports of rectal fullness or pressure or incomplete bowel
evacuation.
Abdominal pain, cramps or distension.
Anorexia, nausea.
Headache.
Many causes and factors contribute to constipation. Among them
are the following:
insufficient fibre and fluid intake
insufficient activity or immobility
irregular defecation habits
change in daily routine
lack of privacy
inaccessible toileting facilities
reliance on other people for assistance
poor gut motility or slow transit times
chronic use of laxatives or enemas
gastrointestinal disorders: irritable bowel syndrome (IBS),
Hirschsprung disease, diverticulosis, pelvic floor dysfunction
coeliac disease
cancer or cancer-related causes
neurological conditions (e.g. Parkinson’s disease), stroke or
paralysis


emotional disturbances such as depression, anxiety or mental
confusion
medications such as opioids, iron supplements, antihistamines,
antacids and antidepressants.
Careful assessment of the person’s habits is necessary before a
diagnosis of constipation is made. A thorough assessment should be
conducted by the nurse to determine if the person is constipated or
at risk of constipation. Box 52.3
 presents cues that should be
used by the nurse when conducting an assessment. While this
information has been designed for the older adult, many of the
elements could be used when assessing any person.
BO X
52.3 Assessment cues to determine
risk of constipation
The priority is to gain an overview of the person’s current
pattern of bowel function and to identify factors that may be
impacting on the person’s normal bowel function:
review dietary fibre intake
discuss impaired mobility or recent reductions in level of
activity
discuss low fluid intake; for example, less than 1.5 L per
day


review medications
identify any surgery or disease that may contribute to
development of constipation.
The person’s normal bowel pattern, toileting preferences and
current status should be determined. This would include:
recent changes in bowel habits or frequency of
movements
consistency/type of stool—number on the Bristol Stool
Chart can be used
normal activities to maintain bowel function (e.g. what
works for them)
presence of faecal incontinence, including soiling
underwear
need for frequent straining during toileting
if recent illness (e.g. stroke), what was their normal prior
bowel pattern
if any laxatives are being taken, what type, frequency and
length of time of use.
Any symptoms of constipation should be identified; for
instance:
nausea, vomiting or rectal pain on defecation
straining during defecation or infrequent bowel
movements
feelings of incomplete emptying after bowel movements
abdominal pain or discomfort


hard stools.
Source: A. Bardsley
. Assessment and treatment options for patients with constipation. British
Journal of Nursing, 26(6), 312–318. https://doi.org/10.12968/bjon.2017.26.6.312.
10 Bardsley, A. (2017). Assessment and treatment options for patients with constipation. British
Journal of Nursing, 26(6), 312–318. https://doi.org/10.12968/bjon.2017.26.6.312.
Constipation can cause health problems for some people. In order to
prevent constipation, nurses have a responsibility to provide
education to the person and their family (see ‘Patient
education
’).
Faecal impaction
Faecal impaction
 is a mass or collection of hardened faeces in
the rectum. Impaction results from prolonged retention and
accumulation of faecal material. In severe impaction, the faeces
accumulate and extend well up into the sigmoid colon and beyond.
Faecal impaction can be recognised by the passage of liquid faecal
seepage (diarrhoea) and no normal stool. The liquid portion of the
faeces seeps out around the impacted mass. Impaction can be
determined after assessing the person’s history and their bowel
movement pattern; the type of stool they have been passing; an
abdominal assessment including inspection of the abdomen,
auscultation for bowel sounds and a gentle palpation of the
abdomen. Only if policy of the organisation permits, a gentle and
cautious digital examination of the rectum is performed to ascertain
the presence of a hardened faecal mass. A digital examination
10


should only ever be performed by the most experienced nurse,
Nurse Practitioner or doctor (if organisation policy permits). Caution
is required during this procedure due to the risks of trauma and
other complications. Should digital examination be contraindicated
and impaction has not been determined, further assessment may be
required such as an abdominal x-ray.
Along with faecal seepage and constipation, symptoms include
frequent but non-productive desire to defecate and rectal pain. A
generalised feeling of illness results; the person becomes anorexic,
the abdomen becomes distended and nausea and vomiting may
occur.
The causes of faecal impaction are usually poor defecation habits
and constipation. The barium used in radiological examinations of
the upper and lower gastrointestinal tracts can also be a causative
factor. Therefore, after these examinations, laxatives or enemas are
usually taken to ensure removal of the barium. Although faecal
impaction should be prevented, special management is required
should it occur and should be ordered by the doctor or Nurse
Practitioner. Management will most likely involve enemas to clear the
rectum; however, it may also include osmotic or stimulant laxatives.
When normal bowel function is restored, a bowel management
program must begin so that the impaction does not occur again (De
Giorgio et al.
).
13 De Giorgio, R., Ruggeri, E., Stanghellini, V., Eusebi, L. H., Bazzoli, F. & Chiarioni, G.
(2015). Chronic constipation in the elderly: A primer for the gastroenterologist. BMC
Gastroenterology, 15, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12876-015-0366-3.
13


In order to prevent faecal impaction, constipation should be avoided
(see previous ‘Patient education
’). Importantly, nurses need to
carefully monitor the person’s bowel functioning, including bowel
sounds, bowel movements and evidence of abdominal distension.
Patient safety competency framework
2 Therapeutic communication
Therapeutic communication is central to
providing safe and responsive nursing practice.
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must
demonstrate therapeutic communication by
using verbal and non-verbal communication
skills to convey respect and empathy and to
encourage the person to express their feelings
and needs (Levett-Jones et al.
).
15 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Discussing bowel functioning can be a difficult
and embarrassing topic for many people. It is
crucial that the nurse and student nurse employ
effective communication skills, adapting
terminology as required to ensure the person
15


feels they can both openly discuss bowel habit
concerns and also understand any confusing
terminology. For example, the nurse may ask a
child, ‘Have you had a poo today?’ as opposed
to ‘Have you had a bowel motion today?’.
Diarrhoea
Diarrhoea
 refers to the passage of liquid faeces and an increased
frequency of defecation. It is the opposite of constipation and results
from rapid movement of faecal contents through the large intestine.
Rapid passage of chyme reduces the time available for the large
intestine to reabsorb water and electrolytes. Some people pass stool
with increased frequency, but diarrhoea is not present unless the
stool is relatively unformed and excessively liquid. The person with
diarrhoea finds it difficult or impossible to control the urge to
defecate for very long. Diarrhoea and the threat of incontinence are
sources of concern and embarrassment. Often, spasmodic cramps
are associated with diarrhoea. Bowel sounds are increased.
Persistent diarrhoea may lead to irritation or pruritis of the anal
region which may extend to the perineum and buttocks. Fatigue,
weakness, malaise and emaciation are the results of prolonged
diarrhoea and are associated with water and electrolyte loss and
malnutrition.


When the cause of diarrhoea is infective irritants in the intestinal
tract, diarrhoea is thought to be a protective flushing mechanism. It
can create serious fluid and electrolyte losses in the body which can
develop within frighteningly short periods of time, particularly in
infants, small children and older adults. Table 52.2
 lists some of
the major causes of diarrhoea and the physiological responses of
the body.
Table 52.2 Major causes of diarrhoea
Patient education
Individual and family teaching to prevent constipation
Educate the person about the importance of a high-fibre
diet (e.g. aim up to 18–30 g of dietary fibre per day).
However, increases should be introduced slowly.
Examples of fibre sources are cereals, nuts and seeds,
wholemeal breads, vegetables (particularly raw
vegetables) and fruits. Encourage the person to chew
their food well.
Educate the person about the function of the bowel and
the importance of adequate fluid intake. The person
should be encouraged to have a fluid intake of 1500–2000
mL of caffeine-free, non-alcoholic fluid in a 24-hour period
unless contraindicated. Examples of fluid include water
and fruit juice. Avoid caffeine, such as coffee, tea and
cola, and limit alcohol usage.


Encourage the person to monitor and record bowel
movements for frequency, character, pattern, episodes of
constipation or faecal soiling, and the use of oral or rectal
laxatives (see Figure 52.5
 for an example of a bowel
habit diary).
Educate the person about the importance of exercise and
promote exercise. For the person who may be bedridden
or confined to a wheelchair, passive exercises should be
encouraged.
Encourage the establishment of a regular time to defecate
and not to delay the urge.
Educate the person about good habits for bowel emptying
(see Box 52.4
).
BO X
52.4 Good habits for bowel
emptying
People should be educated not to delay the
urge to defecate.
The most common time of the day to get the
urge to defecate is first thing in the morning or
following a meal. Olfactory, visual and auditory
privacy should be ensured; otherwise, the
person may suppress the urge to defecate.
The person should be educated as to the best
sitting position for bowel emptying (see Figure


52.6
):
Figure 52.6
Correct sitting position for bowel emptying.
- Lean forward a little and rest your elbows on
your knees.
- Have your knees higher than your hips. You
can do this by lifting your heels. Think of being


on tiptoes. It may help to put a stool under your
feet.
- Push your lower belly out. This helps to relax
your anal sphincter muscles.
Note: for people who have had recent hip surgery,
DO NOT USE this toilet position. Check first with
the doctor.
Sources: A. Bardsley (2017). Assessment and treatment options for patients with
constipation. British Journal of Nursing, 26(6), 312–318, https://doi.org/10.12968/
bjon.2017.26.6.312; Department of Health and Ageing, National Continence
Management Strategy
. Looking After Your Bowel. A Guide to Improving Bowel
Function. Commonwealth of Australia. Retrieved from www.bladderbowel.gov.au/
assets/doc/LookingAfter YourBowel.html; Figure © Continence Foundation of
Australia 2015.
12 Department of Health and Ageing, National Continence Management Strategy
(2013). Looking After Your Bowel. A Guide to Improving Bowel Function.
Commonwealth of Australia. Retrieved from <www.bladderbowel.gov.au>.
Educate the person about medications for the bowel and
the risk of dependence, and encourage them to discuss
their usage of laxatives, stool softeners and enemas with
their doctor.

Practice, 12(7), 1–4. Retrieved from <http://joannabriggs.org/index.html>.
