Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS Standard: Preventing and controlling
healthcare-associated infection
‘The intention of this standard is to reduce the risk of patients
acquiring preventable healthcare-associated infections,
effectively manage infections if they occur, and limit the
development of antimicrobial resistance through prudent use
of antimicrobials as part of antimicrobial stewardship.’
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care
, p. 22)
14 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
Implementing this standard is achieved by the
establishment of evidence-based systems to
support and promote infection prevention and
control, the safe and appropriate prescribing
and use of antimicrobials and the adherence to
11
14


national standards in the reprocessing of
reusable equipment.
Caring for individuals experiencing faecal
elimination disorders will often result in contact
with faeces. Compliance with national hand
hygiene guidelines and occupational health and
safety policies (including the proper use of
personal protective equipment) is imperative to
protect the patients and health care workers.
The irritating effects of diarrhoea increase the risk of perianal skin
breakdown. Therefore, the area around the anal region should be
kept clean and dry and be protected with skin-barrier protective films
or emollients. In addition, a faecal collector can be used if
appropriate (see page 1425).
Real-world practice
Monitoring the person’s bowel movement, including the
colour, consistency, amount, frequency and regularity,
are all part of the nurse’s role. There are conflicting
definitions of the frequency of ‘normal’ bowel sounds in
the literature, with rates varying from 5 to 30 every


minute to 1 every 5 to 10 seconds; however, there was
consensus that a complete lack of bowel sounds was
abnormal (Felder et al.
). A colon that is full of stool
will feel like a firm round mass when palpated. This can
sometimes be confused with a distended bladder,
which will feel like a smooth round mass above the
symphysis pubis. Nurses should question the person
on a daily basis about their bowel function and record
this accurately. Additionally, when questioned, the
person may respond with the word ‘normal’. It is
important to remember that what is normal for one
person may not be for another. Hence, the nurse
needs to question further.
16 Felder, S., Margel, D., Murrell, Z. & Fleshner, P. (2014). Usefulness of
bowel sound auscultation: A prospective evaluation. Journal of Surgical
Education, 71(5), 768–773. Doi: 10.1016/j.jsurg.2014.02.003.
One method of communicating specific amounts could
be by charting ‘½ cup or 1 cup’. In some organisations,
specific codes may be used on bowel charts to
facilitate clear documentation. Describing the stool by
using tools such as the Bristol Stool Form Scale can
be helpful in documentation. It is also important to
remember that a person’s bowel habits can change
while in hospital. For example, a change in exercise
patterns, diet, a reduction in fluid intake and pain may
cause constipation. Additionally, the thought of having
16


to use a bedpan or a communal toilet may cause the
person to withhold from defecating.
—Adapted from Jane Reintges MS, RN, CRRN APRN-bc
Encopresis
Encopresis
, also called faecal incontinence
, refers to the
loss of voluntary ability to control faecal and gaseous discharges
through the anal sphincter. The incontinence may occur at specific
times, such as after meals, or it may occur irregularly. Two types of
bowel incontinence
 are described: partial and major. Partial
incontinence is the inability to control flatus or to prevent minor
soiling. Major incontinence is the inability to control faeces of normal
consistency.
Faecal incontinence is generally associated with impaired functioning
of the anal sphincter or its nerve supply, such as in some
neuromuscular diseases, spinal cord trauma and tumours of the
external anal sphincter muscle.
Functional bowel disorders and faecal incontinence are estimated to
affect 33% of health care seekers in Australia (Ng et al.
). Faecal
incontinence is an emotionally distressing problem that can
ultimately lead to social isolation and loss of quality of life. Several
17


surgical procedures are used for the treatment of faecal
incontinence. These include repair of the sphincter and faecal
diversion (colostomy
 or ileostomy).
17 Ng, K. S., Nassar, N., Hamd, K., Nagarajah, A. & Gladman, M. A. (2015). Prevalence of
functional bowel disorders and faecal incontinence: An Australian primary care survey.
Colorectal Disease, 17(2), 150–159. Doi: 10.1111/codi.12808.
Flatulence
There are three primary sources of flatus: (1) action of bacteria on
the chyme in the large intestine; (2) swallowed air; and (3) gas that
diffuses between the bloodstream and the intestine.
Most gases that are swallowed are expelled through the mouth by
eructation (belching). However, large amounts of gas can
accumulate in the stomach, resulting in gastric distension. The
gases formed in the large intestine are chiefly absorbed through the
intestinal capillaries into the circulation.
Flatulence
 is the presence of excessive flatus in the intestines
and leads to stretching and inflation of the intestines (intestinal
distension). Flatulence can occur in the colon from a variety of
causes, such as foods (e.g. cabbage, onions, spices) or abdominal
surgery. If the gas is propelled by increased colonic activity before it
can be absorbed, it may be expelled through the anus. If excessive


gas cannot be expelled through the anus, it may be necessary to
insert a rectal tube to remove it.
Diagnostic investigations
Clinical inspection of faecal specimens can indicate pathological
conditions such as gastrointestinal haemorrhages, infection and
parasites. Pathological investigations can confirm the presence of
occult blood, infective organisms and parasites.
Faecal specimens
Collection of faecal specimens is described in Chapter 35
.
Attention is also given there to patient education and lifespan
considerations.
Diagnostic examinations
Examinations can be performed to view the gastrointestinal tract via
a direct or an indirect approach.
Direct viewing
The doctor uses instruments such as an endoscope that are
introduced via the mouth to view the upper gastrointestinal tract or


via the rectum to view the lower gastrointestinal tract. See Chapter
35
.
The instrument used for viewing allows inspection of the mucosa,
blood vessels and organ parts.
Indirect viewing
This method relies on radiological examinations such as plain x-ray
or contrast studies (barium or gastrogafin), enemas or defecating
proctograms. In order to enable a viewing of the deeper
gastrointestinal structures, the person is given a contrast medium
such as barium which is either ingested or administered via an
enema. If ingested, the upper gastrointestinal tract is then studied
via an x-ray. The doctor is able to view the lower oesophagus,
stomach and duodenum. If having the barium via an enema, the
lower colon can be viewed.
Patient safety competency framework
1 Person-centred care
Person-centred care indicates that the nursing
student must demonstrate an ability to provide
holistic nursing care that upholds an individual’s
needs and preferences (Levett-Jones et al.
2017).


Faecal elimination patterns can vary greatly
from person to person and the topic can be
embarrassing for some people. The student
nurse should employ therapeutic communication
skills to determine the individual’s
comprehension and preferences for terminology
when discussing elimination patterns, stool
characteristics and toileting preferences and
behaviours.


Nursing management
Assessing
Assessment of faecal elimination includes taking a nursing history;
performing a physical examination of the abdomen, rectum and
anus; and inspecting the faeces. The nurse also should review any
data obtained from relevant diagnostic tests.
Nursing history
A nursing history for faecal elimination helps the nurse ascertain the
person’s normal pattern. The nurse elicits a description of usual
faeces and any recent changes and collects information about any
past or current problems with elimination, the presence of a stoma
and factors influencing the elimination pattern.
Examples of questions to elicit this information are shown in the
‘Assessment interview’. The number of questions to ask is adapted
to the individual person, according to the person’s responses in the
first three categories. For example, questions about factors
influencing elimination might be addressed only to people who are
experiencing problems.


When eliciting data about the person’s defecation pattern, the nurse
needs to understand that the time of defecation and the amount of
faeces expelled are as individual as the frequency of defecation.
Often, the patterns individuals follow largely depend on early training
and on convenience.
Physical examination
Physical examination of the abdomen in relation to faecal elimination
problems includes inspection, auscultation, percussion and palpation
with specific reference to the intestinal tract. Auscultation precedes
palpation because palpation can alter peristalsis. Examination of the
rectum and anus includes inspection and palpation. Physical
examination of the abdomen, rectum and anus is discussed in
Chapter 31
.
Assessment interview
Faecal elimination
Defecation pattern
When do you usually have a bowel movement?
Has this pattern changed recently?


Description of faeces and any
changes
What do your stools usually look like? Have you noticed
any changes in the colour, texture (hard, soft, watery),
shape or odour of your stool recently?
Faecal elimination problems
What problems have you had or do you now have with
your bowel movements (constipation, diarrhoea,
excessive flatulence, seepage or incontinence)?
When and how often does it occur?
What do you think causes it (food, fluids, exercise,
emotions, medications, disease, surgery)?
What have you tried to solve the problem and how
effective was it?
Factors influencing elimination
Use of elimination aids. What routines do you follow to
maintain your usual defecation pattern? Do you use
natural aids such as specific foods or fluids (e.g. a glass
of hot lemon juice before breakfast), laxatives or enemas
to maintain elimination?


Diet. What foods do you believe affect defecation? What
foods do you typically eat? What foods do you avoid? Do
you take meals at regular times?
Fluid. What amount and kind of fluid do you take each day
(e.g. 6 glasses of water, 2 cups of coffee)?
Exercise. What is your usual daily exercise pattern?
(Obtain specifics about exercise rather than asking
whether it is sufficient; ideas of what is sufficient vary
between individuals.)
Medications. What medications do you take? Have you
taken any medications that could affect the intestinal tract
(e.g. iron, antibiotics)?
Stress. Are you experiencing any stress? Do you think
this affects your defecation pattern? How?
Inspecting the faeces
Observe the person’s stool for colour, consistency, shape, amount,
odour and the presence of abnormal constituents. Table 52.1
,
earlier in this chapter, summarises normal and abnormal
characteristics of stool and possible causes. A description of the
stool can also be facilitated by using tools such as the Bristol Stool
Form Scale (see Figure 52.4
).
Diagnostic studies


Diagnostic studies of the gastrointestinal tract include direct
visualisation techniques, indirect visualisation techniques and
laboratory tests for abnormal constituents (see Chapter 35
).
Diagnosing
The nursing diagnosis is the judgment made after conducting a
systematic assessment, collecting both subjective and objective
cues. The nursing diagnosis can be an actual diagnosis or a risk
diagnosis (see Chapter 13
).
Examples of nursing risk diagnoses include:
Risk of constipation related to decreased mobility
Risk of emotional distress related to bowel incontinence.
Examples of actual diagnoses include:
Diarrhoea related to food poisoning as evidenced by frequent
passing of loose watery stool
Faecal impaction related to reduced mobility and overuse of
bulking agents as evidenced by distended abdomen, liquid stool
overflow and 5 days since last normal bowel movement.
Risk of impaired skin integrity related to:
a. prolonged diarrhoea
b. bowel incontinence
c. bowel diversion via a stoma


Low self-esteem related to:
a. stoma
b. faecal incontinence
c. flatulence
d. need for assistance with toileting
Disturbed body image related to:
a. stoma
b. bowel incontinence
Deficient knowledge (bowel training, stoma management) related
to lack of previous experience
Anxiety related to:
a. lack of control of faecal elimination secondary to a stoma
b. response of others to a stoma.
Planning
The major goals for the person with faecal elimination problems are
to:
Maintain or restore normal bowel elimination pattern.
Maintain or regain normal stool consistency.
Prevent associated risks such as fluid and electrolyte imbalance,
skin breakdown, abdominal distension and pain.


Appropriate preventive and corrective nursing interventions that
relate to these must be identified. Specific nursing activities
associated with each of these interventions can be selected to meet
the person’s individual needs. Examples of clinical applications of
these using the nursing diagnosis are shown in ‘Identifying nursing
diagnoses, outcomes and interventions’ and in the ‘Nursing care
plan’ at the end of the chapter.
Lifespan considerations
Factors in potential bowel elimination problems
Children
Successful toilet training can prevent many problems with
elimination. The child and family should be assessed for
‘readiness to train’. Assess the child’s physical, cognitive
and interpersonal skills and parental readiness. Consider:
Does the child have sphincter control (usually by 18 to 24
months)? Does the child understand the meaning of
toileting? Is the child able to express themself and do they
demonstrate interest in learning? Are the parents ready to
work with the child?
Encourage a regular toileting routine for children. When
toilet training, ensure that toddlers can rest their feet
comfortably on the floor or foot stool; a toilet ring can also
be placed over the toilet. Ensure children are not


frightened or pressured while toileting; keep toileting a
positive experience.
An acute episode of dehydration and constipation (often
related to an illness) can lead to chronic stool problems.
Constipation can cause painful defecation, which causes
the child to withhold stool, leading to more severe
constipation, more pain on defecation, more withholding
and so on. Breaking the cycle by helping ease defecation
is important to prevent long-term problems.
Older adults
Poor fluid intake and inability to eat a high-fibre diet, as
well as swallowing or chewing difficulties, are often causes
of constipation.
Medications that are commonly taken by older adults such
as antacids, many antihypertensives, antidepressants,
diuretics and narcotics for pain also contribute to
constipation.
The person receiving tube feedings can experience
diarrhoea. To alleviate it, they require a change of
formula, a change in its strength or a change in the speed
or temperature of tube feeding administration.
The person receiving laxative preparation for x-rays or
other procedures may experience fluid and electrolyte
imbalances due to diarrhoea.
The person with cognitive impairment, such as
Alzheimer’s disease, may be unaware of what and when


they eat or drink, or of their bowel habits. These should be
monitored by the caregiver, whether the person is being
cared for at home or in an institution, to note any special
needs or concerns.
The disabled person or a person with impaired mobility
may have difficulty getting to the bathroom or using a
regular toilet. A raised toilet seat and other devices, such
as bars to assist in ambulation, may be helpful. The
decrease in activity may also contribute to constipation.
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
The person with faecal elimination problems
Implementing
Promoting regular defecation
The nurse can help the person achieve regular defecation by
attending to (a) the provision of privacy, (b) toileting timing, (c)
nutrition and fluids, (d) exercise and (e) positioning. See ‘Patient
education’ for healthy habits related to bowel elimination.


Privacy
Privacy during defecation is extremely important to many people.
The nurse should therefore provide as much privacy as possible for
the person but may need to stay with those who are too weak to be
left alone. Some people also prefer to wipe, wash and dry
themselves after defecating. A nurse may need to provide water and
a washcloth and towel for this purpose.
Timing
A person should be encouraged to defecate when the urge is
recognised. To establish regular bowel elimination, the person and
nurse can discuss when mass peristalsis normally occurs and
provide time for defecation. Many people have well-established
routines. Other activities of daily living should not interfere with the
defecation time.
Patient education
Healthy defecation
Educate the person about healthy bowel functioning.
Establish a regular exercise regimen.
Include high-fibre foods, such as vegetables, fruits and
whole grains, in the diet.
Maintain fluid intake of 1500 to 2000 mL a day in an adult.
Normal daily fluid intake recommendations for children are
dependent on age and weight.


Do not ignore the urge to defecate.
Educate about the correct positioning (see Figure
52.6
).
Allow time to defecate, preferably at the same time each
day.
Educate about the importance of olfactory, visual and
auditory privacy so as not to suppress the urge to
defecate.
Seek medical advice on medications to treat chronic
diarrhoea or constipation.
Nutrition and fluids
The diet for regular normal elimination varies depending on the kind
of faeces the person currently experiences, the frequency of
defecation and the types of foods that they find assist with normal
defecation.
Constipation
Educate the person about the importance of increasing daily fluid
intake and encourage them to drink hot liquids and fruit juices,
especially prune juice. Provide advice about the benefits of fibre in
the diet; that is, foods such as raw fruit, bran products and
wholegrain cereals and bread.
Diarrhoea


Educate the person to maintain an adequate oral intake of fluids and
eat bland food. Eating small amounts can be helpful because it is
more easily absorbed. Excessively hot or cold fluids should be
avoided because they stimulate peristalsis. In addition, highly spiced
foods and high-fibre foods can aggravate diarrhoea. See ‘Patient
education
’ for details about managing diarrhoea.
Patient education
Managing diarrhoea
Educate the person to drink at least 1500 mL (8 glasses)
of water per day to prevent dehydration. The person may
need to consider drinking a few glasses of electrolyte
replacement fluids a day.
Educate the person to eat foods with sodium and
potassium. Many foods, such as crackers, canned soups,
cured meats, contain sodium. Potassium is found in
meats and many vegetables and fruits, especially purple
grape juice, tomatoes, potatoes, bananas, cooked
peaches and apricots.
Encourage the person to increase foods containing
soluble fibre, such as rice, oatmeal and skinless fruits and
potatoes.
Educate the person about avoiding alcohol and beverages
with caffeine, which will dehydrate them further.
Encourage the person to limit foods containing insoluble
fibre, such as high-fibre wholemeal and wholegrain breads
and cereals, and raw fruits and vegetables.


Encourage the person to limit their intake of fatty foods.
Advise the person to thoroughly clean and dry the perianal
area after passing stool to prevent skin irritation and
breakdown. The person should be encouraged to use
soft, unperfumed toilet tissue to clean and dry the area
and to apply a moisturiser, such as zinc-based or paraffin
ointment, or alcohol-free barrier film as needed.
If possible, and with medical advice, the person should be
encouraged to discontinue medications that cause
diarrhoea.
Probiotics may be helpful in the treatment of antibiotic-
associated diarrhoea (Wong et al.
) or to re-establish
healthy gut flora after a case of diarrhoea. The person
should be encouraged to discuss the need for probiotics
with their doctor.
18 Wong, S., Saif, M., O’Driscoll, J., ... Jamous, A. (2015). Use of probiotics in
preventing antibiotic associated diarrhoea and Clostridium difficile associated
diarrhoea in spinal injury centres: An international survey of four western
European countries. International Journal of Probiotics & Prebiotics, 10(2/3),
85–90.
The person should be advised to consult a doctor if
weakness, dizziness or loose stools persist for more than
48 hours.
Flatulence
18


Advise the person to limit carbonated beverages, the use of drinking
straws and chewing gum—all of which increase the ingestion of air.
Gas-forming foods, such as cabbage, beans, lentils, onions and
cauliflower, should also be avoided.
Exercise
Educate the person about regular exercise that helps to develop a
regular defecation pattern. A person with weak abdominal and pelvic
muscles (which impede normal defecation) may be able to
strengthen them with the following isometric exercises.
In a supine position, the person tightens the abdominal muscles
as though pulling them inward, holding them for about 10
seconds and then relaxing them. This should be repeated five to
10 times, four times a day, depending on the person’s health.
Again in a supine position, the person can contract the thigh
muscles and hold them contracted for about 10 seconds,
repeating the exercise five to 10 times, four times a day. This
helps the person confined to bed gain strength in the thigh
muscles, thereby making it easier to use a bedpan.
Positioning
Although the squatting position best facilitates defecation, on a toilet
seat (with the feet positioned on the floor or a low stool) the best
position for some people seems to be leaning forward (see Figure
52.6
).


For the person who has difficulty sitting down and getting up from
the toilet, an elevated toilet seat can be attached to a regular toilet;
however, a foot stool is required to avoid feet dangling.
A bedside commode, a portable chair with a toilet seat and a
receptacle beneath that can be emptied, is often used for the adult
person who can get out of bed but is unable to walk to the
bathroom. Some commodes have wheels and can slide over the
base of a regular toilet when the waste receptacle is removed, thus
providing the person with the privacy of a bathroom. Some
commodes have a seat and can be used as a chair (see Figure
52.7
). Potty chairs are available for children.
Figure 52.7


A commode with overlying seat.
Source: Rick Brady/Pearson Education, Inc.
The person restricted to bed may need to use a bedpan, a
receptacle for urine and faeces. Females use a bedpan for both
urine and faeces; males use a bedpan for faeces and a urinal for
urine.
Home care assessment
Faecal elimination


The individual and the environment
Self-care abilities for toileting: cognitive
impairment; ability to get to the toilet, to manipulate
clothing for toileting, to perform toilet hygiene and
to flush the toilet.
Mechanical aids required: walking frame, walking
stick, wheelchair, raised toilet seat, grab bars,
bedpan, commode.
Mechanical barriers that limit access to the
toilet or are unsafe: distance, poor lighting, stairs,
cluttered pathway to bathroom, narrow doorway for
wheelchair, scatter rugs.
Bowel elimination problem: alterations in
characteristics of faeces, diarrhoea, constipation,
incontinence, presence of stoma and methods of
handling these.
Level of knowledge: hand hygiene, planned bowel
management or training program, effect of
prescribed medications, stoma care, dietary
alterations and fluid and exercise requirements or
restrictions.
Facilities: adequacy of bathroom facilities to
facilitate toilet hygiene and stoma care, and to
contain potentially infectious faecal effluent or stool.
Family
Caregiver availability and skills: people willing
and able to assist with toileting, medications, stoma


care or other prescribed therapeutic measures.
Family role changes and coping: effect on
financial status, parenting and spousal roles,
sexuality, social roles.
Alternative potential primary or respite
caregivers: for example, other family members,
volunteers, church members, paid caregivers or
housekeeping services; available community
respite care (adult daycare, senior centres).
Community
Availability of, and familiarity with, possible
sources of assistance: equipment and supply
companies, financial assistance, home health
agencies.
There are two main types of bedpans: the regular high-back pan and
the slipper, or fracture, pan (see Figure 52.8A
). The slipper pan
has a low back and is used for people unable to raise their buttocks
because of physical problems or therapy that contraindicates such
movement. Many older adults benefit from the use of a slipper pan.
It should be noted that many organisations now have disposable
bedpans and urinals (see Figure 52.8B
). These are made from
paper pulp. The female pans sit inside a plastic receptacle. See
‘Practice guidelines’ for the techniques of giving and removing a
bedpan.


Figure 52.8
A: Plastic high-back pan (top) and plastic slipper pan (bottom). B:
Disposable pan, plastic receptacle and disposable urinal.
Practice guidelines
Giving and removing a bedpan
Provide privacy and organise your work space (toilet
paper, bedpan cover, towels, washcloth, bowl of water).
Wash hands.
Assess the person for pain or discomfort and manage as
appropriate.


Explain to the person the procedure for using a bedpan
and continue to communicate with them throughout the
process.
Don personal protective equipment and disposable gloves.
If the bedpan is metal, warm it by rinsing it with warm
water, and dry.
Adjust the bed to a height appropriate to prevent back
strain.
Elevate the side rail on the opposite side to prevent the
person from falling out of bed.
Ask the person to assist (if their condition permits) by
flexing the knees, resting the weight on the back and
heels and raising the buttocks, or by using a trapeze bar,
if present.
Help transfer the person onto the pan while adhering to
safe transfer principles. If the person is unable to provide
assistance, first assess that there are sufficient trained
staff and equipment available to transfer the person to the
bedpan as necessary.
Place a regular bedpan so that the person’s buttocks rest
on the smooth, rounded rim. Place a slipper pan with the
flat, low end under the person’s buttocks (see Figure
52.9
).
Figure 52.9


Placing a slipper pan under the buttocks.
Source: Rick Brady/Pearson Education, Inc.
For the person who cannot assist, obtain the assistance
of another nurse to help transfer the person onto the
bedpan or place the person on their side. Place the
bedpan against the buttocks (see Figure 52.10
) and
roll the person back onto the bedpan.
Figure 52.10


Placing a regular bedpan under the person’s buttocks.
Source: Rick Brady/Pearson Education, Inc.
To provide a more normal position for the person’s lower
back, elevate the person’s bed to a semi-Fowler’s
position, if permitted. If elevation is contraindicated,
support the person’s back with pillows as needed to
prevent hyperextension of the back.
Cover the person with bed linen to maintain comfort and
dignity.


Provide toilet tissue, place the buzzer within reach, lower
the bed to the low position, elevate the side rail if indicated
and leave the person alone.
Answer the buzzer promptly.
Do not leave anyone on a bedpan longer than 15 minutes
unless they are able to remove the pan themselves.
Lengthy stays on a bedpan can cause pressure injuries.
When removing the bedpan, don personal protective
equipment, such as disposable gloves. Then return the
bed to the position used when giving the bedpan, hold the
bedpan steady to prevent spillage of its contents, cover
the bedpan and place it on the adjacent chair, which you
have covered with a towel.
If the person needs assistance, with gloves on wipe the
person’s perineal area with several layers of toilet tissue.
If a specimen is to be collected or measured, discard the
soiled tissue into a moisture-proof receptacle other than
the bedpan. For females, clean from the urethra towards
the anus to prevent transferring rectal micro-organisms
into the urinary meatus.
Wash the perineal area of dependent people with soap
and water as indicated and thoroughly dry the area.
Offer the person warm water, soap, a washcloth and a
towel to wash their hands.
Assist the person to a comfortable position, empty and
clean the bedpan and return it to the bedside or as per
the organisation’s policy.
Remove and discard your gloves and wash your hands.


Open a window or spray the room with air freshener as
needed to control odour unless contraindicated because
of respiratory problems or allergies.
Document colour, odour, amount and consistency of urine
and faeces, and the condition of the perineal area.
Teaching about medications
The most common categories of medications that can promote
faecal elimination are cathartics and laxatives (also referred to as
aperients), antidiarrhoeals and antiflatulents.
Cathartics and laxatives
Cathartics
 are drugs that induce defecation. They can have a
strong, purgative effect. A laxative is mild in comparison to a
cathartic and it produces soft or liquid stools that are sometimes
accompanied by abdominal cramps. Examples of cathartics are
castor oil, cascara and bisacodyl. Table 52.3
 describes the
different types of cathartics and laxatives.
Table 52.3 Types of cathartics and laxatives
Laxatives are contraindicated in the person who has nausea,
cramps, colic, vomiting or undiagnosed abdominal pain. People need
to be informed about the dangers of laxative use. Continual use of
laxatives to encourage bowel evacuation weakens the bowel’s


natural responses to faecal distension, resulting in chronic
constipation. To eliminate chronic laxative use, it is usually
necessary to teach the person about dietary fibre, regular exercise,
taking sufficient fluids and establishing regular defecation habits. In
addition, any medication regimen should be examined to see
whether it could cause constipation.
Some laxatives are given in the form of suppositories
. These act
by softening the faeces or by stimulating the nerve endings in the
rectal mucosa. The best results can be obtained by inserting the
suppository 30 minutes before the person’s usual defecation time or
when the peristaltic action is greatest, such as after a meal.
Practice guidelines
Faecal elimination
Facilitating toileting
Ensure the person has safe and easy access to the toilet.
Make sure lighting is appropriate, scatter rugs are
removed or securely fastened and assistive devices are in
place.
Educate the person (as needed) about transfer
techniques.
Suggest to the person ways that garments can be
adjusted to make disrobing easier for toileting (e.g. hook
and loop fasteners on clothing).


Educate the person about correct positioning on the toilet
(see Figure 52.6
).
Monitoring bowel elimination pattern
Educate the person about normal bowel functioning (see
Box 52.1
 and Table 52.1
).
Educate the person, if appropriate, to keep a record of
time and frequency of stool passage, any associated pain
and colour and consistency of the stool. The person can
be encouraged to keep a bowel habit diary (see Figure
52.5
).
Dietary alterations
Provide information to the person about required food and
fluid alterations to promote defecation or to manage
diarrhoea.
Medications
Discuss with the person problems associated with overuse
of laxatives, if appropriate, and the use of alternatives to
laxatives, suppositories and enemas.
Discuss with the person the role of fibre supplements if
they are taking a medication that contributes to
constipation.


Measures specific to elimination
problem
Educate the person about specific elimination problems
and management, such as:
− constipation
− diarrhoea.
Community agencies and other
sources of help
Make appropriate referrals to home care or community care
services for assistance with resources such as installation of
grab bars and raised toilet seats, structural alterations for
wheelchair access, home help or home health aid services to
assist with activities of daily living and a continence advisor
for assistance (e.g. the Department of Social Services:
<www.dss.gov.au/our-responsibilities/disability-and-
carers/program-services/for-people-with-disability>).
Provide information about companies or agencies where
durable medical equipment (e.g. raised toilet seats,
commodes, bedpans, urinals) can be purchased, rented
or obtained free of charge, and where medical supplies
such as incontinence pads can be purchased. Suggest


additional sources of information and help such as support
groups or clubs.
Antidiarrhoeal medications
These medications slow the motility of the intestine or absorb excess
fluid in the intestine. Guidelines for using antidiarrhoeals are shown
in Box 52.5
.
BO X
52.5 Guidelines for using
antidiarrhoeal medications
If the diarrhoea persists for more than 3 or 4 days,
determine the underlying cause. Use of a medication such
as an opiate when the cause is an infection, toxin or
poison may prolong diarrhoea.
Long-term use of over-the-counter medications can
produce dependence.
Some antidiarrhoeal agents can cause drowsiness (e.g.
diphenoxylate hydrochloride, loperimide) and should not
be used when driving a car or operating machinery.
Kaolin–pectin preparations may absorb nutrients.
Bulk laxatives and other absorbents may be used to help
bind toxins and absorb excess bowel liquid.


Antidiarrhoeals are not recommended for children (RCH
2017).
Antiflatulent medications
Antiflatulent agents such as simethicone do not decrease the
formation of flatus but they do coalesce the gas bubbles and
facilitate their passage by belching through the mouth or expulsion
through the anus. These agents are frequently combined with an
antacid. Carminatives
 are herbal oils known to act as agents that
help expel gas from the stomach and intestines. Suppositories can
also be given to relieve flatus by increasing intestinal motility.
Decreasing flatulence
There are a number of ways to reduce or expel flatus, including
avoiding gas-producing foods or carbonated drinks, increased
exercise and mobilising. Movement stimulates peristalsis, the
escape of flatus and reabsorption of gases in the intestinal
capillaries.
Enemas
Enemas
 are liquid preparations for rectal administration. Enemas
can be used to deliver topical or systemic treatments or to cause a
bowel motion. The action of an enema, for the purpose of causing a


bowel motion, is to distend the intestine and sometimes to irritate
the intestinal mucosa, thereby increasing peristalsis and the
excretion of faeces and flatus. Enemas are broadly classified as
high-volume (500–1000 mL for an adult) and low-volume enemas
(5–10 mL), but are further classified according to their function, such
as cleansing or retention enemas. Enemas or suppositories should
be avoided where possible in children except in severe
circumstances (RCH 2017).
High-volume enemas
Large-volume soap and water, tap water or hypertonic saline
enemas have been used traditionally to cleanse the colon. They
stimulate peristalsis by increasing the volume in the colon and, in the
case of soap and water enemas, irritate the mucosa. Soap and
water enemas are not recommended as they can cause chemical
colitis (Schmelzer et al.
).
19 Schmelzer, M., Schiller, L., Meyer, R., Rugari, S. & Case, P. (2004). Safety and
effectiveness of large-volume enema solutions. Applied Nursing Research, 17(4), 265–274.
Furthermore, with high-volume water enemas, water absorption,
particularly in the dehydrated individual, is a possibility and increased
fluid overload could be extremely problematic in patients with renal
or cardiac disease.
Low-volume enemas
19


Low-volume enemas containing sodium citrate-sodium lauryl
sulfoacetate-sorbitol base (e.g. Microlax™ 5 mL enema) are easily
administered disposable liquid enemas that act as a lubricant and a
mild stimulant. They initiate a feeling of fullness and ‘urge’, which is a
reflex action to empty the bowel (NPS MedicineWise ).
20 NPS MedicineWise (2014). Sodium Citrate-Sodium Lauryl Sulfoacetate-Sorbitol. Retrieved
from <www.nps.org.au>.
Cleansing enemas
Cleansing enemas are intended to remove faeces. They are given
chiefly to:
prepare the intestine for surgical procedures
prepare the intestine for certain diagnostic tests such as x-ray or
visualisation tests (e.g. colonoscopy)
remove faeces in instances of constipation or impaction.
Cleansing enemas use a variety of solutions. Table 52.4
 lists
commonly used solutions.
Table 52.4 Commonly used enema solutions
Hypertonic solutions (saline, phosphate) exert osmotic pressure,
which draws fluid from the interstitial space into the colon. The
increased volume in the colon stimulates peristalsis and hence
20


defecation. A commonly used hypertonic enema is the commercially
prepared Fleet™ phosphate enema.
Hypotonic solutions (e.g. tap water), on the other hand, exert a
lower osmotic pressure than the surrounding interstitial fluid, causing
water to move from the colon into the interstitial space. Before the
water moves from the colon, it stimulates peristalsis and defecation.
Because the water moves out of the colon, the tap water enema
should not be repeated because of the danger of circulatory
overload when the water moves from the interstitial space into the
circulatory system.
Isotonic solutions, such as physiological (normal) saline 0.9%, are
considered the safest enema solutions to use. They exert the same
osmotic pressure as the interstitial fluid surrounding the colon.
Therefore, there is no fluid movement into or out of the colon. The
instilled volume of saline in the colon stimulates peristalsis.
The amount of solution administered for a high-volume enema will
depend on the age and medical condition of the individual. For
example, people with certain cardiac or renal diseases would be
adversely affected by significant fluid retention that might result from
large-volume hypotonic enemas.
The patient is positioned on their left side in preparation for the
enema. The force of flow of the solution is governed by (a) the
height of the solution container, (b) size of the tubing, (c) viscosity of
the fluid and (d) resistance of the rectum.


The higher the solution container is held above the rectum, the
faster the flow and the greater the force (pressure) in the rectum.
During most adult enemas, the solution container should be no
higher than 30 cm above the rectum. The flow of fluid should be
stopped or slowed if the individual reports any discomfort during the
procedure.
It is important that the nurse recognises that enemas should be
prescribed by the doctor. Organisation policies must be adhered to
in terms of the types of enemas permitted and which health care
professional is permitted to administer them.
Retention enema
A retention enema introduces oil or medication into the rectum and
sigmoid colon. The liquid is retained for a relatively long period (e.g.
1 to 3 hours). An oil retention enema acts to soften the faeces and
to lubricate the rectum and anal canal, thus facilitating passage of
the faeces. Corticosteroids may be given by enema to treat Crohn’s
disease locally and anthelmintic enemas to kill helminths such as
worms and intestinal parasites.
Clinical consideration
Some people may wish to administer their own
enemas. If this is appropriate, the nurse


validates the person’s knowledge of correct
technique and assists as needed.
Skill 52.1
 describes how to administer an enema.
Bowel training programs
For people who have chronic constipation, frequent impactions or
faecal incontinence, bowel training programs may be helpful. The
program is based on factors within the person’s control and is
designed to help the person establish normal defecation. Such
matters as food and fluid intake, exercise and defecation habits are
all considered. Before beginning such a program, people must
understand the rationale and interventions required and want to be
involved. The major phases of the program are as follows:
Determine the person’s usual bowel habits and factors that help
and hinder normal defecation. Maintaining a diary of dietary
intake and a bowel chart to record defecation pattern and stool
consistency and volume (Bristol Stool Form Chart) for a week, if
possible, will assist.
Design a plan with the person that includes the following:
a. Unless contraindicated, increase fluid intake to about 2500 to
3000 mL per day.


b. Increase fibre in the diet in the form of fresh vegetables, fruit,
grains or fibre supplements.
c. Increase intake of hot drinks, especially just before the usual
defecation time.
d. Increase exercise.
Maintain the following daily routine for 2 to 3 weeks:
a. If regular spontaneous defecation does not occur, trial the
administration of a cathartic suppository 30 minutes before
the person’s anticipated defecation time to stimulate
peristalsis.
b. When the person experiences the urge to defecate, assist the
person to the toilet or commode or onto a bedpan.
c. Note the length of time between the insertion of the
suppository and the urge to defecate.
d. Provide the person with privacy for defecation and a time limit
—30 to 40 minutes is usually sufficient.
e. Teach the person to place their feet on the floor or a small
stool, lean forward at the hips, apply pressure on the
abdomen with the hands and bear down for defecation (see
Figure 52.6
). These measures increase pressure on the
colon. Straining should be avoided because it can cause
haemorrhoids.
Provide positive feedback when the person successfully
defecates. Refrain from negative feedback if the person fails to
defecate.


Offer encouragement to the person and convey that patience is
often required. Many people require weeks or months of training
to achieve success.
Faecal incontinence devices
There is a large variety of disposable and non-disposable incontinent
pads and garments on the market which can be used to manage
faecal incontinence. However, more recent innovations aim to
improve the quality of life for sufferers of this condition. Large
volumes of liquid faeces in the bedbound person may be collected in
a faecal incontinence collector pouch (see Figure 52.11
). The
pouch usually incorporates a hydrocolloid skin barrier that adheres
to the perianal area and is designed to prevent progressive perianal
skin irritation and breakdown and frequent linen changes
necessitated by incontinence.
Figure 52.11


A drainable faecal collection pouch.
A faecal collector is secured around the anal opening and may or
may not be attached to drainage. Pouches are best applied before
the perianal skin becomes eroded or ulcerated. If perianal skin
erosion is present, the nurse either (a) applies a moisture-barrier
cream or alcohol-free protective barrier film to the skin to protect it


from faeces until it heals and then applies the pouch, or (b) applies a
hydrocolloid skin barrier underneath the pouch to achieve the best
possible seal.
Nursing responsibilities for people with a rectal pouch include (a)
regular assessment and documentation of the perianal skin status,
(b) emptying the contents as needed and changing the bag every 72
hours or sooner if there is leakage, (c) maintaining the drainage
system and (d) providing explanations and support to the person
and support people.
Commercially available anal plugs (Peristeen™ Anal Plug) may be
preferred by some independent people as a means of managing
their faecal incontinence. A soft expandable foam plug with an
attached string for security is inserted into the anus. Gentle
expansion of the plug against the internal sphincter ensures a seal.
Anal plugs can be worn for up to 12 hours (see Figure 52.12
).
Figure 52.12


Anal Plug.
Source: Provided by Coloplast. © Coloplast.
Intra-anal faecal management systems (Flexi-Seal™ FMS and
Signal™ FMS by ConvaTec) are soft, silicone, water-filled, inflatable
tip catheters which are attached to a drainage bag. They are
designed to be inserted into the rectum and positioned against the
internal anal sphincter to facilitate drainage and containment of
faecal diarrhoea in bed-bound patients. The systems are particularly
useful for containment of diarrhoea caused by infective organisms


such as Clostridium difficile as they protect the perianal skin and
support infection-control practices (Jones et al.
).
21 Jones, S., Towers, V., Welsby, S., Wishin, J. & Bowler, P. (2011). Clostridium difficile
containment properties of a fecal management system: An in vitro Investigation. Ostomy
Wound Management, 57(10), 38–49.
Anal irrigation kits (see Figure 52.13
) have been developed to
assist certain individuals with chronic faecal incontinence or
constipation. Regular rectal irrigation is performed by introducing
lukewarm tap water into the rectum via a rectal catheter while the
person sits on the toilet. The kits are comprised of:
screw-top unit which is connected to a water bag
bag for tepid tap water
pump for activating balloon and flushing water
control unit for regulation of air and water
coated rectal catheter with balloon for insertion into the rectum.
Figure 52.13
21


Peristeen™ Anal Irrigation Device.
Source: Provided by Coloplast. © Coloplast.
The irrigation system is easy to use even if dexterity is poor and can
be used by children over the age of 3 years or adults. It is not
recommended for pregnant or lactating women.


Some people (e.g. post trauma, quadriplegic, paraplegic or post
stroke) may be treated for faecal incontinence with surgical repair of
a damaged sphincter or the insertion of an artificial bowel sphincter.
The artificial sphincter consists of three parts: a cuff around the anal
canal, a pressure-regulating balloon and a pump that inflates the
cuff (see Figure 52.14
). The cuff is inflated to close the sphincter,
maintaining continence. To have a bowel movement, the person
deflates the cuff. The cuff automatically reinflates in 10 minutes.
Management of this device is usually specific to the device; refer to
the instructions provided or contact the manufacturing company for
details.
Figure 52.14


Inflatable artificial sphincter.
Administering enemas and rectal medications may be harmful with
this device in place. Ensure safety of these practices with the device
instruction guide provided by the device manufacturer.


Evaluating
The goals established during the planning phase are evaluated
according to specific desired outcomes, also established in that
phase. Examples of these are shown in ‘Identifying nursing
diagnoses, outcomes and interventions’ earlier in this chapter.
If outcomes are not achieved, the nurse should explore the reasons.
The nurse might consider some or all of the following questions:
Is the person’s fluid intake and diet appropriate?
Is the person’s activity level appropriate?
Are prescribed medications or other factors affecting the
gastrointestinal function?
Do the person and family understand the provided instructions
well enough to comply with the required therapy?
Was sufficient physical and emotional support provided?


SKILL
52.1 Administering an enema
Purpose
To achieve one or more of the following actions:
cleansing or retention.
Assessment
Assess
Gain consent.
Ascertain when the person last had a bowel
movement and the amount, colour and
consistency of the faeces.
Ascertain the person’s diet and fluid intake over
the past 3 days.
Inspect the abdomen for signs of distension.
Palpate the abdomen for hardness and palpable
masses.
Auscultate for bowel sounds.
If the policy of the organisation permits and the
examiner is an experienced Registered Nurse,
Nurse Practitioner or doctor, perform a gentle


digital examination of the anus and rectum for
sphincter control and impaction of faeces.
Determine whether the person can use a toilet or
commode, or must remain in bed and use a
bedpan.
Planning
Before administering an enema, determine that
there is a doctor’s order. In some organisations, a
doctor must order the kind of enema and the time to
give it; for example, the morning of an examination.
Determine if there are any allergies to the
medication, its excipients or the tubing. If a
hypotonic solution is prescribed, determine if there is
a diagnosis of kidney or cardiac disease that
contraindicates the use of a hypotonic solution.
Delegation
Administration of enemas is not usually delegated to
an unlicensed health practitioner such as an
Assistant in Nursing, especially if the enema has
medication content. (Refer to organisation policy.)
Equipment
Disposable linen-saver pad
Bath blanket


Bedpan or commode or very close access to a
toilet
Clean gloves, apron, protective eyewear if
required
Water-soluble lubricant if tubing not pre-
lubricated
Paper towel
Large-volume enema
Disposable solution container with tubing of
correct size and tubing clamp
Correct solution, amount and at body
temperature 37.7°C
Small-volume enema
Pre-packaged container of enema solution with
lubricated tip
Implementation
Preparation
For large-volume enemas select the
appropriately sized tubing depending on the
person (adults 14–30 French gauge).
Lubricate about 5 cm of the rectal tube with a
water-soluble lubricant (some commercially


prepared enema sets already have lubricated
nozzles). Lubrication facilitates insertion through
the sphincters and prevents friction to anal walls.
Run some solution through the connecting tubing
of a large-volume enema set and the rectal tube
to expel any air in the tubing; then close the
clamp. Rationale: air instilled into the rectum,
although not harmful, causes unnecessary
distension.
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation policy. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and how they can cooperate. Gain consent
from the person or person’s family member.
Discuss how the results will be used in
planning further care or treatments. Inform
the person that they may experience a feeling
of fullness while the solution is being
administered but any signs of discomfort
need to be communicated.
2. Perform hand hygiene, don personal
protective equipment—gloves, apron and
protective eye wear if required. Observe
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for person privacy.


4. Assist the adult person to a left lateral
position, with the right leg as acutely flexed as
possible 1 and the linen-saver pad under the
buttocks. Rationale: this position facilitates
the flow of solution by gravity into the sigmoid
and descending colon, which are on the left
side. Having the right leg acutely flexed
provides for adequate exposure of the anus
and helps relax the anal sphincter.
1 Assuming a left lateral position for an
enema. Note the commercially prepared
enema
5. Insert the enema tube.
For people in the left lateral position, lift
the upper buttock to ensure good
visualisation of the anus.


You may be required to perform a gentle
digital rectal examination with a lubricated
gloved finger to determine if there is an
impaction or other mechanical blockage.
Insert the tube smoothly and slowly into
the rectum, directing it towards the
umbilicus. 2 Rationale: the angle follows
the normal contour of the rectum. Slow
insertion prevents spasm of the sphincter.
2 Inserting the enema tube following the
direction of the rectum
Insert the tube 7 to 10 cm. Rationale:
because the anal canal is about 2.5 to 3


cm long in the adult, insertion to this point
places the tip of the tube beyond the anal
sphincter into the rectum.
If resistance is encountered at the internal
sphincter, ask the person to take a deep
breath, then run a small amount of
solution through the tube to relax the
internal anal sphincter.
Never force tube or solution entry. If
instilling a small amount of solution does
not permit the tube to be advanced or the
solution to freely flow, withdraw the tube.
Check for any stool that may have
blocked the tube during insertion. If
present, flush it and retry the procedure. If
resistance persists, end the procedure
and report the resistance to the senior
nurse and doctor.
6. Slowly administer the enema solution.
If a high-volume enema, raise the solution
container and open the clamp to allow
fluid flow. Hold or hang the solution
container no higher than 30 cm above the
rectum. Rationale: the higher the solution
container is held above the rectum, the
faster the flow and the greater the force
(pressure) in the rectum. Administer the


fluid slowly. If the person complains of
fullness or pain, lower the container or use
the clamp to stop the flow for 30 seconds
and then restart the flow at a slower rate.
Rationale: administering the enema
slowly and stopping the flow momentarily
decreases the likelihood of intestinal
spasm and premature ejection of the
solution.
or
Compress a low-volume pliable container
by hand.
After all the solution has been instilled or
when the person cannot hold any more
and feels the desire to defecate (the urge
to defecate usually indicates that sufficient
fluid has been administered), close the
clamp and remove the enema tube from
the anus.
Place the enema tube in a disposable
towel as you withdraw it.
7. Encourage the person to retain the enema.
Ask the person to remain lying down. It is
easier for the person to retain the enema
when lying down than when sitting or
standing, because gravity promotes
drainage and peristalsis.


Request that the person retain the
solution for the appropriate amount of
time, for example 5 to 10 minutes for a
cleansing enema or at least 30 minutes
for a retention enema.
8. Assist the person to defecate.
Assist the person to a sitting position on
the bedpan, commode or toilet. A sitting
position with the feet on the floor or a
stool facilitates the act of defecation.
Ask the person who is using the toilet not
to flush it. The nurse needs to observe the
faeces.
If a specimen of faeces is required, ask
the person to use a bedpan or commode.
9. Document the type and volume, if
appropriate, of enema given. Describe the
results and the patient’s response.
Variation: administering an enema to an
incontinent person
Occasionally, a nurse needs to administer an enema
to a person who is unable to control the external
sphincter muscle and thus cannot retain the enema
solution for even a few minutes. In that case, after


the enema tip is inserted, the person is positioned
on a toilet or commode or assumes a supine
position on a bedpan. The head of the bed can be
elevated slightly, to 30 degrees if necessary, for
easier breathing; pillows support the person’s head
and back.
Evaluation
Perform a detailed follow-up based on findings that
deviated from expected or normal for the person.
Relate findings to previous assessment data if
available. Report significant deviations from
expected to the doctor.


Bowel diversion ostomies
An ostomy
 is an opening for the gastrointestinal or urinary tract
onto the skin of the abdomen. There are many types of intestinal
ostomies. A gastrostomy
 is an opening through the abdominal
wall into the stomach and is used for feeding or deflation of the
stomach. A jejunostomy
 opens through the abdominal wall into
the jejunum and is used for jejunal feeding, while an ileostomy
opens into the ileum and forms a diversion for effluent. A
caecostomy empties from the caecum (the first part of the
ascending colon). An ascending colostomy empties from the
ascending colon, a transverse colostomy from the transverse colon,
a descending colostomy from the descending colon and a
sigmoidostomy from the sigmoid colon.
The divided colostomy consists of two edges of bowel brought out
onto the abdomen but separated from each other (see Figure
52.15
). The opening from the digestive or proximal end is the
colostomy. The distal end in this situation is often referred to as a
mucus fistula, since the proximal section of bowel continues to
secrete mucus. The divided colostomy is often used in situations
where spillage of faeces into the distal end of the bowel needs to be
avoided or when a large amount of mucus is anticipated, such as for
infants born with an imperforate anus or when a rectal tumour is
inoperable and remains in situ.


Figure 52.15
Divided colostomy with two separated stomas.
The double-barrelled colostomy resembles a double-barrelled
shotgun (see Figure 52.16
). In this type of colostomy, the


proximal and distal loops of bowel are sutured together for about 10
cm and both ends are brought up onto the abdominal wall. The
proximal opening will drain effluent and the distal opening will drain
mucus.
Figure 52.16
Double-barrelled colostomy.
Gastrostomies and jejunostomies are generally performed to provide
an alternative feeding route rather than for elimination purposes,
while ileostomies and colostomies are performed for elimination
purposes. Ileostomies and colostomies are often classified according
to (a) their status as permanent or temporary, (b) their anatomical


location (see Figure 52.17
) and (c) the construction of the
stoma
, which is the opening created onto the abdominal wall and
eversion (turning back on itself) of the segment of bowel to form a
stoma. The stoma mucosa is generally red in colour and moist. A
person does not feel any pain from the stoma because there are no
nerve endings in the intestinal or colonic (stoma) mucosa.
Figure 52.17


The anatomical locations of colostomies or an ileostomy.
A colostomy can be either temporary or permanent. Temporary
colostomies are generally performed following traumatic injuries or
inflammatory conditions of the bowel in order to rest a distal
anastomosis (the joining of the intestine or bowel segments distal to


the stoma or disease segment of the colon). Permanent colostomies
are performed to provide a means of permanent elimination when
the rectum or anus is absent as a result of a birth defect or has
been surgically removed because of significant colorectal disease or
malignancy. The location of the colostomy will dictate the
consistency of the stool. Effluent from colostomies sited in the
ascending and transverse colon will be more liquid in consistency
than those sited in the descending and sigmoid colons, which are
more formed and regulated (see ‘Anatomy & physiology
review
’). People with a sigmoid colostomy generally wear a
closed-end appliance and may select to perform colostomy irrigation
as a means of regulating evacuation.
ANATO M Y & PHYSIO LO G Y REVIEW
Small and large intestines
Review the figure and reflect back on your anatomy and
physiology courses.
Questions
1. What are the primary functions of the small intestine?
2. What are the primary functions of the large intestine?
3. What part of the small intestine connects to the colon?
4. What consistency would the stool be in a person with
an ileostomy and why?
5. Compare and contrast the consistency of stool in a
transverse colostomy and a descending colostomy.


6. How would you describe the stool discharged from a
sigmoidostomy?
Source: B. F. Fremgen & S. S. Frucht (2012). Medical Terminology: A Living Language (5th ed.),
Figure 8.6, p. 263. Reproduced with permission of Pearson Education, Inc., Upper Saddle River, NJ.


An ileostomy is usually created in the terminal ileum where the
chyme is more like thickened fluid in consistency. An ileostomy
drainage is constant and cannot be regulated. Ileostomy drainage
contains some digestive enzymes which are corrosive to the skin,
and for this reason people with an ileostomy must wear a drainable
appliance continuously and take special precautions to prevent skin
breakdown. Compared with colostomies, however, odour is minimal
because fewer bacteria are present in the ileum. The length of time
that a person has a colostomy helps to determine the consistency of
the stool, particularly with transverse and descending colostomies.
Over time, the stool becomes more formed because the remaining
functioning portions of the colon tend to compensate by increasing
water reabsorption.
Surgical construction of the stoma
Stoma constructions are described as end (see Figure 52.18
),
loop (ileostomy or colostomy) or divided or double-barrelled
(colostomy) (see Figures 52.15
 and 52.16
). The end stoma is
created when one end of the small or large intestine is exteriorised
onto the anterior abdominal wall and the bowel is everted to expose
mucosa on the outside (see Figure 52.18
). Eversion of the stoma
prevents spontaneous contracture and formation of strictures. An
end stoma or terminal colostomy is permanent and usually flush with
the skin, while an end ileostomy stoma is usually 2 to 3 cm in length
to facilitate liquid drainage into an appliance.


Figure 52.18
End colostomy: the diseased portion of the bowel is removed and a
stoma is created on the abdominal wall.
Source: K. Carville, Silver Chain Group Ltd.
A temporary loop colostomy or ileostomy stoma is created when a
loop of bowel is brought out onto the abdominal wall and may be
supported for 5 to 7 days by a plastic bridge or a piece of rubber
tubing (see Figure 52.19
). A loop stoma has two openings: the
proximal or afferent end, which is active, and the distal or efferent
end, which will not drain stool by mucus from the distal segment of
intestine. The loop colostomy is usually performed in an emergency


procedure and is often situated in the transverse colon. It is a bulky
stoma that is more difficult to manage than an end stoma; however,
it is usually temporary. A loop ileostomy (also known in Australia as
an Abcarian loop) is created in the ileum as a temporary stoma. The
distal opening is usually flush with the skin at the mucocutaneous
junction and may be difficult to visualise. The loop opening facilitates
the drainage of mucus from the distal segment of intestine.
Figure 52.19


Loop colostomy.
Source: Courtesy of Cory Patrick Hartley, RN.
Stoma management
People with faecal diversions or stomas need considerable
psychological support, instruction and physical care initially following
surgery. This section outlines the nurse’s physical interventions for
preoperative education and postoperative stoma assessment and
education to prepare the person for self-care. Many health care
organisations have access to a wound, ostomy and continence
nurse (WOCN), also referred to as a stomal therapy nurse (STN), to
assist these people. The WOCN/STN will visit the person
preoperatively and will educate the person in regard to the
anticipated surgical outcome, recovery and rehabilitation
expectations. The WOCN/STN will demonstrate ostomy appliances
and offer information on how to live with a stoma. The WOCN/STN
will examine the person’s abdomen and involve the person in
selecting the most appropriate site for the anticipated stoma and
appliance. The WOCN/STN will then mark the preferred site, which
will help the surgeon to site the stoma on a level skin surface that is
discrete but facilitates visible self-care.
Every Australian state and territory has at least one ostomy
association or support group; these have amalgamated under the
Australian Council of Stoma Associations (ACSA). The mission of
these associations is to provide support services for ostomates


(people with a stoma) and the distribution of ostomy appliances and
accessories on behalf of the Australian government (see ‘Web
links
’ at the end of this chapter). A person with a new stoma may
experience alterations in body image and concerns in regard to
resuming activities of daily living. Talking with another person who
has gone through a similar experience may help the person realise
that they are not alone and rehabilitation and return to normal
activities of daily living is possible. All of the state and territory
ostomy associations provide visitor services; these may be arranged
directly or via the WOCN/STN.
Clinical manifestations
Screening for bowel (colorectal) cancer
Risk factors
■ Age: > 50
■ Family history: colorectal cancer.
■ Personal health history:
large number of polyps in the bowel
inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s
disease); increased risk if present > 8 years
bowel, ovarian, endometrial cancer
rare genetic disorders (familial adenomatous polyposis,
Lynch syndrome).


■ Lifestyle: overweight, diet high in red meat (especially
processed meats), smokes, drinks alcohol.
Warning signs
■ Early stages, no symptoms.
■ Change in bowel habits (diarrhoea, constipation) or bowel
appearance (narrower stools, mucus in stools).
■ Feeling of fullness, bloating or incomplete emptying in
bowel or rectum; abdominal pain, swelling.
■ Rectal or anal pain; lump in rectum or anus.
■ Rectal bleeding, low red blood cell count.
■ Unexplained weight loss, weakness, fatigue.
Screening tests
■ Faecal occult blood test (FOBT) every 2 years for people
over 50 years.
■ Colonoscopy every 1–2 years for high-risk people (strong
family history or genetic condition associated with bowel
cancer). Note: screening begins at age 50 or 10 years before
the earliest age family member was diagnosed.
Source: Cancer Council NSW
. Bowel Cancer. Retrieved from <www.cancercouncil.com.au/
bowel-cancer/#Whatcausesbowelcancer>.
22 Cancer Council NSW (2016). Bowel Cancer. Retrieved from <www.cancercouncil.com.au>.
22


Stoma and skin care
Care of the stoma and skin is important as the faecal material from
a colostomy or ileostomy is irritating to the peristomal skin. This is
particularly true of stool from an ileostomy, which contains digestive
enzymes. It is important to assess the peristomal skin for irritation
each time the appliance is changed. Any irritation or skin breakdown
needs to be treated immediately. The skin is kept clean by washing
off any effluent and drying thoroughly.
Antegrade continence enema (ACE) procedure
An antegrade continence enema (ACE) procedure, also referred to
as a Malone antegrade continence enema (MACE) procedure,
involves the formation of a caecostomy for insertion of a catheter for
irrigation of the colon for elimination purposes in people with
encopresis or chronic constipation, usually associated with
neurogenic bowel disorders such as spina bifida, myelomeningocele,
Hirschsprung disease or spinal cord injury (Halleran et al.
).
23 Halleran, D., Vilanova-Sanchez, A., Rentea, R. et al. (2019). A comparison of Malone
appendicostomy and cecostomy for antegrade access as adjuncts to a bowel management
program for patients with functional constipation or fecal incontinence. Journal of Pediatric
Surgery, 54, 123–128.
The ACE provides an alternative route for insertion of regular
enemas other than via the anus. This procedure is often preferred
for the management of neurogenic bowel disorders in children. The
surgeon uses the appendix, with its blood supply intact, to fashion a
23


conduit from the caecum to the abdominal surface. The conduit is
usually exteriorised in the right iliac region of the lower abdomen.
The conduit is constructed to form an intussuscepted flap valve (it
folds back on itself) to prevent leakage.
Alternatively, a Chait  (Cook Medical) percutaneous (also referred to
as ‘trapdoor’) caecostomy device may be inserted into the caecum
to facilitate irrigation of the colon and prevention of leakage between
irrigations. The Chait  device is a coiled, small catheter with an
external hinged closure mechanism (see Figure 52.20
). The
coiled tube is inserted into the caecum and left in situ. An adaptor is
attached to the external opening for the purposes of irrigation of the
colon. The child or adult sits on the toilet and the determined amount
of irrigation water or physiological saline solution is inserted into the
caecum via a catheter attached to the bagged fluid. Elimination via
the anus follows but the procedure may take 30–60 minutes.
Enemas/irrigations are undertaken either daily or 2–3 times daily as
determined necessary to avoid encopresis or ensure regular
elimination.
Figure 52.20
®
®


Chait  percutaneous catheter.
Source: Permission for use granted by Cook Medical, Bloomington, Indiana.
A stoma appliance should protect the skin, collect stool, control
odour and be discrete. The appliance consists of a skin barrier
(usually a hydrocolloid) and a pouch (also referred to as a bag).
Some people may prefer to also wear an adjustable stoma belt
which attaches to a stoma appliance to hold it firmly in place (see
®


Figure 52.21
). Appliances can be one piece where the skin
barrier is already attached to the pouch (see Figure 52.22A
) or
can consist of two pieces: a separate pouch and a flange attached
to a skin barrier (see Figure 52.22B
). The pouch fastens to the
flange and can be detached for emptying or cleaning. Appliances
can be closed or drainable (see Figure 52.23
) and are selected
subject to the consistency of the stool. Fluid ileostomy effluent
needs to be drained several times a day when the appliance is one-
third full, while formed colostomy stool may only be evacuated and
require emptying or changing once or twice a day. A drainable
appliance usually has an integrated closure where the end of the
outlet folds onto itself with a self-fastener that secures the end. The
person folds up the end of the outlet of the appliance three or four
times and presses firmly to seal. Alternatively, a separate clip may
be used (see Figure 52.24
).

Adjustable stoma belt.

A: A one-piece stoma appliance or pouching system. B: A two-piece
stoma appliance.
Source: Shirlee Snyder.

A: A closed appliance. B: A drainable appliance.
