high flow: Physiology, efficacy and safety in the acute care setting, a narrative review. Open
Access Emergency Medicine, 11, 109.
Figure 53.16
12


Non-invasive CPAP mask and high-flow oxygen.
Source: © Chalermpon Poungpeth/123RF.
Lifespan considerations
Oxygen delivery equipment Infants
Oxygen hood
An oxygen hood is a rigid plastic dome that encloses an
infant’s head. It provides precise oxygen levels and high


humidity.
The gas should not be allowed to blow directly into the
infant’s face and the hood should not rub against the
infant’s neck, chin or shoulder.
Home care considerations
Home care oxygen equipment
Three major oxygen systems for home care use are
available in most communities: cylinders or tanks of
compressed gas, liquid oxygen and oxygen
concentrators. The latter two are not widely used in
Australia.
1. Cylinders (black cylinders with white
shoulders): (see Figure 53.17
) these are
the system of choice for people who need
oxygen episodically (e.g. on a prn basis).
Advantages are that cylinders deliver litre flows
(1 to 15 L/min) and the oxygen does not
evaporate during storage. Disadvantages are
that the cylinders are heavy and awkward to
move, and the supply company must be notified
when a refill is needed. Oxygen conservation
devices are designed to maximise the


effectiveness of the oxygen delivered. The
device can be placed between the cylinder and
the person to ensure oxygen is delivered as a
pulse during inspiration, thereby reducing
oxygen wastage during exhalation. All cylinders
should be considered empty when they are less
than a quarter full.
Figure 53.17


An ‘E’ cylinder oxygen tank on a wheeled stand.
2. Liquid oxygen: at very low temperatures,
gaseous oxygen can be converted into a liquid,
thereby saving space when storing the oxygen.
Two tanks are needed—a large stationary
container that is filled by the supplier and a
portable unit with a small lightweight tank that is
refilled from the stationary unit for ambulatory
use (see Figure 53.18
). Advantages are that
these reservoirs are lighter in weight and
cleaner in appearance than cylinders and they
are not as difficult to operate. Disadvantages of
liquid oxygen are that many home care medical
supply and service companies are not able to
handle it, oxygen evaporation occurs when the
unit is not used and only low flows (1 to 4 L/min)
can be used or freezing occurs.
Figure 53.18


A portable liquid oxygen supply.
Source: Dennis Hallinan/Alamy Stock Photo.
3. Oxygen concentrators: concentrators are
electrically powered systems that manufacture
oxygen from room air and can deliver a
concentration of about
 oxygen
92% ± 3%


when operating at a flow rate of less than 4
L/min. The concentration falls when the flow
rate increases. Advantages are that they are
more attractive in appearance, resembling
furniture rather than medical equipment; they
eliminate the need for regular delivery of oxygen
or refilling of cylinders; because the supply of
oxygen is constant, they alleviate the individual’s
anxiety about running out of oxygen; and they
are the most economical system when
continuous use is required. Major disadvantages
of a concentrator are that it is expensive; is
heavy to move around (21–26 kg) and it tends
to be noisy; most are powered by electricity (an
emergency back-up unit, for example, an
oxygen tank, must be provided for people for
whom a power failure could be life threatening);
and heat produced by the concentrator motor is
a problem for those who live in caravans, small
houses or warm climates, where air-
conditioners are required. The oxygen
concentrator must also be checked periodically
with an
 analyser to ensure that it is
providing an adequate delivery of oxygen.
Smaller portable, lightweight, 12V battery-driven
concentrators are now available for ambulatory
use.
O2


Another type of oxygen concentrator is the oxygen
enricher. It uses a plastic membrane that allows water
vapour to pass through with the oxygen, thus
eliminating the need for a humidifying device. It is also
thought to filter out bacteria present in the air. The
enricher provides an
 concentration of 40% at all
flow rates, it tends to be quieter than the concentrator,
there is less chance of combustion (since the gas is
only 40% oxygen), it has only two moving parts (thus
decreasing the risk of something going wrong) and a
nebuliser can be operated off the enricher because of
the high flow rate.
Home oxygen support should include:
a 24-hour emergency service
trained personnel to make the initial delivery and
instruct the person in safe, appropriate use of the
oxygen and maintenance of the equipment
at least monthly follow-up visits to check the
equipment and reinstruct the person as necessary
a regular cost review to ensure that the system is
the most cost-effective one for the person, with
routine notification of the doctor or home care
professional if it seems that another system is
more appropriate.
O2


The nurse must ensure the person knows about the
financial reimbursements available from Medicare and
private health insurance agencies. The prescribing
doctor should review the health status of the person at
6 months and record blood gases and pulse oximetry.
NIV with CPAP masks is commonly used in the community setting
for people with sleep apnoea. High-flow oxygen by intranasal
cannula is being used more frequently for neonatal, paediatric and
adult populations. It is more comfortable than the tight-fitting CPAP
mask and so is more easily tolerated by people with respiratory
distress. NIV with high-flow oxygen has been shown to reduce the
length of stay in hospital and the need for endotracheal intubation in
some people with acute respiratory failure (Bell et al.
).
13 Bell, N., Hutchinson, C. L., Green, T. C., Rogan, E., Bein, K. J. & Dinh, M. M. (2015).
Randomised control trial of humidified high flow nasal cannulae versus standard oxygen in the
emergency department. Emergency Medicine Australasia, 27(6), 537–541.
Artificial airways
Artificial airways are inserted to maintain a patent air passage for
people whose airways have become or may become obstructed. A
patent airway is necessary so that air can flow to and from the
lungs. Four of the more common types of airways are
oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal, endotracheal and tracheostomy.
13


Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways
Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways are used to keep the
upper air passages open when they may become obstructed by
secretions or the tongue. These airways are easy to insert and have
a low risk of complications. Sizes vary and should be appropriate to
the size and age of the person.
Selecting the correct size oropharyngeal airway (also known as a
Guedel airway, see Figure 53.19
) is important as an airway that is
too large will stimulate the gag reflex or force the tongue back in the
oropharynx. Conversely, an airway that is too small will not hold the
tongue in the anterior portion of the mouth. Size is determined by
measuring the distance from the corner of the mouth to the angle of
the jaw. As the oropharyngeal airway may stimulate the gag reflex, it
is only used for people with altered levels of consciousness (e.g.
because of general anaesthesia, overdose or head injury). To insert
the airway:
Place the person in a supine or semi-Fowler’s position.
Put on clean gloves.
The airway should be well lubricated with water-soluble gel prior
to inserting.
Hold the lubricated airway by the outer flange, with the distal end
pointing up.
Open the person’s mouth and insert the airway along the top of
the tongue.


When the distal end of the airway reaches the soft palate at the
back of the mouth, rotate the airway 180 degrees downward and
slip it past the uvula into the oral pharynx.
If not contraindicated, place the person in a side-lying position or
with the head turned to the side to allow secretions to drain out
of the mouth.
The oropharynx may be suctioned as needed by inserting the
suction catheter alongside the airway.
Do not tape the airway in place; remove it when the person
begins to cough or gag.
Provide mouth care at least every 2 to 4 hours, keeping suction
available at the bedside.
As appropriate for the person’s condition, remove the airway
every 8 hours to assess the mouth and provide oral care.
Reinsert the airway immediately.
Figure 53.19


Oropharyngeal, or Guedel, airways.
Source: plepraisaeng/123rf.com.
In children less than 8 years of age, there is a risk of damage to the
soft palate if the 180 degree rotation technique is used. Instead the
oropharyngeal airway is inserted under direct vision using a tongue
depressor or a laryngoscope, and with the concave side of the
airway towards the tongue.
Nasopharyngeal airways are tolerated better by people who are
alert. They are inserted through the nares, terminating in the


oropharynx (see Figure 53.20
). When caring for a person with a
nasopharyngeal airway, provide frequent oral and nares care,
repositioning the airway in the other naris every 8 hours or as
ordered to prevent necrosis of the mucosa.
Figure 53.20
A nasopharyngeal airway in place.
Laryngeal mask airway


Laryngeal mask airways (LMA) are increasingly being used in
preference to endotracheal tubes (ETT) to maintain a patent airway,
as they are easier to use, more rapidly inserted and require less
equipment. Like the ETT, an LMA is an oral airway with an inflatable
cuff at the distal end. But unlike the ETT, the cuff seals the
hypopharynx as opposed to the trachea. The LMA can be used in
adults, children and infants. Complications of LMA include gastric
aspiration, partial airway obstruction, coughing or gastric
insufflations.
Endotracheal tubes
Endotracheal tubes are most commonly inserted for people who
have had general anaesthetics or for those in emergency situations
where mechanical ventilation is required. An endotracheal tube is
inserted by the doctor or by a nurse with specialised education. It is
inserted through the mouth or the nose and into the trachea with the
guide of a laryngoscope (see Figure 53.21
). The tube terminates
just superior to the bifurcation of the trachea into the bronchi. The
tube may have an air-filled cuff to prevent air leakage around it,
prevent aspiration and aid with security of the tube. Because an
endotracheal tube passes through the epiglottis and glottis, the
person is unable to speak while it is in place. Nursing interventions
for people with endotracheal tubes are shown in Box 53.3
.
Figure 53.21


An endotracheal tube (ET).
BO X
53.3 Nursing interventions for people
with endotracheal tubes


Assess the person’s respiratory status at least every hour,
or more frequently if indicated. Include respiratory rate,
rhythm, depth, equality of chest excursion and lung
sounds; level of consciousness; and skin colour in your
assessment.
Frequently assess nasal and oral mucosa for redness and
irritation. Report any abnormal findings to the doctor.
Secure the endotracheal tube with a commercially
prepared holder or tape to prevent movement of the tube
further into or out of the trachea. Assess the position of
the tube frequently by auscultation of air entry into both
lungs. Seek immediate assistance if the tube is dislodged
out of the airway or air entry is unequal. If the tube
advances into a main bronchus, it will need to be
repositioned to ensure ventilation of both lungs.
Unless contraindicated, place the person in a side-lying or
semi-prone position as tolerated to prevent aspiration of
oral secretions.
Using sterile technique, suction the endotracheal tube as
needed to remove excessive secretions.
Closely monitor cuff pressure, maintaining a pressure of
20 to 25 mm Hg (or as recommended by the tube
manufacturer) to minimise the risk of tracheal tissue
necrosis, aspiration or tube displacement.
Provide oral and nasal care every 2 to 4 hours. If
necessary, insert a bite block or an oropharyngeal airway
to prevent the person from biting down on an oral
endotracheal tube. Move oral endotracheal tubes to the


opposite side of the mouth daily or as per organisation
protocol, taking care to maintain the position of the tube in
the trachea. This prevents irritation to the oral mucosa.
Provide humidified air or oxygen or a heat moisture
exchange device because the endotracheal tube
bypasses the upper airways, which normally moisten the
air.
If the person is on mechanical ventilation, ensure that all
alarms are enabled at all times because the person
cannot call for help should an emergency occur.
Communicate frequently with the person and their family,
providing a note pad or picture board for the person to
use in communicating.
Tracheostomy
People who need long-term airway support may have a
tracheostomy. A tracheostomy is an opening into the trachea
through the neck. A tube is usually inserted through this opening and
an artificial airway is created. Tracheostomy is done using one of
two techniques: the traditional open surgical method or a
percutaneous insertion. The percutaneous method can be done at
the bedside in a critical care unit. The open technique is done in the
operating room and a surgical incision is made in the trachea just
below the larynx. A curved tracheostomy tube is inserted to extend
through the stoma into the trachea (see Figure 53.22
).


Tracheostomy tubes are plastic and are available in different types,
such as single and double lumen, fenestrated and cuffed or uncuffed
tubes. Regardless of these variations, the principles of care are
similar.
Figure 53.22
A tracheostomy tube in place.
Tracheostomy tubes have an outer cannula that is inserted into the
trachea and a flange that rests against the neck and allows the tube
to be secured in place with tape or ties (see Figure 53.23
). All
tubes also have an obturator, which is used to insert the outer


cannula and is then removed. The obturator may be kept at the
person’s bedside in case the tube becomes dislodged and needs to
be reinserted. Some tracheostomy tubes have an inner cannula that
should be removed and cleaned with warm water and air dried prior
to reinsertion.
Figure 53.23
Components of a tracheostomy tube.


Cuffed tracheostomy tubes are surrounded by an inflatable cuff that
produces an airtight seal between the tube and the trachea. This
seal prevents aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions and air leakage
between the tube and the trachea. Cuffed tubes are often used
immediately after a tracheostomy and are essential when ventilating
a person with a tracheostomy with a mechanical ventilator. Children
do not require cuffed tubes because their tracheas are resilient
enough to seal the air space around the tube.
Low-pressure cuffs (see Figure 53.24
) are commonly used to
distribute a low, even pressure against the trachea, thus decreasing
the risk of tracheal tissue necrosis. They do not need to be deflated
periodically to reduce pressure on the tracheal wall. Air is removed
from the cuff prior to insertion or removal of the tube.
Figure 53.24


A tracheostomy tube with a low-pressure cuff.
A person with a tracheostomy tube is unable to speak as the tube is
below the vocal cords. When a person has a tracheostomy, it can be
a very difficult time for the person and their family. The nurse and
family members may have to adopt a variety of measures to support
communication with the person. Fenestrated tracheostomy tubes
have a decannulation plug that closes the proximal end of the tube,
allowing the breath to pass through the fenestration up past the
vocal cords, allowing the person to talk.
The nurse provides tracheostomy care for the person with a new or
recent tracheostomy to maintain patency of the tube and reduce the
risk of infection. Initially, a tracheostomy may need to be suctioned


(see the section on suctioning that follows) and cleaned as often as
every 1 to 2 hours. After the initial inflammatory response subsides,
tracheostomy care may need to be done only once or twice a day,
depending on the needs of the person. Skill 53.2
 describes
tracheostomy care.
When the person breathes through a tracheostomy, air is no longer
filtered and humidified as it is when passing through the upper
airways; therefore, special precautions are necessary. Heat moisture
exchangers keep the trachea clean, warm and moist (see Figure
53.25
). People with long-term tracheostomies may wear a light
scarf or a moisture protection pad held in place with a cotton tie to
filter air as it enters the tracheostomy. People with tracheostomy
tubes generally are older and, due to age-related physiological
changes, are at greater risk of complications.
Figure 53.25


Heat moisture exchanger.
Lifespan considerations
Tracheostomy care
Infants and children


An assistant should always be present while tracheostomy
care is performed.
General emergency equipment should always be easily
accessible and includes: tracheostomy dilators, suction
equipment and two sterile (one same size and one size
smaller) packaged tracheostomy tubes taped to the child’s
bed so that if the tube dislodges, a new one is available
for immediate reintubation (Bindler et al.
).
14 Bindler, R. C., Ball, J. W., London, M. L. & Davidson, M. W. (2016). Clinical
Skills Manual for Maternity and Pediatric Nursing (5th ed.). Upper Saddle River,
NJ: Pearson.
Older adults
Older adult skin is more fragile and prone to breakdown.
Care of the skin at the tracheostomy stoma is very
important.
Suctioning
When people have difficulty managing their secretions or an airway
is in place, suctioning may be necessary to clear air passages.
Suctioning
 is aspirating secretions through a catheter connected
to a suction machine or wall suction outlet. Suctioning may be
achieved through either open suctioning or closed-suction systems.
Even though the upper airways (the oropharynx and nasopharynx)
14


are not sterile, sterile technique is recommended for all suctioning to
avoid introducing pathogens into the airways.
Home care considerations
Tracheostomy care
For tracheostomies older than 1 month, clean
technique (rather than sterile technique) is used for
tracheostomy care.
Stress the importance of good hand hygiene to the
caregiver.
Tap water may be used for rinsing the inner
cannula.
Teach the caregiver the tracheostomy care
procedure and observe a return demonstration.
Periodically reassess caregiver knowledge and/or
tracheostomy care technique.
Inform the caregiver of the signs and symptoms
that may indicate an infection of the stoma site or
lower airway.
Names and telephone numbers of health care
personnel who can be reached for emergencies or
advice must be available to the person and/or
caregiver.
If the tracheostomy is permanent, provide contact
information for available support groups.


The person and their family should be confident
and competent in care of the tracheostomy prior to
discharge.
Suction catheters may be either open tipped or whistle tipped (see
Figure 53.26
). The whistle-tipped catheter is less irritating to
respiratory tissues, although the open-tipped catheter may be more
effective for removing thick mucus plugs. An oral suction tube, or
Yankauer device, is used to suction the oral cavity (see Figure
53.27
). Most suction catheters have a thumb port on the side to
control the suction. The catheter is connected to suction tubing,
which in turn is connected to a collection chamber and suction
control gauge (see Figure 53.28
).
Figure 53.26


Types of suction catheters. A: Open tipped; B: whistle tipped.
Figure 53.27


Oral (Yankauer) suction tube.
Figure 53.28


A wall suction unit.
Source: Jenny Thomas.
The nurse decides when suctioning is needed by assessing the
person for signs of respiratory distress or evidence that the person
is unable to cough up and expectorate secretions. Dyspnoea,
bubbling or rattling breath sounds, poor skin colour (cyanosis) or


decreased oxygen saturation
 levels (also called
 sat)
may indicate the need for suctioning. Good nursing judgment is
necessary because suctioning irritates mucous membranes and can
increase secretions if performed too frequently. In other words,
suctioning is based on clinical need rather than a fixed schedule.
Oral and oropharyngeal suctioning removes secretions from the
upper respiratory tract. Nasopharyngeal and nasotracheal suctioning
provides closer access to the trachea and requires sterile technique.
Skill 53.3
 outlines oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal suctioning.
Orotracheal suctioning may be required to remove retained
secretions when the person does not have an endotracheal or
tracheostomy tube in situ. Suctioning is the same as oropharyngeal
suctioning with the exception that a disposable Y-suction is passed
further down into the person’s trachea. The Y-suction catheter may
be passed through with a naso- or oropharyngeal artificial airway.
Following endotracheal intubation or a tracheostomy, the trachea
and surrounding respiratory tissues are irritated and react by
producing excessive secretions. Sterile suctioning is necessary to
remove these secretions from the trachea and bronchi to maintain a
patent airway.
There are two methods of suctioning a person with an artificial
airway: open suction system (OSS) and closed suction system
(CSS) (in-line suctioning). OSS occurs when the ventilator circuit is
disconnected and a single-use catheter is used to suction the
artificial airway. The CSS allows the airway to be suctioned without
(SpO2)
O2


disconnecting the circuit as the suction catheter is enclosed in a
plastic sleeve (see Figure 53.29
). The CSS catheter can be
reused.
Figure 53.29
A closed airway suction (in-line) system.


The frequency of suctioning depends on the person’s health and
how recently the intubation was done. Additionally, suctioning may
be necessary in people who have increased secretions because of
pneumonia or inability to clear secretions because of altered level of
consciousness.
Suctioning is associated with several complications: hypoxaemia,
trauma to the airway, hospital-acquired infection and cardiac
dysrhythmia, which is related to the hypoxaemia. The following
techniques are used prior to suctioning to minimise or decrease
these complications:
Hyperinflation
. Hyperinflation is not commonly used in
Australia nor is it recommended as routine practice prior to
suctioning (Credland ).
15 Credland, N. (2016). How to perform open tracheal suction via an endotracheal tube.
Nursing Standard: Official Newspaper of the Royal College of Nursing, 30(35), 36–38.
https://doi.org/10.7748/ns.30.35.36.s46.
Hyperoxygenation
. May be performed by increasing the
oxygen concentration before suctioning and between suction
attempts.
For tracheostomy and endotracheal suctioning, the outer diameter
of the suction catheter should not exceed one-half the internal
diameter of the tracheostomy or endotracheal tube so that hypoxia
can be prevented (Credland 2016; Agency for Clinical Innovation ).
The nurse uses sterile techniques to prevent infection of the
respiratory tract (see Skill 53.4
). The traditional method of
15
16


suctioning an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy is referred to as
the OSS. If a person is connected to a ventilator, CSS systems
should be used. Where the OSS method is required (typically when
the person is breathing spontaneously and not ventilated), the nurse
disconnects the person from the circuit, suctions the airway,
reconnects the circuit and discards the suction catheter.
16 Agency for Clinical Innovation (2014). Suctioning an Adult ICU Patient with an Artificial
Airway: A Clinical Practice Guideline. NSW: ACI. Retrieved from
<www.aci.health.nsw.gov.au>.
With CSS (see Figure 53.29
), the suction catheter attaches to
the ventilator tubing and the person does not need to be
disconnected from the ventilator. The nurse is not exposed to any
secretions because the suction catheter is enclosed in a plastic
sheath. The catheter can be reused as many times as necessary
until the system is changed. The nurse needs to inquire about the
organisation’s policy for changing the CSS.
Chest tubes and drainage systems
If the thin, double-layered pleural membrane is disrupted by lung
disease, surgery or trauma, the negative pressure between the
pleural layers may be lost. The lung then collapses because it is no
longer drawn outward as the diaphragm and intercostal muscles
contract during inhalation. When air collects in the pleural space, it is
known as a pneumothorax
. Blood or fluid in the pleural space, a
haemothorax
, places pressure on lung tissue and interferes with
lung expansion. Chest tubes may be inserted into the pleural cavity


to restore negative pressure and drain collected fluid or blood.
Because air rises, chest tubes for pneumothorax often are placed in
the upper anterior thorax, whereas chest tubes used to drain fluid
generally are placed in the lower lateral chest wall.
Lifespan considerations
Suctioning
Neonates and infants
Suction should not be used in neonates and infants unless
there is an indication of airway obstruction. A large-bore
cannula 10 to 12 Fr is used to suction the mouth and
pharyngeal areas. The suction catheter should not pass
further than 5 cm from the mouth in a term infant. The
suction should be limited to a few seconds duration and
should be less than 100 mm Hg negative pressure.
Prolonged suctioning can cause laryngospasm, a drop in
oxygen levels and bradycardia.
Children
A catheter is used to remove secretions from an older
child’s mouth or nose.
Older adults


Older adults often have cardiac and/or pulmonary
disease, thus increasing their susceptibility to hypoxaemia
related to suctioning. Watch closely for signs of
hypoxaemia. If noted, stop suctioning and
hyperoxygenate.
Home care considerations
Suctioning
Teach the individual and family that the most
important aspect of infection control is frequent
hand washing.
Airway suctioning in the home is considered a clean
procedure.
The catheter or Yankauer should be flushed by
suctioning recently boiled or distilled water to rinse
away mucus, followed by the suctioning of air
through the device to dry the internal surface and,
thus, discourage bacterial growth. The suction
catheter or Yankauer should be allowed to dry and
then be stored in a clean, dry area.
Suction catheters treated in the manner described
above may be reused. It is recommended that
catheters be discarded after 24 hours. Yankauer
suction tubes may be cleaned, boiled and reused.


Lifespan considerations
Suctioning a tracheostomy or endotracheal tube
Infants and children
Have an assistant gently restrain the child to keep the
child’s hands out of the way. The assistant should
maintain the child’s head in the midline position.
Older adults
Do a thorough lung assessment before and after
suctioning to determine effectiveness of suctioning and to
be aware of any special problems.
Home care considerations
Suctioning a tracheostomy or endotracheal tube
Whenever possible, the person should be
encouraged to clear the airway by coughing.


It may be necessary to teach the person to suction
their secretions if they cannot cough effectively.
Clean gloves should be used when endotracheal
suctioning is performed in the home environment.
The nurse needs to educate the caregiver on how
to determine the need for suctioning and the
correct process and rationale underlying the
practice of suctioning to avoid potential
complications of suctioning.
Stress the importance of adequate hydration, as it
thins secretions, which can aid in the removal of
secretions by coughing or suctioning.
When chest tubes are inserted, they must be connected to a sealed
drainage system or a one-way valve that allows air and fluid to be
removed from the chest cavity but prevents air from entering from
the outside. Sterile disposable drainage systems are used to prevent
outside air from entering the chest tube. These may be one-, two- or
three-chamber systems. These systems typically have a suction
control chamber, a water seal chamber and a closed collection
chamber for drainage (see Figure 53.30
). With the water-seal
system, when the person inhales, the water prevents air from
entering the system from the atmosphere. During exhalation,
however, air can exit the chest cavity, bubbling up through the water.
Suction can be added to the system to facilitate removing air and
secretions from the chest cavity. The drainage system should always


be kept below the level of the person’s chest to prevent fluid and
drainage from being drawn back into the chest cavity.
Figure 53.30


A disposable chest drainage system.
Research note
Nurses’ knowledge, skills and self-efficacy when caring
for the person with a tracheostomy or laryngectomy
K. McDonough, J. Crimlisk, P. Nicholas, H. Cabral, E. K. Quinn & S. Jalisi
. Standardizing nurse
training strategies to improve knowledge and self-efficacy with tracheostomy and laryngectomy care.
Applied Nursing Research, 32, 212–216.
17 McDonough, K., Crimlisk, J., Nicholas, P., Cabral, H., Quinn, E. K. & Jalisi, S. (2016). Standardizing
nurse training strategies to improve knowledge and self-efficacy with tracheostomy and laryngectomy
care. Applied Nursing Research, 32, 212–216.
Prevention of complications and serious adverse events for
hospitalised people with a tracheostomy is a priority. Sputum
plugs, infection, inappropriate suctioning technique and
accidental decannulation are a few preventable adverse
events. Indeed, tracheostomy displacement accounts for
around 50% of airway-related deaths. Evidence suggests that
nursing knowledge, confidence and competency caring for
the person may be contributing factors. The authors of this
study sought to demonstrate that dedicated, annual training
would increase the nurses’ knowledge, self-efficacy and
necessary skills associated with tracheostomy and
laryngectomy care. Nurses in the study completed a survey
both before and after they completed the hands-on program.
Findings demonstrated that while the nurses in the study had
17


a very poor understanding of the topic, dedicated hands-on
training increased knowledge, clinical competency and self-
efficacy.
Implications Significant knowledge gaps exist in nurses’
understanding and clinical competence when caring for the
person with a tracheostomy. Annual didactic and hands-on
education will potentially address the problem.
A Heimlich valve may be used for people who are ambulatory (see
Figure 53.31
). The Heimlich valve is a one-way flutter valve that
allows air to escape from the chest cavity but prevents air from re-
entering. The arrow on the housing of the valve should always point
away from the person. At each assessment, observe the inner valve
carefully for movement during exhalation, indicating airflow through
the device. The Heimlich valve is not designed to collect fluid.
Another device that can attach to the chest tube, called the
Pneumostat™, also has a one-way valve and, unlike the Heimlich
valve, has a small built-in collection chamber. It is used exclusively
for people with pneumothorax and small collections of fluid in the
pleural space (see Figure 53.32
).
Figure 53.31


Heimlich chest drain valve.
Source: George Draper/Pearson Education, Inc.
Figure 53.32


The Pneumostat™ is an example of a device often used for people
with a pneumothorax. It uses a one-way valve and has a small
collection chamber.
Nursing responsibilities regarding drainage systems include the
following:
Monitor and maintain the patency and integrity of the drainage
system.
Assess the person’s vital signs, oxygen saturation,
cardiovascular status and respiratory status. Check the breath
sounds bilaterally and check for symmetry of breath sounds.
Observe the dressing site at least every 4 hours. Inspect the
dressing for excessive and abnormal drainage, such as bleeding
or foul-smelling discharge. Palpate around the dressing site and
listen for a crackling sound indicative of subcutaneous
emphysema. Subcutaneous emphysema, which is air in the
subcutaneous tissues, can result from a poor seal at the chest
tube insertion site.
Determine level of discomfort with and without activity and
medicate the person for pain if indicated.
Educate the family to remind and encourage the person to
complete deep breathing and coughing exercises every 2 hours
(this may be contraindicated in people who have had a lung
removed). Have the person sit upright to perform the exercises
and splint the chest around the tube insertion site with a pillow or
with a hand to minimise discomfort.


Reposition the person every 2 hours. When the person is lying
on the affected side, place rolled towels beside the tubing.
Frequent position changes promote drainage, prevent
complications and provide comfort. Rolled towels prevent
occlusion of the chest tube by the person’s weight.
Assist the person with range-of-motion exercises of the affected
shoulder three times per day to maintain joint mobility.
Ensure that the connections are securely taped and that the
chest tube is secured to the person’s chest wall.
Keep the collection device below the person’s chest level.
Frequently check the water seal to ensure that water has not
evaporated. Also check that suction remains patent and at the
prescribed level. The water seal level should fluctuate with
respiratory effort as this reflects changes in intrapleural pressure
and respiration (Tarhan et al.
).
18 Tarhan, M., Gökduman, S. A., Ayan, A. & Dalar, L. (2016). Nurses’ knowledge levels
of chest drain management: A descriptive study. Eurasian Journal of Pulmonology, 18(3),
153–159.
Assess the drainage in the tubing and collection chamber. The
drainage is measured at regularly scheduled times (check the
organisation policy). Mark the date and time at the fluid level on
the drainage chamber. The unit is not replaced until almost full.
Bubbling indicates an air leak. Some systems will continually
bubble when attached to a suction unit.
Avoid aggressive chest tube manipulation (e.g. milking or
stripping the tube). Studies have shown that these techniques do
not improve chest tube patency. If necessary, however, a gentle
technique such as squeezing hand over hand along the tubing
18


and releasing the tubing between squeezes may help improve
patency (Loughran ).
19 Loughran, P. (2019). Stripping or milking of chest tubes. Critical Care Nurse, 39(3),
72–73.
Avoid clamping the chest tube, as this increases the risk of a
tension pneumothorax. Always check organisation policy on
clamping of chest tubes.
If the tube becomes disconnected from the collecting system,
encourage the person to exhale and cough then submerge the
end in 2.5 cm of sterile water to maintain the seal. If the chest
tube is inadvertently pulled out, the wound should be immediately
covered with a dry sterile dressing. If you can hear air leaking out
the site, ensure that the dressing is not occlusive. If the air
cannot escape, this would lead to a tension pneumothorax. A
tension pneumothorax occurs when there is build-up of air in the
pleural space and it cannot escape, causing increased pressure.
This pressure can eventually compromise cardiovascular
function.
When assisting the person to ambulate or when transporting:
a. Keep the water-seal unit below chest level and upright.
b. Disconnect the drainage system from the suction
apparatus before moving the person and make sure the
air vent is open.
Use standard precautions and personal protective equipment
while manipulating the system and assisting with insertion or
removal.
19


Chest tube insertion and removal require sterile technique and must
be done without introducing air or micro-organisms into the pleural
cavity. Removal of a chest tube is a brief but quite painful procedure.
Medicate the person as necessary before the removal. Remove the
dressing around the tube and prepare the dressing that will cover
the insertion site. This will be an occlusive dressing if there is no
purse-string suture around the insertion site to prevent air from
entering the chest. Generally, the doctor performs the removal but,
in some areas, specially trained nurses may be permitted to do so.
Evaluating
Using the goals and desired outcomes identified in the planning
stage of the nursing process, the nurse collects data to evaluate the
effectiveness of interventions. If outcomes are not achieved, the
nurse, individual and support person, if appropriate, need to explore
the reasons before modifying the care plan. For example, if the
outcome ‘Respirations unlaboured and rate is within expected range’
is not met, examples of questions that need to be considered
include the following:
What is the person’s and/or the family’s perception of the
problem?
Is the person complaining of shortness of breath or difficulty
breathing?
Is the person taking medications or performing treatments such
as percussion, vibration and postural drainage as prescribed?


Has the person been exposed to an upper respiratory infection
that is affecting breathing?
Do other factors need to be considered, such as the person’s
psychological stress level?
Examples of questions to consider if the outcome ‘Able to complete
ADLs without fatigue’ is not met include the following:
What other factors may be affecting the person’s ability to
complete ADLs?
Is the person getting adequate sleep? If not, what is interfering
with the person’s rest?
Are there assistive devices (e.g. a shower chair, clothing that is
easy to put on) that could help the person achieve this goal?
Does the person need help with housework and other ADLs?
Is the person’s diet adequate to meet nutritional needs?

Effective airway clearance
Applying critical thinking

suspect that Ms Singh had a very bad cold? Would
you have come to the same conclusion?

distress. What signs might indicate that her condition
is deteriorating into an emergency situation? How
would you handle this?
3. It appears that Ms Singh’s sputum has not been
cultured. In caring for her, what infection-control
guidelines would be needed?

L/minute. What are the considerations for
administering oxygen to a person with COPD?
