and Chronic Kidney Disease: Australian Facts: Morbidity—Hospital Care. Cardiovascular,
diabetes and chronic kidney disease series no. 3. Cat. no. CDK 3. Canberra: AIHW.
Retrieved from <www.aihw.gov.au>.
9


Factors affecting cardiovascular
function
Many factors affect cardiovascular function. Some of these factors
are called risk factors, because, if present, they increase the risk of
cardiovascular disease. Risk factors have been identified for
coronary artery disease, hypertension and peripheral vascular
disease and the majority are the same.
Risk factors
Major risk factors for cardiovascular disease in general have been
classified as non-modifiable (cannot be altered) and modifiable
lifestyle/behavioural risk factors (can be reduced). However, newer,
non-traditional cardiovascular risk factors have also been identified
(see Box 54.1
).
BO X
54.1 Risk factors for coronary heart
disease and targets


Traditional
Non-modifiable risk factors
The first non-modifiable risk factor is heredity. There is a genetic link
for the development of coronary artery disease. That is, if a person
has a parent with heart disease, they are at higher risk. The second
is age. While cardiovascular disorders primarily occur in older
people, they do occur in younger people. Generally, the risk
increases with age, with the highest rate in the 85 years and over
group (AIHW
). The third non-modifiable risk factor is gender.
Through middle adulthood (until menopause), oestrogen has a
protective effect in women, slowing the progress of atherosclerosis
and reducing the risk of cardiovascular disease. This effect is lost at
menopause, but hormone replacement therapy (HRT) may be
beneficial in reducing this risk later in life. Possible benefits from
HRT must be weighed against possible risks. CVD death rates are
1.4 times as high among males compared with females.
10 Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) (2016). Australia’s Health. Australia’s
health series no. 15. Cat. no. AUS 199. Canberra: AIHW.
Women tend to have an acute myocardial infarction (AMI)
 at
an older age than men and are more likely to have complications
(see ‘Research note
’). The presence of chest pain varies
between men and women. More women have pain-free AMIs than
10


men. But they are more likely to experience shortness of breath,
nausea, back pain or unusual fatigue. Research reflects that women
who have an AMI have increased delays in treatment and less
aggressive treatment than men. This results in increased mortality
rates.
Research note
Gender difference in people presenting with acute
coronary syndrome
L. Worrall-Carter, S. McEvedy, A. Wilson & M. A. Rahman (
). Gender differences in presentation,
coronary intervention, and outcomes of 28,985 acute coronary syndrome patients in Victoria,
Australia. Women’s Health Issues, 26(1), 14–20. Doi: 10.1016/j.whi.2015.09.002.
11 Worrall-Carter, L., McEvedy, S., Wilson, A. & Rahman, M. A. (2016). Gender differences in
presentation, coronary intervention, and outcomes of 28,985 acute coronary syndrome patients in
Victoria, Australia. Women’s Health Issues, 26(1), 14–20. Doi: 10.1016/j.whi.2015.09.002.
Annually, acute coronary syndrome (ACS) impacts on
thousands of Australians, with CHD (the main cause of ACS)
being responsible for more deaths than any other disease.
For Australian women, 15% of all deaths will be attributed to
CHD.
While well-developed ACS management guidelines exist,
there is variation in the type of care received by women and
men. This study reviewed all people presenting to Victorian
hospitals with ACS to determine if there are gender
differences in treatment and outcomes. The results showed
11


that women were less likely than men to receive coronary
interventions.
Implications Clinicians should be cognisant that women may
be less likely to receive referral for diagnostic procedure and
that this omission may negatively impact on women’s health
outcomes.
Modifiable risk factors
The modifiable risk factors include high blood cholesterol,
hypertension, tobacco smoking, diabetes, overweight and obesity,
and physical inactivity. The likelihood of developing CVD increases
with the number of risk factors. More than 90% of women have at
least one modifiable CVD risk factor and half the Australian
population have two or three risk factors (AIHW 2016).
High blood cholesterol
A strong link exists between elevated serum lipid levels and the
development of coronary heart disease. Lipoproteins circulate in the
blood and are made up of cholesterol, triglycerides and
phospholipids. A high dietary intake of saturated fats is the most
critical factor for the development of elevated serum lipids. The
Heart Foundation recommends that a diet be rich in fruits and
vegetables, and low in dairy products and saturated and total fat


(National Heart Foundation of Australia and the Cardiac Society of
Australia and New Zealand ) (see Box 54.1
).
12 National Heart Foundation of Australia and the Cardiac Society of Australia and New
Zealand (2012). Reducing Risk in Heart Disease: An Expert Guide to Clinical Practice for
Secondary Prevention of Coronary Heart Disease. Melbourne: National Heart Foundation of
Australia.
Hypertension
Hypertension (or increased blood pressure) increases the risk of
coronary heart disease in several ways. First, it increases the
workload of the heart, increasing oxygen demand and coronary
blood flow. The increased workload also causes hypertrophy of the
ventricles. Over time, this can contribute to heart failure. Secondly,
hypertension causes endothelial damage to the blood vessels, which
stimulates the development of atherosclerosis. In 2017–18, 1 in 5
Australians aged over 18 had high blood pressure (Australian
Bureau of Statistics (ABS)
).
13 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2018). National Health Survey—First Results.
Canberra: ABS.
Tobacco smoking
The cardiovascular system is also affected by cigarette smoking.
Nicotine increases the heart rate, blood pressure and peripheral
vascular resistance, increasing the heart’s workload. Smoking
causes vasoconstriction and, in areas where vessels already are
12
13


narrowed by atherosclerosis, tissue oxygenation can be impaired. In
Australia, the overall smoking rates are continuing to fall, with just
over 13.8% of people smoking daily (ABS 2018).
Diabetes
Type 2 diabetes increases the risk of coronary heart disease,
myocardial infarction, peripheral vascular disease and kidney failure.
Consequently, all patients with CHD should be screened for
diabetes. High blood sugars are linked with accelerated development
of atherosclerosis as well as high levels of serum lipids and
triglycerides. The prevalence of diabetes has increased substantially
in Australia, with an estimated 1 in 20 (1.2 million people) Australians
having diabetes (ABS 2018). Educating people and their families on
how diet, exercise and the administration of oral glucose-lowering
drugs and/or insulin injections contribute to the management of
diabetes is an important nursing activity. Control of blood sugar
levels can greatly reduce risk and slow development of
atherosclerosis.
Overweight and obesity
Overweight and obese people have an increased risk of the
development of cardiovascular disease. In 2017–18, two-thirds
(67%) of Australians over 18 years of age were obese or overweight
(ABS 2018). Within this group, 74.5% of men and 59.7% of women
were classified as obese or overweight (BMI > 30) (ABS 2018).
Compared with people living in major cities (65.0%), people living in


regional areas of Australia (72.4%) are more likely to be overweight
or obese (ABS 2018). Obesity is often accompanied by elevated
serum lipid levels, which increase risk. Additionally, obesity places an
increased workload on the heart, which increases oxygen demand.
An obese individuals’ risk of heart failure and death increases. Waist
circumference, excess abdominal fat and BMI are risk factors for
CVD and type 2 diabetes (ABS 2018) (see Box 54.1
).
Lifespan considerations
Circulation
Children
Blood pressure should be taken routinely on children after
age 3 years.
Heart murmurs, extra sounds detected when listening to
the heart, are common in children, especially in the
preschool years. The vast majority are not associated with
a pathology but are due to normal blood flow or
transitional physiological processes that increase cardiac
output (e.g. anaemia, fever, exercise) (McCance &
Huether 2019).
Older adult
Normal changes of ageing may contribute to problems of
circulation in older adults, even when there is no actual


pathology.
Blood vessels become less elastic and have an increase
in calcification. This results in a restricted blood flow and a
decrease of oxygen and nutrients to tissues (heart,
peripheral and cerebral).
Impaired valve function in the heart is often the result of
increased stiffness and calcification and results in a
decrease in cardiac output.
A decrease of muscle tone in the heart results in a
decrease in cardiac output.
There is a decrease in baroreceptor response to blood
pressure changes, making the heart and blood vessels
less responsive to exercise and stress. This often results
in dizziness, falls, orthostatic hypotension and mental
changes.
A decrease in conduction ability in the heart also makes
the heart less responsive to changes and stresses. This
can also result in dizziness, falls, orthostatic hypotension
and mental changes.
All these factors become important if the person is challenged
by stressors, such as exercise, stress, fever, surgery or other
changes. If challenged, the circulatory system of older adults
is not as effective or as quick to return to normal. People
living with normal changes of ageing and/or pathological
conditions of the circulatory system need to learn to balance
diet, medications and exercise. Nurses have a large part in
working with these people to develop appropriate


interventions and provide teaching to help them maintain
optimal functioning. Teaching people to recognise any
changes or worsening of their condition is very important.
They need to contact the doctor and make any needed
changes. Changing lifestyles and fine-tuning medications can
be critical and nurses can be a part of this in every phase of
the nursing process.
Physical inactivity
Physical activity is associated with a reduction in the risk of death
due to cardiovascular disease (ABS 2018). Physical exercise or
activity increases the heart rate and hence the supply of oxygen in
the body. With regular vigorous exercise, the heart muscle becomes
more powerful and efficient. Aerobic exercise slows the
atherosclerotic process, reducing the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Sedentary people, by contrast, have a higher risk of cardiovascular
disease. Unfortunately, less than half of Australia’s population meet
the recommended physical activity guidelines of 150–300 minutes of
moderate intensity physical activity per week (ABS 2018).
Other factors influencing
cardiovascular function


Other factors that may influence cardiovascular function include
previous health status, stress and coping, dietary factors, alcohol
intake and an elevated homocysteine level.
Health status
In the healthy person, the cardiovascular system (working together
with the respiratory system) is able to provide sufficient oxygen to
meet the body’s needs. Diseases of the cardiovascular system will
often affect the delivery of oxygen to the cells of the body and when
any system or tissue does not get the required oxygen for metabolic
processes, cellular function will be altered. The body has
‘compensatory mechanisms’ that are activated when oxygen
decreases. These mechanisms include increased heart rate,
increased strength of cardiac contraction, vasoconstriction and the
release of certain hormones such as aldosterone. The health status
of a person may affect how the body tolerates the compensation
and the decreased oxygen availability. A person with no significant
health history and with good nutritional status will be more likely to
tolerate short periods of decreased oxygen and the body’s
compensation than a person with multiple disorders and poor
nutritional status.
Most cardiovascular conditions affect how the blood gets to the
tissues. One cardiovascular condition that affects the oxygen-
carrying capacity of the blood is anaemia, described in ‘Blood
alterations’ on page 1499.


Social, economic, psychological,
environmental and cultural factors
Psychosocial factors have been reported to be associated with CHD.
Studies show there is an association between stress, depression,
social isolation, remoteness, socioeconomic disadvantage and a lack
of quality social supports, and CHD (ABS 2018).
Stress causes a neurohormonal response. The stress response
involves a number of interrelated responses and effects. One of the
major effects of stress is the release of adrenal medullary
hormones: adrenaline and noradrenaline. Adrenaline has several
effects including causing the heart to contract more forcefully,
increasing heart rate and stimulating peripheral vasoconstriction.
Noradrenaline causes widespread vasoconstriction, which increases
the blood pressure and increases the oxygen demands of the heart.
CHD typically develops in the frail and elderly, but it is also
disproportionately high in the lower socioeconomic group, in males,
in Indigenous Australians and in groups living in regional and remote
Australia. When compared with people living in major cities,
Australians living in regional and remote areas of Australia generally
report lower levels of health and higher death rates. CHD is the most
common cause of death for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
people (National Heart Foundation of Australia ). The CVD death
rate is reported as 1.3 times higher in remote areas (ABS ). This
has been attributed to the fact that these people are disadvantaged
14
15


in their access to health care and basic necessities such as clean
water and fresh food (ABS 2017). Similarly, people living in regional
and remote areas are more likely to engage in health behaviours
that contribute to CHD, such as tobacco smoking, alcohol
consumption and lower levels of physical activity and fruit intake. As
regional and remote areas also tend to have a greater proportion of
residents of Indigenous background, the influence of these factors
on mortality is complex (ABS 2018).
14 National Heart Foundation of Australia (2018). Coronary Heart Disease. Melbourne:
National Heart Foundation of Australia.
15 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2017). Causes of Death. Canberra: ABS.
Indigenous Australians have a higher prevalence of obesity,
diabetes, smoking and high blood pressure (ABS 2018). Hence, one
of the leading causes of death for Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander people is CHD (Brown & Kritharides ). However, the high
rates of CHD in the Indigenous population are not accounted for by
these risk factors alone. Cultural, historic, environmental,
socioeconomic and social-isolation factors, and the lack of quality
social support all contribute to increased risk in this population
(Brown & Kritharides 2017).
16 Brown, A. & Kritharides, L. (2017). Overcoming cardiovascular disease in Indigenous
Australians. MJA, 206(1), 10–12.
Depression is a mental illness that affects one in four Australians.
There is growing evidence that depression is a modifiable risk factor
for CVD such as CHD, stroke and type 2 diabetes. The risk is
16


directly related to the severity of the depression. Similarly, there is
an association between social isolation and a lack of quality social
support networks and CHD. Involving family and social support
networks in the recovery process is important.
Diet
Diet is a known contributor to hypertension, high blood cholesterol
and overweight and obesity. A healthy diet with adequate calories,
protein and other nutrients is important to maintain good immune
function and increase resistance to disease. There is a relationship
between increased intake of vegetables, fruits and berries, and a
decreased occurrence of CHD. Most non-Indigenous Australian
adults and less than half of Indigenous Australian adults eat the
recommended two serves of fruit and five serves of vegetables daily
(ABS ). Remoteness, availability of food, choice and cost of food,
income and store managers’ attitudes all contribute to poor or
inadequate nutrition for Indigenous Australians (Henryks &
Brimblecombe ).
17 Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) (2016). Australian Health Survey. Canberra: ABS.
18 Henryks, J. & Brimblecombe, J. (2016). Mapping point-of-purchase influencers of food
choice in Australian remote Indigenous communities: A review of the literature. SAGE Open,
6(1), 1–11. Doi: 10.1177/2158244016629183.
Along with certain vitamins and minerals, dietary protein is important
to prevent anaemia. High salt intake can affect blood pressure and
contribute to the development of hypertension. High intake of
17
18


sodium may contribute to hypertension in two ways. First, it may
increase the release of a hormone called natriuretic hormone which
indirectly contributes to hypertension. Additionally, sodium stimulates
vasopressor mechanisms, which cause vasoconstriction. It is
recommended to reduce dietary salt intake to less than 4g/day
(approximately 1600 mg sodium). There is evidence that other
factors such as low potassium, calcium and magnesium intake may
contribute to vasoconstriction and the development of hypertension.
Alcohol
Recent studies suggest that moderate alcohol use (one to two
standard drinks per day) may actually reduce the risk of heart
disease; however, excessive alcohol intake affects oxygenation in
several ways (National Health and Medical Research Council ).
Alcohol is a respiratory depressant, slowing respirations. Alcohol
abusers often are malnourished, increasing their risk of anaemia and
infections. Excess alcohol intake also increases the risk of
hypertension.
19 National Health and Medical Research Council (2014). Alcohol and Health in Australia.
Retrieved from <www.nhmrc.gov.au>.
19


Alterations in cardiovascular
function
Cardiovascular function can be altered by conditions that affect:
the function of the heart as a pump
blood flow to organs and peripheral tissues
the composition of the blood and its ability to transport oxygen
and carbon dioxide.
Three major alterations in cardiovascular function are decreased
cardiac output, impaired tissue perfusion and disorders that affect
the composition or amount of blood available for transport of gases.
Decreased cardiac output
Although the heart normally is able to increase its rate and force of
contraction to increase cardiac output during exercise, fever or other
times of need, some conditions interfere with these mechanisms.
The vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle may become
occluded by atherosclerosis or a blood clot, shutting off the blood
supply to a portion of the myocardium. When this happens, the


tissue becomes necrotic and dies, a condition known as a
myocardial infarction (MI)
 or heart attack. If a large portion of
the heart muscle is affected, particularly in the left ventricle, cardiac
output falls because the affected muscle no longer contracts. Signs
and symptoms of myocardial infarction are variable and may include
the following:
chest pain; substernal and/or radiating to the neck, throat, jaw,
either one or both arms down to the hands
nausea or vomiting
shortness of breath
diaphoresis
pallor
feeling dizzy or light-headed.
Heart failure
 occurs when the heart isn’t able to effectively pump
blood around the body to keep up with the body’s need for oxygen
and nutrients to the tissues. Heart failure usually occurs because of
myocardial infarction, but it may also result from chronic overwork of
the heart, such as in people with uncontrolled hypertension, a
damaged heart valve or extensive arteriosclerosis. It usually
develops slowly over a period of years (chronic heart failure);
however, it can also happen suddenly (acute failure). Heart failure
may be classified as left-sided versus right-sided heart failure,
systolic versus diastolic failure or high-output versus low-output
failure, and acute versus chronic failure. In left-sided heart failure,
the vessels of the pulmonary system become congested or
engorged with blood. This may cause fluid to escape into the alveoli


and interfere with gas exchange, a condition known as pulmonary
oedema.
If the heart failure involves the right side of the heart, there will also
be a ‘congestion’ or build-up of fluid in the liver or legs. Risk factors
for heart failure are CHD, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, diseases of
the heart valves, diabetes or obesity (AIHW 2017). Other diseases
such as myocarditis and cardiomyopathy also can affect the heart
muscle, impairing its ability to contract and pump. Box 54.2
 gives
examples of conditions that may precipitate heart failure.
BO X
54.2 Conditions that may precipitate
heart failure
Conditions that increase preload
Hypervolaemia
Diseases of the heart valve (such as rheumatic heart
disease)
Congenital defects such as patent ductus arteriosus
Conditions that increase afterload


Hypertension
Diabetes and obesity
Conditions that affect myocardial
function
Myocardial infarction
Cardiomyopathy
Coronary artery disease
Diseases of heart muscle (such as alcohol abuse or
infection)
Very irregular or excessively rapid or slow heart rates can decrease
the cardiac output. With irregular or very rapid heart rates, the
ventricles may not fill adequately between beats, so the stroke
volume (amount pumped with each beat) falls. If the heart rate is too
slow, the heart may not be able to increase its stroke volume
enough to maintain the cardiac output. Abnormalities of the heart
rate and rhythm are known as dysrhythmias and can be identified on
the electrocardiogram (ECG).
Alterations in the structure of the heart can affect cardiac output.
Congenital heart defects result in abnormal blood flow and may even
allow venous and arterial blood to mix. The oxygen supply to the
tissues is affected in this case. Acquired heart diseases such as
bacterial endocarditis and rheumatic fever may damage the heart


valves, affecting the flow of blood within the heart and to the great
vessels. For example, if the mitral (bicuspid) valve becomes scarred
and stenotic (constricted), it may not open fully, impairing filling of
the left ventricle. Or, if the mitral valve doesn’t fully close (mitral
insufficiency), blood may escape back or regurgitate into the left
atrium instead of entering the aorta each time the ventricle
contracts. Although heart failure is considered a condition of the
older adult, there are indications that the prevalence is also high in
the middle-aged, male Indigenous population. The rates of
hospitalisation and deaths from heart failure in Aboriginal and Torres
Strait Islander people are two to three times that of the non-
Indigenous population (AIHW 2017).
Impaired tissue perfusion
Atherosclerosis is by far the most common cause of impaired blood
flow to organs and tissues. As vessels narrow and become
obstructed, distal tissues receive less blood, oxygen and nutrients.
Ischaemia
 is a lack of blood supply due to obstructed circulation.
Any artery in the body may be affected by atherosclerosis, although
the effects are often related to coronary arteries, vessels supplying
blood to the brain and arteries in peripheral tissues. Obstruction of
blood flow through the coronary arteries due to narrowing from
atherosclerosis and/or thrombus is called coronary heart disease
(CHD). When blood flow through the arteries is not enough to meet
the oxygen demands of the heart tissue (myocardium), myocardial
ischaemia or infarction occurs. Myocardial infarction is the term used


when the myocardium dies (necrosis). The term acute coronary
syndrome (ACS) is used to represent the clinical syndromes from
unstable angina to acute myocardial infarction (AMI).
One of the most common manifestations of CHD is angina pectoris,
or angina
, the term used to describe the pain associated with
myocardial ischaemia. If the cerebral vessels are affected, the result
may be a transient ischaemic attack (TIA), or stroke. Peripheral
vascular disease leads to ischaemia of distal tissues such as the
legs and feet. Gangrene and amputation may result. Signs of
impaired peripheral arterial circulation may include the following:
decreased peripheral pulses
pale skin colour
cool extremities
decreased hair distribution.
The risk factors for peripheral atherosclerosis are similar to those for
coronary artery disease and include tobacco smoking, high fat
intake, obesity and a sedentary lifestyle. Hypertension and diabetes
also increase the risk of atherosclerosis, particularly if blood
pressure or blood glucose levels are not maintained at near-normal
levels.
Although much less common, other disorders such as vessel
inflammation, arterial spasm and blood clots also can occlude blood
vessels, leading to ischaemia. Tissue oedema can impair flow


through vessels and can increase the distance oxygen and nutrients
must diffuse across to reach cells.
On the venous side, incompetent valves may allow blood to pool in
veins, causing oedema and decreasing venous return to the heart
(see Figure 54.7
). Veins also can become inflamed, reducing
blood flow and increasing the risk of thrombus (clot) formation.
Thrombi may then break loose, becoming emboli. These emboli tend
to travel as far as the pulmonary circulation where they become
trapped in small vessels (pulmonary emboli), occluding blood supply
to the capillary side of the alveolar–capillary membrane. Although
alveolar ventilation to the affected area often remains adequate, no
gas exchange occurs there because of impaired blood flow. Signs of
acute pulmonary embolism can be non-specific and variable, but
may include the following:
sudden onset of shortness of breath
pleuritic chest pain.
Figure 54.7


Vein with competent valve and vein with incompetent valve that
allows blood to pool in the veins.


Source: J. Rice (2012). Medical Terminology: A Word Building Approach (7th ed.), Figure 9.37, p. 298. © 2012.
Reproduced with permission from Pearson Education, Inc., Upper Saddle River, NJ.
Acute coronary syndrome
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS)
 includes ‘a broad spectrum of
clinical presentations, spanning ST-segment-elevation myocardial
infarction, through to an accelerated pattern of angina without
evidence of myonecrosis’ (Chew et al.
). From a clinical
perspective, ACS is classified into syndromes that are characterised
by the presence or absence of ST elevation on the ECG, including
ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), non-ST elevation
myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) and angina pectoris.
20 Chew, D. P., Scott, I. A., Cullen, L., ... Aylward, P. E. G. (2016). National Heart Foundation
of Australia & Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Australian Clinical Guidelines for
the Management of Acute Coronary Syndromes 2016. Heart, Lung and Circulation, 25(9),
895–951.
Patient safety competency framework
6 Evidence-based practice
The Patient Safety Competency Framework
indicates that nursing students must
demonstrate the ability to provide care that
takes into account best available evidence,
clinical expertise and patient’s individual needs,
values and preferences (Levett-Jones et al.
).
20
21


Current evidence suggests that acute coronary
syndromes (ACSs) are the most common
underlying cause of sudden cardiac death and
demonstrate common pathophysiology (Chew et
al. 2016). ACS results from a sudden blockage
of a coronary artery, usually by a blood clot
(thrombosis).
21 Levett-Jones, T., Dwyer, T., Reid-Searl, K., Heaton, L., Flenady,
T., Applegarth, J., Guinea, S. & Andersen, P. (2017). Patient
Safety Competency Framework (PSCF) for Nursing Students.
Sydney. Retrieved from <http://psframework.wpengine.com>.
Skill: all people presenting with suspected ACS
should have a 12-lead ECG performed and the
results interpreted within 10 minutes.
Culturally competent care
There are numerous human-related factors that may impede
seeking medical assistance for a person with ACS. These
factors include older age, being part of an ethnic minority
group, having lower socioeconomic status, being female and
not having family support (Chew et al. 2016).


Blood alterations
As most oxygen is transported to the tissues in combination with
haemoglobin, the problems of inadequate RBCs, low haemoglobin
levels or abnormal haemoglobin structure can affect tissue
oxygenation. Anaemia has several different causes: RBCs are lost
along with other components because of acute or chronic bleeding;
if the diet is deficient in iron or folic acid, haemoglobin and RBCs are
not formed adequately; and some disorders cause RBCs to break
down excessively. People with sickle-cell disease produce an
abnormal form of haemoglobin and may experience tissue
ischaemia during exacerbations of the disease. Signs of anaemia
may include the following:
chronic fatigue
pallor
shortness of breath
hypotension.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: comprehensive care
‘The intention of this standard is to ensure that consumers
receive comprehensive care—that is, coordinated delivery of
the total healthcare required or requested by the patient’
(Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC)
, p. 38).
22


22 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health
Care (ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health
Service Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
All patients with a suspected acute coronary
syndrome should have a 12-lead ECG recorded
and interpreted by an experienced clinician
within 10 minutes of the first emergency clinical
contact. (ACSQHC , p. 4)
23 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC) (2014). Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care
Standard. Sydney: ACSQHC.
Blood volume also affects tissue oxygenation. If the blood volume is
inadequate as in haemorrhage or severe dehydration, the blood
pressure and cardiac output fall and tissues may become ischaemic.
Conversely, people with hypervolaemia (excess blood volume),
which can result from fluid retention or kidney failure, may develop
heart failure and peripheral oedema, leading to tissue ischaemia.
23


Nursing management
Assessing
Nursing assessment of the cardiovascular system status includes a
history, physical examination, cardiac monitoring and review of
relevant diagnostic data.
Nursing history
See Chapter 31
 and the ‘Assessment interview
’ for specific
techniques for obtaining a cardiac history. In addition to the
comprehensive nursing assessment interview, the nurse should
include data regarding:
presence of any symptoms such as pain, shortness of breath,
fatigue, palpitations, cough and fainting. When assessing pain,
remember PQRST (Reid-Searl et al.
). Ask the person:
24 Reid-Searl, K., Dwyer, T. & Moxham, L. (2019a). Nursing Student’s Clinical Survival
Guide (4th ed.). Frenchs Forest, NSW: Pearson Australia.
medications for heart, blood pressure, circulation and cholesterol
lifestyle, including social support, stressors and methods of
coping.
24


Physical assessment
To examine the cardiovascular system, the nurse first inspects the
person. Much information about the cardiovascular system is
obtained by assessing the skin for colour, temperature, hair
distribution, lesions and oedema. People with extensive peripheral
vascular disease may have peripheral cyanosis, cool feet with weak
pulses and shiny, nearly hairless shins and feet. A slow capillary refill
(greater than 2 seconds) may be indicative of hypovolaemia,
peripheral vascular disease or hypothermia. Note the colour of the
person’s tongue, because with central cyanosis it will have a blue or
purple discolouration. With peripheral cyanosis it will remain pink.
Pitting or dependent oedema of the sacrum, feet and ankles may be
noted in people with heart failure. Examine the person’s nails to
determine if there is any evidence of clubbing, which may be a sign
of congenital heart disease or infective endocarditis. Examine the
person’s fluid balance and urine output. In the average person, the
hourly urinary output should exceed 0.5 mL/kg/hour. See Chapter
31
 for specific techniques for assessing the respiratory and
cardiovascular systems.
Assessment interview
Circulation


Current or past cardiovascular
problems
Do you have high blood pressure?
Do you have any history of heart disease such as angina,
heart attack or heart failure? Have you ever had a cardiac
catheterisation, angiogram or angioplasty? Have you ever
been diagnosed with rheumatic fever, endocarditis,
pericarditis or other diseases of the heart? If so, when?
Have you had cardiac surgery or stent placement?
Have you ever been told that you have peripheral vascular
disease? Do you ever develop pain in the calves of your
legs when walking? How far can you walk before it
occurs? What do you do to relieve it? Have you had
surgery on your blood vessels?
Do your feet and ankles ever swell or feel very cold, numb
or tingling? Do you experience pain in your feet? Is the
pain changed by position?
Do you become extremely fatigued with activity? Have
you ever been told that you are anaemic?
Medication history
Have you taken or do you take any over-the-counter or
prescription medications for your heart or blood pressure,
or to increase blood flow?


Do you take any anticoagulants or other medications to
‘thin’ your blood?
Lifestyle
Do you smoke?
Do you exercise? What kind of exercise and how often?
How often do you drink alcoholic beverages such as beer,
wine or spirits? How much do you usually drink at the
time?
Next the nurse evaluates the blood pressure (BP) for both arms (the
results should be within 10 mm Hg of each other) and palpates
peripheral pulses for their rate, rhythm, strength and equality. A lying
and standing blood pressure should also be obtained. There should
be no more than a 15 mm Hg fall in the BP between the lying and
standing readings. If there is, this indicates orthostatic hypotension.
The apical impulse (previously known as the point of maximal
impulse (PMI)), located at the left fifth intercostal space and mid-
clavicular line, is palpated and auscultated. The apical impulse
should normally be about 1 cm by 2 cm and feel like a short, gentle
tap. The impulse will increase in amplitude and duration with high
cardiac output states such as anxiety, fever and anaemia. The apical
pulse is auscultated for rate, rhythm and the quality of heart sounds.
Listen for the ‘lub-bub’ sound of the valves of the heart closing.
Carotid arteries are auscultated for bruits (a sound of turbulence),
which may indicate atherosclerosis and narrowing (see Chapter


31
). Examine the neck for abnormal pulsations and venous
distension. The neck veins may become distended where the person
has congestive cardiac failure, cardiac tamponade or hypervolaemia.
Also important as an indicator of cardiac function is lung sounds.
Begin by examining the person’s breathing rate and pattern. By
auscultating the lungs for adventitious sounds, the nurse assesses
for increased pulmonary vessel pressure secondary to decreased
cardiac output.
Two methods to assess for peripheral vascular disease include the
ankle/brachial index (ABI) and the toe brachial pressure index
(TBPI). These measurements help determine arterial perfusion in
feet and help measure the severity of the disease or establish a
baseline. Box 54.3
 provides an example of an ABI calculation.
BO X
54.3 Calculating an ankle/brachial
index (ABI)
Both assessments use a blood pressure (BP) cuff and a
Doppler ultrasound device to measure the blood pressure
using the person’s brachial pulse and either the posterior
tibial pulse and dorsalis pedis pulse, or the great toe’s distal
pulse (TBPI) (Note: TBPI is not commonly performed in
Australia). The pressure index is calculated by dividing either
the posterior tibial or dorsalis pedis (whichever is highest)


systolic pressure (SBP) by the highest brachial artery SBP of
each arm; for example, a right brachial SBP of 160 and a left
brachial SBP of 120 along with a right dorsalis pedis pressure
of 80 and a left dorsalis pedis pressure of 120. The right ABI
is 0.50 (80 divided by 160) and the left ABI is 1.0 (120 divided
by 120). A normal ABI is between 0.9 and 1.4; < 0.9 indicates
peripheral artery disease.
Source: B. Mitchell, C. Ware, A. McGregor, S. Brown, A. Wells, R. L. Stuart ... M. Mason (
). ASID
(HICSIG)/AICA Position Statement: Preventing catheter-associated urinary tract infections in patients.
Healthcare Infection, 16(2), 45–52.
25 Mitchell, B., Ware, C., McGregor, A., ... Mason, M. (2011). ASID (HICSIG)/AICA Position Statement:
Preventing catheter-associated urinary tract infections in patients. Healthcare Infection, 16(2), 45–52.
Diagnostic studies
Many diagnostic studies are available that can help to identify the
presence of cardiovascular disease. Diagnostic studies may also be
used as screening tools to identify increased risk and then
modifications made to reduce the risk of development of
cardiovascular dysfunction. An example of this is the serum lipid
level. If a person has an elevated serum lipid level, they should be
educated about the effects of diet and the importance of reducing
lipids to reduce the risk of coronary heart disease.
Cardiac monitoring
25


Cardiac monitoring allows continuous observation of the person’s
cardiac rhythm. Cardiac monitoring is a recording of the heart’s
electrical activity. It is used in many instances: for people who have
known or suspected cardiovascular disease, during and after
surgery, to monitor responses to drug therapy and to monitor people
at risk of serious complications such as shock. Electrodes placed on
the person’s chest are attached to a monitor cable and bedside
monitor. The monitor is equipped with alarms used to warn of
potential problems such as very fast, very slow or irregular heart
rates. The alarm limits are set for 20 beats higher and lower than
the person’s baseline rate, often at 100 to 110 and 50 to 55,
respectively, for adults. Many of the cardiac monitors also have the
ability to detect changes to the ST segment. ST segment changes
characteristic of ischaemia are ST segment depression or down-
sloping, and flattening or inversion of the T wave. ST segment
elevation is most commonly associated with acute myocardial injury
or ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). But not all individuals
will present with this ST elevation on the ECG; they will be classified
as non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (non-STEMI or NSTEMI).
All people with chest pain and/or ST segment changes should be
assessed immediately by an appropriately qualified person. For
ambulatory people (in the hospital or at home), the electrodes
connect to a transmitter unit (also called telemetry). This unit
electronically sends the signal to a central monitor for display or to
where the information is to be recorded. Another name for this type
of ambulatory monitoring is the Holter monitor. Electrodes are
attached and the person wears the monitor for 24 hours. A
continuous ECG is recorded and later analysed for irregularities. A


stress ECG may be ordered where the ECG is recorded while the
person participates in progressive exercise.
Electrocardiography most commonly uses 12 ‘leads’ or 12 different
views of the heart. In contrast, cardiac monitoring uses two or three
leads at any given time. See Chapter 35
 for more information
about ECGs.
Clinical consideration
It is important to remember that ECG
monitoring is a recording of the electrical activity
of the heart; it does not reflect mechanical
contraction and cardiac output. ALWAYS
remember to check the person to assess for
cardiac function. Only looking at the ECG
tracing does not give an assessment of the
person’s status.
Blood tests
Specimens of venous blood are taken for several tests that may
reflect some aspect of cardiovascular functioning.


As haemoglobin is the molecule that oxygen attaches to, it gives an
indication of the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. A decreased
haemoglobin increases the risk of oxygen deficit in the tissues when
cardiovascular disease is present.
Measurement of serum electrolytes is important for people with
cardiovascular problems because electrolyte abnormalities such as
hyperkalaemia (higher than normal potassium) and hypokalaemia
(lower than normal potassium) can have a critical effect on the
heart. Serum levels of magnesium, calcium, sodium and phosphorus
are also important to assess.
As previously noted, measurement of enzyme levels in the blood is
an important part of the diagnostic evaluation of people with chest
pain. Certain cardiac-specific enzymes such as creatine kinase-MB
(CK-MB)
 and cardiac-specific troponin
 (cTnT, cTnI), and
myoglobin are released into the blood during an MI. These enzymes
are released into the blood as the cell membrane is damaged.
Elevated levels of these enzymes can help differentiate between an
MI (when the cells actually die) and chest pain from a different
cause such as angina or pleuritic pain.
Haemodynamic studies
Haemodynamics is the study of the forces or pressures involved in
blood circulation. Haemodynamic studies or monitoring procedures
may be performed to evaluate fluid status and cardiovascular
function. Parameters evaluated in haemodynamic studies include


heart rate, arterial blood pressure, central venous pressure,
pressures in the pulmonary vascular system and cardiac output.
Some of these parameters—for example, heart rate, arterial blood
pressure and venous pressure—are measured directly using an
arterial, central venous or pulmonary artery catheter; others such as
the stroke volume and cardiac output are calculated. Haemodynamic
studies are performed in a diagnostic cardiac laboratory and require
informed consent. People in intensive and cardiac care units may
undergo continuous haemodynamic monitoring to evaluate
cardiovascular status and the effect of interventions. Nurses in these
units are responsible for maintaining accurate readings and the
integrity of the system.
Diagnosing
Diagnostic labels that may be relevant for describing circulation
problems include:
Ineffective tissue perfusion (cardiopulmonary): decrease in
oxygen resulting in the failure to nourish the tissues at the
capillary level
Decreased cardiac output: inadequate blood pumped by the
heart to meet metabolic (demands) of the body
Activity intolerance: insufficient physiological or psychological
energy to endure or complete required or desired daily activities.


A clinical example is shown in ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses,
outcomes and interventions’.
Planning
When planning care, the nurse identifies nursing interventions that
will assist the person to achieve these broad goals:
Maintain or improve tissue perfusion.
Maintain or restore an adequate cardiac output.
Obviously, goals will vary according to the diagnosis and defining
characteristics for each individual. Appropriate preventive and
corrective nursing interventions that relate to these must be
identified. Specific nursing activities can be selected to meet the
person’s individual needs.
To promote the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide, the nurse
can optimise cardiac output by reducing stress, planning appropriate
activities and positioning the person for improved vascular blood flow
(see ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and
interventions
’).
IDENTIFYING  NURSING  DIAG NO SES, O UTCO M ES AND
INTERVENTIO NS
People with decreased cardiac output


History Ed Wallace, a 67-year-old retired contractor, has a
history of an acute myocardial infarction 1 year ago. He
presents with shortness of breath.
Implementing
Promoting circulation
Most people in good health give little thought to their cardiovascular
function and will require education. Nurses, because of their
continual presence at the bedside, are able to initiate education. See
‘Patient education
’ for other ways to promote a healthy heart.
Patient education
Promoting a healthy heart
Exercise regularly, participating in at least 30 minutes of
moderate intensity physical activity on at least 5 days of
the week.
Do not smoke. People who quit smoking after a heart
attack can still reduce their risk of death by at least 33%.
Maintain your ideal weight and waist circumference.
Eat a diet low in total fat, saturated fats and cholesterol.


Drink alcohol in moderation, if at all, consuming no more
than 1 cocktail or 1 to 1½ standard glasses of wine or
beer daily.
Reduce stress and manage anger.
Effectively manage diabetes and hypertension,
maintaining blood glucose and blood pressure levels within
normal limits.
If female, discuss with your doctor the advantages and
risks of hormone replacement therapy after menopause
(or after a total hysterectomy).
Consult your doctor about the advisability of low-dose
aspirin therapy to further reduce the risk of cardiovascular
disease.
Formal cardiac rehabilitation programs (CRPs) have been developed
to meet people’s knowledge deficit. CRPs are divided into three
phases: phase I is the initial hospitalisation associated with the
cardiac event; phase II (outpatient) usually starts within 2–4 weeks
after hospital discharge; and phase III is the ongoing maintenance.
While formal CRPs have demonstrated benefits, in Australia,
attendance at these programs is low; fewer females than males
attend and people from regional areas are under-represented. See
‘Culturally competent care
’.
Culturally competent care
Culturally competent cardiac rehabilitation care


What works
Individual, family-based and group-based Indigenous lifestyle
programs with high levels of community ownership have
positive health effects for periods of up to 2 years.
What doesn’t work
Programs that don’t address poverty and the lack of access
to a healthy, affordable food supply.
Source: Closing the Gap Clearinghouse (
). Healthy Lifestyle Programs for Physical Activity and
Nutrition. Produced for the Closing the Gap Clearinghouse. Canberra: Australian Institute of Health
and Welfare (AIHW) & Melbourne: Australian Institute of Family Studies (AIFS).
26 Closing the Gap Clearinghouse (2011). Healthy Lifestyle Programs for Physical Activity and
Nutrition. Produced for the Closing the Gap Clearinghouse. Canberra: Australian Institute of Health
and Welfare (AIHW) & Melbourne: Australian Institute of Family Studies (AIFS).
Immobility is also detrimental to cardiovascular function. Without
exercise of the calf and leg muscles, blood pools in the veins of the
lower extremities. This stagnant blood flow may allow clots to
develop (venous thrombosis). With time, these clots can break loose
and become emboli, eventually lodging in the small vessels of the
pulmonary vascular system. Blood flow and gas exchange in the
lungs is then impaired.
There are many nursing interventions that can help people maintain
cardiac and vascular function. They may be classified as vascular
and cardiac.
26


Vascular
Position with the legs elevated to promote venous return to the
heart. This is particularly important for people with venous
dysfunction. Care should be taken to avoid this position in people
with cardiac dysfunction because it will increase preload and may
stress the dysfunctional heart.
Avoid pillows under the knees or more than 15 degrees of knee
flexion to improve blood flow to the lower extremities and reduce
venous stagnation.
Encourage leg exercises (such as flexion and extension of the
feet, active contraction and relaxation of calf muscles) for a
person on bed rest and promote ambulation as soon as possible.
Encourage or provide frequent position changes.
Cardiac
Position the person in a sitting (high Fowler’s) position to
decrease preload and reduce pulmonary congestion.
Monitor intake and output. Fluid restriction is usually not required
for people with mild to moderate cardiac dysfunction. With
severe heart failure, a fluid restriction may be ordered.
Medications
Many classes of medications are administered to individuals with
cardiovascular disorders. Drugs such as nitrates, calcium channel
blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors reduce


the workload of the heart and prevent vasoconstriction. Various
drugs are used to treat cardiac dysrhythmias. Positive inotropic
drugs such as digitalis are used to increase the contractile strength
of the heart. Beta-adrenergic blocking agents, such as propranolol
or metoprolol, may be given to block the sympathetic nervous
system action on the heart and decrease oxygen consumption.
Direct vasodilators may be used for people with peripheral vascular
disease and sometimes hypertension. Often people are on
numerous medications and it is an important role of the nurse to
help the person understand the purposes, effects and side effects of
the different medications.
Administering medications is an important nursing function. The
nurse is responsible for assessing for the effects of medications and
also for potential complications. Examples include:
When diuretics are administered, the nurse assesses intake and
output, and potassium level (because many diuretics can lower
potassium level).
When positive inotropic medications are administered, the nurse
should assess blood pressure, heart rate, peripheral pulses and
lung sounds as indicators of cardiac output.
When antihypertensive medications are administered, it is critical
for the nurse to monitor blood pressure. Additionally, many
antihypertensive medications can cause postural hypotension.
Preventing venous stasis


When people have limited mobility or are confined to bed, venous
return to the heart is impaired and the risk of venous stasis
increases. Immobility is a problem not only for ill or debilitated
individuals, but also for some travellers who sit with their legs in a
dependent position for long periods in a motor vehicle or an
aeroplane. Venous stasis can lead to thrombus formation and
oedema of the extremities.
Preventing venous stasis is an important nursing intervention to
reduce the risk of complications following surgery, trauma or major
medical problems. See positioning and leg exercises, and anti-
emboli stockings in Chapter 38
. Sequential compression devices
are additional measures to help prevent venous stasis.
Sequential compression devices
People who are undergoing surgery or who are immobilised because
of illness or injury may benefit from a sequential compression device
(SCD) to promote venous return from the legs. SCDs inflate and
deflate plastic sleeves wrapped around the legs to promote venous
flow. The plastic sleeves are attached by tubing to an air pump that
alternately inflates and deflates portions of the sleeve to a specified
pressure. The ankle area inflates first, followed by the calf region
and then the thigh area. This sequential inflation and deflation
assists the leg muscles in moving blood towards the heart (see
Figure 54.8
).
Figure 54.8


The sequential venous compression device enhances venous return.
They are available in knee-high or above-the-knee length.
Source: Beau Lark/Fuse/Getty Images.
The SCD is removed for ambulation and is usually discontinued
when the person resumes activities. SCDs are useful in preventing
thrombi and oedema from venous stasis, but they are not used for
individuals who have arterial insufficiency, cellulitis, infection of the
extremity or pre-existing venous thrombosis.
Skill 54.1
 outlines how to apply a sequential compression device
(SCD).
Patient education
Home care and circulation


Maintaining cardiac output and tissue
perfusion
Teach the symptoms of heart attack and heart failure to
the person and their family and emphasise when to seek
help.
Teach the person about the importance of maintaining
regular physical activity to promote circulation and
vascular health. Emphasise the need to increase activity
levels gradually, with the goal of exercising (brisk walking,
swimming, weight training or medium-paced cycling as
recommended by the care provider) for at least 30
minutes on all, if not most, days of the week.
Teach cardiopulmonary resuscitation or refer for
instruction.
Dietary alterations
Highlight for the individual and the family the benefits of
consuming at least two serves of fruit and five serves of
vegetables daily.
Discuss dietary measures to reduce the risk of
atherosclerosis, including reducing sodium and total and
saturated fats in the diet, reducing weight if obese and
increasing the intake of dietary fibre.


Medications
Instruct the person and family about prescribed
medications, including the effects, the side effects and
administration instructions.
Drug capsule
Low-molecular-weight heparin enoxaparin (Clexane)
Prevention of venous thrombosis
The low-molecular-weight heparins are anticoagulants used
to prevent venous thrombosis after hip, knee or abdominal
surgery. They are also used for individuals at risk of thrombo-
embolus secondary to prolonged bed rest due to acute
illness. These heparins are given subcutaneously either once
a day or every 12 hours. They have a predictable dose
response and do not require lab test monitoring.
Nursing responsibilities
Administration:
Administer deep subcutaneously. Do not give
intramuscularly.
Individuals should be lying down during administration.
Do not expel the air bubble from the pre-filled syringe.
This avoids loss of the drug.


The manufacturer recommends injection into the right
or left anterior lateral or posterior lateral aspect of the
abdominal wall for best absorption.
Alternate between right and left abdomen sites.
Insert the entire length of the needle into a skin fold
created by the thumb and forefinger; hold the skin fold
until the needle is withdrawn.
Do not massage the injection site to minimise bruising.
Do not mix with other injections.
Flexine and regular heparin cannot be used
interchangeably.
Assess baseline laboratory data (e.g. FBC, liver function,
coagulation) and monitor.
Observe for early signs/symptoms of bleeding.
Person and family education
Review how to administer (see above).
Administer at the same time each day.
Report any unusual bleeding or bruising.
Avoid aspirin or NSAIDs.
Note: prior to administering any medications, review all
aspects with a current drug handbook or other reliable
source.
Sequential compression therapy often complements other
preventive measures. The person’s risk level for DVT or pulmonary
embolism often determines the preventive measures used. For


example, individuals at low risk may require only anti-emboli
stockings. People at moderate risk may have both anti-emboli
stockings and sequential therapy as part of their treatment. The
doctor may order anti-emboli stockings, sequential therapy and
anticoagulation therapy for the high-risk person.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is described as the technique
of rescue breathing combined with external chest compression
(Australian Resuscitation Council (ARC)
).
27 Australian Resuscitation Council (2011). The Australian Resuscitation Council. Retrieved
from <www.resus.org.au>.
Figure 54.9
 provides the Australian Resuscitation Council basic
life-support flow chart. A cardiac arrest is the cessation of the heart
pumping and is recognised by the absence of movement and
response from the person who is also not breathing normally (ARC
and New Zealand Resuscitation Council ). Should these occur,
basic life support should be commenced. It is vital that all nurses are
competent to perform basic life support so resuscitation measures
can be initiated immediately when a cardiac arrest occurs. Nurses
also can be instrumental in increasing community awareness of the
need for CPR training and ensuring its availability.

ARC basic life support flow chart.

>. Reproduced with permission from ARC.

Lifespan considerations
Sequential compression devices
Children
As young children tend to be more active, the SCD is
rarely necessary unless the child is immobile (e.g.
comatose).
Older adults
The SCD sleeves may become loose as people move
around in bed. Check that the sleeves are secure and
properly positioned.
Home care considerations
Sequential compression devices
A sequential compression device may be used in
the home. Inform the person or caregiver how to


apply the device correctly and how to operate the
system, including how to respond to the alarm.
Each health care facility has policies and procedures for identifying
the deteriorating person and initiating timely responses and
interventions. In many institutions, this emergency was traditionally
called a cardiac arrest
 and the announcement was referred to as
‘calling the arrest team’. Today, the term ‘arrest team’ may refer to
the ‘resuscitation team’, the ‘cardiac arrest team’, the ‘medical
emergency team (MET)’ or rapid response team (RRT). The
concept of the RRT changes and expands the role of the traditional
cardiac arrest team to allow early identification, assessment and
management of seriously ill people on hospital wards (Dwyer,
Dennett & Jacobs ). Each health care institution has criteria for
calling the RRT or resuscitation team (see Table 54.3
).

There may be a special ‘cardiac arrest’ button near the bed, a
dedicated extension on the phone or a special phone used to
announce the emergency. It is critical that each member of the
30


person care team knows the procedure for activating the rapid
response team. The hospitalised person and their family both play
an important role in recognising clinical deterioration and activating a
timely review and appropriate interventions. Some people have
indicated via an advance directive that should they arrest, they are
not to be resuscitated. It is every person’s right to make an advance
directive of their wishes. If it is the individual’s wish, the doctor
should identify the same on the medical record.
Evaluating
Using the overall goals identified in the planning stage, the nurse
collects data to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions.
Examples of desired outcomes for the identified goals are found in
the ‘Identifying nursing diagnoses, outcomes and interventions’ box
earlier in this chapter.
If desired outcomes are not achieved, the nurse, person and
support person, if appropriate, need to explore the reasons before
modifying the care plan. For example, if the outcome ‘Cardiac pump
effectiveness’ is not achieved, questions to be considered might
include the following:
Have other outcome measures for the goal of maintaining
adequate cardiac output been met?
Are prescribed medications being taken/administered as
ordered?


Are there additional factors that are placing stress on the heart?
Is there a balance between factors that affect cardiac output,
such as preload and afterload?
Are there signs of fluid overload such as weight gain?
Case study
Mrs Gloria Papadopolis reports that she is having increasing
difficulty because she experiences severe pain in her calf
muscles after walking for more than a city block. The pain
subsides if she rests for a few minutes but returns with
activity. Her feet are cool and pale; pedal and posterior tibial
pulses are not palpable and femoral pulses are difficult to
palpate. She lives in a city apartment and uses public
transport to travel across town to visit her husband’s grave
weekly.


Fundamentals of care framework in
context
1. What are the circulatory causes of her leg pain? Which
risk factors would you expect to find in her history to
support this conclusion?
2. Name two nursing diagnoses appropriate for Mrs
Papadopolis. Which would have the highest priority
and why?
3.
 The doctor suggests that Mrs Papadopolis
cease her visits to the cemetery because she has to
walk a long way there to reach the grave site. Would
you agree with this plan? Why or why not? What
considerations or viewpoints influence your choice?
Could the doctor’s suggestion impact on the
therapeutic relationship between the doctor and Mrs
Papadopolis? In what way?
4. Mrs Papadopolis says that she wears support
stockings because her friend told her they help the
circulation in her legs. How would you respond to this
information?


SKILL
54.1 Sequential compression
devices
Purposes
To promote venous return from the legs.
To decrease risk of venous thrombosis and/or
pulmonary embolism.
Assessment
Assess for baseline data:
Cardiovascular status, including heart rate and
rhythm, peripheral pulses and capillary refill.
Colour and temperature of extremities.
Movement and sensation of feet and lower
extremities and Homans’ sign.
Planning


Confirm the type of SCD sleeve. Rationale: both
knee- and thigh-length sleeves are available.
Delegation
Remove and reapply the SCD when performing
hygiene care. The nurse should know the correct
application process for the SCD. This can be
delegated to the Assistant in Nursing. The person
should not have the SCD removed for long periods
of time because the purpose of the SCD is to
promote circulation.
Equipment
Measuring tape
SCD, including disposable sleeves, air pump and
tubing
Implementation
Performance
1. Prior to performing the procedure, introduce
self and verify the person’s identity using
organisation protocol. Explain to the person
what you are going to do, why it is necessary
and the procedure for applying the sequential
compression device. Rationale: the person’s
cooperation and comfort will be increased by


understanding the rationale for applying the
SCD.
2. Perform hand hygiene and observe
appropriate infection-control procedures.
3. Provide for individual privacy and drape the
person appropriately.
4. Prepare the person.
Place the person in a dorsal recumbent or
semi-Fowler’s position.
Measure the person’s legs as
recommended by the manufacturer if a
thigh-length sleeve is required. Rationale:
knee-length sleeves come in just one size;
the thigh circumference determines the
size needed for a thigh-length sleeve.
5. Apply the sequential compression sleeves.
Place a sleeve under each leg with the
opening at the knee.
Wrap the sleeve securely around the leg,
securing the Velcro tabs. Allow two fingers
to fit between the leg and the sleeve. ?
Rationale: this amount of space ensures
that the sleeve does not impair circulation
when inflated.


? Applying a sequential compression device
to the leg
6. Connect the sleeves to the control unit and
adjust the pressure as needed.
Connect the tubing to the sleeves and
control unit, ensuring that arrows on the
plug and the connector are in alignment
and that the tubing is not kinked or
twisted. Rationale: improper alignment or
obstruction of the tubing by kinks or twists
will interfere with operation of the SCD.
Turn on the control unit and adjust the
alarms and pressures as needed. The
sleeve cooling control and alarm should be
on; ankle pressure is usually set at 35 to
55 mm Hg. Rationale: it is important to
have the sleeve cooling control on for
comfort and to reduce the risk of skin
irritation from moisture under the sleeve.


Alarms warn of possible control unit
malfunctions.
7. Document the procedure.
Record baseline assessment data and
application of the SCD. Note control unit
settings.
Assess and document skin integrity and
neurovascular status at least every 8
hours while the SCD is in place. Remove
the unit and notify the doctor if the person
complains of numbness and tingling or leg
pain. These may be symptoms of nerve
compression.
Evaluation
Perform appropriate follow-up assessments,
such as cardiovascular status including pedal
pulses, skin colour and temperature, skin
integrity and neurovascular status, including
movement and sensation.
Compare with the baseline data, if available.
Report significant deviations from normal to the
doctor.


Chapter 54 Review


Chapter highlights
The cardiovascular system transports gases in the blood to and
from the tissues and facilitates the diffusion of gases between
the capillaries and body tissues.
The heart and the blood vessels make up the cardiovascular
system that, together with blood, is the major system for
transporting oxygen and nutrients to the tissues and waste
products away from the tissues for elimination.
The right side of the heart receives deoxygenated blood from the
body and pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary arteries; the
left side receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it
out to the body via the aorta.
Coronary arteries supply oxygen and nutrients to the heart
muscle.
The cardiac cycle is made up of systole and diastole periods.
The cardiac conduction system controls the electrical activity of
the heart and the cardiac cycle: systole, contraction of the heart
muscle and ejection of blood, and diastole, the relaxation period
during which the heart fills with blood.
Cardiac output depends on the stroke volume or amount of blood
ejected during systole and the heart rate.
The systemic blood vessels carry blood to the tissues through a
system of arteries, arterioles and capillaries and return it to the
heart through the venules, veins and the venae cavae.
The blood pressure rises gradually from birth to reach the adult
range in adolescence.


Atherosclerosis causes fatty plaque to develop within arteries.
Decreased cardiac output, impaired tissue perfusion and
disorders affecting the blood are the major cardiovascular
problems that may affect oxygenation.
Cardiac output may fall with a myocardial infarction (MI), heart
failure, dysrhythmias and structural alterations of the heart (e.g.
valve deformities).
The most common cause of impaired blood flow to tissues is
atherosclerosis; this can lead to tissue ischaemia and pain.
Cardiac monitoring is used for continuous observation of the
heart rate and rhythm.
Nursing interventions to promote circulation include using anti-
embolic stockings and sequential compression devices to prevent
venous stasis and oedema, and also administering
cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is used during
cardiopulmonary arrest. Nurses need to be aware of the
hospital’s policies and procedures regarding emergencies.

Chapter 55 Fluid, electrolyte and
acid–base balance
Loretto Quinney, Bronwyn Hayes, Amy Carroll
Learning outcomes
After completing this chapter, you will be able to:
Discuss the function, distribution, movement and regulation of
fluids and electrolytes in the body.
Describe the regulation of acid–base balance in the body,
including the roles of the lungs, the kidneys and buffers.
Identify factors affecting normal body fluid, electrolyte and acid–
base balance.


Discuss the risk factors for and the causes and effects of fluid,
electrolyte and acid–base imbalances.
Collect assessment data related to the person’s fluid, electrolyte
and acid–base balances.
Take a person-centred approach to teaching measures to
maintain fluid and electrolyte balance.
Implement measures to correct imbalances of fluids and
electrolytes or acids and bases such as enteral or parenteral
replacements and blood transfusions.
Use critical thinking and clinical reasoning to evaluate the effect
of nursing and collaborative interventions on the person’s fluid,
electrolyte or acid–base balance.

In good health, a delicate balance of fluids,
electrolytes, acids and bases is maintained in
the body. This balance, or physiological
homeostasis
, depends on multiple
physiological processes that regulate fluid intake
and output and the movement of water and the
substances dissolved in it between the body
compartments.
Almost every illness has the potential to
threaten this balance. Even in daily living,


excessive temperatures or vigorous activity can
disturb the balance if adequate water and salt
intake is not maintained. Therapeutic measures,
such as the use of diuretics or nasogastric
suction, can also disturb the body’s homeostasis
unless water and electrolytes are replaced.


Body fluids and electrolytes
The proportion of the human body composed of fluid is surprisingly
large. Approximately 60% of the average healthy adult’s weight is
water, the primary body fluid. In good health, this volume remains
relatively constant and the person’s weight varies by less than 0.2 kg
in 24 hours, regardless of the amount of fluid ingested.
Water is vital to health and normal cellular function, serving as:
a medium for metabolic reactions within cells
a transporter for nutrients, waste products and other substances
a lubricant
an insulator and shock absorber
one means of regulating and maintaining body temperature.
Age, sex and body fat affect total body water. Infants have the
highest proportion of water, accounting for 70% to 80% of their body
weight. The proportion of body water decreases with age. In the
person older than 60 years of age, it represents only about 50% of
the total body weight. Women also have a lower percentage of body
water than men. Women and older people have reduced body water
due to decreased muscle mass and a greater percentage of fat
tissue. Fat tissue is essentially free of water, whereas lean tissue
contains a significant amount of water. Water makes up a greater
percentage of a lean person’s body weight than an obese person’s.


Distribution of body fluids
The body’s fluid is divided into two major compartments, intracellular
and extracellular. Intracellular fluid (ICF)
 is found within the cells
of the body. It constitutes approximately two-thirds of the total body
fluid in adults. Extracellular fluid (ECF)
 is found outside the cells
and accounts for about one-third of total body fluid. It is subdivided
into compartments. The two main compartments of ECF are
intravascular and interstitial. Intravascular fluid
, or plasma
,
accounts for approximately 20% of the ECF and is found within the
vascular system. Interstitial fluid
, accounting for approximately
75% of the ECF, surrounds the cells. The other compartments of
ECF are the lymph and transcellular fluids. Examples of
transcellular fluid
 include cerebrospinal, pericardial, pancreatic,
pleural, intraocular, biliary, peritoneal and synovial fluids (see Figure
55.1
).
Figure 55.1


Total body fluid represents 40 L in an adult male weighing 70 kg
Intracellular fluid is vital to normal cell functioning. It contains solutes
such as oxygen, electrolytes and glucose, and it provides a medium
in which metabolic processes of the cell take place.
Although extracellular fluid is in the smaller of the two
compartments, it is the transport system that carries nutrients to
and waste products from the cells. For example, plasma carries
oxygen from the lungs and glucose from the gastrointestinal tract to
the capillaries of the vascular system. From there, the oxygen and
glucose move across the capillary membranes into the interstitial
spaces and then across the cellular membranes into the cells. The
opposite route is taken for waste products, such as carbon dioxide
going from the cells to the lungs and metabolic acid wastes going
eventually to the kidneys. Interstitial fluid transports wastes from the
cells by way of the lymph system, as well as directly into the blood
plasma through capillaries.
Composition of body fluids
Extracellular and intracellular fluids contain oxygen from the lungs,
dissolved nutrients from the gastrointestinal tract, excretory products
of metabolism such as carbon dioxide and charged particles called
ions
.


Many salts dissociate in water; that is, break up into electrically
charged ions. The salt sodium chloride breaks up into one ion of
sodium (
) and one ion of chloride (
). These charged
particles are called electrolytes
 because they are capable of
conducting electricity. The number of ions that carry a positive
charge, called cations
, and ions that carry a negative charge,
called anions
, should be equal. Examples of cations are sodium (
), potassium (
), calcium (
) and magnesium (
).
Examples of anions include chloride (
), bicarbonate (
),
phosphate (
) and sulfate (
).
Electrolytes generally are measured in millimoles per litre of water
(mmol/L) or milligrams per 100 millilitres (mg/100 mL). The term
millimoles
 refers to the chemical combining power of the ion or
the capacity of cations to combine with anions to form molecules.
This combining activity is measured in relation to the combining
activity of the hydrogen ion (
). Thus, 1 mmol of any anion equals
1 mmol of any cation. For example, sodium and chloride ions are
equivalent because they combine equally: 1 mmol of
 equals 1
mmol of
 However, these cations and anions are not equal in
weight: 1 mg of
 does not equal 1 mg of
 rather, 3 mg of
 equal 2 mg of
Clinically, the millimole system is most often used in Australia. It also
is important to remember that laboratory tests are usually performed
using blood plasma, an extracellular fluid. These results may reflect
what is happening in the ECF but it generally is not possible to
directly measure electrolyte concentrations within the cell.
