INTERVENTIO NS
The person with altered hydration
Enteral fluid and electrolyte replacement
Fluids and electrolytes can be provided orally in the home and hospital if
the person’s health permits; that is, if the person is not vomiting, has not
experienced an excessive fluid loss and has an intact gastrointestinal
tract and gag and swallow reflexes. The person who is unable to ingest
solid foods may be able to ingest fluids.
Fluid intake modifications
Increased fluids (ordered as ‘push fluids’) are often prescribed for the
person with actual or potential fluid volume deficits arising, for example,


from mild diarrhoea or mild to moderate fevers. Guidelines for helping the
person increase fluid intake are shown in the ‘Practice guidelines’.
Restricted fluids may be necessary for the person who has fluid retention
(fluid volume excess) as a result of renal failure, congestive heart failure,
syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) or
other disease processes. Fluid restrictions vary from ‘nothing by mouth’ to
a precise amount ordered by a doctor. The restriction of fluids can be
difficult for some people, particularly if they are experiencing thirst.
Guidelines for helping the person restrict fluid intake are shown in
‘Practice guidelines’.
Patient education
Home care and fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balance
Monitoring fluid intake and output
Teach and provide the rationale for monitoring fluid intake and
output to the person and family as appropriate. Include how to
use a commode or collection device (‘hat’) in the toilet, how to
empty and measure urinary catheter drainage and how to
count or weigh continence pads.
Instruct and provide the rationale for regular weight monitoring
to the person and family. Weigh at the same time of day, using
the same scale and with the person wearing the same amount
of clothing.
Educate and provide the rationale to the person and family on
when to contact a health care professional, such as in the
cases of a significant change in urine output; any change of 2


kg or more in a 1- to 2-week period; prolonged episodes of
vomiting, diarrhoea or inability to eat or drink; dry, sticky
mucous membranes; extreme thirst; swollen fingers, feet,
ankles or legs; difficulty breathing, shortness of breath or rapid
heartbeat; and changes in behaviour or mental status.
Maintaining food and fluid intake
Instruct the person and family about any diet or fluid
restrictions, such as a low-sodium diet.
Teach family members the rationale for the importance of
offering fluids regularly to the person who is unable to meet
their own needs because of age, impaired mobility or cognition,
or other conditions such as impaired swallowing due to a
stroke.
If the person is on enteral or intravenous fluids and feeding at
home, teach and provide the underlying rationale to caregivers
about proper administration and care. Contact a home health
or home intravenous service to provide services and teaching.
Safety
Instruct and provide the rationale to the person to change
positions slowly if appropriate, especially when moving from a
supine to a sitting or standing position.
Inform and provide the rationale to the person and family about
the importance of good mouth and skin care. Teach the person
to change positions frequently and to elevate the feet on a
stool when sitting for a long period.


Teach the person and family how to care for intravenous
access sites or gastric tubes. Include what to do if tubes
become dislodged.
Medications
Emphasise the importance of and rationale for taking
medications as prescribed.
Instruct the person taking diuretics to take the medication in
the morning. If a second daily dose is prescribed, they should
take it in the late afternoon to avoid disrupting sleep to urinate.
Inform the person about any expected side effects of
prescribed medications and how to handle them (e.g. if a
potassium-depleting diuretic is prescribed, increase intake of
potassium-rich foods; if taking a potassium-sparing diuretic,
avoid excess potassium intake such as using a salt substitute).
Teach the person when to contact their doctor (e.g. if they are
unable to take a prescribed medication or have signs of an
allergic or toxic reaction to a medication).
Measures specific to the person’s
problem
Provide instructions and rationale specific to the person’s fluid,
electrolyte or acid–base imbalance, such as:
‒ fluid volume deficit
‒ risk of fluid volume deficit


‒ fluid volume excess.
Referrals
Make appropriate referrals to home health or community social
services for assistance with resources such as meals, meal
preparation and food, intravenous infusions and access, enteral
feedings and home health aide services to help with ADLs.
Community health organisations and
other sources of help
Provide information about companies or health care
organisations that can provide durable medical equipment such
as commodes, individual transfer chairs or hospital beds for
purchase, for rental or free of charge.
Provide a list of sources for supplies such as catheters and
drainage bags, measuring devices, tube feeding formulas and
electrolyte replacement drinks.
Suggest additional sources of information and help, such as
Diabetes Australia, National Heart Foundation, Dietitians
Association of Australia (DAA) and Lung Foundation Australia.
Although routine supplements for other electrolytes generally are not
recommended, the person who has poor dietary habits, who is
malnourished or who has difficulty accessing or eating fresh fruits and
vegetables may benefit from electrolyte supplements. A daily multiple
vitamin with minerals may achieve the desired goal. A person who


engages in strenuous activity in a warm environment needs to be
encouraged to replace water and electrolytes lost through excessive
perspiration by consuming a sports drink or a commercial fluid and
electrolyte solution.
Dietary changes
Specific fluid and electrolyte imbalances may require simple dietary
changes. For example, the person receiving potassium-depleting diuretics
needs to be informed about foods with a high potassium content (e.g.
bananas, oranges and leafy greens). The person with fluid retention may
need to avoid foods high in sodium. Most healthy people can benefit from
foods rich in calcium.
Oral electrolyte supplements
The person may benefit from oral supplements of electrolytes, particularly
when a medication is prescribed that affects electrolyte balance, when
dietary intake is inadequate for a specific electrolyte, or when fluid and
electrolyte losses are excessive as a result of, for example, excessive
perspiration.
Practice guidelines
Facilitating fluid intake
Explain to the person the reason for the required intake and the
specific amount needed. This provides a rationale for the
requirement and promotes compliance.
Establish a 24-hour plan for ingesting the fluids. For the
hospitalised or long-term care person, half of the total volume


is given during the day shift and the other half is divided
between the evening and night shifts, with most of that
ingested during the evening shift. For example, if 2500 mL is to
be ingested in 24 hours, the plan may specify 7–3 (1500 mL);
3–11 (700 mL); and 11–7 (300 mL). Try to avoid the ingestion
of large amounts of fluid immediately before bedtime to prevent
the need to urinate during sleeping hours.
Set short-term outcomes that the person can realistically meet.
Examples include ingesting a glass of fluid every hour while
awake or a pitcher of water by 12 noon.
Identify fluids the person likes and make available a variety of
those items, including fruit juices, soft drinks and milk (if
allowed). Remember that beverages such as coffee and tea
have a diuretic effect, so their consumption should be limited.
Help the person to select foods that tend to become liquid at
room temperature (e.g. jelly, ice-cream, sorbet, custard), if
these are allowed.
For the person who is confined to bed, supply appropriate
cups, glasses and straws to facilitate appropriate fluid intake
and keep the fluids within easy reach.
Make sure fluids are served at the appropriate temperature:
hot fluids hot and cold fluids very cold.
Encourage the person when possible to participate in
maintaining the fluid intake record. This assists them to
evaluate the achievement of desired outcomes.
Be alert to any cultural implications of food and fluids. Some
cultures may restrict certain foods and fluids and view others
as having healing properties.


Practice guidelines
Helping the person restrict fluid intake
Explain the reason for the restricted intake and how much and
what types of fluids are permitted orally. The person may need
to be informed that ice chips, jelly and ice-cream, for example,
are considered fluid.
Help the person decide the amount of fluid to be taken with
each meal, between meals, before bedtime and with
medications. For the hospitalised or long-term care people, half
the total volume is scheduled during the day shift, when the
person is most active, and receives two meals and most oral
medications. A large part of the remainder is scheduled for the
evening shift to permit fluids with meals and evening visitors.
Identify fluids or fluid-like substances the person likes and
make sure that these are provided, unless contraindicated. A
person who is allowed only 200 mL of fluid for breakfast, for
example, should receive the type of fluid the person favours.
Set short-term goals that make the fluid restriction more
tolerable. For example, schedule a specified amount of fluid at
1- or 2-hourly intervals between meals. The person may prefer
fluids only between meals if the food provided at meal times
helps relieve thirst.
Place allowed fluids in small containers such as a 200 mL juice
glass to allow the perception of a full container.
Periodically offer the person ice chips as an alternative to
water, because ice chips when melted are approximately half of
the frozen volume.
Provide frequent mouth care and rinses to reduce the thirst
sensation.


Instruct the person to avoid ingesting or chewing salty or sweet
foods (hard lollies or gum) because these foods tend to
produce thirst. Sugarless gum may be an alternative for some
people.
Encourage the person when possible to participate in
maintaining the fluid intake record.
Patient education
Promoting fluid and electrolyte balance
Consume six to eight glasses of water daily.
Avoid excess amounts of foods or fluids high in salt, sugar and
caffeine.
Eat a well-balanced diet. Include adequate amounts of milk or
milk products to maintain bone calcium levels.
Limit alcohol intake because it has a diuretic effect.
Increase fluid intake before, during and after strenuous
exercise, particularly when the environmental temperature is
high, and replace lost electrolytes from excessive perspiration
as needed with commercial electrolyte solutions.
Maintain normal body weight.
Learn about and monitor side effects of medications that affect
fluid and electrolyte balance (e.g. diuretics) and ways to handle
side effects.
Recognise possible risk factors for fluid and electrolyte
imbalance, such as prolonged or repeated vomiting, frequent
watery stools, or inability to consume fluids because of illness.
Seek prompt professional health care for notable signs of fluid
imbalance, such as sudden weight gain or loss, decreased


urine volume, swollen ankles, shortness of breath, dizziness or
confusion.
Corticosteroids and many diuretics can cause too much potassium to be
eliminated through the kidneys. For the person taking these medications,
potassium supplements may be prescribed. Instruct the person taking
oral potassium supplements to take the medication with juice to mask the
unpleasant taste and reduce the possibility of gastric distress. Emphasise
the importance of taking the medication as prescribed and seeing their
doctor on a regular basis. As hyperkalaemia can have serious cardiac
effects, the person should never increase the amount of potassium being
taken without an order to do so. In addition, inform the person that most
salt substitutes contain potassium, so it is important to consult with the
doctor before using salt substitutes.
The person who ingests insufficient milk and milk products benefits from
calcium supplements. The recommended daily allowance for calcium is
1000 to 1500 mg. Long-term use of corticosteroid drugs can also cause
calcium loss from the bone and calcium supplements may help reduce
this loss. The person who takes supplemental calcium needs to maintain
a fluid intake of at least 2500 mL per day (unless contraindicated) to
reduce the risk of kidney stones, which are commonly composed of
calcium salts.
The nurse should encourage the person who is malnourished or who has
poor eating habits to take in liquid nutritional supplements. Liquid
nutritional supplements are used with frequency in older adults to bolster
nutritional status and caloric intake. It is very important to be a ‘label
reader’ of the product and to be aware of the contents of the supplement.


Some of them are very high in protein and high in potassium, which may
be contraindicated in an individual with impaired renal function.
Parenteral fluid and electrolyte replacement
Intravenous (IV) fluid therapy is essential when the person is unable to
take food and fluids orally. It is an efficient and effective method of
supplying fluids directly into the intravascular fluid compartment and
replacing electrolyte losses. Intravenous fluid therapy is usually ordered
by the doctor. The nurse is responsible for administering and maintaining
the therapy and for teaching the person and significant others how to
continue the therapy at home if necessary.
Intravenous solutions
Intravenous solutions can be classified as isotonic, hypotonic or
hypertonic. Most IV solutions are isotonic, having the same concentration
of solutes as blood plasma. Isotonic solutions are often used to restore
vascular volume. Hypertonic solutions have a greater concentration of
solutes than plasma; hypotonic solutions have a lesser concentration of
solutes. Table 55.10
 provides examples of IV solutions and nursing
implications.
Table 55.10 Selected intravenous solutions
IV solutions can also be categorised according to their purpose. Nutrient
solutions contain some form of carbohydrate (e.g. dextrose or glucose)
and water. Water is supplied for fluid requirements and carbohydrate for
calories and energy. For example, 1 L of 5% dextrose provides 170
calories. Nutrient solutions are useful in preventing dehydration and


ketosis but do not provide sufficient calories to promote wound healing,
weight gain or normal growth in children. Common nutrient solutions are
5% dextrose in water and 5% dextrose in 0.45% sodium chloride
(dextrose in half-strength saline).
Electrolyte solutions contain varying amounts of cations and anions.
Commonly used solutions are normal saline (0.9% sodium chloride
solution) and Hartmann’s solution (which contains sodium, chloride,
potassium, calcium and lactate).
Lactate is metabolised in the liver to form bicarbonate
 Saline
and balanced electrolyte solutions commonly are used to restore vascular
volume, particularly after trauma or surgery. They also may be used to
replace fluid and electrolytes for the person with continuing losses, for
example because of gastric suction or wound drainage.
Hartmann’s solution is an alkalinising solution that may be given to treat
metabolic acidosis. Acidifying solutions, in contrast, are administered to
counteract metabolic alkalosis. Examples of acidifying solutions are 5%
dextrose in 0.45% sodium chloride and 0.9% sodium chloride solution.
Volume expanders
 are used to increase the blood volume following
severe loss of blood (e.g. from haemorrhage) or loss of plasma (e.g. from
severe burns, which draw large amounts of plasma from the bloodstream
to the burn site). Examples of expanders are dextran, plasma and
albumin.
Venipuncture sites
HCO3−.


The site chosen for venipuncture varies with the person’s age, the length
of time the infusion is to run, the type of solution used and the condition
of veins. For adults, veins in the hand and arm are commonly used; for
infants, dorsal foot veins are often used. Larger veins are preferred for
infusions that need to be given rapidly and for solutions that could be
irritating (e.g. certain medications).
The metacarpal, basilic and cephalic veins are commonly used for
intermittent or continuous infusions (see Figure 55.14B
). The ulna and
radius act as natural splints at these sites and the person has greater
freedom of arm movements for activities such as eating. Although the
basilic and median cubital veins in the antecubital space are convenient
sites for venipuncture, they are usually used for blood draws, bolus
injections of medication and insertion sites for a peripherally inserted
central venous catheter (CVC) (see Figure 55.14A
). See the ‘Practice
guidelines’ for vein selection and general tips for easier IV starts.
Figure 55.14


Commonly used venipuncture sites of the arm (A) and hand (B). A also
shows the site used for a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC)
Practice guidelines
Vein selection
Use distal veins of the arm first.
Use the person’s non-dominant arm whenever possible.
Select a vein that is:
‒ easily palpated and feels soft and full
‒ naturally splinted by bone
‒ large enough to allow adequate circulation around the
catheter.
Avoid using veins that are:
‒ in areas of flexion (e.g. the antecubital fossa)
‒ highly visible, because they tend to roll away from the needle
‒ damaged by previous use, phlebitis, infiltration or sclerosis
‒ continually distended with blood or knotted or tortuous
‒ planned to have an arteriovenous fistula or shunt for  dialysis
in the future (i.e. a person living with chronic  kidney disease)
‒ in a surgically compromised or injured extremity (e.g.
following a mastectomy), because of possible impaired
circulation and discomfort for the person.
When long-term IV therapy or parenteral nutrition is anticipated or the
person is receiving IV medications that are damaging to vessels (e.g.


chemotherapy), a central venous catheter may be inserted. Central
venous catheters
 usually are inserted into the subclavian or jugular
vein, with the distal tip of the catheter resting in the superior vena cava
just above the right atrium (see Figure 55.15
). They may be inserted
at the person’s bedside or, for longer term access, surgically inserted.
Subclavian central venous catheters permit freedom of movement for
ambulation; however, there is greater risk of complications, including
haemothorax or pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, thrombosis and
infection. Assess the person closely for manifestations such as shortness
of breath, chest pain, cough, hypotension, tachycardia and anxiety after
the insertion procedure.
Figure 55.15
Central venous lines with A, subclavian vein insertion and B, left jugular
insertion


Practice guidelines
Tips for inserting IV cannula
Preparation
When starting an IV and inserting an IV cannula the nurse must
first check the written orders. Equipment and supplies are then
prepared and the identity of the person verified.
Important: it is essential the nurse adheres to standard
precautions throughout the procedure, including hand washing and
the provision of a receptacle to place sharps. Personal protective
equipment (PPE) such as gloves and goggles should be applied
prior to commencing the procedure.
Preparing the person
The nurse should appear confident so as to instil trust that will
enable the establishment of a positive relationship with the
person.
The nurse must prepare the person by ensuring they are fully
informed as to the procedure and what is expected of them
during the procedure. For example, the nurse may ask the
person to rest their arm on the armrest of the chair during the
procedure or advise them that they may be required to lower
their arm to enable gravity to assist in filling the veins.
The nurse needs to ensure that the limb where the IV cannula
is to be inserted is warm and that the circulation to the limb is
sufficient to avoid vasoconstriction.
Shaving should not be required as it puts the person at risk of
nicks and cuts and provides entry points for micro-organisms.


Procedure
The nurse needs to ensure there is good light and a
comfortable position to sit while performing the procedure.
The nurse prepares the puncture site by applying the
tourniquet and palpates the distal pulse.
The nurse can instruct the person to make a fist to assist in
distending veins.
The selected site is palpated and insertion site selected.
The site is cleaned with an alcohol wipe.
When commencing to insert the IV cannula the nurse should
rest the heel of their dominant hand on the limb to help stabilise
the insertion site and prevent movement.
The cannula is held between the thumb and index finger.
The skin is pulled taut and the person advised that the needle
of the cannula is about to be inserted. The nurse may say, ‘I’m
about to insert the needle. Don’t move your arm’.
The IV cannula is inserted into the vein.
Watch for first flashback of blood into the flashback chamber,
lower the cannula to almost skin level, advance the cannula a
further 1–2 mm into the vein and stop.
Advance the plastic cannula a short way so that it enters the
vein without piercing through the other side.
Observe for second flashback up the cannula and advance the
cannula forward off the stylet into the vein until the hub is flush
with the skin.
Release the tourniquet and occlude the vein by applying
pressure to the skin surface at the end of the cannula. This will
prevent blood leaking before the extension tube or bung has
been attached.


Attach the primed extension tube or bung. Commence IV
therapy as per fluid order chart.
Post-procedure care
The puncture site needs to be checked for bruising and
bleeding.
IV fluids are adjusted to the correct rate.
The nurse must accurately document the procedure and
commence the fluid balance chart (if required).
With a peripherally inserted central venous catheter (PICC)
, the
catheter is inserted in the basilic or cephalic vein just above or below the
antecubital space of the right arm. The tip of the catheter rests in the
superior vena cava. The risk of pneumothorax is eliminated with PICC.
These catheters frequently are used for long-term intravenous access
when the person will be managing IV therapy at home.
Implantable venous access devices or ports (see Figures 55.16
 and
55.17
) are used for the person with chronic illness who requires long-
term IV therapy (e.g. intermittent medications such as chemotherapy,
total parenteral nutrition and frequent blood samples). The device is
designed to provide repeated access to the central venous system,
avoiding the trauma and complications of multiple venipunctures. Using
local anaesthesia, implantable ports are surgically placed into a small
subcutaneous pocket under the skin, usually on the anterior chest near
the clavicle, and no part of the port is exposed. The distal end of the
catheter is placed in the subclavian or jugular vein. There are different
kinds of implantable venous access devices and they may be tunnelled or
non-tunnelled (Kline & Katrancha ).
19


19 Kline, M. & Katrancha, E. D. (2019). Central venous access devices: An overview for nursing
students. Nursing, 49(7), 63–64.
Figure 55.16


An implantable venous access device: A: components; B: the device in
place
Figure 55.17
An implantable venous access device (right) and a Huber needle with
extension
Special precautions need to be taken with all central lines and venous
access ports to ensure asepsis and cannula patency. Nursing care of the
person with these devices is outlined in ‘Practice guidelines’.
Intravenous equipment


As equipment varies according to the manufacturer, the nurse must
become familiar with the equipment used in each particular health care
organisation.
Practice guidelines
Caring for the person with a venous access device
On insertion, document the date; the site; the brand, gauge
and catheter length; the location of the catheter tip (verified by
x-ray); the length of the external segment; and person
teaching. Do not use the access device until correct placement
has been verified by x-ray.
Site care
Use aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT) and PPE when caring for
central lines and long-term venous access devices. The use of
ANTT and PPE will assist in preventing or reducing the
contamination of the central venous access device with pathogens
able to cause infection (Hoey et al.
).
20 Hoey, A., Edinger-Reeve, M., Anshaw, M., Chan, H. & Konecny, P. (2018). 2101.
Catheter-related infections complicating central venous catheter access device insertion: A
retrospective audit and comparison of two cohorts. Open Forum Infectious Diseases,
5(Suppl 1), S616.
The frequency of dressing changes may vary, depending on
the site and organisation policy. Dressings also should be
changed when loose or soiled.
Assess the site for any redness, swelling, tenderness or
drainage. Compare the length of the external portion of the
20


catheter with its documented length to assess for possible
displacement. Obtain a chest x-ray to determine the catheter
tip’s position if in doubt. Report and document any position
changes or signs of infection.
Follow the health care organisation’s protocol for cleaning
solutions and types of dressings. Isopropyl alcohol or a
combination of alcohol and acetone followed by povidone-iodine
are commonly used to clean the port site.
Before accessing the port, clean an area 5 cm in diameter
around the site with an alcohol-acetone solution on a sterile
cotton swab. Start at the centre of the port site, moving
outwards with a firm, circular motion. Follow with povidone-
iodine solution. Allow the site to air dry. Be sure to check your
hospital policy with regards to the requirements for accessing a
central line port.
Secure the catheter and cover the entry site and external
portion of the catheter with an occlusive dressing.
Provide routine care of the incision site for the implant device
until it is healed. Once it heals, no care is necessary when the
port is idle.
Catheter care and flushing
Change the catheter cap as indicated by organisational
protocol, usually every 3 to 7 days.
Draw back to determine patency of catheter before flushing.
Flush the port with normal saline or as health care organisation
protocol recommends for the specific type of port being used.
After infusing medications or solutions, again flush the port with
saline.


Using a 10 mL syringe, flush the catheter with a solution as
recommended by the organisational policy. The frequency of
flushes between uses depends on the type of catheter.
Remember to flush all lumens for multiple-lumen catheters.
Use a specially designed needle to access an implanted port. A
needle with a 90-degree angle is generally used for infusions
because it is easier to stabilise and more comfortable for the
person. Stabilising the port between the thumb and index finger
of the non-dominant hand, insert the needle through the centre
of the port until the resistance of the platform is felt.
To remove the needle after a treatment, again stabilise the port
and use even pressure to withdraw the needle. Maintain
positive pressure by withdrawing the needle as the last millilitre
of flush solution is being instilled.
Flush idle implanted ports in accordance with the health care
organisation’s protocol or at least every 8 weeks.
Teaching
Provide the person with the following instructions:
Do not allow anyone to take a blood pressure on the arm in
which a PICC line is inserted.
Wear a MedicAlert  tag or bracelet if the device is to be in
place for a long period.
For a PICC, you do not need to restrict activities, except do not
immerse the arm in water. Showering is allowed if the site and
catheter are covered by an occlusive dressing.
For an implanted venous port there are no activity restrictions,
but remember that the port or catheter tip can become
dislodged. Signs of a dislodged catheter tip include pain in the
®


neck or ear on the affected side, swishing or gurgling sounds,
or palpitations. Free movement of the port, swelling or difficulty
accessing the port may indicate port dislodgment. Notify the
doctor should any of these occur or if symptoms of infection
develop.
Solution containers are available in various sizes (50, 100, 250, 500 or
1000 mL); the smaller containers are often used to administer
medications. Most solutions are currently dispensed in plastic bags (see
Figure 55.18
). However, glass bottles may need to be used if the
administered medications are incompatible with plastic. Glass bottles
require an air vent so that air can enter the bottle and replace the fluid
that enters the person’s vein. Some have a tube inside the bottle that
serves as a vent; other containers without air vents require a vent on the
administration set. Air vents usually have filters to prevent contamination
from the air that enters the container. Air vents are not required for plastic
solution bags because the bags collapse under atmospheric pressure
when the solution enters the vein.
Figure 55.18


A plastic intravenous fluid container


It is essential that the solution be sterile and in good condition; that is,
clear. Cloudiness, evidence that the container has been opened
previously or leaks indicate possible contamination. Always check the
expiration date on the label. Return any questionable or contaminated
solutions to the pharmacy or IV therapy department.
Infusion sets usually include an insertion spike, a drip chamber, a roller
valve or screw clamp, tubing with secondary ports and a protective cap
over the cannula adapter (see Figure 55.19
). The insertion spike is
kept sterile and inserted into the solution container when the equipment is
set up and ready to start. The drip chamber permits a predictable amount
of fluid to be delivered. A commonly used drip chamber is the 10 to 20
drops, which delivers macrodrip per millilitre of solution. This information
is found on the package. There are also macrodrip sets which deliver 60
drops per millilitre of solution. The roller valve or screw clamp, which
compresses the lumen of the tubing, controls the rate of the flow. The
protective cap over the cannula adapter maintains the sterility of the end
of the tubing so that it can be attached to a sterile cannula inserted in the
person’s vein.
Figure 55.19


A standard IV administration set


Research note Are there benefits that
support the routine replacement of short
peripheral intravenous catheters
regardless of clinical indication?
C. Stevens, K. A. Milner & J. Trudeau
. Routine versus clinically indicated short peripheral catheter
replacement. Journal of Infusion Nursing, 41(3), 198–204.
21 Stevens, C., Milner, K. A & Trudeau, J. (2018). Routine versus clinically indicated short peripheral catheter
replacement. Journal of Infusion Nursing: The Official Publication of the Infusion Nursing Society, 41(3), 198–
204.
Despite current and high-quality evidence to the contrary, the
current practice in many health care facilities is that short
peripheral catheters (SPCs) are replaced after a certain period of
time—often a 3-day or 96-hour period. An alternative stance is
that SPCs are only replaced when clinically indicated by
assessment of the person’s health status and the integrity of the
intravenous device and dressing; the venue of care was another
influencing factor on this decision. The research team conducted a
high-quality systematic review with analysis and found that there
was no difference in infection or phlebitis rates between people
who had the SPC replaced as required by clinical indicators or
those who had the SPC replaced regardless at a regular time
interval.
Implications A policy of replacing SPCs or peripheral intravenous
cannulas (PIVCs) only when clinically indicated would improve
21


patient care by eliminating unnecessary procedures that hold an
increased risk of infection for the person and an increased risk of
needle-stick injury. Significant savings in equipment, disposables
and workload for staff would also be advantageous.
Most infusion sets include one or more injection ports for administering IV
medications or secondary infusions. Needle-less systems are increasingly
used because they reduce the risk of needle-stick injury and
contamination of the intravenous line. There are various types of needle-
less systems available including blunt cannula devices, Luer-activated
devices and three-way pressure-activated safety valves. With each of
these needle-less systems, a blunt cannula is inserted into a special
injection port or adapter on the IV tubing to administer medications or
secondary infusions (see Figure 55.20
). Many infusion sets include an
in-line filter to trap air, particulate matter and microbes. A special infusion
set may be required if the IV flow rate will be regulated by an infusion
pump.
Figure 55.20


Cannulas used to connect the tubing of additive sets to primary infusions.
A: Threaded-lock cannula; B: Lever-lock cannula
Cannulas and needles are commonly used for intravenous infusions.
Over-the-needle cannulas, also known as angiocaths, are commonly
used for adults. The plastic cannula fits over a needle used to pierce the
skin and vein wall (see Figure 55.21
). Once inserted into the vein, the
needle is withdrawn and discarded, leaving the cannula in place. IV
cannulas allow the person more mobility and rarely infiltrate; that is,
become dislodged from the vein and allow fluid to flow into interstitial
spaces.
Figure 55.21
Schematic of an over-the-needle catheter
Safety devices on IV cannulas are now common. With the original over-
the-needle cannulas, the sharp stylet remained exposed until placed in a
sharps container. This resulted in needle-stick injuries to nurses. The
safety devices for IV cannulas vary. They can be either an active safety
device which requires activation by the nurse or a passive safety device


where the safety feature is automatically activated after the stylet is
removed from the cannula.
Butterfly, or wing-tipped, needles with plastic flaps attached to the shaft
are sometimes used (see Figure 55.22
). The flaps are held tightly
together to hold the needle securely during insertion; after insertion, they
are flattened against the skin and secured with tape.
Figure 55.22


Schematic of a butterfly needle with adapter
IV poles are used to hang the solution container. Some poles are
attached to hospital beds; others stand on the floor or hang from the
ceiling. In the home, plant hangers or robe hooks (even kitchen cabinet
knobs or an S-hook over the top of a door) may be used to hang solution
containers. The height of most poles is adjustable. The higher the solution


container, the greater the force of the solution as it enters the person and
the faster the rate of flow.
Starting an intravenous infusion
Although the doctor is responsible for ordering IV therapy for the person,
the nurse can take a person-centred approach to care by initiating,
monitoring and maintaining the prescribed IV infusion. This is true not
only in hospitals and long-term care facilities, but increasingly in
community-based settings such as clinics and the person’s home.
Before starting an infusion, the nurse determines the following:
a. Correct patient identification by:
asking them to state their name and date of birth
checking these details against the patient’s identification band
and the IV medication/fluid order sheet
checking the patient’s hospital record number is the same as
on the arm band and medication/fluid order sheet.
b. Checks with another nurse against the medication/fluid order
sheet:
the type and amount of solution to be infused
the exact amount (dose) of any medications to be added to a
compatible solution
the rate of flow or the time over which the infusion is to be
completed
the correct medication additive label is completed and signed
by both nurses.


c. Equipment: IV pump with monitor is available, correctly set-up and
functioning; set rate is correct and guard rails are in place.
If solutions are prepared by the pharmacy or another department, the
nurse must verify that the solution supplied exactly matches that which
the doctor ordered.
Understanding the purpose for the infusion is as important as assessing
the person. For example, the nurse may question an order for 5%
dextrose in water at 150 mL/h if the person has peripheral oedema and
other signs of fluid overload.
To perform venipuncture and start an intravenous infusion, see Skill
55.1
.
Regulating and monitoring intravenous infusions
Orders for IV infusions may take several forms: ‘1000 mL every 8 hrs’, or
‘125 mL/h’. The nurse initiating the IV calculates the correct flow rate,
regulates the infusion and monitors the person’s responses. Unless an
infusion-control device is used, the nurse manually regulates the drops
per minute of flow using the roller clamp to ensure that the prescribed
amount of solution will be infused in the correct time span. If the flow is
incorrect, problems such as hypervolaemia, hypovolaemia or inadequate
medication administration can result.
The number of drops delivered per millilitre of solution varies with different
brands and types of infusion sets. This rate, called the drip factor
(sometimes called the drop factor), generally is printed on the package of
the infusion set. Macrodrops commonly have drop factors of 10, 12, 15 or


20 drops/mL; the drop factor for microdrip is always 60 drops/mL (see
Figure 55.23
). In Australia, the macrodrops IV infusion sets used are
those with a 20 drops/mL drip factor.
Figure 55.23
Infusion set spikes and drip chambers: non-vented macrodrip, vented
macrodrip, non-vented microdrip
To calculate flow rates, the nurse must know the volume of fluid to be
infused and the specific time for the infusion. Two commonly used
methods of indicating flow rates are designating the number of millilitres
to be administered in 1 hour (mL/h) and the number of drops to be given
in 1 minute (gtt/min). As l millilitre of fluid displaces 1 cubic centimetre of


space, the volume to be infused in the first method may also be
designated as cubic centimetres per hour (cc/h).
Millilitres per hour
Hourly rates of infusion can be calculated by dividing the total infusion
volume by the total infusion time in hours. For example, if 3000 mL is
infused in 24 hours, the number of millilitres per hour is
Nurses need to check infusions at least every hour to ensure that the
indicated millilitres per hour have infused and that IV patency is
maintained. A strip of adhesive marking the exact time and/or amount to
be infused may be taped to the solution container. Some health care
organisations make pre-marked labels available (see Figure 55.24
).
Figure 55.24
3000 mL  (total infusion volume)
24 h  (total infusion time)
= 125 mL/h


Timing label on an intravenous container. The first time marked (0900
hours) would be correct for a bag hung at 0800 hours with a rate of 100
mL per hour
Source: Elena Dorfman.


Drops per minute
The nurse initiating and monitoring an infusion must regulate the drops
per minute to ensure that the prescribed amount of solution will infuse.
Drops per minute are calculated by the following formula:
If the requirements are 1000 mL in 8 hours and the drip factor is 20
drops/mL, the drops per minute should be
The nurse should round up to the next whole number if the answer is 0.5
or above and round down to the closest whole number when the answer
is less than 0.5.
Approximating this rate as 42 drops/min, the nurse regulates the drops
per minute by tightening or releasing the IV tubing clamp and counting the
drops for 15 seconds, then multiplying that number by 4 (e.g. 10 drops/15
sec).
A number of factors influence flow rate (see Box 55.8
).
BO X
55.8 Factors influencing flow rates
Drops per minute = Total infusion volume  ×  drop factor
Total time of infusion in minutes
1000 mL × 20
8 × 60 min (480) = 41.67 rounded up to 42 drops per minute.


The position of the forearm. Sometimes a change in the
position of the person’s arm decreases flow. Slight pronation,
supination, extension or elevation of the forearm on a pillow
can increase flow.
The position and patency of the tubing. Tubing can be
obstructed by the person’s weight, a kink or a clamp closed too
tightly. The flow rate also diminishes when part of the tubing
dangles below the puncture site.
The height of the infusion bag. Elevating the height of the
infusion bag 5 to 10 cm can speed the flow by creating more
pressure.
Possible infiltration or fluid leakage. Swelling, a feeling of
coldness and tenderness at the venipuncture site may indicate
infiltration.
Relationship of the size of the angiocath to the vein. A cannula
that is too large may impede the infusion flow.
Devices to control infusions
A number of devices are used to control the rate of an infusion. Electronic
infusion devices (EIDs) regulate the infusion rate at pre-set limits. They
also have an alarm that is triggered when the solution in the IV bag is low,
when there is air in the tubing or when the tubing is not high enough.
Another variation is a volume-control set, or burette, which is used if the
volume of fluid administered is to be carefully controlled. The set, which
holds a maximum of 100 mL of solution, is attached below the solution
container and the drip chamber is placed below the set. Volume-control


sets are always used in paediatric settings, where the volume
administered is critical.
A number of assessment tools have been developed to assist the nurse
in their evaluation of the person with an IV cannula in place and IV
therapy in progress. Generally, these tools focus on the assessment of
swelling at the IV cannula site, colour and warmth of the limb into which
the intravenous therapy is being infused and whether the infusion is
causing the person any pain. When using these assessment tools, nurses
may ask the person to rate their discomfort on a scale; for example, 0 to
4 with 0 meaning no symptoms and 4 being very painful. The nurse will
also use this tool to record their observations of the IV cannula site
(Helton, Hines & Best
).
22 Helton, J., Hines, A., Best, J. (2016). Peripheral IV site rotation based on clinical assessment vs
length of time since insertion. Medsurg Nursing, 25(1), 44–49.
An infusion pump (see Figures 55.25
 and 55.26
) delivers fluids
intravenously by exerting positive pressure on the tubing or on the fluid.
In situations where the fluid flow is unrestricted, the pump pressure is
comparable to that of gravity flow. However, if restrictions develop
(increased venous resistance), the pump can maintain the fluid flow by
increasing the pressure applied to the fluid.
Figure 55.25
22


An intravenous infusion pump
Source: Jenny Thomas.
Figure 55.26


Programmable multichannel infusion pumps
Source: Rick Brady/Pearson Education, Inc.
A controller, by contrast, operates solely by gravitational force. The
delivery pressure depends on the height of the container in relation to the


venipuncture site. The container must be at least 76 cm above the
venipuncture site for a controller to work. A controller does not have the
ability to add pressure to the line and to overcome resistances to fluid
flow.
Skill 55.2
 outlines the steps involved in monitoring an intravenous
infusion.
Clinical consideration
It is preferred that flow-rate-control devices are used
when administering IV fluids to all patients. However,
at times, health facilities may not have enough flow-
rate-control devices for all patients. In these
situations, the nurse may have to prioritise patients
for these devices. Remember: a flow-rate-control
device should be used when administering IV fluid to
the older person or child. Both these age groups are
especially at risk of complications of fluid overload,
which can occur with rapid infusion of IV fluids.
Changing intravenous containers, tubing and
dressings

Intravenous solution containers are changed when only a small amount of
fluid remains in the neck of the container and fluid still remains in the drip


chamber. However, all IV bags should be changed every 24 hours,
regardless of how much solution remains, to minimise the risk of
contamination.
To ensure this important step is not missed, it is a good idea to place a
label on the bag when it is first hung. The label should have the name of
the person, the unit number, the time and date the infusion was
commenced and the signatures of the two nurses who checked the IV
fluid prior to commencement.
IV tubing is changed every 48 to 96 hours, depending on health care
organisation protocol, as is the site dressing. In some organisations, the
IV cannula is re-sited every 48 hours to reduce risk of infection and
preserve available venous access sites; however, recent research
indicates that site change should only be considered if clinically indicated
(Stevens et al. 2018). Skill 55.3
 provides guidelines for changing an IV
solution container, tubing and the IV site dressing.
Clinical consideration
The re-spiking of an intravenous flask is always
contraindicated as it carries the risk of causing a
potentially fatal air embolism. This standard
originated from the coronial findings of a 3-year-old
girl who died during emergency transfer (Moritz ).
24 Moritz, D. L. (2018). Coronial consideration of patient deaths in
paramedicine. Australasian Journal of Paramedicine, 15(2), 1–4.
24


When an IV infusion is no longer necessary to maintain the person’s fluid
intake or to provide a route for medication administration, the infusion is
either discontinued and the cannula removed or the cannula is left in
place and converted to a saline or heparin lock. Guidelines for
discontinuing an IV infusion or converting the cannula to a lock are
outlined in Skills 55.4
 and 55.5
 respectively.
Research note What strategies should
be implemented to improve the
experience for people receiving
intravenous therapy and medications in
the home environment?
R. E. Nailon, M. E. Rupp & E. Lyden
. A day in the life of a CVAD. Journal of Infusion Nursing, 42(3), 125–
131.
23 Nailon, R. E., Rupp, M. E. & Lyden, E. (2019). A day in the life of a CVAD. Journal of Infusion Nursing,
42(3), 125–131.
The incidence of people who receive treatment via a central
venous access device (CVAD) in the home environment following
discharge is increasing. A group of nurses used a descriptive
statistics study design to explore the experience of people who
had their CVAD managed at home and the incidence of occlusion
and occurrence of infection. Forty-one (54.7%) of the 75 people
who agreed to participate in the research returned a diary that
23


provided information about CVAD access over a period of 14 days.
The team examined who accessed the CVADs, the purpose for the
access and how the CVAD was accessed. The research team
found that patients had a number of different people access the
CVAD using a wide range of practices and in a number of different
environments. The team found that there was an unusually high
number of occlusions in this population, with the rate being 9.57
per 1000 device days. The team recommended further research to
identify specific strategies that would positively impact on health
outcomes for people with CVAD outside the hospital setting.
Implications Nurses should provide education, demonstrations
and information to family members and carers prior to discharge.
This will support those who access CVADs for people receiving
treatment via a CVAD in the home environment to do so
competently and so avoid complications of infection and occlusion.
Blood transfusions
Intravenous fluids can be effective in restoring intravascular (blood)
volume; however, they do not affect the oxygen-carrying capacity of the
blood. When red and white blood cells, platelets or blood proteins are lost
because of haemorrhage or disease, it may be necessary to replace
these components to restore the blood’s ability to transport oxygen and
carbon dioxide, to clot, to fight infection and to keep extracellular fluid
within the intravascular compartment. A blood transfusion is the
introduction of whole blood or blood components into the venous
circulation.


Blood groups
Human blood is commonly classified into four main groups (A, B, AB and
O). The surface of an individual’s red blood cells contains a number of
proteins known as antigens
 that are unique for each person. Many
blood antigens have been identified, but the antigens A, B and Rh are the
most important in determining blood group or type. Because antigens
promote agglutination or clumping of blood cells, they are also known as
agglutinogens
. The A antigen or agglutinogen is present on the RBCs
of people with blood group A, the B antigen is present in people with
blood group B, and both A and B antigens are found on the RBC surface
in people with group AB blood. Neither antigen is present in people with
group O blood.
Pre-formed antibodies
 to RBC antigens are present in the plasma;
these antibodies are often called agglutinins
. People with blood group
A have B antibodies (agglutinins); A antibodies are present in people with
blood group B; and people with blood group O have antibodies to both A
and B antigens. People with group AB blood do not have antibodies to
either A or B antigens (see Table 55.11
). When blood is transfused, the
blood group of the donor and recipient must match to avoid an antigen–
antibody reaction and destruction (haemolysis) of RBCs.
Table 55.11 The blood groups with their constituent agglutinogens
and agglutinins
Rhesus (Rh) factor
The Rh factor antigen is present on the RBCs of approximately 81% of
the people in Australia (Australian Red Cross Lifeblood ). Blood that
25


contains the Rh factor is known as Rh positive (
); when it is not
present, the blood is said to be Rh negative (
). In contrast to the
ABO blood groups,
 blood does not naturally contain Rh antibodies.
However, on exposure to blood containing Rh factor (e.g. an
 mother
carrying a fetus with
 blood or transfusion of
 blood into a
person who is
), Rh antibodies develop. Subsequent exposures to
 blood place the person at risk of an antigen–antibody reaction and
haemolysis of RBCs.
25 Australian Red Cross Lifeblood (2016a). Retrieved from <www.donateblood.com.au>.
Blood typing and cross-matching
To avoid transfusing incompatible RBCs, both blood donor and recipient
are typed and their blood cross-matched. Blood typing is done to
determine the ABO blood group and Rh factor status. This test is also
performed on pregnant women and neonates to assess for possible
intrauterine exposure of either to an incompatible blood type (particularly
Rh factor incompatibilities).
Culturally competent care
It is important that the nurse understands and effectively manages
complex differences in communication, attitudes, religion, world
views and language. Examples include:
In Australia, the primary cultural or religious issue concerned
with blood is the refusal of members of the Jehovah’s Witness
faith to receive blood or blood products. Blood volume
expanders are acceptable to the person of the Jehovah’s
RH+
Rh−
Rh−
Rh−
RH+
RH+
Rh−
RH+


Witness faith as long as they are not derivatives of blood
(Campbell, Machan & Fisher
).
26 Campbell, Y., Machan, M. D. & Fisher, M. D. (2016). The Jehovah’s Witness
population: Considerations for preoperative optimization of hemoglobin. AANA Journal,
84(3), 173–178.
Christian Scientists do not ordinarily use blood or blood
products (Andrews, Boyle & Collins ).
27 Andrews, M. M., Boyle, J. S. & Collins, J. (2019). Transcultural Concepts in Nursing
Care (8th ed.). Philadelphia: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.
A search of the literature failed to uncover any cultural issues
with Indigenous Australians either receiving or donating blood.
Health care workers may encounter people who have migrated
from countries where giving blood is not culturally acceptable.
One example is members of some isolated tribes from Papua
New Guinea.
As blood typing only determines the presence of the major ABO and Rh
antigens, cross-matching also is necessary prior to transfusion to identify
possible interactions of minor antigens with their corresponding
antibodies. RBCs from the donor blood are mixed with serum from the
recipient; a reagent (Coombs’ serum) is added and the mixture is
examined for visible agglutination. If no antibodies to the donated RBCs
are present in the recipient’s serum, agglutination does not occur and the
risk of transfusion reaction is small.
Selection of blood donors
Screening of blood donors is rigorous. Criteria have been established to
protect the donor from possible ill effects of donation and to protect the
26
27


recipient from exposure to diseases transmitted through the blood. Blood
donors are unpaid volunteers. Potential donors are eliminated by a history
of hepatitis, HIV infection (or risk factors for HIV infection), heart disease,
most cancers, severe asthma, bleeding disorders or convulsions.
Donation may be deferred for people with malaria or who have been
exposed to malaria or hepatitis, or in situations of pregnancy, surgery,
anaemia, high or low blood pressure and certain drugs.
Links to national patient safety standards
NSQHS standard: Blood management
The intention of this standard is to ‘identify risks and put in place
strategies, to ensure that a patient’s own blood is optimised and
conserved, and that any blood and blood products the patient
receives are appropriate and safe’ (Australian Commission on Safety
and Quality in Health Care (ACSQHC)
, p. 56).
28 Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care
(ACSQHC) (2017). National Safety and Quality Health Service
Standards (2nd ed.). Sydney: ACSQHC.
This standard has been designed to assist in clinical
decision making, administering and disposing of
blood and blood products, and the reporting and
investigation of adverse incidents related to blood or
blood product transfusion. It is important to note that
the implementation of this standard ensures the
blood supply in Australia is one of the safest in the
world. Blood products are collected, processed,
stored and delivered under strict guidelines outlined
in the standard. These guidelines are designed to
28


ensure the safety of all concerned through donation,
processing, administering and receiving blood and
blood products (ACSQHC 2017).
This chapter focuses on the maintenance of fluid and
electrolyte balance to facilitate homeostasis. The
infusion of blood and blood products may be an
important part of this process for those patients at
risk of fluid depletion due to blood loss. Safety of the
individual receiving a blood transfusion and practices
of those providing care to such a person are guided
by this standard. Knowledge of the systems used in
the collection, management and delivery of blood and
blood products is imperative to ensure the safety of
both the person receiving the blood product and
other individuals involved in their care.
Blood and blood products for transfusion
Most people do not require transfusion of whole blood. It is more common
for the person to receive a transfusion of a particular blood component
specific to their individual needs. Table 55.12
 lists some of the
common blood products that may be transfused.
Table 55.12 Blood products for transfusion
29 Australian Red Cross Lifeblood (2016b). Red Cells. Retrieved from <www.transfusion.com.au>.


30 Australian Red Cross Lifeblood (2016c). Fact sheet—I Need to Know About Platelets. Retrieved
from <http://resources.transfusion.com.au>.
31 Australian Red Cross Lifeblood (2016d). Fact sheet—I Need to Know About Fresh Frozen
Plasma. Retrieved from <http://resources.transfusion.com.au>.
Transfusion reactions
Transfusion of ABO- or Rh-incompatible blood can result in a haemolytic
transfusion reaction
 with destruction of the transfused RBCs and
subsequent risk of kidney damage or failure. Other forms of transfusion
reaction also may occur, including febrile, allergic, circulatory overload
and sepsis. As the risk of an adverse reaction is high when blood is
transfused, the person must be frequently and carefully assessed before
and during transfusion. Many reactions become evident within 5 to 15
minutes of initiating the transfusion, but they can develop any time during
a transfusion. The nurse can take a person-centred approach to care by
ensuring the person is closely monitored during the initial period of the
transfusion. The transfusion should be stopped immediately if signs of a
reaction develop. Possible transfusion reactions, their clinical signs and
nursing implications are listed in Table 55.13
.
Table 55.13 Transfusion reactions
Administering blood
Special precautions are necessary when administering blood.
When a transfusion is ordered, obtain the blood from the blood bank just
before starting the transfusion. Do not store the blood in the refrigerator
on the nursing unit; lack of temperature control may damage the blood.


Once blood or a blood product is removed from the refrigerator, there is a
limited amount of time to administer it (e.g. packed RBCs should not hang
for more than 4 hours after being removed from the refrigerator). Follow
organisation policies for verifying that the unit is correct for the person.
The blood products obtained from the Australian Red Cross Lifeblood
have barcodes to allow for scanning and machine-readable information on
blood and blood component container labels to help reduce medication
errors.
Blood is usually administered through a #18- to #20-gauge intravenous
cannula; using a smaller cannula may slow the infusion and damage
blood cells (although a smaller-gauge cannula may be necessary for
small children or the person with small, fragile veins). No IV solutions or
drugs should be administered with blood as they may cause the blood
cells to clump or cause clotting. A transfusion should be completed within
4 hours of initiation. The risk of sepsis increases if blood hangs for a
longer period. Blood tubing is changed after every 4 to 6 units per
organisation policy; new intravenous tubing is used following a
transfusion.
To initiate, maintain and terminate a blood transfusion, see Skill 55.6
.
Clinical consideration
Normal saline should always be used when giving a
blood transfusion. If the person has an infusion of
dextrose, stop that infusion and flush the line with
saline prior to initiating the transfusion. Solutions


other than saline can cause damage to the blood
components.
