SKILL
55.1 Starting an intravenous
infusion
Before preparing the infusion, the nurse first verifies
the doctor’s order indicating the type of solution, the
amount to be administered, the rate of flow of the
infusion and if the person has any allergies (e.g. to
tape or povidone-iodine).
Purposes
To supply fluid when the person is unable to take
in an adequate volume of fluids by mouth.
To provide salts and other electrolytes needed to
maintain electrolyte balance.
To provide glucose (dextrose), the main fuel for
metabolism.
To provide water-soluble vitamins and
medications.
To establish a lifeline for rapidly needed
medications.


Assessment
Assess
Vital signs (pulse, respiratory rate and blood
pressure) for baseline data.
Skin turgor.
Allergy to latex (e.g. tourniquet), tape or iodine.
Bleeding tendencies.
Disease or injury to extremities.
Status of veins to determine appropriate
venipuncture site.
Planning
Prior to initiating the IV infusion, consider how long
the person is likely to have the IV, what kinds of
fluids will be infused and what medications the
person will be receiving or is likely to receive. These
factors may affect the choice of vein and cannula
size.
Delegation
This procedure is done by a doctor or a Registered
Nurse who has successfully completed an IV
cannulation competency prior to undertaking the
procedure. Due to the use of sterile technique,
intravenous infusion therapy is not delegated to an
Assistant in Nursing (AIN). An AIN may care for the


person receiving IV therapy and the nurse must
ensure that the AIN knows how to perform routine
tasks such as bathing and positioning without
disturbing the IV. The AIN should also know what
complications or adverse signs, such as leakage,
should be reported to the nurse.
Equipment
Infusion set
Sterile parenteral solution
IV pole
Adhesive or non-allergenic tape
Clean personal protective equipment
Tourniquet
Antiseptic swabs
Antiseptic ointment (check health care
organisational policy)
Intravenous cannula; see Variation at the end of
this procedure for a butterfly (winged-tip) needle
Sterile gauze dressing, transparent occlusive
dressing or dressing as directed by
organisational policy
Arm splint, if required
Towel or pad
Electronic infusion device or pump (The nurse
decides what device is needed as appropriate to
the person’s condition.)


Implementation
Preparation
Prepare the person.
Prior to performing the procedure, take a person-
centred care approach to reduce levels of
anxiety in the person. Introduce yourself and
verify the person’s identity using organisation
protocol. Explain the procedure to the person. A
venipuncture can cause discomfort for a few
seconds, but there should be no discomfort while
the solution is flowing. Use a doll to demonstrate
for children and explain the procedure to the
parents. The person may want to know how long
the process will last. The doctor’s order may
specify the length of time of the infusion; for
example, 1000 mL over 8 hours.
Unless initiating IV therapy is urgent, provide any
scheduled care before establishing the infusion
to minimise movement of the affected limb
during the procedure. Moving the limb after the
infusion has been established could dislodge the
cannula.
Make sure that the person’s clothing or gown can
be removed over the IV apparatus if necessary.
Some organisations provide special gowns that


open over the shoulder and down the sleeve for
easy removal.
Performance
Perform hand hygiene and apply personal protective
equipment:
1. Open and prepare the infusion set.
Remove tubing from the container and
straighten it out.
Slide the tubing clamp along the tubing
until it is just below the drip chamber to
facilitate its access.
Close the clamp.
Leave the ends of the tubing covered with
the plastic caps until the infusion is
started. Rationale: this will maintain the
sterility of the ends of the tubing.
2. Spike the solution container.
Remove the protective cover from the
entry site of the bag.
Remove the cap from the spike and insert
the spike into the insertion site of the bag
or bottle. 1 Follow the manufacturer’s
instructions.


1 Inserting the spike
Source: Elena Dorfman.


3. All intravenous fluids are checked by two
nurses.
4. Apply correct medication additive label signed
by both nurses to the solution container if a
medication is added.
In some health care organisations,
medications and labels are applied in the
pharmacy.
5. Apply a timing label on the solution container.
The timing label may be applied at the time
the infusion is started. Follow organisation
practice. See later discussion of regulating
infusion flow rates and Figure 55.24
.
6. Hang the solution container on the pole.
Adjust the pole so that the container is
suspended about 1 m above the person’s
head. Rationale: this height is needed to
enable gravity to overcome venous
pressure and facilitate flow of the solution
into the vein.
7. Partially fill the drip chamber with solution.
Squeeze the chamber gently until it is half
full of solution. 2


2 Squeezing the drip chamber
Source: Elena Dorfman.
8. Prime the tubing.
Remove the protective cap and hold the
tubing over a container. Maintain the
sterility of the end of the tubing and the
cap.
Release the clamp and let the fluid run
through the tubing until all bubbles are
removed. Tap the tubing, if necessary,
with your fingers to help the bubbles
move. Rationale: the tubing is primed to
prevent the introduction of air into the


person. Air bubbles smaller than 0.5 mL
usually do not cause problems in
peripheral lines, but every effort should be
made to remove all air from the line.
Re-clamp the tubing and replace the
tubing cap, maintaining sterile technique.
For caps with air vents, do not remove the
cap when priming this tubing. The flow of
solution through the tubing will cease
when the cap is moist with one drop of
solution.
When setting up an infusion-control pump,
be sure to follow the manufacturer’s
directions for inserting the tubing, setting
the infusion rate and setting the guard
rails.
Occasionally, IV fluids may be delivered
without a pump; in this instance, a
controller device with a roller clamp will be
used to establish and set the flow.
9. Perform hand hygiene and apply personal
protective equipment again just prior to
contact with the person.
10. Select the venipuncture site.
Use the person’s non-dominant arm,
unless contraindicated (e.g. mastectomy,
fistula for dialysis). Identify possible


venipuncture sites by looking for veins that
are relatively straight, not sclerotic or
tortuous, and avoid venous valves. The
vein should be palpable, but may not be
visible, especially in the person with dark
skin. Consider the cannula length; look for
a site sufficiently distal to the wrist or
elbow that the tip of the cannula will not be
at a point of flexion. Rationale: sclerotic
veins may make initiating and maintaining
the IV difficult. Joint flexion increases the
risk of irritation of vein walls by the
cannula.
Check health care organisation protocol
about shaving if the site is very hairy.
Shaving is not usually recommended
because of the potential for micro-
abrasions, which can increase the risk of
infection.
Place a towel or bed protector under the
extremity to protect linens (or furniture if in
the home).
11. Dilate the vein.
Place the extremity in a dependent
position (lower than the person’s heart).
Rationale: gravity slows venous return
and distends the veins. Distending the


veins makes it easier to insert the needle
properly.
Apply a tourniquet firmly 15 to 20 cm
above the venipuncture site. 3 Explain that
the tourniquet will feel tight. Rationale:
the tourniquet must be tight enough to
obstruct venous flow but not so tight that it
occludes arterial flow. Obstructing arterial
flow inhibits venous filling.
If a radial pulse can be palpated, the
arterial flow is not obstructed. Use the
tourniquet on only one person. This avoids
cross-contamination to other people.


3 Applying a tourniquet
If the vein is not sufficiently dilated:
a. Massage or stroke the vein distal to
the site and in the direction of
venous flow towards the heart.
Rationale: this action helps fill the
vein.
b. Encourage the person to clench
and unclench the fist. Rationale:
contracting the muscles
compresses the distal veins, forcing
blood along the veins and
distending them.
c. Lightly tap the vein with your
fingertips. Rationale: tapping may
distend the vein.
If the preceding steps fail to distend the
vein so that it is palpable, remove the
tourniquet and wrap the extremity in a
warm, moist towel for 10 to 15 minutes.
Rationale: heat dilates superficial blood
vessels, causing them to fill. Then repeat
step 10.
12. Put on clean personal protective equipment
and clean the venipuncture site. Rationale:


personal protective equipment protects the
nurse from contamination by the person’s
blood.
If there is a requirement to draw blood
from the cannula for pathology before IV
therapy is commenced, it is important to
avoid excessive tapping or massage over
the vein and prolonged use of the
tourniquet (greater then 60 seconds).
Rationale: excessive manipulation over
the vein and extended use of a tourniquet
will result in haemolysis of the blood
sample.
Permit the solution to dry on the skin.
Povidone-iodine should be in contact with
the skin for 1 minute to be effective.
13. Insert the cannula and initiate the infusion.
If desired and permitted by organisational
policy, inject 0.05 mL of 1% lidocaine
intradermally over the site where you plan
to insert the IV cannula. Allow 5 to 10
seconds for the anaesthetic to take effect.
Transdermal analgesic creams (e.g. ELA-
Max, EMLA) may also be used, depending
on policy. Allow 30 minutes for the
transdermal analgesic to take effect.


Use the non-dominant hand to pull the
skin taut below the entry site. Rationale:
this stabilises the vein and makes the skin
taut for needle entry. It can also make
initial tissue penetration less painful.
Holding the over-the-needle cannula at a
15- to 30-degree angle with bevel up,
insert the cannula through the skin and
into the vein. Sudden lack of resistance is
felt as the needle enters the vein. Jabbing,
stabbing or quick thrusting should be
avoided because it may cause rupture of
delicate veins (Virhia & Pennycock
).
32 Virhia, P. & Pennycock, J. (2015). Peripheral cannula
in an acute setting. British Journal of Nursing, 24(14
Suppl), S17.
Once blood appears in the lumen of the
needle or you feel the lack of resistance,
lower the angle of the cannula until it is
almost parallel with the skin and advance
the needle and cannula approximately 0.5
to 1 cm further. Holding the needle portion
steady, advance the cannula until the hub
is at the venipuncture site. The exact
technique depends on the type of device
used. Rationale: the cannula is advanced
to ensure that it, and not just the metal
needle, is in the vein.
32


Release the tourniquet.
Put pressure on the vein proximal to the
cannula to eliminate or reduce blood
oozing out of the cannula. Stabilise the
hub with thumb and index finger of the
non-dominant hand.
Remove the protective cap from the distal
end of the tubing and hold it ready to
attach to the cannula, maintaining the
sterility of the end.
Carefully remove the needle, engage the
needle safety device, swap the hub of the
cannula and attach the end of the infusion
tubing to the cannula hub.
Place an IV access cap or extension
tubing that has been flushed with 0.9%
normal saline onto cannular as per health
care organisational policy.
Initiate the infusion.
14. Secure the cannula.
The cannula should be stabilised by the
clinician with a sterile, transparent, semi-
permeable, self-adhesive dressing.
Adhesive tape should not be applied
directly to the site or under the
transparent dressing.


15. Dress and label the venipuncture site and
tubing according to health care organisation
policy. This usually includes date cannula was
inserted and signature of nurse or doctor
inserting cannula.
Unless there is an allergy, a sterile
transparent occlusive dressing is applied.
4 This permits assessment of the site
without disturbing the dressing. This type
of dressing can be left on for 48 to 72
hours, then changed, depending upon the
organisation’s policy.


4 Cover insertion site with transparent
dressing
Source: Patrick Watson.
Discard the tourniquet. Remove soiled
personal protective equipment and discard
appropriately.
Loop the tubing and secure it with tape.
Rationale: looping and securing the
tubing prevent the weight of the tubing or
any movement from pulling on the needle
or cannula.
Label the dressing with the date and time
of insertion, type, gauge of cannula used
and your initials. 5


5 Label IV site with date, time, size of
cannula and initials
Source: Patrick Watson.
16. Ensure appropriate infusion flow.
Apply a disposable foam layered arm
board or plastic splint to splint the joint, as
needed.


Adjust the infusion rate of flow on the
monitor according to the order.
17. Label the IV tubing and date and sign
dressing.
Label the tubing with the date and time of
attachment and your initials. 6 Date and
sign dressing. This labelling may also be
done when the infusion is started.
Rationale: the tubing and dressing is
labelled to ensure that it is changed at
regular intervals (i.e. every 24 to 96 hours
according to health care organisation
policy).


6 Tubing labelled with date, time of
attachment and nurse’s initials Also shown
is a pre-printed label
Source: Elena Dorfman.
In some organisations, the IV cannula site
is also changed every 48 hours, so
knowing the date the cannula was inserted


will assist in ensuring the person’s IV
cannula is changed in accordance with
organisation policy.
18. Document relevant data, including
assessments.
Record the start of the infusion on the
person’s chart. Some organisations
provide a special form for this purpose.
Include the date and time of the
venipuncture; amount and type of solution
used, including any additives (e.g. kind
and amount of medications); container
number; flow rate; type, length and gauge
of the needle or cannula; venipuncture
site, how many attempts were made and
location of each attempt; the type of
dressing applied; and the person’s general
response.
Variation: inserting a butterfly (winged-tip) needle
Hold the needle, pointed in the direction of the
blood flow, at a 30-degree angle, with the bevel
up, and pierce the skin beside the vein about 1
cm below the site planned for piercing the vein.
Once the needle is through the skin, lower the
needle so that it is almost parallel with the skin.
Rationale: lowering the needle reduces the


chances of puncturing both sides of the vein.
Follow the course of the vein and pierce one side
of the vein. Sudden lack of resistance can be felt
as blood enters the needle.
When blood flows back into the needle tubing,
insert the needle to its hub.
Release the tourniquet, attach the infusion and
initiate flow as quickly as possible. Rationale:
attaching the tubing quickly prevents blood from
clotting and obstructing the needle.
Secure the butterfly needle by taping it securely
by the criss-cross (chevron) method. 7 Place a
small gauze square under the needle, if required.
Rationale: the gauze keeps the needle in
position in the vein.


7 Taping the butterfly needle by the chevron method
(N. Nguyen, RN)
Evaluation
The nurse should use sound clinical reasoning when
evaluating the effectiveness of interventions. This is
achieved by evaluating:


skin status at IV site (warm temperature and
absence of pain, redness and swelling)
status of dressing
IV flow rate consistent with that ordered
ability to perform self-care activities;
understanding of any mobility limitations
vital signs compared with baseline level


SKILL
55.2 Monitoring an intravenous
infusion
Purposes
To maintain the prescribed flow rate.
To prevent complications associated with IV
therapy.
Assessment
Assess
Appearance of infusion site; patency of system.
Type of fluid being infused and rate of flow.
Response of the person.
Planning
Review the type of equipment used outside the
person’s room. Read all appropriate materials and
confirm the type of tubing, controller or pump being
used.


Delegation
This procedure should be done by the Registered
Nurse (RN) because it is an important part of
assessment and complications may occur. However,
in some states of Australia, RNs are able to
delegate this task to Enrolled Nurses (EN) who have
undertaken the appropriate educational preparation
and who have been deemed competent by the RN
to perform the task. It is important for the RN to
remember that, if tasks are delegated, the EN works
under the direct or indirect supervision of the RN
and, as a result, the RN is ultimately responsible for
the person’s care (Nursing and Midwifery Board of
Australia ).
33 Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (2013). Nursing Practice
Decision Flow Chart. Retrieved from
<www.nursingmidwiferyboard.gov.au>.
Implementation
Preparation
Gather the pertinent data.
From the doctor’s order, determine the type and
sequence of solutions to be infused.
Determine the rate of flow and infusion schedule.
Performance
33


1. Ensure that the correct solution is being
infused.
If the solution is incorrect, stop the
infusion immediately.
Change the solution to the correct one.
Intravenous solution must be checked by
two nurses. Document and report the
error according to health care organisation
protocol.
2. Observe the rate of flow every hour.
Compare the rate of flow regularly, for
example every hour, against the infusion
schedule and pump reading. Rationale:
infusions that are off schedule can be
harmful to a person.
If the rate is too fast, slow it so that the
infusion will be completed at the planned
time. Rationale: solution administered too
quickly may cause a significant increase in
circulating blood volume (which is about 6
L in an adult). Hypervolaemia may result
in pulmonary oedema and cardiac failure.
If the rate is too slow, check organisation
practice. Some organisations permit
nursing personnel to adjust a rate of flow
by a specified amount. Adjustments above
this rate require a doctor’s order.


Rationale: solution that is administered
too slowly can supply insufficient fluid,
electrolytes or medication for a person’s
needs.
If the rate of flow is 150 mL/h or more,
check the rate of flow more frequently; for
example, every 15 to 30 minutes.
3. Inspect the patency of the IV tubing and
cannula.
Observe the position of the IV solution
and ensure pump is working to deliver the
correct amount of solution and guard rails
are in place.
If using roller-adjusted IV line, adjust
height of pole to ensure appropriate flow.
Rationale: if the IV bag/bottle is too low,
the solution may not flow into the vein
because there is insufficient gravitational
pressure to overcome the pressure of the
blood within the vein.
Observe the drip chamber. If it is less than
half full, squeeze the chamber to allow the
correct amount of fluid to flow in.
Inspect the tubing for pinches, kinks or
obstructions to flow. Sometimes the tubing
becomes caught under the person’s body
and the weight blocks the flow.


If there is leakage of fluid and blockage of
flow, locate the source. If the leak is at the
cannula connection, tighten the tubing into
the cannula. If the leak cannot be
stopped, slow the infusion as much as
possible without stopping it and replace
the tubing with a new sterile set. Estimate
the amount of solution lost, if it was
substantial. The IV cannula may need to
be removed and re-sited. Leaks in lines
put the person at risk of infection, so
careful monitoring of temperature, pulse
and respirations is required.
4. Inspect the insertion site for fluid infiltration.
When an IV cannula becomes dislodged
from the vein, fluid flows into interstitial
tissues, causing swelling. This is known as
infiltration and is manifested by localised
swelling, coolness, pallor and discomfort
at the IV site.
If an infiltration is present, stop the
infusion and notify appropriate personnel
as per your hospital policy. Restart the
infusion at another site or seek the re-
siting of the IV cannula by an experienced
person.


Apply a warm compress to the site of the
infiltration. Rationale: warmth promotes
comfort and vasodilation, facilitating
absorption of the fluid from interstitial
tissues.
5. If the infiltration involves a vesicant drug, it is
called extravasation and other measures may
be indicated. Extravasated vesicant drugs
can cause severe tissue injury or destruction.
The extravasation of a vesicant drug should
be considered an emergency (Coyne et al.
).
34 Coyne, E., Northfield, S., Ash, K. & Brown-West, L. (2019).
Current evidence of education and safety requirements for the
nursing administration of chemotherapy: An integrative review.
European Journal of Oncology Nursing, 41, 24–32.
Stop the infusion immediately. Disconnect
the tubing as close to the cannula hub as
possible and attempt to aspirate any drug
remaining in the hub. If an injectable
antidote is available, the cannula should
remain in place.
The doctor should be notified and, if
ordered, the antidote administered.
The affected arm should be elevated and,
depending on the drug, heat or cold
therapy should be implemented.
34


6. Inspect the insertion site for phlebitis
(inflammation of a vein).
Inspect and palpate the site every 1 to 2
hours or as directed by hospital policy.
Phlebitis can occur as a result of injury to
a vein; for example, because of  -
mechanical trauma or chemical irritation.
Chemical injury to a vein can occur from
intravenous electrolytes (especially
potassium and magnesium) and
medications. The clinical signs are
redness, warmth and swelling at the
intravenous site and burning pain along
the course of a vein.
If phlebitis is detected, discontinue the
infusion and apply warm compresses to
the venipuncture site. Do not use this
injured vein for further infusions.
7. Inspect the intravenous site for bleeding.
Oozing or bleeding into the surrounding
tissues can occur while the infusion is
freely flowing but is more likely to occur
after the needle has been removed from
the vein.
Observation of the venipuncture site is
extremely important for the person who


bleeds readily, such as those receiving
anticoagulants.
8. Teach the person ways to maintain the
infusion system; for example:
Avoid sudden twisting or turning
movements of the arm with the cannula.
Avoid stretching or placing tension on the
tubing.
Notify a nurse if:
a. The flow rate suddenly changes or the
solution stops dripping.
b. The solution container is nearly empty.
c. There is blood in the IV tubing.
d. Discomfort or swelling is experienced
at the IV site.
9. Document all relevant information.
Evaluation
Evaluate the following:
amount of fluid infused according to the schedule
intactness of IV system
appearance of IV site (e.g. dry, tissue infiltration,
discomfort)


urinary output compared with urinary intake
tissue turgor; specific gravity of urine
vital signs and lung sounds compared with
baseline data.


SKILL
55.3 Changing an intravenous
container, tubing and dressing
Purposes
To maintain the flow of required fluids.
To maintain sterility of the IV system and
decrease the incidence of phlebitis and infection.
To maintain patency of the IV tubing.
To prevent infection at the IV site and the
introduction of micro-organisms into the
bloodstream.
Assessment
Assess
Presence of fluid infiltration, bleeding or phlebitis
at IV site.
Allergy to tape or iodine.
Infusion rate and amount absorbed.
Blockages in IV system.


Appearance of the dressing for integrity, moisture
and need for change.
The date and the time of the previous dressing
change.
Planning
Delegation
This procedure includes assessment of the IV site
and should be completed by a Registered Nurse.
Equipment
Container with the correct kind and amount of
sterile solution
Administration set, including sterile tubing and
drip chamber
Timing label
Sterile gauze square for positioning the cannula
For the dressing, follow the organisation’s policy. You
may need:
Clean personal protective equipment
Sterile 5 cm × 5 cm or 10 cm × 10 cm gauze or
transparent dressing
Adhesive remover
Chlorhexidine swabs
Alcohol swabs


Tape
Towel
Note: not all organisation policies will support
dressing IV sites due to risk of infection. Ensure you
check the policy prior to undertaking the procedure.
Implementation
Preparation
Obtain the correct solution container.
Read the label of the new container.
Verify that you have the correct solution, correct
person, correct additives (if any) and correct
dose (number of bags or total volume ordered).
Performance
1. Perform hand hygiene and apply personal
protective equipment.
2. Set up the intravenous equipment with the
new container and label all. See Skill 55.1
,
steps 1 to 8.
Apply a timing label to the container.
Prime the tubing.
Label the tubing as shown in Figure (7) in
Skill 55.1
.


3. Prepare the IV cannula, tape and the
dressing equipment near the person.
Prepare strips of tape as needed for the
type of cannula. For the butterfly needle,
two or three strips of 1.25 cm tape are
needed. Check organisation policy for
specific details relevant to your clinical
area.
Open all equipment: swabs, dressing and
adhesive bandage and ointment.
Rationale: this facilitates access to
supplies after personal protective
equipment is donned.
Place a towel under the extremity.
Rationale: this prevents soiling of bed
linens.
Apply clean personal protective
equipment.
4. Remove the soiled dressing, except the tape
holding the cannula in place.
Remove tape and gauze from the old
dressing one layer at a time. Rationale:
this prevents dislodgment of the cannula
in case tubing becomes entangled
between layers of dressing.
Remove adhesive dressings in the
direction of the person’s hair growth when


possible. Rationale: this minimises
discomfort when adhesive is removed
from the skin.
Discard the used dressing materials in the
appropriate container.
5. Assess the IV site.
Inspect the IV site for the presence of
infiltration or inflammation. Rationale:
inflammation or infiltration necessitates
removal of the IV cannula to avoid further
trauma to the tissues.
Go to step 6 or discontinue and relocate
the IV site if indicated. See Skills 55.1
and 55.4
.
6. Disconnect the used tubing.
Place a sterile swab under the hub of the
cannula. Rationale: this absorbs any
leakage that might occur when the tubing
is disconnected.
Clamp the tubing. With the fourth or fifth
finger of the non-dominant hand, apply
pressure to the vein above the end of the
cannula. Rationale: this helps prevent
blood from coming out of the cannula
during the change of tubing.


Holding the hub of the cannula with the
thumb and index finger of the non-
dominant hand, loosen the tubing with the
dominant hand, using a twisting, pulling
motion. Rationale: holding the cannula
firmly but gently maintains its position in
the vein.
Remove the used IV tubing.
Place the end of the tubing in the basin or
other receptacle.
7. Connect the new tubing and re-establish the
infusion.
Continue to hold the cannula and grasp
the new tubing with the dominant hand.
Swab the cannula cap with an alcohol
wipe.
Remove the protective tubing cap and,
maintaining sterility, insert the tubing end
securely into the cannula hub. Twist it to
secure it.
Open the clamp to start the solution
flowing.
8. Remove the dressing securing the cannula.
When removing the dressing and while
cleaning the site, stabilise the cannula hub


with one hand. Rationale: this prevents
inadvertent dislodgment of the cannula.
9. Clean the IV site.
Start with adhesive remover to remove
adhesive residue. Rationale: removal of
adhesive residue facilitates adherence of
the new dressing.
Then, using chlorhexidine swabs or
alcohol swabs, clean the site, beginning at
the cannula and cleaning outward in a 5
cm diameter. Rationale: cleaning in this
manner prevents contamination of the IV
site from bacteria on the peripheral skin
areas. Antiseptics reduce the number of
micro-organisms present at the site, thus
reducing the risk of infection.
Follow health care organisation protocol
about cleaning procedures.
For a butterfly needle, apply strips of tape
to the wings of the butterfly using the
criss-cross (chevron) method (see Figure
(8) in Skill 55.1
).
Apply a sterile transparent dressing over
the site.
Remove personal protective equipment.
10. Label the dressing and secure IV tubing.


Place the date and time of the dressing
change and your initials either on the label
provided or directly over the top of the
dressing.
Secure IV tubing with tape as required.
11. Regulate the rate of flow of the solution
according to the order on the chart.
12. Document all relevant information.
Record the change of the solution
container, tubing and/or dressing in the
appropriate place on the person’s chart.
Also record the fluid intake according to
organisation practice. Record the number
of the container if the containers are
numbered at the organisation. Also record
your assessments.
Evaluation
Evaluate the following:
status of IV site
patency of IV system
accuracy of flow.


SKILL
55.4 Discontinuing an
intravenous infusion
Purpose
To discontinue an intravenous infusion when the
therapy is complete or when the IV site needs to
be changed.
Assessment
Assess
Appearance of the venipuncture site.
Any bleeding from the infusion site.
Amount of fluid infused.
Appearance of IV cannula.
Planning
Review the doctor’s orders.
Equipment


Clean personal protective equipment
Dry or antiseptic-soaked swabs, according to
organisation practice
Small sterile dressing
Implementation
Performance
1. Prepare the equipment.
Clamp the infusion tubing or turn off
infusion pump. Rationale: clamping the
tubing prevents the fluid from flowing out
of the cannula onto the person or bed.
Loosen the dressing at the venipuncture
site while holding the cannula firmly and
applying counter-traction to the skin.
Rationale: movement of the cannula can
injure the vein and cause discomfort to the
person. Counter-traction prevents pulling
the skin and causing discomfort.
Put on clean personal protective
equipment and hold a sterile gauze above
the venipuncture site.
2. Withdraw the cannula from the vein.
Withdraw the cannula by pulling it out
along the line of the vein. Rationale:


pulling it out in line with the vein avoids
injury to the vein.
Immediately apply firm pressure to the
site, using sterile gauze, for 2 to 3
minutes. Rationale: pressure helps stop
the bleeding and prevents haematoma
formation. Do not use cotton wool swab
as this may leave fibres behind when
removed.
Hold the person’s arm above the body if
any bleeding persists. Rationale: raising
the limb decreases blood flow to the area.
3. Examine the cannula removed from the
person.
Check the cannula to make sure it is
intact. Rationale: if a piece of tubing
remains in the person’s vein it could move
centrally (towards the heart or lungs) and
cause serious problems.
Report a broken cannula to the nurse in
charge or doctor immediately.
If a broken piece can be palpated, apply a
tourniquet above the insertion site.
Rationale: application of a tourniquet
decreases the possibility of the piece
moving until a doctor is notified.


4. Cover the venipuncture site.
Apply the sterile dressing. Rationale: the
dressing continues the pressure and
covers the open area in the skin,
preventing infection.
Discard the IV solution properly, if
infusions are being discontinued, and
discard the used supplies appropriately.
5. Document all relevant information.
Record the amount of fluid infused on the
intake and output record and on the chart,
according to organisation practice. Include
the container number, type of solution
used, time of discontinuing the infusion
and the person’s response.
Evaluation
Evaluate the following:
appearance of the venipuncture site
the pulse
respirations, skin colour, oedema, sputum, cough
and urine output
how the person feels physically and
psychologically.


SKILL
55.5 Changing an intravenous
cannula to an intermittent
infusion lock
Purpose
To permit IV administration of medications or
fluids on an intermittent basis.
Assessment
Assess
Patency of the IV cannula.
Appearance of the site (evidence of inflammation
or infiltration).
Planning
Review the doctor’s order.


A specific order may be written to convert an
intravenous access to a heparin or saline lock.
The order also may be implied; for example, IV
fluids are to be discontinued but the person has
orders for an IV antibiotic every 6 hours or is
receiving analgesics intravenously.
Delegation
Due to the need for sterile technique and technical
complexity, this procedure should be performed by a
Registered Nurse.
Equipment
Intermittent infusion cap or device
Clean personal protective equipment
Sterile 5 cm × 5 cm or 10 cm × 10 cm gauze
Sterile saline for injection (without preservative)
or heparin flush solution (10 units/mL or 100
units/mL) in a prefilled syringe, a 3 mL syringe
with a needle-less infusion device
Alcohol wipe
Tape
Clean kidney dish
Implementation
Preparation
Prepare the person.


Prior to performing the procedure, introduce self
and verify the person’s identity using health care
organisation protocol. Explain the procedure to
the person and the reason for leaving the IV
cannula in place. Changing an IV to a heparin or
saline lock should cause no discomfort other
than that associated with removing tape from the
IV tubing.
Performance
1. Prepare the equipment.
Perform hand hygiene and apply personal
protective equipment.
Assess the IV site (if visible) and
determine the patency of the cannula (see
Skill 55.2
). If the cannula is not fully
patent or there is evidence of phlebitis or
infiltration, discontinue the cannula and
establish a new IV site.
Expose the IV cannula hub and loosen
any tape that is holding the IV tubing in
place or that will interfere with insertion of
the intermittent infusion plug into the
cannula.
Clamp the IV tubing to stop the flow of IV
fluid.
Open the gauze pad and place it under
the IV cannula hub.


Open the alcohol wipe and intermittent
infusion plug, leaving the plug in its sterile
package.
2. Remove the IV tubing and insert the
intermittent infusion plug into the IV cannula.
Put on personal protective equipment.
Stabilise the IV cannula with your non-
dominant hand and use the little finger to
place slight pressure on the vein above
the end of the cannula. Twist the IV tubing
adapter to loosen it from the IV cannula
and remove it, placing the end of the
tubing in a clean kidney dish.
Pick up the intermittent infusion plug from
its package and remove the protective
sleeve from the male adapter, maintaining
its sterility. Insert the plug into the IV
cannula, twisting it to seat it firmly or
engage the Luer-lok.
3. Instil saline or heparin solution as per
organisation policy. Rationale: saline or
heparin are used to maintain patency of the
IV cannula when fluids are not infusing
through the cannula.
4. Tape the intermittent infusion plug in place as
per organisational policy. Rationale: tape


prevents the infusion plug from coming out of
the intravenous cannula. It also promotes
comfort, preventing the plug from catching on
clothing or bedding.
5. Teach the person how to maintain the lock.
Avoid manipulating the cannula or infusion
plug and protect it from catching on
clothing or bedding. A gauze bandage
may be wrapped over the plug when it is
not in use to protect it.
Cover the site with an occlusive dressing
when showering; avoid immersing the site.
Flush the cannula with saline or heparin
solution, as directed.
Notify the nurse or doctor if the plug or
cannula comes out; if the site becomes
red, inflamed or painful; or if any drainage
or bleeding occurs at the site.
6. Document all relevant information.
Evaluation
Evaluate the following:
patency of the cannula
appearance of the site
ease of flushing.


SKILL
55.6 Initiating, maintaining and
terminating a blood transfusion
Purposes
To restore blood volume after severe
haemorrhage.
To restore the oxygen-carrying capacity of the
blood.
To provide plasma factors, such as
antihaemophilic factor (AHF) or factor VIII, or
platelet concentrates, which prevent or treat
bleeding.
Assessment
Assess
Manifestations of hypervolaemia.
Status of infusion site.
Planning


Verify the doctor’s order for transfusion.
Verify the person has consented and signed
consent.
Assess vital signs for baseline data, including
blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and depth
and temperature prior to transfusion.
Determine any known allergies or previous
adverse reactions to blood.
Note specific signs related to the person’s
pathology and the reason for the transfusion. For
example, for an anaemic person, note the
haemoglobin and haematocrit levels.
Delegation
Due to the need for sterile technique and technical
complexity, blood transfusion should be started by a
Registered Nurse.
Equipment
Blood product
Blood administration set and suitable pump with
monitor
IV pole
Venipuncture set containing a #18- to #20-gauge
cannula (if one is not already in place) or, if blood
is to be administered quickly, a larger cannula
Alcohol swabs
Tape


Personal protective equipment
Implementation
Preparation
Prepare the person.
Prior to performing the procedure, introduce self
and verify the person’s identity using health care
organisation protocol.
Explain the procedure and its purpose to the
person. Instruct the person to report promptly
any sudden chills, nausea, itching, rash,
dyspnoea, back pain or other unusual symptoms.
If the person has an intravenous solution
infusing, check whether the cannula is
appropriate to administer blood. The preferred
cannula size is from #18- to #20-gauge and the
solution must be normal saline. Dextrose (which
causes lysis of RBCs), Hartmann’s solution,
medications and other additives and
hyperalimentation solutions are incompatible.
Refer to step 6 below if the infusing solution is
not compatible.
If the person does not have an IV solution
infusing, check organisation policies. In some
organisations, an infusion must be running
before the blood is obtained from the blood bank.


In this case, you will need to perform a
venipuncture on a suitable vein (see Skill
55.1
) and start an IV infusion of normal saline.
Performance
1. Obtain the correct blood component for the
person.
Check the doctor’s order with the
requisition.
Collect the blood from the blood fridge.
Check the requisition form and the blood
bag label according to organisation policy.
Specifically, check the person’s name,
identification number, blood type (A, B, AB
or O) and Rh group, the blood donor
number and the expiration date of the
blood. Observe the blood for abnormal
colour, RBC clumping, gas bubbles and
extraneous material. Return outdated or
abnormal blood to the blood bank.
With another nurse, compare the
laboratory blood record with:
a. the person’s name and
identification number
b. the number on the blood bag label
c. the ABO group and Rh type on the
blood bag label.


If any of the information does not match
exactly, notify the charge nurse and the
blood bank. Do not administer blood until
discrepancies are corrected or clarified.
Sign the appropriate form with the other
nurse according to organisation policy.
Make sure that the blood is left at room
temperature for no more than 30 minutes
before starting the transfusion. Rationale:
RBCs deteriorate and lose their
effectiveness after 2 hours at room
temperature. Lysis of RBCs releases
potassium into the bloodstream, causing
hyperkalaemia. Organisations may
designate different times at which the
blood must be returned to the blood bank
if it has not been started. Rationale: as
blood components warm, the risk of
bacterial growth also increases. If the start
of the transfusion is unexpectedly
delayed, return the blood to the blood
bank. Do not store blood in the unit
refrigerator. Rationale: the temperature of
unit refrigerators is not precisely regulated
and the blood may be damaged.
2. Verify the person’s identity according to
organisation protocol.


Ask the person to state their name and
date of birth.
Check the person’s arm band for name
and ID number. Do not administer blood to
a person without an arm band. The
patient’s hospital record number is
checked to ensure it is the same as on the
arm band and blood order form.
Check details against the person’s
identification band, the blood transfusion
order form and blood bag label.
3. Set up the infusion equipment.
Put on personal protective equipment.
Ensure that the blood filter inside the drip
chamber is suitable for whole blood or the
blood components to be transfused.
Attach the blood tubing to the blood filter,
if necessary. Rationale: blood filters have
a surface area large enough to allow the
blood components through easily but are
designed to trap clots.
Close all clamps on blood transfusion
giving.
4. Prepare the blood bag.
Ensure the bag is intact with no evidence
of leaks or tampering.


There should be no sediment, clots or
discolouration of the blood.
Invert the blood bag gently several times
to mix the cells with the plasma.
Rationale: rough handling can damage
the cells.
Expose the port on the blood bag by
pulling back the tabs. 1
Close the clamp on the IV giving set.
Insert the spike on the giving set into the
blood bag.
Suspend the blood bag.
Open the clamp on the blood-giving set
and prime the tubing.


1 Exposing the port on the blood bag by
pulling back the tabs
5. Establish the blood transfusion.
The blood will run into the drip chamber. If
necessary, squeeze the drip chamber to


re-establish the liquid level with drip
chamber one-third full. (Tap the filter to
expel any residual air within the filter.)
Access IV pump with monitor. Check that
the pump is correctly set up and
functioning.
Connect blood to pump.
Set correct flow rate and ensure guard
rails are in place.
Set the monitor.
6. Observe the person closely for the first 5 to
10 minutes.
Run the blood slowly for the first 15
minutes at 20 drops per minute.
Note adverse reactions, such as chilling,
nausea, vomiting, skin rash or
tachycardia. Rationale: the earlier a
transfusion reaction occurs, the more
severe it tends to be. Identifying such
reactions promptly helps to minimise the
consequences.
Further observations will depend on
hospital policy or the condition of the
patient. Most facilities will require the
recording of blood observations at least
hourly.


Remind the person to call a nurse
immediately if any unusual symptoms are
felt during the transfusion.
If any of these reactions occur, report
these to the nurse in charge and take
appropriate nursing action (see Table
55.13
).
7. Document relevant data.
Record starting the blood, including vital
signs, type of blood, blood unit number,
sequence number (e.g. no. 1 of three
ordered units), site of the venipuncture,
size of the cannula and drip rate.
It is a legislative requirement that the
blood pack donation number is recorded.
This is to enable traceability of the blood
should this be necessary.
8. Monitor the person as per organisation policy.
Fifteen minutes after initiating the
transfusion, check the vital signs of the
person. If there are no signs of a reaction,
establish the required flow rate. Most
adults can tolerate receiving one unit of
blood in 1½ to 2 hours. Do not transfuse a
unit of blood for longer than 4 hours.


Assess the person including vital signs
every 30 minutes or more often,
depending on the health status, until 1
hour post-transfusion. If the person has a
reaction and the blood is discontinued,
send the blood bag and tubing to the
laboratory for investigation of the blood.
9. Terminate the transfusion.
Record vital signs at the completion of the
transfusion.
Put on clean personal protective
equipment.
If no infusion is to follow, clamp the blood
tubing and remove the cannula. If another
transfusion is to follow, clamp the blood
tubing and open the saline infusion arm.
Blood administration sets are changed
within 24 hours or after 4 to 6 units of
blood per organisation protocol.
If the primary IV is to be continued, flush
the maintenance line with saline solution.
Disconnect the blood tubing system and
re-establish the intravenous infusion using
new tubing. Adjust the rate on the monitor.
Discard the administration set according
to organisation practice.
Remove personal protective equipment.


Again monitor vital signs.
10. Follow organisation protocol for appropriate
disposal of the blood bag.
11. Document relevant data.
Record completion of the transfusion, the
amount of blood absorbed, the blood unit
number and the vital signs. If the primary
intravenous infusion was continued,
record connecting it. Also record the
transfusion on the IV flow sheet and fluid
balance chart.
(N. Nguyen, RN)
(N. Nguyen, RN)
Evaluation
Evaluate the following:
changes in vital signs or health status
presence of chills, nausea, vomiting or skin rash.
Evaluating


The nurse should use sound clinical reasoning to
evaluate the effectiveness of interventions. Using
the overall goals identified in the planning stage of
maintaining or restoring fluid balance, maintaining or
restoring pulmonary ventilation and oxygenation,
maintaining or restoring normal balance of
electrolytes and preventing associated risks of fluid,
electrolyte and acid–base imbalances, the nurse
collects data to evaluate the effectiveness of
interventions.
If desired outcomes are not achieved, the nurse, the
person and the support person, if appropriate, need
to explore the reasons. For example, if the outcome
‘Urine output is greater than 1300 mL per day and
within 500 mL of intake’ is not achieved, questions to
be considered may include:
Have other outcome measures for the goal of
achieving fluid balance been met?
Does the person understand and comply with
planned fluid intake?
Is all urinary output being measured?
Are unusual or excessive amounts of fluid being
lost by another route (e.g. gastric suction,
excessive perspiration, fever, rapid respiratory
rate, wound drainage)?


Are prescribed medications being taken or
administered as ordered?


Chapter 55 Review


Chapter highlights
Fluid, electrolyte, acid and base balances in the body are
necessary for health and life.
The body fluid is divided into two major compartments: the
intracellular fluid (ICF) inside the cells and extracellular fluid
(ECF) outside the cells.
Extracellular fluid is subdivided into two compartments:
intravascular (plasma) and interstitial. It constitutes about one-
fourth to one-third of total body fluid.
ECF is in constant motion throughout the body. It is the transport
system that carries nutrients to and waste products from the
cells.
The percentage of total body fluids varies according to the
individual’s age, body fat and sex. The younger the person, the
higher the proportion of water in the body. The less body fat
present, the greater the proportion of body fluid. Post-adolescent
females have a smaller percentage of fluid in relation to total
body weight than do men.
There are two types of body electrolytes (ions): positively
charged ions (cations) and negatively charged ions (anions).
The principal ions of ECF are sodium and chloride; the principal
ions of ICF are potassium and phosphate.
Fluids and electrolytes move among the body compartments by
osmosis, diffusion, filtration and active transport.
The major fluid pressures exerted as part of the movement of
fluid and electrolytes from one compartment to another are


osmotic pressure and hydrostatic pressure.
The three sources of body fluid are fluids taken orally, food
ingested and the oxidation of food. Fluid intake is regulated by
the thirst mechanism.
Fluid output occurs chiefly through excretion of urine, although
body fluid is also lost through sweat, faeces and insensible
vapour loss.
In healthy adults, measurable fluid intake and output should
balance (about 1500 mL per day). The output of urine normally
approximates the oral intake of fluids. Water from food and
oxidation is balanced by fluid loss through the skin, the
respiratory process and faeces.
A number of body systems and organs are involved in regulating
the volume and composition of body fluids: the kidneys, the
endocrine system, the cardiovascular system, the lungs and the
gastrointestinal system. The kidneys are the primary regulator of
fluid and electrolyte balance.
Substances such as the antidiuretic hormone, the renin–
angiotensin–aldosterone system and the atrial natriuretic factor
are also involved in maintaining fluid balance.
Fluid imbalances include:
a. fluid volume deficit (FVD), also referred to as
hypovolaemia
b. fluid volume excess (FVE), also referred to as
hypervolaemia
c. dehydration, a deficit in water and increase in serum
sodium level


d. over-hydration, an excess of water and decrease in serum
sodium level.
The most common electrolyte imbalances are deficits or
excesses in sodium, potassium and calcium.
The acid–base balance (pH range) of body fluids is maintained
within a precise range of 7.35 to 7.45.
Acid–base balance is regulated by buffers that neutralise excess
acids or bases; the lungs, which eliminate or retain carbon
dioxide, a potential acid; and the kidneys, which excrete or
conserve bicarbonate and hydrogen ions.
Acid–base imbalance occurs when the normal 20:1 ratio of
bicarbonate to carbonic acid is upset. Imbalances may be either
respiratory or metabolic in origin; either can result in acidosis or
alkalosis.
Factors that influence an individual’s fluid, electrolyte and acid–
base balance include age, gender and body size, environmental
temperature and lifestyle. Illness, trauma, surgery and certain
medications can place individuals at risk of fluid, electrolyte and
acid–base imbalances.
Fluid, electrolyte and acid–base imbalance is most accurately
determined through laboratory examination of blood plasma.
Assessment relative to fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balances
includes (a) a nursing history; (b) physical examination of the
skin, oral cavity, eyes, jugular vein, veins of the hand and the
neurological system; (c) measurement of body weight, vital signs
and fluid intake and output; and (d) various diagnostic studies of
blood and urine.


A nursing history includes data about the person’s fluid and food
intake; fluid output; signs of fluid, electrolyte and acid–base
imbalances; and medications, therapies or disease processes
that may disrupt these balances.
In many instances, fluids and electrolytes can be provided orally
to the person who is experiencing or at risk of developing fluid
deficits. The nurse needs to establish with the person a 24-hour
plan for ingesting the necessary fluids and to respect the
person’s fluid preferences.
For the person with fluid retention, fluids may need to be
restricted; a schedule and short-term goals that make the fluid
restriction more tolerable need to be developed.
For the person experiencing excessive fluid losses, the
administration of fluids and electrolytes intravenously is
necessary. Meticulous aseptic technique is required when caring
for the person with intravenous infusions.
Preventing complications such as infiltration, phlebitis,
hypervolaemia (circulatory overload) and infection is an important
aspect of intravenous therapy.
The administration of blood transfusions involves accurately
matching and identifying the blood for the individual, correctly
identifying the recipient and monitoring the person throughout the
procedure for transfusion reactions.

Glossary
24-hour food recall
A person’s recall of all the food and beverages consumed during
a typical 24-hour period.
abdominal paracentesis
Removal of fluids from the peritoneal cavity.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health worker
A person who liaises with medical professionals and Indigenous
people to improve the quality of health services.
absorption
The process by which a drug passes into the bloodstream.
accommodation
A process of change whereby cognitive processes mature
sufficiently to allow a person to solve problems that were
previously unsolvable.
accountability
The requirement by decision makers to account for their
decisions. The increase in government control has led to a
demand for heightened scrutiny of government, consistent with


the democratic ideal that those who elect the government are
entitled to call it to account.
accreditation
A status that is conferred on an organisation or a person when
they have been assessed as having met particular standards.
acculturation
The involuntary process that occurs when people adapt to or
borrow traits from another culture.
acid
A substance that releases hydrogen ions (H ) in solution.
acidosis
A condition that occurs with increases in blood carbonic acid or
with decreases in blood bicarbonate; blood pH below 7.35.
action stage
Occurs when a person actively implements behavioural and
cognitive strategies to interrupt previous behaviour patterns and
adopt new ones; this stage requires a great commitment of time
and energy.
active euthanasia
Actions that directly bring about the person’s death with or
without consent.
+


active immunity
A resistance of the body to infection in which the host produces
its own antibodies in response to natural or artificial antigens.
active listening
Involves attending to the person, hearing what is being said and
communicating back to the person that the nurse has heard the
person’s message. Active listening includes verbal and non-
verbal techniques.
active ROM exercises
Isotonic exercises in which the person moves each joint in the
body through its complete range, maximally stretching all muscle
groups within each plane over the joint.
active sense of self
The development of meaning, purpose and direction in one’s life.
active transport
Movement of substances across cell membranes against the
concentration gradient.
activity theory
The best way to age is to stay active physically and mentally.
activity tolerance
The type and amount of exercise or daily activities an individual
can perform.


activity–exercise pattern
Refers to a person’s pattern of exercise, activity, leisure and
recreation.
Acts of Parliament
A body of law passed by the legislature and given royal assent by
the Crown.
actual diagnosis
A problem that is present when the nurse assesses the person.
actual loss
Can be identified by others and can arise either in response to or
in anticipation of a situation.
acupressure
A form of healing in which the therapist exerts finger pressure on
specific sites.
acupuncture
A form of healing in which the therapist applies needles to
stimulate specific sites of the body.
acute confusion
Also called delirium; abrupt onset of confusion with a reversible
cause.
acute coronary syndrome (ACS)


A broad spectrum of clinical presentations, spanning from angina
to acute myocardial infarction.
acute illness
Typically characterised by severe symptoms of relatively short
duration.
acute infections
Those that generally appear suddenly or last a short time.
acute inpatient unit
A ward in a mental health facility that admits individuals who are
generally very mentally unwell.
acute kidney injury
The rapid loss of the kidney’s excretory function. It may be
caused by ischaemia, inflammation or sepsis. It is characterised
by rapid decrease in urine output
, over hours to days, and
increase in blood creatinine and urea. Formerly known as acute
renal failure (Bellomo, Kellum & Ronco ).

756–766.
acute myocardial infarction (AMI)
Sudden heart attack; sudden cardiac tissue necrosis or death of
myocardial cells.

acute pain
Pain that lasts only through the expected recovery period (less
than 6 months), whether it has a sudden or slow onset and
regardless of the intensity.
acute resuscitation plan (ARP)
A form outlining the interventions that should be included and/or
withheld in the event of a respiratory or cardiac arrest.
adaptation
The process of modifying to meet new, changing or different
conditions.
adaptive mechanisms
Learned behaviours that assist an individual to adjust to the
environment.
adherence
The extent to which an individual’s behaviour (e.g. taking
medications, following diets or making lifestyle changes)
coincides with medical or health advice; commitment or
attachment to a regimen.
adolescence
The period during which a person becomes physically and
psychologically mature and acquires a personal identity.
adolescent growth spurt


The period during puberty when sudden and dramatic physical
changes occur.
advance health directive (AHD)
A document that outlines the person’s wishes and requests
regarding their future health care for a variety of medical
conditions, including the decision to prolong life via interventions
such as resuscitation and mechanical ventilation.
adventitious breath sounds
Abnormal or acquired breath sounds.
adverse effects
More severe side effects that may justify the discontinuation of a
drug.
advocate
Individual who pleads the cause of another or argues or pleads
for a cause or proposal.
aerobic
Living only in the presence of oxygen.
aerobic exercise
Any activity during which the body takes in more or an equal
amount of oxygen than it expends.
aesthetic knowing


Providing care and meeting the needs of individuals through
creativity and style.
aetiology
The causal relationship between a problem and its related or risk
factors.
afebrile
Absence of a fever.
affective domain
Known as the ‘feeling’ domain, it is divided into categories that
specify the degree of a person’s depth of emotional response to
tasks; includes feelings, emotions, interests, attitudes and
appreciations.
afterload
The resistance against which the heart must pump to eject blood
into the circulation.
ageing in place
Allowing adults to remain in their own homes as they age.
ageism
Deep and profound prejudice in society against older adults.
agglutinins
Specific antibodies formed in the blood.


agglutinogen
A substance that acts as an antigen and stimulates the
production of agglutinins.
agnostic
A person who doubts the existence of God or a supreme being
or believes the existence of God has not been proven.
agonist
A drug that interacts with a receptor to produce a response.
agonist analgesic
A full agonist, which is a pure opioid drug that binds tightly to mu
receptor sites, producing maximum pain inhibition, an agonist
effect.
alarm reaction
The initial reaction of the body to stress, which alerts the body’s
defences.
algor mortis
The gradual decrease of the body’s temperature after death.
alkalosis
A condition that occurs with increases in blood bicarbonate or
decreases in blood carbonic acid; blood pH above 7.45.
allodynia


When non-painful stimuli (e.g. contact with linen, water or wind)
produces pain.
alopecia
The loss of scalp hair (baldness) or body hair.
alternative medicine
An unrelated group of nonorthodox practices, often with
explanatory systems that do not follow conventional biomedical
explanations.
Alzheimer’s disease
Disease that involves progressive dementia, memory loss and
inability to care for self.
amblyopia
Reduced visual acuity in one eye.
ambulation
The act of walking.
ampoule
A small glass container for individual doses of liquid medications.
anabolism
A process in which simple substances are converted by the
body’s cells into more complex substances (e.g. building tissue,
positive nitrogen balance).


anaemia
A condition in which the blood is deficient in red blood cells or
haemoglobin.
anaerobic
Living only in the absence of oxygen.
anaerobic exercise
Involves activity in which the muscles cannot draw out enough
oxygen from the bloodstream; used in endurance training.
anal stimulation
Stimulation applied to anus for sexual pleasure.
anaphylactic reaction
A severe allergic reaction that usually occurs immediately after
the administration of a drug.
andragogy
The art and science of helping adults learn.
androgyny
Belief that most characteristics and behaviours are human
qualities and not limited to a gender.
anger
An emotional state consisting of a subjective feeling of animosity
or strong displeasure.


angina
Describes the pain associated with myocardial ischaemia.
angiography
A diagnostic procedure enabling x-ray visual examination of the
vascular system after injection of a radiopaque dye.
angle of Louis
The junction between the body of the sternum and the
manubrium; the starting point for locating the ribs anteriorly.
animal-assisted therapy
The use of specifically selected animals as a treatment modality
in health and human service settings.
anions
Ions that carry a negative charge; includes chlorine
,
bicarbonate
, phosphate
 and sulfate

anisocoria
Unequal pupils.
ankylosed
Permanently immobile joints.
anorexia
Lack of appetite.

anorexia nervosa
A disease characterised by a prolonged inability or refusal to eat,

anoscopy
Visual examination of the anal canal using an anoscope (a lighted

antagonist
Drug that inhibits cell function by occupying the drug’s receptor
sites.
antibodies
Immunoglobulins, part of the body’s plasma proteins, defend

anticipatory grief
Grief experienced in advance of the event.
antigen
A substance capable of inducing the formation of antibodies.
anuria
The failure of the kidneys to produce urine, resulting in a total
lack of urination or output of less than 100 mL per day in an
adult.


anxiety
A state of mental uneasiness, apprehension or dread producing
an increased level of arousal caused by an impending or
anticipated threat to self or significant relationships.
aperients
See laxatives.
Apgar score
A scoring system to assess newborn babies.
aphasia
Any defects in or loss of the power to express oneself by speech,
writing or signs or to comprehend spoken or written language
due to disease or injury of the cerebral cortex.
apical pulse
A central pulse located at the apex of the heart.
apical–radial pulse
Measurement of the apical beat and the radial pulse at the same
time.
apnoea
A complete absence of respirations.
apocrine glands


Sweat glands located largely in the axillae and anogenital areas;
they begin to function at puberty under the influence of
androgens.
approximated
Closed tissue surfaces.
aromatherapy
Therapeutic use of essential oils of plants in which odour or
fragrance plays an important part.
arrhythmia
A pulse with an abnormal rhythm.
arterial blood gases (ABGs)
Specimen of arterial blood that assesses oxygenation, ventilation
and acid–base status.
arterial blood pressure
The measure of the pressure exerted by the blood as it pulsates
through the arteries.
arteriosclerosis
A condition in which the elastic and muscular tissues of the
arteries are replaced with fibrous tissue.
ascites
The accumulation of fluid in the abdominal cavity.


asepsis
Freedom from infection or infectious material.
aseptic technique
The method employed to help prevent contamination of wounds
and other susceptible sites by organisms that could cause
infection by ensuring only uncontaminated equipment and fluids
come into contact with sterile/susceptible body sites during
certain clinical procedures.
asphyxiation
Lack of oxygen due to interrupted breathing.
aspiration
The withdrawal of fluid that has abnormally collected (e.g. pleural
cavity, abdominal cavity) or to obtain a specimen (e.g. cerebral

assault
An attempt or threat to touch another person unjustifiably.
assertive communication
Communication that presents the sender’s message while
respecting the rights and dignity of others involved. The content
is non-hostile.
assessing


The process of collecting, organising, validating and recording
data (information) about a person’s health status.
assimilation
The process by which an individual develops a new cultural
identity and becomes like the members of the dominant culture.
assisted suicide
A form of active euthanasia in which individuals are given the

astigmatism
An uneven curvature of the cornea that prevents horizontal and

atelectasis
A condition that occurs when ventilation is decreased and pooled

atheist
One who denies the existence of God.
atherosclerosis
Build-up of fatty plaque within the arteries.
atria
Two upper hollow chambers of the heart.


atrioventricular (AV) node
Conduction pathways that slightly delay transmission of the

atrioventricular (AV) valves
Between the atria and ventricles of the heart, the tricuspid valve

atrophy
Wasting away; decrease in size of organ or tissue (e.g. muscle).
attending
A manner of being present to another or being with another.

attitudes
Mental stance that is composed of many different beliefs; usually
involving a positive or negative judgment towards a person, an
object or an idea.
audit
Examination or review of records.
auditory
Related to or experienced through hearing.
auscultation
The process of listening to sounds produced within the body.


auscultatory gap
The temporary disappearance of sounds normally heard over the

Peak professional college for mental health nurses in Australia.

The independent accrediting authority for nursing and midwifery

authoritarian leader
The individual who makes decisions for the group.
authority
The power given by an organisation to direct the work of others;
the right to act.
autism spectrum disorder
A range of conditions that affect communication, social
interaction and behaviour.
autocratic leader
See authoritarian leader.
automaticity
An electrical impulse and contraction independent of the nervous
system which is generated by the cardiac muscle.


autonomy
The state of being independent and self-directed, without outside
control, to make one’s own decisions.
awareness
The ability to perceive environmental stimuli and body reactions
and to respond appropriately through thought and action.
Ayurveda
Indian system of medicine where illness is viewed as a state of
imbalance between the body’s systems.
Baby Boomers
Generation that includes those born in years 1946–1966.
bacteraemia
Bacteria in the blood.
bacteria
The most common infection-causing micro-organisms.
bactericidal
Bacteria-killing action.
balance
Concept of equilibrium between mental, physical, emotional,
spiritual and environmental components to achieve optimum
wellness.


bandage
A strip of cloth used to wrap some part of the body.
basal metabolic rate (BMR)
The rate of energy utilisation in the body required to maintain
essential activities such as breathing.
base of support
The area on which an object rests.
bases (alkalis)
Have low hydrogen ion concentration and can accept hydrogen
ions in solution.
battery (legal)
The wilful or negligent touching of a person (or the person’s
clothes or even something the person is carrying), which may or
may not cause harm.
bed rest
Strict confinement to bed (complete bed rest) or the person may
be allowed to use a bedside commode or have bathroom
privileges.
behaviourist theory
Includes the careful identification of what is to be taught and the
immediate identification of and reward for correct responses.


beliefs
Interpretations or conclusions that one accepts as true.
beneficence
The moral obligation to do good or to implement actions that
benefit individuals and their support people.
bereavement
A subjective response of a person who has experienced the loss
of a significant other through death.
bevel
The slanted part at the tip of a needle.
bicultural
Used to describe a person who crosses two cultures, lifestyles
and sets of values.
Bier’s block
See intravenous block.
binder
A type of bandage applied to large body areas (abdomen or
chest) or for a specific body part (arm sling); used to provide
support.
bioelectromagnetics


Science that studies how living organisms interact with
electromagnetic fields.
bioethics
Ethical rules or principles that govern right conduct concerning
life.
biofeedback
A stress management technique that brings under conscious
control bodily processes normally thought to be beyond voluntary
command.
biological rhythms
Inner rhythms that appear to control a variety of biological
processes.
biomedical health belief
See scientific health belief.
biomedicine
Term used to describe Western medical practice.
biopsy
The removal and examination of tissue from the living body.
biotransformation
Process by which a drug is converted to a less active form; also
called detoxification.


Biot’s (cluster) respirations
Shallow breaths interrupted by apnoea.
bipolar affective disorder
The name now given for what was once known as manic
depressive psychosis. Describes the recurrent episodes of ‘up
and down’ mood swings, which range from elation and
excitement to sadness and depression.
bladder training
An individual postpones voiding, resists or inhibits the sensation
of urgency and voids according to a timetable rather than
according to the urge to void.
blanch test
A test during which the person’s fingertip is temporarily pinched
to assess capillary refill and peripheral circulation.
blood chemistry
A number of tests performed on blood serum (the liquid portion
of the blood).
blood pressure (BP)
The force exerted on arterial walls by blood flowing within the
vessel.
blood urea nitrogen (BUN)


A measure of blood level of urea, the end product of protein
metabolism.
body image
How a person perceives the size, appearance and functioning of
their body and its parts.
body mass index (BMI)
Indicates whether weight is appropriate for height.
body temperature
The balance between the heat produced by the body and the
heat lost from the body.
boomerang kids
Slang term used for young adults who move back into their
parents’ homes after an initial period of independent living.
bottle mouth syndrome
Describes the decay of an infant’s teeth caused by constant
contact with sweet liquid from a bottle.
boundary
The real or imaginary lines that differentiate one system from
another system or a system from its environment.
bowel (faecal) incontinence


Loss of voluntary ability to control faecal and gaseous discharges
through the anal sphincter.
bradycardia
Abnormally slow pulse rate, less than 60 beats per minute.
bradypnoea
Abnormally slow respiratory rate, usually less than 10
respirations per minute.
braille
Patterns of raised dots that are felt with the fingertips by people
who are vision impaired as an alternative to written text.
brain death
The cessation of circulation to the brain resulting in the entire
brain (including the brainstem) dying.
brand name
The name given to a drug by the drug’s manufacturer.
bruit
A blowing or swishing sound created by turbulence of blood flow.
B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP)
An amino acid polypeptide that is secreted by the ventricles of
the heart in response to excessive stretching.


buccal
Pertaining to the cheek.
buffers
Prevent excessive changes in pH by removing or releasing
hydrogen ions.
bulimia nervosa
An uncontrollable compulsion to eat large amounts of food and
then expel it by self-induced vomiting or by taking laxatives.
bullying
A set of negative behaviours where nurses covertly or overtly
direct their dissatisfaction towards each other and to those less
powerful than themselves.
bundle of His
The right and left bundle branches of the ventricular conduction
pathways.
burden of proof
The duty of proving an assertion.
bureaucratic leader
Does not trust self or others to make decisions and instead relies
on the organisation’s rules, policies and procedures to direct the
group’s work efforts.


burn
Results from excessive exposure to thermal, chemical, electric or
radioactive agents.
burnout
A complex syndrome of behaviours that can be likened to the
exhaustion stage of the general adaptation syndrome; an
overwhelming feeling that can lead to physical and emotional
depletion, a negative attitude and self-concept, and feelings of
helplessness and hopelessness.
calculi
Renal stones.
callus
A localised, thickened, hardened portion of epidermis, resulting
from repetitive friction from footwear.
calorie (c, cal, kcal)
A unit of heat energy equivalent to the amount of heat required
to raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1°C.
cancer pain
Pain associated with cancers; can be related or unrelated to the
disease or its treatment.
cannula


A tube with a lumen (channel) that is inserted into a cavity or
duct and is often fitted with a trocar during insertion; the part of a
needle that is attached to the hub.
capacity to consent
When a person has the ability to understand and use information
to make a decision and then consent to treatment based on the
information provided.
carbohydrate
A compound derived from plants which is critical to the provision
of energy to body cells, in particular glucose for brain
metabolism.
carbon monoxide
An odourless, colourless, tasteless gas that is very toxic.
cardiac arrest
The cessation of heart function.
cardiac output (CO)
The amount of blood ejected by the heart with each ventricular
contraction.
cardiovascular disease (CVD)
Generic term for all diseases and conditions of the heart and
blood vessels.


care coordinator
A nurse who works with the multidisciplinary health care team to
measure the effectiveness of the person’s health care plan and
to monitor outcomes.
caregiver
A role that has traditionally included those activities that assist
the person physically, spiritually and psychologically.
caregiver burden
Responses to long-term stress, such as chronic fatigue, sleeping
difficulties and high blood pressure, in family members who
undertake the care of a person in the home for a long period.
caregiver role strain
Occurs when caregivers experience physical, emotional, social
and financial burdens that can seriously jeopardise their own
health and wellbeing.
caries
Tooth cavities.
caring
Intentional action that conveys physical and emotional security
and genuine connectedness with another person or group of
people.
caring practice


Nursing care that includes connection, empathy, mutual
recognition and involvement.
carminative
An agent that promotes the passage of flatus from the colon.
carrier
A person or animal that harbours a specific infectious agent and
serves as a potential source of infection, yet does not manifest
any clinical signs of disease.
case management
A method for delivering nursing care in which the nurse is
responsible for a caseload of people across the health care
continuum.
catabolism
A process in which complex substances are broken down into
simpler substances (e.g. breakdown of tissue).
cataracts
Opacity of the lens or capsule of the eye.
cathartics
Drugs that induce defecation.
cations


Ions that carry a positive charge; includes sodium
,
potassium
, calcium
 and magnesium
.
central neuropathic pain
Pain resulting from malfunctioning nerves in the central nervous
system.
central venous catheter
Catheter that is usually inserted into the subclavian or jugular
vein, with the distal tip of the catheter resting in the superior vena
cava just above the right atrium.
centre of gravity
The point at which the mass (weight) of the body is centred.
cerumen
The wax-like substance secreted by glands in the external ear
canal.
cerebral palsy
A neurological disorder affecting muscle coordination and body
movement, caused during brain development as a child.
Cervical Screening Test
A test for human papillomavirus (HPV) infection.
change
Process of making something different from what it was.
(Na+)
(K+)
(Ca2+)
(Mg2+)


change agent
Person (or group) who initiates change or who assists others in
making modifications in themselves or in the system.
charismatic leader
Characterised by an emotional relationship between the leader
and the group members; personality of the leader evokes strong
feelings of commitment to both the leader and the leader’s cause
and beliefs.
chart
A formal, legal document that provides evidence of a person’s
care.
charting
The process of making an entry in a patient record.
charting by exception
A documentation system in which only significant findings or
exceptions to norms are recorded.
chemical name
The name by which a chemist knows a drug; describes the
constituents of the drug precisely.
chemical restraints
Medications used to control socially disruptive behaviour.


chemical thermogenesis
The stimulation of heat production in the body through increased
cellular metabolism caused by increases in thyroxine output.
Cheyne–Stokes respirations
Rhythmic waxing and waning of respirations from very deep
breathing to very shallow breathing with periods of temporary
apnoea, often associated with cardiac failure, increased
intracranial pressure or brain damage.
chiropractic
From the Greek meaning ‘done by hand’; involves adjustments of
the spine and joints, and is grounded in the assumption that
maintaining the alignment of the spine and joints facilitates the
flow of energy throughout the body, including the nervous,
circulatory, respiratory, gastrointestinal and limbic systems.
cholesterol
A lipid that does not contain fatty acid but possesses many of the
chemical and physical properties of other lipids.
chronic illness
Illness that lasts for an extended period of time, usually greater
than 6 months.
chronic infections
Infections that occur slowly, over a very long period, and may last
months or years.


chronic pain
Prolonged pain, usually recurring or persisting over 6 months or
longer, and interferes with functioning.
chyme
Digested products that leave the stomach through the small
intestine and then pass through the ileocaecal valve.
circulating nurse
Assists scrub nurses and surgeons during surgery.
circulatory death
Death that can be determined when all the following signs are
evident: immobility, apnoea, absent skin perfusion and absence
of circulation (evidenced by absent arterial pulse for a minimum
of 2 minutes).
civil law
The body of law that deals with relationships between private
individuals; also known as private law.
clean voided urine specimen
Urine specimens for routine urinalysis.
cleaning baths
A type of bath given chiefly for hygiene purposes.
climacteric


The point in development when reproduction capacity in the
female terminates (menopause) and the sexual activity of the
male decreases (andropause).
clinical deterioration
Abnormal vital signs, which may be an early warning of a change
in the person’s physiological wellbeing.
clinical governance
A system of policies, processes and accountabilities directed at
improving patient safety and the quality and effectiveness of
patient care.
clinical incident
Any unplanned event that causes or potentially causes harm to a
patient.
clinical leadership
The process of leading improvements in the safety and quality of
clinical care and the skill set required to motivate and engage
clinical teams.
clinical pathway
See multidisciplinary care plan.
closed awareness
A type of awareness in which the person is unaware of
impending death.


closed captioning
A text version of a spoken part in a movie or television. Closed
captioning is different from subtitling in that it can be turned on or
off.
closed questions
Restrictive questions requiring only a short answer.
closed system
System that does not exchange energy, matter or information
with its environment.
closed-wound drainage system
Consists of a drain connected to either an electric suction or a
portable drainage suction, such as a Hemovac or Jackson-Pratt.
club foot/talipes equinovarus
A congenital deformity in which the affected foot rotates internally
at the ankle.
clubbing
Elevation of the proximal aspect of the nail and softening of the
nail bed.
co-analgesic
Medication that is not classified as a pain medication; however, it
has properties that may reduce pain alone or in combination with


other analgesics, relieve other discomforts, potentiate the effect
of pain medication or reduce the pain medication’s side effects.
code of ethics
