A formal statement of a group’s ideals and values; a set of
ethical principles shared by members of a group, reflecting their
moral judgments and serving as a standard for professional
actions.
cognition
The ability to process information and apply knowledge.
cognitive development
Refers to the manner in which people learn to think, reason and
use language.
cognitive domain
The ‘thinking’ domain, includes six intellectual abilities and
thinking processes: knowing, comprehending, applying,
analysing, synthesising and evaluating.
cognitive skills
Intellectual skills that include problem solving, decision making,
critical thinking and clinical reasoning.
cognitive theory
Recognition of developmental levels of learners and
acknowledgment of the learner’s motivation and environment.


cognitivism
An information-processing theory that deals with how people
perceive, learn, remember and think about information. It sees
learning as taking place within the learner while focusing on
processing rather than behaviour.
collaboration
A collegial working relationship with another health care provider
in the provision of individual care.
collaborative care plan
See multidisciplinary care plan.
collaborative interventions
Actions the nurse carries out in collaboration with other health
team members, such as physiotherapists, social workers,
dietitians and doctors.
collaborator
Nurse working with other individuals and groups for the
assessment, planning, coordination, implementation and
evaluation of care.
collagen
A protein found in connective tissue; a whitish protein substance
that adds tensile strength to a wound.
colloid osmotic pressure


A pulling force exerted by colloids that helps maintain the water
content of blood.
colloids
Substances such as large protein molecules that do not readily
dissolve into true solutions.
colonisation
The presence of organisms in body secretions or excretions in
which strains of bacteria become resident flora but do not cause
illness.
colonoscopy
Viewing of the large intestine.
colostomy
An opening into the colon (large bowel).
common law
The body of principles that evolves from court decisions.
Commonwealth Home Support Programme (CHSP)
Provides a basic level of aged care services to assist people who
are 65 years and over to live independently and remain in their
own homes.
communicable disease
A disease that can spread from one person to another.


communication
The interchange of information between two or more people for
the exchange of ideas or thoughts.
communication disability
Having limitations in expressing thoughts, needs or emotions due
to impaired physical, psychological, developmental or sensory
functions.
communicator
Nurses who identify problems and then communicate these
verbally or in writing to other members of the health team.
community
A collection of people who share some attribute of their lives.
community-based health care (CBHC)
A system that provides health-related services within the context
of people’s daily lives; that is, in places where people spend their
time in the community.
community-based nursing (CBN)
Nursing care directed towards a specific population or group
within the community; primary, secondary or tertiary care may be
provided to individuals or groups.
community health nursing


The synthesis of nursing and public health practice as applied to
promoting and preserving the health of populations.
community mental health nurses
Nurses who provide family support and work with the broader
community in mental health promotion and education.
compassion
Comprises three components: attentiveness, empathy and
‘intelligent’ action.
compassionate leadership
A transformational category of leadership. A compassionate
nursing leader empowers their followers (patients and
colleagues), makes time and space to listen while embracing
risk, establishes clear expectations and builds team and
individual capacity. A compassionate leader is emotionally
intelligent, authentic, open, caring, mindful, kind and respectful.
compensation
When healthy regulatory systems attempt to correct acid–base
imbalances.
compensatory
Counterbalancing.
complementary medicine
See alternative medicine.


complete blood picture (CBP)
See full blood count (FBC).
complete protein
A protein that contains all of the essential amino acids as well as
many non-essential ones.
compliance
The extent to which an individual’s behaviour coincides with
medical or health advice; the ability of the arteries to contract
and expand.
complicated grief
Pathological grief; exists when coping strategies are maladaptive.
compress
A moist gauze dressing applied frequently to an open wound,
sometimes medicated.
computed tomography (CT)
A painless, non-invasive x-ray procedure that has the unique
capability of distinguishing minor differences in the density of
tissues.
concepts
The building blocks of theories.
conceptual framework


A group of related concepts.
concordance
The cooperative involvement of individuals in their treatment
regimen.
concurrent audit
Evaluation of a person’s health care while the person is still
receiving care from the facility.
conduction
The transfer of heat from one molecule to another in direct
contact.
conduction hearing loss
The result of interrupted transmission of sound waves through
the outer and middle ear structures.
confidentiality
Any information a subject relates will not be made public or
available to others without the subject’s consent.
conjunctivitis
Inflammation of the bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva.
connectedness
The state of being socially connected to others; having social
networks.


conscious sedation
A minimal depression of level of consciousness during which the
person retains the ability to consciously maintain a patent airway
and respond appropriately to verbal and physical stimuli.
consequence-based (teleological) theories
The ethics of judging whether an action is moral.
constant fever
A state in which the body temperature fluctuates minimally but
always remains above normal.
constipation
Passage of small, dry, hard stool or passage of no stool for an
abnormally long time.
consultation
A review of the health status of a person by a suitably qualified
health professional.
consultation liaison (CL) nurse
A specialist mental health nurse who is the interface between
medicine and psychiatry.
consultative leader
See democratic leader.
contemplation stage


Stage in which a person acknowledges having a problem,
seriously considers changing a specific behaviour, actively
gathers information and verbalises plans to change the behaviour
in the near future.
continuity theory
Atchley’s theory that people maintain their values, habits and
behaviour in old age.
contract
A written or verbal agreement between two or more people to do
or not do some lawful act.
contractility
The inherent ability of cardiac muscle fibres to shorten or
contract.
contractual obligations
Duty of care established by the presence of an expressed or
implied contract.
contractual relationships
Vary between practice settings; may be as an independent or
employer–employee relationship.
contracture
Permanent shortening of a muscle and subsequent shortening of
tendons and ligaments.


convection
The dispersion of heat by air currents.
conventional medicine
Term used to describe Western medical practice.
coordinating
The process of ensuring that plans are carried out and evaluating
outcomes.
coping
Dealing with change.
coping mechanism
See coping strategy.
coping strategy
An innate or acquired way of responding to a changing
environment or specific problem or situation.
core self-concept
The beliefs and images that are most vital to the person’s
identity.
core temperature
The temperature of the deep tissues of the body (e.g. thorax,
abdominal cavity); relatively constant at 37°C.


corn
A conical, circular, painful, raised area on the toe or foot.
coronary arteries
A network of vessels known as the coronary circulation.
coronary heart disease (CHD)
Heart disease caused by impaired blood flow through the
coronary arteries to the myocardium.
costal (thoracic) breathing
Use of the external intercostal muscles and other accessory
muscles, such as the sternocleidomastoid muscles.
Council of Deans of Nursing and Midwifery (CDNM)
The peak organisation that represents the Deans and Heads of
the Schools of Nursing in universities that offer nursing and
midwifery undergraduate and postgraduate programs throughout
Australia and New Zealand.
counselling
The process of helping a person to recognise and cope with
stressful psychological or social problems, to develop improved
interpersonal relationships and to promote personal growth.
countershock phase
Second part of the alarm reaction in which the changes the body
experienced during the shock phase are reversed.


C-reactive protein (CRP)
A blood test that measures the amount of a protein called C-
reactive protein in the blood.
creatinine
A nitrogenous waste that is excreted in the urine.
creatinine clearance
A test that uses 24-hour urine and serum creatinine levels to
determine the glomerular filtration rate, a sensitive indicator of
renal function.
creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB)
Enzyme that is released into the blood during a myocardial
infarction (MI). CK-MB measurements can be used as an aid in
the diagnosis and treatment of MI.
creativity
Thinking that results in the development of new ideas and
products.
Credé’s manoeuvre
Manual exertion of pressure on the bladder to force out urine.
crepitations
(1) A dry, crackling sound like that of crumpled cellophane,
produced by air in the subcutaneous tissue or by air moving


through fluid in the alveoli of the lungs; (2) a crackling, grating
sound produced by bone rubbing against bone.
criminal law
Deals with actions against the safety and welfare of the public.
criminal negligence
Negligence that goes beyond a mere matter of compensation. In
particular, it shows such disregard for the life and safety of others
as to amount to a crime against the state and conduct that
deserves punishment.
crisis counselling
Therapy focused on solving immediate problems involving
individuals, groups or families in crisis.
crisis intervention
A short-term helping process of assisting individuals to work
through a crisis to its resolution and restore their pre-crisis level
of functioning.
critical analysis
A set of questions one can apply to a particular situation or idea
to determine essential information and ideas and discard
superfluous information and ideas.
critical incidents


Unintended consequences of an action or actions that may result
in harm to recipients of care or staff involved in care delivery.
critical pathways
Multidisciplinary guidelines for individual care based on specific
medical diagnoses designed to achieve predetermined
outcomes.
critical theory
Describes theories that help elucidate how social structures
affect a wide variety of human experiences from art to social
practices.
critical thinking
A cognitive process that includes creativity, problem solving and
decision making.
cross-cultural leadership
Leaders who demonstrate cultural sensitivity help others to
assess, understand and respond appropriately to cultural
differences and similarities; and work towards common
understandings of particular phenomena. Such leaders also help
to effect appropriate cultural change within organisations or
groups of people.
cross-dresser
Individual of one gender (typically male) who dresses in clothing
specific to the opposite gender.


crusted scabies
The immune system fails to control an infestation of scabies and
there is hyperproliferation of mites.
crystalloids
Salts that dissolve readily into true solutions.
cues
Any piece of information or data that influences decisions.
cultural care deprivation
See cultural deprivation.
cultural competence
Within the delivered care the nurse understands and attends to
the total context of the person’s situation and uses a complex
combination of knowledge, attitudes and skills.
cultural deprivation
Lack of culturally assistive, supportive or facilitative acts.
cultural perspective
Recognition that there are many distinct cultures in Australia
which often have different values and beliefs that should be
recognised and appreciated when providing health services.
cultural safety


An outcome of nursing and midwifery education that enables
culturally safe service to be defined by those who receive the
service. The nurse participates in activities that promote cultural
awareness and cultural sensitivity that leads to culturally safe
nursing practice.
culturally appropriate
Application of underlying background knowledge that must be
possessed to provide a given individual with the best possible
health care.
culturally responsive care
To provide quality culturally responsive care, nurses must
become informed about and be sensitive to the culturally diverse
subjective meanings of health, illness, caring and healing
practices (Blackman ).
2Blackman, R. (2011). Understanding culture in practice: Reflections of an Australian
Indigenous nurse. Contemporary Nurse, 37(1), 31–34.
culturally sensitive
Care that demonstrates basic knowledge of and constructive
attitudes towards the health traditions observed in the diverse
cultural groups found in the setting.
culture
A world view and set of traditions used and transmitted from
generation to generation by a particular group (includes related
2


attitudes and institutions); laboratory cultivations of micro-
organisms in a special growth medium.
culture shock
A disorder that occurs in response to transition from one cultural
setting to another.
cumulative effect
The increasing response to repeated doses of a drug that occurs
when the rate of administration exceeds the rate of metabolism
or excretion.
cyanosis
Bluish discolouration of the skin and mucous membranes caused
by reduced oxygen in the blood.
cystoscope
A lighted instrument used to visualise the interior of the urinary
bladder.
cystoscopy
Visual examination of the urinary bladder with a cystoscope.
dacryocystitis
Inflammation of the lacrimal sac.
dandruff
A dry or greasy, scaly material shed from the scalp.


data
Information.
data warehousing
The accumulation of large amounts of data that are stored over
time.
debridement
Removal of infected and necrotic tissue.
decision making
The process of establishing criteria by which alternative courses
of action are developed and selected.
decubitus ulcer
See pressure injury.
deductive reasoning
Making specific observations from a generalisation.
defamation (legal)
A communication that is false, or made with careless disregard
for the truth, and results in injury to the reputation of another.
defecation
Expulsion of faeces from the rectum and anus.
defence mechanisms


Any reaction that serves to protect against something physically
or psychologically harmful.
defining characteristics
Signs and symptoms that must be present to validate a nursing
diagnosis.
dehiscence
The partial or total rupturing of a sutured wound; usually involves
an abdominal wound in which the layers below the skin also
separate.
dehydration
Insufficient fluid in the body.
delirium
Also called acute confusion; abrupt onset of confusion with a
reversible cause.
delusion
A fixed false belief that is firmly sustained despite what
constitutes incontrovertible and obvious proof or evidence to the
contrary. The belief is not one ordinarily accepted by other
members of the person’s culture or subculture.
demand feeding
Child is fed when hungry.


dementia
A global impairment of cognitive function that usually is
progressive and may be permanent; interferes with normal social
and occupational activities.
democratic leader
Encourages group discussion and decision making.
demography
The study of population, including statistics about distribution by
age and place of residence, mortality and morbidity.
dental caries
Tooth decay.
dependent interventions
Activities carried out on the order of a doctor, under a doctor’s
supervision or according to specified routines.
dependent variable
The behaviour, characteristic or outcome that the researcher
wishes to explain or predict.
depression
Feelings of sadness and dejection, often accompanied by
physiological change such as decreased functional activity.
descriptive statistics


Procedures that summarise large volumes of data; used to
describe and synthesise data, showing patterns and trends.
desire phase
Part of the response cycle, which starts in the brain, with
conscious sexual desires.
desired effect
See therapeutic effect.
detoxification
The belief that physical impurities and toxins must be cleared
from the body to achieve better health. See also
biotransformation
.
detrusor muscle
The smooth muscle layers of the bladder.
development
An individual’s increasing capacity and skill in functioning, related
to growth.
developmental stage
Level of achievement for a particular segment of a person’s life.
developmental task
Skill or behaviour pattern learned during stages of development.


diagnosis
A statement or conclusion concerning the nature of some
phenomenon.
Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)
A manual that is published by the American Psychiatric
Association which provides common language and standard
criteria for the classification of mental disorders.
diagnostic overshadowing
Occurs when a health professional attributes unusual behaviour
to a person’s intellectual disability rather than the possibility that it
could be due to a physical cause.
dialysis
A technique by which fluids and molecules pass through a semi-
permeable membrane according to the rules of osmosis.
diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing
Contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm, observed by the
movement of the abdomen, which occurs as a result of the
diaphragm’s contraction and downward movement.
diarrhoea
Defecation of liquid faeces and increased frequency of
defecation.
diastole


The period during which the ventricles relax.
diastolic pressure
The pressure of the blood against the arterial walls when the
ventricles of the heart are at rest.
diet history
A comprehensive assessment of a person’s food intake that
involves an extensive interview by a nutritionist or dietitian.
differentiated practice
A system in which the best possible use of nursing personnel is
based on their educational preparation and resultant skill sets.
differentness
Being different from another person or group of people.
diffusion
The movement of gases or other particles from an area of
greater pressure or concentration to an area of lower pressure or
concentration; the mixing of molecules or ions of two or more
substances as a result of random motion.
digestion
The process of converting food into substances that can be
absorbed and utilised by the body.
direct discrimination


When a person or group is treated less favourably than another
person or group because of their background or certain
characteristics.
directing
A management function that involves communicating the task to
be completed and providing guidance and supervision.
directive interview
A highly structured interview that uses closed questions to elicit
specific information.
disaccharides
Sugars that are composed of double molecules.
discharge planning
The process of anticipating and planning for a person’s needs
after discharge.
discrimination
The differential treatment of individuals or groups.
discussion
An informal oral consideration of a subject by two or more health
care personnel to identify a problem or establish strategies to
resolve a problem.
disease


An alteration in body function resulting in a reduction of
capacities or shortening of the normal lifespan.
disease prevention
Behaviour motivated by a desire to actively avoid illness, detect it
early or maintain functioning within the constraints of illness (also
called health protection).
disengagement theory
Ageing involves mutual withdrawal (disengagement) between the
older person and others in the older adult’s environment.
disinfectant
A chemical preparation capable of killing or inactivating micro-
organisms.
disinfection
The process whereby chemical agents remove or destroy most
pathogens from an object’s surface; this process is unable to
remove all endospores and some viruses.
dissatisfaction problems
Dissatisfaction with sexual encounters despite desire, arousal
and orgasm.
distance learning
Learning in which people communicate effectively across long
distances.


distribution
The transportation of a drug from its site of absorption to its site
of action.
diuresis
See polyuria.
diuretics
Agents that increase urine secretion.
diurnal enuresis
Involuntary urination during the daytime.
diversity
The fact or state of being different.
doctrine of precedent
Rules of law stated in earlier cases which are followed by judges.
To arrive at a ruling, and in order to maintain consistency in a
case, the court applies the same rules and principles applied in
previous, similar cases to the case being heard.
documenting
See charting or recording.
dorsal (supine) position
A back-lying position without a pillow.


dorsal recumbent position
A back-lying position with the head and shoulders slightly
elevated.
drip factor (drop factor)
The number of drops per millilitre of solution delivered for a
particular drip chamber.
drug
A chemical compound taken for disease prevention, diagnosis,
cure or relief, or to affect the structure or function of the body.
drug allergy
An immunological reaction to a drug.
drug dependence
Inability to keep the intake of a drug or substance under control.
drug habituation
A mild form of psychological dependence on a drug.
drug half-life
The time required for the elimination process to reduce the
concentration of a drug to one-half of what it was at initial
administration.
drug interaction


The beneficial or harmful interaction of one drug with another
drug.
drug misuse
Excessive intake of a substance either continually or periodically.
drug tolerance
A condition in which successive increases in the dosage of a
drug are required to maintain a given therapeutic effect.
drug toxicity
The quality of a drug that exerts a deleterious effect on an
organism or tissue.
duty of care
The nurse must have (or should have had) a relationship with the
person that involves providing care and following an acceptable
standard of care.
dysaesthesia
Unpleasant abnormal sensation.
dyslexia
Difficulties with reading and writing.
dysmenorrhoea
Painful menstruation.


dyspareunia
Difficult or painful intercourse.
dysphagia
Difficulty swallowing.
dysphasia
Difficulty finding or selecting the correct words.
dyspnoea
Difficult or laboured breathing.
dysrhythmia
A pulse with an irregular rhythm.
dysuria
Painful or difficult voiding.
eccrine glands
Glands that produce sweat; found over most of the body.
echocardiogram
A non-invasive test that uses ultrasound to visualise structures of
the heart and evaluate left ventricular function.
ecomap
A visualisation of how the family unit interacts with the external
community environment such as schools, religious commitments,


occupational duties and recreational pursuits.
ectoderm
The outer layer of tissue formed in the second week of life.
effleurage
A stroking massage technique.
ego
Includes consciousness and memory, which serve to mediate
between primitive instinctual drives (id), internal social
prohibitions (superego) and reality.
ego defence mechanisms
(Freud) Mental mechanisms that develop as the personality
attempts to defend itself, establish compromises between
conflicting impulses and allay inner tensions.
e-health records (EHRs)
Permit electronic individual data retrieval by caregivers,
administrators, creditors and other people who require the data.
ejaculation
Expulsion of seminal fluid and sperm.
elasticity of the arterial wall
Expansibility or stretching of the vessels.


e-learning (electronic learning)
A type of education where the learning is conducted via
electronic media such as the internet, computers or virtual
classrooms.
elective surgery
Performed when surgical intervention is the preferred treatment
for a condition that is not imminently life threatening or to
improve the person’s life.
electric shock
Occurs when a current travels through the body to the ground
rather than through electric wiring or from static electricity that
builds up on the body.
electrocardiogram (ECG)
A graph of the electric activity of the heart.
electrocardiography
Provides a graphic recording of the heart’s electrical activity.
electroencephalogram (EEG)
A graph of the electrical activity of the brain.
electrolytes
Chemical substances that develop an electric charge and are
able to conduct an electric current when placed in water; ions.


electromyogram (EMG)
A graph of the electrical activity of muscles.
electro-oculogram (EOG)
A graph of the electrical activity of eye-to-eye movement.
elimination
The act of excreting waste products such as faeces or urine from
the body.
elimination half-life
See drug half-life.
Elizabeth Kenny
Early to mid-twentieth century Queensland nurse associated with
poliomyelitis treatment.
emboli
See embolus.
embolus
A blood clot (or a substance such as air) that has moved from its
place of origin and is causing obstruction to circulation elsewhere
(plural: emboli).
embryonic phase
The phase during which the fertilised ovum develops into an
organism with most of the features of a human.


emergency surgery
Surgery that is performed immediately to preserve function or
the life of the person.
emmetropic
Normal refraction so that the eyes focus images on the retina.
emotional intelligence (EI or EQ)
Incorporates five components: knowing one’s emotions,
managing emotions, motivating oneself, recognising emotions in
others and handling relationships. The nurse participates in
activities, such as reflective practice, that lead to development in
these five components of emotional intelligence.
emphysema
A chronic pulmonary condition in which the alveoli are dilated and
distended.
empirical data
Information collected from the observable world.
empirical knowing
Knowledge that comes from science; ranges from factual,
observable phenomena to theoretical analysis.
empowerment
Exists when patients take ownership of their illness and an active
role in their own recovery process.


encopresis
See bowel incontinence.
endocardium
A layer of the heart wall lining the inside of the heart’s chambers
and great vessels.
endoderm
The inner layer of tissue formed in the second week of life.
end-of-life care
Care provided in the final weeks before death.
endogenous
Developing from within.
Endorsed Enrolled Nurse (EEN)
An Enrolled Nurse who has completed an accredited medication
program that is acceptable to the relevant state or territory
registering authority.
enema
A solution introduced into the rectum and sigmoid colon to
remove faeces and/or flatus.
energy
The force that integrates the body, mind and spirit.


Enrolled Nurse (EN)
An associate of the RN who demonstrates competence in the
provision of person-centred care as specified by the registering
authority’s licence to practice, educational preparation and
context of care. Some Australian states call these nurses
Division 2 nurses.
enteral
Through the gastrointestinal system.
enterprise bargaining
Involves negotiations between workers and employers that takes
awards as its starting point and then builds on the award
standard by reference to the needs and circumstances of a
particular trade, industry, enterprise or locality.
entoderm
See endoderm.
enuresis
Involuntary passing of urine in children after bladder control is
achieved.
environment
All of the conditions, circumstances and influences surrounding
and affecting the development of an organism or person.
enzymes


Biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions.
epicardium
The visceral pericardium adhering to the surface of the heart,
forming the heart’s outermost layer.
epidural
Commonly used route for parenteral administration into the
epidural space (the area inside the spinal column but outside the
dura mater).
epidural anaesthesia
An anaesthetic agent into the epidural space.
equianalgesia
Equal analgesia; used when referring to the doses of various
opioid analgesics that provide approximately the same pain relief.
equilibrium
A state of balance.
equity
The separate body of law, developed in the Court of Chancery,
which supplements, corrects and controls the rules of common
law.
erythema
A redness associated with a variety of skin rashes.


erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
A test to help detect inflammation associated with conditions
such as infections, cancers and autoimmune diseases.
erythrocytes
Red blood cells, or RBCs.
eschar
Thick necrotic tissue produced by burning, by a corrosive
application or by death of tissue associated with loss of vascular
supply, bacterial invasion and putrefaction.
essential amino acid
Amino acids that cannot be manufactured in the body and must
be supplied as part of the protein ingested in the diet. Includes
histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine,
threonine, tryptophan and valine.
estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
A test of renal function that estimates the value of the glomerular
filtration rate (GFR), based on an individualised formula that
takes into account factors affecting the GFR including age,
gender, level of creatinine and race.
ethical knowing
Knowledge that focuses on matters of obligation or what should
be done.


ethics
Moral principles that guide behaviour and decision making.
ethnic
Belonging to a specific group of individuals who share a common
social and cultural heritage.
ethnocentrism
The belief that one’s own culture or way of life is better than that
of others.
ethnography
Research that provides a framework to focus on the culture of a
group of people.
eupnoea
Normal, quiet breathing.
evaluating
A planned, ongoing, purposeful activity in which individuals and
health care professionals determine (a) the person’s progress
towards achievement of goals/outcomes, and (b) the
effectiveness of the intervention(s).
Evaluation and Quality Improvement Program (EQuIP)
A comprehensive review of health care standards undertaken by
the Australian Council on Healthcare Standards using a 4-year
cycle of self-assessment and an organisation-wide survey.


evaluation statement
A statement that consists of two parts: a conclusion and
supporting data.
evidence-based practice (EBP)
The use of some form of substantiation in making clinical
decisions.
evisceration
Extrusion of the internal organs.
exacerbation
The period during a chronic illness when symptoms reappear
after remission.
excitement phase
Part of the response cycle, involves vasocongestion and
myotonia.
excoriation
Loss of the superficial layers of the skin.
excretion
Elimination of a waste product produced by the body cells from
the body.
exercise


A type of physical activity; a planned, structured and repetitive
bodily movement performed to improve or maintain one or more
components of physical fitness.
exercise stress test (EST)
A test to assess the response of the respiratory and
cardiovascular systems to exercise.
exhalation (expiration)
The movement of gases from the lungs to the atmosphere.
exogenous
Developing from outside sources.
exophthalmus
A protrusion of the eyeballs with elevation of the upper eyelids,
resulting in a startled or staring expression.
expectorate
To cough and spit out mucus or other materials.
expiration
See exhalation.
extended family
Family that includes the relatives of the nuclear family (e.g.
grandparents, aunts, uncles).


extinction
The failure to perceive touch on one side of the body when two
symmetrical areas of the body are touched simultaneously.
extracellular fluid (ECF)
Fluid found outside the body cells.
exudate
Material, such as fluid and cells, that has escaped from blood
vessels during the inflammatory process and is deposited in
tissue or on tissue surfaces.
eye pointing
The controlled and intentional use of eye gaze to direct another
person’s visual attention to an object for communication
purposes.
fad
A widespread but short-lived interest or practice followed with
considerable zeal.
faecal impaction
A mass or collection of hardened, putty-like faeces in the folds of
the rectum.
faecal incontinence
See bowel incontinence.


faeces (stool)
Body wastes and undigested food eliminated from the bowel.
faith
An active ‘mode of being in relation’ to another or others in which
we invest commitment, belief, love and hope.
false imprisonment
The unlawful restraint or detention of another person against
their wishes.
family
The basic unit of society that consists of those individuals, male
or female, youth or adult, legally or not legally related, genetically
or not genetically related, who are considered by the person to
represent their significant people.
family-centred nursing
Nursing that considers the health of the family as a unit in
addition to the health of individual family members.
fats
Lipids that are solid at room temperature.
fat-soluble vitamins
A, D, E and K vitamins that the body can store.
fatty acids


The basic structural units of most lipids, made up of carbon
chains and hydrogen.
feasibility
The availability of time as well as the material, financial and
human resources needed to investigate a research problem or
question.
febrile
Pertaining to a fever; feverish.
Federation
The politico-legal process of uniting several colonial states within
a national ‘federal’ government, on terms set out in a written
constitution.
feedback
The response or message that the receiver returns to the sender
during communication; the mechanism by which some of the
output of a system is returned to the system as input.
female orgasmic disorder
When the female sexual response stops before orgasm occurs.
female sexual arousal disorder
When lack of vaginal lubrication causes discomfort or pain during
intercourse.


fetal phase
Characterised by a period of rapid growth in the size of the fetus;
both genetic and environmental factors affect its growth.
fever
Elevated body temperature.
fever spike
A temperature that rises to fever level rapidly following a normal
temperature and then returns to normal within a few hours.
fibrin
An insoluble protein formed from fibrinogen during the clotting of
blood.
fidelity
A moral principle that obligates the individual to be faithful to
agreements and responsibilities one has undertaken.
fifth vital sign
Pain assessment.
filtration
Process whereby fluid and solutes move together across a
membrane from one compartment to another.
filtration pressure


The pressure in a compartment that results in the movement of
fluid and substances dissolved in fluid out of the compartment.
fissures
Deep grooves that occur as a result of dryness and cracking of
the skin.
fixation
Immobilisation or the inability of the personality to proceed to the
next developmental stage because of anxiety.
flaccid
Weak or lax.
flatulence
The presence of excessive amounts of gas in the stomach or
intestines.
flatus
Gas or air normally present in the stomach or intestines.
Florence Nightingale
Considered the founder of modern nursing, she was influential in
developing nursing education, practice and administration.
flow sheet
A record of the progress of specific or specialised data such as
vital signs, fluid balance or routine medications; often charted in


graph form.
fluid volume deficit (FVD)
Loss of both water and electrolytes in similar proportions from
the extracellular fluid.
fluid volume excess (FVE)
(hypervolaemia) Retention of both water and sodium in similar
proportions to normal extracellular fluid (ECF).
focus charting
A method of charting that uses key words or foci to describe
what is happening to the individual.
followership
A term coined by Alistair Mant, who recognised that effective
leaders need willing followers.
fontanelles
Unossified membranous gaps in the bone structure of the skull of
a newborn that make moulding of the head possible.
food diary
A detailed record of measured amounts (portion sizes) of all food
and fluids a person consumes during a specified period, usually 3
to 7 days.
food frequency record


A checklist that indicates how often general food groups or
specific foods are eaten.
foot drop
Plantar flexion contracture.
forensic mental health
A subspecialty of mental health in which scientific and clinical
expertise is applied in legal contexts, combining civil, criminal,
correctional and legislative matters.
formal nursing care plan
A written or computerised guide that organises information about
the person’s care.
Fowler’s position
A bed-sitting position with the head of the bed raised 45 to 90
degrees.
friction
Rubbing; the force that opposes motion.
full blood count (FBC)
Specimens of venous blood: includes haemoglobin and
haematocrit measurements, erythrocyte count, leukocyte count,
red blood cell indices and a differential white cell count.
full blood examination (FBE)


See full blood count (FBC).
full disclosure
A basic right, which means that deception, either by withholding
information about a person’s participation in a study or by giving
the person false or misleading information about what
participating in the study will involve, must not occur.
functional strength
Ability of the body to perform work.
fungi
Infection-causing micro-organisms that include yeasts and
moulds.
gait
The way a person walks.
gastrocolic reflex
Increased peristalsis of the colon after food has entered the
stomach.
gastrostomy
An opening through the abdominal wall into the stomach.
gastrostomy tube
A tube that is surgically placed directly into the person’s stomach
and provides a route for administering nutrition and medications.


gauge
Diameter of a shaft.
gender dysphoria
The distress experienced by a person because of incongruity
between their gender identity and their gender assigned at birth.
gender expression
Outward expression of a person’s sense of maleness or
femaleness.
gender identity
A person’s self-image or internal sense of their gender.
genderqueer
A synonym for non-binary. Identifying as genderqueer means the
person does not identify exclusively as male or female.
general adaptation syndrome (GAS)
(Selye) A general arousal response of the body to a stressor
characterised by certain physiological events and dominated by
the sympathetic nervous system.
general anaesthesia
The induced loss of all sensation and consciousness.
Generation Alpha
Those born in years 2010–2024.


Generation X
Those born in years 1965–1979.
Generation Y
Those born in years 1980–1994.
Generation Z
Those born in years 1995–2009.
generativity
Concern for establishing and guiding the next generation.
generic name
A drug name not protected by trademark and usually describing
the chemical structure of the drug.
genital intercourse
Penile/vaginal intercourse (coitus).
genogram
Visual representations of gender and lines of birth descent
through the generations.
geriatrics
Medical care of older adults.
gerontology
The study of ageing and older adults.


gingivitis
Red, swollen gingiva (gums).
glaucoma
A disturbance in the circulation of aqueous fluid; causes an
increase in intraocular pressure.
global self
Refers to the collective beliefs and images one holds about
oneself; the most complete description that individuals can give
of themselves at any one time.
global self-esteem
How much one likes one’s perceived self as a whole.
glomerulus
A tuft of capillaries in the kidney surrounded by Bowman’s
capsule.
glossitis
Inflammation of the tongue.
glycaemic index (GI)
A ranking of carbohydrates on a scale from 0 to 100 according to
the extent to which they raise blood sugar levels after eating.
glycerides


The most common form of lipids, consisting of a glycerol
molecule with up to three fatty acids.
glycogen
The chief carbohydrate stored in the body, particularly in the liver
and muscles.
glycogenesis
The process of glycogen formation.
goals/desired outcomes
A part of a care plan that describes, in terms of observable
individual responses, what the nurse hopes to achieve by
implementing the nursing interventions.
governance
The establishment and maintenance of social, political and
economic arrangements by which practitioners control their
practice, self-discipline, working conditions and professional
affairs.
grand theories
Articulate a broad range of the significant relationships between
the concepts of a discipline.
granulation tissue
Young connective tissue with new capillaries formed in the wound
healing process.


grief
Emotional suffering often caused by bereavement.
grounded theory
Research to understand social structures and social processes;
this method focuses on the generation of categories or
hypotheses that explain patterns of behaviour of people in the
study.
growth
Physical change and increase in size.
guaiac test
A test performed for occult (hidden) blood to detect
gastrointestinal bleeding not visible to the eye.
guided imagery
State of focused attention that encourages changes in attitudes,
behaviour and physiological reactions.
gustatory
Referring to the sense of taste.
Gwendolen Burbidge
Early to mid-twentieth century nurse who wrote the first
Australian nursing textbook.
habit training


Attempts to keep individuals dry by having them void at regular
intervals; also referred to as timed voiding or scheduled toileting.
haematocrit
The proportion of red blood cells (erythrocytes) to the total blood
volume.
haematoma
A collection of blood in a tissue, an organ or a space due to a
break in the wall of a blood vessel.
haemoglobin (Hg)
The red pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
haemoglobin A  (HbA )
Measurement of blood glucose that is bound to haemoglobin.
haemolytic transfusion reaction
Destruction of red blood cells as a result of transfusion of
incompatible blood.
haemoptysis
The presence of blood in the sputum.
haemorrhage
Excessive loss of blood from the vascular system.
haemorrhagic exudate
1C
1C


See sanguineous exudate.
haemorrhoids
Distended veins in the rectum.
haemostasis
Cessation of bleeding.
haemothorax
A collection of blood or fluid in the pleural cavity.
halal
Food prepared according to Islamic (Muslim) dietary laws.
hallucination
An alteration of perception in the absence of a stimulus.
handover
A communication event in which care information is shared and
responsibility and accountability for patient care is formally
handed to another nurse or health care team member.
haustra
Pouches that form in the large intestine when the longitudinal
muscles are shorter than the colon.
haustral churning


Movement of the chyme back and forth within the haustra in the
large intestine.
health
The balance of the person, both within one’s being (physical,
mental and spiritual) and in the outside world (natural, communal
and metaphysical).
health behaviours
The actions a person takes to understand their health state,
maintain an optimal state of health, prevent illness or injury and
reach their maximum physical and mental potential.
health belief
A concept about health that an individual believes to be true.
health-care-associated infections (HAIs)
Infections associated with the delivery of health care services in
a health care facility.
health care system
The totality of services offered by all health disciplines.
health literacy
Ability to read, understand and act on provided health
information.
health promotion


Any activity undertaken for the purpose of achieving a higher
level of health and wellbeing.
health protection
Behaviour motivated by a desire to actively avoid illness, detect it
early or maintain functioning within the constraints of illness.
health risk assessment (HRA)
An assessment and educational tool which indicates a person’s
risk for disease or injury during the next 10 years by comparing
the person’s risk with the mortality risk of the corresponding age,
sex and racial group.
health status
The health of a person at a given time.
heart failure
A condition that develops if the heart cannot keep up with the
body’s need for oxygen and nutrients to the tissues; usually
occurs because of myocardial infarction, but it may also result
from chronic overwork of the heart.
heat balance
The state a person is in when the amount of heat produced by
the body exactly equals the amount of heat lost.
heat exhaustion
Condition where body is stressed by heat.


heat stroke
Life-threatening condition with body temperature greater than
40.5°C.
herbal medicine
Treating illness with herbs.
heritage
The observance of the beliefs and practices of a person’s
acculturated (or modern) belief system.
heritage consistency
The degree to which a person’s lifestyle reflects their respective
tribal culture.
hernia
A protrusion (such as of the intestine through the inguinal wall or
canal).
high Fowler’s position
A bed-sitting position in which the head of the bed is elevated 90
degrees.
high-quality protein
See complete protein.
holism


All living organisms are seen as interacting, unified wholes that
are more than the sums of their parts.
holistic health belief
Holds that the forces of nature must be maintained in balance or
harmony.
holy day
A day set aside for special religious observance.
home care
Providing care in the individual’s home.
Home Care Package
Government-funded program that supports frail older adults to
remain living at home for as long as possible.
home health nursing
Services and products provided to people in their homes that are
needed to maintain, restore or promote their physical,
psychological and social wellbeing.
homeopathy
An alternative therapy based on the theory that the cure for the
disease lies in the disease itself; thus, treatment is with highly
diluted amounts of substances that at a higher concentration
would produce the same symptoms as the disease.


homeostasis
The tendency of the body to maintain a state of balance or
equilibrium while continually changing; a mechanism in which
deviations from normal are sensed and counteracted.
hope
A multidimensional concept that includes perceiving realistic
expectations and goals, having motivation to achieve goals,
anticipating outcomes, establishing trust and interpersonal
relationships, relying on internal and external resources, having
determination to endure and being oriented to the future.
hordeolum (stye)
A redness, swelling and tenderness of the hair follicle and glands
that empty at the edge of the eyelids.
horticultural therapy
Also called gardening or healing garden; adjunct therapy to
occupational therapy and physiotherapy that may involve viewing
nature, visiting a healing garden or wander garden, or actively
gardening.
hospice care
A concept that includes coordinated care and support by health
professionals to terminally ill individuals and their families.
hospital information system (HIS)


Computer software program suite used to manage patient,
financial and administrative data.
hub
The part of a needle that fits onto a syringe.
human research ethics committees (HRECs)
Committees that review research proposals involving human
participants to ensure that they are ethically acceptable and in
accordance with relevant standards and guidelines.
human rights
The rights inherent to all human beings, regardless of race, sex,
nationality, ethnicity, language, religion or any other status.
humanism
Learning that focuses on the feelings and attitudes of learners,
the importance of the individual in identifying learning needs and
taking responsibility for them, and the self-motivation of the
learners to work towards self-reliance and independence.
humanist
A perspective that includes propositions such as the mind and
body are indivisible, people have the power to solve their own
problems and people are responsible for their lives and wellbeing.
humidifiers
Devices that add water vapour to inspired air.


humoral immunity
Antibody-mediated defence; resides ultimately in the B
lymphocytes and is mediated by the antibodies produced by B
cells.
hydrostatic pressure
The pressure a liquid exerts on the sides of the container that
holds it; also called filtration force.
hyperalgesia
Extreme sensitivity to pain.
hypercalcaemia
An excess of calcium in the blood plasma.
hypercapnia
See hypercarbia.
hypercarbia
A condition in which carbon dioxide accumulates in the blood.
hyperchloraemia
An excess of chloride in the blood plasma.
hyperinflation
Giving the person breaths that are 1 to 1.5 times the tidal volume
through the ventilator circuit or via a manual resuscitation bag.


hyperkalaemia
An excess of potassium in the blood plasma.
hypermagnesaemia
An excess of magnesium in the blood plasma.
hypernatraemia
An excess of sodium in the blood plasma.
hyperopia
Abnormal refraction in which light rays focus behind the retina;
long-sightedness.
hyperopic
Having hyperopia.
hyperoxygenation
Done with a manual resuscitation bag or through a ventilator;
increases oxygen flow (usually to 100%) before suctioning and
between suction attempts.
hyperpathia
Heightened response to a painful stimulus; hyperalgesia.
hyperphosphataemia
An excess of phosphate in the blood plasma.
hyperpyrexia


An extremely high body temperature (e.g. 41°C).
hypersomnia
Excessive sleep.
hypertension
An abnormally high blood pressure; over 140 mm Hg systolic
and/or 90 mm Hg diastolic.
hyperthermia
A core temperature greater than 40.6°C.
hypertonic
Solutions that have a higher osmolality than body fluids.
hypertrophy
Enlargement of a muscle or organ.
hyperventilation
Very deep, rapid respirations.
hypervolaemia
Increased blood volume.
hypnotherapy
Application of hypnosis (trance state or altered state of
consciousness) to a medical or psychological disorder.


hypoactive sexual desire disorder
Involves a persistent or recurring absence of sexual thoughts or
lack of interest in sexual activity.
hypocalcaemia
Deficiency of calcium in the blood plasma.
hypochloraemia
Deficiency of chloride in the blood plasma.
hypodermic
Under the skin.
hypodermic syringe
A type of syringe that comes in 2, 2.5, 3 and 5 mL sizes and is
generally calibrated in millilitres.
hypokalaemia
Deficiency of potassium in the blood plasma.
hypomagnesaemia
Deficiency of magnesium in the blood plasma.
hyponatraemia
Deficiency of sodium in the blood plasma.
hypophosphataemia
Deficiency of phosphate in the blood plasma.


hypotension
Blood pressure that is below normal; that is, a systolic reading
consistently between 85 and 110 mm Hg in an adult whose
normal pressure is higher than this.
hypothermia
A core body temperature below the lower limit of normal.
hypothesis
A prediction of the relationship between two or more variables.
hypotonic
Solutions that have a lower osmolality than body fluids.
hypoventilation
Very shallow respirations.
hypovolaemia
An abnormal reduction in blood volume.
hypoxaemia
Reduced oxygen in the blood.
hypoxia
Insufficient oxygen anywhere in the body.
iatrogenic disease
Disease caused unintentionally by medical therapy.


id
The source of instinctive and unconscious psychological urges.
ideal self
How we would prefer to be; the individual’s perception of how
one should behave based on certain personal standards,
aspirations, goals or values.
identification
Perceiving one’s self as similar to and behaving like another
person.
idiosyncratic effect
A different, unexpected or individual effect from the normal one
usually expected from a medication; the occurrence of
unpredictable and unexplainable symptoms.
ileal conduit
Channel created when a segment of the ileum is removed and
the intestinal ends reattached.
ileostomy
An opening into the ileum (small bowel).
illicit drugs
Drugs that are sold illegally; street drugs.
illness


A highly personal state in which the person feels unhealthy or ill;
may or may not be related to disease.
illness behaviour
The course of action a person takes to define the state of their
health and pursue a remedy.
illusion
A distortion of the senses.
imagery
The internal experience of memories, dreams, fantasies and
visions that serve as a bridge connecting body, mind and spirit.
imagination
An important part of preschoolers’ life (the preschooler has an
active imagination and fantasises in play).
imitation
Copying the behaviours and attitudes of another person.
immobility
Prescribed or unavoidable restriction of movement in any area of
a person’s life.
immunity
A specific resistance of the body to infection; it may be natural,
or resistance may develop after exposure to a disease agent.


immunoglobulins
See antibodies.
implementing
The phase of the nursing process in which the nursing care plan
is put into action.
implied contract
A contract that has not been explicitly agreed to by the parties
but that the law nevertheless considers to exist.
impulse control
The ability to control behavioural impetuosity.
incentive spirometers
Devices that measure the flow of air inhaled through the
mouthpiece.
incident report
An employment record of an accident or unusual occurrence.
incident reporting
The system or process for reporting incidents in the workplace.
incomplete protein
Protein that lacks one or more essential amino acids; usually
derived from vegetables.


independent interventions
Activities that the nurse is licensed to initiate as a result of the
nurse’s own knowledge and skills.
independent variable
The presumed cause of or influence on the dependent variable.
Indigenous Australian healing practices
Healing practices linked to culture, people’s beliefs, the land,
spirits, plants and animals, which are deeply embedded in
Aboriginal culture. Linked to traditional healing.
Indigenous health
A holistic view of wellbeing which includes the physical, social,
emotional and cultural wellbeing of the community,
acknowledging the life–death–life cycle.
indirect discrimination
Occurs through systemic approaches or policy that may apply to
everyone but that may effectively disadvantage those with a
disability.
individualised care plan
A plan tailored to meet the unique needs of a specific individual—
needs that are not addressed by the standardised plan.
individualised exercise program


Exercise mode and dose tailored to a specific individual to ensure
greater adherence to the exercise program.
inductive reasoning
Making generalisations from specific data.
infection
The disease process produced by micro-organisms.
inferences
Interpretations or conclusions made based on cues or observed
data.
influence
An informal strategy used to gain the cooperation of others
without exercising formal authority.
informal nursing care plan
A strategy for action that exists in the nurse’s mind.
informed consent
A person’s agreement to accept a course of treatment or a
procedure after receiving complete information, including the
risks of treatment and facts relating to it, from the doctor.
infrared photoenergy therapy
Treatment to improve sensory impairment associated with
peripheral neuropathy.


ingestion
The taking of food or medications into the body via oral route.
ingrown toenail
The growing inwards of the nail into the soft tissues around it;
most often results from improper nail trimming.
inhalation (inspiration)
The act of breathing in; the intake of air or other substances into
the lungs.
inhibiting effect
The decreased effect of one or both drugs.
input
Consists of information, material or energy that enters a system.
inquest
A legal inquiry into the cause or manner of a death.
insensible fluid loss
Fluid loss that is not perceptible to the individual.
insensible heat loss
Heat loss that occurs from evaporation (vaporisation) of moisture
from the respiratory tract, mucosa of the mouth and the skin.
in-service education


Education that is designed to upgrade the knowledge or skills of
employees.
insight
The degree to which a person has an understanding of their
illness or disorder.
insomnia
Inability to obtain a sufficient quality or quantity of sleep.
inspection
The visual examination; that is, assessment by using the sense
of sight.
inspiration
See inhalation.
instrument nurse
Assists the surgeons and maintains control of all instrumentation.
insulin syringe
Similar to a hypodermic syringe, but the scale is specially
designed for insulin: a 100 unit calibrated scale intended for use
with U-100 insulin.
integrated health care system
One that makes all levels of care available in an integrated form
—primary care, secondary care and tertiary care.


integrated report writing
A single patient record containing chronological entries made by
all health care professionals involved in the person’s care.
intellectual disability
Characterised by significant limitations in both intellectual
functioning (reasoning, learning, problem solving) and adaptive
behaviour, which originates before the age of 18.
intention tremor
Involuntary trembling when an individual attempts a voluntary
movement.
intermittent fever
A body temperature that alternates at regular intervals between
periods of fever and periods of normal or subnormal
temperatures.
International Classification of Diseases (ICD)
Classification of diseases, functioning and disability.
internet
A worldwide computer network.
interpersonal communication
One-on-one interactions. Interpersonal communication occurs
within a setting or context (i.e. at the person’s bedside) and
includes verbal and non-verbal communication.


interpersonal skills
All verbal and non-verbal activities people use when
communicating directly with one another.
interpreter
An individual who mediates spoken communication between
people speaking different languages without adding, omitting or
distorting meaning or editorialising.
intersex
Ambiguous gender.
interstitial fluid
Fluid that surrounds the cells.
interview
A planned communication; a conversation with a purpose.
intimacy
A close friendship.
intracellular fluid (ICF)
Fluid found within the body cells; also called cellular fluid.
intradermal
Under the epidermis (into the dermis).
intradermal (ID) injection


The administration of a drug into the dermal layer of the skin just
beneath the epidermis.
intramuscular
Into the muscle.
intramuscular (IM) injections
Injections into muscle tissue that are absorbed more quickly than
subcutaneous injections because of the greater blood supply to
the body muscles.
intraoperative phase
Begins when the person is transferred to the operating table and
ends when the person is admitted to the post-anaesthesia care
unit.
intrapersonal communication
The communication that you have with yourself; another name is
self-talk.
intrapleural pressure
Pressure in the pleural cavity surrounding the lungs.
intrapulmonary pressure
Pressure within the lungs.
intraspinal
Into the spinal cord.


intrathecal
See intraspinal.
intravascular fluid
Plasma.
intravenous
Within a vein.
intravenous block
Anaesthesia used most often for procedures involving the arm,
wrist and hand.
intravenous pyelography (IVP)
X-ray filming of the kidney and ureters after injection of a
radiopaque material into the vein.
introjection
The assimilation of the attributes of others.
ions
Atoms or group of atoms that carry a positive or negative electric
charge; electrolytes.
iron deficiency anaemia
A form of anaemia caused by inadequate supply of iron for
synthesis of haemoglobin.


irrigation (lavage)
A flushing or washing out of a body cavity, organ or wound with a
specified solution that may or may not be medicated.
ischaemia
Deficiency of blood supply caused by obstruction of circulation to
the body part.
ischaemic heart disease (IHD)
A lack of oxygen to the heart muscle.
isokinetic (resistive) exercises
Muscle contraction or tension against resistance.
isometric (static or setting) exercise
Tensing of a muscle against an immovable outer resistance that
does not change muscle length or produce joint motion.
isotonic
Solutions that have the same osmolality as body fluids.
isotonic (dynamic) exercise
Exercise in which muscle tension is constant and the muscle
shortens to produce muscle contraction and active movement.
Jane Bell
Influential late nineteenth to early twentieth century Australian
nurse who promoted professionalism in nursing.


jaundice
A yellowish colour of the sclera, mucous membranes and/or skin.
jejunostomy
An opening through the abdominal wall into the jejunum.
jurisdiction
The scope of the court’s power to examine and determine facts,
interpret and apply the law, make orders and declare judgment.
Jurisdiction may be limited by geographical area, the types of
parties who appear, the type of relief that is sought and the point
to be decided.
justice
Fairness.
keloid
A hypertrophic scar containing an abnormal amount of collagen.
kidneys/ureters/bladder (KUB)
X-ray of the kidneys, ureters and bladder.
kilocalorie (kcal)
See calorie.
kilojoule (kJ)
A metric measurement referring to the amount of energy
required when a force of 1 newton (N) moves 1 kg of weight 1 m


of distance.
kinaesthetic
Refers to awareness of the position and movement of body
parts.
Korotkoff sounds
A series of five sounds produced by blood within the artery with
each ventricular contraction.
kosher
Acceptable or prepared according to Jewish law.
Kussmaul’s breathing
Hyperventilation that accompanies metabolic acidosis in which
the body attempts to compensate (give off excess body acids) by
blowing off carbon dioxide through deep and rapid breathing.
kyphosis
Excessive convex curvature of the thoracic spine.
laissez-faire leader
Recognises the group’s need for autonomy and self-regulation.
lanugo
The fine, woolly hair or down on the shoulders, back, sacrum and
earlobes of the unborn child that may remain for a few weeks
after birth.


lateral position
A side-lying position.
lavage
An irrigation or washing of a body organ, such as the stomach.
law
A rule made by humans that regulates social conduct in a
formally prescribed and binding manner.
laxatives
Medications that stimulate bowel activity and assist faecal
elimination.
leader
A person who influences others to work together to accomplish a
specific goal.
leadership style
Describes traits, behaviours, motivations and choices used by
individuals to effectively influence others.
learning
A change in human disposition or capability that persists over a
period of time and cannot be solely accounted for by growth.
learning need


A desire or a requirement to know something that is presently
unknown to the learner. Learning needs include new knowledge
or information but can also include new skills or physical
activities, or new behaviours or a need to change current
behaviours.
leukocytes
White blood cells.
LGBTI
Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or intersex.
liability
The quality or state of being legally responsible for one’s
obligations and actions, and for making financial restitution for
wrongful acts.
libel
Defamation by means of print, writing or pictures.
libido
Urge or desire for sexual activity.
lifestyle
The values and behaviours adopted by a person in daily life.
lift


An abnormal anterior movement of the chest related to
enlargement of the right ventricle.
line of gravity
An imaginary vertical line running through the centre of gravity.
lipids
Organic substances that are greasy and insoluble in water but
soluble in alcohol or ether.
lipoproteins
Soluble compounds made up of various lipids.
livor mortis
Discolouration of the skin caused by breakdown of the red blood
cells; occurs after blood circulation has ceased; appears in the
dependent areas of the body.
local adaptation syndrome (LAS)
The reaction of one organ or body part to stress.
local anaesthesia
An anaesthetic agent used for minor surgical procedures that is
injected into a specific area.
locus of control (LOC)
A concept about whether people believe their health status is
under their own or others’ control.


long-term memory
The repository for information stored for periods longer than 72
hours and usually weeks and years.
lordosis
An exaggerated concavity in the lumbar region of the vertebral
column.
loss
An actual or potential situation in which a valued ability, object or
person is inaccessible or changed so that it is perceived as no
longer valuable.
lower-quality protein
See incomplete protein.
low Fowler’s position
A bed-sitting position in which the head of the bed is elevated
between 15 and 45 degrees, with or without knee flexion.
Lucy Osburn
Nightingale nurse who started nurse training in Australia in 1868
at the Sydney Hospital.
lumbar puncture
A procedure where cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is withdrawn
through a needle that is inserted into the subarachnoid space of


the spinal canal between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae or
between the fourth and fifth lumbar vertebrae.
lung compliance
Expansibility of the lung.
lung recoil
The tendency of lungs to collapse away from the chest wall.
lung scan
Records the emissions from radioisotopes that indicate how well
gas and blood are travelling through the lungs; also known as a
V/Q (ventilation/perfusion) scan.
maceration
The wasting away or softening of a solid as if by the action of
soaking; often used to describe degenerative changes and
eventual disintegration.
macrominerals
Any of the minerals that people require daily in amounts over 100
mg.
macronutrients
Refers to carbohydrates, fats and protein; they are needed in
large amounts (e.g. hundreds of grams) to provide energy.
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)


A non-invasive diagnostic scanning technique in which the person
is placed in a magnetic field.
maintenance stage
Stage at which a person integrates newly adopted behaviour
patterns into their lifestyle.
male erectile disorder
When a man has erection problems during 25% or more of his
sexual interactions.
male orgasmic disorder
Disorder where a man can maintain an erection but has difficulty
ejaculating.
malnutrition
A disorder of nutrition; insufficient nourishment of the body cells.
management information system (MIS)
Software designed to facilitate the organisation and application of
data used to manage an organisation or department.
manager
One who is appointed to a position in an organisation that gives
the power to guide and direct the work of others.
mandatory competencies


Competencies the nurse must be able to demonstrate
continuously in the workplace.
mandatory reporting
A term used to describe the legislative requirement imposed on
selected classes of people to report suspected cases.
manometer
An instrument used to measure the pressure of fluids or gases.
manubrium
The handle-like superior part of the sternum that joins with the
clavicles.
Mary Evans
Influential Victorian district nurse during the 1960s and 1970s.
mass peristalsis
Involves a wave of powerful muscular contraction that moves
over large areas of the colon; usually occurs after eating.
masturbation
Sexual self-stimulation.
maturity
The state of maximal function and integration; the state of being
fully developed.


mean
A measure of central tendency, computed by summing all scores
and dividing by the number of subjects; commonly symbolised as
x¯ or M.
measures of central tendency
Measures that describe the centre of a distribution of data,
denoting where most of the subjects lie; include the mean,
median and mode.
measures of variability
Measures that indicate the degree of dispersion or spread of the
data; include range, variance and standard deviation.
meatus
An opening, passage or channel.
meconium
The first faecal material passed by the newborn, normally within
24 hours after birth.
median
A measure of central tendency, representing the exact middle
score or value in a distribution of scores; the median is the value
above and below which 50% of the scores lie.
Medicare


Australia’s federal government universal health funding program
(different from the American system of the same name).
medication
A substance administered for the diagnosis, cure, treatment or
relief of a symptom or for prevention of disease.
medication reconciliation
Comparison of medications the person is taking to doctor’s
admission, transfer and/or discharge orders.
meditation
Mental exercise that directs the mind to think inwardly by closing
the sense organs to external stimulation.
memory
The ability to store, retain and recall information.
menarche
Onset of menstruation.
meniscus
The crescent-shaped upper surface of a column of fluid.
menopause
Cessation of menstruation.
menstruation


The monthly discharge of blood through the vagina occurring in
non-pregnant women from puberty to menopause.
Mental Health Act
Contains definitions about mental health and mental illness for
the Act’s jurisdiction.
mental state assessment (MSA)
A clinical assessment that describes the sum total of the
examiner’s observations at the time of the interview or
interaction.
mesoderm
Middle layer of the embryonic tissue that forms during the first 3
weeks of life.
message
What is being communicated by the sender.
metabolic acidosis
A condition characterised by a deficiency of bicarbonate ions in
the body in relation to the amount of carbonic acid in the body;
the pH falls to less than 7.35.
metabolic alkalosis
A condition characterised by an excess of bicarbonate ions in the
body in relation to the amount of carbonic acid in the body; the
pH rises to greater than 7.45.


metabolism
The sum of all physical and chemical processes by which a living
substance is formed and maintained, and by which energy is
made available for use by the organism.
metabolites
End products or enzymes.
metaparadigm
Originates from two Greek words: meta, meaning ‘with’, and
paradigm, meaning ‘pattern’. The four concepts of person,
environment, health and nursing can be superimposed on almost
any work in nursing and are sometimes collectively referred to as
a metaparadigm for nursing.
metered-dose inhaler (MDI)
A hand-held nebuliser, which is a pressurised container of
medication that can be used by the person to release the
medication through a mouthpiece.
microminerals
Any of the minerals that people require daily in amounts under
100 mg.
micronutrients
Vitamins and minerals, which are needed in small amounts (e.g.
milligrams or micrograms) to metabolise energy-providing
nutrients.


micturition
See urination.
mid-level theories
Focus on exploration of concepts such as pain, self-esteem,
learning and hardiness.
midstream urine specimen
Clean voided urine specimen.
millimoles
The chemical combining power of the ion or the capacity of
cations to combine with anions to form molecules.
mineral
Found in organic compounds as an inorganic compound and as a
free ion.
minor
A person who is a child and has not attained the age of majority
of 18 years. A minor is not a separate legal personality and
cannot sue or be sued (subject to legislative and common law
exceptions).
miosis
Constricted pupils.
mixed hearing loss


A combination of conduction and sensorineural loss.
mobility
Ability to move about freely, easily and purposefully in the
environment.
mode
The score or value that occurs most frequently in a distribution of
scores.
model
A standard or example for imitation or comparison; a pattern.
modelling
Observing the behaviour of people who have successfully
achieved a goal that one has set for oneself and, through
observing, acquiring ideas for behaviour and coping strategies.
monosaccharides
Sugars that are composed of single molecules.
monotheism
Belief in the existence of one God.
monounsaturated fatty acid
A fatty acid with one double bond.
mood


The way in which a person describes their feelings at a particular
time.
moral
Relating to right and wrong.
moral behaviour
The way a person perceives the requirements necessary for
people to live together and how they respond to them.
moral development
Process of learning to tell the difference between right and
wrong, and of learning what should and should not be done.
moral rules
Specific prescriptions for actions.
morality
A doctrine or system denoting what is right and wrong in
conduct, character or attitude.
motivation
The desire to learn.
mourning
The process through which grief is eventually resolved or altered.
multidisciplinary care plan


A standardised plan that outlines the care required for individuals
with common, predictable—usually medical—conditions.
Muriel Knox Doherty
New South Wales nurse associated with post World War II
European rebuilding and co-author of long-running nursing
textbook.
muscular dystrophy
A neuromuscular condition that causes a progressive weakening
of muscles.
music therapy
The behavioural science concerned with the systematic
application of music to produce relaxation and desired changes in
emotions, behaviour and physiology.
mutual pretence
A type of awareness in which the individual, family and health
personnel know that the prognosis is terminal but do not talk
about it and make an effort not to raise the subject.
mydriasis
Enlarged pupils.
myocardial infarction (MI)
Heart attack; cardiac tissue necrosis owing to obstruction of
blood flow to the heart.


myocardium
A layer of the heart wall; cardiac muscle cells that form the bulk
of the heart and contract with each beat.
myopia
Abnormal refraction in which light rays focus in front of the retina;
short-sightedness.
myopic
Having myopia.
narcolepsy
An uncontrollable desire for sleep or attacks of sleep during the
day.
narrative charting
A descriptive record of a person’s data, and nursing
interventions, written in sentences and paragraphs.
nasoenteric (nasointestinal) tube
A tube inserted through one of the nostrils, down the
nasopharynx and into the alimentary tract.
nasogastric tube
A tube inserted by way of the nasopharynx and placed into the
person’s stomach for the purpose of feeding the person or to
remove gastric secretions.


nasointestinal tube
See nasoenteric tube.
National Safety and Quality Health Service (NSQHS) Standards
A set of standards to protect the public from harm and to
improve the quality of health service provision.
naturopathic medicine
Practice that focuses on nutrition, herbs, homeopathy,
acupuncture, hydrotherapy, physical medicine, counselling and
minor surgical interventions.
negative feedback
Feedback that inhibits change.
negligence
Failure to behave in a reasonable and prudent manner; an
unintentional tort.
nephrostomy
Diversion of urine from a kidney to a stoma.
nerve block
Chemical interruption of a nerve pathway effected by injecting a
local anaesthetic.
neurogenic bladder


Interference with the normal mechanisms of urine elimination in
which the person does not perceive bladder fullness and is
unable to control the urinary sphincters; the result of impaired
neurological function.
neuropathic pain
The result of a disturbance of the peripheral or central nervous
system that results in pain that may or may not be associated
with an ongoing tissue-damaging process.
nitrogen balance
A measure of the degree of protein anabolism and catabolism;
net result of intake and loss of nitrogen.
nociception
The physiological processes related to pain perception.
nociceptor
A pain receptor.
nocturia
Voiding two or more times at night.
nocturnal emissions
Orgasm and emission of semen during sleep.
nocturnal enuresis
Bed-wetting; involuntary urination at night.


nocturnal frequency
The need for older adults to rise during the night to urinate.
non-assertive communication
A submissive communication style which allows the rights and
feelings of the message sender to be violated.
non-binary
A person who does not exclusively identify as a male or female.
non-directive interview
An interview using open-ended questions and empathetic
responses to build rapport and learn patient concerns.
non-directive leader
See laissez-faire leader.
non-essential amino acid
Amino acids that can be manufactured in the body and do not
need to be supplied by the diet. Includes alanine, arginine,
asparagine, aspartic acid, cysteine, glutamic acid, glutamine,
glycine, proline, serine and tyrosine.
non-maleficence
The duty to do no harm.
non-specific defences


Bodily defences that protect a person against all micro-
organisms, regardless of prior exposure.
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
Drugs that relieve pain by acting on the peripheral nerve endings
to inhibit the formation of the prostaglandins that tend to
sensitise nerves to painful stimuli; have analgesic, antipyretic and
anti-inflammatory effects; include aspirin and ibuprofen.
non-verbal communication
Communication other than words, including gestures, posture
and facial expressions.
norm
An ideal or fixed standard; an expected standard of behaviour of
group members.
normocephalic
Normal head size.
normocephaly
Normal head circumference at birth; usually 35 cm.
NREM (non-REM) sleep
A deep restful sleep rate; also called slow wave sleep.
N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP)


A peptide released from cardiac myocytes that can be measured
to provide prognostic information for people with heart failure,
coronary heart disease and valvular heart disease.
nuclear family
A family of parents and their offspring.
nurse advocate
A nurse who pleads the cause of a person’s rights.
nurse informaticist
An expert who combines computer, information and nursing
science to develop policies and procedures that promote
effective use of computerised records by nurses and other health
care professionals.
nursing
The attributes, characteristics and actions of the nurse providing
care on behalf of, or in conjunction with, the person.
Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia (NMBA)
The board responsible for professional registration, professional
codes, standards and competency issues for all nursing
registrations in Australia.
nursing ethics
Ethical issues that occur in nursing practice.


nursing informatics
Nursing informatics science and practice integrates nursing, its
information and knowledge and their management with
information and communication technologies to promote the
health of people, families and communities worldwide.
nursing intervention
Any treatment, based on clinical judgment and knowledge, that a
nurse performs to enhance patient outcomes.
nursing process
A systematic, rational method of planning and providing nursing
care.
nutrients
Organic or inorganic substances found in food.
nutrition
The sum of all interactions between an organism and the food it
consumes.
nutritive value
The nutrient content of a specified amount of food.
nystagmus
Rapid involuntary rhythmical eye movement.
obese


A body mass index (BMI) greater than 30 kg/m .
obesity
A body mass index (BMI) greater than 30 kg/m .
objective data
Information (data) that is detectable by an observer or can be
tested against an accepted standard; can be seen, heard, felt or
smelled.
obligatory losses
Essential fluid losses required to maintain body functioning.
occult blood
Hidden blood.
oedema
The presence of excess interstitial fluid in the body.
oils
Lipids that are liquid at room temperature.
olfactory
Related to smell.
oliguria
Production of abnormally small amounts of urine by the kidneys.
2
2


oncotic pressure
See colloid osmotic pressure.
one-point discrimination
The ability to sense whether one or two areas of the skin are
being stimulated by pressure.
onset of action
The time after drug administration when the body initially
responds to the drug.
open awareness
A type of awareness in which an individual and others know
about the impending death.
open captioning
Text that appears on screen without the need for special
equipment to see the text.
open disclosure
The open discussion of incidents that have resulted in harm to a
person while receiving health care, with the person, their family,
carers and other support people.
open system
System in which energy, matter and information move into and
out of the system through the system boundary.


open-ended questions
